--- STEM ---
Fellside Foods is a secondary sector tinned-food manufacturer in Country X employing 130 workers. It makes tinned peas and sweetcorn, with revenue of $4.2 million last year and profit of just $84,000 (a 2% margin). Secondary sector employment in Country X fell from 34% to 22% over the past decade as the economy has shifted towards services.

The managing director, Elena Vargas, is choosing between two plans. Plan A is a $900,000 investment in a premium soup and ready-meal range aimed at a growing export market. Plan B is to accept a takeover offer from a supermarket group for $5.2 million and close the site, making all 130 workers redundant. Plan A would retain at least 100 jobs and would take about 18 months to launch.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'opportunity cost'.
    Answer: The value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: value of the next best alternative forgone; arises because resources are scarce and choices must be made

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the shrinking secondary sector creates for Fellside Foods.
    Answer: Problem 1: Weak demand at home [k], the secondary sector's share of employment fell from 34% to 22% over the decade [app], so the domestic market for tinned peas and sweetcorn is unlikely to grow. Problem 2: Thin margins [k], profit of just $84,000 on $4.2 million revenue gives only a 2% margin [app], leaving no cushion for investment or shocks.
    Keywords: secondary sector, 34%, 22%, tinned, $84,000, $4.2 million, 2%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a shrinking secondary sector weakens domestic demand for manufacturers; low profitability leaves businesses unable to respond | application_max_2: secondary employment fell from 34% to 22%; profit of $84,000 on $4.2 million revenue (2% margin); tinned peas and sweetcorn; 130 workers on site

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of Plan A for Fellside Foods.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Access to a growing export market [k], the premium soup and ready-meal range targets rising export demand rather than the shrinking home tinned market [app], which could lift the 2% margin toward sustainable profitability [an]. Benefit 2: Jobs retained [k], Plan A would keep at least 100 of the 130 workers employed [app], preserving skills and local spending around the factory [an].
    Keywords: Plan A, export market, premium, 100, 130, 2%, $900,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: new premium products can reach growing export markets; retaining jobs preserves skills and local income | application_max_2: Plan A is a $900,000 premium soup and ready-meal range; growing export market; at least 100 of 130 workers retained; current $4.2 million revenue and 2% margin | analysis_max_2: premium export sales could raise the 2% margin; kept jobs sustain local spending and avoid redundancy costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fellside Foods should choose Plan A instead of accepting the $5.2 million takeover offer? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Plan A gives the business a future [k]: a premium soup and ready-meal range aimed at a growing export market [app] could transform the 2% margin ($84,000 on $4.2 million revenue) and retain at least 100 of the 130 jobs [an]. However, the takeover is certain money [k]: the $5.2 million offer needs no further capital and lets the owners exit a shrinking sector with a clear gain [app], whereas Plan A commits $900,000 to an unproven export range at a time when secondary employment has already fallen from 34% to 22% [an]. Overall, Plan A is the better choice because $5.2 million is a final exit while a successful premium export brand could be worth more over time and keeps at least 100 jobs in the community [eval], but only if a firm export order or distributor is signed before the $900,000 is spent; otherwise the takeover is the safer option [eval].
    Keywords: Plan A, $5.2 million, $900,000, export market, $84,000, 100, secondary
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Plan A transforms the business through premium export sales; Plan B removes all future risk with certain cash | application_max_2: Plan A $900,000 premium soup/ready-meal range; Plan B $5.2 million takeover closing the site; 2% margin ($84,000 of $4.2 million); secondary employment fell from 34% to 22% | analysis_max_2: premium exports could transform the 2% margin and keep 100+ jobs; unproven export range risks the entire site and 130 jobs | evaluation_max_2: weighs uncertain long-term upside against certain $5.2 million exit; justified conditional recommendation requiring a firm export order first

--- STEM ---
Ashford Grain Co-operative is a primary sector partnership of 14 wheat farmers in Country X, farming 2,300 hectares together and selling 9,000 tonnes of wheat a year to exporters at $240 per tonne. Country X is industrialising fast: manufacturing grew by 8.2% last year, and domestic bakeries and pasta makers now import $30 million of flour annually.

The farmers are considering a $500,000 co-operative flour mill to supply domestic bakeries; flour sells at $360 per tonne, keeping $120 per tonne of added value within the group. The alternative is to continue the exporters' long-standing contracts. The mill would need government approval and a trained miller, and the group currently employs 45 seasonal workers at harvest time. The mill would run in 2 shifts to supply the bakeries year-round.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline why the primary sector's share of employment falls as a country develops.
    Answer: As incomes rise, spending shifts from farm output towards manufactured goods and services; mechanisation and capital equipment replace farm workers, and higher wages in secondary and tertiary activities pull labour out of agriculture [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: spending shifts towards manufactured goods and services as incomes rise; mechanisation/capital replaces farm workers and wages pull labour out

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Ashford Grain Co-operative might build a flour mill.
    Answer: Reason 1: To capture more added value [k], converting wheat at $240 per tonne into flour at $360 per tonne keeps $120 per tonne inside the group [app]. Reason 2: To win domestic business [k], bakeries and pasta makers import $30 million of flour a year, which a local mill could supply [app].
    Keywords: wheat, $240 per tonne, $360 per tonne, $120, $30 million, flour, bakeries
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raises selling price and retains added value locally; a domestic mill can substitute for imports | application_max_2: flour at $360 vs wheat at $240 per tonne ($120 gap); $30 million of flour imported annually; 9,000 tonnes of wheat sold to exporters; bakeries and pasta makers as potential customers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the co-operative might face in building the flour mill.
    Answer: Problem 1: Cost and approvals [k], the $500,000 mill needs government approval and a trained miller [app], so delays could leave members' wheat flowing to exporters meanwhile and cash tied up [an]. Problem 2: Internal disagreement over scale and price [k], the partnership of 14 farmers must agree on flour pricing and quality for bakeries [app], and if demand undercuts the $120 added-value assumption, the mill could run under capacity and strain group relations [an].
    Keywords: $500,000, government approval, trained miller, 14, flour mill, bakeries, wheat
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: building a mill needs capital approval and specialist staff; co-operative decision-making can be slow and divided | application_max_2: $500,000 co-operative flour mill cost; government approval and a trained miller required; 14 wheat farmers in the partnership; flour must meet bakery customers' needs | analysis_max_2: delays leave members reliant on exporters and capital stuck; underuse or disagreement would erode the expected $120 per tonne added value

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ashford Grain Co-operative should invest $500,000 in a flour mill? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A mill keeps far more value onshore [k]: selling flour at $360 per tonne instead of wheat at $240 keeps $120 per tonne inside the group [app], so on 9,000 tonnes a year that is about $1.08 million of added value, potentially repaying the $500,000 within the first year [an]. However, co-operative risk is real [k]: the mill needs government approval and a trained miller, and all 14 members must agree on prices for bakeries and pasta makers [app], and if local buyers keep their contracts for the $30 million of imported flour, the mill could sit underused [an]. Overall, investing is the better choice because Country X is industrialising fast (manufacturing grew 8.2% last year) and the $1.08 million annual added value outweighs the $500,000 cost [eval], but the group should sign bakery supply agreements and secure government approval before committing the funds [eval].
    Keywords: $500,000, $360 per tonne, $240 per tonne, $120 per tonne, $30 million, industrialising, 9,000 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: milling retains $120 per tonne of added value domestically; approval, staffing and member agreement are real obstacles | application_max_2: $360 vs $240 per tonne ($120 added value); $500,000 mill cost and 9,000 tonnes a year; $30 million of flour imported annually; 14 farmers, bakeries and pasta makers as buyers | analysis_max_2: $1.08 million a year of added value could repay the mill quickly; imported-flour contracts could leave the mill underused | evaluation_max_2: weighs large annual added value against approval and demand risk; justified conditional recommendation with supply agreements first

--- STEM ---
Kestrel Construction Ltd is a private limited company founded 6 years ago by Daniel Okafor, building houses and small warehouse units in the town of Marlow. It owns one plot of land near the ring road, large enough for either 12 houses or a single distribution warehouse. The houses would earn $900,000 in revenue over 18 months, while the warehouse would earn $650,000 over 14 months. The business employs 24 site workers and 3 supervisors.

Daniel has only $120,000 saved for materials. He must choose between the housing project and the warehouse, knowing the land cannot do both. He could hire two bricklayers at $450 each per week or lease a concrete mixer for $1,200 a month. Land prices in Marlow have risen 20% since 2023, and the accountant reminded Daniel that scarcity means every choice has an opportunity cost. Either option carries risk, and delays could raise costs by 15%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'land' as a factor of production.
    Answer: Land refers to all natural resources used to produce goods and services, such as the plot near the ring road in Marlow and materials like timber and sand. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Land = all natural resources used in producing goods and services, e.g. the building plot, timber, sand or land itself; Reward any example of a natural resource input used to make goods or services (2 marks for a clear definition with reference to nature)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why land is important to Kestrel Construction Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Land is a basic factor of production that provides natural resources for making goods [k]. Kestrel's only plot near the ring road is large enough for either 12 houses or a single distribution warehouse worth $900,000 or $650,000 of revenue [app]. Reason 2: Without suitable land the business cannot produce or sell anything [k]. With no plot to build on, the $900,000 house scheme and the $650,000 warehouse scheme would both be impossible and Kestrel would earn nothing [app].
    Keywords: Kestrel Construction Ltd, Marlow, $900,000, $650,000, 12 houses, ring road, $120,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Land provides natural resources / site / raw materials needed for production; Without land the firm cannot produce or generate sales revenue | application_max_2: Reference to the single plot being large enough for 12 houses or the warehouse; Reference to the $900,000 (houses) and $650,000 (warehouse) revenue figures / the Marlow site

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways in which opportunity cost affects Kestrel Construction Ltd's decision.
    Answer: Point 1: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made [k]. By choosing the 12 houses, Kestrel gives up the chance to earn $650,000 from the warehouse, so the true cost of the houses includes the lost warehouse revenue [app]. This means Daniel must compare both revenue streams carefully before spending the $120,000 of scarce materials money [an]. Point 2: Scarcity of the single plot means the land cannot serve both projects [k]. Committing the plot to the housing scheme removes the chance to use it for the warehouse, so every scarce input carries a sacrifice [app]. This forces Daniel to recognise that scarcity creates opportunity cost in all of his decisions, not only in this one [an].
    Keywords: Kestrel Construction Ltd, $900,000, $650,000, 12 houses, $120,000, opportunity cost, scarcity
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Opportunity cost = next best alternative forgone when a decision is made; Scarcity = limited resources vs unlimited wants, forcing economic choices | application_max_2: Reference to forgoing the $650,000 warehouse revenue if the 12 houses are chosen (or vice versa); Reference to the single plot / the $120,000 materials finance as scarce resources | analysis_max_2: Analysis of how foregone revenue or profits changes the true cost of each option; Analysis chain linking scarcity -> choice -> sacrifice -> better decision-making

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kestrel Construction Ltd should build the 12 houses rather than the warehouse? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for the houses: Building 12 houses suits Kestrel's construction skills and could earn $900,000 in revenue [k]. That is $250,000 more than the warehouse's $650,000, even though it takes 18 months rather than 14 [app]. However, the scheme ties up $120,000 of scarce materials money and any delay could raise costs by 15%, squeezing the margin for error on a fixed plot [an]. Argument for the warehouse: The warehouse earns $650,000 within 14 months, releasing cash faster for future projects [k]. Land prices have risen 20% since 2023, so completing quickly protects the value of the Marlow plot [app]. But $650,000 is $250,000 less revenue and would leave Kestrel dependent on a single buyer in a weaker warehouse market [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures the housing project offers the higher revenue of $900,000 and matches Kestrel's house-building specialism, so it should proceed only if Daniel secures firm buyer contracts and a contingency for the 15% cost risk [eval]. Otherwise the quicker, lower-risk warehouse would be the wiser choice for a business holding just $120,000 in materials finance [eval].
    Keywords: Kestrel Construction Ltd, $900,000, $650,000, 12 houses, 18 months, 14 months, $120,000, 15%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Houses give higher total revenue ($900,000 vs $650,000); Warehouse gives faster cash return (14 vs 18 months) and matches 20% land price rise | application_max_2: Uses $900,000 / $650,000 / $120,000 / 12 houses / 18 months vs 14 months figures from the stem; Reference to the single Marlow plot and the 15% cost-overrun or 20% price-rise risk | analysis_max_2: Analysis of revenue, cash-flow timing and cost-risk trade-offs between the two schemes; Analysis of how the decision affects scarce materials finance and future projects | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation that is conditional on contracts/cost risk, or favours the warehouse, supported by stem figures; Balanced judgement recognising the risk of the houses scheme vs the security of the warehouse

--- STEM ---
Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd is a private limited company run since 2019 by sisters Priya and Anita Raman. From a workshop in Fenwick it handcrafts oak dining tables and chairs, employing 14 carpenters paid $38,000 per year and 3 apprentices on $16,000 each. Annual output is 900 tables sold at $520 each. The sisters are considering division of labour so each worker specialises in one stage, such as cutting, sanding, joining or finishing.

At present every carpenter builds a whole table alone. Trials show specialised workers can finish a table in 6 hours instead of 11, lifting potential output to 1,240 tables a year. However, several carpenters fear their jobs will become monotonous and their craft skills will narrow. The workshop would need reorganising into 4 stations, and wages currently cost $580,000 a year. Quality complaints must stay below 3% for the plan to succeed.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'labour' as a factor of production.
    Answer: Labour refers to the human effort, both physical and mental, used to produce goods and services, such as the 14 carpenters and 3 apprentices working in the Willow & Pine workshop. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Labour = human effort used in producing goods and services; Reward references to physical/mental effort, or workers such as carpenters, apprentices or staff

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why labour is important to Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Labour performs the skilled work needed to create the product [k]. Willow & Pine employs 14 carpenters at $38,000 per year plus 3 apprentices, whose hands craft the 900 tables sold at $520 each [app]. Reason 2: Without labour the business cannot turn timber into furniture [k]. If the carpenters and apprentices stopped work, the $580,000 wage bill would produce nothing and the 900-table output could not be reached [app].
    Keywords: Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd, 14 carpenters, $38,000, 3 apprentices, 900 tables, $520, $580,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Labour does the physical/mental work of production; Without labour, production is impossible / no goods and services made | application_max_2: Reference to 14 carpenters and 3 apprentices / $38,000 and $16,000 pay; Reference to 900 tables a year at $520 / $580,000 wage bill

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of division of labour for Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd.
    Answer: Point 1: Division of labour means workers specialise in one repeated stage of production [k]. Trials show specialised staff can finish a table in 6 hours instead of 11, lifting potential output to 1,240 tables a year [app]. This raises productivity so the $580,000 wage bill is spread over more units and average labour cost per table falls [an]. Point 2: Specialised workers become faster and more skilled at their single stage [k]. Each of the 4 stations such as cutting or finishing would develop deep expertise, keeping quality complaints below the 3% target [app]. This improves customer satisfaction, protects the brand and supports repeat orders from the Fenwick workshop [an].
    Keywords: Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd, division of labour, 6 hours, 11, 1,240 tables, 4 stations, 900 tables
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Specialisation in one repeated task / stage of production; Workers become quicker and more expert through repetition | application_max_2: Reference to 6 hours vs 11 hours build time and 1,240 tables a year; Reference to 4 stations and the 3% quality complaint threshold | analysis_max_2: Analysis that higher output per worker lowers average cost / raises profit margin; Analysis that fewer errors improve quality, reputation and repeat sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd should introduce division of labour in its workshop? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for division of labour: Specialisation would cut build time from 11 hours to 6 hours per table and could lift output to 1,240 tables a year [k]. Average labour cost per table would fall and revenue could rise sharply if demand holds for oak tables at $520 each [app]. However, gains depend on staff accepting repetitive jobs across 4 stations and on quality complaints staying below 3% [an]. Argument against: Whole-table crafting preserves the craft skills that justify premium pricing and keeps workers engaged [k]. Forcing specialisation could trigger boredom and resignations, risking the loss of experienced $38,000-a-year carpenters [app]. This risk is manageable through job rotation and careful deployment of the 3 apprentices, but it cannot be ignored [an]. Overall, division of labour is the better choice because saving 5 hours per table and the chance to reach 1,240 tables a year clearly outweigh the morale risk, provided the Ashbys consult staff and monitor the 3% quality threshold closely [eval]. Otherwise output gains could be cancelled out by turnover, rework and quality claims [eval].
    Keywords: Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd, division of labour, 6 hours, 11, 1,240 tables, $580,000, 3%, 900 tables
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Division of labour cuts build time (11 to 6 hours) and can raise output (1,240 tables); Whole-table crafting preserves skill, variety and worker engagement | application_max_2: Uses 6 hours vs 11 hours, 1,240 tables, 4 stations and $580,000 wage figures from the stem; Reference to monotony fears and the 3% quality complaints target | analysis_max_2: Analysis of productivity/cost per unit versus motivation and turnover risks; Analysis of quality outcomes and how they affect revenue and reputation | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation supporting specialisation (or retention) conditional on consultation and quality monitoring; Balanced judgement weighing output gains against craft-skill loss and boredom

--- STEM ---
Crossdock Freight Ltd is a logistics business based in the port city of Dunmore, founded 4 years ago by Marcus Reeve. It runs 9 delivery trucks, employing 21 drivers and 6 dispatchers. Revenue last year was $1,750,000 with a profit of $210,000. The company is winning new contracts carrying food from farms to supermarkets across the region, and truck utilisation is already 92% on a typical day.

To meet demand Marcus must add 3 trucks. Buying them would cost $240,000 plus $38,000 a year in maintenance, and they would last 8 years. Leasing would cost $3,600 per truck per month with servicing included. Marcus has $70,000 available now and could borrow the rest at 8% interest. The new contracts promise an extra $400,000 a year in revenue if the trucks arrive before summer.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'capital' as a factor of production.
    Answer: Capital refers to man-made resources used to produce goods and services, such as the trucks, forklifts, tools and depot machinery used by Crossdock Freight Ltd. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Capital = man-made resources used in production (goods used to make other goods); Reward examples such as trucks, machinery, vehicles, tools, equipment or buildings

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why capital equipment is important to Crossdock Freight Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Capital goods such as trucks are the tools that let the business deliver its service [k]. Crossdock runs 9 delivery trucks carrying supermarket food across the region, and truck utilisation is already 92% on a typical day [app]. Reason 2: Without enough capital equipment the firm cannot accept the new contracts [k]. Winning work worth an extra $400,000 a year is impossible unless 3 more trucks are added to the existing 9 [app].
    Keywords: Crossdock Freight Ltd, 9 delivery trucks, 21 drivers, $1,750,000, 92%, $240,000, $3,600
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Capital equipment enables production/delivery of the service; Without adequate capital, output and contract capacity are capped | application_max_2: Reference to 9 delivery trucks and the 92% utilisation rate; Reference to the new food contracts / extra $400,000 a year needing 3 more trucks

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Crossdock Freight Ltd might face if it cannot fund new capital equipment.
    Answer: Point 1: Without capital goods the firm lacks the machinery needed to produce more [k]. Without $240,000 to buy 3 trucks, the new contracts cannot be served and the fleet stays overstretched at 92% utilisation [app]. This leads to late deliveries, penalties and damaged relationships with supermarket customers, which could cost the $400,000 revenue opportunity [an]. Point 2: Relying on overworked capital raises running costs [k]. The existing 9 trucks would work beyond capacity, pushing maintenance above the quoted $38,000 a year and increasing breakdown risk [app]. This eats into the $210,000 profit and could leave Crossdock unable to meet food-safety delivery windows [an].
    Keywords: Crossdock Freight Ltd, $240,000, $38,000, 8 years, $400,000, $70,000, 8% interest
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lack of capital equipment limits production capacity; Overworked/older capital raises maintenance and breakdown costs | application_max_2: Reference to the $240,000 purchase, $38,000 maintenance and 8-year life; Reference to the 92% utilisation and the $400,000 contract opportunity | analysis_max_2: Analysis chain from no new trucks -> lost contracts -> lost revenue and reputation; Analysis chain from overuse -> higher maintenance -> lower profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Crossdock Freight Ltd should buy the 3 trucks rather than lease them? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for buying: Buying for $240,000 plus $38,000 a year maintenance makes the trucks assets lasting 8 years [k]. Owned trucks build equity, lower the true long-run cost per delivery and can be fitted out for the supermarket food contracts [app]. However, with only $70,000 available now, Marcus must borrow $170,000 at 8% interest, adding roughly $13,600 a year to his costs [an]. Argument for leasing: Leasing costs $3,600 per truck per month with servicing included, spreading payments and avoiding big up-front borrowing and maintenance risk [k]. It also gives flexibility to return or upgrade trucks if the new contracts falter [app]. But over a full year, 3 leased trucks cost $129,600 with nothing owned at the end [an]. Overall, buying is the better long-term choice for a stable operator already at 92% utilisation and expecting $400,000 a year in new revenue, provided Marcus secures the loan at 8% and keeps maintenance within $38,000 [eval]. Leasing would suit him only if the contracts were unproven and cash flow were tighter than the current $70,000 suggests [eval].
    Keywords: Crossdock Freight Ltd, $240,000, $3,600, $38,000, 8 years, $70,000, $400,000, 8% interest
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying = ownership, asset lasting 8 years vs monthly lease of $3,600 per truck; Leasing spreads payments and includes servicing; buying needs borrowing at 8% | application_max_2: Uses $240,000 / $70,000 / $170,000 and $38,000 maintenance figures; Uses $3,600 per month leasing rate and the $400,000 projected new revenue | analysis_max_2: Analysis of 8-year cost comparison: leasing $129,600 a year vs buying plus 8% interest; Analysis of capacity/asset value vs cash-flow flexibility and contract risk | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation favouring purchase (or leasing) conditional on loan/contracts; Balanced judgement weighing ownership benefits vs borrowing risk at 8% interest

--- STEM ---
BrightSpark Printing Ltd is an independent commercial printer in the market town of Wexley, started 8 years ago by owner Rachel Dunne. It employs 12 print operators and 2 sales staff, producing catalogues, labels and posters. Last year revenue was $880,000 and profit $96,000. A national online printer has begun undercutting prices by 25% across the region.

Rachel must decide whether to take the risk of buying a high-speed digital press costing $150,000, doubling capacity and cutting unit costs by 18%, or to keep the current presses and compete on service and 24-hour delivery. The bank will lend $100,000 at 9% interest if needed, with a personal guarantee from Rachel. Failure could endanger the business, but standing still may lose 30% of revenue to the cheaper rival within a year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'enterprise' as a factor of production.
    Answer: Enterprise is the risk-bearing and decision-making factor that organises land, labour and capital to produce goods and services, such as Rachel Dunne setting up and running BrightSpark Printing Ltd. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Enterprise = the organising / risk-taking factor of production; Reward references to entrepreneurial risk, decision-making or combining the other factors (land, labour, capital)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why enterprise is important to BrightSpark Printing Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Enterprise organises land, labour and capital into a working business [k]. Rachel decides how the 12 print operators, 2 sales staff and machinery combine to produce catalogues and labels earning $880,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Enterprise drives innovation and response to competition [k]. Facing a national rival undercutting prices by 25%, Rachel must choose how to compete, for example by buying a high-speed press or improving service [app].
    Keywords: BrightSpark Printing Ltd, 12 print operators, $880,000, $96,000, 25%, $150,000, 18%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Enterprise combines and organises the other factors of production; Enterprise creates change/innovation in response to competition or opportunity | application_max_2: Reference to Rachel organising 12 print operators and 2 sales staff at $880,000 revenue; Reference to the 25% undercutting by the online printer and the decision over the press

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Rachel faces when showing enterprise against the online rival.
    Answer: Point 1: Entrepreneurial risk-taking can threaten survival [k]. Buying the $150,000 press with a $100,000 bank loan at 9% interest means failure could leave BrightSpark unable to meet repayments [app]. This would erode the $96,000 profit and could put the 12 print operators out of work [an]. Point 2: Competing on price against a bigger rival squeezes margins [k]. The online firm's 25% price cut may force Rachel to discount up to 30% of revenue to keep clients [app]. This leaves less cash to pay for the new press and weakens long-term investment [an].
    Keywords: BrightSpark Printing Ltd, $150,000, 18%, $100,000, 9% interest, 25%, 30%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Enterprise = risk-taking; risks can threaten business survival; Price competition from a larger rival can erode profit margins | application_max_2: Reference to the $150,000 press and the $100,000 loan at 9% interest; Reference to the 25% undercutting and the possible loss of 30% of revenue | analysis_max_2: Analysis chain from loan repayments -> lower profit -> possible job losses/closure; Analysis chain from discounting -> reduced margins -> less cash for investment

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rachel should buy the high-speed digital press rather than keep the current presses and compete on service? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for buying the press: The $150,000 press doubles capacity and cuts unit costs by 18% [k]. That protects margins against the rival's 25% undercutting and lets BrightSpark quote sharper prices while still delivering in 24 hours [app]. However, with $100,000 borrowed at 9% interest and a personal guarantee, repayments would eat into the $96,000 profit and a soft winter could make the upgrade unaffordable [an]. Argument against buying: Keeping the current presses avoids new borrowing and risk, and superior service with 24-hour turnaround could retain loyal clients without the $150,000 outlay [k]. This keeps Rachel flexible while she studies the online rival's real pricing in Wexley [app]. But standing still risks losing up to 30% of revenue within a year as price-sensitive customers switch away [an]. Overall, Rachel should buy the press if her order book shows at least $150,000 of new long-term contracts, because an 18% unit-cost cut is the strongest defence against a 25% price gap and the press would pay back over its 10-year life [eval]. If the pipeline stays soft she should compete on service first and borrow later once demand is proven [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Press costs $150,000, doubles capacity, cuts unit costs 18%; Keeping presses avoids $100,000 borrowing at 9% but risks losing 30% of revenue | application_max_2: Uses $150,000 / $100,000 / 9% / $96,000 / $880,000 stem figures; Reference to 25% undercutting, 18% cost saving, 24-hour delivery and 30% revenue at risk | analysis_max_2: Analysis of margin protection vs loan-repayment strain and personal guarantee risk; Analysis of capacity gain vs standing still and revenue erosion over a year | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on order pipeline / risk appetite; Balanced judgement weighing cost saving and revenue risk for and against the press

--- STEM ---
Sunvalley Foods Ltd is a food processing company in rural Carlow County, founded 10 years ago by Aoife Brennan. It freezes and packs mixed vegetables for supermarket own-brand ranges, employing 46 production staff plus 4 quality inspectors. Output is 30,000 bags per week across five stages: sorting, washing, cutting, blanching and packing.

Currently workers rotate through all five stages each week. Aoife wants to introduce permanent specialisation, giving each worker one stage. In similar factories this raised output by 40%, but some Sunvalley staff fear boredom and the firm lost 2 workers after a 3-month trial last year. Training one worker for a single stage costs $800, and rejection rates currently stand at 6% of batches. The board must decide by December whether to change.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'division of labour'.
    Answer: Division of labour is where production is split into separate tasks and each worker specialises in one task, such as sorting, washing, cutting, blanching or packing mixed vegetables. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Division of labour = splitting production into small distinct tasks; Each worker specialises in just one repeated task / stage

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why businesses use division of labour.
    Answer: Reason 1: Division of labour breaks production into small tasks so workers specialise [k]. Sunvalley splits its line into five stages — sorting, washing, cutting, blanching and packing — across 46 production staff [app]. Reason 2: It raises productivity and speeds up output [k]. In similar factories specialisation raised output by 40%, which would push Sunvalley well beyond its current 30,000 bags per week [app].
    Keywords: Sunvalley Foods Ltd, 46 production staff, 30,000 bags, specialisation, sorting, washing, cutting, blanching and packing, 40%, $800
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Workers specialise in one repeated task rather than all tasks; Specialisation speeds up work / raises productivity through practice | application_max_2: Reference to the five stages and 46 production staff; Reference to the 40% output gain and 30,000 bags per week from the stem

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Sunvalley Foods Ltd might face after introducing specialisation.
    Answer: Point 1: Repetitive specialist work causes boredom and lowers motivation [k]. Sunvalley already lost 2 workers after a 3-month specialisation trial last year, showing that single-stage work can demoralise the 46 production staff [app]. This raises recruitment and training costs at $800 per replacement and disrupts the 30,000-bag weekly target [an]. Point 2: Over-dependence on key specialists creates bottlenecks [k]. If the cutting specialist is absent, the whole line can stall because each worker masters only one stage [app]. This risks raising rejection rates above the current 6% and jeopardising supermarket own-brand contracts [an].
    Keywords: Sunvalley Foods Ltd, specialisation, 40%, 3-month trial, 2 workers, 6%, 30,000 bags
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Monotony/boredom reduces motivation and can raise labour turnover; Over-specialisation creates dependency on individuals, risking bottlenecks | application_max_2: Reference to the 2 workers lost after the 3-month trial and $800 retraining cost; Reference to the 6% rejection rate / possible contract loss | analysis_max_2: Analysis chain from boredom -> resignations -> higher costs and disrupted output; Analysis chain from absence of a specialist -> line stoppage -> missed orders

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sunvalley Foods Ltd should introduce permanent specialisation on its production line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for specialisation: Giving each of the 46 production staff one of the five stages could raise output by 40%, easing the strain on the 30,000-bag week [k]. Trained specialists make fewer mistakes, which should help push rejection rates below the present 6% [app]. However, boredom could worsen turnover, following the 2 resignations seen in the 3-month trial [an]. Argument against: Keeping job rotation preserves motivation and flexibility [k], and retraining everyone at $800 each would be wasted if staff keep leaving or demand shifts between stages like blanching and packing [app]. But rotation means slower throughput and caps output at 30,000 bags a week for a growing own-brand range [an]. Overall, permanent specialisation is justified if Aoife combines it with job rotation, structured training at $800 per head and close monitoring of the 6% rejection rate, because the 40% output gain is too large to ignore for supermarket contracts [eval]. Imposing rigid single-task roles without staff consultation would only repeat last year's resignations [eval].
    Keywords: Sunvalley Foods Ltd, specialisation, 40%, 2 workers, 3-month trial, 6%, $800, 30,000 bags
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Specialisation can raise output by 40% and reduce mistakes; Rotation preserves motivation; rigid tasks risk turnover and training waste | application_max_2: Uses the 40% figure, 30,000 bags, 6% rejections, $800 training cost and the 2 resignations; Reference to the five stages and 3-month trial from the stem | analysis_max_2: Analysis of productivity gains vs turnover/retraining costs; Analysis of quality and flexibility trade-offs for the supermarket range | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on rotation/consultation/monitoring; Balanced judgement weighing the 40% gain against boredom and resignations

--- STEM ---
FreshPress Laundry Co is a commercial laundry serving 26 hotels and restaurants across Norwick. Founded 5 years ago by Tomasz Nowak, it employs 18 operatives across two shifts at a single depot. Last year it cleaned 4,200 tonnes of linen, about 233 tonnes per worker, but 45 hotel loads were rejected last quarter for poor stain removal.

Tomasz must choose between buying a high-capacity washer costing $85,000, lifting output to 5,100 tonnes a year but using 15% more electricity, or spending $20,000 on staff training to cut re-washes by 30% and reduce wasted water and detergent. He has $90,000 available now. The hotels have asked for better stain removal by March or they will review contracts worth $140,000 a year. The hotels also expect twice-daily deliveries.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'productivity'.
    Answer: Productivity measures how much output is produced per unit of input, usually per worker, such as 4,200 tonnes of linen cleaned divided by 18 operatives at FreshPress Laundry Co. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Productivity = output per worker / per unit of input; Reward formula-style definitions or references to output efficiency per labour unit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why productivity is important to FreshPress Laundry Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: Productivity shows output per worker, so higher productivity lowers average cost per tonne [k]. FreshPress cleans about 233 tonnes per worker per year, so even modest gains across 18 operatives would cut unit costs sharply [app]. Reason 2: High productivity helps meet customer demand and deadlines [k]. The hotels want stain-removal problems fixed by March or they will review contracts worth $140,000 a year, so more output per worker protects that revenue [app].
    Keywords: FreshPress Laundry Co, 18 operatives, 4,200 tonnes, 233 tonnes, 26 hotels, $140,000, 45 hotel loads
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher productivity lowers average/unit costs; Productivity lets the firm meet deadlines and customer demand | application_max_2: Reference to 4,200 tonnes / 233 tonnes per worker / 18 operatives; Reference to the March deadline and the $140,000 hotel contracts

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two differences between productivity and efficiency.
    Answer: Point 1: Productivity measures the quantity of output per unit of input, whereas efficiency measures how well inputs are used with minimal waste [k]. FreshPress cleans 233 tonnes per worker, a productivity measure, while 45 rejected hotel loads and poor stain removal are signs of inefficient work [app]. This shows productivity counts volume but efficiency counts quality and waste [an]. Point 2: Productivity gains can come from more machines or longer hours, but efficiency gains come from better methods [k]. The $85,000 washer would raise output to 5,100 tonnes a year even though it uses 15% more electricity [app]. So FreshPress could lift productivity yet waste more resources if efficiency were ignored [an].
    Keywords: FreshPress Laundry Co, 4,200 tonnes, 233 tonnes, 5,100 tonnes, $85,000, 30%, $20,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Productivity = output per input (volume); efficiency = waste minimisation / quality of input use; Productivity can rise with machines or hours; efficiency requires process improvement | application_max_2: Reference to 233 tonnes per worker vs 45 rejected loads; Reference to the $85,000 washer and its 15% extra electricity use | analysis_max_2: Analysis distinguishing volume/quantity measures from waste/quality measures; Analysis that productivity can rise while efficiency falls, with cost consequences

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tomasz should buy the high-capacity washer rather than spend $20,000 on staff training? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for the washer: The $85,000 washer lifts output to 5,100 tonnes a year, a gain of 900 tonnes [k]. It lets FreshPress take on extra hotel linen and cut turnaround times for its 26 hotels and restaurants [app]. However, it uses 15% more electricity and would absorb nearly all of the $90,000 the business has available, leaving little for maintenance or training [an]. Argument for training: Spending $20,000 on staff training could cut re-washes by 30%, saving water and detergent [k]. It directly addresses the 45 rejected loads that caused the crisis at far lower cost than the washer [app]. But training alone will not raise total capacity or satisfy hotels needing 5,100 tonnes of linen output [an]. Overall, Tomasz should buy the washer because it is the only option that protects the $140,000 contracts, provided he secures an electricity-efficient model, because stain complaints plus lost output together exceed $140,000 a year [eval]. Training should follow in the next quarter to fix quality once the extra capacity is guaranteed [eval].
    Keywords: FreshPress Laundry Co, $85,000, 5,100 tonnes, 15% more electricity, $20,000, 30%, $90,000, $140,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Washer lifts output to 5,100 tonnes (900-tonne gain) at $85,000 and 15% more electricity; Training costs $20,000, cuts re-washes 30% but adds no capacity | application_max_2: Uses $85,000 / $90,000 / $20,000 / 5,100 tonnes / 30% figures from the stem; Reference to the 45 rejected loads and $140,000 contracts and March deadline | analysis_max_2: Analysis of capacity vs quality: extra output does not fix rejects but protects contracts; Analysis of capital use of $90,000 reserve and 15% electricity cost increase | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation prioritising washer (or training) linked to the $140,000 contract threat; Balanced judgement: washer for capacity now, training for quality next

--- STEM ---
Copperfield Foods Ltd is a family food business in the coastal town of Bowen Bay, producing jams, sauces and pickles. It has traded for 7 years under founder Maria Copperfield, employing 9 staff, with revenue of $640,000 last year. Demand for its tomato chutney has grown 30% since winter, and customers keep asking for sugar-free options, though healthier ingredients cost $0.40 more per jar.

Maria has $30,000 to spend and must choose between buying a new boiling kettle line costing $28,000, or launching a sugar-free jam range costing $26,000 for ingredients and jars. She cannot fund both, so either choice means giving up the other. The new range could add $90,000 in sales if it succeeds. The bank manager reminded her that resources are scarce while customer wants are unlimited.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'wants'.
    Answer: Wants are things people desire but do not need to survive, such as jams, sauces and pickles, whose demand exceeds the resources available to supply them. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Wants = desired goods/services not essential for survival; Wants are unlimited; resources to satisfy them are scarce

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why scarcity is a problem for Copperfield Foods Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Scarcity means resources are limited while wants are unlimited [k]. Maria has only $30,000 to spend but wants both a $28,000 kettle line and a $26,000 sugar-free launch [app]. Reason 2: Scarcity forces choices with opportunity costs [k]. Choosing one option means giving up the other, so the scarce $30,000 cannot fund both projects at Copperfield Foods [app].
    Keywords: Copperfield Foods Ltd, 9 staff, $640,000, 30%, $30,000, tomato chutney, $26,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Scarcity = limited resources vs unlimited wants; Scarcity forces trade-offs / economic choices to be made | application_max_2: Reference to the $30,000 budget vs the $28,000 and $26,000 options; Reference to the inability to fund both projects

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways understanding opportunity cost could help Maria make better decisions.
    Answer: Point 1: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone in a decision [k]. If Maria launches the $26,000 sugar-free range, she forgoes the $28,000 kettle line and its extra production capacity [app]. Weighing the $90,000 potential sales against slower production clarifies the true cost of each option [an]. Point 2: Recognising opportunity cost keeps decisions aligned with customer demand [k]. Tomato chutney demand grew 30% and customers ask for sugar-free jars, so choosing the range matches wants and uses scarce ingredients wisely [app]. This raises the chance the $26,000 investment is recovered, rather than spending $28,000 on capacity for a product customers are not asking about [an].
    Keywords: Copperfield Foods Ltd, $30,000, $28,000, $26,000, $90,000, sugar-free, $0.40
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Opportunity cost = next best alternative forgone; Better decisions weigh all alternatives, not only immediate gains | application_max_2: Reference to the $26,000 range vs $28,000 kettle line; Reference to the $90,000 potential sales and the 30% demand growth | analysis_max_2: Analysis linking foregone alternative to true cost of each option; Analysis linking demand signals (30% growth, sugar-free asks) to return on $26,000

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Maria should launch the sugar-free range rather than buy the new kettle line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for the sugar-free range: Launching costs $26,000 and taps proven demand, with chutney sales growing 30% and customers explicitly asking for sugar-free jars [k]. Healthier ingredients cost only $0.40 more per jar, preserving margins while unmet demand is captured [app]. However, $26,000 for ingredients and jars is a near-total commitment of the $30,000 budget and the range has never sold at Copperfield before [an]. Argument for the kettle line: The $28,000 boiling kettle line would raise capacity and protect supply of the existing chutney, safeguarding the 30% growth already in evidence [k]. It is a known product so the investment feels safer, but it creates no new demand and yields no extra revenue by itself [app]. By contrast the range could add $90,000 in sales if it succeeds, more than three times its launch cost [an]. Overall, Maria should launch the sugar-free range because the $90,000 upside against a $26,000 cost and explicit customer demand is compelling, provided she trials small batches to limit risk within her $30,000 budget [eval]. The kettle line can be bought later once range sales prove themselves [eval].
    Keywords: Copperfield Foods Ltd, $30,000, $28,000, $26,000, $90,000, sugar-free, $640,000, 30%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Sugar-free range costs $26,000 vs kettle line $28,000; both fit the $30,000 budget; Range could add $90,000 sales; kettle line adds no direct revenue | application_max_2: Uses $30,000 / $26,000 / $28,000 / $90,000 stem figures; Reference to 30% chutney growth, $0.40 higher ingredient cost and customer demand for sugar-free | analysis_max_2: Analysis of demand-led vs capacity-led investment and payback ($90,000 vs cost); Analysis of risk given an unproven product and a $30,000 ceiling | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation for the range (or kettle) conditional on trial batches and budget limit; Balanced judgement weighing $90,000 upside vs safer capacity expansion

Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd is a woodworking business in the market town of Elmridge, founded 9 years ago by Ben and Clara Ashby. Specialising fully in walnut cabinets would let each worker master one craft, cut waste by 12% and appeal to boutique retailers.     Question: Outline one way specialisation can add value to furniture.
    Answer: By concentrating workers on one craft, output per worker rises and quality improves, so cabinets sell at $1,900 each for far more than the input costs — the difference between selling price and input cost is the added value created [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Specialisation raises skill, output and quality of one task; Added value = difference between selling price and cost of inputs; specialisation widens that gap

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why businesses specialise.
    Answer: Reason 1: Specialisation means workers focus on one product or task [k]. Cedar & Co could let its 10 woodworkers master cabinet-making instead of dividing time with flat-pack pine shelves [app]. Reason 2: Specialisation raises efficiency and adds value [k]. Dedicated cabinet staff could cut waste by 12% and justify premium $1,900 pricing to boutique retailers [app].
    Keywords: Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd, hand-carved walnut cabinets, 10 woodworkers, $720,000, 3,000 flat-pack shelves, $1,900, $85
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Specialisation = focusing on one product/task/market; Specialisation raises skill, speed and quality / reduces waste | application_max_2: Reference to 10 woodworkers and the two ranges ($1,900 cabinets, $85 shelves); Reference to the 12% waste cut and boutique retailer targeting

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways specialisation adds value for Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd.
    Answer: Point 1: Specialised workers develop deeper skills and waste less material [k]. Full-time cabinet makers could cut walnut waste by 12% while mastering the 16-hour build [app]. This lowers unit cost and raises the value added per $1,900 cabinet sold [an]. Point 2: Specialisation enables a stronger brand and premium pricing [k]. Boutique retailers pay more for expert joinery than for general furniture [app]. This helps Cedar & Co capture more value from each of the 60 firm orders for next year, instead of relying on $85 shelves with thin margins [an].
    Keywords: Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd, specialising, 12%, 16 hours, 40 minutes, $9 per board foot, $720,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Specialisation deepens skill, speed and consistency; Specialisation supports brand positioning and premium pricing | application_max_2: Reference to 12% waste cut and 16 hours per cabinet; Reference to boutique retailers, 60 firm cabinet orders and $85 shelves | analysis_max_2: Analysis linking skill/waste reduction to value added per cabinet; Analysis linking brand premium to higher margin per order vs shelves

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd should specialise fully in hand-carved walnut cabinets? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for full specialisation: Concentrating on walnut cabinets lets each of the 10 woodworkers master one craft, cutting waste by 12% and sharpening the brand for boutique retailers [k]. However, with walnut at $9 per board foot and only 60 firm cabinet orders for next year, volume would sit far below the 3,000 flat-pack shelves sold annually [an]. Argument against full specialisation: Keeping both ranges spreads risk, and steady shelf sales of 3,000 units at $85 each generate dependable cash while cabinet demand builds [k]. Specialising too soon could leave the workshop underused and Cedar & Co short of working capital [app]. But splitting focus dilutes craftsmanship, keeps waste high and weakens the added-value story boutique retailers will pay for [an]. Overall, Cedar & Co should specialise fully only once the 60 firm orders are converted into deposits covering at least a full year's production, because the 12% waste saving and $1,900 pricing reward mastery [eval]. Otherwise a gradual transition, keeping shelves until cabinet demand proves itself, is the safer route given demand uncertainty [eval].
    Keywords: Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd, walnut cabinets, $1,900, 16 hours, $9 per board foot, 60 firm cabinet orders, 3,000 flat-pack shelves, 12%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Specialisation cuts waste 12%, builds brand, supports $1,900 pricing; Dual range spreads risk; walnut at $9 per board foot raises input costs | application_max_2: Uses $1,900 / $85 / 16 hours / $9 per board foot / 12% stem figures; Reference to only 60 firm cabinet orders vs 3,000 shelf sales and $720,000 revenue | analysis_max_2: Analysis of added value and margin per cabinet vs shelf volume economics; Analysis of demand uncertainty, walnut cost inflation and working capital risk | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on deposits/conversion of the 60 firm orders; Balanced judgement weighing $1,900-cabinet upside vs risk of losing shelf cash flow

--- STEM ---
QuickQuill Printing Ltd is a print shop in the commuter town of Redford, operating for 6 years. It produces business cards, menus and leaflets for local firms, employing 8 staff and 2 apprentices. Revenue was $520,000 last year, and orders have risen 15% since a rival closed. The shop now turns away work most Saturdays because both presses are fully booked.

Owner Nadia Rahman must choose how to expand. Buying a faster digital press costing $110,000 would raise capacity from 9,000 to 14,000 sheets per hour and last 10 years. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'efficiency'.
    Answer: Efficiency means producing the maximum output from given inputs with the least waste of time, materials or energy, such as QuickQuill Printing Ltd running its presses without idle Saturdays. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Efficiency = maximum output from minimum input / waste; Reward references to minimising waste, time energy or materials in production

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways increased efficiency could benefit QuickQuill Printing Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Higher efficiency means more output from the same inputs [k]. If QuickQuill reduces turnaround times and waste, it could serve the Saturday work it currently turns away and raise effective capacity toward 14,000 sheets an hour [app]. Reason 2: Higher efficiency lowers average costs [k]. Cutting re-prints and idle press time would grow the $520,000 revenue without adding $27,000-a-year staff costs [app].
    Keywords: QuickQuill Printing Ltd, 8 staff, $520,000, 15%, 14,000 sheets, $110,000, $27,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Efficiency raises output per unit of input; Efficiency lowers unit/average costs and waste | application_max_2: Reference to the Saturday backlog and the 9,000 to 14,000 sheets-per-hour upgrade; Reference to $520,000 revenue and $27,000 staff cost comparison

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of expanding QuickQuill Printing Ltd using capital rather than labour.
    Answer: Point 1: Capital investment provides durable, high-output capacity [k]. The $110,000 press lasts 10 years and lifts capacity to 14,000 sheets per hour [app]. This gives QuickQuill the scale to clear the Saturday backlog and capture more of the orders rising 15% since the rival closed [an]. Point 2: Machines produce consistent quality with lower ongoing per-unit costs [k]. Unlike 3 extra operators costing $81,000 a year, the press runs with the existing 8 staff [app]. This protects margins, reduces supervision costs and keeps Saturday turnaround times reliable for business card and leaflet clients [an].
    Keywords: QuickQuill Printing Ltd, $110,000, 14,000 sheets, 10 years, 9,000, $27,000, $130,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Capital goods last for years and offer high, consistent capacity; Machines spread cost over more units / lower per-unit running cost over time | application_max_2: Reference to the $110,000 press, 10-year life and 14,000 sheets per hour; Reference to 3 operators at $27,000 each ($81,000 a year) vs existing 8 staff | analysis_max_2: Analysis linking one-off capital cost to long-run unit cost advantage; Analysis linking capacity, consistency and reliability to winning more orders

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Nadia should buy the faster digital press rather than hire 3 more operators? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for the press: Buying the $110,000 digital press raises capacity from 9,000 to 14,000 sheets per hour and lasts 10 years [k]. It unlocks the Saturday backlog worth about $60,000 a year and scales with the 15% order growth [app]. However, $110,000 of the $130,000 reserves would be spent upfront, leaving little cushion if breakdowns occur [an]. Argument for hiring operators: Three operators add 20% capacity immediately at $81,000 a year with no large upfront outlay [k]. Nadia keeps $130,000 liquid and can scale back staff if demand dips after the rival closure settles [app]. But wages are a permanent cost and never match the press's step-change of 5,000 extra sheets per hour [an]. Overall, Nadia should buy the press because the $60,000 Saturday backlog and 15% growth justify locking in long-term capacity at 10 years, provided she arranges a service contract to manage breakdown risk [eval]. Hiring operators only becomes the better choice if the order pipeline softens or her cash reserves fall below $50,000 [eval].
    Keywords: QuickQuill Printing Ltd, $110,000, 9,000 to 14,000 sheets, 10 years, $27,000, 20% capacity, $130,000, $60,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Press = $110,000, 9,000 to 14,000 sheets/hour, lasts 10 years; Hiring = 20% capacity now for $81,000 a year, keeps cash liquid | application_max_2: Uses $110,000 / $130,000 / $27,000 / $60,000 / 15% figures from the stem; Reference to Saturday backlog, machine breakdowns and staff absence concerns | analysis_max_2: Analysis of one-off vs recurring cost ($110,000 vs $81,000 a year) and payback logic; Analysis of flexibility/liquidity versus capacity step-change and breakdown risk | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation favouring the press (or hiring) conditional on contracts and cash position; Balanced judgement weighing capacity/growth vs liquidity and breakdown risk

--- STEM ---
ClearFlow Water Corporation is a public corporation owned by the Country X government, supplying tap water to 1.8 million households across 6 provinces. Founded in 1994, it employs 3,200 staff and records annual revenue of $420 million, but last year it required a government subsidy of $35 million to cover operating losses at its northern treatment plants.

The government proposes selling ClearFlow to a private investor group for $500 million, arguing the sale would clear part of its $900 million infrastructure debt and fund a $260 million modernisation programme. Private investors expect a profit margin of 12%, compared with ClearFlow's current 2%. Consumers fear water bills could rise by $8 per month, while the 3,200 employees worry about the 400 redundancies planned by the buyer.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'public corporation'.
    Answer: A business organisation owned and controlled by the state or government, usually providing essential goods or services to the public. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Owned and controlled by the government or state; Provides essential goods or services to the public

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the Country X government chose to run ClearFlow as a public corporation.
    Answer: Reason 1: To guarantee essential services to all citizens [k], ClearFlow supplies 1.8 million households across 6 provinces, including remote areas a private firm might avoid [app]. Reason 2: To keep water affordable [k], ClearFlow charges below cost and needed a $35 million subsidy last year rather than pursuing profit like a private owner would [app].
    Keywords: ClearFlow, public corporation, 1.8 million, 6 provinces, $35 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Essential services provided to the whole population; Government controls prices to keep them affordable | application_max_2: Supplies 1.8 million households across 6 provinces; $35 million subsidy to keep water below cost

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems stakeholders may face if ClearFlow is privatised.
    Answer: Problem 1: Consumers may pay higher water bills [k], since the buyer targets a 12% profit margin and would raise bills by $8 per month for 1.8 million households [app], reducing household disposable income and risking payment arrears [an]. Problem 2: Employees may lose their jobs [k], because the buyer plans 400 redundancies among ClearFlow's 3,200 staff [app], cutting household incomes and weakening local communities [an].
    Keywords: ClearFlow, 12%, $8 per month, 1.8 million, 400 redundancies, 3,200, $500 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Consumers face higher prices under private ownership; Employees face job losses and insecurity | application_max_2: 12% profit margin target and $8 monthly bill increases; 400 redundancies planned among 3,200 staff | analysis_max_2: Reduced disposable income may cause arrears; Falling incomes harm local communities

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the Country X government should privatise ClearFlow Water Corporation? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for privatisation is that the $500 million sale [k] would clear much of the government's $900 million infrastructure debt and fund a $260 million modernisation programme [app], which could improve water quality and reliability across the 6 provinces [an]. However, one argument against is that profit-seeking investors [k] would raise bills by $8 per month for 1.8 million households and cut 400 of ClearFlow's 3,200 staff [app], reducing affordability for low-income families and harming public welfare [an]. Overall, the government should not privatise ClearFlow [eval], because water is an essential service and the $35 million annual subsidy costs taxpayers far less than countrywide harm from higher bills and job losses [eval].
    Keywords: ClearFlow, $500 million, $900 million, $260 million, $8 per month, 1.8 million, 400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Privatisation raises funds to pay off debt and invest; Public ownership prioritises essential-service delivery over profit | application_max_2: $500 million sale against $900 million debt and $260 million modernisation; $8 monthly bill rises and 400 redundancies among 3,200 staff | analysis_max_2: Modernisation could improve water quality and reliability; Higher bills and job losses reduce affordability and household welfare | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both privatisation and continued public ownership; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

--- STEM ---
Aldermere City Transit is a bus service provided by Aldermere City Council, a local government authority, operating 45 buses across 12 routes in the town. Last year the service carried 2.4 million passenger journeys and cost $9.6 million to run, with fares covering only 60% of operating costs, so the council topped up $3.8 million from local taxes. It employs 210 drivers and maintenance staff.

A private operator, FastWay Coaches, has offered to run the network for $7.9 million a year, promising 8 newer buses and free Wi-Fi. In return it wants a 25% fare rise, authority to cut the 12 lowest-ridership routes serving rural suburbs, and exclusivity for 7 years. Councillors must decide by March whether to outsource the service, which carries 58,000 pensioners and students using concessionary fares each month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'mixed economy'.
    Answer: An economy containing both a private sector and a public sector, where government and private businesses share the production of goods and services. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Contains both private and public sectors; Government and private businesses share production of goods and services

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Aldermere City Council provides a bus service.
    Answer: Reason 1: To serve areas private firms find unprofitable [k], Aldermere City Transit runs 12 routes covering rural suburbs where ridership is too low for FastWay Coaches to serve alone [app]. Reason 2: To keep transport affordable [k], fares cover only 60% of the $9.6 million cost, with a $3.8 million tax subsidy and concessionary fares for 58,000 pensioners and students [app].
    Keywords: Aldermere City Transit, 12 routes, FastWay Coaches, 60%, $3.8 million, 58,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Council provides services private firms may avoid as unprofitable; Council keeps services affordable for low-income residents | application_max_2: 12 routes covering rural suburbs; 60% cost recovery, $3.8 million subsidy and 58,000 concessionary users

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages for Aldermere residents if the council outsources the service to FastWay Coaches.
    Answer: Problem 1: Fares would rise by 25% [k], making travel unaffordable for the 58,000 pensioners and students who rely on concessionary fares with Aldermere City Transit [app], which may push low-income passengers off buses and into cars, increasing congestion [an]. Problem 2: 12 low-ridership routes would be cut [k], leaving rural suburbs without public transport despite the council's service objective [app], isolating elderly residents and raising their cost of reaching shops and hospitals [an].
    Keywords: 25%, 58,000, Aldermere City Transit, 12, $3.8 million, rural suburbs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher fares exclude low-income passengers; Route cuts remove services from unprofitable areas | application_max_2: 25% fare rise affecting 58,000 concessionary passengers; 12 rural suburb routes to be cut by FastWay | analysis_max_2: Displacement to cars may increase congestion and pollution; Isolation raises living costs and reduces access to services

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Aldermere City Council should outsource its bus service to FastWay Coaches? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for outsourcing is the taxpayer saving [k], because FastWay would run the network for $7.9 million a year, $1.7 million less than the $9.6 million cost, and would deliver 8 newer buses with free Wi-Fi [app], freeing public money for schools and libraries [an]. However, one argument against is the harm to vulnerable passengers [k], since FastWay wants a 25% fare rise and to cut 12 rural routes, undermining the concessionary fares used by 58,000 pensioners and students [app], which conflicts with the council's duty to serve the whole community [an]. Overall, the council should not outsource now [eval], because a $1.7 million annual saving is outweighed by losing 12 routes and pricing out low-income residents, although it could negotiate better terms including fixed fares [eval].
    Keywords: FastWay Coaches, $7.9 million, $9.6 million, 25%, 12, 58,000, Aldermere City Transit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Outsourcing may cut costs and improve equipment; Outsourcing may damage affordability and service coverage | application_max_2: $7.9 million private bid saves $1.7 million against $9.6 million cost; 8 newer buses promised; 25% fare rise and 12 rural route cuts affecting 58,000 concessionary passengers | analysis_max_2: Savings free funds for other public services; Fare rises and route cuts exclude low-income and rural residents | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both outsourcing and continued council control; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

--- STEM ---
Country X's care sector is part of a mixed economy combining private and public providers. Meridian Care Homes is a private company running 3 care homes with 120 beds in the capital, charging residents $1,450 per week and employing 78 qualified nurses and carers. Its waiting list is 25 names and its profit last year was $1.9 million.

The public National Care Trust operates a 200-bed facility in the same city, but its waiting list has grown to 340 people, with average waits of 9 months. The government, which spent $28 million on public care last year, is considering paying Meridian Care Homes $6 million to run 40 additional beds under contract, rather than build a new public ward costing $15 million.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'private sector'.
    Answer: The part of the economy owned and controlled by private individuals and businesses rather than the government, usually aiming to make a profit. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Owned and controlled by private individuals or businesses; Usually aims to make a profit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Country X has a mixed economy in care provision.
    Answer: Reason 1: Private firms add capacity and choice [k], as Meridian Care Homes runs 3 homes with 120 beds and its $6 million contract would open 40 more beds faster than a $15 million public ward [app]. Reason 2: Public provision protects those who cannot pay [k], since the National Care Trust operates 200 beds funded by $28 million of government spending for patients facing 9-month waits [app].
    Keywords: Meridian Care Homes, National Care Trust, 120 beds, $6 million, 200-bed, $28 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Private sector adds capacity and choice; Public sector guarantees access regardless of ability to pay | application_max_2: 120 beds across 3 homes; $6 million for 40 contracted beds versus a $15 million public ward; 200-bed National Care Trust funded by $28 million with 9-month waits

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why stakeholder objectives may conflict in Country X's care sector.
    Answer: Conflict 1: Residents want quality care at fair prices but owners want profit [k], because Meridian charges $1,450 per week and earned $1.9 million profit from 120 beds with 78 staff [app], so cost control may reduce staffing levels and care quality [an]. Conflict 2: Taxpayers want value for money while patients want short waits [k], yet the government must choose between a $6 million contract with Meridian and a $15 million public expansion to clear the 340-person waiting list [app], and funding one option limits money for the other [an].
    Keywords: Meridian Care Homes, $1,450, $1.9 million, 120 beds, $6 million, $15 million, 340
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Owners' profit objective conflicts with residents' quality objective; Taxpayers' value-for-money objective conflicts with patients' access objective | application_max_2: $1,450 weekly fees and $1.9 million profit from 120 beds with 78 staff; Choice between $6 million contract and $15 million ward to clear 340 waiting patients | analysis_max_2: Cost pressure may lower staffing and care quality; Limited public funds force trade-offs between options

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the government should sign the $6 million contract with Meridian Care Homes? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for the contract is that it is cheaper and faster [k], costing $6 million instead of $15 million for a new public ward and adding 40 beds to cut the 340-person waiting list sooner [app], improving care access without raising taxes [an]. However, one argument against is that public money would enrich a profit-making firm [k], whose $1,450 weekly fees and $1.9 million profit show a private objective that may conflict with affordable care for poorer residents [app], weakening long-term public provision [an]. Overall, the government should sign the contract [eval], because $6 million is less than half the public alternative and 9-month waits harm vulnerable people now, provided the contract enforces quality standards and fee caps [eval].
    Keywords: Meridian Care Homes, $6 million, $15 million, 340, $1,450, $1.9 million, National Care Trust
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Contracting private capacity can add beds faster and cheaper; Private profit motive may conflict with affordable public care | application_max_2: $6 million contract adds 40 beds versus $15 million public ward to clear 340 waits; Meridian charges $1,450 per week and earned $1.9 million profit | analysis_max_2: Faster access improves outcomes for waiting patients; Profit orientation may raise long-term costs or reduce equity | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the private contract and public expansion; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

--- STEM ---
Rivermart Stores PLC is a public limited company operating 26 supermarkets across Country X. It employs 1,900 people, reports annual revenue of $310 million and made a profit of $14 million last year, paying shareholders a dividend of $6 million. Opened 21 years ago, it is the country's third-largest supermarket chain. Managers have proposed automating checkouts in 18 stores, requiring a $6 million investment and cutting 150 jobs.

Employees, supported by their union, demand a pay rise of $0.75 per hour, costing about $2.9 million a year. Customers' groups want lower prices, while community groups want Rivermart to keep sourcing local produce from 120 farmers.     Question: Define the term 'shareholders'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Shareholders own shares in the company; Shareholders are part-owners of the business

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why objectives at Rivermart Stores PLC conflict.
    Answer: Conflict 1: Shareholders want higher dividends but employees want higher pay [k], because a $0.75 hourly rise costing $2.9 million a year would cut the $14 million profit available for the $6 million dividend and the automation plan [app]. Conflict 2: Customers want lower prices while owners want profit [k], so with revenue of $310 million across 26 stores, cutting prices to please customers would squeeze the returns shareholders expect [app].
    Keywords: Rivermart Stores PLC, $0.75, $2.9 million, $14 million, $6 million, $310 million, 26
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Shareholder returns objective conflicts with employee pay objective; Customer low-price objective conflicts with owner profit objective | application_max_2: $0.75 hourly rise costing $2.9 million against $14 million profit and $6 million dividend; $310 million revenue across 26 stores must cover any price cuts

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Rivermart Stores PLC if it automates instead of granting the pay rise.
    Answer: Problem 1: 150 employees would lose their jobs [k], because the automation plan cuts roles across 18 of Rivermart's 26 stores [app], damaging morale and increasing recruitment and training costs [an]. Problem 2: Industrial action by the union becomes more likely [k], as workers demanding $0.75 per hour see $2.9 million redirected into a $6 million machine investment [app], risking strikes, higher absenteeism and lost sales [an].
    Keywords: Rivermart Stores PLC, 150, 18, 26, $0.75, $2.9 million, $6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation causes redundancies and job insecurity; Automation provokes union resistance and industrial action | application_max_2: 150 jobs cut across 18 of 26 stores; $2.9 million pay claim set against $6 million automation spend | analysis_max_2: Low morale raises recruitment, training and error costs; Strikes or absenteeism disrupt trading and revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rivermart Stores PLC should invest in automation rather than approve the pay rise? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for automation is lower long-term labour costs [k], because a $6 million investment across 18 stores would cut 150 jobs and support the profit objective on $310 million revenue [app], improving efficiency and helping keep prices competitive for customers [an]. However, one argument against is the damage to stakeholder relations [k], since the union's $0.75 hourly claim costing $2.9 million is under half the automation spend, and cutting 150 of 1,900 staff would worsen morale [app], risking strikes, lost sales and reputational harm [an]. Overall, Rivermart should not automate now [eval], because the $2.9 million pay rise is cheaper than $6 million machines, protects 1,900 jobs and motivates workers to serve customers better [eval].
    Keywords: Rivermart Stores PLC, $6 million, $0.75, $2.9 million, 150, 1,900, $310 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation reduces labour costs and improves efficiency; Automation damages staff morale and union relations | application_max_2: $6 million automation cuts 150 jobs across 18 stores on $310 million revenue; $0.75 hourly claim costs $2.9 million versus automation; 1,900 staff affected | analysis_max_2: Efficiency gains support competitiveness and profit; Worsened morale risks industrial action and lost revenue | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both automation and the pay rise; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures
