--- STEM ---
Nimbus Cycles Ltd is a bicycle retailer in Country X founded 2 years ago by Priya and Daniel. In its first year it made a loss of $25,000, and survival was its only objective. In year two it reached revenue of $480,000, made a profit of $40,000 and holds a 6% share of the city's bicycle market, with 9 employees.

Priya wants to open a second shop in the neighbouring town, costing $180,000, funded by a bank loan. Daniel argues the profit is too small to service the debt and wants to keep the objective of profit maximisation, rebuilding reserves which fell to $30,000.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'survival'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Objective of continuing to trade; Typical of start-ups or crisis periods

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Nimbus Cycles Ltd changed its objective from survival to growth.
    Answer: Reason 1: The business has become financially stable [k], moving from a $25,000 first-year loss to a $40,000 profit and $480,000 revenue in year two [app]. Reason 2: A market opportunity exists [k], because electric-bike sales grew by 45% and its 6% share of the city market leaves room to win neighbouring-town customers [app].
    Keywords: Nimbus Cycles Ltd, $25,000, $40,000, $480,000, 45%, 6%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Financial stability allows objectives to move beyond survival; Market opportunities encourage growth objectives | application_max_2: Move from $25,000 first-year loss to $40,000 profit on $480,000 revenue; 45% growth in electric-bike sales and only 6% market share

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Nimbus Cycles Ltd of pursuing growth as its new objective.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A second shop would reach new customers [k], letting Nimbus sell electric bikes, whose sales grew by 45%, in the neighbouring town [app], increasing revenue beyond the current $480,000 [an]. Benefit 2: Growth spreads risk across two locations [k], so the business no longer depends on one shop paying $4,200 per month rent [app], protecting future profit if city trade slows [an].
    Keywords: Nimbus Cycles Ltd, 45%, $480,000, $4,200, second shop, $40,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Growth reaches new markets and customers; Growth spreads risk across locations | application_max_2: Electric-bike sales grew 45%; neighbouring town is untapped; Single shop rent of $4,200 per month creates concentration risk | analysis_max_2: Revenue potential rises beyond $480,000; Two locations reduce vulnerability to local downturns

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Nimbus Cycles Ltd should pursue growth by opening the second shop? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for growth is that Nimbus has recovered financially [k], turning a $25,000 first-year loss into a $40,000 profit on $480,000 revenue, with electric-bike sales up 45% [app], showing demand strong enough to support a second location [an]. However, one argument against is the financial risk of a $180,000 bank loan [k], because Priya and Daniel hold only $30,000 reserves and a $40,000 annual profit may not cover repayments if trade slows [app], threatening the original shop [an]. Overall, Nimbus should pursue growth by opening the second shop [eval], because a 45% rise in electric-bike sales and two years of improving performance outweigh the debt risk if the loan is spread over several years [eval].
    Keywords: Nimbus Cycles Ltd, $180,000, $30,000, $40,000, 45%, $480,000, second shop
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Growth is justified when demand and stability are proven; Debt-funded growth risks the original business | application_max_2: $25,000 first-year loss recovered to $40,000 profit on $480,000 revenue; electric-bike sales up 45%; $180,000 loan against $30,000 reserves and $4,200 monthly rent | analysis_max_2: Strong demand can fill the second shop and raise revenue; Servicing the loan from limited reserves risks cash flow and failure | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both growth and continued stability/profit maximisation; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

--- STEM ---
Orbit Phones Ltd is an established electronics retailer in Country X with 4 shops and an online store. Annual revenue is $24 million and its profit margin is 9%, earning about $2.16 million last year. Its market share is 14%, compared with TechZone's 22%, the market leader, and industry margins average 8%.

Marketing proposes a 10% price cut on 3,000 phone lines, which it predicts would lift market share to 18% within 12 months and sales volume by 25%. Finance calculates the cut would reduce profit by $1.8 million, leaving about $360,000. Suppliers have offered extended credit of $500,000 if Orbit commits to larger orders. The board meets next month to decide whether market share should replace profit as the main objective.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'profit'.
    Answer: The money left over after total costs are deducted from revenue (sales income). [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Revenue minus total costs; The financial surplus earned by the business

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Orbit Phones Ltd might change its objective from profit to market share.
    Answer: Reason 1: To close the gap with the market leader [k], because TechZone holds 22% and Orbit only 14%, so lifting share to 18% would strengthen its position in Country X [app]. Reason 2: Higher volume could secure cheaper supply [k], with suppliers offering $500,000 extended credit to win Orbit's larger orders if the 10% price cut proceeds [app].
    Keywords: Orbit Phones Ltd, TechZone, 22%, 14%, 18%, $500,000, 10%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Larger market share strengthens competitive position; Volume growth can unlock scale advantages and better supply terms | application_max_2: TechZone on 22% versus Orbit on 14%, target 18%; $500,000 extended credit offered for larger orders after a 10% price cut

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks of Orbit Phones Ltd pursuing market share instead of profit.
    Answer: Risk 1: Profit would nearly disappear [k], because finance calculates the 10% price cut would cost $1.8 million, leaving about $360,000 from $2.16 million [app], reducing retained funds for expansion and dividends [an]. Risk 2: A price war may follow [k], since rival TechZone with 22% share may cut its own prices to defend the lead [app], shrinking Orbit's revenue further below the $24 million baseline [an].
    Keywords: Orbit Phones Ltd, 10%, $1.8 million, $360,000, $2.16 million, TechZone, $24 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Market-share objectives sacrifice short-term profit; Rivals may retaliate with price cuts | application_max_2: $2.16 million profit cut by $1.8 million to about $360,000; TechZone's 22% lead on 3,000 phone lines could trigger a price war | analysis_max_2: Lower retained profit constrains investment and shareholder rewards; Price competition erodes revenue below $24 million

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Orbit Phones Ltd should change its objective from profit to market share? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for pursuing market share is closing the gap with TechZone [k], since a 10% price cut could lift Orbit's share from 14% to 18% and sales volume by 25% across 3,000 lines [app], strengthening its long-term competitive position [an]. However, one argument against is the severe hit to profit [k], because Orbit's $2.16 million profit would fall by $1.8 million to about $360,000 on $24 million revenue [app], leaving little retained profit to fund growth or satisfy shareholders [an]. Overall, Orbit should not switch its objective yet [eval], because sacrificing almost all profit while TechZone may retaliate risks financial stability, so it should cut prices selectively and review share gains each quarter [eval].
    Keywords: Orbit Phones Ltd, TechZone, 10%, 14%, 18%, $1.8 million, $24 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Market-share objective can build long-term competitive strength; Profit objective funds reinvestment and shareholder returns | application_max_2: 10% price cut lifts share 14% to 18% and volume by 25% across 3,000 lines; Profit falls $1.8 million from $2.16 million to about $360,000 on $24 million revenue | analysis_max_2: Larger scale may improve supply terms and position vs TechZone; Profit collapse constrains investment, dividends and resilience to retaliation | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the market-share and profit objectives; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why a business like BrightPath Training might pursue service to the community.
    Answer: Reason 1: The owner's personal values drive the objective [k], as Sofia already runs free cookery classes for 60 disadvantaged teenagers a year while running a profitable $720,000 firm [app]. Reason 2: It strengthens reputation and stakeholder support [k], because reinvesting 70% of profits could double charity partner funding and win community goodwill and local contracts [app].
    Keywords: BrightPath Training, Sofia Marchetti, 60, $720,000, 70%, social enterprise
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Owners' personal values and ethics motivate community objectives; Community objectives build reputation and stakeholder goodwill | application_max_2: Sofia already teaches 60 disadvantaged teenagers a year free; 70% reinvestment could double charity partners' funding

  Qc [6 marks]

Benefit 2: The community and Sofia gain a stronger reputation [k], because BrightPath's 14 staff would be known for social impact rather than profit alone [app], helping win school contracts and motivated workers [an].
    Keywords: BrightPath Training, 70%, 60, 14, $85,000, Sofia Marchetti
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Community members gain skills, training and opportunity; Business reputation and goodwill improve | application_max_2: 70% of profits reinvested, reaching beyond 60 teenagers a year; 14 staff become known for social impact | analysis_max_2: Employability and future incomes of trainees rise; Reputation wins contracts and improves staff motivation

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think BrightPath Training should convert to a social enterprise? Justify your answer.

However, one argument against is the personal financial cost to Sofia [k], because her dividend would fall from $30,000 to $9,000 even though revenue of $720,000 supports the 14 staff and her own wage [app], and reduced drawings could force asset sales or slower growth [an]. Overall, BrightPath should convert to a social enterprise [eval], because the community gain and Sofia's evident commitment outweigh a smaller dividend, provided she keeps a market salary from revenue [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Social enterprise reinvests profits for community benefit; Conversion reduces owners' personal financial reward | application_max_2: 70% of $85,000 profit reinvested; charity funding could double beyond 60 teenagers; Dividend falls from $30,000 to $9,000 on $720,000 revenue supporting 14 staff | analysis_max_2: Trainees gain skills, employability and incomes; Lower drawings may strain Sofia's finances or business growth | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both conversion and keeping the profit objective; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

Country X National Rail Corporation, known as CXNR, is a state-owned public corporation formed in 1987, running 1,100 km of track carrying 86 million passengers a year.     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Transfer of ownership from public to private sector; Usually involves selling a state-owned business

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Country X might keep CXNR as a public corporation.
    Answer: Reason 1: Rail is an essential national service [k], with CXNR carrying 86 million passengers a year across 1,100 km, including 9 million rural journeys private firms may neglect [app]. Reason 2: Public ownership keeps fares affordable [k], shown by fares frozen for 3 years and a $400 million subsidy instead of profit-driven pricing [app].
    Keywords: CXNR, 86 million, 1,100 km, 9 million, $400 million, 3 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Essential national services may be unprofitable for private firms; Public ownership prioritises affordable access over profit | application_max_2: 86 million passengers across 1,100 km including 9 million rural journeys; 3-year fare freeze funded by $400 million subsidy

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of keeping CXNR as a public corporation.

Problem 2: Service quality may stagnate [k], with punctuality of only 81% and fares frozen for 3 years limiting investment in 1,100 km of track [app], frustrating passengers and discouraging rail travel [an].
    Keywords: CXNR, $400 million, $2.1 billion, 81%, 3 years, 1,100 km
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Public corporations often require taxpayer funding; Public ownership may reduce efficiency and investment incentives | application_max_2: $400 million subsidy on $2.1 billion revenue; 81% punctuality and 3-year fare freeze on 1,100 km of track | analysis_max_2: Subsidies have opportunity costs for other public services; Poor reliability and stale investment deter passengers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Country X should privatise CXNR? Justify your answer.

However, one argument against is the harm to passengers and workers [k], since profit-focused owners may raise fares 15-20% and cut 600 jobs, pricing out the 9 million rural passengers who depend on state-supported journeys [app], damaging regional economies and equity [an]. Overall, Country X should not privatise CXNR [eval], because rail is a strategic essential service, so a modest fare rise to shrink the $400 million subsidy is preferable to losing public control [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Privatisation can unlock investment and efficiency; Privatisation risks higher fares and job losses | application_max_2: $700 million promised investment and 5% growth versus $400 million subsidy; 81% punctuality; 15-20% fare rise fears, 600 job cuts, 9 million rural passengers | analysis_max_2: Investment could improve reliability and service growth; Higher fares and job cuts damage access, welfare and regions | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both privatisation and continued public ownership; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

--- STEM ---
In Country X's mixed economy, the StateSea ferry service is a public corporation crossing the Greywater Strait at a flat fare of $11, carrying 520,000 passengers a year on a government subsidy of $6 million. Its journey takes 70 minutes, 15 minutes longer than Harbourline's, and it employs 140 staff. StateSea was founded in 2009 and also holds the island mail contract worth $900,000 a year. The crossings are vital for islanders reaching the mainland for work and hospitals.

Harbourline Ferries Ltd is a private competitor running faster 55-minute crossings at $18 for 340,000 passengers a year, employing 95 people, with profit as its objective. The government is reviewing whether to withdraw StateSea's subsidy and let the private operator serve every route, or keep both services running side by side.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'social objectives'.
    Answer: Targets set by a business to benefit society or the community rather than to make maximum profit, common in the public sector and social enterprises. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Objectives aimed at benefiting society or the community; Common in public sector bodies and social enterprises

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the government keeps a public ferry service alongside a private one.
    Answer: Reason 1: To keep crossings affordable for all [k], StateSea charges a flat $11 fare against Harbourline's $18, so low-income islanders can still cross the Greywater Strait [app]. Reason 2: To guarantee an essential route stays open [k], StateSea carries 520,000 passengers a year and handles the $900,000 island mail contract the profit-focused rival may not sustain [app].
    Keywords: StateSea, Harbourline Ferries Ltd, $11, $18, 520,000, $900,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Public service keeps fares low for low-income users; Public service guarantees essential routes stay open | application_max_2: $11 flat fare versus $18 private fare on the Greywater Strait; 520,000 passengers a year plus $900,000 island mail contract

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why stakeholder objectives conflict on the Greywater Strait.
    Answer: Conflict 1: Harbourline's owners want profit while passengers want low fares [k], because Harbourline's $18 crossing against StateSea's $11 fare shows the gap private owners will not close while 340,000 passengers pay for faster 55-minute journeys [app], directly opposing passengers' affordability objective [an]. Conflict 2: The government wants fiscal savings while island communities want service [k], since withdrawing the $6 million subsidy would cut public spending but end the $11 option used by 520,000 passengers [app], trading taxpayer savings against social access [an].
    Keywords: Harbourline Ferries Ltd, $18, StateSea, $11, 340,000, 520,000, $6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Private owners' profit objective conflicts with passengers' low-fare objective; Government's spending objective conflicts with community service objective | application_max_2: $18 private fare versus $11 public fare across 340,000 versus 520,000 passengers; $6 million subsidy funds the cheaper service and island mail at $900,000 | analysis_max_2: Price gaps directly trade profit against affordability; Subsidy withdrawal harms island access to save public funds

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the government should withdraw StateSea's $6 million subsidy? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for withdrawing the subsidy is the taxpayer saving [k], freeing $6 million a year and letting Harbourline's faster 55-minute service, already carrying 340,000 passengers at $18, compete for the full market [app], which could lower public spending on the strait [an]. However, one argument against is social exclusion [k], since ending subsidised crossings would push StateSea's 520,000 passengers onto $18 fares, a rise of $7 on the $11 flat fare, and risk 140 public-sector jobs [app], cutting off low-income islanders from jobs and hospitals [an]. Overall, the government should keep the subsidy [eval], because affordable transport is a service-to-community objective that the market under-provides, and saving $6 million harms far more residents than it helps [eval].
    Keywords: StateSea, Harbourline Ferries Ltd, $6 million, $18, $11, 520,000, 340,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Withdrawing subsidy saves taxpayer money and encourages competition; Subsidy withdrawal risks exclusion for low-income passengers | application_max_2: $6 million subsidy; Harbourline runs 55-minute crossings at $18 for 340,000 passengers; 520,000 StateSea passengers face a move from $11 to $18 fares; 140 staff at risk | analysis_max_2: Competition and saving public funds may improve efficiency; Higher fares exclude island residents and threaten jobs and access | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both withdrawing and keeping the subsidy; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Objective to increase business size; Can be measured by sales, output, market share or employees

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Delgado & Sons Foods might change its objective from profit to growth.
    Answer: Reason 1: A large market opportunity exists [k], because its 9% share trails the market leader's 27%, so a second line could capture many more regional customers [app]. Reason 2: Growth defends the business competitively [k], since the proposed $700,000 investment to raise capacity by 60% would cut unit costs and strengthen its position in Country X [app].
    Keywords: Delgado & Sons Foods Ltd, 9%, 27%, $700,000, 60%, Marta Delgado
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Market opportunities make a growth objective attractive; Growth strengthens competitive position and scale | application_max_2: 9% share against leader's 27% in the regional ready-meal market; $700,000 second line raising capacity by 60%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to stakeholders if Delgado & Sons pursues growth.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Employees gain job security and possible pay [k], because 60% more capacity would need the 48 current staff and likely more workers, strengthening the case for the $0.80 hourly rise costing $77,000 a year [app], improving morale and retention [an]. Benefit 2: Owners gain long-term wealth [k], since lifting share from 9% to 15% on $9.6 million revenue would grow profits well beyond this year's $1.2 million [app], outweighing the missed $700,000 special dividend [an].
    Keywords: Delgado & Sons Foods Ltd, 60%, 48, $0.80, $77,000, 15%, $1.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Employees benefit from job security and stronger pay claims; Owners benefit from long-term capital growth | application_max_2: 60% capacity rise needs 48 staff and supports the $0.80 rise costing $77,000; Share target 15% on $9.6 million revenue against $1.2 million profit | analysis_max_2: Higher capacity improves morale, retention and pay bargaining position; Share gains compound future profits beyond current levels

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Delgado & Sons Foods should reinvest the $700,000 rather than pay a special dividend? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for reinvesting is the long-term payoff [k], because a $700,000 second line raising capacity by 60% could lift Delgado & Sons from 9% to 15% market share within 2 years [app], growing future profits well beyond the current $1.2 million [an]. However, one argument against is shareholders' immediate reward [k], since Marta's brother, holding 30% of the shares, would receive about $210,000 from a $700,000 special dividend, while reinvesting pays him nothing extra this year [app], straining family relations and owner trust [an]. Overall, the company should reinvest [eval], because 60% capacity growth and a 6-point share gain create more lasting value than a one-off dividend, provided Marta agrees a payment plan with family shareholders [eval].
    Keywords: Delgado & Sons Foods Ltd, $700,000, 60%, 9%, 15%, 30%, $1.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Reinvestment builds long-term capacity and competitive strength; Special dividends reward owners immediately but forgo growth | application_max_2: $700,000 second line raises capacity 60%, lifting share from 9% to 15% in 2 years; Brother holds 30% of shares, so he forgoes about $210,000 this year | analysis_max_2: Capacity and share gains compound future profits beyond $1.2 million; Withholding dividends strains family relationships and owner trust | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both reinvestment and the special dividend; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

SET ID: P1_U1_SET_74
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Harbour & Pine Boat Tours, a guided fishing-trip start-up, was founded 3 years ago by Tom Weaver, a former fishing-boat crew member known for his patience with nervous customers. Based in Country X, it carries 28 passengers a week in summer and 6 in winter at $45 per ticket, earning $58,000 in revenue last year, even though the boat sits completely idle for 4 months each year.

Tom wants to buy a second boat costing $26,000 to double his passenger capacity in summer. The government Coastal Enterprise Scheme offers a $13,000 grant for tourism start-ups in approved premises, plus reduced tax for firms that employ local staff. Alternatively, Tom could keep one boat, refit it for $3,500 during the shutdown and accept steadier but lower long-term growth.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'determination'.
    Answer: A quality of successful entrepreneurs meaning the willingness to persist and keep working towards goals despite setbacks, obstacles or failure [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: willingness to persist despite setbacks; quality of successful entrepreneurs / pursuing goals

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the government Coastal Enterprise Scheme could help Harbour & Pine Boat Tours.
    Answer: Way 1: A $13,000 grant towards a second boat [k], cutting the cash Tom needs for the $26,000 expansion by half [app]. Way 2: Reduced tax for firms employing local staff [k], lowering fixed costs during the 4 idle winter months each year [app].
    Keywords: Coastal Enterprise Scheme, $13,000, $26,000, second boat, 4 months, Tom Weaver, Harbour & Pine Boat Tours, $45
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: grant funding for expansion; reduced tax / approved premises incentives | application_max_2: $13,000 grant vs $26,000 boat cost; 4 idle winter months

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Harbour & Pine Boat Tours of receiving the $13,000 grant.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Lower personal financial risk [k], because the grant halves the $26,000 price of the second boat [app], making Tom's own cash stretch further [an]. Benefit 2: Faster expansion [k], funding capacity for 28 weekly summer passengers to rise as demand grows [app], building extra $45-per-ticket revenue sooner [an].
    Keywords: $13,000, $26,000, second boat, 28 passengers, Harbour & Pine Boat Tours, Tom Weaver, $45
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lowers financial risk; funds faster expansion | application_max_2: halves the $26,000 second boat cost; 28 weekly summer passengers / $45 tickets | analysis_max_2: owner's cash stretches further; revenue grows sooner from higher capacity

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tom should buy a second boat with the grant, or refit the existing boat for $3,500? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying a second boat with the $13,000 grant halves Tom's outlay on the $26,000 expansion [k], doubling capacity for 28 weekly summer passengers and capturing peak-season demand [app], which could lift his $58,000 annual revenue well above current levels [an]. Alternatively, refitting for $3,500 preserves his cash but leaves the boat idle for 4 months each year and caps growth [k], limiting earnings from just 6 winter passengers a week [app], so the business stays stuck at one boat's capacity [an]. Overall, Tom should buy the second boat using the grant [eval], because the $13,000 halves his risk and proven peak demand of 28 summer passengers justifies doubling capacity now [eval].
    Keywords: $13,000, $26,000, $3,500, $58,000, second boat, winter, $45, Tom Weaver, 28
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: grant halves expansion cost / doubles capacity; $3,500 refit preserves cash but caps growth | application_max_2: $13,000 grant vs $26,000 boat; 28 weekly summer passengers / $58,000 revenue / 6 winter passengers | analysis_max_2: captures peak demand and lifts revenue; refit leaves idle months and caps capacity | evaluation_max_2: weighs expansion risk against cautious refit; justified by seasonal demand and grant figures

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U1_SET_75
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Keystone Tutoring, a one-to-one maths and science tuition start-up, was founded 11 months ago by sisters Aisha and Zainab Rahman in Country X. It serves 90 students at $25 per hour and uses a self-designed app to track each student's progress after every lesson. Both sisters are former teachers who built the app after struggling with paper records.

The business earns $4,600 a month after costs and holds $22,000 in its account. They are deciding, in the business plan they are drafting, whether to spend $7,000 on a local radio and social-media campaign aiming to recruit 150 new students, or hire an additional qualified tutor at $2,000 a month so they can take on 60 more students. Each option puts their saved cash at risk while the start-up is young.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'innovation'.
    Answer: The introduction of new ideas, products, services or methods into a business, creating something new or improving an existing offering [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: introducing new ideas/products/services/methods; creating or improving something new

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the Rahman sisters show the characteristics of successful entrepreneurs.
    Answer: Way 1: Innovation [k], shown by developing their own app to track the progress of 90 students after every lesson [app]. Way 2: Initiative [k], shown by founding Keystone Tutoring and building a digital tracking system before any competitor offered one [app].
    Keywords: Keystone Tutoring, 90 students, $25 per hour, Aisha and Zainab Rahman, self-designed app, 11 months ago
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: innovation; initiative / self-starting quality | application_max_2: self-designed app tracking 90 students; founded the business/built the app unprompted

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Keystone Tutoring of preparing a business plan.
    Answer: Benefit 1: It sets measurable objectives [k], such as deciding whether to pursue 150 new students or take on 60 more now [app], focusing effort on one clear route [an]. Benefit 2: It forecasts cash flow [k], showing whether their $22,000 reserve can fund a $7,000 campaign or $2,000 monthly tutor wages [app], avoiding running out of money [an].
    Keywords: $22,000, $7,000, 150 new students, $2,000 a month, business plan, Keystone Tutoring, $25 per hour, 60 more students
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sets objectives/direction; forecasts cash flow / shows viability | application_max_2: 150 new students vs 60 more students; $22,000 reserve / $7,000 campaign / $2,000 a month | analysis_max_2: focuses effort on chosen route; avoids running out of cash

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the Rahman sisters should spend $7,000 on marketing, or hire an additional tutor at $2,000 a month? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Spending $7,000 on a radio and social-media campaign could recruit 150 new students [k], reaching far more families than word of mouth from their current 90 students [app], potentially generating revenue that exceeds the campaign cost [an]. Hiring at $2,000 a month lets them serve 60 more students immediately with no advertising gamble [k], but the fixed wage must be paid monthly before new sign-ups are confirmed [app], squeezing their $22,000 reserve if demand disappoints [an]. Overall, they should hire the additional tutor [eval], because current caseload is already stretching capacity and $2,000 a month is predictable, whereas the $7,000 campaign carries uncertain returns for a young business [eval].
    Keywords: $7,000, $2,000 a month, 150 new students, 60 more students, $22,000, 90 students, Keystone Tutoring, $25 per hour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: campaign recruits via wider reach; tutor adds capacity with predictable monthly cost | application_max_2: $7,000 campaign vs 90 current students / 150 new students; $2,000 a month wage vs $22,000 reserve | analysis_max_2: campaign returns uncertain but potentially large; fixed wage pressures cash before sign-ups confirmed | evaluation_max_2: weighs risky marketing spend against capacity hire; justified recommendation using figures and demand

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U1_SET_76
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Silverline Security Systems has operated in Country X's second-largest city for 7 years, installing and servicing alarm systems. Owner Derek Hale took over from his father and now employs 9 technicians. Revenue reached $380,000 last year, but profit was only $9,000 because of 4 missed-site visits a week, 2 of 9 technicians leaving and a complaint rate of 15% of jobs, partly because Derek avoids delegating decisions to his staff.

Derek sees two paths forward. The government Skills for Enterprise programme would fund 70% of a 12-week management training course costing $8,000, teaching delegation, scheduling and customer care. Alternatively, Derek could sell the business to a national security firm offering $140,000 for the contracts and vans, and pursue a fresh start elsewhere.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'initiative'.
    Answer: The ability to take action and make decisions independently without being told, a characteristic of successful entrepreneurs who spot and act on opportunities [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: taking action without being told; spotting and acting on opportunities / proactive quality

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Silverline Security Systems may be failing despite being established.
    Answer: Reason 1: Poor management [k], because Derek avoids delegation, causing 4 missed-site visits a week and 2 of 9 technicians leaving [app]. Reason 2: Weak customer focus [k], because a complaint rate of 15% of jobs is damaging reputation and repeat business [app].
    Keywords: Silverline Security Systems, 4 missed-site visits, 2 of 9 technicians, 15%, Derek Hale, $380,000, delegation
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: poor management / lack of delegation; poor customer service / high complaints | application_max_2: 4 missed-site visits a week / 2 of 9 technicians left; 15% complaint rate of jobs

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the government's Skills for Enterprise programme could help Derek.
    Answer: Way 1: 70% funding of a 12-week management course [k], cutting Derek's cost to $2,400 of the $8,000 fee [app], making professional training affordable [an]. Way 2: Teaching delegation, scheduling and customer care [k], directly reducing the 4 missed-site visits a week and technician turnover [app], lifting profit from just $9,000 [an].
    Keywords: Skills for Enterprise, 12-week, $8,000, 70%, 4 missed-site visits, $9,000, 2 of 9 technicians, Derek Hale, delegation
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: government funding reduces training cost; teaches delegation/scheduling/customer care | application_max_2: $2,400 cost (30% of $8,000) after 70% funding; 4 missed-site visits / profit only $9,000 | analysis_max_2: makes training affordable for a struggling business; fixes root causes and raises profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Derek should undertake the management training, or sell the business for $140,000? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The Skills for Enterprise course costs Derek only $2,400 after 70% funding [k], directly tackling the poor delegation behind 4 missed visits a week, 2 leavers and 15% complaints [app], which could lift his $9,000 profit substantially [an]. Selling for $140,000 gives Derek immediate, certain cash and escapes the daily stress [k], but gives up a business generating $380,000 of revenue that he has run for 7 years [app], forfeiting all future profit potential [an]. Overall, Derek should undertake the training [eval], because $2,400 is a small risk against the ongoing value of a $380,000-revenue business, and fixing management could raise its worth within a year [eval].
    Keywords: $8,000, $140,000, $380,000, $9,000, Skills for Enterprise, 4 missed-site visits, 15%, 70%, Derek Hale
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: training funded 70% leaves small cost; selling gives certain immediate cash | application_max_2: 4 missed-site visits / 15% complaints / 2 leavers; $140,000 offer / $380,000 revenue / $9,000 profit | analysis_max_2: training fixes root causes and raises profit; selling forfeits future profit potential | evaluation_max_2: weighs certain sale cash against turnaround potential; justified by funding and revenue-profit gap

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U1_SET_77
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Tansy Lane Plant Nursery, a start-up growing bedding plants and hedging shrubs, was founded 2 years ago by Elise Moreau in a semi-rural valley in Country X. It sells to 6 garden centres and 40 households, with annual revenue of $74,000 and 1 part-time weekend worker. Elise wants to hire her first full-time assistant grower at a cost of $1,900 a month including taxes.

The government's First Steps Employment Scheme offers start-ups a tax incentive equal to 20% of a first full-time employee's wages for 2 years, plus a $5,000 grant towards tools and a greenhouse vent system. Elise fears locking in wages before the spring sales peak; her cash reserve is $16,000 and last autumn's frost cut her stock by 18%. She must decide whether to hire now or wait until after the peak.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'tax incentive'.
    Answer: A reduction or exemption in the tax a business has to pay, offered by the government to encourage activities such as hiring staff or investing [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduction/exemption in tax paid; government encouragement e.g. hiring staff

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why governments support start-ups like Tansy Lane Plant Nursery.
    Answer: Reason 1: To reduce unemployment [k], by encouraging Elise to hire her first full-time assistant grower [app]. Reason 2: To boost regional economic growth [k], helping the nursery add $74,000 of revenue while serving 6 garden centres and 40 households locally [app].
    Keywords: Tansy Lane Plant Nursery, $74,000, 6 garden centres, 40 households, Elise Moreau, First Steps Employment Scheme, $1,900 a month
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduce unemployment / create jobs; boost economic growth / entrepreneurship | application_max_2: hiring first full-time assistant grower; $74,000 revenue / 6 garden centres / 40 households

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Tansy Lane Plant Nursery of the government's First Steps Employment Scheme.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Lower wage costs [k], with a tax incentive of 20% of her first full-time employee's $1,900 monthly wages for 2 years [app], saving around $380 a month [an]. Benefit 2: A $5,000 tools and greenhouse grant [k], contributing towards tools and a greenhouse vent system without draining her $16,000 cash reserve [app], preserving working capital before spring [an].
    Keywords: First Steps Employment Scheme, 20%, $1,900 a month, $5,000, $16,000, greenhouse vent system, 18%, Tansy Lane Plant Nursery
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: tax incentive lowers wage costs; tools grant contributes capital | application_max_2: 20% of $1,900 saves about $380 a month; $5,000 grant / $16,000 cash reserve | analysis_max_2: saves wage money for 2 years; preserves working capital before spring peak

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Elise should hire her first full-time employee now, or wait until after the spring sales peak? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Hiring now lets Elise claim the 20% tax incentive and $5,000 tools grant immediately [k], offsetting about $380 of the $1,900 monthly wage and equipping her before orders peak [app], which strengthens the business for spring [an]. However, her cash reserve is only $16,000 and the autumn frost already cut stock by 18% [k], so committing $1,900 a month before spring revenue arrives risks a cash-flow strain [app], leaving little buffer if sales disappoint [an]. Overall, Elise should hire now [eval], because the $5,000 grant plus 20% tax relief discounts the wage cost and 6 garden centres need reliable hedging supply through the spring peak [eval].
    Keywords: 20%, $5,000, $1,900, $16,000, 18%, First Steps Employment Scheme, 6 garden centres, spring, $74,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: hiring now unlocks tax incentive + tools grant; waiting protects cash reserve until demand confirmed | application_max_2: 20% incentive / $5,000 grant / $1,900 wage; $16,000 reserve / 18% stock cut / spring peak | analysis_max_2: grant and relief cut effective wage cost; early commitment risks cash-flow strain | evaluation_max_2: weighs incentive timing against cash risk; justified recommendation using figures and demand

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U1_SET_78
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Larkspur Linens, a handmade linen bedding start-up, was founded 6 months ago by Naomi Carter in Country X. She spent her $13,000 redundancy payment on a sewing contract, fabric and 200 samples, working 2 days a week at a retail shop earning $240 a week alongside the business. She designs each set herself from stone-washed flax supplied by 4 local farms and sells sets at $120 each.

Naomi's business plan, including the market research her lender required, shows fabric flaws from one supplier cause most returns; 30 of the 95 sets sold last month came back with stitching complaints, out of revenue of $11,400. She is deciding whether to resign from her part-time job to run Linens full-time, or keep it while the business grows.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'risk-taking'.
    Answer: A characteristic of successful entrepreneurs meaning being willing to make decisions where the outcome is uncertain, including investing money that could be lost [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: making decisions with uncertain outcomes; willingness to invest money that could be lost

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Naomi shows risk-taking when running Larkspur Linens.
    Answer: Way 1: Investing her redundancy payment [k], spending $13,000 on a sewing contract, fabric and 200 samples [app]. Way 2: Trading secure income for an unproven idea [k], launching a handmade linen range before knowing whether sets at $120 will sell consistently [app].
    Keywords: Larkspur Linens, $13,000, $240 a week, redundancy payment, 200, 95 sets, Naomi Carter
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: financial risk with redundancy pay; launching unproven product / leaving secure income | application_max_2: $13,000 spent on contract, fabric, samples; $120 price point untested at launch

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Larkspur Linens of including market research in its business plan.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Identifying customer preferences [k], such as which sets failed on stitching and why 30 of 95 were returned [app], guiding fabric and supplier choices to cut future returns [an]. Benefit 2: Forecasting demand [k], using last month's sales of 95 sets and $11,400 revenue to plan stock from 4 local farms [app], avoiding costly stockouts or overstock [an].
    Keywords: business plan, market research, 95 sets, $11,400, 30, $120, Larkspur Linens, Naomi Carter
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: identifies customer preferences/problems; forecasts demand/plans stock | application_max_2: 30 of 95 sets returned with stitching complaints; 95 sets / $11,400 revenue / 4 local farms | analysis_max_2: reduces returns by fixing supplier issues; avoids stockouts/overstock, protecting cash

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Naomi should resign from her part-time retail job, or keep it while building Larkspur Linens? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Resigning would free Naomi's full attention for Larkspur Linens [k], letting her resolve the stitching problem behind 30 of 95 returns and rebuild $11,400 monthly revenue faster [app], accelerating growth of a brand she fully controls [an]. However, quitting costs her a guaranteed $240 a week [k], leaving the business as her only income while nearly a third of sets are returned and the supplier issue persists [app], which could push the fragile start-up into a cash crisis [an]. Overall, Naomi should keep her part-time job [eval], because $240 a week still covers essential fabric purchases while she fixes quality and proves repeat sales before committing full-time [eval].
    Keywords: $240 a week, 95 sets, $11,400, 30, Larkspur Linens, Naomi Carter, $120, redundancy payment, $13,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: resigning frees full attention/time; keeping job protects guaranteed income | application_max_2: 30 of 95 sets returned / $11,400 revenue; $240 a week retail wage | analysis_max_2: full-time focus could fix quality and grow faster; quitting risks cash crisis while returns persist | evaluation_max_2: weighs time commitment against income security; justified by return rate and wage figures

--- STEM ---
Beacon Digital Marketing, a social-media and search-marketing agency start-up, was founded 9 months ago by Aaron Silva in Country X's capital. Working from his spare bedroom, he manages 8 client accounts at $900 a month, employs no staff, and revenue stands at $7,200 a month. Aaron wants to sign 20 more clients but cannot afford city-centre office rent of $1,600 a month.

The government's Founders' Incubator Programme offers accepted start-ups shared office space at $320 a month, free Wi-Fi, weekly mentoring from experienced entrepreneurs and meeting rooms for 2 years, before they graduate. Acceptance requires a written business plan and 30 hours of client work per month. Aaron could instead stay at home and save the rent money for a local radio campaign.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'business incubator'.
    Answer: An organisation, often supported by government, that provides start-up businesses with low-cost premises, advice, training and shared services to help them survive and grow [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: low-cost premises/shared services for start-ups; advice, training or mentoring support

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why governments provide business incubators.
    Answer: Reason 1: To reduce start-up failure rates [k], by giving firms like Beacon Digital Marketing space at $320 a month instead of $1,600 city-centre rent [app]. Reason 2: To encourage entrepreneurship and job creation [k], helping agencies grow beyond 8 client accounts and hire staff [app].
    Keywords: Founders' Incubator Programme, $320 a month, $1,600, Beacon Digital Marketing, 8 client accounts, 2 years, 30 hours
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduce start-up failure rate; encourage enterprise/job creation | application_max_2: $320 vs $1,600 rent saving; 8 client accounts / hiring staff

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Beacon Digital Marketing of joining the Founders' Incubator Programme.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Cheap premises [k], at $320 a month for 2 years instead of $1,600 city-centre rent [app], saving $1,280 a month to reinvest in growth [an]. Advantage 2: Weekly mentoring and meeting rooms [k], helping Aaron pitch to new clients beyond his 8 current accounts [app], improving his credibility and win rate [an].
    Keywords: $320 a month, $1,600, weekly mentoring, Founders' Incubator Programme, Aaron Silva, $7,200, 2 years, meeting rooms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cheap/low-cost premises; mentoring and meeting rooms | application_max_2: $320 vs $1,600 ($1,280 monthly saving); meeting clients beyond 8 current accounts | analysis_max_2: savings reinvested in growth; credibility improves client acquisition

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Aaron should move Beacon Digital Marketing into the incubator, or stay working from home? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The incubator offers Aaron office space at $320 a month with mentoring and meeting rooms [k], saving $1,280 a month against $1,600 city-centre rent and letting him host clients professionally [app], which can accelerate signings beyond his current 8 accounts [an]. However, acceptance requires a written business plan and 30 hours of client work per month [k], and leaving home means fixed obligations for 2 years [app], reducing flexibility while revenue is only $7,200 a month [an]. Overall, Aaron should join the incubator [eval], because $320 a month is affordable within $7,200 revenue and professional premises plus mentoring should win more clients faster than a radio campaign alone [eval].
    Keywords: $320 a month, $1,600, $7,200, 8 client accounts, 30 hours, business plan, 2 years, Founders' Incubator Programme, Aaron Silva
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: incubator provides cheap space + mentoring; acceptance requires business plan and monthly hours | application_max_2: $320 vs $1,600 rent / $1,280 monthly saving; 30 hours monthly / 8 client accounts / $7,200 revenue | analysis_max_2: professional premises accelerate client signings; fixed obligations reduce flexibility | evaluation_max_2: weighs low cost against reduced flexibility; justified recommendation based on revenue figures

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U1_SET_80
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Red Kite Falconry Centre, a rural tourism start-up inside a government enterprise zone, opened 10 months ago in Country X and is run by owner Sylvia Brandt. It offers falconry displays for weddings and school visits, welcomed 60 groups in its first year and earned $46,000 in revenue against $58,000 of start-up costs, including $30,000 for 4 trained birds of prey. The zone offers 5 years of reduced business rates and 100% relief on start-up equipment purchases.

Sylvia now wants to open a second display site 40 kilometres away, costing $24,000. Alternatively, she could deepen the existing site with a $9,000 school education programme, which local tourism officers estimate could add $18,000 a year in bookings. She must choose between the two options while her early losses are still being absorbed.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'enterprise zone'.
    Answer: A designated area where the government offers incentives such as reduced taxes or business rates to encourage businesses to locate and grow there [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: designated area with government incentives; reduced tax/rates to encourage location and growth

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why governments create enterprise zones in rural areas.
    Answer: Reason 1: To attract investment to deprived regions [k], bringing businesses like Red Kite Falconry Centre to rural Country X [app]. Reason 2: To create local jobs and income [k], encouraging tourism spending through 60 school and wedding groups in year one [app].
    Keywords: Red Kite Falconry Centre, enterprise zone, 60 groups, rural, Sylvia Brandt, falconry, $46,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: attract investment to deprived areas; create local jobs/income | application_max_2: Red Kite Falconry Centre / rural Country X; 60 school and wedding groups in year one

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Red Kite Falconry Centre of locating in the enterprise zone.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Reduced business rates for 5 years [k], cutting fixed costs while year-one revenue of $46,000 is still below $58,000 of start-up costs [app], easing early losses [an]. Benefit 2: 100% relief on start-up equipment purchases [k], softening the impact of her $30,000 investment in 4 trained birds of prey [app], protecting scarce cash [an].
    Keywords: enterprise zone, $46,000, $58,000, $30,000, 5 years, 100% relief, Red Kite Falconry Centre, 4 trained birds of prey
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduced business rates for 5 years; 100% relief on start-up equipment | application_max_2: $46,000 revenue vs $58,000 start-up costs; $30,000 for 4 birds of prey | analysis_max_2: eases early losses while revenue builds; protects scarce cash / lowers barriers to entry

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sylvia should open a second display site, or invest $9,000 in a school education programme at the existing site? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A second site costing $24,000 would double display capacity and open a fresh market area [k], building on $46,000 revenue from 60 groups in year one [app], potentially boosting long-term growth [an]. The education programme costs only $9,000 [k], and tourism officers estimate it could add $18,000 a year in school bookings [app], returning twice its cost within a single year [an]. Overall, Sylvia should invest $9,000 in the education programme [eval], because it costs less than half the expansion, adds $18,000 a year and suits a business still absorbing its early losses [eval].
    Keywords: $24,000, $9,000, $18,000, $46,000, 60 groups, Red Kite Falconry Centre, education programme, $58,000, enterprise zone
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: second site doubles capacity/opens new market; education programme costs $9,000 with estimated uplift | application_max_2: $24,000 second site vs $9,000 programme; $46,000 revenue / 60 groups / $18,000 a year estimate | analysis_max_2: second site offers growth but heavy upfront cost; programme returns twice its cost in one year | evaluation_max_2: weighs expansion ambition against financial strain; justified by estimated uplift against early losses

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U1_SET_81
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Harborlight Bakery is a sole trader business opened 6 years ago by Priya Raman, baking fresh sourdough loaves and buttery pastries in a rented high-street shop in a busy commuter town. The bakery employs 4 part-time assistants, sells to early-morning office workers and generated $180,000 in sales last year. Priya invested $25,000 of her own savings, works 60 hours a week and carries unlimited liability for all business debts, including the shop's second-hand oven and display cabinets.

Priya's close friend Sofia Marino, a qualified pastry chef, wants to invest $20,000 to become an equal partner taking half of all future profits. Priya must decide whether to remain a sole trader or form a partnership, weighing the extra capital, new recipe ideas and shared workload against sharing profits and losing full control of daily decisions.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'sole trader'.
    Answer: A business owned and controlled by one person who keeps all the profits but bears unlimited liability for the business's debts [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: business owned and controlled by one person; keeps all profits / unlimited liability for debts

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Priya Raman of remaining a sole trader rather than forming a partnership.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Priya keeps all the profits [k], retaining the full benefit of $180,000 in annual sales rather than giving half to Sofia [app]. Advantage 2: She keeps complete control of the business [k], deciding menu, opening hours and suppliers herself without needing Sofia's agreement [app].
    Keywords: $180,000, Priya, Sofia, sourdough, pastries, bakery, $25,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: keeps all profits rather than sharing them; full control of decisions / no partner agreement needed | application_max_2: $180,000 annual sales retained in full; equal partner taking half of profits; menu, opening hours and suppliers

  Qc [6 marks]

It employs 600 staff, spent $50,000,000 last year upgrading pipes and treatment plants and its prices are set by the government water regulator to keep bills affordable for low-income families in the region. The government is considering selling the corporation to private investors.

Private buyers say they would invest $80,000,000 over 4 years to cut leakage by 30%, but warn bills may rise for households and businesses in some areas. The board and union leaders want to keep Northgate in public ownership, arguing water is an essential service that should not be run for private profit.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'public corporation'.
    Answer: A business owned and controlled by the government on behalf of the public, usually created by law to provide essential services without the aim of maximising profit [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: owned and controlled by the government on behalf of the public; provides essential services / not for profit maximisation

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to the region of Northgate remaining in public ownership.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Prices can be kept affordable [k], so the government water regulator can hold down bills for 240,000 households and 9,000 businesses [app]. Advantage 2: Investment focuses on service, not dividends [k], so the $50,000,000 spent on pipes and treatment plants prioritises reliability over shareholder returns [app].
    Keywords: Northgate, 240,000, 9,000 businesses, $50,000,000, regulator, 600 staff, coastal region
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: regulated affordable prices; investment for service rather than profit | application_max_2: 240,000 households and 9,000 businesses; $50,000,000 pipe and treatment upgrades; government water regulator

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to the region of Northgate remaining in public ownership.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: Limited access to capital [k], so the promised $80,000,000 private investment across 4 years could not come from public funds [app], slowing the planned 30% leakage cut [an]. Disadvantage 2: Risk of inefficiency [k], because public corporations face weak competitive pressure and bureaucratic delays [app], leaving 600 staff potentially underdeployed and costs high [an].
    Keywords: $80,000,000, 4 years, 30%, 600 staff, public ownership, $50,000,000, 240,000 households
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: limited public capital for investment; inefficiency / weak competitive pressure and bureaucracy | application_max_2: $80,000,000 over 4 years; 30% leakage cut; 600 staff | analysis_max_2: leakage cut delayed, water loss and costs rise; high costs passed to taxpayers and households

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Northgate Water Corporation should remain in public ownership? Justify your answer.
    Answer: An argument for public ownership is fairness of access [k], because a government-owned corporation can price water affordably for 240,000 households and 9,000 businesses [app], preventing the bill rises private buyers have warned about [an]. An argument for sale is faster funding [k], because $80,000,000 of private investment over 4 years could cut leakage by 30% far sooner [app], modernising ageing pipes quicker [an]. Overall, Northgate should remain in public ownership [eval] because water is an essential service and the regulator plus $50,000,000 of recent public upgrades show public delivery can work without private profit motives [eval].
    Keywords: 240,000, 9,000, $80,000,000, 4 years, 30%, $50,000,000, public ownership
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: affordable pricing / universal service under public ownership; private investment and efficiency argument for sale | application_max_2: 240,000 households and 9,000 businesses; $80,000,000 over 4 years; 30% leakage cut; $50,000,000 recent upgrades | analysis_max_2: public ownership prevents profit-driven bill rises; sale could modernise pipes faster | evaluation_max_2: weighs affordability and accountability against funding and efficiency from a sale

--- STEM ---
Eastvale City Council runs its own refuse collection as a municipal service, employing 120 council workers and collecting waste and recycling from 95,000 households each week across 14 districts and housing estates. The service cost taxpayers $9,600,000 last year and missed 8% of scheduled collections during a staff shortage last winter, leaving streets overflowing for several days in some districts. CleanRight Ltd, a private waste company, has offered to run the service for $8,400,000 a year with strict performance targets and fines for missed collections.

The council must decide by December whether to keep refuse collection as a municipal service or contract it to CleanRight, balancing potential savings of $1,200,000 a year against possible job losses, lower local wages and reduced local accountability to residents.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two types of business organisation in the public sector.
    Answer: Public corporations [1]; municipal services run by local authorities [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: public corporations; municipal services (run by local authorities/councils)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Eastvale residents of keeping refuse collection as a municipal service.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Direct accountability to residents [k], because the council must answer to voters at elections for the service used by 95,000 households [app]. Advantage 2: Local control of standards and jobs [k], so the 120 council workers can be directed to fix the 8% missed collections quickly [app].
    Keywords: Eastvale, 95,000 households, 120 council workers, 8%, municipal service, $9,600,000, refuse collection
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: direct democratic accountability to residents; local control of standards and employment | application_max_2: 95,000 households; 120 council workers; 8% missed collections

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to Eastvale City Council of keeping refuse collection in-house.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: Higher cost to taxpayers [k], because $9,600,000 a year is $1,200,000 more than CleanRight's $8,400,000 offer [app], money unavailable for roads and parks [an]. Disadvantage 2: Capacity and staffing problems [k], shown by 8% missed collections during the staff shortage [app], damaging residents' health and satisfaction [an].
    Keywords: $9,600,000, $8,400,000, $1,200,000, 8%, CleanRight, 120 council workers, Eastvale
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher cost than private alternative; staffing and capacity shortfalls | application_max_2: $9,600,000 in-house cost; $8,400,000 CleanRight offer; $1,200,000 annual difference; 8% missed collections | analysis_max_2: less money available for other council services; health and resident satisfaction damage

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Eastvale City Council should contract refuse collection to CleanRight Ltd? Justify your answer.
    Answer: An advantage of contracting out is the clear saving [k], because the $1,200,000 a year difference between $9,600,000 and $8,400,000 frees money for other services [app], and strict performance targets with fines should end missed collections [an]. A disadvantage is the loss of local control [k], because CleanRight is a private firm whose main aim is profit [app], risking job cuts, lower wages and weaker accountability to 95,000 households [an]. Overall, the council should contract to CleanRight [eval] because the $1,200,000 annual saving plus penalty-backed targets directly fix the 8% missed collections, provided the contract protects the 120 workers and service levels [eval].
    Keywords: CleanRight, $1,200,000, $9,600,000, $8,400,000, 8%, 95,000 households, 120 council workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cost saving with performance targets; loss of local control / private profit motive | application_max_2: $1,200,000 annual saving; $9,600,000 versus $8,400,000; 8% missed collections; 120 council workers | analysis_max_2: targets and fines should restore reliable collections; risk of job losses and weaker accountability | evaluation_max_2: weighs savings and performance targets against accountability and job risks

SET ID: P1_U1_SET_91
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Meridian Can Works is a private limited company (LTD) operating an automated aluminium drink-can plant in an industrial estate for 6 years. The business employs 18 production technicians and engineers, its can output is valued at $4.6 million a year, and sales revenue stands at $4.3 million. Total capital employed is $6.9 million, almost all of it tied up in automated pressing lines imported from overseas suppliers.

Meridian Can Works is considering investing $900,000 of retained profit into a second automated production line to double capacity. However, the board must first decide how to present the company's size when bidding for a government supply contract, since rival Harbor Can & Bottle Co employs 120 workers at a labour-intensive plant but reports a lower margin on each can sold. Directors disagree over whether headcount, value of output or capital employed best reflects the firm's true scale before they commit.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'capital employed'.
    Answer: Capital employed is the total long-term finance invested in a business to fund its operations and assets [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: total long-term finance invested in the business; non-current assets plus working capital (total assets minus current liabilities)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of using number of employees to measure the size of Meridian Can Works.
    Answer: Reason 1: Automation distorts the figure [k], as 18 technicians run lines that produce $4.6 million of cans while a 120-worker rival sells fewer cans [app]. Reason 2: It ignores asset intensity [k], because Meridian's $6.9 million of capital employed is invested in pressing lines rather than wages [app].
    Keywords: 18, technicians, $4.6 million, automated, 120, capital employed, $6.9 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: automation/capital intensity distorts employee numbers; employee count ignores asset or output scale | application_max_2: 18 production technicians; $4.6 million output; $6.9 million capital employed; 120 workers at rival

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of using value of output to measure the size of Meridian Can Works.
    Answer: Problem 1: Value of output ignores how the figure is achieved [k], as producing $4.6 million of cans came from costly automated lines funded by $6.9 million of capital employed [app], which inflates apparent size compared with labour-intensive rivals [an]. Problem 2: Output values can change with prices and stocks [k], so a rise or fall in the $4.6 million figure may reflect can price movements rather than more cans being made [app], giving an unreliable basis for comparing size with Harbor Can & Bottle Co [an].
    Keywords: 4.6, $6.9 million, automated, pressing lines, Harbor Can, capital employed
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: output value ignores asset input/method of production; output value can be distorted by price changes and stock movements | application_max_2: $4.6 million output; $6.9 million capital employed; automated pressing lines; Harbor Can & Bottle Co | analysis_max_2: inflates apparent size relative to labour-intensive rivals; gives unreliable comparison over time or between firms

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Meridian Can Works should invest $900,000 in a second automated production line or continue operating at its current scale? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing $900,000 would double capacity [k] and allow Meridian to convert retained profit into more automated pressing lines [app], spreading fixed costs over more cans and raising long-term profit [an]. However, the rival Harbor Can & Bottle Co employs 120 workers and sells fewer cans at lower margins [k], showing that growth is no guarantee of sales [app], and a second line could leave the firm with surplus output it cannot sell, draining cash [an]. Overall, the investment is worthwhile because the firm can fund it from retained profit without new debt [eval], and doubling automated capacity is the fastest route to winning the government supply contract that would secure steady orders [eval].
    Keywords: $900,000, retained profit, Harbor Can & Bottle Co, government supply contract, automated, $4.6 million, 120
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth increases capacity/output and spreads fixed costs; expansion carries risk if demand does not materialise | application_max_2: $900,000 investment; retained profit; $4.6 million output; government supply contract | analysis_max_2: spreads fixed costs and raises long-term profit; risk of surplus output/cash drain if sales lag | evaluation_max_2: weighs expansion benefits against demand and cash-flow risk, using retained profit and the government contract as the deciding factor

UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
GoldenHive Apiaries is a private limited company (LTD) founded 4 years ago by Rosa and Emilio Varela to keep honeybees and bottle raw honey. Operating from 2 farms in a rural province, the business manages 400 hives, employs 12 beekeepers and packers, and generates $520,000 in annual sales revenue. Demand from supermarkets currently exceeds supply by 30 per cent.

The directors are choosing between two growth paths: building a second extraction and bottling facility on their own land for $180,000, or acquiring Meadowbrook Honey Co, a rival producer with 300 hives and $410,000 in annual revenue, for $450,000. Rosa favours steady organic growth funded by retained profit, while Emilio argues that buying Meadowbrook would instantly add capacity and remove a competitor from the local market.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'external growth'.
    Answer: External growth is the expansion of a business by joining with, or buying, another business rather than by growing from within [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: expansion by merging or acquiring another business; as opposed to internal/organic growth from within

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to GoldenHive Apiaries of growing internally rather than through acquisition.
    Answer: Advantage 1: It is cheaper [k], as a second facility costs $180,000 instead of the $450,000 price for Meadowbrook Honey Co [app]. Advantage 2: It keeps control in the family's hands [k], so Rosa and Emilio Varela avoid culture clash and management issues from absorbing Meadowbrook's staff [app].
    Keywords: $180,000, $450,000, facility, Meadowbrook Honey Co, retained profit, Rosa and Emilio
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: internal growth is cheaper/slower and self-funded; internal growth avoids integration problems/culture clash | application_max_2: $180,000 facility cost; $450,000 acquisition price; Meadowbrook Honey Co; Rosa and Emilio Varela

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems GoldenHive Apiaries might face as a result of rapid growth.
    Answer: Problem 1: Cash-flow strain [k], because $450,000 for Meadowbrook or $180,000 for a new facility must be paid while $520,000 a year of revenue is still being collected from supermarkets [app], so the business could run short of cash and struggle to pay the 12 beekeepers and packers [an]. Problem 2: Communication and coordination problems [k], as managing 2 farms plus an acquired rival would stretch Rosa and Emilio's span of control [app], slowing decisions and risking mistakes such as undelivered orders exceeding the 30 per cent supply gap [an].
    Keywords: $450,000, $180,000, $520,000, beekeepers, Meadowbrook, 2 farms, 30 per cent
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cash-flow/working capital problems from rapid growth; communication/coordination problems (span of control) from growth | application_max_2: $450,000 acquisition; $180,000 facility; $520,000 sales revenue; 12 beekeepers and packers | analysis_max_2: cash shortage prevents payment of wages/bills; slower decisions and more errors across wider operations

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think GoldenHive Apiaries should build its own second extraction and bottling facility or acquire Meadowbrook Honey Co? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Building the $180,000 facility is affordable from retained profit [k] and would add steady output for supermarkets whose demand exceeds supply by 30 per cent [app], letting the family grow at a managed pace with full control of quality [an]. Acquiring Meadowbrook Honey Co for $450,000 would add 300 hives instantly [k] and remove a competitor while adding $410,000 of revenue [app], but integration could bring culture clash and higher debt [an]. Overall, the internal option is better for this business at this stage [eval], because Rosa and Emilio can fund it without borrowing and protect the quality reputation that wins supermarket contracts [eval].
    Keywords: $180,000, $450,000, Meadowbrook Honey Co, 300 hives, retained profit, 30 per cent, $410,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: internal growth is slower but cheaper and keeps control; external growth is faster but costly and risks integration/culture clash | application_max_2: $180,000 facility; $450,000 Meadowbrook price; 300 hives; 30 per cent supply gap | analysis_max_2: managed pace protects quality and control; acquisition adds capacity and revenue quickly but risks debt/clash | evaluation_max_2: weighs cost and control against speed, judging internal growth the safer route at this stage

--- STEM ---
Sungrove Olive Oil is a private limited company (LTD) run by the Peralta family for 9 years, pressing and bottling extra virgin olive oil at a single mill in a dry, sunny province. The business employs 15 workers, crushes about 900,000 kilograms of olives a year and sells $1.4 million worth of oil to restaurants and delicatessens across the country.

Until now Sungrove has bought olives from around 40 local growers at an average price of $0.85 per kilogram. The family plans to secure supplies by purchasing Terra Alta Olive Grove, a 300-hectare primary-sector farm, for $650,000. Some relatives worry about the high upfront cost and last year's fall in oil prices, while others argue that owning the grove would guarantee quality and cut raw material costs.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'backward vertical integration'.
    Answer: Backward vertical integration is when a business takes over or merges with a supplier of its raw materials or earlier-stage inputs [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: integration with a supplier/earlier stage of production; opposite direction from forward vertical integration

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Sungrove Olive Oil of backward vertical integration.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Guaranteed supply [k], as owning the 300-hectare Terra Alta Olive Grove secures the 900,000 kilograms of olives the mill needs each year [app]. Advantage 2: Lower raw material costs [k], since cutting out the 40 local growers buying at $0.85 per kilogram removes their mark-up margins [app].
    Keywords: 900,000, Terra Alta Olive Grove, $0.85, 40 local growers, 300-hectare, kilograms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: secures supply of raw materials; reduces/eliminates supplier mark-up and improves quality control | application_max_2: 900,000 kilograms of olives; Terra Alta Olive Grove; $0.85 per kilogram; 40 local growers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Sungrove Olive Oil of achieving business growth.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Greater market power [k], as selling $1.4 million of olive oil to restaurants gives Sungrove a stronger position to negotiate supply contracts and discounts from bottle and label suppliers [app], lowering average costs and raising profit [an]. Benefit 2: Wider distribution [k], since growth from the 900,000-kilogram harvest would let Sungrove reach more delicatessens beyond its current customer base [app], increasing sales revenue and spreading risk if one buyer stops ordering [an].
    Keywords: $1.4 million, 900,000, delicatessens, restaurants, Terra Alta, 300-hectare
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: larger scale improves market power/bargaining position; growth increases sales revenue and spreads risk | application_max_2: $1.4 million sales; 900,000 kilograms; restaurants and delicatessens; single mill | analysis_max_2: lower average costs raise profit; wider customer base spreads risk and increases revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sungrove Olive Oil should acquire the Terra Alta Olive Grove or continue buying olives from local growers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Acquiring the Terra Alta Olive Grove for $650,000 would guarantee Sungrove a secure supply of 300 hectares of olives [k] and cut the cost of buying from 40 growers at $0.85 per kilogram [app], protecting quality and margins as the business grows [an]. However, the high upfront cost raises financial risk [k], especially after last year's fall in oil prices [app], and owning a farm adds management responsibilities the Peralta family has never handled, which could strain cash flow [an]. Overall, buying the grove is the better decision [eval], because it locks in supply for a mill that crushes 900,000 kilograms a year and secures the quality restaurants expect [eval].
    Keywords: $650,000, Terra Alta Olive Grove, 300-hectare, 40 local growers, 900,000, $0.85
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: backward vertical integration secures supply and quality; integration carries high upfront cost and added complexity | application_max_2: $650,000 purchase price; 300 hectares; 40 growers at $0.85; 900,000 kilograms | analysis_max_2: lower raw material cost/secured quality protects margins; cash-flow strain and management burden raise risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs supply security and quality against financial risk, favouring acquisition for this scale of mill
