--- STEM ---
Redstone Ceramic Tiles is a private limited company (LTD) manufacturing wall and floor tiles at 1 factory for 11 years. Employing 55 technicians alongside 3 kilns firing around the clock, the firm produced tiles worth $3.2 million last year. Almost all output is sold through 3 national wholesalers who each charge a margin of 12 per cent on the trade price.

Founder Miriam Holt is considering opening Redstone's own retail showrooms in 2 cities at a combined cost of $420,000, to sell direct to consumers, builders and architects. She believes cutting out wholesalers would capture their 12 per cent margin, but her financial adviser warns that running showrooms is a tertiary activity needing retail staff, stock control systems and marketing experience she currently lacks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'forward vertical integration'.
    Answer: Forward vertical integration is when a business takes over or merges with a distributor or retailer that sells its products to the final customer [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: integration with a distributor/retailer/next stage towards the customer; opposite direction from backward vertical integration

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Redstone Ceramic Tiles of forward vertical integration.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Capturing the wholesaler margin [k], as selling direct through Redstone's own 2 showrooms would keep the 12 per cent each wholesaler charges [app]. Advantage 2: Better contact with final customers [k], as dealing with consumers, builders and architects directly gives feedback on which tiles sell, instead of relying on 3 distant wholesalers [app].
    Keywords: 12 per cent, wholesalers, 2 cities, showrooms, $420,000, $3.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: captures distributor/retailer margin (higher profit); direct contact with customers improves market feedback/control | application_max_2: 12 per cent margin; 3 national wholesalers; 2 showrooms; consumers, builders and architects

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Redstone Ceramic Tiles of achieving business growth.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Higher revenue [k], as opening 2 showrooms would tap direct sales from consumers and builders in addition to the $3.2 million already produced for wholesalers [app], increasing total sales and spreading income across more customers [an]. Benefit 2: Greater economies of scale [k], as higher output from the factory's 3 kilns would spread fixed costs over more tiles [app], lowering average cost per tile and improving profit on every unit sold [an].
    Keywords: $3.2 million, 2 cities, 3 kilns, 55, 12 per cent, retail showrooms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth increases revenue/sales and customer base; growth enables economies of scale (lower average cost) | application_max_2: $3.2 million output; 2 showrooms; 3 kilns; 55 technicians | analysis_max_2: more revenue and spread risk across customers; fixed costs spread over more units, lowering average cost

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redstone Ceramic Tiles should open its own retail showrooms or continue selling through wholesalers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Opening 2 showrooms at $420,000 would let Redstone capture the 12 per cent margin currently taken by 3 national wholesalers [k], raising profit on the $3.2 million of tiles produced each year [app], and giving direct contact with consumers, builders and architects to plan products [an]. However, showrooms are a tertiary activity requiring retail staff and stock systems Miriam Holt has never managed [k], which risks high costs and slow-moving stock that could erase the margin gain [app], and $420,000 of cash would be tied up with no guarantee of sales [an]. Overall, continuing with wholesalers for now is wiser [eval], because Redstone should test direct selling with one pilot showroom before committing fully [eval].
    Keywords: $420,000, 12 per cent, wholesalers, $3.2 million, 2 cities, Miriam Holt, showrooms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: forward integration captures margin and customer contact; forward integration adds cost/risk in an unfamiliar tertiary activity | application_max_2: $420,000 cost; 12 per cent margin; 3 national wholesalers; $3.2 million output | analysis_max_2: margin capture raises profit and feedback improves products; cash tied up and weak retail skills risk losses | evaluation_max_2: weighs margin capture against unfamiliar retail risk, recommending a cautious pilot before full commitment

VetCare Clinics is a private limited company (LTD) operating 6 veterinary practices across a metropolitan region for 8 years. The business employs 34 vets, nurses and reception staff and generated $2.1 million in revenue last year, making it the second-largest clinic group in the region.

The board has identified 2 possible routes to becoming market leader. It could acquire Paws & Claws Vet Centres, a rival chain of 4 clinics with 22 staff and $1.5 million in revenue, for $1.1 million. Alternatively, it could open 2 brand-new clinics in fast-growing suburbs at a cost of $800,000.     Question: Identify two problems of rapid business growth.
    Answer: 1. Communication problems [1].
2. Cash-flow problems [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: communication problems; coordination problems; cash-flow problems; culture clash

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to VetCare Clinics of business growth.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Increased market share [k], as adding either 4 acquired clinics or 2 new ones would push the current $2.1 million revenue past the market leader [app]. Benefit 2: Greater profits [k], as spreading the 34 existing staff and central marketing costs over more practices lowers average cost per patient [app].
    Keywords: $2.1 million, 34, 6 veterinary practices, Paws & Claws, 2 brand-new clinics, 6 veterinary
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth increases market share; growth increases profit via economies of scale/shared overheads | application_max_2: $2.1 million revenue; 34 vets, nurses and reception staff; 6 veterinary practices; Paws & Claws Vet Centres

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of using value of sales to measure the size of VetCare Clinics.
    Answer: Problem 1: Sales value varies between firms in different sectors [k], as VetCare's $2.1 million and Paws & Claws' $1.5 million say nothing about service quality, prices or client numbers at each of the combined 10 clinics [app], making the measure unreliable for judging the true leader [an]. Problem 2: Sales value ignores profitability and capital employed [k], as a large $2.1 million revenue can hide thin margins or high debt [app], so a bigger revenue figure does not mean a stronger or better-managed business [an].
    Keywords: $2.1 million, $1.5 million, Paws & Claws, 6 veterinary, $1.1 million, 22 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: value of sales ignores profit margins/costs; value of sales is not comparable across sectors or service quality | application_max_2: $2.1 million revenue; $1.5 million Paws & Claws revenue; 6 veterinary practices; 4 clinics | analysis_max_2: misleading measure for comparing the two chains; ignores profitability so size looks bigger than strength

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think VetCare Clinics should acquire Paws & Claws Vet Centres or open two new clinics? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Acquiring Paws & Claws for $1.1 million would add 4 clinics and $1.5 million revenue instantly [k], giving VetCare $3.6 million combined revenue and removing its closest rival [app], a fast route to market leadership [an]. However, Paws & Claws staff fear redundancies and the two chains differ in culture and pay [k], so integration could trigger culture clash, low morale and lost vets [app], which would damage client trust [an]. Opening 2 new clinics for $800,000 is slower but builds organically with chosen staff and culture [eval], and on balance that is the safer decision given the people risks of a takeover [eval].
    Keywords: Paws & Claws, $1.1 million, $1.5 million, $800,000, 2 brand-new clinics, 22 staff, 34
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: external growth is faster, removes rivals, adds instant revenue; external growth risks culture clash/low morale/redundancies | application_max_2: $1.1 million acquisition cost; $1.5 million revenue; 4 clinics, 22 staff; $800,000 for 2 new clinics | analysis_max_2: instant revenue and rival removal give rapid market leadership; culture clash and redundancy fears damage morale and service | evaluation_max_2: weighs speed and rival removal against people/culture risk, favouring organic expansion on balance

--- STEM ---
GreenHaven Plants Plc is a public limited company (PLC) operating a chain of 12 indoor plant nurseries and garden centres for 5 years. The group employs 240 staff across retail, growing and delivery, and annual sales have climbed from $1.1 million in the first year to $3.8 million this year, with 3 new stores opened in the last 12 months.

Growth has created strains. Site managers report that decisions take 6 weeks because every change passes through a long chain of command, and the finance director warns that December cash is tight, with unsold stock worth $240,000 and supplier invoices falling due. The board must decide whether to press ahead with 2 more stores or pause expansion and fix communication, coordination and cash-flow problems first.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State the four methods of measuring business size.
    Answer: 1. Number of people employed [1].
2. Value of output [1].
3. Value of sales [1].
4. Value of capital employed [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: number of people employed; value of output; value of sales; value of capital employed

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems GreenHaven Plants Plc might face as it grows rapidly.
    Answer: Problem 1: Communication problems [k], as a long chain of command means changes take 6 weeks to reach staff in 12 stores with 240 employees [app]. Problem 2: Cash-flow problems [k], as cash is tied up in unsold stock worth $240,000 and supplier invoices fall due before sales revenue arrives [app].
    Keywords: 6 weeks, $240,000, 240 staff, 12 indoor plant, chain of command, $3.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: communication problems (long chain of command/slow messages); cash-flow problems (money tied up in stock/payables-receivables gap) | application_max_2: 6 weeks; $240,000 unsold stock; 12 indoor plant nurseries; 240 staff

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why GreenHaven Plants Plc is able to grow so rapidly.
    Answer: Reason 1: Rising demand for its products [k], as sales have climbed from $1.1 million to $3.8 million, showing customers want indoor plants and garden centre goods across 12 stores [app], so each new store opened adds strong immediate revenue [an]. Reason 2: Access to finance as a public limited company [k], as having 240 staff and $3.8 million sales gives it scale to sell shares and open 3 more stores [app], funding growth faster than a small business could [an].
    Keywords: $1.1 million, $3.8 million, 12 indoor plant, 240 staff, 3 new stores, public limited company
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high demand/rising sales enable growth; Plc status/access to finance enables growth | application_max_2: $1.1 million to $3.8 million sales; 12 indoor plant nurseries; 240 staff; 3 new stores | analysis_max_2: strong demand makes each new store viable; access to capital funds expansion faster than small firms can manage

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think GreenHaven Plants Plc should continue to expand rapidly or pause to fix its internal problems first? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Pausing expansion would let GreenHaven fix its 6-week communication delays and long chain of command [k], so 12 stores with 240 staff can respond to customers quickly [app], preventing mistakes and protecting service quality as it grows [an]. However, GreenHaven's sales have risen from $1.1 million to $3.8 million [k], showing strong demand, so delaying 2 planned stores could lose sales to rivals and leave fixed costs spread over too few stores [app], and cash tied up in $240,000 of unsold stock will worsen if buying slows [an]. Overall, pausing briefly to fix cash-flow and communication is wiser [eval], because $3.8 million of sales will not pay suppliers while December cash is tight [eval].
    Keywords: $3.8 million, 6 weeks, $240,000, 240 staff, 2 more stores, 12 indoor plant, $1.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fixing communication/coordination problems improves efficiency; pausing risks losing momentum to rivals/leaving spare capacity | application_max_2: $3.8 million sales; $240,000 unsold stock; 6 weeks; 240 staff | analysis_max_2: fixing systems prevents service failures and mistakes; pausing risks lost sales and worsening cash position | evaluation_max_2: weighs momentum and demand against internal strain, favouring a short pause to secure cash flow and control

    Answer: Business growth is the increase in the size of a business over time, such as higher sales, more output, more employees or more assets [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increase in size of the business over time; measured by sales/output/employees/capital employed

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why some businesses choose to remain small.
    Answer: Reason 1: To keep quality and customer loyalty [k], as Priya Nair's hand-blended spices sold through 40 delicatessens earn $180,000 a year upheld by loyal customers [app]. Reason 2: To stay in owner's control [k], as remaining a sole trader with 3 part-time assistants keeps decision-making simple and avoids the $150,000 risk of mass expansion [app].
    Keywords: hand-blended, 40 independent delicatessens, 3 part-time assistants, Priya Nair, $180,000, sole trader
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: small firms can focus on quality/customer loyalty/niche markets; owner retains control/avoids complexity and risk of growth | application_max_2: hand-blended spices; 40 independent delicatessens; 3 part-time assistants; Priya Nair

  Qc [6 marks]

Benefit 2: Greater economies of scale [k], as tripling output with an industrial grinder would spread fixed costs like rent and wages over more kilograms of spice [app], lowering average cost per kilogram and improving competitiveness [an].
    Keywords: 3-year, 120 stores, $180,000, $150,000, industrial grinder, 40 independent delicatessens
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth increases sales revenue/profit; growth enables economies of scale (lower average cost) | application_max_2: 3-year exclusive contract; 120 stores; $180,000 annual sales; $150,000 industrial grinder | analysis_max_2: higher profit funds further investment; fixed costs spread over more units, lowering average cost

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Saffron Lane Spice Merchants should accept the supermarket contract or remain a small specialist business? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the 3-year contract to supply 120 stores would transform the business [k], turning $180,000 annual sales into national volumes and justifying the $150,000 industrial grinder and 8 new staff [app], giving stable revenue and a platform for future growth [an]. However, mass production could dilute the hand-blended quality loyal customers love [k], risking the customer loyalty that supports $180,000 a year of sales [app], and over-dependence on one supermarket means losing the contract would leave spare capacity and a $150,000 asset [an].     Keywords: 120 stores, $150,000, $180,000, 40 independent delicatessens, 3-year, hand-blended, Priya Nair
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: large contracts raise revenue and enable economies of scale; growth risks quality dilution and over-dependence on one customer | application_max_2: 120 stores; $150,000 industrial grinder; $180,000 annual sales; 40 independent delicatessens | analysis_max_2: national volume raises revenue and spreads costs; quality dilution and single-customer risk threaten the niche brand | evaluation_max_2: weighs large-scale revenue against brand/quality risk and independence, favouring remaining small at this stage

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Ironbridge Scaffolding Co could overcome the cash-flow problems linked to its rapid growth.

Strategy 2: Negotiate milestone payments [k], asking the client to pay in stages so the $700,000 is not owed entirely upfront [app].
    Keywords: $700,000, 60 days, $2.4 million, 5 different group chats, $48,000, $5.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: overdraft/bank loan to cover short-term gap; stage/milestone payments or tighter credit control | application_max_2: $700,000 upfront spending; 60 days after work starts; $2.4 million contract; $48,000 missing materials

Benefit 2: Greater economies of scale [k], as buying scaffolding and materials in bulk for a $2.4 million project lowers the average cost per job [app], improving profit margins and competitive pricing [an].
    Keywords: $2.4 million, $5.6 million, 78 employees, $700,000, 22 to 78, 18 months
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth increases revenue/market share/security of work; growth enables economies of scale (bulk buying/purchasing economies) | application_max_2: $2.4 million contract; $5.6 million turnover; 78 employees; $700,000 on new scaffolding | analysis_max_2: secured pipeline of work protects jobs and revenue; bulk purchases lower average cost and improve margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ironbridge Scaffolding Co should take a $700,000 bank overdraft to finance the new shopping centre contract or delay taking on this contract? Justify your answer.

    Keywords: $700,000, $2.4 million, 60 days, $48,000, $5.6 million, 5 different group chats, 78 employees
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: overdraft bridges short-term cash gap before payment; overdraft has interest/fees and risks (cost of finance/default) | application_max_2: $700,000 overdraft need; $2.4 million contract; 60 days after work starts; $48,000 missing materials | analysis_max_2: unlocks major revenue and secures employment; interest plus disorganisation could cause default/overruns | evaluation_max_2: weighs overdraft cost and control risk against contract value, favouring taking it with tighter management controls

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Goldenharvest Foods Plc of horizontal integration.

    Keywords: $9 million, $46 million, Roma Pasta Co, 210 staff, $12 million, 2 factories
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration adds market share/scale instantly; horizontal integration removes a competitor at the same stage | application_max_2: $9 million Roma Pasta Co sales; $46 million Goldenharvest sales; Roma Pasta Co; 210 staff

  Qc [6 marks]

    Keywords: 850 staff, $46 million, $12 million, $9 million, Durum Plains Wheat Farm, Roma Pasta Co
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: external growth is fast (speed of expansion); external growth brings scale/bargaining power/economies | application_max_2: 850 staff; $46 million sales; Roma Pasta Co ($12 million); Durum Plains Wheat Farm ($9 million) | analysis_max_2: speed protects market share sooner than organic growth; larger scale lowers average costs and improves negotiating position

  Qd [8 marks]

However, acquiring Durum Plains Wheat Farm for $9 million would secure 35 per cent of durum imports from 1,800 hectares of owned land [k], cutting exposure to volatile overseas prices for the next 10 years [app], protecting margins and supply security [an]. Overall, Roma Pasta Co is the better buy [eval], because Goldenharvest already buys most wheat on contract and a 10-year supply deal could be negotiated instead of a $9 million purchase [eval].

--- STEM ---
Thornwick Paper Mills Ltd operates a newsprint mill in the industrial town of Aldervale, near the northern rail terminus. It employs 210 workers and produced 18,000 tonnes of newsprint last year, generating revenue of $7.2 million. Over the past decade, secondary manufacturing fell from 34% to 21% of employment in Country Y as cheaper overseas paper flooded the market and three local mills closed, with imports now holding about 40% of demand.

Managing Director Helen Marsh is weighing a $2.4 million investment to convert line two into making recycled packaging board, which sells for $1,150 per tonne against $780 for newsprint. --- QUESTIONS ---

    Question: Define the term 'added value'.
    Answer: The difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the inputs used to make it, so the business earns more than it spends on materials and labour [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: difference between selling price and cost of inputs; created by processing or production

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Thornwick Paper Mills might add value by converting to packaging board.
    Answer: Reason 1: The board would raise added value and revenue per tonne [k], because board sells at $1,150 per tonne compared with $780 for newsprint [app]. Reason 2: Diversifying reduces dependence on a shrinking newsprint market [k], since overseas demand is forecast to fall a further 15% next year while 2 regional food manufacturers have already signed board orders [app].
    Keywords: packaging board, newsprint, $1,150, $780, 15%, recycled, Aldervale
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher added value/price per tonne; diversification away from declining market | application_max_2: $1,150 per tonne; $780 for newsprint; fall a further 15%; 2 regional food manufacturers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Thornwick Paper Mills of adding value through a recycled packaging board line.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Higher revenue per unit sold [k], because board earns $1,150 per tonne while newsprint earns $780 [app], so each tonne converted adds value and repays the $2.4 million investment faster [an]. Benefit 2: A more secure order pipeline [k], because board orders from 2 regional food manufacturers are already signed [app], giving steadier sales as overseas newsprint demand keeps falling [an].
    Keywords: packaging board, $1,150, $780, newsprint, $2.4 million, recycled, board orders
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher revenue per unit; more stable order book | application_max_2: $1,150 per tonne; $780 for newsprint; $2.4 million investment; 2 regional food manufacturers | analysis_max_2: each tonne adds revenue to repay the investment; steadier sales as newsprint declines

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Thornwick Paper Mills should convert line two to recycled packaging board rather than continue producing newsprint? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Converting would raise added value [k], since board sells at $1,150 per tonne against $780 for newsprint [app], adding $370 per tonne to revenue that can help repay the $2.4 million investment [an]. However, keeping newsprint continues an established product [k], since line two already produces 18,000 tonnes a year generating $7.2 million in revenue [app], so conversion risks disruption if the 2 regional food manufacturers fall through [an]. Overall, conversion is the stronger option because newsprint demand in Country Y is falling sharply [eval], and the signed board orders plus the higher price per tonne give the mill a far better chance of survival as the secondary sector shrinks [eval].
    Keywords: line two, packaging board, $1,150, $780, newsprint, 18,000 tonnes, $2.4 million, Country Y
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher added value vs continuity/risk of change; conversion risk and disruption | application_max_2: $1,150 per tonne; $780 for newsprint; $2.4 million investment; 18,000 tonnes; $7.2 million in revenue | analysis_max_2: extra revenue per tonne repays the investment; disruption risk if signed orders fall through | evaluation_max_2: weighs declining newsprint market against conversion risk

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the secondary sector in Country X might be shrinking.

    Keywords: castings, 5%, 29%, 18%, secondary sector, engine casings, anodizing

  Qd [8 marks]

However, continuing with raw castings avoids a $3.8 million gamble [k], with 340 workers and $12.6 million in revenue from 9,500 tonnes already secure [app], so anodizing risks heavy losses if carmakers do not switch orders to domestic suppliers [an]. Overall, investment is the better option because Country X's secondary sector has shrunk from 29% to 18% of GDP [eval], meaning staying in low-value raw castings threatens long-term survival unless the plant moves up the value chain [eval].

The board is weighing a $2.6 million investment in a roasted rice-cake snack line, selling at $2,300 per tonne against $950 per tonne for milled rice. Local retailers have agreed trial orders, but the project would halve exports to its traditional bulk buyers in 2 neighbouring countries, which currently take 60% of output.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'opportunity cost'.
    Answer: The next best alternative forgone when a choice is made; what must be given up when one option is chosen over another [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: next best alternative forgone; choices involve giving up something

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Brackenwood's profit margin might have narrowed to 4%.
    Answer: Reason 1: Selling prices are under pressure [k], as milled rice sells at only $950 per tonne [app]. Reason 2: The local industrial base is shrinking [k], as secondary sector employment fell from 31% to 22% over the past decade [app].
    Keywords: milled rice, $950 per tonne, 4%, 31%, 22%, 27,000 tonnes, Riverton
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: price pressure on the product; decline of the industrial/secondary base | application_max_2: $950 per tonne; fell from 31% to 22%; past decade

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Brackenwood of investing in the roasted rice-cake line.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Higher added value per tonne [k], with rice-cakes selling at $2,300 per tonne against $950 for milled rice [app], adding $1,350 per tonne of revenue [an]. Benefit 2: Access to higher-growth retail demand [k], with local retailers already agreeing trial orders [app], broadening the mill beyond bulk export buyers [an].
    Keywords: rice-cake, $2,300 per tonne, $950 per tonne, trial orders, roasted, $2.6 million, $8.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher added value per tonne; access to retail/new market demand | application_max_2: $2,300 per tonne; $950 per tonne; local retailers; trial orders | analysis_max_2: adds $1,350 per tonne of revenue; broadens customer base beyond exporters

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brackenwood Rice Mill should invest in the rice-cake line rather than continue supplying bulk milled rice to exporters? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The rice-cake line would raise added value [k], because rice-cakes sell at $2,300 per tonne against $950 for milled rice [app], adding $1,350 per tonne and potentially reviving the current 4% profit margin [an]. However, staying with bulk exports is safer [k], because 60% of output goes to 2 neighbouring countries that already buy 27,000 tonnes a year [app], and switching to retail packs would halve those exports while the $2.6 million investment strains cash flow [an]. Overall, the rice-cake line is the better gamble because the secondary sector's decline to 22% of employment threatens bulk demand long term [eval], and retailers' trial orders suggest domestic demand that exports alone cannot provide [eval].
    Keywords: rice-cake, $2,300 per tonne, $950 per tonne, 60%, 2 neighbouring countries, $2.6 million, 27,000 tonnes, 4%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher added value vs export continuity; risk of halving exports | application_max_2: $2,300 per tonne; $950 for milled rice; 60% of output; 2 neighbouring countries; 27,000 tonnes | analysis_max_2: adds $1,350 per tonne and lifts the 4% margin; halving exports and cash-flow strain from $2.6 million cost | evaluation_max_2: weighs export loyalty against rising retail demand amid sector decline

--- STEM ---
Brinewell Fisheries is a family-run fishery based in Country X that has landed mackerel for 14 years. It employs 16 crew across 4 boats and catches about 20 tonnes of mackerel a month, selling the fresh fish to a fish merchant at $4 per kilogram. Fuel costs have risen by 18% this year. Sales of fresh mackerel have been flat for a while.

The owner, Priya Nadar, is deciding whether to spend $150,000 on a smoking and filleting unit to sell smoked fillets at $9 per kilogram, with $3 of extra running costs per kilogram. The bank has offered a loan for the equipment. Alternatively, the fish merchant has promised a 3-year fresh contract at $4.40 per kilogram if Brinewell keeps supplying fresh fish. The unit would need 5 extra workers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'added value'.
    Answer: Added value is the difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and inputs used to produce it [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: difference between selling price and cost of bought-in inputs; value created by converting inputs into a finished good or service

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Brinewell Fisheries could increase added value.
    Answer: Way 1: Processing the fish [k], by buying the $150,000 smoking and filleting unit to sell smoked fillets at $9 per kilogram instead of fresh fish at $4 per kilogram [app]. Way 2: Improving presentation and packaging [k], by selling branded, ready-to-eat smoked fillet packs that can command a higher price than the loose fresh fish sold to the fish merchant [app].
    Keywords: mackerel, $150,000, $9 per kilogram, $4 per kilogram, smoked fillets, fish merchant, 20 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing/converting raw materials into a more expensive finished product; improving packaging, branding or presentation to raise the price | application_max_2: $150,000 smoking and filleting unit; smoked fillets at $9 per kilogram; fresh fish at $4 per kilogram; 20 tonnes of mackerel a month

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Brinewell Fisheries of investing in the smoking and filleting unit.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A higher margin per kilogram [k], because smoked fillets sell at $9 per kilogram against $4 per kilogram for fresh fish [app], so even after $3 of extra running costs the business keeps about $2 more per kilogram, raising profit [an]. Benefit 2: Less dependence on one buyer [k], because branded smoked fillet packs can be sold to supermarkets and caterers rather than only the fish merchant [app], spreading the weekly catch across more customers and lowering the risk of losing the merchant's business [an].
    Keywords: $9 per kilogram, $4 per kilogram, $3, fish merchant, $150,000, smoked, filleting
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher selling price/added value raises revenue and profit; processed goods can reach a wider market, reducing reliance on one buyer | application_max_2: smoked fillets at $9 per kilogram; fresh fish at $4 per kilogram; $3 of extra running costs per kilogram; the fish merchant | analysis_max_2: about $2 per kilogram extra margin after running costs lifts profit; wider customer base reduces single-buyer risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brinewell Fisheries should invest in the smoking and filleting unit rather than sign the fresh 3-year contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that smoking captures far more added value [k], because smoked fillets sell at $9 per kilogram with $3 of running costs, leaving $6 per kilogram against $4.40 on the fresh contract [app], so each kilogram earns over $1.60 more, which helps repay the $150,000 loan [an]. On the other hand, the 3-year fresh contract at $4.40 per kilogram is guaranteed income [k] and needs no $150,000 loan, no 5 extra workers and no risk of the smoked packs failing to sell [app]; with fuel costs up 18%, dependable cash flow protects the business [an]. Overall, investing is the better choice only if Priya has secured retail orders for the smoked fillets, since $6 per kilogram beats $4.40 after running costs [eval]; without confirmed orders, the safer 3-year fresh contract is the wiser option while fuel costs stay high [eval].
    Keywords: $150,000, $9 per kilogram, $4.40 per kilogram, 3-year, 18%, smoked fillets, mackerel, fish merchant
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing increases added value and margin per kilogram; the 3-year fresh contract offers certainty and lower risk | application_max_2: $9 per kilogram smoked fillets with $3 running costs; $4.40 per kilogram on the 3-year fresh contract; $150,000 loan for the unit; 18% rise in fuel costs | analysis_max_2: about $1.60 per kilogram extra margin could repay the loan; contract removes debt, staffing and demand risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs higher-margin processing against contract certainty; justified conditional recommendation tied to fuel costs and orders

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U1_SET_112
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Cardew Dairy Farm is a partnership owned by Helen and Marcus Cardew for 9 years in Country X. The farm keeps 60 dairy cows producing about 1,200 litres of milk a day, sold raw to a large creamery at $0.55 per litre. Feed costs have risen by 15% in the past year, squeezing the partners' margins.

The siblings are deciding whether to spend $80,000 on cheese-making and maturing equipment to produce cheddar sold at $15 per kilogram, using 10 litres of milk per kilogram of cheese and $4 of extra running costs per kilogram. The creamery has offered a 2-year raw-milk contract at $0.60 per litre, but cheese would add value and need 4 extra workers once the vat is installed.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by the 'primary sector'.
    Answer: The primary sector is the part of the economy that extracts and harvests natural resources, such as farming, fishing and quarrying [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: extracts, grows or harvests raw materials from nature; examples include agriculture, fishing, forestry and quarrying/mining

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Cardew Dairy Farm might add value to its milk by making cheese.
    Answer: Reason 1: Cheese sells for far more than raw milk [k], because each kilogram of cheddar at $15 is made from 10 litres of milk that the farm currently sells raw at $0.55 per litre, about $5.50 per 10 litres [app]. Reason 2: Cheese lasts much longer [k], because matured cheddar can be stored for months and sold when prices are good, whereas 1,200 litres of raw milk a day must be collected daily or it spoils [app].
    Keywords: $15 per kilogram, $0.55 per litre, cheddar, 1,200 litres, 10 litres, creamery, cheese
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raises the price received per input unit; processed products store longer, cutting waste and smoothing sales | application_max_2: cheddar at $15 per kilogram; raw milk at $0.55 per litre; 1,200 litres of milk a day; 10 litres of milk per kilogram of cheese

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Cardew Dairy Farm of making its own cheese instead of selling raw milk.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A much higher return per litre [k], because cheese at $15 per kilogram uses 10 litres of milk and even after $4 of running costs keeps $11 per kilogram [app], far above the $6 return on the same 10 litres at $0.60 per litre on the 2-year contract, lifting profit [an]. Benefit 2: Greater control over where the product is sold [k], because the farm could sell its cheddar directly at markets and shops instead of depending on the large creamery [app], keeping the full retail margin and avoiding the creamery lowering its $0.55 per litre price [an].
    Keywords: $15, $4, $0.60 per litre, $0.55, creamery, cheddar, 10 litres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher selling price after processing raises profit; selling directly keeps more of the final selling price | application_max_2: $15 per kilogram cheddar; $4 of extra running costs per kilogram; 2-year contract at $0.60 per litre; $0.55 per litre current price | analysis_max_2: $11 per kilogram retained far beats the $6 per 10-litre contract return; direct sales reduce dependence on the creamery's price decisions

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cardew Dairy Farm should make its own cheese rather than accept the 2-year raw-milk contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that cheese adds far more value [k], because each kilogram at $15 is made from 10 litres of milk, so keeping $11 after running costs is far above the $6 return on the same milk at $0.60 per litre [app], meaning the farm could build up capital quickly [an]. However, the 2-year contract is guaranteed income [k], worth about $720 a day from 1,200 litres at $0.60 per litre, with no $80,000 debt, no 4 extra workers to recruit and no risk that the unproven cheddar fails to sell [app]; with feed costs already up 15%, dependable cash matters [an]. Overall, making cheese is the better long-term choice if the partners have secured orders for their cheddar, since $11 per kilogram beats the $6 contract return [eval]; without signed orders, the safer 2-year raw-milk contract at $0.60 per litre is wiser until the cheese proves itself [eval].
    Keywords: $80,000, $15, $0.60 per litre, 1,200 litres, 15%, 2-year, cheddar, $0.55
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing increases added value and margin; the 2-year contract offers certainty and avoids debt | application_max_2: $15 per kilogram cheddar with $4 running costs; $0.60 per litre 2-year contract; 1,200 litres a day (about $720 a day); $80,000 equipment and 4 extra workers | analysis_max_2: $11 retained per kilogram far exceeds the contract return, aiding loan repayment; contract removes finance, staffing and market risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs superior margin against contract security and debt; justified conditional recommendation tied to feed costs and orders

--- STEM ---
Haverfell Quarry is a private limited company operating in Country X that has extracted limestone for 8 years. It employs 34 workers and produces about 500 tonnes of raw stone a month, sold to construction firms at $65 per tonne. Blasting permits have become harder to obtain, and equipment costs have risen. Most sales go to road base and building block manufacturers.

The managing director, Farida Rahman, is deciding whether to spend $450,000 on sawing and polishing machinery to sell cut flagstones at $150 per tonne, with $50 of extra running costs per tonne. A builders' merchant has offered a 2-year contract at $70 per tonne for raw stone, but cut stone would add value and need 6 skilled masons trained on the new saws.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State what is meant by the 'secondary sector'.
    Answer: The secondary sector is the part of the economy that converts raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods, such as manufacturing or construction [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: converts raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods; examples include manufacturing, processing and construction

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Haverfell Quarry could add value to its limestone.
    Answer: Way 1: Cutting and polishing the stone [k], by spending $450,000 on sawing and polishing machinery to sell cut flagstones at $150 per tonne instead of raw stone at $65 per tonne [app]. Way 2: Supplying a tighter specification [k], by delivering uniform, correctly sized flagstones that builders can lay directly, saving them time compared with irregular raw blocks [app].
    Keywords: limestone, $450,000, $150 per tonne, $65 per tonne, flagstones, 500 tonnes, $70 per tonne
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raw materials into a more valuable finished product; improving quality/specification to command a higher price | application_max_2: $450,000 sawing and polishing machinery; flagstones at $150 per tonne; raw stone at $65 per tonne; 500 tonnes of raw stone a month

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Haverfell Quarry of cutting its own flagstones instead of selling raw stone.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A higher price per tonne [k], because cut flagstones sell at $150 per tonne against $65 per tonne for raw stone [app], and even after $50 of extra running costs the quarry keeps $100 per tonne, about $30 above the $70 contract, lifting profit [an]. Benefit 2: Access to new types of buyer [k], because cut flagstones can be sold to landscapers and garden centres as well as construction firms [app], spreading the 500 tonnes a month across more customers and reducing dependence on the builders' merchant [an].
    Keywords: $150 per tonne, $65 per tonne, $50, flagstones, 500 tonnes, construction firms, $70 per tonne
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher selling price after processing increases profit; a wider range of buyers reduces dependence on one customer | application_max_2: flagstones at $150 per tonne; raw stone at $65 per tonne; $50 of extra running costs per tonne; $70 per tonne 2-year contract | analysis_max_2: $100 per tonne retained beats the $70 contract by about $30; new buyer types spread sales and cut single-buyer risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Haverfell Quarry should invest in cut flagstone production rather than accept the 2-year builders' contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that cutting adds real value [k], because flagstones at $150 per tonne keep $100 after $50 running costs, which is $30 per tonne better than the $70 contract [app], so on 500 tonnes a month the quarry could earn around $15,000 extra each month, helping repay the $450,000 machinery loan [an]. On the other hand, the 2-year contract at $70 per tonne is guaranteed income [k], needing no $450,000 loan, no 6 skilled masons to train and no risk that cut-stone buyers fail to appear while blasting permits are harder to obtain [app]; with equipment costs rising, a steady contract protects cash flow [an]. Overall, investing is the stronger choice if the quarry has signed landscaping or garden-centre orders, since $100 per tonne clearly beats $70 [eval]; without confirmed orders, the 2-year contract at $70 per tonne is the safer basis for the business [eval].
    Keywords: $450,000, $150 per tonne, $70 per tonne, 500 tonnes, 2-year, flagstones, $50, limestone
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cutting stone into flagstones increases added value and margin; the 2-year contract gives guaranteed income and avoids debt | application_max_2: flagstones at $150 per tonne; $70 per tonne on the 2-year contract; $450,000 machinery investment; 500 tonnes a month output | analysis_max_2: about $15,000 extra per month could repay the loan; contract avoids loan, staffing and demand risk amid permit problems | evaluation_max_2: weighs higher margin against guaranteed income and permit risk; justified conditional recommendation tied to confirmed orders

SET ID: P1_U1_SET_114
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity

--- STEM ---
Thornapple Orchards is a sole trader business owned by Sofia Lindqvist for 11 years in Country X. It grows apples across 40 hectares, producing about 180 tonnes a year, sold fresh to a wholesaler at $900 per tonne. An early frost last spring cut output by 12%, and storage space is limited. In peak harvest weeks some apples go to waste when the wholesaler cannot collect them.

Sofia is considering spending $95,000 on a juice bottling line to press her apples into bottled juice sold at $2.40 per litre, with about 700 litres of juice from each tonne and $0.50 of extra running costs per litre. The wholesaler has offered a 2-year fresh contract at $1,000 per tonne, but juice would add value and need 3 new workers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'opportunity cost'.
    Answer: Opportunity cost is the benefit forgone from the next best alternative when a choice is made between alternatives [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: value or benefit of the next best alternative given up; arises because resources are scarce and choices must be made

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Thornapple Orchards might add value to its apples by bottling juice.
    Answer: Reason 1: Bottled juice sells for more than fresh apples [k], because each tonne yields about 700 litres of juice at $2.40 per litre, worth roughly $1,680, against $900 per tonne for fresh apples [app]. Reason 2: Bottling uses lower-grade fruit [k], because bruised or graded-out apples that the wholesaler rejects can still be pressed into juice instead of being thrown away [app].
    Keywords: juice, $2.40 per litre, $900 per tonne, 700 litres, $95,000, 180 tonnes, wholesaler
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raises the revenue earned per unit of input; processing allows lower-grade inputs to be used profitably | application_max_2: 700 litres of juice per tonne; juice at $2.40 per litre; fresh apples at $900 per tonne; 180 tonnes a year output

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Thornapple Orchards of bottling apple juice instead of selling fresh apples.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A higher return per tonne [k], because 700 litres of juice at $2.40 per litre bring in about $1,680 per tonne [app], and even after $0.50 per litre of running costs the farm keeps $1,330 per tonne, well above the $1,000 fresh contract, raising profit [an]. Benefit 2: A storable, year-round product [k], because bottled juice can be sold in farm shops and supermarkets long after the harvest [app], smoothing revenue through the year and reducing pressure to sell apples quickly at $900 per tonne when storage space is limited [an].
    Keywords: $2.40 per litre, $0.50, $1,000 per tonne, $900 per tonne, juice, 700 litres, bottling
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher selling price after processing increases profit; processed goods store well, smoothing revenue and cutting waste | application_max_2: juice at $2.40 per litre; $0.50 of extra running costs per litre; $1,000 per tonne on the 2-year fresh contract; fresh apples at $900 per tonne | analysis_max_2: $1,330 per tonne retained beats the $1,000 contract; storable juice smooths cash flow and cuts waste

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Thornapple Orchards should bottle juice rather than accept the 2-year fresh contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that juice adds clearly more value [k], because at $2.40 per litre each tonne yields about $1,680, keeping roughly $1,330 after $0.50 per litre running costs against $1,000 on the 2-year contract [app], so switching could raise profit by around $330 per tonne across the 180 tonnes a year [an]. However, the fresh contract is much safer [k], guaranteeing $1,000 per tonne for 2 years with no $95,000 loan, no 3 new workers and no risk that the farm's bottled juice fails to sell [app]; after the early frost cut output by 12%, dependable cash matters [an]. Overall, bottling is the better choice if Sofia has secured shop or supermarket listings, since $1,330 per tonne beats the $1,000 contract [eval]; without confirmed buyers, the frost-hit farm should take the safety of the 2-year contract at $1,000 per tonne first [eval].
    Keywords: $95,000, $2.40, $1,000 per tonne, 180 tonnes, 12%, 2-year, juice, $0.50
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bottling juice increases added value and revenue per tonne; the 2-year fresh contract offers certainty and avoids debt | application_max_2: juice at $2.40 per litre with $0.50 running costs; $1,000 per tonne on the 2-year contract; $95,000 bottling line and 3 new workers; early frost cut output by 12% | analysis_max_2: around $330 extra per tonne could repay the investment; contract removes finance, staffing and demand risk after the frost | evaluation_max_2: weighs higher juice margin against contract security; justified conditional recommendation linked to confirmed buyers and the frost

--- STEM ---
Woldgate Grain Farm is a partnership owned by Tom and Elsie Brauer for 10 years in Country X. It farms 900 hectares of wheat, harvesting about 4,500 tonnes a year, sold raw in bulk to a milling company at $280 per tonne. A drought last year cut the harvest by 20%, and grain storage is limited.

The partners are considering spending $600,000 on a flour mill to grind their wheat into flour sold at $0.80 per kilogram, with each tonne of wheat yielding about 750 kilograms of flour and $140 of extra running costs per tonne milled. The milling company has offered a 2-year contract at $300 per tonne for raw wheat, but milling would add value and need 7 extra workers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State what is meant by 'industrialisation'.
    Answer: Industrialisation is the process by which a country's economy shifts towards a larger secondary, manufacturing sector as it develops [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth in importance/size of the secondary manufacturing sector; typically involves investment in factories and industry as an economy develops

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Woldgate Grain Farm could add value to its wheat.
    Answer: Way 1: Milling the wheat into flour [k], by spending $600,000 on a flour mill to sell flour at $0.80 per kilogram instead of raw wheat at $280 per tonne [app]. Way 2: Selling branded, consistent-quality flour [k], by supplying bagged flour directly to artisan bakeries, which pay more than raw grain bought in bulk by the milling company [app].
    Keywords: flour, $0.80 per kilogram, $280 per tonne, $600,000, wheat, 750 kilograms, milling company
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raw materials into a higher-priced finished product; branding and packaging can raise the price received | application_max_2: $600,000 flour mill; flour at $0.80 per kilogram; raw wheat at $280 per tonne; 750 kilograms of flour per tonne of wheat

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Woldgate Grain Farm of milling its own flour instead of selling raw wheat.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A higher income per tonne [k], because each tonne of wheat yields about 750 kilograms of flour at $0.80 per kilogram, worth $600 per tonne [app], and even after $140 of extra running costs the farm keeps $460 per tonne, $160 more than the $300 contract, lifting profit [an]. Benefit 2: Less dependence on one buyer [k], because flour can be sold to many bakeries and shops rather than only the milling company [app], spreading the 4,500 tonnes a year across more customers and protecting the farm if the contract price is renegotiated downwards [an].
    Keywords: $0.80 per kilogram, $140, $300 per tonne, $280 per tonne, flour, 750 kilograms, 4,500 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raises revenue per tonne and profit; selling to many buyers reduces reliance on a single customer | application_max_2: $600 per tonne of flour (750 kilograms at $0.80); $140 of extra running costs per tonne; 2-year contract at $300 per tonne; raw wheat at $280 per tonne | analysis_max_2: $460 per tonne retained beats the $300 contract by $160; wider customer base lowers single-buyer risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Woldgate Grain Farm should build its own flour mill rather than accept the 2-year wheat contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that milling captures much more value [k], because flour at $0.80 per kilogram from 750 kilograms per tonne is worth $600 per tonne, keeping $460 after $140 milling costs, beating the $300 contract by $160 per tonne [app], so across 4,500 tonnes a year the extra could approach $720,000 and clear the $600,000 loan [an]. On the other hand, the 2-year contract at $300 per tonne is guaranteed [k], needing no $600,000 loan, no 7 extra workers and no risk that the farm's flour fails to win bakery customers [app]; after drought cut the harvest by 20%, dependable cash is vital [an]. Overall, building the mill is the better choice if the Brauers have forward orders from bakeries, since $460 per tonne beats $300 [eval]; without confirmed buyers, the safer 2-year contract at $300 per tonne protects a drought-hit farm [eval].
    Keywords: $600,000, $0.80 per kilogram, $300 per tonne, 750 kilograms, 4,500 tonnes, 20%, 2-year, drought
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: milling increases added value and margin per tonne; the 2-year contract offers certainty and avoids debt | application_max_2: flour at $0.80 per kilogram (750 kilograms per tonne); $300 per tonne on the 2-year contract; $600,000 flour mill and 7 extra workers; drought cut the harvest by 20% | analysis_max_2: about $720,000 extra a year could clear the $600,000 loan; contract removes finance, staffing and demand risk after the drought | evaluation_max_2: weighs superior milling margin against contract security; justified conditional recommendation linked to orders and the drought

--- STEM ---
Tidemark Prawn Co is a prawn farming business in Country X operating for 6 years. It employs 26 workers across 12 ponds and produces about 140 tonnes of raw prawns a year, sold to an exporter at $6.50 per kilogram. Warming pond temperatures have reduced yields by 8% this season, and prawn feed has also become more expensive this year.

The director, Lena Ortiz, is deciding whether to spend $260,000 on a cooked-and-peeled packing line to sell packs at $13 per kilogram, with $4 of extra running costs per kilogram. The exporter has offered a 2-year raw contract at $7.00 per kilogram, but cooking and peeling would add value and need 5 extra workers; it is skilled, careful work that needs testing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by 'division of labour'.
    Answer: Division of labour is the splitting of a production process into smaller specialised tasks, with each worker responsible for one task [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: production broken into small specialised tasks; workers focus on one task, raising efficiency and output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Tidemark Prawn Co might add value to its prawns by cooking and peeling them.
    Answer: Reason 1: Cooked, peeled prawns sell for far more [k], because packs at $13 per kilogram are exactly double the $6.50 per kilogram the exporter pays for raw prawns [app]. Reason 2: Ready-to-eat packs reach new buyers [k], because cooked prawns can be sold to supermarkets and restaurants rather than only to one exporting firm [app].
    Keywords: prawns, $13 per kilogram, $6.50 per kilogram, $260,000, exporter, 140 tonnes, packing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raises the price received per kilogram; ready-to-eat products reach more customer groups | application_max_2: packs at $13 per kilogram; raw prawns at $6.50 per kilogram; the exporter; 140 tonnes of raw prawns a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Tidemark Prawn Co of cooking and peeling its prawns instead of selling them raw.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A higher net margin [k], because cooked, peeled prawns sell at $13 per kilogram and even after $4 of extra running costs the business keeps $9 per kilogram [app], which is $2 above the $7.00 two-year contract, raising profit [an]. Benefit 2: Less dependence on the exporter [k], because cooked packs can be sold to many supermarkets and restaurants [app], spreading the 140 tonnes a year across more buyers and giving the company more bargaining power over price [an].
    Keywords: $13 per kilogram, $4, $7.00 per kilogram, $6.50, cooked, peeled, $260,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher selling price after processing increases profit; selling to more buyers reduces single-customer dependence | application_max_2: $13 per kilogram packs; $4 of extra running costs per kilogram; $7.00 per kilogram on the 2-year contract; $6.50 per kilogram current price | analysis_max_2: $9 per kilogram retained beats the $7.00 contract by $2; more buyers increase bargaining power and reduce contract risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tidemark Prawn Co should invest in the cooked-and-peeled packing line rather than accept the 2-year exporter contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that processing adds clear value [k], because $13 per kilogram less $4 of running costs leaves $9 per kilogram, which is $2 better than the $7.00 contract [app], so on 140 tonnes a year the extra could reach $280,000, repaying the $260,000 line in about a year [an]. On the other hand, the 2-year contract at $7.00 per kilogram is guaranteed income [k], needing no $260,000 loan, no 5 extra workers and no risk that peeled packs fail food-safety checks or fail to win supermarket shelf space [app]; with yields already down 8%, cash security matters [an]. Overall, investing is the stronger choice if Lena has letters of intent from supermarket buyers, since $9 per kilogram beats $7.00 [eval]; without confirmed orders, the guaranteed $7.00 two-year contract is the safer base while yields recover [eval].
    Keywords: $260,000, $13 per kilogram, $7.00 per kilogram, 140 tonnes, 8%, 2-year, peeled, $4
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cooking and peeling increases added value and margin per kilogram; the 2-year exporter contract offers certainty and avoids debt | application_max_2: $13 per kilogram packs with $4 running costs; $7.00 per kilogram on the 2-year contract; $260,000 packing line and 5 extra workers; yields reduced by 8% this season | analysis_max_2: about $280,000 extra a year could repay the line in about a year; contract removes finance, staffing and food-safety risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs higher processing margin against contract security; justified conditional recommendation linked to food-safety and buyers

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U1_SET_117
UNIT: Unit 1: Understanding Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Copperhill Vineyard is a private limited company in Country X that has grown grapes for 15 years. It employs 38 workers across 120 hectares of vines and harvests about 260 tonnes of grapes a year, sold to a winery at $1,100 per tonne. Irrigation costs have risen by 22% since last summer, squeezing profits. The vineyard has also attracted growing interest from wine importers abroad.

The directors are considering spending $500,000 on a small bottling and labelling line to bottle their own wine at $9 per bottle (750 ml), with about 500 bottles from each tonne and $2.50 of extra running costs per bottle. The winery has offered a 2-year grape contract at $1,250 per tonne, but bottling would add value and need 4 extra cellar workers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'specialisation'.
    Answer: Specialisation is when a worker, business or country concentrates on a narrow range of products or tasks in which it is most efficient [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: focusing on a narrow range of products or tasks; improves efficiency, skill and quality of output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Copperhill Vineyard could add value to its grapes.
    Answer: Way 1: Bottling its own wine [k], by spending $500,000 on a bottling and labelling line to sell wine at $9 per bottle instead of grapes at $1,100 per tonne [app]. Way 2: Creating a distinctive house brand [k], by labelling bottles under the Copperhill Vineyard name, which can command a premium from wine shops and restaurants [app].
    Keywords: wine, $9 per bottle, $1,100 per tonne, $500,000, grapes, 750 ml, winery
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raw materials into a higher-priced finished product; branding and packaging raise the price customers will pay | application_max_2: $500,000 bottling and labelling line; wine at $9 per bottle; grapes at $1,100 per tonne; 500 bottles from each tonne

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Copperhill Vineyard of bottling its own wine instead of selling grapes.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A far higher return per tonne [k], because about 500 bottles at $9 each bring in $4,500 per tonne [app], and even after $2.50 per bottle of running costs the vineyard keeps $3,250 per tonne, well above the $1,250 two-year contract, lifting profit [an]. Benefit 2: A recognisable brand that builds loyalty [k], because own-labelled Copperhill wine can be stocked by shops and served by restaurants [app], widening the market beyond the single winery and supporting repeat sales year after year [an].
    Keywords: $9 per bottle, $2.50, $1,250 per tonne, 500 bottles, wine, bottling, winery
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher selling price after processing increases profit; a brand builds customer loyalty and repeat purchases | application_max_2: 500 bottles per tonne at $9; $2.50 of extra running costs per bottle; $1,250 per tonne on the 2-year grape contract; grapes at $1,100 per tonne | analysis_max_2: $3,250 per tonne retained vs $1,250 under the contract; own brand widens distribution and supports repeat sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Copperhill Vineyard should bottle its own wine rather than accept the 2-year grape contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that bottling transforms the vineyard's earnings [k], because 500 bottles per tonne at $9 bring in $4,500 per tonne, keeping $3,250 after $2.50 per bottle of costs, miles above the $1,250 two-year contract [app], so across 260 tonnes a year the extra could exceed $500,000 and clear the $500,000 loan quickly [an]. However, the 2-year contract at $1,250 per tonne is guaranteed income [k], needing no $500,000 loan, no 4 extra cellar workers and no launch costs to build an unproven brand while irrigation costs have risen 22% [app]. Unsold own-label wine would tie up working capital and could force the vineyard to borrow more [an]. Overall, bottling is the better long-term choice if the directors have secured distribution through shops or restaurants, since $3,250 per tonne beats $1,250 [eval]; without distribution, the safer $1,250 two-year grape contract is wiser for now [eval].
    Keywords: $500,000, $9 per bottle, $1,250 per tonne, 500 bottles, 22%, 2-year, wine, $1,100 per tonne
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bottling wine increases added value and revenue per tonne; the 2-year grape contract offers certainty and avoids debt | application_max_2: 500 bottles per tonne at $9 with $2.50 running costs; $1,250 per tonne on the 2-year grape contract; $500,000 bottling line and 4 extra workers; irrigation costs risen by 22% | analysis_max_2: extra over $500,000 a year could clear the $500,000 loan; unsold stock would tie up working capital and raise debt | evaluation_max_2: weighs superior bottling margin against contract security; justified conditional recommendation tied to distribution deals

--- STEM ---
Redhaven Tomato Farm is a sole trader business run by Dan Whitmore for 8 years in Country X. It grows tomatoes across 25 hectares and produces about 950 tonnes a year, sold fresh to a city market at $750 per tonne. Labour for picking rose by 10% this year, squeezing margins. The farm also grows chilli peppers on a small 3-hectare plot nearby.

Dan is deciding whether to spend $210,000 on a sauce-making and bottling line to produce tomato sauce sold at $3.00 per jar, with about 500 jars from each tonne and $0.60 of extra running costs per jar. The city market has offered a 2-year fresh contract at $820 per tonne, but sauce would add value and need 4 extra workers across the year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State what is meant by 'de-industrialisation'.
    Answer: De-industrialisation is the decline in importance of the secondary, manufacturing sector in an economy, often as services grow [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fall in the share or importance of secondary manufacturing; often linked to growth of the tertiary sector or cheaper imports

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Redhaven Tomato Farm might add value to its tomatoes by making sauce.
    Answer: Reason 1: Sauce sells for more than fresh tomatoes [k], because about 500 jars per tonne at $3.00 per jar bring in $1,500 per tonne, twice the $750 per tonne for fresh tomatoes [app]. Reason 2: Sauce lasts far longer [k], because bottled jars can be stored and sold all year, while fresh tomatoes must be sold quickly at the city market before they spoil [app].
    Keywords: sauce, $3.00 per jar, $750 per tonne, 500 jars, $210,000, 950 tonnes, city market
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raises revenue per tonne of raw input; processed products store longer, reducing waste | application_max_2: 500 jars per tonne at $3.00 per jar; fresh tomatoes at $750 per tonne; 950 tonnes a year output; the city market

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Redhaven Tomato Farm of making tomato sauce instead of selling fresh tomatoes.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A higher return per tonne [k], because 500 jars at $3.00 bring in $1,500 per tonne [app], and even after $0.60 per jar of running costs the farm keeps $1,200 per tonne, $380 above the $820 two-year contract, raising profit [an]. Benefit 2: A stable, year-round sales pattern [k], because bottled sauce can be sold to shops and wholesalers in every season rather than relying on harvest-time prices at the city market [app], smoothing revenue and cutting the amount of unsold fresh tomatoes thrown away [an].
    Keywords: $3.00 per jar, $0.60, $820 per tonne, 500 jars, sauce, city market, $210,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher selling price after processing increases profit; processed goods sell year-round, smoothing revenue | application_max_2: 500 jars at $3.00 per jar; $0.60 of extra running costs per jar; $820 per tonne on the 2-year fresh contract; fresh tomatoes at $750 per tonne | analysis_max_2: $1,200 per tonne retained beats the $820 contract by $380; year-round sales cut waste and smooth cash flow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redhaven Tomato Farm should make tomato sauce rather than accept the 2-year fresh contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that sauce adds clear value [k], because 500 jars at $3.00 keep $2.40 per jar after $0.60 costs, or $1,200 per tonne, which is $380 per tonne better than the $820 contract [app], so across 950 tonnes a year the gain could approach $361,000, repaying the $210,000 line in under a year [an]. However, the 2-year contract at $820 per tonne is guaranteed income [k], needing no $210,000 loan, no 4 extra workers and no marketing push to win shelf space for an unknown sauce, while picking labour has already risen 10% [app]. Fresh tomatoes are also a proven seller for the farm [an]. Overall, sauce is the better choice if Dan has secured supermarket listings, since $1,200 beats $820 per tonne [eval]; without confirmed buyers, the safer 2-year contract at $820 per tonne protects cash flow [eval].
    Keywords: $210,000, $3.00 per jar, $820 per tonne, 500 jars, 10%, 2-year, sauce, $0.60
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: making sauce increases added value and margin per tonne; the 2-year fresh contract offers certainty and avoids debt | application_max_2: 500 jars per tonne at $3.00 with $0.60 costs; $820 per tonne on the 2-year fresh contract; $210,000 line and 4 extra workers; picking labour costs rose by 10% | analysis_max_2: about $361,000 extra a year could repay the $210,000 line in under a year; contract avoids finance, staffing and marketing risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs higher sauce margin against contract security; justified conditional recommendation linked to supermarket listings

Blackcrag Quarry is a partnership between two cousins, Owen and Rhys Blackwood, operating in Country X for 7 years. It employs 22 workers and extracts about 3,000 tonnes of limestone a month, sold raw to a cement maker at $18 per tonne. New haulage rules have added 9% to transport costs. Dust complaints from neighbouring farms have also increased over the past year.

The cousins are deciding whether to spend $300,000 on a crushing and screening plant to sell graded road aggregate at $46 per tonne, with $20 of extra running costs per tonne. The cement maker has offered a 2-year raw contract at $20 per tonne, but grading would add value and need 5 extra workers; the plant would also need a permit and sits close to farmland.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify the four factors of production.
    Answer: Land, labour, capital and enterprise [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: land, labour, capital and enterprise identified; any two of the four named correctly

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Blackcrag Quarry could add value to its limestone.
    Answer: Way 1: Crushing and grading the stone [k], by spending $300,000 on a crushing and screening plant to sell graded road aggregate at $46 per tonne instead of raw stone at $18 per tonne [app]. Way 2: Meeting a tighter specification [k], by supplying consistent, correctly graded aggregate that road builders can use directly, which raw ungraded stone cannot offer [app].
    Keywords: limestone, $46 per tonne, $18 per tonne, $300,000, graded, 3,000 tonnes, cement maker
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing raw materials into a more valuable product; meeting a customer specification raises the price received | application_max_2: $300,000 crushing and screening plant; graded aggregate at $46 per tonne; raw stone at $18 per tonne; 3,000 tonnes of limestone a month

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Blackcrag Quarry of crushing and grading its own stone instead of selling raw stone.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A higher margin per tonne [k], because graded aggregate sells at $46 per tonne against $18 for raw stone [app], and even after $20 of extra running costs the quarry keeps $26 per tonne, above the $20 contract, raising profit [an]. Benefit 2: A wider customer base [k], because graded aggregate can be sold to road builders and councils in addition to the cement maker [app], spreading the 3,000 tonnes a month across more buyers and reducing dependence on one contract [an].
    Keywords: aggregate, $46 per tonne, $20, $18, crushing, 3,000 tonnes, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher selling price after processing increases profit; selling to more customer groups reduces single-buyer dependence | application_max_2: $46 per tonne graded aggregate; $20 of extra running costs per tonne; $20 per tonne on the 2-year raw contract; $18 per tonne raw stone | analysis_max_2: $26 per tonne retained beats the $20 contract; more customer groups cut single-contract dependence

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Blackcrag Quarry should crush and grade its own aggregate rather than accept the 2-year raw contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that grading adds value [k], because aggregate at $46 per tonne keeps $26 after $20 running costs, which is $6 per tonne better than the $20 contract [app], so on 3,000 tonnes a month the extra is about $18,000 a month, enough to repay the $300,000 plant in under two years [an]. However, the 2-year contract at $20 per tonne is guaranteed income [k], needing no $300,000 loan, no 5 extra workers and no permit for a plant near farmland, where complaints could halt operations [app]; with haulage costs already up 9%, a steady contract protects cash flow [an]. Overall, investing is the better choice if the Blackwoods have road-builder orders lined up, since $26 per tonne beats $20 [eval]; without confirmed orders, the $20 two-year contract is the safer option [eval].
    Keywords: $300,000, $46 per tonne, $20 per tonne, 3,000 tonnes, 9%, 2-year, aggregate, farmland
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: grading and crushing increases added value and margin per tonne; the 2-year raw contract offers certainty and avoids debt and permit risk | application_max_2: aggregate at $46 per tonne with $20 running costs; $20 per tonne on the 2-year raw contract; $300,000 plant and 5 extra workers; haulage costs up 9% and farmland permit risk | analysis_max_2: about $18,000 a month extra could repay the $300,000 plant in under two years; contract removes finance, staffing and permit/complaint risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs higher aggregate margin against contract security and permit risk; justified conditional recommendation tied to confirmed road-builder orders

--- STEM ---
Alderbrace Construction Ltd is a private limited company building 30 family homes a year on the edge of Dunmore, a growing town in Country X. The business owns 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries and 6 excavators, and employs 58 site workers plus 7 office staff. Land for a third housing phase was bought for $2.1m last year.

Managing director Priya Nair is deciding whether to buy a new $380,000 mobile crane or to hire 12 additional bricklayers at $520 a week each for the next 3 years. Each bricklayer could lay 340 bricks a day, while the crane would lift loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist. Last year site output rose 11% after new machinery was installed, yet 22 houses from the latest phase remain unsold.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'capital' as a factor of production.
    Answer: Capital is the man-made resources used to produce goods and services, such as Alderbrace's 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries, 6 excavators and hoist, which are used to build homes. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Capital = man-made / human-made resources used to produce goods and services; Reward any suitable examples such as machinery, tools, vehicles, equipment or buildings

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why capital is important to Alderbrace Construction Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Capital gives a business the man-made resources it needs to produce goods and services [k]. Alderbrace owns 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries and 6 excavators to build its 30 family homes a year [app]. Reason 2: Capital raises productivity because machines can work faster and longer than people alone [k]. After new machinery was installed last year, site output rose 11%, showing capital equipment measurably increased production [app].
    Keywords: Alderbrace Construction Ltd, 30 family homes, 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries, 11%, $380,000, 340 bricks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Capital = man-made resources used in production (machinery, vehicles, tools); Capital goods help raise output and productivity | application_max_2: Alderbrace's own assets: 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries, 6 excavators / 30 family homes a year; The 11% rise in site output after new machinery was installed

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of buying the $380,000 mobile crane for Alderbrace.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Capital equipment can increase the speed of production [k]. The crane would lift loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist, allowing the firm to complete phases more quickly [app]. Faster lifting would reduce the time each house spends under construction, raising overall output and helping clear unsold stock sooner [an]. Benefit 2: Machinery raises efficiency by getting more output from existing inputs [k]. A $380,000 crane costs far less over 3 years than hiring 12 bricklayers at $520 a week, which would total $973,440 (12 x $520 x 156 weeks) [app]. Paying once for the crane instead of ongoing wages would cut production costs per house and improve profit margins [an].
    Keywords: Alderbrace Construction Ltd, $380,000, 4 times faster, 22 houses, 12 additional bricklayers, $520, 3 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Machinery/capital equipment can increase speed and output; Machinery can reduce average costs / raise efficiency versus ongoing wages | application_max_2: Crane lifts loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist; Cost comparison: $380,000 crane versus $973,440 to hire 12 bricklayers over 3 years | analysis_max_2: Faster lifting shortens build time, raising output and sales turnover; Lower labour cost per house improves profit margins on the remaining houses

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Alderbrace Construction Ltd should buy the $380,000 mobile crane rather than hire 12 additional bricklayers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for the crane: buying the $380,000 mobile crane gives Alderbrace more capital, which is a man-made resource for production [k]. It would lift loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist, and site output already rose 11% after the previous machinery was installed [app]. This suggests further capital investment would raise productivity and shorten build times, helping shift the 22 houses that remain unsold [an]. Argument for hiring bricklayers: hiring 12 bricklayers at $520 a week is more flexible and avoids a large one-off outlay [k]. However, 12 bricklayers over the next 3 years would cost $973,440 (12 x $520 x 156 weeks), far more than the crane's one-off $380,000 [app]. Yet with 22 houses still unsold, committing cash to the crane is risky if demand weakens, because a specialised crane cannot easily be resold or redeployed [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures the crane is cheaper over 3 years ($380,000 versus $973,440) and matches the 11% output gain from the earlier machinery, so Alderbrace should buy the crane if it can secure buyer interest in the remaining houses [eval]. If demand stays weak, flexible bricklayers would protect the firm's cash, so the decision depends on confirmed sales [eval].
    Keywords: Alderbrace Construction Ltd, $380,000, 12 additional bricklayers, $520, 22 houses, 11%, 4 times faster, 3 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Crane = capital investment; bricklayers = labour, both are factors of production; Capital can raise productivity and reduce unit costs over time | application_max_2: $380,000 crane versus 12 x $520 x 156 weeks = $973,440 over 3 years; 4 times faster lifting / 11% output rise / 22 houses remain unsold / $2.1m land purchase | analysis_max_2: Cost comparison over 3 years favours the crane if demand holds; Fixed capital carries resale/redeployment risk versus flexible labour given unsold stock | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on confirmed demand/buyer contracts for the remaining houses; Balanced judgement recognising flexibility of labour against the crane's cost saving
