--- STEM ---
Alder & Vine Plastering is a partnership founded 6 years ago by Daniela Costa and Ruth Anselm in Country X. The partnership employs 7 plasterers and decorators, and completed $520,000 of work last year. Both owners work long days on-site and handle all the quoting and invoicing themselves.

Daniela and Ruth want to hire a third partner to fund a fleet of plastering machines costing $45,000. Their solicitor warned that adding a partner increases unlimited liability exposure, because each partner is personally liable for all business debts. The alternative is for each owner to lend the business $25,000, keeping the partnership but risking less. They meet tomorrow to decide. Hiring the extra staff needed to run the machines would also increase the annual wage bill.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'unlimited liability'.
    Answer: Unlimited liability means the owners are personally and fully responsible for all the debts of the business [1], with no legal limit on what they can lose, including personal assets [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: owners personally responsible for all business debts; no legal limit on losses, including personal assets

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Alder & Vine of operating as a partnership.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Partners can share the workload and supervise staff jointly [k], so Daniela and Ruth can split responsibility for the 7 plasterers and decorators between them [app]. Benefit 2: More capital is available than for a sole trader [k], which could help fund the $45,000 fleet of plastering machines without heavy borrowing [app].
    Keywords: partnership, $520,000, 7 plasterers, Daniela Costa, Ruth Anselm, $25,000, Alder & Vine Plastering
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: partners share workload and supervision of staff; partnerships can raise more capital than sole traders | application_max_2: 7 plasterers; $45,000; plastering machines; $520,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the solicitor warned about unlimited liability.
    Answer: Reason 1: Every partner is fully liable for all business debts [k], so if the partnership cannot repay money borrowed for the $45,000 machines, Daniela or Ruth could each lose personal savings to cover the full debt [app], threatening their homes and financial security [an]. Reason 2: Joint and several liability means one partner's mistake affects everyone [k], so a single reckless decision on a $520,000 workload could bankrupt both owners [app], creating deep mistrust within the business [an].
    Keywords: unlimited liability, $45,000, $520,000, third partner, plastering machines, business debts, $25,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: each partner fully liable for all business debts; joint and several liability affects all partners | application_max_2: $45,000; $520,000; business debts; plastering machines | analysis_max_2: personal assets of both owners are at risk; one partner's behaviour can bankrupt everyone

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the partners should add a third partner rather than each lend the business $25,000? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Adding a third partner would bring in fresh capital and share the workload [k], fully funding the $45,000 machines and easing supervision of the 7 plasterers [app], strengthening the business without owners lending their own money [an]. However, lending $25,000 each would raise $50,000 in total, more than covering the $45,000 machines [k], while keeping only two owners and limiting each person's exposure to their own loan [app], avoiding the unlimited liability risks of an extra partner [an]. Overall, the partners should each lend $25,000 instead of adding a third partner [eval], because protecting themselves from unlimited liability matters more than the convenience of outside capital [eval].
    Keywords: third partner, $45,000, $25,000, unlimited liability, $520,000, 7 plasterers, plastering machines, partnership
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: third partner injects capital and shares workload; owner loans keep structure simple and exposure limited | application_max_2: $45,000; $25,000; 7 plasterers; plastering machines; unlimited liability; $520,000 | analysis_max_2: fresh capital eases machine purchase and staff supervision; new partner extends unlimited liability exposure to all three | evaluation_max_2: weighs extra capital against unlimited liability spread; recommendation linked to the $45,000 machine cost and $25,000 loans

--- STEM ---
Tallow Tree Bakery is an incorporated private limited company founded 9 years ago by James Whitmore in Country X. The company owns 3 bakeries, employs 26 staff and generated $1.1 million in revenue last year, selling sourdough bread and pastries. The bakeries are famous across the region for their crusty handmade loaves and seasonal treats.

James wants to open 2 more bakeries in neighbouring towns within 18 months. He is choosing between franchising the new outlets, collecting an $8,000 fee and 6% of sales from each franchisee, or keeping them company-owned by funding the $150,000 set-up cost of each bakery through retained profit and a bank loan. James must present his recommendation to the board next month. The neighbouring towns have no bakery offering handmade sourdough at present.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'incorporated'.
    Answer: An incorporated business is a separate legal entity from its owners [1], with its own rights and liabilities, so owners typically benefit from limited liability [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: separate legal entity from its owners; owners usually benefit from limited liability

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Tallow Tree Bakery of franchising the two new outlets.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Expansion with minimal capital outlay [k], because franchisees fund the $150,000 set-up of each bakery while James receives the $8,000 fees and 6% royalties [app]. Benefit 2: Franchisees are motivated owner-operators [k], so each keeps profits from their outlet and personally drives sales of the sourdough bread and pastries [app].
    Keywords: franchising, $8,000, 6%, $150,000, James Whitmore, 3 bakeries, sourdough bread
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rapid expansion without major capital outlay; franchisees are motivated owner-managers | application_max_2: $150,000; $8,000; 6%; sourdough bread; pastries

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Tallow Tree Bakery of keeping the new bakeries company-owned.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The company keeps all the profits [k], since no royalties leak out, so both new bakeries contribute fully to the $1.1 million revenue base [app], boosting funds for future growth [an]. Benefit 2: Full control over quality and pricing [k], so standards stay consistent across the existing 3 bakeries and the 2 new ones [app], protecting the jobs of the 26 staff and the brand reputation [an].
    Keywords: company-owned, retained profit, $1.1 million, 3 bakeries, $150,000, 26 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: company retains 100% of profits; company keeps full control over quality and pricing | application_max_2: $1.1 million; company-owned; 3 bakeries; 26 staff | analysis_max_2: no royalty leakage increases available reinvestment funds; consistent standards protect reputation and staff

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tallow Tree Bakery should franchise the new bakeries rather than keep them company-owned? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Franchising achieves the 18-month expansion without the company funding $300,000 of set-up costs (2 bakeries x $150,000) [k], because franchisees pay their own way while Tallow Tree collects $8,000 fees and 6% royalties [app], adding $16,000 of fee income plus a continuing royalty stream [an]. However, company-owned bakeries keep 100% of profits [k] and guarantee James complete control over quality, prices and brand standards [app], avoiding any franchisee disputes that could damage reputation [an]. Overall, Tallow Tree Bakery should franchise the two new bakeries [eval], because the 18-month target is met faster and cheaper while generating immediate fee income [eval].
    Keywords: franchising, $150,000, $8,000, 6%, 18 months, company-owned, $1.1 million, 2 more bakeries
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: franchising enables fast expansion with low capital outlay; company-owned outlets retain 100% profit and full control | application_max_2: $150,000; $8,000; 6%; 18 months; $1.1 million; company-owned | analysis_max_2: 2 x $150,000 = $300,000 avoided; 2 x $8,000 = $16,000 fee income; full control reduces franchisee dispute risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs expansion speed and fees against lost profits and control; recommendation tied to the 18-month target and fee arithmetic

====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Northpoint Automation Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago in Country X, producing precision components for packaging machines sold across the region. The business employs 28 technicians yet runs 4 automated pressing lines costing $2.4 million. Annual revenue reached $6.2 million with capital employed of $5.1 million, while a nearby rival employs 210 workers producing assembly parts and reports revenue of $1.8 million.

Northpoint has applied for a government manufacturing award shortlisting the region's largest firms. The entry form asks for size, and the directors must decide whether to claim leadership by number of employees, value of output or capital employed. They are also weighing a $400,000 investment to hire 60 assembly workers against keeping their highly automated operation as it is.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'capital employed'.
    Answer: The total value of the long-term finance invested in a business, equal to non-current assets plus working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: total value of long-term finance invested in the business; non-current assets plus working capital (or shareholders' equity and long-term liabilities)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the number of people employed may be a misleading measure of business size for Northpoint Automation.
    Answer: Reason 1: It ignores automation [k], because Northpoint's 28 technicians run 4 pressing lines costing $2.4 million yet produce $6.2 million in revenue while the rival's 210 workers produce just $1.8 million [app]. Reason 2: It ignores capital employed [k], because Northpoint has $5.1 million tied up in assets and pressing lines which the headcount never reveals [app].
    Keywords: 28 technicians, 4 automated pressing lines, $2.4 million, $6.2 million, 210 workers, $1.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: number employed ignores productivity / automation; number employed ignores capital / assets invested | application_max_2: 28 technicians run 4 automated pressing lines; $6.2 million revenue vs rival's 210 workers producing $1.8 million; $5.1 million capital employed / $2.4 million pressing lines

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of using value of sales to measure business size.
    Answer: Limitation 1: Value of sales says nothing about profit or efficiency [k], because Northpoint reports revenue of $6.2 million but sales figures reveal nothing about what it keeps after costs [app], so two firms with equal sales can differ greatly in financial strength [an]. Limitation 2: It hides production and asset scale [k], because the $2.4 million of pressing lines and $5.1 million of capital employed would never appear in a sales figure [app], so a capital-intensive firm can look small beside a labour-intensive rival [an].
    Keywords: $6.2 million, capital employed, $5.1 million, $2.4 million, revenue, pressing lines
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sales value excludes profit / costs; sales value ignores unsold output / assets / capital employed | application_max_2: $6.2 million revenue not the same as profit; $5.1 million capital employed in pressing lines | analysis_max_2: equal-sales firms can differ greatly in financial strength; capital-intensive firms appear small beside labour-intensive rivals

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Northpoint Automation Ltd should invest $400,000 in hiring 60 assembly workers instead of keeping its automated operation? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing in 60 workers would make Northpoint appear larger by the employment measure [k], strengthening its award entry and adding labour capacity it does not currently have [app], which could win larger contracts and push revenue beyond $6.2 million [an]. However, wages would add greatly to costs and reduce productivity [k], because the business's real strength is 28 technicians running $2.4 million of automated pressing lines [app], and 60 extra staff would raise unit costs and slow automated throughput [an]. Overall, Northpoint should keep its automated operation rather than hire 60 workers for appearance [eval], because capital employed, value of output and efficiency are truer indicators of its size than raw headcount [eval].
    Keywords: $400,000, 60 assembly workers, 28 technicians, $2.4 million, $6.2 million, automated pressing lines
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: larger headcount improves ranking on the number-employed measure; extra staff raise wage costs / reduce automation advantage | application_max_2: $400,000 investment and 60 assembly workers; 28 technicians running $2.4 million of pressing lines; $6.2 million revenue | analysis_max_2: bigger headcount may win contracts / award but dilutes productivity; wages erode the automation cost advantage and margins | evaluation_max_2: weighs employment-measure gains against automation productivity in this capital-intensive context

--- STEM ---
Ryecroft Bakeries Ltd is a private limited company founded 7 years ago by Amara Osei in Country X, operating 6 bakeries selling 45,000 loaves a week to households and cafes. The business employs 130 staff, reports annual revenue of $3.4 million and capital employed of $2.1 million. A nearby rival, Hartley & Sons Bakeries, runs 4 bakeries with 85 staff and revenue of $2.2 million, and its owners have offered to merge with Ryecroft, valuing the combined business at $5.8 million.

Amara, Ryecroft's founder, is choosing between accepting Hartley's merger offer or pursuing internal growth instead: opening 2 new bakeries in the south of the city at a cost of $900,000 funded from retained profit. She must weigh faster expansion against losing full control of her family-built brand.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'horizontal integration'.
    Answer: When two businesses at the same stage of production in the same industry join together, for example two bakeries combining their operations [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: two businesses at the same stage of production; in the same industry combining / merging

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Ryecroft Bakeries of merging with Hartley & Sons Bakeries.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Greater market share [k], because combining 6 and 4 bakeries with 130 and 85 staff would create a 10-bakery business dominating the city's bread market [app]. Advantage 2: Economies of scale [k], since buying flour and ingredients for 10 bakeries would let Ryecroft negotiate lower prices than it pays for its own 6 [app].
    Keywords: 6 bakeries, 130 staff, $3.4 million, Hartley & Sons Bakeries, 4 bakeries, 85 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increased market share / reduced competition; economies of scale / lower unit costs / stronger buying power | application_max_2: 6 and 4 bakeries combining to 10 bakeries; 130 and 85 staff combining; $5.8 million combined valuation

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Ryecroft Bakeries might experience after merging with Hartley & Sons.
    Answer: Problem 1: Clash of business cultures [k], because Ryecroft's family-built brand and its working practices may conflict with Hartley's across the 10 combined bakeries [app], causing disputes, confusing staff and risking the loss of loyal customers [an]. Problem 2: Duplication of roles [k], since two sets of bakery managers and delivery staff would overlap across 215 combined employees [app], forcing redundancies, raising short-term costs and damaging morale [an].
    Keywords: family-built brand, Hartley & Sons Bakeries, 6 bakeries, 4 bakeries, 130 staff, 85 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: culture clash between merged firms; duplication of roles / redundancies / integration costs | application_max_2: family-built brand of Ryecroft; Hartley's 4 bakeries and 85 staff joining 6 bakeries and 130 staff | analysis_max_2: culture clash risks disputes and losing loyal customers; redundancies raise short-term costs and damage morale

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ryecroft Bakeries Ltd should merge with Hartley & Sons Bakeries? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Merging would create a 10-bakery business with roughly $5.6 million of combined annual revenue [k], giving Ryecroft instant scale, stronger buying power and a wider customer base without waiting years for organic growth [app], which would raise profits and protect it against larger supermarket bread ranges [an]. However, Amara would lose full control of her family-built brand and face culture clashes [k], since Hartley's 4 bakeries and 85 staff would join her 6 bakeries and 130 staff across 215 combined employees [app], risking redundancies and unhappy customers [an]. The internal growth route, 2 new bakeries for $900,000 from retained profit, keeps full control and grows steadily but more slowly [eval]. Overall, Ryecroft should merge with Hartley because the $5.8 million combined valuation and immediate scale outweigh the slower $900,000 organic route, provided Amara negotiates a clear role for herself and harmonises practices early [eval].
    Keywords: Hartley & Sons Bakeries, $5.8 million, $900,000, retained profit, 2 new bakeries, $3.4 million, family-built brand
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: merger gives scale / market share / economies of scale; merger risks loss of control / culture clash | application_max_2: $5.6 million combined revenue (6 bakeries and 4 bakeries); $5.8 million combined valuation; $900,000 / 2 new bakeries internal growth option; retained profit funding | analysis_max_2: scale raises buying power and protects against supermarket competition; loss of control risks redundancies and unhappy customers | evaluation_max_2: weighs immediate merger scale against slower but controlled organic growth with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Haverstock Furniture Ltd, established 8 years ago in Country X, manufactures wooden office desks and chairs for corporate clients across the region. It employs 40 workers, reports annual revenue of $2.6 million and made a profit of $310,000 last year. Each year it buys 900 cubic metres of oak timber from Suncrest Sawmills at $240 per cubic metre, costing $216,000. The sawmill's owners have offered to sell the business to Haverstock for $1.5 million.

Founder Daniel Whitmore must decide between buying Suncrest Sawmills, a backward vertical integration, to secure the timber supply, or declining and investing $300,000 in a larger showroom to boost sales of finished furniture. He is concerned about managing a sawmill as well as a furniture factory.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'backward vertical integration'.
    Answer: When a business merges with or takes over a supplier at an earlier stage of production, for example a furniture maker buying a sawmill [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: merges with / takes over a supplier; at an earlier stage of production (or moves towards raw materials)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Haverstock Furniture of buying Suncrest Sawmills.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Guaranteed timber supply [k], because the 900 cubic metres of oak Haverstock needs each year would come from its own sawmill instead of a single outside supplier [app]. Benefit 2: Lower net costs [k], because the $240 per cubic metre paid to Suncrest includes its profit margin, which Haverstock would now capture inside the integrated business [app].
    Keywords: 900 cubic metres, $240 per cubic metre, $216,000, Suncrest Sawmills, oak timber, $2.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: secure / guaranteed supply of raw materials; eliminates supplier's profit margin / lower input costs | application_max_2: 900 cubic metres of oak each year; $240 per cubic metre / $216,000 a year; Suncrest Sawmills only outside supplier

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Haverstock Furniture might experience if it buys Suncrest Sawmills.
    Answer: Problem 1: Large capital outlay [k], because paying $1.5 million for the sawmill would absorb nearly five years of its $310,000 annual profit and block the $300,000 showroom alternative [app], stretching the business's finances severely [an]. Problem 2: Lack of expertise and management strain [k], because Daniel Whitmore is already concerned about managing a sawmill as well as a furniture factory [app], so mistakes in both operations could reduce quality and profit [an].
    Keywords: $1.5 million, $310,000, $300,000, showroom, Daniel Whitmore, sawmill
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high purchase cost / strain on finance; management stretch / lack of expertise in the new operation | application_max_2: $1.5 million purchase price vs $310,000 annual profit; $300,000 showroom alternative blocked; Daniel Whitmore's concern about managing both | analysis_max_2: purchase consumes years of profit and limits growth options; stretched management risks falling quality and profit in both businesses

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Haverstock Furniture Ltd should buy Suncrest Sawmills for $1.5 million? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the sawmill would secure supply and cut costs [k]: the $216,000 a year paid at $240 per cubic metre would stay inside the enlarged business, capturing Suncrest's profit margin [app], improving margins on the $2.6 million revenue and reducing dependence on one outside supplier [an]. However, the $1.5 million price equals nearly five years of its $310,000 annual profit [k], and Daniel lacks sawmill management experience while the $300,000 showroom would directly boost furniture sales [app], so the integrated business could lose money for years while he learns an unfamiliar operation [an]. Overall, Haverstock should not buy the sawmill now [eval]; the showroom is the lower-risk option that directly grows revenue, whereas the sawmill would strain cash until timber savings accumulate [eval].
    Keywords: $1.5 million, $216,000, $240 per cubic metre, $310,000, $300,000, $2.6 million, showroom
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: backward integration secures supply and captures supplier margin; large purchase price strains finance / management | application_max_2: $216,000 a year at $240 per cubic metre; $1.5 million price vs $310,000 profit; $300,000 showroom alternative; $2.6 million revenue | analysis_max_2: captured margin improves profitability and supply security; cash strain and unfamiliar operation risk early losses | evaluation_max_2: weighs supply security and margin against capital strain and showroom alternative with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Merrow Vale Cider Ltd is a private limited company founded 6 years ago in Country X, pressing apples from 30 local orchards and selling bottled cider to supermarket chains nationwide. It employs 22 staff across picking, pressing and bottling, produces 600,000 bottles a year and sells them at $2.10 each, giving revenue of $1.26 million and profit of $180,000 last year. Supermarkets add a 50-cent mark-up, selling to consumers at $2.60.

Founder Rosa Merrow is deciding between two growth options: opening 2 own shops at $320,000 each to sell direct at $2.60, keeping the 50 cents supermarkets now take; or keeping supermarkets as the main channel and installing a second pressing line costing $500,000 to raise output to 800,000 bottles a year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'forward vertical integration'.
    Answer: When a business takes over or merges with a firm at a later stage of production, such as a producer opening its own shops to sell directly to consumers [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: takes over / merges with a firm at a later stage of production; moves closer to the final consumer (e.g. own retail outlets)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Merrow Vale Cider of opening its own shops.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Higher margin per bottle [k], because selling at $2.60 direct would keep the 50 cents supermarkets currently add on top of the $2.10 paid to Merrow [app]. Advantage 2: Direct customer relationships [k], because own shops would let Merrow build brand loyalty and gather feedback instead of relying on supermarket shelf space [app].
    Keywords: $2.60, $2.10, 50-cent, 600,000 bottles, supermarkets, $1.26 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: captures the retailer's margin / higher revenue per unit; direct contact with customers / brand control | application_max_2: $2.60 direct price vs $2.10 supermarket price; 50-cent mark-up supermarkets add; 600,000 bottles a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Merrow Vale Cider might face operating its own shops.
    Answer: Problem 1: High set-up cost [k], because 2 shops at $320,000 each would cost $640,000 at once [app], well above the $500,000 pressing-line alternative and likely straining cash reserves while sales build up [an]. Problem 2: Lack of retailing experience [k], because Merrow knows pressing cider, not running tills, displays and shop staff [app], so poor retail management could leave the shops loss-making and damage the brand [an].
    Keywords: $320,000, own shops, $500,000, 2 own shops, pressing line, Rosa Merrow
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high capital cost of opening shops; lack of retailing expertise / new risks | application_max_2: 2 shops at $320,000 each = $640,000; $500,000 pressing-line alternative; Merrow is a cider producer, not a retailer | analysis_max_2: high cost strains cash while sales build up; poor retail management risks losses and brand damage

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Merrow Vale Cider Ltd should open its own 2 shops instead of installing a second pressing line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Own shops would keep the 50-cent mark-up on every bottle sold direct [k], because selling at $2.60 rather than receiving $2.10 would raise revenue from the 600,000 bottles and build direct customer loyalty [app], potentially lifting profit well above $180,000 [an]. However, the shops cost $640,000 against the $500,000 pressing line [k], and raising output to 800,000 bottles would grow revenue to $1.68 million through proven supermarket channels, while Merrow has no retail experience [app], so slow-selling stock and high running costs could erase the saving [an]. Overall, Merrow Vale Cider should install the second pressing line rather than open shops [eval]; it builds on existing supermarket demand with less risk than the $640,000 retail venture [eval].
    Keywords: $2.60, $2.10, 600,000 bottles, 800,000 bottles, $500,000, $320,000, supermarkets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: forward integration captures retailer's margin; shops require capital and retail expertise / risk | application_max_2: $640,000 for 2 shops vs $500,000 pressing line; 600,000 bottles at $2.10 / $2.60; 800,000 bottles / $1.68 million revenue option; $180,000 profit | analysis_max_2: keeping the 50-cent mark-up could lift profit per bottle; retail inexperience risks losses erasing the margin gain | evaluation_max_2: weighs forward integration margins against safer pressing-line expansion with stem figures

====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Ferndell Coffee Co is a private limited company founded 5 years ago by Amara Diallo in Country X. It operates 4 busy cafés in commuter districts serving thousands of breakfast and lunch customers each week, employs 36 staff and reports annual revenue of $1.9 million with profit of $240,000. Lunchtime queues are common and staff report they are working at full capacity, with tills often idle for lack of space to expand seating.

Amara wants to expand into 2 new districts. She can either open 2 more cafés costing $110,000 each from retained profit, or buy Bronze Bean Coffee Co, a rival with 3 cafés and 28 staff, for $850,000 using a bank loan. She must decide which route achieves growth without losing control of her brand.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'internal growth'.
    Answer: Growth achieved by expanding the business's own existing operations, such as opening new outlets or increasing output, rather than by taking over another firm [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth from the business's own existing operations; e.g. opening new outlets / increasing output (not by merger or takeover)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Ferndell Coffee Co of growing internally rather than buying Bronze Bean Coffee Co.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Retained control [k], because opening 2 cafés from Ferndell's own funds would let Amara keep her menu, style and management approach unchanged [app]. Advantage 2: No new debt or interest [k], because internal growth from retained profit avoids the bank loan needed for the $850,000 Bronze Bean purchase [app].
    Keywords: 2 new districts, $110,000, retained profit, Bronze Bean Coffee Co, $850,000, bank loan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: keeps control of decisions / brand / culture; no loan / interest payments (self-financed) | application_max_2: 2 new cafés from retained profit; $850,000 Bronze Bean price needing a bank loan; Amara wants to avoid losing control of her brand

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of internal growth for Ferndell Coffee Co.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: Slower expansion [k], because opening 2 cafés requires finding, fitting out and staffing sites while Bronze Bean's 3 cafés would be trading from day one [app], delaying Ferndell's entry into the new districts [an]. Disadvantage 2: Drains retained profit [k], because Ferndell's annual profit is only $240,000 against the $220,000 needed for 2 cafés [app], leaving almost nothing in reserve if sales prove slow [an].
    Keywords: $240,000, $110,000, retained profit, Bronze Bean Coffee Co, 2 more cafés, $1.9 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: internal growth is slower than acquisition; self-financing drains reserves / limits funds | application_max_2: Bronze Bean's 3 cafés trading from day one; $240,000 annual profit vs $220,000 needed for 2 cafés; retained profit funding the expansion | analysis_max_2: delay in entering new districts cedes ground to rivals; thin reserves leave the business vulnerable if sales are slow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ferndell Coffee Co should buy Bronze Bean Coffee Co instead of opening 2 new cafés? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying Bronze Bean would give Ferndell an instant footprint [k], because 3 ready-made cafés with 28 staff and a customer base would be added to Ferndell's own 4 cafés and 36 staff immediately [app], pushing revenue well beyond $1.9 million [an]. However, the $850,000 price must be funded by a bank loan [k], and interest would burden a business earning only $240,000 profit a year, while Ferndell would inherit Bronze Bean's staff, leases and working practices [app], risking cultural friction and reduced control of the brand [an]. Overall, Ferndell should open the 2 new cafés rather than buy Bronze Bean [eval], because the internal $220,000 route from retained profit avoids loan risk and overstretching a business with $240,000 annual profit [eval].
    Keywords: Bronze Bean Coffee Co, $850,000, bank loan, $1.9 million, $240,000, retained profit, 2 new districts
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: takeover gives instant scale / customer base; loan-funded acquisition adds debt and integration risk | application_max_2: Bronze Bean: 3 cafés, 28 staff, $850,000; Ferndell: 4 cafés, 36 staff, $1.9 million revenue, $240,000 profit; $220,000 internal cost from retained profit | analysis_max_2: instant scale could lift revenue quickly; loan interest and integration friction could erode profit and control | evaluation_max_2: weighs speed and convenience of takeover against cost and control of organic growth with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Stornaway Appliances Ltd is a private limited company founded 12 years ago in Country X, selling household appliances such as washing machines and refrigerators. In the last 3 years it grew from 4 stores to 26 by buying 3 rival chains across the country. It now employs 380 staff across checkout, warehouse and delivery operations, with revenue of $14.5 million, but profit fell from $1.3 million to $700,000. Customer complaints have risen by 40% and absenteeism has also doubled.

The board is deciding whether to continue expanding by acquiring Halcyon Retail, 8 stores with 95 staff, for $2.0 million, or to pause takeovers for 2 years and consolidate: improve training, standardise procedures across stores and rebuild morale and customer service.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'external growth'.
    Answer: Growth achieved by merging with or taking over another business, rather than by expanding the business's own internal operations [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth by merging with / taking over another business; as opposed to internal (organic) growth

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits Stornaway Appliances gained from growing externally.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Rapid expansion [k], because buying 3 rival chains took Stornaway from 4 stores to 26 in just 3 years, far faster than building shops itself [app]. Benefit 2: Established customer bases [k], because acquiring 3 chains brought their stores, staff and shoppers overnight rather than starting each outlet from scratch [app].
    Keywords: 4 stores to 26, 3 rival chains, $14.5 million, 380 staff, 26
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fast growth / saves time vs organic expansion; acquires existing outlets, customers and staff | application_max_2: 4 stores to 26 in 3 years via 3 rival chains; revenue of $14.5 million; 380 staff

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Stornaway Appliances is experiencing from its rapid growth and how each might be overcome.
    Answer: Problem 1: Poor communication across 26 stores and 380 staff [k], because decisions no longer reach shop floors quickly, shown by customer complaints rising 40% [app], so regular written briefings and store manager meetings should be introduced [an]. Problem 2: Low morale and rising absenteeism [k], because rapid change has doubled absence and squeezed profit from $1.3 million to $700,000 [app], so staff training and standardised procedures should be used to rebuild engagement [an].
    Keywords: 40%, $1.3 million, $700,000, 380 staff, 4 stores to 26, absenteeism has also doubled
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: communication problems in large/growing organisations; low morale / absenteeism / control problems from rapid growth | application_max_2: 40% rise in customer complaints; absenteeism doubled; profit fell from $1.3 million to $700,000 | analysis_max_2: clearer briefings and meetings would cut errors and complaints; training and standardised procedures would restore morale and profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Stornaway Appliances should pause acquisitions and consolidate instead of buying Halcyon Retail for $2.0 million? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Consolidating would fix Stornaway's problems directly [k]: pausing for 2 years to improve training, standardise procedures and rebuild morale would tackle the 40% rise in complaints and doubled absenteeism across 26 stores [app], restoring profitability back toward the $1.3 million previously earned [an]. However, buying Halcyon Retail would add 8 stores and 95 staff for $2.0 million [k], quickly growing revenue and market share while rivals may be expanding too, and the profits from fixing the core business would not arrive until later [app], whereas waiting 2 years may permanently cede ground to competitors [an]. Overall, Stornaway should pause acquisitions and consolidate [eval], because acquiring Halcyon before fixing communication and morale would simply repeat the same failures on a larger, $2.0 million scale [eval].
    Keywords: Halcyon Retail, $2.0 million, 40%, $1.3 million, $700,000, 4 stores to 26, absenteeism has also doubled
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: consolidation / pausing growth to fix internal problems; acquisition adds scale but also integration risk | application_max_2: 40% rise in complaints and doubled absenteeism; $1.3 million to $700,000 profit fall; Halcyon Retail: 8 stores, 95 staff, $2.0 million; 26 stores, 380 staff | analysis_max_2: fixing communication and morale could restore profitability; buying Halcyon now multiplies integration problems on a larger scale | evaluation_max_2: weighs pausing to consolidate against buying Halcyon, using stem figures, with a justified recommendation

--- STEM ---
Inkwell & Ivy Bookbinders is a partnership founded 9 years ago in Country X by Elena Marchetti and Ruth Adeyemi. It employs 6 craftspeople who hand-bind leather journals using traditional stitching and locally sourced leather. The partnership makes 1,500 journals a year, sold at $95 each for revenue of $142,500, and has a growing waiting list of 2,000 orders from shops and individual buyers. Both partners work 55 hours a week, mostly alone in a small rural workshop.

Elena believes demand justifies expansion: hire 10 more binders, move to larger premises costing $300,000 and raise output to 6,000 journals a year. Ruth prefers to keep the workshop small, charging a premium and maintaining personal quality and control, fearing growth would dilute the brand.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two methods of measuring business size.
    Answer: Number of people employed and value of output (other valid answers: sales revenue or capital employed) [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: number of people employed; value of output / sales revenue / capital employed

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Inkwell & Ivy Bookbinders has remained small.
    Answer: Reason 1: Owners' preference for quality and control [k], because Ruth wants to keep the personal, hand-made finish that 6 craftspeople can guarantee across just 1,500 journals a year [app]. Reason 2: Limited capital [k], because moving to larger premises costing $300,000 is far beyond a partnership earning revenue of $142,500 a year [app].
    Keywords: 6 craftspeople, 1,500 journals, $142,500, $300,000, Ruth, $95
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: owners value control / quality / lifestyle over growth; limited capital / finance for expansion | application_max_2: Ruth's desire to maintain personal quality and control; $300,000 premises vs $142,500 annual revenue; 6 craftspeople / 1,500 journals a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages Inkwell & Ivy Bookbinders might face if it expands to 6,000 journals a year.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: Loss of personal quality [k], because raising output to 6,000 journals with 10 new, less experienced binders would make each journal less individual [app], weakening the hand-bound reputation that lets it charge $95 each [an]. Disadvantage 2: Overstretched finances [k], because $300,000 of premises plus wages for 16 craftspeople would far exceed current revenue of $142,500 [app], leaving the partners stretched far beyond their 55-hour week with heavy debt [an].
    Keywords: 6,000 journals, $95, $300,000, $142,500, 55 hours, 10 more binders
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: expansion can dilute quality / brand / craftsmanship; expansion strains finance and management capacity | application_max_2: 6,000 journals a year with 10 new binders; $300,000 premises and 16 craftspeople vs $142,500 revenue; $95 price reliant on quality reputation | analysis_max_2: diluted quality weakens the premium reputation and pricing power; debt and workload strain threaten survival if demand falls short

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Inkwell & Ivy Bookbinders should expand to 6,000 journals a year? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Expansion would let Inkwell & Ivy meet its 2,000-order waiting list [k]: 6,000 journals at $95 each would generate about $570,000 a year instead of $142,500 [app], transforming the partnership and its ability to serve eager customers [an]. However, growth would risk the hand-bound quality behind the brand [k], since 10 new, less experienced binders may not match the standards of the existing 6, and the $300,000 premises must be financed against current revenue of $142,500 [app], undermining the premium $95 positioning [an]. Overall, the partners should expand cautiously in stages rather than jump straight to 6,000 journals [eval], serving the waiting list while keeping quality control and avoiding over-commitment of their $142,500 business base [eval].
    Keywords: 2,000 orders, $95, $142,500, $300,000, 6,000 journals, 10 more binders
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth can meet unmet demand / raise revenue; growth can dilute quality and strain finance | application_max_2: 2,000-order waiting list; $570,000 potential revenue at $95 each vs current $142,500; $300,000 premises and 10 new binders | analysis_max_2: serving the waiting list could transform revenue and profitability; diluted quality and debt risk undermining the premium brand | evaluation_max_2: weighs revenue upside against quality and finance risks with stem figures, recommending staged expansion

--- STEM ---
Elmridge Precision Tools Ltd is a private limited company founded 11 years ago in Country X, employing 48 workers making drill bits for industrial clients. Last year it reported revenue of $2.9 million, value of output of $3.1 million and capital employed of $4.4 million. Its nearest rival, Halstead Tools Plc, employs 620 workers with revenue of $28 million and capital employed of $19 million. Revenue per worker at Elmridge is about $60,000; at Halstead it is about $45,000.

The board is considering a $500,000 investment in automated drilling lines, which would cut 18 jobs but raise value of output from $3.1 million to $4.5 million. Directors also wonder which measure best shows Elmridge's size when applying for a regional manufacturing award.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'value of output'.
    Answer: The total monetary worth of the goods and services produced by a business over a period of time, whether or not they have been sold [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: total monetary worth of goods/services produced; over a period of time, including unsold output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of using value of sales to measure business size.
    Answer: Limitation 1: It ignores production and unsold output [k], because Elmridge's output of $3.1 million exceeds its sales of $2.9 million, so sales understate the size of its production [app]. Limitation 2: It says nothing about assets or investment [k], because Elmridge's $4.4 million of capital employed is completely invisible in a sales figure [app].
    Keywords: $3.1 million, $2.9 million, $4.4 million, value of output, revenue
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sales exclude unsold output / production scale; sales ignore capital employed / asset base | application_max_2: output $3.1 million vs revenue $2.9 million; $4.4 million capital employed never appears in sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why value of output may be a better measure of business size than number of employees for Elmridge.
    Answer: Reason 1: It shows productivity and automation [k], because Elmridge's 48 workers produce $3.1 million of drill bits, a highly productive output-per-worker figure [app], so headcount would make the firm look far smaller than it really is [an]. Reason 2: It gives a fairer comparison with Halstead Tools Plc [k], because Halstead's 620 workers against Elmridge's 48 hides the fact that Elmridge earns about $60,000 revenue per worker versus Halstead's about $45,000 [app], so output reveals efficiency, not just headcount [an].
    Keywords: 48 workers, $3.1 million, Halstead Tools Plc, 620 workers, about $60,000, about $45,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: output reflects productivity / automation, not headcount; output allows fairer like-for-like comparison between firms | application_max_2: 48 workers producing $3.1 million of output; Halstead: 620 workers, about $45,000 revenue per worker; Elmridge about $60,000 revenue per worker | analysis_max_2: headcount makes capital-intensive Elmridge look smaller than it is; output reveals relative efficiency and effective scale

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Elmridge Precision Tools Ltd should invest $500,000 in automated drilling lines, cutting 18 jobs but raising value of output to $4.5 million? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Automation would raise Elmridge's value of output from $3.1 million to $4.5 million [k], an increase of about 45% that would strengthen its regional award application and competitiveness against Halstead [app], improving efficiency, output quality and profit despite the $500,000 cost [an]. However, cutting 18 of 48 jobs would remove over one-third of the workforce [k], leaving 30 employees, damaging morale and risking the loss of experienced drill-bit specialists [app], with harm to staff welfare and the firm's local reputation [an]. Overall, Elmridge should invest in the automated drilling lines [eval], because the output and efficiency gains secure long-term competitiveness and the remaining workforce can be retrained for higher-skilled roles [eval].
    Keywords: $500,000, 18 jobs, $3.1 million to $4.5 million, 48 workers, Halstead Tools Plc, value of output
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: automation raises output / efficiency / competitiveness; automation costs jobs / risks morale and skills | application_max_2: $500,000 investment; 18 of 48 jobs cut; value of output rises from $3.1 million to $4.5 million; Halstead Tools Plc rival | analysis_max_2: higher output and efficiency lift the award case and competitiveness; job cuts and morale loss risk skills and reputation | evaluation_max_2: weighs output/efficiency gains against job losses with stem figures, recommending investment with retraining

--- STEM ---
Briskfield Foods Ltd is a private limited company founded 7 years ago in Country X, producing chilled ready meals such as lasagne, cottage pie and curries sold through supermarkets and convenience stores nationwide. It employs 52 staff and reports annual revenue of $4.7 million with profit of $520,000 last year. Each year it buys 700 tonnes of mixed vegetables from Delmara Farms at $1,100 per tonne, costing $770,000.

Two takeover targets are on offer: Delmara Farms, the vegetable grower, asking $950,000, a backward vertical integration; or Callum Fresh Meals Ltd, a rival ready-meal maker with 30 staff and revenue of $2.3 million, asking $1.1 million, a horizontal integration. Briskfield can afford only one of these two established businesses and must choose.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'takeover'.
    Answer: When one business acquires a controlling interest in another business and takes over its assets, operations and management [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: one business acquires a controlling interest in another; takes over its assets / operations / management

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Briskfield Foods of buying Callum Fresh Meals Ltd.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Increased market share [k], because combining with a rival of $2.3 million revenue would add to Briskfield's $4.7 million, creating a business near $7.0 million in sales [app]. Advantage 2: Economies of scale [k], because producing more ready meals with shared kitchens, buying and distribution would cut average costs per meal [app].
    Keywords: Callum Fresh Meals Ltd, $2.3 million, $4.7 million, 30 staff, $1.1 million, 52 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increased market share / reduced rivalry; economies of scale / lower unit costs | application_max_2: $2.3 million rival revenue + $4.7 million Briskfield revenue = about $7.0 million; 30 staff and ready-meal production combining with 52 staff

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Briskfield Foods of buying Delmara Farms instead.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Guaranteed vegetable supply [k], because the 700 tonnes of mixed vegetables Briskfield needs each year would come from its own farm [app], securing uninterrupted ready-meal production through every season [an]. Advantage 2: Capturing the supplier's margin [k], because the $770,000 a year paid at $1,100 per tonne includes Delmara's profit [app], which Briskfield would now keep, boosting its $520,000 profit [an].
    Keywords: Delmara Farms, 700 tonnes, $1,100 per tonne, $770,000, $520,000, $950,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: secures supply of essential inputs; captures supplier margin / integrated cost savings | application_max_2: 700 tonnes of mixed vegetables each year; $770,000 a year at $1,100 per tonne; $520,000 annual profit | analysis_max_2: secured supply protects production continuity; captured margin lifts profit above $520,000

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Briskfield Foods Ltd should buy Delmara Farms instead of Callum Fresh Meals Ltd? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying Delmara Farms would secure supply and save money [k]: the $770,000 a year paid at $1,100 per tonne would stay within the enlarged business and Delmara's profit margin would be captured [app], potentially lifting profit well above $520,000 while guaranteeing vegetable supply [an]. However, Callum Fresh Meals offers scale and market share [k]: adding its $2.3 million revenue and 30 staff to Briskfield's $4.7 million would create a near $7.0 million chilled-ready-meal business [app], with shared costs, stronger buying power and fewer rivals [an]. Overall, Briskfield should buy Callum Fresh Meals rather than Delmara Farms [eval], because horizontal integration transforms its competitive position and revenue, while vegetables at $1,100 per tonne are a known market price it can keep buying externally [eval].
    Keywords: Delmara Farms, Callum Fresh Meals Ltd, $770,000, $1,100 per tonne, $520,000, $2.3 million, $4.7 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: backward integration secures supply / captures margin; horizontal integration adds scale / market share / economies | application_max_2: $770,000 a year at $1,100 per tonne for 700 tonnes; Delmara: $950,000 asking price; Callum: $2.3 million revenue, 30 staff, $1.1 million asking price; Briskfield: $4.7 million revenue, $520,000 profit, 52 staff | analysis_max_2: captured supplier margin and secure supply lift profit; rival acquisition builds scale and purchasing power | evaluation_max_2: weighs backward vs horizontal integration with stem figures, recommending Callum Fresh Meals

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why high employee turnover might be a problem for this business.

    Keywords: trainers, gym, hourly, health centers, fitness, turnover, 30%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increased recruitment expenses; reduced customer satisfaction/service quality | application_max_2: fitness trainers; gym members; class instructors; 4 health centers

  Qc [6 marks]

Benefit 2: Better budget predictability [k], allowing labor expenses of $450,000 to be calculated accurately across 4 health centers [app], reducing cash flow uncertainty [an].
    Keywords: gym, fitness, wages, salary, off-peak, $450,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: income security/predictable pay; better financial predictability/budgeting | application_max_2: off-peak gym seasons; 4 health centers; $450,000 labor expenses; instructors | analysis_max_2: increases motivation/lowers resignations; reduces cash flow uncertainty

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think introducing fixed monthly salaries is a better motivation method for this business than an 'Employee of the Month' bonus scheme? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A fixed monthly salary provides guaranteed income security [k], motivating hourly-paid gym trainers during off-peak seasons [app] and reducing trainer turnover costs [an]. However, an 'Employee of the Month' bonus scheme creates competitive drive [k] for individual instructors teaching gym classes [app], but may demotivate non-winning staff who feel the $50 award is unfairly distributed [an].     Keywords: trainers, gym, turnover, bonus, salary, $50, off-peak
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guaranteed income security; competitive drive/demotivation of non-winners | application_max_2: gym trainers; off-peak seasons; 30% turnover; $50 bonus | analysis_max_2: reduces turnover costs; creates demotivation/jealousy among staff | evaluation_max_2: weighs basic financial security against small individual bonus in high-turnover gym context

--- STEM ---
A custom furniture manufacturing enterprise operates as a Partnership with 2 workshop facilities, employing 35 skilled carpenters and 10 warehouse staff. Operating for 8 years, the firm generates $2.1m in annual revenue and pays carpenters using a piece-rate system ($45 per completed wooden table). While daily output volume is high, customer product returns due to poor finishing and flawed wood assembly have increased by 25% over the past year.

Carpenters rush through assembly work to maximize individual piece-rate earnings, ignoring safety guidelines and quality inspection checks. According to Herzberg's two-factor theory, hygiene factors like workplace safety and working conditions are failing, while motivators like job recognition are absent. The partners must decide whether to replace piece-rate wages with profit-sharing schemes or implement job enrichment by giving carpenters full responsibility for entire furniture design and assembly projects from raw timber to final polish.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'piece-rate payment'.
    Answer: A payment system where workers are paid a fixed amount for each unit of output produced [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fixed payment per unit produced; wage tied directly to output volume

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two hygiene factors according to Herzberg's theory that might be demotivating workers in this workshop.
    Answer: Factor 1: Poor working conditions and safety [k], as carpenters ignore safety guidelines in workshop facilities [app]. Factor 2: Unfair wage structure [k], as $45 piece-rate wages encourage rushing rather than fair compensation for quality woodworking [app].
    Keywords: carpenters, workshop, $45, piece-rate, wooden, timber
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working conditions/safety; wage structure/pay conditions | application_max_2: workshop facilities; $45 piece-rate; carpenters; wooden tables

  Qc [6 marks]

Sales consultants are paid purely on a commission basis ($1,200 per vehicle sold), with total annual commission payouts reaching $800,000.

However, reliance on commission pay has created aggressive internal competition, where sales consultants pressure customers and refuse to share showroom duties. Customer service ratings have dropped by 35%, and annual staff turnover among sales consultants has reached 40%. According to Taylor's scientific management theory, financial rewards drive effort, but sales staff report severe income insecurity during low-demand winter months. The HR director must decide whether to replace pure commission pay with a basic fixed salary plus lower sales bonuses or introduce a team profit-sharing scheme based on quarterly showroom targets.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'commission'.
    Answer: Payment made to an employee based on a percentage of sales value or number of units sold [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: payment based on percentage of sales value; payment per unit/vehicle sold

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to this dealership of paying sales consultants purely on commission.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: Income insecurity during low-demand periods [k], as sales consultants earn lower commission in winter months when electric vehicle sales drop [app]. Disadvantage 2: Poor customer service quality [k], as sales staff rush customers to close sales quickly rather than explaining maintenance packages [app].
    Keywords: consultants, electric vehicles, showroom, winter, commission, dealership
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: income insecurity/unpredictable pay; poor customer service/aggressive tactics | application_max_2: electric vehicle sales; maintenance packages; winter months; sales consultants

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to this business of introducing a basic fixed salary alongside lower sales bonuses.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Improved job and income security [k], reducing financial anxiety for 22 sales consultants during slow winter months [app], which lowers annual staff turnover rates [an]. Benefit 2: Encourages better customer engagement [k], as staff are willing to perform non-selling showroom duties [app], raising customer satisfaction ratings and brand loyalty [an].
    Keywords: consultants, salary, bonuses, showroom, winter, turnover
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: income security/lower staff turnover; encourages non-selling duties/better customer service | application_max_2: 22 sales consultants; showroom duties; winter months; customer satisfaction ratings | analysis_max_2: lowers staff turnover rates; raises customer satisfaction and brand loyalty

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think introducing a basic fixed salary plus lower bonuses is better for this dealership than a team profit-sharing scheme? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A basic fixed salary plus bonuses provides guaranteed financial stability [k], reducing 40% consultant turnover during slow sales periods [app] and lowering recruitment expenses [an]. On the other hand, a team profit-sharing scheme encourages teamwork across 3 showrooms [k], motivating consultants to share vehicle lead details [app], but individual high-performing staff may feel unrewarded if team profits fall [an]. Overall, a basic salary plus lower bonuses is better because pure commission creates severe income anxiety [eval]; providing basic financial security directly resolves the 40% staff turnover problem while preserving individual incentive [eval].
    Keywords: consultants, salary, bonuses, profit-sharing, turnover, commission
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guaranteed financial stability/lower turnover; promotes teamwork/lack of individual reward link | application_max_2: 40% consultant turnover; 3 showrooms; electric vehicle sales; commission payouts | analysis_max_2: lowers recruitment expenses; demotivates top sales performers | evaluation_max_2: weighs basic income security against collective team incentives in high-value retail context

Operating for 5 years, the business generates $1.8m in annual sales revenue producing artisan sourdough bread and baked pastries, with wage overheads totaling $600,000.

Bakery line workers perform repetitive slicing and packaging tasks while paid hourly wages ($18 per hour). Due to extreme boredom and lack of job satisfaction, worker absenteeism has reached 18%, and production line flours and dough are frequently wasted due to careless handling. Applying Herzberg's two-factor theory, hygiene factors like basic hourly pay are satisfied, but motivators like achievement and meaningful work are lacking. The partners are evaluating whether to introduce job rotation across mixing, baking, and packaging stations or implement job enrichment by training line workers to create new pastry recipes and manage quality assurance inspections.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'job rotation'.
    Answer: Swapping workers between different tasks of similar difficulty levels to reduce monotony and boredom [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: swapping workers between different tasks; tasks at similar skill/responsibility level to reduce boredom

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two motivators according to Herzberg's theory that are missing for bakery line workers in this business.
    Answer: Motivator 1: Meaningful work and responsibility [k], as workers perform repetitive slicing and packaging of sourdough bread without decision-making input [app]. Motivator 2: Sense of achievement and recognition [k], as line staff receive no praise for reducing flour waste in the bakery [app].
    Keywords: bakery, sourdough, bread, pastries, slicing, packaging, flour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: meaningful work/responsibility; sense of achievement/recognition | application_max_2: sourdough bread; slicing and packaging; bakery line workers; flour waste

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to this bakery business of implementing job rotation.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Reduced workplace boredom and monotony [k], as 30 line workers rotate between dough mixing, baking, and packaging stations [app], lowering the 18% absenteeism rate [an]. Benefit 2: Greater workforce flexibility [k], allowing line staff to cover for absent colleagues across both production facilities [app], preventing bakery output delays [an].
    Keywords: baking, mixing, packaging, bakery, rotation, absenteeism
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduces boredom/monotony; increases workforce flexibility/multiskilling | application_max_2: 30 line workers; mixing, baking, packaging; 18% absenteeism; production facilities | analysis_max_2: lowers absenteeism rates; prevents output delays and production bottlenecks

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think implementing job enrichment is better for this bakery partnership than introducing job rotation? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Job enrichment grants higher responsibility [k], empowering workers to design pastry recipes and manage quality checks [app], which increases pride in work and cuts flour waste [an]. However, job rotation swaps staff across mixing and packaging stations [k], reducing task boredom for 30 line workers [app] without requiring expensive retraining expenses [an]. Overall, job enrichment is better because simple task rotation does not add true responsibility [eval]; giving workers genuine ownership over baking quality directly provides Herzberg motivators, solving high absenteeism and dough waste [eval].
    Keywords: bakery, enrichment, rotation, pastries, recipes, mixing, packaging, absenteeism
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: adds genuine responsibility/pride in craftsmanship; reduces boredom at low cost/increases flexibility | application_max_2: pastry recipes; quality assurance checks; mixing and packaging stations; 18% absenteeism | analysis_max_2: cuts raw material flour waste; avoids expensive retraining overheads | evaluation_max_2: weighs psychological job ownership against low-cost task variety in food production context

  Qb [4 marks]

    Keywords: chain of command, shop floor, middle managers, hierarchy, pricing

    Keywords: delayering, middle managers, wage overheads, retail, stores

--- STEM ---
Ironvale Fasteners Co is a private limited company employing 96 workers at its steel bolt and nut factory in Country X. Output reached 1.8 million units last year, up 12% on the previous 12 months. Priya Nair, the operations manager, reports that 34% of bolts failed quality checks in March, and two line supervisors resigned after a dispute over overtime. Workers are paid a time rate of $9.50 per hour and work 44 hours per week.

Priya is considering two ways to improve motivation on the shop floor. Option A: switch the 60 line workers to a piece rate of $0.09 per approved bolt, based on Taylor's scientific management. Option B: keep the time rate and invest $18,000 in a recognition scheme, giving monthly certificates and a $150 bonus for the team with the lowest defect rate, linked to Herzberg's theory. She must decide before the new contract is signed in 6 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'Maslow's hierarchy of needs'.
    Answer: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a theory that arranges human needs in five levels — physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation — where lower-level needs must be met before higher-level needs can motivate employees [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Needs are arranged in a hierarchy or levels (physiological to self-actualisation); Lower-level needs must be satisfied before higher-level needs motivate

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why a well-motivated workforce is important to Ironvale Fasteners Co.
    Answer: A well-motivated workforce matters because motivated workers produce more output per hour, raising productivity so Ironvale can grow beyond 1.8 million units with the same 96 workers [k]. Higher productivity spreads fixed costs over more bolts, lowering the average cost per unit and protecting the margin needed to fund the $18,000 scheme [app]. Second, motivated workers take greater care and make fewer mistakes [k]. Fewer errors mean the 34% defect rate seen in March should fall, so fewer bolts are scrapped and Ironvale's reputation with its new contract customer is protected [app].
    Keywords: 1.8 million, 96 workers, 34%, $18,000, Ironvale Fasteners Co, piece rate, $9.50
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Motivated workers are more productive / higher output per worker; Motivated workers make fewer errors / take greater care | application_max_2: Reference to 1.8 million units output / 96 workers; Reference to 34% defect rate in March / scrap and reputation

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Ironvale Fasteners Co might face if it introduces the piece rate (Option A).
    Answer: First, a problem is that piece rate can reduce quality [k]. Paying $0.09 per approved bolt pushes workers to produce bolts as fast as possible, so defect rates could climb above the 34% recorded in March [app], and higher defects would damage Ironvale's standing with clients, leading to lost orders and rework costs [an]. Second, piece rate rewards individual speed, not teamwork [k]. Taylor's scientific management treats each worker separately, so experienced staff may refuse to help the slower of the 60 line workers [app], and the friction could trigger more disputes like the one that cost the factory two supervisors, raising labour turnover [an].
    Keywords: piece rate, $0.09, 34%, 60 line workers, Taylor's scientific management, two line supervisors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Piece rate can push workers to rush / quality may fall; Piece rate rewards individual effort / weakens teamwork | application_max_2: Reference to $0.09 per approved bolt / 34% defect rate in March; Reference to Taylor's scientific management / 60 line workers / two supervisors resigned | analysis_max_2: Chain from rushing to more defects to lost orders / rework costs; Chain from individual reward to friction to disputes / higher labour turnover

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ironvale Fasteners Co should switch to the piece rate (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A follows Taylor's scientific management: paying $0.09 per approved bolt links pay directly to output, so the 60 line workers would be driven to maximise production and Ironvale could lift output above 1.8 million units [k]. Because only approved bolts are paid, workers also carry the quality risk themselves, creating a direct incentive to avoid the defects that reached 34% in March [app]. Higher throughput would spread fixed costs over more units, improving efficiency and competitiveness [an]. However, Option B targets Herzberg's theory and Maslow's esteem needs [k]. Monthly certificates and a $150 team bonus reward the whole team for the lowest defect rate while keeping the $9.50 per hour base pay unchanged, so the $18,000 cost is predictable [app]. This addresses the overtime dispute and low morale directly, whereas piece rate could inflame them further [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better choice [eval] because Ironvale's central problem is quality — a 34% failure rate — and Herzberg shows pay alone does not remove dissatisfaction; recognition and team effort do [eval].
    Keywords: piece rate, $0.09, 1.8 million, 34%, $18,000, $150, $9.50, 60 line workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Taylor's scientific management: pay linked to output motivates effort; Herzberg: motivators (recognition) / hygiene factors (pay) distinction | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $0.09 per approved bolt / 60 line workers / 1.8 million units; Reference to Option B: $18,000 scheme / $150 team bonus / $9.50 per hour | analysis_max_2: Chain from piece rate to throughput to lower fixed cost per unit / efficiency; Chain from recognition scheme to morale / quality improvement vs overtime dispute | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence (34% defects and morale vs higher output)

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U2_SET_42
UNIT: Unit 2: People in Business
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Copperfield Electronics Assembly is a public limited company that builds circuit boards for home appliances in Country X. The factory employs 210 production-line workers and 18 quality inspectors. Annual revenue reached $26 million last year, but average labour turnover on the assembly line hit 22%, with 58 workers leaving in 12 months. Pay is a salary of $1,450 per month and staff describe the work as repetitive.

Managing Director Elena Brooks is choosing between two motivation strategies. Option A: apply Taylor's scientific management more strictly — time-and-motion studies, a 10-week training programme for new hires, and a piece rate of $2.10 per tested board. Option B: introduce job rotation between three assembly stations every 4 hours, plus a $90 monthly attendance bonus. Elena must present her recommendation to the board in 10 days.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'Taylor's scientific management'.
    Answer: Taylor's scientific management is the theory that workers are motivated principally by money, using time-and-motion studies to find the one best way to do each job and paying a piece rate linked to how much each worker produces [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Workers motivated mainly / principally by money; Time-and-motion studies identify the one best way / pay linked to output via piece rate

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why labour turnover on the assembly line is high at Copperfield Electronics Assembly.
    Answer: One reason is that the work is repetitive, so workers become bored and see no challenge in the job [k]. Repeating the same assembly stations all day adds no variety or new skills, removing Herzberg's motivators such as responsibility, so the 210 production-line workers drift towards quitting — 58 left in the last 12 months [app]. A second reason is that pay does not reward effort [k]. A salary of $1,450 per month is paid regardless of output, so productive and unproductive workers earn the same, and turnover has hit 22% [app].
    Keywords: assembly line, 210, 58 workers, $1,450, 22%, salary, repetitive
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Repetitive work causes boredom / removes Herzberg's motivators; Salary is fixed regardless of output, so effort is not rewarded | application_max_2: Reference to 58 workers leaving in 12 months / 210 production-line workers; Reference to $1,450 per month salary / 22% turnover

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Copperfield Electronics Assembly of introducing Option B (job rotation).
    Answer: One benefit is reduced boredom [k]. Moving each worker between three assembly stations every 4 hours adds variety and fresh skills to a repetitive job [app], and less boredom means fewer errors and fewer absences, helping the 210 production-line workers sustain daily output [an]. A second benefit is greater flexibility [k]. With every worker trained on three stations, cover is available whenever colleagues are absent, so the 18 quality inspectors receive a steadier flow of comparable boards [app], reducing bottlenecks and protecting the $26 million annual revenue [an].
    Keywords: job rotation, three assembly stations, every 4 hours, 210, $26 million, 18 quality inspectors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Job rotation adds variety / reduces boredom; Job rotation makes workers multi-skilled / flexible cover | application_max_2: Reference to three assembly stations every 4 hours / repetitive work; Reference to 210 production-line workers / 18 quality inspectors / $26 million revenue | analysis_max_2: Chain from variety to lower boredom to fewer errors / absences / sustained output; Chain from multi-skilling to flex cover to steady flow / protected revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Copperfield Electronics Assembly should introduce Option A? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A is built on Taylor's theory that money drives effort: a piece rate of $2.10 per tested board would reward fast workers, so tested output per worker should rise above current levels [k]. Time-and-motion studies and a 10-week training programme would also standardise methods for new hires, helping stabilise a workforce that lost 58 workers in 12 months [app]. Higher tested output spreads overheads over more boards, improving cost efficiency [an]. However, Option B tackles why people are leaving — repetitive, unchallenging work [k]. Job rotation between three assembly stations every 4 hours adds variety, and the $90 monthly attendance bonus rewards presence without raising the $1,450 basic salary bill unpredictably [app]. Retention of skilled assemblers also protects quality, which the 18 inspectors police on every board before it reaches home-appliance clients [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the stronger choice [eval] because 58 workers left in 12 months mainly from monotony, and Herzberg's theory shows adding variety keeps people better than paying more for the same dull job [eval].
    Keywords: piece rate, $2.10, 58 workers, 10-week training programme, three assembly stations, every 4 hours, $90 monthly attendance bonus, $1,450, 22%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Taylor's scientific management: link pay to output via piece rate; Herzberg: hygiene factors vs motivators / variety reduces dissatisfaction | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $2.10 per tested board / 10-week training programme; Reference to Option B: three assembly stations every 4 hours / $90 monthly attendance bonus / $1,450 salary | analysis_max_2: Chain from piece rate to higher tested output to lower unit overheads; Chain from rotation to retention of skilled assemblers to protected quality / fewer leavers | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence (58 leavers, 22% turnover, salary vs piece rate)
