UNIT: Unit 2: People in Business
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Halcyon Ceramics Ltd employs 78 workers at its pottery factory near Country X's capital city. The factory produces 3,400 hand-decorated plates per month. Workers are paid $11.20 per hour and eat in a cramped canteen with no heating. Absenteeism reached 9% last winter and 11 workers resigned in the last 6 months. The production director, Marcus Vale, wants to raise morale before a large export order.

Marcus is weighing two investments. Option A: spend $40,000 improving hygiene factors — a heated canteen, better lockers and a quiet rest room — reflecting Herzberg's view that conditions must be adequate before motivators can work. Option B: spend the same $40,000 on motivators — job enrichment, monthly recognition boards and team leaders with responsibility for quality on each kiln line. He must decide this month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'Herzberg's two-factor theory'.
    Answer: Herzberg's two-factor theory states that job satisfaction and dissatisfaction come from different factors: hygiene factors such as pay and conditions prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators such as recognition, responsibility and advancement create satisfaction and encourage effort [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Job satisfaction and dissatisfaction arise from different factors; Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two hygiene factors Halcyon Ceramics Ltd should improve.
    Answer: One hygiene factor is working conditions [k]. The canteen has no heating and lockers are poor, so making these comfortable would remove a daily irritation, helping to cut the 9% absenteeism recorded last winter [app]. A second hygiene factor is rest and recovery space [k]. A quiet rest room for the 78 workers would ease fatigue during long kiln shifts, so people return to work on the 3,400 hand-decorated plates with more care rather than after a miserable break [app].
    Keywords: cramped canteen, Absenteeism reached 9%, 78 workers, 3,400, hygiene factors, $11.20
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Working conditions are a hygiene factor; Rest or facilities are hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction | application_max_2: Reference to cramped canteen with no heating / lockers; Reference to 9% absenteeism / 78 workers / 3,400 plates

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Halcyon Ceramics Ltd of spending the $40,000 on motivators (Option B).
    Answer: One benefit is greater responsibility and esteem [k]. Giving team leaders responsibility for quality on each kiln line meets Maslow's esteem level and gives workers a real voice in standards [app], so workers take ownership of each batch and defect rates on the 3,400 plates should fall [an]. A second benefit is recognition of good performance [k]. Monthly recognition boards make strong performance visible and job enrichment adds variety to decorating work [app], and motivated workers are more productive and less likely to join the 11 who resigned in the last 6 months [an].
    Keywords: job enrichment, kiln line, 3,400, $40,000, 11 workers resigned, team leaders
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Responsibility and esteem are motivators / create satisfaction; Recognition and job enrichment are motivators | application_max_2: Reference to team leaders on each kiln line / responsibility for quality; Reference to monthly recognition boards / job enrichment / 11 workers resigned | analysis_max_2: Chain from responsibility to ownership to lower defect rates; Chain from recognition to motivation to higher productivity / lower turnover

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Halcyon Ceramics Ltd should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A is strongly supported by Herzberg: hygiene factors like a heated canteen and better lockers do not motivate on their own, but when they are poor they create dissatisfaction that blocks everything else [k]. The $40,000 would immediately improve daily life for all 78 workers, directly tackling the discomfort behind last winter's 9% absenteeism and the 11 resignations in 6 months [app]. Fixing dissatisfaction first stabilises the team before a demanding export order [an]. However, Option B adds only true motivators — job enrichment, recognition boards and team-leader responsibility — which Herzberg argues create genuine satisfaction and extra effort [k]. The pay of $11.20 per hour is presumably adequate, so further comfort may simply become the new normal, whereas motivators keep adding satisfaction [app]. Motivators build long-term engagement and quality ownership across the export order's production run [an]. Overall, I think Halcyon should choose Option A first [eval] because Herzberg is explicit that hygiene factors must be adequate before motivators can work — you cannot enrich jobs for workers shivering in an unheated canteen [eval].
    Keywords: $40,000, Absenteeism reached 9%, 11 workers resigned, 78 workers, $11.20, 3,400, job enrichment
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction / are prerequisites; Herzberg: motivators create satisfaction / extra effort | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: heated canteen / lockers / rest room / $40,000; Reference to Option B: job enrichment / recognition boards / $11.20 per hour | analysis_max_2: Chain from removing dissatisfaction to stabilised team / export readiness; Chain from motivators to long-term engagement / quality ownership | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence (9% absenteeism, 11 resignations vs $11.20 pay adequacy)

Merryfield Confectionery is a private limited company making chocolate truffles in Country X. It employs 64 production-line workers across 2 shifts and 9 packaging staff. Pay is $10.60 per hour on both shifts.

The owner, Dana Whitmore, is considering either Option A: promote 2 experienced line workers to team-leader posts at $13.80 per hour, creating advancement on Herzberg's list of motivators, or Option B: keep everyone on $10.60 and introduce a profit-sharing scheme paying 4% of annual profit into a staff bonus fund shared equally. She needs to decide before the autumn rush.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'motivators'.
    Answer: Motivators, in Herzberg's two-factor theory, are factors such as recognition, responsibility, advancement and the work itself that create job satisfaction and encourage employees to work harder and better [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Motivators create job satisfaction (not just prevent dissatisfaction); Examples: recognition / responsibility / advancement / the work itself

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Merryfield Confectionery's line workers feel 'stuck'.
    Answer: One reason is the near absence of promotion opportunities [k]. With only 9 packaging staff and 5 quality assurance inspectors above the line, there are few senior roles to aim for, so ambition stalls on the production floor [app]. A second reason is a lack of responsibility and recognition [k]. Workers make truffles with no say in quality decisions and no advancement path, so Herzberg's motivators are missing — which helps explain why 17 resigned in the past year [app].
    Keywords: advancement, 9 packaging staff, 5 quality assurance, 17 resigned, $10.60, promotion
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Few promotion opportunities / career progression available; Lack of responsibility or recognition (Herzberg's motivators missing) | application_max_2: Reference to 9 packaging staff and 5 QA inspectors above the line / no chance of promotion; Reference to 17 resigned in the past year / feeling 'stuck'

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Merryfield Confectionery of Option A (promoting 2 line workers to team-leader posts).
    Answer: One benefit is a visible signal that effort is rewarded [k]. Promoting 2 experienced line workers to team-leader posts at $13.80 per hour shows 64 colleagues that loyalty can lead to advancement [app], and the post costs only $3.20 per hour more while strongly lifting esteem and retention on the line [an]. A second benefit is better on-the-job leadership [k]. Team leaders drawn from the line know the truffle process intimately and can take responsibility for shift quality [app], reducing the load on the 5 quality assurance inspectors and protecting the $4.2 million sales revenue [an].
    Keywords: team-leader posts, $13.80, 64, 5 quality assurance, $4.2 million, 2 experienced line workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Promotion signals effort is rewarded / advancement is a Herzberg motivator; Team leaders provide leadership / responsibility on the line | application_max_2: Reference to 2 experienced line workers to team-leader posts at $13.80 per hour / 64 colleagues; Reference to 5 quality assurance inspectors / $4.2 million sales | analysis_max_2: Chain from visible advancement to esteem to better retention; Chain from internal leaders to better shift quality to protected revenue / less QA load

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Merryfield Confectionery should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A applies Herzberg's advancement motivator and Maslow's esteem needs [k]. Promoting 2 experienced line workers to team-leader posts at $13.80 per hour shows the whole line that effort leads somewhere, so staff should commit more strongly before the autumn rush [app]. Giving leaders authority over shift quality also builds skills in-house and eases supervision pressure on Dana Whitmore [an]. However, Option B shares financial success with everyone [k]. Keeping everyone on $10.60 avoids internal pay friction, and the 4% of annual profit is split equally, so even packaging staff participate in the reward [app]. But profit depends on factors beyond worker effort, such as cocoa and sugar costs, so the 4% fund may be small per person and weakly linked to individual performance [an]. Overall, I think Option A is the better first step [eval] because advancement and responsibility are true motivators that directly answer why 17 resigned, while an equal profit share would be felt only weakly on the line [eval].
    Keywords: team-leader posts, $13.80, $10.60, 4% of annual profit, 17 resigned, $4.2 million, 64, 2 experienced line workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Herzberg: advancement and responsibility are motivators; Profit-sharing rewards company-wide success, not individual effort | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: two promotions at $13.80 per hour / team-leader posts; Reference to Option B: $10.60 base / 4% of annual profit shared equally | analysis_max_2: Chain from visible promotion to commitment / skills built in-house; Chain from equal profit share to weak individual link / depends on external costs | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence (17 resigned, autumn rush vs equal shares for all staff)

--- STEM ---
Northgate Textiles is a private limited company weaving denim fabric in Country X. The mill employs 130 weavers across 3 production lines and pays a time rate of $8.90 per hour. Last year the mill produced 2.6 million metres of denim, but customer rejections reached 7.5% of orders. Managing Director Sofia Grant believes workers put in little discretionary effort because pay is not linked to results.

Sofia is considering Option A: replace the time rate with a piece rate of $0.07 per accepted metre across all 3 lines, following Taylor's scientific management. Option B: keep $8.90 per hour and introduce a team bonus of $220 per month for each line that keeps rejections below 5%. The board meets in 2 weeks to decide.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'bonus'.
    Answer: A bonus is an additional financial reward paid on top of normal wages or salary when an employee or team reaches a set target, such as an output level, quality standard or sales figure [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Extra / additional financial reward on top of normal pay; Paid for reaching a target (output / quality / sales)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Northgate Textiles should not rely on the time rate alone.
    Answer: One reason is that time rate pays for hours, not results [k]. At $8.90 per hour, fast weavers earn the same as slow ones, so there is little incentive to push beyond the 2.6 million metres produced last year [app]. A second reason is that time rate ignores quality [k]. Workers are paid the same however many metres are rejected, so nothing in the pay system discourages the 7.5% rejection rate that is costing orders [app].
    Keywords: time rate, $8.90, 2.6 million metres, 7.5%, piece rate, team bonus
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Time rate pays for hours not results / low incentive to work harder; Time rate ignores quality / does not discourage waste | application_max_2: Reference to $8.90 per hour / 2.6 million metres; Reference to 7.5% rejection rate / costing orders

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two possible problems with Option A (a piece rate of $0.07 per accepted metre).
    Answer: One problem is quality risk [k]. Paying $0.07 per accepted metre pushes weavers to rush, and disputes over what counts as 'accepted' could rise, so rejections could climb above 7.5% [app], damaging Northgate's reputation with denim buyers and inviting more rejected orders [an]. A second problem is unstable incomes [k]. Piece rate pay swings with machine stoppages and order books, so the 130 weavers could take home very different amounts each week [app], which may demotivate cautious workers and increase labour turnover at the mill [an].
    Keywords: piece rate, $0.07, 7.5%, 130 weavers, accepted metre, Northgate Textiles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Piece rate can encourage rushing / quality falls; Piece rate incomes vary week to week / unstable | application_max_2: Reference to $0.07 per accepted metre / 7.5% rejections; Reference to 130 weavers / machine stoppages / order books | analysis_max_2: Chain from rushing to more rejections to damaged reputation / lost orders; Chain from income instability to demotivation to higher turnover

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Northgate Textiles should switch to the piece rate (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A follows Taylor's scientific management by linking pay to output [k]. At $0.07 per accepted metre, fast weavers earn more, so output should rise above 2.6 million metres a year, and because rejected metres are unpaid, workers also shoulder part of the quality risk behind the 7.5% rejection rate [app]. Higher throughput would spread fixed costs over more metres, cutting unit cost [an]. Option B, by contrast, keeps the $8.90 per hour base and adds a $220 monthly team bonus per line for holding rejections below 5% [k]. This targets Northgate's real emergency — 7.5% rejections — with a shared team goal, and earnings do not swing with machine stoppages, keeping the 130 weavers financially secure [app]. A team bonus also builds cooperation on the line, which Taylor's individual piece rate undermines [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better choice [eval] because the urgent problem is a 7.5% rejection rate, and the $220 team bonus attacks that directly while keeping pay stable for the 130 weavers [eval].
    Keywords: $0.07, 2.6 million metres, 7.5%, $8.90, $220, 5%, 130 weavers, team bonus
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Taylor's scientific management: output-linked pay motivates; Team bonus builds cooperation / shared goal vs individual competition | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $0.07 per accepted metre / 2.6 million metres / 7.5%; Reference to Option B: $220 per line per month / 5% target / $8.90 base | analysis_max_2: Chain from piece rate to higher throughput to lower unit cost; Chain from team bonus to cooperation to lower rejections without pay instability | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence (7.5% rejections vs throughput incentive)

--- STEM ---
Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting is a private limited company producing brake housings for motorbikes in Country X. The plant cast 240,000 brake housings last year. It employs 84 machine operators and 12 health-and-safety inspectors across 2 shifts. Last year 27 accidents were reported, more than double the 13 recorded 2 years ago. Workers mention stress, noise at 95 decibels and fear of burns from molten metal. Pay is $12.40 per hour.

Managing Director Viktor Lam must choose between two options. Option A: invest $55,000 in extra safety — extraction fans, heat shields and quieter machines — targeting Maslow's safety needs. Option B: raise all 96 workers' pay by 8% to $13.39 per hour, arguing that a stronger financial reward will lift morale. A safety audit is due in 8 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'motivation'.
    Answer: Motivation is the factors inside and around a job that encourage employees to behave in ways that achieve business objectives, such as working hard, taking care over quality and staying with the employer [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Motivation is the drive / factors that encourage employees to work well; Motivated employees work hard / take care / stay with the employer

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting should invest in safety before raising pay.
    Answer: One reason is Maslow's hierarchy of needs [k]. With 27 accidents last year, noise at 95 decibels and fear of burns from molten metal, workers cannot move up the hierarchy towards esteem and self-actualisation while they feel physically unsafe [app]. A second reason is that accidents destroy productivity and cost money [k]. Every injury means lost shifts and investigation time across the 2 shifts, so preventing injuries is cheaper and more reliable than enduring them [app].
    Keywords: 27 accidents, 95 decibels, molten metal, Maslow, 2 shifts, $55,000, $12.40
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Maslow: safety needs must be met before higher needs motivate; Accidents cost money / lost time / investigations | application_max_2: Reference to 27 accidents / 95 decibels / fear of burns from molten metal; Reference to 2 shifts / 84 machine operators

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting of choosing Option A (investing $55,000 in extra safety).
    Answer: One benefit is fewer accidents [k]. Extraction fans, heat shields and quieter machines would cut exposure to fumes, burns and noise, so the 27 accidents reported last year should fall towards the 13 seen 2 years ago [app], keeping the 84 machine operators productive and the 2 shifts running on schedule [an]. A second benefit is a stronger audit outcome [k]. The improvements directly answer the safety audit due in 8 weeks and show the workforce that management takes its duties seriously [app], which should lift confidence, morale and willingness to stay at the plant [an].
    Keywords: $55,000, 27 accidents, 13, 84 machine operators, 2 shifts, safety audit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Extra safety reduces accidents / exposure to fumes, burns, noise; Visible commitment to safety improves confidence and morale | application_max_2: Reference to 27 accidents last year / 13 two years ago / $55,000; Reference to 8-week safety audit / 84 machine operators / 2 shifts | analysis_max_2: Chain from fewer accidents to sustained productivity / shifts on schedule; Chain from passing the audit to higher morale / retention

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A targets the real problem: fear [k]. Maslow's hierarchy shows safety needs must be met before higher motivation is possible, and with 27 accidents more than double the 13 recorded 2 years ago, plus 95 decibel noise, no pay rise makes molten metal safer [app]. The $55,000 covers physical safeguards used by all 96 workers, and passing the 8-week safety audit protects production of the 240,000 brake housings a year [an]. Option B is simpler — 8% more pay, $13.39 per hour for every worker, no machinery changes [k]. Herzberg would class this as a hygiene factor: welcome, but it prevents dissatisfaction rather than creating motivation, so the fear of burns persists [app]. It also permanently raises the wage bill by $0.99 per hour per worker regardless of safety outcomes [an]. Overall, I think Option A is the right choice [eval] because the stem's own evidence — double the accidents and dangerous noise — points to unmet safety needs that Option B cannot fix, however welcome $13.39 per hour feels [eval].
    Keywords: $55,000, 27 accidents, 13, 95 decibels, $13.39, 8 weeks, Maslow's safety needs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Maslow: safety needs before higher-order motivation; Herzberg: pay is a hygiene factor, preventing dissatisfaction not creating motivation | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $55,000 / extraction fans / heat shields / safety audit; Reference to Option B: 8% rise to $13.39 per hour / all 96 workers | analysis_max_2: Chain from physical safeguards to fewer accidents / audit passed / output protected; Chain from pay rise to temporary relief but unchanged fear / permanent extra cost | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence (27 vs 13 accidents, 95 decibels vs $13.39)

--- STEM ---
Clearway Glassworks is a private limited company making laboratory glass tubing in Country X. It employs 52 glass-blowers and 14 packers. Output averages 9,500 metres of tubing per month at a defect rate of 4%. Pay is a salary of $1,380 per month for blowers. The owner, Helena Ortiz, notes that quit rates among young blowers reach 15% a year and blames low pay.

Helena is considering two reward options for the blowers. Option A: a profit-sharing scheme paying 3% of annual profit, about $70,000 this year, split equally among all 66 staff. Option B: an individual bonus of $60 per month for each blower whose defect rate stays under 2%, payable for up to 5 months per year. She wants a decision at the June review.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'teamworking'.
    Answer: Teamworking is organising employees into groups that share responsibility for a task or goal, pooling skills, supporting one another and taking collective ownership of the result [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Employees organised into groups sharing responsibility for a task/goal; Pool skills / support one another / collective ownership

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Clearway Glassworks could use Maslow's hierarchy of needs to motivate its glass-blowers.
    Answer: One way is to meet safety needs [k]. A second way is to meet esteem needs [k]. Recognising blowers whose defect rate is under 2% with a certificate would make them feel respected and valued, matching the pride Herzberg says esteem-level recognition creates [app].
    Keywords: 15%, defect rate, 2%, glass-blowers, $1,380, quit rates
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Safety needs must be met (protection, equipment, safe conditions); Esteem needs: recognition / respect / achievement | application_max_2: Reference to molten glass / 15% annual quit rate among young blowers; Reference to defect rate under 2% / recognition with a certificate

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of Option B (an individual bonus of $60 per month for defects under 2%).
    Answer: One drawback is weakened teamwork [k]. Paying $60 only for personal sub-2% months rewards individual effort over group success [app], so experienced blowers may stop helping juniors whose defect rates run closer to 4%, eroding the shared skills the workshop needs [an]. A second drawback is the temptation to hide defects [k]. Blowers chasing $60 could pass flawed tubes on to the 14 packers for shipment [app], and faulty laboratory tubing reaching hospitals would mean returns, lost contracts and a damaged reputation far costlier than the bonus pool [an].
    Keywords: $60, 2%, 4%, 14 packers, individual bonus, Clearway Glassworks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Individual rewards can undermine teamwork / helping colleagues; Individual rewards can encourage hiding defects / cutting corners | application_max_2: Reference to $60 per month / sub-2% defect target / juniors near 4%; Reference to 14 packers / laboratory tubing reaching hospitals | analysis_max_2: Chain from individual reward to rivalry to lost shared learning / rising 4% rate; Chain from hiding defects to faulty tubes to returns / lost contracts

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Clearway Glassworks should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A is straightforward and equal: 3% of annual profit, about $70,000 this year, split equally among all 66 staff, gives blowers and packers the same stake [k]. On Herzberg's view, financial reward is a hygiene factor — a profit share will not by itself create lasting drive — but it signals the firm values everyone and costs nothing until profits exist [app]. Equal sharing, however, links blower effort only weakly to the payout: each of the 66 staff receives roughly $1,060 whether or not their own defects fell [an]. Option B ties $60 per qualifying month directly to quality: under 2% defects, up to 5 months a year, worth $300 extra for top blowers [k]. It attacks the actual 4% defect rate with a clear personal target and leaves the $1,380 salary untouched [app]. But it ignores the packers entirely, may breed rivalry among the 52 blowers, and does not address why quit rates hit 15% a year [an]. Overall, I think Clearway should choose Option A first, then layer Option B on next year [eval] because equal profit sharing builds firm-wide loyalty at predictable cost, while the individual bonus can be added once defect data is reliable [eval].
    Keywords: 3% of annual profit, $70,000, 66 staff, $60, 2%, 4%, 15%, $1,380
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Herzberg: financial reward is a hygiene factor, not a true motivator; Equal profit sharing links pay weakly to individual effort | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: 3% of annual profit / $70,000 / split equally among 66 staff; Reference to Option B: $60 per month / under 2% / 5 months a year / $1,380 salary | analysis_max_2: Chain from equal split to weak effort link / shared stake but diluted incentive; Chain from personal quality target to lower 4% defect rate but rivalry risk / packers excluded | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence ($70,000 pool, 4% defect rate, 15% quit rate)

Marlin Rope & Twine Factory is a private limited company in Country X producing marine rope from synthetic fibre. It employs 44 spinners, 16 finishers and 6 office staff.     Answer: Profit sharing is a financial reward in which a portion of the business's profit is paid out to employees, usually as a bonus, so staff benefit when the company succeeds and lose when it does not [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A portion of the business's profit is paid to employees; Usually paid as a bonus; reward depends on company success

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two non-financial methods Marlin Rope & Twine could use to motivate its spinners.
    Answer: One non-financial method is job rotation [k]. Alternating spinners between spinning and finishing every 3 months varies the routine and cuts boredom behind the 11% absenteeism rate across 820,000 metres of annual output [app]. A second non-financial method is giving responsibility through team leaders [k]. Appointing 4 spinners at $280 per month extra to lead quality checks and train new starters would satisfy Herzberg's responsibility motivator and plug the skill gaps left by 3 experienced spinners retired recently [app].
    Keywords: job rotation, 3 months, 820,000, 11%, team leaders, $280, spinning and finishing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Job rotation varies tasks / reduces boredom; Responsibility / team leadership is a Herzberg motivator | application_max_2: Reference to 11% absenteeism / 820,000 metres output; Reference to 4 team leaders at $280 per month / 3 experienced spinners retired

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of Option B (appointing 4 team leaders at $280 per month extra).
    Answer: One advantage is faster transfer of skills [k]. Four experienced spinners can coach new starters on quality while spinning and finishing continue as normal [app], preserving craft knowledge lost when 3 experienced spinners retired and protecting the $540,000 export contract [an]. A second advantage is stronger motivation of the leaders themselves [k]. The role brings recognition and responsibility — Herzberg's key motivators — beyond money [app], which should lift effort and morale across the 44 spinners as quality checks are enforced consistently each shift [an].
    Keywords: team leaders, $280, experienced spinners retired, $540,000, 44 spinners
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Experienced staff coach/train newcomers / transfer skills; Responsibility and recognition are Herzberg motivators | application_max_2: Reference to 4 team leaders / $280 per month extra / 3 experienced spinners retired; Reference to $540,000 export contract / 44 spinners | analysis_max_2: Chain from coaching to retained skill / protected contract delivery; Chain from leader motivation to consistent quality / plant-wide morale

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marlin Rope & Twine should choose Option B? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option B creates 4 team-leader roles at $280 per month extra — about $1,120 per month, small against $540,000 of export revenue and $3.1 million annual output [k]. Responsibility and recognition are Herzberg motivators, so the chosen leaders should work harder and lift the 44 spinners around them through quality checks and onboarding of new starters [app]. This directly targets the skill gaps from 3 retirements and the 11% absenteeism problem before the 9-month export contract begins [an]. Option A, by contrast, spreads skills wider [k]. Job rotation between spinning and finishing every 3 months builds flexibility so anyone can cover either role, though it does nothing about pay, leadership or the loss of specialist mentors [app]. Rotation is free to implement and affects all 44 spinners equally, whereas only 4 get the extra responsibility [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better choice [eval] because the urgent issue is skill loss and quality leadership on a $540,000 contract — 4 motivated team leaders fix that now, while rotation can be added later [eval].
    Keywords: team leaders, $280, $540,000, job rotation, 44 spinners, 11%, 3 months, $3.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Herzberg: responsibility and recognition are motivators; Job rotation builds multi-skilling and flexibility | application_max_2: Reference to Option B: 4 team leaders / $280 per month / quality checks / training new starters; Reference to Option A: spinning and finishing every 3 months / all 44 spinners | analysis_max_2: Chain from team leaders to retained skills / protected export contract on time; Chain from rotation to flexible cover but no fix for absenteeism or skill gaps | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence (11% absenteeism, 3 retirements vs free rotation)

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U2_SET_49
UNIT: Unit 2: People in Business
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Redbank Paper Mill is a public limited company producing corrugated cardboard in Country X. The mill employs 118 workers across 3 shifts and pays $10.10 per hour. Output is 1.4 million square metres per quarter, and fibre waste reached 8.5% of raw material last quarter. Fibre recycling trials recovered a further 3% last quarter. The operations director, Tomas Lindqvist, wants to cut waste before the annual shareholders' meeting in June.

He is considering two approaches. Option A: a job enrichment programme letting line teams decide on quality checks and stop the line when defects appear, plus a weekly feedback board. Option B: an across-the-board pay rise of 5% to $10.61 per hour for all 118 workers, on the argument that better-paid staff work with more care. Costings are due in 3 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'hygiene factors'.
    Answer: In Herzberg's two-factor theory, hygiene factors are job-related conditions such as pay, working conditions, company policy and supervision; if they are inadequate they cause dissatisfaction, but improving them does not by itself create motivation [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Conditions such as pay / working conditions / policy / supervision; Their absence causes dissatisfaction; improving them does not by itself motivate

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of using pay alone to motivate workers at Redbank Paper Mill.
    Answer: One limitation is that pay is a hygiene factor [k]. Raising wages to $10.61 per hour stops dissatisfaction but soon becomes the expected norm, so the extra motivation fades after the first few pay packets [app]. A second limitation is that pay does not change behaviour at the machine [k]. Workers can be paid 5% more yet still watch waste run at 8.5% of raw material, because money adds no authority to stop the line or set quality checks [app].
    Keywords: pay rise, $10.61, 8.5%, 5%, 118 workers, $10.10
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Pay is a hygiene factor — becomes expected norm / effect fades; Money alone does not give authority to change working methods | application_max_2: Reference to $10.61 per hour / 5% pay rise / $10.10 per hour; Reference to 8.5% fibre waste / all 118 workers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two arguments in favour of Option A (the job enrichment programme).
    Answer: One argument is responsibility and ownership [k]. Letting line teams decide on quality checks and stop the line meets Herzberg's responsibility motivator and gives crews real authority over defects [app], so problems are fixed at source and the 8.5% fibre waste figure should fall sharply [an]. A second argument is shared visibility of results [k]. A weekly feedback board shows waste and output figures to all 118 workers, turning improvement into a shared challenge [app], and shared visibility plus ownership should cut waste per 1.4 million square metres produced each quarter [an].
    Keywords: job enrichment, 8.5%, 118 workers, 1.4 million, weekly feedback board, fibre waste
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Job enrichment adds responsibility / authority over work; Feedback/visibility of results motivates improvement | application_max_2: Reference to line teams deciding on quality checks / stop the line; Reference to weekly feedback board / 118 workers / 8.5% fibre waste | analysis_max_2: Chain from team authority to problems fixed at source to lower 8.5% waste; Chain from visible figures to shared challenge to lower waste per quarter

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redbank Paper Mill should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A gives teams the authority and the information to act [k]. Stop-the-line power and a weekly feedback board target the actual problem — 8.5% fibre waste — and add Herzberg motivators such as responsibility, achievement and recognition rather than a one-off wage bump [app]. Cutting waste by even a couple of percentage points across 1.4 million square metres per quarter would save far more than a 5% pay rise costs [an]. Option B is simpler and universal [k]. A 5% rise to $10.61 per hour rewards all 118 workers equally, is easily understood and looks decisive before the June shareholders' meeting [app]. However, Herzberg warns pay is only a hygiene factor, so workers may welcome $10.61 briefly then coast, and the higher wage bill is permanent with no guaranteed fall in waste [an]. Overall, I think Option A is the better choice [eval] because the mill's central problem is waste, not pay — enrichment fixes it at source and builds a quality culture within the 3 weeks available [eval].
    Keywords: job enrichment, 8.5%, 118 workers, $10.61, 5%, 1.4 million, weekly feedback board, $10.10
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Herzberg: motivators create lasting satisfaction; pay is hygiene; Job enrichment = stop-the-line authority / feedback / responsibility | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: job enrichment / weekly feedback board / stop the line; Reference to Option B: 5% rise to $10.61 per hour / all 118 workers / June shareholders' meeting | analysis_max_2: Chain from empowerment to lower fibre waste to savings vs pay-rise cost; Chain from pay rise to temporary boost / permanent bill / coasting risk | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence (8.5% waste vs 5% pay rise, 3 weeks)

--- STEM ---
Westbrook Industrial Coatings is a private limited company painting steel tanks and beams in Country X. It employs 58 spray-painters and 8 QA inspectors across 2 lines. Annual revenue is $5.6 million and rejections average 6%. Rejections cost an estimated $340,000 last year. Painters are paid $11.90 per hour. Managing Director Grace Ellison sees 20% staff turnover in the painting booths and wants to improve motivation before quoting for a 3-year infrastructure contract.

She is weighing two options. Option A: a share-ownership scheme granting paint-shop staff shares worth up to $4,000 each after 2 years' service. Option B: a job-enrichment programme letting 10 coach painters lead daily briefings and approve first-off checks, plus $75 monthly recognition bonuses. Grace must decide in 4 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'share ownership'.
    Answer: Share ownership is a financial reward in which employees are given or can buy shares in the company, making them part-owners who gain when the business is profitable and its shares rise in value [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Employees are given or can buy shares in the company; They become part-owners / gain from profit and rising share value

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the 20% staff turnover in the painting booths should concern Westbrook Industrial Coatings.
    Answer: One reason is replacement cost [k]. Recruiting and training a spray-painter is expensive, and constant turnover means juniors keep leaving before mastering the spray technique [app]. A second reason is rising rejections [k]. New painters make more mistakes, so the 6% rejection rate and the $340,000 it cost last year could climb further as 20% of the 58 spray-painters are replaced [app].
    Keywords: 20%, 58 spray-painters, 8 QA inspectors, 6%, $340,000, staff turnover
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Replacement means recruitment and training costs recur; Inexperienced staff make more mistakes / quality falls | application_max_2: Reference to 20% turnover / 58 spray-painters; Reference to 6% rejections / $340,000 cost last year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two strengths of Option B (the job-enrichment programme).
    Answer: One strength is immediate motivation through responsibility [k]. Ten coach painters lead daily briefings and approve first-off checks — Herzberg's responsibility and recognition motivators in action [app], and coach-led checks catch spray faults early, helping to cut the 6% rejection rate on tanks and beams [an]. A second strength is visible, targeted recognition [k]. The $75 monthly recognition bonuses reward genuine achievement without raising everyone's pay bill — ten coaches at $75 is only $750 per month [app], while daily briefings spread best practice to new painters far faster [an].
    Keywords: 10 coach painters, $75, 6%, first-off checks, daily briefings, 20%, 2 lines
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Responsibility and recognition are Herzberg motivators; Targeted bonuses reward achievement without universal pay rise | application_max_2: Reference to 10 coach painters / daily briefings / first-off checks / $75 per month; Reference to 6% rejection rate / tanks and beams | analysis_max_2: Chain from coach-led checks to earlier fault detection to lower rejection rate; Chain from daily briefings to faster skill spread to protected quality and lower turnover

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Westbrook Industrial Coatings should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A offers a $4,000 shareholding after 2 years' service — a long-term stake aligning paint-shop staff with company success on a possible 3-year infrastructure contract [k]. Shares make employees part-owners with a reason to protect quality, echoing Maslow's esteem needs and Herzberg's recognition of achievement [app]. But 2 years is a long wait to change behaviour now, the 20% turnover may not improve before the quote in 4 weeks, and share value depends on the $5.6 million revenue holding up [an]. Option B applies Herzberg's motivators — responsibility and recognition — straight away [k]. Ten coach painters lead daily briefings and approve first-off checks, and $75 monthly recognition bonuses reward the 10 coaches directly, costing just $750 per month [app]. It directly attacks the 6% rejection rate and 20% turnover before the infrastructure quote is signed, and can be running inside the 4 weeks available [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better first step [eval] because responsibility and recognition fix the booth problems immediately, while share ownership's 2-year vesting is too slow to cut 20% turnover before the quote [eval].
    Keywords: $4,000, 2 years, 20%, 6%, $75, 10 coach painters, 3-year infrastructure contract, 4 weeks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Share ownership aligns employees with company success / long-term stake; Herzberg: responsibility and recognition are motivators acting quickly | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $4,000 after 2 years / paint-shop staff; Reference to Option B: 10 coach painters / $75 bonuses / $750 per month / 4 weeks | analysis_max_2: Chain from share vesting to weak short-term pull / turnover persists until decision in 4 weeks; Chain from coach scheme to faster fault detection to improved rejections and retention before quote | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem evidence (2-year vesting vs 4-week deadline, 20% turnover, 6% rejections)

--- STEM ---
Northgate Fashion Stores is a retail clothing chain operating 5 stores across a regional shopping district, employing 26 full-time sales assistants and 4 store managers. Annual revenue stands at $3.1m, and assistants are paid a time-rate wage of $13 per hour. Last year staff turnover among assistants reached 28%, and customer feedback cited slow fitting-room service and unhelpful styling advice.

The directors are deciding between two options for next year's peak season. Option one is a 4% commission on each assistant's monthly sales, which would lift top sellers' pay by around $300 a month but cut low sellers' pay. Option two keeps the time-rate wage and adds non-financial methods: job enrichment through window-display styling, teamworking incentives, and training leading to promotion to supervisor. The board meets in 3 weeks and wants a clear recommendation.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'motivation'.
    Answer: Motivation is the willingness of people to work hard and apply effort in their jobs, driven by internal and external factors [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: employees' willingness to work hard and apply effort; driven by internal and external factors

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Northgate Fashion Stores of introducing a 4% commission for sales assistants.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Higher sales revenue [k], as commission-based pay pushes assistants to sell more in the 5 stores during the peak season [app]. Advantage 2: Lower fixed wage cost for weak sellers [k], as 4% commission lifts top sellers' pay by $300 a month while poor performers earn less than the $13 per hour wage [app].
    Keywords: $3.1m, 5 stores, 4% commission, $300, $13 per hour, peak season, time-rate wage
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher sales revenue; pay linked to output lowers fixed wage cost | application_max_2: 5 stores; peak season; $300 a month; $13 per hour

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to this business of the non-financial package instead of commission.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Improved customer service [k], as training and window-display styling give assistants the skills customers asked for in feedback [app], which should lift customer satisfaction and loyalty [an]. Benefit 2: Better retention and a promotion pipeline [k], as job enrichment and training leading to promotion to supervisor motivate ambitious assistants [app], reducing the 28% staff turnover and its recruitment costs [an].
    Keywords: job enrichment, window-display styling, training, promotion to supervisor, 28%, teamworking incentives, customer feedback
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: improved customer service skills; better retention and promotion pathway | application_max_2: customer feedback; window-display styling; promotion to supervisor; 28% staff turnover | analysis_max_2: raises customer satisfaction and loyalty; reduces recruitment costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Northgate Fashion Stores should introduce the 4% commission rather than keep the time-rate wage with the non-financial package? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Commission rewards high sellers [k], lifting top pay by around $300 a month and driving sales across the 5 stores during the peak season [app], which could push revenue beyond $3.1m [an]. On the other hand, the non-financial package attacks the root causes [k]: job enrichment, teamworking incentives and training leading to promotion address the feedback about styling advice [app], building loyalty and cutting the 28% turnover [an]. Overall, Northgate should keep the time-rate wage with the non-financial package rather than introduce commission [eval], because its service and retention problems stem from low engagement rather than low pay; the package protects experienced assistants and the $3.1m revenue base more reliably than commission pressure, though a small peak-season bonus could be added later to sharpen effort [eval].
    Keywords: 4% commission, $300, $3.1m, 28%, 5 stores, non-financial methods, job enrichment, promotion to supervisor
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: commission drives sales but income varies; non-financial package tackles engagement and retention | application_max_2: $300 a month; $3.1m; 28% turnover; 5 stores; peak season | analysis_max_2: could push revenue beyond $3.1m; cutting turnover reduces recruitment costs | evaluation_max_2: weighs engagement-led problems against pay-led incentives; recommends retention-first approach with optional seasonal bonus

The company proposes spending $300,000 on improved bunks and crew rotation, while the union wants the offending trawler stood down until safety is independently checked. Owner Markus Hale must decide which offer to accept before the season's final month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'strike'.
    Answer: A form of industrial action in which employees refuse to work to pressure the employer to meet their demands [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: employees refuse to work; a form of industrial action to pressure the employer

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why 41 of 54 crew voted to strike.
    Answer: Reason 1: Rest-break failures [k], with rest hours on the newest trawler dropping below 6 between trips [app]. Reason 2: Safety incidents [k], including 2 near-miss accidents logged in March [app].
    Keywords: Sea Workers United, 54 crew, 41 voted, below 6, 2 near-miss accidents, newest trawler, March
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: inadequate rest/welfare provision for crew; safety concerns/near-miss accidents | application_max_2: rest hours; newest trawler; below 6 between trips; 2 near-miss accidents; March

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why settling the dispute quickly would benefit Northwind Fishing.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Protects revenue [k], avoiding about $600,000 in lost catch during peak prawn season [app], safeguarding the $8.2 million annual turnover [an]. Benefit 2: Protects crew safety [k], addressing rest hours on the newest trawler after 2 near-miss accidents [app], reducing the risk of a serious injury and future disruption [an].
    Keywords: 6 trawlers, $600,000, $8.2 million, newest trawler, 2 near-miss accidents, peak prawn season
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: avoids lost revenue/catch during peak season; addresses underlying safety concerns | application_max_2: $600,000 in lost catch; $8.2 million annual turnover; newest trawler; 2 near-miss accidents | analysis_max_2: safeguards turnover and cash flow; reduces risk of serious injury and further industrial action

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Northwind Fishing should stand down the offending trawler until safety is independently checked, rather than only improve bunks? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Standing down the trawler removes the immediate risk [k], protecting the 54 crew after 2 near-miss accidents in March [app], which is what the union's 41-vote strike mandate demands [an]. However, the $300,000 bunk improvement [k] would fix rest-hour shortages across all 6 trawlers [app], whereas a stand-down risks part of the $600,000 peak-season catch [an]. Overall, Northwind should stand the trawler down [eval] because crew safety outweighs one vessel's season profit [eval], ideally paired with the $300,000 rotation investment.
    Keywords: Newest trawler, 54 crew, 2 near-miss accidents, 41, $300,000, $600,000, Sea Workers United
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: standing down removes risk pending independent safety check; bunk improvements address rest shortages across fleet | application_max_2: 54 crew; 2 near-miss accidents in March; 41-vote strike mandate; $300,000 bunk improvement; $600,000 peak-season catch | analysis_max_2: eliminates risk of serious injury and forced shutdown later; stand-down may forfeit catch while bunks fix all vessels | evaluation_max_2: weighs immediate safety against lost catch revenue; justified stand-down recommendation prioritising safety

--- STEM ---
Coral Ridge Hotel is a 4-star resort in a coastal tourist town in Country X, operating 120 guest rooms and 3 restaurants. The hotel employs 95 staff, of whom 60 are full-time and 35 are part-time. The head chef, who was paid $54,000 a year, resigned after 6 years. The general manager must decide whether to promote Marco, a section chef on $42,000 a year with 5 years' service, or recruit externally.

Marco knows the kitchen brigade and the summer menu but has never run a whole kitchen. The hotel placed a job advertisement in the regional newspaper costing $350 and received 24 applications within 2 weeks. Of these, 9 came from existing staff and 15 from outside the hotel. The advertised salary for the new head chef is $55,000 a year. The summer season lasts 14 weeks, with occupancy averaging 90%, and the wage bill already totals $2.4 million a year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'external recruitment'.
    Answer: External recruitment is the process of hiring new workers from outside the business, for example through job advertisements, instead of promoting existing employees. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Hiring new workers from outside the business; Attracting outside candidates, for example through job advertisements, rather than promoting existing staff

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Coral Ridge Hotel placed a job advertisement in the regional newspaper.
    Answer: Placing a job advertisement informs potential candidates outside the hotel about the head chef vacancy, widening the pool beyond the 9 internal applicants [k]. Advertising at a cost of $350 attracted 15 external applications within 2 weeks, giving the manager a wider choice of experienced chefs [app]. An advertisement can set out the salary and the requirements of the role [k], which filters for candidates willing to lead 3 restaurants at the advertised salary of $55,000 a year [app].
    Keywords: regional newspaper, $350, 24 applications, $55,000, 2 weeks, 3 restaurants, Marco
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: The advert informs potential candidates that a vacancy exists, widening the applicant pool; The advert sets out the salary and requirements, attracting suitable applicants and filtering out unsuitable ones | application_max_2: The advert cost $350 and attracted 15 external applications within 2 weeks; $55,000 salary is advertised for managing 3 restaurants

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Coral Ridge Hotel of promoting Marco to head chef.
    Answer: Promoting Marco is cheaper and quicker than external recruitment [k], because the hotel avoids the $350 advertising cost and the time spent interviewing unknown applicants [app], so the new head chef can be in post before the 14-week summer season and the wage bill of $2.4 million is not strained further [an]. Internal promotion also rewards loyalty and motivates other staff [k]. Marco has 5 years' service and knows the kitchen brigade and the summer menu, so service can continue smoothly across the 3 restaurants [app]. Because guests will find familiar quality during a season when occupancy averages 90%, reviews and repeat bookings are more likely to hold up [an].
    Keywords: Marco, 5 years, $350, kitchen brigade, 14 weeks, 90%, 3 restaurants, $2.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Internal promotion is cheaper and quicker than external recruitment; Promoting internally rewards and motivates loyal existing staff | application_max_2: $350 advertising avoided; Marco has 5 years' service; Marco knows the kitchen brigade and the summer menu across the 3 restaurants | analysis_max_2: Head chef in post before the 14-week peak, avoiding disruption at high occupancy; Continuity of quality protects reputation, reviews and revenue during the 90% occupancy season

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Coral Ridge Hotel should promote Marco or recruit a new head chef externally? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Promoting Marco is cheaper and faster [k]. Marco has 5 years' service, knows the kitchen brigade and the summer menu, and the promotion costs about $13,000 a year more ($55,000 minus $42,000) rather than $350 of advertising plus weeks of interviews [app]. Staying with Marco protects food quality and cover during the 14-week peak when occupancy averages 90% [an]. However, Marco has never run a whole kitchen, and external candidates may bring broader experience across several kitchens and fresh menu ideas [k]. The 15 external applications include chefs prepared to accept $55,000; a stronger outsider could lift standards and motivate the brigade across the 3 restaurants [app]. An external hire might also introduce new routines that improve standards, but risks upsetting established staff and losing continuity during the busiest season [an]. Overall, the hotel should promote Marco because the risk and cost of external hiring so close to the 14-week season are too high, and his 5 years here make him the safest pair of hands [eval]. If the board wanted a long-term transformation of the menu, an external search after the summer would be wiser, but this vacancy must be filled immediately [eval].
    Keywords: Marco, 14 weeks, 90%, $55,000, 5 years, 3 restaurants, $42,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Internal promotion: cheaper, faster, known candidate, motivates staff; External recruitment: wider pool, fresh skills/experience, but costlier and riskier | application_max_2: Marco: 5 years' service; knows brigade and menu; promotion costs about $13,000 a year more; 15 external applications; $55,000 salary; 90% occupancy; 14-week season | analysis_max_2: Internal pick protects quality and continuity during peak season; External pick could raise standards but disrupt staff and delay the start date | evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement justified by timing, cost and risk; Recognises when external recruitment would become the better option

--- STEM ---
BrightPath Logistics runs a parcel distribution depot in Country X, employing 78 staff: 50 full-time drivers and warehouse operatives earning $15 an hour, and 28 part-time workers earning $12 an hour. Parcel volumes rise by 45% during the 10-week pre-Christmas peak, when the depot handles 9,600 parcels a week. Last year, 140 parcels were damaged and 12 were lost because staff were overstretched.

The operations manager must choose between hiring 20 additional part-time workers for the peak only or 10 additional full-time staff all year on a salary of $31,200. Part-time workers are paid only for hours worked but cannot drive heavy vehicles or operate the new forklifts. Full-time staff receive 6 weeks of training and would stay after the peak ends. The recruitment budget is $4,000 and advertising costs $180 per vacancy. The depot expects similar volumes next peak season.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'part-time employment'.
    Answer: Part-time employment is a job in which the employee works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee, often on flexible or reduced shifts, and is paid for the hours worked. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee; Paid for the hours worked, often on flexible or reduced shifts

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to BrightPath Logistics of hiring 20 additional part-time workers for the peak.
    Answer: Part-time workers are paid only for the hours they work [k], so during the 10-week pre-Christmas peak, when volumes rise by 45% to 9,600 parcels a week, the depot pays extra wages only when the extra capacity is actually needed [app]. Additional part-time staff reduce the overload on the existing 78 staff [k], helping to prevent repeats of the 140 damaged and 12 lost parcels that occurred last year [app].
    Keywords: 10-week, 45%, 9,600 parcels, 78 staff, 140, $12 an hour, 9,600
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Pay only for the hours worked; labour cost flexes with demand; Extra staff relieve pressure and reduce errors/losses | application_max_2: 10-week peak; volumes rise 45% to 9,600 parcels a week; $12 an hour; 140 damaged and 12 lost parcels last year; 78 existing staff

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of employing 10 additional full-time staff all year.
    Answer: Full-time staff can be trained and trusted with demanding tasks [k]. The 50 current full-time drivers and operatives already handle heavy vehicles and forklifts, and new full-time hires would receive 6 weeks of training [app], widening the pool of skilled staff available all year, not just in December [an]. Full-time staff remain after the peak, giving the depot stable capacity [k]. Ten full-time salaries cost $312,000 a year (10 x $31,200), but these staff can cover quieter months and stand in for absences [app], reducing reliance on agency cover and repeated seasonal recruitment every December [an].
    Keywords: $31,200, 6 weeks, 10-week, $15 an hour, 45%, 140, $4,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Full-time staff can receive full training and handle more demanding tasks; Full-time staff provide year-round stable capacity and continuity | application_max_2: 6 weeks of training; heavy vehicles and forklifts; 50 current full-time staff; 10 x $31,200 = $312,000 a year; stays after the peak ends | analysis_max_2: Wider skilled pool all year reduces bottlenecks and dependence on December cover; Year-round presence lowers agency costs and re-recruitment effort

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think BrightPath Logistics should hire 20 additional part-time workers for the peak or 10 additional full-time staff all year? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Hiring 20 part-time workers is cheaper and more flexible [k]. At $12 an hour part-timers cost less than the $15 full-time rate and are paid only for hours worked, and 20 vacancies at $180 each total $3,600, still inside the $4,000 recruitment budget [app]. Bringing in extra hands should stop the 140 damaged and 12 lost parcels that overstretched staff caused last year [an]. However, part-time staff cannot drive heavy vehicles or operate forklifts [k], so the depot would still rely on its 50 full-time staff for the hardest tasks and might repeat the same overload in January returns or other peaks [app]. Full-time hires at $31,200 each would stay year-round, receive 6 weeks of training and cut the need to re-recruit every December [an]. Overall, the depot should hire the 20 part-time peak workers because demand is temporary and $312,000 of annual salary for year-round cover is hard to justify for a peak that lasts 10 weeks [eval]. If volumes stayed high all year, or forklift-certified full-time staff were urgently needed, the full-time option would become worth the extra cost [eval].
    Keywords: 20 additional part-time, 10-week, 9,600, $4,000, $12 an hour, $31,200, 45%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Part-time: flexible, cheaper per hour, suits short peaks; Full-time: permanent, trained, versatile but costly year-round | application_max_2: $12 vs $15 an hour; $180 per vacancy; 20 vacancies = $3,600 inside $4,000 budget; 10 x $31,200 = $312,000; 10-week peak; 9,600 parcels; 140 damaged and 12 lost | analysis_max_2: Cheap flexible capacity matched to a known 10-week peak reduces overload and parcel losses; Full-time gives year-round skill and stability but overspends for a temporary need | evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement justified by the temporary nature of the peak and the cost arithmetic; Recognises the circumstances in which the full-time option would be preferable

Meadowbrook Day Nursery is a private nursery in Country X caring for 48 children aged 2 to 5 years. Of these applications, 18 enclosed a curriculum vitae (CV) and 12 completed the nursery's application form, which asks 8 standard questions about qualifications, experience and childcare training. CVs vary widely in layout and detail, making comparison slow, while the forms give consistent information. However, the forms reveal less about personality. Interview panels cost $120 per candidate in staff time and the total recruitment budget for this role is $800.

--- QUESTIONS ---

    Question: Define 'application form'.
    Answer: An application form is a standard document produced by the business that applicants complete to provide details such as personal information, qualifications and experience, allowing the employer to compare candidates fairly. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Standard document produced by the employer for applicants to complete; Gathers consistent information (qualifications, experience, personal details) to aid fair comparison

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Meadowbrook Day Nursery might prefer the application forms when shortlisting.
    Answer: Application forms present every candidate's information in the same format [k]. With 30 applications received in 3 weeks, the owner can scan the 12 completed forms quickly against the 8 standard questions instead of comparing 18 different CV layouts [app]. Forms ensure the nursery gets the specific information it needs [k]. The form's questions on qualifications, experience and childcare training directly test whether applicants meet the requirements for caring for children aged 2 to 5 [app].
    Keywords: 30 applications, 3 weeks, 18 enclosed a curriculum vitae, application form, 8 standard questions, $250, 48 children
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Forms give a consistent, directly comparable format; Forms gather specific job-relevant information the employer chooses | application_max_2: 30 applications in 3 weeks; 12 forms versus 18 CVs; 8 standard questions; Qualifications, experience and childcare training questions; children aged 2 to 5

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of inviting shortlisted candidates for an interview.
    Answer: Interviews let the owner probe claims made on the forms or CVs [k]. With $120 of staff time per candidate and a total budget of $800 (minus $250 already spent on the advertisement), the nursery can interview only the strongest candidates and check their claims face to face [app], which reduces the risk of hiring unsuitable staff for the 48 children [an]. Interviews also give candidates the chance to ask questions about the role [k]. Discussing the $26,000 full-time salary, the 9 existing full-time practitioners and daily duties helps both sides judge fit before the autumn term [app], lowering the chance of an early resignation and the $120 per-interview cost being wasted [an].
    Keywords: 30 applications, $120, application form, $26,000, 9 full-time practitioners, autumn term, 48 children
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interviews verify/probe candidate claims and reveal interpersonal qualities; Interviews allow two-way communication; candidates can ask questions and judge fit | application_max_2: $120 per candidate; $800 budget; $250 spent on the advertisement; $26,000 salary; 9 full-time colleagues; autumn term deadline | analysis_max_2: Better screening reduces risk of unsuitable hires around young children; Two-way fit assessment lowers early turnover and wasted recruitment spend

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Meadowbrook Day Nursery should shortlist using the CVs or the application forms? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Application forms give consistent information the nursery can compare quickly [k]. The 12 completed forms answer the 8 standard questions directly, so the owner can shortlist confidently before paying $120 per interview from the remaining budget [app]. This reduces the risk of hiring someone unsuitable to work with the 48 children aged 2 to 5 [an]. However, CVs reveal more about personality, motivation and experiences such as first-aid courses, and the 18 CVs received may contain stronger candidates than the forms show [k]. A detailed CV might reveal qualities the standard form cannot capture, and rejecting them all could leave the nursery choosing only from the form-fillers [app]. Over-reliance on the form alone could cause the nursery to miss the most enthusiastic applicant for the role [an]. Overall, the nursery should shortlist using the application forms because consistency and the 8 targeted questions suit a safeguarding-critical childcare role, and the budget does not stretch to interviewing widely from an unverified CV pool [eval]. If strong candidates emerge on the forms, CVs can be read as supporting evidence, but the form should remain the primary tool [eval].
    Keywords: application form, 18 enclosed a curriculum vitae, 8 standard questions, $120, 48 children, autumn term, 30 applications
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Application forms: consistent, comparable, fast to process; CVs: richer picture of personality/motivation, but variable layout and detail | application_max_2: 12 completed forms vs 18 CVs; 8 standard questions; $120 per interview; $800 budget; 48 children aged 2 to 5; children need safe, vetted carers; autumn term deadline | analysis_max_2: Forms speed shortlisting and cut the risk of unsuitable hires in a care setting; CVs may hide stronger candidates; form-only shortlisting risks lower quality of hire | evaluation_max_2: Reasoned overall judgement anchored to budget, safeguarding and comparability; Acknowledges the CV's value as secondary evidence

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Face-to-face (or video) meeting between applicant and employer; Used to assess suitability, skills and attitude for the role

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Tekworks Electronics should test the 12 assemblers before hiring them.

Testing reduces the risk of costly mistakes and rework [k]. With the line due to reach 400 units a month within 4 months, hiring untested assemblers risks faulty devices and a damaged relationship with the new client [app].
    Keywords: $45, 98%, 35 applicants, 1,100 repaired devices, $190, 12 electronics assemblers, 2 workshops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Tests measure actual job skills directly rather than claimed ability; Testing identifies unsuitable candidates and reduces hiring errors and rework | application_max_2: Soldering and fault-finding; 98% fault-free requirement; 35 invited applicants; $45 assessment; 400 units a month within 4 months

  Qc [6 marks]

Interviews also let candidates ask about the job [k], so shortlisted applicants can understand the 400-unit monthly target, the 6-week hiring deadline and working patterns [app], meaning expectations match reality and the $3,000 recruitment budget is not wasted on someone who resigns quickly [an].
    Keywords: $190, 64 people, $3,000, 400 units, 6 weeks, $25 per candidate, 30-minute panel interview
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interviews assess communication, attitude and team fit; Interviews let candidates ask questions and form realistic expectations | application_max_2: Devices priced at $190; team of 64 across 2 workshops; 400-unit monthly target; 6-week deadline; $3,000 budget | analysis_max_2: Better fit reduces turnover and disruption in the new line; Realistic expectations reduce early resignations, saving recruitment cost

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tekworks Electronics should use practical assessments or panel interviews to select the 12 assemblers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Practical assessments directly measure the exact skills the assembly line needs [k]. A $45 assessment for 35 applicants costs $1,575, leaving $1,425 of the $3,000 budget, and shows who can actually solder to the 98% fault-free standard [app]. Choosing by observed skill rather than talk minimises rework and protects delivery of 400 units a month within 4 months [an]. However, practical tests alone cannot show how candidates communicate under pressure or fit into the 64-person team [k]. The $25 interview would reveal reliability and willingness to start within 6 weeks; running both costs $70 per applicant, or $2,450 for 35, still within budget [app]. A brilliant solderer who quits after a week would leave the line short-staffed and waste selection time [an]. Overall, practical assessments are the essential tool because the role is skill-critical and the client's 98% fault-free clause leaves no margin for unsuitable technicians [eval]. Interviews should be added only as a brief final check for the chosen 12, not as the main basis of selection [eval].
    Keywords: practical assessment, $45, 98%, $3,000, 400 units, 12 electronics assemblers, 4 months
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Practical tests show real soldering/fault-finding competence; Interviews assess communication, reliability and team fit | application_max_2: $45 x 35 = $1,575; $3,000 budget; $70 per applicant combined; 98% fault-free; 400 units a month; 4 months; 6-week start; 2 workshops of 64 people | analysis_max_2: Test-first selection minimises rework and quality failure for the new client; Interview-only selection risks hiring polished speakers who cannot solder | evaluation_max_2: Clear judgement: practical assessments are essential, interviews secondary; Notes that running both still fits the $3,000 budget

--- STEM ---
Sunfield Care Home is a residential care home in Country X providing 60 places for elderly residents. It is staffed by 38 full-time carers earning $13.50 an hour and 12 part-time night staff. The senior care supervisor, who retires soon, coordinates rotas for 50 staff, reviews care plans and keeps medication records up to date.

The home has a recruitment budget of $650. One candidate is Priya, a senior carer earning $14.25 an hour with 7 years at the home and all leadership training completed; she would accept promotion at $15.50 an hour. The alternative is an external advertisement costing $300, likely to attract applicants, some holding nursing qualifications. Resident occupancy is 93%. Last year an unsuitable external hire resigned within 4 months, costing $2,100 in agency cover and another advertisement. The manager wants continuity of care for the 60 residents.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'recruitment'.
    Answer: Recruitment is the process of identifying that a business needs a new employee, attracting suitable candidates and filling the vacancy. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifying the need for a new employee / a vacancy; Attracting and selecting a suitable candidate to fill it

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of recruiting the senior care supervisor internally.
    Answer: Internal recruitment is cheaper and quicker [k]. The home avoids the external $300 advertising cost and weeks of interviews, staying within its $650 budget while keeping the rota fully covered [app]. The internal candidate is a known quantity [k]. Priya has 7 years at Sunfield and has completed all leadership training, so the manager can predict her reliability and medication-record accuracy at 93% occupancy across the 60 places [app].
    Keywords: $300, $650, Priya, 7 years, 93%, 60 places, $13.50 an hour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Internal recruitment is cheaper and quicker; no external advertising cost; Internal candidates are known to the business, so performance and reliability can be predicted | application_max_2: $300 advertising avoided; $650 budget respected; $14.25 current pay; Priya: 7 years, all leadership training done; 93% occupancy; 60 places

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of recruiting the senior care supervisor externally.
    Answer: External recruitment brings skills the home currently lacks [k]. Some applicants may hold nursing qualifications, adding clinical oversight that neither Priya nor the other carers can offer today [app], which could raise care standards across the home's 60 places [an]. A wider choice of candidates [k]. A $300 advertisement could attract hundreds of applications, giving the manager genuine choice rather than relying on a single internal candidate [app], which increases the chance of appointing a strong leader able to cut the agency costs that hit $2,100 last year [an].
    Keywords: $300, Priya, $2,100, 93%, $650, 7 years, 50 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: External recruitment brings in new skills/qualifications not held internally; External recruitment widens the applicant pool and gives genuine choice | application_max_2: Possible nursing-qualified applicants; $300 advertisement; $2,100 agency cover spent last year after a weak hire; 60 places | analysis_max_2: Added clinical oversight could lift standards of care for all residents; Wider pool raises the odds of a stronger appointment and lower agency spend

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sunfield Care Home should promote Priya or recruit a senior care supervisor externally? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Promoting Priya is cheaper, safer and immediate [k]. She has 7 years at the home and all leadership training, asking only $15.50 an hour instead of $14.25 ($1.25 more, about $2,600 a year for 2,080 full-time hours), versus $300 of external advertising plus the risk of another failure like last year's $2,100 agency cover bill [app]. Appointing Priya keeps continuity of care at 93% occupancy, protects rota planning for 50 staff and rewards loyalty [an]. However, promoting internally excludes outsiders with nursing qualifications who could lift clinical oversight and challenge stale routines [k]. External advertising attracts a far wider field, and the strongest candidate might improve medication records, care planning and morale beyond Priya's level [app]. If Priya's promotion simply re-shuffles existing problems rather than solving them, the home could be worse off within months [an]. Overall, the home should promote Priya because she is known, trained, immediately available and far cheaper than another external failure, which matters most at 93% occupancy with vulnerable residents [eval]. An external search after the budget recovers, or next time a clinical skill gap appears, would be the sensible way to add outside expertise later [eval].
    Keywords: Priya, $15.50, $2,100, 93%, $300, 7 years, $650
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Internal: cheaper, immediate, known, motivates staff; External: fresh skills and wider pool, but higher risk and cost | application_max_2: Priya: 7 years, all training done; $14.25 to $15.50 ($1.25 more, about $2,600 a year); $300 external advertising; $2,100 spent last year; 93% occupancy; rotas for 50 staff | analysis_max_2: Continuity protects resident care and avoids disruption while the vacancy is open; External hire could add nursing skills but risks another costly mis-hire | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation tied to continuity, cost and risk; Identifies when external recruitment would become the better option

--- STEM ---
Riverview Leisure Centre is a public leisure facility in Country X with 2 swimming pools, a gym and a sports hall, employing 40 full-time staff. Attendances rose 18% last year to 210,000 visits, so opening hours increased to 14 hours a day, 7 days a week.

The manager must decide between recruiting 8 part-time lifeguards to cover the new evening and weekend sessions at $11.50 an hour, or 4 full-time lifeguards on $24,500 a year. Full-time lifeguards would also open and close the pools and complete gym induction checks. Part-time staff can supervise only 1 pool each and work 30-minute shifts. Full-time contracts include 5 weeks of annual leave. The recruitment budget is $900, of which $280 would be spent on advertising. The centre wants the new staff in place before the summer holidays begin.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'full-time employment'.
    Answer: Full-time employment is a job in which the employee works the standard number of hours each week set by the employer, usually around 35 to 40 hours, on an ongoing basis. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Works the full/standard working week (about 35-40 hours); On an ongoing, usually permanent basis for the business

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of hiring 8 part-time lifeguards for the evening and weekend sessions.
