Eight part-time lifeguards provide scheduling flexibility [k], covering 30-minute shifts and just 1 pool each across 2 pools, and they can cover for one another at short notice [app].
    Keywords: $11.50 an hour, 14 hours a day, 30-minute shifts, 1 pool, $24,500, 8 part-time lifeguards, 210,000 visits
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Pay only for the hours needed; labour cost matches demand; Flexible shifts and more staff provide cover and resilience | application_max_2: $11.50 an hour; 14-hour days; evenings and weekends; 1 pool each; 30-minute shifts; 2 pools; $24,500 full-time alternative

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of hiring 4 full-time lifeguards instead.
    Answer: Full-time lifeguards can take on wider duties [k]. They would open and close the pools and complete gym induction checks, tasks that part-timers on 30-minute shifts cannot practically handle [app], giving consistent standards at both ends of the 14-hour day [an]. Four full-time staff are also easier to train and supervise than 8 part-timers [k]. At $24,500 each, totalling $98,000 a year, they receive 5 weeks of annual leave arranged around demand and stay year-round [app], which lowers induction and turnover costs and strengthens safety compliance [an].
    Keywords: $24,500, gym induction checks, 5 weeks, 14 hours a day, 2 swimming pools, 30-minute shifts, full-time
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Full-time staff take on wider, end-to-end duties; Fewer staff are easier to train, supervise and retain | application_max_2: Open and close duties; gym induction checks; 30-minute shifts impractical; $24,500 each, $98,000 total; 5 weeks annual leave; 14-hour day | analysis_max_2: End-of-day cover improves pool safety and consistent standards; Lower turnover and training burden; stronger safety compliance

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Riverview Leisure Centre should hire 8 part-time lifeguards or 4 full-time lifeguards? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Hiring 8 part-time lifeguards costs less and flexes with demand [k]. At $11.50 an hour, covering only evenings and weekends is cheaper than $98,000 a year of full-time salaries, and 30-minute shifts slot neatly around peak attendance from 210,000 visits [app]. Part-time cover keeps the pools staffed into busy sessions without exhausting the $900 recruitment budget [an]. However, part-time staff cannot open and close or complete gym induction checks properly [k], so the 14-hour day would still stretch the 40 existing full-time staff further, or require tighter supervision [app]. Four full-time lifeguards on $24,500 each would handle openings, closings and induction checks, with 5 weeks of leave rosterable around the summer peak [an]. Overall, the centre should hire the 4 full-time lifeguards because open/close and gym induction duties are essential to safe 14-hour days, and 8 part-timers would leave those duties uncovered [eval]. If attendances proved erratic after summer, some evening shifts could be converted to part-time once core full-time cover was secure [eval].
    Keywords: 8 part-time lifeguards, 4 full-time lifeguards, $11.50 an hour, $24,500, 14 hours a day, 210,000 visits, gym induction checks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Part-time: cheaper per hour, flexible, suits peaks; Full-time: committed, wider duties, end-to-end responsibility | application_max_2: $11.50 an hour vs $24,500 ($98,000 total); 210,000 visits; $900 budget; Open/close and gym induction duties; 5 weeks leave; 14-hour days; 2 pools | analysis_max_2: Cheaper flexible cover, but leaves opening/closing and induction uncovered; Full-time option guarantees daily end-to-end safety cover | evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation justified by non-negotiable safety duties; Acknowledges replacing some shifts with part-time later if demand is volatile

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Online advertising is cheaper than print; Online advertising reaches wider and younger audiences quickly | application_max_2: $150 online vs $400 print; save $250; $600 budget; Over 55 newspaper readership; 13 weeks; March to May | analysis_max_2: Savings improve cost-effectiveness and free budget for other hiring needs; Wider reach accelerates filling the 3 roles before the peak season

  Qd [8 marks]

--- STEM ---
Northgate Coach Travel is an intercity coach operator in Country X running 24 daily routes between 5 cities, employing 70 people. It has 44 full-time coach drivers on $34,000 a year and 26 office and depot staff.

The company has won an airport shuttle contract requiring 8 drivers within 8 weeks. The operations director must choose between two-round interviews (a 15-minute telephone screening followed by a 30-minute panel interview costing $140 per shortlisted candidate) or a single 20-minute informal chat with the owner, which is free. The contract requires drivers to hold a valid licence, a 5-year clean driving record and good customer-service skills. The interview budget is $1,400 and 40 drivers applied within 2 weeks. Round-one telephone screening at 15 minutes per candidate takes about 10 hours in total. Panel members include the operations director and the health and safety officer.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline two advantages of using interviews to select candidates.
    Answer: Interviews let the panel assess communication and customer-service skills face to face, and allow candidates to explain their 5-year clean driving record and route knowledge. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Assesses communication and interpersonal skills directly; Allows candidates to explain experience and driving history

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using two-round interviews to select the 8 airport drivers.
    Answer: Telephone screening cheaply filters out unsuitable applicants [k], so the 15-minute first round can eliminate anyone lacking a valid licence or the 5-year clean record before staff time is spent, narrowing the 40 applicants to a serious shortlist [app]. Structured panel interviews give every shortlisted driver the same 30-minute question set [k], making customer-service answers directly comparable and enabling a fair choice of the strongest 8 within the $1,400 budget [app].
    Keywords: 15-minute, 40 drivers, $1,400, $140, 5-year clean driving record, 24 daily routes, 8 drivers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Screening removes unqualified applicants early at low cost; Structured interviews make assessments fair and comparable | application_max_2: 15-minute screening; 40 applicants in 2 weeks; 5-year clean record; valid licence; $140 per shortlisted candidate; $1,400 budget; 30-minute panel interview

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Northgate Coach Travel might face with a single informal chat.
    Answer: Informal chats follow no fixed agenda [k], so each of the 40 applicants may be asked different questions and answers cannot be compared consistently when picking the 8 airport drivers [app], raising the risk of a biased or lucky selection for a safety-critical role [an]. A single chat also reveals little depth [k]. In 20 minutes the owner cannot verify driving records, licences or claim histories before trusting drivers with passengers on 24 daily routes [app], risking poor service that could damage, or even lose, the new airport contract [an].
    Keywords: 20-minute informal chat, 40 drivers, $140, 24 daily routes, 5-year clean driving record, $34,000 a year, airport shuttle contract
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Informal chats lack standard questions, so comparisons are inconsistent and biased; A short chat cannot verify key facts or test judgement in depth | application_max_2: 40 applicants; 8 drivers; 20 minutes only; no record checks mentioned; 24 daily routes; 5-year clean record required; airport contract at stake | analysis_max_2: Inconsistent comparison risks unsafe or unsuitable hires; Unverified selection risks reputational and contract loss

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Northgate Coach Travel should use two-round interviews or a single informal chat to select the 8 airport drivers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Two-round interviews cost a little but are far more reliable [k]. The 15-minute telephone screening clears the 40 applicants cheaply, and the $1,400 budget covers panel interviews for up to 10 finalists at $140 each (10 x $140 = $1,400), selecting the strongest 8 on merit [app]. Structured, recorded answers protect the company from unfair-selection claims and let panel members probe customer-service skills properly [an]. However, the 20-minute informal chat is free, fast and might secure drivers within days, which helps if routes must start within 8 weeks [k]. For internal candidates from the 44 existing drivers it could work, but it cannot test new applicants consistently against licence and the 5-year clean-record requirement [app]. Saving $1,400 means little if an unfit driver causes an incident on the 24 daily routes [an]. Overall, the company should run two-round interviews because the airport contract demands verified records and strong customer-service skill, and the process fits the $1,400 budget exactly [eval]. The informal chat could follow the panel decision as a courtesy introduction, but never as the selection method [eval].
    Keywords: two-round interviews, 20-minute informal chat, $1,400, $140, 40 drivers, 8 weeks, airport shuttle contract
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Two-round interviews: thorough, fair, verifiable, structured selection; Informal chat: free, fast, but unstructured and unreliable for unknown applicants | application_max_2: 15-minute telephone screening; $140 per finalist; $1,400 budget; 40 applicants; 8 drivers; 8-week deadline; 24 daily routes; 5-year clean record; 44 existing drivers | analysis_max_2: Better evidence protects passengers, brand and the new contract; The free/fast appeal is outweighed by the risk of unsafe hires | evaluation_max_2: Clear recommendation justified by contract requirements and budget arithmetic; Notes the limited legitimate role of an informal chat (courtesy, not selection)

The Reading Nook is an independent bookshop in Country X employing 7 staff: the owner, 2 full-time weekend managers on $21,500 a year, 3 part-time assistants on $9.50 an hour and 1 weekend cashier. Shop sales are $780,000 a year, with footfall peaking on Saturdays at 900 customers.

If the best applicants are inexperienced, she should choose the one who connects with customers and train them on stock in the first weeks [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Studying the job in detail: tasks, duties and responsibilities; Identifying the skills and qualifications needed to perform it

  Qb [4 marks]

It also produces an accurate job description and person specification [k], so the firm's 75 recent enquiries can be screened against the current demands before interviews are booked [app].
    Keywords: job analysis, 3 new contracts, 75 enquiries, 10 more officers, night, $220 online and $500 in print, 8 weeks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the actual, current duties of the job; Forms the basis of an accurate job description and person specification | application_max_2: Night car-park patrols; radio equipment; incident reports; duties absent from old documents; 3 new contracts; 75 enquiries received; 10 officers needed within 8 weeks

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kestrel Security Services should carry out a fresh job analysis or re-use last year's job description and person specification? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A fresh job analysis is essential because the contracts changed [k]. A small share of the $1,200 budget spent now prevents repeat hiring, client disputes and lost contracts later [an]. Overall, the firm should carry out a fresh job analysis because the risk of appointing officers unsuited to night patrols and incident reporting far outweighs 60 staff-hours, and any cost gap can be closed by choosing the $220 online advert over print [eval].   Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Harbourview Hotels Group might choose to dismiss the 3 supervisors.

Reason 2: Dismissal signals that poor performance is not tolerated [k], which could motivate the remaining 207 staff and help reverse the rise to 78 complaints a year [app].
    Keywords: 3 supervisors, complaints, resort hotels, 78, housekeeping, 4 coastal

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Clearline Contact Centre of the higher legal minimum wage.

    Keywords: $9.00, $296,400, 5%, $480,000, utilities, 150

    Keywords: 2 years, 84%, $9.00, utilities, 91%, $296,400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: improved motivation / retention; avoids legal penalties / complies with the law | application_max_2: pay frozen 2 years / 91% to 84% quality scores; $9.00 from January / utilities client | analysis_max_2: better call quality / lower recruitment costs; avoids fines and damage to reputation / margin protected

  Qd [8 marks]

--- STEM ---
Northgate Freight Services is a haulage firm in Country X operating 6 depots and a fleet of 140 trucks with 260 drivers. Head office issued a 46-page written handbook last year covering new fuel-saving and roadside safety rules, plus weekly emails. After one driver missed a loading note and $30,000 of refrigerated goods were rejected, the board debated how to communicate the revised rules: keep the written handbook and emails, or hold 30-minute depot briefings between shifts at $25 per driver per briefing. The handbook cost $18,000 to print and translate.

The board must decide how all 260 drivers receive the revised rules from June. Written methods give a permanent record and reach every driver regardless of shift, but may never be read; verbal briefings give instant feedback but clash with night runs. Insurers want evidence that every driver was informed of the safety changes.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'written communication'.
    Answer: Written communication is the exchange of information through written words, such as letters, emails, reports and handbooks [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exchange of information through written words; examples: letters, emails, reports, handbooks

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of written communication for Northgate Freight Services.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Permanent record [k]; the 46-page handbook and weekly emails prove to insurers that all 260 drivers received the safety rules [app]. Advantage 2: Consistent message [k]; every driver at the 6 depots reads the same fuel-saving and loading instructions regardless of shift pattern [app].
    Keywords: 46-page, 260 drivers, 6 depots, handbook, insurers, emails

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of written communication for Northgate Freight Services and how it could overcome each.
    Answer: Limitation 1: No immediate feedback [k]; drivers cannot ask about the revised loading rules electronically, so misunderstanding like the missed loading note goes unnoticed [app], which is why a short question-and-answer session should follow each handbook update [an]. Limitation 2: Risk of being ignored [k]; a 46-page handbook translated into several languages is unlikely to be read in full [app], so key rules should be summarised on one page with a signature or reply email to confirm receipt [an].
    Keywords: loading note, $30,000, 46-page, handbook, 260, briefings
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: no immediate feedback / cannot ask questions; may not be read / ignored / too long | application_max_2: missed loading note / $30,000 rejected goods; 46-page handbook / translated versions | analysis_max_2: follow-up Q&A session catches misunderstandings; one-page summary with confirmation proves receipt

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Northgate Freight Services should rely on written communication rather than verbal depot briefings for the revised rules? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Written communication is the stronger primary method [k]; the $18,000 handbook gives insurers evidence that all 260 drivers received the rules, and reaches night-shift drivers that briefings miss [app]. However, the $30,000 rejected load shows written messages can simply be overlooked [k], and briefings at $25 per driver cost $6,500 per session but guarantee understanding and instant feedback [app]. A short briefing after each handbook update would close the feedback gap for high-risk rules [an], but weekly briefings for all content would be an expensive recurring cost for 6 depots [an]. On balance, Northgate should rely on written communication as the primary method with brief, targeted briefings for the safety-critical rules [eval], because the insurer evidence requirement outweighs the convenience of verbal sessions for 260 dispersed drivers [eval].
    Keywords: $18,000, 260, $30,000, $25 per driver, 6 depots, handbook, insurer
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: written gives permanent record / insurer evidence; written can be overlooked / briefings guarantee understanding | application_max_2: $18,000 handbook / 260 drivers / night shifts; $30,000 rejected load / $6,500 per briefing / 6 depots | analysis_max_2: targeted briefings close the feedback gap for critical rules; weekly briefings are a high recurring cost across 6 depots | evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation: written primary plus targeted briefings; justified by insurer evidence and 260 dispersed drivers

--- STEM ---
Whitehaven Dairies processes 120,000 litres of milk a week across 2 lines with 90 workers in Country X. Line output has fallen 8% this year and the quality team blames unclear daily targets. The factory displays paper wall charts showing output, wastage and allergen changeovers, plus posters for hygiene rules. Directors debate spending $14,000 on 4 digital displays cycling live targets versus refreshing paper charts for $900 a year. Allergen mistakes rose to 11 last quarter and one recall cost $22,000.

The board must pick a visual upgrade before winter peak in 6 weeks. Digital displays update automatically and show live data but need power, care and staff training; paper charts are cheap and familiar but fade and rely on staff reading them. Yield must recover from 92% to at least 97% to hit the $6.8m annual plan.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'visual communication'.
    Answer: Visual communication is the exchange of information through images, such as charts, diagrams, posters, signs and video [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exchange of information through images; examples: charts, diagrams, posters, signs, video

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of visual communication on the dairy factory floor.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Fast, universal understanding [k]; charts showing output and allergen changeovers are understood quickly by all 90 workers regardless of language [app]. Advantage 2: Continuous targets [k]; daily visual targets remind packing-line staff of the 92% to 97% yield gap without a meeting [app].
    Keywords: 90 workers, charts, 92%, 97%, allergen, yield
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: understood quickly / universal / fewer words needed; continuous reminder of targets / standards | application_max_2: 90 workers / language mix / allergen changeovers; 92% to 97% yield / packing-line staff

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of the dairy's paper wall charts and posters and how the factory could overcome each.
    Answer: Limitation 1: Charts go stale [k]; paper figures fade and are updated only weekly, so the 8% output fall was spotted late [app], which is why live digital displays or a daily supervisor update board would keep targets current [an]. Limitation 2: One-way only [k]; posters broadcast hygiene rules but cannot check understanding after 11 allergen mistakes last quarter [app], so short toolbox talks or quizzes should accompany the posters [an].
    Keywords: 8%, allergen mistakes, charts, posters, hygiene, yield
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: paper charts fade / go out of date / not live; one-way communication / no feedback or understanding check | application_max_2: 8% output fall spotted late / weekly update; 11 allergen mistakes last quarter / hygiene posters | analysis_max_2: live displays or daily update boards keep targets current; toolbox talks or quizzes confirm understanding

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Whitehaven Dairies should invest $14,000 in 4 digital displays rather than keep replacing paper charts? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Digital displays give automatic, live targets across both lines [k]; with yield at 92% against a 97% target, instant visibility could recover the 8% output fall within the 6-week run-up to winter peak [app]. However, $14,000 is a large outlay for a plant already absorbing a $22,000 recall from 11 allergen mistakes [k], while refreshed paper charts cost only $900 a year and are familiar to all 90 workers [app]. Live displays also need power, care and basic training, adding hidden costs [an], but paper charts risk another undetected yield slide and a missed $6.8m annual plan [an]. On balance, Whitehaven should invest in the 4 digital displays [eval], because the $22,000 recall and the 97% yield requirement show that stale information is costing more than the screens cost [eval]; paper can remain as backup at each line.
    Keywords: $14,000, 92%, 97%, $22,000, $900, 6 weeks, $6.8m
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: digital displays give live automatic targets; digital costs more / paper is cheap and familiar | application_max_2: 92% to 97% yield / 8% output fall / 6 weeks / 2 lines; $14,000 / $22,000 recall / $900 a year / 90 workers / 11 allergen mistakes | analysis_max_2: hidden costs of power, care and training for screens; paper risks undetected yield slide and missed $6.8m plan | evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation: invest in digital displays; justified by recall cost, yield gap and $6.8m plan, with paper as backup

Cardinal Retail Group operates 30 stores and 2 distribution centres in Country X with 1,400 staff. The board votes in 3 weeks. An intranet would reach all staff instantly, cut printing costs of $7,200 a year and record who read what; but 252 staff would miss out without alternatives.     Question: Define 'electronic communication'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exchange of information using technology; examples: email, intranet, messaging apps, video calls

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of electronic communication for Cardinal Retail Group.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Instant reach [k]; an intranet reaches all 1,400 staff across 30 stores and 2 distribution centres in seconds [app]. Advantage 2: Cost saving and records [k]; switching paper memos to the app saves $7,200 a year in printing and shows who has read each message [app].
    Keywords: 1,400 staff, 30 stores, $7,200, intranet, noticeboard, $1,500

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two barriers to electronic communication for Cardinal Retail Group and how each could be overcome.
    Answer: Barrier 1: Staff without access [k]; 18% of staff, about 252 people, have no smartphone or home computer [app], so noticeboards and printed memos must remain for them alongside the app [an]. Barrier 2: IT failure [k]; a 6-hour outage delayed 38 deliveries worth $22,000 [app], so backup paper procedures and offline access to critical information are essential during week-one rollout [an].
    Keywords: 18%, 252, 6-hour, $22,000, noticeboard, 1,400 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lack of staff access / digital divide; IT failure / system outage | application_max_2: 18% / 252 people without smartphone or computer; 6-hour outage / 38 deliveries / $22,000 | analysis_max_2: keep noticeboards and memos for those excluded; offline backups / paper fallback protects operations

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cardinal Retail Group should replace noticeboards with a staff intranet? Justify your answer.

However, about 252 staff (18%) have no smartphone or home computer [k], and a 6-hour IT outage already delayed $22,000 of deliveries, so removing noticeboards entirely would silence a fifth of the workforce and leave no fallback [app].     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: intranet is instant / cheap per message / provable receipt; removing noticeboards excludes 18% / no outage fallback | application_max_2: 1,400 staff / 30 stores / $7,200 / $1,500 a month; 252 staff / 18% / 6-hour outage / $22,000 / 2 distribution centres | analysis_max_2: value only if most staff actually use the intranet; huddles cost nothing but cannot prove receipt | evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation: intranet plus retained noticeboards and huddles; justified by the 18% excluded and the outage risk

--- STEM ---
Brightstack Software is a private limited company in Country X that grew from 40 to 85 developers and support staff in 3 years, with revenue of $3.2m. Staff turnover hit 22% and 3 product launches slipped last year. The founders communicate by one-way email memos, and staff say they never hear why decisions are made. The operations director proposes monthly all-staff meetings plus an anonymous suggestion box and quarterly pulse surveys costing $9,000 a year. Two founders prefer keeping email-only memos to protect coding time.

The board decides this month. Meetings consume 1 hour of 85 staff time monthly, costed at $4,400 per session but building feedback, surfacing training needs and improving morale. Email memos are quick and free but give no response channel and may be ignored. The business must decide before 20 new hires start in July.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'two-way communication'.
    Answer: Two-way communication is communication in which the receiver can respond and give feedback to the sender [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: receiver can respond / feedback to sender; contrasts with one-way communication

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of two-way communication for Brightstack Software.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Feedback highlights problems early [k]; pulse surveys would have surfaced the training needs behind the 3 slipped product launches [app]. Benefit 2: Staff feel valued [k]; giving 85 developers a voice could help reverse the 22% staff turnover [app].
    Keywords: 3 product launches, 22%, 85, turnover, surveys, $3.2m
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: feedback highlights problems / training needs; staff feel valued / higher motivation and retention | application_max_2: 3 slipped product launches / pulse surveys; 85 developers / 22% turnover

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two barriers to two-way communication at Brightstack Software and how each could be overcome.
    Answer: Barrier 1: Fear of the founders [k]; junior developers may not challenge two founders who favour email memos [app], so anonymous suggestion boxes and surveys let staff speak safely, surfacing problems early [an]. Barrier 2: Time pressure [k]; 85 busy developers lose 1 hour per monthly meeting, $4,400 per session [app], so keeping sessions short, focused and followed by written summaries protects coding time while still inviting feedback [an].
    Keywords: 85, $4,400, email memos, anonymous suggestion box, monthly, turnover
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: hierarchy / fear of seniors silences staff; time cost / meeting overload | application_max_2: two founders favour email memos / anonymous suggestion box; 1 hour monthly / $4,400 per session / 85 staff | analysis_max_2: anonymous channels let staff speak safely; short focused sessions plus written summary protect coding time

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brightstack Software should introduce monthly two-way meetings and surveys rather than keep one-way email memos? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Two-way communication fixes the root problem [k]; with 22% turnover and 3 slipped launches, anonymous feedback would surface training needs and rebuild trust before 20 new hires arrive in July [app]. However, monthly meetings cost $4,400 per session plus $9,000 a year for surveys [k], and two founders argue email preserves coding time across a team grown from 40 to 85 in 3 years [app]. Meetings with a written summary give every voice a route into decisions [an], while memos remain free and fast but leave staff unheard and jumping ship [an]. On balance, Brightstack should introduce the meetings and surveys [eval], because reversing 22% turnover and protecting the July intake outweighs a $4,400 monthly time cost, with memos kept for routine updates only [eval].
    Keywords: $4,400, 22%, 3 product launches, $9,000, 20 new hires, 85, email memos
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: two-way fixes root problems / feedback channels; meetings cost staff time / memos are free and fast | application_max_2: 22% turnover / 3 slipped launches / 20 new hires / July; $4,400 per session / $9,000 surveys / 40 to 85 / 3 years | analysis_max_2: written summaries give every voice a route into decisions; memos unheard staff increase turnover | evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation: adopt meetings and surveys; justified against turnover, launch slips and 20 new hires; memos for routine updates

--- STEM ---
Corvid Electronics Ltd runs an electronics assembly plant in the industrial city of Brannock, Country X. It employs 140 production workers assembling smart-home controllers, with output of 96,000 units and revenue of $4.8 million last year. Workers are paid a time rate of $9.50 per hour, and average output is 25 controllers per worker per hour. Absenteeism on the line reached 11% last year.

Managing Director Priya Raman is considering switching assemblers to a piece rate of $0.38 per completed unit, which her production manager estimates would lift output by 20% to about 115,000 units. The works council has warned that 60 of the 140 workers oppose the change, fearing rushed work and lower safety. She must decide before next month's production cycle begins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'motivation'.
    Answer: The internal desire and external incentives that encourage employees to work hard and commit to achieving a business's objectives [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: internal and external factors encouraging effort; commitment to achieving business objectives

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Corvid Electronics might want employees who are well motivated.
    Answer: Reason 1: A motivated workforce raises output and productivity [k], because each of the 140 production workers currently completes only 25 controllers per hour and output stands at 96,000 units [app]. Reason 2: Motivation reduces absenteeism and disruption [k], because absenteeism on the line reached 11% last year [app].
    Keywords: Corvid Electronics Ltd, 140 production workers, 96,000 units, $9.50, 25 controllers, 11%, $4.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher productivity/output; lower absenteeism/turnover | application_max_2: 140 production workers; 25 controllers per hour; 96,000 units; 11% absenteeism

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Corvid Electronics Ltd of introducing piece rate payment.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Piece rate links pay directly to output [k], because workers earn $0.38 per completed unit instead of just $9.50 per hour [app], so faster assemblers are rewarded and output could rise by 20% towards 115,000 units [an]. Advantage 2: It encourages a stronger work pace on the line [k], because only 25 controllers per worker per hour are completed now [app], so beating that level adds revenue on every unit above the threshold [an].
    Keywords: $0.38, $9.50, 25 controllers, 20%, 115,000 units, piece rate, 140 production workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: pay linked to output; stronger work incentive/pace | application_max_2: $0.38 per completed unit; $9.50 per hour; 20% output lift; 115,000 units; 25 controllers per worker per hour | analysis_max_2: faster assemblers rewarded, output rises towards target; each extra unit above 25 per hour adds revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Corvid Electronics Ltd should introduce piece rate payment rather than continue with the time rate? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Introducing piece rate would directly reward effort [k], since at 25 units per hour a worker earns exactly $9.50 and every extra unit adds $0.38 [app], so faster assemblers earn more and output could rise by 20% [an]. However, piece rate risks quality and safety problems [k], because 60 of the 140 workers oppose the change and absenteeism is already 11% [app], so rushed work could raise defect rates and harm the reputation of the controllers [an]. Overall, piece rate should be introduced but with quality checks and a safety review [eval], because the output gains are substantial for a line already suffering 11% absence and low hourly output [eval].
    Keywords: piece rate, time rate, $0.38, $9.50, 25 controllers, 20%, 11%, 60
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: piece rate rewards effort vs risks quality/safety; time rate gives security but no output incentive | application_max_2: 25 units per hour earns $9.50; $0.38 per additional unit; 60 of the 140 workers oppose; 11% absenteeism; 20% output lift | analysis_max_2: faster assemblers earn more and output rises; rushed work raises defects and damages reputation | evaluation_max_2: weighs output/motivation gains against safety and quality risks

--- STEM ---
Stonyhurst Steel Fabrication operates a steel beam fabrication yard on the outskirts of Calderfield, Country X, employing 85 welders and fabricators. Output last year reached 3,400 tonnes of structural beams for building sites, generating $6.1 million in revenue. Workers earn $11.00 per hour, but the yard has recorded 3 minor accidents this year and staff turnover has reached 18%.

Operations Director Marcus Hale must use a $120,000 improvement budget. He is considering installing new washrooms, a canteen and improved safety guards, or raising hourly pay by $1.25 per hour, which would cost the yard about $221,000 per year. A recent survey showed only 34 of the 85 welders were satisfied with yard conditions. He wants to fix what workers say is wrong before the most experienced welders leave.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'hygiene factors'.
    Answer: Aspects of work that do not actively motivate employees but, if poor, cause dissatisfaction; Herzberg argued these include pay, working conditions and job security [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: prevent dissatisfaction rather than motivate; examples: pay, working conditions, job security

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two hygiene factors that could be causing dissatisfaction at Stonyhurst Steel Fabrication.
    Answer: Reason 1: Poor working conditions and safety are hygiene factors [k], because the yard has recorded 3 minor accidents this year and pay is only $11.00 per hour [app]. Reason 2: Weak workplace facilities cause dissatisfaction [k], because a recent survey showed only 34 of the 85 welders were satisfied with yard conditions [app].
    Keywords: Stonyhurst Steel Fabrication, 85 welders, $11.00, 3 minor accidents, 18%, washrooms, Calderfield
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working conditions/safety as hygiene factors; facilities/pay as hygiene factors | application_max_2: 3 minor accidents this year; $11.00 per hour; 34 of the 85 welders; 18% turnover

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Stonyhurst Steel Fabrication of improving hygiene factors before raising pay.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Better safety reduces accidents and lost time [k], because the yard recorded 3 minor accidents this year [app], so improved guards and facilities cut injury risk and keep the 85 welders productive [an]. Benefit 2: Improving conditions tackles the root cause of low morale cheaply [k], because only 34 of the 85 welders are satisfied with yard conditions [app], so fixing washrooms and a canteen for $120,000 addresses dissatisfaction before an extra $221,000 a year wage bill is needed [an].
    Keywords: $120,000, washrooms, canteen, $1.25, $221,000, 18%, 3 minor accidents
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: safety improvements cut accidents and absence; conditions address root cause of dissatisfaction | application_max_2: 3 minor accidents this year; 34 of the 85 welders; $120,000 improvement budget; $221,000 per year wage cost | analysis_max_2: guards cut injury risk and lost productive time; fixing facilities for $120,000 avoids a $221,000 annual wage increase

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Stonyhurst Steel Fabrication should spend the $120,000 on facilities and safety rather than raise hourly pay by $1.25? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Spending $120,000 on facilities would remove clear hygiene problems [k], because only 34 of the 85 welders are satisfied and the yard recorded 3 minor accidents this year [app], so better washrooms, a canteen and guards could cut turnover from 18% and protect the safety of the experienced crew [an]. However, a $1.25 hourly rise would raise every worker's pay now [k], because it costs about $221,000 per year across 85 welders earning $11.00 per hour [app], so it is expensive but directly competitive in a tight labour market [an]. Overall, the $120,000 should go on facilities and safety first [eval], because Herzberg showed hygiene factors must be fixed before pay motivates anyone, and accidents and turnover are the urgent problems [eval].
    Keywords: $120,000, washrooms, $1.25, $221,000, 85 welders, 18%, 3 minor accidents
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: hygiene factors must be fixed before motivation rises; pay rise vs facilities trade-off | application_max_2: $120,000 improvement budget; $1.25 per hour; $221,000 per year; 34 of the 85 welders satisfied; 3 minor accidents this year; 18% turnover | analysis_max_2: facilities cut turnover and protect the experienced crew; pay rise is expensive but competitive in a tight labour market | evaluation_max_2: weighs one-off facility spend against ongoing wage cost; prioritises hygiene over pay as per Herzberg

--- STEM ---
Redbrook Food Processing Ltd operates a vegetable canning factory in the market town of Vellamo, Country X, employing 110 line workers and 12 supervisors. Last year it canned 5.2 million tins of mixed vegetables, generating revenue of $3.9 million. A forklift incident in March injured 2 workers, and a health and safety audit rated two production lines as high risk.

Human resources manager Daniel Okafor has a $125,000 investment fund to raise motivation. He is considering spending $80,000 on machine guarding and forklift safety upgrades for the two high-risk lines, or $45,000 on a leadership and esteem programme for the 12 supervisors. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'Maslow's hierarchy of needs'.
    Answer: Maslow's five-level model of motivation, which suggests people must satisfy lower-level needs such as safety before they can be motivated by higher-level needs such as esteem [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: five levels of needs in a hierarchy; lower needs must be satisfied before higher ones motivate

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Redbrook Food Processing should take safety needs seriously.
    Answer: Reason 1: Meeting safety needs removes a source of fear and anxiety [k], because a forklift incident in March injured 2 workers and two lines were rated high risk [app]. Reason 2: Safe workers are more productive workers [k], because the factory employs 110 line workers canning 5.2 million tins a year [app].
    Keywords: Redbrook Food Processing Ltd, 110 line workers, 12 supervisors, forklift, 2 workers, 5.2 million tins, high risk
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: safety needs sit low in the hierarchy and cause fear if unmet; safe conditions enable productivity and motivation | application_max_2: forklift incident in March injured 2 workers; two lines rated high risk; 110 line workers; 5.2 million tins

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Redbrook Food Processing Ltd of spending $80,000 on safety upgrades.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Better safety protects the workforce [k], because 2 workers were injured in March and two lines are rated high risk [app], so fewer injuries mean fewer absences and steadier canning output [an]. Advantage 2: A safer workplace raises morale and trust [k], because the 110 line workers would see the company investing in their welfare [app], increasing their effort towards the 5.2 million tins target [an].
    Keywords: $80,000, 2 workers, high risk, 110 line workers, $125,000, 5.2 million tins, March
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fewer injuries and absences; higher morale and trust in the employer | application_max_2: 2 workers injured in March; two lines rated high risk; 110 line workers; 5.2 million tins target | analysis_max_2: fewer injuries means steadier output and less disruption; feeling valued raises effort towards the production target

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redbrook Food Processing Ltd should spend $80,000 on safety upgrades rather than $45,000 on a leadership programme for the 12 supervisors? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Spending $80,000 on safety would meet the most basic needs first [k], because a forklift incident injured 2 workers and two production lines are rated high risk [app], so safer lines would cut injuries, absences and lost output across the 110-worker workforce [an]. However, the leadership programme could still raise motivation [k], because for only $45,000 it would meet the esteem needs of the 12 supervisors [app], giving them recognition and responsibility that could cascade into better line management [an]. Overall, the safety upgrades should take priority [eval], because Maslow's hierarchy puts safety before esteem and the injured workers show the need is urgent [eval].
    Keywords: $80,000, $45,000, 12 supervisors, 2 workers, high risk, forklift, 110 line workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Maslow: safety needs before esteem; esteem needs of supervisors vs safety of shop floor | application_max_2: $80,000 safety upgrade; $45,000 leadership programme; 12 supervisors; 2 workers injured in March; two lines rated high risk; 110-worker workforce | analysis_max_2: safer lines cut injuries, absences and lost output; esteem programme cascades recognition into better supervision | evaluation_max_2: weighs urgent safety need against cheaper esteem investment

--- STEM ---
Tansy Garment Works operates a sewing factory in the coastal city of Port Azene, Country X, employing 130 sewing machinists who make workwear shirts. Last year output reached 78,000 garments and revenue was $2.6 million. Machinists are paid a salary of $520 per month, and the defect rate has crept up to 4% this year.

Owner-manager Lucia Fernandes is choosing between two options. Option one is an 8% bonus, worth $41.60 per month per machinist, for machinists whose team beats 650 garments a week with a defect rate below 2%. Option two is an across-the-board 5% pay rise, costing about $40,560 per year. Her quality manager says defects at 4% are costing about $90,000 a year in rework. She wants to lift motivation and cut defects without adding too much cost.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'bonus'.
    Answer: An additional payment given to workers, usually for good performance or reaching a target, on top of their regular pay [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: additional payment on top of regular pay; linked to performance or targets

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways an 8% bonus could motivate the machinists at Tansy Garment Works.
    Answer: Reason 1: A bonus links pay to performance [k], because the 8% bonus of $41.60 per month is paid on top of the $520 salary for teams beating 650 garments a week [app]. Reason 2: A bonus rewards quality as well as quantity [k], because teams must also keep defects below 2% to qualify [app].
    Keywords: Tansy Garment Works, 8% bonus, $41.60, $520, 650 garments, 2%, 130 sewing machinists
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: pay linked to performance motivates effort; rewarding quality and quantity drives both behaviours | application_max_2: 8% bonus of $41.60 per month; $520 salary; 650 garments a week; defect rate below 2%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Tansy Garment Works of offering an 8% bonus rather than a 5% pay rise.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The bonus is paid only for extra results [k], because it is conditional on beating 650 garments a week with defects below 2% [app], so the $40,560 a year cost of a pay rise is only incurred when output improves [an]. Benefit 2: It improves quality as well as output [k], because the 4% defect rate costs about $90,000 a year in rework [app], so rewarding defects below 2% directly cuts waste and rework [an].
    Keywords: 650 garments, 2%, $40,560, 4%, $90,000, $41.60, 8% bonus
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: conditional payment targets money at performance; quality rewards cut rework and waste | application_max_2: conditional on 650 garments a week; defects below 2%; $40,560 per year pay rise cost; 4% defect rate costing about $90,000 | analysis_max_2: pay rise cost only incurred when output rises; rewarding low defects cuts the $90,000 rework bill

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tansy Garment Works should offer the 8% bonus rather than a 5% across-the-board pay rise? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The 8% bonus would target motivation at performance [k], because machinists must beat 650 garments a week with a defect rate below 2% to earn the extra $41.60 [app], so money is spent only when output rises and the 4% defect rate is controlled [an]. However, a 5% pay rise would be simpler and more equal [k], because at about $40,560 per year it would lift the pay of all 130 sewing machinists unconditionally [app], which could reduce resentment and feel fairer to slower teams [an]. Overall, the 8% bonus is the better choice [eval], because it drives both output and quality, which have slipped to 4% defects and $90,000 of rework costs [eval].
    Keywords: 8% bonus, $41.60, 650 garments, 2%, $40,560, 130 sewing machinists, 4%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: performance-linked bonus vs across-the-board rise; fairness and simplicity of equal pay | application_max_2: 650 garments a week target; defect rate below 2%; $41.60 extra per month; $40,560 per year rise cost; 130 sewing machinists; 4% defects, $90,000 rework | analysis_max_2: bonus spend only when output and quality improve; equal rise reduces resentment but does not target performance | evaluation_max_2: weighs performance incentive against fairness of equal rise

Quillon Bottling Co operates a soft-drink bottling plant in the inland town of Marram, Country X, employing 96 production staff, including a quality assurance team of 18.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'motivators'.
    Answer: Factors in Herzberg's theory, such as achievement, recognition and responsibility, that actively create satisfaction and motivate employees to work harder [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Herzberg motivators create satisfaction; examples: achievement, recognition, responsibility

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Quillon Bottling Co of having a well-motivated quality assurance team.
    Answer: Reason 1: Well-motivated QA staff catch faults early [k], because the plant fills 24 million bottles a year and missed defects could force costly recalls [app]. Reason 2: Motivation reduces resignations [k], because 3 QA staff have already resigned in 6 months citing boredom [app].
    Keywords: Quillon Bottling Co, 24 million bottles, quality assurance team, 3 QA staff, 6 months, 9%, 18 QA staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: motivated staff catch faults and maintain quality; motivation lowers turnover and recruitment cost | application_max_2: 24 million bottles a year; 3 QA staff resigned in 6 months; quality assurance team of 18

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Quillon Bottling Co of using Herzberg's motivators for the QA team.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Recognition gives QA staff a sense of achievement [k], because 3 QA staff resigned in 6 months citing boredom [app], so awards and certificates could make them feel valued and stay [an]. Advantage 2: Responsibility increases commitment [k], because team leader roles hand the 18 QA staff responsibility for line decisions [app], raising motivation and supporting the quality behind 24 million bottles a year [an].
    Keywords: 3 QA staff, 6 months, 18 QA staff, team leader roles, 24 million bottles, $6,000, recognition
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: recognition creates achievement and loyalty; responsibility deepens commitment and quality | application_max_2: 3 QA staff resigned in 6 months; 18 QA staff team leader roles; 24 million bottles a year; boredom cited in resignations | analysis_max_2: feeling valued reduces resignations and recruitment cost; responsibility raises motivation and protects output quality

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Quillon Bottling Co should introduce a recognition programme rather than a 7% pay rise for the quality assurance team? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A recognition programme would provide the motivators Herzberg identified [k], because costing just $6,000 it directly attacks the boredom that made 3 QA staff resign in 6 months [app], so morale could improve for a fraction of the pay rise cost [an]. However, a 7% pay rise would also matter [k], because the QA staff earn $30,000 each and the rise costs about $37,800 a year for all 18 [app], and Herzberg regarded adequate pay as a necessary hygiene factor [an]. Overall, the recognition programme should be introduced first [eval], because the resignations were driven by lack of recognition, a true motivator, rather than by inadequate pay at $30,000 [eval].

--- STEM ---
Ironmarsh Canning Ltd runs a fish canning factory in the port town of Sandbar, Country X, employing 65 canning line workers. Last year it processed 2,900 tonnes of sardines into 4.6 million tins, generating $5.5 million in revenue. Managing Director Theo Barros wants to lift productivity on the lines, which have fallen to 78% of capacity.

A management consultant has proposed applying Taylor's scientific management fully: time studies to set a standard time of 45 seconds per tin, carefully timed rest breaks of 10 minutes every 2 hours, and a piece rate of $0.11 per tin. Union representatives say 45 seconds per tin is too fast to sustain and want 60 seconds per tin with a joint review every 3 months. Theo must recommend an approach to the board at its meeting on 14 July.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'Taylor's scientific management'.
    Answer: Taylor's approach to management which uses scientific time studies to find the most efficient way to do a job, then applies standard tasks and financial incentives to raise productivity [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: time studies find the one best way to do a job; standard tasks and financial incentives raise productivity

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Ironmarsh Canning Ltd might adopt Taylor's scientific management.
    Answer: Reason 1: Time studies set standard tasks [k], because the consultant proposes a standard time of 45 seconds per tin on every line [app]. Reason 2: It raises output through financial incentive [k], because the proposed piece rate of $0.11 per tin rewards faster workers directly [app].
    Keywords: Taylor's scientific management, 45 seconds per tin, piece rate, $0.11, 4.6 million tins, time studies, 2,900 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: time studies define standard tasks and pace; financial incentives motivate higher output | application_max_2: standard time of 45 seconds per tin; piece rate of $0.11 per tin; 78% of capacity; 4.6 million tins

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Ironmarsh Canning Ltd of adopting Taylor's scientific management fully.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Standard times remove guesswork from planning [k], because a time study sets 45 seconds per tin as the measured standard [app], so output per line becomes predictable and scheduling the 4.6 million tins improves [an]. Benefit 2: Piece rate aligns pay with output [k], because workers earn $0.11 per completed tin instead of a flat wage [app], so the 2,900 tonnes of sardines flow through faster and unit labour cost falls [an].
    Keywords: 45 seconds per tin, $0.11, 4.6 million tins, 2,900 tonnes, piece rate, time studies, Taylor's scientific management
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: standard times enable predictable planning; piece rate aligns pay with output | application_max_2: 45 seconds per tin standard; $0.11 per completed tin; 4.6 million tins per year; 2,900 tonnes of sardines | analysis_max_2: predictable output improves scheduling and capacity use; pay linked to output raises pace and cuts unit labour cost

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ironmarsh Canning Ltd should adopt Taylor's scientific management with a 45-second standard rather than accept the union's 60-second proposal? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Adopting Taylor's system at 45 seconds per tin would raise productivity [k], because the standard comes from time studies and the $0.11 piece rate rewards faster work [app], so the factory could close the gap to full capacity and lift output beyond its 78% level [an]. However, forcing 45 seconds risks conflict and low morale [k], because union representatives say it is too fast to sustain and want 60 seconds with a joint review every 3 months [app], so imposing the rate could trigger stoppages and quality shortcuts [an]. Overall, Ironmarsh should adopt Taylor's approach but pilot 45 seconds and review it jointly [eval], because time studies and piece rate are proven tools, yet a negotiated phase protects morale and the 4.6 million tins output [eval].
    Keywords: Taylor's scientific management, 45 seconds, $0.11, 4.6 million tins, 60 seconds, time studies, piece rate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Taylor's system raises productivity via time studies and pay; imposing a rate risks conflict and morale damage | application_max_2: 45 seconds per tin standard; $0.11 piece rate; 78% of capacity; union wants 60 seconds with joint review; 4.6 million tins output | analysis_max_2: full capacity planning improves with standard times; imposition risks stoppages and quality shortcuts | evaluation_max_2: weighs productivity gain against morale and union conflict

  Qb [4 marks]

Reason 2: It creates a sense of ownership across the firm [k], because all 54 staff, from 48 assemblers to 6 office staff, would receive roughly $889 each [app].

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Brightstead Superstores might introduce the piece rate for warehouse pickers.

Reason 2: It could help cut labour turnover [k], easing the 28% turnover that leaves $3,100 a month of replacement and refund costs [app].
    Keywords: piece rate, $0.11, 800 items, $440, 28%, $3,100, warehouse pickers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: pay linked to output encourages effort; helps reduce labour turnover | application_max_2: 800 items per shift; $440 a week; 28% turnover; $3,100 a month

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Brightstead Superstores of keeping the time rate and adding the weekly accuracy bonus.

Benefit 2: Cautious, accurate pickers keep a stable income [k], because $11.50 per hour is guaranteed on a 38-hour week with an extra $40 weekly team bonus only above 97% accuracy [app], which should lift morale and hold turnover below 20% [an].
    Keywords: time rate, $11.50, $40, 97%, 6%, $3,100, order error rate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rewards quality and accuracy, not just speed; income security maintains morale | application_max_2: 6% error rate; $3,100 a month; $11.50 per hour; $40 weekly team bonus; 97% accuracy | analysis_max_2: fewer errors reduce refund and replacement costs; secure pay plus bonus supports morale and retention

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brightstead Superstores should replace the time rate with a piece rate for warehouse pickers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching links pay to output [k]; at $0.11 per item an average picker earns about $440 a week, matching the current $437 time rate [app], so fast pickers are rewarded and productivity should rise [an]. However, piece rate can encourage rushing [k]; with errors already at 6% and costing $3,100 a month, paying per item could push accuracy below the 97% the bonus scheme demands [app], increasing refunds and damaging customer trust [an]. Overall, Brightstead should keep the time rate and add the $40 team bonus instead [eval], because online grocery fulfilment depends on correct orders, not just fast ones [eval].
    Keywords: piece rate, $0.11, $440, $437, 97%, 6%, $3,100, $40 weekly team bonus
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: piece rate rewards output speed; piece rate risks poor quality and rushing | application_max_2: $0.11 per item; $440 a week; $437; 6%; $3,100 a month | analysis_max_2: output-linked pay should raise picker productivity; rushing increases errors, refunds and customer harm | evaluation_max_2: weighs higher output against order accuracy and fulfilment quality

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Casa Verde Restaurants might replace the fixed Christmas bonus with a profit-sharing scheme.
    Answer: Reason 1: Profit sharing links rewards to business performance [k], so staff have an incentive to control costs and grow profit beyond $240,000 [app]. Reason 2: It makes the reward affordable in weak years [k], because the pool is 20% of profit rather than a guaranteed $47,500 cost [app].
    Keywords: profit-sharing scheme, 20%, $240,000, $47,500, $48,000, 190 full-time staff, fixed Christmas bonus
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: links pay to business performance; variable cost adjusts to profitability | application_max_2: $240,000 profit; 20% of profit; $47,500

  Qc [6 marks]

Benefit 2: It feels fair across roles [k], because waiting staff and chefs receive the same $250 rather than a share diluted by seniority or hours [app], supporting goodwill and teamwork during the busiest season [an].
    Keywords: Christmas bonus, $250, 190, $47,500, waiting staff, guaranteed
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guaranteed income for employees; equal treatment across roles | application_max_2: $250; 190 staff; waiting staff and chefs | analysis_max_2: certainty helps winter budgeting; equal pay supports goodwill in peak season

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Casa Verde Restaurants should replace the fixed Christmas bonus with a profit-sharing scheme? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Profit sharing aligns everyone with profit [k]; this year 20% of $240,000 would pay $48,000, slightly more than the $47,500 fixed bonus [app], and if profit reached $300,000 the pool would rise to $60,000, rewarding strong performance [an]. However, staff prefer certainty [k]; in a weak year with little profit, 190 employees could receive nothing instead of $250 each [app], demoralising the waiting staff who already earn modest tips [an]. Overall, Casa Verde should switch to profit sharing [eval], because it caps costs at 20% of profit and turns rewards into a shared performance goal, provided staff are shown how their actions cut waste [eval].

He is weighing two rewards for the 12 senior employees: a share ownership scheme gifting 4% of company shares, vesting over 5 years, worth about $15,000 per person at today's valuation, or a one-off cash bonus of $3,000 each, costing $36,000. The senior managers favour the shares; the supervisors are unsure which reward they would prefer.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'share ownership'.
    Answer: A financial reward where employees are given or sold shares in the business, making them part-owners entitled to dividends and any rise in share value [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: employees receive shares in the business; gain dividends and share-value growth

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Ashbourne Home & DIY might introduce the share ownership scheme for senior staff.
    Answer: Reason 1: Shares tie senior staff to long-term performance [k], since the 4% stake vests over 5 years, so managers gain only if the company keeps growing in value beyond $4.5 million [app]. Reason 2: It defends leadership talent against the national chain [k], because $15,000 per person in shares is a stronger reason to stay than a one-off $3,000 bonus [app].
    Keywords: share ownership, 4%, 5 years, $4.5 million, $15,000, $3,000, national chain
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: long-term performance alignment; retention of key staff vs competitors | application_max_2: 4% stake vests over 5 years; $4.5 million; $15,000 per person; $3,000 bonus

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of the share ownership scheme over the one-off bonus for Ashbourne.
    Answer: Benefit 1: It builds genuine part-ownership thinking [k], because senior staff would hold a 4% stake worth about $15,000 each at today's $4.5 million valuation [app], making them care about profit of $520,000 and how it grows [an]. Benefit 2: It costs no immediate cash [k], unlike the $36,000 bonus paid from wages or savings now [app], preserving cash as the national chain prepares its June opening [an].
    Keywords: share ownership, 4%, $15,000, $4.5 million, $520,000, $36,000, June
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ownership mindset improves decisions; no immediate cash outflow | application_max_2: 4% stake; $15,000; $4.5 million; $520,000; $36,000 bonus | analysis_max_2: owners-in-waiting manage profit carefully; cash preserved ahead of competitive threat

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ashbourne Home & DIY should introduce the share ownership scheme rather than pay the one-off $3,000 bonus? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Share ownership secures long-term commitment [k]; gifting 4% of shares vesting over 5 years, worth about $15,000 per senior manager versus $3,000 cash now [app], should keep all 12 leaders loyal past the national chain's June opening [an]. However, shares carry risk [k]; if profit falls from $520,000 after the opening, the $4.5 million valuation could drop, making the $15,000 worth less than it appears [app], and younger supervisors may prefer cash today [an]. Overall, Ashbourne should introduce the share ownership scheme [eval], because it is the deeper motivator for retention, provided vesting over 5 years is explained clearly to the unsure supervisors [eval].
    Keywords: share ownership, 4%, 5 years, $15,000, $3,000, $4.5 million, June, 12 senior
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: shares retain key staff long term; share value can fall, reducing reward | application_max_2: 4%; 5 years; $15,000; $3,000; $520,000; $4.5 million | analysis_max_2: vesting period locks in loyalty beyond the June threat; valuation risk may weaken the reward | evaluation_max_2: weighs long-term retention value against immediate reward certainty

--- STEM ---
Amberfold Day Spa is a premium spa and beauty salon in Country X employing 27 staff in total, including 15 therapists paid $12.60 per hour on 25-hour weeks. Client retention stands at 72% across the last year and no therapist has been promoted in 3 years, and several experienced therapists have resigned to work at upmarket spas in the capital city.

Owner Ines Barbosa is choosing between two rewards to retain her team. Option A is $9,600 a year of off-the-job training in new treatments, plus a promotion path to senior therapist at $14.20 per hour, with 4 senior posts expected within 18 months. Option B is an across-the-board 6% pay rise for the 15 therapists, costing about $14,700 a year. Both options cost under $15,000 annually.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'training'.
    Answer: The process of teaching employees the skills, knowledge and behaviours they need to carry out their jobs effectively, so performance improves [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: teaching skills, knowledge or behaviours; aimed at improving job performance

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Amberfold Day Spa might choose Option A, the training and promotion path.
    Answer: Reason 1: Off-the-job training widens therapists' skills [k], letting the spa offer new treatments that support the current 72% client retention [app]. Reason 2: A promotion path motivates ambitious staff [k], creating 4 senior posts at $14.20 per hour within 18 months instead of a flat $14,700 pay rise across the board [app].
    Keywords: off-the-job training, 72%, 4 senior posts, $14.20, $9,600, senior therapist, Option A
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: training widens service offer and skills; promotion prospects motivate ambitious staff | application_max_2: 72% client retention; 4 senior posts; $14.20 per hour; $14,700

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the 6% pay rise for the 15 therapists.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Every therapist gains immediately [k], because 6% on $12.60 per hour raises base pay for all 15 on 25-hour weeks, not just the 4 promoted to senior posts [app], feeling fair and transparent [an]. Benefit 2: It is simple to administer [k], costing about $14,700 a year with no courses to schedule or cover staffing for training days [app], avoiding disruption to client bookings [an].
    Keywords: 6% pay rise, $12.60, 15 therapists, 25-hour weeks, $14,700, Option B
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: equal benefit for all therapists; simple to administer and apply | application_max_2: 6%; $12.60 per hour; 15 therapists; 25-hour weeks; about $14,700 a year | analysis_max_2: fairness spreads morale across the whole team; no cover or scheduling disruption needed

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Amberfold Day Spa should fund the training and promotion path rather than the 6% pay rise? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A builds lasting capability [k]; $9,600 of off-the-job training plus 4 senior posts at $14.20 per hour within 18 months gives therapists growth and the spa a deeper skill base for the 72% returning clients [app], lifting service quality and retention [an]. However, a pay rise is felt by all now [k]; the $14,700 option reaches all 15 therapists at once, whereas only 4 gain promotion and others wait [app], which may demotivate those overlooked [an]. Overall, Amberfold should fund the training and promotion path [eval], because skills and careers motivate more deeply than a one-off raise, with a pay review after 18 months if retention stalls [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $9,600, $14.20, 72%, $14,700, 18 months, promotion path
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: training and promotion build long-term motivation; pay rise benefits all immediately | application_max_2: $9,600; 4 senior posts; $14.20; 72%; $14,700; 15 therapists | analysis_max_2: skills deepen service quality and repeat custom; instant fair pay avoids leaving anyone out | evaluation_max_2: weighs deep, career-based motivation against broad, immediate reward

--- STEM ---
Brewhurst Bottling Co is a private limited company in the port town of Carrick, Country X, bottling craft soft drinks for 90 supermarket customers. It employs 74 staff: 64 bottling operatives in 8 teams of 8, 8 supervisors, 1 general manager and 1 office manager. Output reached 1.5 million bottles last year across 2 production shifts.

The board is reviewing the company's span of control. Supervisors currently manage 8 operatives each, and quality checks take 3 hours a day per line. Directors propose widening the span to 12 operatives per supervisor and removing 2 supervisors, saving $58,000 a year in wages (2 x $29,000). However, a March trial lifted output per shift by only 4% while customer complaints doubled from 11 to 22 a month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'span of control'.
    Answer: Span of control is the number of subordinates that one manager is directly responsible for, such as Brewhurst's 8 supervisors each managing 8 bottling operatives. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Span of control = number of subordinates reporting directly to one manager; Can be wide (many staff per manager) or narrow (few staff per manager)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Brewhurst Bottling Co of widening the span of control to 12 operatives per supervisor.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A wider span of control means each supervisor manages more operatives, so fewer supervisors are needed [k]. Removing 2 supervisors would save $58,000 a year in wages (2 x $29,000) [app]. Benefit 2: Fewer supervisors can speed up communication between directors and operatives [k]. The March trial lifted output per shift by 4%, suggesting operatives can work well with less direct supervision [app].
    Keywords: Brewhurst Bottling Co, $58,000, 12 operatives per supervisor, 64 bottling operatives, output per shift, 4%, 2 supervisors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Wider span of control = more subordinates per manager, fewer managers needed overall; Fewer managers can reduce wage costs and speed up communication | application_max_2: Saving $58,000 a year by removing 2 supervisors (2 x $29,000); March trial raised output per shift by 4%; 64 operatives would be covered by fewer supervisors at 12 each

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks for Brewhurst of widening the span of control to 12 operatives per supervisor.
    Answer: Drawback 1: Supervisors with more operatives to oversee have less time to monitor each one [k]. Quality checks already take 3 hours a day per line, so spreading one supervisor over 12 operatives could stretch supervision even further [app]. Weaker supervision may let defects reach dispatch, damaging relationships with the 90 supermarket customers [an]. Drawback 2: A wider span of control can leave operatives without enough support or guidance [k]. Customer complaints doubled from 11 to 22 a month during the March trial [app]. Rising complaints could mean more returns and penalty charges, wiping out the $58,000 wage saving [an].
    Keywords: Brewhurst Bottling Co, 3 hours a day, 11 to 22, 90 supermarket customers, $58,000, 12 operatives, March trial
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Wider span gives each subordinate less supervision and support; Supervisors may become overloaded, so guidance and discipline weaken | application_max_2: Quality checks already take 3 hours a day per line; proposal is 12 operatives per supervisor; Complaints doubled from 11 to 22 a month during the March trial; 90 supermarket customers | analysis_max_2: Less supervision raises the risk of defects reaching customers, harming supermarket relationships; Complaint and return costs could exceed the $58,000 wage saving

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brewhurst should widen the span of control to 12 operatives per supervisor rather than keep 8 operatives each? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for widening: a wider span of control cuts the number of supervisors Brewhurst needs [k]. Removing 2 supervisors would save $58,000 a year in wages (2 x $29,000), and the March trial lifted output per shift by 4% with 64 bottling operatives working in teams [app]. Lower wage costs would raise profit on 1.5 million bottles a year, helping Brewhurst price competitively for its 90 supermarket customers [an]. Argument for keeping 8 supervisors: the current narrow span lets supervisors monitor quality checks that take 3 hours a day per line [k]. The March trial doubled complaints from 11 to 22 a month while output rose only 4%, showing operatives may need closer supervision [app]. Wider spans could overload supervisors, harm quality and lose supermarket contracts that depend on reliable supply [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Brewhurst should not widen the span yet, because complaints doubling to 22 a month and only a 4% output gain outweigh the $58,000 saving; it should fix the causes of complaints first [eval]. If complaint and quality data improve over the next 3 months, widening the span could then be reconsidered [eval].
    Keywords: Brewhurst Bottling Co, $58,000, 12 operatives per supervisor, 11 to 22, 4%, 90 supermarket customers, 3 hours a day, 8 operatives each
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Wider span reduces manager numbers and wage costs; Narrower span allows closer supervision and support | application_max_2: $58,000 yearly saving from removing 2 supervisors (2 x $29,000); March trial output per shift up only 4%; Quality checks take 3 hours a day per line; complaints doubled from 11 to 22 a month | analysis_max_2: Lower wages raise per-bottle profit and competitive pricing across 1.5 million bottles; Overloaded supervisors could damage quality and lose supermarket contracts | evaluation_max_2: Recommendation not to widen yet, tied to the 22 complaints per month and the 4% gain; Conditional reconsideration if complaint and quality data improve over 3 months

--- STEM ---
Hallowmere Furniture Co is a private limited company in the market town of Brantwell, Country X, making oak dining furniture for 35 furniture retailers. It employs 84 people across design, cutting, assembly and finishing. Orders pass through 5 management levels, from workshop floor to managing director, before any price change or material substitution is approved.

Last year the company lost 14 orders worth $96,000 because quotes took 9 days to approve. Managing director Ruth Ellison proposes shortening the chain of command so department heads can approve quotes up to $4,000 without director sign-off. The sales manager supports this, but 2 senior managers warn that junior staff could approve underpriced work and that rushed sign-off might raise material waste, already 7% of timber.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'chain of command'.
    Answer: Chain of command is the line of authority through which orders and decisions pass from senior managers to junior staff, such as Hallowmere's quotes passing through 5 management levels before approval. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Chain of command = line of authority/communication from top to bottom of the hierarchy; Shows who answers to whom and who may give orders

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Hallowmere Furniture Co of its long chain of command.
    Answer: Problem 1: A long chain of command slows down decision-making because every decision passes through many levels [k]. Quotes took 9 days to approve, and the company lost 14 orders worth $96,000 last year [app]. Problem 2: A long chain of command can distort messages as they travel down or up the levels [k]. Orders pass through 5 management levels before approval, so instructions may arrive late or changed [app].
    Keywords: Hallowmere Furniture Co, 5 management levels, 9 days, $96,000, 14 orders, 35 furniture retailers, $4,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Long chains slow decision-making and approvals; Messages can be distorted or delayed as they pass through levels | application_max_2: Quotes took 9 days to approve; 14 orders worth $96,000 lost last year; 5 management levels from workshop floor to managing director

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Hallowmere of shortening the chain of command so department heads can approve quotes up to $4,000.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Shorter chains of command speed up decisions [k]. Approving quotes up to $4,000 at department level would cut the 9-day approval time and help save some of the 14 lost orders worth $96,000 [app]. Faster quotes would help Hallowmere win more repeat orders from its 35 furniture retailers before rivals respond [an]. Benefit 2: Shortening the chain gives department heads more responsibility [k]. Releasing routine decisions up to $4,000 lets the managing director focus on larger contracts and strategy [app]. Senior staff would build judgement and motivation, providing cover when directors are absent [an].
    Keywords: Hallowmere Furniture Co, $4,000, 9 days, $96,000, 14 orders, 35 furniture retailers, managing director
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Shorter chains speed up decisions and approvals; Delegating routine authority develops junior managers and frees senior time | application_max_2: Quotes took 9 days; 14 orders worth $96,000 lost last year; Department heads could approve quotes up to $4,000 without director sign-off | analysis_max_2: Faster quotes protect repeat orders from the 35 furniture retailers; Delegated responsibility develops staff and frees the managing director for strategy

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hallowmere should shorten the chain of command rather than keep director sign-off for all quotes? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for shortening: shortening the chain of command speeds up decisions [k]. Letting department heads approve quotes up to $4,000 would cut the 9-day approval time that cost Hallowmere 14 orders worth $96,000 last year [app]. Faster approvals would protect revenue from the 35 furniture retailers and sharpen competitiveness [an]. Argument for keeping sign-off: keeping director sign-off protects against underpriced work [k]. The 2 senior managers warn that junior staff could approve below-cost quotes, and material waste already stands at 7% of timber [app]. Mistakes at department level could erode profit faster than the time saved wins new orders [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Hallowmere should shorten the chain for quotes up to $4,000 only, because the $96,000 lost orders and 9-day delays are proven costs, while the risk can be managed with a minimum price list and weekly checks [eval]. If waste or underpricing rises after the change, the limit should be lowered or director sign-off restored [eval].
    Keywords: Hallowmere Furniture Co, $4,000, 9 days, 14 orders, $96,000, 7% of timber, 2 senior managers, 35 furniture retailers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Short chains speed decisions; long chains give control and consistency; Delegated limits must be controlled to prevent underpricing | application_max_2: $4,000 approval limit; 9-day approval time; 14 orders worth $96,000 lost; 2 senior managers' warning; material waste already 7% of timber; 35 furniture retailers | analysis_max_2: Faster quotes protect revenue and competitiveness with retailers; Underpricing or waste at department level could outweigh the time savings | evaluation_max_2: Recommends shortening only for quotes up to $4,000, with price-list floor and weekly checks; Conditional reversal if waste or underpricing rises after the change
