--- STEM ---
Wexmoor Care Homes Ltd runs 6 residential care homes in Country X, employing 240 carers, 9 care managers and a head of care. Each home has just 2 management levels below the head of care, with an average of 27 staff per manager. Annual carer turnover has risen to 26%, and 41% of leavers in exit surveys cited 'no career progression'.

The board is debating the hierarchy. Option one creates a senior carer grade, adding a third level and a promotion path for 36 experienced carers at $2,400 a year extra each, costing $86,400 a year. Option two keeps 2 levels and gives all carers a 4% pay rise costing $151,000 a year. The head of care argues promotion paths matter more to retention than flat pay.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'hierarchy'.
    Answer: Hierarchy is the levels of authority and responsibility in a business, from senior managers at the top to junior staff at the bottom, such as Wexmoor's carers reporting through care managers to the head of care. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Hierarchy = levels of authority/responsibility in an organisation; Staff at higher levels hold more authority over those below

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why a clear hierarchy is important to Wexmoor Care Homes Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: A hierarchy clarifies who is responsible for what [k]. Wexmoor's 240 carers report through 9 care managers to one head of care, so each home knows its lines of authority [app]. Reason 2: A hierarchy should give staff a promotion path [k]. With only 2 management levels, 41% of leavers cited no career progression, so clearer levels could help retain carers [app].
    Keywords: Wexmoor Care Homes Ltd, 240 carers, 9 care managers, head of care, 41% of leavers, 2 management levels, 26%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Hierarchy defines responsibilities and lines of authority; Hierarchy provides promotion paths that aid retention and motivation | application_max_2: 240 carers report through 9 care managers to one head of care across 6 homes; Only 2 management levels; 41% of leavers cited no career progression

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of adding a third level (senior carer grade) to Wexmoor's hierarchy.
    Answer: Drawback 1: Adding a level lengthens the chain of command and can slow decisions [k]. A third level would sit between the 240 carers and the head of care, adding another step for approvals and information to travel [app]. Longer lines could delay responses to care-home incidents where minutes matter [an]. Drawback 2: A new grade raises payroll costs [k]. The senior carer grade would cost $86,400 a year (36 experienced carers at $2,400 extra each) [app]. If the grade does not cut the 26% turnover, Wexmoor would carry higher wages without the promised savings [an].
    Keywords: Wexmoor Care Homes Ltd, third level, $86,400 a year, 36 experienced carers, 240 carers, $2,400, 26%, head of care
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Extra levels lengthen the chain of command and slow decisions; Extra levels add management cost and may narrow spans further | application_max_2: A third level would sit between 240 carers and the head of care; $86,400 a year for 36 experienced carers at $2,400 extra each | analysis_max_2: Longer decision lines could delay urgent care responses, risking resident safety; If turnover stays at 26%, the $86,400 grade cost is paid without retention benefits

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wexmoor should create the senior carer grade rather than give all carers a 4% pay rise? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for the senior carer grade: it adds a third level to the hierarchy and creates a visible promotion path [k]. 36 experienced carers would gain $2,400 a year extra each, costing $86,400 a year, and 41% of leavers cited no career progression as the reason for leaving [app]. A targeted grade could lift retention of the most skilled carers and protect care quality [an]. Argument for the 4% pay rise: it rewards all carers fairly rather than a chosen few [k]. The 4% rise across 240 carers costs $151,000 a year, nearly double the grade's $86,400, but it avoids resentment among carers passed over for senior posts [app]. However, a flat rise does not fix the missing progression that drives leavers, so turnover may stay near 26% [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Wexmoor should create the senior carer grade because 41% of leavers point to missing progression and $86,400 a year is cheaper than $151,000; it should be paired with clear selection criteria to limit resentment [eval]. If turnover does not fall within a year, the 4% rise for all carers should be reconsidered [eval].
    Keywords: Wexmoor Care Homes Ltd, senior carer grade, $86,400, $151,000, 41% of leavers, 240 carers, 26%, $2,400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A promotion grade motivates and retains high performers; A flat pay rise rewards everyone equally but may ignore progression needs | application_max_2: $2,400 extra each for 36 experienced carers = $86,400 a year; 4% rise for 240 carers costs $151,000 a year; 41% of leavers cite no career progression; turnover 26% | analysis_max_2: Targeted grade tackles the stated reason for leaving and should lift retention; Flat rise is costlier and may not fix progression, so turnover could persist | evaluation_max_2: Recommends the senior carer grade at $86,400 a year, with clear selection criteria; Reconsider the 4% rise if turnover does not fall within a year

If complaint levels rise after flattening, some supervisory posts should be reinstated [eval].
    Keywords: Ravenglass Retail Co, $780,000, $21m, 3 levels, 6 levels, about 25, about 7, 2 store managers

--- STEM ---
Redharrow Engineering Ltd is a steel fabrication business in the industrial town of Corvessa, Country X, employing 160 staff across cutting, welding and painting at 3 sites. It has a tall hierarchy of 7 levels with 4 middle management layers between the managing director and the shop floor. Each team leader manages 7 operatives. Last year revenue was $14m and profit was $1.1m.

The board proposes delayering, removing 2 middle management layers, a production manager and 2 shift supervisors per site, 9 posts in total, saving $342,000 a year. Span of control would widen to 14 operatives per team leader. Output targets would pass directly from directors to team leaders. The managing director warns that delayering may overload team leaders, and 2 of them have already asked for clearer written targets.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'delayering'.
    Answer: Delayering is the removal of one or more levels of management from a hierarchy to create a flatter structure, such as Redharrow removing a production manager and 2 shift supervisors per site. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delayering = removing levels/layers of management from the hierarchy; Creates a flatter structure with wider spans of control

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Redharrow Engineering Ltd is considering delayering.
    Answer: Reason 1: Delayering reduces the cost of management layers [k]. Removing 9 posts would save $342,000 a year from the cost of running the 7-level hierarchy [app]. Reason 2: Delayering shortens the chain of command so decisions reach the shop floor faster [k]. Output targets would pass directly from directors to team leaders, bypassing the 4 middle management layers [app].
    Keywords: Redharrow Engineering Ltd, $342,000 a year, 9 posts, 7 levels, 4 middle management layers, team leaders, $14m
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delayering cuts management/salary costs; Delayering shortens the chain of command and speeds decisions | application_max_2: 9 posts removed would save $342,000 a year; Output targets would pass directly from directors to team leaders; 4 middle layers bypassed

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of delayering for Redharrow Engineering Ltd.
    Answer: Drawback 1: Delayering widens spans of control and can overload team leaders [k]. Each team leader would manage 14 operatives instead of 7 across cutting, welding and painting at 3 sites [app]. Overloaded leaders may miss safety and quality checks, risking rework and accidents on steel lines [an]. Drawback 2: Delayering removes experienced managers and their knowledge [k]. The 9 removed posts include production managers and shift supervisors whose site know-how would be lost [app]. Losing that experience could slow problem-solving on urgent orders and raise costly errors [an].
    Keywords: Redharrow Engineering Ltd, 14 operatives per team leader, 9 posts, 3 sites, team leaders, 2 shift supervisors per site, $1.1m
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delayering widens spans of control and can overload managers; Delayering loses experienced management knowledge and can damage morale | application_max_2: Span would widen from 7 to 14 operatives per team leader; 9 posts removed: a production manager and 2 shift supervisors per site across 3 sites | analysis_max_2: Overloaded leaders may miss safety/quality checks, causing rework and accidents; Loss of site know-how could slow problem-solving and raise errors

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redharrow should delayer by removing the 2 middle layers rather than keep the current 7-level hierarchy? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for delayering: delayering removes costly management layers [k]. Removing 9 posts would save $342,000 a year, lifting profit from $1.1m on $14m of revenue [app]. Shorter chains of command would let output targets pass directly from directors to team leaders, speeding response to order changes [an]. Argument against delayering: delayering widens spans and can overload leaders [k]. Team leaders would manage 14 operatives instead of 7, and 2 of them have already asked for clearer written targets [app]. Without clearer targets and support, safety and quality could fall on steel lines, costing more than the $342,000 saving [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Redharrow should delayer, because the $342,000 yearly saving is significant against $1.1m profit, but only with written targets, training and phased removal of the layers [eval]. If team leaders cannot cope within 2 quarters, one supervisory layer should be reinstated [eval].
    Keywords: Redharrow Engineering Ltd, $342,000 a year, $1.1m, $14m, 14 operatives, 9 posts, 7 levels, clearer written targets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delayering cuts costs and shortens the chain of command; Delayering widens spans and can overload remaining managers | application_max_2: $342,000 a year saving; profit $1.1m on revenue $14m; 9 posts removed across 3 sites; Span widens from 7 to 14 operatives; 2 team leaders have asked for clearer written targets | analysis_max_2: Saving materially lifts the $1.1m profit and speeds target-setting; Overloaded leaders without clear targets risk safety and quality costs exceeding savings | evaluation_max_2: Recommends delayering with written targets, training and phased removal; Conditional reinstatement of a supervisory layer if leaders cannot cope

Overbrook Farms Ltd is an arable farm outside the market town of Dunwick, Country X, growing wheat and barley on 320 hectares. It employs 18 full-time workers plus 2 mechanics. Owner and managing director Sarah Vane works 70-hour weeks, personally approving every tractor repair, seed order and holiday request. Last year output was worth $2.3m and overtime rose 18% because decisions waited for Sarah.

Sarah must decide whether to delegate routine decisions to farm manager Tom Ilsley, letting him approve repairs up to $1,500 and all holiday requests, or to hire an assistant farm manager at $38,000 a year. Tom has run the machinery fleet for 6 years and passed his management course in March. Workers respect him, but Sarah recalls 2 costly repair mistakes last winter.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'delegation'.
    Answer: Delegation is the passing of authority down the hierarchy to subordinates to perform tasks and make decisions, such as Sarah letting Tom approve repairs up to $1,500 and all holiday requests. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delegation = passing authority/tasks down from manager to subordinate; Subordinate is accountable for the task, manager remains responsible overall

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Sarah of delegating routine decisions to Tom Ilsley.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Delegation frees the manager's time for more important work [k]. Sarah works 70-hour weeks and personally approves every tractor repair, seed order and holiday request, so delegation would cut her workload [app]. Advantage 2: Delegation develops the subordinate's skills and motivation [k]. Tom has run the machinery fleet for 6 years and passed his management course in March, so trusted responsibility would build his judgement and confidence [app].
    Keywords: Overbrook Farms Ltd, 70-hour weeks, Tom Ilsley, $1,500, 6 years, management course, holiday requests
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delegation frees managers to focus on strategic work; Delegation develops and motivates subordinates | application_max_2: Sarah works 70-hour weeks, approving every repair, seed order and holiday request; Tom has 6 years running the fleet and passed his management course in March

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages for the farm of delegating to Tom Ilsley.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: The manager remains accountable for mistakes made by the subordinate [k]. Sarah recalls 2 costly repair mistakes last winter, so handing Tom repair sign-off up to $1,500 carries real financial risk [app]. A repeat mistake on a $1,500 repair could escalate into crop losses at the height of the season [an]. Disadvantage 2: Delegation can fail if the subordinate is not ready or supported [k]. Tom has passed his management course, but approving repairs across a $2.3m output still demands judgement under cost pressure [app]. Poor decisions could push overtime, already up 18%, even higher as errors are fixed late [an].
    Keywords: Overbrook Farms Ltd, 2 costly repair mistakes, $1,500, $2.3m, 18%, Tom Ilsley, management course
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delegator remains accountable for subordinates' mistakes; Delegation may fail without the right skills, support and limits | application_max_2: 2 costly repair mistakes last winter; repairs delegated up to $1,500; Output worth $2.3m; overtime rose 18%; Tom passed his management course in March | analysis_max_2: A repeat repair mistake could escalate into crop losses at peak season; Poor decisions could push overtime above the existing 18% rise as errors are corrected

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sarah should delegate routine decisions to Tom Ilsley rather than hire an assistant farm manager at $38,000 a year? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for delegating to Tom: delegation passes authority to a trusted subordinate at no wage cost [k]. Tom has run the machinery fleet for 6 years and passed his management course in March, and Sarah works 70-hour weeks with decisions waited on her [app]. Delegating repairs up to $1,500 and holiday requests would cut her workload and rebuild Tom's motivation without the $38,000 salary [an]. Argument for hiring an assistant: an assistant farm manager adds extra capacity rather than stretching existing staff [k]. Hiring at $38,000 a year would bring in fresh judgement while Tom keeps handling the machinery fleet he knows [app]. However, hiring raises fixed costs on output worth $2.3m, and 2 costly repair mistakes last winter suggest Sarah's approval bottleneck, not Tom's competence, is the real problem [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Sarah should delegate to Tom, because his 6 years of fleet experience and March management course make him ready, and $38,000 a year is better spent only if delegation fails [eval]. If Tom makes costly errors beyond $1,500 or turnover rises among the 18 full-time workers, she should reconsider the hire [eval].
    Keywords: Overbrook Farms Ltd, Tom Ilsley, $1,500, $38,000 a year, 6 years, 70-hour weeks, 18%, $2.3m
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delegation empowers existing trusted staff at little cost; Hiring adds capacity but raises fixed wage costs | application_max_2: Tom: 6 years on the machinery fleet, passed his management course in March; repairs up to $1,500; Assistant manager $38,000 a year; Sarah works 70-hour weeks; overtime rose 18% | analysis_max_2: Delegation cuts Sarah's workload and costs nothing beyond current wages; Hiring adds judgement and capacity but raises fixed costs on $2.3m output | evaluation_max_2: Recommends delegating to Tom based on his experience and course, with $38,000 held in reserve; Reconsider hiring if Tom errs above $1,500 or worker turnover rises

--- STEM ---
Westmoor Bus Co is a private limited company running 14 coach routes between 5 towns in Country X. It employs 96 drivers and 12 office staff, carrying 1.9 million passengers a year. A new route to the coastal resort of Pelwyke starts in June. The operations manager, Dale Mercer, usually allocates drivers and vehicles on the morning of each shift.

Last month, 22 services ran late or were cancelled because no spare driver had been scheduled, and 3 corporate clients warned they would switch suppliers unless punctuality rose above 90%. Dale argues that planning routes months ahead is impossible in this business. The board must decide whether to introduce a quarterly planning system covering driver rotas, vehicle servicing and Pelwyke timetables, costing $27,000 to set up, or to keep day-to-day allocation.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'planning' as a role of management.
    Answer: Planning is setting objectives and deciding in advance how to achieve them, such as Westmoor deciding its June Pelwyke timetables, driver rotas and vehicle servicing ahead of the new route. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Planning = setting objectives and deciding how to achieve them in advance; Involves forecasting, target-setting and preparing resources before action

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why planning is important to Westmoor Bus Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: Planning ensures enough resources are available when needed [k]. Last month 22 services ran late or were cancelled because no spare driver had been scheduled [app]. Reason 2: Planning sets targets that guide the business and measure performance [k]. 3 corporate clients warned they would switch unless punctuality rose above 90%, a target only planning can deliver [app].
    Keywords: Westmoor Bus Co, 22 services, 90%, 3 corporate clients, Pelwyke, 96 drivers, 14 coach routes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Planning ensures resources are ready when needed; Planning sets targets and direction for the business | application_max_2: 22 services late or cancelled last month for lack of scheduled spare drivers; 96 drivers; 3 corporate clients demanding punctuality above 90%; Pelwyke route starts in June

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Westmoor of introducing the quarterly planning system costing $27,000.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Planning ahead prevents resource shortfalls and costly disruption [k]. A quarterly system covering driver rotas, vehicle servicing and Pelwyke timetables would avoid repeats of the 22 services that ran late or were cancelled last month [app]. Fewer cancellations would protect revenue from 1.9 million passengers a year [an]. Benefit 2: Planning builds client confidence and protects contracts [k]. Meeting the 90% punctuality threshold the 3 corporate clients demand would secure their repeat business [app]. Retaining those contracts stabilises income and supports the June Pelwyke launch [an].
    Keywords: Westmoor Bus Co, $27,000, 22 services, 90%, 1.9 million passengers, 3 corporate clients, Pelwyke, driver rotas
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Planning prevents shortfalls and disruption; Planning builds reliability, trust and contract retention | application_max_2: Quarterly system covers driver rotas, vehicle servicing and Pelwyke timetables; setup cost $27,000; 22 late or cancelled services last month; 90% punctuality demanded by 3 corporate clients | analysis_max_2: Avoiding cancellations protects revenue from 1.9 million passengers a year; Meeting the 90% threshold retains corporate contracts and stabilises income

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Westmoor should introduce the quarterly planning system rather than keep day-to-day allocation? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for the planning system: planning means deciding in advance how to achieve objectives [k]. However, flexibility has already produced 22 failures in one month, and 3 clients are ready to switch suppliers, so the current approach is visibly failing [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Westmoor should introduce the quarterly planning system because 22 failures and the 90% client ultimatum show that day-to-day allocation is not working, and $27,000 is a small price against losing 3 corporate contracts [eval]. If the system proves too rigid or costly after 2 quarters, it should be adjusted rather than abandoned [eval].
    Keywords: Westmoor Bus Co, $27,000, 22, 90%, 3 corporate clients, 14 coach routes, 1.9 million passengers, Pelwyke
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Planning = deciding in advance how to achieve objectives; Day-to-day allocation is flexible but reactive and unplanned | application_max_2: $27,000 setup cost; covers driver rotas, vehicle servicing, Pelwyke timetables; 22 late or cancelled services last month; 3 corporate clients demanding 90% punctuality; 14 routes; 1.9 million passengers a year | analysis_max_2: Fewer cancellations protect passenger revenue and corporate contracts; Day-to-day allocation is failing, as shown by 22 failures and client ultimatums | evaluation_max_2: Recommends introducing the system, weighing $27,000 against losing 3 contracts; Adjust rather than abandon if the system proves too rigid after 2 quarters

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Organising matches resources to tasks and deadlines; Organising avoids clashes and protects existing commitments | application_max_2: Only 4 CNC machines, all booked solid for 8 weeks; 3 urgent orders worth $1.4m due in 6 weeks; 40 existing engineering firm customers must not be disrupted

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying adds permanent capacity and asset ownership; Owning capacity reduces dependency on outsiders/competitors | application_max_2: $210,000 used machine vs $18,000 a month rival hire ($54,000 over 3 months); 3 urgent orders worth $1.4m; 4 CNC machines currently booked solid; 40 engineering firm customers | analysis_max_2: Extra capacity lets Pembroke chase further urgent orders, raising long-term revenue; In-house work protects confidentiality and quality versus outsourcing to a rival

  Qd [8 marks]

Glenmore Dairy Co is a private limited company in Country X making fresh milk and yoghurt for 9 supermarket chains. General manager Ravi Menon leads 46 employees across pasteurising, packing and quality control, processing 18,500 litres of milk a day. Last year revenue reached $1.32 million. Ravi uses a democratic leadership style: a works council meets every Friday and staff ideas shaped last year's new yoghurt flavour, which lifted sales by 12%.

Glenmore has just won a contract requiring 22,000 litres a day from January, needing a new pasteuriser costing $85,000. The launch schedule allows only 6 weeks. Ravi is weighing a switch to autocratic leadership so he can impose decisions quickly, or keeping the democratic style workers are used to despite slower meetings.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'autocratic leadership'.
    Answer: Autocratic leadership is a style of leadership where the leader makes decisions alone without consulting employees and issues clear, direct instructions that staff are expected to follow. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Leader makes decisions alone/without consulting employees; Clear one-way instructions/close control of subordinates

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of a democratic leadership style for Glenmore Dairy Co.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Democratic leadership involves employees in decision-making, so employee ideas are used [k]; Glenmore staff suggested the new yoghurt flavour, which lifted sales by 12% [app]. Advantage 2: Employees who are consulted often feel valued, raising morale and motivation [k]; the Friday works council keeps 46 employees engaged in daily operations [app].
    Keywords: Glenmore Dairy Co, every Friday, new yoghurt flavour, 12%, 46 employees, 18,500 litres, works council
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Employees are involved in/consulted about decisions; Involvement can raise motivation/morale/commitment | application_max_2: Staff-suggested new yoghurt flavour lifted sales by 12%; Friday works council keeps 46 employees engaged

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of Glenmore Dairy Co switching to an autocratic leadership style.
    Answer: Problem 1: Autocratic leaders decide alone, so employees lose influence over decisions affecting their work [k]; Ravi's Friday works council, where the 46 employees currently influence decisions, would be pushed aside [app], which could lower morale and cause staff to resist the change [an]. Problem 2: Decisions made without consultation ignore useful employee input [k]; staff knowledge of pasteurising and packing shaped the yoghurt flavour that raised sales [app], so ignoring it risks weaker decisions on the new line and delays the ramp-up to 22,000 litres a day [an].
    Keywords: Glenmore Dairy Co, every Friday, yoghurt flavour, 22,000 litres, 46 employees, $85,000, pasteurising
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Autocratic style means the leader decides alone/little employee input; Consultation brings useful employee knowledge/ideas | application_max_2: Friday works council where 46 employees influence decisions; Staff knowledge of pasteurising and packing shaped the yoghurt flavour | analysis_max_2: Lower morale, resistance to change, possible higher labour turnover; Weaker decisions/delays in ramping up to 22,000 litres a day

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ravi should switch Glenmore Dairy Co to autocratic leadership for the new contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One reason for switching is speed: autocratic leadership means the leader decides alone and issues direct instructions [k]; the new contract requires 22,000 litres a day within 6 weeks and a pasteuriser costing $85,000, so fast unquestioned decisions could keep the launch on schedule [app], reducing the risk of late delivery penalties and protecting the $1.32 million revenue base [an]. However, Glenmore's democratic culture produced the staff-suggested yoghurt flavour, which lifted sales by 12%, and the Friday works council keeps 46 employees committed [k]; sidelining it now could lower motivation just when extra effort is needed for the ramp-up [app], so errors and staff turnover could rise precisely when reliability matters most [an]. On balance, a time-limited use of tighter direction during the 6-week launch makes sense, with democratic consultation restored once running [eval], because permanent autocratic control would damage the culture that made the yoghurt launch successful [eval].
    Keywords: 22,000 litres, $85,000, yoghurt flavour, 12%, every Friday, 46 employees, $1.32 million, 18,500 litres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Autocratic leadership = quick unilateral decisions/direct instructions; Democratic leadership = consultation/employee involvement, stronger commitment | application_max_2: 22,000 litres a day within 6 weeks; pasteuriser costing $85,000; Yoghurt flavour lifted sales by 12%; Friday works council; 46 employees | analysis_max_2: Faster decisions keep launch on schedule/protect contract and revenue; Sidelining consultation risks lower morale, errors and turnover during ramp-up | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (speed of autocratic vs motivational benefits of democratic); Justified recommendation: time-limited autocracy, then return to democratic

--- STEM ---
Cypress Bay Hotel Co is a private limited company in Country X operating a 60-room coastal hotel. General manager Paula Duarte leads 28 staff across reception, housekeeping, kitchen and events, with revenue of $1.05 million last year and a gross profit of $410,000. Paula uses a democratic leadership style, holding a weekly 30-minute briefing where employees raise ideas; staff redesigned the breakfast menu this year, raising sales by 9%.

The events manager has resigned and Paula must choose a replacement. Marco, a reception supervisor, would continue her democratic style with the 6-person events team. An external candidate, Lidia, would use a laissez-faire style, giving the experienced team freedom to run events themselves. The events calendar is fully booked with 14 weddings between May and September, and wedding customers pay $12,000 deposits each.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'democratic leadership'.
    Answer: Democratic leadership is a leadership style where the leader consults employees and involves them in decision-making, using their views before deciding. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Leader consults/involves employees in decisions; Decisions consider employee views before being made

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of democratic leadership for Cypress Bay Hotel Co.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Democratic leaders share decision-making with employees, using their ideas [k]; staff redesigned the breakfast menu, which raised sales by 9% [app]. Advantage 2: Involvement in decisions can improve morale and commitment [k]; the weekly 30-minute briefing keeps Paula's 28 staff engaged across reception, housekeeping, kitchen and events [app].
    Keywords: Cypress Bay Hotel Co, breakfast menu, 9%, 30-minute briefing, 28 staff, democratic, $1.05 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Decisions are shared/employees consulted, so ideas are used; Involvement can raise morale/commitment/motivation | application_max_2: Staff redesigned the breakfast menu, raising sales by 9%; Weekly 30-minute briefing keeps 28 staff engaged

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems a laissez-faire style could cause for Cypress Bay's events team.
    Answer: Problem 1: Laissez-faire leaders give employees freedom with little guidance or support [k]; Lidia would let the 6-person events team run weddings with minimal direction [app], so tasks could be missed during the busy season when 14 weddings overlap [an]. Problem 2: Without regular checking, standards can slip [k]; the team would oversee events where customers pay $12,000 deposits with little supervision [app], raising the risk of complaints or refund demands that cut gross profit [an].
    Keywords: Cypress Bay Hotel Co, 14 weddings, $12,000 deposits, May and September, 6-person events team, laissez-faire, breakfast menu
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire = minimal guidance, full freedom for employees; Little monitoring leads to inconsistent standards | application_max_2: 6-person events team given freedom over weddings; $12,000 deposits at stake with little supervision | analysis_max_2: Missed tasks/delays during overlap of 14 weddings; Complaints/refund demands reducing gross profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Paula should promote Marco, the democratic supervisor, or appoint Lidia, the laissez-faire external candidate, as events manager? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Lidia would give the experienced 6-person events team freedom to manage the 14 weddings themselves [k]; with the calendar booked between May and September and customers paying $12,000 deposits, empowered staff could respond flexibly to each couple's wishes [app], protecting customer satisfaction and repeat business [an]. However, Marco's democratic style matches the hotel's existing culture: Paula's weekly briefing kept 28 staff engaged and staff ideas lifted breakfast sales by 9% [k]; promoting Marco would preserve consistency, and he already knows the weddings schedule and hotel standards [app], avoiding disruption in the busiest trading season [an]. On balance, promoting Marco with an agreed plan to give the events team more autonomy as the season develops is the safer choice [eval], because Lidia's hands-off style risks uneven delivery if any of the 6 staff falls behind on a May wedding [eval].
    Keywords: 14 weddings, $12,000 deposits, May and September, 6-person events team, breakfast menu, 9%, 28 staff, laissez-faire
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire gives autonomy to skilled, experienced staff; Democratic keeps consultation/consistency with existing culture | application_max_2: 14 weddings between May and September; $12,000 deposits; Marco's democratic approach; weekly briefing; breakfast sales up 9%; 28 staff | analysis_max_2: Autonomy improves responsiveness and customer satisfaction; Consistency reduces disruption/errors during peak season | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both candidates/styles; Justified recommendation (promote Marco with phased autonomy)

--- STEM ---
Seaward Printworks is a private limited company in Country X producing marketing brochures, packaging and catalogues for 25 business customers. It is led by production director Omar Haddad, who manages 22 printers and finishers. Output last year was 940,000 printed items, with revenue of $1.28 million and unit costs of $0.86.

Omar has always kept close control of daily schedules. He now employs 5 senior designers who are highly skilled and self-motivated, and they complain that his daily checks slow them down. Omar is deciding whether to move to a laissez-faire style for the design team, letting them set their own deadlines and client meetings, or keep close control until the end of the year, when a $95,000 digital press is installed.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'laissez-faire leadership'.
    Answer: Laissez-faire leadership is a leadership style where the leader gives employees freedom to make their own decisions and organise their own work, with very little supervision or guidance. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Employees given freedom to make decisions/organise their own work; Little supervision/guidance from the leader

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of laissez-faire leadership for Seaward Printworks.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives employees freedom to organise their own work [k]; Seaward's 5 senior designers could set schedules around each client brief instead of waiting for daily checks [app]. Advantage 2: Autonomy can raise motivation and creativity among skilled staff [k]; the designers would have freedom to propose layouts for the brochures and catalogues, where fresh ideas win print contracts [app].
    Keywords: Seaward Printworks, 5 senior designers, brochures, catalogues, laissez-faire, daily checks, $1.28 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Freedom/autonomy to organise own work with minimal supervision; Autonomy can raise motivation/creativity | application_max_2: 5 senior designers could set schedules around client briefs; Design ideas for brochures and catalogues win print contracts

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of Seaward Printworks adopting a laissez-faire style for the design team.
    Answer: Problem 1: Laissez-faire leaders avoid close monitoring, so poor work can go unnoticed [k]; the 5 senior designers could miss deadlines on client jobs without Omar's daily checks [app], leading to late delivery to one of the 25 business customers [an]. Problem 2: Inconsistent standards can reduce quality [k]; with no review before files reach the press, errors could pass into production [app], wasting output and reprints against the $1.28 million revenue [an].
    Keywords: Seaward Printworks, 25 business customers, daily checks, $95,000, digital press, 940,000 printed items, senior designers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire leaders avoid monitoring, so problems go unnoticed; Inconsistent standards reduce quality | application_max_2: 5 senior designers may miss client-job deadlines without daily checks; Errors could pass into production without review | analysis_max_2: Late delivery damages relations with the 25 business customers; Reprints/waste cut revenue of $1.28 million

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Omar should move the design team to laissez-faire working now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Omar should give the design team laissez-faire freedom now because the 5 senior designers are highly skilled and self-motivated [k]; removing daily checks would let them meet client briefs faster and improve the brochures and catalogues behind the $1.28 million revenue [app], lifting motivation and the quality of creative work [an]. However, the $95,000 digital press arriving at year-end will change workflows and client expectations [k]; keeping close control until then would let Omar set standards consistently during the changeover [app], avoiding costly mistakes when the new press is commissioned [an]. On balance, a middle path of agreed weekly reviews instead of daily checks until the press is installed captures most of the motivation benefit while limiting risk [eval], and would still protect the 940,000 printed items during the transition [eval].
    Keywords: 5 senior designers, $95,000, digital press, $1.28 million, 940,000 printed items, laissez-faire, daily checks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire frees skilled, self-motivated staff to self-manage; Close control suits periods of change/new equipment installation | application_max_2: 5 senior designers highly skilled/self-motivated; daily checks slow them; $95,000 digital press at year-end; 940,000 printed items; $1.28 million revenue | analysis_max_2: Freedom lifts motivation, speed and design quality; Close control reduces errors during the press changeover | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (freedom now vs control until year-end); Justified recommendation (weekly reviews until press installed)

--- STEM ---
Coppergrove Assembly Ltd is a private limited company in Country X assembling small household kitchen appliances. It employs 54 workers on two production lines, producing 3,800 units a month with revenue of $2.1 million last year. Shift supervisor Adam Kone ran the lines under a laissez-faire style, giving workers freedom and rarely interfering.

Output has fallen to 3,400 units a month and error rates have risen from 2% to 5%. New production manager Lucia Ferreira wants to introduce a democratic style with daily 10-minute briefings and worker input on targets, while Adam argues freedom keeps experienced line staff motivated. Adam has run the lines for 6 years, and the line staff trust him. Lucia estimates her plan could restore output to 3,800 units within 3 months.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'motivation'.
    Answer: Motivation is the internal desire or willingness of employees to work hard and perform well in order to achieve business objectives. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Motivation is the willingness/desire to work hard/perform well; Motivation drives effort towards business objectives

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways motivation affects the performance of Coppergrove Assembly Ltd.
    Answer: Point 1: A motivated workforce is more productive and achieves higher output [k]; this matters because output has fallen from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month [app]. Point 2: Motivated workers take more care and make fewer mistakes [k]; with the error rate up from 2% to 5%, fewer errors would save wasted appliances [app].
    Keywords: Coppergrove Assembly Ltd, 3,800 units, 3,400 units, 2% to 5%, $2.1 million, two production lines, 54 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Motivated workers are more productive/achieve higher output; Motivated workers make fewer errors/higher quality work | application_max_2: Output has fallen from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month; Error rate has risen from 2% to 5%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of laissez-faire leadership shown by Coppergrove Assembly Ltd.
    Answer: Problem 1: Laissez-faire leaders provide little guidance or control, so workers may lack direction and standards [k]; under Adam's freedom the lines slipped from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month [app], showing output was not being maintained [an]. Problem 2: Without intervention, quality drifts [k]; errors rose from 2% to 5% with nobody correcting working methods [app], increasing waste and eating into the $2.1 million revenue [an].
    Keywords: Coppergrove Assembly Ltd, laissez-faire, 3,800, 3,400, 2% to 5%, $2.1 million, Adam Kone, two production lines
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Little guidance/control from laissez-faire leaders; Quality declines without supervision/intervention | application_max_2: Lines slipped from 3,800 to 3,400 units a month; Error rate rose from 2% to 5% without correction | analysis_max_2: Falling productivity/output against targets; More waste/rework reducing revenue of $2.1 million

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Lucia should introduce democratic leadership at Coppergrove Assembly Ltd? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Democratic leadership involves workers in decisions through consultation and shared information [k]; Lucia's daily 10-minute briefings would let the 54 line workers discuss targets and contribute ideas [app], which should rebuild commitment and could return output to 3,800 units within 3 months [an]. However, Adam argues the experienced line staff value the freedom they already have and their motivation relies on it [k]; replacing freedom with daily briefings could resent workers who prefer autonomy [app], so motivation might fall further before it improves, with errors possibly worsening [an]. On balance, introducing democratic briefings while keeping some team freedom, and reviewing progress after 3 months against the 3,800-unit target, is the better choice [eval], because the democratic approach directly addresses why output fell without removing autonomy completely [eval].
    Keywords: democratic style, 10-minute briefings, 54 workers, 3,800 units, 3,400 units, 2% to 5%, 3 months, $2.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Democratic = consultation/shared decision-making; Laissez-faire = freedom/autonomy valued by experienced staff | application_max_2: Daily 10-minute briefings; worker input on targets; 54 line workers; Output fell to 3,400 units; error rate 5%; target 3,800 within 3 months | analysis_max_2: Involvement rebuilds commitment and output; Abrupt removal of freedom may demotivate and raise resistance | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (democratic briefings vs existing laissez-faire freedom); Justified recommendation with review period/partial autonomy retained

--- STEM ---
Gannet Logistics Ltd is a private limited company running a distribution depot in Country X. It employs 96 warehouse operatives and drivers on night and day shifts, moving about 1,450 pallets a week. Revenue last year was $6.4 million. Wages start at $11.80 per hour, and last year 23 operatives left the company. The night shift runs from 10pm to 6am, and Gannet pays a $1.90 night-shift allowance on top of the base rate.

A union, the Country X Transport Workers Union (CXTWU), has approached Gannet asking to be recognised for collective bargaining on pay and night-shift allowances. Managing director Sana Iqbal is unsure: recognition could mean higher wage bills, but she worries about recruitment and morale. She must decide within 8 weeks whether to agree.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'trade union'.
    Answer: A trade union is an organisation of workers formed to protect and advance their members' interests, such as pay, conditions and job security, by negotiating collectively with employers. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Organisation of workers/employees; Protects/advances members' interests (pay, conditions) via collective negotiation

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why employees at Gannet Logistics Ltd might want to join the CXTWU.
    Answer: Reason 1: A trade union negotiates collectively on behalf of members, giving them a stronger voice than negotiating alone [k]; 96 operatives and drivers could together bargain for better night-shift allowances than any one worker could [app]. Reason 2: Unions provide members with advice and representation in disputes [k]; with 23 operatives leaving last year, staff may want union support on pay and conditions issues [app].
    Keywords: Gannet Logistics Ltd, 96 warehouse operatives, 1,450 pallets, $11.80 per hour, night-shift allowances, 23 operatives, $6.4 million, CXTWU
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Collective bargaining gives a stronger voice than individual negotiation; Advice/representation/support in disputes or grievances | application_max_2: 96 operatives and drivers bargaining for night-shift allowances; 23 operatives left last year; pay and conditions concerns

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects on Gannet Logistics Ltd of its employees joining the CXTWU.
    Answer: Effect 1: The business may face pressure to raise pay [k]; recognition for collective bargaining on pay could push the $11.80 hourly wage upward [app], raising labour costs against revenue of $6.4 million [an]. Effect 2: A union can improve communication and handling of grievances [k]; formalising representation could address the causes behind 23 operatives leaving [app], lowering recruitment and training costs [an].
    Keywords: Gannet Logistics Ltd, $11.80 per hour, $6.4 million, 23 operatives, collective bargaining, 96 warehouse operatives, night and day shifts
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Union pressure pushes up pay/wage bills; Union involvement can improve grievance handling/communication | application_max_2: Collective bargaining on the $11.80 hourly wage and night-shift allowances; Representation could address why 23 operatives left | analysis_max_2: Higher labour costs squeeze profit margins; Better relations/higher retention saves recruitment and training costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sana should recognise the trade union at Gannet Logistics Ltd? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Sana should recognise the union because members can negotiate collectively for fair pay and conditions [k]; the union's proposal targets pay and night-shift allowances for the 96 employees on $11.80 per hour [app], which could raise morale and reduce the loss of 23 operatives a year, saving recruitment and training costs [an]. However, recognition could raise labour costs: the union may push wages above $11.80 per hour across 1,450 pallets a week [k]; higher settlements and possible industrial action during disputes could disrupt the depot and squeeze the $6.4 million revenue [app], which could force price rises or job losses [an]. On balance, recognising the union with a clear bargaining framework is the better option [eval], because the turnover cost of 23 leavers a year and the value of fair treatment outweigh manageable negotiation costs [eval].
    Keywords: $11.80 per hour, $6.4 million, 1,450 pallets, 23 operatives, 96 warehouse operatives, collective bargaining, 8 weeks, night-shift allowances
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Collective bargaining gives members a stronger, unified voice; Recognition can raise wage bills and dispute costs | application_max_2: Pay and night-shift allowances; 96 employees on $11.80 per hour; 23 operatives left last year; 1,450 pallets a week; $6.4 million revenue | analysis_max_2: Better morale, lower turnover and reduced recruitment/training costs; Higher wages and possible disruption squeeze margins | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (recognition benefits vs higher costs/disruption); Justified recommendation (recognise with clear bargaining framework)

--- STEM ---
Mallowgate Flour Ltd is a private limited company in Country X operating a flour mill employing 118 workers. It produces 240 tonnes of flour a week for bakeries nationwide, with revenue of $5.6 million last year. The National Mill and Food Workers Union (NMFWU) represents 74 of the workers.

The union balloted members: 81% voted for strike action over pay and the 40-minute unpaid lunch break. Mallowgate has offered a 2.5% pay rise, but the union demands 6% and paid breaks. Formal talks broke down after 7 weeks of negotiation in November. A 10-day strike is planned from 2 December, with the mill holding a contract worth $900,000 a year to supply a national bakery chain, Country X's largest bread buyer.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'industrial action'.
    Answer: Industrial action is action taken by employees, such as a strike or a work-to-rule, to pressure their employer during an industrial dispute, usually organised through a trade union. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Action by employees/workers against the employer (e.g. strike); Taken to pressure the employer during a dispute, usually via a trade union

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects industrial action could have on Mallowgate Flour Ltd.
    Answer: Effect 1: Industrial action halts or slows production [k]; a 10-day strike would stop the mill producing its 240 tonnes of flour a week [app], so orders for the national bakery chain worth $900,000 a year may not be fulfilled. Effect 2: Industrial action damages reputation and customer confidence [k]; bakeries relying on weekly flour supplies may switch to rival mills during a 10-day stoppage [app], risking the loss of long-term customers and revenue.
    Keywords: Mallowgate Flour Ltd, 10-day strike, 240 tonnes, $900,000, $5.6 million, NMFWU, 118 workers, 2 December
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Industrial action stops/slows production; Industrial action damages reputation/customer confidence | application_max_2: 10-day strike would stop 240 tonnes a week of flour; Bakery chain contract worth $900,000 a year at risk

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects a strike would have on the employees of Mallowgate Flour Ltd.
    Answer: Effect 1: Striking workers lose pay for days not worked [k]; during a 10-day strike from 2 December the 74 union members would forfeit wages while the dispute continues [app], squeezing household budgets even though the 6% demand is the union's goal [an]. Effect 2: Industrial action shows solidarity and strengthens the union's bargaining position [k]; with 81% of voting members backing the strike, the union negotiates from a position of strength [app], increasing the chance the employer improves the 2.5% offer or grants paid breaks [an].
    Keywords: Mallowgate Flour Ltd, 74 of the workers, 81%, 6%, 2.5%, 10-day strike, 2 December, 40-minute unpaid lunch break
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Strikers lose pay for days not worked; Industrial action demonstrates solidarity/strengthens bargaining position | application_max_2: 10-day strike from 2 December; 74 union members would forfeit wages; 81% of voting members backed the strike; 2.5% offer vs 6% demand | analysis_max_2: Financial hardship/loss of income for striking workers; Stronger position to win a better offer (6% or paid breaks)

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Mallowgate Flour Ltd should agree to the union's demands of a 6% pay rise and paid lunch breaks? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Agreeing would end the threat to stop production [k]; a settlement would protect the bakery-chain contract worth $900,000 a year and keep 240 tonnes a week flowing [app], avoiding the $5.6 million revenue base being disrupted by a 10-day stoppage [an]. However, conceding 6% is far above the 2.5% offered, and paid breaks add hours that currently go unpaid [k]; lifting the offer to 6% across 118 workers and adding paid breaks would materially raise the wage bill [app], which could force price rises or job cuts at the mill [an]. On balance, Mallowgate should negotiate a compromise, such as a phased rise reaching 6% over two years with a shorter paid break [eval], because outright refusal guarantees a 10-day stoppage while full capitulation sets a costly precedent [eval].
    Keywords: $900,000 a year, 240 tonnes, $5.6 million, 2.5%, 6%, 10-day strike, 81%, paid breaks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Industrial action pressures the employer; settlement protects production; Concession raises wage costs and may set a precedent for future claims | application_max_2: $900,000 a year bakery-chain contract; 240 tonnes a week; 10-day strike risk; 2.5% offer vs 6% demand; 118 workers; $5.6 million revenue | analysis_max_2: Settlement avoids stopped production, lost orders and lost revenue; Full concession strains margins and invites further claims | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (concede fully vs refuse vs compromise); Justified recommendation: negotiated compromise/phased settlement

--- STEM ---
Hollymoor Garment Co is a private limited company in Country X employing 132 machinists and cutters in one factory. Annual revenue is $3.7 million and the factory produces 26,000 garments a month. The Garment Workers Union represents 98 employees.

Workers have complained about noise averaging 88 decibels near the cutting machines and poor ventilation. The union wants the company to sign a collective agreement covering ear protection, extraction fans and a joint health and safety committee, estimated at $52,000. Director Elena Petrova must decide whether to sign the agreement or keep the current basic safety measures. She has two weeks to respond before the union calls a meeting of all 132 employees. The factory runs two full shifts daily and cannot afford production stoppages.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'collective bargaining'.
    Answer: Collective bargaining is the process by which a trade union negotiates with an employer on behalf of all its members to agree pay, working hours and conditions of employment. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Union negotiates with employer on behalf of members; Agreement covers pay/working hours/conditions for the group

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of collective bargaining for workers at Hollymoor Garment Co.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Collective bargaining lets the union negotiate on behalf of all members, giving workers more power than negotiating alone [k]; the 98 employees the union represents could jointly press for ear protection and extraction fans rather than complaining individually [app]. Benefit 2: Collective agreements can fix clear, agreed standards [k]; a signed deal with a joint committee would make the noise target and ventilation arrangements binding on the company [app].
    Keywords: Hollymoor Garment Co, 98 employees, 88 decibels, extraction fans, ear protection, $52,000, 132 machinists
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Union negotiates on behalf of members, stronger together; Agreements fix clear, binding standards | application_max_2: 98 employees represented; joint press for ear protection and extraction fans; Joint health and safety committee would make arrangements binding

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects on Hollymoor Garment Co of signing the health and safety agreement.
    Answer: Effect 1: Signing the agreement increases short-term costs [k]; ear protection, extraction fans and a joint committee are estimated at $52,000 [app], reducing profit against annual revenue of $3.7 million [an]. Effect 2: A safer workplace can reduce accidents, absences and staff turnover [k]; cutting noise from 88 decibels and improving ventilation would make machinists healthier [app], protecting output of 26,000 garments a month [an].
    Keywords: Hollymoor Garment Co, $52,000, 88 decibels, $3.7 million, 26,000 garments, health and safety committee, extraction fans
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Agreed safety measures raise short-term costs; Safer workplaces reduce accidents, absence and turnover | application_max_2: $52,000 estimated cost against revenue of $3.7 million; Noise at 88 decibels; ventilation; 26,000 garments a month | analysis_max_2: Lower profit/higher costs in the short term; Healthier, more stable workforce protects output

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Elena should sign the collective health and safety agreement? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Signing the agreement would address a serious, immediate risk and show the business values its workers [k]; the $52,000 for ear protection, extraction fans and a joint committee is about 1.4% of annual revenue of $3.7 million [app], which is affordable and would tackle the 88-decibel noise directly, cutting accidents, absence and possible compensation claims while protecting 26,000 garments a month [an]. However, a signed collective agreement sets a formal precedent of joint decision-making [k]; once the health and safety committee exists, the company must consult on future changes, and ongoing costs could rise beyond the $52,000 initial estimate [app], limiting management flexibility [an]. On balance, Elena should sign the agreement because the safety risk is measurable at 88 decibels and the cost is modest relative to revenue [eval]; the alternative of waiting for an injury could mean costs far above $52,000 plus reputational damage [eval].
    Keywords: $52,000, $3.7 million, 88 decibels, 26,000 garments, 98 employees, health and safety committee, extraction fans
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Safer workplace protects employees and reduces absence/accidents; Collective agreements create ongoing consultation obligations | application_max_2: $52,000 ≈ 1.4% of $3.7 million revenue; 88-decibel noise; 26,000 garments a month; 98 union employees | analysis_max_2: Prevents accidents/claims and protects output and reputation; Ongoing committee costs and reduced management flexibility | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (sign vs keep current measures); Justified recommendation (sign) with cost justification

--- STEM ---
Cove & Crumb Café is a private limited company in Country X operating 4 cafés in two seaside towns. It employs 34 staff, including 11 baristas on $9.60 an hour: 7 full-time and 4 part-time. Union membership at the cafés stands at 18 staff. Revenue last year was $1.9 million, and the union has campaigned for the new national minimum wage of $10.25 an hour, effective 1 April.

Owner Dana Whitlock must decide whether to raise the 11 baristas to $10.25 an hour now and absorb the extra cost, or offset it by cutting 40 staff hours a week across the four cafés. July is the peak month with revenue of $310,000, and the cafés trade 11 hours a day on summer tourists.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'minimum wage'.
    Answer: The minimum wage is the lowest hourly rate of pay that employers are legally required to pay workers, set by the government to protect low-paid employees. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Minimum wage is a legal minimum hourly pay rate; Set by government to protect/benefit low-paid workers

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the minimum wage rise on workers at Cove & Crumb Café.
    Answer: Effect 1: Low-paid workers receive higher pay [k]; the 11 baristas currently on $9.60 an hour will earn at least $10.25 from 1 April [app]. Effect 2: Higher pay can improve living standards and motivation [k]; better wages may reduce turnover among the 34 staff who rely on café wages [app].
    Keywords: Cove & Crumb Café, $9.60, $10.25, 11 baristas, $1.9 million, 34 staff, 1 April
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Minimum wage raises pay for the lowest-paid workers; Higher pay can improve living standards/motivation | application_max_2: 11 baristas rise from $9.60 to $10.25 an hour from 1 April; 34 staff rely on café wages; union campaigned for the rise

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the minimum wage rise could cause for Cove & Crumb Café.
    Answer: Problem 1: Labour costs rise [k]; raising 11 baristas from $9.60 to $10.25 adds cost across the four cafés on revenue of $1.9 million [app], which could force price increases or tighter margins [an]. Problem 2: To control costs the business may cut hours [k]; removing 40 staff hours a week across the cafés would stretch remaining staff during 11-hour days [app], causing longer queues in July and dissatisfied tourists [an].
    Keywords: Cove & Crumb Café, $9.60, $10.25, 11 baristas, $1.9 million, 40 staff hours, July, $310,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Minimum wage raises labour/operating costs; Businesses may respond by cutting hours/jobs/prices rise | application_max_2: 11 baristas rising from $9.60 to $10.25; $1.9 million revenue; 40 staff hours a week cut; 11-hour trading days; July peak | analysis_max_2: Tighter margins or price increases reduce competitiveness; Understaffing causes queues and lost tourist sales in July

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Dana should absorb the minimum wage increase or cut 40 staff hours a week to offset it? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Absorbing the increase shows the business values its staff and protects service [k]; in July, revenue reaches $310,000 and the cafés trade 11 hours a day on summer tourists [app], so full staffing avoids queues and protects the café's reputation at peak season [an]. However, raising 11 baristas from $9.60 to $10.25 raises costs across four cafés on $1.9 million of revenue [k]; cutting 40 staff hours a week would limit the wage rise and help keep the cafés profitable in a competitive market [app], but would stretch remaining staff in the peak summer [an]. On balance, Dana should absorb the increase through July and review rosters in quieter months [eval], because losing tourist trade in the best revenue month would cost more than the extra wages [eval].
    Keywords: $310,000, July, 11 hours a day, $10.25, $9.60, 11 baristas, four cafés, 40 staff hours, $1.9 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Absorbing wages protects morale/service quality; Cutting hours limits the cost increase but risks service | application_max_2: $310,000 July revenue; cafés trading 11 hours a day; 11 baristas to $10.25; four cafés; $1.9 million revenue; 40 staff hours a week | analysis_max_2: Full staffing in peak season protects sales/reputation; Hour cuts save money but risk understaffing and lost tourists | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (absorb cost vs cut hours); Justified hybrid recommendation tied to seasonality

Benefit 2: Unions support and represent members in disputes with their employer [k]; nurses could get legal advice and representation if injured at work [app].
    Keywords: Elmtree Dental Practice, needle-stick injuries, 7 recorded, 12 dental nurses, BDNA, $2.6 million, internal staff forum

  Qb [4 marks]

Advantage 2: Consultation can improve morale and acceptance of change [k]; discussing the script over 3 weeks would make the 48 call agents more willing to use it properly [app].
    Keywords: Brightcall Teleservices Ltd, 3.2%, 48 call agents, 1,300 calls a day, 3 weeks, new claims script, agents have suggested
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Employee ideas are used in decisions; Consultation improves morale/acceptance of change | application_max_2: Agents' suggested wording could cut the 3.2% complaints; 3 weeks of consultation keeps 48 call agents engaged/accepting change

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of imposing the script autocratically.

Problem 2: Imposed change can cause resistance and lower morale [k]; 48 call agents facing mandatory compliance and daily checks may resent the script [app], increasing errors and call times above the 6 minutes average [an].

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Maya should impose the new script autocratically or consult the agents democratically first? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Imposing the script autocratically is fast and gives Maya control [k]; the regulator expects the script live within 5 weeks, so immediate instructions with daily checks would guarantee compliance on time [app], avoiding penalties or sanctions for missing the deadline [an]. However, consultation would harness the agents' own suggestions [k]; spending 3 weeks consulting the 48 call agents before launch could improve the script and cut the 3.2% complaint rate and the 6 minutes per call average [app], though views may be slow to gather and the 5-week deadline could be missed [an]. Brancott Bakery Co operates a wholesale bakery in Country X supplying 24 supermarkets across the region. It employs 96 production staff working three shifts to produce around 31,000 loaves a week. Sales of a new wholegrain loaf have fallen 18% after staff failed to follow the updated recipe. Night-shift workers rarely attend briefings, and the canteen board is read by fewer than 1 in 5 staff.   Qb [4 marks]

    Answer: Reason 1: Effective internal communication ensures all employees understand how to do their jobs correctly [k], so the 96 production staff follow the updated wholegrain recipe and output stays at around 31,000 loaves a week [app]. Reason 2: It allows information to reach staff who miss meetings [k], so night-shift workers who rarely attend briefings would still receive recipe changes through the canteen board or a daily messaging group [app].
    Keywords: Brancott Bakery Co, 96 production staff, 31,000 loaves, night-shift workers, daily messaging group, canteen board, 18%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Ensures employees understand tasks and work to standard; Allows information to reach all staff, including those who miss meetings | application_max_2: 96 production staff must follow the updated wholegrain recipe to keep output at 31,000 loaves a week; Night-shift workers rarely attend briefings and would need recipe changes via the canteen board or messaging group

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for the bakery of Priya paying staff to stay for a 15-minute briefing at the start of every shift.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Every worker receives the same instructions face to face [k], so night-shift staff who missed verbal briefings in the past would hear the updated recipe directly [app], reducing the risk of mistakes and helping reverse the 18% fall in wholegrain loaf sales [an]. Benefit 2: Two-way questions can be asked and answered immediately [k], so workers can clarify the content of the 15-minute briefing before starting production across the three shifts [app], preventing wasted flour, time and effort on the 31,000-loaf target [an].
    Keywords: 15-minute briefing, night-shift, 18%, three shifts, 31,000, updated recipe, wholegrain loaf
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Face-to-face briefings give every worker the same direct message; Two-way communication allows immediate questions and clarification | application_max_2: Night-shift staff who missed verbal briefings would hear the updated recipe directly; The 15-minute briefing covers all three shifts before production begins on the 31,000-loaf target | analysis_max_2: Fewer mistakes reverse the 18% fall in wholegrain loaf sales; Clarified instructions prevent wasted flour, time and effort

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Priya should create a daily messaging group instead of paying staff to stay for 15-minute briefings? Justify your answer.

Overall, Priya should pay staff to stay for the 15-minute briefing instead [eval], because face-to-face briefings are more reliable for a production workforce and the extra wages are small compared with lost sales and wasted output from the 18% decline [eval].
    Keywords: daily messaging group, 96 production staff, three shifts, night-shift workers, 18%, 1 in 5, 15-minute briefing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Electronic written methods like messaging groups are fast and cheap; Written messages can be ignored and give no guarantee of understanding | application_max_2: Messaging group reaches 96 production staff across three shifts including night-shift workers at almost no extra wages; The canteen board is read by fewer than 1 in 5 staff, suggesting written notices are ignored | analysis_max_2: Wider reach of recipe changes could reverse the 18% sales fall; An ignored messaging group repeats the failure and recipe errors continue | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the messaging group and paid briefings; Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

Redmarsh Construction Ltd is building a 9-storey office block in Country X. The site employs 74 workers, including 26 contract migrants whose first language is not English. Falls from height remain the biggest risk, with 2 scaffolders injured last year. Safety rules are communicated through coloured posters and hazard signs around the site, plus a 20-minute verbal safety talk each Monday led by the site manager.

After 3 near-miss incidents in one month, the safety officer proposes weekly 10-minute toolbox talks using a translator, at a cost of $60 per session.     Question: Define the term 'visual communication'.
    Answer: Visual communication is the passing of information through images, such as signs, posters, charts, diagrams, photographs or videos, rather than through words alone. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Communication using images, symbols or diagrams; Examples include posters, signs, charts and videos

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of visual communication on the construction site.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Signs and posters communicate safety rules instantly without spoken language [k], which is vital because 26 contract migrants on site have a first language other than English [app]. Advantage 2: Visual warnings are permanent and cannot be forgotten [k], so coloured hazard signs around the site constantly remind the 74 workers of the dangers of working at height on the 9-storey block [app].
    Keywords: coloured posters, hazard signs, 26 contract migrants, 74 workers, 9-storey, 20-minute, multilingual
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Images communicate quickly without spoken language; Visual messages are permanent and always visible | application_max_2: 26 contract migrants have a first language other than English; Coloured hazard signs remind the 74 workers on the 9-storey block

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why visual communication alone may not be enough on the site.
    Answer: Reason 1: Posters and signs cannot check understanding [k], so the 26 contract migrants might misread hazard warnings even in their own language [app], leaving the safety officer unable to tell whether workers understand the risks [an]. Reason 2: Visual methods cannot answer questions [k], so workers cannot clarify site rules beyond the 20-minute Monday talk without stopping work [app], meaning misunderstandings about falls from height and scaffolding could persist undetected [an].
    Keywords: posters, hazard signs, 26 contract migrants, multilingual signage, 20-minute, toolbox talks, 3 near-miss
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Visual methods are one-way and cannot check understanding; Visual methods cannot answer questions or give feedback | application_max_2: 26 contract migrants might misread existing coloured posters and hazard signs; Only the 20-minute Monday talk allows any spoken explanation of the rules | analysis_max_2: The safety officer cannot tell whether workers understand the risks; Unchecked misunderstandings about falls from height may go undetected

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the project manager should spend $4,800 on multilingual signs instead of hiring a translator for toolbox talks? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for the multilingual signs is that they cost $4,800 once [k] and would be on display in all areas permanently, covering the 26 contract migrants and the other 48 workers [app], so safety instructions would always be visible where the danger actually occurs on the 9-storey block [an]. However, one argument against is that signs are one-way [k] and cannot check that workers understand, as shown by the 3 near-miss incidents in one month despite existing posters [app], whereas a translator at $60 per session would let migrants ask questions and get answers face to face [an]. Overall, the site should fund both, but if only one option is possible, the multilingual signs are the better spend [eval], because they protect every worker every day, matching the 40% fall in accident rates seen on similar sites after signage was introduced [eval].
    Keywords: $4,800, $60, multilingual signs, 26 contract migrants, 3 near-miss, 40%, 74 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Visual methods are permanent, always visible and cheap over time; Verbal two-way methods check understanding and allow questions | application_max_2: $4,800 once for multilingual signs covering 26 contract migrants and 48 other workers; 3 near-miss incidents in one month despite existing posters and signs | analysis_max_2: Permanent visible signs protect workers where the danger occurs; Existing one-way signs failed to prevent near misses, so interaction is needed | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the signs and the translator-led toolbox talks; Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

  Qb [4 marks]

Advantage 2: It creates shareable written records [k], so task boards and shared files would replace the single spreadsheet now updated by one senior developer [app].
    Keywords: 19 work from home, 5 different countries, shared chat channel, weekly video meeting, project management platform, $1,150, 43 staff

Problem 2: Email is slow for urgent decisions [k], so the 19 staff working from home across 5 different countries must wait hours for replies instead of seeing tasks and deadlines on a shared board [app], reducing productivity and morale [an].

  Qd [8 marks]

However, one argument against is that staff already suffer 'message overload' [k], and the platform would add another channel on top of the shared chat and email rather than removing them [app], which could reduce attention and cut the personal contact of the weekly video meeting [an].     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Centralised task boards improve clarity and accountability; Too many communication channels create overload | application_max_2: $1,150 per month platform versus slow unclear email chains; 14 deadlines slipped and 31 complaints blamed on email last quarter | analysis_max_2: Live shared task visibility makes coordination faster and clearer; Adding a channel without removing email worsens message overload | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the platform's clarity and the risk of overload; Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures
