PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U2_SET_164
UNIT: Unit 2: People in Business
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Hathersage Garden Centre employs 18 staff in a rural location and is busiest at weekends and during the spring planting season, when customer numbers double. The owner wants to replace 4 full-time checkout employees who resigned, but weekend trade now generates 60% of weekly revenue and weekday mornings are quiet, with fewer than 50 customers by noon. The planting season typically begins in February and lasts until early May when the weather is favourable.

The owner is considering recruiting 8 part-time employees working Saturday, Sunday and Wednesday shifts instead of 4 full-time replacements. Full-time replacements would have cost $108,000 a year, so part-time staff at $11.50 per hour would save an estimated $12,000 a year, but full-time staff would offer more consistent service and need less supervision and training overall.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'part-time employee'.
    Answer: A part-time employee is a worker contracted for fewer hours per week than a full-time employee, for example weekend or reduced weekday shifts. Pay and benefits are usually calculated pro rata against full-time staff. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee; Pay and benefits usually pro rata against full-time staff

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Hathersage Garden Centre of recruiting part-time employees.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Part-time staff can be rostered for the busiest periods, such as weekends when customer numbers double [k], matching labour to the pattern in which weekend trade now generates 60% of weekly revenue [app]. Benefit 2: Part-time employees at $11.50 per hour cost less than full-time replacements [k], saving an estimated $12,000 a year against the $108,000 full-time bill [app]. [4]
    Keywords: part-time employees, weekend trade, 60%, $11.50, $12,000, spring planting season
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Can be rostered to match peak trading periods; Lower total wage cost than full-time staff | application_max_2: Covers weekends when numbers double and 60% of revenue is earned; Saves about $12,000 a year versus the $108,000 full-time bill

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks to Hathersage Garden Centre of replacing the 4 full-time checkout employees with part-time staff.
    Answer: Drawback 1: Replacing 4 full-time employees with 8 part-time workers doubles the number of people to train and supervise [k], increasing the workload for the owner of an 18-staff business [app], so induction and supervision costs could erode the projected $12,000 annual saving [an]. Drawback 2: Part-time staff often lack the product knowledge of full-time workers [k], so service quality during the spring planting season could slip [app], risking the garden centre's reputation and repeat custom [an]. [6]
    Keywords: 8 part-time employees, 4 full-time replacements, 18 staff, $12,000, spring planting season, Wednesday shifts
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: More part-time staff means more training and supervision; Part-time staff may lack full product knowledge | application_max_2: 8 part-time recruits to train versus 4 full-time at an 18-staff business; Service quality at risk during the spring planting season | analysis_max_2: Induction and supervision costs may offset the $12,000 saving; Poorer customer advice could reduce reputation and repeat sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hathersage Garden Centre should recruit 8 part-time employees instead of replacing the 4 full-time checkout employees? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Hathersage Garden Centre should recruit the part-time employees because they can be concentrated on the weekend trade that generates 60% of weekly revenue [k], letting the centre serve doubled customer numbers without paying for idle hours on quiet weekday mornings [app]. The estimated $12,000 annual saving against the $108,000 full-time cost also protects margins [an]. However, 8 part-time workers mean more rotas, training and supervision than 4 full-time staff [k], and less experienced checkout staff may give poorer advice during the spring planting season rush [app], which could damage customer loyalty and reduce the very weekend sales that make the model work [an]. Overall, on balance the owner should recruit the part-time staff for Saturday, Sunday and Wednesday cover but retain one experienced full-time supervisor to train them [eval]. This captures the $12,000 saving and flexibility while limiting the risk of poorer customer service during the critical planting season [eval].
    Keywords: 8 part-time employees, 60%, $12,000, 4 full-time replacements, spring planting season, Wednesday, $11.50
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Part-time staff can be rostered around peaks; More part-timers increase supervision and training needs | application_max_2: Targets 60% of weekly revenue at weekends; Saves about $12,000 a year versus the $108,000 full-time bill | analysis_max_2: Matching labour to demand protects margins and service at peaks; Inexperienced staff could reduce loyalty and weekend sales | evaluation_max_2: Balanced judgement favouring part-time cover with retained experience; Weighs wage saving against service risk in the planting season

Quillfern Software Ltd employs 55 developers and analysts creating accounting packages for small businesses in Country X. The company has grown by 25% in two years and now serves 40 small business clients. It now wants to hire 5 graduate analysts to support this growth and has shortlisted 20 candidates. The HR manager has proposed a half-day assessment centre with group exercises, a presentation and an in-tray task, costing $3,000 in total.

The technical director argues that a structured 45-minute panel interview is cheaper at $400 in total and enough to judge each candidate, while the HR manager believes behaviour and teamwork shown at an assessment centre better predict job performance. The board must decide which method to use before offers are made in September.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'assessment centre'.
    Answer: An assessment centre is a selection method in which candidates complete a series of tasks and exercises, such as group discussions, presentations and problem-solving activities, while trained assessors observe and score their performance. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Candidates complete a series of tasks and exercises; Assessors observe and score performance across the activities

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using an assessment centre for the 5 graduate analyst roles.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Assessment centres use several exercises, such as group work, a presentation and an in-tray task, so assessors observe candidates over a longer period [k], giving a fuller and fairer picture than one 45-minute interview when choosing between 20 candidates [app]. Benefit 2: Group exercises reveal teamwork and communication skills [k], which Quillfern Software Ltd needs in graduate analysts supporting 40 small business clients [app]. [4]
    Keywords: assessment centre, 20 candidates, group exercises, in-tray task, $3,000, 5 graduate analysts
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Multiple exercises show behaviour over a longer period; Reveals teamwork and communication skills | application_max_2: Richer comparison across 20 shortlisted candidates; Matches the needs of analysts supporting 40 small business clients

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of a structured panel interview over an assessment centre for selecting the graduate analysts.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A 45-minute panel interview costs only $400 in total [k], compared with $3,000 for the assessment centre [app], so the company spends far less at a time when the 55-person business is investing in growth [an]. Advantage 2: Panel interviews are quicker to arrange and give each candidate direct time to discuss motivation and career goals [k], helping the technical director judge commitment to the analyst role [app], which speeds up offers before the September start [an]. [6]
    Keywords: panel interview, $400, $3,000, 45-minute, 55 developers, September
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Much lower cost than an assessment centre; Quicker to arrange and gives candidates direct time | application_max_2: $400 versus $3,000 for the 20-candidate shortlist; Direct discussion of motivation for the analyst role | analysis_max_2: Preserves cash for a 55-person business investing in growth; Faster decisions mean offers before the September start

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Quillfern Software Ltd should run the assessment centre rather than rely on panel interviews for the 5 graduate analyst roles? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Quillfern Software Ltd should run the assessment centre because exercises such as group tasks, a presentation and an in-tray activity reveal how all 20 candidates actually behave [k], not just how they answer questions in a 45-minute interview [app]. For 5 graduate analysts supporting 40 small business clients, seeing teamwork and problem-solving in practice reduces the risk of an expensive mis-hire [an]. However, the technical director is right that $3,000 is much more than $400 [k], and a poorly organised assessment centre can feel repetitive or intimidating to able candidates [app], causing them to withdraw and accept offers elsewhere at a time of 25% growth [an]. Overall, on balance the company should hold the assessment centre, because at $150 per candidate the extra $2,600 is modest against the cost of a wrong appointment, and structured interviews can still be kept within the day [eval]. This combined approach best predicts which 5 candidates will succeed with small business clients before the September start [eval].
    Keywords: assessment centre, $3,000, $400, 20 candidates, 5 graduate analysts, 45-minute, September
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Assessment centres reveal real behaviour across exercises; Panel interviews are cheaper and quicker | application_max_2: Observes teamwork across 20 candidates for 5 roles; $3,000 versus $400 cost and risk to candidate experience | analysis_max_2: Better prediction of on-the-job performance for analysts; Poorly run process could deter talented candidates during growth | evaluation_max_2: Weighs $150 per candidate against cost of a mis-hire; Concludes assessment centre plus interviews is the best route

Benefit 2: Converting 6 full-time roles to 20 hours per week saves an estimated $56,000 a year [k], at the $9 hourly rate [app]. [4]
    Keywords: 90%, $56,000, $9, July and August, 20 hours per week, part-time
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Rostered to match seasonal demand; Reduces total wage cost | application_max_2: Covers 90% occupancy peak weeks in July and August; Saves about $56,000 a year at the $9 hourly rate

[6]
    Keywords: 6 full-time housekeeping roles, part-time, 70 bedrooms, $56,000, 90%, 20 hours

  Qd [8 marks]

Conversions should fall back to natural wastage if too many resign, limiting the operational risk [eval].
    Keywords: 6 full-time housekeeping roles, $56,000, $9, 90%, 35%, 70 bedrooms, part-time
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Matching labour hours to seasonal demand; Experienced staff may resign over reduced hours | application_max_2: 35% winter versus 90% summer occupancy; $56,000 annual saving at the $9 hourly rate | analysis_max_2: Avoids paying idle hours in the off-season; Loss of experienced staff threatens peak-season service | evaluation_max_2: Balanced judgement favouring conversion with retention safeguards; Falls back to natural wastage to limit operational risk

--- STEM ---
Brackmere City Council employs 1,150 staff delivering waste collection, leisure centres and social care in Country X. The council uses a standard application form for all vacancies and received 260 applications for 8 administrative officer posts last year. Councillors have asked whether the council should accept CVs instead, arguing the form is outdated and discourages younger applicants from applying.

The form guarantees every candidate supplies the same information, supporting fair, consistent shortlisting and the council's equal opportunities policy. Moving to CVs could modernise recruitment, but officers estimate rewriting the process would cost $4,500 and take 3 months, and 90% of councils in comparable regions still use application forms for consistency and legal defensibility. The form is also translated into 2 community languages.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'curriculum vitae (CV)'.
    Answer: A curriculum vitae (CV) is a written summary prepared by a job applicant listing their personal details, qualifications, work history and skills. It is sent to employers when advertisements invite applications rather than use a standard form. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Written summary listing personal details, qualifications and work history; Prepared by the applicant rather than the employer

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Brackmere City Council of continuing to use a standard application form.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A standard form means every applicant supplies the same information in the same order [k], so shortlisting the 260 applications for the 8 administrative officer posts is consistent and fair [app]. Benefit 2: Using the form supports the council's equal opportunities policy [k], helping it demonstrate non-discriminatory shortlisting to staff and regulators [app]. [4]
    Keywords: application form, 260, 8 administrative officer posts, equal opportunities policy, Brackmere City Council, social care
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Every applicant supplies the same information in the same format; Supports equal opportunities and defensible shortlisting | application_max_2: Consistent shortlisting of 260 applications for 8 posts; Demonstrates non-discrimination to staff and regulators

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two arguments for the council accepting CVs instead of application forms.
    Answer: Argument 1: CVs let applicants present their experience in a modern, personal format [k], encouraging younger applicants who see the paper form as outdated [app], helping the council compete for talent in social care and leisure roles [an]. Argument 2: Accepting CVs reduces the effort needed for well-prepared applicants [k], so strong candidates in a tight labour market may be more willing to apply to Brackmere City Council [app], widening the pool beyond the 260 received last year [an]. [6]
    Keywords: CVs, younger applicants, application form, 260, administrative officer, Brackmere City Council
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CVs present experience in a modern, personal format; Reduces effort for well-prepared applicants | application_max_2: May attract younger applicants put off by the paper form; Could widen the pool beyond 260 applications | analysis_max_2: Helps compete for talent in social care and leisure roles; Larger, stronger pool raises quality of appointments

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brackmere City Council should continue using application forms rather than accept CVs? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Brackmere City Council should continue using application forms because 260 applications for 8 administrative officer posts must be shortlisted consistently [k], and the form guarantees comparable information on every candidate, matching the council's equal opportunities policy and its 2 community languages translation [app]. Rewriting the process would cost $4,500 and take 3 months, and with 90% of comparable councils still using forms, the legal and reputational risk of changing outweighs the benefits [an]. However, accepting CVs could modernise recruitment and attract younger applicants put off by the paper form [k], which matters for filling roles quickly in social care and leisure [app], and the $4,500 cost is modest for an organisation employing 1,150 staff [an]. Overall, on balance the council should keep the application form for now because consistency, translations and legal defensibility outweigh the modernising appeal of CVs [eval]. A limited CV pilot for hard-to-fill posts could be considered later as a measured compromise [eval].
    Keywords: application form, 260, $4,500, 90%, equal opportunities policy, 1,150, 2 community languages
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Application forms standardise shortlisting and support equal opportunities; CVs may attract younger applicants and modernise the process | application_max_2: Fair shortlisting of 260 applicants for 8 posts with language translations; $4,500 rewrite cost and 3-month timeline against 90% peer benchmark | analysis_max_2: Consistency and legal defensibility protect the council; Modest cost and youth appeal make CVs attractive in shortage areas | evaluation_max_2: Balanced judgement favouring retention of the application form; Suggests a limited CV pilot as a measured compromise

--- STEM ---
Redmoor Refrigerated Foods Ltd is a private limited company operating a cold-storage distribution depot in Country X for 6 years. The business employs 84 warehouse workers and drivers storing chilled foods for 40 supermarket customers, generating annual sales revenue of $2.6 million. Staff turnover reached 28% last year and accident-related absences cost the business $45,000.

The operations manager must train 16 new pickers before the busy summer season, when depot volumes rise by 35%. Option one is a 2-day induction course costing $400 per worker, covering safety rules and stock systems. Option two is a 5-day induction costing $950 per worker, adding supervised shifts and a mentor for each new picker. A decision is required by 15 June so training can start before orders peak.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'induction training'.
    Answer: Training given to new employees when they first join a business, introducing them to the organisation's culture, policies, safety rules and their duties so they can settle in quickly [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: training given to new employees on joining the business; introduces policies, safety rules and the duties of the role

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Redmoor Refrigerated Foods should provide induction training for the 16 new pickers.
    Answer: Reason 1: New staff learn the depot's safety rules and procedures from day one [k], reducing the risk of accidents like those already costing $45,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Induction helps new pickers settle quickly into their roles [k], which matters because turnover is already 28% ahead of a summer season that raises volumes by 35% [app].
    Keywords: induction, 16 new pickers, $45,000, 28%, 35%, Redmoor Refrigerated Foods, summer season
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: teaches safety rules and procedures; helps new staff settle and integrate quickly | application_max_2: accident-related absences already costing $45,000; 28% turnover and 35% summer volume rise

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of choosing the 5-day induction for the 16 new pickers.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A 5-day induction gives each picker supervised shifts and a mentor [k], so mistakes are caught and corrected before they affect chilled orders for the 40 supermarket customers [app], reducing costly errors and waste during the 35% summer surge [an]. Advantage 2: It shows new staff the firm values them [k], improving morale in a workforce already facing 28% turnover [app], lowering the cost and disruption of replacing pickers later [an].
    Keywords: 5-day induction, supervised shifts, mentor, 16 new pickers, 40 supermarket customers, 35%, 28%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: longer induction allows closer supervision and mentoring; demonstrates the employer values new employees | application_max_2: supervised shifts and a mentor for each picker; 40 supermarket customers and 28% turnover | analysis_max_2: catches errors early, protecting orders and reducing waste; improves morale and retention, cutting replacement costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redmoor Refrigerated Foods should approve the 5-day induction rather than the 2-day induction? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for: the 5-day induction costs $950 per worker [k], so 16 pickers cost $15,200, adding supervised shifts and mentors that address the safety problems behind the $45,000 absence cost [app], reducing accidents and errors during the 35% summer peak [an]. Argument against: the 2-day induction costs only $400 per worker [k], so 16 pickers cost $6,400, an $8,800 saving against the $15,200 option when turnover is already 28% [app], risking wasted spend if pickers leave soon after joining [an]. Overall, the 5-day induction is the stronger choice because the mentoring and safety benefits outweigh the $8,800 saving in an accident-hit peak season [eval], although the depot should also tackle the causes of 28% turnover to protect its investment [eval].
    Keywords: 5-day induction, 2-day induction, $950 per worker, $400 per worker, 16 new pickers, $45,000, 35%, 28%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: longer induction adds mentoring and supervision; longer induction costs more per worker | application_max_2: 16 x $950 = $15,200 versus 16 x $400 = $6,400; $8,800 difference; $45,000 absence cost and 35% summer rise | analysis_max_2: reduces accidents and errors during the peak; savings could outweigh benefits if staff leave quickly | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing mentoring benefits against extra cost; conditional judgement linking decision to tackling 28% turnover

Ironbarrow Foundry Ltd is a manufacturing business in Country X founded 11 years ago, casting and machining components for agricultural machinery. It employs 96 factory workers at its foundry, generating annual sales revenue of $3.4 million. Eight experienced casting operators currently run the manual milling machines.

The company has bought 6 computer numerical control (CNC) milling machines costing $78,000 each, which can triple output per shift. The operations director wants on-the-job training: the 16 workers selected to run the new machines would be coached by experienced operators during normal production, at an estimated cost of $5,000. The finance director prefers a 4-day off-the-job college course costing $1,800 each, taking the 16 workers away from the production line. A decision is needed this month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'on-the-job training'.
    Answer: Training carried out at the employee's normal workplace while they perform their job, often by observing or being coached by an experienced colleague [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: training at the employee's normal workplace; learning while doing the job, usually with an experienced colleague

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of on-the-job training for Ironbarrow Foundry.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Workers learn on the actual machines used in production [k], so the 16 workers selected gain directly practical experience on equipment costing $78,000 each [app]. Advantage 2: Output continues while training takes place [k], avoiding the lost working time of a 4-day college course [app].
    Keywords: on-the-job training, CNC, 16 workers selected, $78,000, 4-day, production line, Ironbarrow Foundry
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: practical learning on real equipment; production can continue during training | application_max_2: 16 workers selected for machines costing $78,000 each; 4-day off-the-job course would remove workers from the line

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Ironbarrow Foundry may face if it relies only on on-the-job training.
    Answer: Problem 1: Training quality depends on the coaching skills of existing staff [k], and with only 8 experienced casting operators to share the role [app], bad habits may be passed on to the new CNC operators [an]. Problem 2: Training during production can slow output and distract supervisors [k], delaying the tripled output per shift the machines should deliver [app], weakening the return on the $78,000 machines [an].
    Keywords: on-the-job training, Eight experienced casting operators, CNC, triple, 16 workers, $78,000, production line
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: depends on the coaching ability of existing staff; can disrupt or slow production while learning | application_max_2: only 8 experienced casting operators; tripled output per shift and $78,000 machines | analysis_max_2: risk of passing on bad habits and poor CNC practice; delays in realising the machines' output gains

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ironbarrow Foundry should use on-the-job training rather than the off-the-job college course? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for: on-the-job training costs only $5,000 [k], far below the $28,800 needed for 16 off-the-job course fees at $1,800 each [app], saving the foundry $23,800 while workers learn on running machines [an]. Argument against: the college course gives structured, expert-led teaching away from production pressure [k], which is valuable for staff using $78,000 CNC machines where mistakes damage parts [app], whereas coaching from just 8 busy operators risks inconsistent learning [an]. Overall, on-the-job training is the better value option for introducing the new machines [eval], provided Ironbarrow Foundry adds short off-the-job refresher courses later to keep CNC skills up to date [eval].
    Keywords: on-the-job training, $5,000, $1,800, college course, 16 workers, $78,000, off-the-job, CNC
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: on-the-job training is cheaper and workplace-relevant; off-the-job training offers structured expert teaching | application_max_2: $5,000 in-house cost versus 16 x $1,800 = $28,800; $23,800 saving; 8 operators coaching 16 workers | analysis_max_2: saves money and keeps production moving; expert teaching reduces costly machine errors | evaluation_max_2: justified value-for-money recommendation; conditional refinement proposing later refresher training

  Qb [4 marks]

Difference 2: Dismissal happens because of the employee's conduct or capability [k], as with the supervisor found sleeping in the yard for the third time [app].
    Keywords: redundant, dismiss, 5 showroom staff, sleeping in the yard, kitchen and bathroom showroom, gross misconduct, north branch
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: redundancy reflects business need, not employee fault; dismissal reflects the employee's conduct or capability | application_max_2: 5 showroom staff roles ending as the showroom closes; supervisor sleeping in the yard for the third time

Overall, dismissing the supervisor while making the 5 showroom staff redundant is correct [eval], because the showroom closure is a genuine redundancy and the supervisor's conduct justifies dismissal [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: defending may cost more than settling; weak procedure makes losing at tribunal likely | application_max_2: $25,000 fees versus $18,000 settlement; no formal warnings; 4 years' service; male colleagues kept jobs | analysis_max_2: settlement preserves cash and $5.2 million revenue; likely loss would add 12 months' pay compensation

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brackenmoor Textiles should settle Amina's claim rather than defend it? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for: settling for $18,000 caps the cost of the dispute [k], avoiding $25,000 legal fees plus possible 12 months' pay in compensation [app], saving at least $7,000 and ending bad publicity for the factory [an]. Argument against: defending the claim could clear the firm's name if dismissal was genuinely about performance [k], and Amina has only 4 years' service so compensation may be modest [app], but the missing warnings make this risky with 120 machinists watching [an]. Overall, settling and reinstating Amina with retraining is the sensible choice [eval], because the weak procedure makes losing likely and it restores a skilled worker to the floor [eval].
    Keywords: $18,000, $25,000, 12 months' pay, 4 years' service, 120 machinists, formal warnings, reinstate, tribunal
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: settlement caps cost and ends the dispute; defending may be cheaper only if the firm wins | application_max_2: $18,000 settlement versus $25,000 fees plus compensation; 4 years' service; 120 machinists watching the outcome | analysis_max_2: saves at least $7,000 and avoids publicity damage; reinstatement restores skilled labour and morale | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to settle given weak procedure; overall judgement balancing cost, optics and staff relations

--- STEM ---
Oxbrow Steel Co is a private steel components factory in Country X trading for 14 years, employing 88 workers including 30 machine operators. Annual revenue is $3.8 million. In the last 12 months, 7 workers suffered hand or arm injuries on two ageing pressing machines; at the last inspection 6 months ago a guard was found missing on both machines. The national health and safety authority issued a prohibition notice with a deadline of 8 weeks.

Option one is to stop both machines and fit modern safety guards and emergency stops at $22,000 each, retraining operators. Option two is to keep the machines running, paying a specialist $4,000 to produce risk assessments to satisfy the authority at its follow-up visit. The directors estimate lost output of $9,000 per week during any shutdown.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'health and safety'.
    Answer: The legal duty of employers to protect the welfare of employees at work, including safe machinery, proper training, equipment and working conditions [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: legal duty to protect employee welfare at work; covers safe machinery, training, equipment and conditions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two consequences for Oxbrow Steel Co if it fails to comply with the health and safety notice.
    Answer: Consequence 1: The authority can keep the machines stopped [k], halting output estimated at $9,000 per week on the two pressing machines [app]. Consequence 2: The company may face prosecution and fines [k], putting the $3.8 million annual revenue and 7 injured workers' claims at risk [app].
    Keywords: health and safety, $9,000 per week, prohibition notice, $3.8 million, 7 workers, ageing pressing machines, 8 weeks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: authority can prohibit machinery use and prosecute; fines and legal action may follow | application_max_2: $9,000 per week lost output on two pressing machines; $3.8 million revenue at risk; 7 injured workers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Oxbrow Steel Co of fitting modern safety guards.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Modern guards and emergency stops prevent hand injuries [k], addressing the harm to the 7 workers on the two ageing machines [app], reducing absence, compensation claims and staff fear [an]. Benefit 2: Compliance with the prohibition notice protects production [k], avoiding an 8-week shutdown that could cost up to $72,000 [app], safeguarding the $3.8 million revenue stream [an].
    Keywords: safety guards, emergency stops, 7 workers, $22,000, prohibition notice, $3.8 million, 8 weeks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guards and emergency stops remove the hazard; compliance avoids prohibition and fines | application_max_2: 7 workers injured on two ageing machines; 8 weeks at $9,000 per week = $72,000 potential downtime loss | analysis_max_2: fewer injuries, claims and lost working days; legal compliance keeps revenue flowing

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Oxbrow Steel Co should fit modern safety guards rather than rely on risk assessments alone? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for: the guards cost $22,000 each [k], $44,000 for two machines, removing the hazard behind 7 injuries and preventing further notices [app], and five weeks of shutdown at $9,000 per week would exceed the guards' total cost [an]. Argument against: risk assessments cost only $4,000 [k], satisfying the authority at its follow-up visit while the machines keep running and revenue holds near $3.8 million [app], but relying on paperwork alone leaves operators exposed to further injury and prosecution [an]. Overall, fitting the guards is the responsible and ultimately cheaper choice [eval], because it removes the root cause of the injuries and keeps the factory legally operating [eval].
    Keywords: $22,000, $9,000 per week, $4,000, 7 workers, prohibition notice, $3.8 million, safety guards, risk assessments
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guards remove the physical hazard; risk assessments satisfy paperwork but not safety | application_max_2: $22,000 each = $44,000 for two machines; $4,000 assessment versus $9,000 per week shutdown and $3.8 million revenue | analysis_max_2: five weeks of downtime exceeds the guards' cost; unsafe operation risks further injuries and prosecution | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring the guards; overall judgement on legal and moral responsibility

Kettlebrook Coaches Ltd runs 12 bus routes in Country X, operating for 16 years and employing 54 drivers and 6 office staff. Fares revenue last year was $2.9 million, and ridership fell 3% last year on the two busiest routes. Option one is to raise fares by 8% from April, offsetting the extra wage cost of roughly $118,000 a year. Option two is to freeze fares and cut 9 driver overtime shifts per week, saving about $115,000 a year, but peak-time services may be reduced. The directors must announce their decision at the fare review in 6 weeks.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'legal minimum wage'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lowest pay rate an employer may legally pay; set by the government / employment law

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the minimum wage rise on Kettlebrook Coaches.
    Answer: Effect 1: Wage costs rise by roughly $118,000 a year [k], because 45 of the 60 staff are on or near the $9.00 minimum [app]. Effect 2: Peak-time services may be reduced [k], since freezing fares would require cutting 9 driver overtime shifts per week to save about $115,000 [app].
    Keywords: minimum wage, $118,000, 45 of the 60 staff, $9.00, $10.50, overtime, fares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: raises wage costs; forces fare rises or service cuts | application_max_2: 45 of 60 staff on or near $9.00 minimum; $118,000 increase; 9 overtime shifts per week to save $115,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Kettlebrook Coaches of raising fares rather than cutting overtime.
    Answer: Benefit 1: An 8% fare rise generates about $232,000 a year on $2.9 million revenue [k], comfortably covering the $118,000 wage rise [app], protecting the 12 bus routes [an]. Benefit 2: Keeping driver overtime maintains peak-time services [k], retaining the 54 drivers and their passengers [app], safeguarding revenue and the firm's reputation [an].
    Keywords: raise fares, 8%, $118,000, overtime, 12 bus routes, 54 drivers, fares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fare rise generates revenue to cover costs; retaining overtime keeps peak services running | application_max_2: 8% of $2.9 million = $232,000, above the $118,000 rise; 54 drivers keep their overtime and passengers | analysis_max_2: protects all 12 routes from cuts; stable services retain passengers and reputation

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kettlebrook Coaches should raise fares rather than cut overtime shifts? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for: an 8% fare rise yields about $232,000 a year against $118,000 of extra wages [k], comfortably funding the legal minimum wage increase while protecting the 12 bus routes [app], keeping services reliable and drivers fully paid [an]. Argument against: higher fares may deter price-sensitive passengers [k], who could switch away after the 8% increase [app], risking lower ridership and revenue despite the higher prices [an]. Overall, raising fares is justified because it funds the legal increase without cutting services that 45 of the 60 staff depend on [eval], although the firm should monitor passenger numbers and adjust fares if demand falls [eval].
    Keywords: 8%, $118,000, minimum wage, 12 bus routes, fares, overtime, $10.50, 45 of the 60 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fare rise funds the wage increase directly; higher fares risk losing price-sensitive passengers | application_max_2: 8% of $2.9 million = $232,000 versus $118,000 cost; 12 routes protected; 45 of 60 staff on or near minimum | analysis_max_2: revenue surplus covers the wage rise and service quality; fare increase could reduce ridership and revenue | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to raise fares; conditional judgement to adjust if demand falls

--- STEM ---
Clearspan Contact Centre is a private limited company in Country X handling billing and technical queries for telecom providers. It employs 140 customer service agents across 2 shifts and last year generated $4.2 million in revenue. Agents currently earn a fixed monthly salary of $1,150, wages account for $1.9 million of annual costs, staff turnover reached 22%, and average customer satisfaction stands at 78%. The average agent completes 3,000 calls a month, with 7 minutes spent on each call.

Operations director Lena Ortiz is comparing two reward proposals. Option 1 keeps the fixed salary and introduces a 'Star Agent' recognition scheme with monthly awards and certificates, costing $25,000 a year. Option 2 replaces the salary with $400 a month plus $0.25 per completed call, so an average agent would earn $1,150 a month and a top performer completing 3,600 calls would earn $1,300.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'salary'.
    Answer: A fixed regular payment to an employee, usually expressed as an annual amount paid monthly [1], which does not vary with the number of hours worked or the output produced [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fixed regular payment, usually monthly; does not vary with hours worked or output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Clearspan Contact Centre might introduce the output-based pay option.
    Answer: Reason 1: Output-based pay links an agent's earnings directly to productivity [k], so an agent completing 3,600 calls would earn $1,300 a month instead of the fixed $1,150 [app]. Reason 2: Agents who complete more calls are financially rewarded for their effort [k], which should motivate the 140 agents to raise call output above the current 3,000 calls a month [app].
    Keywords: Clearspan Contact Centre, $0.25, $1,150, $1,300, 3,600, 3,000, Star Agent, 140
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: pay linked directly to output and productivity; financial reward for extra effort motivates workers | application_max_2: $0.25 per completed call; $1,300 a month for 3,600 calls; $1,150 fixed salary; 3,000 calls a month

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the output-based pay option could cause for Clearspan Contact Centre.
    Answer: Problem 1: Agents may rush calls to raise their call count [k], so the 7 minutes per call could be cut at the expense of quality, hurting the 78% customer satisfaction rating [app], which could damage Clearspan's reputation with telecom providers [an]. Problem 2: Pay would become unstable for slower agents [k], as an agent completing only 2,500 calls would earn $1,025 a month, below the current $1,150 salary [app], so low-earning agents may leave and turnover could rise above 22% [an].
    Keywords: $0.25, 7 minutes, 78%, $1,150, 22%, 3,000, telecom providers, $4.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: workers rush work to maximise pay, reducing quality; variable pay creates income insecurity | application_max_2: 7 minutes per call; 78% customer satisfaction; $1,025 a month on 2,500 calls; 22% turnover | analysis_max_2: damages reputation with telecom providers; low earners may resign, raising turnover above 22%

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Clearspan Contact Centre should replace the fixed salary with output-based pay instead of keeping the salary and adding the Star Agent recognition scheme? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Output-based pay would reward agents for exceeding 3,000 calls a month [k], as completing 3,600 calls would raise pay from $1,150 to $1,300, directly rewarding effort [app], which could lift productivity and protect the $4.2 million revenue [an]. However, the salary option gives income stability [k], agents keep a certain $1,150 a month and the $25,000 Star Agent scheme recognises effort without encouraging rushed calls [app], helping retention and satisfaction above 78% [an]. Overall, Clearspan should keep the fixed salary and introduce the Star Agent recognition scheme [eval], because agents already have income security and recognition improves service quality rather than raw call volume [eval].
    Keywords: Star Agent, $25,000, $1,150, $1,300, 3,600, 3,000, 78%, $4.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: output-based pay motivates higher productivity; recognition schemes motivate without harming quality | application_max_2: $1,300 for 3,600 calls; $25,000 Star Agent scheme; $1,150 salary; 78% satisfaction; $4.2 million | analysis_max_2: higher output could lift or protect revenue; recognition supports retention and call quality | evaluation_max_2: weighs productivity gain against quality and retention risk; reaches a justified recommendation tied to stem figures

--- QUESTIONS ---

    Question: Define 'piece rate'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: paid a fixed amount per unit produced; pay varies directly with output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the piece rate option for Torr Vale Distribution Centre.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Pay would be linked directly to output [k], so a picker completing 18 orders an hour would earn $17.10 compared with $14.50 an hour now [app]. Benefit 2: Effort is financially rewarded [k], which should motivate pickers to raise productivity beyond the 1.35 million orders handled last year without closer supervision [app].
    Keywords: Torr Vale Distribution Centre, $0.95, $17.10, $14.50, 1.35 million orders, 18 orders an hour, $3.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: pay linked directly to output; financial reward for effort motivates productivity | application_max_2: $0.95 per order; $17.10 for 18 orders an hour; $14.50 an hour; 1.35 million orders

  Qc [6 marks]

Problem 2: Picker income would become unpredictable [k], as a picker producing only 12 orders an hour would earn $11.40, below the $14.50 hourly rate [app], so weaker staff may leave and the 17% turnover could worsen [an].
    Keywords: $0.95, 3%, $11.40, $14.50, 17%, 2 national supermarket chains, $3.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rushing reduces quality and accuracy; variable pay creates income insecurity | application_max_2: 3% error rate; $11.40 for 12 orders an hour; $14.50 hourly rate; 17% turnover | analysis_max_2: risks losing supermarket orders; higher turnover and recruitment costs

  Qd [8 marks]

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: piece rate directly rewards higher output; team recognition motivates without encouraging rushing | application_max_2: $17.10 an hour for fast pickers; $14.50 current hourly pay; $300 weekly team award; 3% error rate; 17% turnover | analysis_max_2: higher output protects revenue without extra supervision; errors and turnover risk undermines supermarket contracts | evaluation_max_2: weighs productivity incentive against accuracy and retention risk; justified recommendation tied to stem figures

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of the current salary-plus-commission scheme at Brightspur Field Sales.

Advantage 2: The 3% commission links pay to performance [k], adding about $1,000 a month on top of salary and motivating representatives to close more sales above the current average [app].

  Qc [6 marks]

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: commission-only pay rewards and motivates top sellers; recognition motivates at low cost without income risk | application_max_2: $1,650 at current average; $8,000 Star Performer scheme; $9.6 million sales; 20% turnover; 24 representatives | analysis_max_2: commission-only could lift sales but risks resignations; recognition protects morale and relationships cheaply | evaluation_max_2: weighs short-run selling incentive against retention risk; justified recommendation tied to stem figures

The sales director is choosing between two motivation proposals. Option 1 introduces a share ownership scheme offering senior consultants 400 shares each, worth $25 a share today and vesting after 3 years, a benefit worth about $10,000 each. Option 2 introduces a monthly 'Star Seller' bonus of $700 for any consultant selling 3 or more cars in a month, above the current average of 2 cars per consultant per month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'share ownership'.
    Answer: A scheme in which employees are given or allowed to buy shares in the company they work for [1], making them part-owners who benefit when the company performs well [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: employees receive or buy shares in the company; employees benefit when company performs well

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of the share ownership scheme for Highgate Motors.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Employees become part-owners of the business [k], so senior consultants receiving 400 shares at $25 each gain directly if the share value rises [app]. Advantage 2: Share ownership encourages long-term loyalty [k], as the shares vest only after 3 years, giving senior consultants a strong reason to stay rather than leave for rival showrooms [app].
    Keywords: Highgate Motors, 400 shares, $25 a share, 3 years, $10.8 million, 30 sales consultants
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: employees become part-owners with a stake in success; vesting periods encourage long-term retention | application_max_2: 400 shares each; $25 a share; vesting after 3 years; 3 showrooms

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems with the share ownership scheme for Highgate Motors.
    Answer: Problem 1: The shares may never rise in value [k], so senior consultants could wait 3 years for shares still worth $25 and feel unrewarded [app], weakening the motivational effect of the scheme [an]. Problem 2: Only senior consultants qualify [k], so the rest of the 30 sales consultants gain nothing [app], which could breed jealousy and reduce team spirit across the 3 showrooms [an].
    Keywords: $25 a share, 3 years, 30 sales consultants, 3 showrooms, $10,000, share ownership, 19%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: share values can fall or stay flat, weakening rewards; schemes limited to some staff can damage morale | application_max_2: $25 a share; 3 years; 30 sales consultants; 3 showrooms | analysis_max_2: flat share price undermines motivation; jealousy reduces team spirit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Highgate Motors should introduce the share ownership scheme instead of the monthly Star Seller bonus? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Share ownership links consultants' wealth to the whole business [k], as 400 shares worth $25 each ($10,000) reward long-term loyalty and align senior staff with growth in the $10.8 million revenue [app], improving retention beyond the current 19% turnover [an]. However, the reward is distant and uncertain [k], whereas the $700 Star Seller bonus is immediate and earned by selling just 1 car above the 2-car monthly average [app], motivating every consultant now and lifting sales beyond 720 cars [an]. Overall, Highgate should introduce the monthly Star Seller bonus [eval], because it motivates all 30 consultants immediately and share ownership can be added later for senior staff [eval].
    Keywords: share ownership, $10,000, $700, Star Seller, 2 cars, $10.8 million, 19%, 30 sales consultants
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: share ownership aligns staff with long-term business success; immediate bonuses motivate performance more directly | application_max_2: 400 shares worth $25 each; $10,000 per senior consultant; $700 monthly bonus; 2 cars per month average; $10.8 million revenue | analysis_max_2: share scheme aids retention but pays off only later; immediate bonus can lift sales above 720 cars | evaluation_max_2: weighs long-term loyalty against immediate motivational impact; justified recommendation tied to stem figures

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of job enrichment for Copperline Hotels Group.

Benefit 2: Enriched jobs develop employees' skills [k], so experienced housekeepers can cover a wider range of duties without extra supervisors [app].
    Keywords: Copperline Hotels Group, welcome packs, linen ordering, 2 hotels, 180 guest rooms, $11 an hour

Option 2 keeps a salary but adds output-based pay of $700 basic plus $18 per sale closed; an average agent closing 30 sales a month would earn $1,240, while a stronger agent closing 45 sales would earn $1,510 and a weak agent closing only 20 sales would earn $1,060.

--- QUESTIONS ---

    Question: Define 'training'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: developing employee skills and knowledge; improves current job performance and adaptability

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the off-the-job training option for Calderwood Telesales.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Off-the-job training develops agents' selling techniques away from the desk [k], targeting a rise in the success rate from 2% to 3%, worth about 32,400 sales a year [app]. Benefit 2: Time on the 2-day course is an investment in all 60 agents at $300 each [k], and raising the whole team's skills protects the $6.5 million in sales the business depends on [app].
    Keywords: Calderwood Telesales, 2-day, $18,000, $300 per agent, 32,400, 2%, $6.5 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: off-the-job training builds new skills away from work pressures; training improves capability across the whole team | application_max_2: 2% to 3%; 32,400 sales a year; 2-day course costing $18,000; $300 per agent

  Qc [6 marks]

Problem 2: Weaker agents would be pushed below the present salary [k], as an agent closing only 20 sales a month would earn $1,060 against today's $1,250 [app], so morale may fall and the 24% turnover could rise further [an].
    Keywords: $18 per sale, $1,250, 24%, $1,060, 21,600, $6.5 million, 60 outbound agents
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: commission per sale encourages pressure selling; output pay is insecure for weaker performers | application_max_2: $18 per sale; $1,060 on 20 sales a month; $1,250 fixed salary; 24% turnover | analysis_max_2: pressure selling damages reputation and contracts; poor earners may quit, worsening turnover

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Calderwood Telesales should fund the off-the-job training course instead of introducing output-based pay? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Training tackles the root cause of weak results [k], lifting the success rate from 2% to 3%, around 10,800 extra sales a year, a permanent gain for all 60 agents [app], which protects and could grow the $6.5 million in sales revenue [an]. However, the $18,000 cost is certain while the 3% target is not [k], whereas output pay costs nothing until agents actually close sales and rewards high performers up to $1,510 a month [app], though it risks pressure selling and income anxiety [an]. Overall, Calderwood should fund the 2-day training course [eval], because it raises the whole team's ability without risking the 24% turnover climbing higher [eval].
    Keywords: 2-day, $18,000, $1,510, 24%, $6.5 million, 32,400, 2%, training course
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: training addresses root cause and builds permanent capability; output pay rewards only realised sales but risks behaviour | application_max_2: 2% to 3% success rate; $18,000 training cost; $1,510 a month for strong agents; 24% turnover; $6.5 million sales | analysis_max_2: extra 10,800 sales could grow revenue; pressure selling risk could worsen turnover | evaluation_max_2: weighs certain training cost against uncertain conversion gain; justified recommendation tied to stem figures

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of job rotation for Elmridge Fulfilment Co.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Variety reduces boredom and fatigue [k], as pickers move between picking, packing and loading during the demanding 8-week peak [app]. Benefit 2: Rotation makes workers multi-skilled [k], so full-time and seasonal staff can cover absent colleagues anywhere in the warehouse without slowing order processing [app].
    Keywords: Elmridge Fulfilment Co, picking, packing and loading, 8-week peak, 120 full-time pickers, 80 seasonal workers, $13 an hour

Alderfen Supermarkets operates 14 branches across Country X and employs 4,800 people. The chief executive reviews a weekly written report from each branch passed up through the regional layer before it reaches her desk on a Monday morning.

The board is considering removing the regional director layer and having branch managers report directly to the operations director in the capital. This would delayer the business from six levels to five and widen the operations director's span of control from 4 to 14. The decision must be made before the busy winter trading season, when weekly sales across the 14 branches reach $9.6 million.

    Question: Define the term 'span of control'.
    Answer: The number of subordinates directly supervised and answerable to one manager on a given level of the organisation [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the number of employees directly supervised by one manager; can be wide (many subordinates) or narrow (few subordinates) depending on the work

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why widening the operations director's span of control from 4 to 14 might help Alderfen.
    Answer: Reason 1: Fewer layers speed up decisions [k], because branch stock problems currently travel through a regional director before reaching the operations director, and removing that layer shortens the business from six levels to five [app]. Reason 2: A wider span cuts management costs [k], because four regional director posts would be removed, saving salary across 14 branches that already generate $9.6 million in weekly winter sales [app].
    Keywords: 14 branches, operations director, six levels to five, regional directors, $9.6 million, 4 to 14
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fewer management layers mean quicker decisions and a shorter chain of command; removing a layer reduces management salary costs | application_max_2: chain shortens from six levels to five; 14 branches under one operations director generating $9.6 million weekly

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Alderfen may face if it removes the regional director layer.
    Answer: Problem 1: The operations director may become overloaded [k], because instead of reviewing 4 regional reports she would now receive a weekly written report from each of the 14 branches [app], so urgent stock decisions could still be delayed across $9.6 million of weekly winter sales [an]. Problem 2: Branch managers lose local support and guidance [k], because regional directors currently visit the 3 or 4 branches they each oversee and understand local conditions [app], so branch-specific problems could go unnoticed until they damage branch performance [an].
    Keywords: span of control from 4 to 14, weekly written report, 14 branches, six levels to five, $9.6 million, regional directors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a manager supervising too many staff becomes overloaded / span too wide; removing a layer removes local support, coaching and quality checks | application_max_2: operations director would review reports from all 14 branches instead of 4 regions; regional directors currently oversee 3 or 4 branches each and know local conditions | analysis_max_2: overload slows urgent decisions and errors slip through; loss of local support lets branch problems grow before being noticed

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Alderfen should remove the regional director layer to create a flatter structure? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Removing the regional director layer would shorten the chain from six levels to five and cut management costs [k], since one operations director could receive the weekly written report from each of the 14 branches directly [app], so decisions on winter stock reaching $9.6 million could be faster and cheaper [an]. However, a span of 14 is very wide compared with today's 4, and the operations director may miss problems in individual branches [k], especially as regional directors currently know local conditions across the 3 or 4 branches they each visit [app], so service and stock control could slip during the busiest season [an]. Overall, Alderfen should keep the regional director layer through the winter at least [eval], because protecting branch performance across $9.6 million of weekly winter sales matters more than the salary saving from delayering [eval].
    Keywords: regional director layer, six levels to five, 14 branches, $9.6 million, regional directors, 4 to 14
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delayering shortens the chain of command / cuts management costs; a span of 14 is too wide / risks overload and loss of local knowledge | application_max_2: from six levels to five with reports from all 14 branches; $9.6 million weekly winter sales and 3 or 4 branches per regional director | analysis_max_2: faster, cheaper decisions versus slower branch problem detection; salary savings versus protection of sales during peak season | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to peak winter trading and branch supervision

Caspian Bay Hotels Group operates 22 hotels in 6 countries from its head office in Country X's capital. The group employs 3,600 people. The chain of command runs from the group chief executive through the operations director, 6 country general managers, 22 hotel managers and then 4 department heads in each hotel covering front office, housekeeping, food and beverage and maintenance, ending with team leaders on the floor.

A guest recently waited 9 days for a repairs decision after a burst pipe at the harbour hotel because the request travelled from the hotel manager through the country general manager to head office and back.     Question: Define the term 'chain of command'.

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of a clear chain of command for Caspian Bay Hotels Group.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Everyone knows who to report to [k], so the 4 department heads in each of the 22 hotels know whether to contact the hotel manager or head office for decisions [app]. Benefit 2: Accountability is clear at every level [k], so after the burst pipe the failure can be traced from team leaders up through the hotel manager and country general manager to head office over the 9 days [app].
    Keywords: 22 hotels, 6 countries, 4 department heads, hotel manager, head office, 9 days
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: clear reporting lines so employees know who to report to / take orders from; clear accountability at each level of the organisation | application_max_2: 4 department heads in each of the 22 hotels; burst pipe decision traced through hotel manager and general manager over 9 days

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of keeping all spending above $500 with head office.
    Answer: Problem 1: Slow decisions in emergencies [k], because the burst pipe request took 9 days to travel from the hotel manager through the country general manager and back for approval of spending above $500 [app], leaving guests facing cold rooms and damaging the group's reputation [an]. Problem 2: Hotel managers become demotivated [k], because they cannot approve even routine $600 repairs without head office [app], so they feel their experience is ignored and may leave for a rival group [an].
    Keywords: 9 days, hotel manager, head office, $500, burst pipe, country general manager
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a long chain slows urgent decisions; lack of authority demotivates local managers | application_max_2: burst pipe took 9 days for approval above $500; hotel manager cannot approve routine spending without head office | analysis_max_2: slow repairs damage the guest experience and reputation; demotivated managers may leave / stop taking initiative

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Caspian Bay should give hotel managers authority to spend up to $3,000 locally? Justify your answer.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: local authority speeds up decisions / fixes the long chain; weaker central control risks overspending / loss of budget discipline | application_max_2: $3,000 local authority versus $500 with head office; 22 hotel managers across 6 countries; 9-day burst pipe delay | analysis_max_2: faster repairs improve guest experience and loyalty; uncontrolled spending may blow group budgets | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation balancing speed of service against cost control

    Keywords: 5 factories, 3 directors, 2,300, Country Y, head office, functional

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: verbal communication allows instant two-way feedback; verbal communication reaches workers who do not read written material | application_max_2: daily 10-minute briefings versus emailed PDF briefings; 260 subcontractors and only 54% readership of the PDFs

  Qc [6 marks]

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think dynamic pricing is a better strategy for Sentinel than a fixed $25 monthly fee? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Dynamic pricing captures more value at peak times [k], because match-day demand lets Sentinel charge 20% more to 9,000 homes [app], raising $5.4m revenue and funding better monitoring technology [an]. However, a fixed $25 fee protects subscriber trust [k], and price-sensitive subscribers may leave rather than accept variable bills [an], putting the 11% share at risk [app].     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: varied prices can maximise peak revenue; fixed prices are simpler and protect trust | application_max_2: 20% peak increase; $25 fixed fee; 9,000 homes; 11% share | analysis_max_2: higher revenue vs risk of losing price-sensitive subscribers; peak loads predictable enough to manage | evaluation_max_2: weighs peak-event revenue against subscriber trust and churn in this market

Conversely, establishing wholly owned overseas dealerships retains complete control over $4,500 prices and brand image [k] within the $600,000 budget [app], but requires massive capital outlays and incurs full financial risk if sales volume falls below 3,000 units [an]. Overall, a joint venture is better because entering foreign Asian markets involves complex legal and channel barriers [eval]; partnering with an established local distributor mitigates entry risks far more effectively than building independent dealerships alone [eval].
    Keywords: joint venture, distributor, motorcycles, dealerships, electric, $4,500, $600,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: local channel access/mitigates regulatory risk; retains complete brand and price control/high capital outlay and full risk | application_max_2: $4,500 electric motorbikes; foreign import trade laws; $600,000 strategy budget; 3,000 units volume baseline | analysis_max_2: reduces foreign market entry risks; incurs full financial risk and heavy capital outlays | evaluation_max_2: weighs joint venture local partner expertise against direct ownership brand control in international motor vehicle market entry

--- STEM ---
Amber Grove Juices is a private limited company in Country X that presses cold-pressed mango and passionfruit juice. Sales of its signature mango juice have risen from 40,000 bottles in 2023 to 68,000 bottles in 2025, a growth-stage product life cycle. The owner, Lena Duarte, employs 14 staff and sells mainly through 30 independent grocers and one supermarket chain across two regions.

The supermarket has offered to stock mango juice in 45 more stores if Amber Grove installs a second bottling line costing $90,000. Alternatively, Lena could spend $18,000 on a regional television and social media advertising campaign to lift sales further. Either option risks stretching cash flow this year, and the mango juice is entering late growth, so she must decide quickly before summer demand peaks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'growth stage' of the product life cycle.
    Answer: The growth stage is the stage of the product life cycle when sales rise rapidly and the product becomes more widely known, so revenue and usually profit increase [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sales rise rapidly after introduction as the product gains acceptance; revenue and profit increase as sales grow

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Amber Grove Juices of its mango juice being in the growth stage.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Rising sales grow revenue [k], because bottle sales rose from 40,000 in 2023 to 68,000 in 2025 [app]. Benefit 2: A strong growth-stage product attracts bigger distribution deals [k], shown by the supermarket offer to stock mango juice in 45 more stores [app].
    Keywords: mango juice, 40,000, 68,000, 2023, 2025, 45 more stores, supermarket, growth-stage
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth stage brings rising revenue/profit; growth-stage popularity attracts distributors, retailers and wider acceptance | application_max_2: bottle sales rose from 40,000 in 2023 to 68,000 in 2025; supermarket offer to stock mango juice in 45 more stores

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Amber Grove Juices might face as its mango juice enters late growth.
    Answer: Problem 1: Production capacity may not keep pace with demand [k], because sales rose from 40,000 to 68,000 bottles a year on one line [app], risking empty shelves that could cost the new supermarket contract and the 30 grocers [an]. Problem 2: Cash flow could be stretched by expansion [k], because the $90,000 bottling line and $18,000 campaign both absorb cash this year [app], leaving Amber Grove short of working capital before summer demand peaks [an].
    Keywords: 40,000, 68,000, $90,000, $18,000, supermarket, cash flow, 45 more stores, late growth
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rapid growth strains capacity/production; growth-stage expansion pressures cash flow/working capital | application_max_2: sales rose from 40,000 to 68,000 bottles; $90,000 bottling line and $18,000 campaign absorb cash this year | analysis_max_2: risk losing the new supermarket contract and existing 30 grocers if stock runs out; short of working capital before summer demand peaks

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Amber Grove Juices should install the second bottling line rather than spend $18,000 on advertising? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that the second bottling line locks in growth [k], because the supermarket will stock mango juice in 45 more stores once it is installed [app], turning current capacity into supply for over two regions and converting 68,000-bottle sales into lasting profit [an]. On the other hand, advertising is far cheaper [k]: $18,000 spreads the word across the region without borrowing and keeps options open if growth slows [app], making it a lower-risk way to push mango juice before it exits late growth [an]. Overall, the bottling line is the better choice because $90,000 unlocks 45 more stores of guaranteed distribution, a much larger prize than the $18,000 campaign can deliver [eval], although Amber Grove should only proceed if cash flow stays positive and sales hold above 60,000 bottles a year [eval].
    Keywords: $90,000, $18,000, 45 more stores, supermarket, 68,000, late growth, mango juice, cash flow
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bottling line secures distribution and capacity for growth; advertising is cheaper and flexible but less certain | application_max_2: supermarket offer of 45 more stores tied to installing the line; $18,000 advertising option vs $90,000 bottling line cost | analysis_max_2: guaranteed extra distribution could convert growth-stage sales into lasting profit; advertising spreads awareness with less debt but does not add capacity | evaluation_max_2: weighs guaranteed distribution against cheaper flexible spending; justified choice with a cash-flow safeguard condition

--- STEM ---
Old Harbour Biscuits is a partnership in Country X making digestive and ginger biscuits since 2004. Its best-selling digestive biscuit sells 120,000 packs a year at $2.40 each; after years of maturity, sales have been flat for 3 years and the market is saturated. The two partners employ 22 staff and supply 55 independent grocers and 8 cafes across the southern region, with profits easing from $96,000 to $70,000 a year.

The partners are considering two options: relaunching the digestive biscuit with three new flavours and a modern wrapper costing $45,000, or cutting the price by 15% to $2.04 to stimulate sales. Their main competitor cut prices last year and gained 8% market share. They cannot afford both options and must decide by the end of the month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'saturation' in the product life cycle.
    Answer: Saturation is the stage of the product life cycle when the market is full of the product, sales stop rising and competition is intense, so revenue flattens [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: market is full / market no longer growing; sales flatten and competition is intense

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems a saturated market creates for Old Harbour Biscuits.
    Answer: Problem 1: Flat sales cap revenue [k], because digestive biscuit sales have been stuck at 120,000 packs a year for 3 years [app]. Problem 2: Rivals undercut and take share [k], because the main competitor cut prices and gained 8% market share [app].
    Keywords: 120,000 packs, $2.40, 3 years, saturated, 8%, market share, digestive
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: saturation means flat/plateauing sales and revenue; saturation means intense competition eroding share | application_max_2: digestive biscuit sales stuck at 120,000 packs a year for 3 years; competitor price cut gained it 8% market share

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Old Harbour Biscuits of relaunching with three new flavours and new packaging.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A relaunch can re-stimulate demand [k], because three new flavours and a modern wrapper give existing buyers a reason to try the biscuits again [app], which can reverse 3 years of flat sales supplied to 55 grocers and 8 cafes [an]. Benefit 2: Fresh packaging can support a better price [k], because buyers link modern packaging with improved quality [app], lifting margins as profits eased from $96,000 to $70,000 and offsetting the $45,000 wrapper cost [an].
    Keywords: three new flavours, modern wrapper, $45,000, $96,000, $70,000, 55 independent grocers, 8 cafes, flat
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: extension strategies such as new flavours re-stimulate demand; rebranding/repackaging can refresh product appeal and support pricing | application_max_2: three new flavours and a modern wrapper for $45,000; profits eased from $96,000 to $70,000 a year | analysis_max_2: can reverse flat sales and protect supply to 55 grocers and 8 cafes; higher perceived quality offsets wrapper costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Old Harbour Biscuits should relaunch with new flavours rather than cut the price by 15%? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that relaunching refreshes the product [k], because three new flavours and a modern wrapper costing $45,000 give buyers a reason to repurchase [app], reviving the 120,000-pack-a-year business and rebuilding profits that eased from $96,000 to $70,000 [an]. On the other hand, the 15% price cut to $2.04 is simpler and faster [k]: it directly answers the competitor that gained 8% market share and could lift volume quickly [app], but each pack earns $0.36 less, so profit per pack falls [an]. Overall, the relaunch is the better choice because cutting price only matches a rival and erodes margins, while new flavours defend share properly and could restore the $96,000 peak profit level [eval], but the partners should track sales weekly and switch to pricing action if the relaunch has not lifted packs within 3 months [eval].
    Keywords: $45,000, 15%, $2.04, $2.40, 120,000, 8%, three new flavours, $96,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: extension strategy (new flavours/packaging) refreshes a maturing product; price cuts stimulate volume but reduce margin per unit | application_max_2: relaunch costs $45,000 vs 15% price cut to $2.04; competitor gained 8% market share after a price cut | analysis_max_2: new flavours can revive demand and rebuild profits from $70,000 toward $96,000; price cuts win volume at the cost of $0.36 per pack margin | evaluation_max_2: weighs brand refresh against reactive price matching; justified choice plus a measurable review condition

Sales peaked at 30,000 units in 2021 and fell to 9,000 units in 2025, placing both products in the decline stage of the product life cycle. The business employs 38 staff, holds $260,000 of unsold stock, and annual revenue has halved from $2.4 million to $1.2 million over three years.

The directors are considering either an extension strategy, releasing a combined DVD/MP3 media centre with smart streaming for $120,000 of retooling, or discontinuing the range and selling the factory machinery to raise about $180,000.     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sales fall steadily; product is outdated/replaced so revenue and profit shrink

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Everline Audio's products are in the decline stage.
    Answer: Reason 1: Technology is outdated [k], because DVD players and MP3 players have been replaced by streaming and online content [app]. Reason 2: Unit sales keep shrinking [k], with sales falling from 30,000 units in 2021 to 9,000 units in 2025 [app].
    Keywords: DVD players, MP3 players, 30,000 units, 9,000 units, 2021, 2025, decline stage, 11 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: products become outdated as technology moves on; sales fall steadily in the decline stage | application_max_2: DVD/MP3 players replaced by modern alternatives; sales fell from 30,000 units in 2021 to 9,000 units in 2025

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Everline Audio of launching the media centre as an extension strategy.
    Answer: Benefit 1: It can win back lapsed customers [k], because a DVD/MP3 media centre with smart streaming updates the old range for existing owners [app], slowing the slide from 30,000 units to 9,000 units a year and protecting the 38 staff [an]. Benefit 2: It keeps the factory productive [k], because $120,000 of retooling reuses the plant and 11 years of manufacturing experience [app], preserving $1.2 million of annual revenue instead of shutting down for a machinery sale [an].
    Keywords: $120,000, media centre, DVD/MP3, smart streaming, 30,000, 9,000, 38 employees, extension strategy
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: extension strategies extend a declining product life; extension reuses existing resources/knowhow | application_max_2: media centre with smart streaming for $120,000 of retooling; reuses factory built over 11 years | analysis_max_2: can slow the sales slide and protect jobs and revenue; cheaper than starting from scratch; keeps plant productive

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Everline Audio should launch the media centre rather than discontinue the range? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that the extension strategy buys time [k], because the media centre with smart streaming refreshes an outdated range for only $120,000 of retooling [app], which could recover some of the fall from 30,000 units in 2021 to 9,000 units and keep the 38 staff employed [an]. On the other hand, discontinuing is cleaner [k], because selling the machinery for about $180,000 frees cash and ends the $260,000 unsold-stock problem [app], letting shareholders redeploy money instead of backing a shrinking DVD/MP3 market [an]. Overall, Everline should discontinue the range because four years of decline, down to 9,000 units from a 30,000 peak, show demand is structurally gone; taking the $180,000 is safer than risking $120,000 of further losses [eval], but if confirmed pre-orders for the media centre top 12,000 units the board should approve the launch instead [eval].
    Keywords: $120,000, $180,000, $260,000, media centre, smart streaming, 9,000, 38 employees, extension strategy
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: extension strategies can prolong but not reverse structural decline; discontinuing releases cash and ends losses | application_max_2: $120,000 retooling vs selling machinery for about $180,000; sales fell from 30,000 units (2021) to 9,000 (2025); $260,000 of unsold stock | analysis_max_2: media centre may recover some demand but DVD/MP3 market keeps shrinking; discontinuing frees $180,000 and stops cash drain on dead stock | evaluation_max_2: weighs extension risk against clean exit; justified exit recommendation with a clear trigger for reversal
