    Question: Explain two benefits to Redcurrent Energy of launching first in one region.
    Answer: Benefit 1: It cuts launch cost and risk [k], because a one-region campaign costs $30,000 instead of $95,000 nationwide [app], conserving cash after $210,000 of development [an]. Benefit 2: It provides real sales feedback before scaling [k], because 6 months of regional data reveal whether a $1.50 can with $0.60 of canning and distribution sells at volume [app], letting Redcurrent fix problems before reaching 1,200 campuses [an].
    Keywords: $30,000, $95,000, $1.50, 6 months, one region, 16 to 24, $0.60, 78%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: regional launches limit cost and risk of new product failure; regional launches give real market evidence before expansion | application_max_2: $30,000 one-region campaign vs $95,000 nationwide advertising; $1.50 price with $0.60 canning and distribution cost | analysis_max_2: conserves cash after $210,000 of unrecovered development spend; 6 months of data shows whether per-can economics work at scale

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redcurrent Energy should launch nationwide rather than start in one region? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that the nationwide launch maximises impact [k], because 1,200 university stores and campuses reach the 16 to 24 student market immediately [app], with $95,000 of advertising building rapid awareness while Redcurrent is first mover [an]. On the other hand, the one-region launch protects cash [k], because a $30,000 campaign limits risk after $210,000 of development and only 300 students of trial evidence [app], letting Redcurrent refine the $1.50 price and $0.60 per-can cost before national exposure [an]. Overall, Redcurrent should start in one region because unrecovered development of $210,000 and uncertain acceptance mean $95,000 should only be committed after 6 months of real sales data prove demand [eval], but if early sales beat 70% of target within 3 months the rollout nationwide should follow immediately [eval].
    Keywords: $95,000, $30,000, $210,000, 1,200 university stores, $1.50, 300 trial students, 6 months, 78%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: national launch builds fast awareness but risks cash; regional launch limits risk and provides market proof | application_max_2: $95,000 nationwide advertising vs $30,000 regional campaign; $210,000 development already spent; reach via 1,200 university stores | analysis_max_2: full launch spends before demand is proven; regional data verifies $1.50 pricing and $0.60 per-can economics | evaluation_max_2: weighs speed and scale vs risk and evidence; justified regional-first choice with a numeric escalation trigger

--- STEM ---
Harvest Crown Cereals is a public limited company in Country X making the nation's best-selling corn flakes since 2001. Sales fell from 95,000 boxes a week in 2022 to 58,000 boxes a week in 2025 as rivals launched new variants and ran price promotions. The business employs 240 staff across 2 factories and holds 19% market share, down from 26% three years ago.

Management wants an extension strategy to revive the brand. Option one is a $500,000 relaunch with high-protein and honey variants and a new box design, with $310,000 allocated to design and factory changeover. Option two is a $180,000 promotional drive of free samples and price reductions for 8 weeks. Both aim to extend the product life cycle and defend the 19% share.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two extension strategies a business could use.
    Answer: Two extension strategies are relaunching the product with new variants or additional features [1]; running sales promotions such as free samples or price reductions to revive demand [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relaunch with new variants/features/flavours; sales promotions such as free samples or price reductions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Harvest Crown Corn Flakes may have moved towards decline.
    Answer: Reason 1: Changing consumer tastes [k], because buyers shifted towards high-protein and healthier cereals offered by rivals [app]. Reason 2: Stronger rival products [k], because rivals launched new variants and promotions, cutting Harvest Crown share from 26% to 19% [app].
    Keywords: corn flakes, 26%, 19%, 58,000, 95,000, 2001, rivals, extension strategy
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: consumer tastes change away from the product; rival new entrants/variants erode demand | application_max_2: buyers want high-protein/healthier cereals; market share fell from 26% to 19% as rivals launched new variants and promotions

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Harvest Crown of the $500,000 relaunch with new variants.
    Answer: Benefit 1: It attracts buyers back [k], because high-protein and honey variants meet current health trends [app], reversing the slide from 95,000 to 58,000 boxes a week [an]. Benefit 2: A new box design refreshes shelf presence [k], because packaging that stands out stops rivals dominating the display [app], helping rebuild the 19% market share towards the previous 26% [an].
    Keywords: $500,000, high-protein, honey, 95,000, 58,000, 19%, new variants, box design
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: extension strategies (new variants) attract returning and new buyers; extension strategies refresh packaging and shelf appeal | application_max_2: high-protein and honey variants for $500,000 including new box design; sales fell from 95,000 to 58,000 boxes a week | analysis_max_2: can reverse weekly sales decline and protect 240 jobs; can rebuild 19% share towards earlier 26% level

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harvest Crown Cereals should relaunch with new variants rather than run the promotional drive? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One side is that the relaunch can permanently refresh demand [k], because high-protein and honey variants with a new box design cost $500,000 but extend the life cycle properly [app], reversing the slide from 95,000 to 58,000 boxes a week and rebuilding 19% share towards 26% [an]. On the other hand, the $180,000 promotional drive is cheaper and faster [k], because free samples and 8 weeks of price reductions spike weekly volume immediately [app], costing less than the $310,000 design and changeover portion of the relaunch and defending share while deeper plans are prepared [an]. Overall, Harvest Crown should relaunch with new variants because the decline is structural, not seasonal; the promotion only rents demand for 8 weeks while the relaunch rebuilds the brand for the next decade [eval], but if board cash is tight, running the $180,000 drive first to fund the relaunch is a sensible bridge [eval].
    Keywords: $500,000, $180,000, $310,000, 95,000, 58,000, 19%, 26%, high-protein
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relaunch (real extension strategy) addresses structural decline; promotion gives short-term volume spike but no permanent fix | application_max_2: $500,000 relaunch with $310,000 design and changeover vs $180,000 promotional drive; sales fell from 95,000 (2022) to 58,000 boxes a week (2025); share 26% to 19% | analysis_max_2: new variants can rebuild weekly sales and share durably; promotion rents demand for 8 weeks at lower cost and risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs durable brand revival against cheap quick volume; justified relaunch with a funding-bridge exception

--- STEM ---
Queensbridge Deli & Rotisserie is a family-run deli and hot-food counter operating for 6 years in Queensbridge market square, employing 9 staff and serving around 420 roast-chicken meals a week. Each meal costs $8 to make, and the owner prices it using cost-plus pricing with a 25% mark-up, giving a selling price of $10. Weekly meal revenue is therefore $4,200 and weekly mark-up profit is $840.

A new supermarket deli opened nearby in March, charging $9.50 for a comparable meal and attracting price-sensitive shoppers. The owner employs a part-time assistant at $12 an hour to cope with the lunch rush of 240 meals between 12:00 and 14:00. The owner must decide whether to keep 25% cost-plus pricing and promote quality, or switch to competitive pricing aligned with the supermarket at $9.50. The decision will be reviewed at the end of September, after 8 weeks of trading data.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'mark-up'.
    Answer: A mark-up is the amount added to the cost of a product to arrive at its selling price, usually expressed as a percentage of cost; for example, adding 25% to the $8 cost gives a price of $10 [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the amount added to the cost of a product to set the selling price; usually expressed as a percentage of cost

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Queensbridge Deli & Rotisserie of keeping cost-plus pricing.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A guaranteed profit margin [k], as the 25% mark-up on the $8 cost gives $2 per meal and about $840 a week at 420 meals [app]. Advantage 2: Simplicity [k], as the owner can set prices in minutes without tracking the supermarket's $9.50 price every day [app].
    Keywords: cost-plus pricing, 25%, $8, $10, $4,200, $840, competitive pricing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guarantees a profit margin on every unit sold; simple and quick way to set selling prices | application_max_2: 25% mark-up on the $8 cost gives $2 per meal; $840 weekly mark-up profit at 420 meals; supermarket charges $9.50

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of keeping 25% cost-plus pricing instead of switching to competitive pricing.
    Answer: Problem 1: A price above the rival [k], as cost-plus ignores the supermarket's $9.50 meal and leaves the deli at $10 [app], so price-sensitive shoppers may switch, cutting weekly volume and the $840 mark-up profit [an]. Problem 2: No signal from the market [k], as cost-plus only covers the $8 cost plus 25% and ignores what shoppers will pay [app], so falling demand may go unnoticed until the September trading review [an].
    Keywords: supermarket, $9.50, $10, price-sensitive, 25%, September, competitive pricing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cost-plus ignores competitors' prices and market demand; price set above the rival loses sales | application_max_2: $9.50 supermarket meal versus the deli's $10 price; price-sensitive shoppers; 8 weeks of trading data by September | analysis_max_2: cuts weekly volume and the $840 mark-up profit; prevents early detection of falling demand until the review

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Queensbridge Deli & Rotisserie should keep 25% cost-plus pricing rather than switch to competitive pricing? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Keeping cost-plus protects the margin [k]: the 25% mark-up yields $2 per meal and about $840 a week at 420 meals [app], and dropping to $9.50 would wipe out $0.50 per meal and roughly $210 a week of profit at 420 meals [an]. However, competitive pricing matches shopper expectations [k]: aligning to the supermarket's $9.50 would win back the price-sensitive lunch trade lost since March [app], potentially restoring volume and protecting the deli's footfall [an]. Overall, Queensbridge should keep cost-plus at $10 rather than match $9.50 for now [eval], because its speed, quality and market-square location remain proven at $10 and a $0.50 cut costs $210 a week before extra sales are guaranteed [eval]. The owner should promote quality and convenience, and review the September trading data before switching.
    Keywords: 25%, $9.50, $10, $840, 420, cost-plus pricing, competitive pricing, supermarket
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cost-plus protects a planned unit margin; competitive pricing defends share against a rival | application_max_2: 25% mark-up gives $2 per meal / $840 weekly profit; $9.50 supermarket price; $0.50 cut costs about $210 a week at 420 meals | analysis_max_2: cutting to $9.50 immediately reduces profit even before sales response; matching $9.50 could win back price-sensitive shoppers and restore volume | evaluation_max_2: weighs guaranteed margin against competitive threat; recommends keeping cost-plus with a review; quantifies $210 a week at risk from a $0.50 price cut

--- STEM ---
Bluewater Frozen Foods is a discount frozen-food retailer that opened its first 3 stores this year in the southern province, backed by $900,000 of owners' capital. Its biggest line is a 1kg bag of frozen vegetables sold at $3.50 using penetration pricing, compared with $6.00 at the national supermarket chain. Unit cost is $2.75, so each bag earns only $0.75. First-month sales reached 9,000 bags across the 3 stores.

The board is deciding whether to hold the $3.50 launch price for a further 6 months to build a 15% local market share, or switch to competitive pricing at $5.25, trusting that Bluewater's local sourcing and fresher stock can win shoppers without such a deep discount. Last week, 68% of surveyed shoppers said price was the main reason they switched. The board meets in 3 weeks to decide.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'market share'.
    Answer: Market share is the proportion of total sales in a market held by one business or brand, usually expressed as a percentage of total market sales; it shows how well a business is performing against its rivals [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the proportion of total market sales held by one business or brand; usually expressed as a percentage of total market sales

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Bluewater Frozen Foods of holding the $3.50 penetration price.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Rapid share growth [k], as $3.50 continues to undercut the national chain's $6.00, drawing the 68% of shoppers who switched for price and lifting the 3 stores toward the 15% local market share target [app]. Advantage 2: High volume drives store traffic [k], as 9,000 bags sold in month 1 means more shoppers also buy other groceries on the same trip [app].
    Keywords: $3.50, $6.00, 9,000, 3 stores, 15%, penetration pricing, 68%, $2.75
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: builds market share quickly; high sales volume increases store traffic and basket size | application_max_2: $3.50 price versus the national chain's $6.00; 68% switched for price; 9,000 bags sold in month 1 across 3 stores; 15% share target

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of Bluewater Frozen Foods holding the $3.50 penetration price.
    Answer: Problem 1: Very thin margins [k], as the unit cost is $2.75, so each bag earns only $0.75 [app], which delays recovery of the $900,000 of owners' capital for longer [an]. Problem 2: Risk of a price war [k], as holding a deep discount invites rivals to match $3.50 [app], leaving Bluewater with thinner margins and no lasting share gain [an].
    Keywords: $2.75, $0.75, $900,000, $3.50, 15%, $5.25, penetration
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: penetration prices give very low profit margins; rivals may match the low price, triggering a price war | application_max_2: unit cost $2.75 gives only $0.75 margin per bag; $900,000 owners' capital; $3.50 launch price | analysis_max_2: slower recovery of owners' capital; no lasting share gain if rivals match price, only thinner margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Bluewater Frozen Foods should hold the $3.50 penetration price rather than switch to competitive pricing at $5.25? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Holding $3.50 keeps the volume engine running [k]: $3.50 against the national chain's $6.00 pulled in 9,000 bags in month 1, and 68% of surveyed shoppers switched for price, supporting the push to 15% local market share [app], which builds scale, buying power and brand presence for future growth [an]. However, switching to $5.25 protects profit [k]: lifting the price into the competitive zone raises the margin from $0.75 to $2.50 per bag [app], turning thin trading into healthier cash to fund more stores [an]. Overall, Bluewater should hold $3.50 only until the 15% share target is met, then move towards $5.25 [eval], because penetration pricing is a launch tactic rather than a permanent strategy, and share won cheaply now must eventually convert into profit [eval].
    Keywords: $3.50, $5.25, $6.00, 9,000, 68%, 15%, penetration pricing, $2.75
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: low penetration price wins volume and share quickly; switching to competitive pricing restores unit margin | application_max_2: $3.50 versus $6.00; 9,000 bags in month 1; 68% switched for price; $5.25 switching raises margin from $0.75 to $2.50 | analysis_max_2: share and scale strengthen buying power and future brand presence; extra $1.75 per bag funds expansion and healthier cash flow | evaluation_max_2: recommends time-limited price hold then switch to competitive pricing; recognises penetration pricing is a launch tactic, not permanent strategy

--- STEM ---
Tidemark Marine Instruments launched the 'Lookout Pro', a kayak-mounted sonar fish finder, 5 months ago. Production cost is $140 per unit. At launch, price skimming set the price at $499 for early adopters, against around $210 for standard fish finders from rivals. Month 1 sales were 240 units, but monthly sales had fallen to 90 by month 5 as the enthusiast market filled.

Development cost of $85,000 must also be recovered. The board is deciding whether to keep the $499 price for the remaining 600 units in stock, or cut to $299 to attract mainstream anglers before next summer's fishing season. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'price-inelastic demand'.
    Answer: Price-inelastic demand is when demand for a product changes proportionately less than its price; customers are not very responsive to price changes, often because they see few close substitutes [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: demand changes proportionately less than price; customers are not very responsive, often due to few substitutes

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Tidemark Marine Instruments of using price skimming at launch.
    Answer: Advantage 1: High margins from early adopters [k], as enthusiasts paid $499 against a $140 production cost, earning $359 per unit [app]. Advantage 2: Quick recovery of development spend [k], as the strong $499 price generated cash early, helping recover the $85,000 development cost while monthly sales peaked at 240 in month 1 [app].
    Keywords: $499, $140, 240, $85,000, price skimming, Lookout Pro
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high profit margins from early adopters; recovers development costs quickly | application_max_2: $499 price against $140 production cost gives $359 per unit; $85,000 development cost; 240 units sold in month 1

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Tidemark Marine Instruments of cutting the price from $499 to $299.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A wider mainstream market [k], as cutting to $299 makes the Lookout Pro affordable to ordinary anglers, not just the 90-a-month enthusiasts [app], lifting volume toward the 300-unit monthly capacity before the season [an]. Advantage 2: Faster clearance of remaining stock [k], as 600 units are unsold and mainstream anglers are more price-aware than enthusiasts [app], converting slow stock into cash before summer [an].
    Keywords: $499, $299, 600, 300, $210, Lookout Pro, 90
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: opens the mass market and lifts sales volume; clears remaining stock more quickly | application_max_2: $499 to $299 targets mainstream anglers; monthly sales fell to 90; 600 units in stock; 300-unit monthly capacity | analysis_max_2: raises volume toward capacity and total sales; converts unsold stock into cash before the season

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tidemark Marine Instruments should keep the $499 price rather than cut to $299? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Keeping $499 defends the margin [k]: each Lookout Pro still earns $359 per unit, and the 240 units sold in month 1 prove demand exists at this level among enthusiasts [app], so the remaining 600 units would yield the highest possible return per unit [an]. However, cutting to $299 would revive volume [k]: mainstream anglers would respond to a $200 lower price, and with sales down to 90 a month, cash would arrive faster to fund the next product [app], though each unit's margin falls by $200 [an]. Overall, Tidemark should cut to $299 [eval], because enthusiast demand has dried up from 240 to 90 units a month and 600 units at $299 (earning $159 each) beat unsold stock sitting at $499 [eval].
    Keywords: $499, $299, $140, 240, 90, 600, Lookout Pro
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high launch price protects unit margin and brand image; lower price revives demand once early-adopter market fills | application_max_2: $499 gives $359 per unit; 240 units in month 1; sales fell to 90 a month; 600 units remaining | analysis_max_2: keeps maximum return per unit on remaining stock; cutting to $299 restores volume and cash flow at a $200 margin cost | evaluation_max_2: recommends cutting to $299 as the enthusiast segment is exhausted; quantifies $159 margin per unit at $299 versus unsold stock at $499

--- STEM ---
Harrington Fuels operates a petrol station with a convenience shop on the northern approach road, facing 3 rival stations within 2 kilometres. It prices unleaded petrol at $1.45 per litre, exactly matching its nearest rival, and accepts a fuel margin as low as $0.06 per litre. Most profit comes from the shop, where 1,400 extra customers a week buy drinks, snacks and car accessories; shop revenue last year was $86,000, and annual fuel volume is around 950,000 litres.

The station manager is deciding whether to keep matched pricing or raise petrol to $1.49, relying on shop sales to hold customer numbers. A $0.04 rise would add an estimated $38,000 a year to fuel margin but risks losing shoppers to rivals. The regional manager reviews pricing on 30 June.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'competitive pricing'.
    Answer: Competitive pricing is setting the selling price in line with rivals' prices for similar products, rather than basing the price purely on costs or demand; the business charges what the market already pays [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: setting the price in line with rivals' prices for similar products; not based purely on costs or demand

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Harrington Fuels of matching rivals' fuel prices.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Protects customer numbers [k], as matching the nearest rival at $1.45 per litre stops drivers switching, keeping fuel volume at around 950,000 litres a year [app]. Advantage 2: Steady forecourt and shop traffic [k], as matching keeps Harrington the habit stop for local drivers, sustaining the 1,400 extra shop customers a week [app].
    Keywords: $1.45, 1,400, $86,000, $0.06, 3 rival stations, matched pricing, 950,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: prevents loss of customers to rivals; sustains regular footfall and habitual custom | application_max_2: $1.45 per litre matches the nearest rival; 950,000 litres a year; 1,400 extra shop customers a week; shop revenue $86,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of Harrington Fuels matching rivals' fuel prices.
    Answer: Problem 1: A razor-thin fuel margin [k], as the $0.06 margin per litre leaves no cushion against rising wholesale fuel costs [app], squeezing overall profit if shop sales dip [an]. Problem 2: No price-based differentiation [k], as charging exactly $1.45 gives drivers no price reason to prefer Harrington [app], so the business must win entirely on shop appeal and service [an].
    Keywords: $0.06, $1.45, $1.49, 2 kilometres, 950,000, matched pricing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fuel margins become extremely thin; no price differentiation from rivals | application_max_2: $0.06 per litre margin; exactly $1.45 matching the nearest rival | analysis_max_2: profit is squeezed if shop sales fall or costs rise; must win customers on shop appeal rather than fuel price

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harrington Fuels should keep matching rivals at $1.45 rather than raise petrol to $1.49? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Keeping matched pricing protects the shop engine [k]: at $1.45 the station stays the default stop, and the 1,400 weekly shop customers generate the $86,000 shop revenue where margins are far healthier than fuel's $0.06 per litre [app], so total profit is more secure even with flat fuel margins [an]. However, raising to $1.49 adds guaranteed profit [k]: a $0.04 rise on 950,000 annual litres would add around $38,000 a year to fuel margin if volume holds [app], though losing only modest footfall to the 2 rivals within 2 kilometres could erase it through lost shop sales [an]. Overall, Harrington should keep $1.45 [eval], because the shop is the real profit centre and a $0.04 rise risks the footfall that makes the whole site viable [eval].
    Keywords: $1.45, $1.49, $0.06, 1,400, $86,000, 950,000, 2 kilometres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: matching price protects footfall and shop-dependent profit; raising price adds direct margin if volume holds | application_max_2: $1.45 matched price; 1,400 weekly shoppers; $86,000 shop revenue; $1.49 gives $0.04 rise; 950,000 litres = about $38,000 a year | analysis_max_2: shop margins far healthier than fuel's $0.06, so footfall protects total profit; lost footfall could wipe out the $38,000 gain through lost shop sales | evaluation_max_2: recommends keeping $1.45 to protect the shop profit centre; quantifies the $38,000 gain against footfall risk from 2 rivals within 2 kilometres

--- STEM ---
Willowmere Home & Furniture operates a 7,000 m² out-of-town warehouse selling sofas, beds and dining sets. Every bank holiday it runs promotional pricing, cutting selected lines by 20% for 4 days; a bestselling three-seat sofa marked $1,200 sells at $960 during these events. The April event drew 3,800 visitors and sold 420 sofas, lifting April revenue to $980,000 against $610,000 in March. The marketing manager reports that 55% of event sales came from repeat bargain-hunters.

The board is deciding whether to extend promotional pricing to every weekend in July and August, or restrict it to the 6 bank holiday weekends a year to protect full prices. Warehouse costs are unchanged either way, and summer stock stands at 2,900 sofas. The board meets in 5 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'promotional pricing'.
    Answer: Promotional pricing is reducing the selling price of a product for a short period to boost sales, attract customers or clear stock; the price returns to normal after the promotion ends [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reducing the price for a short period; used to boost sales, attract customers or clear stock; price returns to normal afterwards

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Willowmere Home & Furniture of promotional pricing.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A strong short-term sales boost [k], as the April event sold 420 sofas at $960 and lifted April revenue to $980,000 against $610,000 in March [app]. Advantage 2: Attracts new and repeat visitors [k], as the event drew 3,800 visitors, widening Willowmere's customer base [app].
    Keywords: promotional pricing, $960, April, $980,000, $610,000, 3,800, $1,200
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: boosts sales quickly during the promotion; attracts new and repeat customers | application_max_2: April event sold 420 sofas; revenue rose to $980,000 from $610,000; 3,800 visitors attended the April event; $960 sale price

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of extending promotional pricing to every summer weekend for Willowmere.
    Answer: Problem 1: Lost margin on every sale [k], as the $1,200 sofa sells at $960, giving up $240 per sofa [app], so 2,900 summer sofas at 55% bargain-hunter reliance could forfeit deep margin [an]. Problem 2: Customers wait for discounts [k], as 55% of event sales already came from repeat bargain-hunters [app], so everyday $1,200 prices may stop selling at full price [an].
    Keywords: $1,200, $960, 55%, July and August, 2,900 sofas, promotional pricing, 20%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: margin is sacrificed on every discounted unit; customers become trained to wait for sales, damaging full-price demand | application_max_2: $1,200 sofa sells at $960, losing $240 per unit; 55% of event sales from repeat bargain-hunters; 2,900 sofas in stock | analysis_max_2: extending discounts across the summer could cost a very large share of margin; full-price sales collapse once bargain behaviour becomes the norm

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Willowmere Home & Furniture should extend promotional pricing to every summer weekend rather than keep bank-holiday events only? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Every-weekend discounting would shift summer stock fast [k]: sale events could clear part of the 2,900-sofa stock at $960, adding weekly volume, as April's event pushed revenue to $980,000 against a $610,000 March [app], converting floor stock to cash before the autumn delivery cycle [an]. However, constant sales would damage the everyday price [k]: with 55% of event sales from repeat bargain-hunters, extending discounts risks training customers to never pay $1,200, and margin lost at $240 per sofa across 2,900 sofas amounts to $696,000 [app], wiping out the April-style revenue gain if full prices stop selling [an]. Overall, Willowmere should not discount every weekend [eval]; it should keep bank-holiday promotions and add at most one mid-summer event, protecting the everyday $1,200 price while still capturing some impulse volume [eval].
    Keywords: $1,200, $960, 55%, 2,900 sofas, promotional pricing, $980,000, July and August, 20%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: frequent promotions clear stock and lift short-term cash; constant promotions destroy everyday price integrity and margin | application_max_2: April event sold 420 sofas, revenue $980,000 vs $610,000 March; 55% of event sales from repeat bargain-hunters; 2,900 sofas at $240 off = $696,000 at risk | analysis_max_2: summer volume converts stock to cash before the autumn cycle; loss of full-price sales outweighs the promotion revenue gain | evaluation_max_2: rejects every-weekend discounting; recommends keeping bank holidays plus one mid-summer event; quantifies $696,000 margin at risk across 2,900 sofas

--- STEM ---
The Rialto Theatre, a 900-seat city-centre venue run as a private limited company, stages musicals and classic plays. Its box office uses dynamic pricing: peak Saturday seats are $42, midweek seats $24, and day-of unsold seats drop to $12 at 16:00. Last season, average occupancy was 68%, weekday evenings ran at 45% capacity, and Saturdays sold out in 9 of 22 weekends. Annual ticket revenue was $1,150,000 across all performances.

The board is deciding whether to widen the dynamic range — Saturdays at $48, weekdays at $20 and day-of at $8 — or move to a flat $28 ticket price to simplify sales and marketing. The marketing manager warns that a flat price could cut revenue by an estimated $95,000 a year. The board votes on 20 August.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'demand'.
    Answer: Demand is the quantity of a product or service that consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price, in a given time period, within a given market [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quantity of a product consumers are willing and able to buy; at a given price, in a given time period, within a given market

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to The Rialto Theatre of dynamic pricing.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Maximises peak-slot revenue [k], as Saturday seats at $42 sold out in 9 of 22 weekends, so higher Saturday prices load income when demand is strongest [app]. Advantage 2: Fills off-peak capacity [k], as weekday seats at $24 and day-of seats at $12 lift occupancy from the 45% weekday level toward the 68% season average [app].
    Keywords: dynamic pricing, $42, $24, $12, 45%, 68%, 900-seat
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: charges more when demand is high, maximising peak revenue; day-of discounts fill seats that would otherwise stay empty | application_max_2: $42 Saturday seats sold out in 9 of 22 weekends; weekday occupancy at 45% versus 68% season average; $12 day-of price

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of dynamic pricing for The Rialto Theatre.
    Answer: Problem 1: Customer resentment [k], as fans paying $42 for Saturdays while others pay $12 day-of may feel the pricing is unfair [app], damaging loyalty and word-of-mouth promotion [an]. Problem 2: Complex administration [k], as the box office must manage three price tiers and drop seats to $12 at 16:00 each day [app], adding staffing and systems cost and risking pricing errors [an].
    Keywords: $42, $24, $12, 16:00, dynamic pricing, weekday, Saturdays
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: perceived unfairness can damage customer relationships; managing multiple price tiers adds cost and complexity | application_max_2: Saturday $42 versus day-of $12 perception gap; three tiers with a 16:00 daily price drop | analysis_max_2: loyalty and word-of-mouth promotion suffer; higher administration cost and pricing errors

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think The Rialto Theatre should widen the dynamic pricing range rather than adopt a flat $28 ticket? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Widening the dynamic range captures peak demand [k]: Saturdays at $48 on sold-out weeks and weekday seats at $20 to lift the 45% weekday occupancy both push ticket revenue above the current $1,150,000 [app], provided the revenue gain exceeds the flat-price alternative the marketing manager estimated at $95,000 a year [an]. However, the flat $28 ticket is simpler and fairer [k]: one price ends resentment between $42 Saturday payers and $12 day-of buyers and removes the daily 16:00 price change [app], though it could cut revenue by an estimated $95,000 a year [an]. Overall, The Rialto should widen the dynamic range rather than adopt $28 flat [eval], because weekends sell out while weekdays sit at 45% — dynamic pricing is the only lever that monetises scarcity and fills spare seats at once [eval].
    Keywords: dynamic pricing, $48, $20, $28, $95,000, $1,150,000, 45%, Saturdays
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: dynamic pricing captures peak demand and fills off-peak seats; a flat price is simpler and perceived as fairer | application_max_2: $48 Saturdays and $20 weekday seats against 45% weekday occupancy; flat $28 ticket estimated to cut revenue by $95,000 a year; $1,150,000 current revenue | analysis_max_2: widening the range can push revenue above the current $1,150,000; flat pricing sacrifices an estimated $95,000 a year in revenue | evaluation_max_2: recommends widening the dynamic range over a flat $28 price; uses weekend sell-outs versus 45% weekday occupancy as decisive reasoning

--- STEM ---
Hartley & Rye Artisan Bakery operates 2 shops in a market town, employing 14 bakers and assistants. It sells an everyday staple cottage loaf for $3.20 and a premium heritage-grain sourdough for $5.50. When staple prices rose 10% last year, unit sales slipped 2%, but a 10% rise in the premium loaf cut unit sales by 14%. Loyal weekly customers number around 1,100. Price notices would change on 1 September.

The owner is deciding whether to raise all bread prices by a further 10% this year, or raise only the staple loaf, leaving the premium sourdough at $5.50. The premium loaf generates 38% of shop revenue, and the wholesale butter contract renews in 3 months. The owner is meeting her accountant on Friday.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'price elasticity of demand'.
    Answer: Price elasticity of demand describes how responsive demand for a product is to a change in its price: demand is price-elastic when a price change leads to a proportionately larger change in quantity demanded, and price-inelastic when quantity changes proportionately less [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: describes how responsive demand is to a change in price; elastic = quantity changes proportionately more than price; inelastic = proportionately less

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why demand for Hartley & Rye's staple cottage loaf is price-inelastic.
    Answer: Reason 1: Bread is a necessity [k], as everyday bread is a staple bought weekly by around 1,100 loyal customers, so the 10% price rise last year cut sales by only 2% [app]. Reason 2: Limited local choice [k], as with only 2 shops in the market town, weekly routines kept shoppers buying despite the rise [app].
    Keywords: staple, cottage loaf, 10%, 2%, 1,100, 2 shops, $3.20
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: everyday bread is a necessity or habit purchase; limited local substitutes keep customers buying | application_max_2: 10% rise last year cut staple sales by only 2%; around 1,100 loyal weekly customers; 2 shops in the market town

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why demand for the premium heritage-grain sourdough is price-elastic.
    Answer: Reason 1: It is a luxury, not a necessity [k], as the $5.50 heritage-grain loaf is a premium choice, so buyers are more price-aware than cottage-loaf buyers [app], making demand fall sharply when price rises [an]. Reason 2: Substitutes are close at hand [k], as shoppers can switch to the $3.20 cottage loaf or other bread options [app], so the 10% rise cut premium unit sales by 14% [an].
    Keywords: $5.50, premium, $3.20, 14%, sourdough, 10%, heritage-grain
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: premium products are luxuries that customers cut back on when prices rise; close substitutes make switching easy | application_max_2: $5.50 heritage-grain premium loaf; 10% rise cut premium sales by 14%; cottage loaf at $3.20 | analysis_max_2: premium spend is discretionary and drops sharply with price rises; easy substitution drives the 14% fall in sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hartley & Rye should raise all bread prices by 10% rather than only the staple loaf? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising everything rides on the inelastic staple [k]: cottage-loaf sales fell just 2% on a 10% rise last year, so lifting $3.20 to $3.52 would hold volume and lift revenue from around 1,100 weekly customers [app], protecting margin on the highest-volume line [an]. However, lifting the premium sourdough ignores its elasticity [k]: the premium loaf generates 38% of revenue and its sales already fell 14% on the last 10% rise, so a further rise risks steeper losses on the line that matters most [app], eroding revenue despite the higher unit price [an]. Overall, Hartley & Rye should raise only the staple loaf and leave the premium sourdough at $5.50 [eval], because the data shows a price-inelastic staple and a price-elastic premium line, exactly the opposite of what an across-the-board rise needs [eval].
    Keywords: staple, cottage loaf, 2%, 14%, 38%, $5.50, $3.20, 1,100, premium
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: inelastic demand allows price rises with little volume loss; elastic demand means price rises cause steep volume losses | application_max_2: staple fell 2% on a 10% rise; $3.20 to $3.52; premium loaf generates 38% of revenue; sales fell 14% on the last 10% rise | analysis_max_2: staple rise protects margin on the highest-volume line; premium rise erodes revenue and risks losing the line generating 38% of revenue | evaluation_max_2: recommends staple-only increase, leaving the premium sourdough at $5.50; grounds the recommendation in the opposite elasticities shown by the sales data

--- STEM ---
Redhill Everyday Value, a discount supermarket chain with 4 stores in one province, is launching its own-brand tomato soup. It employs 210 staff across the 4 stores. The soup costs $1.10 per tin to produce. Applying a 20% cost-plus mark-up gives a launch price of $1.32. The market leader charges $1.49 and the cheapest rival charges $1.19. Category manager Theo Lambert must set the price this month.

Forecasts suggest sales of 380,000 tins in year 1 at $1.32, or 600,000 tins at $1.19, matching the cheapest rival under competitive pricing. At $1.32 the tin earns $0.22 margin, worth $83,600; at $1.19 margin is $0.09, worth $54,000. Theo argues that volume and share matter most in own-brand launches, while the finance director prefers protecting margin in year 1. Leadership meets tomorrow to decide.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'cost-plus pricing'.
    Answer: Cost-plus pricing sets the selling price by adding a fixed percentage mark-up to the unit cost of a product, so the business covers its costs and earns a planned profit on every unit, regardless of demand or rivals' prices [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: adds a fixed percentage mark-up to the unit cost; guarantees costs are covered plus a planned profit regardless of demand or rivals

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Redhill Everyday Value of launching the soup at $1.32.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A guaranteed margin on every tin [k], as the 20% mark-up adds $0.22 to the $1.10 cost, giving $83,600 of margin at the 380,000-tin forecast [app]. Advantage 2: Simplicity and certainty [k], as Theo Lambert can hold $1.32 without watching the $1.19 and $1.49 rival prices daily [app].
    Keywords: 20%, $1.32, $1.10, $0.22, 380,000, $83,600, cost-plus mark-up
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guarantees a planned profit margin per unit; simple to set and hold without constant rival monitoring | application_max_2: 20% mark-up on $1.10 gives $1.32; $83,600 forecast margin; 380,000 tins forecast; rivals at $1.19 and $1.49

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Redhill Everyday Value of launching the soup at $1.19 to match the cheapest rival.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Undercutting the market leader [k], as $1.19 matches the cheapest rival and undercuts the $1.49 market leader [app], drawing bargain-seeking switchers to the own-brand soup [an]. Advantage 2: Higher launch volume [k], as 600,000 tins are forecast at $1.19 compared with 380,000 at $1.32 [app], building share and repeat buying early [an].
    Keywords: $1.19, $1.49, 600,000, own-brand, competitive pricing, $54,000, market leader
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: matching the cheapest rival attracts price-sensitive switchers; lower launch price drives higher volume and share | application_max_2: $1.19 versus $1.49 market leader; 600,000 tins forecast at $1.19 versus 380,000 at $1.32 | analysis_max_2: switchers from the $1.49 leader build trial; higher volume builds share and repeat buying early

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redhill Everyday Value should launch the soup at $1.32 cost-plus rather than $1.19 to match the cheapest rival? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Launching at $1.32 banks the planned margin [k]: $0.22 per tin at the 380,000-tin forecast yields $83,600, which is $29,600 more profit than the $54,000 forecast at $1.19 [app], so cost-plus delivers the stronger year-1 cash result [an]. However, launching at $1.19 wins the market [k]: 600,000 tins would seize shelf share and pull buyers from the $1.49 market leader [app], building the loyalty and scale that own-brand launches need to survive [an]. Overall, Redhill should launch at $1.19 rather than $1.32 [eval], because own-brand success depends on volume and share in year 1, and the $29,600 profit sacrifice buys 220,000 additional tins of trial and repeat custom [eval].
    Keywords: $1.32, $1.19, 380,000, 600,000, $83,600, $54,000, own-brand, market leader, cost-plus
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cost-plus secures the planned margin and year-1 cash; competitive pricing wins volume and share in launches | application_max_2: $1.32 gives $0.22 per tin and $83,600 at 380,000 tins; $1.19 gives $54,000 at 600,000 tins; market leader at $1.49 | analysis_max_2: cost-plus yields $29,600 more year-1 profit despite lower volume; $1.19 builds loyalty and scale needed for own-brand survival | evaluation_max_2: recommends launching at $1.19 for volume and share; quantifies the $29,600 profit sacrifice for 220,000 extra tins of trial

--- STEM ---
Cindervale Ceramic Company, a private limited company founded by Priya Anand, has developed a premium artisan pizza oven for back gardens. Production cost is $380 per unit. Development took 4 years and cost $260,000. Founder Priya Anand must choose a launch price for next spring: a price skimming start at $950 targeting enthusiasts, or a penetration start at $520, below the market leader's comparable oven at $640.

Forecasts suggest 900 units in year 1 at $950, or 1,700 units at $520. Skimming would earn a $570 margin per oven; penetration only $140 per oven, worth $238,000 across 1,700 units. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'penetration pricing'.
    Answer: Penetration pricing is setting an initially low price for a new product to attract customers quickly, build market share fast, and discourage rivals from entering the market [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: initially low price for a new product; aims to build market share quickly and deter rival entry

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Cindervale Ceramic of launching at $520 penetration pricing.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Faster share capture [k], as $520 undercuts the market leader's $640 comparable oven and should shift the forecast 1,700 units in year 1 [app]. Advantage 2: Deters rival entry [k], as a low price makes the premium back-garden oven niche unattractive to competitors watching from the sidelines [app].
    Keywords: $520, $640, 1,700, penetration, market leader, $380
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: wins market share quickly against the leader; low price discourages rivals from entering | application_max_2: $520 versus the market leader's $640; 1,700-unit forecast; annual capacity of 1,800 units

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Cindervale Ceramic of launching at $950 with price skimming.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A high margin on every oven [k], as $950 minus the $380 production cost leaves $570 per unit [app], so even 900 units would generate $513,000 of margin, covering the $260,000 development spend [an]. Advantage 2: A premium brand image [k], as a high launch price signals quality and exclusivity to enthusiast buyers [app], supporting Priya Anand's positioning as a premium artisan brand [an].
    Keywords: $950, $380, $570, 900, $260,000, price skimming, premium
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high profit margin per unit early in the product's life; a high price builds a premium, exclusive brand image | application_max_2: $950 minus $380 cost leaves $570 per oven; 900 units forecast; $260,000 development cost | analysis_max_2: 900 units at $570 yields $513,000, comfortably recovering development costs; premium image supports the brand's artisan positioning

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cindervale Ceramic should launch at $520 penetration rather than $950 price skimming? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Penetration at $520 attacks the leader directly [k]: at $520 the oven undercuts the $640 comparable model, and the 1,700-unit forecast beats the 900-unit skimming forecast, giving Cindervale scale, references and a foothold in a new market [app], though the margin falls to $140 per oven, worth just $238,000 [an]. However, skimming at $950 banks the money [k]: $570 per oven across the 900-unit forecast yields $513,000, recovering the $260,000 development cost while annual capacity is only 1,800 units [app], before easing prices later for mainstream buyers [an]. Overall, Cindervale should launch at $950 price skimming rather than $520 penetration [eval], because the oven took 4 years and $260,000 to develop, sales capacity is tight at 1,800 units, and the enthusiast segment will pay early — chasing volume now risks thin $140 margins with no cash buffer [eval].
    Keywords: $520, $950, $640, 1,700, 900, $260,000, 1,800, price skimming, penetration
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: penetration wins share and scale quickly at thin margins; skimming maximises early margin and recovers development costs | application_max_2: $520 versus $640 leader; 1,700-unit forecast; $238,000 margin at $140 per oven; $950 skimming: $570 per oven × 900 units = $513,000; $260,000 development cost; 1,800 capacity | analysis_max_2: penetration builds scale but leaves only $238,000 of margin against $260,000 development cost; skimming recovers the $260,000 spend while keeping capacity manageable | evaluation_max_2: recommends launching at $950 with price skimming; cites tight capacity and development cost recovery as decisive factors

PAPER: Paper 1

--- STEM ---
Saltmarsh Cove Hotel, a 120-room coastal resort owned by a public limited company, struggles with off-season occupancy of only 38% in January and February. Room price is the single biggest factor in guests' booking decisions, according to its own survey of 1,400 past guests. The sales director proposes two routes to lift the off-season: promotional pricing — 25% off, rooms from $160 down to $120 for 6 weeks — or dynamic pricing — weekends at $260, midweeks at $130, day-before rates from $90 — all off-season.

Last year's January–February revenue was $640,000, and the forecast is 55% occupancy with promotional pricing versus 60% with dynamic pricing. Part-time hours would rise by 480 hours a month under dynamic pricing if occupancy reaches 60%. The hotel employs 46 full-time staff and 30 part-time. The board meets on 10 December to choose.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'dynamic pricing'.
    Answer: Dynamic pricing is the practice of changing a product's price flexibly and frequently in response to changes in demand and market conditions, rather than keeping a fixed price [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: prices change flexibly and frequently; in response to demand and market conditions rather than a fixed price

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Saltmarsh Cove Hotel of promotional pricing for the off-season.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Lifts occupancy quickly [k], as cutting rooms from $160 to $120 for 6 weeks directly targets the 38% January–February slump [app]. Advantage 2: Simple to communicate [k], as one clear 25% off message is easy for guests and staff to understand, with no tiered pricing to manage [app].
    Keywords: $160, $120, 38%, 55%, 25%, 6 weeks, promotional pricing, off-season
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lifts occupancy and attracts price-sensitive guests quickly; simple single-price message that is easy to advertise and sell | application_max_2: $160 to $120 for 6 weeks in January and February against 38% occupancy; 25% off; forecast 55% occupancy versus 60% dynamic

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Saltmarsh Cove Hotel of dynamic pricing for the off-season.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Maximises weekend revenue [k], as weekends priced at $260 capture high-demand leisure breaks while midweeks at $130 widen weekday appeal [app], raising yield per available room [an]. Advantage 2: Day-before discounts fill unsold rooms [k], as rates from $90 at short notice monetise rooms that would otherwise stand empty [app], lifting occupancy toward 60% above the $640,000 baseline [an].
    Keywords: $260, $130, $90, dynamic pricing, 60%, $640,000, weekends, midweeks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: raises yield by charging more on high-demand dates; short-notice discounting fills rooms that would otherwise be empty | application_max_2: $260 weekends and $130 midweeks; $90 day-before rates; forecast 60% occupancy versus $640,000 last year and 38% occupancy | analysis_max_2: lifts yield per room across the trading week; fills unsold rooms and lifts revenue above the $640,000 baseline

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Saltmarsh Cove Hotel should use promotional pricing rather than dynamic pricing for the off-season? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Promotional pricing is simple and proven to pull off-season guests [k]: 25% off brings $160 rooms down to $120 for 6 weeks and forecasts 55% occupancy against last year's 38%, lifting revenue above the $640,000 baseline simply by making January and February visibly cheaper [app], with no retraining on day-by-day tiered pricing or revenue software [an]. However, dynamic pricing captures more value [k]: weekends at $260 and midweeks at $130, with day-before rates from $90, could reach the forecast 60% occupancy [app], holding weekend prices high instead of discounting busy dates [an]. Overall, Saltmarsh Cove should adopt dynamic pricing rather than promotional pricing [eval], because 60% occupancy beats 55% and yield per room stays higher, though the 25% promotion should be kept as a fallback for the quietest weeks [eval].
    Keywords: promotional pricing, dynamic pricing, 25%, 38%, 55%, 60%, $640,000, $120, $260
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: promotions are simple and reliably lift off-season demand; dynamic pricing maximises yield and can reach higher occupancy | application_max_2: 25% off: $160 to $120 for 6 weeks; forecast 55% occupancy versus 38%; $260 weekends, $130 midweeks, $90 day-before; forecast 60% occupancy; $640,000 baseline | analysis_max_2: promotion lifts revenue above baseline but sacrifices yield on all rooms; dynamic pricing holds busy dates high and fills midweeks at $130 | evaluation_max_2: recommends dynamic pricing, citing 60% forecast occupancy over 55%; keeps the promotion as a fallback for the quietest weeks

  Qd [8 marks]

--- STEM ---
BrightBuy Supermarkets operates 14 stores across Country X, employing 420 workers and generating $9.6 million in annual revenue. The weekly marketing budget is $18,000. Cereal is a key traffic-driving aisle for weekly family grocery shops and BrightBuy wants to win it back from rivals. To lift slow cereal sales, currently 300 boxes per store per week and 25% below target, the marketing manager must choose between two sales promotions for the own-brand cornflakes range.

Option 1 is BOGOF (buy one, get one free) on own-brand cornflakes, costing an estimated $7,500 per week and expected to double unit sales. Option 2 is a 20% price reduction from $4.00 to $3.20 per box, costing around $5,800 per week with only modest sales growth expected. The board wants higher sales volume while protecting profit margins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'sales promotion'.
    Answer: Short-term incentives designed to encourage customers to purchase a product, such as price reductions, BOGOF offers, competitions or free gifts [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: short-term incentives to encourage product purchase; examples include price reductions, BOGOF offers, competitions or free gifts

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why BrightBuy Supermarkets might use sales promotion to increase breakfast cereal sales.
    Answer: Reason 1: Sales promotion can encourage immediate purchases and product trial [k], helping the supermarket lift its 300 boxes per store per week, currently 25% below target across 14 stores [app]. Reason 2: Promotions can pull customers away from rival supermarkets [k], which matters when BrightBuy generates $9.6 million in revenue and wants to protect its share of household grocery spending [app].
    Keywords: 300 boxes, 25%, 14 stores, $9.6 million, cereal, BOGOF
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: encourages immediate purchases and product trial; pulls customers away from rival supermarkets | application_max_2: 300 boxes per store per week; 25% below target; 14 stores across Country X; $9.6 million annual revenue

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to BrightBuy Supermarkets of using BOGOF on its own-brand cornflakes.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: BOGOF reduces the profit earned on each promotional sale [k], because the second box is given free, and with cornflakes priced at $4.00 per box the supermarket sacrifices half the revenue per promotional pack [app], squeezing the margin that covers store and staffing costs [an]. Disadvantage 2: Customers may become conditioned to expect free offers [k], damaging sales of regular-priced lines once the $7,500 weekly promotion ends [app], leaving the 25% shortfall to reappear without continual discounting [an].
    Keywords: BOGOF, $4.00, $7,500, own-brand, cornflakes, 25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduces profit per promotional sale because the second unit is free; customers become conditioned to expect free offers | application_max_2: $4.00 per box price; $7,500 weekly promotion cost; own-brand cornflakes; 25% below target | analysis_max_2: squeezes the margin that covers store and staffing costs; post-promotion sales drop back without continual discounting

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think a BOGOF offer or a 20% price reduction to $3.20 is the better sales promotion for this supermarket? Justify your answer.
    Answer: BOGOF is widely understood and doubles the perceived value of each pack [k], and at an estimated $7,500 per week it should lift cereal volume well above 300 boxes per store per week across the 14 stores [app], clearing slow stock and closing the 25% gap to target [an]. However, a 20% price reduction from $4.00 to $3.20 costs only $5,800 per week [k], is simpler to operate on shelf and keeps customers paying something for every box [app], preserving more margin than giving a full box away [an]. Overall, BOGOF is the better promotion because the board's key objective is restoring sales volume, and the extra $1,700 per week is justified if double-unit sales are achieved [eval], though a shorter trial period would limit the conditioned-expectation risk [eval].
    Keywords: BOGOF, $7,500, $5,800, 300 boxes, $4.00, $3.20
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: BOGOF doubles perceived value and is easy to understand; price reduction is simpler, cheaper and preserves per-unit margin | application_max_2: $7,500 per week BOGOF cost; 20% price reduction to $3.20; 300 boxes per store per week; 14 stores across Country X | analysis_max_2: lifts volume, clears slow stock and closes the 25% target gap; protects margin and avoids customers expecting free goods | evaluation_max_2: weighs volume-driving impact of BOGOF against margin protection of the price cut; justifies the choice against the board's volume objective while noting the extra cost risk

Reason 2: Positive press coverage is often seen as more believable than paid advertising [k], and a well-handled story for the 150 local business leaders and journalists at the charity dinner could reframe the hotel's reputation [app].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rebuilds trust and credibility more cheaply than advertising; positive press coverage seen as more believable than paid advertising | application_max_2: 3 key guests complaining publicly about breakfast service; poor breakfast service; 150 local business leaders and journalists; charity dinner

  Qc [6 marks]

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: associates the hotel with a good cause and generates favourable publicity; reaches opinion leaders directly at relatively low cost | application_max_2: 150 local business leaders and travel journalists; $12,000 charity dinner cost; $15,000 newspaper campaign; 62% average occupancy | analysis_max_2: repairs breakfast-service damage through word-of-mouth recommendations; coverage could exceed the printed audience, lifting occupancy above 62%

    Keywords: $12,000, $15,000, 62%, 150, breakfast, $2.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: PR rebuilds damaged trust through independent, credible coverage; newspaper adverts reach a broad audience with a controlled message | application_max_2: $12,000 charity dinner with 150 opinion leaders; four full-page adverts at $15,000; 62% average occupancy; breakfast complaints from 3 key guests | analysis_max_2: credible third-party coverage turns critics into advocates and lifts occupancy; direct advertising guarantees controlled reach but cannot buy credibility | evaluation_max_2: weighs third-party editorial credibility against controllable mass-reach advertising; judges fit to an image-repair problem and notes the $8,000 follow-up headroom

  Qb [4 marks]

Reason 2: Association with a successful national team transfers positive feelings to the brand [k], strengthening the image of the new Thunder boot range among young football buyers [app].
    Keywords: Thunder, national football team, 6 months, 2 years, Summit Sports, headline kit sponsor
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exposes the brand to huge audiences at matches; transfers positive feelings from a successful team to the brand | application_max_2: Thunder logo on shirts and training wear; 6-month build-up; 2-year sponsorship term; new Thunder boot range

Disadvantage 2: If the team performs poorly or suffers a scandal, the brand image suffers [k], damaging the Thunder range's launch just as $4 million of first-year sales is forecast [app], threatening the revenue projections underpinning the deal [an].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: long-term, high-cost commitment that strains launch-stage cash; brand image suffers if the team performs poorly or faces a scandal | application_max_2: $350,000 over 2 years; $500,000 launch budget; Thunder range launch; $4 million first-year sales forecast | analysis_max_2: launch-stage cash strained before any boot is sold; revenue projections underpinning the deal threatened by poor team form

  Qd [8 marks]

  Qb [4 marks]

Reason 2: Social content resonates strongly with the target demographic [k], and 16 to 28 year-olds who frequent corner shops and gyms are heavy social media sharers likely to react to a humorous challenge [app].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reaches huge audiences at very low cost per viewer; resonates with the target demographic on social media | application_max_2: $18,000 video with 3 micro-influencers; 900,000 combined followers; 16 to 28 year-olds; corner shops and gyms

Disadvantage 2: Negative reactions can spread as fast as positive ones [k], and a clumsy mango-flavoured stunt could generate viral criticism among health-conscious young buyers [app], harming the brand before any controlled TV alternative could correct the story [an].

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think viral marketing or national television advertising is the better way to launch the mango-flavoured drink? Justify your answer.

--- STEM ---
PureWeight Foods is a private limited company producing 'LeanLine' weight-loss biscuits promoted as 'clinically proven to burn belly fat'. It employs 60 workers, sales reached $1.8 million last year, and Trading Standards has flagged the pack claim as potentially misleading promotion. A routine inspection also found 500g packets averaging only 450g, breaching weights and measures law.

The managing director must choose between two options. Option 1 is to withdraw all LeanLine stock, reprint packaging with revised claims and recalibrate the filling machinery at a cost of $80,000, halting the promotion for 2 months. Option 2 is to continue selling current stock with the existing promotion unchanged and contest the ruling, risking fines and compensation claims with legal costs estimated at $25,000, but protecting $600,000 of near-term sales.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'misleading promotion'.
    Answer: Promotion that gives consumers a false or deceptive impression about a product, such as untrue claims about what it can do, which consumer protection law prohibits [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: promotion giving a false or deceptive impression about a product; prohibited by consumer protection legislation

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two legal controls that PureWeight Foods must comply with regarding LeanLine biscuits.
    Answer: Control 1: Weights and measures law requires packets to contain the stated weight [k], so 500g packs filled to an average of only 450g break the law and can trigger enforcement by Trading Standards [app]. Control 2: Misleading promotion law forbids untrue or unproven product claims [k], so the claim that LeanLine is 'clinically proven to burn belly fat' is unlawful unless the company holds genuine clinical evidence [app].
    Keywords: 500g, 450g, Trading Standards, LeanLine, weights and measures, clinically proven
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: weights and measures law requires packets to contain the stated weight; misleading promotion law forbids untrue or unproven claims | application_max_2: 500g packs filled to an average of 450g; Trading Standards enforcement; 'clinically proven to burn belly fat' claim; LeanLine weight-loss biscuits

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to PureWeight Foods of withdrawing and reprinting the LeanLine packaging immediately.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Immediate withdrawal stops the unlawful promotion at once [k], avoiding fines and compensation claims that could exceed the $80,000 reprint cost [app], protecting the $600,000 of near-term sales from being frozen by enforcement action [an]. Benefit 2: Revised claims restore consumer trust and legal safety [k], reassuring buyers that reformulated packaging with honest weight-loss wording is compliant [app], safeguarding the brand while $1.8 million of annual revenue is at stake [an].
    Keywords: $80,000, $600,000, $1.8 million, Trading Standards, LeanLine, packaging
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: immediate withdrawal stops the unlawful promotion and avoids fines; revised claims restore consumer trust and legal safety | application_max_2: $80,000 reprint cost; $600,000 of near-term sales; LeanLine packaging with revised claims; $1.8 million of annual revenue | analysis_max_2: avoids enforcement freezing near-term sales; safeguards brand reputation while $1.8 million of annual revenue is at stake

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think PureWeight Foods should withdraw and reprint now, or contest the Trading Standards ruling? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Withdrawing and reprinting stops the breach immediately [k], sacrificing only $80,000 and 2 months of promotion to avoid fines, compensation claims and a stop on $600,000 of sales [app], and it signals to regulators and customers that PureWeight takes consumer protection seriously [an]. However, contesting the ruling could keep the strong 'clinically proven to burn belly fat' promotion in place and defend $600,000 in near-term sales for legal costs of about $25,000 [k], which is commercially tempting if the clinical claim is genuinely defensible [app], but a known loss would bring heavier penalties and lasting reputational damage [an]. Overall, withdrawal is the better option because breaching weights and measures and misleading promotion laws risks prosecution, recalls and destroyed consumer trust, far outweighing $25,000 of legal savings [eval], and a compliant relaunch can retain most sales with an honest message [eval].
    Keywords: $80,000, $25,000, $600,000, 2 months, Trading Standards, LeanLine
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: withdrawal stops the breach and avoids fines and reputational damage; contesting could keep the promotion running for around $25,000 legal costs | application_max_2: $80,000 reprint and 2 months without promotion; $600,000 of near-term sales; 'clinically proven to burn belly fat' claim; $25,000 estimated legal costs | analysis_max_2: signals consumer protection commitment and avoids enforcement freezes; a known loss brings heavier penalties and lasting reputational damage | evaluation_max_2: weighs $25,000 legal saving against prosecution, recall and trust-destruction risk; judges fit to legal reality: honest relaunch can retain most near-term sales

An online marketplace offers to sell her moisturisers for a 5% commission plus a 3% delivery fee. A nationwide supermarket chain has offered shelf space in 25 stores, ordering 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit, paying 60 days late and charging $1,200 a year in listing fees.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'retailer'.
    Answer: A retailer is a business that buys goods from producers or wholesalers and sells them in small quantities to final consumers [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sells goods to final consumers in small quantities; buys from producers/wholesalers rather than manufacturing

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Meadowsweet Skincare might sell through the supermarket chain.
    Answer: Reason 1: Supermarkets attract very large numbers of shoppers [k], so shelf space in 25 stores would expose her moisturisers to far more buyers than 3 high-street beauty shops [app]. Reason 2: Supermarkets are trusted, convenient places to buy everyday items [k], and an order of 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit would give a predictable, regular flow of revenue [app].
    Keywords: Meadowsweet Skincare, 25 stores, 3 high-street beauty shops, 2,400 units, $9 per unit, $410,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: supermarkets reach many/more customers (wider exposure); regular bulk orders give predictable demand and revenue | application_max_2: 25 stores; 3 high-street beauty shops; 2,400 units a month; $9 per unit

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Meadowsweet Skincare would face by selling through supermarkets.
    Answer: Problem 1: The supermarket pays 60 days late [k], so selling 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit means waiting 2 months for around $21,600 in income [app], which could create cash-flow difficulties [an]. Problem 2: Supermarkets squeeze suppliers on price [k], charging $1,200 a year in listing fees on top of a low unit price [app], reducing the profit available to reinvest in the brand [an].
    Keywords: 60 days, 2,400 units, $9 per unit, $1,200, $6,800, Priya Nair
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: late payment/long credit terms strain cash flow; supermarkets negotiate low prices and may charge listing fees | application_max_2: 60 days late; 2,400 units a month; $9 per unit; $1,200 a year in listing fees | analysis_max_2: cash-flow difficulties paying suppliers/wages; lower margins reduce funds for marketing and growth

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Meadowsweet Skincare should launch its own website to sell directly to consumers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Selling direct through its own website would give Meadowsweet Skincare full control over pricing, branding and customer data [k], avoiding the supermarket's 60-day late payment and $1,200 a year listing fees on the 2,400-unit monthly order [app], allowing more profit to be reinvested in marketing and quality [an]. However, a supermarket chain would give her instant access to shoppers in 25 stores [k], and an order of 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit would generate around $21,600 a month before fees [app], which a new website with unknown traffic may take years to match [an]. Overall, launching her own website is the better option [eval] because the $6,800 build cost is small next to a year's listing fees and it builds a direct customer relationship the brand needs [eval], while she can still approach supermarkets later with better terms.
    Keywords: $6,800, 25 stores, 2,400 units, 60 days, $1,200, $9 per unit, Meadowsweet Skincare
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: direct channel gives control of price, brand and customer relationships; indirect channel gives instant reach and sales volume through established retailers | application_max_2: 60 days late; $1,200 a year listing fees; 2,400 units a month; 25 stores; $9 per unit; $6,800 | analysis_max_2: more profit reinvested and stronger brand without intermediaries; a new website may take years to match supermarket volume | evaluation_max_2: weighs control/independence against instant supermarket reach; justified recommendation tied to the $6,800 build cost and listing fees

  Qb [4 marks]

    Keywords: 9% commission, northern port, 2 neighbouring countries, Crimson Chilli Foods, $5.20, Daniel Okoro

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Crimson Chilli Foods of accepting the wholesaler's offer.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The wholesaler would buy 60,000 bottles a year at $3.40 [k], adding a confirmed export order on top of the 4,500 bottles sold locally each week [app], making production planning easier [an]. Benefit 2: The wholesaler collects the bottles monthly from the factory [k], so Crimson Chilli avoids shipping costs, transport risk and import paperwork [app], protecting its local operation's margins [an].
    Keywords: 60,000 bottles, $3.40, 4,500 bottles, collected monthly, $3.75, Crimson Reaper
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: wholesaler provides a large regular order; wholesaler takes on transport and collection risk | application_max_2: 60,000 bottles a year; $3.40; 4,500 bottles; collected monthly from the factory | analysis_max_2: confirmed order eases production planning and scheduling; no shipping costs/paperwork/risk to manage

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Crimson Chilli Foods should export through the agent rather than the wholesaler? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The agent would charge only 9% commission on completed orders [k], keeping Crimson Chilli in full control of its price, brand and paperwork in the 2 neighbouring countries [app], preserving the margin on each of the 4,500 bottles it could sell each week and beyond [an]. However, the wholesaler offers a guaranteed 60,000 bottles a year at $3.40 with monthly collection from the factory [k], removing all transport risk and giving a predictable export order Daniel Okoro can plan around [app], which would support investment in extra production capacity [an]. Overall, the agent is the better first step into the export market [eval] because it limits financial risk while the firm tests demand in the 2 new countries [eval], although the wholesaler may suit the firm once the market is proven.
    Keywords: 9% commission, $3.40, 60,000 bottles, 2 neighbouring countries, 4,500 bottles, northern port, Crimson Reaper
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: agent = low-risk market testing, commission-only payment; wholesaler = guaranteed volume with transport risk passed on | application_max_2: 9% commission; 2 neighbouring countries; 60,000 bottles a year; $3.40; 4,500 bottles | analysis_max_2: keeps control, margins and brand while testing markets; guaranteed volume supports planning and investment | evaluation_max_2: weighs agent's lower risk against the wholesaler's guaranteed order; justified recommendation tied to testing the two new markets

Foxhollow Dairy Farm is a family partnership milking 120 cows and bottling 3,200 litres a week. A refrigerated van delivers to 3 village shops, and 30% of output goes to retail supermarkets at $0.85 per litre, but they return unsold cartons and pay 30 days late. The family is considering selling more through a farm gate shop and a simple website at $1.60 per litre.

A regional wholesaler has offered to collect 4,000 litres a week at $0.95 per litre but requires a $14,000 bottling-line upgrade. Farm gate customers pay up front and receive next-day delivery for $4 per order, yet weekend sales have averaged only 900 litres a week. The family must decide which channel keeps the milk fresh and profitable.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'direct selling'.
    Answer: Direct selling is when a producer sells its goods straight to the final customer without using any intermediary such as a wholesaler or retailer [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: producer sells straight to the final consumer; no intermediary (wholesaler/retailer) involved

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Foxhollow Dairy Farm of selling through its own farm gate shop and website.
    Answer: Reason 1: The farm keeps the full $1.60 per litre [k], almost double the $0.85 per litre that retail supermarkets pay [app]. Reason 2: Farm gate customers pay up front [k], so the farm avoids the 30-day wait for supermarket payment and the cost of returned unsold cartons [app].
    Keywords: $1.60 per litre, $0.85, pay up front, 30 days, 3 village shops, Foxhollow Dairy Farm, $4 per order
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: producer keeps the full price/no share taken by intermediaries; immediate/up-front payment improves cash flow | application_max_2: $1.60 per litre; $0.85 per litre; pay up front; 30 days; returned unsold cartons

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of accepting the wholesaler's offer.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The wholesaler would collect 4,000 litres a week [k], more than the 3,200 litres the farm currently bottles, so spare capacity on the refrigerated van would be used [app], increasing total weekly revenue [an]. Benefit 2: The wholesaler pays $0.95 per litre [k], which is higher than the $0.85 per litre supermarkets pay [app], improving the return on every litre collected [an].
    Keywords: 4,000 litres, 3,200 litres, $0.95, $0.85, $14,000, 900 litres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: wholesaler offers a larger, more stable weekly volume; wholesaler pays more than the supermarkets | application_max_2: 4,000 litres a week; 3,200 litres; $0.95 per litre; $0.85 per litre | analysis_max_2: spare capacity is used, raising total revenue; better price improves margin per litre

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Foxhollow Dairy Farm should accept the wholesaler's offer rather than expand direct selling? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The wholesaler offers to collect 4,000 litres a week at $0.95 per litre [k], using the 800 litres of spare capacity and paying more than the $0.85 supermarkets pay [app], providing stable, growing revenue after the $14,000 upgrade [an]. However, direct selling at $1.60 per litre nearly doubles the price per litre [k], and customers pay up front with $4 delivery per order [app], building cash flow and brand loyalty that a wholesaler cannot match [an]. Overall, the farm should accept the wholesaler [eval] because 4,000 litres at $0.95 (around $3,800 a week) beats direct sales of 900 litres at $1.60 (around $1,440 a week) while weekend demand remains small [eval], keeping the farm gate shop open for loyal customers.
    Keywords: 4,000 litres, $0.95, $1.60, 900 litres, $14,000, pay up front, 3 village shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: wholesaler gives volume, capacity use and stable revenue; direct selling gives a higher price and up-front payment | application_max_2: 4,000 litres; $0.95; $0.85; $1.60 per litre; 900 litres; $14,000 | analysis_max_2: stable growing revenue using spare capacity; direct selling builds cash flow and loyalty but demand is limited | evaluation_max_2: quantified comparison: about $3,800 vs $1,440 a week; justified recommendation linked to weekend demand of 900 litres
