--- STEM ---
VoltEdge Electronics is a private limited company operating 2 high-street shops selling televisions, laptops and small appliances. Last year revenue was $1.9 million, with online sales of $640,000 through its own website. Only 4 in 10 computer buyers say they trust paying online without seeing the product first, and 18% of online orders are returned within 14 days.

Nationwide online rivals charge lower prices and offer 24/7 ordering. Switching to online-only would save $220,000 a year in rent and wages but lose the walk-in trade worth $1.26 million last year. Delivering a 55-inch television costs $120 per unit, and many customers complain about delivery times. The owners must decide whether to close the 2 shops and trade online only, or keep both channels open.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two benefits of e-commerce for businesses.
    Answer: Businesses can sell to a wider market, reaching customers across the country or the world [1], and businesses can trade 24/7 without the costs of running staffed physical shops at all hours [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: wider market reach (national/worldwide sales); trades 24/7/lower overheads than physical shops

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for VoltEdge Electronics of switching to online-only sales.
    Answer: Reason 1: Trading online only would remove the shops' fixed costs [k], saving $220,000 a year in rent and wages [app]. Reason 2: A website is open at all hours [k], serving customers nationwide and supporting the $640,000 of online revenue already achieved [app].
    Keywords: $220,000, $640,000, 24/7, VoltEdge Electronics, $1.9 million, 2 high-street shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: online-only removes high fixed costs of physical shops; 24/7 trading reaches a wider market | application_max_2: $220,000 a year; $640,000; 24/7; $1.9 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems VoltEdge Electronics would face by closing its 2 shops.
    Answer: Problem 1: Customers cannot see or test products before buying online [k], and only 4 in 10 buyers trust paying online without seeing the item first [app], so demand for televisions and laptops could fall [an]. Problem 2: Bulky televisions cost $120 per unit to deliver [k], and 18% of online orders are returned within 14 days [app], adding delivery and returns costs that erode margins [an].
    Keywords: 4 in 10, $120, 18% of online orders, 14 days, 55-inch, $1.26 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customers cannot see/test before purchase (trust issue); delivery and returns add costs | application_max_2: 4 in 10; $120 per unit; 18% of online orders; 14 days; 55-inch television | analysis_max_2: demand for high-value goods may fall; delivery and returns costs reduce profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think VoltEdge Electronics should close its 2 shops and trade online only? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Closing the 2 shops would save $220,000 a year in rent and wages [k] and let VoltEdge trade 24/7 nationwide, building on the $640,000 of online revenue already achieved [app], raising profit and freeing cash for marketing [an]. However, the shops generated $1.26 million of sales last year [k], and closing them would lose test-before-buy customers, only 4 in 10 of whom trust paying online, facing $120 delivery charges on 55-inch televisions and an 18% return rate [app], likely cutting total revenue by far more than the $220,000 saving [an]. Overall, VoltEdge should keep both channels [eval] because losing $1.26 million of walk-in revenue to save $220,000 is a poor trade [eval], while growing the website alongside the shops.
    Keywords: $220,000, $640,000, $1.26 million, 4 in 10, $120, 18%, 55-inch, 24/7
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: online-only saves fixed costs and allows 24/7 national reach; shops provide test-before-buy and customer trust | application_max_2: $220,000; $640,000; $1.26 million; 4 in 10; $120; 18% | analysis_max_2: higher profit and freed cash for marketing; lost walk-in revenue likely exceeds the saving | evaluation_max_2: weighs the $220,000 saving against $1.26 million shop revenue; justified recommendation to keep both channels

--- STEM ---
Citybasket Grocery is a private limited company running 3 neighbourhood supermarkets and an online delivery service launched 18 months ago. The average online basket is $54, and each van route costs $68 in fuel, driver wages and boxes. Customers pay a $5 delivery charge, but 60% abandon their basket when they see the fee.

The owners propose a $65 minimum order for free delivery within 8 kilometres instead of the $5 charge. Fuel prices have risen 19% this year, and 240 deliveries are made weekly, only 80 of them worth $65 or more. Driver wages absorb half of route costs, and complaints about delivery punctuality rose 15% last month. The owners must decide whether the new rule protects margins or drives away online customers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'logistics'.
    Answer: Logistics is the planning and management of the movement and storage of goods, including transport, warehousing and delivery from producer to consumer [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: planning/managing the movement of goods; includes transport, warehousing and delivery

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Citybasket Grocery of offering free delivery on orders above $65.
    Answer: Reason 1: Free delivery encourages customers to add items to their basket [k], lifting the average $54 order toward $65 or more [app]. Reason 2: Larger orders spread the $68 delivery cost across more items [k], improving the margin on each of the 240 deliveries made weekly [app].
    Keywords: $54, $65, $68, 240 deliveries, Citybasket Grocery, 8 kilometres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: free delivery incentivises larger baskets; larger orders dilute the fixed cost of delivery | application_max_2: $54; $65; $68; 240 deliveries

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Citybasket Grocery would face with the $65 free-delivery rule.
    Answer: Problem 1: Only 80 of them reach $65 or more among the 240 deliveries made weekly [k], so two-thirds of current customers would not qualify for free delivery [app], risking lost orders and more abandoned baskets [an]. Problem 2: Fuel prices have risen 19% this year and driver wages absorb half of route costs [k], so a $65 order may not cover the $68 cost of each route [app], wiping out the delivery margin [an].
    Keywords: $65, 240 deliveries, 80 of them, 19%, $68, $5, 8 kilometres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: most current orders fall below the threshold; free delivery can cost more than it returns on marginal orders | application_max_2: 80 of them; $65 or more; 240 deliveries; 19%; $68; half of route costs | analysis_max_2: two-thirds of customers lose the incentive, orders fall; delivery margin is wiped out as costs exceed revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Citybasket Grocery should introduce the $65 minimum for free delivery? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Free delivery above $65 would encourage customers to add more to their average $54 basket [k], increasing revenue per delivery and helping to cover the $68 route cost [app], so the online channel could become profitable as basket sizes grow [an]. However, only 80 of them reach $65 or more among the 240 weekly deliveries [k], so two-thirds of customers gain nothing, and with 60% already abandoning baskets at the $5 charge, some may switch to rivals [app], risking a fall in delivery volume [an]. Overall, the owners should introduce the $65 rule [eval] because raising basket sizes is the best lever to offset the 19% fuel cost rise [eval], provided they monitor abandoned baskets closely after the change.
    Keywords: $65, $54, $68, 80 of them, 60%, 19%, 240 deliveries, 15%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a free-delivery minimum lifts average basket size; many orders below the threshold risk lost volume | application_max_2: $54; $68; 80 of them; 240 deliveries; 60%; 19% | analysis_max_2: bigger baskets cover route costs, lifting profit; abandonment and rival switching may cut volume | evaluation_max_2: weighs basket-size incentive against two-thirds not qualifying; recommendation tied to offsetting the 19% fuel cost rise

--- STEM ---
Petalpost Florists is a partnership running 2 shops in the commercial district, selling bouquets for birthdays, weddings and everyday gifts. The spring wedding season will bring 340 online bouquets over the next 3 months. A competitor has been accused of buying fake reviews, which the partners refuse to do. The partners must decide whether to keep promoting delivery or concentrate on the 2 shops.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'intermediary'.
    Answer: An intermediary is a person or business, such as a wholesaler, retailer or agent, that links the producer of a product with the final consumer in the channel of distribution [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: links producer to final consumer; examples: wholesaler, retailer or agent

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Petalpost Florists of promoting online bouquet orders.
    Answer: Reason 1: Online orders average $52 per bouquet [k], which is $6 more than the $46 walk-in average [app]. Reason 2: A website is open all day and night [k], capturing sales during the spring wedding season, which will bring 340 online bouquets over the next 3 months [app].
    Keywords: $52, $46, 340 online bouquets, 3 months, 40%, Petalpost Florists
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: online orders have a higher average value; 24/7 availability widens exposure and sales | application_max_2: $52; $46; 340 online bouquets; 3 months

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages for Petalpost Florists of delivering online orders.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: Online buyers cannot see or touch the flowers before dispatch [k], and 12% are refunded within 48 hours because the flowers arrive bruised or smaller than the photographs suggest [app], adding courier and refund costs [an]. Disadvantage 2: Each courier delivery costs the firm $7 [k], while 9 complaints last month mentioned misleading photos [app], damaging the firm's reputation and future sales [an].
    Keywords: 12%, 48 hours, $7, 9 complaints, fake reviews, bruised
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customers cannot see/touch before buying; refunds and damaged goods erode margins | application_max_2: 12%; 48 hours; $7; 9 complaints; photographs | analysis_max_2: refund and courier costs reduce profit; reputation suffers from misleading photos/complaints

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Petalpost Florists should keep promoting online delivery rather than concentrate on its 2 shops? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Keeping delivery would exploit the 40% of monthly bouquet revenue already coming online at an average of $52 per order [k], capturing the 340 wedding bouquets over the coming 3 months with round-the-clock ordering [app], growing sales beyond what the 2 shops can handle [an]. However, 12% of online orders are refunded within 48 hours and each delivery costs $7 [k], while online buyers cannot see or touch the flowers and 9 complaints mentioned misleading photos [app], eroding profit and risking the reputational damage that fake-review accusations against rivals also show [an]. Overall, Petalpost should keep promoting delivery while tightening quality control [eval] because higher online revenue outweighs refund costs if it photographs honestly and packs carefully [eval], while refusing to buy fake reviews at all times.
    Keywords: 40%, $52, 340, 12%, $7, 9 complaints, 2 shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: online channel already substantial and higher value; refunds, delivery cost and reputation risks | application_max_2: 40%; $52; 340; 12%; $7; 9 complaints | analysis_max_2: sales beyond physical capacity/24-7 ordering; margin erosion and reputational damage | evaluation_max_2: weighs online growth against refund and reputation risks; justified recommendation tied to honest photography and quality control

--- STEM ---
Nettlemead Jewellery is a sole trader business handcrafting silver rings and earrings from a workshop in the market town. Elena Marchetti sells about 210 pieces a month at $48 each through craft fairs and 2 boutique gift shops, which pay her $26 per piece wholesale. She is considering selling online.

An online marketplace charging 15% commission plus $300 a month would reach 3 million registered buyers, but her pieces would sit alongside 900 similar sellers. Her own website would cost $2,400 to build, with 2% card fees and full control over branding, but she estimates only 60 visitors a day. Six loyal customers have said they would not buy jewellery online without seeing it in person. Elena must decide which online route grows sales.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two limitations of selling through an online marketplace.
    Answer: The marketplace charges a commission on every sale [1], and the seller's products appear alongside many competing sellers, reducing control over branding and pricing [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: marketplace takes commission/a share of each sale; little control over branding/direct customer relationships

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Nettlemead Jewellery of joining the online marketplace.
    Answer: Reason 1: The marketplace reaches 3 million registered buyers [k], giving far wider exposure than craft fairs and 2 boutique gift shops [app]. Reason 2: The marketplace provides advertising and ready-made demand [k], so Elena could start selling online without first paying $2,400 to build her own website [app].
    Keywords: 3 million, 2 boutique gift shops, $2,400, Nettlemead Jewellery, 15% commission, 60 visitors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: huge existing customer base/reach; marketplace provides infrastructure and traffic | application_max_2: 3 million; 2 boutique gift shops; $2,400; 210 pieces

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Nettlemead Jewellery of building its own website.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Her own website avoids the 15% commission plus $300 a month [k], so on $48 pieces the marketplace would take $7.20 each versus only about $0.96 in card fees on her own site [app], leaving more profit per piece [an]. Benefit 2: A personal website gives full control over branding and presentation [k], letting her tell her handcrafted story to buyers instead of competing with 900 similar sellers [app], strengthening loyalty and repeat purchases [an].
    Keywords: 15% commission, $300, $48, 2% card fees, 900 similar sellers, $26 per piece, $2,400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower selling costs/no commission; full control of brand and customer experience | application_max_2: 15% commission; $300; $48; 2% card fees; 900 similar sellers | analysis_max_2: more profit per piece at volume; stronger brand differentiation and loyalty

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Nettlemead Jewellery should build its own website rather than join the marketplace? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Her own website would avoid the 15% commission and $300 a month [k], saving about $7.20 per $48 piece, roughly $1,500 a month on 210 pieces [app], keeping more margin and full control of her brand and customer list [an]. However, the marketplace offers 3 million ready buyers compared with her estimate of 60 visitors a day on a new site [k], and six loyal customers have said they would not buy jewellery online without seeing it first [app], so a personal site may mean slow sales and a poor return on the $2,400 build cost [an]. Overall, Elena should build her own website but keep selling at craft fairs [eval], because the $1,500 monthly commission saving compounds quickly against a one-off $2,400 build cost [eval], while the fairs supply the traffic a new site needs.
    Keywords: 15% commission, $300, $48, 210 pieces, $2,400, 60 visitors, 3 million, Six loyal customers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: own website = lower fees and brand control; marketplace = ready audience and trust | application_max_2: 15% commission; $300; $48; 210 pieces; $2,400; 60 visitors; 3 million | analysis_max_2: commission saving compounds at 210 pieces a month; new site may be too quiet to pay back its cost | evaluation_max_2: weighs about $1,500 a month of fee savings against the ready marketplace audience; justified recommendation: own website plus craft fairs

--- STEM ---
Coppertree Bakery is a family-owned bakery chain operating 6 outlets across Country X, employing 34 staff and generating $780,000 in annual revenue. Most customers are office workers aged 25-45 buying lunchtime rolls. The other two outlets sit on industrial estates with little footfall. Sales of lunchtime rolls and salads have fallen by 12% over 18 months as more companies let staff work from home.

The owners plan to launch a gluten-free baked goods range, including croissants, rolls and cakes, but must decide whether to spend $15,000 on a secondary research report from a market analysis agency, or carry out their own primary research with 300 regular customers. They also must choose between launching in all 6 outlets at once or trialling the range in 2 outlets first.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'market research'.
    Answer: The systematic process of collecting, analysing and interpreting information about a market, including customer needs and demand [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: collecting and analysing information about a market; understanding customers' needs and demand

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: market research costs money and time; customer tastes change quickly | application_max_2: interviewing customers across both stores; restructured range of 1,800 lines | analysis_max_2: less cash left for new stock purchases; range could still miss future demand

    Keywords: market research, smart home devices, 1,800 product lines, 15%, 2 stores, $2.4 million

--- STEM ---
Silverpine Youth Hostels is a national hostel chain operating 14 hostels across Country X, from coastal cities to mountain towns, welcoming 38,000 guests each year. The marketing manager wants to survey 400 guests about a proposed $250,000 refurbishment of its dormitories before next summer, adding bunk pods, laundry rooms and study corners.

One option is random sampling: selecting 400 guests at random from the full guest list. The other is quota sampling: interviewing guests in each age and gender group until 400 responses are gathered. The accuracy of the results will depend on the sample size, the wording of the questions and possible bias. Guests aged 16-24 make up 55% of bookings, so a flawed sample could mislead the chain into building features guests ignore.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'random sampling'.
    Answer: A sampling method in which every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected, usually using a random number generator [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: every member of the population has an equal chance; selection is random, for example using random numbers

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Silverpine Youth Hostels of using random sampling for its guest survey.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Every guest on the full list has an equal chance of selection [k], so the 400 respondents are likely to represent the 38,000 guests fairly [app]. Advantage 2: It reduces the risk of bias [k] compared with hand-picking guests from just one hostel [app].
    Keywords: Silverpine Youth Hostels, 14 hostels, 38,000 guests, 400, random sampling, $250,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: equal chance of selection for all; reduces risk of bias | application_max_2: 400 respondents representing 38,000 guests; compared with hand-picking from one hostel

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of Silverpine's market research data.
    Answer: Factor 1: Sample size [k] - surveying only 40 guests instead of 400 would poorly represent the 16-24 group that makes up 55% of bookings [app], producing unreliable results and a wasted $250,000 refurbishment [an]. Factor 2: Wording of the questions [k] - leading or confusing questions would bias answers about dormitory facilities [app], so the chain builds features guests do not want [an].
    Keywords: sample size, wording of the questions, 400, 55%, 16-24, $250,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sample size affects accuracy; wording of questions can bias answers | application_max_2: 40 instead of 400 poorly represents the 16-24 group; leading questions bias answers about dormitories | analysis_max_2: unreliable results waste the $250,000 refurbishment; biased answers mean building unwanted features

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Silverpine Youth Hostels should use random sampling rather than quota sampling for the dormitory survey? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Random sampling gives every guest on the full list an equal chance of selection [k], producing an unbiased, representative picture of the 38,000 annual guests [app], which should guide the $250,000 refurbishment wisely [an]. However, quota sampling would guarantee enough responses from each age and gender group [k], for example the 16-24 segment at 55% of bookings [app], and can be completed faster at busier hostels [an]. Overall, random sampling is the better choice [eval] because the full guest list already exists, making it cheap and unbiased [eval].
    Keywords: random sampling, quota sampling, 38,000 guests, $250,000, 55%, 16-24
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: random sampling gives equal chance and low bias; quota sampling ensures group representation | application_max_2: 400 random respondents from the full guest list; 16-24 segment at 55% of bookings | analysis_max_2: unbiased representative data guides the $250,000 decision; quota is faster at busier hostels | evaluation_max_2: weighs representativeness against speed and group quotas; justified recommendation for random sampling

  Qb [4 marks]

    Answer: Benefit 1: Loyal customers give repeat, predictable sales [k], email members visit 11 times a year [app]. Benefit 2: Retaining customers costs less than attracting new ones [k], cheaper than replacing the 20% lunch trade lost to the mall rival [app].
    Keywords: Kettleworth Coffee Co, 7 coffee shops, 4,200 customers, $4.80, 11 times a year, 20%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: repeat, predictable sales; cheaper to retain than attract new customers | application_max_2: email members visiting 11 times a year; 20% lunch trade lost to the mall rival

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of the loyalty card over staff training as a response to the lost trade.
    Answer: Advantage 1: It directly rewards repeat visits [k], a free drink after 8 stamps gives 4,200 weekly customers a reason to return [app], quickly rebuilding visit frequency [an]. Advantage 2: It produces usable data [k], stamp redemptions show which of the 7 shops keep loyal customers [app], guiding future promotion spending [an].
    Keywords: loyalty card, 8 stamps, 4,200 customers, 7 shops, $18,000, 11 times a year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: directly rewards repeat purchases; produces measurable redemption data | application_max_2: free drink after 8 stamps for 4,200 weekly customers; redemption data across the 7 shops | analysis_max_2: quickly rebuilds visit frequency; data guides future promotion spending

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kettleworth Coffee Co should introduce the loyalty card rather than invest in staff training? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The loyalty card costs $18,000 but directly incentivises repeat visits [k] from 4,200 weekly customers spending $4.80 each [app], quickly replacing the 15% fall in repeat visits since March [an]. However, staff training costs just $9,500 and tackles the root cause of service quality [k], improving experience across all 7 shops [app], building loyalty that stamps alone cannot buy, though its effect is slower [an]. Overall, introduce the loyalty card now [eval] because visit frequency must be rebuilt urgently while the mall rival gains ground [eval], adding training in the next quarter.
    Keywords: $18,000, $9,500, 4,200 customers, $4.80, 15%, 7 shops, 11 times a year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: loyalty card directly incentivises repeat visits; training tackles root cause of service quality | application_max_2: $18,000 card cost vs $9,500 training cost; 4,200 weekly customers spending $4.80 each; 15% fall since March | analysis_max_2: card quickly replaces lost repeat visits; training builds deeper loyalty across all 7 shops but slower | evaluation_max_2: weighs urgent frequency rebuilding against root-cause improvement; justified recommendation to introduce the loyalty card now

--- STEM ---
Saffron Dune Spices is a private limited company in Country X that blends and packs saffron-based spice jars. It sells 42,000 jars a year at $6.50 each, generating $273,000 in revenue, and employs 18 workers. Domestic sales have slipped since two supermarkets launched own-brand blends at lower prices, cutting Saffron Dune's market share from 15% to 11%.

A distributor in neighbouring Country Y has offered to sell 60,000 jars a year at $5.20 per jar if Saffron Dune licences its brand to a local bottler, or enters a joint venture with a Country Y importer. Country Y charges a 12% import tariff on finished spice jars and customers there prefer milder flavours. Saffron Dune must decide whether to stay purely domestic, licence its brand or form the joint venture.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'licensing'.
    Answer: An agreement where a business (the licensor) grants another business (the licensee) the right to produce or sell its product using its brand, patent or process, usually in exchange for a fee or royalty [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: one business grants another the right to use its brand/patent/process; in exchange for a fee or royalty

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two opportunities for Saffron Dune Spices of expanding into Country Y.
    Answer: Opportunity 1: Entering Country Y gives Saffron Dune access to a much larger customer base [k], because the distributor could sell 60,000 jars a year at $5.20, worth about $312,000 in extra revenue [app]. Opportunity 2: Selling abroad reduces dependence on the domestic market [k], which matters because Saffron Dune's domestic market share has already slipped from 15% to 11% [app].
    Keywords: 60,000 jars, $5.20, Country Y, 15%, 11%, 42,000 jars, $273,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: access to a larger market / more customers abroad; spreads risk / reduces reliance on the domestic market | application_max_2: 60,000 jars a year at $5.20 / about $312,000 extra revenue; domestic share fell from 15% to 11% / revenue $273,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Saffron Dune Spices could face if it expands into Country Y.
    Answer: Problem 1: Country Y shoppers prefer milder flavours [k], so the existing saffron blends may not appeal and recipes may need reformulating to win buyers [app], increasing costs and risking a launch that fails to cover the entry investment [an]. Problem 2: The 12% import tariff on finished spice jars [k] would add about $0.62 to each $5.20 jar [app], cutting margins or pushing prices up so local competitors stay cheaper [an].
    Keywords: milder, 12% import tariff, $5.20, saffron, $6.50, Country Y, 42,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cultural differences / tastes differ between countries; tariffs raise the cost of selling abroad | application_max_2: Country Y prefers milder flavours / recipes need reformulating; 12% import tariff on $5.20 jar / about $0.62 added per jar | analysis_max_2: higher costs / launch may fail to cover entry investment; margins squeezed or prices raised / lose competitiveness

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Saffron Dune Spices should enter Country Y through licensing or a joint venture? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Licensing its brand to a local bottler would let Saffron Dune sell in Country Y without paying the 12% import tariff, because the jars would be filled locally [k], and could generate 60,000 jars at $5.20, about $312,000 a year, with little capital at risk [app]. However, licensing gives limited control over quality and over the milder recipe adaptation [an]. A joint venture with the Country Y importer would share the risk and bring market knowledge for the milder-flavour demand [k], while giving closer oversight and shared decision-making over the 60,000-jar plan [app], yet it locks capital into a long-term partnership and exposes Saffron Dune to the partner's performance [an]. Overall, licensing is the better first step given the share slide to 11% at home, because it is quick and low-risk [eval]; if Country Y orders exceed 60,000 jars a year, converting to a joint venture would then protect the brand [eval].
    Keywords: 60,000 jars, $5.20, 12% import tariff, milder, 11%, Country Y
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: licensing = local firm produces/sells for a fee, low capital risk; joint venture = shared ownership/risk with local partner and shared knowledge | application_max_2: 60,000 jars at $5.20 / about $312,000 a year for licensing; 12% import tariff avoided locally / milder flavours / share fell to 11% | analysis_max_2: licensing avoids tariff and keeps capital free but weakens quality control; joint venture shares risk and adds local knowledge but locks capital in | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two entry methods; conditions/sequence suggested (license first, convert to JV if successful)

--- STEM ---
Tandoori Flame is a private limited company that runs 6 fast-casual tandoori restaurants in Country X, two in the capital and four in regional towns. Each outlet averages $410,000 in annual revenue, so the chain generated about $2.46 million last year and employs 84 staff across the six sites. Growth has slowed across Country X and two rival chains have opened competing restaurants near its two best-performing locations.

A group of investors in Country Z has asked to open Tandoori Flame outlets there under an international franchise agreement costing an upfront $40,000 per outlet plus 6% of annual sales. A company-owned Country Z restaurant would cost about $320,000 to open, and local customers prefer milder spice levels and different side dishes. The board must choose between the franchise programme and opening its own outlet.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'international franchising'.
    Answer: A business (the franchisor) allows entrepreneurs in a foreign country (franchisees) to trade there using its brand, format and support in return for upfront fees and ongoing royalties [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: franchisee in another country trades under the franchisor's brand/system; in return for upfront fees and ongoing royalty payments

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Tandoori Flame might use international franchising to expand into Country Z.
    Answer: Reason 1: Franchising allows rapid expansion abroad without Tandoori Flame funding each outlet itself [k], avoiding the roughly $320,000 opening cost of its own Country Z restaurant [app]. Reason 2: Each franchisee pays an upfront $40,000 fee plus 6% of annual sales [k], giving Tandoori Flame a steady royalty income on top of the $2.46 million domestic revenue [app].
    Keywords: $40,000, 6%, $320,000, $2.46 million, Country Z, $410,000, 84 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fast growth abroad with less capital investment; upfront fees and ongoing royalty income for the franchisor | application_max_2: avoids about $320,000 cost of own outlet; $40,000 upfront plus 6% of annual sales / on top of $2.46 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Tandoori Flame could face if it expands into Country Z.
    Answer: Problem 1: Country Z customers prefer milder spice levels and different side dishes [k], so the menu must change from the format that works in Country X [app], risking weak sales and food waste if the adaptation is judged wrongly [an]. Problem 2: Operating in Country Z means unfamiliar local laws and regulations [k], such as different food hygiene and employment rules that franchisees must follow [app], adding compliance delays and unexpected costs against the $410,000 average outlet revenue [an].
    Keywords: milder spice levels, side dishes, Country Z, $410,000, $2.46 million, 6 fast-casual
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cultural differences / tastes and preferences differ abroad; unfamiliar laws and regulations / compliance burden | application_max_2: milder spice levels and different side dishes; franchisees must follow local rules / $410,000 average outlet revenue | analysis_max_2: weak sales and food waste if menu is wrong; compliance delays and added costs squeeze margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tandoori Flame should use international franchising or open its own outlet in Country Z? Justify your answer.
    Answer: International franchising would deliver $40,000 per outlet upfront plus 6% of annual sales [k], giving Tandoori Flame fee income without paying the $320,000 needed for its own restaurant [app], which also spreads risk across local franchisees rather than one $320,000 bet [an]. A company-owned outlet would give full control over the milder menu adaptation, service and standards [k], but the $320,000 cost would concentrate all losses in Tandoori Flame in an unfamiliar country [app], and any mistake on compliance or sourcing would hit the chain directly [an]. Overall, franchising is the better route now, because local partners understand Country Z tastes and share the risk while regular royalties build on the $2.46 million domestic base [eval]; a company-owned outlet should only follow once outlet sales prove the brand travels well [eval].
    Keywords: $40,000, 6%, $320,000, milder, Country Z, $2.46 million, $410,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: franchising = fees plus royalties, low capital commitment, shared risk; own outlet = full control over quality/service but full cost and risk | application_max_2: $40,000 upfront plus 6% royalties per franchised outlet; $320,000 to open own outlet / built on $2.46 million base | analysis_max_2: franchise spreads risk and earns ongoing royalty income; own outlet concentrates cost and loss risk on Tandoori Flame | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two options; conditions for a later company-owned move (proven outlet demand)

Country W has 120,000 cycling commuters and its distributors want to stock Kestrel bicycles, but riders there prefer lighter aluminium frames over steel designs.     Question: Define 'localising products'.
    Answer: Adapting a product, such as its design, features, ingredients or packaging, to suit the tastes, laws and conditions of a foreign market rather than selling an identical product everywhere [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: product adapted to suit local tastes/laws/conditions; rather than selling an identical product in every market

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two opportunities for Kestrel Cycles of entering Country W.
    Answer: Opportunity 1: Country W has 120,000 cycling commuters [k], a much larger potential market than the shrinking domestic one [app]. Opportunity 2: Establishing itself abroad diversifies revenue away from Country X [k], where sales fell 9% over the past 2 years, helping secure demand and jobs for the 46 workers [app].
    Keywords: 120,000, 9%, $2.72 million, 8,000, Country W, 46 workers, $340
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: larger market / more potential customers abroad; diversification / less reliance on domestic demand | application_max_2: 120,000 cycling commuters in Country W; domestic sales fell 9% over 2 years / 46 workers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Kestrel Cycles could face if it enters Country W.
    Answer: Problem 1: Country W riders prefer lighter aluminium frames [k], so current steel models are unlikely to sell and Kestrel would need a $400,000 redesign [app], delaying entry and adding $55 to every unit cost [an]. Problem 2: A 14% import tariff on finished bicycles [k] would add about $48 to each $340 bike [app], forcing higher prices that could make Kestrel uncompetitive against local Country W brands [an].
    Keywords: aluminium, $400,000, $55, 14%, $340, 120,000, 8,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: different consumer tastes / preferences abroad (cultural differences); tariffs raise the landed cost of exports | application_max_2: riders prefer lighter aluminium frames / steel models unsuitable; 14% tariff adds about $48 to each $340 bike | analysis_max_2: redesign delays entry and raises unit costs by $55; higher prices make Kestrel uncompetitive locally

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kestrel Cycles should localise its bicycles for Country W or export its current model? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Localising the range would match Country W riders' preference for lighter aluminium frames [k], making the bicycles far more attractive across a commuter population of 120,000 [app], and it avoids the commercial failure of shipping steel models that dealers expect to remain unsold [an]. Exporting the current steel range avoids the $400,000 redesign and $55 higher unit cost [k], but a 14% tariff lifts each $340 bike by about $48 [app], and steel frames clash with local tastes, so volumes may be too low to profit [an]. Overall, localisation is the stronger option because $400,000 is only about 15% of annual revenue and unlocks the much larger Country W market [eval], while simply exporting the current model risks unsold stock and tariff-inflated prices [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: localising adapts the product to local tastes and conditions; exporting sells the standard product abroad (with tariff cost) | application_max_2: aluminium-frame preference / 120,000 commuters; $400,000 redesign, $55 extra unit cost, 14% tariff adds about $48 to $340 | analysis_max_2: localising raises appeal and avoids unsold stock; exporting keeps costs down but tariff and tastes suppress demand | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two options; weighs redesign cost (~15% of revenue) against market size

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two opportunities for Amber Brook Cheese of exporting to Country V.
    Answer: Opportunity 1: Exporting brings a firm order for 15,000 wheels a year [k], roughly $360,000 in extra revenue on top of its flat $672,000 domestic sales [app].     Keywords: 15,000 wheels, $24, $672,000, $28, 25 workers, Country V, 24,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: larger market / additional sales revenue abroad; diversification / less dependence on the domestic economy | application_max_2: 15,000 wheels a year at $24 / about $360,000 extra revenue; domestic revenue flat at $672,000 / 25 workers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Amber Brook Cheese could face if it exports to Country V.

Problem 2: Country V requires its own food-safety certification and labelling rules [k], which take up to 9 months to complete [app], delaying the first export order and tying up cash in compliance before any revenue arrives [an].

  Qd [8 marks]

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exporting gains extra revenue and volume in a new market; duties and freight reduce the effective export price and margin | application_max_2: 15,000 wheels / about $360,000 extra revenue (~$1.03 million total); $2.40 duty and $3 freight / about $18.60 vs $28 domestic | analysis_max_2: extra volume helps absorb fixed costs and offset 18% milk-cost rise; weaker margin and certification delay risk cash flow | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation with conditions; recommendation sensitive to duty/freight negotiations

Revenue last year was $884,000 from 13,000 customers spending an average of $68 a year. Repeat purchase rates are 45%, but a rival brand has launched a similar range priced 15% below Lumen's products and is advertising heavily on television and online.

The marketing manager must recommend a new marketing strategy. Option A is a national social media influencer campaign costing $60,000 to attract new customers across the country.     Question: Define 'marketing strategy'.
    Answer: A long-term plan for how a business will use the marketing mix to reach its chosen target market and achieve its marketing objectives, such as gaining share or loyalty [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: long-term plan for using the marketing mix; aims at a target market and marketing objectives

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Lumen Haircare needs a clear marketing strategy before choosing between the two options.
    Answer: Reason 1: A marketing strategy sets out which customers and which mix to target [k], so the $60,000 campaign and the $25,000 loyalty scheme are aimed deliberately rather than wastefully [app]. Reason 2: A planned strategy links promotion to measurable sales objectives [k], letting the 14 retail stores track whether either option lifts revenue above $884,000 [app].
    Keywords: $60,000, $25,000, 14 retail stores, $884,000, 13,000 customers, 15%, $68
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: strategy identifies the target market and marketing mix; strategy sets measurable objectives and direction | application_max_2: the $60,000 campaign vs $25,000 loyalty scheme differ; target is to lift revenue above $884,000 across 14 retail stores

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways a well-chosen marketing strategy could help Lumen Haircare counter the rival's 15% lower prices.
    Answer: Way 1: A loyalty programme rewarding repeat purchases [k] would raise the 45% repeat-purchase rate by giving existing customers a reason to stay despite the rival's discount [app], defending the base of 13,000 customers rather than rebuying lost ones at great cost [an]. Way 2: Consistent, high-quality premium marketing [k] could strengthen Lumen's brand image so shoppers feel its price is justified [app], reducing pressure to match the rival's 15% price cut across the 14 retail stores [an].
    Keywords: 45%, 13,000, 15%, 14 retail stores, Lumen, loyalty
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: loyalty/relationship marketing retains existing customers; strong brand image differentiates from lower-priced rivals | application_max_2: 45% repeat-purchase rate / base of 13,000 customers; rival priced 15% below / across 14 retail stores | analysis_max_2: higher repeat rate defends revenue without matching price cuts; premium image supports price and protects margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Lumen Haircare should choose the influencer campaign or the loyalty programme? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The influencer campaign costing $60,000 [k] could reach a far wider audience than the 13,000 current customers [app], building awareness and winning new buyers away from the rival [an]. The loyalty programme costs less than half as much at $25,000 [k], and by lifting the 45% repeat-purchase rate it protects the customers who already spend about $68 a year [app], which is cheaper than replacing customers lost to the rival [an]. Overall, the loyalty programme is the better first move because its $25,000 cost is affordable given limited cash and it directly defends Lumen's most profitable relationships [eval]; the influencer campaign should follow once retention improves and awareness converts into loyal buyers [eval].
    Keywords: $60,000, $25,000, 45%, 13,000, $68, $884,000, 15%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: influencer campaign builds awareness and reach at higher cost; loyalty programme retains existing customers at lower cost | application_max_2: $60,000 campaign vs $25,000 loyalty programme; 45% repeat-purchase rate / $68 average annual spend / 13,000 customers | analysis_max_2: campaign widens reach and wins new customers; loyalty defence is cheaper than replacing churned customers | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two options; sensible sequencing suggested (loyalty first, campaign later)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two consequences for The Paper Lantern Bookshop if it does not respond to changing customer needs.
    Answer: Consequence 1: Footfall, already down 22% over 3 years [k], would keep falling as customers choose rivals that meet their needs better [app], pushing annual revenue below $323,000 [an]. Consequence 2: Without understanding customer needs [k], the bookshop may stock unwanted titles and miss requests for events and recommendations [app], wasting shelf space and cash while customers defect to online sellers [an].
    Keywords: 22%, 3 years, $323,000, 19,000, online, footfall
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ignoring needs loses sales and customers to rivals; poor marketing leads to wasted stock and missed opportunities | application_max_2: footfall down 22% over 3 years / revenue $323,000; customers want events and recommendations / online rivals | analysis_max_2: revenue falls further without a response; wasted stock and cash; customers defect to online sellers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think The Paper Lantern Bookshop should employ a part-time marketing assistant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Employing an assistant for $14,000 a year [k] would put someone in place to identify customer needs and organise events and recommendations [app], directly tackling the 22% footfall decline and building customer loyalty [an]. However, the bookshop still owes $26,500 and wages cannot be used to repay that debt [k], so the $14,000 adds a fixed cost before any extra sales arrive [app], and if sales do not respond the hire strains cash further [an]. Overall, hiring the assistant is justified because $14,000 is under 4.5% of the $323,000 revenue and directly reverses the 22% slide by rebuilding the relationships that keep bookshops alive [eval]; the owners should set a 6-month sales target and review it to protect cash [eval].
    Keywords: $14,000, $26,500, 22%, $323,000, events, 9 staff, 3 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: marketing builds loyalty and relationships that defend sales; extra wages are a fixed cost and compete with debt repayment | application_max_2: $14,000 a year assistant / tackles 22% footfall decline; debts of $26,500 / $323,000 revenue (under 4.5%) | analysis_max_2: assistant reverses footfall decline and builds loyalty; hire strains cash if sales do not respond | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation; sensible safeguard suggested (6-month sales target review)

The marketing manager believes honest promotion would build customer trust and loyalty over time.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'misleading promotion'.
    Answer: Advertising, packaging or other promotion that is false or exaggerated, or leaves out important information, so consumers are deceived about a product's qualities, price or performance [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: promotion that is false or exaggerated; leaves out important information so consumers are deceived

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Summit Grill Co must obey legal controls over marketing.
    Answer: Reason 1: Misleading claims can trigger a fine of up to $50,000 [k], more than four times the $12,000 cost of an honest campaign [app]. Reason 2: Legal controls protect consumers from being deceived [k], so complying preserves the public trust on which $902,500 of annual barbecue sales depend [app].
    Keywords: $50,000, $12,000, $902,500, 9,500, $95, misleading, smoke-free
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: legal controls prevent false/misleading claims to consumers; compliance avoids fines and reputational damage | application_max_2: $50,000 fine vs $12,000 cost of honest campaign; $902,500 annual revenue depends on consumer trust

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Summit Grill Co could face if it keeps the smoke-free claim.
    Answer: Problem 1: The regulator could impose a $50,000 fine [k], equivalent to roughly 526 barbecues at $95 each [app], cancelling a large slice of annual profit [an]. Problem 2: Customers who discover the smoke-free claim is false may stop trusting the brand [k], cutting the 9,500 units sold last year [app], damaging reputation and making an honest relaunch far harder [an].
    Keywords: $50,000, $95, 9,500, smoke-free, $902,500, 31 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: regulators can fine businesses for misleading promotion; misleading claims destroy consumer trust and loyalty | application_max_2: $50,000 fine / about 526 units at $95 each; 9,500 units sold last year at risk | analysis_max_2: fine wipes out profit on hundreds of units; lost trust cuts sales and complicates relaunch

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Summit Grill Co should withdraw the smoke-free campaign? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Withdrawing the campaign and launching an honest low-smoke advertisement costs $12,000 [k], affordable against $902,500 of revenue and removing the threat of a $50,000 fine [app], which is more than four times the relaunch cost [an]. Keeping the slogan would save $12,000 today [k], but Summit Grill would risk the fine, possible legal action and a collapse in customer trust across its 31-worker operation [app], cutting into sales of 9,500 units [an]. Overall, withdrawing is clearly the right decision because honest promotion with redesigned packaging builds the trust and loyalty needed to protect future sales [eval]; the $12,000 is far cheaper than the regulator's fine and the long-term cost of a deceived customer base [eval].
    Keywords: $12,000, $50,000, $902,500, 9,500, smoke-free, 31 workers, $95
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: withdrawing and correcting misleading claims restores trust; keeping misleading claims risks fines and reputational damage | application_max_2: $12,000 reprint/redesign vs $50,000 fine against $902,500 revenue; 9,500 units / 31 workers at stake | analysis_max_2: fine is over four times the relaunch cost; withdrawal is low risk; keeping the claim risks sales collapse and harder recovery | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation; honest low-smoke positioning builds long-term trust and loyalty

--- STEM ---
Fable & Flint Fine Stationery is a private limited company in Country X producing hand-bound notebooks sold through 5 premium stationery shops. It makes 6,000 notebooks a year at $45 each, generating $270,000 in revenue, and employs 11 skilled bookbinders and packers. Domestic growth has slowed and the owners have identified Country V, with 400,000 potential buyers, as a promising overseas market.

They must recommend a marketing strategy for Country V: either position the notebooks as a luxury niche product sold in 12 exclusive shops at $60 each, or sell them through supermarkets and department stores at $32 each for the mass market. Labelling in the local language is required either way before launch. The two owners disagree about which positioning best fits the brand.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'target market'.
    Answer: The specific group of consumers a business aims its marketing mix at, identified through market research as most likely to buy the product [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the specific group of consumers aimed at; identified through market research as likely buyers

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Fable & Flint Fine Stationery of identifying a clear target market for Country V.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A defined target market focuses promotion and budget where it works best [k], so the $60 luxury positioning reaches the hand-bound buyers among the 400,000 potential buyers rather than everyone [app]. Benefit 2: Knowing the target market helps match product and price to customer needs [k], such as offering premium notebooks at $60 in 12 exclusive shops for affluent professionals [app].
    Keywords: 400,000, $60, 12 exclusive shops, $45, Country V, $270,000, 6,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: marketing resources are used more efficiently; product/price can be tailored to the intended buyers | application_max_2: $60 luxury positioning / 400,000 potential buyers; 12 exclusive shops / affluent professionals

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Fable & Flint could face when entering Country V.
    Answer: Problem 1: Country V requires labelling in the local language [k], so every notebook and box must be reprinted before sale [app], adding cost and delaying the launch while stock sits ready but unsellable [an]. Problem 2: Choosing the wrong positioning [k], for example pushing a $60 luxury notebook through supermarkets to mass-market shoppers not seeking hand-bound quality [app], would waste the marketing budget and blur the premium image built through the 5 premium stationery shops [an].
    Keywords: local language, $60, $32, supermarkets, hand-bound, 5 premium stationery shops, $45
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: unfamiliar local regulations/language requirements abroad; wrong positioning wastes marketing spend and damages brand image | application_max_2: labelling in the local language required; $60 luxury product misplaced in supermarkets / image built in 5 shops | analysis_max_2: reprinting adds cost and delays launch; confused positioning erodes brand and wastes budget

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fable & Flint should enter Country V with the luxury niche strategy or the mass-market strategy? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The luxury niche option, $60 notebooks in 12 exclusive shops [k], matches the hand-bound positioning that earned $270,000 from 6,000 notebooks at $45 in Country X [app], protecting the premium brand image and preserving margins [an]. The mass-market option, supermarkets at $32 [k], could reach far more of the 400,000 potential buyers [app], but selling at $32, well below the domestic $45, risks cheapening the brand and undermining loyalty [an]. Overall, the luxury niche route is the stronger recommendation because it plays to Fable & Flint's craftsmanship, keeps the $45-to-$60 price ladder and avoids discounting [eval]; a limited supermarket line could follow later once Country V demand is proven [eval].
    Keywords: $60, $45, $32, 400,000, 12 exclusive shops, supermarkets, 6,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: niche strategy targets a small premium segment with premium pricing; mass-market strategy targets the whole market with low prices | application_max_2: 12 exclusive shops at $60 / brand built at $45, 6,000 notebooks; supermarkets at $32 vs 400,000 potential buyers | analysis_max_2: niche protects brand image and margins; mass-market maximises reach but risks brand erosion | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two strategies; sensible sequencing suggested (prove niche first, expand later)

--- STEM ---
Hearthside Foods is a private limited company in Country X producing chilled ready meals sold through 9 supermarkets. Last year it sold 250,000 meals at $5.40 each, generating $1.35 million in revenue, and employs 27 workers at its kitchen and cold-chain dispatch. The business wants to enter Country U, a neighbouring market three times the size of Country X, through an import distributor it has already signed.

The marketing manager must devise the marketing mix for Country U: either a premium range at $6.80 per meal targeted at affluent urban households, with gift-style packaging in specialist shops, or a family value range at $4.40 per meal aimed at price-sensitive shoppers in large supermarket chains. The distributor favours the family value option for the launch.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'marketing mix'.
    Answer: The combination of elements a business uses to market its products, usually product, price, place and promotion, to achieve its marketing objectives [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: combination of elements used to market products; product, price, place and promotion

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two elements of the marketing mix Hearthside Foods should consider for Country U.
    Answer: Element 1: Price — the premium option charges $6.80 per meal while the family value option charges $4.40 [k], and Country U shoppers are reported to be price-sensitive, so pricing must match the target segment [app]. Element 2: Place — the meals could go through specialist shops or large supermarket chains [k], with the family value range gaining reach across a market three times the size of Country X [app].
    Keywords: $6.80, $4.40, three times, supermarket, $5.40, $1.35 million, 9 supermarkets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: price must reflect costs and what the target segment will pay; place/distribution must reach the target customers | application_max_2: $6.80 premium vs $4.40 family value / price-sensitive shoppers; specialist shops vs supermarket chains / market three times the size

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Hearthside Foods could face entering Country U.
    Answer: Problem 1: Country U shoppers are price-sensitive [k], so premium $6.80 meals may sell slowly and stock could build up in the distributor's freezers [app], cutting margins and potentially ending the trial with unsold inventory [an]. Problem 2: Relying on a single import distributor [k] gives that partner control over pricing and shelf placement [app], so Hearthside loses direct contact with Country U customers and may struggle to build its brand or gather feedback [an].
    Keywords: price-sensitive, $6.80, distributor, $4.40, Country U, supermarket
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: price-sensitivity limits demand for premium prices abroad; intermediaries control distribution and customer access | application_max_2: $6.80 premium meals may not sell to price-sensitive shoppers; single import distributor controls pricing/placement | analysis_max_2: excess stock and markdowns destroy trial economics; weak brand-building and no direct customer feedback

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hearthside Foods should launch the premium or the family value range in Country U? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The family value range at $4.40 per meal [k] matches Country U's price-sensitive shoppers and the distributor's plan to list in supermarket chains [app], giving the best chance of high volume in a market three times the size of Country X [an]. The premium range at $6.80 [k] protects margins and suits affluent urban households, but the distributor doubts demand at that price and freezer stock could pile up unsold [app], forcing markdowns that destroy the premium positioning [an]. Overall, launching family value is the sensible first move because it maximises reach and builds operational scale in Country U, generating cash and brand recognition [eval]; a premium gift line can follow once the brand is established [eval].
    Keywords: $4.40, $6.80, price-sensitive, supermarket, three times, $1.35 million, 250,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: family value range fits price-sensitive mass markets; premium range protects margins but limits volume | application_max_2: $4.40 family value / distributor favours it / supermarket chains; $6.80 premium / affluent urban households / doubts over demand | analysis_max_2: family value maximises volume and reach at scale; premium risks unsold stock and markdowns | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two options; sensible sequencing suggested (value range first, premium later)

--- STEM ---
Ironwood Smokehouse is a private limited company in Country X producing smoked sausages and cured meats sold through 11 delicatessens. A food importer in Country S has shown strong interest in stocking Ironwood products in delicatessens and gourmet shops across that country.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customers repeatedly buy the same brand; rather than switching to rival brands / because of trust or satisfaction

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways a domestic loyalty scheme could help Ironwood Smokehouse build customer loyalty.
    Answer: Way 1: Points or discounts for repeat purchases [k] reward the habit behind 168,000 pack sales a year [app]. Way 2: Tasting evenings for loyal customers [k] build personal relationships and give shoppers direct reasons to keep choosing the brand at $2.50 per pack over rivals [app].
    Keywords: 168,000 packs, 11 delicatessens, $2.50, $420,000, loyalty, Ironwood, 168,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rewards/discounts encourage repeat purchases; events build relationships and deepen attachment to the brand | application_max_2: 168,000 pack sales a year / 11 delicatessens; $2.50 per pack / shoppers choose it over rivals

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Ironwood Smokehouse could face if it exports to Country S.

Problem 2: The importer offers just $2.20 per pack [k], 30 cents below the domestic price of $2.50 [app], so margins thin exactly when new-market costs rise, risking losses on every export order [an].
    Keywords: $90,000, $2.20, $2.50, $420,000, Country S, 14 workers, 20,000 packs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: entering foreign markets requires significant upfront investment; exporters often accept lower prices/margins from intermediaries | application_max_2: $90,000 setup / about 21% of $420,000 revenue / 14 workers; $2.20 importer price / 30 cents below the domestic $2.50 | analysis_max_2: cash drained before overseas sales begin; thin margins risk losses on export volume

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ironwood Smokehouse should export to Country S or invest in a domestic loyalty scheme? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Exporting offers 20,000 packs a year at $2.20, about $44,000 in extra revenue [k], opening a new market beyond the 11 delicatessens [app], but the $90,000 setup would take more than 2 years of export revenue to recover [an]. The loyalty scheme costs just $30,000 [k] and should raise repeat purchases from the existing 168,000-pack base while deepening relationships with delicatessen partners [app], delivering steadier returns at lower risk [an]. Overall, investing in the domestic loyalty scheme is the better recommendation now [eval], because protecting and deepening the local 168,000-pack franchise is cheaper, faster and builds exactly the relationships that would make exporting viable later [eval].
    Keywords: $90,000, $2.20, 20,000 packs, $30,000, 168,000, $420,000, 11 delicatessens
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exporting enters a new market but at high setup cost and lower price; loyalty scheme retains and deepens existing customers more cheaply | application_max_2: 20,000 packs at $2.20 / about $44,000 extra revenue / $90,000 setup; $30,000 loyalty scheme / existing 168,000-pack base / 11 delicatessens | analysis_max_2: export investment recovers in over 2 years at $44,000 a year; loyalty delivers steadier returns at lower risk | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between the two options; sequencing suggested (local loyalty now, export later)

--- STEM ---
Fernbrook Cleaning Co is a private limited company in Country X that has sold liquid laundry detergent for 9 years. It employs 34 staff and last year generated revenue of $2.3 million from 18,000 households. The company is now developing a concentrated detergent refill tablet designed to dissolve in existing bottles at home. Demand for low-waste refill solutions is growing across Country X as households try to cut plastic use.

Development has so far cost $260,000, covering laboratory testing, safety certification and pack design, with a further $150,000 needed for a factory trial run. The tablet will retail at $6.50 for a 3-month supply, but 4 of 30 trial households said the tablets dissolved too slowly. The directors must decide whether to proceed to a national launch in March or abandon the project.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'new product development'.
    Answer: New product development is the process by which a business creates, tests and launches new products or significantly improves existing ones, moving from idea generation through design, testing and test marketing to commercial launch. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies new product development as creating or improving products; Refers to stages such as idea generation, testing or launch

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Fernbrook Cleaning Co might benefit from launching the refill tablet.
    Answer: Reason 1: Developing a new product can meet changing customer needs and attract new customers [k]; the refill tablet is aimed at 18,000 households already using Fernbrook's liquid detergent, so launching it could capture that base with a more convenient, eco-friendly option [app]. Reason 2: A successful new product can increase revenue and give a competitive advantage [k]; since the tablet will retail at $6.50 for a 3-month supply, a national launch could add a profitable line on top of Fernbrook's $2.3 million revenue base [app].
    Keywords: Fernbrook, refill tablet, 18,000 households, $6.50, $2.3 million, 3-month
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises a new product can meet changing customer needs; Recognises a new product can increase revenue or competitiveness | application_max_2: Links the tablet to the 18,000 existing households or $2.3 million revenue; Links the $6.50 price point or 3-month supply to incremental sales potential

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Fernbrook Cleaning Co may face if it proceeds to the national launch in March.
    Answer: Problem 1: Developing new products is costly and the outcome is uncertain [k]; Fernbrook has already spent $260,000 and needs a further $150,000 for the trial run, so a failed launch would write off $410,000 [app]; this matters because the loss would reduce retained profit and limit funds available to support the core liquid detergent range [an]. Problem 2: Product weaknesses found in testing may not be fixed in time [k]; 4 of 30 trial households reported that the tablets dissolved too slowly, so a March launch could trigger complaints and returns [app]; this could damage Fernbrook's reputation and reduce sales of its existing detergents as customers lose trust in the brand [an].
    Keywords: Fernbrook, $260,000, $150,000, March, 4 of 30, dissolved too slowly
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises development costs and uncertainty of success; Recognises that unresolved design flaws cause complaints or returns | application_max_2: Uses the $260,000 spent and $150,000 trial-run cost; Uses the 4 of 30 slow-dissolving trial households | analysis_max_2: Explains impact of failure on retained profit or core range; Explains impact of complaints on brand reputation and existing sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fernbrook Cleaning Co should proceed to the national launch in March? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Proceeding makes sense because Fernbrook has already invested heavily [k]; it has spent $260,000 and faces a further $150,000, totalling around $410,000 [app]; walking away would waste that investment, whereas a launch into the growing eco refill market could add a profitable new line and strengthen the brand with 18,000 existing households [an]. However, the trial flaw is a serious warning [k]; 4 of 30 households found the tablets dissolved too slowly, and launching in March without reformulation risks disappointing early adopters [app]; poor first impressions could trigger complaints, damage the brand and drag down sales of the $2.3 million core detergent business [an]. Overall, Fernbrook should delay the March launch briefly to fix the dissolution problem and retest rather than abandon the project entirely [eval]; this protects the $410,000 committed while avoiding a damaging failed launch [eval].
    Keywords: Fernbrook, March, $260,000, $150,000, 4 of 30, 18,000 households, $2.3 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Understands development costs and sunk investment; Understands the risk of launching an unproven product | application_max_2: Uses the $260,000 and $150,000 figures; Uses the 4 of 30 slow-dissolving households or March timing | analysis_max_2: Analyses the upside of launching into the eco refill trend; Analyses the downside of complaints or brand damage to the core range | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options; Considers a middle course such as delaying rather than abandoning

--- STEM ---
Granary & Grain Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that has made traditional wheat pasta for 12 years. Last year it launched VerdeProtein, a plant-based protein pasta aimed at gym-goers and vegetarians, after spending $340,000 on two years of development. The company employs 48 staff and VerdeProtein generated just $75,000 in its first 6 months.

VerdeProtein packs contain 28g of protein per 100g, roughly double traditional wheat pasta. VerdeProtein is now stocked in 120 supermarkets, and sales in July reached 5,600 packs at $2.80 each, so the product is in the introduction stage of the product life cycle. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the 'introduction stage' of the product life cycle.
    Answer: The introduction stage is the first stage of a product's life cycle after launch, when the product is first offered to the market and sales are usually low because awareness is limited and customers have not yet tried it. Promotion and distribution are still being built up and the product often makes losses at this stage. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies it as the launch stage when sales are low; Notes that awareness or distribution is still being built

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why sales of VerdeProtein are likely to be low during the introduction stage.
    Answer: Reason 1: In the introduction stage the product is new to the market and customer awareness is low [k]; only 22% of shoppers surveyed by Granary & Grain could identify VerdeProtein [app]. Reason 2: Consumers are reluctant to buy an unfamiliar product without proof or promotion [k]; VerdeProtein is stocked in 120 supermarkets and July sales reached just 5,600 packs at $2.80 each, so customer habit and shelf presence are still developing [app].
    Keywords: VerdeProtein, Granary & Grain, 22%, 120 supermarkets, 5,600 packs, $2.80, introduction stage
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises that awareness is low for a newly launched product; Recognises that customers are reluctant to try unknown products | application_max_2: Uses the 22% brand-awareness figure; Uses the 120 supermarkets or 5,600 July packs figure

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits VerdeProtein could gain from strong promotional support during the introduction stage.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Promotion increases awareness and trial among the target market [k]; allocating part of the $60,000 budget to social media and in-store tasting could lift the 22% recognition figure and persuade gym-goers to try VerdeProtein [app]; wider trial would generate word of mouth and repeat purchases, building early momentum as the product moves towards growth [an]. Benefit 2: Promotion can shift demand and help recover development costs [k]; with July sales of 5,600 packs at $2.80 producing only about $15,680 a month, stronger promotion could close the gap on the $340,000 development spend faster [app]; rising sales also reassure supermarkets to keep stocking the product and avoid delisting [an].
    Keywords: $60,000, 22%, 5,600 packs, $2.80, $340,000, 120 supermarkets, VerdeProtein
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises that promotion builds awareness and trial; Recognises that promotion can lift sales or recover costs | application_max_2: Uses the $60,000 promotional budget or 22% awareness figure; Uses the 5,600 July packs or $2.80 price figure | analysis_max_2: Explains how trial leads to repeat purchase and growth; Explains how rising sales support supermarket listings and faster recovery of costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Granary & Grain Foods Ltd should spend the full $60,000 promoting VerdeProtein during the introduction stage? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Spending now is justified because promotion matters most in the introduction stage [k]; with only 22% of shoppers recognising VerdeProtein and just $75,000 of revenue in 6 months, investment is needed before rivals copy the recipe [app]; allocating the $60,000 across social media and in-store tasting could build awareness and trial, moving VerdeProtein towards growth and protecting the $340,000 spent on development [an]. However, the introduction stage usually brings losses [k]; sales of 5,600 packs in July at $2.80 yield only around $15,680 a month [app], so committing all $60,000 at once could strain cash flow when returns are unproven, and poorly targeted spending aimed at gym-goers may be wasted [an]. Overall, Granary & Grain should spend the $60,000 but in stages, linked to awareness and sales milestones [eval]; this balances the need to build the new brand against financial prudence while the product is unproven [eval].
    Keywords: $60,000, 22%, $75,000, 5,600 packs, $2.80, $340,000, VerdeProtein, 120 supermarkets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Understands promotion is most critical at introduction; Understands introduction-stage losses and cash-flow pressure | application_max_2: Uses the 22% awareness, $75,000 6-month revenue or 5,600 July packs figure; Uses the $60,000 budget or $340,000 development cost figure | analysis_max_2: Analyses how promotion could build awareness and move VerdeProtein towards growth; Analyses the risk of overspending or targeting errors draining cash flow | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options; Considers a staged spending approach linked to milestones

--- STEM ---
Wildroot Brew Co is a private limited company in Country X that launched a fermented kombucha drink 18 months ago. Bottle sales have risen from 30,000 in its first quarter to 190,000 in the latest quarter, and the company employs 26 staff. The product is in the growth stage of the product life cycle. Wildroot's kombucha is brewed from organic tea, raw sugar and live cultures at its plant in Country X.

Wildroot sells through 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains at $3.20 per 500ml bottle. Profit last year was $180,000. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the 'growth stage' of the product life cycle.
    Answer: The growth stage is the phase in which a product's sales and profits rise rapidly as awareness spreads, the product is accepted by the market and distribution widens. Competitors often enter the market at this stage as the product proves successful. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies rapid growth in sales or profits; Notes rising customer acceptance or widening distribution

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Wildroot Brew Co's kombucha sales are rising rapidly in the growth stage.

Reason 2: Wider distribution makes the product easy to buy [k]; Wildroot is stocked in 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains, so growing numbers of customers can buy a 500ml bottle at $3.20 [app].
    Keywords: Wildroot, 30,000, 190,000, 340 independent health stores, 2 supermarket chains, $3.20, growth stage
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises growing acceptance and word-of-mouth awareness; Recognises that wider distribution increases sales | application_max_2: Uses the 30,000 to 190,000 bottle sales rise; Uses the 340 independent health stores, 2 supermarket chains or $3.20 price

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits Wildroot Brew Co could gain by investing $400,000 in extra brewing tanks now.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Extra capacity lets the business meet rising demand and avoid lost sales [k]; with quarterly sales up from 30,000 to 190,000 bottles, current tanks are stretched, so extra capacity would let Wildroot fill every order before rival Zing launches in 6 months [app]; this would strengthen supermarket relationships and secure shelf space that might otherwise go to competitors [an]. Benefit 2: Higher volume spreads fixed costs and lifts profit [k]; increasing output to serve the 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains at $3.20 per bottle would grow revenue above its current level and raise the $180,000 profit [app]; economies of scale on ingredients and bottling would further reduce unit costs and improve margins [an].
    Keywords: $400,000, 30,000, 190,000, Zing, 6 months, $3.20, $180,000

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wildroot Brew Co should invest $400,000 of retained profit in extra brewing tanks? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing is attractive because the growth stage is the moment to capture market share [k]; sales have risen from 30,000 to 190,000 bottles per quarter and distribution spans 340 independent health stores and 2 supermarket chains [app]; added capacity would let Wildroot supply demand fully, lock in volume and defend supermarket shelf space before Zing launches in 6 months, building on the $180,000 profit already achieved [an]. However, the investment carries real risk [k]; the $400,000 would come from retained profit, and if Zing wins share or consumer tastes change, Wildroot could be left with excess capacity and lower cash reserves [app]; raising the price to $3.60 to protect margins might slow the sales momentum that makes expansion worthwhile [an]. Overall, Wildroot should invest the $400,000 now [eval]; the sixfold sales rise and the imminent rival launch make speed more valuable than preserving cash, and failing to expand risks permanently losing supermarket shelf space [eval].
    Keywords: Wildroot, $400,000, 190,000, Zing, 6 months, $180,000, $3.60, 340 independent health stores
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Understands the competitive logic of investing at the growth stage; Understands the risk of tying up retained profit in capacity | application_max_2: Uses the 30,000 to 190,000 sales rise, 340 stores or 2 supermarket chains; Uses the $400,000 investment, Zing's 6-month launch or the $3.60 price rise option | analysis_max_2: Analyses how capacity supports demand and market-share defence; Analyses the risk of excess capacity or price rises slowing momentum | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options; Considers timing relative to Zing's entry or the price-rise alternative
