--- STEM ---
Amberfields Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that produces QuickQuick instant noodle pots. The brand is 14 years old and sales have been flat at around 900,000 pots a year for 3 years, placing the market at maturity. The company employs 72 staff and QuickQuick generated $2.7 million revenue last year, sold as 112,500 cases of 8 pots at $24 per case.

Amberfields holds a 16% share of the instant noodle market, down from 21% four years ago, as two rivals undercut its price by $0.10 per pot. The marketing manager must recommend an extension strategy, a new spicy variant and festival multipack, or a permanent wholesale price cut to match rivals. The board has $150,000 available.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the 'maturity stage' of the product life cycle.
    Answer: The maturity stage is the phase in which sales growth slows and levels off as the market becomes saturated with the product and competition intensifies. Sales remain high but plateau, and businesses typically focus on defending market share and extending the product's profitable life. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies sales growth slowing or levelling off; Notes high but flat sales amid heavy competition

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two features of the maturity stage of the product life cycle shown by QuickQuick.
    Answer: Feature 1: Sales are high but flat, with little growth [k]; QuickQuick sales have been flat at around 900,000 pots a year for 3 years [app]. Feature 2: Competition is intense and prices come under pressure [k]; two rivals undercut QuickQuick by $0.10 per pot and its share has slipped from 21% to 16% [app].
    Keywords: QuickQuick, 900,000 pots, $0.10 per pot, 21%, 16%, maturity
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises plateauing or flat sales at maturity; Recognises intensified competition and price pressure | application_max_2: Uses the flat 900,000 pots a year figure; Uses the $0.10 undercut or 21% to 16% share slide

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of an extension strategy for QuickQuick instant noodle pots.
    Answer: Benefit 1: An extension strategy prolongs the product life cycle and defends revenue [k]; a new spicy variant and festival multipack could reverse the share slide from 21% to 16% without resorting to a permanent $0.10 price cut, keeping QuickQuick relevant as tastes change [app]; maintaining sales of around 900,000 pots a year would protect $2.7 million of revenue and the jobs of 72 staff [an]. Benefit 2: It creates fresh promotional opportunities at relatively low cost [k]; with the board's $150,000 available, new variants can be advertised and displayed in store to win back lapsed buyers [app]; renewed attention can lift repeat purchase rates and slow the drift towards saturation [an].
    Keywords: QuickQuick, 21%, 16%, 900,000 pots, $2.7 million, $150,000, 72 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises that extension strategies prolong the life cycle or defend share; Recognises extension strategies create promotional freshness | application_max_2: Uses the 21% to 16% share slide, 900,000 pots or $2.7 million revenue; Uses the $150,000 board budget or the spicy variant and festival multipack | analysis_max_2: Explains how variants protect revenue and jobs or slow decline; Explains how promotion refreshes the brand and drives repeat purchase

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Amberfields Foods Ltd should use an extension strategy rather than cut its wholesale price permanently? Justify your answer.
    Answer: An extension strategy is the stronger option [k]; a new spicy variant and festival multipack would refresh the brand and appeal to the 900,000 pots a year that QuickQuick still sells, rebuilding the share that slipped from 21% to 16% without eroding margins across the whole range [app]; focused promotion using the $150,000 budget protects the $2.7 million revenue and avoids a $0.10 cut lowering profit on every case sold [an]. However, a price cut responds to rivals immediately [k]; matching the $0.10 undercut would win back price-sensitive buyers who switched and could restore volume quickly, an outcome the $150,000 extension plan cannot guarantee [app]; deep cuts, though, risk a price war and signal that QuickQuick is a cheap brand, weakening its position further [an]. Overall, Amberfields should choose the extension strategy over a permanent price cut [eval]; it protects profit per pot and rebuilds brand appeal, whereas a permanent cut sacrifices long-term profitability for only temporary volume [eval].
    Keywords: extension strategy, $150,000, 21%, 16%, $0.10, 900,000 pots, $2.7 million, QuickQuick
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Understands extension strategies refresh the product or defend share; Understands price cuts respond to rivals but erode margins | application_max_2: Uses the 21% to 16% share slide, 900,000 pots or $2.7 million revenue; Uses the $150,000 budget, $0.10 undercut or spicy variant and festival multipack | analysis_max_2: Analyses how variants and promotion rebuild share without cutting margin; Analyses how permanent price cuts affect profit or invite a price war | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options; Considers short-term volume recovery against long-term margin damage

--- STEM ---
Cascade Beverages is a private limited company in Country X that bottles Cascade Cola, launched 19 years ago. The market is now saturated: sales peaked at 18 million bottles in 2021 and last year reached 12.5 million bottles at $1.50 each, a fall of over 30%. The company employs 88 staff.

The marketing director proposes an extension strategy built on redesign: Cascade Zero, a sugar-free cola in new recyclable bottles, at a development and promotion cost of $380,000. The alternative is launching two new flavours in the existing packaging at $180,000. Cascade Zero would add an estimated $0.35 of extra cost per bottle, and the board must choose between the two options. Cascade plans to keep production at its existing Country X bottling plant whichever option it selects.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the 'saturation stage' of the product life cycle.
    Answer: The saturation stage is the point at which the market is full of the product and virtually everyone who wants one already has it, so sales peak and then begin to fall. Further growth can only come from extension strategies or from reaching new customer segments. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the market as full of the product; Notes sales peaked and began to fall

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Cascade Beverages wants to use an extension strategy at this stage.
    Answer: Reason 1: The market is saturated, so organic growth has stalled [k]; sales peaked at 18 million bottles in 2021 and have fallen to 12.5 million last year, a drop of over 30% [app]. Reason 2: Extension strategies refresh the product and attract new buyers [k]; a sugar-free variant in new recyclable bottles could appeal to health-conscious customers, while new flavours could target different tastes [app].
    Keywords: Cascade Cola, 18 million bottles, 12.5 million bottles, over 30%, Cascade Zero, extension strategy
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises that saturated markets stall organic growth; Recognises that extension strategies refresh products and attract buyers | application_max_2: Uses the 18 million peak versus 12.5 million bottles or over 30% fall; Uses the sugar-free Cascade Zero or recyclable bottles proposal

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Cascade Beverages could face with the proposed extension strategies.
    Answer: Problem 1: Extension strategies require heavy investment with no guaranteed payoff [k]; Cascade Zero would cost $380,000 against $180,000 for the two new flavours, and the extra $0.35 per bottle would raise unit costs [app]; if the sugar-free cola fails to win share, the larger spend would intensify losses in a market already down over 30% [an]. Problem 2: New flavours can fail if they miss customer tastes [k]; the existing-packaging option at $180,000 offers little shelf differentiation in a crowded cola market, so trial may be slow [app]; weak adoption would leave Cascade with disappointing sales and less money for future launches [an].
    Keywords: Cascade Zero, $380,000, $180,000, $0.35, over 30%, two new flavours
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises heavy investment and uncertain payoff; Recognises new variants may miss customer tastes | application_max_2: Uses the $380,000 Cascade Zero cost or $0.35 extra per bottle; Uses the $180,000 two-flavour alternative | analysis_max_2: Explains consequence of failure in a falling market on losses or viability; Explains how slow trial undermines extension success or future launches

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cascade Beverages should launch Cascade Zero in redesigned recyclable bottles rather than two new flavours? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cascade Zero is the stronger choice [k]; a sugar-free cola in redesigned recyclable bottles targets two powerful trends, health and sustainability, and would stand out on shelves in a saturated market where sales have fallen over 30% to 12.5 million bottles a year [app]; a visible, differentiated relaunch could rebuild the brand, attract new buyers and restart growth, justifying the $380,000 investment despite the extra $0.35 per bottle [an]. However, the two new flavours cost only $180,000 [k]; launching them in existing packaging keeps costs low and spreads risk across two products, which is safer if health trends shift again or Cascade Zero underperforms [app]; a failed relaunch would leave the board having spent more than double for no gain [an]. Overall, Cascade should back Cascade Zero [eval]; the differentiation and brand revival it offers outweigh the higher cost, provided the board sets clear sales targets and reviews performance after 12 months [eval].
    Keywords: Cascade Zero, $380,000, $180,000, 12.5 million bottles, $0.35, over 30%, $1.50
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Understands how redesigned differentiated extensions rebuild brands; Understands the cost and risk trade-offs between options | application_max_2: Uses the over 30% fall to 12.5 million bottles or $380,000 Cascade Zero cost; Uses the $180,000 two-flavour alternative or $0.35 extra cost | analysis_max_2: Analyses how differentiation and trends could restart growth; Analyses the risk of overspending or underperformance on relaunch | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options; Considers monitoring and review as a condition of the decision

Bridgewater Office Machines Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that has manufactured office fax machines for 16 years, employing 30 staff. Unit sales peaked at 14,000 machines in 2019 and fell to 3,600 last year as businesses switched to email and scanning. Revenue fell from $1.4 million to $380,000 over the same period.

The machines are now in the decline stage of the product life cycle, and Bridgewater holds $140,000 of unsold stock. The managing director proposes an extension strategy, a Wi-Fi internet fax model costing $220,000 to develop, or stopping fax production and converting the workshop to servicing machines and selling scanners, which would affect 18 production workers.     Question: Define the 'decline stage' of the product life cycle.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies sales and profits falling in this phase; Notes the product becomes obsolete or is replaced by alternatives

  Qb [4 marks]

Reason 2: Customers are leaving the category altogether [k]; revenue dropped from $1.4 million to $380,000 over the same period, leaving Bridgewater with $140,000 of unsold stock [app].
    Keywords: Bridgewater, 14,000 machines, 3,600, $1.4 million, $380,000, $140,000, fax machines
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises technological obsolescence as a cause of decline; Recognises that falling demand reduces revenue and leaves unsold stock | application_max_2: Uses the 14,000 to 3,600 machines sales fall; Uses the $1.4 million to $380,000 revenue fall or $140,000 stock figure

Problem 2: The fax segment itself is shrinking [k]; even a Wi-Fi fax targets a category collapsing from 14,000 to 3,600 units a year, so it may only cannibalise existing orders rather than win new customers [app]; spending $220,000 to prolong a dying product could delay the necessary shift into servicing and scanners [an].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises development cost and uncertain return; Recognises shrinking markets limit extension potential | application_max_2: Uses the $220,000 development cost or $380,000 revenue figure; Uses the 14,000 to 3,600 units fall or $140,000 unsold stock | analysis_max_2: Explains consequence of failure on losses or viability; Explains cannibalisation risk and delayed strategic shift

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Bridgewater Office Machines should develop the Wi-Fi internet fax model? Justify your answer.

Overall, Bridgewater should stop fax production and convert rather than develop the Wi-Fi model [eval]; the collapse in demand shows extension is unlikely to succeed, and conversion repositions the business around what customers now buy [eval].

The brand launched 8 years ago and sales reached 600,000 bars a year at $8.50, but have plateaued for 2 years. The company employs 44 staff and repeat purchases have slipped from 38% to 29% of customers over 12 months.

  Qb [4 marks]

Strategy 2: Entering a new geographical market extends the life cycle [k]; exporting Nettle & Sage to Country Z, costed at $150,000 for licensing and promotion, would expose the bars to customers who have never encountered them [app].
    Keywords: Nettle & Sage, 3 new scents, 50g travel-size bar, $4.00, Country Z, 38%, 29%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises product variation as an extension strategy; Recognises entering new markets as an extension strategy | application_max_2: Uses the 3 new scents, 50g travel-size bar or $4.00 price details; Uses the Country Z export option or the 38% to 29% repeat-purchase slip

--- STEM ---
Emberglow Candle Co is a private limited company in Country X making scented candles for 6 years. For the first 4 years it sold own-brand candles in gift shops at $14, with modest sales. Last year it relaunched as the premium brand Maison Ember, with luxury packaging and a stronger fragrance story, selling 180,000 candles at $22 each and lifting revenue to $3.96 million. The relaunch involved rebuilding the name, scent profiles and artwork over 6 months with a packaging design agency.

Repeat purchases rose from 19% to 34% after the relaunch, and the company employs 39 staff. Rival Lumen Homeware sells similar candles at $12. Moving Maison Ember into supermarkets at a lower $9 price would double volume but may damage the premium brand image Emberglow has built.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'brand image'.
    Answer: Brand image is the set of beliefs, perceptions and feelings consumers hold about a particular brand, formed by its name, logo, packaging, advertising, quality and customer experiences. It shapes whether buyers notice, trust and choose that brand over competitors. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies brand image as consumer perception or beliefs about a brand; Notes it is shaped by name, packaging, advertising, quality or experience

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways a strong brand image can help Emberglow Candle Co.
    Answer: Way 1: A strong brand image increases loyalty and repeat purchases [k]; after the Maison Ember relaunch, repeat purchases rose from 19% to 34%, showing customers formed a favourable premium perception [app]. Way 2: It allows the business to charge a higher price [k]; Maison Ember sells 180,000 candles at $22 each against a rival at $12, lifting revenue to $3.96 million [app].
    Keywords: Maison Ember, 19%, 34%, $22, $12, $3.96 million, Emberglow
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises strong brand image increases loyalty or repeat purchase; Recognises strong brand image supports premium pricing | application_max_2: Uses the 19% to 34% repeat-purchase rise; Uses the $22 price, $12 rival price, 180,000 candles or $3.96 million revenue

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems that might result from moving Maison Ember into supermarkets at $9.
    Answer: Problem 1: A much lower price erodes premium positioning [k]; selling Maison Ember at $9 instead of the $22 gift-shop price signals a mass-market product and clashes with the luxury packaging and fragrance story behind the relaunch [app]; supermarket bargain displays could make loyal gift-shop buyers question the value of what they paid [an]. Problem 2: Supermarket channels cut profit per candle [k]; moving to volume at $9 doubles volume but takes far less margin per unit than $22, squeezing profitability unless costs fall sharply [app]; the $3.96 million revenue stream could shift from high-margin gift shops to high-volume, low-margin sales, so total profit may fall even if revenue doubles [an].
    Keywords: $9, $22, Maison Ember, luxury packaging, Lumen Homeware, $12, $3.96 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises low prices erode premium positioning or perceived exclusivity; Recognises supermarket margins or volume-margin trade-offs | application_max_2: Uses the $9 supermarket price versus $22 gift-shop price or luxury packaging; Uses the $3.96 million revenue or doubled-volume framing | analysis_max_2: Explains how discounting damages brand trust or perceived value; Explains how margin shift can reduce total profit despite higher volume

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Emberglow Candle Co should move Maison Ember into supermarkets at $9? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Supermarket distribution is tempting [k]; at $9 Maison Ember would undercut rival Lumen Homeware at $12 and roughly double volume, lifting revenue well beyond the current $3.96 million and placing the brand in front of far more shoppers [app]; for a young brand, supermarket shelf space would raise awareness and introduce Maison Ember to a wider demographic [an]. However, it risks the premium image [k]; discounting to $9 erodes the exclusivity created by luxury packaging and the fragrance story that justified $22 gift-shop pricing and drove repeat purchases from 19% to 34% [app]; cannibalising gift-shop sales at less than half the margin could reduce total profit despite higher volume, and recovering premium positioning later is very difficult [an]. Overall, Emberglow should not move Maison Ember into supermarkets at $9 [eval]; the brand's value rests on premium scarcity and perception, so a separate value line, not the Maison Ember range itself, would be the safer route if supermarket entry is ever pursued [eval].
    Keywords: Maison Ember, $9, $12, $22, $3.96 million, 19%, 34%, Lumen Homeware
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Understands the volume and awareness benefits of supermarket distribution; Understands the premium-image risk of deep discounting | application_max_2: Uses the $9 price, $12 Lumen Homeware price or doubled-volume framing; Uses the $3.96 million revenue, $22 gift-shop price or 19% to 34% repeat rise | analysis_max_2: Analyses awareness and revenue upside of mass distribution; Analyses margin erosion, cannibalisation and premium-image damage | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options; Considers a separate value line as an alternative to discounting the premium brand

--- STEM ---
Sunhaven Vitamins Ltd is a private limited company in Country X selling children's multivitamin gummies. It sells 900,000 bottles a year at $11.50, generating $10.35 million in revenue, with 26 employees. Pharmacies are the main seller, and each bottle contains 60 gummies, roughly a two-month supply for a child aged 4 to 10. Complaints show 3,800 opened bottles were found by children despite child-resistant caps, including one near-miss incident.

Sunhaven plans a redesigned pack: a resealable child-safe pouch with bold dosing information and bright fruit graphics, costing $110,000 plus $0.22 more per unit. Retooling for the changeover would cost $75,000. Parents in trials rated the new pack 4.6 out of 5, and pharmacy sales could rise by an estimated 12%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'packaging'.
    Answer: Packaging is the materials and design used to contain, wrap, protect and present a product for sale. It serves functional purposes such as protection and safety and marketing purposes such as attracting attention, providing information and reinforcing brand identity. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies packaging as materials or design used to contain or protect the product; Notes functional or marketing roles such as safety, information or branding

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two roles of packaging for Sunhaven's children's multivitamin gummies.
    Answer: Role 1: Packaging protects the product and keeps children safe [k]; the redesigned resealable child-safe pouch directly addresses the 3,800 opened-bottle complaints and the near-miss incident, reducing the chance of harm [app]. Role 2: Packaging communicates information and promotes the product [k]; bold dosing information shows parents the correct dose clearly, while bright fruit graphics make the product appealing, with trial parents rating the pack 4.6 out of 5 [app].
    Keywords: Sunhaven, 3,800, child-safe, bold dosing information, bright fruit graphics, 4.6 out of 5
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises protection or safety as a packaging role; Recognises information or promotion as a packaging role | application_max_2: Uses the 3,800 opened-bottle complaints or near-miss incident; Uses the bold dosing information, bright fruit graphics or 4.6 out of 5 rating

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits Sunhaven Vitamins would gain from the packaging redesign.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Improved safety can cut complaints and liability [k]; a resealable child-safe pouch would directly address the 3,800 opened-bottle incidents, protecting children and reducing the risk of expensive claims or product recalls [app]; this safeguards the brand's reputation with parents, the key buyers in pharmacy purchases [an]. Benefit 2: The redesign can lift sales and profit [k]; trials scored the new pack 4.6 out of 5 and pharmacy sales could rise by an estimated 12% on $10.35 million of revenue [app]; clearer dosing and stronger shelf stand-out use packaging as promotion, encouraging repeat purchase and cushioning the $0.22 extra unit cost [an].
    Keywords: 3,800, child-safe, 4.6 out of 5, 12%, $10.35 million, $0.22, Sunhaven
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recognises improved safety reduces complaints or liability; Recognises redesign can lift sales or repeat purchase | application_max_2: Uses the 3,800 opened-bottle incidents or child-safe pouch; Uses the 4.6 out of 5 rating, 12% estimated pharmacy sales rise or $10.35 million revenue | analysis_max_2: Explains how safety protects reputation and parental trust; Explains how packaging promotion supports repeat purchase or absorbs unit cost

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sunhaven Vitamins should go ahead with the packaging redesign? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The redesign is justified [k]; child safety is non-negotiable, and the current child-resistant caps have failed, with 3,800 opened bottles found by children and one near-miss, so a resealable child-safe pouch directly fixes a real risk [app]; together with bold dosing information, bright fruit graphics and a 4.6 out of 5 parent rating, the change would build trust and could lift pharmacy sales by an estimated 12% on $10.35 million of revenue [an]. However, the costs are significant [k]; the $110,000 development spend plus $75,000 retooling and $0.22 more per unit will squeeze margins on 900,000 bottles a year, roughly $198,000 of extra annual unit cost before any sales increase [app]; if the projected 12% uplift does not appear, the investment will not pay back quickly [an]. Overall, Sunhaven should proceed with the redesign [eval]; the safety imperative and strong trial feedback outweigh the $0.22 cost increase, and for a children's health product reputational damage is far costlier than the redesign [eval].
    Keywords: Sunhaven, 3,800, $110,000, $75,000, $0.22, 4.6 out of 5, 12%, $10.35 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Understands packaging's protective and marketing roles; Understands the cost implications of a redesign | application_max_2: Uses the 3,800 incidents, near-miss or child-safe pouch details; Uses the $110,000, $75,000 or $0.22 figures and 4.6 out of 5 rating | analysis_max_2: Analyses how safety and redesign drive trust and pharmacy sales; Analyses the margin impact of added unit costs | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified recommendation that weighs both options; Considers safety and reputation as decisive over pure cost

--- STEM ---
Foxbury Flour Mills is a private limited company in Country X, founded 9 years ago by siblings Dana and Cole Foxbury. It mills wheat into flour for 60 bakeries across the region, employing 24 millers and drivers, and last year milled 9,000 tonnes of flour. The company uses cost-plus pricing, applying a 25% markup to a production cost that has risen from $0.80 per kilogram to $0.88 and now $0.96.

The cost-plus price has therefore moved from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram. Keeping the 25% markup would lift the price to $1.20. Rival Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 per kilogram, and two large bakeries warned they will switch suppliers if prices rise again. Cole wants to hold at $1.10 and absorb the extra cost, while Dana wants the full increase passed on. The directors must decide within one month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'cost-plus pricing'.
    Answer: Cost-plus pricing is a pricing method in which a business calculates the total cost of producing a product and then adds a percentage markup to set the selling price. This ensures all production costs are covered and a profit margin is built in [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Business calculates the total cost of making the product; Adds a percentage markup to the cost to set the selling price

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Foxbury Flour Mills uses cost-plus pricing.
    Answer: Cost-plus pricing ensures that all production costs are covered and a profit is made [k], which is vital when wheat costs have risen from $0.80 to $0.96 per kilogram [app]. It is also straightforward to calculate and easy to update as costs change [k], as shown by the price moving from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram and possibly to $1.20 [app].
    Keywords: Foxbury, $0.80, $0.96, $1.10, $1.20, 25% markup, 9,000 tonnes, $1.00
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Covers production costs and guarantees a profit margin; Simple to calculate and adjust when costs change | application_max_2: Wheat cost has risen from $0.80 to $0.88 and now $0.96 per kilogram; Price moved from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram and could rise to $1.20 with the 25% markup

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Foxbury Flour Mills may face if it raises its price to $1.20 per kilogram.
    Answer: A higher price could make Foxbury uncompetitive against rivals [k], because Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 per kilogram [app], so the two large bakeries may switch suppliers, cutting Foxbury's sales volume [an]. A price rise could also damage Foxbury's relationships with long-standing customers [k], as two of its 60 bakery buyers have already warned they will switch [app], leaving capacity under-used across the 9,000 tonnes milled and reducing revenue [an].
    Keywords: Harborpoint Flour, $1.15, $1.20, 60 bakeries, 9,000 tonnes, Foxbury, $1.10
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: May become uncompetitive / rivals may be cheaper; May damage customer relationships / lose goodwill and long-standing buyers | application_max_2: Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 per kilogram, below the proposed $1.20; Two of Foxbury's 60 bakery customers have already warned they will switch suppliers | analysis_max_2: Sales volume and revenue fall if bakeries switch to Harborpoint; Under-used milling capacity across the 9,000 tonnes milled reduces recovery of fixed costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Foxbury Flour Mills should raise its price to $1.20 per kilogram, in line with cost-plus pricing, or hold the price at $1.10 per kilogram? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising the price to $1.20 maintains the 25% markup on the higher wheat cost of $0.96 [k], preserving the profit Foxbury earns on each of its 9,000 tonnes of flour [app], protecting cash flow and avoiding erosion of margins [an]. However, holding at $1.10 keeps Foxbury close to Harborpoint Flour's $1.15 price [k], helping Foxbury retain its 60 bakery customers and avoid losing the two large buyers who warned they will switch [app], protecting long-term revenue and market share [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to raise the price in line with cost-plus pricing [eval], because repeated input cost rises from $0.80 through $0.88 to $0.96 cannot be absorbed indefinitely without destroying profit, and the price must reflect true costs to remain sustainable [eval].
    Keywords: $1.20, $1.10, 25% markup, $0.96, 9,000 tonnes, Harborpoint Flour, $1.15, 60 bakeries
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cost-plus keeps the markup intact and protects profit; Holding the price protects share and keeps the price close to the rival | application_max_2: $0.96 wheat cost with 25% markup gives $1.20; margin must cover 9,000 tonnes; Holding at $1.10 stays near Harborpoint Flour at $1.15; two of 60 bakeries threatening to switch | analysis_max_2: Raising preserves margin and protects cash flow; Holding protects long-term volume, share and customer relationships | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation that costs rose repeatedly ($0.80 to $0.88 to $0.96) so absorption is unsustainable; Acknowledges the risk of losing the two large bakery buyers and weighs it against margin protection

--- STEM ---
Harborview Electrical is a private limited company in Country X, founded 6 years ago by owner Priya Nair. It sells televisions, refrigerators and small appliances from two high-street shops, employing 16 staff including delivery drivers. Last year it sold 2,400 televisions at an average price of $599 against a unit cost of $410, generating $1.44 million in revenue and a profit of $0.30 million.

National chain ValueMart has cut its television prices to $549 and runs match-any-price weekend promotions. Priya can either hold $599 and rely on free delivery and expert advice, or lower to $549 to match ValueMart. Matching cuts Harborview's profit margin per television from $189 to $139, and she fears sales could fall by 20% if the higher price is held. She must set the television price for the key summer trading period.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'competitive pricing'.
    Answer: Competitive pricing is a pricing method where a business sets its prices at or close to the prices charged by its competitors, rather than basing the price only on its own costs, so that it remains attractive to customers in the market [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Price is set at or close to competitors' prices; Focus is on matching the market rather than the business's own costs

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of competitive pricing for Harborview Electrical.
    Answer: Competitive pricing keeps Harborview's televisions attractive next to ValueMart, which has cut prices to $549 [k], helping Harborview defend its position against a rival running match-any-price weekend promotions [app]. It also helps prevent losing customers to cheaper competitors [k], protecting Harborview's 2,400 television sales and $1.44 million annual revenue [app].
    Keywords: ValueMart, $549, Harborview, 2,400, $1.44 million, $599, $189
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Keeps the product attractive against rivals' prices; Helps prevent loss of customers to cheaper competitors | application_max_2: ValueMart has cut television prices to $549 and runs match-any-price weekends; Harborview sold 2,400 televisions and earned $1.44 million in revenue last year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of competitive pricing for Harborview Electrical.
    Answer: Matching ValueMart at $549 cuts the profit margin per television from $189 to $139 [k], meaning $50 is lost on every set while the cost stays at $410 [app], squeezing Harborview's $0.30 million profit across its 2,400 sales [an]. Competitive pricing also makes Harborview dependent on rivals' decisions [k], so ValueMart's match-any-price weekends may force repeated price cuts [app], eroding margins in the two shops without any guarantee of extra volume [an].
    Keywords: $549, $189, $139, $410, $0.30 million, ValueMart, match-any-price
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Margins are squeezed because price is set by rivals; The business becomes dependent on competitors' pricing decisions | application_max_2: Matching $549 cuts the margin from $189 to $139 against a $410 unit cost; ValueMart runs match-any-price weekend promotions | analysis_max_2: Profit is squeezed across the 2,400 televisions sold, threatening the $0.30 million profit; Repeated reactive price cuts erode margins without guaranteeing more volume

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harborview Electrical should lower its television price to $549 to match ValueMart, or hold at $599? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Matching at $549 would cut the profit margin per television from $189 to $139 [k], reducing profit on the 2,400 sets sold and threatening the $0.30 million annual profit [app], limiting funds available for the free-delivery offer and in-store advice [an]. However, holding $599 risks losing customers to ValueMart and its match-any-price weekend promotions [k], potentially cutting television sales by the 20% Priya fears across the two shops [app], shrinking Harborview's market share in its local market [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to hold at $599 but add clearer value such as free delivery and expert advice [eval], because matching a national chain's discount triggers a price war Harborview cannot win on size, while superior service justifies the $50 premium for local buyers [eval].
    Keywords: $549, $599, $189, $139, 2,400, $0.30 million, ValueMart, $1.44 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Matching protects volume but erodes margin per unit; Holding the price risks losing customers / market share to the rival | application_max_2: Margin falls from $189 to $139 at $549 against $410 cost; 2,400 televisions sold, $0.30 million profit, ValueMart match-any-price weekends, 20% feared sales fall | analysis_max_2: Matching funds shrink (delivery, advice) and erodes per-unit margin; Holding risks sales volume and local market share | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation balancing margin erosion against share loss; Recognises Harborview cannot win a price war on size against a national chain, so service must carry the premium

--- STEM ---
Turnbridge Fitness Centre is a new private limited company in Country X, opened 4 months ago by owner Marcus Yuen. It offers a gym, pool and studio classes with capacity for 1,500 members and employs 22 full-time trainers and reception staff. Rival Capital Fitness charges $45 per month, has 900 members, and Turnbridge has spent $80,000 on launch advertising so far.

To attract members quickly, Marcus is considering penetration pricing: $25 per month for the first 3 months, after which membership rises to $42 per month. The centre has just 240 members against a year-end target of 600 and needs to build loyalty quickly. His business partner prefers launching at the standard $42 price to protect profit margins, while Marcus wants the low launch price to undercut Capital Fitness and fill the gym fast.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'penetration pricing'.
    Answer: Penetration pricing is a pricing method where a new product or business is launched at a low price to attract customers quickly and gain market share, with the price usually rising later once the product is established [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Launch price is set low to attract customers quickly; Aim is to gain market share, with price typically rising later

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of penetration pricing for Turnbridge Fitness Centre.
    Answer: Penetration pricing attracts customers quickly and builds market share [k], helping Turnbridge move from just 240 members towards its year-end target of 600 [app]. The low opening price of $25 per month also undercuts Capital Fitness's $45 price [k], giving price-sensitive customers a clear incentive to switch or join [app].
    Keywords: 240 members, 600, $25, Capital Fitness, $45, Turnbridge, penetration pricing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Attracts customers quickly / builds market share fast; Low price undercuts rivals and attracts price-sensitive customers | application_max_2: Turnbridge has only 240 members versus a year-end target of 600; $25 per month undercuts Capital Fitness at $45 per month

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of penetration pricing for Turnbridge Fitness Centre.

    Keywords: $25, $42, $80,000, 3 months, 240 members, Capital Fitness, $45
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Profit per customer is reduced by the low price; Customers may leave when the price later rises | application_max_2: $25 per month earns $17 less than the $42 standard price; $80,000 launch advertising spend and a 3-month offer period | analysis_max_2: Slower recovery of the $80,000 launch spend squeezes cash flow; Post-offer churn makes membership income and cash flow unpredictable

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Turnbridge Fitness Centre should launch at $25 per month using penetration pricing or open at the standard $42? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Launching at $25 per month would attract members quickly and undercut Capital Fitness's $45 price [k], helping Turnbridge close the gap from 240 members towards its target of 600 and fill the 1,500-capacity gym [app], building loyalty before the price rises to $42 after the 3-month offer [an]. However, an opening price of $42 would protect profit margins from day one [k], earning $17 more per member each month and repaying the $80,000 launch spend faster [app], preserving cash for running costs and new equipment [an]. Overall, the stronger position is penetration pricing at $25 for 3 months [eval], because the gym is only 4 months old and needs volume, habit and word of mouth to compete with Capital Fitness's 900 established members, and margins can be restored at $42 once loyalty is built [eval].
    Keywords: $25, $42, Capital Fitness, $45, 240 members, 600, 1,500, $80,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Penetration launch undercuts rivals and drives quick volume; Standard opening protects margins and cash from day one | application_max_2: 240 members versus target of 600; 1,500 capacity; $25 undercuts Capital Fitness's $45; $42 earns $17 more per member; helps repay the $80,000 launch spend | analysis_max_2: Penetration builds loyalty and word of mouth before price rises to $42; Standard opening preserves cash for running costs and equipment | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation based on the gym being only 4 months old and needing volume and habit; Recognises Capital Fitness's 900 established members and weighs $17 per-member margin against growth speed

--- STEM ---
Vertex Drone Works is a private limited company in Country X founded 3 years ago by engineer-entrepreneur Lena Okafor. It designs camera drones for professional surveyors and employs 18 hardware engineers and flight technicians. Last year Vertex sold 1,100 drones at $1,500 each, earning $1.65 million revenue, with research and development spending of $220,000.

The flagship Vertex Pro X1 uses a survey-grade camera and was developed at a cost of $180,000. The board is choosing between price skimming at $2,400 per unit for the first 12 months, aimed at surveying firms and early adopters, or penetration pricing at $1,500 per unit to undercut rivals immediately.     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: New product launched at a high price; High profits earned early / price lowered later as product establishes

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of price skimming for Vertex Drone Works.

It also helps recover the $180,000 development cost of the new model quickly [k], turning the 300 pre-orders at $2,400 into $720,000 of early revenue [app].
    Keywords: Vertex Pro X1, $2,400, $1,050, $180,000, $1,500, $220,000, $1.65 million, 300 units
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: High profit per unit / high margins from premium buyers; Recovers research and development costs quickly | application_max_2: $2,400 price versus $1,050 production cost gives a $1,350 margin; 300 pre-orders at $2,400 worth $720,000 towards the $180,000 development cost

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of price skimming for Vertex Drone Works.

Competitors may also copy the drone quickly [k], because a high price with strong early margins signals a profitable market [app], forcing Vertex to cut prices sooner and reducing the benefit of skimming [an].
    Keywords: $2,400, Vertex Pro X1, 300 units, $1,500, 1,100 drones, $1,050, pre-orders
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: High price limits the number of buyers / appeals only to early adopters; High profit signals attract competitor entry and copying | application_max_2: $2,400 price for the Vertex Pro X1 may deter surveying firms outside the 300 pre-orders; Strength of margins invites rivals to copy, ending the skimming window in the first 12 months | analysis_max_2: Slower adoption limits early revenue and delays cost recovery; Earlier-than-planned price cuts erode the expected skimming benefit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Vertex Drone Works should launch the Vertex Pro X1 at $2,400 using price skimming or at $1,500 using penetration pricing? Justify your answer.

However, penetration pricing at $1,500 would undercut rivals immediately [k], matching the company's volume drone already selling 1,100 units a year at $1,500 and protecting the $1.65 million revenue line [app], which reduces the risk of weak launch sales and speeds adoption [an]. Overall, the stronger choice is price skimming at $2,400 [eval], because Vertex's customers are professional surveyors who value survey-grade accuracy over price, and early adopters expect to pay a premium for a genuinely new flagship product [eval].
    Keywords: $2,400, $1,500, $180,000, 300 units, Vertex Pro X1, $1.65 million, $1,050
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Penetration undercuts rivals to win adoption quickly; Skimming earns premium margins from early adopters | application_max_2: 300 pre-orders at $2,400 worth $720,000 towards the $180,000 development cost; margin $1,350 per unit; 1,100 drones a year already sold at $1,500; penetration matches the $1.65 million revenue line | analysis_max_2: Skimming funds future research and holds premium positioning for 12 months; Penetration cuts launch risk and speeds adoption but sacrifices margin | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation referencing the professional surveyor customer base and early adopters; Weighs survey-grade differentiation and pre-order evidence against the appeal of a lower launch price

--- STEM ---
Ambertide Resort & Spa is a private limited company in Country X, a 120-room beach resort with a spa and three restaurants, established 11 years ago by the Verma family. It employs 85 staff across operations, food and beverage, and maintenance. Peak-season occupancy, from December to April, reaches 85% at $220 per room per night, while off-peak occupancy, from June to September, falls to 45%.

To lift off-peak trade, general manager Ravi Verma proposes promotional pricing: a three-night package at $150 per night with breakfast included and a free dinner worth $45 for each stay, aimed at families. He estimates the promotion could raise off-peak occupancy from 45% to 70%, costing about $12,000 in advertising. Director Meera Verma prefers keeping the standard $220 rate to protect the resort's premium image and profit per room.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'promotional pricing'.
    Answer: Promotional pricing is a pricing method where a business lowers its price for a limited time, or offers a special package or discount, to boost sales volume, often in a quiet period or to clear stock [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Price is lowered for a limited time / special offer made; Aim is to boost sales volume, often in quiet periods or to clear stock

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two aims of promotional pricing for Ambertide Resort & Spa.
    Answer: Promotional pricing aims to increase sales during quiet periods [k], helping Ambertide lift off-peak occupancy from 45% towards the proposed 70% with its $150 three-night package [app]. It also aims to attract new customer groups such as families [k], using the free dinner worth $45 to make the deal more appealing [app].
    Keywords: off-peak, 45%, 70%, $150, $45, three-night, Ambertide
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Increase sales / lift occupancy in a quiet period; Attract new customer groups to the business | application_max_2: Off-peak occupancy expected to rise from 45% to 70% with the three-night package; Free dinner worth $45 aimed at attracting families

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of promotional pricing for Ambertide Resort & Spa.
    Answer: Selling rooms at $150 instead of the standard $220 reduces the profit earned per room per night [k], and breakfast and the free dinner worth $45 add further cost [app], so each guest contributes far less, weakening off-peak profit even if occupancy rises [an]. Frequent promotions also train customers to expect lower prices [k], as families wait for the deal rather than book at $220 [app], damaging the resort's premium image and long-run profit per room [an].
    Keywords: $150, $220, $45, promotional pricing, 120-room, 45%, 70%, $12,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower price reduces profit per sale / margins are squeezed; Customers learn to expect discounts / brand image suffers | application_max_2: $150 package versus $220 standard rate; breakfast and a free dinner worth $45 add cost; Families may wait for the deal rather than book at $220 | analysis_max_2: Weaker off-peak profit per room even if occupancy rises to 70%; Brand image damage reduces long-run pricing power and profit per room

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ambertide Resort & Spa should run the promotional package ($150 per night with breakfast and a free dinner) or keep the standard $220 rate? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The promotional package would lift off-peak occupancy from 45% towards 70% [k], filling more of the 120 rooms in June to September, where occupancy is just 45% at the standard $220 rate [app], raising total room revenue and keeping staff busy through the quiet season [an]. However, keeping $220 protects the premium image and profit per room [k], avoiding over-reliance on discounts and the $12,000 advertising spend, and avoiding training families to expect deals [app], which protects long-term margin and brand strength [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to run the promotional package for the off-peak months only [eval], because 70% occupancy across 120 rooms (84 rooms) earns far more than 45% (54 rooms) at $220, even with the added $45 dinner cost [eval].
    Keywords: $150, $220, 45%, 70%, 120-room, $12,000, off-peak, $45
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Promotion fills rooms in quiet periods and attracts new customers; Keeping the standard rate protects premium image and margin | application_max_2: Off-peak occupancy 45% to 70%; 120 rooms (84 versus 54 rooms filled); $150 rate with breakfast; $220 standard rate; $12,000 advertising spend; free dinner worth $45 per stay | analysis_max_2: Higher occupancy raises total room revenue and covers staff through quiet months; Holding rate avoids deal-expectation and protects long-run margin and brand | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation weighting 84 rooms at $150 against 54 rooms at $220; Recognises the dinner cost ($45) and advertising ($12,000) but still favours the promotion

--- STEM ---
Crosswinds Airways is a private limited company in Country X operating short-haul flights to 14 destinations. Founded 7 years ago by the Sandoval family, it employs 260 staff including 90 pilots and cabin crew. Last year it carried 240,000 passengers at an average fare of $150, earning $36 million in revenue. Peak-weekend flights run at 82% occupancy, while off-peak midweek flights average 54%.

The board is considering replacing the flat $150 fare with dynamic pricing: fares could rise to $260 on busy flights 48 hours before departure and fall to as low as $89 on empty midweek flights, with demand-adjustment software costing $35,000 per year. Director Elena Sandoval worries that passengers dislike unpredictable fares and may switch to FaresAir, which charges a flat $140. Chairman Marco Sandoval argues dynamic pricing will fill off-peak seats and lift average fares.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'dynamic pricing'.
    Answer: Dynamic pricing is a pricing method where prices are changed continuously in response to demand, supply and other market conditions, so the price differs between times, situations or customers [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Prices are changed continuously in response to conditions; Price differs between times, situations or customers

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of dynamic pricing for Crosswinds Airways.
    Answer: Dynamic pricing maximises revenue from passengers willing to pay more [k], lifting fares to as much as $260 on busy flights 48 hours before departure [app]. It also fills empty seats by lowering prices [k], with off-peak midweek fares falling to as low as $89 to attract price-sensitive passengers when occupancy averages 54% [app].
    Keywords: $260, 48 hours, $89, 54%, dynamic pricing, 240,000, $150
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Maximises revenue from passengers willing to pay more; Lowers price to fill empty seats / increase off-peak occupancy | application_max_2: Fares could rise to $260 on busy flights 48 hours before departure; Off-peak fares could fall to as low as $89 with occupancy at 54%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of dynamic pricing for Crosswinds Airways.
    Answer: Passengers may resent unpredictable fares [k], feeling overcharged close to departure when the fare may reach $260 instead of $150 [app], damaging loyalty and pushing flyers to FaresAir [an]. Dynamic pricing also requires investment and ongoing cost [k], such as the $35,000 per year demand-adjustment software [app], adding fixed cost that must be recouped across the 14 routes served [an].
    Keywords: $260, $150, $35,000, FaresAir, 14 destinations, 82%, 54%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Passengers resent unpredictable or seemingly unfair fares; Requires investment in systems / ongoing software costs | application_max_2: Fares may jump from $150 to $260 near departure; $35,000 per year demand-adjustment software across 14 destinations | analysis_max_2: Loyalty damage pushes passengers to FaresAir's $140 flat fare; Software cost must be recouped, squeezing margins on weaker routes

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Crosswinds Airways should introduce dynamic pricing or keep the flat $150 fare? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Dynamic pricing would raise revenue where demand is highest [k], lifting fares to $260 on busy peak flights and to as low as $89 on empty midweek flights [app], so total fare revenue should rise above the current $36 million while 82% peak occupancy is monetised effectively [an]. However, the flat $150 fare is predictable and trusted [k], avoiding customer frustration and the risk that price-sensitive passengers switch to FaresAir, whose flat $140 is $10 cheaper [app], protecting Crosswinds' reputation on the 14 routes it serves [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to introduce dynamic pricing [eval], because peak flights at 82% occupancy are already selling out and fares should reflect that scarcity, while $89 off-peak fares will win new passengers that a flat $150 fare drives away [eval].
    Keywords: $260, $89, $150, $36 million, 82%, 54%, FaresAir, 14 destinations
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Dynamic pricing monetises high-demand seats and fills empty ones; Flat fare is predictable and trusted by regular passengers | application_max_2: Peak fares to $260, off-peak to $89; revenue could exceed $36 million; 82% peak occupancy; FaresAir flat $140 is $10 cheaper; flat $150 predictable across 14 destinations | analysis_max_2: Higher peak fares monetise scarcity of seats at 82% occupancy; Flat fare protects reputation and avoids losing passengers to FaresAir | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation that selling-out peak flights should charge more; Weighs FaresAir switching risk and the flat $150's predictability against revenue gain

--- STEM ---
Copperhill Pharmacy is a private limited company in Country X, run by owners Ade and Ruth Boateng for 5 years. It has 2 branches and employs 11 pharmacists and assistants, generating $1.1 million in annual revenue, of which $600,000 comes from prescription medicines. A large supermarket pharmacy chain operates 500 metres from the main branch.

Demand for prescription pain relief is price-inelastic: customers must fill prescriptions and few leave over small rises. Demand for vitamins, shampoos and cold remedies is price-elastic: many substitutes exist and a small rise can cut sales sharply. Ruth wants to raise the price of a common prescription medicine from $12.50 to $13.50, an 8% rise. Ade prefers holding prescription prices and instead discounting vitamins by 10% from $9.00 to $8.10 to win price-sensitive shoppers from the supermarket rival.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'price-elastic demand'.
    Answer: Price-elastic demand is when demand for a product is sensitive to price changes: a small rise in price leads to a relatively large fall in quantity demanded, and a small fall leads to a relatively large rise in demand [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Demand is sensitive to price changes; Small price rise causes a larger fall in quantity demanded (and vice versa)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why demand for prescription medicines at Copperhill Pharmacy is price-inelastic.
    Answer: Prescription medicines are necessities for patients [k], so customers must fill their prescriptions even if Copperhill raises a common pain relief from $12.50 to $13.50 [app]. There are few close substitutes for many prescribed drugs [k], so the 2 branches lose very few of the $600,000 in prescription sales when prices rise slightly [app].
    Keywords: prescription, $12.50, $13.50, $600,000, 2 branches, price-inelastic, 8%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Prescription medicines are necessities; Few close substitutes for prescribed drugs | application_max_2: $12.50 to $13.50 rise (8%) on a common pain relief; Little risk to the $600,000 of prescription revenue across the 2 branches

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two factors that make demand for the vitamins sold by Copperhill Pharmacy price-elastic.
    Answer: Vitamins have many close substitutes available [k], since supermarkets and the large chain 500 metres away also sell competing brands [app], so a small price rise can send Copperhill's vitamin customers elsewhere [an]. Vitamins are also non-essential purchases that customers cut back on easily [k], so a 10% discount from $9.00 to $8.10 would likely draw in price-sensitive shoppers [app], increasing vitamin sales volume and footfall into the 2 branches [an].
    Keywords: vitamins, 500 metres, 10%, $9.00, $8.10, prescription, $1.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Many close substitutes exist for vitamins; Vitamins are non-essential / customers can postpone or switch purchases | application_max_2: Supermarket and the large chain 500 metres from the main branch sell competing brands; Proposed 10% discount from $9.00 to $8.10 to win price-sensitive shoppers | analysis_max_2: Small price change shifts demand to rivals, so volume falls sharply; Discounting pulls in shoppers, lifting vitamin sales and store footfall

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Copperhill Pharmacy should raise the price of the common prescription medicine to $13.50, or hold prescription prices and discount vitamins to $8.10? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising the prescription price to $13.50 (an 8% rise) would raise revenue without losing many customers [k], because essential prescription demand is price-inelastic and few patients will change pharmacy over a $1.00 rise [app], lifting the $600,000 prescription line across the 2 branches [an]. However, holding prescription prices and cutting vitamins by 10% to $8.10 would attract price-sensitive shoppers from the competing chain 500 metres away [k], competing on a range where demand is price-elastic [app], lifting footfall and the chance that customers buy higher-margin over-the-counter goods as well [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to hold prescription prices and discount the vitamins [eval], because an 8% rise on an inelastic essential risks customer trust and community goodwill, while winning elastic, everyday shoppers defends Copperhill's total $1.1 million revenue across both branches [eval].
    Keywords: $13.50, $12.50, $8.10, $9.00, 500 metres, $600,000, $1.1 million, 8%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Inelastic essentials can bear a price rise without losing many customers; Elastic goods respond to discounts, attracting price-sensitive shoppers | application_max_2: $12.50 to $13.50, an 8% rise; $600,000 prescription revenue across 2 branches; Vitamins cut 10% from $9.00 to $8.10; supermarket chain 500 metres away | analysis_max_2: Price rise lifts the protected prescription revenue with minimal volume loss; Discounting lifts footfall and cross-selling of higher-margin goods | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation weighting trust on an inelastic essential against elastic everyday shoppers; Weighs $1.1 million total revenue across both branches, not just the prescription line

--- STEM ---
Sable & Sparrow Fashion is a private limited company in Country Z specialising in winter coats, founded 6 years ago by owner Freya Lindqvist. It has 2 stores and employs 12 sales assistants, generating $980,000 in annual revenue. Each winter coat costs $60 to buy and sells at $90, a 50% markup. As spring approaches, 600 coats remain unsold, and storage costs $2 per coat per month, $1,200 in total.

Freya is considering promotional pricing: a 25% end-of-season discount, falling to $67.50, which still covers the $60 cost with $7.50 profit per coat. Her partner favours holding the standard $90 price to protect the brand's premium image, though up to 40% of the 600 coats may remain unsold by next winter. The two must decide before the spring collection arrives.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two reasons why a retailer might discount stock at the end of a season.
    Answer: Two reasons are: to convert unsold seasonal stock into cash quickly, and to free up storage and display space before the next season's stock arrives [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Convert unsold stock into cash quickly; Free up storage or display space for the new season

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Sable & Sparrow Fashion might use promotional pricing on its coats.
    Answer: Promotional pricing converts unsold stock into cash quickly [k], allowing Sable & Sparrow to turn the 600 unsold coats into revenue instead of paying storage costs of $1,200 per month [app]. It also attracts bargain-seeking customers into the stores [k], and a 25% discount to $67.50, which is still above the $60 cost, can encourage sales without pricing below cost [app].
    Keywords: 600 coats, $1,200, 25%, $67.50, $60, Sable & Sparrow, $90
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Converts unsold stock into cash quickly; Attracts bargain-seeking customers / boosts footfall and sales | application_max_2: 600 coats remain unsold; storage costs $2 per coat per month ($1,200 total); 25% discount to $67.50 still covers the $60 cost, retaining $7.50 profit per coat

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks for Sable & Sparrow Fashion of using promotional pricing on the coats.
    Answer: A 25% discount to $67.50 leaves only $7.50 profit per coat [k], far below the $30 profit earned at the standard $90 price [app], so deep discounts would erode margins despite clearing the 600 coats [an]. Customers may also learn to expect discounts and wait for sales [k], which could leave up to 40% of the 600 coats unsold by next winter [app], weakening the effectiveness of the promotion and damaging the brand's premium image [an].
    Keywords: $67.50, $90, $7.50, $60, 40%, 600 coats, 25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Margins are eroded by the discounted price; Customers expect discounts / wait for sales instead of buying at full price | application_max_2: $67.50 leaves $7.50 profit per coat versus $30 at $90; Up to 40% of the 600 coats may remain unsold by next winter | analysis_max_2: Lower per-unit profit weakens total contribution from the clearance; Deal-expectation harms full-price sales and the premium brand image

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sable & Sparrow Fashion should sell the remaining coats at a 25% promotional discount ($67.50) or hold the standard $90 price? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The 25% promotional discount to $67.50 clears the 600 unsold coats [k], avoiding storage costs of $1,200 per month and the risk that 40% of the coats become unsaleable by next winter [app], converting dead stock into $40,500 of cash (600 × $67.50) while still earning $7.50 per coat [an]. However, holding $90 keeps the full $30 margin per coat and protects the premium image [k], but with the spring collection arriving, unsold coats still cost $1,200 a month to store and may require an even deeper cut later [app], weakening margins further [an]. Overall, the stronger position is the 25% promotional clearance [eval], because $67.50 still covers the $60 cost and the opportunity cost of holding $90 through spring outweighs the extra $22.50 margin per coat [eval].
    Keywords: $67.50, $90, $60, 600 coats, $1,200, 40%, 25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Clearance converts unsold stock into cash and avoids storage cost; Holding price preserves per-unit margin and premium image | application_max_2: 600 coats at $67.50 = $40,500; $7.50 profit per coat after $60 cost; Holding $90 keeps $30 margin; storage $1,200 per month; up to 40% unsaleable | analysis_max_2: Clearance frees cash and avoids deeper future cuts; Holding protects image but storage and later markdown risk erode returns | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation weighting cash freed now against margin per coat; Weighs $22.50 extra margin at $90 against storage cost and unsaleable risk (40%)

--- STEM ---
Pinnacle Audio Labs is a private limited company in Country Y founded 2 years ago by founder Theo Mensah, designing wireless headphones for commuters. It employs 9 product designers and engineers and has spent $120,000 developing its noise-cancelling Aria headphones. Production costs are $140 per unit and 1,500 pre-orders have been received at the proposed $399 launch price.

A rival, SoundWave, sells a similar headphone at $249, undercutting Pinnacle's plan by $150. The board must choose between price skimming at $399, capturing early adopters before competitors respond, or a competitive $249 to match SoundWave and win share from day one. At $399 the margin is $259 per unit; at $249 the margin is $109. Sales director Ivy Brooks prefers $249, while Theo believes the headphones' battery life justifies the premium.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two reasons why a business might launch a new product at a high price.
    Answer: Two reasons are: to recover research and development costs quickly, and to earn high profits from early adopters who are willing to pay a premium for a new product [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recover development costs quickly; Earn high profits from early adopters / premium buyers

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Pinnacle Audio Labs of price skimming its Aria headphones at $399.
    Answer: Price skimming at $399 maximises the early profit per unit [k], earning a $259 margin over the $140 production cost, far above the $109 margin at $249 [app]. It also recovers the $120,000 development spend quickly [k], because 1,500 pre-orders at $399 would generate $598,500 [app].
    Keywords: $399, $140, $109, $120,000, 1,500, $249, pre-orders
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Maximises early profit per unit / high margins; Recovers development costs quickly | application_max_2: $399 price versus $140 production cost gives a $259 margin (vs $109 at $249); 1,500 pre-orders at $399 worth $598,500 against $120,000 development spend

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Pinnacle Audio Labs of launching at $399 instead of matching SoundWave at $249.
    Answer: A price $150 above the rival may deter the price-sensitive majority [k], so Pinnacle could fall short of 1,500 pre-orders as commuters choose SoundWave's similar headphones at $249 [app], depressing launch volume and the revenue needed to cover the $120,000 development cost [an]. A premium launch price also risks an early price cut if demand disappoints [k], prompting a move towards $249 soon after launch [app], which can damage Pinnacle's credibility with early adopters and retailers [an].
    Keywords: $399, $249, $150, 1,500, SoundWave, $120,000, $140
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Price far above rivals deters the price-sensitive majority; Weak demand may force an early price cut | application_max_2: $399 is $150 above SoundWave at $249, risking the 1,500 pre-orders; If demand disappoints, Pinnacle must cut towards $249 soon after launch | analysis_max_2: Lower launch volume slows recovery of the $120,000 development cost; An early price cut damages credibility with early adopters and retailers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Pinnacle Audio Labs should launch the Aria headphones at $399 using price skimming or at $249 matching SoundWave? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Price skimming at $399 would yield a $259 margin per unit [k], and with 1,500 pre-orders at $399 Aria could generate $598,500, repaying the $120,000 development spend rapidly [app], funding future models and rewarding Pinnacle's 9 designers for a genuinely differentiated flagship [an]. However, matching SoundWave at $249 would maximise launch volume [k], trading the $109 margin for far wider adoption among commuters and cutting the $150 price gap to rivals [app], which could convert the everyday market and build the Aria brand quickly [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to launch at $399 with price skimming [eval], because Aria's battery life and noise-cancelling quality give early adopters a real reason to pay a premium, and high initial margins protect a small 9-person company from a price war with SoundWave [eval].
    Keywords: $399, $249, $150, 1,500, $120,000, SoundWave, $140, 9 product designers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Skimming maximises early margin and funds recovery of development cost; Matching the rival maximises adoption and market share from day one | application_max_2: $399 gives $259 margin; 1,500 pre-orders worth $598,500 versus $120,000 development spend; $249 gives $109 margin; cuts the $150 gap to SoundWave and wins broader commuter volume | analysis_max_2: Skimming funds future models and rewards the differentiation investment; Matching builds share and brand quickly but sacrifices per-unit margin | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation based on product differentiation and early adopter willingness to pay; Weighs vulnerability of a small 9-person company to a SoundWave price war against share ambitions

Quayside Ferry Co is a private limited company in Country Z, running commuter ferries across the Kessler Strait since 2018.     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Raises fares when demand is highest / maximises peak revenue; Lower prices encourage off-peak travel / spread demand | application_max_2: Peak fares $15 and off-peak $9, versus 88% peak occupancy; Off-peak services run at just 38% occupancy

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of dynamic pricing for Quayside Ferry Co.

Dynamic pricing also requires investment and ongoing cost [k], such as the $40,000 per year software licence [app], which must be paid even if off-peak demand stays at 38% occupancy [an].
    Keywords: $15, $12, $40,000, 500,000, 38%, 88%, flat $12
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Customers resent unpredictable fare changes; Requires investment in systems / ongoing software cost | application_max_2: Peak fare $15 is $3 above the flat $12 fare; rival speedboat charges $13; $40,000 per year software; off-peak occupancy stuck at 38% | analysis_max_2: Loyalty damage among 500,000 annual passengers pushes them to the rival speedboat; Software cost must be recouped; weak off-peak demand may not cover it

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Quayside Ferry Co should introduce dynamic pricing ($15 peak, $9 off-peak) or keep the flat $12 fare? Justify your answer.

Overall, the stronger position is dynamic pricing [eval], because peak occupancy is 88% and fares should reflect that scarcity, while $9 off-peak fares will win price-sensitive passengers without abandoning peak revenue [eval].
    Keywords: $15, $9, $12, $6.0 million, $6.3 million, $40,000, 88%, 38%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Dynamic pricing monetises high-demand peak seats; Flat fare is predictable and protects loyalty | application_max_2: Revenue rises from $6.0 million to $6.3 million: 300,000 peak at $15 + 200,000 off-peak at $9; $40,000 software cost; 25% fuel increase; rival speedboat at $13 versus flat $12 | analysis_max_2: Extra $300,000 covers software cost and fuel increase; Flat fare protects reputation and passenger base against the $13 rival | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation based on 88% peak occupancy signalling scarcity; Weighs rival switching risk and commuter preference for predictability against revenue gain

--- STEM ---
Wickmere Fruit Juices is a private limited company in Country X, owned by Carla Jimenez for 5 years. It presses apple and berry juices and sells 32,000 bottles a month to supermarkets at $2.40 each, generating $920,000 in annual revenue. The company holds a 4% share of the regional juice market, well behind market leader Purevale on 21%, and sales grew by 9% last year.

Carla must set the aims of next year's promotion with a budget of $35,000. Her marketing manager has proposed either an informative campaign explaining the new low-sugar recipe to existing customers, costed at $16,000, or a persuasive campaign using lifestyle posters and television advertising aimed at rival brand switchers, costed at $27,000. The campaign must also improve customer loyalty and support the launch of a new 750ml family-size bottle planned for the spring.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'promotion'.
    Answer: Promotion is communicating with customers to inform, persuade or remind them about a product in order to encourage sales [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: communicating with customers/informing or persuading them; to encourage sales or remind them of the product

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two aims Wickmere Fruit Juices could have for its promotion.
    Answer: Aim 1: To inform existing customers about the new low-sugar recipe [k], giving clear details of what has changed in the juices they already buy [app]. Aim 2: To persuade rival brand switchers to buy Wickmere juices instead [k], helping the company grow from its 4% market share against Purevale's 21% [app].
    Keywords: low-sugar recipe, 32,000 bottles, 4%, 21%, Purevale, supermarkets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: to inform customers/explain the product or its changes; to persuade customers to buy or switch brands | application_max_2: low-sugar recipe; existing customers; 4% market share; Purevale's 21%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Wickmere Fruit Juices of setting clear aims for its promotion.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Clear aims allow Carla to choose between the informative and persuasive proposals [k], so the $35,000 budget goes to the option that fits the business best [app], reducing wasted spending on the wrong method [an]. Benefit 2: Clear aims provide measurable targets, such as continued growth in bottles sold [k], letting Carla check whether sales stay ahead of the recent 9% rise [app], which helps judge whether the campaign succeeded [an].
    Keywords: $35,000, 750ml, family-size bottle, low-sugar recipe, 9%, loyalty
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: aims focus budget on a suitable promotional method; aims provide measurable targets to evaluate success | application_max_2: informative and persuasive proposals; $35,000 budget; recent 9% rise; 32,000 bottles | analysis_max_2: reduces wasted expenditure on an unsuitable method; enables the business to judge campaign success afterwards

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wickmere Fruit Juices should choose the informative campaign or the persuasive campaign? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The informative campaign explains the new low-sugar recipe to existing customers [k], targeting the buyers of the 32,000 bottles sold each month [app], which should protect repeat sales and the recent 9% growth [an]. However, the persuasive campaign uses lifestyle posters and television advertising to reach rival brand switchers [k], going beyond Wickmere's 4% share against Purevale's 21% [app], which could accelerate growth of the family-size bottle if it succeeds [an]. Overall, the informative campaign is the safer choice because Carla's first priority should be keeping existing customers as the recipe changes [eval], and with a budget of $35,000 the cheaper $16,000 option leaves headroom to support the 750ml family-size bottle launch [eval].
    Keywords: $16,000, $27,000, 4%, Purevale, 32,000 bottles, 750ml, low-sugar recipe, $35,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: informative campaign: informs existing customers, lower risk; persuasive campaign: wider reach, can attract new customers | application_max_2: $16,000 informative campaign; persuasive campaign at $27,000; 4% share against Purevale's 21%; 750ml family-size bottle launch | analysis_max_2: protects repeat sales and recent 9% growth; could accelerate family-size bottle success via switchers | evaluation_max_2: weighs lower-risk retention against higher-risk persuasion; justified choice given the $35,000 budget constraint

One uses informative advertisements in technology magazines explaining the 90km battery range, the 2-year warranty and the crash-tested frame. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'informative advertising'.
    Answer: Advertising that provides factual information about a product, such as its features or price, to help customers make an informed decision [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: advertising that gives factual information; helps customers make informed decisions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two differences between informative and persuasive advertising.
    Answer: Difference 1: Informative advertising gives factual information about a product [k], such as the 90km battery range, the 2-year warranty and the crash-tested frame [app]. Difference 2: Persuasive advertising aims to convince customers by appealing to emotions and desires [k], using television and billboards showing freedom and prestige [app].
    Keywords: 90km battery range, 2-year warranty, crash-tested frame, freedom and prestige, television and billboards, technology magazines
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: informative advertising gives factual information; persuasive advertising appeals to emotions to convince | application_max_2: 90km battery range; 2-year warranty; crash-tested frame; television and billboards

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Aldermont Cycles of using persuasive advertising for the new commuter e-bike.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Persuasive advertisements can build a desirable brand image [k], presenting the commuter e-bike as a symbol of freedom and prestige [app], which differentiates it from ordinary bicycles and encourages buyers to pay $1,850 [an]. Advantage 2: Television and billboard advertising reaches a mass audience [k], creating awareness of the new commuter e-bike beyond the single showroom [app], which should increase enquiries and showroom footfall before winter [an].
    Keywords: commuter e-bike, freedom and prestige, television and billboards, single showroom, $1,850
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: builds brand image/desire for the product; reaches large audiences quickly | application_max_2: freedom and prestige; television and billboards; $1,850; single showroom | analysis_max_2: differentiates the product and supports premium pricing; raises enquiries and footfall ahead of launch

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Aldermont Cycles should use informative advertising or persuasive advertising for the new e-bike launch? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The informative campaign suits a high-price product like the $1,850 e-bike, because readers of technology magazines want hard facts such as the 90km range and 2-year warranty [k], giving technically minded buyers the confidence to visit the single showroom and test-ride [app], which lowers the risk of wasted visits [an]. However, the persuasive campaign on television and billboards reaches a much wider audience [k], embedding the e-bike as a symbol of freedom and prestige [app], which could pull in aspirational buyers who would never read technology magazines [an]. Overall, Aldermont should choose informative advertising because the $32,000 must justify a considered, high-involvement purchase rather than impulse desire [eval], and prestige imagery alone rarely convinces someone spending $1,850 without technical proof [eval].
    Keywords: $1,850, 90km, 2-year warranty, technology magazines, single showroom, $32,000, freedom and prestige
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: informative ads: supports high-involvement decisions; persuasive ads: wider emotional reach/aspiration | application_max_2: $1,850 e-bike; 90km range and 2-year warranty; technology magazines; single showroom | analysis_max_2: reduces risk of unsuitable buyers visiting showroom; broadens reach beyond technical readers | evaluation_max_2: weighs considered purchase against mass emotional reach; justified preference for technical proof at this price point
