--- STEM ---
Bramfield Supermarket is a private limited company in Country X with 6 branches and 480 staff. It generated $14.6 million in revenue last year, and breakfast cereals account for 11% of all sales. Annual marketing expenditure is $210,000, of which $60,000 has been allocated to cereal promotions over the next quarter. Rival discounters have been cutting staple prices aggressively across the region, winning back families on tight budgets.

The marketing manager wants to increase cereal sales by 20% in the next quarter. Two options are available: a buy-one-get-one-free (BOGOF) offer across 14 cereal brands, or a straight 15% price reduction on the same 14 brands. Suppliers have agreed to fund half of the cost of whichever promotion is chosen this quarter.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'sales promotion'.
    Answer: Short-term incentives used to encourage customers to buy a product or to boost sales of it, such as discounts or special offers [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: short-term incentives to buy; used to boost sales of a product

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Bramfield Supermarket of using a BOGOF offer on cereal.
    Answer: Advantage 1: BOGOF can rapidly increase sales volume [k], helping the supermarket reach its target of a 20% rise in cereal sales across the 6 branches [app]. Advantage 2: BOGOF attracts customers into the supermarket [k], where they may buy other products alongside the 14 cereal brands [app].
    Keywords: BOGOF, 14 cereal brands, 20%, 6 branches, $60,000, breakfast cereals, 11%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rapidly increases sales volume; attracts customers into the store (footfall) | application_max_2: 20% rise in cereal sales; 6 branches; 14 cereal brands; breakfast cereals

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Bramfield Supermarket of the suppliers funding half the promotion.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Funding halves the supermarket's net cost of the promotion [k], so the $60,000 allocation stretches further whichever option is chosen [app], keeping money available within the wider $210,000 marketing budget [an]. Benefit 2: Suppliers fund the activity because higher sales also benefit their own brands [k], so they share the risk on the 14 cereal brands [app], which strengthens the long-term trading relationship [an].
    Keywords: $60,000, $210,000, Suppliers have agreed to fund half, 14 brands, half of the cost
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduces supermarket's net promotional cost; shared risk with suppliers seeking higher sales | application_max_2: $60,000 allocation; $210,000 marketing expenditure; 14 cereal brands; fund half of the cost | analysis_max_2: keeps budget available for other marketing; strengthens supplier relationships and cooperation

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Bramfield Supermarket should use the BOGOF offer or the 15% price reduction on its cereal brands? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The BOGOF offer creates a strong short-term incentive, because shoppers pay full price for one box and receive a second box free [k], which could push cereal sales up sharply towards the 20% target across all 14 brands [app], clearing stock quickly and drawing in price-conscious families [an]. However, the 15% price reduction is simpler for staff and customers to understand [k], lowering the shelf price of every box without giving away extra units [app], protecting margins if BOGOF would halve the value of each sale at higher volume [an]. Overall, Bramfield should choose BOGOF because the suppliers fund half the cost either way, making the free extra units affordable [eval], and a dramatic offer is more likely to achieve a 20% quarterly uplift than a modest 15% discount during rival price cuts [eval].
    Keywords: BOGOF, 15% price reduction, 14 brands, $60,000, 20%, 6 branches
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: BOGOF: strong instant incentive, drives volume; price reduction: simple, protects unit margins/understanding | application_max_2: 20% target across 14 brands; suppliers funding half of either option; $60,000 allocation; rival discounters cutting prices | analysis_max_2: clears stock quickly, attracts price-sensitive shoppers; simpler administration and preserves margins per unit | evaluation_max_2: weighs dramatic volume-driving offer against simpler discount; justified choice given shared funding and rival price pressure

--- STEM ---
Thistlebrook Snacks is a private limited company in Country X, owned by Devon Okafor for 3 years. It produces baked lentil and chickpea snacks sold at $1.60 per 150g bag through 900 convenience stores, generating $780,000 in annual revenue. A new chilli-lime flavour is due to launch in May, and its target market is health-conscious commuters who eat on the way to work.

To promote the new flavour, the sales manager is choosing between two options. The first is distributing 10,000 free 50g sample bags at railway stations and gyms, costing $14,000. The second is running a competition where shoppers enter the code inside packs to win a $5,000 holiday voucher, costing $17,000 in prizes and administration over three months.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'free samples'.
    Answer: Free trial-size giveaways of a product offered to customers so they can taste or test it before buying [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: free trial-size giveaways/samples of a product; allow customers to test before buying

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Thistlebrook Snacks of distributing 10,000 free sample bags.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Free samples let potential customers try the new chilli-lime flavour before buying [k], encouraging first-time trial among health-conscious commuters [app]. Advantage 2: Samples handed out at railway stations and gyms reach the target market directly [k], where 900 convenience stores can turn fresh awareness into repeat purchases [app].
    Keywords: chilli-lime flavour, 10,000 free 50g sample bags, $14,000, railway stations and gyms, 900 convenience stores, health-conscious commuters
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lets customers try before buying (trial); targeted distribution reaches the intended market | application_max_2: chilli-lime flavour; health-conscious commuters; railway stations and gyms; 900 convenience stores

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Thistlebrook Snacks could face when running the competition.
    Answer: Problem 1: The competition costs $17,000, more than the $14,000 needed for samples [k], and the code inside packs means only people who already buy the snacks can enter [app], so it may not attract new customers at all [an]. Problem 2: Competition entries depend entirely on customer participation [k], and a hidden or unclear code could mean very few entries [app], wasting the $5,000 prize money and three months of administration [an].
    Keywords: $17,000, $5,000, code inside packs, three months, chilli-lime flavour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher cost than alternatives/aims at existing buyers only; success depends on customer participation and clarity of entry method | application_max_2: $17,000 total cost; code inside packs; $5,000 holiday voucher; three months of administration | analysis_max_2: may fail to attract new customers; wasted prize spend and effort if participation is low

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Thistlebrook Snacks should use free samples or the in-pack competition to promote the new chilli-lime flavour? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Free samples cost $14,000 and put the new chilli-lime flavour directly into the hands of health-conscious commuters at railway stations and gyms [k], generating word-of-mouth and immediate trial at the 900 convenience stores [app], which should drive first-time purchases and launch momentum [an]. However, the competition costs $17,000 yet reaches only buyers who already pick up a 150g bag [k], making it a tool for loyalty and repeat purchase rather than new trial [app], so it suits retention more than launch awareness [an]. Overall, Thistlebrook should choose free samples because the central challenge is getting the new flavour tried, not retaining existing buyers [eval], and the lower cost frees $3,000 to support distribution across the 900 stores [eval].
    Keywords: $14,000, $17,000, 900 convenience stores, health-conscious commuters, railway stations and gyms, chilli-lime flavour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: samples: drive trial among new customers; competition: rewards existing buyers, builds repeat purchases | application_max_2: $14,000 samples cost; $17,000 competition cost; 900 convenience stores; health-conscious commuters | analysis_max_2: stimulates first-time purchase and launch awareness; better suited to retention than trial | evaluation_max_2: weighs launch trial against loyalty repeat purchase; justified choice given target of launching a new flavour

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Elmwick Teas of using point-of-sale displays in delis.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Displays make the Elmwick brand more visible at the moment of purchase [k], helping more than 3 in 10 shoppers notice Elmwick on deli shelves [app]. Advantage 2: Displays for all 240 delis cost $18,000 [k], which fits within the $22,000 promotion budget [app].
    Keywords: 240 delis, 3 in 10, $18,000, $22,000, point-of-sale displays
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increases brand visibility at the point of purchase; affordable/high reach per unit of spend | application_max_2: 3 in 10 shoppers; 240 delis; $18,000; $22,000 promotion budget

  Qc [6 marks]

Benefit 2: A branded infuser keeps the Elmwick name visible in customers' homes [k], reinforcing loyalty every time tea is brewed [app], which should defend the $1.3 million annual revenue [an].
    Keywords: $6.80, tea infuser, $1.3 million, 2 tins, 240 delis
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: gift increases units purchased per visit; gift keeps brand visible at home, builds loyalty | application_max_2: $6.80 tins; every 2 tins purchased; tea infuser; $1.3 million annual revenue | analysis_max_2: raises average transaction value; protects revenue through repeat loyalty

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Elmwick Teas should choose the free branded tea infuser gift or the point-of-sale displays? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The point-of-sale displays attack the core problem identified by research: only 3 in 10 shoppers notice Elmwick on deli shelves [k], and better visibility across 240 stores should convert passing shoppers into buyers at $6.80 per tin [app], directly lifting sales volume and against the below-target repeat rate [an]. However, the free tea infuser gift with every 2 tins turns loyal shoppers into visible brand ambassadors at home [k], rewarding repeat purchase and keeping Elmwick in the kitchen cupboard [app], which deepens relationships that shelf signage cannot [an]. Overall, Elmwick should choose point-of-sale displays because awareness is the bottleneck the research exposes [eval], and at $18,000 it fits the $22,000 budget while leaving $4,000 for deli cooperation and restocking support [eval].
    Keywords: 3 in 10, $18,000, $22,000, tea infuser, 240 delis, $6.80
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: displays: increase visibility at moment of purchase; gift: rewards loyalty, increases purchase frequency | application_max_2: only 3 in 10 shoppers notice the brand; 240 delis; $6.80 per tin; $18,000 display cost | analysis_max_2: converts shoppers into buyers at shelf; builds deeper home-based brand loyalty | evaluation_max_2: weighs shelf visibility against in-home loyalty; justified choice given research bottleneck and budget fit

    Question: Define 'viral marketing'.

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Harbour & Lark Streetwear of using social media to promote its products.

    Keywords: $9,000, 13 to 24, 85% of sales, 38,000 followers, graphic hoodies

    Question: Explain two problems Harbour & Lark Streetwear could face from the viral stunt.

    Keywords: $2,500, 500 artist-designed hoodies, 2 micro-influencers, 38,000 followers, viral stunt
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: unpredictable/uncontrollable whether content goes viral; negative publicity risk spreads fast online | application_max_2: 500 artist-designed hoodies; $2,500; 2 micro-influencers; 38,000 followers | analysis_max_2: wasted spend if the video never trends; reputation damage weakens existing customer trust

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harbour & Lark Streetwear should choose the $9,000 paid social media campaign or the $2,500 viral stunt? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The paid campaign spends $9,000 on 3 months of targeted advertisements aimed at 13 to 24 year olds [k], delivering predictable, measurable reach into the website and social pages behind 85% of revenue [app], making sales impact easier to forecast and optimise [an]. However, the viral stunt costs only $2,500 and could reach far more people if the drop video is shared widely [k], creating buzz around the limited 500-unit run that no fixed advertising budget could buy [app], punching far above its weight for a bootstrapped brand with no marketing staff [an]. Overall, Zoe should choose the paid campaign because reliable, targeted reach matters more than lottery-odds virality [eval], and her limited budget cannot comfortably absorb $2,500 on a stunt that may never trend [eval].
    Keywords: $9,000, $2,500, 13 to 24, 85% of sales, $45, 500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: paid social ads: predictable, measurable targeting; viral stunt: potentially huge reach, low certainty | application_max_2: $9,000 for 3 months; 13 to 24 year olds; 85% of revenue; $2,500 viral stunt | analysis_max_2: forecastable, optimisable return on ad spend; cheap high-impact buzz if video is shared widely | evaluation_max_2: weighs reliable targeting against low-odds high-reward virality; justified choice given limited budget and no marketing staff

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Embergate Cinema of offering a 25% price reduction on Monday to Thursday tickets.

Advantage 2: Lower prices can fill the half-empty weekday screenings [k], using spare capacity across the 4 screens to grow ticket sales [app].
    Keywords: 25% price reduction, $8.25, Monday to Thursday, 4-screen, half-empty
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower price attracts price-sensitive customers; fills spare capacity and lifts sales volume | application_max_2: $8.25; Monday to Thursday; half-empty; 4 screens

  Qc [6 marks]

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: free gift adds perceived value without cutting price; competition creates excitement and repeat visits | application_max_2: $11; Monday to Thursday; $260,000; season pass | analysis_max_2: lifts food and drink income; converts one-off visits into repeat loyalty

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Embergate Cinema should use the 25% price reduction or the free popcorn and competition promotion for January? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The 25% price reduction to $8.25 directly attacks the 28% Monday to Thursday attendance fall [k], using a simple, visible discount that price-sensitive customers instantly understand [app], which should fill the 4 half-empty screens and protect contribution above variable costs [an]. However, the popcorn-and-competition offer costs only $9,000 and keeps the $11 price intact [k], preserving the $1.045 million ticket revenue base and protecting the $260,000 food and drink spend [app], while the season pass competition builds repeat visits and loyalty [an]. Overall, Embergate should choose the free popcorn and competition because it protects margins better than a 25% price cut would [eval], and it builds lasting weekday habits rather than training customers to wait for discounts [eval].

--- STEM ---
Verdano Botanicals is a private limited company in Country X producing natural skincare, including the 'GlowBoost' vitamin C serum. It employs 34 workers and sold 12,000 bottles last year at $24 each, earning $288,000 in revenue. The serum's label claims it 'erases wrinkles in 7 days, clinically proven'. A routine Trading Standards inspection flagged the claim as unproven, and the advertising regulator warned Verdano that keeping it risks a $40,000 fine.

The GlowBoost serum is Verdano's best-seller, accounting for 45% of revenue. The marketing manager proposes changing the claim to 'reduces the look of fine lines over 8 weeks', which a dermatologist-supported trial backs. The founder worries sales could fall because the stronger claim drove purchases. Alternatively, Verdano could keep the current claim and fund an $80,000 clinical trial, hoping to prove it or risk the fine.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'misleading promotion'.
    Answer: Misleading promotion is advertising or promotion that gives consumers a false or exaggerated impression of a product or service, such as claiming benefits that cannot be proved, which legal controls can ban or punish. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Promotion that gives a false/exaggerated impression of a product; Legal controls can ban/fine/punish such claims

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways legal controls over marketing might affect Verdano Botanicals.
    Answer: Way 1: Verdano must stop or change claims that cannot be proved [k]; Trading Standards has flagged the GlowBoost 'erases wrinkles in 7 days, clinically proven' claim, so the label and advertising may have to change [app]. Way 2: Verdano faces sanctions if it does not comply [k]; keeping the current claim could bring a $40,000 fine and force changes to the serum that generates 45% of its revenue [app].
    Keywords: Verdano Botanicals, GlowBoost, Trading Standards, $40,000, 45%, 12,000 bottles, $288,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: False/unsubstantiated claims must be withdrawn or corrected; Sanctions include fines, label changes and public warnings | application_max_2: Trading Standards flagged the GlowBoost 'clinically proven' claim; Keeping the claim risks a $40,000 fine; serum is 45% of revenue

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Verdano Botanicals might face if it keeps the current '7 days' claim.
    Answer: Problem 1: Regulators can fine the business for an unproven claim [k]; keeping 'erases wrinkles in 7 days' risks the $40,000 fine Verdano has been warned about [app], which would cut profits on the serum producing 45% of its $288,000 revenue [an]. Problem 2: Consumer trust falls when claims prove false [k]; customers bought 12,000 bottles last year partly because of the strong claim [app], so losing trust could cut repeat purchases and damage the whole Verdano brand [an].
    Keywords: erases wrinkles in 7 days, $40,000, 45%, $288,000, 12,000 bottles, GlowBoost, Trading Standards
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Unproven claims breach advertising/misleading-promotion rules; False claims damage consumer trust and repeat purchase behaviour | application_max_2: $40,000 fine warning; serum is 45% of $288,000 revenue; 12,000 bottles bought partly because of the strong claim | analysis_max_2: Fine directly reduces profit on the key product; Lost trust reduces repeat sales and brand equity

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Verdano Botanicals should change its promotion to 'reduces the look of fine lines over 8 weeks' or keep the current claim and fund an $80,000 clinical trial? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Changing the claim to 'reduces the look of fine lines over 8 weeks' would match the dermatologist-supported evidence [k]; Verdano could keep selling GlowBoost serum, worth 45% of $288,000 revenue, without risking the $40,000 fine [app], protecting profits quickly although sales may soften because the new claim is weaker [an]. However, an $80,000 clinical trial could prove the stronger claim and keep the message that drove 12,000 bottles of annual sales [k]; but the trial may fail, the $80,000 outlay is heavy for a firm earning $288,000 a year, and the fine could still arrive meanwhile [app], so the payback is uncertain [an]. On balance, Verdano should change the claim now and treat the trial as a later investment [eval], because avoiding the $40,000 fine and regulatory action outweighs the uncertain sales boost from a stronger claim [eval].
    Keywords: $80,000, 8 weeks, 45%, GlowBoost, $40,000, $288,000, 12,000 bottles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Promotions must be capable of substantiation; An 8-week improvement claim is supported by dermatologist evidence | application_max_2: 45% of $288,000 revenue from GlowBoost; 12,000 bottles a year; $80,000 trial cost vs $40,000 fine risk | analysis_max_2: Changing the claim protects revenue/profit and avoids sanctions; Trial is costly and may still fail, leaving the fine risk unresolved | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (compliance now vs proving the stronger claim); Justified recommendation: change claim now, review trial later

--- STEM ---
Tinkerhill Toys is a private limited company in Country X making wooden pull-along toys for children aged 1-3. Employing 28 workers, it sold 9,000 'Turbo Fox' toys last year at $18 each, generating $162,000 in revenue. A safety inspection found the Turbo Fox's small wheel fails the small-parts choke test, and the product regulator has ordered corrective action before any further sales.

Around 2,400 unsold units remain in Tinkerhill's warehouse. The quality manager estimates a full nationwide recall, refunding all buyers, would cost $180,000 including $18,000 logistics. The alternative is a targeted programme: redesign the wheel with a new $22,000 mould, recall only warehouse stock, and post free wheel replacements to owners, costing about $60,000 in total. Both options stop sales for weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'dangerous goods'.
    Answer: Dangerous goods are products that can harm consumers because of a defect or hazard, such as parts that pose a choking risk, which legal controls can ban or force a business to recall. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Products that can harm/injure consumers through defects or hazards; Legal controls can ban sales or force recalls

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why legal controls over dangerous goods matter to Tinkerhill Toys.
    Answer: Reason 1: They protect children from unsafe products [k]; the Turbo Fox wheel fails the small-parts choke test for children aged 1-3, so without controls the toy could injure a child [app]. Reason 2: They protect the business from legal liability [k]; if Tinkerhill ignored the regulator's order, sales would stop and it could face prosecution over the 9,000 toys already sold [app].
    Keywords: Tinkerhill Toys, Turbo Fox, children aged 1-3, 9,000, $18, $162,000, small-parts choke test
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Unsafe products can injure consumers, especially children; Non-compliance leads to enforcement, fines or prosecution | application_max_2: Turbo Fox wheel fails the small-parts choke test; toys for children aged 1-3; Regulator ordered corrective action; 9,000 toys already sold

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems caused for Tinkerhill Toys by the regulator's corrective-action order.
    Answer: Problem 1: Sales of its best-selling toy have to stop [k]; no Turbo Fox sales until the defect is fixed, threatening $162,000 of annual revenue from 9,000 toys [app], which could leave Tinkerhill unable to pay its 28 workers [an]. Problem 2: Fixing the defect is expensive [k]; the new wheel mould costs $22,000 and a full recall would cost $180,000 against revenue of $162,000 [app], wiping out a year's takings if the wrong option is chosen [an].
    Keywords: 2,400 unsold units, $180,000, $22,000, $60,000, Turbo Fox, $162,000, small-parts choke test
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Legal corrective action halts sales until defects are fixed; Recall/redesign costs fall on the business | application_max_2: $162,000 revenue from 9,000 toys now at risk; 28 workers to pay; $22,000 mould; $180,000 full recall vs revenue of $162,000 | analysis_max_2: Stopped sales threaten cash flow and wage payment; Fix costs can consume a full year's revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tinkerhill Toys should carry out a full nationwide recall or a targeted wheel-replacement programme? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A full recall would refund all buyers and remove every hazardous toy [k]; it costs about $180,000 including $18,000 logistics, fully addressing the risk from 9,000 sold toys [app], safeguarding the brand's reputation with parents and retailers [an]. However, a targeted programme — redesigning the wheel with a $22,000 mould, recalling the 2,400 unsold units, and free wheel replacements for owners — costs only about $60,000 [k]; it leaves Tinkerhill with more cash but depends on owners responding to the notice, so some defective toys could stay in use [app], creating ongoing risk of injury and prosecution [an]. On balance, Tinkerhill should do the full recall [eval], because the $180,000 cost is recoverable from future sales, whereas an injury to one child would destroy the brand and could cost far more in damages [eval].
    Keywords: $180,000, $60,000, $22,000, Turbo Fox, 2,400 unsold units, $18, $162,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Full recall removes the hazard entirely for all owners; Targeted schemes depend on consumer response and leave residual risk | application_max_2: $180,000 full recall (incl. $18,000 logistics) vs $60,000 targeted programme; 2,400 unsold units; $22,000 mould; 9,000 toys already sold | analysis_max_2: Recall protects brand, customers and avoids damages claims; Targeted option conserves cash but leaves defective toys in use | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (certainty vs cost); Justified recommendation: full recall to protect brand and children

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Pre-packed goods must match the stated weight; Trading standards can enforce with fines/prosecution | application_max_2: 40-pack sample averaged 460g vs labelled 500g (8% underweight); 60 days to comply or face $18,000 fine and possible prosecution

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Exporting adds logistical and compliance costs; Limited knowledge of foreign markets increases risk | application_max_2: $12,000 labelling + $1.50 per case freight ($37,500) on 25,000 cases; Single Neighbourland distributor; Solmar Fizz unknown locally | analysis_max_2: Costs erode margin to about $150,500; Distributor dependence weakens control of local sales

--- STEM ---
Kilnworth Ceramics is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing floor and wall tiles, employing 70 workers. Last year it generated $2.1 million in domestic revenue, but cheaper imported tiles arriving next year will squeeze margins. A construction materials group in Westmark, a foreign country, has proposed a 50/50 joint venture to build a $3.2 million tile plant there, supplying its building projects and exporting regionally.

Under the deal, the Westmark group provides land and 300 local workers, while Kilnworth provides tile technology and $1.4 million in cash from its $1.9 million retained profit. If the venture succeeds, Kilnworth expects annual dividends of $350,000 from year 3. Alternatively, Kilnworth could spend $900,000 on a second kiln at home, lifting annual output by 25% and defending its domestic share.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'joint venture'.
    Answer: A joint venture is an agreement between two or more businesses to work together on a specific project or market, sharing costs, risks and rewards, usually through a jointly owned enterprise. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Two or more businesses collaborating on a project/market; Costs, risks and rewards are shared between partners

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two opportunities for Kilnworth Ceramics of the Westmark joint venture.
    Answer: Opportunity 1: Entry into a new market [k]; the Westmark partner provides land and 300 local workers plus regional distribution, so Kilnworth can sell tiles in Westmark and beyond without building from scratch [app]. Opportunity 2: Risk and cost sharing [k]; the $3.2 million plant is built together, so Kilnworth funds only $1.4 million and expects dividends of about $350,000 a year from year 3 [app].
    Keywords: Kilnworth Ceramics, Westmark, 50/50, $3.2 million, $350,000, $2.1 million, 70 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Joint ventures give market access through local partners; Costs and risks of entry are shared between partners | application_max_2: Partner provides land and 300 local workers plus distribution; $3.2 million plant; Kilnworth funds $1.4 million; $350,000 expected dividends

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Kilnworth Ceramics of the Westmark joint venture.
    Answer: Problem 1: Shared control means compromise [k]; as a 50/50 partner Kilnworth must agree major decisions with the Westmark group, whose priorities may differ [app], causing conflict and slower decisions [an]. Problem 2: Heavy use of scarce cash [k]; the $1.4 million comes from its $1.9 million retained profit and could be lost if Westmark demand disappoints [app], leaving little reserve if domestic revenue of $2.1 million falls against cheaper imports [an].
    Keywords: $1.4 million, $1.9 million, Westmark, $3.2 million, 50/50, $2.1 million, Kilnworth Ceramics
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Joint ventures require shared decision-making/control; Capital contributed by partners is at risk if the venture fails | application_max_2: 50/50 control with a foreign partner of differing priorities; $1.4 million from $1.9 million retained profit; $2.1 million domestic revenue | analysis_max_2: Conflict over decisions slows progress and erodes the venture; Cash tied up leaves no buffer against import competition

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kilnworth Ceramics should form the Westmark joint venture or spend $900,000 on a second kiln at home? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The joint venture opens a new market and growth beyond Country X [k]; with $1.4 million of Kilnworth's $1.9 million retained profit and partner-supplied land and 300 workers, year-3 dividends of about $350,000 would comfortably exceed the return on a $900,000 kiln [app], and exports spread risk beyond a domestic market squeezed by cheaper imports [an]. However, the second kiln lifts annual output by 25% at home at $900,000 [k]; it stays fully under Kilnworth's control, with no partner conflict, and directly defends its $2.1 million domestic revenue against imported tiles arriving next year [app], though it does nothing to open new markets or spread risk [an]. On balance, the Westmark joint venture is the stronger move [eval], because it tackles both the import threat and the need for growth, while the kiln only defends the status quo [eval].
    Keywords: $900,000, 25%, $1.4 million, $350,000, $2.1 million, Westmark, $1.9 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Joint ventures give access to foreign markets with shared risk; Internal expansion keeps full control but ties capital to one market | application_max_2: $1.4 million cash, $350,000 expected year-3 dividends vs $900,000 kiln; Second kiln raises output 25%; $2.1 million domestic revenue at risk | analysis_max_2: JV diversifies markets and can outrun the import threat; Kiln protects home share but no new revenue streams | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (JV abroad vs domestic expansion); Justified recommendation: form the Westmark joint venture

--- STEM ---
Cilento Pasta Co is a private limited company in Country X making jarred pasta sauces, employing 40 staff. Domestic revenue reached $1.6 million last year. A food importer in Ostresh, a foreign country, wants to produce and sell Cilento sauces locally under licence, paying an 8% royalty on local sales. The importer forecasts year-1 local sales of $700,000, which would pay Cilento $56,000 in royalties.

Licensing would need no new factory investment, and it would avoid the breakages that ruined 6% of a trial export consignment earlier this year. The alternative is for Cilento to open its own sales office in Ostresh, costing $180,000 in year 1, which keeps full control of recipes and pricing but commits the firm to a risky new market. Both options start next year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'licensing'.
    Answer: Licensing is an agreement where a business gives another firm the right to produce or sell its product or brand in a market, in return for a fee or a royalty on sales. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Another firm gets permission to produce/sell the product or brand; The licence holder pays fees/royalties in return

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Cilento Pasta Co of licensing production to the Ostresh importer.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Low investment with quick income [k]; the importer forecasts $700,000 of year-1 local sales, so Cilento receives $56,000 in royalties at 8% with no factory spend [app]. Benefit 2: Local production avoids export losses [k]; 6% of a trial consignment was damaged in transit, so Ostresh-made sauces arrive fresher and cheaper than shipped jars [app].
    Keywords: Cilento Pasta Co, Ostresh, 8%, $56,000, $700,000, 6%, $1.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Licensing earns royalties without capital investment; Local production removes shipping costs and breakage | application_max_2: $700,000 forecast year-1 sales; 8% royalty = $56,000; 6% of trial consignment damaged in transit

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Cilento Pasta Co of licensing production to the Ostresh importer.
    Answer: Problem 1: Loss of control over the product [k]; once the importer produces Cilento sauces locally, quality may slip and harm the brand across Ostresh [app], undoing the reputation behind $1.6 million of annual domestic sales [an]. Problem 2: Royalties are a small share of profit [k]; 8% of $700,000 is only $56,000 a year, so success in Ostresh enriches the importer far more than Cilento [app], and exiting the agreement later could be difficult and costly [an].
    Keywords: $180,000, Ostresh, 6%, Cilento Pasta Co, 8%, $700,000, 40 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Licensing transfers production control to another firm; The licensor keeps only royalties, not the full profit margin | application_max_2: Importer controls local production of Cilento sauces; 8% of $700,000 = $56,000 vs $180,000 own-office cost | analysis_max_2: Quality slips damage brand reputation and sales; Most upside value accrues to the licensee, weakening Cilento's returns

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cilento Pasta Co should license production to the Ostresh importer or open its own sales office there? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Licensing is cheaper and faster [k]; $56,000 of royalty income from $700,000 of local sales arrives with no $180,000 setup cost and avoids the 6% breakage problem that ruined the trial consignment [app], giving steady returns while Cilento keeps its $1.6 million domestic business in focus [an]. However, Cilento's own sales office keeps full control of recipes, quality and pricing [k]; it costs $180,000 in year 1 but captures the whole profit margin in Ostresh and builds direct customer relationships [app], delivering far more income long term if the market grows [an]. On balance, Cilento should license first and review after two years [eval], because $56,000 of low-risk income beats a $180,000 untested commitment in a foreign market Cilento knows little about [eval].
    Keywords: $180,000, $56,000, $700,000, 8%, 6%, Ostresh, $1.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Licensing gives low-risk entry using a local partner; Own operations keep full control and full margin but higher risk | application_max_2: $56,000 royalty on $700,000 sales vs $180,000 office cost; 6% transit breakages; $1.6 million domestic base | analysis_max_2: Licensing protects cash and tests the market; Own office offers greater long-term profit and control | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (licensing vs own office); Justified recommendation: license first, review later

--- STEM ---
Tandoor & Thyme is a private limited company in Country X running 12 fast-casual curry houses, each selling $350,000 a year on average, with total revenue of $4.2 million. It employs 210 staff. A franchise group in Farovia, a foreign country, has offered to open 8 outlets there under international franchise: an initial fee of $75,000 per outlet plus a 5% royalty on sales. The group forecasts first-year Farovia sales of $2.6 million.

The franchise deal would bring Tandoor & Thyme $600,000 of initial fees and $130,000 of year-1 royalties, with very little capital invested. The alternative is to open 3 company-owned outlets in Farovia at $900,000 each, costing $2.7 million, keeping all profits and full control of recipes and branding, but tying up cash and taking about 2 years to break even.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'franchising'.
    Answer: Franchising is an agreement where a franchisor allows franchisees to use its brand, products and business methods in return for an initial fee and ongoing royalties on sales. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Franchisor licenses brand/methods to franchisees; Franchisee pays initial fees plus ongoing royalties

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Tandoor & Thyme of international franchising in Farovia.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Fast growth with little capital [k]; 8 franchise outlets cost Tandoor & Thyme nothing to build yet bring $75,000 of fees each, worth $600,000 upfront [app]. Benefit 2: Recurring royalty income [k]; 5% of forecast $2.6 million first-year Farovia sales gives $130,000 a year with local operators running sites and staff [app].
    Keywords: Tandoor & Thyme, Farovia, $75,000, $600,000, $130,000, 5%, $2.6 million, 12 fast-casual curry houses
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Franchising enables rapid expansion without large capital outlay; Ongoing royalties provide recurring income | application_max_2: 8 outlets x $75,000 fee = $600,000 upfront; 5% of forecast $2.6 million year-1 sales = $130,000 royalties

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Tandoor & Thyme of international franchising in Farovia.
    Answer: Problem 1: Loss of control over quality [k]; franchisees run the kitchens, so poor curries or service could damage the brand behind $4.2 million of domestic revenue [app], erasing the home market's trust in Tandoor & Thyme [an]. Problem 2: Franchise income is shared and capped [k]; Tandoor & Thyme keeps only the fees and 5% royalties, so $730,000 of year-1 income is far below what company-owned outlets would earn [app], limiting funds for further expansion [an].
    Keywords: $600,000, $130,000, Farovia, 5%, 8 outlets, international franchise, $4.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Franchisors cede operational control to franchisees; Franchisor income is limited to fees and royalties | application_max_2: Franchisees run Farovia kitchens; brand built on $4.2 million domestic revenue; $600,000 fees + $130,000 royalties = $730,000, not the outlet profits | analysis_max_2: Quality slips damage reputation and home sales; Limited income restricts reinvestment and growth

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tandoor & Thyme should enter Farovia by international franchising or by opening company-owned outlets? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Franchising 8 outlets brings $600,000 of fees plus $130,000 of year-1 royalties with no capital at risk [k]; Tandoor & Thyme keeps its $4.2 million domestic business focused while partners handle Farovia's sites, with standards enforced through training [app], and expansion is fast without debt [an]. However, 3 company-owned outlets at $900,000 each cost $2.7 million [k]; they keep full profit and tight control of recipes, branding and service — vital for a cuisine-led brand — but drain cash and take about 2 years to break even [app], straining the 12 domestic houses if Farovia disappoints [an]. On balance, international franchising is the better first step for Tandoor & Thyme [eval], because $730,000 with near-zero capital beats betting $2.7 million before Farovia demand is proven [eval].
    Keywords: $2.7 million, $600,000, $130,000, $900,000, $4.2 million, Farovia, 210 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Franchising offers low-capital, fast international growth; Company ownership keeps full control and full profits | application_max_2: $600,000 fees + $130,000 royalties vs $2.7 million for 3 owned outlets; 12 domestic houses, $4.2 million revenue, 210 staff | analysis_max_2: Franchising funds growth from partners' capital; Owned outlets maximise long-term profit but strain cash and risk | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (franchising vs company-owned); Justified recommendation: franchise first, own outlets later

--- STEM ---
Cascabel Foods is a private limited company in Country X producing ready-to-eat meals. Its best-seller 'Double Chilli Beef' sells 95,000 packs a year at $4.60 each. The firm plans to enter Zandrivia, a foreign market where shoppers prefer milder flavours and smaller single portions. Domestic revenue is $1.9 million, and the firm employs 54 workers across two factories.

One option is to sell the standard 'Double Chilli Beef' 500g pack unchanged, forecast to sell 60,000 packs at $4.20 in year 1, worth $252,000. The other is to localise: create a mild 'Zandrivia Chicken' recipe in 350g packs, costing $150,000 in reformulation and packaging, forecast to sell 140,000 packs at $3.80, worth $532,000 in year 1. Zandrivia's regulator also requires allergen labels in its own language.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'localising a product'.
    Answer: Localising a product is adapting it to the tastes, culture, laws or conditions of a particular market, rather than selling an identical product everywhere. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Adapting a product to a specific local market; Covers taste, portion, culture or legal requirements

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Cascabel Foods might localise its meals for Zandrivia.
    Answer: Reason 1: Local tastes differ [k]; Zandrivia shoppers prefer milder flavours, so a mild 'Zandrivia Chicken' recipe should sell better than the fiery 'Double Chilli Beef' they do not know [app]. Reason 2: Legal rules differ [k]; Zandrivia's regulator requires allergen labels in its own language, so a localised pack is needed to sell legally there at all [app].
    Keywords: Cascabel Foods, Zandrivia, Zandrivia Chicken, Double Chilli Beef, milder flavours, 95,000 packs, $4.60
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Markets differ in taste, culture and usage habits; Foreign markets may have product/label legal requirements | application_max_2: Zandrivia prefers milder flavours; 'Zandrivia Chicken' planned; Allergen labels required in Zandrivia's own language

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Cascabel Foods might face if it localises for Zandrivia.
    Answer: Problem 1: Localising costs money up front [k]; the new recipe and 350g packaging need $150,000 before any Zandrivia sale is made [app], so profit is delayed and cash is tied up on two factories already running [an]. Problem 2: The sales forecast may prove wrong [k]; if the mild recipe matches only the standard pack forecast of 60,000 rather than 140,000 units, the localised range loses money despite its $532,000 vs $252,000 projected revenue [app], leaving obsolete packaging and stock [an].
    Keywords: $150,000, 350g, Zandrivia Chicken, milder flavours, allergen labels, 54 workers, Cascabel Foods
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Localising requires reformulation/packaging investment; Sales forecasts for new products are uncertain | application_max_2: $150,000 reformulation and packaging cost for 350g 'Zandrivia Chicken'; 140,000-pack forecast worth $532,000 vs 60,000 packs worth $252,000 | analysis_max_2: Upfront cost strains cash and delays profit; If forecast is missed, the localised range makes a loss

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cascabel Foods should localise its meals for Zandrivia or sell the standard 'Double Chilli Beef' pack unchanged? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Localising fits Zandrivia's milder taste preference [k]; 140,000 packs of 'Zandrivia Chicken' at $3.80 could bring $532,000 in year 1, far above the standard pack's expected 60,000 packs worth $252,000 [app], and meeting allergen-label rules protects the brand legally in Zandrivia [an]. However, the standard pack needs no new recipe or packaging, avoiding the $150,000 upfront cost [k]; it simply extends 'Double Chilli Beef', which sells 95,000 packs a year at home [app], keeping production simple but ignoring local tastes and legal labelling, so Zandrivia sales may stay slow and repeat orders may never come [an]. On balance, Cascabel should localise [eval], because the forecast $280,000 uplift in year-1 revenue comfortably exceeds the $150,000 cost [eval].
    Keywords: $150,000, $252,000, $532,000, 60,000 packs, 140,000 packs, $4.20, $3.80
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Localising matches products to local tastes and laws; Standardisation is cheaper but may ignore local needs | application_max_2: $532,000 forecast (140,000 packs at $3.80) vs $252,000 (60,000 packs at $4.20); $150,000 reformulation/packaging; allergen labels required | analysis_max_2: Localising wins more Zandrivia sales and legal compliance; Standard pack saves cash but risks poor acceptance | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (localise vs standardised product); Justified recommendation: localise; uplift exceeds cost

--- STEM ---
Brightflame Heaters is a private limited company in Country X making electric convector heaters. It sold 6,500 heaters at $65 each last year, generating $422,500 in revenue and employing 32 workers. Its supplier flagged that a wiring defect affected 2 production batches; 1,800 of the sold heaters came from these batches, and heaters from them can overheat and pose a fire risk.

The product regulator has ordered Brightflame to stop sales and act. A full nationwide recall and refund of all 6,500 buyers would cost about $482,500 including $60,000 logistics. A targeted programme — repairing the 1,800 defective units via home visits at $25 each ($45,000) plus a public safety notice — costs around $60,000 but relies on owners responding to the notice.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'faulty goods'.
    Answer: Faulty goods are products that are not made or supplied to a satisfactory standard: they are defective, unsafe or do not work as they should, giving consumers rights to repair, replacement or refund. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Goods that are defective/not of satisfactory standard; Consumers gain rights to repair, replacement or refund

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why legal controls over faulty goods matter to Brightflame Heaters.
    Answer: Reason 1: They protect consumers from harm [k]; a wiring defect in 2 production batches can make convector heaters overheat, creating a real fire risk in homes [app]. Reason 2: They protect the firm from enforcement [k]; the regulator has already stopped Brightflame's sales, and ignoring this could bring prosecution and fines on top of $422,500 of annual revenue at risk [app].
    Keywords: Brightflame Heaters, 6,500 heaters, $65, $422,500, 1,800, 2 production batches, electric convector heaters
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Unsafe products can injure consumers and damage property; Legal controls enable regulators to stop sales and prosecute | application_max_2: Wiring defect in 2 batches; 1,800 sold heaters can overheat; Regulator ordered a stop to sales; $422,500 revenue at risk

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems with Brightflame Heaters relying only on a targeted repair programme.
    Answer: Problem 1: Owners may not respond [k]; the $45,000 repair programme depends on people opening the safety notice, so some of the 1,800 defective heaters could stay in use [app], leaving Brightflame exposed to a fire and enormous damages claims [an]. Problem 2: Trust and reputation suffer [k]; buyers who feel the recall was half-hearted may avoid Brightflame heaters, jeopardising all $422,500 of annual revenue [app], and the regulator could judge the action inadequate and tighten restrictions [an].
    Keywords: $482,500, $60,000, $45,000, 1,800, Brightflame Heaters, $65, 32 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Owner response is uncertain, leaving residual risk; Perceived half-measures damage brand trust | application_max_2: $45,000 repairs depend on 1,800 owners responding; All $422,500 of annual revenue depends on brand trust | analysis_max_2: Residual fires cause devastating damages and liability; Lost trust cuts sales and may trigger further enforcement

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brightflame Heaters should do a full nationwide recall or the targeted repair programme? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A full recall would refund all 6,500 buyers and remove every at-risk heater from homes [k]; it costs about $482,500 including $60,000 logistics, more than last year's $422,500 revenue, but guarantees the defect cannot hurt anyone and keeps the regulator fully satisfied [app], protecting the brand and avoiding unlimited liability [an]. However, the targeted programme repairs the 1,800 defective units at $25 each ($45,000) plus a public notice, around $60,000 in total [k]; it is far cheaper and focuses money on the actual risk, keeping cash for the business and its 32 workers [app], but it relies on owners responding and may miss some defective heaters in use [an]. On balance, Brightflame should do the full recall [eval], because the firm can survive one bad year of lost revenue but cannot survive a house fire traced to its heaters [eval].
    Keywords: $482,500, $60,000, $45,000, 1,800, $422,500, 6,500 heaters, $25
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Full recall eliminates the hazard and liability entirely; Targeted repair is cheaper but relies on owner response | application_max_2: $482,500 full recall (incl. $60,000 logistics) vs $60,000 targeted; 1,800 defective units at $25 = $45,000; $422,500 annual revenue | analysis_max_2: Recall protects life, brand and regulatory standing; Targeted option preserves cash but leaves residual risk | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (certainty vs cost); Justified recommendation: full recall to eliminate risk

--- STEM ---
Ferncombe Cheese Co is a family-run cheese maker founded 9 years ago in a rural valley in Country X. It employs 14 staff and produces 60 tonnes of handmade cheese a year. Around 70% of output is sold through Marlowe Wholesale Foods, a national wholesaler that charges an 18% margin and supplies 45 independent shops, while the farm shop sells the remaining 30% at $14 per kg. The wholesaler pays $9 per kg.

Annual revenue last year was $630,000. Marlowe Wholesale Foods has offered to buy an extra 15 tonnes a year if Ferncombe invests $90,000 in a new maturing room, using up all spare winter capacity. Alternatively, Ferncombe could spend $45,000 expanding its farm shop and expect to sell 4 more tonnes each year at $14 per kg.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'wholesaler'.
    Answer: A wholesaler is a business that buys goods in large quantities from producers and sells smaller quantities to retailers or other businesses [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: buys goods in large quantities/bulk from producers; sells in smaller quantities to retailers or other businesses

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Ferncombe Cheese Co of selling through Marlowe Wholesale Foods.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Marlowe Wholesale Foods buys in bulk, so Ferncombe can sell large volumes of its 60 tonnes a year without visiting every shop itself [k], reaching 45 independent shops in one commercial deal rather than 45 separate ones [app]. Benefit 2: A wholesaler holds stock and breaks bulk close to the 45 independent shops [k], giving Ferncombe a steady outlet that helped it earn $630,000 in annual revenue [app].
    Keywords: Ferncombe Cheese Co, Marlowe Wholesale Foods, 45 independent shops, 60 tonnes, $630,000, farm shop
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: buys in bulk, allowing the producer to sell large volumes without many separate visits; holds stock and breaks bulk, providing a convenient and steady outlet | application_max_2: reaching 45 independent shops through one deal; helping earn $630,000 annual revenue

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Ferncombe Cheese Co of relying on Marlowe Wholesale Foods.
    Answer: Problem 1: Marlowe charges an 18% margin, so Ferncombe receives only $9 per kg from wholesale sales instead of $14 per kg at the farm shop [k], cutting the revenue earned on the 70% of output sold through the wholesaler [app], which leaves less profit available to invest in the maturing room or farm shop expansion [an]. Problem 2: Relying on one wholesaler gives Marlowe strong bargaining power over a small producer [k], so its offer of an extra 15 tonnes a year could tie up all spare capacity in a low-margin channel [app], weakening Ferncombe's independence and pricing power over time [an].
    Keywords: Marlowe, 18%, $9 per kg, farm shop, 70%, 15 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the wholesaler takes a margin, so the producer receives a lower price per unit; reliance on a single buyer gives that buyer bargaining power over a small producer | application_max_2: 18% margin means Ferncombe gets $9 per kg instead of $14 per kg; 70% of output goes wholesale; the extra 15 tonnes offer would tie up spare winter capacity | analysis_max_2: less profit per kg reduces funds available for reinvestment; dependence on one buyer weakens independence and long-term pricing power

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ferncombe Cheese Co should accept the wholesaler's offer of an extra 15 tonnes a year? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting would secure a reliable bulk buyer for an extra 15 tonnes a year [k]. At $9 per kg this is about $135,000 a year of extra revenue (15,000 kg x $9), using spare winter capacity that would otherwise go unused [app], and it would strengthen the relationship with Marlowe, encouraging them to keep Ferncombe in the 45 independent shops [an]. However, the offer requires $90,000 for a new maturing room and commits the extra output to the wholesale channel at just $9 per kg, far below the $14 per kg paid at the farm shop [k]. Expanding the farm shop for $45,000 could sell 4 more tonnes at $14 per kg, about $56,000 a year, for half the investment [app], though accepting both options is impossible while winter capacity is tight [an]. Overall, Ferncombe should accept the offer, because $135,000 of secure extra revenue outweighs the sacrificed direct sales if the firm can finance the maturing room without strain [eval], but it should keep at least part of output for the higher-margin farm shop to preserve direct customer relationships [eval].
    Keywords: Marlowe Wholesale Foods, 15 tonnes, $90,000, $45,000, $14, farm shop, maturing room
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: accepting secures a reliable bulk buyer for extra volume; however, it locks spare capacity into a lower-margin channel and requires heavy new investment | application_max_2: 15 tonnes at $9 per kg gives about $135,000 a year (15,000 kg x $9); farm shop alternative: $45,000 for 4 tonnes at $14 per kg, about $56,000 a year; maturing room costs $90,000 | analysis_max_2: accepting strengthens the wholesaler relationship and uses spare capacity, lifting revenue; however, lower margin per kg, commitment of limited capacity and investment risk reduce flexibility | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing $135,000 revenue gain against $90,000 outlay and lower margins; overall judgement that balances short-term revenue against independence and channel mix

--- STEM ---
Brightwick Candles is a small business in Country X making scented soy candles in a home workshop. Founded 3 years ago, it employs 6 staff and makes about 8,000 candles a month. Sales last year reached $240,000, with 75% of revenue coming from three regional distributors supplying 12 gift shops and 25% from weekend craft fairs.

The owner is considering an e-commerce website costing $15,000 to build and $400 a month to run, expecting online sales of $60,000 in the first year. Demand is highest at Christmas, so the workshop currently turns away seasonal orders. However, she worries about postage costs eating profits on single candles, online payment fraud and customers not trusting a brand they cannot smell first. She could instead spend $6,000 on extra craft fair pitches.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'channel of distribution'.
    Answer: The route taken by goods or services from the producer to the final consumer, which may involve intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers or may be direct [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the route goods take from producer to consumer; may involve intermediaries or be direct to the consumer

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways e-commerce could benefit Brightwick Candles.
    Answer: Benefit 1: An e-commerce website would let Brightwick sell its candles directly to consumers across the country, beyond the 12 gift shops supplied through its distributors [k], so the expected $60,000 of first-year online sales would add a new revenue stream on top of the $240,000 earned last year [app]. Benefit 2: Selling online means the shop is open 24 hours a day at a running cost of only $400 a month [k], so Brightwick can take orders outside craft fair weekends without paying for extra pitches [app].
    Keywords: Brightwick Candles, 12 gift shops, $240,000, $60,000, $400 a month, 8,000 candles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: e-commerce widens market reach beyond existing physical outlets; online sales are open continuously at low running cost | application_max_2: expected $60,000 first-year online sales would add to last year's $240,000; reaching beyond the 12 gift shops at $400 a month running cost

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems e-commerce could cause Brightwick Candles.
    Answer: Problem 1: Customers cannot smell soy candles before buying online [k], so some orders, especially for the $60,000 first-year target, could end in disappointment, returns and refund costs, while postage on single candles would eat the margin [app], eroding profit on small orders [an]. Problem 2: E-commerce exposes the business to online payment fraud and cyber-security risks [k], so Brightwick must pay for secure payment processing plus $400 a month hosting on top of the $15,000 build cost [app], diverting cash from the $6,000 extra craft fair pitches it could alternatively secure [an].
    Keywords: $15,000, $400 a month, $6,000, craft fairs, 12 gift shops, soy
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customers cannot inspect/test the product before buying online; payment fraud and cyber-security risks are inherent to e-commerce | application_max_2: postage on single candles eats the margin; first-year online target is $60,000; $15,000 build cost plus $400 a month hosting, compared with spending $6,000 on craft fairs | analysis_max_2: returns and refund handling erode profit on small online orders; extra security and hosting costs drain cash that could be used for proven fair sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brightwick Candles should launch its own e-commerce website? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Launching the website would widen Brightwick's market beyond the 12 gift shops and weekend craft fairs it already uses [k]. If online sales reach the expected $60,000 in the first year, they would add about a quarter to last year's $240,000 revenue [app], while the 24-hour shopfront keeps selling when fairs are closed, helping a 3-year-old business grow quickly [an]. However, the website costs $15,000 plus $400 a month to run, and customers cannot smell soy candles before buying [k]; fraud, postage on single candles and refund handling could erode the thin margins Brightwick makes on weekend fair sales [app]. At the same time, $6,000 on extra craft fair pitches would grow the channel that already delivers 25% of revenue [an]. Overall, Brightwick should launch the website, because $60,000 of new annual revenue outweighs the setup cost if it prices delivery sensibly and takes secure payments [eval], but it should keep the craft fairs as a face-to-face showcase and review the website's return on investment after 12 months [eval].
    Keywords: Brightwick Candles, e-commerce website, $15,000, $60,000, $240,000, 12 gift shops, craft fairs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: owning a website widens market reach beyond existing physical channels; however, setup and running costs plus inability to inspect goods online are risks | application_max_2: expected $60,000 first-year online sales versus $240,000 revenue last year; $15,000 build cost, $400 a month running cost, $6,000 alternative craft fair spend | analysis_max_2: 24-hour shopfront supports fast growth beyond fair weekends; fraud, postage and refunds could erode margins; fair channel is proven and cheap to expand | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing $60,000 extra revenue against $15,000 plus running costs; overall judgement recommending launch with delivery priced sensibly and a 12-month review

--- STEM ---
Solmara Herbal Teas is a private limited company in Country X blending organic herbal teas from locally grown herbs. Founded 6 years ago, it employs 20 staff and produces 90 tonnes a year. Exports to Country Y account for $520,000 of annual revenue, sold through a single distributor that stocks 40 shops but has cut prices by 12%.

A speciality food agent has offered to represent Solmara in Country Y, promising introductions to 150 speciality shops in return for 8% commission on sales. Buyers at two recent trade fairs requested free samples, and Country Y retailers praised the light leafy flavours. Alternatively, Solmara could open its own sales office in Country Y, costing $85,000 a year plus travel, keeping full control of pricing, promotion and branding.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'agent'.
    Answer: A person or firm that acts on behalf of a business to arrange sales in a market, earning a commission but not taking ownership of the goods [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: acts on behalf of another business to arrange sales; earns a commission and does not own the goods

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Solmara Herbal Teas of appointing an agent in Country Y.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The agent already knows the Country Y food trade and speciality food retailers [k], so Solmara could reach 150 speciality shops instead of the 40 stocked by its current distributor [app]. Benefit 2: The agent is paid only a commission on actual sales [k], so Solmara pays 8% of sales rather than committing $85,000 a year plus travel to its own office [app].
    Keywords: Solmara Herbal Teas, Country Y, 150 speciality shops, 8% commission, $85,000, 40 shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an agent has local market knowledge and buyer relationships; an agent costs only commission, so no fixed cost is incurred before sales are made | application_max_2: access to 150 speciality shops instead of the 40 currently stocked; 8% commission is paid only on sales, unlike the $85,000 a year office cost

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Solmara Herbal Teas of opening its own sales office in Country Y.
    Answer: Benefit 1: An own office gives Solmara full control over pricing, promotion and branding in Country Y [k], so it could stop the 12% price cuts and hold prices steady across the 150 target shops [app], protecting its premium image and margins on the 90 tonnes it produces a year [an]. Benefit 2: A permanent office builds direct relationships with retailers and gives fast response to market changes [k], so Solmara can gather feedback and launch new herbal blends quickly [app], strengthening retailer loyalty and long-term export sales [an].
    Keywords: Solmara, $85,000 a year, 90 tonnes, 150 speciality shops, 12%, Country Y
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: own office gives full control over pricing, promotion and branding; a permanent office enables direct retailer relationships and fast feedback | application_max_2: reversing the 12% price cuts across 150 target speciality shops; responding quickly for the 90 tonnes of annual production with locally gathered feedback | analysis_max_2: price control protects premium image and margins; direct relationships build loyalty and sustain long-term export sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Solmara Herbal Teas should appoint the agent in Country Y? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Appointing the agent would cost only 8% commission on actual sales [k], which on $520,000 of annual exports is about $41,600 a year, far less than the $85,000 office cost plus travel [app], and would immediately open doors to 150 speciality shops, triple the 40 shops currently served [an]. However, an agent is not an employee, so Solmara would keep less control over how its tea is presented and priced [k]; the 12% price cutting could continue if the agent chases volume, and Solmara's brand could be weakened in Country Y [app], which may reduce its ability to charge premium prices later [an]. Overall, the agent is the better first step, because it limits risk while testing demand across 150 shops and costs under half the office budget [eval], although Solmara should sign the agent on a renewable 12-month contract and review results before committing to a permanent office [eval].
    Keywords: Solmara Herbal Teas, agent, 8% commission, $85,000, 150 speciality shops, Country Y, $520,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an agent is paid commission only on sales, limiting fixed cost and risk; an agent is not an employee, so the principal has less control over presentation and pricing | application_max_2: 8% commission on $520,000 is about $41,600 a year versus $85,000 a year for an office; 150 speciality shops reachable versus the 40 shops currently stocked; 12% price cuts may persist | analysis_max_2: commission-only payment limits downside risk while expanding distribution; weak control over the agent could damage premium branding and pricing power | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring the agent as lower risk while testing the market; overall judgement with a review condition before committing to a permanent office

--- STEM ---
Brancott Catering Co is a private limited company providing mobile event catering for weddings and corporate parties in Country X. Founded 4 years ago, it employs 8 staff and generated $322,000 last year from 46 events, with an average value of $7,000 per event. Word of mouth supplies most bookings.

A hotel group in the capital has offered to refer wedding clients in return for a 12% fee on every referred booking. Most enquiries arrive by phone or social media message, and summer Saturdays fill up 6 months ahead. Alternatively, Brancott could spend $7,500 on its own website with online booking, targeting corporate clients directly; the owner expects 2 extra events a month worth about $7,000 each, while venue referrals might add 15 events a year but at lower margins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'e-commerce'.
    Answer: Buying and selling goods or services over the internet, for example through a website, app or online booking platform [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: buying and selling goods or services over the internet; carried out through a website, app or online platform

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why selling services directly to customers suits a service business such as Brancott Catering Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: Services are intangible and cannot be stored or transported, so they are normally sold direct from provider to customer [k], matching how Brancott already wins most of its 46 events through word of mouth [app]. Reason 2: Selling direct lets Brancott meet clients personally to plan each event [k], so each $7,000 event can be tailored to the customer's menu, budget and schedule [app].
    Keywords: Brancott Catering Co, 46 events, $322,000, $7,000, word of mouth, weddings
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: services are intangible and cannot be stocked, so direct selling is typical; direct sale enables personal consultation and tailoring of the service | application_max_2: most of Brancott's 46 events already come through word of mouth; each event is worth about $7,000 and needs personal planning

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks for Brancott Catering Co of relying on hotel-group referrals.
    Answer: Drawback 1: The hotel group would take a 12% fee on every referred booking [k], so on 15 referred events a year at $7,000 each Brancott would pay about $12,600 in fees, cutting the margin left for ingredients and staff [app], weakening profit per event over time [an]. Drawback 2: Referred clients are effectively loyal to the hotel rather than to Brancott [k], so if the hotel ends the partnership or switches caterer, Brancott could lose those 15 events a year without owning the customer relationships [app], making future revenue less predictable [an].
    Keywords: hotel group, 12% fee, $7,000, 15 events, 46 events, $322,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an intermediary takes a fee that reduces the producer's margin per sale; reliance on a referral partner creates dependency and weakens the producer's direct customer relationships | application_max_2: 12% of 15 referred events at $7,000 each is about $12,600 a year; loss of referred clients if the hotel switches caterer or ends the deal | analysis_max_2: fees directly reduce profit retained per event; dependency makes revenue unpredictable and weakens Brancott's bargaining position

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brancott Catering Co should rely on referrals from the hotel group? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Relying on the hotel group would bring about 15 extra events a year worth roughly $105,000 at $7,000 each, with almost no marketing effort from Brancott [k]. Even after paying the 12% fee of about $12,600 a year, the referred bookings would add useful volume while Brancott builds its pipeline [app], and hotel clients could introduce Brancott to premium wedding customers it could not reach alone [an]. However, the 12% fee would recur every year, costing far more than a one-off $7,500 website plus modest hosting [k], while the owner expects 2 extra corporate events a month from the website at about $7,000 each, roughly $168,000 a year with no commission taken [app]. Owning that channel gives Brancott customer data, direct repeat bookings and full margin [an]. Overall, Brancott should not rely on hotel referrals as its main channel; it should invest in the website and accept hotel referrals only as a short-term top-up while online enquiries build [eval], because owning its own marketing channel protects margins and customer relationships in the long run [eval].
    Keywords: Brancott Catering Co, hotel group, 12%, $7,500, $322,000, word of mouth, 46 events
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: hotel referrals deliver predictable extra volume with little marketing effort; however, the recurring fee exceeds a one-off investment in an own website | application_max_2: 15 referred events x $7,000 = about $105,000 a year, fee about $12,600 a year; website expected 2 extra events a month at $7,000 = about $168,000 a year, no commission | analysis_max_2: referrals can add volume quickly and access premium wedding clients; own website builds customer data, direct repeat bookings and full margin | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation against relying mainly on referrals; balanced judgement favouring the website with referrals as a short-term top-up

--- STEM ---
Torncliffe Kayak Co is a private limited company making touring kayaks in Country X. Founded 11 years ago, it employs 28 staff and builds about 850 kayaks a year, selling them at an average price of $1,150. Revenue last year was $977,500, with 80% of sales through 22 independent watersports retailers and the rest at the factory showroom.

Each kayak is built by hand in under 3 weeks and carries a 5-year hull guarantee. The directors want to sell more kayaks online. A national online marketplace would charge 15% commission on each sale and already receives 2 million visits a month. Alternatively, Torncliffe could build its own website for $30,000, plus about $90 per kayak for delivery and packaging, keeping the full selling price but having to attract customers itself.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'direct to consumer'.
    Answer: Selling goods or services straight to the final customer without intermediaries such as wholesalers or retailers, for example through a factory shop or website [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: selling straight to the final consumer; no intermediaries such as wholesalers or retailers involved

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits Torncliffe Kayak Co could gain from selling kayaks directly to consumers online.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Selling direct removes the retail margin built into the 80% of sales currently made through 22 independent watersports retailers [k], so Torncliffe keeps the full $1,150 average price per kayak rather than the lower trade price [app]. Benefit 2: A direct online channel reaches paddlers nationwide who never visit a watersports shop [k], expanding the market beyond the 850 kayaks a year currently built [app].
    Keywords: Torncliffe Kayak Co, 22 independent watersports retailers, $1,150, 850 kayaks, 80%, factory showroom
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: selling direct avoids paying intermediary margins; a direct online channel widens geographic market reach | application_max_2: full $1,150 kept instead of the trade price after retailer margins; expanding beyond 850 kayaks a year and the current 80% retailer share

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Torncliffe Kayak Co might face selling through an online marketplace.
    Answer: Problem 1: The marketplace charges 15% commission on each sale [k], so on a $1,150 kayak each sale would cost Torncliffe about $172.50, far more than the $90 delivery and packaging for its own website [app], leaving a lower margin per boat and less profit to reinvest [an]. Problem 2: Marketplace listings appear side by side with rival brands, encouraging price comparison [k], so Torncliffe may have to discount its touring kayaks to win sales [app], eroding the premium brand image built over 11 years [an].
    Keywords: 15% commission, $1,150, 2 million visits, $30,000, $90 per kayak, $977,500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: marketplaces charge commission on every sale, reducing margin; marketplace listings expose products to direct price comparison with rivals | application_max_2: 15% of $1,150 is about $172.50 per kayak, versus $90 delivery on its own website; pressure to discount touring kayaks on the same screen as rival brands | analysis_max_2: commission directly reduces margin and funds available for reinvestment; price-comparison pressure can erode premium positioning built over 11 years

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Torncliffe Kayak Co should sell through the national online marketplace rather than its own website? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The marketplace already receives 2 million visits a month [k], giving Torncliffe instant access to a huge paddling audience without first spending $30,000 on its own website [app]. For a firm building about 850 kayaks a year, even a modest conversion rate could lift online volume while Torncliffe learns which models sell best without upfront promotion spend [an]. However, the 15% commission costs about $172.50 per $1,150 kayak, almost double the $90 delivery for own-site orders, and the marketplace owns the customer data and shopping experience [k]. A Torncliffe website would keep the full margin, let it retarget accessory sales and control its branding, but it would take time and ongoing promotion to attract visitors [app]; over hundreds of sales the commission bill would quickly dwarf the $30,000 build cost [an]. Overall, Torncliffe should start with the marketplace only as a 12-month trial to build awareness [eval], then shift sales to its own website once enough online orders cover the $30,000 build cost, which at about $172.50 saved per kayak needs only around 174 online sales [eval].
    Keywords: Torncliffe Kayak Co, online marketplace, 15% commission, $30,000, $1,150, 22 independent watersports retailers, $977,500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a marketplace provides instant access to a large existing audience; however, its commission exceeds the per-order cost of own-site delivery and it owns customer data | application_max_2: 2 million visits a month versus an $30,000 own-website build cost; 15% commission on $1,150 is about $172.50 per kayak versus $90 delivery on own website | analysis_max_2: marketplace gives fast exposure with low upfront cost and risk; commission accumulates quickly; own website keeps margin, data and brand control over time | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation: trial the marketplace for 12 months, then migrate to own website; clear judgement based on roughly 174 sales to cover the $30,000 build cost
