--- STEM ---
Fernbrook Press is a private limited company producing organic fruit juices in Country X. Founded 5 years ago, it employs 12 staff and presses 30,000 litres a month. It sells mainly through 60 independent shops supplied by one wholesaler, with revenue last year of $480,000.

In January, Fernbrook launched a subscription website offering 4 weekly deliveries at $18 per box, costing $12,000 to set up. The wholesaler takes 14 days to pay invoices, squeezing cash flow each month, and spring is the busiest season. After 4 months, subscriptions reached 300 households, but 3% of boxes arrived damaged and some subscribers cannot taste the juice before buying. The wholesaler has just offered to extend coverage to 65 shops if Fernbrook guarantees weekly deliveries.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'retailer'.
    Answer: A business that sells goods in small quantities directly to consumers, usually from a shop or other consumer-facing premises [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sells goods in small quantities directly to consumers; typically operates from a shop or consumer-facing premises

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Fernbrook Press of selling juice directly to consumers through its subscription website.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A subscription gives Fernbrook a predictable, recurring revenue stream [k], with 300 households signed up in 4 months each paying for 4 weekly deliveries at $18 per box [app]. Benefit 2: Selling direct removes the wholesaler's margin and the retailer's mark-up [k], so Fernbrook keeps more of the $18 box price and can reach health-conscious households nationwide beyond the 60 independent shops it supplies now [app].
    Keywords: Fernbrook Press, 30,000 litres, $18 per box, 300 households, 60 independent shops, subscription website
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: subscriptions provide predictable recurring revenue; selling direct keeps more of the selling price by removing intermediary margins | application_max_2: 300 households in 4 months, 4 weekly deliveries at $18 per box; keeping more of the $18 price and reaching beyond the 60 independent shops

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two threats that buying juice on a subscription website poses to consumers.
    Answer: Threat 1: Online buyers cannot taste or inspect juice before paying [k], so they risk buying flavours they do not enjoy, unlike in the 60 independent shops where they can sample first [app], which can cause disappointment or wasted boxes [an]. Threat 2: Delivery can fail or arrive damaged [k], as shown by the 3% of subscription boxes that arrived damaged [app], so consumers pay for juice they cannot use and may face refund delays and inconvenience [an].
    Keywords: 3% of boxes, 60 independent shops, subscription website, $18 per box, 300 households, 4 weekly deliveries
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: online shoppers cannot inspect or test products before buying; delivery problems can damage goods before they reach the customer | application_max_2: no tasting before buying, unlike the 60 independent shops; 3% of subscription boxes arrived damaged | analysis_max_2: buying untried flavours risks disappointment and wasted spend; damaged deliveries mean paying for unusable juice and refund delays

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fernbrook Press should prioritise its subscription website over extending wholesale shop coverage? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The subscription website could transform Fernbrook from a supplier dependent on one wholesaler into a brand with direct customer relationships [k]. The 300 households signed up in 4 months already generate recurring revenue, and the $12,000 setup is modest against $480,000 of annual revenue [app]. Direct sales also give Fernbrook data on flavours and delivery timing to plan the 30,000 litres it presses each month [an]. However, e-commerce brings real threats for consumers and for the business: 3% of boxes arrived damaged and buyers cannot taste first [k], which can drive refunds, complaints and bad reviews [app], while the wholesaler's offer to extend coverage to 65 shops would secure immediate in-store volume in 5 more shops with tasting that builds trust [an]. Overall, Fernbrook should not abandon the website, but it should prioritise the wholesale expansion for 12 months to fix quality and delivery reliability [eval], then reinvest in subscriptions once damaged-box rates fall, because reputation for a fresh product cannot be repaired cheaply after early failures [eval].
    Keywords: Fernbrook Press, subscription website, 300 households, $12,000, 65 shops, 3% of boxes, 60 independent shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: subscriptions build direct customer relationships and recurring revenue; however, e-commerce carries consumer threats that can damage reputation | application_max_2: 300 households in 4 months and $12,000 setup against $480,000 revenue; wholesaler offer to extend coverage to 65 shops in return for guaranteed weekly deliveries | analysis_max_2: direct sales give Fernbrook valuable data to plan production and delivery; damaged boxes and refunds can destroy early-stage reputation and push customers back to shops | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation: prioritise fixing delivery reliability and wholesale coverage first; balanced view that subscriptions should resume priority once quality metrics improve

--- STEM ---
Rusthaven Engineering Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 10 years ago, building stainless-steel dough mixers and ovens for commercial bakeries. It employs 22 staff and sells about 45 machines a year at an average price of $28,000, with revenue last year of $1,260,000.

Each machine is delivered within 8 weeks of order and includes a 2-year parts warranty. Currently sales are handled by an agent who earns a 6% commission and knows the bakery trade well. Alternatively, Rusthaven could employ a full-time technical sales representative at $55,000 a year to visit and demonstrate machines to around 90 bakery owners. The representative would keep the full margin, but the salary would be paid whatever the sales result.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'place' in the marketing mix.
    Answer: In the marketing mix, place refers to where and how goods and services are made available to customers, that is the channels of distribution used to reach them [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: refers to where and how products/services are made available to customers; concerns the channels of distribution used to reach the customer

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Rusthaven Engineering Ltd of using an agent to sell its bakery machines.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The agent already knows the bakery trade and its buyers [k], so Rusthaven gains immediate access to bakery owners it might never reach alone [app]. Benefit 2: The agent is paid only a 6% commission on machines actually sold [k], so Rusthaven carries no fixed salary cost and avoids the risk of paying $55,000 a year before any sales are made [app].
    Keywords: Rusthaven Engineering Ltd, agent, 6% commission, bakery trade, $55,000, 90 bakery owners
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an agent brings local or trade market knowledge and buyer relationships; an agent is paid commission only, so there is no fixed cost before sales are made | application_max_2: access to bakery owners through the agent's trade knowledge; 6% commission only, avoiding a guaranteed $55,000 a year salary

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Rusthaven Engineering Ltd of employing its own technical sales representative rather than an agent.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A technical representative would demonstrate machines to around 90 bakery owners, giving live technical walkthroughs and trials [k], which is ideal for a $28,000 machine that bakeries want to see working before buying [app], raising the conversion of demonstrations into sales [an]. Benefit 2: The representative works exclusively for Rusthaven [k], so pricing, messaging and service are fully controlled by Rusthaven rather than by an outside agent acting for its own commission [app], protecting margins and brand image on every $28,000 sale [an].
    Keywords: technical sales representative, $55,000 a year, 90 bakery owners, 6% commission, $28,000, $1,260,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a technical representative can demonstrate complex products directly to buyers; an exclusive representative gives the firm control over pricing and messaging | application_max_2: live demonstrations to around 90 bakery owners for a $28,000 machine; Rusthaven keeps control of every $28,000 sale instead of relying on a commission-driven agent | analysis_max_2: technical demonstrations build buyer confidence and lift conversion rates; full control over the sales process protects margins and brand consistency

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rusthaven Engineering Ltd should replace the agent with its own sales representative? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Replacing the agent with a representative at $55,000 a year would cost less than the 6% commission last year, about $75,600 on $1,260,000 of revenue [k], saving around $20,600 a year before counting extra sales from 90 bakery-owner demonstrations [app]. A dedicated representative could build direct relationships, feed back market information and sell the full range of machines with live technical support [an]. However, the $55,000 salary is a fixed cost paid even in a weak year, when the agent would have cost nothing, and the agent's trade contacts and motivation to close deals could be lost [k]; commission may push an agent to sell more aggressively than a salaried employee [app], so revenue could fall below $1,260,000 during the transition [an]. Overall, Rusthaven should replace the agent, because $75,600 of commission exceeds the $55,000 salary and direct control suits high-value technical machines [eval], but it should set clear sales targets and keep the agent on a handover period of a few months to protect customer relationships [eval].
    Keywords: Rusthaven Engineering Ltd, agent, 6% commission, $55,000, 90 bakery owners, $1,260,000, $28,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a fixed salary can cost less than percentage commission on current revenue; however, a salary is paid regardless of sales, unlike commission, and incumbent trade contacts are lost | application_max_2: 6% commission on $1,260,000 is about $75,600 a year versus $55,000 for a representative; saving about $20,600 a year, plus upside from demonstrations to 90 bakery owners | analysis_max_2: dedicated representative builds direct relationships and gathers market intelligence; transition risk: fixed cost, lost agent motivation and possible revenue dip below $1,260,000 | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring replacement given the commission saving and control benefits; balanced judgement recommending targets and a short handover period to manage risk

--- STEM ---
Rowanhill Knitwear is a private limited company designing and knitting wool sweaters and cardigans in Country X. Founded 8 years ago, it employs 40 staff and sells through 80 independent clothes shops and 2 department stores. Revenue last year was $2.4 million.

Half of revenue comes from sweaters and cardigans sold in autumn and winter, so stock must be ready by September. The directors must choose a route to grow sales. They could launch their own online shop at a cost of $40,000, with packaging and postage adding about $6 per garment, or they could sign a deal with Haversham Wholesale, which would place Rowanhill Knitwear in 120 shops but demand a 20% discount on trade prices. Online trials suggest 5% of parcels would come back as returns, and customers cannot try garments before buying.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'distribution'.
    Answer: The process of getting goods from the producer to the final customer, including transport, storage and the channels used, such as wholesalers, retailers or direct sales [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the process of getting goods from producer to consumer; includes transport, storage and the channels of distribution used

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Rowanhill Knitwear might face if it launches its own online shop.
    Answer: Problem 1: Customers cannot try sweaters and cardigans before buying [k], so the expected 5% return rate would add postage, repackaging and refund costs on top of the $40,000 setup [app]. Problem 2: Knitwear is seasonal and visual, so Rowanhill must keep improving photography and website content to compete online [k], adding ongoing spending beyond the $6 per garment packaging and postage [app].
    Keywords: Rowanhill Knitwear, $2.4 million, 80 independent clothes shops, $40,000, $6 per garment, 2 department stores
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customers cannot try on garments before buying, increasing returns; online fashion needs continuous website and photography investment | application_max_2: 5% returns on top of the $40,000 setup cost; $6 per garment packaging and postage reduces margin per item

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits Rowanhill Knitwear would gain by signing with Haversham Wholesale.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Haversham Wholesale would place Rowanhill Knitwear in 120 shops, 50% more than the 80 independent clothes shops it supplies now [k], quickly growing sales volume and total revenue beyond $2.4 million [app], strengthening its market position before rivals react [an]. Benefit 2: Haversham manages ordering, warehousing and delivery to shops [k], taking over logistics so Rowanhill's 40 staff can focus on design and knitting [app], lowering strain on the business while the 2 department store relationships continue [an].
    Keywords: Haversham Wholesale, 120 shops, 20% discount, 80 independent clothes shops, $2.4 million, 2 department stores
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a wholesaler places the brand in far more shops, growing volume and revenue; a wholesaler handles ordering, storage and delivery to retailers | application_max_2: 120 shops versus the current 80, lifting revenue beyond $2.4 million; 40 staff freed to focus on design while 2 department stores still hold the range | analysis_max_2: wider distribution grows volume faster than internal sales effort could; outsourced logistics reduces operational strain and supports continuity

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rowanhill Knitwear should sign with Haversham Wholesale rather than launch its own online shop? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Signing with Haversham Wholesale would instantly widen distribution from 80 to 120 shops, so sales could rise well beyond $2.4 million without the $40,000 website build or the 5% return headache [k]. The wholesaler handles logistics and reorders, letting Rowanhill focus on design, and shop stock is financed by Haversham rather than Rowanhill [app], spreading risk and supporting faster national coverage [an]. However, Haversham demands a 20% discount on trade prices, so Rowanhill would earn less per garment and remain dependent on one intermediary for growing shop distribution [k]; the online shop would keep full price and customer data, with $6 packaging per parcel, though 5% returns and no try-on would deter some buyers [app], and online traffic and trust take years to build [an]. Overall, Rowanhill should sign with Haversham now, because immediate volume into 120 shops beats waiting for online traction [eval], but it should renegotiate the 20% discount after 12 months of results and start building its online presence once cash flow improves [eval].
    Keywords: Rowanhill Knitwear, Haversham Wholesale, 120 shops, 20% discount, $40,000, 80 independent clothes shops, $6 per garment
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: wholesale delivers immediate wider distribution with logistics handled by the intermediary; however, it demands a discount on trade prices and creates dependency on one intermediary | application_max_2: distribution from 80 to 120 shops versus the $40,000 website build; 20% discount on trade prices; own website keeps full price at $6 packaging per parcel with 5% returns | analysis_max_2: immediate volume, lower capital risk and outsourced logistics favour wholesale now; own website would retain margin, data and independence but takes years to attract online shoppers | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring Haversham Wholesale in the short term; overall judgement recommending a 12-month discount review and phased online investment

--- STEM ---
Saltpan Lobster Co is a family fishing business in Country X, founded 7 years ago, employing 8 fishermen on 2 boats. It lands about 30 tonnes of live lobsters a year. Around 80% are sold to a wholesale fish market at $14 per kg and 20% go directly to 12 local restaurants at $22 per kg. Revenue last year was $468,000.

The owners could spend $25,000 on a refrigerated van to deliver live lobsters to 20 more restaurants each week. The 2 boats fish 5 days a week, weather permitting, and landings peak in July and August. However, lobsters sold wholesale need no marketing or extra staff, payments arrive reliably, and the wholesale market currently takes every lobster the boats land.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'intermediary'.
    Answer: An independent business that helps move goods from producer to consumer, for example wholesalers, retailers or agents, earning a margin or commission for its role [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an independent business between producer and consumer; includes wholesalers, retailers or agents, earning a margin or commission

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why selling lobsters directly to restaurants suits a perishable product such as live lobsters.
    Answer: Reason 1: Live lobsters are perishable, so every hour of transit matters [k], meaning short direct trips to the 12 local restaurants keep them fresher than a longer journey through the wholesale fish market [app]. Reason 2: Selling direct removes intermediary handling and margins [k], so Saltpan can charge $22 per kg instead of $14 per kg, keeping an extra $8 per kg on every lobster sold direct [app].
    Keywords: Saltpan Lobster Co, $22 per kg, $14 per kg, 12 local restaurants, 30 tonnes, live lobsters
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: perishable goods need the shortest possible channel to stay fresh; selling direct avoids the intermediary's margin or mark-up | application_max_2: short direct trips to 12 local restaurants keep lobsters fresher than the wholesale route; $22 per kg direct versus $14 per kg wholesale, an extra $8 per kg

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why wholesale markets remain important to fishing businesses such as Saltpan Lobster Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: The wholesale fish market takes the full catch whatever the volume [k], giving Saltpan a guaranteed outlet for the 24 tonnes a year that currently go through it [app], securing reliable weekly cash flow without finding 32 individual direct buyers [an]. Reason 2: Selling wholesale needs no van, extra staff or marketing [k], avoiding the $25,000 refrigerated van and the daily effort of chasing $22-per-kg restaurant orders [app], keeping overheads low and letting the 8 fishermen focus on fishing [an].
    Keywords: wholesale fish market, 80%, $14 per kg, 30 tonnes, $25,000, 2 boats
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a wholesale market guarantees an outlet for the entire catch; wholesale sales require no extra vehicle, staff or marketing spend | application_max_2: 24 tonnes a year (80% of 30 tonnes) currently go through the wholesale market; avoids the $25,000 refrigerated van and daily management of restaurant orders | analysis_max_2: guaranteed outlet secures consistent revenue and working capital; lower overheads let the business concentrate on fishing rather than distribution

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Saltpan Lobster Co should buy the refrigerated van and sell more lobsters directly to restaurants? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the van would let Saltpan supply 20 more restaurants directly at $22 per kg [k]; shifting 6 tonnes a year from the wholesale rate to the direct rate would add about $48,000 of revenue (6,000 kg x $8 extra per kg) without catching more lobster [app]. Fresher deliveries would also build restaurant loyalty and justify premium menu pricing [an]. However, the van costs $25,000 and brings fuel, insurance and maintenance costs, and the direct channel only works if 20 restaurants order reliably every week [k]; dropped or forgotten orders would leave perishable stock worthless [app], and the wholesale market still guarantees an outlet for any unsold catch and pays reliably [an]. Overall, Saltpan should buy the van, because moving more volume to the $22-per-kg direct channel clearly beats $14 per kg for a freshness-critical product [eval], but only after the 20 restaurants commit to standing weekly orders, with the wholesale market kept as a fallback for unsold stock [eval].
    Keywords: Saltpan Lobster Co, refrigerated van, $25,000, $22 per kg, 20 more restaurants, $14 per kg, 30 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: direct supply to restaurants commands a higher price for perishable seafood; however, it requires vehicle investment and reliable weekly ordering by buyers | application_max_2: shifting 6 tonnes from $14 to $22 per kg adds about $48,000 a year (6,000 kg x $8); the van costs $25,000 and must serve 20 more restaurants reliably each week | analysis_max_2: higher margin and fresher delivery strengthen restaurant relationships and revenue per kg; if restaurants cancel or volumes vary, perishable stock is lost and the van becomes a fixed burden | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to buy the van only with confirmed standing weekly orders; balanced judgement retaining the wholesale market as an outlet for unsold stock

--- STEM ---
Tidemill Electrical is a private limited company running 2 independent electrical goods shops in country towns in Country X. Founded 15 years ago, it employs 26 staff. Revenue last year was $1.8 million, but sales have fallen 12% over 2 years as online discounters undercut its prices.

The directors could build a website with click-and-collect for $35,000 plus $1,500 a month to maintain, letting customers order online and collect in store. It stocks about 1,400 product lines from 3 national suppliers. An online rival sells a $700 television for $549. The alternative is to remain a specialist high street retailer: 70% of Tidemill's customers say expert advice and free installation of kitchen appliances are why they shop there, and installation earns $300,000 a year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'click-and-collect'.
    Answer: A service where a customer orders goods online and collects them in person from a shop or depot at a chosen time [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: order placed online, typically paid for in advance; goods collected in person from a shop or depot

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two threats e-commerce poses to Tidemill Electrical.
    Answer: Threat 1: Online discounters carry lower store overheads and can undercut high street prices [k], as the rival selling a $700 television for $549 shows, helping drive Tidemill's 12% sales fall over 2 years [app]. Threat 2: Customers who buy online skip the shop entirely [k], so Tidemill loses walk-in trade that supports its $300,000 a year of kitchen appliance installation business [app].
    Keywords: Tidemill Electrical, $1.8 million, 12%, $700 television, $549, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: online discounters can undercut physical shops because they have lower overheads; online buying removes the store visit, cutting walk-in trade for physical retailers | application_max_2: a $700 television sold online for $549 undercuts Tidemill's pricing; the 12% sales fall over 2 years and the $300,000 installation income both reflect store traffic

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits Tidemill Electrical could gain from a click-and-collect website.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Click-and-collect lets Tidemill sell online while still driving customers into its two country-town shops [k], protecting footfall and upselling the kitchen appliance installation that already earns $300,000 a year [app], defending revenue and margins [an]. Benefit 2: Click-and-collect removes home delivery costs and waiting times [k], making online buying attractive for heavy items such as televisions and washing machines at a running cost of only $1,500 a month [app], improving convenience and customer loyalty [an].
    Keywords: click-and-collect, $35,000, $1,500 a month, $300,000, kitchen appliances, Tidemill Electrical
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: click-and-collect combines online ordering with in-store collection; click-and-collect avoids home delivery costs and delays | application_max_2: in-store collection drives upselling of the $300,000 a year installation service; $1,500 a month running cost for heavy items such as televisions and washing machines | analysis_max_2: store visits protect add-on sales and margins that pure delivery would lose; convenience versus home delivery can win back price-checking customers and build loyalty

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tidemill Electrical should invest in a click-and-collect website? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing in click-and-collect would let Tidemill compete online while keeping its two shops relevant [k]; at $35,000 build cost and $1,500 a month running cost, it is cheaper than losing 12% of a $1.8 million business, about $216,000 of revenue at risk [app], and it converts browsing into store visits where advice and installation can be sold [an]. However, Tidemill cannot match online prices such as $549 for a $700 television, so price-led buyers may still leave [k]; the website only works if stock is visible online and collection is easy, and at $18,000 a year running cost the system must win back meaningful volume [app], otherwise the investment becomes an expensive brochure [an]. Overall, Tidemill should invest, prioritising click-and-collect over price cuts because its differentiator, advice and installation valued by 70% of customers, cannot be copied by online rivals [eval], and it should review sales versus the $216,000 at risk after 12 months [eval].
    Keywords: Tidemill Electrical, click-and-collect, $35,000, $1.8 million, $549, 70%, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: click-and-collect lets a physical retailer compete online while retaining store visits; however, the firm cannot match online discounters on price alone | application_max_2: $35,000 setup plus $1,500 a month ($18,000 a year) versus about $216,000 revenue at risk from a 12% fall on $1.8 million; the $549 rival television example shows price competition is unwinnable; advice and installation valued by 70% of customers is the firm's edge | analysis_max_2: click-and-collect protects footfall and installation upselling worth $300,000 a year; execution risk: poor stock visibility or collection experience would make it an expensive brochure | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to invest in click-and-collect rather than cut prices; balanced judgement requiring a 12-month review against the $216,000 revenue at risk

--- STEM ---
Copperhole Bakery is a private limited company operating 4 bakery outlets across Country X. It employs 28 staff, generates $520,000 in annual revenue and sells its best-known sourdough loaf to around 3,500 customers each week. The owners are considering opening a fifth outlet in the Riverside district, 12 km from the nearest existing store, and have set aside $7,500 for market research. They want the business to be market-orientated, making what customers want rather than what the owners prefer.

The owners must decide between conducting their own primary research — a questionnaire posted to 400 Riverside households plus follow-up interviews with 30 residents — and buying a secondary research report on Country X bakery spending, priced at $3,000, alongside free government statistics on local household incomes. Internal records show sourdough sales rose 18% last year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'market research'.
    Answer: The process of collecting, recording and analysing information about customers, competitors and the market to inform business decisions [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: collecting, recording and analysing information; about customers, competitors or the market to inform decisions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Copperhole Bakery should conduct market research before opening a fifth outlet.
    Answer: Reason 1: To find out whether Riverside residents actually want a new bakery [k] before committing $7,500 and signing a lease on the fifth outlet [app]. Reason 2: To discover what products and prices Riverside customers would prefer [k], so the new branch can sell items like its best-known sourdough loaf rather than the owners guessing demand [app].
    Keywords: Copperhole Bakery, Riverside, $7,500, sourdough, fifth outlet, $520,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: identify customer demand or needs before committing resources; reduce the risk of a poor business decision | application_max_2: $7,500 research budget for the fifth outlet; Riverside district located 12 km from the nearest existing store; best-known sourdough loaf

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using questionnaires as a primary research method for Copperhole Bakery.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Questionnaires gather first-hand, up-to-date information directly from target customers [k], for example the 400 Riverside households receiving the posted questionnaire [app], so the replies reflect current local demand rather than outdated national trends [an]. Benefit 2: They can reach many respondents in writing at low cost [k], such as 400 households compared with only 30 face-to-face interviews [app], giving a larger evidence base to set alongside internal records showing sourdough sales rose 18% last year [an].
    Keywords: questionnaire, Riverside, households, sourdough, internal records, 18%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: collects first-hand, up-to-date primary data; can reach a large sample at relatively low cost | application_max_2: 400 Riverside households receiving the posted questionnaire; 30 follow-up face-to-face interviews; internal records show sourdough sales rose 18% | analysis_max_2: reflects current local demand for the new outlet; larger sample improves the reliability of the evidence base

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Copperhole Bakery should rely on primary research rather than secondary sources when deciding on the fifth outlet? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Primary research provides specific, current data on Riverside residents' preferences [k], for example from the 400 posted questionnaires and 30 follow-up interviews [app], which reduces the risk of opening where demand is weak [an]. However, secondary sources are quicker and cheaper [k]; the $3,000 report and free government statistics on local household incomes [app] would arrive without weeks of fieldwork [an]. Overall, primary research is the better choice for this location decision [eval] because only it can reveal local tastes and likely footfall in Riverside, which national statistics cannot show [eval].
    Keywords: Riverside, questionnaire, $3,000, government statistics, household incomes, $7,500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: primary research is specific and up to date; secondary research is quicker and cheaper but less specific | application_max_2: $3,000 secondary report on Country X bakery spending; free government statistics on local household incomes; 400 posted questionnaires and 30 follow-up interviews | analysis_max_2: reduces risk of opening where demand is weak; secondary data avoids weeks of fieldwork | evaluation_max_2: weighs specificity of primary data against cost and speed of secondary data; justifies primary research for a location-specific decision

Keswick Outdoors Ltd is a private limited company selling camping and hiking equipment from 3 stores across Country X. It employs 45 full-time staff, generated $1.1 million in revenue last year, and camping stoves accounted for 22% of total sales. The marketing manager is planning the summer launch of a new lightweight stove, the Trailflame, aimed at weekend hikers aged 25–40, and wants evidence before committing to a $60,000 production run.

The manager must choose between two primary research methods: running 4 focus groups of 8 hikers each, costing $1,800 in total including refreshments and venue hire, or carrying out an observation of shopper behaviour at the camping aisles of its 3 stores over 6 weekends using a trainee researcher.   Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Keswick Outdoors should conduct primary research before launching the Trailflame stove.
    Answer: Reason 1: To test whether weekend hikers actually want a lightweight stove like the Trailflame [k] before committing to production and promotion costs [app]. Reason 2: To gather up-to-date information on what hikers look for in a stove [k], such as weight, price and features, since stoves already account for 22% of store sales [app].
    Keywords: Trailflame, hikers, 22%, camping, 3 stores, $1.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: identify whether demand exists for a new product; gather up-to-date information for a specific decision | application_max_2: Trailflame aimed at weekend hikers; camping stoves account for 22% of sales; 3 stores across Country X

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using focus groups to research the Trailflame stove.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Focus groups bring a small number of target customers together to discuss their views in depth [k], for example 4 groups of 8 hikers talking about the Trailflame [app], giving detailed qualitative feedback on design and price expectations [an]. Benefit 2: The moderator can probe unexpected opinions and ask follow-up questions [k], unlike a written questionnaire, helping Keswick explore hikers' reactions for $1,800 across all 4 groups [app] and refine the stove before launch [an].
    Keywords: focus groups, hikers, Trailflame, $1,800, camping, stores
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: detailed qualitative feedback from target consumers; moderator can probe and ask follow-up questions | application_max_2: 4 focus groups of 8 hikers each; Trailflame lightweight stove aimed at weekend hikers; $1,800 total cost | analysis_max_2: detailed feedback on design and price expectations; helps refine the stove before launch

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Keswick Outdoors should use focus groups rather than observation to research the Trailflame launch? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Focus groups generate detailed discussion with target customers [k]; 4 groups of 8 hikers at $1,800 in total [app] reveal opinions and reasons, helping Keswick set the Trailflame's features and price [an]. However, observation records real behaviour without asking questions [k]; watching shoppers at the camping aisles across 3 stores over 6 weekends [app] shows what hikers actually pick up and buy, avoiding answers people give just to please the moderator [an]. Overall, focus groups are the better first step for this launch [eval] because they explain the reasons behind preferences, which observation alone cannot provide, although observation could confirm the findings later [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: focus groups give in-depth qualitative reasons; observation records actual behaviour without questioning | application_max_2: 4 groups of 8 hikers at $1,800 in total; camping aisles of its 3 stores over 6 weekends; Trailflame aimed at weekend hikers | analysis_max_2: reveals opinions behind hikers' preferences for features and price; avoids answers given just to please the moderator | evaluation_max_2: weighs qualitative depth of focus groups against behavioural truth of observation; justifies focus groups as first step with observation as confirmation

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U3_SET_153
UNIT: Unit 3: Marketing
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Hallowdene Clothing Co is a private limited company manufacturing school uniforms and workwear in Country X. It employs 120 machinists in its main factory, generated $2.4 million in revenue last year and winter jackets account for 30% of total sales. The company wants to survey customers about a new winter jacket range for 2027 and has chosen a sample of 400 respondents from its database of 6,500 recent buyers.

The marketing manager, newly promoted from production, must decide between random sampling — selecting 400 names using a computerised random number generator — and quota sampling, choosing respondents to match the database profile of 55% female, 45% male and 40% aged over 50. The questionnaire will be posted with a prepaid reply envelope and costs $2,000 to print and post, and results will guide the winter range launch.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'quota sampling'.
    Answer: Selecting a sample in which respondents are chosen to fill set quotas matching the characteristics of the target market, such as age and gender [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: respondents chosen to fill fixed quotas; quotas match the characteristics of the target market such as age or gender

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of Hallowdene Clothing's questionnaire results.
    Answer: Factor 1: A low or biased response rate [k]; if only a fraction of the 400 chosen names reply, the views of 6,500 recent buyers will be poorly represented [app]. Factor 2: Leading or unclear questions can bias the answers [k]; if the questionnaire nudges respondents towards the new winter jacket range, the 30% winter jacket share of sales may appear more popular than it is [app].
    Keywords: sample, 400, 6,500, winter jacket, questionnaire, 55% female
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: low or biased response rate reduces accuracy; leading or unclear questions bias the answers | application_max_2: sample of 400 chosen from 6,500 recent buyers; winter jackets account for 30% of sales; prepaid reply envelope questionnaire

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of random sampling for this survey.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Every name in the database has an equal chance of selection [k], so the 400 chosen from 6,500 recent buyers by random number generator [app] are less likely to be biased by the sampler's personal preferences [an]. Benefit 2: It is simple and quick to administer [k]; generating the sample costs nothing extra beyond the $2,000 printing and postage [app], leaving budget to chase replies and raise the response rate that drives accuracy [an].
    Keywords: random, 6,500, recent buyers, $2,000, questionnaire, 400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: every member of the population has an equal chance of selection; simple and quick to administer | application_max_2: 400 names from 6,500 recent buyers; random number generator selection; $2,000 to print and post the questionnaire | analysis_max_2: avoids bias from the sampler's personal preferences; frees budget to chase replies and improve response rate

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hallowdene Clothing should use quota sampling rather than random sampling for its questionnaire? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Quota sampling ensures the sample mirrors the target market [k]; choosing respondents to match the database profile of 55% female, 45% male and 40% aged over 50 [app] guarantees older buyers are heard, which pure chance might miss [an]. However, random sampling avoids interviewer bias in who is approached [k]; a random number generator applied to all 6,500 recent buyers [app] gives every customer an equal, impartial chance of selection [an]. Overall, quota sampling is the better choice for this winter jacket survey [eval] because buying habits differ sharply between these gender and age groups, so matching the profile matters more than statistical impartiality [eval].
    Keywords: quota, random, 55% female, 45% male, 40% aged over 50, 6,500, winter jacket
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quota sampling matches the sample to target market characteristics; random sampling gives every member an equal chance | application_max_2: database profile of 55% female, 45% male and 40% aged over 50; random number generator applied to 6,500 recent buyers; new winter jacket range | analysis_max_2: guarantees views from older buyers who pure chance might miss; impartial selection avoids interviewer bias | evaluation_max_2: weighs representative profile of quota sampling against impartiality of random sampling; justifies quota sampling because buying habits differ by gender and age

--- STEM ---
Rushmere Creamery is a private limited company producing premium ice cream and frozen yoghurt in Country X. It employs 65 staff at its creamery, generates $1.6 million in annual revenue and sells to 240 independent shops in 12 regions. The owners want to launch a dairy dessert aimed at children and are choosing between two research options.

Option one is a secondary market research report on the Country X dairy dessert sector, priced at $5,000, plus free government statistics on household spending and the owners' own internet research on rival brands. Option two is primary research: 500 questionnaires posted to households in 3 cities, costing $9,500 including printing, postage and analysis by an external firm. The owners worry that published secondary data may be out of date or not specific enough.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'secondary market research'.
    Answer: The use of information that has already been collected by someone else, such as government statistics, internet sources, market research reports and internal records [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: information already collected by someone else; examples include government statistics, internet sources, reports or internal records

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Rushmere Creamery of using secondary market research.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Secondary data is cheap and quick to access [k]; government statistics are free and the report costs $5,000, far less than the $9,500 needed for primary fieldwork [app]. Benefit 2: It can show the size and trends of the whole dairy dessert sector [k] before Rushmere commits to producing a new dessert for its 240 independent shops [app].
    Keywords: secondary, $5,000, government statistics, report, 240, $9,500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cheap and quick to access compared with primary research; shows overall market size and sector trends | application_max_2: free government statistics plus a $5,000 report; 240 independent shops currently supplied; dairy dessert aimed at children

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of relying on secondary market research for this launch.
    Answer: Limitation 1: Secondary data may not be specific to the new dairy dessert [k]; the report covers the whole Country X dairy dessert sector, not children's reactions to Rushmere's recipe [app], so decisions rest on general rather than tailored evidence [an]. Limitation 2: Secondary data can be out of date [k]; government statistics on household spending may be a year or two old, which the owners already worry about [app], meaning spending patterns may have shifted before the launch [an].
    Keywords: secondary, dairy dessert, government statistics, $5,000, household spending, children
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: secondary data may not be specific to the business's needs; secondary data may be out of date | application_max_2: report covers the whole Country X dairy dessert sector; government statistics on household spending a year or two old; children's reaction to Rushmere's recipe unknown | analysis_max_2: decisions rest on general rather than tailored evidence; spending patterns may have shifted before launch

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rushmere Creamery should buy the secondary report and use internet research rather than conduct primary research for its dairy dessert launch? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Secondary research is cheaper and faster [k]; at $5,000 plus free government statistics and internet research it costs $4,500 less than the $9,500 primary survey [app], freeing cash to market the launch through 240 independent shops [an]. However, primary research reveals exactly what children and parents in the 3 target cities think [k]; 500 questionnaires [app] would show likely demand and preferred flavours, reducing the risk of a failed launch [an]. Overall, primary research is the safer choice for this new product launch [eval] because no existing data covers children's preferences for this exact dairy dessert, so the $4,500 saving is poor value against a failed launch [eval].
    Keywords: secondary, $5,000, $9,500, government statistics, 500, dairy dessert, 240 independent shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: secondary research is cheaper and faster; primary research reveals specific current preferences | application_max_2: $5,000 report plus free government statistics and internet research; $9,500 cost of 500 questionnaires in 3 cities; 240 independent shops to supply | analysis_max_2: frees cash to market the launch; shows likely demand and preferred flavours, reducing failure risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs cost saving of secondary data against specificity of primary data; justifies primary research because no existing data covers this exact product

--- STEM ---
Brightwash Launderette is a sole trader business in Country X offering self-service washing and drying to city-centre residents. It runs 8 machines, employs 6 staff and generates $95,000 in annual revenue. Owner Daniela Ruiz keeps detailed internal records of daily wash volumes and peak hours, and she has noticed that Tuesday afternoons are far quieter than Saturdays, when queues sometimes form outside the shop.

Daniela wants to become more market-orientated and is deciding between analysing her internal records and free government statistics on local household numbers in the city centre, and paying $1,200 for a primary survey of 150 local residents about new services such as dry cleaning and ironing. She has no marketing department, limited time and no previous research experience.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'market-orientated business'.
    Answer: A business that focuses on identifying and satisfying customer needs and wants before producing or selling its products or services [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: identifies customer needs and wants first; satisfies those needs through its products or services

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Brightwash Launderette could become more market-orientated.
    Answer: Way 1: By using market research to find out what customers actually want [k], such as the proposed survey of 150 local residents about dry cleaning and ironing [app]. Way 2: By acting on its own internal records of customer behaviour [k], for example noticing that Tuesday afternoons are far quieter than Saturdays [app].
    Keywords: Brightwash Launderette, 150 local residents, dry cleaning, ironing, internal records, Tuesday afternoons
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: find out what customers want through market research; act on information about existing customer behaviour | application_max_2: proposed survey of 150 local residents; new services such as dry cleaning and ironing; internal records showing quieter Tuesday afternoons than Saturdays

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using internal records as secondary market research for Brightwash Launderette.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Internal records are free and already available to the business [k]; Daniela's logs of daily wash volumes and peak hours [app] cost nothing to analyse compared with paying $1,200 for a new survey [an]. Benefit 2: Internal records show real, recent behaviour rather than opinions [k]; the fact that Tuesday afternoons are far quieter than Saturdays [app] lets Daniela target promotions or adjust staffing on quiet days [an].
    Keywords: internal records, Tuesday afternoons, peak hours, $1,200, wash volumes, Saturdays
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: internal records are free and already available; internal records show actual rather than stated behaviour | application_max_2: logs of daily wash volumes and peak hours; $1,200 cost of the proposed primary survey; Tuesday afternoons far quieter than Saturdays | analysis_max_2: saves $1,200 compared with commissioning new research; enables targeted promotions or staffing changes on quiet days

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brightwash Launderette should invest $1,200 in primary research rather than rely on internal records and government statistics? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Primary research would directly reveal current customer wants [k]; the $1,200 survey of 150 local residents [app] shows demand for dry cleaning and ironing before Daniela buys any equipment [an]. However, internal records and government statistics cost little and already exist [k]; free government statistics on local household numbers combined with daily wash volumes [app] give a quick picture without spending the $1,200 or Daniela's limited time [an]. Overall, the primary survey is worthwhile for the new services decision [eval] because records only show what customers already use — not whether they want ironing or dry cleaning — so the $1,200 buys genuinely new information [eval].
    Keywords: internal records, $1,200, 150 local residents, government statistics, dry cleaning, wash volumes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: primary research reveals current customer wants directly; secondary sources cost little and already exist | application_max_2: $1,200 survey of 150 local residents; free government statistics on local household numbers; daily wash volumes from internal records | analysis_max_2: shows demand for dry cleaning and ironing before equipment purchase; gives a quick picture without spending $1,200 or limited time | evaluation_max_2: weighs new insight from primary research against cost and convenience of secondary data; justifies the $1,200 survey because records cannot show demand for new services

--- STEM ---
Ellsworth Electronics is a private limited company operating 3 high-street electronics shops in Country X. It employs 24 sales staff, generates $1.8 million in annual revenue and its most popular item is a $120 wireless speaker, which comes with a 3-month free returns policy. The owners want structured feedback on customer service across all 3 shops and are designing a short survey.

They must choose between a written questionnaire left at each till, with a prize draw entry for returning it, or face-to-face interviews conducted by the shop manager for 2 weeks, lasting about 4 minutes each. The questionnaire cost $800 to print and design; interviews cost nothing beyond staff time but take staff off the shop floor during the busy period before Christmas.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'questionnaire'.
    Answer: A written set of questions used to collect information from respondents, either in person, by post or electronically [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a written set of questions; used to collect information from respondents

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Ellsworth Electronics might prefer a questionnaire for gathering customer feedback.
    Answer: Reason 1: Questionnaires can reach many customers without taking staff off the shop floor [k]; 3 high-street electronics shops can leave them at each till for 2 weeks [app]. Reason 2: Written answers are easy to summarise and compare [k], for example feedback on the $120 wireless speaker, since all customers answer the same printed questions [app].
    Keywords: questionnaire, till, $120, wireless speaker, $800, shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reaches many customers at low cost; answers are easy to summarise and compare consistently | application_max_2: 3 high-street electronics shops; questionnaire left at each till for 2 weeks; $120 wireless speaker

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of interviewing customers face-to-face.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Interviews let the interviewer ask follow-up questions and clarify confusing answers [k], so a 4-minute conversation with a customer who bought the $120 wireless speaker can uncover problems a printed form would miss [app], producing richer detail for the owners [an]. Advantage 2: In-person response rates are usually higher [k], because customers face the shop manager directly rather than ignoring a till form [app], so Ellsworth gathers more completed feedback across its shops [an].
    Keywords: interviews, 4 minutes, $120, questionnaire, wireless speaker, till
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: interviewer can probe and clarify answers; response rates are usually higher face-to-face | application_max_2: 4-minute interviews conducted by the shop manager; $120 wireless speaker; till questionnaire with prize draw | analysis_max_2: produces richer detail than a printed form; gathers more completed feedback across the shops

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ellsworth Electronics should use the questionnaire rather than face-to-face interviews for its customer service survey? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Questionnaires are cheap and wide-reaching [k]; at $800 to print, 3 high-street electronics shops can survey customers for 2 weeks without removing staff from the shop floor [app], generating a large volume of comparable responses [an]. However, interviews produce deeper, more honest insight [k]; the shop manager's 4-minute conversations [app] can probe the reasons behind low service scores, although they cost staff time on the floor [an]. Overall, the questionnaire is the better primary tool here [eval] because Ellsworth needs broad feedback across 3 shops, not deep insight into a small number of customers [eval].
    Keywords: questionnaire, $800, interviews, till, $120, high-street
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: questionnaires are cheap with wide reach; interviews produce deeper, more qualitative insight | application_max_2: $800 to print the questionnaire; 3 high-street electronics shops over 2 weeks; shop manager's 4-minute interviews | analysis_max_2: generates a large volume of comparable responses; probes reasons behind low service scores | evaluation_max_2: weighs breadth of questionnaire responses against depth of interview insight; justifies the questionnaire for broad feedback across 3 shops

--- STEM ---
Harborview Grand Hotel is a 4-star seaside hotel with 140 rooms in Country X. It employs 95 staff, generates $3.2 million in annual revenue and 30% of guests use the leisure facilities, especially during the busy summer season. The owners are considering a $250,000 refurbishment of the spa, adding a sauna and new treatment rooms, and want guest feedback before committing.

They must choose between running 2 focus groups of 10 guests each in the hotel lounge, at a cost of $1,500 including refreshments and a moderator, or conducting 40 individual 15-minute interviews at check-in. The front office manager has offered to run the interviews free of charge, but departing guests may feel rushed when leaving and unable to comment in detail.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'focus group'.
    Answer: A small group of people selected from the target market who are brought together to discuss their views and feelings about a product, service or advertisement [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: small group drawn from the target market; brought together to discuss views on a product, service or advertisement

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Harborview Grand Hotel of using focus groups before the spa refurbishment.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Focus groups reveal detailed opinions in guests' own words [k], such as what the 10 spa-using guests in each group want from the $250,000 refurbishment [app]. Benefit 2: Group discussion sparks ideas one guest would not think of alone [k], helping the owners decide which facilities matter most, given that 30% of guests use the leisure facilities [app].
    Keywords: focus groups, spa, $250,000, 30%, refurbishment, guests
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reveals detailed opinions in participants' own words; group interaction sparks ideas individuals may not generate | application_max_2: 2 focus groups of 10 guests each; $250,000 spa refurbishment; 30% of guests use the leisure facilities

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of focus groups for this research.
    Answer: Limitation 1: Opinions from a focus group may not represent all guests [k]; 20 guests across 2 groups is a tiny sample of the hotel's guests [app], so refurbishment choices could reflect a vocal minority [an]. Limitation 2: Dominant speakers can sway the views of others [k]; in a group of 10 guests each, quieter guests may simply agree aloud [app], producing misleading feedback on which facilities to upgrade first [an].
    Keywords: focus groups, 2, 10 guests, $1,500, spa, refurbishment
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: small sample may not represent the whole population; dominant participants can influence others' views | application_max_2: 2 focus groups of 10 guests each; 140 rooms at the seaside hotel; spa refurbishment facilities to upgrade | analysis_max_2: refurbishment choices could reflect a vocal minority; quieter guests agreeing aloud produces misleading feedback

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harborview Grand Hotel should use focus groups rather than individual interviews to research the spa refurbishment? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Focus groups generate rich, interactive discussion [k]; 2 groups of 10 guests at $1,500 [app] let guests build on each other's ideas about the spa, helping the owners avoid wasting the $250,000 refurbishment on the wrong facilities [an]. However, individual interviews at check-in avoid group pressure [k]; 40 free 15-minute interviews run by the front office manager [app] reach more guests and let each speak freely without louder guests dominating [an]. Overall, focus groups are better for redesigning the spa [eval] because the interactive format suits open-ended discussion of facilities, whereas interviews would suit measuring satisfaction scores [eval].
    Keywords: focus groups, $1,500, refurbishment, interviews, 15-minute, spa, $250,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: focus groups generate interactive discussion; individual interviews avoid group pressure and reach more people | application_max_2: 2 groups of 10 guests at $1,500; 40 free 15-minute interviews at check-in by the front office manager; $250,000 spa refurbishment | analysis_max_2: interactive format surfaces ideas about which facilities to fund; interviews let quieter guests speak freely at no cost | evaluation_max_2: weighs interactive depth of focus groups against reach and neutrality of interviews; justifies focus groups for open-ended spa redesign decisions

--- STEM ---
Cobblestone Kitchen is a private limited company running a casual dining restaurant in Country X. It employs 18 staff, serves 320 meals per week and generates $680,000 in annual revenue. The owner, Priya Nair, is reviewing the menu with her chef and wants to know which dishes diners actually finish, and how best to present the findings as a simple bar chart or written summary for the kitchen team.

She must choose between employing a researcher to carry out an observation of diners for 4 weeks, recording what is ordered and how much is left on each plate, at a cost of $2,400, or handing out a one-page questionnaire with the bill. She is also unsure whether 200 responses would be more useful than 80 completed questionnaires for judging menu changes.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'observation'.
    Answer: A primary research method where researchers watch and record how consumers behave, such as what shoppers pick or diners leave, rather than asking them questions [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: watching and recording consumer behaviour; carried out rather than asking consumers questions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of observation as a research method for Cobblestone Kitchen.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Observation records actual behaviour, not just what people say [k]; the researcher sees which of the 320 meals per week are left unfinished [app]. Advantage 2: Diners behave naturally because they are unaware of being watched [k], avoiding the inaccurate answers a questionnaire attached to the bill might receive [app].
    Keywords: observation, 320 meals, questionnaire, bill, diners, $2,400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: records actual behaviour rather than stated opinions; consumers unaware of being observed behave naturally | application_max_2: 320 meals per week served; researcher observing diners for 4 weeks; questionnaire handed out with the bill

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of presenting the research findings as a bar chart rather than raw numbers.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Charts make patterns immediately visible [k]; a bar chart of leftover portions per dish [app] lets the chef spot unpopular dishes at a glance [an]. Benefit 2: Visual results are easier for staff without research training to understand [k]; showing 4 weeks of observations as bars [app] supports faster decisions on which dishes to remove from the menu [an].
    Keywords: bar chart, chef, 4 weeks, dishes, menu, diners
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: charts make patterns visible at a glance; visual results are easier for non-specialists to understand | application_max_2: bar chart of leftover portions per dish; 4 weeks of observation findings; chef deciding which dishes to remove | analysis_max_2: chef can spot unpopular dishes at a glance; supports faster menu decisions

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cobblestone Kitchen should use observation rather than a questionnaire to research its menu? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Observation shows real behaviour [k]; watching diners for 4 weeks at $2,400 reveals which dishes are ordered and how much is left [app], giving truthful evidence for menu changes the chef can trust [an]. However, a questionnaire is far cheaper and captures opinions [k]; a one-page form with the bill could collect views from many of the 320 weekly diners [app], explaining why dishes are disliked rather than just how often they are finished [an]. Overall, observation is the better method for this menu review [eval] because diners may claim to like a dish yet leave it unfinished, and the $2,400 cost is modest against $680,000 annual revenue [eval].
    Keywords: observation, questionnaire, $2,400, 320, diners, $680,000, bill
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: observation records actual behaviour; questionnaire is cheaper and captures stated opinions | application_max_2: 4 weeks of observation at $2,400; one-page questionnaire handed out with the bill; 320 meals per week | analysis_max_2: gives truthful, behaviour-based evidence for menu changes; questionnaire explains why dishes are disliked | evaluation_max_2: weighs truthful behaviour data against cheap opinion data; justifies observation because diners may leave disliked dishes unfinished

--- STEM ---
Northquay Fitness Club is a private limited company running a gym and pool in Country X. It has 1,800 members, employs 22 staff and generates $540,000 in annual revenue. Membership renewals fell 8% last year, mainly among newer joiners, and the manager wants to survey members before changing the membership packages and pricing.

The manager must choose between random sampling — emailing a questionnaire to 300 members chosen by a random number generator — and quota sampling, selecting 300 members to mirror the club profile of 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30. The survey software costs $300 per month and the results will be shown as colourful charts on the club notice board and in the member email newsletter.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'random sampling'.
    Answer: Selecting a sample from a population in which every member has an equal chance of being chosen, for example by using a random number generator [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: every member of the population has an equal chance; selection by chance, e.g. random number generator

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Northquay Fitness Club may face in getting accurate survey results.
    Answer: Problem 1: A low response rate [k]; if only a fraction of the 300 emailed members reply, the reason for the 8% fall in renewals will not be explained accurately [app]. Problem 2: Biased or dishonest answers [k]; members wanting cheaper fees may exaggerate complaints about the current membership packages [app], so the results overstate the problem.
    Keywords: 300, membership packages, 8%, renewals, questionnaire, survey
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: low response rate reduces representativeness; biased or dishonest answers distort results | application_max_2: 300 emailed members; 8% fall in membership renewals; current membership packages

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using quota sampling for this survey.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Quota sampling guarantees the sample reflects key member groups [k]; selecting 300 members to match 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30 [app] ensures older members' views are heard [an]. Benefit 2: It avoids the cost and complexity of random selection [k]; picking members by quota from the 1,800-name membership list needs no separate random process [app], saving staff time for a small club [an].
    Keywords: quota, 300, 60% aged under 30, 40% aged over 30, membership, members
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guarantees representation of key groups; avoids the cost and complexity of random selection | application_max_2: 300 members mirroring 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30; 1,800 members at the club; manager wants to change membership packages | analysis_max_2: ensures older members' views are included; saves staff time at a small club

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Northquay Fitness Club should use quota sampling rather than random sampling for its member survey? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Quota sampling ensures both age groups are fairly represented [k]; mirroring 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30 in the sample of 300 [app] reveals whether the 8% renewal fall is driven by young or older members [an]. However, random sampling gives every member an equal chance [k]; emailing 300 members chosen by random number generator [app] avoids the manager unknowingly favouring familiar faces at the gym [an]. Overall, quota sampling is the better choice here [eval] because age-related differences in package preferences are the key question, and quotas guarantee both groups are heard [eval].
    Keywords: quota, random, 60%, 40%, 300, 8%, membership packages
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quota sampling guarantees representative sub-groups; random sampling gives every member an equal chance | application_max_2: 60% aged under 30 and 40% aged over 30 profile; 300 members chosen by random number generator; 8% renewal fall last year | analysis_max_2: reveals whether renewals fell among young or older members; avoids favouring familiar faces at the gym | evaluation_max_2: weighs representative quotas against impartial random selection; justifies quota sampling because age differences drive package preferences

--- STEM ---
Wetherby Furniture Co is a private limited company manufacturing sofas and dining sets in Country X. It employs 85 staff, generates $2.1 million in annual revenue and sells through 5 independent retailers across the region. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'sample'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a group of people selected from the target market or population; used to take part in market research

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two factors that may limit the accuracy of Wetherby Furniture Co's survey results.
    Answer: Factor 1: The response rate was low [k]; only 220 of the 600 questionnaires were returned [app], so the sample may not represent all buyers. Factor 2: Incomplete answers [k]; several questionnaires were only half completed [app], leaving gaps in the data on quality, delivery times and value for money.
    Keywords: 600, 220, questionnaires, quality, delivery times, value for money
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: low response rate limits representativeness; incomplete questionnaires leave gaps in the data | application_max_2: 220 of the 600 questionnaires returned; questionnaires only half completed; satisfaction with quality, delivery times and value for money

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of presenting the survey results as charts rather than a written table.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Charts make comparisons between questions instantly clear [k]; a bar chart for each of the 3 questions [app] shows at a glance whether satisfaction with quality, delivery times or value for money is lowest [an]. Benefit 2: Visual results are more engaging for the board than columns of figures [k]; the manager can highlight the 220 returned responses visually [app], supporting faster, better-informed decisions on where to improve [an].
    Keywords: bar chart, written table, 3 questions, quality, delivery times, 220, value for money
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: charts make comparisons clear at a glance; visual results are more engaging for non-specialists | application_max_2: bar chart for each of the 3 questions; 220 returned responses on quality, delivery times and value for money; presented to the board | analysis_max_2: lowest-scoring question identified at a glance; supports faster, better-informed improvement decisions

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wetherby Furniture Co should present the survey results as bar charts rather than a written table? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Bar charts make the findings easy to interpret quickly [k]; a chart for each of the 3 questions [app] reveals weak spots such as delivery times without board members reading columns of numbers [an]. However, a written table preserves the exact figures [k]; the table shows precisely how the 220 returned questionnaires rated each question [app], which matters if the board wants exact percentages rather than visual impressions [an]. Overall, bar charts are the better choice for the board meeting [eval] because decisions about sofas and dining sets need immediate insight, not precision to one decimal place, and charts communicate to non-specialists more effectively [eval].
    Keywords: bar chart, written table, 3 questions, 220, sofas, dining sets, survey
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bar charts are quick to interpret; a written table preserves exact figures | application_max_2: a chart for each of the 3 questions; 220 returned questionnaires; satisfaction with quality, delivery times and value for money | analysis_max_2: reveals weak spots such as delivery times without reading tables; preserves precise percentages for detailed scrutiny | evaluation_max_2: weighs immediacy and accessibility of charts against precision of tables; justifies bar charts for a board decision on sofas and dining sets

--- STEM ---
Duskmere Appliances is a retailer of household white goods operating for 6 years in Country X, employing 22 staff across 2 stores. Annual revenue fell from $540,000 to $470,000 over the past 18 months as rising unemployment reduced real household incomes. Shoppers are trading down from premium washing machines priced at $650 to budget models at $310, and rival chains now run $25 weekly promotions on entry-level lines.

The owner is considering two responses to these changing consumer spending patterns. Option 1 is to cut the price of the $310 budget washing machine by 15% to protect footfall in both stores. Option 2 is to launch an own-label budget range across both stores, costing $90,000 in stock and packaging. The board must decide which option best matches how customers are now spending.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'consumer spending patterns'.
    Answer: The ways in which consumer expenditure on goods and services changes over time [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: consumer expenditure on goods and services; changes over time

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why consumer spending at Duskmere Appliances has fallen.
    Answer: Reason 1: Rising unemployment reduces household disposable incomes [k], so shoppers are trading down from $650 premium machines to $310 budget models, cutting revenue from $540,000 to $470,000 [app]. Reason 2: Lower real incomes make consumers more price-sensitive [k], shifting purchases towards rival chains running $25 weekly promotions [app].
    Keywords: Duskmere, $540,000, $470,000, $650, $310, $25, washing machines, 18 months
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rising unemployment reduces household incomes; consumers more price-sensitive / trade down | application_max_2: $650 premium machines; $310 budget models; $540,000 to $470,000; $25 weekly promotions

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Duskmere Appliances of launching the own-label budget range.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Attracts price-sensitive budget shoppers [k] who are trading down from $650 premium machines, defending the $470,000 revenue [app], which can help the business recover sales volume in both stores [an]. Advantage 2: Differentiates Duskmere from rivals who only run $25 promotions [k], giving shoppers a reason to choose its 2 stores and trust the own-label brand [app], which can increase long-term repeat sales [an].
    Keywords: own-label, $90,000, $310, $25, $470,000, budget, Duskmere
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: attracts price-sensitive budget shoppers; differentiates from rivals / builds own brand | application_max_2: trading down from $650; defending the $470,000 revenue; $25 promotions; 2 stores | analysis_max_2: recovering sales volume in both stores; increasing long-term repeat sales via own-label loyalty

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think launching the own-label budget range is a better response to changing consumer spending patterns than cutting the price of the $310 budget washing machine by 15%? Justify your answer.

--- STEM ---
Millbrook Roastery is a private limited company in Country X that roasts speciality coffee beans. It sells 250 g bags online and to 12 independent cafés, employing 9 staff.     Question: Define the term 'marketing strategy'.
    Answer: A marketing strategy is a long-term plan setting out how a business will use the marketing mix to achieve its marketing objectives, such as increasing sales, market share or customer loyalty [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a long-term plan for using the marketing mix; designed to achieve marketing objectives such as higher sales or market share

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Millbrook Roastery must respond to the supermarket's own-label launch.
    Answer: Reason 1: A clear response helps Millbrook keep customers who might switch to cheaper coffee [k], which matters because its sales have already fallen 8% in 6 months [app]. Reason 2: Responding protects Millbrook's position against a much larger rival [k], important when revenue of $340,000 and 12 café accounts are now under threat from $7 own-label bags [app].
    Keywords: own-label coffee, $7, $12, 8%, $340,000, 12 independent cafés, Millbrook Roastery
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: failing to respond risks losing customers to rivals; a response protects market share and the business's position | application_max_2: sales already fallen 8% in 6 months; supermarket own-label at $7 against Millbrook's $12; $340,000 revenue and 12 café accounts

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of choosing the premium brand image campaign.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A strong brand image lets Millbrook justify charging $12 rather than matching the $7 own-label coffee [k], keeping a higher margin on every 250 g bag sold through its 12 café customers [app], which protects the $340,000 revenue better than a price war would [an]. Advantage 2: New packaging, storytelling and a loyalty card strengthen the brand image and recognition [k], encouraging repeat buyers at a time when sales have fallen 8% [app], so customers return more often over the 12-month campaign rather than switching to the supermarket [an].
    Keywords: premium brand image, $12, $7, 250 g, loyalty card, 8%, 12
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a strong brand image supports premium pricing; packaging and loyalty schemes build recognition and repeat custom | application_max_2: charging $12 against $7 own-label coffee with loyal café customers; loyalty card aimed at repeat buyers after an 8% sales fall | analysis_max_2: protects margin and revenue better than matching the cheap rival; increases repeat purchase frequency and defends the customer base

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Millbrook Roastery should invest in the premium brand image campaign rather than the promotional pricing campaign? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Argument for: the $18,000 premium brand image campaign [k] includes new packaging, storytelling and a loyalty card aimed at repeat buyers who already accept the $12 price [app], defending Millbrook's premium position instead of chasing the supermarket's $7 own-label coffee [an]. Argument against: the promotional pricing campaign cutting the bag to $9 for 6 months [k] costs an estimated $15,000 in lost margin but could win back price-sensitive shoppers put off since sales fell 8% in 6 months [app], although margins would thin and customers may leave once prices rise again [an].     Keywords: $18,000, premium brand image, loyalty card, $12, $15,000, promotional pricing, 8%, $340,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: brand image campaigns aim to differentiate and build loyalty; promotional pricing cuts margin to stimulate short-term demand | application_max_2: $18,000 premium campaign with loyalty card against $15,000 lost margin and a $9 bag price; sales already down 8% in 6 months; $340,000 revenue at stake against $7 own-label | analysis_max_2: premium positioning defends margin and the cafe relationships; price cuts may only pull forward demand and erode long-term pricing power | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing brand investment against short-term price response; conditional judgement with a monitoring and contingency caveat

Larkfield Farm Shop is a family-run farm shop in Country X outside Wexford, selling local meat, vegetables, cheese and preserves.
