Reason 2: An online retailer can sustain discounting far better than a small shop [k], so a price war Peregrine cannot afford could drag on regardless of the 12% revenue fall already seen [app].
    Keywords: 25%, 40 bestselling, $18,000, $190,000, 12%, online retailer

--- STEM ---
Fern & Fable Bookshop is an independent bookshop in the market town of Corby Vale, Country X. It employs 9 staff and earned $620,000 in annual revenue in 2025, with its 40,000 loyalty members spending an average of $18 per visit. Owner Daniel Herrera is considering opening a second branch in the nearby town of Ashford, which has 48,000 residents and 3 existing bookshops.

Before committing, Daniel has budgeted $85,000 for market research. His assistant proposes either Option 1: a random sample of 300 names drawn from Ashford's electoral register, costing $4,800 and taking 3 weeks, or Option 2: a quota sample of 300 people interviewed on Ashford's high street, with age and gender quotas set to match the town's population, costing $2,600 and taking 1 week. The findings will be presented to his two senior managers with charts and graphs.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'random sampling'.
    Answer: Random sampling is a way of choosing people for research in which every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected [1]. Names are drawn at random from a complete list, such as an electoral register [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: every member of the population has an equal chance of selection; names drawn at random from a complete list such as an electoral register

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Fern & Fable Bookshop should carry out market research before opening in Ashford.
    Answer: Reason 1: Market research would show whether demand in Ashford can support another bookshop alongside the 3 existing bookshops [k], helping Daniel judge whether his $620,000 revenue could be repeated in a town of 48,000 people [app]. Reason 2: Research reduces the risk of wasting the $85,000 budget [k], because the findings would reveal what Ashford's 48,000 residents want before he commits to a lease or stock [app].
    Keywords: Fern & Fable Bookshop, Ashford, 48,000, 3 existing bookshops, $620,000, $85,000, Daniel
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: research reveals demand and customer preferences; research reduces the risk of a bad or costly decision | application_max_2: 48,000 residents and 3 existing bookshops; $620,000 revenue and $85,000 research budget

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems with using the quota sample instead of the random sample for Ashford.
    Answer: Problem 1: Quota sampling lets interviewers choose who to approach [k], so shoppers questioned on Ashford's high street may over-represent people free during the day and under-represent workers and commuters [app], making the results less representative of the town [an]. Problem 2: Quotas usually only match age and gender [k], not income or reading habits, so a sample of 300 high-street visitors may not reflect all 48,000 residents [app], which could lead to the wrong decision about opening the branch [an].
    Keywords: Ashford, quota sample of 300 people, high street, 48,000, 3 weeks, $2,600, 1 week
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: interviewer bias: the interviewer selects who to approach; quotas may not produce a fully representative sample | application_max_2: high street intercepts on 300 people; age and gender quotas set to match the town's population | analysis_max_2: high-street sample under-represents workers and commuters; unrepresentative data could lead to a wrong branch decision

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Daniel should choose Option 1 (the random sample) instead of Option 2 (the quota sample)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option 1 would give every adult in Ashford an equal chance of selection [k], so the sample of 300 names from the electoral register would be more representative of the 48,000 residents [app], making the findings more reliable for a decision involving the $85,000 budget [an]. However, Option 2 is cheaper and far faster [k]: interviewing 300 high-street shoppers with age and gender quotas costs $2,600 and takes 1 week, against $4,800 and 3 weeks for Option 1 [app], giving Daniel quicker answers before the lease decision is due [an]. Overall, Daniel should choose Option 1, the random sample [eval], because representativeness matters more than speed for a major commitment, and the extra $2,200 cost is small next to the $85,000 research budget [eval].
    Keywords: Option 1, Option 2, 300, electoral register, 48,000, $4,800, $2,600, $85,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection; quota sampling is quicker and cheaper but less representative | application_max_2: 300 names from Ashford's electoral register, costing $4,800 and taking 3 weeks; 300 people on Ashford's high street, costing $2,600 and taking 1 week | analysis_max_2: random sample gives more reliable, representative findings; quota sample delivers faster answers but risks bias and mis-selection | evaluation_max_2: weighs representativeness against speed and cost; reaches a justified recommendation tied to the $85,000 budget and stem figures

Sorrel & Sage Haircare is a private limited company in Country X that manufactures professional shampoos and conditioners. She must choose between Option 1: a random sample of 400 names drawn from the national register of electors, costing $3,500 and taking 4 weeks, and Option 2: a quota sample of 400 women questioned in salons, split into 3 age bands (18 to 24, 25 to 39 and 40 to 55) in the same proportions as the national population, costing $2,100 and taking 10 days. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'quota sampling'.
    Answer: Quota sampling is a method of choosing people for research where the interviewer selects people so that the sample fills set quotas for different groups [1]. The quotas reflect the proportions of those groups in the population, such as age and gender [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: interviewer selects people to fill set quotas for groups; quotas reflect the proportions of those groups in the population

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Sorrel & Sage Haircare might use quota sampling rather than random sampling.
    Answer: Reason 1: Quota sampling guarantees that key groups are represented [k], so the sample of 400 women would include all 3 age bands in the same proportions as the national population [app]. Reason 2: Quota sampling is quicker and cheaper [k], costing $2,100 and taking 10 days against $3,500 and 4 weeks for the random sample [app].
    Keywords: Sorrel & Sage Haircare, 400, 3 age bands, $2,100, 10 days, $3,500, salons, colour-protect shampoo
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quota sampling guarantees representation of key groups; quota sampling is quicker and cheaper than random sampling | application_max_2: 3 age bands matching national population proportions; $2,100 and 10 days versus $3,500 and 4 weeks

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of the colour-protect shampoo research.
    Answer: Factor 1: The size of the sample affects accuracy [k], so a sample of 400 women is likely to give more reliable results than a much smaller group [app], meaning the findings are more trustworthy for the launch decision [an]. Factor 2: Who is approached affects accuracy [k], as women questioned in salons may already buy haircare from salons and differ from other women, introducing bias [app], which could overstate demand for the colour-protect shampoo [an].
    Keywords: 400, salons, colour-protect shampoo, 3 age bands, $1.35 million, 340 hair salons, 18 to 55
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sample size influences the reliability of the findings; bias arises if the people approached are not typical of the population | application_max_2: sample of 400 women; women questioned in salons may differ from other women | analysis_max_2: larger sample gives more trustworthy findings; salon visitors may overstate demand for the new shampoo

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Priya should use the quota sample instead of the random sample? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The quota sample reaches exactly the target market [k]: questioning 400 women in salons, split across the 3 age bands in national proportions, gives relevant results for a colour-protect shampoo [app], so the launch decision would rest on the views of likely buyers [an]. However, the random sample from the national register of electors would give every woman an equal chance of selection [k], avoiding the bias of salon visitors and producing more representative data for $3,500 [app], at the cost of a 4-week delay before the launch [an]. Overall, Priya should use the quota sample [eval], because it costs $2,100, takes only 10 days, and focuses on the salon channel through which the shampoo will be sold [eval].
    Keywords: Option 1, Option 2, 400, 3 age bands, salons, $2,100, $3,500, 10 days
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quota sampling targets the intended market segments directly; random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection | application_max_2: 400 women in salons across 3 age bands in national proportions; national register of electors, costing $3,500 and taking 4 weeks | analysis_max_2: quota data reflects likely buyers and suits the launch decision; random data is less biased but delays the launch by 4 weeks | evaluation_max_2: weighs relevance and speed of quota sampling against representativeness of random sampling; recommendation justified with the stem's cost and timing figures

It employs 22 staff and generates $780,000 in annual revenue. Owner Marcus Adebayo is considering a new gluten-free range and wants to research demand first.

His daughter suggested surveying the 60 customers queuing on Saturday morning, which would cost nothing at all but would only reach loyal buyers. Marcus prefers a random sample of 250 customers from his loyalty card database of 9,500 members, sending questionnaires at a cost of $900. So far 23 out of 60 Saturday customers said they would buy gluten-free, roughly 38%, but he worries this is not representative of his wider customer base.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'bias'.
    Answer: Bias is a factor that distorts research findings away from the true picture [1]. It can arise when the sample is unrepresentative or when questions are worded to push respondents towards a particular answer [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bias distorts research findings away from the true picture; causes include unrepresentative samples and leading questions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the Saturday-morning survey may be biased.
    Answer: Reason 1: The Saturday survey only reaches loyal, regular customers [k], so the 60 people queuing on Saturday morning are not representative of the customers of all 45 shops and 12 school canteens [app]. Reason 2: The sample is self-selecting [k], as only people who happened to visit on that Saturday were asked, so the 23 out of 60 figure may not reflect the wider customer base [app].
    Keywords: Briarwood Artisan Bakery, Saturday morning, 60, 45 shops, 12 school canteens, 23 out of 60, 9,500 members
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bias arises when the sample is not representative of the population; self-selecting samples over-represent the most engaged people | application_max_2: 60 Saturday-morning queue customers versus 45 shops and 12 school canteens; 23 out of 60 interested in the gluten-free range

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of Marcus's gluten-free research.
    Answer: Factor 1: The sample size affects accuracy [k], so the views of only 60 Saturday customers are less reliable than those of a random sample of 250 from the loyalty database [app], making the roughly 38% figure less dependable [an]. Factor 2: Who is in the sample affects accuracy [k], because Saturday shoppers may be unusually loyal or health-conscious [app], unlike a random sample of the 9,500-member loyalty database, so demand for the gluten-free range could be overestimated [an].
    Keywords: 60, 250, 9,500, roughly 38%, gluten-free, $900, loyalty card database
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sample size affects the reliability of the results; sample selection affects representativeness and can introduce bias | application_max_2: 60 Saturday customers versus 250 loyalty members drawn at random; 9,500-member loyalty card database | analysis_max_2: small sample makes the roughly 38% figure less dependable; unrepresentative sample could overestimate demand for the gluten-free range

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marcus should rely on the Saturday survey instead of the loyalty-card random sample? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The Saturday survey costs nothing and gives immediate results [k], with 23 out of 60 customers, roughly 38%, already showing interest in a gluten-free range [app], which could save the bakery time and the $900 mailing cost [an]. However, the sample is small and biased towards loyal customers [k], whereas a random sample of 250 from the 9,500 loyalty members would better represent his wider customer base across 45 shops [app], giving a more accurate picture before investing in new equipment and ingredients [an]. Overall, Marcus should use the loyalty-card random sample [eval], because spending $900 now is worthwhile to avoid producing a gluten-free range that his wider customers may not buy [eval].
    Keywords: Saturday morning, 23 out of 60, roughly 38%, 250, 9,500, $900, 45 shops, gluten-free
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: small, self-selected samples are cheaper but unrepresentative; random sampling from a full customer list is more representative | application_max_2: 23 out of 60 Saturday customers, roughly 38%, interested in gluten-free; 250 random customers from 9,500 loyalty members, costing $900 | analysis_max_2: Saturday survey saves money but risks a wrong launch decision; larger random sample gives a truer picture of wider demand across 45 shops | evaluation_max_2: weighs free quick results against the value of representative data; justified recommendation tied to the $900 cost and gluten-free launch risk

--- STEM ---
Stormhaven Fitness Club is a private leisure club in Country X with 2,400 members and 35 full-time staff, generating $1.1 million a year. Membership director Ellie Kaminski is considering extending opening hours to 24 hours a day, seven days a week, at an extra staffing cost of $60,000 a year.

Ellie drafts a questionnaire asking 'Would you not love the convenience of a 24-hour gym?' and plans to hand it to 150 members as they leave a class. Her assistant suggests neutral wording ('How often would you use a 24-hour gym, if offered?') and a random sample drawn from the full membership database, costing $400 to mail. Ellie worries the owners will use the results to approve the $60,000 increase in staffing costs.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'questionnaire'.
    Answer: A questionnaire is a set of written questions used to collect information from people [1]. It is a common method of primary research and can be given to large numbers of respondents by post, online or face to face [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a set of written questions used to collect information; a primary research method usable for large numbers of respondents

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the wording of Ellie's question matters.
    Answer: Reason 1: Leading questions suggest the answer the researcher wants [k], so 'Would you not love the convenience of a 24-hour gym?' pushes members towards a yes [app]. Reason 2: Loaded wording produces unreliable data [k], meaning the 150 responses collected may not reflect true member demand for the 24-hour option [app].
    Keywords: Stormhaven Fitness Club, 24-hour gym, 150, 2,400, $60,000, questionnaire, Ellie Kaminski
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: leading questions push respondents towards a desired answer; loaded wording makes responses unreliable | application_max_2: 'Would you not love the convenience of a 24-hour gym?'; 150 responses planned

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two factors that could make the questionnaire results inaccurate.
    Answer: Factor 1: Leading questions bias the answers [k], so members asked 'Would you not love the convenience of a 24-hour gym?' may agree to please the staff, inflating apparent demand for 24-hour opening [app], which could persuade the owners to approve $60,000 extra staffing costs [an]. Factor 2: Who is asked affects the accuracy [k], because questioning only members leaving a class at one time of day may over-represent certain groups and miss many of the 2,400 members [app], so the results may not generalise to the whole membership [an].
    Keywords: 24-hour gym, 150, 2,400, $60,000, $400, questionnaire, Ellie Kaminski
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: leading questions bias responses in favour of a preferred answer; an unrepresentative sample produces findings that do not generalise | application_max_2: 'Would you not love the convenience of a 24-hour gym?'; 150 members leaving a class, from a membership of 2,400 | analysis_max_2: inflated demand could trigger a $60,000 staffing decision; findings may not generalise to the whole membership

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the club should use Ellie's questionnaire as drafted instead of the assistant's revised version? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Ellie's version is simple, needs no postage and is quick to hand out as classes end [k], so it could gather 150 responses almost free before the owners' meeting [app], letting the club act fast on the $60,000 staffing decision [an]. However, the leading wording and a sample of only gym-leavers would bias the results [k], whereas the assistant's neutral wording mailed to a random sample of all 2,400 members would cost $400 but produce far more trustworthy data [app], so the owners would not be misled into spending $60,000 a year on opening hours few members use [an]. Overall, the club should use the assistant's revised questionnaire [eval], because accurate data is worth the extra $400 when $60,000 a year in staffing costs is at stake [eval].
    Keywords: Ellie, 150, 2,400, $400, $60,000, 24-hour gym, questionnaire, random sample
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: neutral, non-leading wording produces more reliable data; random samples are more representative than convenient ones | application_max_2: Ellie's leading question handed to 150 members as they leave a class; assistant's neutral wording mailed to a random sample of all 2,400 members, costing $400 | analysis_max_2: Ellie's version is fast but biased and could mislead the owners; the assistant's version gives trustworthy data to inform the $60,000 decision | evaluation_max_2: weighs speed and zero mailing cost against accuracy and representativeness; recommendation justified by the $400 cost against $60,000 at stake

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the timing of Snowdrift's market research matters.
    Answer: Reason 1: Consumer behaviour changes with the seasons [k], so a January survey in a covered market would understate demand from people buying ice cream at the beach in July [app]. Reason 2: Research at the wrong time can mislead [k], as the 22% of 200 shoppers (44 people) found in winter may be far lower than peak summer demand for a new vegan gelato [app].
    Keywords: Snowdrift Ice Cream Co, January, July, 200, 22%, 44, vegan gelato
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: consumer behaviour and demand vary with the seasons; mis-timed research can understate peak demand | application_max_2: January survey in a covered market; 22% of 200 shoppers, 44 people, low winter demand

  Qc [6 marks]

    Keywords: January, July, 200, 250, 180 shops, 25 hotels, covered market, bar chart
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: timing and location of the survey shape who responds; sample size affects the reliability of the findings | application_max_2: 200 shoppers in a covered market in January versus 250 beach-goers in July; 180 shops and 25 hotels supplied by Snowdrift | analysis_max_2: unrepresentative winter sample biases the demand estimate; bar chart may misjudge interest in the vegan gelato

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sofia should launch the vegan gelato at Easter based on the January survey instead of repeating the research in July? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Launching at Easter would catch the spring sales period [k], and the January survey shows 22% of 200 shoppers, 44 people, interested in the vegan gelato [app], which could give Snowdrift a first-mover advantage in its 180 shops and 25 hotels [an]. However, the survey was taken in winter when ice cream demand is lowest [k], so a repeat survey of 250 beach-goers and market-stall visitors in July would cost $1,300 but reflect true peak-season demand [app], reducing the risk of the Easter launch flopping [an].     Keywords: Easter, January, July, 200, 22%, 44, $1,300, vegan gelato
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: timing affects the validity of research findings; seasonal products need season-specific demand data | application_max_2: 22% of 200 shoppers, 44 people, interested in vegan gelato; repeat survey of 250 beach-goers in July, costing $1,300, delaying launch by 5 months | analysis_max_2: early Easter launch captures spring demand but risks overestimating it; July survey reflects peak-season demand and reduces launch risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs speed to market against the accuracy of July data; recommendation justified by the seasonal nature of ice cream demand

--- STEM ---
Hazel & Wren Furniture Co is a family-run furniture retailer in Country X with 4 showrooms, 64 staff and $2.3 million in annual revenue. The directors are preparing this year's customer survey results for the board. Of 500 customers asked why they chose the store, 42% came for price, 27% for quality, 19% for delivery speed and 12% for design.

A junior manager has drawn a line graph of the percentages, while the senior manager proposes a bar chart. The finance director wants a table of the raw numbers: 210 for price, 135 for quality, 95 for delivery speed and 60 for design, and wonders whether to cut delivery charges. The board must agree on the presentation method at Friday's meeting before approving the $40,000 budget for a new delivery fleet.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'sample size'.
    Answer: Sample size is the number of people included in a research sample [1]. Generally, the larger the sample, the more representative and reliable the findings are likely to be [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the number of people included in a research sample; larger samples tend to be more representative and reliable

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the choice between a bar chart and a line graph matters for these results.
    Answer: Reason 1: A bar chart is best for comparing separate categories [k], so price, quality, delivery speed and design can be compared side by side from the 500 responses [app]. Reason 2: A line graph implies a trend over time [k], so placing 42%, 27%, 19% and 12% on a line could suggest a progression that does not exist between four separate reasons [app].
    Keywords: Hazel & Wren Furniture Co, bar chart, line graph, 500, 42%, 27%, 19%, 12%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bar charts compare separate categories; line graphs imply a trend over time | application_max_2: four separate reasons from 500 customers; 42%, 27%, 19% and 12% are categories, not a time series

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways tables and charts could help the board decide about the delivery fleet.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A bar chart shows the comparison at a glance [k], so the board can instantly see that 210 customers chose price against only 95 citing delivery speed [app], which questions whether delivery speed justifies the $40,000 fleet budget [an]. Benefit 2: A table of raw numbers adds precision [k], showing 210, 135, 95 and 60 exactly rather than percentages alone [app], so directors can verify the figures before allocating the budget or cutting delivery charges [an].
    Keywords: bar chart, 210, 95, 135, 60, $40,000, delivery fleet
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: charts communicate comparisons quickly at a glance; tables present exact raw figures for verification | application_max_2: 210 for price, 135 for quality, 95 for delivery speed and 60 for design; $40,000 delivery fleet budget | analysis_max_2: chart reveals delivery speed is a lower priority than price; table allows directors to verify figures before committing $40,000

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the board should present the results as a bar chart instead of a line graph? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A bar chart fits categorical data [k]: the four reasons, price 42%, quality 27%, delivery speed 19% and design 12%, are distinct categories, not points in a sequence [app], so the board would not misread the figures as a trend and could weigh delivery charges fairly [an]. However, a line graph might look neater in a presentation to non-specialists [k], since the values fall in an tidy sequence from 42% down to 12% [app], but it still implies change over time that does not exist and could confuse the decision on the $40,000 delivery fleet [an]. Overall, the board should use the bar chart [eval], supported by the finance director's table of 210, 135, 95 and 60 for exact figures [eval].
    Keywords: bar chart, line graph, 42%, 27%, 19%, 12%, $40,000, table
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bar charts correctly present categorical comparisons; line graphs are designed for trends over time | application_max_2: price 42%, quality 27%, delivery speed 19% and design 12%; raw figures 210, 135, 95 and 60 in a table | analysis_max_2: bar chart avoids the false implication of a trend; line graph could confuse the fleet and delivery-charges decision | evaluation_max_2: weighs visual simplicity against data accuracy; recommendation justified with stem figures and the role of the table

  Qb [4 marks]

--- STEM ---
The Arncliffe Bay Hotel is a private limited company in Country X with 120 rooms and 48 staff, generating $2.6 million a year. General manager Carla Jensen wants to understand why occupancy fell from 74% to 61% last year, a drop of 13 percentage points, before the summer season.

Option 1 is an online survey emailed to 2,000 past guests, with a 15% expected response rate (300 replies) at a cost of $300. Option 2 is observation with short interviews of 120 departing guests over 4 weeks, at a cost of $1,900, giving an instant impression of guest opinions but capturing mostly leisure guests in the high season. Carla will present the findings to the owners as a table and bar chart.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'observation'.
    Answer: Observation is a method of primary research in which researchers watch how people behave rather than asking them questions [1]. It records real behaviour, such as what customers choose or how they move around a business [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: researchers watch how people behave rather than asking questions; records real behaviour to inform decisions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the expected 15% response rate matters.
    Answer: Reason 1: A low response rate shrinks the sample [k], so only about 300 of the 2,000 emailed guests may reply, which weakens the reliability of the findings [app]. Reason 2: A low response rate may bias the results [k], as only guests motivated enough to reply answer, so their views may not represent all past guests of the Arncliffe Bay Hotel [app].
    Keywords: The Arncliffe Bay Hotel, 2,000, 15%, 300, $2.6 million, 74%, 61%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: low response rate reduces the effective sample size; respondents may be unrepresentative, introducing bias | application_max_2: about 300 of 2,000 emailed guests expected to reply; Arncliffe Bay Hotel's 120 rooms and falling occupancy

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of either option.
    Answer: Factor 1: Sample size affects reliability [k], so 300 online replies give more data than 120 departing-guest interviews, though the smaller sample allows deeper questions [app], influencing how confidently the owners interpret the fall from 74% to 61% [an]. Factor 2: Who is included affects accuracy [k], as the interviews capture mainly leisure guests while the online survey hears only from past guests bothered to reply [app], so both samples are biased in different ways and neither fully represents everyone who might book [an].
    Keywords: 300, 120, 74%, 61%, leisure guests, 2,000, bar chart
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: larger samples generally give more reliable findings; biased samples distort findings and do not generalise | application_max_2: 300 online replies versus 120 departing-guest interviews; interviews mostly capture leisure guests | analysis_max_2: sample size shapes confidence in interpreting the 74% to 61% fall; each option is biased differently, so neither is fully representative

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Carla should use the online survey instead of observing and interviewing departing guests? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The online survey is far cheaper and reaches more people [k]: 300 replies from 2,000 past guests at a cost of $300 would give a broad spread of views on why occupancy fell [app], letting the owners analyse trends across room types and seasons before the summer [an]. However, option 2's observation of departing guests shows real, immediate behaviour and detail [k], interviewing 120 leisure guests would reveal in depth why they rated the hotel as they did [app], whereas the 15% online response rate risks hearing only from already-disappointed guests and misdiagnosing the 74% to 61% drop [an]. Overall, Carla should use the online survey [eval], because 300 responses at $300 give the widest and cheapest evidence, and the owners can always commission follow-up interviews if the table and bar chart raise questions [eval].
    Keywords: online survey, 2,000, 300, $300, 120, $1,900, 74%, 61%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: online surveys are cheap and reach large numbers; observation and interviews yield richer but narrower evidence | application_max_2: 300 replies expected from 2,000 past guests, costing $300; 120 departing leisure guests observed over 4 weeks, costing $1,900 | analysis_max_2: online breadth supports trend analysis across the whole past customer base; low response rate risks hearing only from disappointed guests | evaluation_max_2: weighs breadth and cost of online data against depth of interviews; recommendation justified with stem figures and practical follow-up

Focus groups with 24 customers rated the sample jeans 8 out of 10 for quality and said they would pay $95. Till data shows denim sells 9,000 units a year at $60, generating $540,000 a year. A survey of 600 customers found 61%, 366 people, interested, though a recent industry report said only 12% of shoppers actually buy sustainable denim. Lena must choose between a full range launch costing $120,000 and a 3-store trial costing $45,000.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'focus group'.
    Answer: A focus group is a small group of people brought together to discuss a product, advertisement or idea [1]. A moderator leads the discussion so the business can gather detailed opinions and reactions [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a small group discussing a product, advertisement or idea; led by a moderator to gather detailed opinions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Birch & Bloom Clothing Co used focus groups for the denim launch.
    Answer: Reason 1: Focus groups give detailed qualitative feedback [k], so the 24 customers could explain in depth why they rated the sample jeans 8 out of 10 for quality [app]. Reason 2: They reveal attitudes a survey cannot [k], as the discussion showed the customers would pay $95 a pair for recycled cotton denim [app].
    Keywords: Birch & Bloom Clothing Co, 24, 8 out of 10, $95, 9,000, $540,000, focus groups
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: focus groups provide detailed qualitative opinions; focus groups reveal attitudes and motivations surveys cannot | application_max_2: 24 customers rated the sample jeans 8 out of 10; customers said they would pay $95 a pair

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Lena could use the research findings to decide on the launch.
    Answer: Use 1: The findings can test demand before committing [k], as 61% of 600 customers, 366 people, interested and the 8 out of 10 focus-group rating suggest genuine interest [app], though the industry report's 12% actual buying rate warns against over-confidence [an]. Use 2: The findings can shape the launch approach [k], comparing the $120,000 full launch with the $45,000 3-store trial against denim's current 9,000 units at $60, or $540,000 a year [app], so Lena can judge whether a limited trial protects the business if sustainable denim disappoints [an].
    Keywords: 600, 61%, 366, 12%, $120,000, $45,000, $540,000, 9,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: research findings can test demand before a costly decision; research findings can inform the scale and approach of a launch | application_max_2: 61% of 600 customers, 366 people, interested; 12% industry purchase rate; $120,000 full launch versus $45,000 3-store trial; 9,000 units at $60 = $540,000 | analysis_max_2: gap between stated interest and actual buying warns against over-confidence; a limited trial de-risks the launch decision

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Lena should commit to the full range launch instead of the 3-store trial? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A full launch would seize first-mover advantage [k]: 61% of 600 surveyed customers, 366 people, showed interest and focus groups rated the jeans 8 out of 10 at $95 a pair [app], so an immediate nationwide launch across 7 stores could capture autumn demand before competitors copy the range [an]. However, the industry report suggests only 12% of shoppers actually buy sustainable denim [k], so the $45,000 3-store trial lets Lena test real sales before committing $120,000 [app], protecting the $540,000 current denim business while gauging true demand [an]. Overall, Lena should run the 3-store trial first [eval], because the gap between 61% stated interest and 12% actual buying makes a cautious launch the safer use of the budget [eval].
    Keywords: full range launch, 3-store trial, 600, 61%, 12%, $120,000, $45,000, 8 out of 10
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: research evidence can support a full launch decision; trial launches reduce risk when evidence is uncertain | application_max_2: 61% of 600 customers, 366 people, interested; jeans rated 8 out of 10 at $95; 3-store trial costing $45,000 versus full launch at $120,000 | analysis_max_2: full launch could capture autumn demand ahead of competitors; trial de-risks the decision and protects the existing $540,000 denim sales | evaluation_max_2: weighs speed and first-mover gain against risk and evidence quality; recommendation justified by the 61% interest versus 12% purchase gap

--- STEM ---
Redfield Energy Drinks is a private limited company founded 6 years ago by twin sisters Priya and Nina Rao. It produces a natural mango and lime energy drink sold in 1,800 convenience stores across Country X, employing 46 full-time staff at a bottling plant. Annual revenue reached $3.6 million last year, up 8% on the previous year, and the drink holds 9% of the youth energy drink market behind two multinational rivals.

The marketing director has $120,000 for the next 12 months and must choose between sponsoring the Country X national basketball league for $100,000, with logos on courtside boards and team shirts for one season, or a six-month social media campaign costing $110,000 aimed at 18-24 year-olds. A smaller trial of the sponsorship raised brand awareness by 14% in the capital city.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'sponsorship'.
    Answer: A business paying to support an event, team or individual in exchange for displaying its name or logo to a wide audience, gaining publicity and brand awareness [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: paying to associate the business name with an event, team or individual; gaining publicity and brand awareness from the association

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Redfield Energy Drinks of sponsoring the national basketball league rather than running social media adverts.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Sponsorship provides repeated exposure of the Redfield name [k] to 18-24 year-old basketball fans through courtside boards and team shirts across one season [app]. Benefit 2: Association with the national league gives the drink a healthy, energetic image [k] that appeals to the young buyers it must win over from two multinational rivals [app].
    Keywords: Redfield Energy Drinks, $100,000, national basketball league, 1,800 convenience stores, 9%, 14%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sponsorship gives repeated, wide exposure to the brand name; association with an event or league builds a positive image | application_max_2: courtside boards and team shirts reaching fans across a season; winning young buyers from two multinational rivals

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why sponsorship may not increase sales for Redfield Energy Drinks.
    Answer: Reason 1: The $100,000 fee uses most of the $120,000 budget [k], leaving only $20,000 for everything else that drives purchase decisions [app], so awareness may rise without enough in-store support to convert it into sales [an]. Reason 2: Sponsorship reaches mainly basketball fans [k], a narrower audience than the 1,800 convenience stores across Country X [app], so many young buyers outside the sport never see the logo and buying habits do not change [an].
    Keywords: $100,000, $120,000, national basketball league, 1,800 convenience stores, 18-24, 9%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sponsorship consumes most of the promotional budget; sponsorship reaches a limited, self-selected audience | application_max_2: $100,000 of the $120,000 budget leaves $20,000 for other uses; basketball fans are narrower than 1,800 convenience stores nationwide | analysis_max_2: awareness may rise without converting into sales without in-store support; non-fans never see the logo so buying habits do not change

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redfield Energy Drinks should sponsor the national basketball league? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The sponsorship would build positive brand awareness [k] among 18-24 year-old fans through courtside boards and shirts all season [app], helping Redfield close the gap on two multinational rivals at 9% market share [an]. However, the $110,000 social media campaign [app] would reach 18-24 year-olds precisely for six months with clicks and sales tracked directly [k], converting awareness into purchases faster [an]. Overall, Redfield should sponsor the basketball league [eval] because the 14% awareness lift shown in the trial is hard evidence rather than speculation, and an image built over a season outlasts a six-month advert run [eval].
    Keywords: $100,000, $110,000, 18-24, 14%, 9%, national basketball league
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sponsorship builds brand awareness and positive image; social media advertising allows precise targeting and measurable results | application_max_2: courtside boards and shirts reaching 18-24 year-olds all season; $110,000 six-month social media campaign targeting 18-24 year-olds | analysis_max_2: awareness may help Redfield take share from two multinational rivals; tracked clicks and sales may convert awareness into purchases faster | evaluation_max_2: weighs trial evidence of a 14% awareness lift against social media measurability; justified recommendation to sponsor the league based on durable image and hard evidence

--- STEM ---
Marlowe & Bright Biscuits is a private limited company that has baked cream crackers and fruit biscuits in the eastern region for 9 years. It employs 58 factory staff and supplies 320 supermarkets across Country X. Annual sales revenue was $5.4 million last year, but a social media complaint about an underweight pack spread after a customer posted photos, and sales fell 11% in the last quarter. The affected batch was certified at 200g but averaged 187g.

The managing director has $25,000 to repair the company's image before the holiday season. Option one is a public relations campaign — a factory open day for 40 food retailers and journalists plus a press release, costing $16,000. Option two is a newspaper advertising campaign across 8 regional papers costing $22,000. The board also wants the pack-weight complaint investigated while the campaign runs.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'public relations'.
    Answer: The part of marketing that builds a favourable image and goodwill with the public through unpaid coverage such as press events, open days and news stories, rather than paid advertising [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: building a favourable image and goodwill with the public; gaining publicity through events, press coverage and press releases, not paid adverts

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Marlowe & Bright Biscuits of the public relations campaign rather than newspaper advertising.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Coverage earned through the open day and press release carries more credibility than paid advertising [k] because 40 food retailers and journalists would experience the bakery first-hand [app]. Benefit 2: The campaign costs $16,000 against $22,000 for newspapers [k], saving $6,000 while reaching the decision-makers behind 320 supermarket listings [app].
    Keywords: public relations campaign, $16,000, $22,000, 40 food retailers, press release, 320 supermarkets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: earned coverage is more credible than paid advertising; public relations is cheaper than press advertising | application_max_2: 40 food retailers and journalists experiencing the bakery first-hand; $16,000 PR cost versus $22,000 newspaper adverts, reaching 320 supermarket decision-makers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks to Marlowe & Bright Biscuits of relying on public relations to repair its image.
    Answer: Drawback 1: Marlowe & Bright cannot control what journalists write [k] after the open day [app], so coverage could rehash the 187g pack-weight story instead of celebrating the bakery, deepening distrust rather than repairing it [an]. Drawback 2: Public relations reaches only the 40 attending retailers and journalists [k] compared with 8 regional papers [app], so most supermarket buyers never hear the company's side and sales may keep falling [an].
    Keywords: public relations campaign, open day, 187g, 40 food retailers, 8 regional papers, 320 supermarkets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a business cannot control what journalists publish; public relations reaches a limited, targeted audience only | application_max_2: open day coverage could rehash the 187g pack-weight story; only 40 attendees reached versus 8 regional papers and 320 supermarkets | analysis_max_2: uncontrolled coverage could deepen distrust instead of repairing the image; limited reach means most buyers never hear the company's side, so sales keep falling

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marlowe & Bright Biscuits should run the public relations campaign rather than the newspaper advertising? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The PR campaign would rebuild credibility [k] by letting 40 food retailers and journalists see the bakery and the 200g pack quality first-hand [app], which could win back the 320 supermarket listings lost after an 11% fall in quarterly sales [an]. However, newspaper advertising across 8 regional papers [app] would reach far more of the public at once with a message the company fully controls [k], though at $22,000 it costs $6,000 more than the $16,000 PR option [an]. Overall, Marlowe & Bright should choose the PR campaign [eval] because trust, not awareness, is the problem this 187g batch created, so third-party voices will persuade sceptical shoppers better than paid adverts [eval].
    Keywords: $16,000, $22,000, 40 food retailers, 8 regional papers, 11%, 187g
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: public relations rebuilds credibility through third-party endorsement; paid advertising gives wide reach and full control of the message | application_max_2: 40 food retailers and journalists seeing 200g pack quality first-hand; 8 regional papers reaching far more of the public for $22,000 | analysis_max_2: credible coverage could win back 320 supermarket listings lost after the 11% fall; advertising costs $6,000 more but delivers controlled, wider exposure | evaluation_max_2: weighs controlled wide reach against credible third-party persuasion; justified recommendation to choose PR because the problem is trust, not awareness

--- STEM ---
Mango Flash Snacks is a private limited company producing baked plantain chips for 4 years, sold in 850 corner shops and school canteens across Country X. It employs 23 workers and generated $880,000 in revenue last year. Packets retail at $1.50. Owner Dani Reyes plans to launch a chilli-mango flavour aimed at 13-19 year-olds this spring and has set a target of 60,000 extra packets in the first month.

The launch budget is $45,000. Option one is a 6-week viral video campaign: a 30-second clip of friends trading Mango Flash packets costing $15,000 to produce, seeded to 4 student influencers with 2.3 million combined followers. Option two is a 3-week evening television campaign costing $40,000, expected to reach 1.1 million viewers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'viral marketing'.
    Answer: A promotional method where a message, usually a short video, spreads rapidly from person to person online as viewers choose to share it, giving wide reach at very low cost [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a message spreads rapidly online from person to person; viewers choose to share it, giving wide reach at low cost

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Mango Flash Snacks of the viral video campaign rather than television advertising.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Viral video costs only $15,000 [k], one third of the $45,000 budget, far below the $40,000 television alternative, so the rest can fund stock and distribution [app]. Benefit 2: If viewers share the clip it spreads from person to person [k], reaching 13-19 year-olds through the 4 student influencers' 2.3 million combined followers [app].
    Keywords: $15,000, $45,000, 2.3 million, 4 student influencers, 13-19 year-olds, chilli-mango
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: viral video is low cost compared with television advertising; pass-along sharing can multiply the audience exponentially | application_max_2: $15,000 versus $40,000 leaves budget for stock and distribution; reach aimed at 13-19 year-olds via 4 student influencers with 2.3 million followers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks for Mango Flash Snacks of choosing the viral video campaign.
    Answer: Risk 1: Success depends on viewers choosing to share [k], so if the 30-second clip fails to engage, reach stays far below the 2.3 million influencer followers [app], and the spring target of 60,000 extra packets may be missed entirely [an]. Risk 2: A viral message can spread for the wrong reasons [k]; a clip misread as mocking students could damage the brand with exactly the 13-19 year-olds it wants to recruit [app], turning a launch into a costly public relations problem [an].
    Keywords: $15,000, 2.3 million, 30-second clip, 60,000, 13-19 year-olds, 4 student influencers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sharing is voluntary, so reach is uncertain; viral content can be misread and backfire | application_max_2: clip may fall flat with 2.3 million influencer followers; misread clip could offend the 13-19 year-old target audience | analysis_max_2: 60,000 extra packet target may be missed entirely; a backlash would turn the launch into a public relations problem

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Mango Flash Snacks should run the viral video campaign? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The viral campaign would cost $15,000 [app] and its pass-along nature suits the 13-19 year-olds who live on social media [k], so a genuinely funny clip could reach far beyond the 2.3 million influencer followers at almost no extra cost [an]. However, television for $40,000 guarantees reach to 1.1 million evening viewers [app] with a message the company fully controls [k], de-risking the spring launch of the chilli-mango flavour [an]. Overall, Mango Flash should run the viral clip and bank the $25,000 saving [eval] because the target audience lives online and the saving can fund launch stock and school canteen sampling [eval].
    Keywords: $15,000, $40,000, 2.3 million, 1.1 million, 13-19 year-olds, 60,000 extra packets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: viral marketing suits digitally native young audiences at low cost; television advertising guarantees reach with full message control | application_max_2: $15,000 viral budget versus $40,000 television reach of 1.1 million viewers; 13-19 year-old social media audience for the chilli-mango launch | analysis_max_2: a shareable clip could multiply reach beyond the 2.3 million followers; television de-risks the launch with controlled, guaranteed exposure | evaluation_max_2: weighs uncertain pass-along reach against guaranteed controlled exposure; justified recommendation to run the viral campaign and bank the $25,000 saving

--- STEM ---
Scarlet Meadow Fashion is a private limited company founded 8 years ago, designing streetwear for 18-30 year-olds. It runs 5 stores in Country X, employs 64 staff and generated $7.2 million in revenue last year. The brand won a national design award in 2024. The directors want to sell online in two neighbouring markets, Country V and Country W, where online clothing sales are growing 15% a year among 18-30 year-olds.

The marketing manager has $150,000 and must choose between one global mega-influencer campaign costing $130,000 run identically in both countries, or local campaigns costing $140,000 in total — two regional celebrities plus a launch event in each capital city. Country V buyers trust local celebrity endorsement, while Country W has stricter advertising rules requiring pre-clearance of promotional content.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'advertising'.
    Answer: Paid-for promotion of a product or brand through media such as television, newspapers or social media, designed to inform or persuade customers to buy [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: paid-for promotion of a product or brand; designed to inform or persuade customers to buy

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Scarlet Meadow Fashion of the global mega-influencer campaign.
    Answer: Advantage 1: One campaign is produced and purchased once [k], costing $130,000 to cover Country V and Country W instead of two separate local shoots [app]. Advantage 2: A single mega-influencer with a huge following gives instant, massive reach [k], building rapid awareness among the 18-30 year-olds the brand wants in both growing markets [app].
    Keywords: $130,000, $150,000, Country V, Country W, mega-influencer, 18-30 year-olds
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: one global campaign is cheaper and simpler than running two local campaigns; a mega-influencer gives instant, massive reach | application_max_2: $130,000 covering both Country V and Country W instead of two local shoots; fast awareness among 18-30 year-olds in both growing markets

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks for Scarlet Meadow Fashion of the global mega-influencer campaign.
    Answer: Drawback 1: An identical advert ignores local differences [k]; Country V buyers trust local celebrity endorsement [app], so a foreign mega-influencer may feel irrelevant and fail to persuade them to buy [an]. Drawback 2: Country W requires pre-clearance of promotional content [k]; a global campaign shot without local approval could be rejected or banned there [app], wasting most of the $130,000 before a single online sale is made [an].
    Keywords: Country V, Country W, $130,000, pre-clearance, local celebrity endorsement, mega-influencer
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a standardised campaign ignores local preferences and culture; strict advertising rules abroad can block foreign campaigns | application_max_2: Country V buyers trust local celebrity endorsement over foreign faces; Country W requires pre-clearance that a global shoot may not have | analysis_max_2: the foreign face may fail to persuade Country V buyers to purchase; pre-clearance failure could waste the $130,000 before any sale is made

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Scarlet Meadow Fashion should run the global mega-influencer campaign or the two local campaigns? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The global campaign would cost $130,000 [app] and give one consistent brand message across both markets [k], saving $10,000 against the local option and simplifying management [an]. However, the local campaigns at $140,000 [app] use trusted regional celebrities and launch events [k], matching Country V's preference for local faces and clearing Country W's pre-clearance rules, which should convert awareness into faster online sales [an]. Overall, Scarlet Meadow should run the two local campaigns [eval] because the extra $10,000 buys legal certainty in Country W and credibility in Country V, the two barriers most likely to block a $7.2 million brand breaking into these markets [eval].
    Keywords: $130,000, $140,000, Country V, Country W, $150,000, pre-clearance
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a global campaign gives a consistent message across markets at lower cost; local campaigns match local tastes and legal rules | application_max_2: $130,000 global campaign versus $140,000 local campaigns; regional celebrities and launch events matching Country V and clearing Country W rules | analysis_max_2: the global option saves $10,000 and simplifies management; local campaigns should convert awareness into faster online sales | evaluation_max_2: weighs $10,000 saving and consistency against legal certainty and local credibility; justified recommendation to run the two local campaigns

Alderwick Preserves Co is a partnership of two brothers, Theo and Jonah Marchetti, making rose-hip and quince jams by hand since 2015. A distributor in neighbouring Country V offers to stock 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 per jar if Alderwick meets Country V food-safety labelling within 6 months, with the contract running for 3 years.     Question: Define 'export'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: selling goods produced in the home country to overseas customers; extending the market beyond domestic borders

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two opportunities for Alderwick Preserves Co of exporting to Country V.
    Answer: Opportunity 1: The order would add sales beyond the stagnant domestic market [k] — 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 is about $153,000 of new revenue [app]. Opportunity 2: Entering Country V spreads risk [k], so if two domestic supermarket chains force the 12% discount, the brothers still have a second market to sell into [app].
    Keywords: 30,000 jars, $5.10, 12% price discount, Country V, 2%, 95,000 jars
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exporting adds sales beyond the domestic market; selling into a second country spreads risk | application_max_2: 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 is about $153,000 of new revenue; a second market cushions the 12% discount demanded by supermarket chains

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Alderwick Preserves Co of exporting to Country V.

Problem 2: Freight adds $24,000 a year [k] and the $5.10 jar price is $1.30 below the domestic $6.40 [app], squeezing margins so the order may add little profit even when the factory is full [an].
    Keywords: $9,000, $24,000, $5.10, $6.40, 6 months, Country V
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: export markets impose labelling and certification requirements; freight costs and lower overseas prices squeeze margins | application_max_2: $9,000 certification and 6-month labelling deadline for Country V; $5.10 export price versus $6.40 domestic, plus $24,000 freight | analysis_max_2: failure to certify wastes the fee and strains cash flow; thin margins mean the order may add little profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Alderwick Preserves Co should start exporting to Country V? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Exporting would open a Country V market while domestic sales crawl at 2% [k], with 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 worth about $153,000 even after $24,000 freight — roughly $129,000 before certification [app]. However, the $5.10 price is $1.30 below domestic $6.40 [app] and the $9,000 certification carries a real risk of rejection within 6 months [k], so refusal would waste the fee and six months of planning [an], while the domestic slide continues unchecked [an]. Overall, Alderwick should accept the export order [eval] because a second market reduces dependence on supermarkets demanding 12% discounts, and the numbers still add up after certification [eval].
    Keywords: $5.10, $6.40, $24,000, $9,000, 30,000 jars, 12%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exporting opens overseas markets when domestic demand stagnates; certification deadlines and lower export prices carry real risk | application_max_2: $153,000 of export revenue at $5.10 after $24,000 freight; $5.10 price is $1.30 below domestic $6.40 | analysis_max_2: roughly $129,000 remains before certification; rejected paperwork would waste the $9,000 certification fee | evaluation_max_2: weighs overseas growth and reduced supermarket dependence against price and certification risk; justified recommendation to export because the numbers work after costs

--- STEM ---
Halloran Cycle Works is a private limited company founded 10 years ago by Sofia Lindqvist, producing electric cargo bicycles for delivery riders. It employs 72 workers, generated $9.8 million in revenue last year and sells each bike at $4,100, with domestic demand now flat. Country W, where e-bike deliveries grew 22% last year, has no domestic producer and the boom is driven by courier firms switching from vans to cargo bikes.

The board wants to enter Country W and must choose between a joint venture with Weidler Logistics, a local company with 40 depots, costing $1.2 million for a 50% share, or building its own assembly plant in Country W for $3.5 million. Country W also charges a 12% tariff on imported bicycles, ruling out simple exporting.

    Question: Define 'joint venture'.
    Answer: Two or more businesses agreeing to work together on one project or market, sharing capital, risks, decision-making and profits [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: two or more businesses working together on one project or market; sharing capital, risks, control and profits

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two opportunities for Halloran Cycle Works of entering Country W through a joint venture with Weidler Logistics.
    Answer: Opportunity 1: The joint venture gives instant local knowledge and distribution [k] through Weidler's 40 depots across Country W [app]. Opportunity 2: Sharing the $1.2 million cost means half the capital at risk [k] instead of $3.5 million for its own plant, preserving cash for product development [app].
    Keywords: $1.2 million, $3.5 million, 40 depots, Weidler Logistics, Country W, 22%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a joint venture provides local knowledge and distribution channels; sharing capital halves the financial risk of entry | application_max_2: Weidler's 40 depots give nationwide distribution in Country W; $1.2 million for 50% versus $3.5 million for its own assembly plant

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Halloran Cycle Works of entering Country W.
    Answer: Problem 1: A 12% tariff on imported bicycles [k] makes shipping finished bikes from Country X costly [app], raising the retail price and dampening demand among cost-conscious delivery riders [an]. Problem 2: Sharing a joint venture halves control [k]; Halloran must agree every major decision with Weidler Logistics [app], risking slow decisions and erosion of the 10-year brand it built on technical quality [an].
    Keywords: 12% tariff, Weidler Logistics, $1.2 million, $3.5 million, Country W, $4,100
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: import tariffs raise the cost of selling abroad; joint ventures mean shared control and compromise | application_max_2: 12% tariff on imported bicycles entering Country W; every major decision must be agreed with Weidler Logistics | analysis_max_2: higher retail prices dampen demand among delivery riders; slow decisions and compromised control could erode the 10-year brand

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Halloran Cycle Works should enter Country W through a joint venture rather than build its own plant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The joint venture would halve the capital at risk — $1.2 million for 50% [app] — and bring instant local knowledge [k] through Weidler's 40 depots [app], letting Halloran enter the 22% growth market quickly before Weidler's rivals move [an]. However, building its own plant for $3.5 million keeps full control and all the profits [k], while a partner might push its own fleet priorities and erode Halloran's 10-year brand reputation [an]. Overall, Halloran should choose the joint venture [eval] because with a 12% import tariff ruling out simple exporting, shared risk and local expertise are worth more than owning every profit [eval].
    Keywords: $1.2 million, $3.5 million, 40 depots, 22%, 12% tariff, Weidler Logistics

Opportunity 2: Bellano knows Country S labelling and retail networks [k], so the cream can reach buyers immediately, earning 7% royalties on forecast sales of 120,000 tubes a year [app].
    Keywords: $70,000, Bellano Cosmetics, 7% royalties, 120,000 tubes, Country S, $8.00
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: licensing avoids the capital cost of direct exporting; the local licensee provides market knowledge and distribution | application_max_2: no $70,000 set-up or shipping documentation needed for Country S; 7% royalties on forecast sales of 120,000 tubes a year

  Qc [6 marks]

Drawback 2: Royalties of 7% [k] yield only $67,200 a year on sales of 120,000 tubes at $8.00 [app], far below the margin Fernwell earns on its own 260,000 tubes, limiting the upside of going overseas [an].
    Keywords: 7%, $8.00, 120,000 tubes, 260,000 tubes, Bellano Cosmetics, 2017
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the licensor loses control of quality and brand presentation; royalties are a small share of overseas sales value | application_max_2: dilution risk to the shea-butter formula and its 2017 reputation; 7% of 120,000 tubes at $8.00 yields about $67,200 a year | analysis_max_2: brand damage would hit loyal buyers in both markets; the royalty stream limits the financial upside of overseas expansion

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fernwell Skincare should license the cream to Bellano Cosmetics rather than export directly? Justify your answer.

    Keywords: $70,000, 120,000 tubes, $8.00, 7%, Country S, 900,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: licensing gives low-cost, low-risk entry with local expertise; exporting keeps control and full margin but costs capital and effort | application_max_2: no $70,000 set-up; 7% royalties on 120,000 tubes at $8.00; 900,000-view video driving demand in Country S | analysis_max_2: steady royalty income without export risk; quality-control loss could damage the brand if Bellano cuts corners | evaluation_max_2: weighs low-risk royalty income against lost control and lower returns; justified recommendation to license first, with the option to renegotiate later

    Keywords: $35,000, 5%, $420,000, Country Z, 2 million, international franchises

Benefit 2: Halal certification and local-language labels remove barriers to purchase [k], opening distribution far wider than the current limited export range [app].
    Keywords: 60,000 jars, 30%, Country Z, halal-certified, low-salt pastes, $95,000

--- STEM ---
A manufacturing company operates as a Private Limited Company, producing custom packaging boxes in a single factory employing 80 production workers. Operating for 5 years, the factory uses batch production to manufacture 100,000 cardboard boxes per week. The factory incurs weekly fixed costs of $15,000 and total variable costs of $45,000, selling each box at a wholesale price of $0.80. Due to manual assembly errors, the current defect rate is 4%, leading to wasted raw materials and customer complaints.

To improve efficiency, the operations manager is considering investing $350,000 in an automated flow production line. Alternatively, the company is evaluating adopting Lean Production techniques, specifically Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory management, to eliminate raw material storage costs and reduce cardboard waste across the assembly plant.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the total cost per box. Show your working.
    Answer: Total Cost = Fixed Costs ($15,000) + Variable Costs ($45,000) = $60,000 [1]. Average Cost per box = $60,000 / 100,000 units = $0.60 per box [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: correct formula/method step; $0.60 per box

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems caused by the 4% defect rate in box manufacturing.
    Answer: Problem 1: Wasted raw materials [k], increasing unit costs for cardboard paper supplies [app]. Problem 2: Damage to brand reputation [k], leading to lost orders from packaging clients [app].
    Keywords: cardboard, boxes, defect, packaging, defect rate, 100,000, customer
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: wasted raw materials/increased unit costs; damaged reputation/lost sales | application_max_2: cardboard paper supplies; packaging clients; 4% defect rate

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to this business of introducing Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory management.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Reduced warehouse storage costs [k], as cardboard rolls are delivered only when needed for production [app], lowering fixed overheads across the factory [an]. Benefit 2: Reduced risk of inventory damage [k], as fewer raw packaging materials sit in storage [app], minimizing wasted stock and improving cash flow [an].
    Keywords: cardboard, inventory, boxes, JIT, storage, waste, Just-In-Time
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduced storage costs/space; reduced risk of damaged/obsolete inventory | application_max_2: cardboard rolls; factory warehouse; packaging materials | analysis_max_2: lowers fixed overheads; minimizes wasted stock/improves cash flow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think introducing automated flow production is better for this business than relying on Lean Production techniques? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Automated flow production reduces reliance on manual assembly workers [k], eliminating the 4% defect rate in cardboard boxes [app] and lowering average unit costs below $0.60 over time [an]. However, automated machinery requires a heavy capital investment of $350,000 [k], increasing initial financial risk for the factory [app] and creating downtime during installation [an]. Overall, automated flow production is better because fixing manual assembly errors at high volumes (100,000 boxes weekly) requires machine precision [eval], making technological automation more reliable at scale than procedural lean changes [eval].
    Keywords: boxes, defect, $350,000, cardboard, factory
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: eliminates manual defects/lowers unit costs; high initial capital cost/financial risk | application_max_2: 4% defect rate; $350,000 investment; 100,000 boxes weekly; $0.60 unit cost | analysis_max_2: lowers average unit costs over time; creates financial risk/downtime | evaluation_max_2: weighs high capital outlay against high-volume precision needs in packaging context

Weekly factory fixed costs stand at $50,000, while total variable costs equal $110,000. The company sells jeans to retail buyers at $12.00 per unit, facing a 4% defect rate due to stitching errors.

With rising fabric prices pushing total variable costs higher, executive directors are evaluating operational strategies to reduce average unit costs. The plant manager proposes introducing performance-related pay for sewing operators to boost labor productivity, while the operations chief advocates installing automated laser cutting machines costing $400,000 to eliminate material fabric waste.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State the formula for Average Cost per unit.
    Answer: Average Cost = Total Cost / Total Output (or Fixed Cost per unit + Variable Cost per unit) [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Total Cost / Total Output; Fixed Cost per unit + Variable Cost per unit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the total weekly cost and the average cost per pair of jeans. Show your working.
    Answer: Total weekly cost = Fixed costs ($50,000) + Variable costs ($110,000) = $160,000 [k]. Average cost per pair = $160,000 / 20,000 pairs of jeans = $8.00 per pair [app]. The $8.00 average uses the 20,000 pairs produced weekly across the 150 sewing operators [app]. Combining fixed and variable costs gives the $160,000 total [k].
    Keywords: jeans, $50,000, $110,000, 20,000, denim, sewing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates Total Cost ($160,000); $8.00 per pair of jeans | application_max_2: 20,000 pairs of jeans weekly; $160,000 total weekly cost

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways higher labor productivity among sewing machine operators can reduce average unit costs.
    Answer: Way 1: Spreads fixed costs over more output [k], as 150 operators sewing more than 20,000 pairs weekly spreads $50,000 fixed costs thinner [app], lowering average fixed cost per unit [an]. Way 2: Reduces stitching error rate [k], cutting the 4% defect rate in denim fabric [app], which minimizes wasted raw materials and lowers unit variable costs [an].
    Keywords: jeans, sewing, operators, denim, defect, stitching
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: spreads fixed costs over higher output; reduces defect rates/wasted materials | application_max_2: 150 sewing operators; 20,000 pairs weekly; 4% defect rate; denim fabric | analysis_max_2: lowers average fixed cost per unit; minimizes wasted raw materials and variable costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think introducing performance-related pay is a better strategy for reducing average costs than installing $400,000 automated laser cutting machines? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Introducing performance-related pay motivates 150 sewing machine operators [k], raising weekly jeans output beyond 20,000 pairs [app] and lowering average costs below $8.00 without heavy capital outlays [an]. Conversely, installing $400,000 laser cutting machinery eliminates fabric waste [k] and lowers the 4% defect rate [app], but requires high initial financing that increases fixed costs [an]. Overall, installing laser cutting machinery is better because denim fabric represents the main variable cost [eval]; automating precise fabric cuts guarantees material savings whereas pay incentives can lead to rushed, sloppy stitching errors [eval].
    Keywords: jeans, laser, $400,000, denim, sewing, operators, performance-related
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: motivates workers/lowers fixed cost per unit without capital outlay; eliminates material waste/high initial capital cost | application_max_2: 150 sewing machine operators; $8.00 unit cost; $400,000 laser cutters; 4% defect rate | analysis_max_2: lowers average costs without capital debt; increases initial fixed overheads | evaluation_max_2: weighs labor motivation against technological waste reduction in garment manufacturing sector

--- STEM ---
A beverage bottling plant operates as a Private Limited Company, producing canned sparkling water distributed to retail supermarkets. Operating for 4 years, the factory employs 35 production workers and produces 120,000 aluminum cans per week. The plant incurs weekly fixed costs of $30,000, total variable costs of $48,000 for ingredients and cans, and sells each canned drink at $0.90 per unit. Operating with a 2% defect rate due to faulty capping machinery, the factory currently operates close to its break-even point.

To increase the margin of safety and protect profit margins, the operations team is analyzing break-even metrics. Management is debating whether to reduce variable costs by switching to cheaper aluminum casing suppliers, or increase weekly output to 180,000 cans by adding a night shift to benefit from purchasing economies of scale on bulk raw material orders.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'margin of safety'.
    Answer: The amount by which actual sales output exceeds the break-even level of output [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: amount by which actual sales/output exceeds; break-even level of output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the weekly break-even output in cans. Show your working.
    Answer: Variable cost per can = $48,000 / 120,000 cans = $0.40 [k]. Contribution per unit = Wholesale price ($0.90) - Variable cost ($0.40) = $0.50 per can [app]. Break-even output = Fixed costs ($30,000) / Contribution ($0.50) = 60,000 cans per week [app], the level where total revenue equals total costs [k].
    Keywords: cans, $30,000, $48,000, $0.90, sparkling water, 120,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates unit contribution ($0.50); 60,000 cans per week | application_max_2: $0.90 selling price per can; $48,000 variable costs across 120,000 cans

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to this business of increasing its margin of safety.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Financial protection against falling demand [k], ensuring the plant covers $30,000 fixed costs even if canned sparkling water sales drop [app], reducing insolvency risk [an]. Benefit 2: Operational cushion during machinery breakdowns [k], allowing the factory to remain profitable even if faulty capping machinery reduces output below 120,000 cans [app], maintaining cash flow stability [an].
    Keywords: cans, sparkling water, capping, margin of safety, break-even
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: financial protection against falling sales/demand; operational cushion during output disruptions | application_max_2: $30,000 fixed costs; canned sparkling water; faulty capping machinery; 120,000 cans | analysis_max_2: reduces insolvency risk; maintains cash flow stability

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think switching to cheaper aluminum casing suppliers is a better strategy for this bottling plant than adding a night shift to achieve purchasing economies of scale? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching to cheaper aluminum suppliers lowers variable costs below $0.40 per can [k], reducing the 60,000 unit break-even point [app] and increasing profit margins immediately [an]. However, cheaper aluminum casings may increase the 2% capping defect rate [k], damaging brand reputation among retail supermarkets [app] and leading to cancelled orders [an]. Conversely, adding a night shift to produce 180,000 cans unlocks bulk purchasing discounts on raw aluminum for 35 workers, spreading $30,000 fixed costs over higher output. Overall, adding a night shift is better because it preserves canned drink quality [eval]; bulk purchasing discounts lower average costs without risking defective aluminum cans or customer complaints [eval].
    Keywords: cans, aluminum, capping, defect, night shift, suppliers, break-even
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lowers variable costs/lowers break-even point; unlocks bulk purchasing discounts/spreads fixed costs | application_max_2: $0.40 per can; 60,000 break-even point; 2% defect rate; 180,000 cans | analysis_max_2: increases profit margins immediately; spreads fixed costs over higher output | evaluation_max_2: weighs raw material cost-cutting against volume expansion through bulk purchasing in beverage sector

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think expanding the existing factory is better for this e-bike manufacturer than building a second smaller assembly plant? Justify your answer.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: identifies fixed costs ($40,000) and variable costs ($75,000); $115,000 total weekly cost | application_max_2: $40,000 fixed costs; $75,000 variable costs / 250,000 syringes
