--- STEM ---
A custom leather footwear workshop operates as a Partnership, handcrafting leather work boots in a small facility with 15 artisan shoemakers. Operating for 7 years, the workshop uses job production to produce 200 pairs of boots per week. Weekly fixed costs stand at $6,000, while total variable costs reach $14,000 for premium leather hides and steel toe caps. Each pair sells for a wholesale price of $140, but manual cutting errors lead to a 4% defect rate.

With rising wholesale orders from safety equipment distributors, the partners need to boost weekly capacity. The production partner proposes transitioning from job production to batch production using computer-controlled leather cutting machinery costing $80,000. Alternatively, the firm is considering adopting Just-In-Time (JIT) component delivery for leather hides and steel caps while expanding job production with 10 additional shoemakers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'batch production'.
    Answer: A production method where a set quantity of identical products are made together before switching machinery to make another set [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: producing a set quantity of identical products together; switching machinery/tooling to manufacture a different set

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the weekly profit made by the workshop. Show your working.
    Answer: Total revenue = 200 pairs x $140 = $28,000 [k]. Total cost = Fixed costs ($6,000) + Variable costs ($14,000) = $20,000 [k]. Weekly profit = $28,000 - $20,000 = $8,000 [app], earned by selling leather work boots to safety equipment distributors [app].
    Keywords: boots, $140, $6,000, $14,000, shoemakers, leather
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates Total Revenue ($28,000) or Total Cost ($20,000); $8,000 weekly profit | application_max_2: 200 pairs of boots weekly; $140 wholesale price per pair

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks to this workshop of adopting Just-In-Time (JIT) component delivery.
    Answer: Drawback 1: Risk of delivery delays [k], as late arrivals of steel toe caps interrupt assembly for 15 artisan shoemakers [app], halting boot production [an]. Drawback 2: Loss of bulk purchasing discounts [k], as ordering leather hides in smaller frequent parcels increases variable material costs [app], squeezing profit margins [an].
    Keywords: boots, leather, shoemakers, toe caps, JIT, hides
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: risk of supply chain delays/production halts; loss of bulk purchasing discounts/higher unit costs | application_max_2: steel toe caps; 15 artisan shoemakers; leather hides; work boots | analysis_max_2: halts boot assembly lines; squeezes weekly profit margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think transitioning to batch production using computer-controlled cutting machinery is better for this workshop than expanding job production? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Transitioning to batch production standardizes leather cutting [k], eliminating manual cutting errors that cause the 4% defect rate [app] and lowering average unit costs below $100 per pair [an]. However, purchasing $80,000 machinery increases fixed overheads [k] and risks losing the handcrafted custom brand reputation among safety distributors [app], creating initial debt burdens [an]. Overall, transitioning to batch production is better because satisfying commercial safety distributor contracts requires higher output volume beyond 200 pairs weekly [eval]; mechanized cutting ensures uniform product dimensions far more efficiently than hiring 10 manual shoemakers [eval].
    Keywords: boots, batch, leather, $80,000, shoemakers, defect, cutting
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: standardizes cutting/lowers unit costs; high capital outlay/risk of losing handcrafted reputation | application_max_2: 4% defect rate; $80,000 machinery; safety equipment distributors; 200 pairs weekly | analysis_max_2: lowers average unit costs below $100; creates debt burdens and reduces custom appeal | evaluation_max_2: weighs capital machinery cost against volume expansion needs in commercial footwear sector

--- STEM ---
A commercial cardboard container factory operates as a Private Limited Company, manufacturing heavy-duty corrugated shipping boxes for industrial clients. Operating for 8 years, the plant employs 65 assembly line workers and produces 80,000 corrugated boxes per week. The factory incurs weekly fixed costs of $20,000 for building lease and machinery depreciation, while total variable costs reach $48,000 for paper pulp and adhesives. Each shipping box sells for a wholesale price of $1.10. Quality reports show a 3% defect rate caused by faulty gluing machinery.

With rising paper pulp costs pushing total variable costs up by 15%, management is evaluating cost reduction measures. The plant manager proposes investing $160,000 in automated gluing equipment to lower variable labor and adhesive waste, while the financial controller recommends renegotiating the factory lease to lower weekly fixed costs to $15,000.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'variable costs'.
    Answer: Costs that change directly in proportion with the level of output produced by a business [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: costs that change directly; in proportion with the level of output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the average total cost per corrugated shipping box at current output. Show your working.
    Answer: Total weekly cost = Fixed costs ($20,000) + Variable costs ($48,000) = $68,000 [k]. Average total cost = $68,000 / 80,000 corrugated boxes = $0.85 per box [app], based on the current weekly output of 80,000 boxes [app]. Adding fixed and variable costs gives the $68,000 total [k].
    Keywords: boxes, $20,000, $48,000, 80,000, corrugated, pulp
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates Total Weekly Cost ($68,000); $0.85 per box | application_max_2: $20,000 fixed costs; $48,000 variable costs / 80,000 boxes

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways a 15% increase in paper pulp costs affects the factory's operational cost structure.
    Answer: Way 1: Increases total variable costs [k], raising weekly material expenditure for paper pulp above $48,000 [app], which increases total production expenses [an]. Way 2: Increases average cost per unit [k], pushing unit production costs above $0.85 per shipping box [app], which squeezes gross profit margins [an].
    Keywords: boxes, paper, pulp, variable, corrugated, gluing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increases total variable costs; increases average unit cost/squeezes profit margins | application_max_2: paper pulp material; above $48,000 variable costs; above $0.85 average cost; corrugated shipping boxes | analysis_max_2: raises total weekly production expenses; squeezes gross profit margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think investing $160,000 in automated gluing equipment is a better operational strategy for this factory than renegotiating the lease to lower fixed costs? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing $160,000 in automated gluing equipment eliminates adhesive waste and fixes the 3% defect rate [k], reducing variable costs for paper pulp across 80,000 boxes weekly [app] and lowering average costs below $0.85 [an]. Conversely, renegotiating the factory lease cuts weekly fixed costs to $15,000 [k] for 65 workers [app], but fails to address raw material waste or machinery defects [an]. Overall, investing in automated gluing equipment is better because raw materials represent the largest cost component [eval]; eliminating gluing defects and material waste cuts average costs far more permanently than a modest fixed lease reduction [eval].
    Keywords: boxes, gluing, $160,000, lease, $15,000, defect, paper
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: eliminates material waste/lowers variable unit cost; reduces fixed overheads/does not fix operational waste | application_max_2: $160,000 gluing equipment; 3% defect rate; 80,000 boxes weekly; $15,000 fixed lease | analysis_max_2: lowers average unit costs below $0.85; fails to address raw material waste or machinery defects | evaluation_max_2: weighs variable waste reduction through technology against fixed lease cost reduction

--- STEM ---
A commercial laundry processing facility operates as a Public Limited Company, cleaning linen items for hotel chains. Operating for 10 years, the central laundry employs 100 industrial laundry operators and processes 200,000 linen items per week. Weekly fixed overheads stand at $40,000 for rent and equipment leases, while total variable costs equal $80,000 for water, detergents, and electricity. The firm charges hotels $0.70 per processed item, but experiences a 4% damage defect rate due to manual pressing errors.

With utility prices pushing variable energy costs higher, the operations director is seeking ways to reduce average unit costs. The plant manager suggests introducing productivity bonuses for 100 laundry operators to increase weekly throughput to 250,000 items, while the chief engineer recommends installing automated continuous tunnel washers costing $300,000 to reduce water and detergent usage.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State the formula for Total Cost.
    Answer: Total Cost = Fixed Costs + Total Variable Costs (or Average Cost x Total Output) [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed Costs + Total Variable Costs; Average Cost x Total Output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the average cost per linen item at current weekly output (200,000 units). Show your working.
    Answer: Total cost = Fixed costs ($40,000) + Variable costs ($80,000) = $120,000 [k]. Average cost = $120,000 / 200,000 linen items = $0.60 per item [app], based on the current weekly throughput of 200,000 items [app]. Adding fixed and variable costs gives the $120,000 total [k].
    Keywords: linen, $40,000, $80,000, 200,000, laundry, detergents
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates Total Cost ($120,000); $0.60 per item | application_max_2: $40,000 fixed overheads; $80,000 variable costs / 200,000 items

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why increasing weekly throughput from 200,000 to 250,000 items reduces average fixed cost per item.
    Answer: Reason 1: Spreads fixed overheads over a larger volume [k], spreading $40,000 rent and machinery leases across 250,000 linen items instead of 200,000 [app], dropping fixed cost per unit from $0.20 to $0.16 [an]. Reason 2: Maximizes industrial facility capacity [k], utilizing washing machinery more continuously across 100 operators [app], improving total operational efficiency [an].
    Keywords: linen, laundry, washers, fixed, overheads, throughput
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: spreads fixed overheads over larger output volume; maximizes facility/machinery capacity utilization | application_max_2: $40,000 rent and leases; 250,000 linen items; $0.20 to $0.16 unit cost; 100 laundry operators | analysis_max_2: drops fixed cost per unit; improves total operational efficiency

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think introducing productivity bonuses is a better strategy for reducing average costs than installing $300,000 automated tunnel washers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Productivity bonuses motivate 100 laundry operators to process 250,000 items weekly [k], lowering average fixed costs per item without heavy capital outlay [app] and boosting total revenue from hotel contracts [an]. Conversely, installing $300,000 automated tunnel washers directly reduces water and detergent variable costs [k] and lowers the 4% damage defect rate [app], but requires heavy initial debt financing [an]. Overall, installing automated tunnel washers is better because utility and detergent expenses represent the major variable cost [eval]; automating wash cycles guarantees permanent utility savings whereas productivity bonuses may cause rushed handling that increases linen damage [eval].
    Keywords: linen, washers, $300,000, bonuses, laundry, defect, operators
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lowers fixed cost per unit without debt; reduces variable utility waste/high initial capital cost | application_max_2: 100 laundry operators; $300,000 tunnel washers; 4% damage defect rate; water and detergent variable costs | analysis_max_2: boosts total revenue from hotel contracts; requires heavy initial debt financing | evaluation_max_2: weighs labor productivity incentives against automated utility waste reduction in commercial service context

--- STEM ---
A commercial paint manufacturing facility operates as a Private Limited Company, producing interior wall paint packaged in 5-liter plastic buckets. Operating for 5 years, the plant employs 40 factory technicians and produces 50,000 paint buckets per week. Weekly fixed costs stand at $30,000, while total variable costs reach $75,000 for pigments, chemical resins, and buckets. The wholesale price is $2.50 per bucket, but automated filling errors cause a 2% spillage defect rate. The factory currently operates close to its break-even point.

To increase the margin of safety and protect against raw material price volatility, management is analyzing break-even metrics. The operations team is debating whether to reduce variable costs by sourcing lower-grade chemical resins, or increase weekly production output to 75,000 buckets by running weekend shifts to secure bulk purchasing economies of scale on chemical orders.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'break-even point'.
    Answer: The level of sales output at which total revenue exactly equals total costs, resulting in zero profit and zero loss [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: level of output/sales where total revenue equals total cost; resulting in zero profit and zero loss

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the weekly break-even output in 5-liter paint buckets. Show your working.
    Answer: Variable cost per bucket = $75,000 / 50,000 buckets = $1.50 [k]. Contribution per unit = Wholesale price ($2.50) - Variable cost ($1.50) = $1.00 per bucket [app]. Break-even output = Fixed costs ($30,000) / Contribution ($1.00) = 30,000 buckets per week [app], the level where total revenue equals total costs [k].
    Keywords: paint, buckets, $30,000, $75,000, $2.50, 5-liter, break-even
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates unit contribution ($1.00); 30,000 buckets per week | application_max_2: $2.50 wholesale price per bucket; $75,000 variable costs across 50,000 buckets

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways reducing variable costs lowers the break-even point for this factory.
    Answer: Way 1: Increases contribution per unit [k], as lowering pigment and resin costs below $1.50 increases unit contribution above $1.00 [app], requiring fewer sales to cover $30,000 fixed costs [an]. Way 2: Expands margin of safety [k], increasing the gap between current output (50,000 buckets) and the lower break-even volume [app], reducing financial risk during sales downturns [an].
    Keywords: paint, buckets, break-even, resins, pigments
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increases contribution per unit/covers fixed costs faster; expands margin of safety/reduces financial risk | application_max_2: pigment and resin costs; $1.50 variable cost; $30,000 fixed costs; 50,000 buckets current output | analysis_max_2: requires fewer unit sales to break even; reduces financial risk during market downturns

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think sourcing lower-grade chemical resins is a better strategy for increasing the margin of safety than running weekend shifts to gain bulk purchasing economies of scale? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Sourcing lower-grade chemical resins lowers variable costs below $1.50 per bucket [k], immediately reducing the 30,000 unit break-even point [app] and expanding profit margins [an]. However, inferior resins damage paint quality and increase the 2% spillage defect rate [k], leading to customer complaints from hardware stores [app] and lost sales [an]. Conversely, running weekend shifts to produce 75,000 buckets unlocks bulk purchasing discounts on raw chemical resins for 40 technicians, spreading $30,000 fixed costs over higher output. Overall, running weekend shifts is better because maintaining paint opacity and quality is critical [eval]; bulk purchasing discounts lower unit costs without compromising chemical resin standards or risking brand reputation [eval].
    Keywords: paint, buckets, resins, break-even, shifts, defect, chemical
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lowers variable cost/lowers break-even point; gains bulk purchasing discounts/spreads fixed costs | application_max_2: $1.50 variable cost; 30,000 break-even point; 2% spillage defect rate; 75,000 buckets weekend output | analysis_max_2: immediately expands profit margins; spreads fixed costs over higher output | evaluation_max_2: weighs raw material quality compromise against volume expansion through bulk purchasing in chemical manufacturing

--- STEM ---
A commercial solar panel assembly plant operates as a Public Limited Company, manufacturing photovoltaic solar modules for commercial buildings. Operating for 6 years, the facility employs 120 assembly technicians and produces 2,000 solar modules per week. Weekly fixed costs stand at $100,000, and total variable costs reach $300,000 for silicon cells, tempered glass, and aluminum frames. Each solar module sells at $250 wholesale, with a 3% defect rate.

To achieve technical and purchasing economies of scale, the executive board plans to double weekly plant output to 4,000 modules. However, the plant manager warns that doubling output on a single factory site risks triggering managerial and communication diseconomies of scale. The board must decide whether to double capacity by expanding the existing plant or building a second smaller assembly facility in a neighboring region.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'diseconomies of scale'.
    Answer: Factors that cause average costs per unit to rise as the scale of production increases beyond an optimal point [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: factors that cause average unit costs to rise; as scale of production increases beyond optimal point

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the average cost per solar module at current weekly output (2,000 units). Show your working.
    Answer: Total cost = Fixed costs ($100,000) + Variable costs ($300,000) = $400,000 [k]. Average cost per module = $400,000 / 2,000 solar modules = $200 per module [app], using the current weekly output of 2,000 modules [app]. Adding fixed and variable costs gives the $400,000 total [k].
    Keywords: solar, modules, $100,000, $300,000, silicon, 2,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates Total Cost ($400,000); $200 per module | application_max_2: $100,000 fixed costs; $300,000 variable costs / 2,000 modules

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways purchasing economies of scale can benefit this factory if output is expanded.
    Answer: Way 1: Bulk purchasing discounts [k], securing lower unit prices on silicon cells and tempered glass orders [app], which reduces total variable costs below $300,000 [an]. Way 2: Increased supplier bargaining power [k], negotiating better credit terms for large material quantities [app], which improves cash flow management [an].
    Keywords: solar, modules, silicon, glass, economies, purchasing
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bulk purchasing discounts/lower unit material costs; increased supplier bargaining power/better credit terms | application_max_2: silicon cells and tempered glass; $300,000 variable costs; photovoltaic solar modules; doubled output (4,000 units) | analysis_max_2: reduces total variable costs; improves corporate cash flow management

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think expanding the existing solar panel factory is better for this firm than building a second smaller assembly facility? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Expanding the existing factory maximizes purchasing economies of scale on silicon cells [k], dropping average unit costs below $200 per module [app] and boosting profit margins on $250 wholesale sales [an]. However, doubling output in one plant creates managerial communication breakdowns [k] among 120 assembly technicians [app], increasing defect rates above 3% during wiring checks [an]. Overall, building a second smaller assembly facility is better because high-tech photovoltaic assembly requires strict quality coordination [eval]; operating two specialized regional plants prevents manager overload and maintains tight quality control far better than an unwieldy single facility [eval].
    Keywords: solar, modules, factory, silicon, diseconomies, assembly
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: purchasing economies/lowers average costs; managerial diseconomies/communication and quality bottlenecks | application_max_2: silicon cells and tempered glass; $200 average cost; 120 assembly technicians; 3% defect rate | analysis_max_2: boosts profit margins on wholesale sales; increases defect rates during wiring checks | evaluation_max_2: weighs purchasing economies of scale against managerial diseconomies in renewable energy manufacturing

--- STEM ---
A precision optics manufacturer operates as a Private Limited Company, producing glass camera lenses for digital security systems. Operating for 7 years, the factory employs 50 optical technicians and manufactures 20,000 lenses per week. The plant incurs weekly fixed costs of $35,000 and total variable costs of $50,000 for optical glass and anti-reflective coatings. Lenses sell to security camera makers at $6.00 each. Final end-of-line inspections reveal a 6% defect rate due to lens surface scratching and coating misalignments.

Because defective security lenses cause customer returns and damage commercial supplier contracts, the operations director demands immediate quality improvements. The quality manager recommends replacing end-of-line Quality Control inspection with a comprehensive Quality Assurance system across all grinding and coating stages. Alternatively, the board is evaluating investing $220,000 in automated laser scanning inspection hardware.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'quality assurance'.
    Answer: A system of managing quality where processes are designed to prevent defects from occurring at every stage of production [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: system of managing quality to prevent defects; at every stage of production

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the total weekly cost of manufacturing 20,000 lenses. Show your working.
    Answer: Total weekly cost = Fixed costs ($35,000) + Variable costs ($50,000) = $85,000 [k]. This covers 20,000 lenses manufactured weekly in the precision optics factory [app], so average cost = $85,000 / 20,000 = $4.25 per lens [app]. Adding fixed and variable costs gives the $85,000 total [k].
    Keywords: lenses, $35,000, $50,000, 20,000, optical, glass
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: identifies fixed costs ($35,000) and variable costs ($50,000); $85,000 total weekly cost | application_max_2: $35,000 fixed costs; $50,000 variable costs / 20,000 lenses

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems caused by relying solely on end-of-line Quality Control inspection for this lens manufacturer.
    Answer: Problem 1: Wastes raw materials and labor [k], as scratched optical glass lenses are identified only after complete grinding and anti-reflective coating [app], driving up total unit costs [an]. Problem 2: High inspection labor expenses [k], paying inspectors to check 20,000 lenses weekly [app], which increases factory fixed costs [an].
    Keywords: lenses, glass, scratching, coating, inspection, defect
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: wastes raw materials/labor after full assembly; high inspection labor expenses/does not prevent defects | application_max_2: scratched optical glass lenses; anti-reflective coating stage; 20,000 lenses weekly; 6% defect rate | analysis_max_2: drives up total unit costs; increases factory fixed overheads

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think implementing a Quality Assurance system is a better strategy for this lens manufacturer than investing $220,000 in automated laser scanning inspection hardware? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Quality Assurance trains 50 optical technicians to prevent lens scratching at the grinding stage [k], eliminating the 6% defect rate at the source [app] and reducing total weekly costs below $85,000 [an]. Conversely, investing $220,000 in laser scanning hardware detects surface misalignments instantly [k], but still catches defective lenses after assembly [app], wasting expensive optical glass and coatings [an]. Overall, implementing Quality Assurance is better because precision optics demand zero-defect standards [eval]; preventing defects during grinding avoids wasting expensive anti-reflective coatings far more effectively than merely discarding faulty lenses faster [eval].
    Keywords: lenses, glass, Quality Assurance, laser, $220,000, defect
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: prevents defects at source/reduces scrap waste; instant automated detection/still results in component scrap | application_max_2: 50 optical technicians; 6% defect rate; $220,000 laser scanners; optical glass and coatings | analysis_max_2: reduces total weekly manufacturing costs; wastes expensive materials before rejecting flawed lenses | evaluation_max_2: weighs defect prevention culture against automated end-of-line detection in optical device manufacturing

--- STEM ---
An aircraft component manufacturing plant operates as a Public Limited Company, producing aluminum turbine blades for commercial jet engines. Operating for 12 years, the foundry employs 150 specialized machinists and manufactures 5,000 turbine blades per week. The plant incurs weekly fixed costs of $150,000 and total variable costs of $350,000 for aerospace-grade aluminum alloy and machining coolant. Each blade sells for $120.00, but casting flaws result in a 5% defect rate during safety testing.

With aviation safety regulators issuing strict zero-defect mandates, the executive board demands immediate operational overhaul. The plant director must choose a quality strategy: implementing Total Quality Management (TQM) with Kaizen continuous improvement groups empowering 150 machinists, or hiring additional Quality Control inspection teams to inspect turbine blades at every single machining station.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'Kaizen'.
    Answer: A Japanese business philosophy of continuous improvement where workers continuously make small, incremental improvements to processes [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: philosophy of continuous improvement; workers make small incremental improvements to processes

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the average cost per turbine blade. Show your working.
    Answer: Total cost = Fixed costs ($150,000) + Variable costs ($350,000) = $500,000 [k]. Average cost per blade = $500,000 / 5,000 turbine blades = $100.00 per blade [app], using the current weekly output of 5,000 blades [app]. Adding fixed and variable costs gives the $500,000 total [k].
    Keywords: turbine, blades, $150,000, $350,000, aluminum, 5,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates Total Cost ($500,000); $100.00 per blade | application_max_2: $150,000 fixed costs; $350,000 variable costs / 5,000 blades

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why achieving zero defects is critical for this aerospace component manufacturer.
    Answer: Reason 1: Compliance with aviation safety regulators [k], preventing severe legal sanctions and loss of commercial manufacturing licenses [app], protecting company survival [an]. Reason 2: Eliminates expensive material waste [k], stopping the loss of aerospace-grade aluminum alloy from the 5% defect rate [app], which lowers unit production costs below $100.00 [an].
    Keywords: turbine, blades, aluminum, regulators, alloy
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: regulatory compliance/prevents license loss; eliminates expensive material scrap/lowers unit costs | application_max_2: aviation safety regulators; aerospace-grade aluminum alloy; 5% defect rate; $100.00 unit cost | analysis_max_2: protects company survival and contracts; lowers unit production costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think implementing Total Quality Management (TQM) is a better strategy for this manufacturer than hiring additional Quality Control inspection teams? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Implementing TQM empowers 150 machinists through Kaizen groups [k], eliminating casting flaws in aluminum turbine blades at the root cause [app] and achieving zero defects [an]. Conversely, hiring additional Quality Control inspection teams at every workstation catches defective blades before safety testing [k], but increases weekly fixed costs above $150,000 [app] while still wasting expensive aluminum alloy [an]. Overall, TQM is better because aerospace components require absolute zero-defect perfection [eval]; instilling a total quality culture among machinists eliminates defect creation entirely, saving expensive alloy waste far better than paying inspectors to scrap flawed blades [eval].
    Keywords: turbine, blades, TQM, Kaizen, machinists, aluminum, inspection
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: empowers workforce/eliminates defects at root cause; catches defects before shipping/increases inspection fixed costs and scrap waste | application_max_2: 150 specialized machinists; aluminum turbine blades; $150,000 fixed costs; aerospace-grade aluminum alloy | analysis_max_2: achieves zero-defect production; increases weekly fixed overheads while continuing scrap waste | evaluation_max_2: weighs root-cause defect elimination through TQM against costly multi-stage inspection teams in aerospace manufacturing

--- STEM ---
An industrial battery manufacturing enterprise operates as a Private Limited Company, producing lithium-ion energy storage packs for electric commercial vehicles. Operating for 6 years, the facility employs 80 battery assembly technicians and produces 1,000 battery packs per week. The plant incurs weekly fixed costs of $60,000 and total variable costs of $240,000 for raw lithium, cobalt, and steel casings. Battery packs sell to vehicle assembly plants for $350 each. The factory records a 3% defect rate during final voltage testing.

With urban redevelopment increasing factory lease renewal costs, the board must relocate operations. The directors are debating relocation options: moving to a rural industrial zone adjacent to major highway freight corridors and lithium raw material suppliers, or relocating offshore to a developing country offering 35% lower technician wages but requiring long sea freight transport to vehicle assembly clients.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two location factors that influence where a manufacturing business chooses to locate.
    Answer: 1. Proximity to raw material suppliers and transport links [1].
2. Cost and availability of skilled labor [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: proximity to raw material suppliers/transport links; cost/availability of skilled labor; site lease/land cost; proximity to target market/customers

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the weekly profit made by the battery plant. Show your working.
    Answer: Total revenue = 1,000 packs x $350 = $350,000 [k]. Total cost = Fixed costs ($60,000) + Variable costs ($240,000) = $300,000 [k]. Weekly profit = $350,000 - $300,000 = $50,000 [app], earned by selling lithium-ion battery packs to vehicle assembly plants [app].
    Keywords: battery, $350, $60,000, $240,000, lithium, cobalt
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates Total Revenue ($350,000) or Total Cost ($300,000); $50,000 weekly profit | application_max_2: 1,000 battery packs weekly; $350 price per pack

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to this manufacturer of locating near lithium raw material suppliers and highway corridors.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Reduces raw material freight expenses [k], lowering variable transport costs for heavy raw lithium and cobalt [app], which increases profit margins [an]. Advantage 2: Enables rapid Just-In-Time delivery to clients [k], shipping 1,000 battery packs quickly via highway freight corridors to commercial vehicle assembly plants [app], preventing supply chain delays [an].
    Keywords: battery, lithium, cobalt, highway, freight, suppliers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduces raw material transport costs; enables fast delivery/prevents supply chain delays | application_max_2: raw lithium and cobalt; highway freight corridors; commercial vehicle assembly plants; 1,000 battery packs | analysis_max_2: increases weekly profit margins; prevents supply chain delays

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think relocating to a rural industrial zone near highway corridors is a better location decision for this business than relocating offshore? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Relocating to a rural industrial zone maintains fast highway transport of 1,000 battery packs to vehicle assembly plants [k], avoiding expensive sea freight for heavy lithium packs [app] and protecting client relationships [an].     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates new Total Variable Cost ($420,000); calculates new Total Cost ($570,000) | application_max_2: $420,000 variable cost from 600,000 x $0.70; $570,000 total cost with unchanged $150,000 fixed overheads

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two causes of managerial diseconomies of scale experienced by this metal stamping business.
    Answer: Cause 1: Poor communication channels [k], as messages take longer to pass between shift supervisors and quality engineers across three production lines [app], increasing decision-making time [an]. Cause 2: Lack of coordination [k], leading to uncoordinated shift handovers that cause a 4% defect rate in steel brackets [app], raising unit waste costs [an].
    Keywords: supervisors, brackets, steel, engineers, diseconomies, lines
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: poor communication / long chain of command; weak coordination / lack of control over large workforce | application_max_2: three production lines; shift supervisors and quality engineers; 4% defect rate; steel brackets | analysis_max_2: increases decision-making time; raises unit waste costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think investing $400,000 in hydraulic stamping presses is a better strategy to lower unit costs than restructuring into autonomous production cells? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Hydraulic stamping presses deliver technical economies of scale [k], increasing output speed and lowering variable costs per steel bracket below $0.70 [app], which drives down average total costs [an]. However, spending $400,000 increases fixed overheads and does not resolve the managerial communication breakdown among 120 technicians [app], risking continued defect waste [an]. Restructuring into autonomous production cells improves coordination directly [k]. Overall, restructuring management is better because current cost increases stem from communication breakdown [eval]; fixing coordination across three production lines removes the 4% defect rate before investing $400,000 in extra equipment [eval].
    Keywords: hydraulic, presses, brackets, steel, $400,000, cells
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delivers technical scale economies / reduces unit cost; high capital outlay / fails to address underlying managerial coordination issues | application_max_2: $0.70 variable cost; $400,000 capital outlay; 120 technicians; 4% defect rate | analysis_max_2: drives down average total costs; risks continued defect waste and high financial risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs technical equipment scale economies against organizational restructuring in resolving plant inefficiency

A frozen food processing firm operates as a Private Limited Company, manufacturing pre-baked frozen pizza crusts for supermarket brands. Operating for 5 years, the facility employs 35 production workers and processes 80,000 pizza crusts monthly. The wholesale selling price is $1.40 per crust.

Due to rising flour supply costs, variable costs per crust are projected to increase by 15%. To protect gross profit margins, the operations manager is considering expanding monthly production to 150,000 crusts to secure purchasing economies of scale on bulk flour orders. Alternatively, the firm is considering automating the pizza topping line with automated cheese dispensers costing $90,000.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the current average cost per frozen pizza crust. Show your working.
    Answer: Average Cost = Total Cost / Output = $80,000 / 80,000 units = $1.00 per crust [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: correct formula (Total Cost / Output); $1.00 per crust

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the new total variable cost if production increases to 150,000 crusts at the current $0.70 variable cost per unit. Show your working.
    Answer: Total Variable Cost = Output (150,000) x Variable Cost per unit ($0.70) = $105,000 [k]. This uses the flour, yeast and cheese variable cost of $0.70 per crust [app] applied to the planned 150,000 crust output [app], confirming the expanded scale calculation [k].
    Keywords: pizza, crusts, flour, yeast, cheese, $0.70, $24,000, 150,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: correct formula (Output x Unit VC); $105,000 | application_max_2: $105,000 variable cost from 150,000 x $0.70; $0.70 per crust variable cost (flour, yeast, cheese)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways purchasing economies of scale can lower average unit costs for this frozen food manufacturer.
    Answer: Way 1: Bulk material discounts [k], purchasing flour, yeast, and cheese in larger quantities to negotiate lower unit prices below $0.70 [app], reducing variable cost per crust [an]. Way 2: Spreading fixed costs [k], spreading $24,000 monthly overheads across 150,000 pizza crusts [app], lowering fixed cost per unit produced [an].
    Keywords: flour, yeast, cheese, pizza, crusts, $24,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bulk buying discounts on raw materials; spreading fixed costs over higher output volume | application_max_2: flour, yeast, and cheese; $0.70 unit variable cost; $24,000 monthly overheads; 150,000 pizza crusts | analysis_max_2: reduces variable cost per unit; lowers average fixed cost per unit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think expanding monthly output to 150,000 crusts is a better operational strategy than investing $90,000 in automated cheese dispensers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Expanding output to 150,000 crusts achieves purchasing economies of scale on bulk flour [k], lowering unit variable costs below $0.70 [app] and spreading fixed costs to maximize profit margins at the $1.40 selling price [an]. However, expanding volume requires securing major new supermarket supply contracts; if sales remain at 80,000 crusts [app], cold storage holding costs will rise [an]. Automated cheese dispensers directly reduce cheese waste [k]. Overall, expanding output volume is better because pizza crust manufacturing operates on narrow margins [eval]; bulk material discounts lower average costs far more effectively than automated topping equipment alone [eval].
    Keywords: pizza, crusts, flour, cheese, $90,000, dispensers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: achieves purchasing scale economies / spreads fixed overheads; risk of overproduction / direct waste reduction without sales expansion | application_max_2: $0.70 variable cost; $1.40 selling price; supermarket supply contracts; $90,000 capital outlay | analysis_max_2: lowers average unit manufacturing costs; increases cold storage holding costs | evaluation_max_2: weighs volume scale economies against targeted automation investment in frozen food manufacturing

--- STEM ---
A beverage bottling plant operates as a Private Limited Company, canning organic sparkling fruit water sold to retail grocery chains across the whole country. Operating for 4 years, the factory employs 30 technicians and produces 120,000 cans per month. Monthly fixed overheads stand at $36,000, while variable costs per unit are $0.50 (aluminum cans, fruit extract, and carbonated water). Each can sells for $1.10 wholesale. Currently, monthly sales volume matches monthly output at 120,000 cans.

To raise profitability, the commercial director is evaluating a proposal to increase the wholesale selling price from $1.10 to $1.30 per can. Alternatively, the plant is considering investing $60,000 in energy-efficient aluminum canning equipment to reduce variable cost per unit to $0.40 while maintaining the $1.10 selling price.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'contribution per unit'.
    Answer: The selling price per unit minus the variable cost per unit [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit; amount each unit contributes toward covering fixed costs

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the current monthly break-even output level in cans. Show your working formula.
    Answer: Contribution per unit = $1.10 - $0.50 = $0.60 per can [k]. Break-even Output = Fixed Costs ($36,000) / Contribution ($0.60) = 60,000 cans per month [k], using the $36,000 monthly fixed overheads [app] and $0.50 variable cost per can of sparkling fruit water [app].
    Keywords: cans, sparkling, fruit water, bottling, $36,000, $0.50, $1.10, 120,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates contribution per unit ($0.60); calculates break-even output (60,000 cans) | application_max_2: $0.60 contribution from $1.10 price minus $0.50 variable cost; 60,000 cans break-even from $36,000 fixed costs

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways break-even analysis can help this beverage bottling plant make operational decisions.
    Answer: Way 1: Margin of safety measurement [k], showing sales of 120,000 cans exceed the break-even output by 60,000 cans [app], giving the plant a buffer before losses occur [an]. Way 2: Pricing and cost decisions [k], testing the effect of raising price to $1.30 or cutting variable cost to $0.40 [app], supporting profitable operational planning [an].
    Keywords: cans, sparkling, fruit water, bottling, 120,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: understands margin of safety (sales above break-even before losses); understands break-even analysis tests pricing and cost decisions | application_max_2: 120,000 actual sales exceed 60,000 break-even level; $1.30 price rise and $0.40 variable cost option; sparkling fruit water; bottling plant | analysis_max_2: provides buffer against falling retail demand; supports informed pricing and cost decisions

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think increasing the selling price to $1.30 per can is a better operational strategy to improve financial performance than investing $60,000 to lower unit variable cost to $0.40? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Increasing price to $1.30 raises contribution to $0.80 per can ($1.30 - $0.50) [k], reducing break-even output to 45,000 cans ($36,000 / $0.80) [app] and expanding margin of safety without capital outlay [an]. However, raising prices risks losing retail grocery chain contracts [k] if competitors maintain lower prices, reducing sales below 120,000 cans [an]. Lowering variable cost to $0.40 raises contribution to $0.70 for a $60,000 outlay [app]. Overall, lowering variable cost is better because beverage markets are price-sensitive [eval]; maintaining the $1.10 retail price protects sales volume while permanently reducing break-even risk [eval].
    Keywords: cans, $1.30, $0.40, $60,000, bottling
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increases unit contribution / lowers break-even point; risk of reduced demand / capital outlay requirement | application_max_2: selling price $1.30 per can; break-even 45,000 cans; retail grocery chain contracts; $60,000 capital outlay | analysis_max_2: expands margin of safety without capital cost; risks sales drop if retail buyers switch to competitors | evaluation_max_2: weighs price elasticity risks against capital expenditure in beverage bottling sector

--- STEM ---
A solar panel assembly facility operates as a Public Limited Company, manufacturing residential roof solar modules. Operating for 5 years, the facility employs 45 assembly technicians and produces 2,000 solar panels per month. Monthly fixed overheads total $120,000, including factory lease and robotic maintenance contracts. Variable costs per panel are $180 (photovoltaic cells, aluminum frames, and glass covers). Each solar panel sells for $300 wholesale. Monthly sales volume currently equals 2,000 units.

Due to rising global photovoltaic cell import costs, variable costs per panel are expected to rise to $210. To maintain profitability, management is debating whether to increase the wholesale selling price to $330 per panel or negotiate a $20,000 reduction in monthly factory fixed costs with the landlord.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'break-even output'.
    Answer: The total level of production/sales output at which total revenue equals total costs, resulting in zero profit and zero loss [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: output level where total revenue equals total costs; resulting in neither profit nor loss

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the current break-even output per month before the variable cost increase. Show your working.
    Answer: Contribution per unit = $300 - $180 = $120 per panel [k]. Break-even Output = Fixed Costs ($120,000) / Contribution ($120) = 1,000 panels per month [k], using the $120,000 monthly fixed overheads [app] and $180 photovoltaic cell variable cost per solar panel [app].
    Keywords: panels, solar, $300, $180, $120,000, photovoltaic, 2,000, assembly
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates contribution per unit ($120); calculates break-even output (1,000 panels) | application_max_2: $120 contribution from $300 price minus $180 variable cost; 1,000 panels break-even from $120,000 fixed overheads

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain the impact on the break-even output level if variable costs rise to $210 per panel while selling price remains $300.
    Answer: New Contribution = $300 - $210 = $90 per panel [k]. New Break-even Output = $120,000 / $90 = 1,334 panels per month [k]. This is 334 more panels than the current break-even of 1,000 [app], narrowing the margin of safety from 1,000 to 666 panels [app] and increasing operational financial risk [an]. A higher break-even also means the solar panel assembly plant must sell more units each month to avoid losses [an].
    Keywords: panels, solar, $210, $300, photovoltaic, $120,000, assembly
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates new contribution ($90) or new break-even point (1,334 panels); explains operational impact (narrowed margin of safety / higher risk) | application_max_2: $210 variable cost; 1,334 panels break-even; solar panel assembly; margin of safety narrowed to 666 panels | analysis_max_2: increases operational financial risk; requires higher sales volume to avoid losses

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think increasing the selling price to $330 per panel is a better strategy to maintain margin of safety than negotiating a $20,000 fixed cost reduction? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Increasing price to $330 restores contribution to $120 per panel ($330 - $210) [k], maintaining the original 1,000 panel break-even output ($120,000 / $120) [app] and preserving profit margins [an]. However, raising prices by $30 risks losing commercial installation contracts to rival solar module assembly plants, reducing monthly sales below 2,000 units [an]. Negotiating a $20,000 fixed cost reduction lowers fixed overheads to $100,000 [k] without customer pushback [app]. Overall, fixed cost reduction is better because solar energy markets are highly competitive [eval]; avoiding price hikes protects the 2,000 unit sales volume while lowering break-even risk safely [eval].
    Keywords: solar, panels, $330, $20,000, fixed costs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: restores unit contribution / maintains break-even point; lowers fixed overheads / avoids price elasticity demand loss | application_max_2: $330 selling price; 1,000 panel break-even; $20,000 fixed cost reduction; 2,000 monthly sales volume | analysis_max_2: preserves unit profit margins; risks losing installation contracts to competitors | evaluation_max_2: weighs price increase demand risks against fixed overhead cost reductions in solar equipment sector

    Answer: Contribution per unit = $2.50 - $1.00 = $1.50 per pair [k]. New Break-even Output = New Fixed Costs ($45,000) / Contribution ($1.50) = 30,000 pairs per month [k], using the $45,000 renewed factory lease [app] and $2.50 wholesale selling price per pair of soles [app].
    Keywords: soles, rubber, $45,000, footwear, $2.50, $1.00, athletic, 70,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: uses correct contribution ($1.50); calculates new break-even output (30,000 pairs) | application_max_2: $1.50 contribution from $2.50 price minus $1.00 variable cost; 30,000 pairs break-even from $45,000 fixed costs

  Qd [8 marks]

  Qb [4 marks]

    Answer: New Contribution = $600 - $350 = $250 per scooter [k]. New Break-even Output = $100,000 / $250 = 400 e-scooters per month [k], based on bulk purchase discounts reducing lithium battery pack costs to $350 [app] and unchanged $100,000 monthly fixed overheads [app].
    Keywords: e-scooters, lithium, battery, $600, $350, bulk purchase, commuter, assembly
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates new contribution ($250); calculates new break-even output (400 e-scooters) | application_max_2: $250 contribution from $600 price minus $350 battery discount; 400 e-scooters break-even from $100,000 fixed overheads

--- STEM ---
An automotive foundry operates as a Private Limited Company, casting iron brake discs for commercial vehicle manufacturers. Operating for 12 years, the foundry employs 70 metalworkers and casts 30,000 brake discs per month. Monthly fixed overheads total $90,000, while variable costs equal $150,000 ($5.00 per disc in scrap iron and alloy additives). Each brake disc sells for $12.00 wholesale.

Currently, the foundry relies on end-of-line Quality Control (QC) inspection. However, thermal stress during cooling causes a 6% defect rate, resulting in 1,800 cracked brake discs scrapped monthly, costing $9,000 in wasted metal. To improve production quality, management is debating whether to introduce Total Quality Management (TQM) with Kaizen quality circles across casting shifts or purchase automated ultrasonic crack detection testing machinery costing $150,000.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'Total Quality Management (TQM)'.
    Answer: An organization-wide operational approach focused on continuous quality improvement in all processes, aiming for zero defects through total employee involvement [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: organization-wide continuous quality improvement approach; aims for zero defects through employee involvement

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two operational drawbacks to this foundry of relying on Quality Control (QC) inspection.
    Answer: Drawback 1: High scrap costs [k], scrapping 1,800 cracked brake discs monthly and losing $9,000 in wasted metal [app]. Drawback 2: Fails to correct defect causes [k], inspecting discs after thermal cooling without preventing cracking during casting [app].
    Keywords: brake discs, foundry, cracked, $9,000, 1,800, iron
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high material waste / scrap costs; does not identify or correct root causes of defects | application_max_2: 1,800 cracked brake discs; $9,000 wasted metal; thermal cooling process; casting iron discs

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Kaizen quality circles can assist this business in achieving zero defects.
    Answer: Way 1: Continuous worker problem-solving [k], holding regular meetings where 70 metalworkers suggest adjustments to cooling temperatures [app], eliminating thermal stress cracks [an]. Way 2: Empowering factory workforce [k], encouraging casting operators to take responsibility for mold preparation quality [app], reducing rework expenses [an].
    Keywords: Kaizen, metalworkers, cooling, brake discs, foundry
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: regular small-group problem solving for continuous improvement; empowering workers to take ownership of process quality | application_max_2: 70 metalworkers; cooling temperatures / thermal stress; mold preparation quality; iron brake discs | analysis_max_2: eliminates thermal stress cracks; reduces scrap and rework expenses

  Qd [8 marks]

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the total monthly cost of wasted silicon raw materials caused by the 3% defect rate. Show your working.
    Answer: Defective Units = 100,000 x 3% = 3,000 chips [k]. Wasted Material Cost = 3,000 chips x $4.00 variable cost = $12,000 per month [k], based on the 3% dust contamination defect rate [app] and the $4.00 silicon wafer variable cost per chip [app].
    Keywords: microchips, silicon, cleanroom, $12,000, 3,000, wafers, $4.00, automotive
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: calculates defective units (3,000 chips); calculates total monthly material waste cost ($12,000) | application_max_2: 3,000 defective chips from 100,000 x 3%; $12,000 monthly waste from $4.00 variable cost per chip

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Job production is slow / low output rate; High unit costs / high wages for skilled craftspeople | application_max_2: 14-20 weeks per organ; 6 organs on the order book delayed; $85,000 average chapel organ price; 40% capacity used for 18 months | analysis_max_2: Delays to existing customers damages loyalty and could lose sales; High prices restrict demand / shrink the potential market

Bramblewood Preserves is a partnership run by Diane Whitmore and Marcus Bell in Country X, producing bottled fruit jams and chutneys. The firm makes 8 flavours in batches of 2,400 jars, with each batch taking one full day on the shared kettle and filling line. It employs 14 workers and sold 310,000 jars last year at an average selling price of $3.20 per jar.

A national supermarket chain has offered a three-year contract for 60,000 jars of strawberry jam per month, but only if the firm guarantees monthly deliveries. Diane and Marcus debate whether to increase batch size and buy a second kettle for $55,000, or keep producing mainly through farmers' markets, where loyal stall customers pay full price. Either route would reshape the partnership.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two disadvantages of batch production.
    Answer: Time is lost between batches when machinery must be reset, cleaned and switched to a different product [1]. Stock of finished goods or work-in-progress can build up between batches, raising storage costs and the risk of unsold output [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Setup / changeover time lost between batches; Work-in-progress or finished stock builds up / storage costs and risk of unsold stock

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of batch production for Bramblewood Preserves.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Batch production allows many different products to be made on shared equipment [k]. One kettle and filling line can produce all 8 flavours in runs of 2,400 jars, keeping fixed costs low for a small partnership [app]. Advantage 2: Batch production lets the firm switch easily when demand changes [k]. If strawberry sells faster than chutney, Diane and Marcus can allocate more batch days to strawberry and fewer to slow-selling flavours [app].
    Keywords: 8 flavours, 2,400 jars, farmers' markets, 60,000 jars, $3.20, strawberry jam
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Different products made on the same machinery / flexibility of product range; Easy to switch production when demand changes | application_max_2: 8 flavours produced on one shared kettle and filling line; batches of 2,400 jars; Strawberry vs chutney demand; farmers' markets vs supermarket

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of increasing batch size for the supermarket contract.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Larger batches spread setup costs across more jars [k]. Filling 60,000 jars a month in fewer, bigger runs would cut the cost per jar and help cover the $55,000 second kettle [app], which improves profit margins on the contract and frees cash for expansion [an]. Benefit 2: Bigger batches raise total capacity [k]. The existing line making 2,400 jars a day cannot reach 60,000 jars a month alone, so a second kettle lifts daily capacity and supports guaranteed monthly deliveries [app], reducing the risk of losing the three-year contract to a rival supplier [an].
    Keywords: $55,000, 60,000 jars, 2,400 jars, three-year contract, strawberry jam, 8 flavours
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Larger batches spread fixed / setup costs over more units, lowering unit cost; Larger batches / extra capacity increase potential output | application_max_2: 60,000 jars per month for three years; $55,000 second kettle; Current line makes 2,400 jars per day, insufficient alone for 60,000 jars per month | analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs improve margins and cash for expansion; Extra capacity secures monthly deliveries and protects the contract from rivals

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Diane and Marcus should buy the second kettle and take the supermarket contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arguments for taking the contract: it guarantees 60,000 jars per month for three years, far more than the 310,000 jars sold last year [k]. At $3.20 per jar, 60,000 jars gives monthly revenue of $192,000, dwarfing farmers' market sales [app]. This steady cash flow would repay the $55,000 kettle quickly and fund further growth [an]. Arguments against: relying on one supermarket hands the chain power to squeeze prices, and failing to deliver risks losing the contract and the kettle investment [k]. The firm may lose its farmers' market brand identity, with 8 flavours shrinking towards strawberry only [app]. Dependence on one buyer is dangerous if the chain cuts the contract after a year, leaving an expensive second kettle under-used [an]. Overall, with forecast revenue near $192,000 per month and a quick return on the investment, taking the contract is sensible provided they negotiate a price guarantee and keep some farmers' market presence [eval]. However, if the supermarket refuses price protection or demands exclusivity, remaining small protects margins and flexibility [eval].
    Keywords: 60,000 jars, $3.20, $55,000, 310,000 jars, three-year contract, farmers' markets, strawberry jam
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large orders can guarantee revenue and support economies of larger batches; Dependence on one large buyer increases risk / customer has negotiating power | application_max_2: 60,000 jars per month x $3.20 = $192,000 per month; 310,000 jars last year; $55,000 second kettle; three-year contract; farmers' markets at risk | analysis_max_2: Steady cash flow aids investment and growth; Loss of brand identity and over-dependence on one buyer | evaluation_max_2: Conditional judgement; justified by citing revenue and capital-cost figures; Notes circumstances under which decision should be reversed

--- STEM ---
SoftWeave Paper Products Ltd, a private limited company in Country X, manufactures paper tissues and kitchen roll on one continuous flow production line. The line runs 16 hours a day, 6 days a week, producing 1,200 packs per hour, and employs 38 machine operators plus 6 maintenance staff. Last year the firm sold 9.6 million packs at $2.40 each.

Demand is rising and SoftWeave is considering adding a second continuous line costing $1.15 million, rather than paying overtime or outsourcing overflow to a competitor's factory. The new line would double capacity to 2,400 packs per hour but would deepen dependence on a single supplier of recycled paper pulp. The directors must decide by next month, before the autumn peak trading season begins, and want a recommendation backed by the figures.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two advantages of flow production.
    Answer: Flow production can produce very large quantities quickly through a continuous process [1]. Unit costs are low because output is high and machinery keeps running, spreading fixed costs [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Very high output / continuous production; Low unit cost / fixed costs spread over huge output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why flow production suits SoftWeave Paper Products Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Paper tissues are a standardised, identical product sold in huge volumes, which suits continuous production [k]. The line already outputs 1,200 packs per hour and SoftWeave sold 9.6 million packs last year, volumes that job or batch production could not match economically [app]. Reason 2: Flow production uses capital equipment intensively with very few changeovers [k]. With only tissues and kitchen roll to make, the single line and its 38 machine operators can run 16 hours a day without costly resetting [app].
    Keywords: 1,200 packs per hour, 9.6 million packs, $2.40, 16 hours a day, 38 machine operators, kitchen roll
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Standardised, identical products suit flow production; Capital intensive, few changeovers / machinery used continuously | application_max_2: 1,200 packs per hour; 9.6 million packs sold; $2.40 per pack; 38 machine operators; 16 hours a day line running tissues and kitchen roll

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks of adding a second flow production line.
    Answer: Risk 1: The $1.15 million investment raises fixed costs sharply [k]. If demand dipped below the doubled capacity of 2,400 packs per hour, the new line would still incur machine and building costs [app], squeezing profit margins and lengthening the time needed to recoup the money invested [an]. Risk 2: A second line deepens dependence on a single supplier of recycled paper pulp [k]. Any disruption to pulp deliveries would halt twice as much output as before, stopping both lines together [app], which could lose key supermarket customers to rivals during the outage [an].
    Keywords: $1.15 million, 2,400 packs per hour, recycled paper pulp, single supplier, 1,200 packs per hour, $2.40
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: High capital cost / fixed costs rise with a second line; Dependence on one supplier / supply disruption risk | application_max_2: $1.15 million cost; doubled capacity of 2,400 packs per hour; Single supplier of recycled paper pulp; both lines depend on pulp | analysis_max_2: Idle capacity squeezes margins / delays recouping the investment; Losing pulp supply halts all output, risking customers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think SoftWeave should add the second production line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arguments for adding the line: demand is rising and the present line already runs 16 hours a day, 6 days a week, so it has no spare capacity [k]. A second line doubling capacity to 2,400 packs per hour could lift sales beyond 9.6 million packs without overtime or outsourcing premiums [app]. Higher output would lower average costs and could win new supermarket contracts [an]. Arguments against: outsourcing overflow is flexible, so SoftWeave pays only for the output it needs and avoids the $1.15 million outlay and the single-supplier pulp risk [k]. If demand fell, outsourcing could simply be cut back [app]. Keeping cash free also funds marketing and shields the firm from over-commitment to one pulp supplier [an]. Overall, if rising demand is confirmed by firm supermarket orders, the second line offers the lowest long-run unit cost and is worth funding [eval]. However, if demand is seasonal or unproven, outsourcing overflow first limits risk until the trend is certain [eval].
    Keywords: $1.15 million, 2,400 packs per hour, 9.6 million packs, 16 hours a day, $2.40, single supplier, recycled paper pulp
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Flow production lowers unit cost at high volumes / justifies investment; Outsourcing offers flexibility without capital outlay | application_max_2: 16 hours a day, 6 days a week, 1,200 packs per hour, 9.6 million packs; $1.15 million cost; 2,400 packs per hour capacity; single pulp supplier | analysis_max_2: Lower average costs and new contracts from expanded capacity; Flexibility of outsourcing vs fixed commitment and supplier risk | evaluation_max_2: Justified conditional judgement based on evidence of demand; Reversal condition stated if demand is unproven

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U4_SET_44
UNIT: Unit 4: Operations Management
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Calver Caravans Ltd manufactures recreational caravans in a large factory in Country X. Currently, 42 workers operate as one long flow line, fitting panels, wiring and interiors in sequence. Workers wait on the previous stage 11% of the time, quality complaints cost $18,000 last year, and the line produced 380 caravans in total at an average cost of $9,800 per unit, below the target margin.

The production manager proposes replacing the flow line with 6 self-contained cells, each staffed by 7 multi-skilled workers building one caravan from shell to finish. The changeover would cost $140,000 and take 6 weeks, but each cell could complete a caravan in 26 working days and fix defects inside the cell. Initial staff training would take 5 days per worker.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'cell production'.
    Answer: Cell production is a method of production where the process is split into groups (cells) of workers, each responsible for completing a whole product or a major part of it [1]. Each cell is self-managing and responsible for quality at its own stage [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Production split into groups/cells of workers completing whole products or major parts; Cells are self-managing / responsible for quality at their stage

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of cell production for Calver Caravans Ltd.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Cell production reduces waiting and movement between stages [k]. With 42 workers split into 6 self-contained cells, each caravan is built start-to-finish in one place, cutting the 11% idle time found on the flow line [app]. Advantage 2: Communication within a small cell is easier [k]. A 7-person cell can spot and fix wiring and panel faults immediately instead of passing defects down the line [app].
    Keywords: 6 self-contained cells, 7 multi-skilled workers, 11%, 380 caravans, $9,800, 42 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Less waiting/movement between stages / reduced idle time; Easier communication within small teams / defects fixed at source | application_max_2: 42 workers into 6 cells; eliminates 11% waiting time; 7 multi-skilled workers per cell; wiring and panel faults spotted early

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways cell production could improve quality and costs at Calver Caravans Ltd.
    Answer: Quality improvement: each cell owns the caravan from shell to finish and checks its own work [k]. Caravans completed in 26 working days within one cell are inspected by the same team that built them, so wiring and panel faults are caught earlier [app], reducing rework and warranty claims after delivery [an]. Cost improvement: multi-skilled workers can cover several tasks [k]. Coverage within each 7-person cell keeps output near 380 caravans a year flowing without overtime or temporary labour [app], lowering the average cost below $9,800 per caravan [an].
    Keywords: 26 working days, $9,800, 380 caravans, $140,000, 6 weeks, 7 multi-skilled workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cells responsible for quality at their stage / own-check inspection; Multi-skilled teams cover absences / flexibility of labour | application_max_2: 26 working days per caravan; faults caught within the cell; 7-person cells keep output near 380 caravans flowing | analysis_max_2: Earlier fault detection cuts rework and warranty costs; Less overtime/temp labour lowers average cost per caravan

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Calver Caravans Ltd should replace the flow line with cell production? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arguments for switching: cell production attacks the 11% idle time caused by waiting between flow-line stages [k]. Each of the 6 cells can build a whole caravan in 26 working days with defect-fixing inside the cell, cutting rework and potentially lifting output above 380 caravans a year [app]. Lower unit costs would strengthen competitiveness against imports [an]. Arguments against: the switch costs $140,000 and takes 6 weeks [k], during which production could fall and the order book suffer delays [app]. Multi-skilling 42 workers requires training time and some staff may resist the change [an]. Overall, because cells remove the 11% idle time and embed quality at a one-off cost of $140,000, the change is justified if cash flow allows and workers support it [eval]. However, if demand is uncertain or workers resist strongly, introducing cells one at a time over six months is the lower-risk route [eval].
    Keywords: $140,000, 6 weeks, 11%, 26 working days, 380 caravans, $9,800, 6 self-contained cells
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cell production reduces idle time/waiting and improves quality ownership; Switching production methods involves capital cost, disruption and training | application_max_2: 11% idle time; 26 working days per caravan; 6 cells of 7 workers; $140,000 cost; 6 weeks changeover; current output 380 caravans at $9,800 | analysis_max_2: Lower unit cost strengthens competitiveness vs imports; Disruption, training cost and staff resistance could delay the gains | evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement based on cash flow and worker buy-in; Alternative phased implementation acknowledges uncertainty

UNIT: Unit 4: Operations Management

--- STEM ---
Suncourt Flowers is a family-owned company in Country X growing cut roses and lilies for 3 national supermarket chains. It currently harvests each morning and stores up to 4 days of unsold flowers in a chilled cold store costing $3,600 per week to run. Last year wastage from unsold stock was 9% of output, and at peak the cold store holds $28,000 of flowers grown on 6 hectares.

The operations manager proposes switching to just-in-time, harvesting and delivering twice daily so supermarkets receive flowers within 8 hours of cutting. Hauliers would charge $700 per extra trip. The chains reserve the right to cancel standing orders at 48 hours notice. Suncourt's two regular hauliers need reliability checks before any change is agreed.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two advantages of low inventory levels for a business.
    Answer: Storage and warehousing costs fall because the business holds little stock [1]. Less working capital is tied up in unsold goods, and waste from obsolete or unsold stock is reduced [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower storage / warehousing costs; Less capital tied up in stock / less obsolete or wasted stock

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of switching to just-in-time for Suncourt Flowers.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Just-in-time would cut cold-store costs [k]. Harvesting and delivering twice daily so flowers reach shelves within 8 hours could remove the $3,600 weekly cold-store cost and shrink the $28,000 of flowers held at peak [app]. Benefit 2: Just-in-time also reduces waste [k]. The 9% of output lost to unsold stock should fall because flowers are cut only to known demand [app].
    Keywords: $3,600, $28,000, 9%, twice daily, 8 hours, just-in-time
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: JIT reduces storage / warehousing costs; JIT reduces waste / obsolete and unsold stock | application_max_2: Cold store costs $3,600 per week; holds $28,000 of flowers at peak; 9% of output wasted; twice daily harvest to demand

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks of just-in-time for Suncourt Flowers.
    Answer: Risk 1: Production for delivery can be stopped by transport failures [k]. Harvesting and delivering twice daily means any missed trip or vehicle breakdown leaves the supermarkets without flowers and Suncourt with no route to market for that day's cut [app], risking lost sales and penalties from the 3 national supermarket chains [an]. Risk 2: JIT depends on reliable partners and offers no protection against cancellations [k]. If a chain cancels its standing order at 48 hours notice, cut flowers already harvested for that order may have no other buyer [app], turning low stock levels into immediate write-offs with no time to find new customers [an].
    Keywords: twice daily, 48 hours notice, 3 national supermarket chains, 8 hours, 9% of output, $700 per extra trip
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Supply or transport delays can halt production / delivery; Dependence on reliable suppliers/customers; no fallback for cancellations | application_max_2: Twice daily harvests; $700 per extra haulier trip; 3 supermarket chains; Chains can cancel at 48 hours notice; flowers perish quickly | analysis_max_2: Missed deliveries mean lost sales and damaged supermarket relationships; Late cancellations create unsaleable perishable stock with no fallback

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Suncourt Flowers should switch to just-in-time? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arguments for switching: JIT removes the $3,600 weekly cold-store cost and shrinks the $28,000 peak stock, freeing working capital [k]. Fresher flowers within 8 hours of cutting improve shelf life and would delight supermarket buyers, strengthening the 3 contracts [app]. Higher quality and lower waste could lift margins on every stem sold [an]. Arguments against: JIT leaves the firm exposed to haulier delays and to chains cancelling at 48 hours notice [k]. Extra haulier trips at $700 add cost, and one missed twice-daily delivery could sour relationships with supermarkets [app]. Cancellation shortly after cutting could leave perishable stock unsold despite low inventory [an]. Overall, JIT suits a high-frequency, perishable product with 9% wastage and costly storage, so adopting it is justified provided hauliers prove reliable and chains sign minimum-order commitments [eval]. However, if the chains refuse minimum-order terms, holding a small back-up supply of one day's flowers is prudent insurance [eval].
    Keywords: $3,600, $28,000, 9%, 8 hours, $700, 48 hours notice, 3 national supermarket chains
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: JIT lowers storage costs and waste, suits perishable high-turnover goods; JIT risks halted operations and dependence on reliable supply and demand | application_max_2: $3,600 per week cold store; $28,000 peak stock; 9% wastage; 8 hours freshness; $700 per extra trip; 48 hours notice cancellations; 3 national chains | analysis_max_2: Lower costs and fresher stock strengthen margins and contracts; Transport failures and cancellations risk lost sales and unsold stock | evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement; conditions attached to the decision; Insurance via minimal back-up supply acknowledges residual risk
