--- STEM ---
Rushton Paper Mill Ltd, a private limited company in Country X, produces 26,000 tonnes of kraft paper a year on a 10-year-old machine. Last year the mill scrapped 2,080 tonnes as trimmings and off-spec rolls, equal to 8% of output, and spent $150,000 disposing of waste. Worker morale is low, the mill employs 120 workers on 3 shifts, and shop-floor ideas are rarely collected.

The operations director proposes a kaizen programme of small, continuous improvements, with weekly team meetings and a suggestion scheme, targeting a 25% cut in waste over 12 months. The alternative is a single immediate investment of $250,000 in a new laser trimmer, which would cut trimming waste by 40% at once but require board approval and about 8 weeks of commissioning time.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two ways kaizen can reduce waste in a factory.
    Answer: Workers suggest small, continuous improvements to processes and layouts, reducing unnecessary motion, waiting and handling [1]. Regular review and team feedback spot defects early, lowering reject rates and scrap [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Small continuous worker-led improvements to processes / layouts; Early spotting of defects / reduced motion, waiting, handling and rejects

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why kaizen could suit Rushton Paper Mill Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Kaizen costs little to start [k]. It avoids the $250,000 upfront laser trimmer and asks only for meeting time and a suggestion scheme, which suits a mill watching cash flow [app]. Reason 2: Kaizen empowers workers and lifts morale [k]. With morale low and ideas rarely collected, weekly team meetings give operators a voice, raising engagement and quality awareness across the shop floor [app].
    Keywords: weekly team meetings, $250,000, $150,000, Rushton Paper Mill Ltd, shop-floor, suggestion scheme
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Kaizen involves low-cost, continuous small improvements; Kaizen involves and motivates all employees / raises morale | application_max_2: Avoids $250,000 laser trimmer; low-cost meetings and suggestion scheme; Low morale and rarely collected shop-floor ideas

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of achieving a 25% cut in waste through kaizen.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Waste disposal and lost material costs fall [k]. Cutting 8% wastage by a quarter saves about 520 tonnes of paper a year and reduces part of the $150,000 disposal bill [app], directly lifting profit without new machinery or debt [an]. Benefit 2: A 25% waste cut frees up machine capacity [k]. With 26,000 tonnes sold a year, reclaiming 520 tonnes of sellable paper raises effective output and reduces reliance on the 10-year-old machine running flat out [app], helping the mill meet orders on time and avoid lost custom [an].
    Keywords: 2,080 tonnes, 8% of output, $150,000, 26,000 tonnes, 25%, $250,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Less waste lowers disposal / material / scrap costs; Less waste raises effective capacity / output from same resources | application_max_2: 25% of 2,080 tonnes = 520 tonnes saved; part of $150,000 disposal bill; 26,000 tonnes annual output; 10-year-old machine | analysis_max_2: Lower costs directly improve profit without debt; Extra capacity helps meet orders and protects customer relationships

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rushton Paper Mill Ltd should adopt kaizen instead of buying the laser trimmer? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arguments for kaizen: it attacks the same 8% wastage at low cost, avoiding the $250,000 trimmer outlay [k]. Weekly team meetings and a suggestion scheme build a culture of continuous improvement and lift morale on the shop floor [app]. Because kaizen is gradual, savings build over 12 months without debt or long machine downtime [an]. Arguments for the trimmer: it would cut trimming waste by 40% at once, beating the 25% kaizen target in year one [k]. A full year of gradual kaizen may under-deliver if meetings fade or workers mistrust the scheme [app]. Kaizen also demands sustained management commitment, whereas the trimmer is a one-off purchase [an]. Overall, kaizen is the better first step given its low cost, morale gains and 25% target, with the trimmer deferred until 12-month results are visible [eval]. However, if the board demands a guaranteed, fast 40% waste cut and cash is available, buying the trimmer now is the stronger choice [eval].
    Keywords: 8%, $250,000, $150,000, 2,080 tonnes, 25%, 40%, weekly team meetings
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Kaizen gives steady low-cost improvement with worker involvement; Capital investment gives immediate, guaranteed but costly waste reduction | application_max_2: 8% waste; 25% kaizen target; $150,000 disposal bill; $250,000 laser trimmer cutting waste 40% at once | analysis_max_2: Kaizen builds culture and avoids debt; savings are gradual and uncertain; Trimmer gives certainty and speed but high cost and less culture change | evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement; both options weighed with stem figures; States the circumstance under which the alternative is preferred

--- STEM ---
Thornfield Garden Tools Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making hand trowels, forks and rakes. Workers move parts between 3 separate buildings, and changeovers between product sizes take 55 minutes. Scrap from metal offcuts cost $95,000 last year, and late deliveries cost $30,000 in penalty fees. Orders are forecast at 38,000 units next year, with 4 national retailers already on the order book.

The owner is considering adopting lean production: cutting waste, reorganising the workflow into a single flow and involving workers in continuous improvement, at an initial cost of $60,000 for training and layout changes. The alternative is to carry on as before and rely on a new sales manager to boost revenue within 6 months.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'lean production'.
    Answer: Lean production is an approach to production that aims to reduce or eliminate waste of all kinds, such as time, materials, stock, movement and defects, from the production process [1]. It also aims to produce only what is needed, when it is needed, using fewer resources [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Approach aimed at eliminating/reducing waste (time, materials, stock, movement, defects); Produces only what is needed, when needed, using fewer resources

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of lean production for Thornfield Garden Tools Ltd.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Lean production reduces waste and cost [k]. Cutting the $95,000 metal-offcut scrap through tighter layouts and worker suggestions would directly improve profit [app]. Benefit 2: Lean production shortens changeover times [k]. Reducing the 55 minutes needed to change between trowel, fork and rake sizes lets Thornfield switch products faster and serve varied orders [app].
    Keywords: lean production, $95,000, 55 minutes, 3 separate buildings, $60,000, Thornfield Garden Tools Ltd
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lean reduces waste and costs; Lean reduces changeover / setup times and speeds flow | application_max_2: $95,000 scrap from metal offcuts; 55-minute changeovers between trowel, fork and rake sizes

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways lean production could help Thornfield meet next year's forecast of 38,000 units.
    Answer: Way 1: Lean removes delays between processes [k]. Reorganising into a single flow instead of 3 separate buildings cuts transport time and waiting between stages [app], so throughput rises without overtime and the 38,000 units forecast becomes achievable [an]. Way 2: Lean reduces late deliveries [k]. Smoother flow and faster 55-minute changeovers mean orders ship on time, helping avoid repeat $30,000 penalty fees [app], which keeps key retail customers loyal and protects future orders [an].
    Keywords: 38,000 units, 3 separate buildings, 55 minutes, $30,000, $95,000, single flow
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lean reduces waiting/transport/movement waste between processes; Lean smooths flow, reduces delays and late deliveries | application_max_2: Single flow replaces 3 separate buildings; throughput rises; 55-minute changeovers; avoids $30,000 penalty fees | analysis_max_2: Higher throughput without overtime supports 38,000 units forecast; On-time delivery protects customer loyalty and repeat orders

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Thornfield Garden Tools Ltd should adopt lean production? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arguments for adopting lean: it tackles waste directly, with $95,000 scrap, 55-minute changeovers and $30,000 penalty fees all reducible [k]. A one-off $60,000 for training and layout changes could recover its cost within a year and lift capacity towards 38,000 units [app]. Involving workers in continuous improvement should raise motivation and ownership on the shop floor [an]. Arguments for the sales-manager alternative: that route could boost revenue quickly without reorganising production or spending $60,000 upfront [k]. If workers resist change or meetings fade, lean savings may not materialise [app]. A new sales manager may also open new retail accounts that increase orders immediately [an]. Overall, lean production attacks the root causes of waste and should underpin sustainable growth towards 38,000 units, so adopting it now is justified if the owner commits to training and follow-through [eval]. However, if cash is tight, rolling the changes out gradually, department by department, limits risk while still capturing savings [eval].
    Keywords: $60,000, $95,000, $30,000, 55 minutes, 38,000 units, single flow, lean production
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lean addresses root-cause waste and can be employee-driven; Lean carries upfront cost, culture change and uncertain payoff | application_max_2: $95,000 scrap; $30,000 penalty fees; 55-minute changeovers; $60,000 training and layout cost; 38,000 units forecast | analysis_max_2: Sustainable cost and capacity gains underpin growth; Quick revenue boost possible but does not fix waste; risk of failed rollout | evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement citing investment cost and waste figures; Acknowledges risk and proposes staged alternative

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U4_SET_48
UNIT: Unit 4: Operations Management
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Spinwell Vinyl Ltd is a private limited company in Country X pressing vinyl records. It currently presses in batches of 2,000 records, changing labels and jackets between runs; the machine presses 4,000 records per working day and the firm sold 820,000 records last year. Independent artists order runs of 500-1,000 records, paying premium prices. Its cutting machines are serviced every 6 weeks under a fixed maintenance contract.

A major label has offered a three-year contract for 120,000 records per month of a new compilation album, the largest single order in the firm's history. Spinwell could keep batch production, adding night shifts at overtime cost, or invest $900,000 in a dedicated flow line pressing only that title at 15,000 records per day. The board meets next week to decide.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two disadvantages of flow production.
    Answer: Flow production is inflexible, making it expensive and time-consuming to switch the product made [1]. It requires very large capital investment and high output volumes to justify the specialist machinery [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Inflexible / hard and costly to switch products; High capital investment / needs high volumes to break even

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why batch production suits independent record orders.
    Answer: Reason 1: Batch production can switch between small, varied runs [k]. Runs of 500-1,000 records for independent artists need different labels and jackets, and changing over between batches makes these variations practical [app]. Reason 2: Batch production suits premium-priced, lower-volume work [k]. Pressing 500-1,000 at a time avoids overproducing unsold records while capturing the premium prices independent artists will pay [app].
    Keywords: 500-1,000, batches of 2,000, 4,000 records, independent artists, 820,000 records, premium prices
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Batch production handles small varied runs / changeovers between products; Batch suits premium-price, low-volume work / avoids overproduction | application_max_2: 500-1,000 record runs need different labels and jackets; Premium prices paid by independent artists

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of investing in the dedicated flow line.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A flow line slashes unit cost for the compilation [k]. Pressing 15,000 records per day of a single title removes the repeated changeovers of labels and jackets that slow batch runs today [app], so the very large 120,000 records per month contract becomes highly profitable [an]. Benefit 2: A flow line guarantees the label's monthly volumes [k]. At 15,000 records per day the line completes 120,000 records in 8 working days [app], giving the major label dependable supply throughout its three-year contract [an].
    Keywords: 15,000 records per day, 120,000 records per month, three-year contract, $900,000, 4,000 records per working day, labels and jackets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Flow production lowers unit cost at high volume / no changeovers; Flow production guarantees supply / dependable high output | application_max_2: 15,000 records per day of one title; no label/jacket changeovers; 120,000 records in 8 working days; 120,000 per month demand | analysis_max_2: Lower unit cost makes the compilation contract highly profitable; Dependable supply secures the three-year contract and future business

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Spinwell Vinyl Ltd should invest $900,000 in the dedicated flow line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arguments for the flow line: the three-year contract for 120,000 records per month guarantees predictable, enormous volume that batch production with changeovers cannot match [k]. The flow line at 15,000 records per day finishes the monthly quota in 8 working days, leaving capacity to serve other clients [app]. Lower unit costs would transform margins on the compilation and attract future major-label work [an]. Arguments against: the $900,000 outlay ties up cash in one title for one customer, and a flow line is inflexible [k]. Batch production with night shifts keeps flexibility to serve independent artists ordering 500-1,000 records at premium prices [app]. A compilation flop would leave a costly dedicated line under-used, dragging down profit [an]. Overall, because the contract alone amounts to 1.44 million records a year against only 820,000 sold last year, a dedicated flow line is justified provided the label signs a firm minimum-purchase clause [eval]. However, if the label will not commit beyond one year, staying with flexible batch production plus night shifts is the safer option [eval].
    Keywords: $900,000, 120,000 records per month, 15,000 records per day, three-year contract, 500-1,000, 4,000 records, 820,000 records
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Dedicated flow line suits very high-volume, stable demand; Batch keeps flexibility for varied, premium-priced small runs | application_max_2: 120,000 per month x 36 months; 15,000/day = 8 days to fulfil; $900,000; 820,000 records last year; 500-1,000 artist runs at premium prices | analysis_max_2: Lower unit cost and guaranteed supply win profit and future contracts; Single-customer, single-title dependence risks stranded investment if demand falls | evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement; compares 1.44 million contract volume vs 820,000 past sales; Stated reversal condition if contract commitment is weak

--- STEM ---
CaseCraft Ltd is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing phone cases under contract for 2 smartphone brands. Eight months ago it adopted just-in-time, holding almost no stock, and it now orders moulded parts from a single overseas supplier with a 12-week lead time and no local alternative.

Two supplier failures have since halted the assembly line for 3 days each, costing about $96,000 in lost output and forcing air-freighted parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment. The brands pay on a net-30 basis, which squeezes cash flow further. The operations manager, who joined 6 months ago, now debates abandoning just-in-time and rebuilding a 3-week stock of moulded parts costing $120,000, or keeping just-in-time and qualifying a second overseas supplier before the next smartphone model launch.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline two disadvantages of just-in-time production.
    Answer: If suppliers fail to deliver on time, production must stop because there is no stock to fall back on [1]. The business becomes heavily dependent on reliable suppliers, and any disruption can halt output completely [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Supply delays halt / stop production with no stock fallback; Heavy dependence on reliable suppliers

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks of just-in-time shown by CaseCraft's experience.
    Answer: Risk 1: Just-in-time leaves no stock to absorb supplier disruption [k]. Both halts followed supplier failures, and with a 12-week lead time CaseCraft could not quickly replace moulded parts from scratch [app]. Risk 2: A single overseas supplier creates dangerous dependence [k]. The need to air-freight parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment shows how one failing source can sharply raise costs and stress the two smartphone brands [app].
    Keywords: 12-week lead time, $18,000, $96,000, 3 days each, moulded parts, air-freighted
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Supply disruption halts production when no stock is held; Dependence on a single/unreliable supplier is risky | application_max_2: 12-week lead time; line halted for 3 days each time; Air-freighted parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of qualifying a second overseas supplier while keeping just-in-time.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A second supplier reduces the chance of a halted line [k]. If one supplier fails, CaseCraft can switch orders across, avoiding 3-day stoppages like the two that cost $96,000 in lost output [app], protecting the two smartphone contracts and future renewals [an]. Benefit 2: A second supplier keeps the benefits of just-in-time [k]. Just-in-time still avoids the $120,000 needed to rebuild a 3-week stock, plus storage costs [app], so the firm keeps its lean cash flow while gaining resilience [an].
    Keywords: 3-week stock, $120,000, $96,000, 12-week lead time, $18,000, just-in-time
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Multiple suppliers reduce risk of stoppage / increase resilience; Qualifying a second supplier preserves low-stock / lean advantages | application_max_2: Two halts cost $96,000; avoiding repeat losses protects contracts; Avoids $120,000 3-week stock and storage costs | analysis_max_2: Protects the two smartphone contracts and reputation; Maintains low working capital and lean cash flow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think CaseCraft Ltd should abandon just-in-time? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arguments for abandoning: two supplier failures in 8 months stopped the line for 6 days in total and cost $96,000 in lost output plus $18,000 air-freight bills [k]. Rebuilding a 3-week stock of parts costing $120,000 would let the line run through most disruptions and protect the two smartphone contracts [app]. Predictability and customer trust may outweigh stock-holding costs [an]. Arguments against abandoning: a 3-week stock ties up $120,000 that could be used elsewhere and adds storage costs, eroding the savings just-in-time created [k]. Qualifying a second overseas supplier attacks the same risk at lower cost while keeping working capital free [app]. Large stock also raises obsolescence risk for phone-specific parts [an]. Overall, abandoning just-in-time entirely is not justified; qualifying a second supplier plus a small emergency stock of critical parts is cheaper and safer than either extreme [eval]. However, if no second supplier can be qualified within 3 months, rebuilding the 3-week stock is a necessary stopgap [eval].
    Keywords: $120,000, $96,000, 3 days each, 12-week lead time, just-in-time, $18,000, 2 smartphone brands
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: JIT risk: halted production, dependence on suppliers; Stock holding costs: capital tied up, storage, obsolescence | application_max_2: Two halts x 3 days; $96,000 lost output; $18,000 air-freight; $120,000 3-week stock; 12-week lead time; 8 months experience | analysis_max_2: Stock gives predictability and protects customer contracts; Second supplier preserves lean benefits at lower cost; obsolescence risk of stock | evaluation_max_2: Justified conditional judgement favouring second supplier / small emergency stock; Stated fallback if supplier cannot be qualified quickly

--- STEM ---
Calloway Rods is a sole-trader fishing-rod workshop in Country X run by Sam Whitaker, building bespoke trout and salmon rods. Each rod is made to the angler's specification in about 7 days, sells at $340, and the workshop produced 260 rods last year with a 6-week waiting list and a part-time assistant who varnishes each rod.

Sam's supplier of hand-built cork grips has cut prices for identical grip designs ordered in batches. Local angling shops have asked to stock 3 standard models. Sam could keep full job production, switch the 3 standard models to batches of 40 and keep bespoke work on top, or go fully batch and drop custom orders completely, ending a decade of one-off builds. The shops want an answer within 3 months.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline two advantages of batch production.
    Answer: Batch production allows a range of different products to be made on shared machines, keeping some flexibility between runs [1]. Unit costs are lower than job production because larger quantities spread fixed and setup costs [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Different products made in batches on shared machinery / flexibility of range; Lower unit cost than job production / setup costs spread over batch

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why batch production might help Calloway Rods.
    Answer: Reason 1: Batch production lowers unit costs for standard lines [k]. Making 3 standard models in batches of 40 would spread labour and machine time across 120 rods, cutting average cost per rod compared with one-off builds [app]. Reason 2: Batch production can supply local angling shops reliably [k]. Stocking 3 standard models in predictable batches of 40 matches exactly what the shops have asked for and relieves the 6-week waiting list [app].
    Keywords: batches of 40, 3 standard models, $340, 260 rods, angling shops, bespoke
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower unit cost from larger runs / shared fixed costs; Predictable stock supply for retailers | application_max_2: 3 standard models x 40 = 120 rods per batch cycle; Angling shops asked for 3 standard models; 6-week waiting list

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Calloway Rods could face if it switched fully to batch production.
    Answer: Problem 1: Unique bespoke work would disappear [k]. Dropping custom orders means giving up the $340 bespoke trout and salmon rods and the loyal customers behind the 6-week waiting list [app], shrinking the firm's premium reputation with serious anglers [an]. Problem 2: Batch production risks unsold stock [k]. If the 3 standard models do not sell in batches of 40, capital is tied up in rods that angling shops cannot shift [app], raising storage costs and waste if designs fall out of fashion [an].
    Keywords: $340, 6-week waiting list, 260 rods, batches of 40, 3 standard models, bespoke
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Loss of custom/bespoke work and premium reputation; Risk of unsold stock / capital tied up in batches | application_max_2: $340 bespoke trout and salmon rods; 6-week waiting list; 3 standard models in batches of 40 held as stock | analysis_max_2: Eroding bespoke reputation reduces premium pricing power; Unsold batches tie up cash and raise storage/obsolescence costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sam should switch the three standard models to batch production alongside the bespoke work? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arguments for switching: producing 3 standard models in batches of 40 spreads setup costs, frees capacity for bespoke rods and shortens the 6-week waiting list [k]. Supplier discounts on identical hand-built cork grips ordered in batches cut material costs further [app]. The angling shops' request widens the market beyond the 260 rods sold last year [an]. Arguments against: splitting production could dilute the bespoke reputation that supports $340 pricing [k]. Batch runs of 40 unsold models tie up cash, and savings only materialise if grips are ordered for proven demand [app]. Overproducing one design would leave expensive unsold stock [an]. Overall, adding 3 standard batch models alongside bespoke work captures shop demand and supplier discounts without abandoning the firm's identity, so the partial switch is justified [eval]. However, Sam should keep batches small and monitor sell-through before expanding, protecting workshop flexibility [eval].
    Keywords: batches of 40, 3 standard models, 6-week waiting list, $340, 260 rods, angling shops, cork grips
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Batch suits standard models / spreads setup costs, frees capacity; Risks: diluted bespoke identity, unsold stock, tied-up capital | application_max_2: Batches of 40 for 3 standard models; 6-week waiting list; 260 rods last year; Supplier discounts on identical cork grips; $340 bespoke price | analysis_max_2: Wider market and lower costs while retaining bespoke identity; Overproduction and reputation dilution risk if demand misjudged | evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement favouring partial switch; Safeguard suggested: small batches and sell-through monitoring

--- STEM ---
Brackenhill Biscuits Ltd is a family-owned biscuit manufacturer in Country X that has produced shortbread and cream crackers for 11 years. Last year the business invested $480,000 in an automated wrapping and packing line using robotic arms, capable of sealing 120 packs per minute. The new equipment replaced 3 manual packing benches and 15 jobs. The owning family wants the business to stay cost-competitive against larger rivals importing cheaper biscuits.

Since the line began operating in March, output has risen from 38,000 to 52,000 packs per week, and faulty seals have fallen from 4% to 1% of packs. The operations manager estimates the investment will pay for itself in under 3 years, although the 15 redundant packers received only statutory pay and morale among the remaining 60 factory workers has dipped.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'automation'.
    Answer: Automation is the use of machines and technology to control and carry out production processes with little or no human input [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Use of machines/technology to carry out tasks or control processes; Little or no human involvement or intervention in the process

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Brackenhill Biscuits of automating its packing line.
    Answer: First, the line raised productivity [k], sealing 120 packs per minute and lifting weekly output from 38,000 to 52,000 packs [app]. Second, product quality improved [k], as faulty seals fell from 4% to 1% of packs [app].
    Keywords: Brackenhill Biscuits, $480,000, 120 packs per minute, 38,000, 52,000, 4% to 1%, packing line
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher productivity/output per period; Improved and more consistent product quality or fewer errors | application_max_2: Line seals 120 packs per minute and weekly output rose from 38,000 to 52,000 packs; Faulty seals fell from 4% to 1% of packs

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages for Brackenhill Biscuits of introducing the automated line.
    Answer: First, redundancies [k]: the business made 15 packers redundant, so they received only statutory pay [app], and lower morale among the remaining 60 factory workers could raise absenteeism and errors [an]. Second, high capital outlay [k]: $480,000 had to be spent before the estimated payback of under 3 years [app], so if weekly output falls short of 52,000 packs the family may struggle to recover the cost and stay competitive against imports [an].
    Keywords: Brackenhill Biscuits, $480,000, redundant packers, statutory pay, 60 factory workers, under 3 years, 52,000 packs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Redundancies and loss of jobs; High initial capital cost of the investment | application_max_2: 15 packers made redundant and paid only statutory pay; morale dipped among the remaining 60 factory workers; $480,000 was invested with payback estimated at under 3 years | analysis_max_2: Poorer morale could increase absenteeism and mistakes on the line; If demand or output falls below 52,000 packs per week, repaying the investment becomes harder and threatens competitiveness

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brackenhill Biscuits should invest in automated mixing and baking equipment as well? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes, further automation should raise productivity [k]; the packing line lifted output from 38,000 to 52,000 packs per week and cut faulty seals from 4% to 1% [app]; extending the same technology to mixing and baking could remove more errors, lower unit costs and keep biscuits cheaper than imports [an]. However, automation destroyed jobs [k]; this project cost $480,000, made the 15 redundant packers leave on statutory pay and soured morale among the remaining 60 factory workers [app]; repeating that scale of disruption in mixing and baking, where timing and temperature need judgement, could deepen absenteeism and hurt consistency [an]. Overall I recommend phased investment in automated mixing first, with skilled staff retrained and supervising [eval]; baking should keep human oversight for now, so automating both stages fully would be premature given the morale damage already seen [eval].
    Keywords: Brackenhill Biscuits, $480,000, 38,000, 52,000, 4% to 1%, redundant packers, 60 factory workers, under 3 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation raises productivity and reduces errors; Automation causes redundancies, high capital cost and morale problems | application_max_2: Output rose from 38,000 to 52,000 packs per week; faulty seals fell from 4% to 1%; $480,000 invested, 15 packers redundant on statutory pay, morale dipped among 60 remaining workers | analysis_max_2: More automation could cut unit costs and errors and improve competitiveness against imports; Over-automation in baking could damage morale and product consistency, risking mistakes | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both sides and reaches a clear, justified recommendation; Conditional decision (phased approach) supported by stem figures

--- STEM ---
Cinderford Brickworks is a brick manufacturer in Country X that has supplied builders for 14 years, producing facing and engineering bricks for housebuilders across the region. Two years ago the owners spent $250,000 installing a mechanised extrusion machine and automatic wire-cutter, allowing operators to feed clay rather than mould bricks by hand. The yard now employs 74 workers, 30 of whom run the machines.

Output has risen from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week, and reject bricks have fallen from 7% to 3%. Hourly wages of $11.50 for machine operators tempt the business to recruit 6 more workers this year, but clay prices have climbed 12%. The kilns are now the production bottleneck, and the owners have delayed a planned wage rise until 2027 while they repay the machine loan.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'mechanisation'.
    Answer: Mechanisation is the use of machines to carry out work that was previously done by hand, with workers still operating or controlling the machines [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Use of machines to replace or assist manual labour; Human operators still control or supervise the machines

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Cinderford Brickworks introduced mechanised machines.
    Answer: First, to raise output [k]; the mechanised extruder and wire-cutter lifted production from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week [app]. Second, to cut waste [k]; reject bricks fell from 7% to 3% after the machines were installed [app].
    Keywords: Cinderford Brickworks, $250,000, mechanised extrusion machine, 140,000, 210,000, 7% to 3%, 74 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: To increase output/productivity; To reduce waste, rejects and human error | application_max_2: Production rose from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week; Reject bricks fell from 7% to 3%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Cinderford Brickworks may face from its mechanisation.
    Answer: First, dependence on skilled operators [k]: the business relies on 30 of its 74 workers to run the machines at $11.50 per hour [app], so any absence or breakdown could stop extrusion and widen the kiln bottleneck [an]. Second, rising input costs [k]: clay prices have climbed 12% [app], squeezing margins and making it harder to recover the $250,000 outlay without raising brick prices for builders [an].
    Keywords: Cinderford Brickworks, $250,000, run the machines, $11.50, 12%, 210,000 bricks per week, 140,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Dependence on specialist operators and machine breakdowns; Higher costs or repayment burden after investment | application_max_2: 30 of 74 workers run the machines at $11.50 per hour; Clay prices have climbed 12% after $250,000 was spent | analysis_max_2: Absences or breakdowns halt output and delay deliveries to builders; Squeezed margins limit funds for kiln upgrades and may force price rises that risk losing customers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cinderford Brickworks should now invest in mechanising the kilns as well? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes, mechanising the kilns would attack the bottleneck [k]; the yard already lifted output from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week and cut rejects from 7% to 3% by mechanising extrusion [app]; applying the same approach to firing could raise capacity and stabilise quality while builder demand keeps growing [an]. However, machines reduce rather than increase labour needs [k]; the business has already spent $250,000 and pays operators $11.50 per hour amid a 12% clay price rise [app], and another large outlay plus recruiting 6 more workers risks overstretching cash if the housing market slows [an]. Overall I recommend phased kiln mechanisation funded largely from retained profit, because the proven 50% output gain outweighs the cost risk, provided the new recruits are trained to operate the machines before phase two begins [eval]; if clay costs keep climbing, phase two should be delayed rather than debt-financed [eval].
    Keywords: Cinderford Brickworks, $250,000, 140,000, 210,000, 7% to 3%, 12%, $11.50, 6 more workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Mechanisation raises capacity and reduces rejects; High capital cost and cash-flow strain | application_max_2: Output rose from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week; rejects fell from 7% to 3%; $250,000 already spent, $11.50 hourly wages, clay prices up 12%, plan to recruit 6 more workers | analysis_max_2: Mechanised kilns could remove the bottleneck and meet growing builder demand with consistent quality; Extra capital spending could strain cash and threaten the business if housing demand slows or clay costs rise further | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both sides and reaches a clear, justified recommendation; Conditional decision supported by stem figures

--- STEM ---
Dunmere Plastics Ltd is an injection-moulding business in Country X producing plastic housings for washing machines, lawnmowers and dishwashers, trading for 8 years. The factory runs two 8-hour shifts, five days a week. It recently installed CAM software costing $320,000 to control its 8 moulding machines directly from programs written by the production office. CAM programs also log every machine fault automatically.

Machine set-up time has fallen from 45 minutes to 12 minutes, and scrap has fallen from 9% to 4% of output. Annual output is now 950,000 housings, exported to 3 countries. Orders from 2 washing-machine plants account for 80% of output. The managing director is considering extending CAM to the final assembly robot, which would displace 12 of the 120 employees.

    Question: Define 'CAM (computer-aided manufacturing)'.
    Answer: CAM is the use of computer software to control machines and manufacturing processes directly during production [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Computer software controls machines/processes; Used to plan and run manufacturing directly in production

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of CAM for Dunmere Plastics Ltd.
    Answer: First, faster set-ups [k]; machine set-up time fell from 45 minutes to 12 minutes [app]. Second, less waste [k]; scrap fell from 9% to 4% of output [app].
    Keywords: Dunmere Plastics Ltd, $320,000, 45 minutes, 12 minutes, 9% to 4%, 950,000 housings, 8 moulding machines
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Reduced machine set-up/changeover time; Reduced scrap/waste and errors | application_max_2: Set-up time fell from 45 minutes to 12 minutes; Scrap fell from 9% to 4% of output

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Dunmere Plastics may face if it extends CAM to the final assembly robot.
    Answer: First, job losses and morale [k]: extending CAM to assembly would displace 12 of the 120 employees [app], which could damage motivation, raise turnover and harm the business's reputation as an employer [an]. Second, high extra cost and risk [k]: after spending $320,000 on moulding CAM, another system must be bought and integrated [app], so if exports to the 3 countries slow, the investment may take longer to repay and strain cash flow [an].
    Keywords: Dunmere Plastics Ltd, $320,000, 12 of the 120 employees, 950,000 housings, 3 countries, 8 moulding machines, 80% of output
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Redundancies/job losses harming morale and reputation; High additional capital cost and repayment risk | application_max_2: Assembly CAM would displace 12 of the 120 employees; $320,000 already spent on the moulding CAM system | analysis_max_2: Displaced workers may leave, reducing goodwill and raising training costs for remaining staff; Extra investment is risky if export demand in the 3 countries weakens, delaying payback

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Dunmere Plastics should extend CAM to the final assembly robot? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes, assembly CAM would compound the gains [k]; moulding CAM already cut set-ups from 45 to 12 minutes and scrap from 9% to 4%, with 950,000 housings exported to 3 countries [app]; extending computer control to assembly could deliver the same consistency at the final stage and help win larger export contracts [an]. However, assembly CAM would displace 12 of the 120 employees [app]; the moulding system already cost $320,000 [k], and forcing 12 redundancies could lower morale, raise absenteeism and increase long-run labour costs among those remaining [an]. Overall I recommend extending CAM to assembly only if the 12 affected workers are retrained or redeployed [eval]; the quality and export benefits justify the move, but rushing it without reskilling would risk the workforce goodwill the business still needs [eval].
    Keywords: Dunmere Plastics Ltd, $320,000, 12 of the 120 employees, 45 minutes, 12 minutes, 9% to 4%, 950,000 housings, 3 countries
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAM improves consistency, speed and waste reduction; Redundancies harm morale and reputation | application_max_2: Set-up fell 45 to 12 minutes; scrap fell 9% to 4%; 950,000 housings exported to 3 countries; Assembly robot would displace 12 of 120 employees; moulding CAM cost $320,000 | analysis_max_2: Consistent final assembly could win larger export contracts and cut customer complaints; Forcing 12 redundancies could reduce morale and raise long-run labour costs | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both sides and reaches a clear, justified recommendation; Conditional decision supported by stem figures

--- STEM ---
Aldercroft Auto Components is a private limited company in Country X producing suspension brackets and exhaust flanges for 2 car assembly plants. It employs 240 workers at a single factory on an industrial estate. Two years ago the business invested $1.2 million in a CIM system linking its design office, 14 CNC machines, quality scanners and a stock control database.

The system passes CAD designs straight to CAM files, schedules machine use automatically and flags defects on the line. Defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5%, and average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days, helping both assembly plants cut buffer stock. However, CIM needs 2 full-time IT technicians on $38,000 salaries, and the $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'CIM (computer-integrated manufacturing)'.
    Answer: CIM is the use of a single computer system to link and control all stages of production, from design through manufacture to quality and stock control [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Computer systems link and control production stages together; Covers design, manufacture, quality and stock/inventory control in one integrated system

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of CIM for Aldercroft Auto Components.
    Answer: First, better product quality [k]; defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5% after the system was installed [app]. Second, faster delivery [k]; average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days, helping both assembly plants cut buffer stock [app].
    Keywords: Aldercroft Auto Components, $1.2 million, 6% to 1.5%, 21 to 9 days, 14 CNC machines, 240 workers, 2 car assembly plants
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Improved quality/fewer defects; Faster lead time/quicker deliveries | application_max_2: Defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5%; Average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks or costs of CIM for Aldercroft Auto Components.
    Answer: First, dependence on specialist staff [k]: CIM needs 2 full-time IT technicians on $38,000 salaries [app], so if they leave, the whole production line could stall until replacements are found and trained [an]. Second, financial risk [k]: the $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan [app], so the business must keep the 2 assembly plants' orders profitable enough to meet interest payments, or face cash-flow pressure if orders fall [an].
    Keywords: Aldercroft Auto Components, $1.2 million, $38,000, 2 full-time IT technicians, 14 CNC machines, 2 car assembly plants, 6% to 1.5%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Dependence on scarce specialist IT staff; High capital cost financed by borrowing | application_max_2: 2 full-time IT technicians required on $38,000 salaries; $1.2 million financed by a bank loan | analysis_max_2: If technicians leave or the system fails, production stops and deliveries to both assembly plants are jeopardised; Loan repayments strain cash flow; falling orders would make the debt harder to service

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Aldercroft Auto Components should roll CIM out to a second production hall? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes, rolling CIM out to a second hall would replicate proven gains [k]; defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5% and lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days [app]; a second hall could cut buffer stocks for both assembly plants, win more orders and spread the fixed costs of the CIM system [an]. However, the first $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan and the system already needs 2 IT technicians on $38,000 salaries [app]; duplicating it doubles loan pressure, and one technical failure could halt even more limited IT capacity [an], even though integration usually lifts productivity [k]. Overall I recommend a phased second-hall rollout funded from operating surplus rather than new borrowing [eval], because the 4.5-point defect fall and 12-day lead-time cut are compelling, but only once the 2 technicians confirm the system is stable [eval].
    Keywords: Aldercroft Auto Components, $1.2 million, $38,000, 6% to 1.5%, 21 to 9 days, 2 car assembly plants, 14 CNC machines, 240 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CIM raises quality and speed across production; High capital cost and dependence on specialist staff | application_max_2: Defects fell from 6% to 1.5%; lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days; $1.2 million financed by bank loan; 2 IT technicians on $38,000 salaries | analysis_max_2: Second hall would spread fixed costs, cut buffer stock and win more assembly-plant orders; New borrowing or a single system failure could strain cash and halt production | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both sides and reaches a clear, justified recommendation; Conditional decision supported by stem figures

Dorchester Village Stores operates 6 grocery supermarkets in Country X, employing 145 staff. Last year it spent $180,000 installing EPOS tills in all 6 stores. Each checkout now scans barcodes, records sales by the hour and updates a central stock database automatically. The head office believes EPOS will free staff from manual stock counts.

EPOS data shows fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% of stock within 4 months. The system flags when any of 400 key product lines drop below 2 weeks of expected sales. Trading on a Saturday can reach $38,000 per store, so managers worry automatic orders may over-buy perishables before quiet weekdays.   Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of EPOS for Dorchester Village Stores.
    Answer: First, reduced wastage [k]; fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% of stock within 4 months [app]. Second, better reordering [k]; the system flags when any of 400 key product lines drop below 2 weeks of expected sales [app].
    Keywords: Dorchester Village Stores, $180,000, 12% to 7%, EPOS, 400 key product lines, 2 weeks of expected sales, $5,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower wastage/better stock control; Automatic reordering and sales data capture | application_max_2: Fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% within 4 months; EPOS flags product lines below 2 weeks of expected sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Dorchester Village Stores holds inventories.

Second, to balance wastage against availability [k]; fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% after EPOS began tracking sales [app], showing that accurate stock data lets the business hold the right amount instead of over-ordering perishables [an].

  Qd [8 marks]

--- STEM ---
Tannersley Glassworks is a glass bottle manufacturer in Country X that has supplied soft-drink bottlers for 16 years. Its 120 workers produced 240,000 bottles per week, an average of 2,000 bottles per worker per week. After installing 2 new furnaces and an extra forming machine costing $900,000, the factory made 288,000 bottles per week with 96 workers. The factory operates three shifts, six days a week.

That equals 3,000 bottles per worker per week, a 50% rise in productivity, and annual output is now about 15 million bottles, up from 12.5 million. The $900,000 was borrowed from a bank. Overtime would cost $16 per hour time-and-a-half, while a furnace would take 18 months to install but last 25 years. Bottlers want an extra 40,000 bottles a week under contract.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'productivity'.
    Answer: Productivity is the output produced per worker, or per other input, over a given time period [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Output per worker/per input; Measured over a period of time

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two differences between production and productivity.
    Answer: First, what they measure [k]; production is total output, which rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week, while productivity is output per worker, which rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker [app]. Second, how each is increased [k]; production can be raised by adding workers or overtime, while productivity rose because 96 workers replaced 120 after the new machines arrived [app].
    Keywords: Tannersley Glassworks, 240,000 bottles, 288,000 bottles, 2,000 bottles, 3,000 bottles, 120 workers, 96 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Production = total output; productivity = output per worker/per input; Production can be raised by more inputs; productivity by more efficient use of inputs | application_max_2: Total output rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week; Output per worker rose from 2,000 to 3,000 after the workforce fell from 120 to 96

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Tannersley Glassworks of the rise in productivity.
    Answer: First, lower labour cost per bottle [k]; output rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week while the workforce fell from 120 to 96 [app], so fixed costs are spread over more units and the business can improve profit to help repay the $900,000 loan [an]. Second, stronger competitiveness [k]; each of the 96 remaining workers now produces 3,000 bottles per week [app], so unit costs fall and Tannersley can undercut rivals to win the contract for an extra 40,000 bottles a week [an].
    Keywords: Tannersley Glassworks, 240,000, 288,000, 120 workers, 3,000 bottles, $900,000, 40,000 bottles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher output per worker lowers average cost per unit; Improved efficiency and competitiveness | application_max_2: Output rose 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week while staff fell from 120 to 96; Each worker now produces 3,000 bottles per week | analysis_max_2: Fixed costs are spread over more bottles, improving profit and ability to repay the bank loan; Lower unit costs strengthen competitiveness and support winning the extra 40,000 bottles contract

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tannersley Glassworks should raise output further by overtime or by buying a third furnace? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes, a third furnace would replicate the gains [k]; productivity already rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker after the 2 new furnaces were installed [app]; a third furnace would last 25 years and help supply bottlers the extra 40,000 bottles a week under contract [an]. However, overtime is more flexible right now [k]; the $900,000 was borrowed and overtime at $16 per hour time-and-a-half adds capacity without new long-term debt [app]; but overtime raises labour cost per bottle and cannot match machine efficiency or consistent quality [an]. Overall I recommend buying the third furnace, financed partly from retained profit, because the proven 50% productivity rise shows machines outperform overtime [eval]; if demand softens before contracts are signed, delay the furnace and use overtime as a stop-gap [eval].
    Keywords: Tannersley Glassworks, $900,000, 240,000, 288,000, 2,000, 3,000, 50%, $16 per hour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Investment in capital machinery raises productivity long term; Overtime adds capacity quickly but at higher unit cost | application_max_2: Productivity rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker after 2 new furnaces; $900,000 loan outstanding; overtime at $16 per hour time-and-a-half; furnace would take 18 months and last 25 years | analysis_max_2: A third furnace locks in capacity and consistency to fulfil the 40,000 bottles weekly contract; Overtime protects cash flow now but erodes unit economics and quality consistency | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options and reaches a clear, justified recommendation; Conditional decision supported by stem figures

  Qb [4 marks]

Second, secure more inputs [k]; buying more milk from the 26 local farms or signing new suppliers would let the 3 existing vats run closer to full capacity [app].
    Keywords: Dunnock Cheese Co, 18,000 kg, 3 pasteurising vats, fourth vat, $150,000, 25%, 26 local farms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Increase capacity/capital equipment; Secure more inputs (raw materials, labour) or use existing capacity fully | application_max_2: Fourth vat costing $150,000 would raise capacity by 25% (18,000 kg to 22,500 kg); Milk comes from 26 local farms via 3 pasteurising vats

  Qc [6 marks]

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Reducing waste/improving input efficiency; Better planning and scheduling of labour and capital | application_max_2: 180,000 litres of milk bought at $0.42 per litre each month; 40 workers and 3 vats in use; orders worth $9,000 a month turned away | analysis_max_2: Better yields spread the milk cost over more cheese, raising profit per kg; Smarter scheduling raises output without new capital spending, easing pressure on the $150,000 decision

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Dunnock Cheese Co should buy the fourth vat now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes, the fourth vat would capture lost sales [k]; the vats are fully booked and the business turns down orders worth $9,000 a month [app]; a 25% capacity increase to 22,500 kg would lift revenue above $198,000 and push profit beyond $27,000 [an]. However, milk and cheesemaker supplies are limited [k]; the 26 local farms already supply 180,000 litres a month, and hiring skilled cheesemakers locally is hard [app]; spending $150,000 without guaranteed inputs could leave an expensive vat idle and strain cash [an]. Overall I recommend buying the fourth vat only after securing extra milk contracts and at least one cheesemaker [eval]; demand clearly exists, but the vat will not pay for itself if inputs stay capped [eval].
    Keywords: Dunnock Cheese Co, $150,000, 25%, $198,000, $27,000, 180,000 litres, 26 local farms, $0.42
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Capacity investment captures unmet demand; Input constraints (raw materials, labour) can idle new capital | application_max_2: Turns down orders worth $9,000 a month; sales $198,000, profit $27,000; 26 farms supply 180,000 litres at $0.42; cheesemaker supply limited; vat costs $150,000 | analysis_max_2: A 25% capacity rise to 22,500 kg would lift revenue and profit; Without extra milk or labour the vat sits idle, wasting $150,000 and worsening cash flow | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both sides and reaches a clear, justified recommendation; Conditional decision supported by stem figures

Quillbrook Pens Ltd is a small manufacturer in Country X producing luxury brass fountain pens, employing 28 workers. Pens retail at $180 each and are popular with corporate gift buyers.   Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Quillbrook Pens Ltd holds inventories.
    Answer: First, to meet seasonal demand [k]; EPOS sales data from 40 stockist shops shows November demand spikes sharply [app]. Second, to avoid lost sales [k]; running out of stock in October would lose the season's sales [app].
    Keywords: Quillbrook Pens Ltd, November, 500 pens, 3 months of raw materials, EPOS sales data, 40 stockist shops, $7,500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Meet expected/seasonal demand and avoid stockouts; Keep production running between deliveries | application_max_2: EPOS data from 40 stockist shops shows November demand spikes; Running out of stock in October would lose the season's sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of holding too much inventory for Quillbrook Pens Ltd.

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Quillbrook Pens Ltd should build inventory to 4 months' supply or arrange faster deliveries from the brass supplier? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes, higher inventory protects the season [k]; EPOS sales data from 40 stockist shops shows November demand spikes, and running out of stock in October would lose the season's sales [app]; 4 months' supply would let the factory run batches of 500 pens ahead of orders [an]. However, faster deliveries may be smarter [k]; 3 months of raw materials already cost $7,500 per month to store in 900 square metres [app], and tighter deliveries would cut storage cost and obsolescence risk without tying up more cash, provided the brass supplier can deliver within days [an]. Overall I recommend negotiating faster deliveries as the primary plan, keeping 3 months of stock as the November buffer [eval]; this secures the season while avoiding a permanent storage burden, with 4 months' supply used only as a one-off for the busiest weeks [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Holding inventory avoids stockouts and lost seasonal sales; Faster replenishment reduces storage cost and cash tied up | application_max_2: EPOS data shows November spikes; October stockouts would lose the season's sales; Storage costs $7,500 per month; space limited to 900 square metres; 3 months of materials on hand | analysis_max_2: 4 months' supply secures production ahead of the November gift season; Faster deliveries cut storage cost and free working capital without stockout risk | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options and reaches a clear, justified recommendation; Conditional/hybrid decision supported by stem figures

--- STEM ---
Meridian Ceramic Tiles is a private limited company founded 6 years ago by founder Priya Raman, manufacturing glazed ceramic floor tiles at a factory outside Capital City, Country X. Each box of tiles sells for $30, with variable costs of $18 per box. Annual fixed costs are $72,000. The factory produces 9,000 boxes a year and employs 24 workers.

Priya is considering investing $40,000 in a new kiln that would cut variable costs to $14 per box but raise annual fixed costs to $96,000. Alternatively, she could keep the current kiln and raise the selling price to $33 per box. She worries about how high output must be before the business breaks even under each option, and whether the price rise would put off regular builders' merchants.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'total costs'.
    Answer: Total costs are the full cost of producing a given level of output, found by adding fixed costs to total variable costs (Meridian's $72,000 fixed costs plus the variable cost of every box made). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed costs do not change with output, e.g. rent and salaries; Total costs = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit x output)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Priya of calculating break-even output before deciding on the new kiln.
    Answer: Benefit 1: break-even output shows Priya the minimum number of boxes she must sell before making a profit [k]; with the new kiln, fixed costs of $96,000 divided by the $16 contribution gives 6,000 boxes, so she can check whether the current 9,000 boxes a year still leaves a safe cushion [app]. Benefit 2: it lets her compare the options on equal terms [k]; keeping the current kiln needs $72,000 divided by $12 = 6,000 boxes, while the $33 selling price option needs $72,000 divided by $15 = 4,800 boxes, so she can see which option leaves the biggest margin of safety [app].
    Keywords: $96,000, 9,000 boxes, $72,000, $33, new kiln, $14 per box
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even output identifies the output needed to cover all costs; Break-even can be used to compare options / assess risk before investing | application_max_2: Applies figures: $96,000 fixed costs, $16 contribution, 6,000 boxes break-even; Applies figures: $72,000 / $12 = 6,000 boxes; $72,000 / $15 = 4,800 boxes at the $33 price

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of break-even analysis for Priya's investment decision.
    Answer: Limitation 1: break-even analysis assumes all output is sold, which may not happen [k]; if builders' merchants buy fewer boxes than the 9,000 a year forecast, revenue will fall short while the $96,000 fixed costs of the new kiln remain unchanged, so the calculated break-even output gives false comfort [app][an]. Limitation 2: break-even analysis assumes costs and revenue move in straight lines [k]; if the new kiln cuts variable costs to $14 per box only at full efficiency, or if discounts push the $33 selling price lower than expected, the $16 contribution would shrink and the true break-even output would be higher than the 6,000 boxes calculated [app][an].
    Keywords: $96,000, 9,000 boxes, $14 per box, $33, builders' merchants, $72,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even assumes all output is sold; Break-even assumes linear (straight-line) costs and revenue | application_max_2: Applies to builders' merchants buying fewer than 9,000 boxes with fixed costs unchanged; Applies to the $14 per box variable cost and $33 price risk shifting the $16 contribution | analysis_max_2: Explains that unsold output means the break-even figure overstates safety; Explains that a lower contribution pushes the break-even output above 6,000 boxes

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Priya should invest in the new kiln? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Priya could invest in the new kiln because it lowers the cost of every box made [k]. Cutting variable costs to $14 per box lifts contribution to $16, so break-even output stays at 6,000 boxes ($96,000 divided by $16) and profit rises from $36,000 to $48,000 a year (9,000 boxes x $16, minus $96,000) [app][an]. However, the $40,000 must be paid up front and fixed costs would rise to $96,000; if sales slip below 6,000 boxes the loss would be deeper than before, and the 3,000-box margin of safety is thin [app][an]. Conversely, keeping the current kiln and raising the price to $33 would cut break-even output to 4,800 boxes ($72,000 divided by $15) and could yield $63,000 profit (9,000 x $15, minus $72,000), but only if builders' merchants accept the higher price [k][eval]. Overall, because variable-cost savings are under Priya's control while a price rise depends on uncertain demand in a competitive market, the evidence favours the kiln - provided she is confident of holding at least 9,000 boxes of annual sales; otherwise the safer short-term move is the price rise, whose 4,800-box break-even output is more forgiving [eval].
    Keywords: $14 per box, $96,000, $40,000, 9,000 boxes, $33, new kiln, $18 per box
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: New kiln: contribution $16, break-even $96,000 / $16 = 6,000 boxes; Price rise: contribution $15, break-even $72,000 / $15 = 4,800 boxes, profit potential $63,000 | application_max_2: New kiln profit $48,000 vs current $36,000 at 9,000 boxes; Current kiln fixed costs $72,000 and 3,000-box margin of safety | analysis_max_2: Identifies that higher fixed costs deepen losses if sales fall below 6,000 boxes; Analyses that the price-rise option depends on demand holding at $33 | evaluation_max_2: Justified overall recommendation tied to Priya's demand confidence and control over costs

--- STEM ---
Copper Kettle Preserves is a partnership opened 3 years ago by founders Nadia and Theo Barlow, making artisan strawberry jam in a small kitchen in Millbrook, Country X. Each jar sells for $6, variable costs are $2.50 per jar, and fixed costs are $21,000 a year. The business currently makes 7,000 jars a year and sells them at farmers' markets and local shops.

Nadia and Theo are deciding whether to supply a national supermarket chain with 10,000 jars a year at a bulk price of $4.50 per jar. Theo fears the lower price would squeeze contribution per jar, while Nadia argues the extra volume would spread fixed costs over more jars and lift the margin of safety. They want a break-even calculation before signing anything.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the break-even output for Copper Kettle Preserves. You are advised to show your working.
    Answer: Break-even output = Fixed costs / (Price - Variable cost) = $21,000 / ($6.00 - $2.50) = $21,000 / $3.50 = 6,000 jars per year. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even formula: fixed costs divided by contribution per unit; Contribution per jar = $6.00 - $2.50 = $3.50

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Nadia and Theo should calculate the margin of safety before signing the supermarket contract.
    Answer: Reason 1: the margin of safety shows how far sales can fall before the partnership makes a loss [k]; at 7,000 jars a year and a break-even output of 6,000 jars, the cushion is only 1,000 jars, so relying on the bulk contract's lower price could be risky if the supermarket cuts orders [app]. Reason 2: it tests whether the contract improves security [k]; selling 17,000 jars in total (7,000 plus the 10,000 bulk jars) against the same 6,000-jar break-even output would lift the margin of safety to 11,000 jars, reducing the chance of losses [app].
    Keywords: 7,000 jars, 10,000 jars, margin of safety, $2.50 per jar, national supermarket chain, $21,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Margin of safety = actual output - break-even output; A larger margin of safety means lower risk of losses | application_max_2: Applies figures: 7,000 - 6,000 = 1,000 jars current cushion; Applies figures: combined 17,000 jars gives an 11,000-jar margin of safety

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using break-even analysis for the contract decision.
    Answer: Benefit 1: break-even analysis shows the output at which total revenue equals total costs [k]; the $4.50 bulk jar leaves only $2.00 contribution ($4.50 - $2.50), so 10,500 jars at the bulk price alone would be needed to cover the $21,000 fixed costs - warning the partners that the deal is only worthwhile alongside their existing sales [app][an]. Benefit 2: break-even analysis supports a like-for-like comparison of options [k]; selling 10,000 bulk jars adds $20,000 contribution (10,000 x $2.00) to the current $3,500 profit (7,000 x $3.50 - $21,000), showing the total profit would rise to $23,500 [app][an].
    Keywords: $4.50 per jar, $21,000, $2.50 per jar, 10,000 jars, contribution per jar, 7,000 jars
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even compares fixed and variable costs with revenue; Break-even allows objective comparison of options | application_max_2: Applies figures: $2.00 contribution, 10,500 bulk jars to cover $21,000 fixed costs; Applies figures: $20,000 added contribution, profit rising from $3,500 to $23,500 | analysis_max_2: Explains the bulk deal only covers fixed costs if existing premium sales continue; Explains the contract lifts total profit despite a lower per-jar margin

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Copper Kettle Preserves should accept the supermarket contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the contract would secure a guaranteed weekly outlet for 10,000 jars and spread the $21,000 fixed costs over far more units [k]. Selling 10,000 bulk jars at $4.50 adds $20,000 contribution (10,000 x $2.00) to the current $3,500 profit, lifting the total to around $23,500, and the combined margin of safety would rise to 11,000 jars [app][an]. However, the bulk price of $4.50 leaves only $2.00 contribution per jar, far below the $3.50 earned on premium jars; 10,500 bulk jars would be needed merely to cover the $21,000 fixed costs, and the supermarket may demand an even lower price after the first year [app][an]. Conversely, keeping only premium farmers' market sales protects the brand but caps growth and leaves the 1,000-jar margin of safety exposed to poor weather and festival cancellations [k][eval]. Overall, the partnership should accept the contract only if production capacity and jar quality can be maintained at 17,000 jars a year and the $4.50 price and shelf-life terms are written into a fixed two-year agreement; if the supermarket's price or volume is uncertain, Nadia and Theo should negotiate first rather than sign [eval].
    Keywords: $4.50 per jar, $21,000, 10,000 jars, $2.50 per jar, margin of safety, 7,000 jars, supermarket
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Bulk contribution $2.00 per jar vs $3.50 premium contribution; Bulk break-even 10,500 jars; current profit $3,500 | application_max_2: Applies figures: 10,000 x $2.00 = $20,000 added contribution, profit ~$23,500; Applies figures: combined 17,000 jars gives 11,000-jar margin of safety | analysis_max_2: Analyses that fixed costs are spread thinner at 17,000 jars but the margin per jar falls; Analyses the risk of price pressure or order cuts from the supermarket | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on capacity, quality and a fixed contract

--- STEM ---
Silverline Window Frames is a public limited company listed on the Country X stock exchange, operating a single factory in Riverside Industrial Estate for 8 years. It sells each triple-glazed window unit for $450, with variable costs of $270 per unit. Yearly fixed costs are $810,000. Last year it sold 6,000 units to housebuilders across Country X.

The board is debating an automated cutting line that would raise annual fixed costs to $1,050,000 but cut variable costs to $240 per unit and lift capacity to 7,500 units. Some directors favour the machine for its lower unit cost; others fear higher break-even output if sales slip. The finance director has asked for break-even figures for both options before the board votes.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State what is meant by 'average cost'.
    Answer: Average cost is the total cost of producing a given output divided by the number of units produced - the cost per unit (at 6,000 units with total costs of $2,430,000, the average cost is $405). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Average cost = total cost / output; Average cost includes both fixed and variable elements per unit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the board wants break-even figures for both options.
    Answer: Reason 1: to judge the extra risk from higher fixed costs before approving the machine [k]; the automated cutting line raises fixed costs to $1,050,000, so break-even output climbs to 5,000 units ($1,050,000 / $210) compared with 4,500 units today ($810,000 / $180), showing sales must hold above 5,000 units [app]. Reason 2: to protect shareholders' funds and dividends [k]; at 6,000 units the margin of safety would fall from 1,500 units to 1,000 units, so the board can decide whether the risk of dividend cuts is acceptable [app].
    Keywords: $1,050,000, $810,000, 6,000 units, $450, $240 per unit, 7,500 units
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even figures reveal the sales needed to avoid losses; Higher fixed costs raise break-even output and risk | application_max_2: Applies figures: $1,050,000 / $210 = 5,000 units vs $810,000 / $180 = 4,500 units; Applies figures: margin of safety falls from 1,500 to 1,000 units at 6,000 sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Analyse two ways the board could use a break-even chart to present the options.
    Answer: Way 1: the chart's total revenue line (units sold x $450) and total cost line show exactly where they cross for each option [k]; the machine option's cost line starts at $1,050,000 and rises less steeply (variable cost $240 vs $270), so the crossing moves from 4,500 to 5,000 units, and directors can see the shift at a glance [app][an]. Way 2: the vertical gap between the two lines at 6,000 units shows profit and margin of safety [k]; the current set-up shows a profit of $270,000 at 6,000 units against $210,000 with the machine, and the loss zone above 5,000 units is visible immediately, making the comparison persuasive to shareholders [app][an].
    Keywords: $450, $270 per unit, $240 per unit, 6,000 units, $1,050,000, $810,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even chart plots total revenue and total cost against output; The intersection shows break-even output; the gap shows profit or loss | application_max_2: Applies figures: revenue line $450 per unit, cost line rising $240 vs $270 per unit; Applies figures: profit $270,000 current vs $210,000 with machine at 6,000 units | analysis_max_2: Explains why the flatter cost line moves the intersection right to 5,000 units; Explains that the chart makes profit differences visible to non-financial directors

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the board should approve the automated cutting line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The board could approve the line because it cuts variable costs to $240 per unit and lifts capacity to 7,500 units, helping Silverline win larger housebuilder contracts [k]. At full capacity of 7,500 units the machine would earn $525,000 profit (7,500 x $210 contribution, minus $1,050,000 fixed costs) compared with about $540,000 today at the same volume - so the case rests on winning more orders, not on lower costs alone [app][an]. However, at the current 6,000 units the machine would cut profit from $270,000 to $210,000, average cost rises from $405 to $415, and break-even output climbs to 5,000 units with only a 1,000-unit margin of safety [app][an]. Conversely, approve the line too late and a rival with cheaper units could undercut Silverline, whose current $405 average cost and thin 1,500-unit cushion leave little room against leaner competitors [k][eval]. Overall, the board should not approve the line now: the figures show it only beats the current option above 8,000 units, which exceeds its own 7,500-unit capacity, so no realistic output justifies it yet; the directors should wait until housebuilders sign firm orders for at least 7,000 units a year, or renegotiate the machine's price or financing, before voting in favour [eval].
    Keywords: $240 per unit, $270 per unit, 6,000 units, 7,500 units, $1,050,000, $810,000, $450
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Machine option: contribution $210, break-even 5,000 units, profit $210,000 at 6,000; Current option: contribution $180, break-even 4,500 units, profit $270,000 at 6,000 | application_max_2: Applies figures: machine profit at 7,500 units = $525,000; Applies figures: average cost $405 current vs $415 with machine | analysis_max_2: Identifies the indifference output of 8,000 units lies beyond the 7,500-unit capacity; Links higher fixed costs to a deeper loss zone below 5,000 units | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation: delay approval until contracted volume or price improves
