--- STEM ---
Wanderlust Caravan Park is a family-run partnership in Sunnyvale, Country X, operating 60 tourer pitches since 2015. Pitch fees are $25 per night, variable costs such as utilities and laundry are $9 per pitch per night, and fixed costs are $64,000 a year. Last season the park logged 5,500 occupied pitch-nights, mainly from visiting families and retirees.

The owners are weighing two expansion ideas for next season: building 20 new pitches, which would raise fixed costs to $114,000, or adding a heated swimming pool that would raise fixed costs to $80,000 and allow fees to rise to $29 per night. They want to know how many extra bookings each option needs to cover its costs before committing their own money.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by 'total revenue'.
    Answer: Total revenue is the money a business receives from selling its output, calculated as price per unit multiplied by quantity sold (at Wanderlust last season, 5,500 pitch-nights x $25 = $137,500). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Total revenue = price x quantity sold; Total revenue is the top-line income before any costs are deducted

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the owners could use total revenue and total cost figures to choose between the two options.
    Answer: Way 1: compare the break-even outputs of the two options [k]; the 20 new pitches need $114,000 covered, meaning 7,125 pitch-nights at $16 contribution, whereas the pool option needs only 4,000 pitch-nights at $20 contribution ($80,000 / $20), so the pool requires fewer extra bookings [app]. Way 2: compare profit at last season's 5,500 pitch-nights [k]; the pool option would earn 5,500 x $20 - $80,000 = $30,000 profit, while the pitch-building option would make 5,500 x $16 - $114,000 = a $26,000 loss, showing revenue alone does not decide the choice when costs differ so sharply [app].
    Keywords: 5,500, $25 per night, $29 per night, $114,000, $80,000, 20 new pitches
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even output = fixed costs / contribution per unit; Profit = total revenue - total costs | application_max_2: Applies figures: new pitches 7,125 pitch-nights vs pool 4,000 pitch-nights; Applies figures: pool profit $30,000 vs pitch option $26,000 loss at 5,500 pitch-nights

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of break-even analysis for a seasonal caravan park.
    Answer: Limitation 1: break-even analysis assumes all output is sold at the stated price [k]; caravan occupancy is seasonal and weather-dependent, so the 5,500 pitch-nights of last season may not repeat, and fixed costs of $64,000 must still be paid when pitches stand empty, making the 4,000 pitch-night break-even point unreliable [app][an]. Limitation 2: break-even analysis assumes variable costs and prices stay constant [k]; the $9 per pitch cost of utilities and laundry could rise in peak months and peak fees might need discounting to attract families, shifting the break-even point for either expansion option and invalidating precisely the calculation the owners need [app][an].
    Keywords: 5,500, $64,000, $9 per pitch per night, $25 per night, 60 tourer pitches, last season
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even assumes all output is sold; Break-even assumes constant costs and prices (linearity) | application_max_2: Applies figures: 5,500 pitch-nights may not repeat; $64,000 fixed costs continue off-season; Applies figures: $9 per pitch variable cost and fee discounting would shift break-even | analysis_max_2: Explains empty pitches still incur fixed costs so calculated safety is overstated; Explains changing costs invalidate the linear chart used for the decision

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the owners should build the 20 new pitches? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The owners could build the pitches and unlock capacity they cannot currently offer in the busy summer weeks [k]; the option raises fixed costs to $114,000, giving a break-even output of 7,125 pitch-nights ($114,000 / $16) - but at full 80-pitch occupancy about 7,300 pitch-nights would be possible, suggesting strong demand could make it profitable [app][an]. However, last season the park took 5,500 pitch-nights, so at current demand the pitch option would turn a $26,000 loss (5,500 x $16 - $114,000), and the park would need roughly 1,600 more pitch-nights a year (+29%) just to break even on the expansion [app][an]. Conversely, the swimming pool option raises fixed costs to only $80,000, keeps break-even at 4,000 pitch-nights, lifts fees to $29 per night and would have earned about $30,000 profit last season - $6,000 more than the park actually made - while attracting precisely the families and retirees who already visit [k][eval]. Overall, on the evidence the owners should not build the new pitches now: the pool option is cheaper, lowers risk, raises fees, improves last season's profit by $6,000 and keeps break-even at 4,000 pitch-nights, whereas the pitches gamble $114,000 on demand rising well beyond anything yet achieved; only if they secure advance bookings above 7,125 pitch-nights for next season should the pitch plan proceed [eval].
    Keywords: $114,000, $80,000, 5,500, $29 per night, 20 new pitches, heated swimming pool, $25 per night
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Pitch option: break-even 7,125 pitch-nights vs current 5,500 taken; Pool option: break-even 4,000 pitch-nights, fees $29, profit $30,000 | application_max_2: Applies figures: 5,500 x $16 - $114,000 = $26,000 loss on pitch option; Applies figures: pool profit $30,000 vs $24,000 current profit | analysis_max_2: Links the $114,000 fixed-cost commitment to needing 29% more pitch-nights; Explains the pool raises revenue per existing night without needing extra occupancy | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation: pool preferred unless contracted bookings exceed 7,125 pitch-nights

--- STEM ---
RedRock Brickworks is a private limited company that has fired clay bricks for housebuilders near Quarrying Town, Country X, for 14 years under managing director Sofia Andrade. Each pack of 500 bricks sells for $180, variable costs are $120 per pack, and fixed costs are $360,000 a year. Last year the yard sold 8,000 packs to builders across the south of the country.

Sofia is considering switching to a cheaper clay source that would cut variable costs to $105 per pack but add $45,000 a year for transport and storage. The alternative is a two-year supply deal with a national builder guaranteeing 9,500 packs a year at $170 per pack. She wants break-even outputs for both options calculated before the board meets.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'break-even chart'.
    Answer: A break-even chart is a graph plotting total revenue and total cost against output; the point where the two lines intersect is the break-even output, above which the business makes a profit and below which it makes a loss. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even chart plots total revenue and total cost lines against output; The intersection shows break-even output; profit above, loss below

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Sofia wants break-even outputs for both options.
    Answer: Reason 1: to compare the riskiness of the two options on one measure [k]; the cheaper clay source lifts fixed costs to $405,000 but cuts variable costs to $105 per pack, giving break-even output of 5,400 packs ($405,000 / $75) against 6,000 packs today, while the bulk deal needs 7,200 packs ($360,000 / $50) - showing which option leaves more safety margin [app]. Reason 2: to support a sound pricing and capacity negotiation [k]; the supply deal guarantees 9,500 packs at $170, giving margin of safety of 2,300 packs over its 7,200-pack break-even, so Sofia can negotiate transport, storage and payment terms from a position of knowledge [app].
    Keywords: $105 per pack, $170 per pack, 9,500 packs, 8,000 packs, two-year supply deal, $360,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even output identifies the sales needed to cover costs; Break-even comparison of options reveals which is safer | application_max_2: Applies figures: cheaper clay $405,000 / $75 = 5,400 packs; deal $360,000 / $50 = 7,200 packs; Applies figures: 9,500 packs guaranteed gives 2,300-pack margin of safety

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Analyse two limitations of relying only on break-even analysis for this decision.
    Answer: Limitation 1: break-even analysis assumes costs behave in straight lines [k]; the cheaper clay adds a flat $45,000 for transport and storage regardless of volume, and clay, diesel or wage costs could jump mid-contract, so the 5,400-pack break-even would no longer hold and RedRock could face losses at output it believed was safe [app][an]. Limitation 2: break-even analysis assumes all output is sold at a single constant price [k]; the supply deal locks 9,500 packs at $170, but builders may squeeze the price at renewal or order less in a housing slump, and last year's actual sales of 8,000 packs might already have been uneven across the year, so margin-of-safety figures flatter or misstate the risk [app][an].
    Keywords: $45,000, $170 per pack, 9,500 packs, 8,000 packs, $120 per pack, $180
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even assumes linear costs and revenue; Break-even assumes constant price and single-product sales | application_max_2: Applies figures: flat $45,000 transport/storage and cost jumps undermining 5,400-pack break-even; Applies figures: $170 per pack contract price may be cut at renewal; 8,000 packs sold unevenly | analysis_max_2: Explains non-linear costs push true break-even above the calculated 5,400 packs; Explains price and volume risk makes margins of safety over-optimistic

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think RedRock Brickworks should sign the two-year supply deal? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Sofia could sign the deal because it guarantees orders for 9,500 packs a year for two years, giving the kiln and workforce a stable, predictable workload [k]; at $170 per pack the deal contributes $50 per pack, giving a 7,200-pack break-even ($360,000 / $50) and a 2,300-pack margin of safety, revenue of $1,615,000 and profit of about $115,000 a year [app][an]. However, that profit of $115,000 is below the $120,000 RedRock earned last year on 8,000 packs, and far below the $195,000 available from the cheaper clay source (8,000 packs x $75 - $405,000 fixed costs), which also has the lower 5,400-pack break-even output and a 2,600-pack margin of safety [app][an]. Conversely, the cheaper clay route exposes RedRock to volatile transport costs and an unproven supplier for two years, whereas the national builder's contract de-risks planning, staffing and any bank loan for the yard [k][eval]. Overall, Sofia should not sign the deal as it stands: it offers less profit than the clay switch and less profit than current operations, and its 7,200-pack break-even exceeds the 6,000 packs currently comfortable; she should pursue the cheaper clay supply first, keeping the $170-per-pack deal as a fallback only if the clay trial fails or the builder raises the offer towards $180 per pack [eval].
    Keywords: $170 per pack, 9,500 packs, $105 per pack, $45,000, 8,000 packs, two-year supply deal, $180
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Deal: $50 contribution, 7,200-pack break-even, profit $115,000; Clay switch: $75 contribution, 5,400-pack break-even, profit $195,000 | application_max_2: Applies figures: deal profit $115,000 vs current $120,000 vs clay $195,000; Applies figures: clay option fixed costs $405,000 with $45,000 transport/storage | analysis_max_2: Analyses the deal's guaranteed volume against its lower per-pack return; Analyses that clay risk must be weighed against contract certainty | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation: clay preferred; deal only as fallback or at a higher price

--- STEM ---
RedKite Adventure Park is an outdoor adventure business opened 4 years ago by founder Marcus Bell in Country X's Lake District. Entry tickets cost $15 per visitor, variable costs such as instructor wages and equipment upkeep are $6 per visitor, and fixed costs are $54,000 a year. The park welcomed 6,750 visitors last year, mostly school groups and families during the summer season.

Marcus is deciding between two improvements for next year: new safety harnesses that add $9,000 a year to fixed costs, or a cafe that adds $13,500 to fixed costs and lets him charge $3 extra per entry. He must show his co-owner that the chosen option keeps the park comfortably above break-even output at current visitor numbers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the break-even output and the margin of safety for RedKite Adventure Park. You are advised to show your working.
    Answer: Break-even output = $54,000 / ($15 - $6) = $54,000 / $9 = 6,000 visitors; margin of safety = 6,750 - 6,000 = 750 visitors per year. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even output = fixed costs / contribution per unit; contribution = $9; Margin of safety = actual output - break-even output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Marcus needs to know the margin of safety.
    Answer: Reason 1: the margin of safety shows how far visitor numbers can fall before the park starts making losses [k]; with 6,750 visitors against a 6,000-visitor break-even point, the cushion is only 750 visitors, so one poor summer month or a cancelled school-group contract could push the park into loss [app]. Reason 2: it tests whether the improvements are affordable [k]; adding the harnesses raises fixed costs to $63,000 and break-even output to 7,000 visitors - 250 above last year's attendance - whereas the cafe option gives a 1,125-visitor cushion, so Marcus can judge which choice is safest for the park [app].
    Keywords: 6,750 visitors, $54,000, $15 per visitor, $6 per visitor, $9,000, $13,500, break-even output
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Margin of safety = actual output - break-even output; A small margin of safety means a small sales drop creates a loss | application_max_2: Applies figures: 6,750 - 6,000 = 750-visitor cushion; Applies figures: harnesses raise break-even to 7,000; cafe option gives 1,125 cushion

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using break-even analysis to choose between the two improvements.
    Answer: Benefit 1: break-even analysis quantifies the minimum attendance each option requires [k]; the harness option lifts fixed costs to $63,000 and breaks even at 7,000 visitors ($63,000 / $9), 250 more than last year, while the cafe option breaks even at 5,625 visitors ($67,500 / $12), comfortably below current demand, so the choice becomes measurable rather than a guess [app][an]. Benefit 2: break-even analysis shows the profit effect at current attendance [k]; the cafe option yields 6,750 x $12 contribution - $67,500 = $13,500 profit, versus $6,750 profit today (6,750 x $9 - $54,000), giving Marcus a clear figure to present to his co-owner [app][an].
    Keywords: 6,750 visitors, $13,500, $9,000, $3 extra, $6 per visitor, $15 per visitor, $54,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even output = fixed costs / contribution per unit; Lower break-even output and higher profit are preferred | application_max_2: Applies figures: harnesses 7,000 visitors vs cafe 5,625 visitors break-even; Applies figures: cafe profit $13,500 vs current $6,750 | analysis_max_2: Explains quantified break-even turns a judgement call into a measurable comparison; Explains profit at 6,750 visitors shows the cafe option clearly outperforms today's position

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marcus should buy the new safety harnesses? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Marcus could buy the harnesses because safety should not be traded off against cost; they protect visitors, staff morale and the park's reputation against the serious risk of a harness failure [k]; they add only $9,000 a year to fixed costs, which is modest next to the $54,000 already committed, and could lower insurance claims and premiums [app][an]. However, buying the harnesses alone lifts break-even output to 7,000 visitors ($63,000 / $9), which is 250 more than the 6,750 visitors of last year; the margin of safety would turn negative, so at current demand the park would lose about $2,250 and the improvement would not pay for itself [app][an]. Conversely, funding the harnesses through the cafe option - extra fixed costs of $13,500 but $3 extra per entry, contribution $12, break-even 5,625 visitors and an $18 entry price - would produce about $13,500 profit at 6,750 visitors, easily covering the harness cost and keeping a 1,125-visitor cushion [k][eval]. Overall, Marcus should buy the harnesses, but not in isolation: the park must introduce the cafe (or an equivalent price rise) in the same season, because harnesses alone push break-even output 250 visitors above proven attendance; buying them together keeps safety non-negotiable while keeping RedKite profitable and comfortably above break-even [eval].
    Keywords: $9,000, $13,500, 6,750 visitors, $3 extra, new safety harnesses, $15 per visitor, $54,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Harness option alone: fixed costs $63,000, break-even 7,000 visitors, 250 above current demand; Cafe option: contribution $12, break-even 5,625 visitors, profit $13,500 | application_max_2: Applies figures: harness-only profit about -$2,250 at 6,750 visitors; Applies figures: cafe option leaves 1,125-visitor margin of safety | analysis_max_2: Links rising fixed costs to break-even output exceeding proven demand; Identifies that combining both options funds safety while restoring a safe margin of safety | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation: buy harnesses only together with the cafe or a price rise

--- STEM ---
Amber Valley Candle Co is a small private limited company making soy candles in Ashford, Country X, owned by sisters Lena and Maja Okoro. A large candle sells for $12, variable costs are $5 per candle, and fixed costs are $42,000 a year. Candles are sold through local boutiques and gift shops, and last year 7,500 were sold.

The sisters are comparing two sales channels for next year: a hotel chain willing to buy 6,000 candles at $10 per candle, or launching an online shop that adds $7,000 a year to fixed costs while keeping the $12 price. They want both options' break-even outputs compared, and to know how many extra candles the online shop must sell to cover its costs.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'break-even analysis'.
    Answer: Break-even analysis is a technique that compares a business's fixed costs and variable costs with its revenue to find the output at which total revenue equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Compares total costs and total revenue; Finds the output at which profit is zero

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the sisters want break-even outputs for both options.
    Answer: Reason 1: to see which option clears the $42,000 fixed costs most easily [k]; the online shop keeps the $12 price and $7 contribution but lifts fixed costs to $49,000, so break-even output rises to 7,000 candles ($49,000 / $7) against 6,000 candles today, whereas the hotel deal, at only $10 per candle, gives $5 contribution and an 8,400-candle break-even - a much heavier target [app]. Reason 2: to judge whether the hotel's guaranteed volume is worth the lower price [k]; 6,000 candles at $5 contribution add only $30,000 towards the $42,000 fixed costs, so the sisters can see the hotel offer alone cannot carry the business [app].
    Keywords: $42,000, $10 per candle, 6,000 candles, $12, $7,000, hotel chain
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even identifies the output covering all costs; Comparing options on break-even output shows which is safer or needier of volume | application_max_2: Applies figures: online $49,000 / $7 = 7,000 candles; hotel $5 contribution, 8,400 candles; Applies figures: 6,000 candles x $5 = $30,000 contribution vs $42,000 fixed costs

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of break-even analysis for the candle business.
    Answer: Limitation 1: break-even analysis assumes all produced candles are sold at the marked price [k]; if the hotel cuts its order below 6,000 candles or boutiques reduce stock after a slow season, the $42,000 fixed costs remain while revenue falls, so the calculated 6,000-candle break-even and 1,500-candle margin of safety would overstate the business's real safety [app][an]. Limitation 2: break-even analysis assumes costs and prices stay fixed and move in straight lines [k]; soy wax, jars and fragrance can rise in price and Amber Valley may need to discount candles in quieter gift-shop months, which would narrow the $7 contribution, shift break-even output upward and make the single-chart comparison between the online shop and the hotel misleading [app][an].
    Keywords: $42,000, 6,000 candles, $12, $5 per candle, 7,500, hotel chain
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even assumes all output is sold; Break-even assumes constant costs, prices and linear relationships | application_max_2: Applies figures: hotel order below 6,000 leaves $42,000 fixed costs uncovered; Applies figures: rising input costs narrow the $7 contribution and lift break-even | analysis_max_2: Explains unsold stock turns the paper margin of safety into a loss; Explains cost or price changes invalidate the straight-line chart comparison

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the sisters should open the online shop? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The sisters could open the online shop because it widens their market beyond Ashford and keeps the healthy $12 price [k]; the shop adds $7,000 a year to fixed costs, lifting break-even output to 7,000 candles ($49,000 / $7), which is just 500 below last year's 7,500 sales, so it needs only about 1,000 extra candles a year to justify itself [app][an]. However, if online sales merely match the 7,500 candles sold today, profit would fall from $10,500 to $3,500 (7,500 x $7 - $49,000), and any delivery problems or website costs could erase even that [app][an]. Conversely, the hotel option looks worse on paper - $5 contribution per candle, an 8,400-candle break-even, and only $30,000 contribution from the promised 6,000 candles - so online is clearly the stronger of the two growth routes despite thinner online margins after postage [k][eval]. Overall, the sisters should open the online shop, but only with a modest digital marketing push and a clear sales target of at least 1,000 extra candles a year; if they cannot commit to that volume, they should stay with the boutique channel and treat the online plan as a six-month trial, so a weak online launch cannot absorb the $7,000 fixed costs [eval].
    Keywords: $7,000, $12, 6,000 candles, online shop, $10 per candle, $42,000, 7,500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Online option: fixed costs $49,000, break-even 7,000 candles; Hotel option: $5 contribution, 8,400-candle break-even | application_max_2: Applies figures: flat sales yield $3,500 profit vs $10,500 today; Applies figures: 1,000 extra candles needed to cover the $7,000 extra fixed costs | analysis_max_2: Analyses that online sales barely below today's 7,500 erase most profit; Analyses the hotel offer cannot carry the $42,000 fixed costs on its own | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation: proceed online with a 1,000-candle target or a limited trial

--- STEM ---
Maplewood Mattress Co is a private limited company in Country X producing pocket-sprung mattresses in a single factory owned by managing director Owen Hartley. Each mattress sells for $320, variable costs are $190 per mattress, and fixed costs are $780,000 a year. Output last year was 6,500 mattresses, sold to furniture retailers and bed specialists across the region and built a loyal base.

Owen is weighing a redesigned spring unit that would add $100,000 to fixed costs but cut variable costs to $160 per mattress. Alternatively, a marketing campaign costing $65,000 a year would, he hopes, lift sales to 7,200 mattresses at the current price. He wants both options' break-even outputs and margins of safety compared before deciding which route to take this year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'total contribution'.
    Answer: Total contribution is the amount left from total revenue after variable costs are deducted - contribution per unit multiplied by units sold (Maplewood: 6,500 x $130 = $845,000) - which first covers fixed costs and then becomes profit. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Total contribution = contribution per unit x units sold; Contribution goes towards fixed costs, then profit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Owen wants break-even outputs and margins of safety compared for the two options.
    Answer: Reason 1: to test whether committing $100,000 of extra fixed costs is safe [k]; the spring unit lowers break-even output from 6,000 to 5,500 mattresses ($880,000 / $160), doubling the margin of safety to 1,000 mattresses at last year's output, so Owen can see the risk has actually fallen [app]. Reason 2: to test the campaign's gamble honestly [k]; the campaign raises fixed costs to $845,000 and break-even output to 6,500 mattresses ($845,000 / $130), and only the hoped-for 7,200 sales would leave a 700-mattress cushion, which is riskier than the spring unit [app].
    Keywords: $780,000, $100,000, $65,000, 6,500 mattresses, $160 per mattress, 7,200 mattresses
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher fixed costs raise break-even output; lower variable costs lower it; Margin of safety measures the cushion above break-even | application_max_2: Applies figures: spring unit 5,500 mattresses break-even, 1,000 margin of safety; Applies figures: campaign 6,500 mattresses break-even, 700 cushion only at 7,200 sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Analyse two effects the redesigned spring unit would have on Maplewood's costs and break-even output.
    Answer: Effect 1: variable cost per mattress falls from $190 to $160 [k]; each sale then contributes $160 instead of $130, so a larger share of every order goes towards the $880,000 fixed costs and profit, meaning each additional mattress beyond break-even is worth $30 more to the business [app][an]. Effect 2: break-even output falls from 6,000 to 5,500 mattresses ($880,000 / $160) [k]; Owen's risk of losses at weak demand shrinks, the margin of safety doubles to 1,000 mattresses, and profit at 6,500 mattresses rises from $65,000 (6,500 x $130 - $780,000) to $160,000 (6,500 x $160 - $880,000), although the $100,000 extra fixed cost must be paid whatever sales do [app][an].
    Keywords: $190 per mattress, $160 per mattress, redesigned spring unit, $780,000, 6,500 mattresses, $100,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Redesigned unit lowers variable cost per unit, raising contribution; Break-even output = fixed costs / contribution per unit | application_max_2: Applies figures: contribution $160 vs $130; $880,000 fixed costs; Applies figures: break-even 5,500; profit $160,000 vs $65,000 at 6,500 mattresses | analysis_max_2: Explains each extra sale contributes $30 more after the redesign; Explains lower break-even deepens safety but the $100,000 fixed cost is unavoidable

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Owen should choose the redesigned spring unit? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Owen could choose the spring unit because it cuts variable costs by $30 per mattress and gives certain, controllable savings rather than hoped-for sales [k]; break-even output falls to 5,500 mattresses, the margin of safety doubles to 1,000, profit at last year's 6,500 mattresses rises from $65,000 to $160,000, and the saving applies to every future mattress sold [app][an]. However, the unit adds $100,000 to fixed costs, which must be paid even in a bad year; if sales fell below 5,500 mattresses the loss would be larger than today, and the 1,000-mattress cushion, though doubled, is still modest for a big-ticket product [app][an]. Conversely, the campaign option could lift sales to 7,200 mattresses and produce $91,000 profit (7,200 x $130 - $845,000), so it offers growth the spring unit alone cannot unlock - but its 6,500-mattress break-even exactly equals last year's output, leaving zero cushion unless the 7,200 sales actually materialise [k][eval]. Overall, Owen should choose the redesigned spring unit: it reduces break-even output, doubles the margin of safety, raises profit by $95,000 at current volumes and does not depend on an advertising bet; if the campaign is run later from that stronger position, any growth in sales would stack further profit on top, whereas committing to the campaign first risks an empty cushion of zero at last year's output [eval].
    Keywords: $160 per mattress, $190 per mattress, $100,000, 6,500 mattresses, $65,000, 7,200 mattresses, redesigned spring unit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Spring unit: contribution $160, break-even 5,500, margin of safety 1,000, profit $160,000; Campaign: fixed costs $845,000, break-even 6,500, profit $91,000 at 7,200 sales | application_max_2: Applies figures: current profit $65,000 rises to $160,000 with the spring unit; Applies figures: campaign break-even of 6,500 equals last year's sales | analysis_max_2: Analyses that fixed $100,000 commitment deepens losses below 5,500 mattresses; Analyses the campaign's dependence on uncertain demand for its 700-mattress cushion | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation: spring unit chosen; campaign can follow later

--- STEM ---
Northgate Paper Bags is a partnership founded 5 years ago by founders Ben and Idris Whitmore in Country X, producing recycled paper shopping bags for supermarkets. Each thousand-bag batch sells for $90, variable costs are $55 per batch, and fixed costs are $52,500 a year. Last year the workshop sold 2,500 batches across the north of the country and employed nine full-time staff members.

The partners are debating a larger premises costing $17,500 extra a year in fixed costs, allowing annual output to rise to 3,200 batches, or accepting a six-month bulk order from a wholesaler at $80 per batch. Both options carry risk, and they want to know how each affects break-even output and the margin of safety before committing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State what is meant by 'total fixed cost'.
    Answer: Total fixed cost is the sum of all costs that do not vary with output in the short run, such as rent, insurance and salaries - Northgate's $52,500 a year stays the same whether 1 or 3,200 batches are made. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run; Examples include rent, insurance and salaries

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the partners should calculate break-even output for the two options.
    Answer: Reason 1: to see how the extra premises cost changes the sales needed to avoid losses [k]; the larger site lifts fixed costs to $70,000, so break-even output rises to 2,000 batches ($70,000 / $35) against 1,500 batches today, showing the business must gain around 500 extra batches just to stand still [app]. Reason 2: to compare the bulk order honestly [k]; at $80 per batch contribution is only $25, giving a 2,100-batch break-even ($52,500 / $25), so the partners can see that filling the order with bulk sales alone would leave only a thin cushion at 2,500 batches [app].
    Keywords: $52,500, $17,500, 2,500 batches, $90, $80 per batch, $55 per batch, 3,200 batches
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even output = fixed costs / contribution per unit; Comparison of break-even across options reveals relative risk | application_max_2: Applies figures: larger premises $70,000 / $35 = 2,000 batches vs 1,500 today; Applies figures: bulk order contribution $25, break-even 2,100 batches

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of break-even analysis when comparing the premises and the bulk order.
    Answer: Limitation 1: break-even analysis assumes output is sold at one constant price, yet the two options use different prices [k]; blending $90 supermarket batches with $80 wholesale batches changes the average contribution, so a single break-even figure misleads the partners about true safety ($25 contribution on bulk batches versus $35 normally) [app][an]. Limitation 2: break-even analysis assumes all output is sold and costs stay linear [k]; moving to a larger premises assumes supermarkets actually buy 3,200 batches, and costs such as transport, storage and extra power on a bigger site may rise faster than output, so the 2,000-batch break-even is only a guide and unsold batches would turn the expansion into a loss [app][an].
    Keywords: $80 per batch, $90, 3,200 batches, $17,500, six-month bulk order, $52,500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even assumes constant price; multiple products/prices distort it; Break-even assumes all output sells and costs are linear | application_max_2: Applies figures: $25 bulk contribution vs $35 normal contribution; Applies figures: 3,200 batches assumed; larger-site costs may exceed $70,000 | analysis_max_2: Explains blended pricing makes one break-even figure unreliable for the mix; Explains demand shortfall at 3,200 batches or non-linear costs create losses

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Northgate Paper Bags should move to the larger premises? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The partners could move because supermarket demand is growing and capacity is the constraint [k]; the larger premises raises fixed costs to $70,000 and lifts capacity to 3,200 batches, giving a 2,000-batch break-even output and, at 3,200 batches, a margin of safety of 1,200 batches and profit of $42,000 (3,200 x $35 - $70,000) [app][an]. However, at last year's 2,500 batches the bigger site would earn only $17,500 profit (2,500 x $35 - $70,000), halving the current $35,000 profit, and the partners would need around 3,000 batches just to match today's earnings - unproven demand for a business employing nine staff [app][an]. Conversely, the six-month bulk order at $80 per batch is safer in the short run: contribution of $25 per batch still beats doing nothing new, and it would build the cash and track record needed to support the premises move later, without betting $17,500 extra every year on untested capacity [k][eval]. Overall, the partners should move to the larger premises only if at least one or two supermarkets sign volume commitments consistent with 3,000-3,200 batches a year; if not, they should take the bulk order first, bank the $25-per-batch contribution, and revisit the move in 12 months when the extra demand is proven rather than hoped for [eval].
    Keywords: $17,500, 3,200 batches, 2,500 batches, $80 per batch, larger premises, $52,500, $55 per batch
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Larger premises: fixed costs $70,000, break-even 2,000 batches, profit $42,000 at 3,200; Bulk order: contribution $25, break-even 2,100 batches | application_max_2: Applies figures: profit halves to $17,500 at 2,500 batches on the larger site; Applies figures: ~3,000 batches needed to match the current $35,000 profit | analysis_max_2: Analyses the jump from fixed-cost certainty to demand-dependent returns; Analyses the bulk order as a lower-risk bridge to finance expansion | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation: move only with contracted volume; otherwise take the bulk order first

--- STEM ---
Hillybrook Honey Farm is a family business in Country X's hill country, bottling wildflower honey in 500g jars since 2012. Each jar sells for $8, variable costs are $3.00 per jar, and fixed costs are $36,000 a year. The farm filled 9,000 jars last year and sells them at farm shops, markets and a small online store.

The owners are considering a new bottling line that raises fixed costs to $60,000 but cuts variable costs to $2.00 per jar, or raising the jar price to $9 to fund a quality certification. A poor, wet summer this year has made them cautious. They also wonder whether break-even figures can be trusted when honey sales swing with the weather and tourism numbers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'total variable cost'.
    Answer: Total variable cost is the sum of all costs that change directly with output, found by multiplying variable cost per unit by units made (Hillybrook last year: $3.00 x 9,000 jars = $27,000 - more jars means proportionally higher variable costs). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Variable costs change directly with output; Total variable cost = variable cost per unit x output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the owners want break-even figures for the new bottling line.
    Answer: Reason 1: to check whether the line is affordable at current demand [k]; the bottling line raises fixed costs to $60,000 and cuts variable costs to $2.00 per jar, so contribution becomes $6.00 and break-even output jumps to 10,000 jars ($60,000 / $6.00) - 1,000 jars more than the 9,000 filled last year [app]. Reason 2: to compare the line fairly against the certification price rise [k]; raising the price to $9 also gives $6.00 contribution but keeps fixed costs at $36,000, so break-even output would be 6,000 jars - a far safer cushion than the line offers [app].
    Keywords: $2.00 per jar, $60,000, 9,000 jars, $9, $36,000, new bottling line
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even output = fixed costs / contribution per unit; Higher fixed costs raise break-even output even when variable costs fall | application_max_2: Applies figures: line break-even $60,000 / $6.00 = 10,000 jars vs 9,000 filled; Applies figures: $9 price gives $6.00 contribution, break-even 6,000 jars

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why break-even analysis has limitations for a weather-dependent honey farm.
    Answer: Limitation 1: break-even analysis assumes all jars produced are sold [k]; a wet summer reduces both the honey crop and tourist footfall at farm shops and markets, so if only, say, 6,000 jars are sold, the $36,000 fixed costs would outstrip revenue and the calculated 7,200-jar break-even would never reveal that risk [app][an]. Limitation 2: break-even analysis assumes prices and unit costs stay constant [k]; a poor harvest raises honey cost per jar, and discounting to shift slow-moving stock narrows the $5.00 contribution, dragging break-even above 7,200 jars and eroding the 1,800-jar margin of safety precisely when demand is weakest [app][an].
    Keywords: $36,000, 9,000 jars, $8, $3.00 per jar, weather, tourism
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Break-even assumes all output is sold; Break-even assumes constant prices and costs (straight lines) | application_max_2: Applies figures: weak sales of 6,000 jars leave $36,000 fixed costs uncovered; Applies figures: narrower $5.00 contribution lifts break-even above 7,200 jars | analysis_max_2: Explains weather losses make the static chart overstate safety; Explains cost increases and price discounting push the true break-even upwards

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the owners should buy the new bottling line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The owners could buy the line because it cuts variable costs to $2.00 per jar, lifting contribution to $6.00 and preparing Hillybrook for growth if honey demand recovers or tourism rises [k]; it also improves consistency and speed for online-store orders, and every future jar carries a lower unit cost [app][an]. However, at last year's 9,000 jars the line would raise fixed costs to $60,000 and give break-even output of 10,000 jars ($60,000 / $6.00), producing a loss of about $6,000 (9,000 x $6.00 - $60,000) and a negative margin of safety of 1,000 jars - it cannot pay for itself without finding 1,000 extra jars a year [app][an]. Conversely, raising the jar price to $9 to fund quality certification also yields $6.00 contribution but keeps fixed costs at $36,000, so break-even output falls to 6,000 jars, the margin of safety widens to 3,000 jars and profit rises from $9,000 to $18,000 at unchanged volume [k][eval]. Overall, the owners should not buy the bottling line at present - with a poor, wet summer and fragile tourism, committing to $60,000 fixed costs with break-even 1,000 jars above proven sales is too risky; they should raise the jar price to $9 and pursue certification first, and revisit the line only when annual sales are demonstrably above 10,000 jars or the line's cost falls substantially [eval].
    Keywords: $60,000, $2.00 per jar, 9,000 jars, $9, new bottling line, $36,000, honey sales
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Bottling line: fixed costs $60,000, contribution $6.00, break-even 10,000 jars; Price rise to $9: contribution $6.00, break-even 6,000 jars, profit $18,000 | application_max_2: Applies figures: line yields ~$6,000 loss at 9,000 jars, margin of safety -1,000; Applies figures: $9 price doubles profit from $9,000 to $18,000 at 9,000 jars | analysis_max_2: Analyses that break-even 1,000 jars above proven sales makes the line unsafe this year; Analyses that the $9 price route reaches the same contribution without extra fixed costs | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation: price rise and certification first; line only above 10,000-jar sales

--- STEM ---
Hartwell Flour Milling Co is a private limited company founded 9 years ago by Daniel Whitmore, operating a flour mill in Country X. It employs 45 workers and mills 600 tonnes of flour a month. Last year revenue was $3.6 million and profit was $420,000. Daniel is considering expanding output to 900 tonnes a month to win a long-term contract with a national bakery chain.

Option A is to sign the contract and buy grain in bulk at $240 a tonne instead of the usual $310, saving $70 a tonne. Option B is to keep output at 600 tonnes and serve small local bakeries. Widening the mill warehouse costs $95,000, which Daniel would need to finance before the first delivery arrives in 4 months.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'purchasing economies of scale'.
    Answer: Purchasing economies of scale are the cost advantages a business gains by buying inputs in large quantities, because suppliers offer bulk discounts so the cost of each unit of materials purchased falls [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying inputs in large quantities / bulk; Suppliers offer discounts, so cost per unit of materials falls

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Hartwell Flour Milling Co of purchasing economies of scale.
    Answer: One benefit is lower grain costs [k]. Buying at $240 a tonne instead of $310 saves $70 a tonne, a saving of $63,000 a month on 900 tonnes, which cuts Hartwell's average cost per tonne of flour [app]. A second benefit is stronger competitiveness [k]. With cheaper flour, Hartwell can price its bid for the national bakery chain contract more aggressively than its larger rival, protecting its $3.6 million revenue base [app].
    Keywords: Hartwell Flour Milling Co, $240, $310, $70, $3.6 million, national bakery chain, 900 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying in bulk lowers the cost of inputs; Lower input costs can improve competitiveness / prices | application_max_2: Reference to $240 a tonne vs $310, saving $70 a tonne; Reference to $63,000 a month saved on 900 tonnes / national bakery chain contract

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Hartwell Flour Milling Co might face if it expands output to 900 tonnes a month.
    Answer: One problem is the strain on cash [k]. Widening the mill warehouse costs $95,000, and grain must be paid for before the first delivery arrives, so Hartwell's cash position could tighten even though profit was $420,000 last year [app], and if the contract start is delayed the mill would carry the extra debt without the expected revenue [an]. A second problem is diseconomies of scale [k]. Running at 900 tonnes means more lorries, more staff and busier shifts each day [app], and without additional supervisors, miscommunication could raise flour waste and breach the bakery chain's quality requirements [an].
    Keywords: $95,000, 900 tonnes, $420,000, Hartwell, national bakery chain, $70, warehouse
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large expansion strains cash / requires upfront finance; Diseconomies of scale: coordination and communication problems as output rises | application_max_2: Reference to $95,000 warehouse cost / payment before first delivery; Reference to 900 tonnes output / $420,000 profit last year | analysis_max_2: Chain from $95,000 upfront spend to tight cash to risk if contract delayed; Chain from larger scale to miscommunication/waste to quality risk with national bakery chain

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hartwell Flour Milling Co should sign the contract and expand to 900 tonnes a month? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, signing the contract gives Hartwell a reliable national customer and protects its $3.6 million revenue base [k]. Bulk grain at $240 a tonne instead of $310 saves $70 a tonne, worth $63,000 a month on 900 tonnes [app]. Lower input costs create purchasing economies of scale, so average cost falls and profit can rise above the $420,000 earned last year, making Hartwell more competitive against its rival [an]. However, expanding is not risk-free [k]. Widening the warehouse costs $95,000 before the first delivery in 4 months, cash must be found while the mill pays for grain up front, and running a bigger mill could bring poor communication and flour waste [app]. If the bakery chain delays or cancels, Hartwell would carry high fixed costs with sales below 900 tonnes, squeezing profit and possibly threatening the mill's future [an]. Overall, I think Hartwell should sign the contract [eval]. The $63,000 monthly saving is large next to the $95,000 one-off warehouse cost, which would be recovered in about 6 weeks of running at the new volume, and purchasing economies at this size clearly outweigh the coordination risks for a well-established mill [eval].
    Keywords: Hartwell Flour Milling Co, $240, $310, $70, $95,000, $420,000, 900 tonnes, national bakery chain
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Purchasing economies of scale reduce average cost when buying in bulk; Growth carries risks such as diseconomies of scale and cash strain | application_max_2: Reference to $240 vs $310 a tonne, $70 saving worth $63,000 a month on 900 tonnes; Reference to $95,000 warehouse cost, delivery in 4 months, $3.6 million revenue, $420,000 profit | analysis_max_2: Chain from bulk saving to lower average cost to higher profit and competitiveness; Chain from $95,000 upfront spend and bigger scale to cash strain or waste to risk if contract lost | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on signing the contract; Weighs both options using stem figures ($63,000 saving vs $95,000 cost and 4-month delay)

--- STEM ---
Sunvale Soft Drinks is a private limited company based in Country X, producing premium sparkling fruit drinks. It employs 38 workers, makes 2 million bottles a year and earned revenue of $3.1 million last year with a profit of $280,000. Its advertising budget last year was $150,000, spent on radio adverts in three cities. The managing director, Priya Raman, wants Sunvale to become a national brand rather than a regional favourite.

Option A is a national television and billboard campaign costing $600,000, expected to add 1.2 million bottles of annual sales worth about $1.8 million in extra revenue. Option B is a regional campaign costing $120,000, expected to add 400,000 bottles worth about $600,000 in extra revenue. The board has 3 months to decide before the summer season begins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'marketing economies of scale'.
    Answer: Marketing economies of scale are cost advantages where the cost of advertising and promotion is spread over a larger volume of sales, so the marketing cost per unit falls as the business grows [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Advertising/promotion cost is spread over more units sold; Marketing cost per unit falls as output and sales rise

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Sunvale Soft Drinks of using a national campaign.
    Answer: One benefit is a much wider audience [k]. A $600,000 national television and billboard campaign would put Sunvale's drinks in front of customers across the whole country, far more than the $150,000 a year now spent on three cities [app]. A second benefit is spreading the advertising cost over more sales [k]. Adding 1.2 million bottles to the 2 million already sold would spread the campaign cost over far more units, lowering the marketing cost per bottle [app].
    Keywords: Sunvale Soft Drinks, $600,000, $150,000, national television, 1.2 million bottles, 2 million, $1.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: National advertising reaches a much wider audience; Marketing cost is spread over more units sold / cost per unit falls | application_max_2: Reference to $600,000 national campaign vs $150,000 spent on three cities; Reference to 1.2 million extra bottles added to 2 million current sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Sunvale Soft Drinks might face if it spends $600,000 on the television and billboard campaign.
    Answer: One problem is the high upfront cost [k]. Paying $600,000 is four times Sunvale's $150,000 advertising budget and more than twice its $280,000 profit, so financial strain is a serious risk [app]. If sales do not rise as expected, cash flow would suffer and other investment plans would be delayed [an]. A second problem is poor targeting [k]. A national television and billboard campaign cannot be tailored to specific towns or income groups [app], so money could be wasted on viewers who never buy premium fruit drinks, lowering the return on the campaign spend [an].
    Keywords: $600,000, $280,000, television and billboard campaign, $150,000, 2 million bottles, Sunvale
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A large upfront campaign strains cash flow and profit; Mass campaigns cannot be targeted precisely / risk wasted spend | application_max_2: Reference to $600,000 vs $150,000 budget and $280,000 profit; Reference to national television and billboard campaign / premium sparkling fruit drinks | analysis_max_2: Chain from $600,000 spend to cash-flow strain to delayed investment if sales disappoint; Chain from broad targeting to wasted spend to lower return on the campaign

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sunvale Soft Drinks should launch the national campaign? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, the $600,000 campaign could transform Sunvale from a regional seller into a national brand [k]. It would add about 1.2 million bottles a year, worth $1.8 million in extra revenue, three times the campaign cost [app], and the higher volume would spread advertising and fixed costs over more units, lowering the marketing cost per bottle through marketing economies of scale [an]. On the other hand, the risk is real [k]. The campaign costs four times the $150,000 advertising budget of last year and over twice the $280,000 profit Sunvale earned, so if extra sales fall short of 1.2 million bottles the money would be wasted and cash flow could be damaged [app]. A safer route is the $120,000 regional campaign, expected to add 400,000 bottles worth $600,000 in extra revenue, growing the brand without crippling the business [an]. Overall, I think Sunvale should launch the national campaign [eval]. The expected $1.8 million extra revenue dwarfs the $600,000 cost, and without national visibility the brand may never escape regional obscurity; spend can be trimmed later if the response disappoints [eval].
    Keywords: Sunvale Soft Drinks, $600,000, $1.8 million, $150,000, $280,000, 1.2 million bottles, $120,000, 400,000 bottles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Marketing economies of scale: cost per unit falls as advertising is spread over more sales; Large campaigns carry cash-flow and targeting risks | application_max_2: Reference to $600,000 cost, 1.2 million extra bottles, $1.8 million expected revenue; Reference to $150,000 budget, $280,000 profit, $120,000 regional alternative with 400,000 extra bottles | analysis_max_2: Chain from higher volume to marketing cost spread over more units to lower cost per bottle; Chain from $600,000 upfront cost to cash-flow risk to potential harm if sales disappoint | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on the national campaign; Weighs both options using stem figures ($1.8 million vs $600,000; $120,000 alternative)

--- STEM ---
Wexford Steel Co is a private limited company in Country X supplying rolled steel to builders and fabricators. It employs 84 staff at one depot and produced 4,000 tonnes of steel product last year, with revenue of $11.5 million and profit of $900,000. Director Aaron Blake wants to install a new electric furnace to lift capacity to 6,500 tonnes a year and cut unit costs.

Wexford's bank will lend $2.5 million at 7% interest a year, while smaller rivals typically pay 11%. Option A is to borrow the $2.5 million now and fit the furnace; the extra 2,500 tonnes would be sold under a 5-year supply deal. Option B is to decline the loan, keep producing 4,000 tonnes a year and avoid $175,000 of annual interest.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'financial economies of scale'.
    Answer: Financial economies of scale are cost advantages where large businesses can borrow money at lower interest rates and on better terms than smaller businesses, because lenders view them as less risky [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large businesses pay lower interest rates on loans; Lenders see larger, safer businesses as less risky

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Wexford Steel Co of financial economies of scale.
    Answer: One benefit is cheaper borrowing [k]. Wexford would pay 7% interest rather than the 11% typical for smaller rivals, saving $100,000 a year on a $2.5 million loan [app]. A second benefit is funding expansion from outside savings [k]. Access to a $2.5 million loan lets Wexford buy the electric furnace and raise output from 4,000 to 6,500 tonnes without waiting years to save the cash from revenue [app].
    Keywords: Wexford Steel Co, 7%, 11%, $2.5 million, 4,000, 6,500 tonnes, electric furnace
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Larger firms borrow at lower interest rates; Cheaper, easier finance funds growth and investment | application_max_2: Reference to 7% vs 11%, saving $100,000 a year on $2.5 million; Reference to electric furnace / capacity lifted from 4,000 to 6,500 tonnes

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks to Wexford Steel Co of borrowing $2.5 million at 7% interest.
    Answer: One risk is the fixed interest cost [k]. Interest of $175,000 a year must be paid even in a downturn [app], so if steel orders fall, Wexford could struggle to cover payments and last year's $900,000 profit would shrink fast, raising the danger of insolvency [an]. A second risk is over-committing to one customer [k]. The 5-year supply deal depends on the extra 2,500 tonnes being sold [app], and if demand does not materialise, Wexford would be left paying for an underused furnace while still owing the bank $2.5 million [an].
    Keywords: $2.5 million, 7%, $175,000, $900,000, 5-year supply deal, 2,500 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interest must be paid regardless of trading conditions; Debt creates repayment/insolvency risk if revenue falls | application_max_2: Reference to $175,000 a year interest / $900,000 profit last year; Reference to 5-year supply deal / extra 2,500 tonnes / $2.5 million loan | analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed interest to pressure on profit to risk of insolvency in a downturn; Chain from reliance on one deal to underused capacity to cash strain while still owing the bank

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wexford Steel Co should borrow the $2.5 million? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, borrowing at 7% shows a clear financial economy of scale [k]. Paying $175,000 interest a year instead of $275,000 at the 11% rate rivals typically pay saves $100,000 a year, and the furnace lifts capacity from 4,000 to 6,500 tonnes under a 5-year supply deal [app]. That extra scale would spread fixed costs, such as the depot and management, over more tonnes, lowering average cost and helping Wexford win further building-sector contracts [an]. On the other hand, debt adds pressure [k]. Even at 7%, Wexford commits $175,000 a year for many years, and profit of $900,000 last year could evaporate if construction demand falls or the 5-year deal is renegotiated smaller [app]. Staying at 4,000 tonnes avoids any risk to the 84 staff and keeps Wexford flexible if orders drop [an]. Overall, I think Wexford should borrow the $2.5 million [eval]. The guaranteed 5-year supply deal secures the extra 2,500 tonnes of sales, and the four percentage point interest advantage saves $100,000 a year, making expansion decisively worthwhile for an established supplier [eval].
    Keywords: Wexford Steel Co, $2.5 million, 7%, 11%, $175,000, 4,000, 6,500 tonnes, 5-year supply deal
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Financial economies of scale: larger firms borrow at lower interest rates; Debt increases fixed financial commitments and risk | application_max_2: Reference to 7% vs 11%, $175,000 vs $275,000 interest, saving $100,000 a year; Reference to 5-year supply deal, 6,500 tonnes vs 4,000 tonnes, $900,000 profit, 84 staff | analysis_max_2: Chain from lower interest and extra scale to lower average cost to more competitiveness; Chain from fixed interest commitments to pressure on $900,000 profit to insolvency risk if demand falls | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on borrowing the $2.5 million; Weighs both options using stem figures ($100,000 saving vs fixed $175,000 interest risk)

--- STEM ---
Carrick Pharmaceuticals is a private limited company in Country X making generic painkillers. It employs 120 workers and produces 80,000 packs a year, earning revenue of $8.4 million and profit of $950,000. Late deliveries and missed orders have doubled since last year. Output has outgrown the office; general managers now cover marketing, production planning and finance at the same time.

Option A is to appoint three specialists, a marketing director, a production manager and a finance analyst, at a combined cost of $260,000 a year. They would aim to cut pack wastage from 9%, roughly $90,000 lost a year, to 3%. Option B is to keep the current generalist structure and postpone hiring until annual profit passes $1.1 million. The two owners disagree about the risk.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'managerial economies of scale'.
    Answer: Managerial economies of scale are cost advantages where a larger business can afford specialist managers for particular functions, whose expertise reduces waste and improves decisions as the business grows [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large businesses can afford specialist managers; Specialist expertise reduces waste and improves decisions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Carrick Pharmaceuticals of hiring specialist managers.
    Answer: One benefit is better decisions in each function [k]. A dedicated marketing director, production manager and finance analyst would each give expert attention to their area instead of roles being covered by stretched generalists at a business employing 120 workers [app]. A second benefit is lower wastage [k]. Targeting wastage from 9% to 3% would cut roughly $60,000 of the $90,000 lost each year, protecting part of the $950,000 profit [app].
    Keywords: Carrick Pharmaceuticals, marketing director, production manager, finance analyst, 120 workers, 9%, $90,000, $950,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Specialist managers make better decisions in their function; Specialists reduce waste and errors in the business | application_max_2: Reference to 120 workers / general managers covering marketing, production planning and finance; Reference to wastage cut from 9% to 3% / $90,000 lost a year / $950,000 profit

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Carrick Pharmaceuticals might face from hiring the three specialists.
    Answer: One problem is the salary cost [k]. The three specialists cost $260,000 a year, which would cut profit from $950,000 to roughly $690,000 before any savings are made [app]. If wastage does not fall as planned, Carrick would carry the extra payroll with no financial benefit in return [an]. A second problem is duplicated authority [k]. Adding a production manager above existing supervisors could create conflict over who makes decisions [app], and slow early coordination between new and existing managers could delay the very efficiency gains the hires are meant to deliver [an].
    Keywords: $260,000, $950,000, specialists, 120 workers, $90,000, wastage
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Senior specialists are expensive and reduce short-term profit; New managers can create conflict or duplication of authority | application_max_2: Reference to $260,000 combined annual salaries / profit $950,000 to about $690,000; Reference to a production manager above existing supervisors / current generalist structure | analysis_max_2: Chain from $260,000 salary cost to lower profit to pressure if savings do not materialise; Chain from overlapping authority to conflict or slow coordination to delayed efficiency gains

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Carrick Pharmaceuticals should hire the three specialists now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, managerial economies of scale apply as Carrick grows [k]. At 120 workers producing 80,000 packs a year, general managers are stretched across marketing, production planning and finance; specialists could cut wastage from 9% to 3%, saving about $60,000 a year of the $90,000 now lost [app]. Expert coordination would also reduce late deliveries and missed orders, protecting the $8.4 million revenue and supporting further efficient growth [an]. On the other hand, the cost is heavy [k]. Paying $260,000 a year would drop profit from $950,000 to about $690,000, and the two owners disagree; if savings fall short, waiting until annual profit passes $1.1 million, as Option B suggests, would be the safer route [app]. Duplicated authority and slow decisions between new and existing managers are also possible at this size [an]. Overall, I think Carrick should hire the three specialists now [eval]. The wastage saving plus better marketing and financial control make $260,000 good value against a $950,000 profit, and postponing to $1.1 million simply lets more waste accumulate [eval].
    Keywords: Carrick Pharmaceuticals, $260,000, $950,000, 120 workers, 80,000 packs, $90,000, 9%, 3%, $8.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Managerial economies of scale: specialists improve decisions and reduce waste as firms grow; Hiring costs reduce short-term profit and carries integration risks | application_max_2: Reference to 120 workers, 80,000 packs, wastage cut from 9% to 3%, about $60,000 of the $90,000 saved; Reference to $260,000 salaries, profit $950,000 to about $690,000, Option B threshold of $1.1 million, $8.4 million revenue | analysis_max_2: Chain from specialist expertise to less waste and fewer errors to protected revenue and margin; Chain from $260,000 payroll to lower profit to risk if savings fall short / postponed hiring | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on hiring now versus Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($260,000 vs $950,000 profit and 9% to 3% wastage)

--- STEM ---
Silverline Electronics is a private limited company in Country X assembling home circuit-breaker panels. It employs 30 workers on manual assembly at $11 an hour, working 40 hours a week, producing 6,000 units a month; manual labour costs about $13,200 a week. Revenue last year was $5.6 million and profit was $700,000. Demand now exceeds capacity. Chloe Navarro, the managing director, believes the line would pay for itself through lower labour cost per unit, while the production manager fears defects during installation.

Option A is to buy an automated assembly line costing $1.8 million, run it with 8 operators, and raise output to 14,000 units a month. Option B is to stay with manual assembly, hire 12 extra workers at $11 an hour, and raise output to 8,500 units a month. The directors want the decision within 6 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'technical economies of scale'.
    Answer: Technical economies of scale are cost advantages where a large business can afford advanced machinery and production techniques that lower the average cost per unit as output rises [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large businesses can afford advanced/automated machinery; Specialist techniques lower average cost per unit as output rises

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Silverline Electronics of buying the automated assembly line.
    Answer: One benefit is higher output from fewer workers [k]. The line runs with 8 operators instead of 30 workers on manual assembly, lifting output from 6,000 to 14,000 units a month [app]. A second benefit is lower labour cost per unit [k]. Labour would fall from about $13,200 a week to about $3,520 a week, so the labour cost of each circuit-breaker panel would drop sharply as volume rises [app].
    Keywords: Silverline Electronics, 8 operators, 30 workers, 6,000, 14,000 units, $1.8 million, $11
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automated machinery raises output with fewer workers; Labour cost per unit falls as volume rises | application_max_2: Reference to 8 operators vs 30 workers / output 6,000 to 14,000 units a month; Reference to $13,200 a week labour vs about $3,520 a week / $11 an hour

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Silverline Electronics might face if it buys the automated assembly line.
    Answer: One problem is the purchase price [k]. Paying $1.8 million would consume a large share of cash and is more than twice last year's $700,000 profit, so Silverline would likely need a loan or director funding [app]. If faults appear during installation, Silverline could pay interest while producing nothing, threatening profit [an]. A second problem is training and reliability [k]. The 8 operators must learn new controls, and a breakdown would halt production of up to 14,000 units a month [app], so one technical failure could cost far more than manual assembly ever would [an].
    Keywords: $1.8 million, $700,000, 14,000 units, automated assembly line, 6,000, circuit-breaker
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Advanced machinery is expensive and strains cash flow; Automation brings training needs and breakdown risk | application_max_2: Reference to $1.8 million cost vs $700,000 profit last year; Reference to 8 operators needing training / 14,000 units a month at risk | analysis_max_2: Chain from $1.8 million spend to reliance on borrowing to profit pressure if installation fails; Chain from breakdown or poor training to halted production to heavy cost of failure

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Silverline Electronics should buy the automated assembly line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, technical economies of scale strongly favour the purchase [k]. The $1.8 million line raises output from 6,000 to 14,000 units a month, more than double, while manual labour falls from 30 workers to 8 operators [app]. Spreading fixed costs, such as factory rent and management, over more units lowers average cost per unit, and demand already exceeds capacity, so the extra panels can be sold without deep discounting [an]. On the other hand, the price tag is heavy [k]. At $1.8 million, the line is more than twice last year's $700,000 profit and would probably need borrowed money or director funding [app]. Option B, hiring 12 extra workers at $11 an hour to reach 8,500 units a month, is cheaper now, keeps flexibility and avoids installation defects that the production manager fears [an]. Overall, I think Silverline should buy the automated assembly line [eval]. Demand exceeds capacity and technical economies scale so well that the extra output of 5,500 units a month over Option B would quickly justify the $1.8 million, while Option B cannot match the fall in average cost per unit [eval].
    Keywords: Silverline Electronics, $1.8 million, 6,000, 14,000 units, 30 workers, 8 operators, $700,000, 8,500 units
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale: automation lowers average cost per unit as output rises; Automation requires heavy upfront investment and carries installation risk | application_max_2: Reference to $1.8 million line, output 6,000 to 14,000 units, 30 workers to 8 operators; Reference to $700,000 profit, Option B of 12 extra workers at $11 an hour for 8,500 units | analysis_max_2: Chain from automation to spread fixed costs over more units to lower average cost per unit; Chain from $1.8 million upfront cost to financing risk to possible harm if installation fails | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on buying the automated line; Weighs both options using stem figures (14,000 vs 8,500 units; $1.8 million vs $700,000 profit)

--- STEM ---
The Meadowlark Dairy Co-operative in Country X is owned by 60 member farms. It collects and processes 150,000 litres of milk a day and employs 55 staff; the co-operative pays members $0.42 per litre collected. Last year revenue was $9.8 million and the surplus paid to members was $640,000. The board is weighing how to scale up processing capacity.

Option A is to build a new central plant costing $4 million, cutting average cost from $0.58 to $0.49 per litre and lifting capacity to 240,000 litres a day. Option B is to upgrade the existing line for $1.2 million, raising capacity to 190,000 litres a day. Members are split on whether a bigger plant risks paying farmers late; some fear coordination problems and slow decisions across a doubled site.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'scale of production'.
    Answer: Scale of production is the size of a business's output, meaning how large the operation is and the volume of goods or services it produces [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Scale of production refers to the size of output / the volume produced; It shows how large the business operation is

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Meadowlark of increasing its scale of production.
    Answer: One benefit is lower average cost [k]. A new central plant would cut average cost from $0.58 to $0.49 per litre, saving 9 cents on every one of 240,000 litres processed each day [app]. A second benefit is greater capacity for member farms [k]. Capacity rising from 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day means all 60 member farms can sell more milk through the co-operative instead of seeking outside buyers [app].
    Keywords: Meadowlark Dairy Co-operative, $0.58, $0.49, 240,000 litres, 150,000 litres, 60 member farms, $4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Larger scale can reduce average cost per unit; Larger scale gives more capacity and output | application_max_2: Reference to average cost $0.58 to $0.49 per litre / 9 cents saved; Reference to capacity 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day / 60 member farms

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two diseconomies of scale Meadowlark might face at a large central plant.
    Answer: One diseconomy is poor communication [k]. A bigger site with more drivers, engineers and member farms means messages travel further, and a quality problem in one shift could reach the board days late [app]. Slow reaction would waste more milk than the current 150,000-litres-a-day operation, hitting the $9.8 million revenue [an]. A second diseconomy is slow decision-making [k]. More layers of approval at a plant nearly twice the size mean routine decisions, such as buying parts or changing shifts, take longer [app], so the co-operative becomes sluggish just as larger rivals cut their prices [an].
    Keywords: 150,000 litres, 240,000 litres, $4 million, 60 member farms, Meadowlark Dairy Co-operative, $0.49
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Poor communication as organisations grow larger; Slow decision-making as more layers of management are added | application_max_2: Reference to doubled/larger site vs current 150,000 litres a day / $9.8 million revenue; Reference to central plant / 60 member farms / more layers of approval | analysis_max_2: Chain from longer message routes to delayed response to wasted milk and lost revenue; Chain from more approval layers to slower decisions to sluggish response to rivals' price cuts

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Meadowlark Dairy Co-operative should build the large central plant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, bigger scale brings real economies [k]. The $4 million plant lifts capacity from 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day and cuts average cost from $0.58 to $0.49 per litre; on 240,000 litres a day, that 9-cent saving is about $21,600 a day [app]. Purchasing power for packaging, fuel and milk-collection logistics would also improve, supporting the $9.8 million revenue and the $640,000 surplus paid to members [an]. On the other hand, co-operatives fail when members feel ignored [k]. A plant 60% larger could bring poor communication and slower decisions across 60 farms, and if 240,000 litres cannot be sold profitably, member milk could be paid late, as some members fear [app]. Option B, upgrading the existing line for $1.2 million to reach 190,000 litres a day, is a cheaper and safer step that still adds capacity and avoids a doubled site [an]. Overall, I think Meadowlark should build the central plant [eval]. The $0.49 average cost and an extra 90,000 litres of daily capacity offer savings far beyond the $1.2 million upgrade, provided the board appoints extra supervisors to keep communication clear [eval].
    Keywords: Meadowlark Dairy Co-operative, $4 million, $0.58, $0.49, 240,000 litres, 150,000 litres, $640,000, $1.2 million, 60 member farms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Larger scale of production can deliver economies of scale and lower average cost; Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and slow decision-making in large organisations | application_max_2: Reference to $4 million plant, $0.58 to $0.49 per litre, capacity 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day; Reference to $1.2 million upgrade to 190,000 litres, $9.8 million revenue, $640,000 surplus, 60 member farms | analysis_max_2: Chain from lower average cost and scale to better member surplus and competitiveness; Chain from larger, doubled site to coordination problems to risk of late payment to members | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on building the central plant; Weighs both options using stem figures ($21,600 a day saving vs $1.2 million cheaper upgrade)
