--- STEM ---
Quickhaul Courier Services is a private limited company in Country X delivering parcels for online retailers. It has grown from 40 employees 18 months ago to 210 today, handling 15,000 parcels a day, with revenue of $6.3 million last year. Late deliveries have risen from 5% to 12% and two major clients have complained. Drivers report that messages from head office arrive too late to act on, and meeting notes are lost between depots.

Option A is to sign a national contract worth $1.4 million a year, pushing the workforce to about 400. Option B is to split Quickhaul into 3 regional divisions of around 70 staff, each with its own operations manager. The founder, Jess Marino, must decide before the contract signing deadline in 6 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two diseconomies of scale.
    Answer: Poor communication, such as instructions from head office arriving late or being lost between depots [1]; slow decision-making, as more layers of management delay each approval [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Poor communication as the business grows larger; Slow decision-making as more management layers are added

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Quickhaul Courier Services of splitting into regional divisions.
    Answer: One benefit is better communication [k]. Divisions of around 70 staff would have shorter chains of command, so messages between depots and drivers would arrive on time and fewer parcels would be missed [app]. A second benefit is faster decision-making [k]. Each division's operations manager could approve routes and shifts without waiting for head office, helping to cut the 12% late-delivery rate back toward 5% [app].
    Keywords: Quickhaul Courier Services, 70 staff, 12%, 5%, 210, 15,000 parcels
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Smaller divisions shorten communication channels; Delegated decisions are made faster at division level | application_max_2: Reference to divisions of around 70 staff / lost messages between depots; Reference to 12% late deliveries vs 5% / operations manager per division

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Quickhaul Courier Services of signing the national contract.
    Answer: One benefit is secure revenue [k]. The national contract is worth $1.4 million a year, giving Quickhaul predictable income on top of its current $6.3 million revenue [app]. Guaranteed volume would spread fixed costs, such as vehicles and depots, over more parcels a day, lowering average cost per delivery [an]. A second benefit is stronger market position [k]. With about 400 staff and 15,000-plus parcels a day, Quickhaul could win more online-retail contracts from rival couriers [app], and greater scale could unlock purchasing economies when buying fuel, tyres and packaging [an].
    Keywords: $1.4 million, national contract, 15,000 parcels a day, about 400, Quickhaul Courier Services
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A large contract secures predictable revenue; Greater scale spreads fixed costs and unlocks purchasing economies | application_max_2: Reference to $1.4 million a year contract / $6.3 million revenue; Reference to about 400 staff / 15,000 parcels a day | analysis_max_2: Chain from guaranteed volume to spread fixed costs to lower average cost per delivery; Chain from national scale to purchasing economies and stronger negotiating position

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Quickhaul Courier Services should sign the national contract worth $1.4 million a year? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, signing the contract secures $1.4 million of annual revenue [k]. It would push the workforce from 210 to about 400 and lock in a large online retailer, helping Quickhaul spread fixed costs over 15,000-plus parcels a day and benefit from purchasing economies on fuel and vehicle parts [app]. This scale could secure Quickhaul's position as a national courier and lift profit above its current level [an]. On the other hand, growing to about 400 staff risks serious diseconomies of scale [k]. Deliveries are already 12% late, up from 5%, and drivers say head-office messages arrive too late; expanding to near double today's 210 as one organisation would likely worsen communication further [app]. Splitting into 3 regional divisions of around 70 staff, each with its own operations manager, would shorten chains of command and speed up decisions before capacity is stretched [an]. Overall, I think Quickhaul should sign the national contract only after splitting into regional divisions [eval]. The $1.4 million revenue is too valuable to refuse, but the rise from 5% to 12% late shows the current structure is already failing; divisions protect service quality while keeping the contract's scale [eval].
    Keywords: Quickhaul Courier Services, $1.4 million, 210, about 400, 12%, 5%, 70 staff, 3 regional divisions
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large contracts secure revenue and scale economies (purchasing, fixed cost spreading); Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and slow decisions as firms grow | application_max_2: Reference to $1.4 million a year contract, workforce 210 to about 400, 15,000 parcels a day; Reference to deliveries 5% to 12% late, 3 regional divisions of around 70 staff | analysis_max_2: Chain from contract volume to fixed costs spread over more parcels to lower average cost and higher profit; Chain from larger single organisation to worse communication to rising late deliveries | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation combining or choosing between the options; Weighs both options using stem figures ($1.4 million vs 5% to 12% late deliveries)

--- STEM ---
Driftwood Timber Co is a private limited company in Country X turning pine logs into fence panels. It employs 64 workers and produced 120,000 panels last year, with revenue of $1.92 million and a profit of $210,000. Total production costs were $1.71 million, equal to an average cost of $14.25 per panel. Driftwood's customers are two national builders' merchants who want 30% more panels next year.

Option A is to invest $350,000 in a larger kiln and an automated panel conveyor, lifting output to 200,000 panels a year and cutting waste from 12% of timber to 5%; the bank will lend at 8%. Option B is to keep current methods and repair the existing kiln for $40,000. The owner, Ruth Ellison, worries a bigger works may strain supervision.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'efficiency'.
    Answer: Efficiency is producing the maximum possible output from a given amount of inputs, or minimising waste of time, materials and money in the production process [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Efficiency means maximum output from given inputs; Efficiency means minimising waste of resources

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Driftwood Timber Co could improve its efficiency.
    Answer: One way is investing in a larger kiln and conveyor [k]. Automating the movement of panels would lift output from 120,000 to 200,000 panels a year using the same 64 workers [app]. A second way is cutting timber waste [k]. Reducing waste from 12% to 5% of timber would get far more panels from each log, so the same raw materials would produce more saleable output [app].
    Keywords: Driftwood Timber Co, 120,000, 200,000 panels, 64 workers, 12%, 5%, $350,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation can raise output from the same inputs; Reducing waste increases usable output from the same materials | application_max_2: Reference to output lifted from 120,000 to 200,000 panels / 64 workers unchanged; Reference to waste cut from 12% to 5% of timber

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Driftwood Timber Co might face if it expands to 200,000 panels a year.
    Answer: One problem is higher supervisory strain [k]. A works operating at two-thirds more output needs tighter supervision, and without it the quality of fence panels could fall [app]. Defects found by the two national builders' merchants would damage Driftwood's reputation and future orders [an]. A second problem is larger fixed costs [k]. The $350,000 kiln and conveyor add to overheads at a works that currently earns $210,000 profit, and if demand from builders' merchants falls short of target, the extra capacity would be underused [app], leaving high fixed costs spread over fewer panels and raising average cost instead of lowering it [an].
    Keywords: 200,000 panels, $350,000, $210,000, $14.25, 120,000 panels, builders' merchants
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Rapid growth strains supervision and can reduce quality; Extra capacity raises fixed costs, which must be justified by demand | application_max_2: Reference to two national builders' merchants / output rose 120,000 to 200,000 panels; Reference to $350,000 investment vs $210,000 profit | analysis_max_2: Chain from weaker supervision to defects to damaged reputation and lost orders; Chain from extra capacity to underused fixed costs to rising average cost if demand disappoints

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Driftwood Timber Co should invest $350,000 in the kiln and conveyor? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, the investment lifts efficiency at a bigger scale [k]. Output would rise from 120,000 to 200,000 panels a year and waste would fall from 12% to 5%, so far more usable timber comes from each log and the average cost of $14.25 per panel should fall [app]. Technical economies like this lower average cost as output rises, and the bank would lend at 8% under Option A, so the extra capacity can be financed affordably [an]. On the other hand, expansion carries real risk [k]. Driftwood earned only $210,000 profit on revenue of $1.92 million, so $350,000 is about 1.7 times last year's profit [app]. If the two national builders' merchants do not take the extra 30% of panels, fixed costs would be spread over too few panels, profit would fall and the loan would be hard to repay [an]. Overall, I think Driftwood should invest the $350,000 [eval]. The 12% to 5% waste saving and automated output gain are decisive for a business facing a 30% demand increase, and the 8% bank loan is affordable; Option B only delays an inevitable decision [eval].
    Keywords: Driftwood Timber Co, $350,000, 120,000, 200,000 panels, $14.25, 12%, 5%, $210,000, 30%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale lower average cost as output rises; Large investments raise fixed costs and financing risk | application_max_2: Reference to 120,000 to 200,000 panels, waste 12% to 5%, average cost $14.25, bank lends at 8%; Reference to $350,000 vs $210,000 profit, $1.92 million revenue, 30% more panels wanted by two builders' merchants | analysis_max_2: Chain from waste reduction and automation to lower average cost to higher profit; Chain from underused capacity to fixed costs spread over fewer panels to falling profit and loan pressure | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on the $350,000 investment; Weighs both options using stem figures (waste 12% to 5% vs $350,000 cost and 30% demand rise)

--- STEM ---
Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing industrial cleaning granules. It employs 150 workers and last year output was 220,000 kg, with revenue of $1.9 million, total costs of $1.32 million and a profit of $580,000. The present average cost is $6.00 per kg (total cost $1.32 million divided by 220,000 kg), and managers already report slow decisions between the two halls.

Option A is to spend $2.2 million on a third production hall to lift output to 330,000 kg a year, projecting average cost near $5.10 per kg. Option B is to keep two halls, keep output at 220,000 kg and protect the $580,000 profit. Bank lending for Option A would run for 8 years at 6%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the average cost per kg last year when total costs were $1.32 million and output was 220,000 kg.
    Answer: Average cost = total cost / output = $1,320,000 / 220,000 kg = $6.00 per kg [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Average cost = total cost divided by output; Correct substitution: $1,320,000 / 220,000 = $6.00 per kg

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd of building the third production hall.
    Answer: One benefit is lower average cost [k]. Lifting output from 220,000 to 330,000 kg a year would spread fixed costs over 50% more units, projecting average cost near $5.10 per kg instead of $6.00 [app]. A second benefit is greater capacity to accept orders [k]. A third hall would let Saltmarsh take on larger contracts from industrial customers without turning work away to rival suppliers [app].
    Keywords: Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd, 220,000 kg, 330,000 kg, $5.10, $6.00, third production hall
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Larger scale spreads fixed costs, lowering average cost; More capacity enables larger orders / new customers | application_max_2: Reference to output 220,000 to 330,000 kg / average cost $6.00 to $5.10 per kg; Reference to third production hall / industrial cleaning granules customers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two diseconomies of scale Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd might face after building the third production hall.
    Answer: One diseconomy is slow decision-making [k]. With three halls, approvals for maintenance, shifts and purchases would pass through more managers, so routine decisions take longer [app]. That could delay urgent repairs and cut availability of the halls below plan [an]. A second diseconomy is poor communication [k]. A workforce expanding beyond 150 workers would need clearer reporting lines [app], and without them mistakes in handling industrial cleaning granules could cause accidents or rejected batches [an].
    Keywords: third production hall, 220,000 kg, 150 workers, Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd, $5.10, industrial cleaning granules
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Slow decision-making as more management layers are added; Poor communication as the workforce grows larger | application_max_2: Reference to three halls / more managers for decisions; Reference to 150 workers / handling industrial cleaning granules | analysis_max_2: Chain from more approval layers to slower decisions to delayed repairs and lost output; Chain from unclear reporting lines to mistakes/accidents to rejected batches and higher cost

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd should build the third production hall? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, greater scale would cut average cost [k]. Output would rise from 220,000 to 330,000 kg a year, with average cost projected near $5.10 per kg against $6.00 now; on 330,000 kg that is roughly $297,000 saved each year [app]. The 6% bank loan over 8 years is manageable against a $580,000 profit, and the extra capacity strengthens Saltmarsh's position with industrial buyers [an]. On the other hand, the risk is concentrated [k]. Paying $2.2 million for the hall with only $580,000 a year of profit means it pays for itself slowly, and fixed interest of about $132,000 a year at 6% would bite hard if orders stall [app]. Diseconomies such as slow decisions across three halls and weaker communication could also erode the projected $5.10 saving [an]. Overall, I think Saltmarsh should build the third hall [eval]. The $297,000 annual saving is about half of the $580,000 profit, the 6% loan is affordable and Option B locks in $6.00 average cost forever; with clear reporting lines, the risks are controllable [eval].
    Keywords: Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd, $2.2 million, 220,000 kg, 330,000 kg, $5.10, $6.00, $580,000, 6%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher scale of production lowers average cost through economies of scale; Large investments raise fixed financial commitments and financing risk | application_max_2: Reference to output 220,000 to 330,000 kg, average cost $6.00 to $5.10, saving about $297,000 a year; Reference to $2.2 million cost, $580,000 profit, 6% loan over 8 years | analysis_max_2: Chain from lower average cost at larger scale to about $297,000 annual saving to stronger profit; Chain from fixed interest of about $132,000 a year to pressure on profit if orders stall | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on building the third hall; Weighs both options using stem figures ($297,000 saving vs $2.2 million cost and $580,000 profit)

--- STEM ---
Clayborne Tiles Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making ceramic floor tiles. It employs 92 workers and produces 400,000 tiles a year. Fixed costs are $480,000 and the variable cost is $2.60 a tile. Revenue last year was $1.6 million and profit was $80,000. Demand from builders is rising by 20% a year and the order book is full until spring.

Option A is to build a fourth kiln for $1.5 million, lifting output to 550,000 tiles; fixed costs would rise to $640,000 and variable cost would hold at $2.60, giving an average cost of about $3.76 a tile. Option B is to keep three kilns, use overtime, raise output to 460,000 tiles at a variable cost of $2.85, giving an average cost near $3.89. The directors must decide within a month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the total variable cost when output is 400,000 tiles and the variable cost is $2.60 per tile.
    Answer: Total variable cost = variable cost per unit x output = $2.60 x 400,000 = $1,040,000 [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Total variable cost = variable cost per unit multiplied by output; Correct calculation: $2.60 x 400,000 = $1,040,000

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Clayborne Tiles Ltd of building the fourth kiln.
    Answer: One benefit is lower average cost [k]. Holding variable cost at $2.60 while fixed costs rise only to $640,000 gives an average cost of about $3.76 a tile, below Option B's $3.89 [app]. A second benefit is extra capacity to fill the order book [k]. Output of 550,000 tiles a year would let Clayborne meet builder demand growing by 20% a year without turning orders away [app].
    Keywords: Clayborne Tiles Ltd, $2.60, $640,000, $3.76, $3.89, 550,000 tiles, fourth kiln
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher output with stable variable cost lowers average cost; Extra capacity allows the business to accept more orders | application_max_2: Reference to $2.60 variable cost held / fixed costs $640,000 / $3.76 vs $3.89; Reference to output 550,000 tiles / demand rising 20% a year / order book full until spring

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Clayborne Tiles Ltd might face if it keeps three kilns and uses overtime under Option B.
    Answer: One problem is the higher variable cost [k]. Overtime raises the variable cost from $2.60 to $2.85 a tile, adding 25 cents on every one of 460,000 tiles, about $115,000 a year of extra cost [app]. That would wipe out the $80,000 profit unless prices rise, which could lose sales to rivals [an]. A second problem is worker fatigue and low morale [k]. Sustained overtime lowers motivation and concentration [app], so defects could rise and deliveries to builders could slip, damaging Clayborne's reputation just as the order book is fullest [an].
    Keywords: $2.85, $2.60, 460,000 tiles, $80,000, overtime, Option B
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Overtime raises variable cost per unit; Overtime lowers morale and motivation, risking defects and delays | application_max_2: Reference to variable cost $2.60 to $2.85 / 25 cents x 460,000 tiles / about $115,000 a year; Reference to $80,000 profit / order book full until spring / three kilns | analysis_max_2: Chain from higher variable cost to $115,000 extra cost to loss of the $80,000 profit or higher prices; Chain from overtime fatigue to defects and late deliveries to damaged reputation with builders

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Clayborne Tiles Ltd should build the fourth kiln? Justify your answer.
    Answer: On one hand, the fourth kiln delivers real economies of scale [k]. Output rises from 400,000 to 550,000 tiles, fixed costs climb from $480,000 to $640,000, yet average cost falls to about $3.76 a tile against $3.80 now and $3.89 under overtime [app]. Spreading higher fixed costs over 37.5% more tiles lowers average cost, and $1.5 million buys durable capacity for a business whose orders are full until spring and whose demand is growing 20% a year [an]. On the other hand, $1.5 million is a large commitment for a firm earning $80,000 profit [k]. The fourth kiln probably needs borrowing, and if builder demand slows, output near 550,000 tiles would not materialise, leaving Clayborne with underused fixed costs of $640,000 [app]. Option B costs nothing up front, keeps flexibility and lifts output to 460,000 tiles, though at $2.85 a tile its average cost is worse [an]. Overall, I think Clayborne should build the fourth kiln [eval]. Average cost of $3.76 against $3.89, plus capacity for 20% annual demand growth, outweighs the $1.5 million outlay; the firm should negotiate the loan before committing [eval].
    Keywords: Clayborne Tiles Ltd, $1.5 million, $480,000, $640,000, 400,000, 550,000 tiles, $3.76, $2.85
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Larger scale spreads fixed costs, lowering average cost (economies of scale); Large investments raise financing risk and fixed cost commitments | application_max_2: Reference to output 400,000 to 550,000 tiles, fixed costs $480,000 to $640,000, average cost $3.76 vs $3.89, $1.5 million kiln; Reference to $80,000 profit, demand rising 20% a year, order book full until spring, Option B with overtime at $2.85 | analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed costs spread over 37.5% more tiles to lower average cost to stronger profit per tile; Chain from $1.5 million outlay to financing strain to risk if demand slows and capacity lies underused | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on building the fourth kiln; Weighs both options using stem figures ($3.76 vs $3.89 average cost; $1.5 million vs $80,000 profit)

--- STEM ---
Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago by the Ferreira family in Country X. It employs 42 workers making premium boxed chocolates at its Bellport factory. Last year it sold 1.4 million boxes at $8 each, earning revenue of $11.2 million. Recently, complaints about broken pralines have risen to 240 a month, and 18% of boxes failed final inspection in May.

Managing Director Carla Ferreira must decide between two options before the Christmas gifting range ships in 10 weeks. Option A is quality control: adding an end-of-line inspection team to catch faulty boxes before dispatch, costing $60,000 a year. Option B is quality assurance: building checks into every production stage and training 30 workers to inspect recipes, enrobing and packaging, costing $95,000 to set up but cutting rework.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by 'quality assurance'.
    Answer: Quality assurance is a system of building quality into every stage of production, from raw materials to dispatch, so that faults are prevented rather than just detected [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality is built into every stage of production; Faults are prevented rather than just detected

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why quality is important to Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd.
    Answer: First, quality is important because high-quality chocolates satisfy customers and build loyalty [k]. With complaints already at 240 a month, fixing quality would protect the Christmas gifting range and encourage shoppers to reorder Hazelmere boxes [app]. Second, quality is important because poor quality wastes resources [k]. The 18% of boxes failing final inspection contain wasted ingredients and labour, so improving quality lowers costs and protects the $11.2 million revenue [app].
    Keywords: 240, 18%, $11.2 million, Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd, 1.4 million boxes, Christmas gifting range
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality builds customer satisfaction and loyalty; Quality reduces waste, rework and costs | application_max_2: Reference to 240 complaints a month / Christmas gifting range; Reference to 18% failing final inspection / $11.2 million revenue

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd might face if it introduces quality control (Option A).
    Answer: First, quality control checks products at the end of production, so faults are only detected after costs have been added [k]. With 18% of boxes already failing final inspection, even a larger inspection team would simply find more faulty boxes without stopping them being made, raising rework and scrap [app]. This would increase costs rather than remove the root cause of the defect problem, squeezing profit [an]. Second, quality control adds a permanent wage bill for inspectors [k]. The extra team costs $60,000 a year on top of existing wages for 42 workers, and that money cannot also train 30 production workers [app]. The ongoing expense reduces funds available for improvements such as Option B, limiting long-term competitiveness [an].
    Keywords: quality control, $60,000, 18%, 42 workers, end-of-line inspection, final inspection
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality control checks at the end of production; faults detected late; Quality control adds a permanent staffing cost | application_max_2: Reference to 18% failing final inspection; Reference to $60,000 a year / 42 workers / 30 workers to train | analysis_max_2: Chain from late detection to rework and scrap to higher costs and squeezed profit; Chain from inspector wages to fewer funds for training to weaker long-term competitiveness

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd should introduce quality assurance (Option B) rather than quality control (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A, quality control, would catch faulty boxes at the end of the line, protecting customers quickly before dispatch [k]. At $60,000 a year it is cheaper up front and would visibly cut complaints during the 10 weeks before the Christmas gifting range ships [app]. This rapid protection is valuable given the reputation risk at peak season [an]. However, Option B, quality assurance, prevents defects at every stage rather than detecting them afterwards [k]. Training 30 of the 42 workers to check recipes, enrobing and packaging costs $95,000 to set up, but it attacks the rework behind the 18% failure rate directly [app]. Preventing faults earlier reduces wasted ingredients, rework and complaints, protecting Hazelmere's $11.2 million revenue more sustainably than end-of-line checks [an]. Overall, I think Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd should choose Option B [eval] because prevention is cheaper than failure: the $95,000 is less than two years of Option A at $60,000 a year, after which Option B is cheaper and errors fall further [eval].
    Keywords: quality assurance, quality control, $60,000, $95,000, 240, 18%, Christmas gifting range, $11.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality control detects faults at end of production; Quality assurance prevents faults at every stage | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $60,000 a year / 10 weeks / Christmas gifting range; Reference to Option B: $95,000 / 30 of 42 workers / 18% failure rate / $11.2 million revenue | analysis_max_2: Chain from end-of-line detection to rapid reputation protection at peak season; Chain from prevention at source to less rework/waste to protected revenue and lower long-run cost | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($60,000 vs $95,000, 18% failure, 240 complaints)

This directly addresses the root cause of the 5% return rate and would reassure the retailer ahead of the $400,000 order review [app]. Timberline Joinery is a partnership owned by brothers Adam and Eli Kovac, manufacturing fitted wardrobes and kitchens at its Kilndown workshop in Country X. It employs 25 workers, producing 1,150 units last year and earning revenue of $3.6 million. Rework caused by finish flaws affects 9% of units, and a national housebuilder has offered a contract worth $900,000 a year if consistent quality can be evidenced by independent assessment.

The partners must decide in 6 weeks, before signing the housebuilder contract. Option A: pay $70,000 for an external quality audit and a 12-month certification, renewable each year, proving standards to buyers and reducing the need to prove quality for every new order. Option B: keep weekend in-house checks costing $5,000, with no external validation and no proof to show the housebuilder, but immediate savings.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by 'quality control'.
    Answer: Quality control is the inspection of finished goods at the end of production to check they meet required standards, allowing faulty items to be removed or reworked before sale [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Inspection of finished goods at the end of production; Faulty items are removed or reworked before sale

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Timberline Joinery of winning the housebuilder contract.
    Answer: First, the contract would raise revenue and profit [k]. At $900,000 a year it is a 25% uplift on the $3.6 million earned last year, adding significant sales income [app]. Second, the contract would secure regular orders and market presence [k]. Supplying a national housebuilder across its developments would raise Timberline's profile and reputation in Country X, attracting further large buyers [app].
    Keywords: $900,000, $3.6 million, housebuilder, 1,150 units, 9%, 25 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Increased revenue and profit; Reputation / regular orders / market presence | application_max_2: Reference to $900,000 a year / $3.6 million revenue; Reference to national housebuilder

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Timberline Joinery of paying for external certification (Option A).
    Answer: First, certification gives independent proof that quality standards are met [k]. The housebuilder requires evidence of consistent quality, and a 12-month certificate from external auditors satisfies that demand without repeated checks for every order [app]. Securing this independent approval makes the $900,000 contract far more likely, lifting revenue by a quarter [an]. Second, external audits identify weaknesses in production processes [k]. Auditors would examine how the 25 workers prepare, fit and finish each unit and flag the flaws causing 9% rework [app]. Fixing these weaknesses would cut waste and rework costs, improving efficiency and protecting profit margins [an].
    Keywords: external quality audit, $900,000, 9%, 25 workers, $70,000, housebuilder
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Independent / external proof of quality standards; Audits identify process weaknesses to correct | application_max_2: Reference to 12-month certification / housebuilder's requirement for evidence; Reference to 25 workers / 9% rework / $900,000 contract | analysis_max_2: Chain from certification to accepted evidence to contract secured; Chain from audit findings to less rework and waste to lower costs and higher profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Timberline Joinery should pay $70,000 for external certification (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A costs $70,000 for a 12-month certification, renewable each year, but it provides independent proof of quality standards [k]. The housebuilder has explicitly offered $900,000 a year if quality can be evidenced, so certification converts directly into a contract worth 25% of the $3.6 million earned last year [app]. Winning it would stabilise the order book for 25 workers and build a reputation attracting further buyers [an]. However, Option B keeps weekend in-house checks at only $5,000, saving $65,000 in the short run and preserving cash for materials and wages [k]. The $5,000 checks can still reduce some finish flaws, but they offer no external validation, so the housebuilder may award the contract elsewhere [app]. Losing $900,000 of annual revenue to save $65,000 would be poor financial logic for the Kovac brothers [an]. Overall, I think Timberline Joinery should choose Option A [eval] because the $70,000 cost is outweighed many times over by the $900,000 contract and the lasting credibility certification brings [eval].
    Keywords: $70,000, $5,000, $900,000, $3.6 million, housebuilder, 9%, 25 workers, 12-month certification
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Certification = independent external proof of quality standards; In-house checks are cheaper but unverified externally | application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $70,000 / 12-month certification / renewable annually; Reference to Option B: $5,000 weekend checks / no external validation / $900,000 contract at risk | analysis_max_2: Chain from certification to evidence to secured contract and sales pipeline; Chain from weak validation to contract lost to lost $900,000 revenue exceeding $65,000 saved | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($70,000 vs $5,000, $900,000 contract, $3.6 million revenue)

--- STEM ---
Rosedale Knitwear is a private limited company producing knitwear for retailers in Country X. It employs 110 workers at its Rivergate factory and knitted 600,000 garments last year, selling at an average of $15 each for revenue of $9 million. Complaints and returns over stitching faults reached 12,000 garments last quarter, and its main overseas customer, a fashion retail group taking 60% of output, has demanded a corrective action plan.

Managing Director Sara Okafor must act within 5 weeks, ahead of the retailer's supplier audit. Option A: hire 6 more inspectors for $54,000 a year to double-check finished garments. Option B: introduce quality assurance at every stage, from yarn inspection to knitting, linking and pressing, with retraining for all 110 workers, costing $80,000 as a one-off.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'quality'.
    Answer: Quality is the extent to which a product meets or exceeds customer expectations and requirements, consistently and without faults [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality is meeting customer expectations and requirements; Quality means consistency / absence of faults or defects

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Rosedale Knitwear should reduce the number of faulty garments.
    Answer: First, faulty garments create rework and returns costs [k]. With returns at 12,000 garments last quarter, each faulty item wastes yarn, machine time and labour, so fewer faults would lower production costs [app]. Second, faults damage reputation with customers [k]. The overseas fashion retail group taking 60% of output has demanded a corrective action plan, so persistent faults could lose Rosedale its largest customer [app].
    Keywords: 12,000, 60%, $9 million, 110 workers, Rosedale Knitwear, 600,000 garments
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Faults create rework, returns and waste costs; Faults damage reputation and customer relationships | application_max_2: Reference to 12,000 garments returned last quarter; Reference to 60% of output / overseas fashion retail group

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Rosedale Knitwear might face if it hires 6 more inspectors (Option A).
    Answer: First, inspection at the end of production only detects faults; it does not prevent them [k]. Double-checking finished garments would not stop stitching faults occurring during linking, so the 12,000 returns might continue [app]. Rework and scrap costs would persist, squeezing profit margins [an]. Second, hiring 6 inspectors raises costs without fixing processes [k]. The extra $54,000 a year is a permanent wage bill that does not reduce the fault rate itself [app]. Higher overheads reduce funds for training and could force price rises, weakening competitiveness against rival suppliers [an].
    Keywords: $54,000, 12,000, 6 more inspectors, quality assurance, 110 workers, stitching faults
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: End-of-line inspection detects but does not prevent faults; Additional permanent staffing cost | application_max_2: Reference to 12,000 returns / stitching faults in linking; Reference to $54,000 a year / 6 more inspectors | analysis_max_2: Chain from late detection to persistent defects to continuing rework costs and lower profit; Chain from higher overheads to less training funds / price rises to weaker competitiveness

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rosedale Knitwear should introduce quality assurance (Option B)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option B builds quality into every stage, from yarn inspection to pressing, preventing stitching faults rather than catching them afterwards [k]. Retraining all 110 workers costs $80,000 as a one-off but attacks the root cause of the 12,000 returns, protecting the relationship with the retail group taking 60% of output [app]. Fewer returns would cut rework costs and safeguard the $9 million revenue earned last year [an]. However, Option A hires 6 inspectors at $54,000 a year, is simpler to introduce within 5 weeks and would intercept faulty garments before they reach the retailer [k]. But the fault rate itself would persist, and two years of $54,000 totals $108,000 — more than Option B's single $80,000 payment [app]. Only Option B permanently reduces the 60% customer's risk of lost trust and meets its demand for a corrective action plan [an]. Overall, I think Rosedale Knitwear should choose Option B [eval], because prevention aligns with the audit and is cheaper over two years [eval].
    Keywords: quality assurance, $80,000, $54,000, 12,000, 60%, $9 million, 110 workers, 5 weeks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality assurance prevents faults at source at every stage; Quality control detects faults after production / at the end | application_max_2: Reference to Option B: $80,000 one-off / retraining 110 workers / every stage; Reference to Option A: $54,000 a year / 6 inspectors / 5 weeks / 12,000 returns | analysis_max_2: Chain from prevention to fewer returns to protected retailer relationship and revenue; Chain from annual inspection wages to higher 2-year cost ($108,000) vs one-off $80,000 | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($54,000 vs $80,000, 12,000 returns, 60% of output)

--- STEM ---
Bramblewick Honey is a sole trader business owned by Yusuf Rahman on his 22-hectare farm in Country X, bottling honey from 80 hives delivered weekly. He produces 36,000 jars a year sold at $5 each, giving revenue of $180,000, through farmers' markets and 14 local shops. A supermarket chain wants to list his honey in 30 stores but requires batch testing before each delivery, following two complaints of incorrectly blended honey.

Yusuf must decide within 4 weeks. Option A: pay a laboratory to test every delivery batch for $8,000 a year, a quality control approach of checking finished jars. Option B: buy a refractometer and jarring equipment for $6,000 as a one-off and introduce quality assurance checklists for extraction, straining and jarring at each stage.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two costs of poor quality to a business.
    Answer: Poor quality leads to customer complaints and returns, raising costs [1]. It damages reputation, losing customers and sales [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Complaints, returns or rework costs; Damaged reputation / lost customers and sales

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Bramblewick Honey of improving quality before supplying the supermarket chain.
    Answer: First, higher quality would help secure the new contract [k]. Listing in 30 stores would massively expand sales beyond his 14 local shops, multiplying market reach [app]. Second, consistent quality protects reputation [k]. With complaints of incorrectly blended honey already recorded, proving reliable jars to the supermarket would earn repeat, larger orders [app].
    Keywords: 30 stores, 14 local shops, $180,000, 36,000 jars, incorrectly blended honey, supermarket chain
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality helps secure new contracts / sales growth; Quality protects and builds reputation | application_max_2: Reference to 30 supermarket stores vs 14 local shops; Reference to incorrectly blended honey complaints

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Yusuf might face if he relies on laboratory testing of finished batches alone (Option A).
    Answer: First, testing finished batches detects faults but does not prevent them [k]. Blending and straining errors would already have happened by the time the laboratory approves a batch, so jars of incorrectly blended honey could still slip through to the 30 stores [app]. A rejected batch would destroy honey he has already paid to produce and jar [an]. Second, the laboratory fee is a permanent annual cost [k]. Paying $8,000 a year cuts into the $180,000 revenue from jars sold at $5 each, eroding his small margin [app]. Over two years the $16,000 total exceeds the $6,000 cost of Option B's equipment [an].
    Keywords: $8,000, $6,000, 30 stores, $180,000, laboratory, incorrectly blended honey, $5 each
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Finished-product testing detects faults but does not prevent them; Laboratory testing is an ongoing annual cost | application_max_2: Reference to 30 stores / incorrectly blended honey / extraction, straining and jarring stages; Reference to $8,000 a year / $180,000 revenue / $5 per jar | analysis_max_2: Chain from late detection to spoiled produced stock to lost value; Chain from $8,000 fee to lower margin to $16,000 two-year cost exceeding Option B

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Yusuf Rahman should choose quality assurance (Option B)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option B costs $6,000 once and introduces quality assurance checklists at extraction, straining and jarring, preventing faults at source [k]. This directly prevents the incorrectly blended honey problem before jars reach the 30 stores, and the equipment remains his indefinitely with no recurring fee [app]. Over two years Option A costs $16,000 against $6,000 for Option B, leaving more cash for Yusuf to fund growth [an]. However, Option A uses an independent laboratory, which may reassure the supermarket more than self-checks [k]. Independent test certificates give the chain objective proof that each delivery meets its batch requirements, though waiting for approval could delay dispatch to stores [app]. The $8,000 a year fee is also ongoing, and a failed batch wastes both the fee and the production cost of that batch [an]. Overall, I think Yusuf should choose Option B [eval], provided the supermarket accepts documented QA procedures: it prevents faults, saves $10,000 over two years and builds lasting capability [eval].
    Keywords: quality assurance, $6,000, $8,000, $180,000, 30 stores, 14 local shops, extraction, incorrectly blended honey
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality assurance prevents faults at source at each stage; Independent laboratory testing offers objective third-party proof | application_max_2: Reference to Option B: $6,000 one-off / extraction, straining, jarring checklists / refractometer; Reference to Option A: $8,000 a year laboratory / 30 stores / batch testing requirement | analysis_max_2: Chain from QA checklists to prevention to fewer rejected batches and protected sales; Chain from independent testing to supermarket confidence vs recurring $8,000 fee and wasted batches | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($6,000 vs $8,000 a year, 30 stores, $180,000 revenue)

Starling Cosmetics is a private limited company formulating organic skincare creams at its Harborne laboratory facility in Country X. Director Priya Nair must decide within 8 weeks, ahead of the regulator's audit. Option A: add 2 laboratory technicians to test every batch before release, a quality control approach costing $48,000 a year.   Qb [4 marks]

With 320 complaints of skin irritation in 6 months, quality failures would deter new buyers and cut the $6.3 million revenue [app].
    Keywords: 4,000 jars, $90,000, 320, $6.3 million, skin irritation, Starling Cosmetics
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality protects customer safety / prevents recalls; Quality protects reputation and sales | application_max_2: Reference to recall of 4,000 jars / $90,000 recall cost; Reference to 320 complaints / $6.3 million revenue

Preventing faults at source would cut recalls and scrap, saving money and protecting the brand [an]. Second, TQM encourages continuous improvement and employee suggestions [k]. The suggestion scheme empowers 54 workers to report risks and propose safer handling [app]. Engaged workers take greater care, reducing the 320 complaints and satisfying the regulator ahead of its audit [an].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: TQM involves every department / all employees share responsibility for quality; TQM encourages continuous improvement and employee suggestions | application_max_2: Reference to formulation, filling, packaging and warehousing / monthly review meetings; Reference to suggestion scheme / 54 workers / 320 complaints | analysis_max_2: Chain from cross-department targets to early error detection to fewer recalls and lower cost; Chain from worker involvement to greater care to fewer complaints and regulator confidence

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Starling Cosmetics should introduce Total Quality Management (Option B)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option B costs $75,000 to implement, more than the $48,000 a year cost of Option A, but TQM prevents defects across every department rather than only catching them in the laboratory before release [k]. Monthly review meetings and quality targets shared by 54 workers would tackle why the contaminated batch reached 4,000 jars in the first place [app]. However, Option A, quality control, is quicker and cheaper in year one, adding 2 technicians who pass or fail every batch independently [k]. Over two years Option A costs $96,000, exceeding Option B's $75,000, while Option B leaves the business a permanent quality culture [an]. Overall, I think Starling Cosmetics should choose Option B [eval] because TQM removes causes of failure system-wide and costs less over two years [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: TQM prevents defects across all departments / whole business approach; Quality control detects defects before release / at the end of production | application_max_2: Reference to Option B: $75,000 / 54 workers / monthly review meetings / suggestion scheme; Reference to Option A: $48,000 a year / 2 technicians / batch testing / 8-week audit | analysis_max_2: Chain from cross-department prevention to fewer contaminated batches to protected revenue and regulator confidence; Chain from recurring $48,000 lab fee to $96,000 over two years exceeding $75,000 to Option B better value | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($48,000 vs $75,000, 4,000 jars, $6.3 million revenue)

Ferndale Tiles is a private limited company manufacturing ceramic wall and floor tiles at its Kilnvally factory in Country X. A hotel group has offered a $600,000 contract if quality can be proven, after 2 container loads were returned because tiles cracked in transit and 4% of tiles failed finish inspection.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline the difference between quality control and quality assurance.
    Answer: Quality control checks finished products at the end of production and removes faulty items [1]. Quality assurance builds quality into every stage of production so faults are prevented before they occur [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality control = checks finished goods / removes faulty items at the end; Quality assurance = builds quality into every stage / prevents faults

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Ferndale Tiles of obtaining external certification (Option A).
    Answer: First, certification proves quality objectively to buyers [k]. The hotel group offering $600,000 wants proof before placing orders, and an external audit provides independent evidence [app]. Second, certification strengthens reputation and competitiveness [k]. Winning the $600,000 contract would lift revenue above the $4.4 million earned last year and open further large hotel projects [app].
    Keywords: $600,000, $4.4 million, hotel group, 12-month certification, $45,000, 2.2 million tiles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Independent proof/evidence of quality standards; Stronger reputation / competitive advantage | application_max_2: Reference to $600,000 hotel group contract; Reference to $4.4 million revenue / 2.2 million tiles

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Ferndale Tiles of building its own quality assurance system (Option B).

Checking clay preparation, glazing, firing and packing would catch the flaws causing tiles to crack, rather than discovering them after dispatch [app]. Preventing the 4% finish failures would cut returns and rework, raising profit [an]. Second, a documented system makes quality consistent and trainable [k]. Written procedures let all 85 workers follow the same checks every shift, so quality does not depend on memory [app]. Consistent routines lower waste and help Ferndale keep the hotel contract worth $600,000 year after year [an].
    Keywords: quality assurance, $22,000, clay preparation, 4%, $600,000, 85 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quality assurance prevents faults at source at each stage; Documented procedures make quality consistent and trainable | application_max_2: Reference to clay preparation, glazing, firing and packing / 4% finish failures; Reference to 85 workers / $600,000 hotel contract | analysis_max_2: Chain from stage-by-stage checks to fewer cracks/rejects to lower rework cost and higher profit; Chain from written procedures to consistent quality to lower waste and a stable $600,000 contract

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ferndale Tiles should pay for external certification (Option A) rather than build its own quality assurance system (Option B)? Justify your answer.

Building internal capability also raises staff ownership of quality, not just audit paperwork [an]. Overall, I think Ferndale Tiles should choose Option B [eval], because it prevents faults permanently and costs less, unless the hotel group rejects uncertified systems, in which case Option A is a necessary $45,000 investment to secure the $600,000 contract [eval].

It employs 64 workers and produced 24,000 units last year at $250 each, earning $6 million. Bench tests show 7% of units fail, costing $180,000 a year in rework, and warranty claims are rising. A developer considering an order of 8,000 panels wants evidence of a defect-reduction plan.

The owners must decide in 6 weeks before the developer decides on the order. Option A: add tester overtime for $25,000 a year to clear the inspection backlog, keeping the current end-of-line quality control. Option B: adopt Total Quality Management over 12 months, forming cross-functional teams, a suggestion scheme and a supplier quality programme, costing $85,000.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two costs a business might incur to improve quality.
    Answer: Installing inspection and testing equipment is one cost of improving quality [1]. Training workers to check their own work at each stage is another cost [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Testing or inspection equipment / laboratory fees; Training costs for staff on quality checks

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why reducing the failure rate matters to Osprey Electronics.
    Answer: First, a lower failure rate cuts rework costs [k]. Failures already cost $180,000 a year, so fixing processes would release funds for wages and materials [app]. Second, fewer defects build customer trust and win orders [k]. The developer weighing an 8,000-panel order, worth $2 million at $250 each, will favour a supplier with a credible defect-reduction plan [app].
    Keywords: defect-reduction plan, $180,000, 8,000 panels, $250, 7%, Osprey Electronics
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower defects cut rework / waste costs; Lower defects build trust and help win orders | application_max_2: Reference to $180,000 a year rework cost; Reference to developer's 8,000-panel order / $250 per unit

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of adopting Total Quality Management (Option B) at Osprey Electronics.
    Answer: First, TQM prevents defects at source by making everyone responsible for quality [k]. Cross-functional teams covering assembly, testing and dispatch would find why 7% of units fail before panels are built [app]. Eliminating root causes would shrink the $180,000 rework bill and free capacity for new orders [an]. Second, TQM extends into the supply chain [k]. The supplier quality programme audits bought-in components, stopping faulty inputs reaching the test bench [app]. Fewer incoming faults raise first-pass test rates and strengthen the bid for the 8,000-panel order [an].
    Keywords: Total Quality Management, $85,000, cross-functional teams, suggestion scheme, supplier quality programme, 7%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: TQM prevents defects at source / all employees responsible; TQM extends quality into supplier relationships | application_max_2: Reference to cross-functional teams / 7% unit failures / suggestion scheme; Reference to supplier quality programme / 8,000-panel order | analysis_max_2: Chain from root-cause elimination to lower rework bill to freed capacity and orders; Chain from supplier audits to fewer incoming faults to higher first-pass pass rates and contract wins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Osprey Electronics should adopt Total Quality Management (Option B)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option B costs $85,000 over 12 months, more than the $25,000 a year of Option A, but it prevents defects at source through cross-functional teams, a suggestion scheme and supplier checks [k]. The 7% failure rate and $180,000 rework cost both point to process faults, and only TQM removes those causes rather than managing a backlog [app]. Eliminating rework quickly offsets the $85,000 programme and makes the 8,000-panel, $2 million developer order far more secure [an]. However, Option A keeps end-of-line control with overtime at $25,000 a year, cheaper immediately and clears the inspection backlog within weeks [k]. But a year of $25,000 still leaves the 7% fail rate untouched, the $180,000 rework bill standing and customer confidence flat [app]. Clearing a backlog is not the same as curing the process disease, and the developer wants evidence of reduction that inspection alone does not provide [an]. Overall, I think Osprey Electronics should adopt Option B [eval], with Option A only as a temporary supplement; the $85,000 buys prevention, the $2 million contract and falling rework costs [eval].
    Keywords: Total Quality Management, $85,000, $25,000, 7%, $180,000, 8,000 panels, $6 million, suggestion scheme
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: TQM = prevention across the whole business incl. suppliers; Quality control / inspection = detects faults at the end / short-run relief | application_max_2: Reference to Option B: $85,000 / 12 months / cross-functional teams / supplier quality programme; Reference to Option A: $25,000 a year / tester overtime / inspection backlog / 7% failures | analysis_max_2: Chain from root-cause prevention to lower rework to protected developer contract ($2 million); Chain from inspection-only to unchanged 7% failure and $180,000 rework to weak customer confidence | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($25,000 vs $85,000, 7% failures, $180,000 rework, 8,000 panels)

--- STEM ---
Thornhill Vineyards is a family-owned wine estate at its Kilmara site in Country X, producing 140,000 bottles a year from 60 hectares of vines and employing 30 staff. Wines sell at $14 a bottle, earning revenue of $1.96 million. Inconsistent fermentation means 6% of bottles are rejected at bottling, and two vintages scored poorly with critics. A supermarket chain has proposed an own-label listing worth $800,000 a year, conditional on consistent quality and an annual external audit.

The family must decide in 9 weeks. Option A: hire a full-time quality manager for $45,000 a year to run end-of-line quality control at bottling. Option B: implement winery-wide quality assurance with TQM principles, covering vine-to-bottle procedures, staff training and lab checks at each stage, costing $70,000 to set up.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'repeat business'.
    Answer: Repeat business is when customers return to buy from the same business again, usually driven by satisfaction with the quality and service received [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Customers return to buy from the same business again; Driven by satisfaction with quality and service

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why consistent quality is important for the supermarket listing at Thornhill Vineyards.
    Answer: First, the supermarket listing would provide reliable, high-volume sales [k]. It is worth $800,000 a year, nearly a 41% uplift on the $1.96 million revenue, and guarantees a route to market for part of the 140,000 bottles [app]. Second, consistent quality protects reputation [k]. Two poorly scored vintages and a 6% rejection rate show how quickly standards can slip, risking withdrawal of the listing [app].
    Keywords: $800,000, supermarket chain, 6%, $1.96 million, 140,000 bottles, Thornhill Vineyards
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Consistent quality secures large, stable sales contracts; Consistent quality protects reputation and avoids losing listings | application_max_2: Reference to $800,000 a year own-label listing / $1.96 million revenue; Reference to 6% rejected at bottling / poorly scored vintages

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of relying on end-of-line quality control at bottling only (Option A).
    Answer: First, bottling-stage checks detect faults after they have been created [k]. Fermentation and vineyard problems arise months earlier, so rejecting faulty bottles at the end still wastes wine, glass and labour [app]. 6% of 140,000 bottles is 8,400 bottles lost every year [an]. Second, a single quality manager is a single point of failure [k]. One hire cannot continuously cover vineyard, cellar and bottling, so errors outside those hours go unchecked [app]. Poor processes persist, critic scores stay low and the supermarket may cancel the $800,000 own-label deal [an].
    Keywords: $45,000, 6%, 140,000 bottles, end-of-line quality control, $800,000, fermentation
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: End-of-line control detects faults after they occur / after value added; Reliance on one manager creates a single point of failure / limited coverage | application_max_2: Reference to fermentation / vine-to-bottle stages / 6% rejection / 140,000 bottles; Reference to $800,000 own-label listing / critics / end-of-line quality control | analysis_max_2: Chain from late rejection to 8,400 wasted bottles a year to lost revenue and profit; Chain from incomplete coverage to unchecked faults to poor critic scores and lost listing

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Thornhill Vineyards should implement quality assurance and Total Quality Management (Option B)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option B costs $70,000 once and rebuilds quality from vine to bottle, with procedures, staff training and lab checks at each stage, so fermentation faults are caught before bottling [k]. This directly targets the 6% rejection rate, 8,400 bottles a year, and gives the supermarket an audit-ready record for the $800,000 own-label listing [app]. Preventing rejects also saves wine, bottles and labour, protecting the $1.96 million revenue [an]. However, Option A hires a quality manager for $45,000 a year, $90,000 over two years, to run end-of-line checks at bottling and is simple to start within 9 weeks [k]. But it only filters faulty bottles after months of wasted work, leaves fermentation uncontrolled and does nothing for critic confidence [app]. The listing depends on an annual external audit, which a bottling-only filter cannot support [an]. Overall, I think Thornhill Vineyards should choose Option B [eval] because it removes the causes of rejects, satisfies the audit and costs less than two years of Option A [eval].
    Keywords: quality assurance, TQM principles, $70,000, $45,000, 6%, $800,000, 140,000 bottles, fermentation
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option B = quality assurance / TQM across the whole process; Option A = end-of-line quality control / filtering at bottling | application_max_2: Reference to Option B: $70,000 / vine-to-bottle / staff training / lab checks; Reference to Option A: $45,000 a year / end-of-line checks / 9 weeks / critic scores | analysis_max_2: Chain from vine-to-bottle prevention to fewer rejects (8,400 bottles) to protected $1.96 million revenue and listing; Chain from bottling-only filter to uncontrolled fermentation to failed annual audit and jeopardised $800,000 deal | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($70,000 vs $45,000 a year, 6% rejection, $800,000 listing)

--- STEM ---
Redbank Brickworks Ltd has manufactured clay bricks for housebuilders in Country X for 9 years. It currently operates one kiln on a 3-hectare site 38 km from its clay quarry, and pays $420,000 each year in fuel and road transport for 17,000 tonnes of clay. Sales reached $2.6 million last year across 210 customers, but rising diesel prices are squeezing margins.

The quarry owner offered the company a 5-hectare plot beside the quarry at a subsidised rent of $30,000 a year, 25% below the current site rent. However, the quarry plot is 60 km from the main motorway, and wages there would be $1,700 a month compared with $2,100 at the current site. The board must decide whether to relocate the kiln beside the quarry or remain at the current site.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'raw materials'.
    Answer: Raw materials are the basic inputs a business buys in and uses in the production of its goods or services, for example clay used to make bricks [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: raw materials are the basic inputs used in production; they are transformed into finished goods or services

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Redbank Brickworks might relocate the kiln beside the quarry.
    Answer: Reason 1: Locating beside the quarry removes the 38 km haulage of 17,000 tonnes of clay each year, cutting the $420,000 fuel and road transport bill [k], which matters because diesel prices are rising and squeezing margins [app]. Reason 2: The quarry plot costs just $30,000 a year in rent, 25% below the current site, and wages there are $1,700 a month against $2,100 at the current site [k], saving money every month the kiln operates [app].
    Keywords: 17,000, $420,000, 38 km, $30,000, $1,700, $2,100, clay quarry
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: removes or reduces transport costs of raw materials; lower rent or lower wages near the supplier | application_max_2: $420,000 transport per year / 17,000 tonnes of clay / 38 km; $30,000 rent, 25% below current site / $1,700 vs $2,100 wages

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Redbank Brickworks could face if it relocates beside the quarry.
    Answer: Problem 1: The quarry plot is 60 km from the main motorway [k], so delivering finished bricks to 210 customers may take longer and cost more in fuel than today [app], eating into the $30,000 rent saving and squeezing the already-thin margins [an]. Problem 2: Moving an operating kiln means a costly shutdown and rebuild [k], during which Redbank could fail to deliver bricks to its 210 customers for weeks [app], risking lost orders and damage to customer relationships built over 9 years [an].
    Keywords: 60 km, 210 customers, $30,000, 9 years, clay quarry, $420,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: longer delivery distances to customers from the remote site; shutdown and relocation costs / disruption to production | application_max_2: 60 km from the main motorway / 210 customers; kiln move / 9 years of customer relationships | analysis_max_2: higher transport costs erode the $30,000 rent saving and margins; missed deliveries risk lost orders and reputational damage

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redbank Brickworks should relocate the kiln beside the quarry? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Relocating beside the quarry would eliminate 38 km of clay haulage per trip and cut the $420,000 annual transport bill on 17,000 tonnes of clay [k], while the subsidised $30,000 rent and $1,700 monthly wages add further savings [app]. However, staying put keeps the kiln close to the motorway and to the 210 customers, protecting delivery times [k], and it avoids the 60 km stretch to the motorway absorbing the $30,000 rent saving [app]. Relocation could strengthen competitiveness as diesel prices rise [an], but a kiln rebuild would halt production in the short term [an]. On balance, Redbank should relocate, because the $420,000 yearly transport saving outweighs the one-off move costs and the motorway distance [eval]; it should plan the move in stages to guarantee customer deliveries throughout [eval].
    Keywords: $420,000, 17,000, 38 km, $30,000, $1,700, 210 customers, 60 km, 9 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relocation removes transport and lowers rent and wages; staying preserves customer proximity and avoids disruption | application_max_2: $420,000 transport, 17,000 tonnes of clay, 38 km / $30,000 rent, $1,700 wages; 210 customers, 60 km from the motorway | analysis_max_2: savings improve competitiveness as diesel prices rise; rebuild halts production and threatens customer deliveries | evaluation_max_2: weighs $420,000 yearly transport saving against one-off move costs and motorway risk; justified recommendation with a staged move to protect deliveries

--- STEM ---
Harbor & Finch Accountants is a partnership of 14 accountants serving 260 small business clients in Country X. It is deciding between renewing the lease on its city-centre office at $95,000 a year and moving to a business park on the edge of town at $58,000 a year. Walk-in enquiries generated 60 new clients last year, and the city-centre office is a 5-minute walk from the main bank branch and clients’ lawyers.

The business park offers free parking, faster internet and 40% lower rent, but is 12 km from the financial district. Staff travel would rise by 25 minutes each way, and the partners must choose where to base the firm from next April. The decision will affect walk-in trade, staff morale and overheads for years.

    Question: Define 'accessibility'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: how easily a location can be reached by customers/staff/suppliers; includes road access, parking and transport links

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Harbor & Finch might move to the business park.
    Answer: Reason 1: Moving would cut rent from $95,000 to $58,000 a year, a saving of $37,000 at 40% lower rent [k], freeing cash to invest in faster internet and better client software [app]. Reason 2: The business park offers free parking and faster internet [k], which suits 260 small business clients who drive to appointments instead of using the congested city centre [app].
    Keywords: $95,000, $58,000, 40% lower rent, free parking, 260 small business clients, business park
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower rent reduces fixed costs; free parking / faster internet improves client and staff access | application_max_2: $95,000 to $58,000 saving / 40% lower rent; free parking and faster internet / 260 small business clients

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Harbor & Finch could face if it moves to the business park.
    Answer: Problem 1: The city-centre office generated 60 walk-in clients last year [k]; moving 12 km away to the edge of town could lose much of this spontaneous trade [app], reducing revenue from new client acquisition in the first year after the move [an]. Problem 2: Staff face 25 minutes extra travel each way [k], which may lower morale and make recruiting qualified accountants harder [app], threatening the service quality that 260 small business clients expect from 14 partners [an].
    Keywords: 60, 12 km, 25 minutes, 260 small business clients, edge of town, $95,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: loss of walk-in/passing trade away from the city centre; longer commute reduces morale and recruitment appeal | application_max_2: 60 walk-in clients / 12 km to the edge of town; 25 minutes extra travel each way / 260 small business clients / 14 partners | analysis_max_2: lost walk-in trade cuts new client revenue; longer journeys weaken recruitment and client service quality

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harbor & Finch should move to the business park? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Moving saves $37,000 a year, 40% off the $95,000 rent, and brings free parking and faster internet for the 260 small business clients who visit in person [k], improving cash flow and productivity after the move [app]. However, it risks losing the 60 walk-in clients generated last year, a key source of new business from the city centre [k], and staff face 25 minutes of extra travel each way, which may hurt morale and recruitment [app]. Keeping the city-centre office preserves walk-in trade and easy access to the banks and lawyers that 260 small business clients use [an], while the move could lift margins if even half the walk-in work were replaced [an]. On balance, the partnership should move to the business park, because the $37,000 annual saving outweighs the walk-in risk if local marketing replaces it [eval]; it should keep a small city-centre meeting room for client visits [eval].
    Keywords: $95,000, $58,000, 40% lower rent, 60, 260 small business clients, 25 minutes, free parking, business park
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: move cuts fixed costs and adds parking and faster internet; staying preserves walk-in trade and central access | application_max_2: $95,000 rent / 40% lower / free parking and faster internet / 260 small business clients; 60 walk-in clients last year / 25 minutes extra travel | analysis_max_2: city centre preserves walk-in trade and bank/lawyer access; move lifts margins if walk-in work is replaced | evaluation_max_2: weighs $37,000 yearly saving against 60 lost walk-in clients; justified recommendation to move, with conditions to replace walk-in trade

--- STEM ---
Lumen & Co Fashion runs 6 stores in Country X and is choosing the site for a new flagship. Retail rents in the capital rose 6% last year. Site A is on the busy high street with footfall of 9,500 people a day, but rent is $14,000 a month and just 45 parking spaces are nearby. Site B is an out-of-town retail park unit with rent of $8,500 a month, 320 free parking spaces and a cinema next door, but footfall is only 2,200 a day.

Both options would need $180,000 of fit-out costs. Site A sits two doors from a direct competitor, while Site B has none nearby. The board must decide where to open the new flagship in March, balancing footfall, rent, parking and competition carefully.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'footfall'.
    Answer: Footfall is the number of people passing through or visiting a retail location during a given period, indicating the potential customer traffic for a shop [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: number of people passing through/visiting a location; indicates potential customer traffic for a shop

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Site A might suit the new flagship.
    Answer: Reason 1: Site A offers footfall of 9,500 people a day against just 2,200 at Site B [k], giving the flagship far more natural exposure to fashion shoppers at no extra marketing cost [app]. Reason 2: Site A sits two doors from a direct competitor [k], so opening there lets Lumen defend its share of high street shoppers in the capital and respond to rival promotions [app].
    Keywords: 9,500, 2,200, Site A, two doors, direct competitor, high street, 6 stores
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high footfall brings more potential customers; proximity to competitor supports defensive positioning | application_max_2: 9,500 people a day vs 2,200 at Site B; two doors from a direct competitor / high street / capital

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of opening at Site A.
    Answer: Drawback 1: Site A's rent of $14,000 a month exceeds Site B's $8,500 by $5,500 [k], adding $66,000 a year of extra fixed costs before the first garment is sold [app], which raises the sales the flagship needs to break even on its $180,000 fit-out [an]. Drawback 2: With only 45 parking spaces nearby, car-borne shoppers may choose Site B's 320 free spaces instead [k], diverting customers to the retail park with the cinema next door [app], weakening the flagship's early sales in March [an].
    Keywords: $14,000, $8,500, 45 parking spaces, 320 free parking spaces, $180,000, 9,500, March
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher rent raises fixed costs and break-even point; limited parking deters car-borne customers | application_max_2: $14,000 vs $8,500, i.e. $5,500 more per month / $66,000 a year; 45 parking spaces vs 320 at Site B / cinema next door / $180,000 fit-out | analysis_max_2: higher break-even sales needed to cover the fit-out; lost car-borne customers weaken early sales in March

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Lumen & Co Fashion should open the flagship at Site A? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Site A delivers footfall of 9,500 people a day, more than four times Site B's 2,200 [k], which should drive far stronger walk-in sales for a fashion flagship investing $180,000 in fit-out [app]. However, Site A costs $14,000 a month in rent, $66,000 a year more than Site B's $8,500, and only 45 parking spaces may frustrate car-borne shoppers [k], who could defect to Site B's 320 free spaces and cinema destination [app]. Site A's two-door proximity to a direct competitor risks constant price comparison and discounting [an], while Site B offers lower overheads and exclusive trade nearby but far fewer passing shoppers [an]. On balance, Lumen should open at Site A, because footfall is the strongest driver of fashion retail revenue and outweighs the rent gap if the fit-out attracts attention [eval]; it should negotiate a rent reduction and arrange evening parking for shoppers [eval].
    Keywords: 9,500, 2,200, $14,000, $8,500, 45 parking spaces, 320 free parking spaces, $180,000, two doors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: footfall advantage of Site A; rent and parking disadvantages of Site A | application_max_2: 9,500 vs 2,200 footfall / $180,000 fit-out; $14,000 vs $8,500 rent / 45 vs 320 parking spaces / two doors from a direct competitor / cinema next door | analysis_max_2: competitor proximity forces price comparison and discounting; Site B offers lower overheads but far less passing trade | evaluation_max_2: weighs 9,500 daily footfall against $66,000 extra yearly rent and 45 parking spaces; justified recommendation for Site A conditional on rent negotiation and parking solutions

Goldengrain Bakery Ltd operates a large bakery in a residential area of Country X, employing 85 workers and producing 11,000 loaves a day for 140 local shops. Night shifts run from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Neighbours complained about overnight noise from the ovens and delivery lorries. The local council has warned it will enforce noise limits of 45 decibels at the site boundary after 9 p.m. unless the company invests in acoustic insulation costing $120,000 or relocates.

The current site has good road access and cheap power at $0.09 per kWh. The alternative site on the industrial estate costs $35,000 a year more in rent but already meets the noise rules. The board must decide between upgrading the current site and moving to the estate.

    Question: Define 'planning permission'.
