  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Goldengrain Bakery might choose acoustic insulation over relocation.
    Answer: Reason 1: Acoustic insulation costs $120,000 once, far less than buying and fitting out a new bakery [k], and it keeps the current site's cheap power at $0.09 per kWh and its established position near 140 local shops [app]. Reason 2: Upgrading avoids any shutdown of the 11,000 loaves a day output [k], so customer deliveries to 140 local shops continue uninterrupted overnight [app].
    Keywords: $120,000, $0.09, 140 local shops, 11,000, acoustic insulation, industrial estate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: one-off upgrade costs less than relocation; avoids shutdown and preserves current site advantages | application_max_2: $120,000 acoustic insulation / $0.09 per kWh power; 11,000 loaves a day / 140 local shops / overnight delivery

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Goldengrain Bakery could face if it relocates to the industrial estate.
    Answer: Problem 1: The estate site costs $35,000 a year more in rent [k], which squeezes the margin on every one of the 11,000 loaves produced daily [app], reducing cash available to replace ovens and maintain quality standards [an]. Problem 2: Relocating 85 workers and the delivery fleet would interrupt nightly production [k], so orders may be missed for weeks while the new site is commissioned [app], risking lost contracts with the 140 local shops [an].
    Keywords: $35,000, 11,000, 85 workers, 140 local shops, 9 p.m., industrial estate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher rent adds to annual fixed costs; relocation disrupts production and distribution | application_max_2: $35,000 a year more in rent / 11,000 loaves a day; 85 workers / 140 local shops / nightly production | analysis_max_2: lower margins reduce cash for reinvestment; missed deliveries risk losing contracts with the 140 local shops

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Goldengrain Bakery should install acoustic insulation rather than relocate? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Acoustic insulation at $120,000 is a one-off cost that keeps 11,000 loaves a day flowing overnight [k], protecting the $0.09 per kWh power advantage and the location near 140 local shops [app]. However, the council's 45 decibels limit may tighten further, and insulation may not solve noise from 10 p.m. delivery lorries [k], exposing the bakery to enforcement action if limits are breached [app]. Relocating to the industrial estate guarantees legal compliance and removes neighbour complaints permanently [an], but costs $35,000 a year extra for years and risks lost customers during the move [an]. On balance, Goldengrain should install the insulation first, since $120,000 once breaks even against $35,000 of extra annual rent in about 3.4 years [eval]; moving remains sensible only if noise still exceeds 45 decibels after the upgrade [eval].
    Keywords: $120,000, 45 decibels, 11,000, $0.09, $35,000, 140 local shops, 10 p.m., industrial estate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: insulation is a one-off cost preserving the site; moving guarantees compliance but adds rent and disruption | application_max_2: $120,000 insulation / $0.09 per kWh / 140 local shops / 11,000 loaves; 45 decibels limit / 10 p.m. delivery lorries / $35,000 extra rent | analysis_max_2: moving guarantees compliance but adds $35,000 yearly and disruption; enforcement risk remains if noise persists after insulation | evaluation_max_2: weighs $120,000 one-off vs $35,000 a year (break-even ~3.4 years); justified recommendation to insulate first, relocate only if limits still breached

--- STEM ---
VoltEdge Assembly Ltd is a private limited company in Country X assembling 140,000 phone chargers a year for domestic retailers, employing 230 workers with average wages of $520 a month. A competitor relocated to Country Z last year and cut labour costs by 55%, undercutting VoltEdge on price and winning 12 new retail contracts. VoltEdge supplies chargers within 48 hours of order.

VoltEdge is now considering moving production to Country Z, where wages average $230 a month, but the new legal environment requires extra safety inspections costing $90,000 a year, and import tariffs of 8% would apply to chargers brought back into Country X. Shelf space with the retailers would take 6 months to win back. The chief executive must recommend staying put or relocating.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'wage costs'.
    Answer: Wage costs are the total payments a business makes to its workforce in return for their labour, including hourly wages, salaries, overtime and bonuses [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: total payments made to the workforce; includes wages, salaries and overtime

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why VoltEdge might relocate production to Country Z.
    Answer: Reason 1: Wages average $230 a month in Country Z compared with $520 in Country X [k], cutting the monthly wage bill across 230 workers by about $66,700 [app]. Reason 2: The competitor that moved cut labour costs by 55% [k], so relocating would help VoltEdge match rival prices and win back the 12 retail contracts lost to the competition [app].
    Keywords: $230, $520, 230 workers, 55%, Country Z, 12 new retail contracts, 140,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower wage costs reduce expenses; competitor relocation creates pressure to match prices | application_max_2: $230 vs $520 wages / 230 workers / about $66,700 a month; competitor cut labour costs by 55% / 12 retail contracts

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems VoltEdge could face if it relocates to Country Z.
    Answer: Problem 1: Chargers brought back into Country X would face 8% import tariffs [k], which would raise the landed cost of the 140,000 chargers sold to domestic retailers [app], potentially erasing much of the monthly wage saving of about $66,700 [an]. Problem 2: The new legal environment demands safety inspections costing $90,000 a year [k], adding compliance work and management time beyond the current Country X regime [app], which could delay production ramp-up and weaken VoltEdge's 48-hour delivery promise in the first year [an].
    Keywords: 8%, 140,000, $90,000, Country Z, 48 hours, legal environment, 230 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: import tariffs raise landed cost of goods; new legal environment adds inspection and compliance costs | application_max_2: 8% import tariffs / 140,000 chargers a year; $90,000 a year inspections / 48-hour delivery promise | analysis_max_2: tariffs could wipe out the wage saving on domestic sales; compliance delays weaken service and ramp-up

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think VoltEdge should relocate production to Country Z? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Relocating would cut wages from $520 to $230 a month, saving about $66,700 every month across 230 workers [k], and would help VoltEdge match the competitor that cut labour costs by 55% to win back 12 new retail contracts [app]. However, 8% import tariffs would apply to chargers brought back into Country X [k], adding duty on the 140,000 units sold to domestic retailers each year [app]. The wage saving of roughly $800,400 a year dwarfs the $90,000 inspection cost, but tariffs could still squeeze margins if buyers resist higher prices [an], while relocating risks disrupting the 48-hour delivery that won VoltEdge its contracts [an]. On balance, VoltEdge should relocate gradually, moving half of production first to test tariff and compliance costs [eval]; if Country X sales hold up, it can shift fully and capture the savings [eval].
    Keywords: $520, $230, 55%, 8%, 140,000, $90,000, Country Z, 48 hours
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: wage saving is the main benefit of relocating; tariffs and inspections are the main costs of relocating | application_max_2: $230 vs $520, about $66,700 a month / 230 workers / 55% cut by competitor / 12 new retail contracts; 8% tariffs / 140,000 chargers / $90,000 inspections / 48-hour delivery | analysis_max_2: $800,400 yearly wage saving dwarfs $90,000 inspection cost; tariffs may squeeze margins and disrupt 48-hour deliveries | evaluation_max_2: weighs $66,700 monthly saving and 55% competitor advantage against 8% tariffs and $90,000 inspections; justified recommendation to relocate gradually with a half-first trial

--- STEM ---
Crumb & Co Bakehouse supplies 180 supermarket stores in Country X, selling around 24 million rolls a year. Ahead of the December peak, the company must decide whether to build up an inventory of 400,000 extra frozen rolls in October, costing $0.06 per roll per month to store, or rely on just-in-time deliveries from daily production, which risks empty shelves if demand spikes. Last year, empty shelves cost an estimated $95,000 of lost sales.

Storage at its chilled warehouse costs $6,800 a month and capacity is limited to 500,000 rolls. The bakery currently runs 2 production lines and could increase output by 30% in November. The owner wants to avoid both stockouts during the peak and excess storage costs, and must set the festive plan soon.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'inventory'.
    Answer: Inventory is the stock of goods and materials a business holds to support production or sale, including raw materials, work in progress and finished goods [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: stock of goods and materials held by a business; includes raw materials, work in progress and finished goods

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Crumb & Co might build a festive inventory of 400,000 rolls.
    Answer: Reason 1: Building an inventory of 400,000 extra rolls meets the sudden surge in December demand across 180 supermarket stores [k], avoiding stockouts that cost an estimated $95,000 of lost sales last year [app]. Reason 2: Holding finished rolls in chilled storage smooths production across the 2 lines [k], letting the bakery run steadily instead of chasing just-in-time orders daily at peak time [app].
    Keywords: 400,000, 180 supermarket stores, $95,000, 2 production lines, just-in-time, 24 million rolls, 500,000 rolls
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: inventories meet sudden or seasonal demand spikes; finished goods stock smooths production and avoids stoppages | application_max_2: 400,000 extra rolls / 180 supermarket stores / $95,000 lost sales; 2 production lines / December peak / just-in-time deliveries

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs of holding the extra festive inventory.
    Answer: Problem 1: Chilled storage costs $6,800 a month, and holding 400,000 rolls adds $0.06 per roll per month, about $24,000 a month [k], so the pre-Christmas build could add more than $30,000 of storage costs before January [app], cutting the margin on festive sales [an]. Problem 2: Storage capacity is limited to 500,000 rolls and unsold rolls tie up cash [k], so if December demand disappoints, rolls may be left in chilled storage needing to be sold later at a discount [app], reducing cash available for flour and January wages [an].
    Keywords: $0.06, $6,800, 400,000, 500,000 rolls, $95,000, 180 supermarket stores
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: storage and handling costs of holding inventories; cash tied up / risk of unsold stock needing discounting | application_max_2: $6,800 a month / $0.06 per roll per month / about $24,000 a month; capacity 500,000 rolls / 400,000 extra rolls | analysis_max_2: storage costs above $30,000 erode festive margins; unsold rolls tie up cash needed for January expenses

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Crumb & Co should build the festive inventory rather than rely on just-in-time deliveries? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Building the 400,000-roll inventory protects the 180 stores from December stockouts [k], and last year empty shelves cost $95,000 of lost sales, far above the roughly $30,000 storage cost for the period [app]. However, relying on just-in-time production of around 24 million rolls a year would keep storage costs near zero and make the bakery leaner [k], leaving only the chilled warehouse's $6,800 a month within its 500,000-roll capacity [app]. A partial build covering the peak, combined with 30% higher output from the 2 lines in November, meets surge demand and limits excess stock [an], but if stores over-order, chilled capacity is wasted and cash is tied up in unsold rolls [an]. On balance, Crumb & Co should build the festive inventory, because the $95,000 loss risk outweighs about $30,000 of storage and capacity can absorb the surge [eval]; it should scale the order to each store's December forecast [eval].
    Keywords: 400,000, $95,000, $6,800, 500,000 rolls, 180 supermarket stores, 24 million rolls, just-in-time, $0.06
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: inventory guards against stockouts during demand spikes; just-in-time keeps inventory costs minimal | application_max_2: 400,000-roll inventory / $95,000 lost sales / 180 stores; just-in-time / 24 million rolls a year / $6,800 a month / 500,000-roll capacity | analysis_max_2: partial build with 30% extra November output meets the surge efficiently; over-ordering wastes chilled capacity and ties up cash | evaluation_max_2: weighs $95,000 stockout risk against about $30,000 storage cost and 500,000-roll capacity; justified recommendation to build stock scaled to store-level forecasts

--- STEM ---
Stonebridge Builders Merchants holds inventories of cement, blocks and timber for 320 trade customers in Country X. Its supplier offered an 8% discount on orders above 900 tonnes of cement, but the company currently stores only 260 tonnes in a warehouse rented at $2,400 a month. Extra security and insurance for the larger stock would cost $1,150 a month. The merchant also holds $210,000 of goods insured under one policy.

Cement older than 90 days hardens and must be written off, and the business turns over around 300 tonnes each month. Cash tied up in the bigger inventory would be $74,000, delaying a planned forklift replacement budgeted at $28,000. The owner must decide whether to accept the supplier’s discount or keep smaller, more frequent orders.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'obsolescence'.
    Answer: Obsolescence is the process by which items lose usefulness or value because they become outdated or spoiled, for example cement hardening if stored too long [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: items lose usefulness/value over time; caused by becoming outdated or spoiled

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Stonebridge might accept the 8% bulk-buy discount.
    Answer: Reason 1: An 8% discount on 900 tonnes lowers the price of the merchant's key input for its 320 trade customers [k], improving margins or allowing it to pass savings on as sharper trade prices [app]. Reason 2: Buying in bulk reduces the frequency of deliveries and admin per tonne [k], freeing staff to serve trade counter customers during busy mornings [app].
    Keywords: 8%, 900 tonnes, 320 trade customers, 260 tonnes, cement, $2,400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bulk-buying lowers average purchase cost; fewer, larger deliveries reduce admin and handling | application_max_2: 8% discount on 900 tonnes / 320 trade customers; 260 tonnes currently stored / cement trade

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs of holding 900 tonnes of cement at Stonebridge.
    Answer: Problem 1: Extra security and insurance cost $1,150 a month on top of $2,400 a month of warehouse rent [k], so carrying the larger stock adds $3,550 a month of holding costs [app], which erodes the 8% discount if cement turns over slowly [an]. Problem 2: Cement older than 90 days hardens and must be written off [k], so stock bought in bulk could spoil before the merchant sells through its usual 300 tonnes a month [app], turning part of the $74,000 cash investment into waste [an].
    Keywords: $1,150, $2,400, 900 tonnes, 90 days, 300 tonnes, $74,000, 8%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: storage, security and insurance costs rise with stock size; perishable inventories can spoil and be written off | application_max_2: $1,150 extra security and insurance / $2,400 rent / $3,550 total; cement older than 90 days / 300 tonnes each month / $74,000 cash tied up | analysis_max_2: holding costs erode the 8% discount if turnover slows; spoiled cement wastes the $74,000 investment

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Stonebridge should accept the 8% bulk-buy discount? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the discount on 900 tonnes could cut the cost of cement for 320 trade customers and lift margins [k], and with turnover of around 300 tonnes each month, the store could clear 90 days' worth of stock if sales hold up [app]. However, extra security and insurance of $1,150 a month plus $2,400 rent make $3,550 a month of carrying costs [k], and cement older than 90 days hardens and must be written off [app]. The discount only pays if sales stay near 300 tonnes a month and stock moves within 90 days [an], but a slow quarter would leave Stonebridge paying $3,550 monthly for unsellable cement, while $74,000 of cash tied up would delay the $28,000 forklift replacement [an]. On balance, Stonebridge should accept the discount only with phased deliveries [eval]; if the supplier cannot split the order, it should keep smaller orders rather than risk spoilage [eval].
    Keywords: 8%, 900 tonnes, 300 tonnes, 90 days, $74,000, $28,000, $1,150, 320 trade customers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bulk discount improves margin if turnover is steady; holding costs and spoilage risk can wipe out the saving | application_max_2: 8% discount on 900 tonnes / 320 trade customers / 300 tonnes a month / 90 days; $1,150 security and insurance + $2,400 rent = $3,550 a month / $74,000 cash tied up / $28,000 forklift | analysis_max_2: discount viable only if sales hold near 300 tonnes a month and stock moves within 90 days; slow quarter leaves unsellable cement and $3,550 monthly costs | evaluation_max_2: weighs 8% discount and margin gain against $3,550 monthly carrying costs and 90-day spoilage risk; justified recommendation for phased deliveries or smaller orders

--- STEM ---
Delta Foods Cannery exports canned tomatoes from Country X to 5 countries inside the Arca trade bloc, paying tariffs of 12% on each shipment. Sales reached $3.4 million last year, but growth has stalled as overseas buyers seek cheaper suppliers. Last year tariffs cost the business $408,000, and tomato purchases alone cost $1.3 million. The board is considering building a $2.1 million canning plant inside the bloc, which would eliminate tariffs and cut delivery times from 21 days to 4 days.

The alternative is expanding the existing Country X factory for $700,000 and continuing to pay tariffs on every shipment. Wages inside the bloc are 30% higher than in Country X. The directors must decide which plan to fund at next month’s board meeting.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'trade bloc'.
    Answer: A trade bloc is a group of countries that agree to reduce or remove tariffs and trade barriers between member countries to encourage trade between them [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: group of countries with reduced or removed trade barriers; created to encourage trade between members

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Delta Foods might build the plant inside the trade bloc.
    Answer: Reason 1: Building inside the bloc eliminates the 12% tariff on each of its 5 bloc-country markets [k], saving the $408,000 a year paid in duties last year [app]. Reason 2: Delivery times would fall from 21 days to 4 days [k], giving overseas buyers fresher canned tomatoes and more reliable supply than Country X competitors can offer [app].
    Keywords: 12%, $408,000, 21 days to 4 days, trade bloc, $3.4 million, 5 countries
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: eliminates tariffs on exports to member countries; shorter delivery times improve reliability and freshness | application_max_2: 12% tariff / $408,000 last year / 5 countries; 21 days to 4 days delivery / bloc-country markets

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of the bloc plant compared with the domestic expansion.
    Answer: Problem 1: The $2.1 million bloc plant costs $1.4 million more than the $700,000 domestic expansion [k], tying up far more capital before the first tariff-free can is exported [app], which raises financial risk if bloc growth does not resume [an]. Problem 2: Wages inside the bloc run 30% higher than in Country X [k], permanently raising the cost of every can produced for the 5 bloc markets [app], which erodes the $408,000 of tariff savings if buyers resist higher prices [an].
    Keywords: $2.1 million, $700,000, 30% higher, $408,000, 5 countries, Country X
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: much higher capital cost vs domestic expansion; higher wage costs inside the bloc | application_max_2: $2.1 million vs $700,000, i.e. $1.4 million more; 30% higher wages / 5 bloc markets / $408,000 tariff saving | analysis_max_2: extra capital raises financial risk if growth stays stalled; higher wages erode the $408,000 tariff saving

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Delta Foods should build the plant inside the trade bloc? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The bloc plant would remove the 12% tariffs that cost $408,000 last year and cut delivery from 21 days to 4 days across the 5 bloc markets [k], helping the stalled $3.4 million export business grow again [app]. However, it costs $2.1 million against $700,000 for domestic expansion, a difference of $1.4 million before the first can is exported [k], and 30% higher wages inside the bloc permanently raise running costs [app]. If Delta can pass on savings, the plant could pay back within several years [an], but if growth stays stalled, the larger debt and wage bill could outweigh the saving [an]. On balance, Delta should build the bloc plant, provided projected bloc sales rise above $3.4 million within two years [eval]; if orders do not materialise, the cheaper domestic expansion is the safer choice [eval].
    Keywords: 12%, $408,000, $2.1 million, $700,000, 30% higher, $3.4 million, 21 days to 4 days, 5 countries
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bloc plant removes tariffs and speeds delivery; domestic expansion costs far less capital | application_max_2: 12% tariffs / $408,000 last year / 21 days to 4 days / 5 bloc markets; $2.1 million vs $700,000 / 30% higher wages / $3.4 million sales | analysis_max_2: payback possible if savings are passed on and sales recover; stalled growth leaves larger debt and wage bill unaffordable | evaluation_max_2: weighs $408,000 tariff saving and faster delivery against $1.4 million extra capital and 30% higher wages; justified recommendation conditional on sales exceeding $3.4 million within two years

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Silkharbour might relocate one factory to Country Y.
    Answer: Reason 1: The currency in Country Y is 20% weaker [k], which would make shirts made there cheaper for Asia and Europe buyers and help restore margins lost when the dollar strengthened by 14% [app]. Reason 2: Wages are 35% lower in Country Y [k], significantly cutting labour cost on the relocated factory's share of the 420,000 shirts produced each year [app].
    Keywords: 20% weaker, 35% lower, 14%, 420,000, Country Y, Asia and Europe, 70%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: weaker foreign currency lowers export prices; lower wages reduce production costs | application_max_2: 20% weaker currency / 14% dollar strengthening / margins 11% to 6%; 35% lower wages / 420,000 shirts a year / Asia and Europe buyers

  Qc [6 marks]

Problem 2: The dollar's 14% strengthening may reverse [k], so relocating could prove premature if the currency falls back and export competitiveness returns [app], leaving the new factory underused with higher fixed costs [an].
    Keywords: 3 factories, 3 days, 14%, Country Y, 420,000, Asia and Europe, 70%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relocation disrupts supply chains and compliance; exchange rates can reverse, making relocation premature | application_max_2: 3 factories / 3 days domestic supplier delivery / Asia and Europe buyers; 14% dollar strengthening / Country Y currency is 20% weaker | analysis_max_2: disruption risks buyer penalties and lost orders; reversed currency leaves the new factory underused and costly

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Silkharbour should relocate one factory to Country Y? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Relocating one factory would let Silkharbour produce in a currency 20% weaker with wages 35% lower, directly countering the 14% dollar strengthening that squeezed margins from 11% to 6% [k], and would help defend its 70% export share to Asia and Europe buyers [app]. However, keeping all 3 factories in Country X preserves 3-day delivery from domestic suppliers [k], and relocating before the dollar move proves lasting could freeze capital in a factory that later proves unnecessary [app]. The relocation hedges against further dollar strength and restores export competitiveness [an], but the 18% fall in Asian orders could reflect changing buyer demand, which a new factory would not fix [an].     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relocation hedges currency and wage costs; keeping factories preserves supply reliability | application_max_2: 20% weaker currency / wages 35% lower / 14% dollar strengthening / margins 11% to 6%; 70% export share / 3 factories / 3-day domestic deliveries / 18% fall in Asian orders | analysis_max_2: relocation hedges further dollar strength and restores competitiveness; Asian order fall may reflect demand, not just currency, so a factory alone may not fix it | evaluation_max_2: weighs currency and wage advantage against 3-day supply security and risk of premature move; justified recommendation to relocate one factory, keeping Country X as a domestic supplier base

--- STEM ---
Saltrunner Surfboards is a sole trader business owned by Marco Deleanu, shaping bespoke surfboards in a small coastal workshop in Country X for 6 years. Saltrunner employs 3 skilled shapers and produces 220 custom boards a year, each hand-shaped over 9 hours and sold at $1,450, generating annual revenue of $319,000. Fixed costs are $4,000 a month and materials cost $180 per board.

A national surf retailer has offered a 2-year contract for 800 identical boards a year at $620 each. Marco could accept by introducing batch production with 2 Computer-Aided Design templates and $55,000 of new machinery, or he could refuse and keep shaping one-off boards for his loyal custom customers. He must decide before the retailer's order deadline on 30 September.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'job production'.
    Answer: Producing one-off, often unique products, each made to the individual requirements of a specific customer [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: one-off / single items are produced at a time; products are made to the individual customer's specification

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why job production suits Saltrunner's surfboards.
    Answer: Reason 1: Job production makes one-off items to individual specifications [k], which suits boards ordered in personal sizes and designs by Saltrunner's 220 custom boards a year [app]. Reason 2: Job production supports skilled craftsmanship [k], allowing each $1,450 board to be hand-shaped over 9 hours to the buyer's exact dimensions [app].
    Keywords: 220 custom boards a year, $1,450, 9 hours, hand-shaped, $319,000, custom customers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: job production customises each item to the customer's order; job production relies on skilled labour producing one-off items | application_max_2: 220 custom boards a year are ordered to personal designs; each $1,450 board is hand-shaped over 9 hours

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to Saltrunner of switching to batch production for the retailer contract.
    Answer: Problem 1: Switching to batch production would standardise the boards [k], but the retailer's 800 identical boards differ completely from the individual designs ordered by loyal custom customers [app], so the hand-shaping skills built over 6 years could be lost [an]. Problem 2: Batch production with $55,000 of new machinery raises fixed costs [k], and each contract board sells at only $620 instead of $1,450 [app], so Saltrunner could treble volume yet earn less cash per unit [an].
    Keywords: 800 identical boards, $55,000, $620, $1,450, 6 years, one-off boards, 2-year contract
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: batch production standardises output and loses per-item customisation; batch production usually needs capital investment in machinery | application_max_2: the retailer wants 800 identical boards, unlike bespoke custom work; $55,000 machinery and only $620 per board against $1,450 today | analysis_max_2: loss of skills and differentiation built up over 6 years; higher volume but much thinner margin per board

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Saltrunner Surfboards should accept the 800-board retailer contract and switch to batch production? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the contract would raise revenue sharply [k], since 800 boards a year at $620 would bring $496,000 compared with today's $319,000 [app], so capacity use and cash flow would improve significantly [an]. However, batch production with $55,000 of machinery weakens the bespoke position [k]; loyal clients who pay $1,450 each for a hand-shaped one-off board may feel Saltrunner has gone mass market [app], so premium orders could fall below today's levels [an]. Overall, Saltrunner should decline the contract for now [eval], because protecting a $319,000-a-year bespoke reputation with only 3 skilled shapers beats taking on $55,000 of machinery debt for thin $620 margins [eval].
    Keywords: 800 identical boards, $620, $1,450, $55,000, $319,000, 2-year contract, one-off boards
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: batch production raises volume and capacity utilisation at low unit cost; batch production risks losing differentiation and premium pricing | application_max_2: 800 boards at $620 = $496,000 a year, above the current $319,000; $55,000 machinery and a drop from $1,450 to $620 per board | analysis_max_2: cash flow benefit weighed against margin per unit; brand dilution could erode the premium custom segment | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the figures and the sole-trader scale of the business

--- STEM ---
Sunpepper Hot Sauce Co is a private limited company founded 4 years ago by Lena Ortiz in Country X, employing 14 production staff in one factory. Sunpepper cooks 6,000 litres of premium chilli sauce a month in batches of 750 litres, selling each 250 ml bottle at $6.40 and generating monthly revenue of $153,600. It makes 12 varieties, best known for smoky chipotle, mango habanero and lime leaf.

A supermarket chain has listed Sunpepper's smoky chipotle sauce nationally, forecasting sales of 72,000 bottles a month, three times current output. Lena could install a continuous flow production line costing $480,000, or buy 2 additional 750-litre vats for $60,000 and hire 6 staff at $1,150 a month to triple batch capacity. She must decide within 8 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'batch production'.
    Answer: Producing a set quantity of identical items, completing each stage for the whole batch before moving to the next batch [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a batch is a set number of identical items produced together; each stage is completed for the batch before production switches

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of batch production for Sunpepper.
    Answer: Reason 1: Batch production allows different varieties to be made [k], which suits Sunpepper's 12 varieties, since each 750-litre batch can focus on one recipe [app]. Reason 2: Batch production spreads set-up costs across many units [k], lowering the average cost per bottle across the 24,000 bottles sold each month at $6.40 [app].
    Keywords: 12 varieties, 750-litre vats, 6,000 litres, $6.40, 250 ml, $153,600
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: batch production can switch between varieties or recipes; batch production spreads set-up costs over many units | application_max_2: each 750-litre batch is devoted to one of the 12 varieties; 24,000 bottles a month (6,000 litres at 250 ml) at $6.40 each

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to Sunpepper of its current batch production.
    Answer: Problem 1: Batch production needs downtime between batches [k], so cleaning and resetting vats across 12 varieties loses production hours in a factory making only 6,000 litres a month [app], leaving too little capacity to serve the supermarket listing [an]. Problem 2: One error can spoil a whole batch [k], and a faulty recipe could waste all 750 litres in a run before anyone notices [app], creating unsold stock and cash flow pressure against $153,600 monthly revenue [an].
    Keywords: 12 varieties, 750 litres, 6,000 litres, $153,600, 72,000 bottles, $6.40
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: batches need changeover time for cleaning and resetting; a single fault can ruin an entire batch | application_max_2: 12 varieties mean frequent vat changeovers in a small factory; all 750 litres in a batch would be lost to one error | analysis_max_2: changeover downtime prevents meeting the 72,000-bottle forecast; wasted batches directly damage cash flow against $153,600 revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sunpepper Hot Sauce Co should install the $480,000 flow production line rather than expand batch capacity? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The supermarket forecasts 72,000 bottles a month, three times current output [k]; buying 2 additional 750-litre vats at $60,000 and hiring 6 staff at $1,150 adds only $6,900 a month in wages [app], far cheaper than $480,000 [an]. However, a flow line would cut unit costs and fill 72,000 bottles smoothly every month [k], avoiding 24 changeovers and protecting the national listing [app], building long-term volume beyond the chipotle sauce [an]. Overall, Sunpepper should expand batch capacity first [eval], keeping 12 varieties flexible for local shops while proving the supermarket volume before committing $480,000 [eval].
    Keywords: 72,000 bottles, $480,000, $60,000, $1,150, smoky chipotle, 750-litre vats, 12 varieties, $153,600
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: flow production cuts unit cost for one standardised product at high volume; expanding batch capacity keeps variety and flexibility at lower cost | application_max_2: 72,000 bottles a month (three times current) vs 2 vats at $60,000 and 6 staff at $1,150; $480,000 line vs $6,900 a month extra wages (6 x $1,150) | analysis_max_2: capital cost difference between the two options and when each breaks even; variety flexibility versus single-product flow efficiency and listing security | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to cash flow, the 8-week decision window and listing risk

--- STEM ---
Cindergate Canning Co is a private limited company in Country X, founded 5 years ago, employing 46 factory workers in one plant. It makes 125,000 cans of chopped tomatoes a day on a continuous flow production line, 5 days a week, selling to national supermarkets and wholesalers across Country X. Last year Cindergate sold 32.5 million cans at $0.85 each, and fixed costs are $210,000 a month.

A supermarket has offered a 3-year contract for 45 million cans a year at $0.82 per can. The board is deciding between installing a second fully automated flow line costing $6.5 million, or keeping one line and running Saturday and Sunday shifts, adding $38,000 a month in overtime and maintenance. The contract starts in May, 9 months away.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'flow production'.
    Answer: Producing large quantities of standardised products continuously, with work moving from one stage to the next on an assembly line [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: continuous production of standardised / identical products; output moves through stages, typically on an assembly line

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of flow production for Cindergate.
    Answer: Reason 1: Flow production allows very high volumes [k], enabling Cindergate's continuous line to make 125,000 cans a day [app]. Reason 2: Flow production lowers average cost per unit [k], so each of the 32.5 million cans sold last year carried only a small share of the $210,000 monthly fixed costs [app].
    Keywords: 125,000 cans, 32.5 million cans, $210,000, $0.85, $0.82
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: flow production achieves very high output volumes; flow production lowers average cost per unit | application_max_2: 125,000 cans a day on one continuous line; 32.5 million cans a year spreading $210,000 fixed costs

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of flow production for Cindergate.
    Answer: Problem 1: Flow production needs high capital investment [k], and a second automated line would cost $6.5 million in one payment [app], stretching cash reserves built from last year's 32.5 million cans [an]. Problem 2: A breakdown stops the whole line [k], so one fault in the continuous process could halt all 125,000 cans a day worked by 46 factory workers [app], missing supermarket deliveries and triggering penalties [an].
    Keywords: $6.5 million, 125,000 cans, 46 factory workers, 32.5 million cans, $210,000, 5 days a week
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: flow production requires very high capital investment; in flow production one fault stops the entire line | application_max_2: $6.5 million for a second automated line; one fault could halt 125,000 cans a day across 46 workers | analysis_max_2: cash flow strain and risk of under-used capacity; lost output and delivery penalties under time pressure

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cindergate Canning Co should install a second flow line rather than run Saturday and Sunday shifts? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Running weekends would meet the contract cheaply [k]: moving to 7 days raises capacity from 32.5 million to 45.5 million cans a year, covering the 45 million needed for only $38,000 a month in overtime [app], protecting cash ahead of the 9-month deadline [an]. However, weekend working strains workers and machinery [k], and the 3-year contract at $0.82 per can is worth about $110.7 million in revenue [app], so automation's reliability and lower long-run unit costs could protect margins on such a valuable deal [an]. Overall, Cindergate should run Saturday and Sunday shifts first [eval], keeping the $6.5 million uncommitted until the supermarket contract proves repeatable at $0.82 per can [eval].
    Keywords: 125,000 cans, $0.82, $0.85, $6.5 million, $38,000, 45 million cans, $210,000, 32.5 million cans
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: overtime/weekend working raises capacity without capital spending; automation lowers long-run unit cost and improves reliability | application_max_2: 7 days yields 45.5 million cans a year, covering the 45 million contract for $38,000 a month; 3-year contract worth about $110.7 million (45 million x $0.82 x 3) | analysis_max_2: $38,000 per month vs $6.5 million capital outlay, cash timing; reliability and unit-cost benefits versus workforce fatigue and maintenance | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the 9-month deadline and contract risk

--- STEM ---
Thornwick Garments Ltd is a private limited company in Country X employing 85 sewing machinists making hard-wearing workwear for factories and logistics firms in one factory. Last month the factory produced 42,000 garments, up from 38,000 six months ago, after 12.5 hours of weekly overtime per machinist were approved. Total hours worked rose from 12,750 to 17,000 a month, and quality complaints rose from 1.2% to 1.9% of garments.

The owner could hire 12 more machinists at $520 per week to raise output, or invest $95,000 in 20 computerised sewing machines and a staff training programme to raise productivity and hold defects down. The largest customer, a national retailer, wants 55,000 garments a month within 12 months; overtime is already unpopular with the machinists.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'production'.
    Answer: The process of transforming resources such as labour, land and capital into goods and services [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: production is the process of making goods / providing services; production converts inputs (factors of production) into outputs

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the fall in productivity from 2.98 to 2.47 garments per hour matters to Thornwick.
    Answer: Reason 1: Lower productivity means more labour hours per garment [k], so total hours rose from 12,750 to 17,000 a month to produce only 42,000 garments [app]. Reason 2: Falling productivity raises unit labour cost [k], and with complaints up from 1.2% to 1.9% of garments, rework makes each of the 42,000 garments more expensive [app].
    Keywords: 12,750 to 17,000, 1.2% to 1.9%, 42,000 garments, 38,000, 85 sewing machinists
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower productivity raises input per unit of output; lower productivity increases average / unit cost | application_max_2: hours rose from 12,750 to 17,000 while output rose only from 38,000 to 42,000; complaints rose from 1.2% to 1.9% of garments adding rework cost

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Thornwick of investing in the 20 computerised sewing machines rather than hiring 12 more machinists.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Machines raise output without adding proportional wages [k], since 20 computerised sewing machines would lift output towards the 55,000 garments the national retailer wants without adding 12 x $520 weekly wages [app], so unit labour cost falls [an]. Benefit 2: Machines improve consistency [k], reducing the 1.9% complaint rate that appeared once 12.5 extra weekly hours were worked [app], so rework falls and the retailer relationship is protected [an].
    Keywords: $95,000, 20 computerised sewing machines, 55,000 garments, $520, 12 more machinists, 1.9%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: capital investment raises capacity without proportional wage increases; machines improve consistency and reduce errors | application_max_2: 20 computerised sewing machines towards the 55,000-garment target; complaints at 1.9% after 12.5 overtime hours per machinist | analysis_max_2: unit labour cost falls as output rises without 12 x $520 wages; fewer defects means less rework and a protected key account

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Thornwick Garments should invest in the 20 computerised sewing machines rather than hire 12 more machinists? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing $95,000 in 20 computerised machines would attack the productivity problem directly [k]; output could reach 55,000 garments a month within 12 months without permanently adding 12 x $520 a week to the wage bill [app], so unit costs fall and quality improves as manual overtime is replaced [an]. However, machines take time to install and machinists may fear job losses [k], whereas hiring 12 machinists at $520 a week adds capacity quickly and keeps 85 skilled operators in work [app], avoiding disputes and protecting output during changeover [an]. Overall, Thornwick should invest in the machines [eval], because productivity has already fallen from 2.98 to 2.47 garments per hour and overtime cannot sustainably deliver the national retailer's 55,000-garment target [eval].
    Keywords: $95,000, 20 computerised sewing machines, 55,000 garments, 12 more machinists, $520, 42,000 garments, 1.9%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: technology investment raises productivity and quality; hiring adds quick capacity but raises permanent wage costs | application_max_2: $95,000 for 20 machines vs 55,000 garments needed within 12 months; 12 machinists at $520 a week would cost $6,240 a week in extra wages | analysis_max_2: productivity recovery versus speed and disruption of installation; permanent wage cost versus one-off capital saving over time | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the productivity decline and retailer deadline

--- STEM ---
Brightfold Packaging Ltd is a private limited company in Country X employing 40 machine operators and 5 supervisors, producing corrugated postal boxes in brown, white and branded print in one plant. Last month the plant produced 480,000 boxes. Fixed costs are $96,000 a month and materials cost $0.31 per box; boxes sell at $0.95 each. Labour productivity was 12,000 boxes per operator per month.

Brightfold's main customer placed a rush order for 720,000 boxes next month, 50% above current output. The operations manager proposes hiring 20 additional operators at $2,050 per month each, while the general manager proposes upgrading 6 forming machines for $120,000 to raise productivity to 18,000 boxes per operator. One of the two plans must be chosen within 3 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'productivity'.
    Answer: A measure of output per unit of input, usually output per worker per period [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: productivity is output per worker / per unit of input; higher productivity means more output from the same resources

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Brightfold of raising labour productivity to 18,000 boxes per operator.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Higher productivity spreads fixed costs over more output [k], so the $96,000 monthly fixed costs would be shared across 720,000 boxes instead of 480,000 [app]. Benefit 2: Higher productivity raises capacity without extra staff [k], allowing 40 operators to meet the 720,000-box rush order instead of 60 [app].
    Keywords: 720,000 boxes, 480,000, $96,000, 18,000 boxes per operator, $0.95, $0.31
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher productivity lowers average / unit cost; higher productivity raises capacity without extra labour | application_max_2: $96,000 fixed cost spread over 720,000 boxes rather than 480,000; 40 operators at 18,000 boxes each = 720,000 without hiring

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Brightfold may face if it hires 20 additional operators instead of upgrading the machines.
    Answer: Problem 1: Extra operators raise wage costs permanently [k], adding 20 x $2,050 = $41,000 a month to the payroll [app], squeezing margins once the rush order ends [an]. Problem 2: More staff need more supervision and space [k], and 60 operators on one line exceed the capacity of the 5 supervisors and the plant floor [app], creating congestion, more defects and overtime costs [an].
    Keywords: 20 additional operators, $2,050, 5 supervisors, 40 machine operators, 720,000 boxes, $0.31
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: hiring adds permanent wage costs; more staff require more supervision and workspace | application_max_2: 20 x $2,050 = $41,000 a month added to the payroll; 60 operators vs only 5 supervisors on one line | analysis_max_2: margins are squeezed once the rush order finishes; supervision strain raises defect and overtime risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brightfold Packaging should upgrade the 6 forming machines rather than hire 20 extra operators? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The $120,000 upgrade would let the existing 40 operators reach 720,000 boxes (40 x 18,000) [k], and equals about 3 months of the $41,000 monthly wage bill for 20 new operators [app], so within a quarter the upgrade is cheaper and margins recover [an]. However, machines need installation time and the rush order is due next month [k], whereas hiring 20 operators at $2,050 each can be done within the 3-week decision window [app], securing the customer's rush order immediately [an]. Overall, Brightfold should upgrade the machines [eval], because the bottleneck is equipment rather than effort, and the rush order can be covered by short-term overtime from the current 40 operators while installation is completed [eval].
    Keywords: $120,000, 720,000 boxes, 20 additional operators, $2,050, 18,000 boxes per operator, 5 supervisors, 40 machine operators
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: capital upgrade lowers long-run unit labour cost; hiring is quicker but adds permanent wage cost | application_max_2: 40 operators x 18,000 = 720,000 boxes with no extra hires; $120,000 equals about 3 months of $41,000 wages (20 x $2,050) | analysis_max_2: recovery time of the $120,000 upgrade versus ongoing wage drain; speed of hiring versus disruption of machine installation | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the 3-week window and equipment bottleneck

Ironbark Furniture Works is a partnership founded 9 years ago by two brothers in Country X, employing 34 workers making three product lines: bespoke fitted wardrobes at $4,800 each (25 a month), oak dining chairs made in batches of 600 a month at $210 each, and pine stools on a flow line at 2,000 a month at $34 each. Monthly sales revenue averages $314,000.

The stool flow line is overloaded with 1,400 stools on backorder, while the wardrobe line has spare capacity. The partners could invest $150,000 in a second stool pressing machine to raise stool output to 3,200 a month, or move 4 chair-batch workers onto the stool line and keep total employment unchanged. Orders are due next month.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two advantages of flow production.
    Answer: Flow production allows very high output volumes [1]; it lowers average unit costs through standardisation and continuous working [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: flow production achieves very high output volume; flow production lowers average unit cost through standardisation

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Ironbark uses different production methods for its three product lines.
    Answer: Reason 1: Job production suits one-off custom work [k], fitting fitted wardrobes made to each customer's room at $4,800 and about 25 a month [app]. Reason 2: Flow production suits identical high-volume products [k], ideal for 2,000 pine stools a month at $34, while chairs are batch-made at 600 a month to balance volume and choice [app].
    Keywords: fitted wardrobes, $4,800, 25 a month, 2,000 a month, batches of 600, $34
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: job production suits one-off, customised products; flow production suits standardised high-volume products | application_max_2: wardrobes at $4,800, about 25 a month, made to room measurements; stools at $34 on a flow line, 2,000 a month; chairs batched at 600 a month

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to Ironbark of investing in the second stool pressing machine.
    Answer: Problem 1: The press creates over-dependence on one low-margin line [k], since stools sell at only $34 each against $4,800 wardrobes [app], so recovering the $150,000 depends on volumes that may not last [an]. Problem 2: The press commits capital with one fault point [k], and with the flow line already missing 1,400 stools on backorder, a machine breakdown could halt stool output entirely [app], pushing deliveries past the orders due next month [an].
    Keywords: $150,000, 1,400 stools on backorder, $34, $4,800, 2,000 a month, pine stools
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: capital is committed to one product line, raising risk; flow lines are vulnerable to breakdown stoppages | application_max_2: stools at $34 each versus $4,800 bespoke wardrobes; backorder already 1,400 stools; press costs $150,000 | analysis_max_2: recovery risk if stool demand fades; single point of failure pushing deliveries beyond next month

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ironbark Furniture Works should invest in the second stool pressing machine rather than move 4 chair-batch workers onto the stool line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The second press would lift stool output to 3,200 a month [k], clearing the 1,400-stool backorder and supporting the $314,000-a-month sales run rate reliably [app], so flow efficiency and delivery would recover quickly [an]. However, $150,000 in one payment strains partner cash [k], while moving 4 chair-batch workers keeps chairs flowing, which sell at $210 each and earn $126,000 a month [app], and avoids debt if stool demand fades [an]. Overall, Ironbark should move the 4 chair-batch workers first [eval], solving the backorder without new debt, and commit to the $150,000 press only if backorders persist for two more months [eval].
    Keywords: $150,000, 1,400 stools on backorder, 3,200 a month, $314,000, $210, batches of 600, 2,000 a month
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: investment raises flow capacity for high-volume standard goods; reallocating existing staff is cheaper and more flexible | application_max_2: press lifts output to 3,200 a month vs 1,400-stool backorder; chairs sell at $210 each earning about $126,000 a month | analysis_max_2: capacity and reliability versus cash flow strain; flexibility and zero debt versus delivery risk next month | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to backorder size and partner cash position

Honeywick Artisan Bakery is a private limited company in Country X employing 18 bakers and 6 counter staff, producing fresh bread, rolls and pastries for 9 local shops across the town and two neighbouring villages. Last year the bakery produced 780,000 loaves and rolls, 8% more than the previous year, while the wage bill rose 15% to $540,000. The owners report each baker shapes 5% fewer loaves per hour than two years ago.

The owners could buy a $70,000 spiral dough mixer to lift weekly output from 15,000 to 21,000 loaves and free bakers for skilled pastry work, or pay overtime to cover the 600 loaves a week the 9 shops are short. The decision must be made by the end of the month.

    Question: Outline the difference between production and productivity.
    Answer: Production is the total output made in a period, whereas productivity measures output per worker or per input used [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: production is the total output made; productivity is output per worker / per unit of input

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Honeywick's labour productivity has fallen even though production rose.
    Answer: Reason 1: Production can rise while productivity falls if more labour is used [k], because total output rose 8% to 780,000 loaves while the wage bill rose 15% to $540,000 [app]. Reason 2: Productivity falls when output per worker decreases [k], and each baker now shapes 5% fewer loaves per hour than two years ago [app].
    Keywords: 780,000 loaves, $540,000, 5% fewer loaves, 18 bakers, 15%, 8%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: total output can rise while output per worker falls; productivity measures output per worker, not total output | application_max_2: output rose 8% to 780,000 while the wage bill rose 15% to $540,000; each baker shapes 5% fewer loaves per hour than two years ago

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Honeywick of buying the $70,000 spiral dough mixer instead of paying overtime.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The mixer raises output without permanent extra wages [k], lifting weekly output from 15,000 to 21,000 loaves, enough to cover the 600-loaf shortfall and grow [app], spreading the $70,000 over years of output [an]. Benefit 2: The mixer removes heavy manual kneading [k], freeing the 18 bakers to focus on pastries and quality [app], so productivity per hour rises and overtime is not needed [an].
    Keywords: $70,000, 15,000 to 21,000 loaves, 600 loaves, 18 bakers, 9 local shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: machinery raises capacity without permanent wage inflation; machinery reduces physical strain and frees labour | application_max_2: output lifts from 15,000 to 21,000 loaves a week, covering the 600 shortfall; 18 bakers freed from manual kneading for pastries and quality work | analysis_max_2: $70,000 spread over years versus open-ended overtime premiums; productivity per hour recovers, easing the wage-bill pressure

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Honeywick Artisan Bakery should buy the spiral dough mixer rather than pay overtime? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The $70,000 mixer would raise weekly output from 15,000 to 21,000 loaves [k], covering the 600-loaf weekly shortfall with capacity to spare for the 9 local shops [app], so Honeywick can grow without open-ended overtime premiums [an]. However, $70,000 is a large one-off outlay for a small bakery [k], while overtime spending would fall automatically if orders soften, unlike the fixed mixer cost [app], so the mixer raises cash flow risk if demand fades [an]. Overall, Honeywick should buy the mixer [eval], because bakers already shape 5% fewer loaves per hour than two years ago and overtime only deepens the fatigue behind the productivity slide [eval].
    Keywords: $70,000, 15,000 to 21,000 loaves, 600 loaves, 18 bakers, 9 local shops, 780,000 loaves, $540,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: machinery raises capacity and productivity sustainably; overtime is flexible but deepens fatigue and wage costs | application_max_2: $70,000 mixer lifts output from 15,000 to 21,000 loaves, covering 600 shortfall; bakers shape 5% fewer loaves per hour; overtime cost falls if demand fades | analysis_max_2: long-run saving versus short-run cash flow strain; productivity recovery versus risk of weakening demand | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to productivity decline and demand risk

--- STEM ---
Wychwood Naturals Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 6 years ago, employing 22 staff making 15 varieties of natural skincare at an average of $12 per jar. Output runs in weekly batches of 300 jars per variety, fully traceable; batch changeovers take 6 hours each week, and last quarter 2 batches were rejected after a mislabelled allergen, costing $9,600 in write-offs.

A regional pharmacy chain wants weekly delivery of 1,500 jars of tea-tree soap and lavender balm, 8 months a year. Wychwood could cut its range to the 6 best-selling varieties and run batches of 800 jars using $85,000 of new moulding equipment, or keep all 15 varieties and stay flexible for its 28 local shops.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two disadvantages of batch production.
    Answer: It requires downtime between batches for cleaning and changeovers [1]; one error can spoil an entire batch [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: changeover downtime between batches / set-up time lost; one fault can ruin a whole batch

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why cutting the range to 6 varieties and running batches of 800 jars could help Wychwood.
    Answer: Reason 1: Larger batches cut changeover time [k], so the 6 hours lost each week resetting 15 varieties would fall, freeing capacity for the pharmacy's 1,500 jars a week [app]. Reason 2: Fewer varieties reduce allergen-management risks [k], lowering the chance of rejecting whole runs like the 2 batches that cost $9,600 last quarter [app].
    Keywords: 1,500 jars, 6 hours, $9,600, 800 jars, 15 varieties, 6 best-selling varieties
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: larger batches reduce changeover downtime; fewer varieties reduce the risk and cost of errors | application_max_2: 6 hours weekly changeover across 15 varieties would fall; capacity freed for the pharmacy's 1,500 jars a week

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Wychwood of keeping all 15 varieties and smaller batches.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A broad range serves more segments [k], keeping 28 local shops stocked with all 15 varieties at $12 each rather than only the top 6 [app], so loyal shop buyers do not switch to rivals [an]. Benefit 2: Batches of 300 jars limit write-off exposure [k], so a mislabelled batch costs a fraction of an 800-jar run [app], protecting cash flow and the $9,600 type of loss [an].
    Keywords: 28 local shops, 15 varieties, $12, 300 jars, 800 jars, $9,600
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a wider range appeals to more customer segments; smaller batches reduce the cost of errors | application_max_2: 28 local shops buy the full 15 varieties at $12 per jar; 300-jar batches vs 800-jar batches for error exposure | analysis_max_2: retention of shop contracts and loyal buyers; lower write-off cost protects cash flow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wychwood Naturals should cut its range to 6 varieties and invest $85,000 in the moulding equipment? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cutting to 6 varieties and buying $85,000 of moulding equipment would slash changeover losses [k], letting Wychwood supply the pharmacy's 1,500 jars a week at $12 (an extra $18,000 a week) with 800-jar batches [app], lifting output and margin for 8 months a year [an]. However, dropping 9 of the 15 varieties risks the 28 local shops that stock the full range [k], whose buyers may migrate to rivals once niche items disappear [app], eroding shop contracts and spreading risk away from retail [an]. Overall, Wychwood should cut the range and buy the equipment [eval], because the pharmacy's 1,500-jar weekly order for 8 months a year is large and repeatable, while niche volumes at $12 are easily outweighed by the extra $18,000 a week [eval].
    Keywords: $85,000, 1,500 jars, $12, 28 local shops, 6 best-selling varieties, 8 months, $9,600
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: consolidating volumes lowers unit cost and changeover waste; narrowing range risks losing segments and channel diversity | application_max_2: $85,000 moulding equipment; 800-jar batches; pharmacy 1,500 jars a week at $12 = $18,000 a week; 28 local shops and 15 varieties; risk of losing niche buyers | analysis_max_2: capacity and margin gain versus channel concentration risk; contract certainty for 8 months a year versus local shop loyalty | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to pharmacy revenue size vs local shop risk

--- STEM ---
Elmsworth & Cross Watchmakers Ltd is a private limited company founded 12 years ago by two horologists in Country X, employing 9 master watchmakers and selling hand-built watches at $9,500 each. Elmsworth sold 240 watches last year, generating revenue of $2.28 million; each watch takes 30 hours to assemble and regulate, and waiting lists run to 7 months. Elmsworth's clients are collectors who value heritage and discretion.

The owners could launch a $1,800 everyday automatic watch made on a small flow production line costing $900,000 with 12 new assembly staff, or stay exclusively with hand-built watches and raise prices by 15% to clear the 7-month backlog and shorten waiting lists. The board meets in December to decide between the two plans.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two disadvantages of flow production.
    Answer: It requires very high capital investment in machinery [1]; a breakdown stops the whole production line [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: flow production needs very high capital investment; in flow production one breakdown halts the whole line

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why job production suits Elmsworth & Cross's luxury watches.
    Answer: Reason 1: Job production makes one-off items to exact specification [k], suiting the 30 hours of individual assembly and regulation each $9,500 watch requires [app]. Reason 2: Job production supports premium craftsmanship and pricing [k], letting 9 master watchmakers sell genuinely hand-built watches to clients who wait 7 months [app].
    Keywords: 30 hours, $9,500, 9 master watchmakers, 240 watches, 7 months
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: job production makes one-offs to individual specification; job production enables premium craftsmanship and pricing | application_max_2: 30 hours per watch at $9,500 each; 9 master watchmakers; 7-month waiting lists

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks to Elmsworth & Cross of launching the $1,800 flow-made watch.
    Answer: Problem 1: The $900,000 line with 12 new assembly staff is a heavy fixed commitment [k], and if the everyday watch disappoints, the cost cannot easily be repaid at $1,800 each, roughly a fifth of the luxury price [app], so one weak launch damages cash flow [an]. Problem 2: A cheaper line can blur exclusivity [k], diluting the hand-built reputation that supports $2.28 million of annual sales [app], so loyal collectors may question what the brand now stands for [an].
    Keywords: $1,800, $900,000, 12 new assembly staff, $2.28 million, $9,500, flow production line
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: flow lines need large fixed capital commitments that are hard to exit; product-line extensions can dilute brand positioning | application_max_2: $900,000 line and 12 staff vs a $1,800 selling price; reputation underpins $2.28 million annual sales at $9,500 | analysis_max_2: low selling price makes recouping the line slow; brand dilution could erode the core luxury customer base

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Elmsworth & Cross Watchmakers should launch the $1,800 flow-made watch rather than only raise prices by 15%? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising prices by 15% would grow revenue without new risk [k], since 240 watches at $10,925 would bring about $2.62 million, roughly $342,000 more a year [app], while protecting the exclusive hand-built positioning [an]. However, the $1,800 watch could reach far more buyers than 240 a year [k], and the $900,000 line with 12 new assembly staff could open a larger market and spread brand awareness [app], building long-term demand beyond the waiting list [an]. Overall, Elmsworth & Cross should raise prices and hold the flow line under review [eval], because exclusivity underpins the $9,500 price, and $342,000 of low-risk extra revenue beats betting $900,000 on an unproven mass market [eval].
    Keywords: $1,800, $900,000, $9,500, $2.28 million, 240 watches, 15%, 12 new assembly staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: price rises lift revenue with no capital risk; a flow-made entry range can expand market reach at scale | application_max_2: 240 watches at $10,925 = about $2.62 million, +$342,000 a year; $900,000 line, 12 staff, $1,800 selling price vs $9,500 luxury price | analysis_max_2: low-risk margin gain versus scalable but unproven demand; brand exclusivity versus audience growth | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the figures and the waiting-list position

--- STEM ---
Kilnworth Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company in Country X employing 36 production workers and 4 packers making ceramic tableware for hotel groups and restaurant chains. Last week the factory produced 27,000 plates and bowls on one 8-hour shift, five days a week; labour productivity was 750 pieces per worker. Sales have grown steadily for three years, and two hotel groups want 40,500 pieces a week next year.

Kilnworth could add a second 8-hour shift with 36 new workers at $485 a week each to reach 54,000 pieces a week, or install a new shuttle kiln for $260,000 to raise productivity to 1,150 pieces per worker. Both options would begin after the January delivery window, and the cheaper option must be chosen by February.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the labour productivity of Kilnworth's production workers last week. Show your working.
    Answer: Labour productivity = output / workers = 27,000 / 36 = 750 pieces per worker per week [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: labour productivity = output / number of workers; 27,000 / 36 = 750 pieces per worker

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Kilnworth of installing the new shuttle kiln rather than adding a second shift.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The kiln raises productivity per worker [k], lifting output from 750 to 1,150 pieces per worker with the same 36 production workers [app]. Benefit 2: The kiln avoids recurring shift wages [k], saving 36 x $485 = $17,460 a week compared with a second shift [app].
    Keywords: 1,150 pieces per worker, 750 pieces, 36 production workers, $485, $260,000, 40,500 pieces
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: machinery raises output per worker; machinery avoids recurring wage costs of extra shifts | application_max_2: 750 to 1,150 pieces per worker with 36 production workers; 36 x $485 = $17,460 a week saved versus a second shift

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Kilnworth may face if it adds a second shift with 36 new workers.
    Answer: Problem 1: A second shift roughly doubles labour cost [k], adding 36 x $485 = $17,460 a week to the payroll before overtime and supervision [app], squeezing margins on price-sensitive hotel contracts [an]. Problem 2: New workers need training and quality checks [k], and with only 4 packers to handle 54,000 pieces a week [app], breakages and delivery delays could hit both hotel groups [an].
    Keywords: 36 new workers, $485, 54,000 pieces, 4 packers, 40,500 pieces, 8-hour shift
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a second shift adds permanent recurring labour cost; new workers require training and quality supervision | application_max_2: 36 x $485 = $17,460 a week extra payroll; only 4 packers for 54,000 pieces a week | analysis_max_2: margins squeezed on price-sensitive hotel contracts; packing bottleneck causes breakages and late deliveries

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kilnworth Ceramics should install the new shuttle kiln rather than add a second shift? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The $260,000 kiln would lift productivity to 1,150 pieces per worker [k], so the existing 36 workers make 41,400 pieces a week and cover the hotel groups' 40,500 target [app], avoiding $17,460 a week of second-shift wages [an]. However, a second shift with 36 new workers would reach 54,000 pieces a week [k], giving spare capacity if both hotel groups expand beyond 40,500 [app], whereas the kiln's 41,400 leaves little headroom [an]. Overall, Kilnworth should install the kiln [eval], because a second shift would cost about $907,920 a year in wages against a one-off $260,000, and confirmed demand is only 40,500 pieces [eval].
    Keywords: $260,000, 1,150 pieces per worker, 40,500 pieces, 54,000 pieces, $485, 36 new workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: capital investment raises productivity without recurring wages; a second shift doubles capacity but doubles labour cost | application_max_2: kiln: 1,150 x 36 = 41,400 pieces per week, covering 40,500 needed; second shift: 54,000 pieces a week; 36 x $485 = $17,460 a week (~$907,920 a year) | analysis_max_2: headroom for growth versus cheaper one-off outlay; recurring wage cost versus capital outlay | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to confirmed demand of 40,500 pieces

--- STEM ---
Brackenfell Woodcraft is a family-run furniture business founded 9 years ago by Helen Marchetti in Country X. It employs 26 workers making handcrafted oak dining tables and chairs, with output of 140 tables a month and annual revenue of $620,000. It sells directly to local hotels, restaurants and homes across the capital region, and the workshop has three separate areas for cutting, sanding and assembly, with parts travelling 14 metres between them.

The production manager proposes kaizen, a programme of continuous small improvements costing about $6,500 a year in training and suggestion rewards. The alternative is a one-off investment of $95,000 in a computer-controlled sanding machine that would cut sanding time by 35%. Helen must decide which route to fund before the new financial year starts.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'kaizen'.
    Answer: A Japanese term meaning continuous, small, ongoing improvements to production processes, involving employees at every level rather than one-off large changes [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: continuous or ongoing small improvements; involves employees/everyone contributing ideas

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Brackenfell Woodcraft might introduce kaizen.
    Answer: Reason 1: Kaizen involves all employees in spotting small, ongoing improvements [k], which suits a 26-worker workshop where parts travel 14 metres between cutting, sanding and assembly [app]. Reason 2: Kaizen costs very little in capital spending [k], at about $6,500 a year compared with a $95,000 machine [app].
    Keywords: 26 workers, 140 tables a month, $620,000, 14 metres, $6,500, handcrafted oak dining tables
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: continuous small improvements by all staff; low-cost approach needing no major capital outlay | application_max_2: 26 workers; 14 metres between work areas; $6,500 a year; $95,000 sanding machine

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Brackenfell Woodcraft of choosing kaizen rather than the computer-controlled sanding machine.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Kaizen preserves cash [k], because $6,500 a year is far cheaper than the $95,000 sanding machine [app], leaving money free for timber and wages [an]. Benefit 2: Kaizen builds a culture where all 26 workers contribute improvement ideas [k], applied across the 140 tables a month passing through cutting, sanding and assembly [app], cutting rework and defects over time [an].
    Keywords: 26 workers, $6,500, $95,000, 140 tables a month, 14 metres, computer-controlled sanding machine
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: kaizen needs little capital, freeing cash flow; kaizen engages and motivates all employees | application_max_2: $6,500 a year; $95,000 sanding machine; 26 workers; 140 tables a month | analysis_max_2: cash saved can be spent on materials and wages; ongoing employee ideas reduce defects and rework

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brackenfell Woodcraft should introduce kaizen instead of buying the computer-controlled sanding machine? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Kaizen spreads the cost at about $6,500 a year [k], engaging all 26 workers in improving the flow of 140 tables a month across workshop areas 14 metres apart [app], so savings build steadily while cash stays available for materials [an]. However, the sanding machine would cut sanding time by 35% immediately [k], lifting capacity on a $620,000 revenue business far faster than gradual kaizen steps [app], which could win larger hotel orders and raise output [an]. Overall, Brackenfell Woodcraft should introduce kaizen first [eval], because low-cost cultural change suits a family-run workshop better than a $95,000 commitment before waste is removed [eval].
    Keywords: $6,500, $95,000, 140 tables a month, $620,000, 14 metres, 35%, 26 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: kaizen is low-cost and gradual with staff involvement; automation gives an immediate, measurable time saving | application_max_2: $6,500 a year; 35% cut in sanding time; $620,000 revenue; $95,000 machine; 14 metres between areas | analysis_max_2: cash preserved funds materials and wages; faster sanding lifts capacity and wins larger orders | evaluation_max_2: weighs low-cost gradual improvement against immediate machine productivity gain

--- STEM ---
Selbrook Foods Ltd is a chilled ready-meal company in Country X, employing 48 workers at its Merriton factory near the rail depot. It produces 9,500 meals a day for supermarkets and made revenue of $1.8 million last year. Fresh vegetables currently arrive in bulk every Monday, and demand peaks sharply before weekends. The cold store holds about 6 days of stock, costing $4,300 a month to run.

The operations director proposes just-in-time deliveries from the main vegetable supplier, arriving four times a day and cutting cold-store stock to half a day. The purchasing manager argues this adds $900 a month in transport costs and any late delivery would stop the production line. Selbrook must decide before signing the new three-year supply contract.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'just-in-time'.
    Answer: A stock management approach in which raw materials and components are delivered only when they are needed in production, rather than being held in inventory [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: materials delivered only when needed; reduces or eliminates inventory holding

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Selbrook Foods Ltd might introduce just-in-time deliveries.
    Answer: Reason 1: JIT reduces the cost of holding inventory [k], because cutting stock from 6 days to half a day would slash much of the $4,300 monthly cold-store cost [app]. Reason 2: JIT keeps ingredients fresher [k], which matters because chilled meals receive fresh vegetables in bulk every Monday and demand peaks before weekends [app].
    Keywords: 9,500 meals a day, $1.8 million, $4,300, 6 days of stock, four times a day, cold store
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduces inventory holding costs and space; perishable inputs arrive fresher and spoil less | application_max_2: 6 days of stock; $4,300 a month; fresh vegetables in bulk every Monday; half a day

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Selbrook Foods Ltd of introducing just-in-time deliveries.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Lower storage costs [k], as cold-store stock falls from 6 days to half a day against a current $4,300 monthly bill [app], freeing cash for other uses [an]. Benefit 2: Fresh ingredients support consistent quality [k], protecting the chilled ready-meal reputation with supermarket buyers who receive 9,500 meals a day [app], which should secure loyal, repeat orders [an].
    Keywords: $4,300, 6 days, half a day, 9,500 meals a day, chilled ready-meal company, four times a day
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: JIT cuts storage and holding costs; fresher inputs improve product quality | application_max_2: 6 days of stock; $4,300 a month; 9,500 meals a day; half a day | analysis_max_2: cash tied up in stock is freed for other uses; better quality protects supermarket relationships and repeat orders

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Selbrook Foods Ltd should switch to just-in-time deliveries? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Just-in-time means vegetables arrive four times a day [k], cutting the cold store from 6 days of stock to half a day and reducing the $4,300 monthly cost [app], so cash tied up in stock drops and ingredients stay fresher [an]. However, deliveries add $900 a month in transport and any late arrival would stop a line producing 9,500 meals a day [k], so four trucks a day leave no buffer when traffic delays suppliers [app], risking lost sales and supermarket penalties [an]. Overall, Selbrook should adopt just-in-time from its main vegetable supplier [eval], because chilled meals spoil quickly and freshness outweighs the $900 delivery cost, provided late-delivery penalties are written into the three-year contract [eval].
    Keywords: $4,300, $900, 9,500 meals a day, half a day, four times a day, 6 days of stock, three-year supply contract
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: JIT cuts inventory cost and improves freshness; JIT creates vulnerability to supply delays with no buffer stock | application_max_2: four times a day; $4,300 monthly cold-store cost; $900 a month transport; 9,500 meals a day; three-year supply contract | analysis_max_2: less cash held in stock and fresher ingredients; a single late delivery halts output and loses sales | evaluation_max_2: weighs freshness and storage savings against transport cost and supply risk
