--- STEM ---
Quenby Electronics Ltd assembles industrial control panels for factories across Country X, employing 132 staff at its Westhaven plant. The panels range from small machine controllers to large motor-control cabinets for food processors, and most customers are regional engineering firms. Panels are built on a flow line where each worker repeats a single task. Output is 260 panels a month, the defect rate is 5.5%, and last year revenue reached $2.4 million.

The operations manager proposes cell production, forming 6 cells of 6 workers, each completing a whole panel from start to finish. The finance director warns that reorganisation costs $38,000 and output would fall by 12% during changeover. Any defects reaching customers trigger penalty clauses. Quenby must vote on the proposal at its board meeting next month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'cell production'.
    Answer: A production method in which workers are organised into small self-contained groups or 'cells', each responsible for completing a whole product or a major section of it [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: workers grouped into small self-contained teams/cells; each cell completes a whole unit or major part

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Quenby Electronics Ltd might introduce cell production.
    Answer: Reason 1: Teams take ownership of a complete panel [k], replacing the flow line where each of the 132 staff repeats a single task in isolation [app]. Reason 2: Cell production usually improves quality [k], helping cut the current 5.5% defect rate as workers check their own output [app].
    Keywords: 132 staff, 260 panels a month, 5.5%, 6 cells of 6 workers, flow line, $2.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: whole-task ownership raises motivation and accountability; built-in checks reduce defects and rework | application_max_2: 132 staff; flow line; 5.5% defect rate; single task

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Quenby Electronics Ltd of introducing cell production.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Higher motivation [k], because 6 cells of 6 workers each complete whole panels rather than repeating single tasks [app], which lifts morale and effort [an]. Benefit 2: Fewer defects [k], tackling the 5.5% defect rate on the 260 panels a month built on the flow line [app], cutting rework and protecting $2.4 million of revenue [an].
    Keywords: 6 cells, 6 workers, whole panel, 260 panels a month, single task, $2.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cells increase variety and ownership, boosting motivation; cells reduce defects through team responsibility | application_max_2: 6 cells of 6 workers; single task; 5.5% defect rate; 260 panels a month | analysis_max_2: motivated teams work harder and stay with the firm; fewer defects cut rework cost and protect revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Quenby Electronics Ltd should introduce cell production? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cell production gives 6 cells of 6 workers ownership of completed panels [k], attacking the 5.5% defect rate on 260 panels a month built on a single-task flow line [app], improving quality and cutting rework as teams learn together [an]. However, reorganisation costs $38,000 and output would fall by 12% (roughly 31 panels a month) during changeover [k], risking missed delivery slots and penalty clauses while staff learn new cell roles [app], which would strain cash and customer trust [an]. Overall, Quenby should vote yes [eval], because the $38,000 outlay is small against $2.4 million of annual revenue and defect-driven losses [eval].
    Keywords: $38,000, 12%, 260 panels a month, 5.5%, 6 cells, $2.4 million, 132 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cell production improves ownership, teamwork and quality; reorganisation carries direct cost and temporary output loss | application_max_2: 6 cells of 6 workers; 5.5% defect rate; $38,000; 12% fall in output; $2.4 million revenue | analysis_max_2: fewer defects reduce penalty clauses and rework cost; temporary output loss risks missed deliveries and cash strain | evaluation_max_2: weighs long-run quality and teamwork gains against short-term cost and disruption

--- STEM ---
Tallowmere Chocolates is a family business in Country X founded 12 years ago, employing 37 workers who make 18,000 boxes of chocolates a month. Most sales go to national supermarket chains, with two export orders to neighbouring countries. Before last Easter it produced 60,000 seasonal boxes in advance; 14,500 were still unsold by May and sat in a rented warehouse costing $2,100 a month. Annual revenue is $1.1 million.

The owner proposes lean production with a make-to-order approach for seasonal lines, making boxes only against confirmed retailer orders. The sales director warns this could leave shelves empty in peak weeks and lose impulse sales of about $48,000. The board must decide which system to use for the next Easter season, with production planning starting in December.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'lean production'.
    Answer: A production approach that aims to minimise waste at every stage of the production process, producing only what customers demand while using resources efficiently [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: aims to eliminate or minimise waste; produces only what is needed / matches customer demand

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Tallowmere Chocolates might adopt a make-to-order approach for seasonal boxes.
    Answer: Reason 1: Make-to-order prevents overproduction [k], avoiding a repeat of 14,500 unsold boxes from the 60,000 made in advance [app]. Reason 2: Make-to-order reduces storage needs [k], easing the $2,100 monthly cost of renting warehouse space for unsold stock [app].
    Keywords: 60,000, 14,500, $2,100, 18,000 boxes, make-to-order approach, confirmed retailer orders
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: avoids overproduction, a key lean waste; cuts the cost of storing excess output | application_max_2: 14,500 unsold boxes; 60,000 seasonal boxes; $2,100 a month; rented warehouse

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Tallowmere Chocolates of a make-to-order approach.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Less unsold stock [k], sparing the business another 14,500 boxes from the 60,000 made in advance sitting in storage [app], which cuts waste costs and protects the $1.1 million revenue margin [an]. Benefit 2: Better cash flow [k], because making against confirmed retailer orders avoids money being tied up each month in the output of 18,000 boxes [app], freeing cash for ingredients and wages [an].
    Keywords: 14,500, $2,100, $1.1 million, 18,000 boxes of chocolates a month, 60,000, make-to-order approach
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: make-to-order removes the risk of unsold output; cash is not tied up in finished goods stock | application_max_2: 14,500 unsold boxes; 60,000 seasonal boxes; 18,000 boxes of chocolates a month; $1.1 million | analysis_max_2: lower storage and write-off costs raise margins; freed cash improves liquidity for wages and ingredients

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tallowmere Chocolates should make seasonal boxes only against confirmed retailer orders? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A make-to-order approach means producing only against confirmed retailer orders [k], which would prevent a repeat of 14,500 of 60,000 pre-made Easter boxes going unsold and paying $2,100 a month for storage [app], releasing cash and cutting waste dramatically [an]. However, empty shelves in peak weeks could forfeit impulse sales of about $48,000 [k], and a strict make-to-order system cannot serve unplanned supermarket top-up orders when demand spikes [app], risking lost display space and goodwill [an]. Overall, Tallowmere should switch largely to make-to-order [eval], because the certain saving on 14,500 unsold boxes outweighs the speculative $48,000, provided a modest flexible reserve is kept for peak weeks [eval].
    Keywords: $48,000, 14,500, $2,100, 60,000, $1.1 million, make-to-order approach, confirmed retailer orders
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: make-to-order removes overproduction and storage waste; strict make-to-order risks empty shelves and lost impulse sales | application_max_2: 14,500 unsold boxes; 60,000 seasonal boxes; $2,100 a month; $48,000 impulse sales; $1.1 million revenue | analysis_max_2: freed cash and lower storage raise margins and liquidity; missed peak demand damages supermarket display and goodwill | evaluation_max_2: weighs certain waste savings against speculative impulse-sales losses

--- STEM ---
Silverbeck Ice Cream Co makes tubs of ice cream in Country X, employing 29 workers on a three-stage line with two shifts. A recent time study found the mixing tank sat idle 35% of each shift waiting for ingredients, and 4.2% of tubs were rejected for temperature faults, costing $6,800 a month in scrapped product. Daily output averages 3,200 litres, demand peaks in the hot summer months, and the business supplies hotel freezers and corner shops.

The production manager proposes kaizen workshops to redesign the ingredient route and add a mixing-schedule board, costing $3,400. The owner favours an $88,000 automated ingredient-dosing machine arriving in 8 months. Both options aim to cut waiting and defects. Silverbeck must choose one investment this quarter.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'waste' in a production context.
    Answer: Any activity, time or resource used in production that does not add value for the customer, for example waiting time, defects, excess inventory and unnecessary motion [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: something that does not add value; examples include waiting, defects or excess stock

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two types of waste that kaizen workshops could cut at Silverbeck Ice Cream Co.
    Answer: Waste 1: Waiting [k], shown by the mixing tank sitting idle 35% of each shift waiting for ingredients to arrive [app]. Waste 2: Defects [k], shown by 4.2% of tubs rejected for temperature faults costing $6,800 a month [app].
    Keywords: 35%, 4.2%, $6,800, mixing tank, temperature faults, waiting for ingredients
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: waiting waste: idle time while resources wait; defects waste: faulty output requiring scrap or rework | application_max_2: mixing tank idle 35% of each shift; 4.2% of tubs rejected; $6,800 a month; waiting for ingredients

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Silverbeck Ice Cream Co of the kaizen workshops.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Very low cost [k], at $3,400 compared with $88,000 for the automated machine [app], so payback is fast and cash stays available [an]. Benefit 2: Worker-led solutions stick [k], engaging the 29 workers around the daily 3,200-litre output [app], which sustains lower waste and defect rates over time [an].
    Keywords: $3,400, $88,000, 29 workers, 3,200 litres, 35%, 4.2%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: kaizen is inexpensive and quick to implement; kaizen gains employee ownership of improvements | application_max_2: $3,400; $88,000; 29 workers; 3,200 litres | analysis_max_2: fast payback preserves cash for other needs; staff ownership sustains long-term defect reduction

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Silverbeck Ice Cream Co should fund the kaizen workshops rather than the automated ingredient-dosing machine? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Kaizen workshops cost $3,400 [k], and by attacking waiting (the tank is idle 35% of each shift) and defects (4.2% of tubs, $6,800 a month scrapped) they could pay back within months [app], cutting both waste types immediately while cash is preserved [an]. However, the $88,000 machine arrives in 8 months [k] and would remove dosing errors permanently, whereas workshops depend on staff discipline and ideas [app], so savings may be partial and slow to appear [an]. Overall, Silverbeck should fund the kaizen workshops first [eval], because at nearly 26 times the cost the machine can follow once the process has been redesigned [eval].
    Keywords: $3,400, $88,000, 35%, 4.2%, $6,800, 8 months, kaizen
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: kaizen is low-cost and immediate but depends on staff; automation is costly and delayed but removes errors permanently | application_max_2: $3,400; $88,000 machine; 35% idle time; $6,800 a month; 8 months | analysis_max_2: cheap fix cuts both waiting and defects quickly; automation removes dosing errors at far higher cost and delay | evaluation_max_2: weighs low-cost immediate kaizen savings against high-cost permanent automation

Benefit 2: Less obsolete stock [k], tackling the $38,000 of parts stored over 8 months [app], reducing write-off risk and freeing cash for development [an].

Wrenthorpe Clothing Co makes workwear garments in Country X, employing 58 machinists paid by output. Orders come mainly from construction companies. The floor manager proposes cell production, arranging workstations into U-shaped cells so each cell completes a garment in one area. The owner warns the change would disrupt the busy spring season and cost $9,000 in layout work. A pilot cell could trial the layout first. They must agree the plan before the new spring contract of 11,000 garments begins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'efficiency'.
    Answer: Producing a given level of output using the minimum possible resources, such as time, labour and materials, with no unnecessary waste [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: minimum input/resources for a given output; avoiding waste of time, labour or materials

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Wrenthorpe Clothing Co might introduce cell production.
    Answer: Reason 1: Cells cut motion waste [k], removing much of the 30 metres of walking each garment requires between 45 metres of cutting, sewing, pressing and packing benches [app]. Reason 2: Cells reduce defects [k], helping cut the 6% defect rate as each team checks a whole garment [app].
    Keywords: 30 metres, 6%, 45 metres, 58 machinists, U-shaped cells, cell production
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cells eliminate unnecessary movement/motion waste; cells improve quality through team ownership of each unit | application_max_2: 30 metres of walking per garment; 45 metres of floor; 6% defect rate; cutting, sewing, pressing and packing

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Wrenthorpe Clothing Co of cell production.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Less walking time [k], saving part of the 30 metres per garment across 45 metres of floor [app], so machinists sew more units within the spring contract of 11,000 garments [an]. Benefit 2: Better teamwork [k], as 58 machinists work in U-shaped cells around one area per garment [app], speeding communication and cutting errors [an].
    Keywords: 30 metres, 6%, 58 machinists, 11,000 garments, U-shaped cells, 45 metres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cells cut unnecessary movement, raising output per worker; cells strengthen teamwork and communication | application_max_2: 30 metres of walking per garment; 45 metres of floor; 58 machinists; 11,000 garments | analysis_max_2: more sewing time per shift raises output on the spring contract; tighter teams communicate faster and make fewer errors

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wrenthorpe Clothing Co should introduce cell production next month? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cell production would end the 30 metres of walking per garment [k], freeing sewing time across 45 metres of floor to support the spring contract of 11,000 garments [app], directly lifting output per machinist and cutting the 6% defect rate [an]. However, the change costs $9,000 and risks disrupting the busy spring season [k], when all 58 machinists must relearn layouts and output may dip [app], possibly missing early delivery deadlines [an]. Overall, Wrenthorpe should introduce cell production next month as a single pilot cell [eval], since $9,000 is recoverable through lower defects and walking time, and full rollout can follow the spring peak [eval].
    Keywords: $9,000, 11,000 garments, 30 metres, 6%, 58 machinists, 45 metres, cell production
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cells remove motion waste and improve team output; reorganisation carries cost and temporary disruption | application_max_2: 30 metres of walking per garment; 11,000 garments; $9,000 layout cost; 6% defect rate; 58 machinists | analysis_max_2: freed sewing time raises output for the spring contract; layout change risks missed deadlines during spring | evaluation_max_2: weighs long-run efficiency gain against short-term cost and disruption risk

--- STEM ---
Copperbeech Toys Ltd assembles wooden building sets in Country X, employing 41 workers on a flow production line. Timber supplies come from two local sawmills, and sales have grown steadily for four years. Inspectors check only finished boxes, and 7% of sets fail final inspection, so they are reworked at a cost of $5,600 a month. The operations manager proposes lean production cells with in-process checks at each stage, ending final-only inspection. The owner notes the change requires $24,000 of training and may slow throughput at first, with 41 workers learning new cell roles. Both options aim to protect the Christmas season. They must decide whether to reorganise before Christmas peak production begins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'flow production'.
    Answer: A production method in which products move continuously along a line or sequence of stages, used to make large volumes of identical items [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: continuous movement along a line/stages; used for large volumes of identical products

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Copperbeech Toys Ltd might switch to in-process checks at each stage.
    Answer: Reason 1: Defects are caught early [k], ending final-only inspection on a line where 7% of sets fail at the end [app]. Reason 2: Rework costs fall [k], cutting the $5,600 a month spent fixing rejected wooden building sets [app].
    Keywords: 7%, $5,600, 26,000 sets, flow production line, in-process checks, $980,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: in-process checks catch defects at the source; early detection reduces rework and scrap cost | application_max_2: 7% of sets fail final inspection; $5,600 a month; final-only inspection; wooden building sets

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Copperbeech Toys Ltd of switching to lean cells with in-process checks.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Lower rework cost [k], removing much of the $5,600 a month spent on the 7% of sets failing final inspection [app], which lifts margins on $980,000 of revenue [an]. Benefit 2: Smoother Christmas output [k], because stopping errors at each stage protects the flow toward 26,000 sets a year [app], avoiding bottlenecks before the peak [an].
    Keywords: 7%, $5,600, $24,000, 41 workers, 26,000 sets, Christmas
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: early quality checks cut rework and scrap; steady flow protects output at peak times | application_max_2: $5,600 a month; 7% of sets fail; $980,000 revenue; 26,000 sets a year | analysis_max_2: saved rework cost directly raises profit margins; fewer bottlenecks secure the Christmas order book

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Copperbeech Toys Ltd should reorganise into lean cells before Christmas? Justify your answer.
    Answer: In-process checks at each stage [k] would catch defects before the 7% that currently fail final inspection, saving $5,600 a month of rework on 26,000 sets a year [app], protecting the pre-Christmas build when demand is highest [an]. However, reorganisation requires $24,000 of training [k] and throughput may slow at first, with 41 workers learning new cell roles [app], risking short-term delays to the Christmas order book [an]. Overall, Copperbeech should reorganise before Christmas [eval], because letting 7% defects reach final inspection in peak season would be worse, and the $24,000 is repaid by about four to five months of rework savings [eval].
    Keywords: $24,000, $5,600, 7%, 26,000 sets, $980,000, 41 workers, in-process checks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: in-process inspection reduces defects and rework; reorganisation carries training cost and slower throughput at first | application_max_2: 7% failing final inspection; $5,600 a month; $24,000 training; 26,000 sets a year; 41 workers | analysis_max_2: saved rework cost protects margins during peak season; initial throughput dip risks Christmas deliveries | evaluation_max_2: weighs training cost and disruption against rework savings and peak-season quality

--- STEM ---
Wychwood Furniture Co is a private limited company in Country X making flat-pack wardrobe doors and drawer fronts for 12 furniture retailers. It has traded for 8 years and employs 34 workers, including 18 on manual cutting benches. Last year the company sold 240,000 doors at $28 each, earning revenue of $6,720,000, but 6% of doors failed quality checks and were reworked at a cost of $95,000.

The managers are comparing two options. Option A is to keep hand-cutting and add a second shift. Option B is to spend $900,000 on CAM-controlled CNC routers and edgebanders, which would replace 10 cutting jobs, raise output to 300,000 doors a year and cut the defect rate to 2%. The machines would cost $120,000 a year to maintain but save $210,000 a year in wasted board.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'computer-aided manufacturing (CAM)'.
    Answer: Computer-aided manufacturing is the use of computer-controlled machines and software to carry out production processes such as cutting and assembly, rather than doing them by hand. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAM = use of computers and software to control manufacturing machinery and processes; CAM programs guide machines such as CNC routers and edgebanders automatically

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Wychwood Furniture Co of using CAM-controlled machines.
    Answer: Benefit 1: CAM machines cut and edge doors to the same measurements every time, removing human error [k]. The defect rate would fall from 6% of doors to 2%, saving costly rework [app]. Benefit 2: CAM-controlled routers work continuously and faster than hand cutting [k]. Output would rise from 240,000 doors a year to 300,000, helping Wychwood serve its 12 retailers [app].
    Keywords: Wychwood Furniture Co, 6% of doors, 2%, 240,000 doors, 300,000, CAM-controlled CNC routers, 12 furniture retailers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAM gives consistent, accurate output and removes human error; CAM machines work faster and continuously, raising output | application_max_2: Defect rate falls from 6% to 2%, cutting rework costs; Output rises from 240,000 to 300,000 doors a year for 12 retailers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Wychwood Furniture Co could face if it buys the CAM-controlled machines.
    Answer: Problem 1: The machines are expensive to buy and run [k]. Option B costs $900,000 plus $120,000 a year in maintenance, a heavy outlay for one factory [app]. If sales stay flat, these fixed costs may take years to recover and strain cash flow [an]. Problem 2: CAM removes labour from the cutting benches [k]. Replacing 10 cutting jobs from 34 workers would make staff redundant [app]. Redundancy payments and lower morale among remaining workers could reduce productivity [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $900,000, $120,000 a year, 10 cutting jobs, 34 workers, Option A, $210,000 a year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: High capital and running costs for CAM equipment; CAM machines replace manual jobs, leading to redundancies | application_max_2: Option B costs $900,000 plus $120,000 a year in maintenance; 10 cutting jobs would be replaced from 34 workers | analysis_max_2: Fixed costs rise, squeezing profit and cash flow if sales do not grow; Redundancy costs and lower morale can reduce productivity and damage the workforce

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wychwood Furniture Co should buy the CAM-controlled machines rather than add a second shift? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Case for Option B: CAM would make production faster and more accurate [k]. Output would rise from 240,000 to 300,000 doors a year while defects fall from 6% to 2%, and the $210,000 a year board saving less $120,000 a year maintenance still leaves about $90,000 a year before rework savings [app]. Lower unit costs would let Wychwood price competitively and win larger orders from its 12 retailers [an]. Case for Option A: keeping hand-cutting avoids the $900,000 investment and protects the 10 cutting jobs [k]. A second shift keeps 18 manual benches running with no redundancy costs, but the 6% defect rate would stay [app]. Staying manual would keep rework at $95,000 a year and leave Wychwood vulnerable to rivals with fewer defects [an]. Overall, Wychwood should buy the CAM machines because the defect saving and $210,000 annual board saving outweigh the maintenance cost and the 10 lost jobs [eval]. If retailer demand weakens, the company could lease rather than buy the machines outright [eval].
    Keywords: Wychwood Furniture Co, Option A, Option B, $900,000, $210,000 a year, $120,000 a year, 6%, 12 furniture retailers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAM gives faster, more consistent production than hand methods; Keeping manual cutting avoids capital cost and redundancies | application_max_2: Output rises to 300,000 doors; defects fall from 6% to 2%; $210,000 board saving less $120,000 maintenance; Option A avoids $900,000 spend; $95,000 a year rework cost would continue; 18 manual benches kept | analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs improve competitiveness and retailer orders; Manual operation preserves rework cost burden and weaker quality position | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation based on stem figures (defect saving and $210,000 outweigh costs); Condition suggested for the alternative (lease if demand weakens)

====================================================================================================
PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U4_SET_122
UNIT: Unit 4: Operations Management
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Ondara Convenience Stores is a private limited company operating 4 convenience stores in Country X for 6 years. It employs 58 staff and earns annual sales revenue of $9.6 million. Each store relies on handwritten stock books, and a full stock-take takes 2 days per store every month. Shrinkage from theft and missing stock costs the company $84,000 a year.

The owners are comparing two options. Option A is to keep the manual system and hire 1 part-time stock clerk per store at $19,000 a year each. Option B is to spend $260,000 on EPOS tills linked to a central stock database, which scan every sale and reorder stock automatically, cutting shrinkage by 60% and reducing the monthly stock-take to 4 hours per store.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'electronic point of sale (EPOS)'.
    Answer: Electronic point of sale is a computerised till system that scans barcodes, records each sale and updates sales and stock records automatically at the checkout. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: EPOS = computerised till that records sales electronically; Linked to stock records so inventory updates automatically

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Ondara Convenience Stores of installing EPOS tills.
    Answer: Benefit 1: EPOS records every sale instantly, so stock figures are always up to date [k]. Reordering would be automatic, replacing the 2 days per store monthly stock-take with a 4 hours per store task [app]. Benefit 2: EPOS creates a detailed sales record that helps ordering decisions [k]. Shrinkage of $84,000 a year would be expected to fall by 60%, saving about $50,400 a year [app].
    Keywords: Ondara Convenience Stores, $84,000 a year, 60%, 2 days per store, 4 hours per store, $260,000, 4 convenience stores
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: EPOS keeps stock records accurate and current in real time; Detailed sales data supports better ordering and pricing decisions | application_max_2: Monthly stock-take falls from 2 days to 4 hours per store; Shrinkage of $84,000 reduced by 60% (about $50,400 a year saved)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Ondara Convenience Stores could face if it installs EPOS tills.
    Answer: Problem 1: EPOS requires a large upfront payment [k]. Option B costs $260,000, a big outlay for a business earning $9.6 million a year [app]. If the system underperforms, the money is hard to recover and cash flow suffers [an]. Problem 2: Staff must learn to use the new system [k]. With 58 staff across 4 stores, training and early till errors could frustrate customers [app]. Poor training could slow service and lose regular shoppers [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $260,000, $9.6 million, 58 staff, 4 convenience stores, Option A, $19,000 a year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: EPOS needs a large upfront capital payment; Staff require training to operate EPOS correctly | application_max_2: Option B costs $260,000 against $9.6 million annual revenue; 58 staff across 4 stores need retraining and support | analysis_max_2: High fixed investment reduces liquidity and financial flexibility; Disruption and customer frustration during changeover could offset savings

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ondara Convenience Stores should install EPOS tills rather than hire stock clerks? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Case for EPOS: EPOS automates sales recording and reordering [k]. It would cut shrinkage by 60% (about $50,400 a year from $84,000) and turn the 2 days per store stock-take into a 4 hours per store task, while 4 clerks would cost $76,000 a year (4 x $19,000) [app]. Accurate, live stock data would help Ondara avoid empty shelves across its 4 stores [an]. Case for clerks: Option A avoids the $260,000 outlay and keeps records checked by people who know each store [k]. Four part-time clerks at $19,000 a year each would cost $76,000 a year and could also serve customers, but would not cut shrinkage or speed up tills [app]. Clerks alone leave the shrinkage problem and the 2-day stock-takes untouched [an]. Overall, Ondara should install EPOS because the $50,400 shrinkage saving plus avoided clerk costs of $76,000 a year (about $126,400 in total) recovers the $260,000 outlay in roughly 2 years [eval]. If staff are unsure about the system, the owners could trial EPOS in 1 store first [eval].
    Keywords: Ondara Convenience Stores, Option A, Option B, $260,000, $19,000 a year, $84,000 a year, 60%, 4 convenience stores
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: EPOS automates sales recording and stock reordering; Manual clerks keep records but cannot prevent shrinkage electronically | application_max_2: 60% shrinkage cut (~$50,400 of $84,000), stock-take falls from 2 days to 4 hours per store; 4 clerks at $19,000 each = $76,000 a year vs Option B $260,000 outlay | analysis_max_2: Live stock data reduces stockouts and over-ordering across stores; Clerks retain old problems (shrinkage, slow stock-takes), weakening the manual option | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (save ~$126,400 a year, recovery in about 2 years); Suggestion to de-risk the decision (trial in one store first)

--- STEM ---
Breckfield Pump Works is a private limited company in Country X making water pumps for farms for 11 years. It employs 85 workers and produces 1,400 pumps a month. Annual sales revenue is $11.2 million. Errors between the design office and the factory floor mean 8% of pumps need reworking before dispatch.

The directors are choosing between two options. Option A is to keep the existing separate CAD and CAM machines with 2 standalone inspection stations. Option B is to spend $2.4 million on a CIM system linking the design office, 6 CNC machines, automated scanners and the stock control database, which would cut rework from 8% to 3% and raise output to 1,750 pumps a month. Training 12 staff would cost $36,000.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM)'.
    Answer: Computer-integrated manufacturing is the linking of all production stages - design, machining, quality inspection and stock control - into one computer-controlled system that shares information automatically. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CIM links design, production, inspection and stock in one computer system; Information flows automatically between stages without manual paperwork

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Breckfield Pump Works of installing a CIM system.
    Answer: Benefit 1: CIM shares design data directly with the machines, removing manual re-entry [k]. Rework would fall from 8% of pumps to 3%, saving materials and labour [app]. Benefit 2: Linking all stages in one system speeds up the whole production flow [k]. Output would rise from 1,400 pumps a month to 1,750 pumps a month, a 25% increase [app].
    Keywords: Breckfield Pump Works, 8% of pumps, 3%, 1,400 pumps a month, 1,750 pumps a month, 6 CNC machines, $2.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CIM removes manual data transfer errors between design and production; An integrated flow speeds up the process from planning to dispatch | application_max_2: Rework falls from 8% to 3% of pumps; Output rises from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps a month (a 25% increase)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Breckfield Pump Works could face if it installs a CIM system.
    Answer: Problem 1: CIM costs a great deal of money up front [k]. Option B requires $2.4 million plus $36,000 to train 12 staff [app]. Borrowing that sum would add interest payments and raise financial risk for the company [an]. Problem 2: CIM depends on all its linked parts working together [k]. A fault in 1 of the 6 CNC machines or in the shared database could stop the whole line [app]. One breakdown could halt deliveries to farm customers and breach supply commitments [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $2.4 million, $36,000, 12 staff, 6 CNC machines, Option A, 85 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CIM requires very high capital investment and training spend; Integrated systems can fail as a whole if one component breaks | application_max_2: Option B costs $2.4 million plus $36,000 to train 12 staff; 6 CNC machines and one shared database are all linked together | analysis_max_2: High borrowing increases interest burden and financial risk; A single-point failure could stop production and lose farm customer contracts

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Breckfield Pump Works should install the CIM system rather than keep the separate machines? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Case for CIM: CIM links design, machining, inspection and stock in 1 system [k]. It would cut rework from 8% to 3% and raise output from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps a month, a 25% increase on $11.2 million of revenue [app]. Fewer errors and higher output would raise profit and let Breckfield take on more farm contracts [an]. Case for keeping separate machines: Option A avoids the $2.4 million cost and the $36,000 training bill [k]. The existing CAD and CAM machines and 2 inspection stations already work, so there is no disruption or retraining [app]. Staying with separate machines keeps the 8% rework rate and the 1,400 pumps a month output limit [an]. Overall, Breckfield should install CIM, because cutting rework from 8% to 3% and lifting output by 25% outweighs the upfront cost over time [eval]. The directors could phase the system in over 12 months to limit disruption [eval].
    Keywords: Breckfield Pump Works, Option A, Option B, $2.4 million, $36,000, 8% to 3%, 1,750 pumps a month, $11.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CIM integrates all stages to cut errors and speed flow; Separate machines avoid capital cost and retraining | application_max_2: Rework falls from 8% to 3%; output rises from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps (+25%) on $11.2 million revenue; Option A avoids $2.4 million and $36,000 training; 8% rework and 1,400 pumps limit remain | analysis_max_2: Lower rework and higher output raise profit and capacity for farm contracts; Keeping separate machines preserves status quo inefficiencies and output ceiling | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (rework and 25% output gain outweigh cost); Practical phasing suggestion to reduce risk (12-month phased rollout)

--- STEM ---
Sandpiper Bakery Co is a private limited company in Country X supplying supermarket loaves for 9 years. It employs 46 staff working 6 days a week and bakes 90,000 loaves a week. Weekly fixed costs are $28,000 and total variable costs are $36,000. The wholesale price is $1.10 per loaf and hand-wrapping damages 2% of loaves every week.

The family owners are comparing two options. Option A is to keep hand-wrapping and hire 6 extra wrapping staff at $400 a week each. Option B is to buy an automated wrapping line for $720,000, which seals 140 bags a minute, halves the damage rate to 1% and replaces 9 hand-wrapping jobs earning $420 a week each. The line would need $54,000 a year in maintenance.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'automation'.
    Answer: Automation is the use of machines and computer-controlled systems to carry out tasks previously done by people, with little or no human involvement. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation = machines doing tasks with little or no human input; Often computer-controlled and capable of continuous running

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Sandpiper Bakery Co of buying the automated wrapping line.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Automated wrapping machines work continuously and consistently [k]. The line seals 140 bags a minute and would halve the damage rate from 2% of loaves to 1% [app]. Benefit 2: Automation cuts the number of workers needed for wrapping [k]. Replacing 9 jobs earning $420 a week each would save $3,780 a week in wages [app].
    Keywords: Sandpiper Bakery Co, 140 bags a minute, 2% of loaves, 1%, 9 hand-wrapping jobs, $420 a week, 90,000 loaves a week
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation gives consistent output and fewer damaged products; Automation replaces labour, lowering wage costs | application_max_2: Damage rate halves from 2% to 1% of 90,000 loaves a week; 9 jobs at $420 a week saved = $3,780 a week

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Sandpiper Bakery Co could face if it buys the automated wrapping line.
    Answer: Problem 1: The line is expensive to purchase [k]. Option B costs $720,000 plus $54,000 a year in maintenance [app]. Heavy fixed outlays reduce profit in the early years and increase the risk if supermarket orders fall [an]. Problem 2: Automation would make 9 hand-wrapping workers redundant [k]. Losing 9 of 46 staff could lead to redundancy payments and lower morale among the rest [app]. The remaining team may resist the change, slowing production [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $720,000, $54,000 a year, 9 hand-wrapping jobs, 46 staff, Option A, $400 a week
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation needs a large capital purchase and running costs; Automation makes workers redundant | application_max_2: Option B costs $720,000 plus $54,000 a year in maintenance; 9 of 46 staff would lose their jobs | analysis_max_2: High fixed costs squeeze early profit and cash flow; Redundancy costs and resistance may slow production and hurt quality

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sandpiper Bakery Co should buy the automated wrapping line rather than hire 6 extra wrapping staff? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Case for the automated line: automation removes human error and works faster than people [k]. It seals 140 bags a minute, halves damage from 2% to 1% of 90,000 loaves and saves $3,780 a week on 9 jobs (plus about $990 a week in avoided wasted loaves) [app]. Lower unit costs would protect Sandpiper's margins when selling at $1.10 per loaf to supermarkets [an]. Case for hiring staff: Option A keeps jobs and avoids the $720,000 purchase and $54,000 annual maintenance [k]. Six extra staff at $400 a week each cost only $2,400 a week and preserve flexibility if orders change [app]. Hand-wrapping keeps damage at 2% and delivers nowhere near the consistency of 140 bags a minute [an]. Overall, Sandpiper should buy the automated line, because $3,780 a week wage savings plus reduced waste exceed the $2,400 weekly cost of extra staff [eval]. If the family fears supermarket demand dropping, leasing the line could reduce the risk [eval].
    Keywords: Sandpiper Bakery Co, Option A, Option B, $720,000, $54,000 a year, 140 bags a minute, 90,000 loaves a week, $1.10 per loaf
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation is faster and more consistent than manual work; Manual hiring avoids capital outlay and keeps flexibility | application_max_2: Line seals 140 bags/minute, halves damage 2% to 1%, saves $3,780 a week on 9 jobs; 6 staff at $400 a week = $2,400 a week; avoids $720,000 and $54,000 a year maintenance | analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs protect margins on $1.10 supermarket loaves; Manual option keeps 2% damage and weaker consistency | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (wage savings plus waste reduction exceed extra staff cost); Suggestion to reduce risk (lease the line if demand is uncertain)

--- STEM ---
Sorrel & Main Fashion Co is a private limited company in Country X making school uniforms for 20 schools for 14 years. Option B is to spend $140,000 on CAD software and 2 workstations, plus $18,000 a year in licences, which would cut pattern preparation from 2 weeks to 2 days and reduce cutting waste from 9% to 6% of fabric.

  Qb [4 marks]

Benefit 2: CAD nests pattern pieces efficiently on screen to cut fabric waste [k]. Cutting waste would fall from 9% to 6% of fabric, saving about $27,000 a year on $900,000 of fabric [app].
    Keywords: Sorrel & Main Fashion Co, 2 weeks to 2 days, 9% to 6%, $900,000, 20 schools, 3 pattern cutters, $140,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAD improves accuracy and consistency of designs; CAD reduces material waste through efficient layouts | application_max_2: Pattern time falls from 2 weeks to 2 days across 20 schools; Waste falls from 9% to 6%, about $27,000 saved a year on $900,000 fabric spend

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Sorrel & Main Fashion Co could face if it adopts CAD.

These set-up and running costs cut profit in the early years [an]. Problem 2: CAD depends on computers working [k]. If a workstation fails, pattern work stops until repaired and cutting cannot start without patterns [app]. Delays would hold up uniform deliveries to 20 schools and risk school contracts [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $140,000, $18,000 a year, 3 pattern cutters, 2 workstations, Option A, 52 machinists
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAD needs capital spend, annual licences and retraining; CAD output depends on working hardware and software | application_max_2: Option B costs $140,000 plus $18,000 a year in licences and 3 retrained cutters; Failure of 1 of the 2 workstations would stop all pattern work | analysis_max_2: Fixed set-up costs reduce early profit margins; System failure delays cutting, risking late deliveries and school contracts

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sorrel & Main Fashion Co should adopt CAD rather than keep hand-drawn patterns? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Case for CAD: CAD creates designs on screen that can be changed instantly [k]. It would cut pattern preparation from 2 weeks to 2 days and reduce waste from 9% to 6%, saving about $27,000 a year on $900,000 of fabric [app]. Faster turnaround and less waste would raise profit on school uniform orders worth part of $7.3 million of revenue [an]. Case for hand-drawn patterns: Option A avoids the $140,000 cost and the $18,000 yearly licences [k]. The 3 pattern cutters already serve 20 schools and need no retraining or computers [app]. Hand methods keep the 2-week pattern cycle and the 9% waste rate, so savings stay slow to arrive [an]. Overall, Sorrel & Main should adopt CAD, because pattern time cut from 2 weeks to 2 days and about $27,000 a year in fabric savings outweigh licence costs [eval]. The directors could buy 1 workstation first to test staff acceptance [eval].
    Keywords: Sorrel & Main Fashion Co, Option A, Option B, $140,000, $18,000 a year, 2 weeks to 2 days, 9%, $900,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAD speeds up and improves accuracy of pattern design; Hand-drawn patterns avoid capital cost and retraining | application_max_2: Pattern time 2 weeks to 2 days; waste 9% to 6%; about $27,000 a year saved on $900,000 fabric; Option A avoids $140,000 and $18,000 yearly licences; 3 cutters serve 20 schools already | analysis_max_2: Faster turnaround and lower waste raise profit on $7.3 million revenue; Hand methods preserve slow 2-week cycle and 9% waste, limiting savings | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (time and $27,000 fabric saving); Practical low-risk first step suggested (trial one workstation)

--- STEM ---
Warrenfield Farm Shops is a private limited company running 3 farm shops in rural Country X for 7 years, selling milk, cheese, eggs and preserves. It employs 24 staff and average monthly sales revenue is $85,000 per shop. Fresh stock is ordered by hand from notebook records and 12% of fresh stock is thrown away each month as unsold waste.

The owners are comparing two options. Option A is to keep handwritten records and add 1 ordering day per week per shop. Option B is to spend $96,000 on EPOS tills with a stock-control system that tracks sales in real time and suggests reorder quantities, expected to cut fresh-stock waste from 12% to 5% of stock and shrinkage by 40%. Some loyal cash-paying customers rarely use cards.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'stock control'.
    Answer: Stock control is the process of ordering, storing and monitoring a business's stock so it has enough to meet customer demand without holding too much. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Stock control = managing the ordering, holding and monitoring of inventory; Aim is the right stock at the right time with minimum waste

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Warrenfield Farm Shops of installing EPOS with stock control.
    Answer: Benefit 1: EPOS records every sale as it happens [k]. Stock levels would update in real time, so notebook records are replaced and reordering becomes automatic [app]. Benefit 2: Live sales data shows exactly what sells [k]. Fresh-stock waste would fall from 12% to 5% of stock across the 3 farm shops [app].
    Keywords: Warrenfield Farm Shops, 12% of fresh stock, 5% of stock, 3 farm shops, $85,000 per shop, real time, $96,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: EPOS gives accurate, up-to-date stock records in real time; Sales data allows automated, needs-based reordering | application_max_2: Fresh-stock waste falls from 12% to 5% of stock; Real-time tracking replaces handwritten notebook records in 3 shops

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Warrenfield Farm Shops could face if it installs EPOS.
    Answer: Problem 1: EPOS tills cost money to buy and run [k]. Option B requires $96,000, a large sum for 3 rural shops earning $85,000 a month each [app]. The outlay may take years to recover from waste savings [an]. Problem 2: Some customers pay cash and rarely use cards [k]. EPOS could make loyal cash-paying customers feel unwelcome or unable to pay as before [app]. Lost goodwill in small rural communities could cut sales sharply [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $96,000, 3 farm shops, $85,000, Option A, 24 staff, 12% of fresh stock
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: EPOS needs significant upfront and ongoing investment; EPOS may not suit customers who prefer paying cash | application_max_2: Option B costs $96,000 against 3 shops earning $85,000 a month each; Loyal cash-paying customers rarely use cards at these rural shops | analysis_max_2: High fixed outlay strains cash flow of small rural shops; Alienating cash customers risks losing loyal local sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Warrenfield Farm Shops should install EPOS rather than keep handwritten records? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Case for EPOS: EPOS links the till to live stock records [k]. It would cut monthly fresh-stock waste from 12% to 5% and shrinkage by 40% across 3 shops averaging $85,000 in sales each month [app]. Better stock data would cut waste costs and free staff from notebooks to serve customers [an]. Case for handwritten records: Option A costs nothing and keeps ordering simple for 24 staff [k]. Adding 1 ordering day per week per shop would catch waste earlier without new technology [app]. Handwritten records also keep personal contact with local suppliers, but waste would stay near 12% and shrinkage untracked [an]. Overall, Warrenfield should install EPOS, because waste falling from 12% to 5% saves far more than an extra ordering day costs [eval]. The owners could keep notebook records as backup and train staff gradually to retain loyal cash customers [eval].
    Keywords: Warrenfield Farm Shops, Option A, Option B, $96,000, 12% of fresh stock, 5% of stock, 40%, $85,000 per shop
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: EPOS gives real-time stock visibility and automated reordering; Manual records cost nothing but keep errors and waste | application_max_2: Waste falls 12% to 5%, shrinkage cut by 40%, across 3 shops at $85,000 monthly sales each; Option A adds 1 ordering day per week per shop, no capital cost, 24 staff unchanged | analysis_max_2: Lower waste and shrinkage directly protect profit margins; Manual system leaves 12% waste and shrinkage untracked | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (waste saving outweighs ordering-day cost); Suggestion to de-risk (keep notebook backup, train staff gradually)

Amberdale Dye Works is a private limited company in Country X dyeing wool and cotton yarn for knitwear factories for 10 years.   Qb [4 marks]

Benefit 2: Machines can work longer and more evenly than hand-stirring [k]. Batches of 400 kg would be dyed more consistently, lifting output quality for knitwear customers [app].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Machines repeat precise settings, improving consistency; Mechanisation raises output per worker and allows longer running | application_max_2: Reject costs fall 70%, about $50,400 a year saved from $72,000; 400 kg batches dyed more consistently for knitwear factories

    Keywords: Option B, $480,000, $45,000 a year, 2 fewer dye hands, 30 workers, Option A, $5.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Mechanisation requires large capital and running costs; Mechanisation reduces the number of workers required | application_max_2: Option B costs $480,000 plus $45,000 a year in maintenance; 2 fewer dye hands out of 30 workers would be needed | analysis_max_2: High fixed costs reduce profit and strain cash flow; Redundancy payments and lost skills could hurt early quality and morale

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Mechanisation gives exact, repeatable process control; Retraining avoids capital cost and keeps jobs | application_max_2: Rejects fall 70% (~$50,400 saved), wages drop $34,000, net about $39,400 after $45,000 maintenance; Option A avoids $480,000, keeps 30 workers, but $72,000 reject cost persists | analysis_max_2: Net annual savings and consistency strengthen competitiveness with knitwear factories; Manual retraining leaves high reject costs and weaker consistency | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (net $39,400 plus 70% reject cut outweighs retraining); Practical transition suggestion (keep one manual vat for delicate batches)

--- STEM ---
Glen Carrick Water Co is a private limited company in Country X bottling spring water for 5 years. It employs 28 workers on 2 shifts and bottles 1.2 million litres a month, selling at $0.55 per litre. Annual revenue is $7.92 million and capping and labelling are done by hand, with 4% of bottles leaking at the cap.

The board is comparing two options. Option A is to hire 8 extra bottle-hand workers at $16,000 a year each to raise output to 1.5 million litres a month. Option B is to invest $1.1 million in an automated capping and labelling line, replacing 6 jobs, cutting leaks from 4% to under 1%, raising output to 1.8 million litres a month and costing $85,000 a year to run.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'productivity'.
    Answer: Productivity is a measure of how efficiently a business uses its resources, usually output per worker or output per unit of input over a given time. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Productivity = output per worker or per unit of input over time; Higher productivity means more output from the same resources

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Glen Carrick Water Co of installing the automated line.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The line works continuously without fatigue or error [k]. Leaking caps would fall from 4% of bottles to under 1%, cutting wasted water and complaints [app]. Benefit 2: Automation raises output with no extra labour [k]. Output would rise from 1.2 million to 1.8 million litres a month, a 50% increase [app].
    Keywords: Glen Carrick Water Co, 4% of bottles, under 1%, 1.2 million litres, 1.8 million litres, 28 workers, $1.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automated lines run continuously with consistent quality; Automation raises output per worker sharply | application_max_2: Leaks fall from 4% to under 1% of bottles; Output rises from 1.2 million to 1.8 million litres a month (+50%)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Glen Carrick Water Co could face if it installs the automated line.
    Answer: Problem 1: The line requires a very large investment [k]. Option B costs $1.1 million to buy plus $85,000 a year to run [app]. High fixed costs raise financial risk if sales growth slows [an]. Problem 2: 6 jobs would be replaced [k]. Making 6 of 28 workers redundant means redundancy payments and staff resentment [app]. Negative publicity or disputes could harm the company's local reputation [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $1.1 million, $85,000 a year, replacing 6 jobs, 28 workers, Option A, $16,000 a year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation needs a very large capital outlay and running costs; Automation replaces existing worker jobs | application_max_2: Option B costs $1.1 million plus $85,000 a year to run; 6 of 28 workers would be made redundant | analysis_max_2: High fixed costs increase financial risk if demand slows; Redundancies cost money and could harm morale and local reputation

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Glen Carrick Water Co should invest in the automated line rather than hire 8 more workers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Case for the automated line: automation means machines doing work once done by people [k]. At $0.55 per litre the extra 0.6 million litres a month is worth about $3.96 million a year in revenue at full capacity [an]. Output would still rise to 1.5 million litres a month (+25%) and 36 workers keep their jobs with morale high [app]. Leaks would stay near 4% and capacity stays below the automated option [an]. If demand is uncertain, the board could phase installation over 6 months [eval].
    Keywords: Glen Carrick Water Co, Option A, Option B, $1.1 million, 1.8 million litres, 1.5 million litres, $0.55 per litre, 4% of bottles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation raises output with minimal labour and high consistency; Manual hiring avoids capital outlay and protects jobs | application_max_2: Output 1.2m to 1.8m litres (+50%); leaks 4% to under 1%; $85,000 a year running cost; Option A adds 8 workers at $16,000 = $128,000 a year, output 1.5m litres (+25%) | analysis_max_2: Extra 0.6 million litres a month is about $3.96 million a year revenue at $0.55 per litre; Manual option leaves 4% leaks and lower capacity ceiling | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (+50% output and leak reduction); Risk mitigation suggested (phase installation over 6 months)

--- STEM ---
Ferrymead Packaging Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making printed cardboard boxes for toy makers for 13 years. It employs 44 workers. Box designs are drawn by hand and test prototypes take 3 weeks to make. 7% of prototypes fail customer tests, wasting about $45,000 a year in board and printing. Last year revenue was $6.1 million.

The owners are comparing two options. Option A is to keep hand-drawing and build prototypes in-house as now. Option B is to spend $220,000 on CAD box design plus CAM to drive a cutting table, which would cut prototype time from 3 weeks to 3 days, reduce prototype failures from 7% to 2% and let customers approve designs on screen. Licences and running costs would be $38,000 a year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'production'.
    Answer: Production is the process of converting inputs such as land, labour, capital and enterprise into goods and services that can be sold to customers. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Production = turning inputs/resources into goods and services; It combines the factors of production to create output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Ferrymead Packaging Ltd of using CAD and CAM.
    Answer: Benefit 1: CAD lets designs be edited on screen and approved instantly [k]. Prototype time would fall from 3 weeks to 3 days and customers can approve designs on screen [app]. Benefit 2: A CAM cutting table follows the CAD design exactly [k]. Prototype failures would fall from 7% to 2%, saving about $32,000 a year in wasted board and printing [app].
    Keywords: Ferrymead Packaging Ltd, 3 weeks to 3 days, 7% to 2%, $45,000 a year, $220,000, $6.1 million, 44 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAD allows instant digital editing and customer approval of designs; CAM reproduces CAD designs exactly, reducing errors | application_max_2: Prototype time falls from 3 weeks to 3 days; Failures fall from 7% to 2%, saving about $32,000 a year of $45,000 waste

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Ferrymead Packaging Ltd could face if it adopts CAD and CAM.
    Answer: Problem 1: CAD and CAM cost money to buy and run [k]. Option B needs $220,000 up front plus $38,000 a year in licences and running costs [app]. These fixed set-up costs reduce profit in the early years on $6.1 million of revenue [an]. Problem 2: Workers must learn new skills [k]. The 44 workers, used to hand-drawing, would need training on CAD software and the CAM cutting table [app]. Training time and early mistakes could delay orders for toy-maker customers [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $220,000, $38,000 a year, 44 workers, Option A, $6.1 million, 3 weeks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAD/CAM needs capital outlay plus annual licences and running costs; Staff need training to use CAD and CAM effectively | application_max_2: Option B needs $220,000 plus $38,000 a year in licences and running costs; 44 workers used to hand-drawing need retraining | analysis_max_2: Fixed set-up costs reduce early profitability; Training disruption and early errors could delay customer orders

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ferrymead Packaging Ltd should adopt CAD and CAM rather than keep hand-drawn designs? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Case for CAD and CAM: CAD lets designs be edited, stored and shared digitally [k]. Prototype time would fall from 3 weeks to 3 days, failures from 7% to 2% and waste from $45,000 to about $13,000 a year [app]. Faster approval cycles would help Ferrymead win repeat orders from toy makers beyond the current $6.1 million revenue [an]. Case for hand-drawing: Option A avoids the $220,000 investment and the $38,000 yearly licence costs [k]. Existing hand skills keep prototypes flexible for unusual one-off boxes with no computer dependence [app]. Hand-drawing keeps the 3-week prototype cycle and the $45,000 a year waste burden [an]. Overall, Ferrymead should adopt CAD and CAM, because prototypes cut from 3 weeks to 3 days and about $32,000 a year waste saving outweigh licence costs [eval]. In quiet seasons the firm could run fewer CAM hours to keep costs down [eval].
    Keywords: Ferrymead Packaging Ltd, Option A, Option B, $220,000, $38,000 a year, 3 weeks to 3 days, $45,000 a year, $6.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: CAD/CAM gives fast digital design, approval and exact cutting; Hand-drawing avoids capital and licence costs and keeps flexibility | application_max_2: Prototypes 3 weeks to 3 days; failures 7% to 2%; waste falls from $45,000 to about $13,000 a year; Option A avoids $220,000 and $38,000 yearly licences; hand skills kept | analysis_max_2: Faster approval and lower waste improve competitiveness and revenue growth; Hand-drawing keeps the 3-week cycle and $45,000 yearly waste burden | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (time saving plus about $32,000 waste saving); Suggestion to scale usage sensibly (fewer CAM hours in quiet seasons)

--- STEM ---
Norbury Fasteners Co is a private limited company in Country X making steel bolts and rivets for bridge builders for 15 years. It employs 70 workers across 3 shifts and produces 18 million fasteners a year, with annual revenue of $8.4 million. Quality inspectors currently check only 10% of bolts by hand and miss 3% of faulty fasteners.

The directors are comparing two options. Option A is to hire 4 more inspectors at $24,000 a year each to raise manual checking to 20% of output. Option B is to spend $650,000 on an automated optical inspection system checking 100% of fasteners at 2,000 per minute, cutting escape faults from 3% to 0.5%, replacing 5 inspector jobs ($130,000 a year in wages) and costing $60,000 a year in maintenance.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'efficiency'.
    Answer: Efficiency is the ability to produce the maximum output from the resources used, minimising waste of time, materials and effort. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Efficiency = most output from given resources with least waste; Higher efficiency lowers unit costs and raises competitiveness

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Norbury Fasteners Co of installing automated optical inspection.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The system checks every fastener rather than a sample [k]. Inspection would rise from 10% of bolts to 100% of output, at 2,000 per minute [app]. Benefit 2: Automated optics are far more reliable than the human eye [k]. Escape faults would fall from 3% to 0.5%, protecting bridge-builder customers [app].
    Keywords: Norbury Fasteners Co, 10% of bolts, 100% of fasteners, 2,000 per minute, 3%, 0.5%, 18 million fasteners
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automated inspection checks 100% of output, not samples; Machine vision is more accurate and consistent than humans | application_max_2: Inspection rises from 10% of bolts to 100% at 2,000 per minute; Escape faults fall from 3% to 0.5% across 18 million fasteners a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Norbury Fasteners Co could face if it installs the automated system.
    Answer: Problem 1: The system is a major purchase [k]. Option B costs $650,000 plus $60,000 a year in maintenance [app]. Heavy fixed costs reduce profit if fastener demand from bridge projects weakens [an]. Problem 2: 5 inspector jobs would be replaced [k]. Making 5 of 70 workers redundant costs redundancy payments and may cause disputes [app]. Losing experienced inspectors could hurt quality if the system needs recalibration [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $650,000, $60,000 a year, replacing 5 inspector jobs, 70 workers, Option A, $130,000 a year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automated systems need large capital and maintenance spend; Automation replaces existing worker jobs | application_max_2: Option B costs $650,000 plus $60,000 a year in maintenance; 5 of 70 workers (inspector jobs worth $130,000 a year) would be replaced | analysis_max_2: High fixed costs increase financial risk when demand is weak; Redundancies cost money and risk skill loss for recalibration and edge cases

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Norbury Fasteners Co should install the automated inspection system rather than hire 4 more inspectors? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Case for the automated system: automation replaces human checks with machine precision [k]. It would inspect 100% of 18 million fasteners at 2,000 per minute and cut escape faults from 3% to 0.5%, while saving $130,000 a year in inspector wages [app]. Reliable quality would protect contracts with bridge builders and cut rejects and returns [an]. Case for hiring inspectors: Option A avoids the $650,000 outlay and adds only $96,000 a year in wages (4 workers at $24,000) [k]. Manual checking would rise to 20% of output, yet 80% of fasteners would still go unchecked [app]. Extra inspectors keep human judgement for difficult cases but leave escape faults far above 0.5% [an]. Overall, Norbury should install the automated system, because checking 100% of output and cutting escape faults sixfold outweigh the $650,000 cost over time [eval]. If a major bridge contract is won or lost, the directors could lease the system [eval].
    Keywords: Norbury Fasteners Co, Option A, Option B, $650,000, 100% of fasteners, 3% to 0.5%, 2,000 per minute, $130,000 a year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Automation checks every unit with machine precision; Manual hiring is cheaper upfront but samples only | application_max_2: 100% inspection at 2,000 per minute; faults 3% to 0.5%; $130,000 a year wage saving; Option A: $650,000 avoided; 4 inspectors at $24,000 = $96,000 a year; only 20% checked | analysis_max_2: Full-output inspection secures bridge-builder contracts and cuts return costs; Manual option leaves 80% of output unchecked and high escape faults | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (100% inspection and sixfold fault cut outweigh cost); Practical condition for the alternative (lease the system if demand is uncertain)

--- STEM ---
Marshfield Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making oak dining tables. It employs 26 carpenters and produced 1,950 tables last year, which is 75 per carpenter, generating revenue of $975,000 at an average price of $500 per table. The business holds $96,000 of seasoned oak in storage to keep production running if suppliers are late, and it stores finished tables in a rented warehouse costing $700 per month.

Managing Director Ruth Ellison wants to raise output. One option is a $240,000 CNC routing machine that would cut sanding time by 40% and lift output per carpenter to 95 tables a year. The alternative is hiring 8 more carpenters at $21,600 each per year, which would raise total production to 2,550 tables a year, but the wage bill would increase permanently.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'productivity'.
    Answer: The output produced per worker, or per unit of input, over a given time period, showing how efficiently resources are used to produce goods or services [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: output per worker or per unit of input; measured over a given period of time

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Marshfield Furniture Ltd of increasing productivity.
    Answer: Reason 1: Higher productivity lowers the labour cost per table [k], because output per carpenter would rise to 95 tables a year at an average price of $500, spreading the same wage bill across more tables [app]. Reason 2: Higher productivity raises revenue and profit [k], because the $240,000 CNC routing machine lifts output per carpenter from 75 to 95 tables a year without any extra wages [app].
    Keywords: 95 tables a year, CNC routing machine, $240,000, 26 carpenters, $500, seasoned oak
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lowers unit or labour cost per item; higher revenue and profit from same inputs | application_max_2: 95 tables a year; $500 per table; $240,000; CNC routing machine

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Marshfield Furniture Ltd holds inventories.
    Answer: Reason 1: Holding inventories keeps production running without interruption [k], because $96,000 of seasoned oak is stored so carpenters are not idle if timber suppliers are late [app], which protects delivery dates and customer orders since the carpenters remain fully employed [an]. Reason 2: Holding finished-goods inventories lets the business meet sudden demand [k], so tables made in advance can be dispatched quickly from the rented warehouse costing $700 per month [app], which avoids losing sales when customers want immediate delivery [an].
    Keywords: seasoned oak, $96,000, rented warehouse, $700 per month, 75 per carpenter, $500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ensures uninterrupted production; helps meet sudden or unexpected demand | application_max_2: $96,000 seasoned oak; rented warehouse; $700 per month | analysis_max_2: protects delivery dates and customer orders; avoids lost sales when customers want immediate delivery

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marshfield Furniture Ltd should buy the CNC routing machine rather than hire 8 more carpenters? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the CNC routing machine would raise productivity [k]; output per carpenter would rise from 75 to 95 tables a year, so 26 carpenters would make 2,470 tables worth $1,235,000 at $500 each [app], lowering unit labour cost and helping repay the $240,000 investment [an]. Hiring 8 more carpenters would raise production instead [k]; 34 carpenters at 75 tables a year would make 2,550 tables worth $1,275,000 [app], but wages would permanently rise by $172,800 a year and productivity per carpenter would stay flat [an]. Overall, the CNC machine is the better option because it raises output per worker rather than adding permanent wages [eval], and its $240,000 one-off cost is cheaper than $172,800 of extra wages every year while demand for oak tables stays steady [eval].
    Keywords: CNC routing machine, 8 more carpenters, $21,600, 95 tables a year, $240,000, 2,550 tables a year, $500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: productivity gains versus simply hiring more inputs; permanent wage costs versus one-off investment | application_max_2: 95 tables a year; $500; $240,000; $21,600 each per year; 2,550 tables a year | analysis_max_2: unit labour cost falls and repays the investment; permanent wage rise of $172,800 a year versus one-off machine cost | evaluation_max_2: weighs productivity versus production and judges one-off cost preferable; justified overall recommendation with reference to figures

--- STEM ---
Dunwick Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing dried pasta. It employs 60 staff and produced 720,000 packs last year, which is 12,000 packs per employee, generating revenue of $2.88 million at $4 per pack. The firm supplies 24 regional supermarkets and orders flour weekly from a single supplier. The business made a profit of $96,000 last year, a margin of about 3.3%.

The supplier offers an 8% discount on any single order above 400 tonnes of flour, saving Dunwick $28,800 on its 500-tonne annual usage. Storing the extra flour would require a rented silo costing $1,350 per month, insurance of $240 per month and a one-off security upgrade of $3,000, and $360,000 of working capital would be tied up in the flour.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'inventory'.
    Answer: Goods and materials a business holds in stock, including raw materials, work in progress and finished goods, held to support production and sales [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: goods and materials held in stock; includes raw materials, work in progress and finished goods

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Dunwick Foods Ltd might hold a flour inventory.
    Answer: Reason 1: A flour inventory ensures uninterrupted production [k], because holding 400 tonnes would keep the pasta lines running even if the weekly delivery from the single supplier were late [app]. Reason 2: Buying in bulk cuts material costs [k], because the supplier's 8% discount saves $28,800 on a 400-tonne order against its 500-tonne annual usage [app].
    Keywords: 400 tonnes, 8% discount, $28,800, 500-tonne annual usage, 12,000 packs, single supplier
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ensures uninterrupted production; bulk-buy discounts reduce costs | application_max_2: 400 tonnes; 8% discount; $28,800; 500-tonne annual usage

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs Dunwick Foods Ltd would face if it held a large flour inventory.
    Answer: Cost 1: Storage and security costs reduce profit [k], because the rented silo would cost $1,350 per month and insurance $240 per month, around $19,080 a year [app], which eats into the $28,800 discount and squeezes a 3.3% profit margin [an]. Cost 2: Capital tied up in stock cannot be used elsewhere [k], because $360,000 of working capital would be locked in flour instead of paying suppliers or wages [app], which could force Dunwick to delay other payments or borrow at interest [an].
    Keywords: $1,350 per month, $240 per month, $360,000, 400 tonnes, $28,800, $3,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: storage and security costs; capital tied up in stock | application_max_2: $1,350 per month; $240 per month; $360,000; $3,000 security upgrade | analysis_max_2: storage costs eat into the discount and margin; capital unavailable for other uses or borrowing needed

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Dunwick Foods Ltd should place the one-off 400-tonne bulk order to gain the 8% discount? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Placing the bulk order would cut costs [k]; the 8% discount saves $28,800 a year on flour for a firm making 720,000 packs [app], leaving about $9,720 after the $19,080 of storage and insurance, and it secures supply from a single supplier [an]. However, the order ties up resources [k]; $360,000 of working capital would be locked in flour and the one-off $3,000 security upgrade adds to first-year cost [app], which could strain cash flow even though pasta keeps well and will not become obsolete quickly [an]. Overall, Dunwick should place the order [eval], because the first-year net gain is still positive at $6,720 ($28,800 - $19,080 - $3,000) and the saving repeats every year while the flour will not spoil quickly [eval].
    Keywords: 8% discount, $28,800, $1,350 per month, $240 per month, $360,000, $3,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cost saving from bulk discount versus cash-flow strain; risk of tying up a large amount of working capital | application_max_2: $28,800; 8% discount; $360,000; $3,000 | analysis_max_2: net saving after storage is about $9,720 a year; first-year net gain is $6,720 after the security upgrade | evaluation_max_2: justified decision to place the order given the positive net gain; acknowledges the cash-flow risk but concludes positively

--- STEM ---
Saltwick Electronics Ltd is a manufacturer of electric fans in Country X. It employs 75 workers and assembled 15,000 fans last year, which is 200 fans per worker, generating revenue of $1.5 million at $100 per fan. It sells through 15 electrical wholesalers across Country X and made a profit of $120,000 last year. Its electric motors are imported from overseas with a 10-week lead time.

The board must decide how many motors to store. A large order of 9,000 motors would cost $90,000 and attract a 12% discount, saving $10,800, but next year's models may use a redesigned motor, making current stock obsolete. Storage costs $640 per month and security $150 per month, and $90,000 of working capital would be tied up in the motors.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'production'.
    Answer: The process of converting inputs such as labour, materials and machinery into goods or services that can be sold to customers [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: converting inputs into goods or services; inputs include labour, materials and machinery

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Saltwick Electronics Ltd might hold a large inventory of electric motors.
    Answer: Reason 1: Motors ensure uninterrupted production [k], because with a 10-week lead time the factory cannot wait months if the overseas supplier is late or short of stock [app]. Reason 2: Motors help meet sudden demand [k], because if a hot summer drove orders above the 200 fans per worker expected output, fans could be assembled immediately from stock [app].
    Keywords: 10-week lead time, 200 fans per worker, 15,000 fans, 9,000 motors, electric fans, wholesalers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ensures uninterrupted production; helps meet sudden demand | application_max_2: 10-week lead time; 200 fans per worker; 15,000 fans

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs Saltwick Electronics Ltd would face if it held 9,000 motors.
    Answer: Cost 1: Storage and security costs reduce profit [k]; the motors would cost $640 per month to store and $150 per month to secure, about $9,480 a year [app], which absorbs nearly all of the $10,800 discount on the $1.5 million fan business [an]. Cost 2: Obsolescence risk [k]; if next year's models use a redesigned motor, the 9,000 motors could become unsellable [app], forcing Saltwick to write off up to $90,000 of stock and erase the saving [an].
    Keywords: $640 per month, $150 per month, $10,800, 9,000 motors, $1.5 million, $90,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: storage and security costs; obsolescence risk on stock | application_max_2: $640 per month; $150 per month; $10,800; 9,000 motors | analysis_max_2: storage absorbs nearly all of the discount; write-off risk if the model is redesigned

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Saltwick Electronics Ltd should order the 9,000 motors to gain the 12% discount? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Ordering the 9,000 motors would secure supply and save money [k]; the 12% discount is worth $10,800 off the $90,000 order [app], covering roughly a year of storage ($9,480) and protecting fan output ahead of peak summer sales [an]. However, the order is risky [k]; storage and security cost $790 a month and next year's redesigned motor could make the whole stock obsolete [app], which would write off $90,000 for a saving of only $10,800 [an]. Overall, Saltwick should not place the full order [eval], because the downside is far larger than the upside - losing $90,000 outweighs the $1,320 net annual benefit after storage costs [eval].
    Keywords: 9,000 motors, 12% discount, $10,800, $90,000, $640 per month, $150 per month, redesigned motor
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guaranteed supply and discount benefit; obsolescence risk is asymmetric | application_max_2: $10,800; $90,000; $640 per month; $150 per month | analysis_max_2: discount barely covers a year of storage ($9,480); potential $90,000 write-off for a $10,800 saving | evaluation_max_2: asymmetric risk, reject the full order; justified overall recommendation with reference to figures

  Qb [4 marks]
