Reason 2: Finished goods protect valuable orders [k], because the dresses are worth $450,000 at the selling price and being late risks the retailer cancelling the order [app].
    Keywords: 9,000 summer dresses, 1 June, $450,000, 240 per machinist, 28,800 garments, summer lines

  Qc [6 marks]

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: storage and security costs; obsolescence of unsold stock | application_max_2: $1,800 per month; $400 per month; after August; 9,000 summer dresses | analysis_max_2: around $6,600 over three months cuts margin; write-off risk exceeds the holding cost

  Qd [8 marks]

However, holding them carries costs [k]; warehouse and security charges of $2,200 per month from March to May plus the risk that dresses unsold after August become obsolete [app], which adds cost to a business with an $108,000 annual profit [an]. Overall, Brimfield should manufacture the dresses in advance [eval], because missing the June deadline could cost the entire $450,000 order and the $6,600 three-month holding cost is small in comparison [eval].
    Keywords: 9,000 summer dresses, 1 June, $450,000, $1,800 per month, $400 per month, after August, weekly batches
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: securing the order versus holding costs; late delivery risks losing the contract | application_max_2: 1 June; $450,000; $1,800 per month; after August | analysis_max_2: weekly batches risk missing the deadline; $6,600 holding cost is small against the $450,000 order | evaluation_max_2: weighs deadline security against holding costs; justified overall recommendation with reference to figures

--- STEM ---
Kettleworth Canning Co is a manufacturer of tinned tomatoes and sweet corn in Country X. It employs 80 cannery workers and produced 4.8 million tins last year, which is 60,000 tins per worker, generating revenue of $6 million at an average of $1.25 per tin. Its tins are sold to 9 supermarket chains across the country, and its profit last year was $210,000. Its single tinplate supplier has a 12-week delivery lead time.

Last winter a 3-week supply interruption stopped line two and cost Kettleworth about 40,000 tins of lost output, worth $50,000. Operations director Maria Santos proposes raising the reserve from the current 2 weeks to 6 weeks of raw materials. This would cost $2,100 per month extra storage, $350 per month extra insurance, and tie up $480,000 of working capital.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two reasons why businesses hold inventories.
    Answer: To keep production running without interruption if supplies are delayed; to meet sudden or unexpected demand from customers [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ensures uninterrupted production; helps meet sudden or unexpected demand

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Kettleworth Canning Co should increase its raw material reserve to 6 weeks.
    Answer: Reason 1: A larger reserve prevents production stoppages [k], because the single tinplate supplier has a 12-week delivery lead time and one 3-week interruption already stopped line two [app]. Reason 2: A larger reserve protects revenue [k], because last winter's interruption cost 40,000 tins of lost output, worth $50,000 at $1.25 a tin [app].
    Keywords: 12-week delivery lead time, line two, 40,000 tins, $50,000, $1.25, 9 supermarket chains
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: prevents production stoppages; protects revenue and output | application_max_2: 12-week delivery lead time; line two; 40,000 tins; $50,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs of raising the reserve from 2 weeks to 6 weeks.
    Answer: Cost 1: Extra storage costs reduce profit [k]; the 6-week reserve adds $2,100 per month of storage and $350 per month of insurance, about $29,400 a year [app], which is more than half of last winter's $50,000 loss repeated within a single year [an]. Cost 2: Capital tied up [k]; raising the reserve from 2 weeks to 6 weeks locks up $480,000 of working capital [app], which cannot be used for new lines or repairs and might have to be borrowed at interest [an].
    Keywords: $2,100 per month, $350 per month, $480,000, 6 weeks, line two, 4.8 million tins
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: extra storage and insurance costs; capital tied up in stock | application_max_2: $2,100 per month; $350 per month; $480,000; 6 weeks | analysis_max_2: about $29,400 a year, more than half the prior loss; capital unavailable for other uses or borrowing needed

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kettleworth Canning Co should raise its raw material reserve from 2 weeks to 6 weeks? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising the reserve would protect production and revenue [k]; a 6-week reserve covers supplier delay and avoids a repeat of last winter's 3-week stoppage that cost 40,000 tins worth $50,000 [app], which exceeds the extra holding cost of $29,400 a year [an]. However, the reserve is not free [k]; storage and insurance cost $2,450 per month and $480,000 of working capital would be tied up in tinplate and tomatoes [app], and the money could instead earn interest or fund line two while a second supplier is found [an]. Overall, Kettleworth should raise the reserve [eval], because one avoided stoppage saves $50,000 against $29,400 a year of holding costs, and with 12-week lead times another delay is likely, not rare [eval].
    Keywords: 6 weeks, 12-week delivery lead time, 40,000 tins, $50,000, $480,000, $2,100 per month, $350 per month
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: protection of production versus opportunity cost of capital; alternative uses of funds | application_max_2: $50,000; 40,000 tins; $480,000; $2,100 per month | analysis_max_2: holding cost of $29,400 is below one stoppage loss of $50,000; capital could earn interest or fund repairs elsewhere | evaluation_max_2: justified decision to raise the reserve; weighs risk of stockouts against holding costs

--- STEM ---
Aldenbrook Print Co is a commercial printing business in Country X producing catalogues and leaflets. It employs 30 print operators and produced 1.8 million catalogues last year, which is 60,000 per operator, generating revenue of $720,000 at $0.40 per copy. The presses run one shift a day and it sells to over 200 local firms. The business made a profit of $61,200 last year.

A national retailer has offered an order for 900,000 catalogues over 6 months, worth $360,000. Aldenbrook can take it by running its current presses on overtime at time and a half, costing an extra $54,000 in wages, or invest $150,000 in a second-hand press that would raise output per operator by 30% but needs a full year to install and train staff.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two ways a business could increase productivity.
    Answer: Investing in new or better machinery and technology; training workers or improving their skills [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: new or better machinery and technology; training workers to improve skills

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why higher productivity matters to Aldenbrook Print Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: Higher productivity lowers cost per catalogue [k], because producing 60,000 catalogues per operator at $0.40 per copy spreads wages across more output [app]. Reason 2: Higher productivity wins more business [k], because raising output per operator by 30% helps Aldenbrook fulfil the retailer's 900,000-catalogue order worth $360,000 [app].
    Keywords: 60,000 per operator, $0.40 per copy, 900,000 catalogues, $360,000, output per operator by 30%, 1.8 million catalogues
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower unit cost per item; win orders and compete | application_max_2: 60,000 per operator; $0.40 per copy; output per operator by 30%; 900,000 catalogues

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Aldenbrook Print Co of investing in the second-hand press.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The press raises productivity [k]; output per operator would rise by 30% to about 78,000 catalogues a year with no extra wages [app], which lowers unit costs and increases profit on every copy printed [an]. Benefit 2: The press adds long-term capacity [k]; once installed, the one-off $150,000 cost compares favourably with the $54,000 overtime premium that recurs whenever orders spike [app], so Aldenbrook can take repeat work such as the retailer's $360,000 order at lower marginal cost [an].
    Keywords: $150,000, second-hand press, output per operator by 30%, $54,000, $360,000, 900,000 catalogues
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: productivity gain lowers unit cost; long-term capacity versus recurring overtime | application_max_2: output per operator by 30%; $150,000; $54,000; $360,000 | analysis_max_2: about 78,000 catalogues per operator lowers unit cost; one-off press cost versus recurring overtime premium

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Aldenbrook Print Co should invest in the second-hand press rather than use overtime? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing in the press would raise productivity permanently [k]; output per operator would rise by 30% to about 78,000 catalogues a year [app], cutting the labour cost of future retailer work without time and a half on every shift [an]. However, overtime suits the immediate order better [k]; the press costs $150,000 and needs a full year to install and train staff, while the retailer needs 900,000 catalogues within 6 months [app], so the overtime premium of $54,000 is far cheaper now and keeps the presses busy immediately [an]. Overall, Aldenbrook should use overtime rather than rush into the press [eval], because the immediate order is only $360,000 and the $96,000 difference between the two options can be kept as cash now, with the press worth buying later if the retailer renews the contract [eval].
    Keywords: second-hand press, $150,000, $54,000, 900,000 catalogues, $360,000, overtime, output per operator by 30%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: permanent productivity versus flexible overtime; timing of the order versus installation lead time | application_max_2: $150,000; $54,000; 900,000 catalogues; $360,000 | analysis_max_2: 30% rise means about 78,000 catalogues per operator; $96,000 difference keeps cash in the business now | evaluation_max_2: weighs short-term cash and timing against long-term productivity; justified overall recommendation with reference to figures

--- STEM ---
Holloway Toys Ltd is a toy manufacturer in Country X, run by owner Gary Whitmore. It employs 60 workers and produced 480,000 toys last year, which is 8,000 per worker, generating revenue of $2.4 million at an average of $5 per toy. Around 70% of its annual sales take place in November and December, and last Christmas stockouts cost an estimated $30,000 in lost sales.

For next Christmas the board forecasts orders of 320,000 toys in the peak two months. It can build the toys from August onwards and store them in a warehouse costing $2,600 per month with $500 per month extra insurance, or keep the current production rate and add night shifts in October and November at 25% above the normal hourly wage of $9.00, plus hire 15 casual workers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State the difference between production and productivity.
    Answer: Production is the total output of goods or services produced, whereas productivity is the output per worker or per unit of input over a given period [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: production is total output of goods or services; productivity is output per worker or per unit of input

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Holloway Toys Ltd might build a finished-goods inventory before Christmas.
    Answer: Reason 1: Building an inventory meets sudden seasonal demand [k], because the board forecasts orders of 320,000 toys in the peak two months, far above what normal production would cover [app]. Reason 2: An inventory prevents stockouts at the peak [k], because around 70% of annual sales fall in November and December and toys made from August would be ready, protecting the $30,000 of lost sales suffered last Christmas [app].
    Keywords: 320,000 toys, November and December, 70%, 480,000 toys, 8,000 per worker, $30,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: meets seasonal or sudden demand; prevents stockouts at the peak | application_max_2: 320,000 toys; November and December; $30,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs Holloway Toys Ltd would face from building this Christmas inventory from August.
    Answer: Cost 1: Storage and security reduce profit [k]; the warehouse costs $2,600 per month and extra insurance $500 per month, about $9,300 over three months [app], cutting the margin on 480,000 toys sold at an average of $5 [an]. Cost 2: Capital and obsolescence risk [k]; building the extra 160,000 toys beyond normal output ties up roughly $400,000 of working capital if each toy costs $2.50 to make [app], and toys that fall out of fashion cannot be sold next year [an].
    Keywords: $2,600 per month, $500 per month, 480,000 toys, $5 per toy, 320,000 toys, November and December
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: storage and insurance costs; capital tied up and obsolescence risk | application_max_2: $2,600 per month; $500 per month; 480,000 toys; $5 per toy | analysis_max_2: about $9,300 over August to October; roughly $400,000 of working capital locked in stock

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Holloway Toys Ltd should build the Christmas inventory from August rather than add night shifts in October and November? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Building the inventory from August would secure the peak [k]; toys ready before November allow Holloway to fill the 320,000-toy forecast in the peak two months [app], where current output would meet only about half, winning the peak revenue and keeping retailers loyal [an]. However, building stock early carries costs [k]; warehouse and insurance cost $2,600 and $500 per month respectively and about $400,000 of working capital would be tied up in extra toys [app], while night shifts at 25% above $9.00 an hour plus 15 casual workers flex cost only when demand arrives [an]. Overall, Holloway should build the inventory from August [eval], because the peak represents about 70% of annual sales worth roughly $1.68 million and the $9,300 three-month holding cost is tiny against losing that revenue [eval].
    Keywords: August, 320,000 toys, night shifts, $9.00, $2,600 per month, 70%, 25% above
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: securing the peak versus flexible overtime; cash tied up versus lost sales | application_max_2: 320,000 toys; $2,600 per month; $9.00; November and December | analysis_max_2: current output covers only about half of the forecast; peak represents about 70% of sales, roughly $1.68 million | evaluation_max_2: weighs holding cost against lost peak revenue; justified overall recommendation with reference to figures

--- STEM ---
Dunfell Dairy Ltd is a milk processing business in Country X, supplying 60 supermarkets. It employs 40 workers and processed 4 million litres of milk last year, which is 100,000 litres per worker, generating revenue of $3.2 million at $0.80 per litre. Fresh milk keeps for only 5 days, and the company holds 2 days of chilled output in its cold store.

The operations manager, Priya Shah, proposes raising the chilled inventory to 4 days to cover sudden demand from a new supermarket contract worth $180,000 a year. This would need a second cold room costing $5,400 a year to run, plus $260 per week of extra power, and unsold milk that passes its date is written off, which wastage already reached $22,000 last year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'obsolescence'.
    Answer: When inventory can no longer be sold because it is out of date, spoiled or replaced by a newer design, so it has to be written off [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: inventory becomes out of date or unusable; has to be written off and cannot be sold

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Dunfell Dairy Ltd holds 2 days of chilled milk inventory.
    Answer: Reason 1: Chilled inventory ensures uninterrupted supply [k], because holding 2 days of output covers the gap between pasteurising and delivery even if a supermarket order arrives suddenly [app]. Reason 2: Chilled inventory meets sudden demand [k], because the new supermarket contract worth $180,000 a year could be supplied faster than 5 days of shelf life would allow extra production [app].
    Keywords: 2 days, $180,000, 5 days, chilled, $0.80 per litre, 60 supermarkets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ensures uninterrupted supply; helps meet sudden demand | application_max_2: 2 days; $180,000; 5 days

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs of raising the chilled inventory from 2 days to 4 days.
    Answer: Cost 1: Higher running costs reduce profit [k]; the second cold room costs $5,400 a year plus $260 per week of extra power, around $18,920 a year [app], which cuts margins on 4 million litres sold at $0.80 per litre [an]. Cost 2: Greater wastage and obsolescence [k]; milk passing its 5-day date is written off and wastage already reached $22,000 last year [app], so holding 4 rather than 2 days raises the risk of unsold, date-expired milk [an].
    Keywords: $5,400, $260 per week, $22,000, 5 days, 4 million litres, $0.80 per litre
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher running costs of cold storage; greater waste and write-off risk | application_max_2: $5,400; $260 per week; $22,000; 5 days | analysis_max_2: about $18,920 a year against margins on $3.2 million of sales; longer chilled cover raises the write-off risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Dunfell Dairy Ltd should raise its chilled inventory from 2 days to 4 days? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising the chilled inventory would help win the supermarket contract [k]; 4 days of cover lets Dunfell supply the new customer worth $180,000 a year reliably [app], far outweighing the $18,920 of added cold-room and power costs [an]. However, higher stock risks more waste [k]; milk keeps only 5 days and wastage hit $22,000 last year [app], so if demand does not materialise, extra chilled litres could be written off rather than sold [an]. Overall, Dunfell should raise the inventory to 4 days [eval], because the potential $180,000 contract is nearly ten times the $18,920 holding cost, and the spoilage risk can be managed with strict stock rotation and sales forecasts [eval].
    Keywords: 4 days, $180,000, 5 days, $22,000, $5,400, $260 per week
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: contract security versus spoilage risk; opportunity cost of cold-room spending | application_max_2: $180,000; $5,400; $260 per week; 5 days | analysis_max_2: contract is nearly ten times the $18,920 holding cost; spoilage risk can be managed with rotation and forecasting | evaluation_max_2: justified decision to raise the chilled inventory; weighs contract value against spoilage risk

--- STEM ---
Barrowfield Builders Merchants is a building materials supplier in Country X, selling cement, blocks and timber to 340 trade customers, including 12 housebuilders. It employs 25 staff and sold 2,600 tonnes of cement last year, generating revenue of $780,000 at $300 per tonne. The business stores cement in a rented yard costing $1,950 per month.

Its supplier offers a 10% discount on any single order above 1,000 tonnes. At the purchase price of $250 per tonne, a 1,000-tonne order would save $25,000, but the yard would need extending at $3,600 per month plus $550 per month extra security, security staff would patrol the yard nightly, and $250,000 of working capital would be tied up in cement that damp could spoil. Extra forklift handling would also be needed at the yard.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline two benefits to a business of increasing productivity.
    Answer: Lowers unit or labour cost per item so profit margins improve; allows the business to produce more with the same resources, meeting customer demand faster [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower unit or labour cost per item; more output from the same resources

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Barrowfield Builders Merchants might hold a large cement inventory.
    Answer: Reason 1: Cement stock keeps supply uninterrupted [k], because 340 trade customers expect immediate collection and running out loses regular trade to rival yards [app]. Reason 2: Cement stock meets sudden demand [k], because a 1,000-tonne order could be supplied from the yard straight away instead of waiting for the supplier [app].
    Keywords: 340 trade customers, 1,000-tonne order, $300 per tonne, 2,600 tonnes, housebuilders, rented yard
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: keeps supply uninterrupted; helps meet sudden demand | application_max_2: 340 trade customers; 1,000-tonne order; $300 per tonne

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs Barrowfield would face from the 1,000-tonne cement inventory.
    Answer: Cost 1: Storage and security costs reduce profit [k]; extending the yard would cost $3,600 per month and extra security $550 per month, about $49,800 a year [app], which is double the $25,000 discount being chased [an]. Cost 2: Capital tied up [k]; a 1,000-tonne order locks up $250,000 of working capital at $250 per tonne [app], which cannot fund other stock and may force borrowing at interest [an].
    Keywords: $3,600 per month, $550 per month, $250,000, 1,000-tonne order, $250 per tonne, $25,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: storage and security costs; capital tied up in stock | application_max_2: $3,600 per month; $550 per month; $250,000; $250 per tonne | analysis_max_2: about $49,800 a year, double the $25,000 discount; capital unavailable for other stock or borrowing needed

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Barrowfield Builders Merchants should place the 1,000-tonne bulk order to gain the 10% discount? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The bulk order would cut material costs [k]; the 10% discount saves $25,000 on a 1,000-tonne order at $250 per tonne [app], and guaranteed cement supply protects trade for 340 customers in a busy building market [an]. However, the holding costs exceed the saving [k]; yard extension and security cost $49,800 a year and $250,000 of working capital would be tied up in stock that damp could spoil [app], which is more than the $25,000 saved and far more than its current $1,950 per month yard rent [an]. Overall, Barrowfield should not place the full order [eval], because annual holding costs of $49,800 are nearly twice the $25,000 discount, so accepting the deal would reduce profit - unless the extension is needed for under 6 months or the supplier delivers in stages [eval].
    Keywords: 1,000-tonne order, 10% discount, $25,000, $250 per tonne, $3,600 per month, $550 per month, $1,950 per month
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bulk discount benefit versus holding costs; opportunity cost of tied-up capital | application_max_2: $25,000; $3,600 per month; $550 per month; $250,000 | analysis_max_2: $49,800 a year is nearly twice the $25,000 saving; extension would break even at about 6 months of holding costs | evaluation_max_2: justified rejection of the full bulk order; weighs discount against holding costs and spoilage risk

--- STEM ---
Corven Auto Components Ltd is a manufacturer of CNC-machined suspension knuckles in Country X. It employs 90 workers and produced 45,000 knuckles last year, which is 500 per worker, generating revenue of $8.1 million at $180 per knuckle. The company sells 70% of its output to one car assembly plant under a delivery contract with penalty clauses.

The plant allows no more than 2 late deliveries a year, and any line stoppage is charged at $2,000 per hour. Corven currently holds 3 weeks of finished knuckles. The stores manager proposes raising this to 6 weeks, adding 2,600 knuckles to stock, which means $2,900 per month extra storage, $380 per month extra security and $260,000 of working capital tied up. The plant is also considering a suspension redesign next year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two types of inventory a manufacturing business might hold.
    Answer: Raw materials; work in progress; finished goods (any two) [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: raw materials; work in progress or finished goods

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Corven Auto Components Ltd holds 3 weeks of finished knuckles.
    Answer: Reason 1: Finished stock keeps Corven within its contract terms [k], because the plant allows no more than 2 late deliveries a year and charges $2,000 per hour for any line stoppage [app]. Reason 2: Finished stock helps cover sudden demand [k], because 70% of sales go to one car assembly plant whose schedule can change at short notice [app].
    Keywords: 2 late deliveries, $2,000 per hour, 70%, 45,000 knuckles, 3 weeks, suspension knuckles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: stay within delivery contract terms; covers sudden demand from the customer | application_max_2: 2 late deliveries; $2,000 per hour; 70%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs of raising the finished-knuckle inventory from 3 weeks to 6 weeks.
    Answer: Cost 1: Storage and security costs reduce profit [k]; the extra 3 weeks add $2,900 per month of storage and $380 per month of security, about $39,360 a year [app], which is a permanent cost on an $8.1 million business [an]. Cost 2: Capital and obsolescence risk [k]; the extra 2,600 knuckles tie up about $260,000 of working capital at $100 each [app], and if the plant redesigns its suspension next year this stock could become unsellable and be written off [an].
    Keywords: $2,900 per month, $380 per month, 2,600 knuckles, $260,000, 3 weeks, $8.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: storage and security costs; capital tied up and obsolescence risk | application_max_2: $2,900 per month; $380 per month; 2,600 knuckles; $260,000 | analysis_max_2: about $39,360 a year is a permanent cost; redesign next year could write the stock off

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Corven Auto Components Ltd should raise its finished-parts inventory from 3 weeks to 6 weeks? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising the inventory would strengthen the contract [k]; 6 weeks of cover would cut the risk of late deliveries beyond the plant's limit of 2 a year, avoiding $2,000 per hour stoppage charges [app], and protecting 70% of revenue worth $5.67 million a year [an]. However, the extra stock is expensive and risky [k]; storage and security cost $39,360 a year and $260,000 would be tied up in 2,600 knuckles while the plant may redesign its suspension next year [app], which could write off the batch with no alternative buyer [an]. Overall, Corven should not raise the inventory to 6 weeks yet [eval], because the redesign risk could erase far more than the $39,360 annual saving on penalties, so keeping 3 weeks and agreeing tighter schedule-sharing with the plant is safer until the redesign decision is known [eval].
    Keywords: 6 weeks, 2 late deliveries, $2,000 per hour, 70%, $260,000, 2,600 knuckles, 3 weeks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: contract protection versus redesign and obsolescence risk; opportunity cost of tied-up capital | application_max_2: 2 late deliveries; $2,000 per hour; $260,000; 2,600 knuckles | analysis_max_2: protecting 70% of revenue, about $5.67 million a year; redesign could write off $260,000 of stock | evaluation_max_2: justified decision to hold at 3 weeks until redesign known; weighs penalty risk against obsolescence risk

--- STEM ---
Kindred Vale Dairy Co is a private limited company in Country X founded 6 years ago by Renata Vidal. It bottles fresh milk and plain yoghurt for 25 local shops, employs 18 workers and produced 200,000 litres last year. Fixed costs were $120,000 and variable costs $0.40 per litre, giving an average cost of $1.00. It sells to local shops at $1.20 per litre.

A national supermarket chain has offered a three-year contract that would lift output to 320,000 litres a year. Fixed costs would rise only to $160,000, bulk buying of bottles and lids would cut variable costs by $0.05 per litre, and six extra staff would be needed. The supermarket would pay $1.05 per litre, and Renata must decide whether to sign the contract or keep supplying local shops.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'average cost'.
    Answer: Average cost is the total cost of production divided by the number of units produced, showing the cost of producing one unit of a good or service. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Average cost = total cost divided by output (cost per unit); Expressed as the cost of producing one unit of output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the supermarket contract could reduce Kindred Vale's average cost.
    Answer: Reason 1: The contract spreads fixed costs over a much larger output [k]. Fixed costs would rise only to $160,000 while output reaches 320,000 litres, so fixed cost per litre falls from $0.60 to $0.50 [app]. Reason 2: Bulk buying of bottles and lids is a purchasing economy of scale [k]. Cutting variable costs by $0.05 per litre lowers variable cost from $0.40 to $0.35, so average cost falls from $1.00 to $0.85 per litre [app].
    Keywords: Kindred Vale Dairy Co, 200,000 litres, 320,000 litres, $160,000, $0.05 per litre, $1.20 per litre, $1.05 per litre, bulk buying
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Spreading fixed costs over a larger output lowers average cost; Purchasing/bulk-buying economies lower variable cost per unit | application_max_2: Fixed costs $120,000 rising only to $160,000 while output reaches 320,000 litres (fixed cost per litre $0.60 to $0.50); Variable cost falls $0.40 to $0.35 per litre; average cost falls $1.00 to $0.85

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Kindred Vale should consider before signing the contract.
    Answer: Problem 1: The supermarket would pay only $1.05 per litre [k]. That is below the $1.20 paid by local shops, so each extra litre earns a smaller margin even though average cost falls [app], meaning Kindred Vale must sell far more litres just to lift total profit [an]. Problem 2: A bigger operation strains management [k]. Employing six extra staff alongside the single plant risks slower decisions and low morale among the 18 existing workers [app], which could cause mistakes and waste that push average cost back up [an].
    Keywords: Kindred Vale Dairy Co, 320,000 litres, $1.05 per litre, $1.20 per litre, 18 workers, $120,000, $0.40 per litre
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A lower price reduces the margin/profit earned per unit; Rapid growth can cause diseconomies of scale (poor communication, low morale, slow decision-making) | application_max_2: $1.05 supermarket price versus $1.20 paid by local shops; 18 existing workers with six extra staff needed at the single plant | analysis_max_2: Thinner margin per litre means many more litres must be sold to raise total profit; Poor coordination or low morale causes errors and waste, raising average cost

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kindred Vale Dairy Co should sign the three-year supermarket contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Signing the contract should spread fixed costs over a larger output [k]: average cost falls from $1.00 to $0.85 as output reaches 320,000 litres with fixed costs of $160,000 [app], so profit rises from $40,000 locally to about $64,000 a year, an extra $24,000 [an]. However, dependence on one buyer is risky [k]: the supermarket pays only $1.05 per litre versus $1.20 for local shops, and losing the contract after three years would leave Kindred Vale with a half-empty plant and committed fixed costs of $160,000 [app], which could push average cost back above $1.00 and threaten survival [an]. Overall [eval], the figures favour signing, provided the contract guarantees volumes for three years and the $0.05 saving from bulk buying is secured in writing [eval]; without those safeguards, Renata should expand more gradually.
    Keywords: Kindred Vale Dairy Co, 320,000 litres, $160,000, $1.05 per litre, $1.20 per litre, bulk buying, three-year contract
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Economies of scale: fixed costs spread over larger output lower average cost; Risk of over-dependence on a single large customer | application_max_2: 320,000 litres output, fixed costs $160,000, average cost $0.85 versus $1.00; $1.05 supermarket price versus $1.20 local; profit $40,000 rising to about $64,000 | analysis_max_2: Lower average cost at higher output lifts annual profit by about $24,000; Losing the contract leaves $160,000 fixed costs spread over fewer litres, sharply raising average cost | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures and reaches a justified position (sign with safeguards); Clear overall judgement linked to conditions, not a one-sided answer

--- STEM ---
Torvion Helmets Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making reinforced cycling helmets for export dealers. It employs 26 workers at its Briarport factory and produced 40,000 helmets last year. Fixed costs were $240,000, variable cost was $9 per helmet and each helmet sold for $17, giving an average cost of $15.00. Orders from two European distributors would fill extra capacity if Torvion could supply it.

The board is weighing two options. A new injection-moulding machine costing $600,000 would lift capacity to 60,000 helmets a year, cut variable cost to $7.50 and raise fixed costs to $330,000. Alternatively, Torvion could keep its three older presses and outsource up to 20,000 extra helmets a year at $12 each, paying only for units actually needed.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'fixed costs'.
    Answer: Fixed costs are costs that do not vary with the level of output in the short run, such as rent, insurance and lease payments, which must still be paid even if nothing is produced. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed costs do not change with the level of output in the short run; They must be paid even if output is zero (e.g. rent, leases, insurance)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages Torvion Helmets Ltd would gain from buying the new machine.
    Answer: Reason 1: It creates technical economies of scale [k]. The machine cuts variable cost from $9 to $7.50 per helmet and lifts capacity to 60,000 helmets, so average cost falls from $15.00 to $13.00 [app]. Reason 2: It spreads fixed costs over more units [k]. Although fixed costs rise to $330,000, spreading them over 60,000 helmets gives $5.50 each instead of $6.00 at 40,000 helmets [app].
    Keywords: Torvion Helmets Ltd, 40,000 helmets, 60,000 helmets, $600,000, $7.50, $12 each, Briarport, $330,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale: new machinery lowers unit production cost; Spreading higher fixed costs over greater output lowers fixed cost per unit | application_max_2: Variable cost falls $9 to $7.50; average cost falls $15.00 to $13.00 at 60,000 helmets; Fixed cost per helmet falls from $6.00 ($240,000/40,000) to $5.50 ($330,000/60,000)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Torvion might outsource helmets instead of buying the machine.
    Answer: Reason 1: It avoids heavy capital expenditure [k]. Outsourcing at $12 each means Torvion pays only for the extra units actually needed, so it keeps $600,000 rather than borrowing for a machine [app], protecting cash flow while the European distributors' orders are uncertain [an]. Reason 2: It avoids the risk of excess fixed costs [k]. Fixed costs of $330,000 would still be due even if the 60,000-helmet capacity went unfilled [app], and underused machinery would push average cost back above $13.00, wiping out the expected saving [an].
    Keywords: Torvion Helmets Ltd, $600,000, $12 each, $330,000, 60,000 helmets, $7.50, European distributors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Outsourcing avoids large capital outlay and preserves cash/liquidity; Unused capacity still incurs fixed costs, raising average cost | application_max_2: $12 each for outsourced helmets versus $600,000 machine cost; $330,000 fixed costs regardless of output; capacity of 60,000 helmets | analysis_max_2: Flexible output lets Torvion match supply to confirmed orders, protecting cash flow; If capacity is underfilled, fixed cost per helmet rises and the $2.00 unit saving disappears

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Torvion Helmets Ltd should buy the new injection-moulding machine? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the machine secures technical economies of scale [k]: variable cost falls from $9 to $7.50 and average cost from $15.00 to $13.00, adding $2.00 per helmet — about $120,000 a year at 60,000 helmets [app], more than repaying the $600,000 cost within five years [an]. However, demand could fall short [k]: if Torvion produced only 40,000 helmets a year, fixed costs of $330,000 spread over fewer units would push average cost to about $15.75 [app], worse than today's $15.00 and higher than the $12 outsourcing price for the marginal units [an]. Overall [eval], buying is justified if the two European distributors commit to volumes near 60,000 helmets; otherwise outsourcing at $12 each, which still leaves a $5.00 margin per helmet, is the safer option [eval].
    Keywords: Torvion Helmets Ltd, $600,000, 60,000 helmets, $7.50, $12 each, $330,000, $15.00, European distributors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale reduce variable and average cost per unit; Low demand spreads fixed costs over fewer units, raising average cost | application_max_2: Average cost falls $15.00 to $13.00; $2.00 saving worth about $120,000 a year at 60,000 helmets; At 40,000 helmets average cost would be about $15.75; outsourcing price $12 each | analysis_max_2: $120,000 annual saving would recover the $600,000 machine within five years; Underfilled capacity removes the $2.00 saving and can exceed current average cost | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and gives a justified, conditional recommendation; Clear overall judgement tied to demand commitments

UNIT: Unit 4: Operations Management

--- STEM ---
Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co is a private limited company in Country X producing tomato sauces and passata for 30 delicatessens. Founded 5 years ago, it employs 11 workers and makes 240,000 jars a year. Variable costs are $1.10 per jar, of which tomatoes account for $0.50. Fixed costs are $66,000 and jars sell at $2.00; own-label orders are growing quickly across all thirty delicatessens.

A growers' co-operative has offered a two-year contract for 120 tonnes of tomatoes at $800 per tonne, compared with $1,000 per tonne bought weekly, a saving of $24,000 a year. Deliveries would arrive quarterly, so Marazzi would lease cold storage at $10,000 a year, cutting the tomato portion of variable cost from $0.50 to $0.40 per jar.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'variable costs'.
    Answer: Variable costs are costs that change directly with the level of output, rising when more units are produced and falling when fewer are produced, such as raw materials, components and packaging. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Variable costs change with the level of output; Examples: raw materials, components, packaging, direct labour per unit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits the co-operative tomato contract could bring Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: It is a purchasing economy of scale [k]. Buying 120 tonnes at $800 per tonne instead of $1,000 saves $200 per tonne, worth $24,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: It lowers the variable cost of every jar [k]. The tomato portion falls from $0.50 to $0.40, so variable cost drops from $1.10 to $1.00 per jar and average cost falls from about $1.38 to about $1.32 [app].
    Keywords: Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co, 120 tonnes, $800 per tonne, $1,000 per tonne, $24,000 a year, $0.50, $1.10 per jar, cold storage
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Bulk purchasing earns lower prices (purchasing economies of scale); Lower variable cost per unit reduces average cost | application_max_2: $200 per tonne saving on 120 tonnes = $24,000 a year; Tomato portion of variable cost falls $0.50 to $0.40; variable cost $1.10 to $1.00 per jar; average cost about $1.38 to $1.32

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of signing the two-year tomato contract.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: It adds a new fixed cost [k]. Leasing cold storage at $10,000 a year must be paid even if jar sales fall below 240,000 [app], so the net saving drops to $14,000 and average cost rises if output dips [an]. Disadvantage 2: It locks Marazzi into one supplier [k]. If spot prices fall below $800 per tonne or the co-operative's quality slips, Marazzi must still honour the two-year deal [app], risking higher costs or inconsistent sauces across its 30 delicatessen customers [an].
    Keywords: Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co, $10,000 a year, 240,000 jars, $800 per tonne, 30 delicatessens, two-year contract, $1,000 per tonne
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: New fixed commitments must be paid regardless of output; Long-term supply contracts remove flexibility if prices or quality change | application_max_2: $10,000 a year cold-storage lease; output currently 240,000 jars; Fixed price $800 per tonne for two years; supplies 30 delicatessens | analysis_max_2: Fixed lease is unavoidable, so falling sales raise average cost and shrink the saving to $14,000; Lock-in risks paying above market price or poor quality, harming margins and reputation

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co should sign the two-year tomato contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Signing brings clear purchasing economies of scale [k]: the $200 per tonne saving is worth $24,000 a year, more than covering the $10,000 cold-store lease, so net costs fall by $14,000 a year [app] and profit rises from $150,000 to about $164,000, with average cost dropping to about $1.32 [an]. However, the two-year commitment is risky [k]: if tomato prices fall below $800 per tonne or demand from the 30 delicatessens weakens, the fixed lease and price would become a burden [app], and bulk quarterly deliveries could raise wastage, eroding the $0.10 saving per jar [an]. Overall [eval], the contract is worth signing because the saving exceeds the lease cost by $14,000 a year — about 9% extra profit — provided Marazzi negotiates quality guarantees and an exit clause before committing [eval].
    Keywords: Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co, $800 per tonne, $10,000 a year, $24,000 a year, 240,000 jars, $1.10 per jar, two-year contract
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Purchasing economies of scale reduce input and average costs; Fixed commitments and supplier lock-in create risk | application_max_2: $24,000 annual saving versus $10,000 lease; net $14,000 saving; Profit rises $150,000 to about $164,000; average cost falls to about $1.32 per jar | analysis_max_2: Net saving improves profit by about 9% and lowers variable cost per jar; Weak demand or falling spot prices could make the fixed lease and price uncompetitive | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified recommendation; Overall judgement with a clear condition (quality guarantee/exit clause)

UNIT: Unit 4: Operations Management

--- STEM ---
Peregrine Outdoor Co is a private limited company in Country X designing rucksacks and hiking jackets. It employs 34 staff at one factory and sold 90,000 units last year, earning revenue of $4.5 million. Fixed costs are $1.8 million, variable cost is $22 per unit, selling price is $50 and average cost is $42. Demand has grown by 15% a year for three years, and its two largest customers have asked about faster northern deliveries.

The board is considering a second northern factory, doubling capacity to 180,000 units a year. Fixed costs would rise to $3.24 million, while bulk buying of fabric would cut variable cost to $20 per unit. The board must weigh economies of scale against slower communication, duplicated management and integration costs across two sites.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'economies of scale'.
    Answer: Economies of scale are the cost advantages a business gains as it increases the scale of production, so that the average cost of each unit falls as output rises. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Average cost per unit falls as the scale/output of production increases; Examples: purchasing, technical, financial, marketing and managerial economies

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits Peregrine Outdoor Co would gain from economies of scale if it doubles capacity.
    Answer: Reason 1: Purchasing economies would lower variable cost [k]. Bulk buying of fabric cuts variable cost from $22 to $20 per unit, saving $2.00 on each of 180,000 units — $360,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Fixed costs are spread over more output [k]. Fixed costs rise only to $3.24 million, so the fixed cost per unit drops from $20 to $18 and average cost falls from $42 to $38 [app].
    Keywords: Peregrine Outdoor Co, 90,000 units, 180,000 units, $1.8 million, $3.24 million, variable cost to $20, average cost is $42
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Purchasing (bulk-buying) economies lower variable cost per unit; Spreading fixed costs over greater output lowers average cost | application_max_2: Variable cost $22 to $20; saving $2.00 x 180,000 units = $360,000 a year; Fixed cost per unit $20 to $18 ($1.8m/90,000 vs $3.24m/180,000); average cost $42 to $38

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Peregrine might face from operating two factories.
    Answer: Problem 1: Diseconomies of scale can emerge [k]. Slower communication between a northern site and head office, plus duplicated management, could delay decisions and cause errors [app], pushing average cost up instead of down [an]. Problem 2: Fixed costs nearly double [k]. Fixed costs rise to $3.24 million, so if demand fails to reach 180,000 units, the extra fixed cost is spread over fewer units [app], pushing average cost above $42 and reducing profit below $720,000 [an].
    Keywords: Peregrine Outdoor Co, $3.24 million, 180,000 units, 90,000 units, $1.8 million, average cost is $42, two sites
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Diseconomies of scale: poor communication, low morale, slow decision-making as firms grow; Higher fixed costs raise the output needed to cover them | application_max_2: Duplicated management and slower communication across two sites; Fixed costs $1.8 million rising to $3.24 million; capacity of 180,000 units | analysis_max_2: Delays and errors from weaker communication erode the cost savings of scale; If demand stays below 180,000 units, fixed cost per unit rises and the $4.00 saving is reversed

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Peregrine Outdoor Co should open the second northern factory? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Opening the factory secures economies of scale [k]: average cost falls from $42 to $38, a $4.00 saving per unit worth about $720,000 a year at 180,000 units [app], and profit could rise from $720,000 to about $2.16 million [an]. However, the gains depend on filling the extra capacity [k]: at only 90,000 units a year, fixed costs of $3.24 million would push average cost to about $56 [app], and duplicated management across two sites could cause diseconomies of scale, with slower decisions eroding the saving [an]. Overall [eval], the expansion is justified if the two largest customers commit to northern volumes and faster deliveries, since the $4.00 unit saving and delivery advantage outweigh moderate diseconomy risk; Peregrine should sign those orders before committing to the factory [eval].
    Keywords: Peregrine Outdoor Co, 180,000 units, $3.24 million, $4.5 million, average cost is $42, variable cost to $20, second northern factory, two largest customers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Economies of scale lower average cost as output rises; Diseconomies of scale and excess fixed costs threaten growth benefits | application_max_2: Average cost falls $42 to $38; saving worth about $720,000 a year at 180,000 units; profit could rise towards $2.16 million; At 90,000 units average cost would be about $56; fixed costs $3.24 million | analysis_max_2: $4.00 saving per unit and doubled capacity drive profit from $720,000 towards $2.16 million; Unfilled capacity makes fixed costs per unit rise, reversing the scale benefit | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and gives a justified, conditional recommendation; Clear overall judgement linked to securing customer commitments first

--- STEM ---
Ironbark Furniture Co is a private limited company in Country X making flat-pack and solid-oak wardrobes. It employs 38 workers at its Kilndown workshop and produced 6,500 wardrobes last year, earning revenue of $2.6 million. It sells through 15 furniture stores across the region. Owner Ray Castellane personally manages production, buying and sales. Profit was $325,000, fixed costs were $455,000 and variable cost was $280 per wardrobe, with oak prices rising 8% this year.

A national retail chain has offered a contract for 2,500 wardrobes a year at $380 each. Ray could hire a specialist operations director at $85,000 a year to run the enlarged factory, lifting output to 9,000 wardrobes, or decline the contract and remain owner-managed at the current scale.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'total cost'.
    Answer: Total cost is the complete cost of producing a given level of output, equal to fixed costs plus variable costs. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Total cost = fixed costs + variable costs; It rises as more units are produced because variable costs increase

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of hiring a specialist operations director.
    Answer: Reason 1: It creates a managerial economy of scale [k]. A dedicated operations director can plan 9,000 wardrobes a year and negotiate better buying deals for the retail chain order, relieving Ray Castellane of production decisions [app]. Reason 2: The fixed salary cost is spread over a larger output [k]. At $85,000 a year, the director costs only about $9.44 per wardrobe across 9,000 units [app].
    Keywords: Ironbark Furniture Co, 6,500 wardrobes, 9,000 wardrobes, $85,000 a year, operations director, $380 each, Kilndown, 2,500 wardrobes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Managerial economies of scale: specialist managers improve efficiency and decision-making; Fixed salary costs can be spread over greater output | application_max_2: Director manages the 2,500-wardrobe retail chain order plus current production, lifting output to 9,000; $85,000 salary spread over 9,000 wardrobes = about $9.44 per wardrobe

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of accepting the retail chain contract.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: The contract price is below the current selling price [k]. At $380 per wardrobe versus the $400 Ironbark earns now, it gives up $20 on each of the 2,500 contract wardrobes [app], so profit depends on tight cost control and high volume [an]. Disadvantage 2: A national chain demands reliability [k]. Supplying 2,500 wardrobes a year means late or faulty deliveries risk penalties and contract loss [app], which could add rework costs and damage Ironbark's reputation with other buyers [an].
    Keywords: Ironbark Furniture Co, $380 each, 2,500 wardrobes, $2.6 million, $455,000, Kilndown, national retail chain
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A lower contract price reduces the margin earned per unit; Large customers impose strict quality and delivery requirements, with penalties for failure | application_max_2: $380 contract price versus $400 current average selling price on 2,500 wardrobes; 2,500 wardrobes a year required under the retail chain contract | analysis_max_2: $20 lower price per unit means volume and efficiency must compensate to keep profit growing; Penalties or lost orders from missed deadlines could erase the extra profit entirely

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ironbark Furniture Co should hire the operations director and take the contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Hiring the director unlocks a managerial economy of scale [k]: fixed costs rise only to $540,000 while output reaches 9,000 wardrobes, so average cost falls from $350 to $340 [app] and profit rises from $325,000 to about $490,000, an extra $165,000 a year [an]. However, the chain pays just $380 per wardrobe — below the $400 Ironbark gets now [k] — and the $85,000 salary is payable even if the 2,500-unit order shrinks [app], so any cancellation or quality failure could quickly wipe out the gain and leave Ironbark with unwanted fixed costs [an]. Overall [eval], signing is justified because the $40 contract margin still beats the $340 average cost and the extra $165,000 outweighs the $85,000 salary risk, provided quality at the enlarged factory stays high enough to avoid penalties [eval].
    Keywords: Ironbark Furniture Co, $380 each, $85,000 a year, 9,000 wardrobes, 6,500 wardrobes, $455,000, national retail chain, operations director
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Managerial economies of scale improve decisions and lower average cost; Fixed commitments (salaries) and lower prices increase financial risk | application_max_2: Fixed costs rise to $540,000, average cost falls $350 to $340, profit rises $325,000 to $490,000; $380 contract price versus $400 current price; $85,000 salary; 2,500-unit order | analysis_max_2: $10 lower average cost across 9,000 units plus the extra volume lifts profit by about $165,000; Shrinkage or cancellation of the order leaves fixed costs underused, eroding profit | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified position; Clear overall judgement with an explicit condition (quality maintained)

--- STEM ---
Sorrel & Rye Milling Co is a partnership in Country X founded 7 years ago by sisters Priya and Nadia Menon. It mills 1,600 tonnes of plain flour a year for 40 bakeries, employs 24 workers and earns revenue of $1.2 million, selling at $750 per tonne; it supplies supermarkets' own-label bakeries as well as independents. Fixed costs are $190,000 and variable cost is $480 per tonne.

Wheat is bought weekly at $300 per tonne, about 2,080 tonnes a year. A growers' co-operative offers an annual contract for 2,000 tonnes at $270 per tonne, payable within 30 days, a saving of $60,000 a year. Quarterly deliveries would need extra silo space costing $500 a month, and Nadia wants lower input costs to protect margins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'purchasing economies of scale'.
    Answer: Purchasing economies of scale are the cost benefits gained when inputs are bought in bulk, because suppliers offer lower prices per unit on larger orders. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Bulk buying inputs lowers the price paid per unit; Example: discounts for large orders or annual contracts with suppliers

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits the co-operative wheat contract could bring Sorrel & Rye Milling Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: A lower input price [k]. Buying 2,000 tonnes at $270 instead of $300 saves $30 per tonne, or $60,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: A lower variable cost per tonne of flour [k]. The saving works out at about $37.50 per tonne of flour, cutting variable cost from $480 to about $442.50 and lowering average cost from $598.75 to $565 [app].
    Keywords: Sorrel & Rye Milling Co, 1,600 tonnes, 2,000 tonnes, $270 per tonne, $300 per tonne, $60,000 a year, $500 a month, plain flour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Purchasing economies: bulk contracts earn lower input prices; Lower variable cost per unit reduces average cost | application_max_2: $30 per tonne x 2,000 tonnes = $60,000 a year saving; Variable cost falls roughly $37.50 per tonne of flour; average cost falls $598.75 to $565

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of signing the annual wheat contract.
    Answer: Drawback 1: It adds a storage fixed cost [k]. Leasing silo space at $500 a month costs $6,000 a year even if flour sales fall [app], cutting the net saving to $54,000 and raising average cost if output dips below 1,600 tonnes [an]. Drawback 2: It demands faster payment [k]. Paying within 30 days ties up a cash outflow of $540,000 a year on the wheat bill (2,000 tonnes x $270) [app], straining working capital if the 40 bakeries pay late [an].
    Keywords: Sorrel & Rye Milling Co, $500 a month, 2,000 tonnes, $270 per tonne, about 2,080 tonnes, 40 bakeries, $60,000 a year, plain flour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Storage and handling add fixed costs that do not fall with output; Large up-front payments strain cash flow and working capital | application_max_2: $500 a month extra silo cost = $6,000 a year; net saving falls to $54,000; 30-day payment terms on a $540,000 annual wheat bill; sales needed from 40 bakeries | analysis_max_2: Fixed silo cost must be paid regardless of sales, so weak demand lifts average cost; Faster payment outpaces bakery receipts, risking cash-flow shortfalls

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sorrel & Rye Milling Co should sign the co-operative wheat contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Signing delivers clear purchasing economies of scale [k]: the $30 per tonne saving is worth $60,000 a year, so even after the $6,000 silo lease, net costs fall by $54,000 and average cost drops from $598.75 to $565 per tonne [app], lifting profit from $242,000 to about $296,000 [an]. However, the contract's 30-day payment terms create real risk [k]: the mill would pay $540,000 a year within a month of delivery, and quarterly bulk deliveries could strain cash flow if the 40 bakeries pay late [app], while being locked in for a year prevents buying elsewhere if a cheaper offer emerges [an]. Overall [eval], signing is justified — the $54,000 net saving raises the margin per tonne from about $151 to $185 — provided the sisters confirm bakery payment terms and negotiate quality checks on each quarterly delivery [eval].
    Keywords: Sorrel & Rye Milling Co, $270 per tonne, $300 per tonne, $60,000 a year, $500 a month, 2,000 tonnes, 40 bakeries, 1,600 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Purchasing economies of scale lower variable and average cost; Contractual payment terms and lock-in create cash-flow and flexibility risk | application_max_2: $60,000 a year saving less $6,000 lease = $54,000 net; average cost falls $598.75 to $565; 30-day payment on a $540,000 annual bill; 2,000 tonnes at $270 per tonne | analysis_max_2: Net saving raises profit from $242,000 to about $296,000 and lifts margin per tonne from $151 to $185; Slow bakery payments or lock-in at $270 could outweigh the $30 saving if prices fall | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified position; Clear overall judgement with conditions (payment terms confirmed, quality checks)

--- STEM ---
Eastport Cannery Ltd is a private limited company in Country X canning baked beans and chopped tomatoes for two supermarket chains. It employs 58 workers at its Eastport plant and canned 3.6 million tins last year. Fixed costs were $540,000, variable cost was $0.28 per tin and tins sell at $0.52, giving an average cost of $0.43. It is one of the region's largest canneries.

An automated high-speed line costing $800,000 would lift capacity to 4.4 million tins, cut variable cost to $0.20 and raise fixed costs to $660,000. It could be part-funded by a bank loan, and could be installed during the spring shutdown. Demand for canned goods has grown steadily since last year, and two supermarket chains have hinted at larger orders, but neither contract is signed.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'technical economies of scale'.
    Answer: Technical economies of scale are the cost advantages gained from using larger or more advanced machinery and production processes, which lower the cost of producing each unit. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Larger/advanced machinery lowers cost per unit; Example: automation, mass production equipment, specialist machines

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the new automated canning line.
    Answer: Reason 1: It cuts variable cost per tin [k]. Automation lowers variable cost from $0.28 to $0.20, saving $0.08 per tin — $352,000 a year at 4.4 million tins [app]. Reason 2: It spreads fixed costs over more output [k]. Capacity rises to 4.4 million tins, so average cost falls from $0.43 to $0.35 [app].
    Keywords: Eastport Cannery Ltd, 3.6 million tins, 4.4 million tins, $800,000, $0.20, $660,000, $0.43
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale: automation lowers variable cost per unit; Higher output spreads fixed costs, lowering average cost | application_max_2: Variable cost $0.28 to $0.20; saving $0.08 x 4.4 million tins = $352,000 a year; Capacity 4.4 million tins; average cost falls $0.43 to $0.35

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks of installing the automated line now.
    Answer: Risk 1: The $800,000 cost strains finances [k]. Eastport would likely need a bank loan, adding interest repayments that raise fixed costs beyond $660,000 [app], squeezing profit if tin prices or demand fall [an]. Risk 2: Extra capacity may go unfilled [k]. Neither supermarket contract is signed, so output could stay near 3.6 million tins [app], in which case fixed costs of $660,000 give an average cost of about $0.38 — better than $0.43 but not the targeted $0.35 [an].
    Keywords: Eastport Cannery Ltd, $800,000, $660,000, 3.6 million tins, 4.4 million tins, $0.43, bank loan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large capital investments increase debt and fixed commitments; Unfilled capacity leaves fixed costs under-recovered, raising average cost | application_max_2: $800,000 line cost likely financed by bank loan; fixed costs rise to $660,000; No signed orders; current output only 3.6 million tins | analysis_max_2: Loan interest adds to fixed costs, so weak demand makes the line a burden; At 3.6 million tins average cost is about $0.38, not the $0.35 planned

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Eastport Cannery Ltd should install the automated line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Installing the line secures technical economies of scale [k]: average cost falls to $0.35 at 4.4 million tins and profit could rise from $324,000 to about $748,000 a year, an extra $424,000 [app], recovering much of the $800,000 cost within two years [an]. However, the order book is unconfirmed [k]: at today's 3.6 million tins, average cost would be about $0.38 and fixed costs of $660,000 would pressure cash flow until orders are signed [app], and demand below 3.6 million tins would push average cost back toward $0.43 [an]. Overall [eval], Eastport should install the line only once at least one supermarket chain commits in writing to extra volume — the potential $424,000 gain outweighs the loan risk if capacity is filled, but installing speculatively would risk debt service on underused machinery [eval].
    Keywords: Eastport Cannery Ltd, $800,000, 4.4 million tins, 3.6 million tins, $0.43, $660,000, bank loan, two supermarket chains
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale lower average cost and raise profit; Unfilled capacity and loan commitments create financial risk | application_max_2: Average cost $0.43 to $0.35; profit $324,000 to $748,000 (extra $424,000); $800,000 cost; At 3.6 million tins average cost is about $0.38; fixed costs $660,000; neither contract signed | analysis_max_2: $424,000 extra profit would recover the investment in about two years; Unconfirmed demand leaves fixed costs under-recovered and cash flow strained | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified, conditional recommendation; Clear overall judgement tied to securing a signed order first

UNIT: Unit 4: Operations Management

--- STEM ---
Amberfield Packaging Ltd is a private limited company in Country X packing cardboard cartons for food producers. It has traded for 9 years, employs 46 workers and packed 1,000,000 cartons last year, earning revenue of $1.6 million. Fixed costs are $300,000, variable cost is $0.60 and average cost is $0.90.

A national grocery chain has shortlisted Amberfield to supply another 1,000,000 cartons a year, doubling capacity to 2,000,000 cartons. Serving it needs a second plant costing $500,000, which the bank would finance at 7.5% interest thanks to its track record; a start-up rival was quoted 11%. Fixed costs would rise to $520,000 and bulk buying would cut variable cost to $0.55. The chain would decide by next quarter, and Amberfield would need to begin building within six months to keep the contract.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'financial economies of scale'.
    Answer: Financial economies of scale are the advantages larger or more established businesses gain when raising finance, such as lower interest rates and better access to loans and share issues. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Established/larger firms borrow more cheaply (lower interest rates); Better access to finance: loans, debentures, share issues at lower cost

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of the bank finance for the second plant.
    Answer: Reason 1: Cheaper borrowing than rivals [k]. At 7.5% interest the $500,000 loan costs $37,500 a year, while a start-up rival quoted 11% would pay $55,000 — saving $17,500 a year [app]. Reason 2: The finance unlocks rapid expansion [k]. A second plant doubling capacity to 2,000,000 cartons enables the grocery chain contract without waiting years to accumulate profit [app].
    Keywords: Amberfield Packaging Ltd, 1,000,000 cartons, 2,000,000 cartons, $500,000, 7.5% interest, 11%, $520,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Established firms get lower interest rates (financial economies of scale); Access to finance enables investment that retained profit cannot fund quickly | application_max_2: 7.5% interest = $37,500 a year versus 11% = $55,000; saving $17,500 a year; Capacity doubles to 2,000,000 cartons; second plant costing $500,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the expansion could cause.
    Answer: Problem 1: Higher fixed costs and debt [k]. Fixed costs rise to $520,000 and the $37,500 interest is an unavoidable yearly outflow [app], so profit could fall sharply if the grocery chain order is delayed or cut, even though average cost falls toward $0.81 [an]. Problem 2: Diseconomies of scale may appear [k]. Running two sites duplicates management and slows communication [app], which could cause packing errors or late deliveries to the national chain and risk the contract that justified the investment [an].
    Keywords: Amberfield Packaging Ltd, $520,000, $500,000, 7.5% interest, 2,000,000 cartons, national grocery chain, $0.55
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Debt and higher fixed costs increase financial risk; Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and slow decisions in larger firms | application_max_2: Fixed costs rise to $520,000; $37,500 annual interest on the $500,000 loan; Two sites with duplicated management; national grocery chain contract | analysis_max_2: If the order slips, fixed costs and interest still fall due, cutting net profit below the $0.81 average-cost plan; Errors or late deliveries could lose the contract, leaving spare capacity and debt

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Amberfield Packaging Ltd should borrow $500,000 and build the second plant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Borrowing to expand brings financial economies of scale [k]: at 7.5%, interest is $37,500 a year — far cheaper than the 11% a start-up rival would pay — and doubling capacity to 2,000,000 cartons cuts average cost from $0.90 to $0.81 [app], lifting profit before interest from $700,000 to about $1.58 million [an]. However, the loan creates fixed commitments [k]: if the grocery chain order is smaller or later than expected, the $520,000 fixed costs and interest still fall due, and operating two sites could cause diseconomies of scale, such as slower communication and packing errors for the national chain [app], eroding the $0.09 saving per carton [an]. Overall [eval], Amberfield should proceed, because even after $37,500 interest, profit after interest of about $1.54 million comfortably exceeds $700,000 today — but it should secure the chain's order in writing before drawing the loan and phase the second plant's ramp-up to protect quality [eval].
    Keywords: Amberfield Packaging Ltd, $500,000, 7.5% interest, 11%, 2,000,000 cartons, $520,000, national grocery chain, 1,000,000 cartons
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Financial economies: established firms borrow at lower interest rates; Debt and diseconomies of scale create expansion risk | application_max_2: 7.5% interest = $37,500 a year versus 11% ($55,000); average cost falls $0.90 to $0.81; Fixed costs rise to $520,000; profit before interest rises $700,000 to about $1.58 million; $500,000 loan | analysis_max_2: Doubling capacity spreads fixed costs and bulk buying cuts $0.05 per carton, lifting profit by about $880,000; Underfilled capacity or poor coordination raises average cost and threatens the national contract | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified position; Clear overall judgement with conditions (signed contract first, phased ramp-up)

--- STEM ---
Larkhill Soft Drinks Ltd is a private limited company in Country X brewing elderflower and ginger cordials. It employs 28 staff, sells 750,000 bottles a year in 400 regional shops and earns revenue of $1.5 million. Fixed costs are $420,000, variable cost is $0.80 per bottle and marketing spending is $90,000 a year, reaching about 120,000 households. It is known locally for its distinctive glass swing-top bottles.

A media agency proposes a national television campaign costing $400,000 over 2 years, reaching an estimated 3 million households; sales could rise by 20%. Larkhill hopes a national supermarket listing would follow wider awareness. Alternatively, five separate regional television slots are priced at $120,000 each, and Larkhill could simply continue its local promotions.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'marketing economies of scale'.
    Answer: Marketing economies of scale are the cost advantages gained when advertising and promotion costs are spread over a larger output, lowering the marketing cost per unit sold. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cost of advertising/promotion spread over more units lowers marketing cost per unit; Example: one national campaign cheaper per customer than many regional campaigns

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the national television campaign.
    Answer: Reason 1: A wider reach at lower cost per household [k]. The $400,000 campaign reaches an estimated 3 million households for about $0.13 each, versus $0.75 per household on the current local campaign [app]. Reason 2: Sales could rise nationally [k]. If sales grow by 20% to 900,000 bottles, revenue rises from $1.5 million to $1.8 million and the fixed campaign cost is spread over more bottles [app].
    Keywords: Larkhill Soft Drinks Ltd, 750,000 bottles, $400,000, 3 million households, 120,000 households, $120,000 each, 400 regional shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: One national campaign reaches more customers at lower marketing cost per customer; Higher sales volume spreads fixed marketing costs, lowering cost per unit | application_max_2: $0.13 per household ($400,000/3 million) versus $0.75 per household local spending; 20% sales rise = 900,000 bottles; revenue $1.5 million to $1.8 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons Larkhill might keep its local promotions instead.
    Answer: Reason 1: The campaign may not pay back [k]. At an extra $110,000 a year above current spending, Larkhill needs roughly 92,000 extra bottles a year just to break even [app] — about 12% growth — and if the forecast 20% fails, profit falls below today's $480,000 [an]. Reason 2: National reach may be wasted without distribution [k]. Advertising to 3 million households means little while bottles sell in only 400 regional shops [app], because unavailable stock turns awareness into lost sales rather than revenue [an].
    Keywords: Larkhill Soft Drinks Ltd, $90,000 a year, 750,000 bottles, 400 regional shops, $400,000, 3 million households, 120,000 households
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Marketing spend is a fixed cost; weak sales growth leaves it under-recovered; Advertising is ineffective without distribution to meet demand | application_max_2: Extra $110,000 a year required; break-even needs about 92,000 extra bottles (12%); 400 regional shops only; bottles/revenue at risk if national demand cannot be supplied | analysis_max_2: If growth is under 12%, the campaign adds cost without enough contribution to cover it; Awareness without stock loses sales and damages brand, wasting the $400,000

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Larkhill Soft Drinks Ltd should spend $400,000 on the national campaign? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The national campaign offers marketing economies of scale [k]: it reaches 3 million households at about $0.13 each — far cheaper than $0.75 per household locally — and saves $200,000 against five separate regional slots at $120,000 each [app], so if sales rise by 20% as forecast, the extra $1.20 contribution per bottle covers the extra spend within two years [an]. However, the risk of weak returns is real [k]: at only 10% sales growth, Larkhill gains just 75,000 bottles of contribution, about $90,000 a year, which fails to cover the extra $110,000 a year above current local spending [app], leaving Larkhill worse off than continuing its $90,000 local promotions [an]. Overall [eval], Larkhill should proceed only if national retailers sign listings and the agency stages payments — the reach and $200,000 saving versus regional slots justify the spend once distribution is secured; without it, local promotion remains safer [eval].
    Keywords: Larkhill Soft Drinks Ltd, $400,000, 3 million households, $120,000 each, $90,000 a year, 750,000 bottles, 400 regional shops, 120,000 households
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Marketing economies of scale: wider reach at lower cost per customer; Marketing is a fixed cost; returns depend on distribution and sales growth | application_max_2: $0.13 per household nationally versus $0.75 locally; $200,000 cheaper than five regional slots at $120,000 each; At 10% growth contribution is about $90,000 a year, below the extra $110,000 a year cost | analysis_max_2: At 20% growth the extra contribution repays the additional spend within two years; Slow sales or poor distribution leaves the fixed campaign cost unrecovered | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified, conditional recommendation; Clear overall judgement tied to securing national distribution first
