====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Garside Cement Ltd is a private limited company producing cement at a Country X plant for 20 years and employing 260 workers. The firm supplied 480,000 tonnes last year and earned $14 million of revenue. After a second kiln opened, coordination loss between the shifts caused 2 kiln stoppages and average costs rose from $27 to $31 per tonne.

The board is considering buying Tarnfell Cement's neighbouring plant for $5.2 million, a horizontal integration removing its closest rival and adding capacity. Alternatively, Garside could stay independent, invest $800,000 in shift-planning software and reorganise into 3 production cells, aiming to cut average costs back to $27 per tonne by next year. The board meets in five weeks to choose between the two plans.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'fixed costs'.
    Answer: Fixed costs are costs that do not vary with the level of output, such as rent and insurance, and must be paid even if nothing is produced [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: costs that do not change with output level; examples: rent, insurance, salaries of managers (must be paid regardless of output)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two diseconomies of scale affecting Garside.
    Answer: Problem 1: Coordination loss [k], because the two shifts operating the second kiln cannot synchronise maintenance and loading, causing 2 kiln stoppages [app]. Problem 2: Rising average cost [k], because stoppages and poor coordination pushed average cost from $27 to $31 per tonne, about $1.92 million extra at 480,000 tonnes [app].
    Keywords: Garside Cement Ltd, coordination loss, 2 kiln stoppages, $27 to $31, 480,000 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: coordination loss (failure to align across departments/shifts); rising average costs as scale increases (diseconomies of scale) | application_max_2: 2 kiln stoppages between the shifts; average cost rose from $27 to $31 per tonne / 480,000 tonnes

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Garside of buying Tarnfell Cement's plant.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Horizontal integration removes its closest rival [k], because buying Tarnfell's neighbouring plant for $5.2 million adds capacity and ends direct local price competition [app], spreading fixed costs over more tonnes [an]. Benefit 2: Potential economies of scale [k], as shared purchasing of fuel and maintenance across two plants lowers average cost from the $31 peak [app], lifting profit on the $14 million revenue towards the $27 target [an].
    Keywords: horizontal integration, Tarnfell Cement, $5.2 million, $31, $14 million, 480,000 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration removes a competitor/gains share and capacity; economies of scale (purchasing/technical savings) reduce average cost | application_max_2: $5.2 million for Tarnfell Cement's neighbouring plant; average cost $31 peak / $14 million revenue target of $27 | analysis_max_2: fixed costs spread over more output lowers average cost; removing a rival raises pricing power and margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Garside should buy Tarnfell Cement's plant or reorganise internally? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying Tarnfell gives instant capacity and removes the closest rival [k], because $5.2 million secures a neighbouring plant and ends its competition, pushing Garside towards economies of scale [app], which could cut average cost below the current $31 per tonne [an]. However, internal reorganisation is cheaper and fixes the real cause [k], because $800,000 of shift-planning software plus 3 production cells would end the coordination loss and 2 kiln stoppages driving costs from $27 to $31 [app], saving about $1.92 million a year at 480,000 tonnes without any integration risk [an]. Overall, I think Garside should reorganise internally first [eval], because buying another plant before fixing coordination would simply double the diseconomies that are already costing it margin [eval].
    Keywords: $800,000, 3 production cells, $5.2 million, Tarnfell Cement, $27, $31, 2 kiln stoppages
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration adds capacity/removes rival but risks importing its problems; internal reorganisation fixes coordination/communication cheaply and directly | application_max_2: $5.2 million takeover of Tarnfell Cement / 480,000 tonnes / $14 million revenue; $800,000 software and 3 production cells / 2 kiln stoppages / $27 to $31 | analysis_max_2: takeover raises scale quickly to unlock economies of scale; fixing coordination restores average cost (~$1.92 million a year saving) without takeover risk | evaluation_max_2: reasoned judgement on takeover vs reorganisation, justified with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Thornby Hotels Ltd runs 9 mid-range hotels across Country X and employs 720 staff. Revenue was $16 million last year, down from $19 million two years ago, and occupancy fell to 66%. Guest satisfaction slipped to 71%, and 6 levels of management slowed decision-making, with pricing and refurbishment approvals now taking 8 weeks.

A rival group, Kestreldon Hotels, offers to sell its 4 hotels totalling 340 rooms for $9 million, a horizontal integration promising economies of scale in marketing and bulk buying. Alternatively, Thornby could delayer, removing 2 management levels and saving an estimated $650,000 a year, then reinvest the savings in its existing 9 hotels. The board meets next month to decide which route reverses the decline, and time is short.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'delayering'.
    Answer: Delayering is the removal of one or more levels of management from a business hierarchy, shortening the chain of command and widening spans of control [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: removing levels of management from the hierarchy; shortens chain of command / widens span of control / speeds decisions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems caused by slow decision-making at Thornby.
    Answer: Problem 1: Lost competitiveness [k], because 8-week approval cycles for pricing and refurbishments let rivals react fast, contributing to occupancy falling to 66% and revenue dropping from $19 million to $16 million [app]. Problem 2: Falling guest satisfaction and morale [k], because 6 levels of management distance staff from decisions, and satisfaction slipped to 71% [app].
    Keywords: Thornby Hotels Ltd, 8 weeks, 6 levels, 66%, 71%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lost competitiveness (rivals react faster); low morale/satisfaction as decisions take too long | application_max_2: 8-week approvals and revenue fall from $19 million to $16 million / occupancy 66%; 6 levels of management / satisfaction slipped to 71%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Thornby of delayering 2 management levels.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Faster decisions [k], because removing 2 of the 6 levels shortens the chain of command between 720 staff and senior managers [app], ending the 8-week approval delays for pricing and refurbishment [an]. Benefit 2: Lower overheads [k], because delayering saves an estimated $650,000 a year in management salaries [app], directly improving profit at a time when revenue has fallen to $16 million [an].
    Keywords: delayer, 2 management levels, $650,000, 720 staff, 8 weeks, 6 levels
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: faster decision-making (shorter chain of command); lower overhead costs (fewer managers to pay) | application_max_2: removing 2 of 6 management levels / 720 staff; $650,000 a year saved / 8-week delays / revenue $16 million | analysis_max_2: quicker refurbishment and pricing response improves occupancy/competitiveness; cost savings flow straight to profit when revenue is falling

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Thornby should buy the 4 Kestreldon hotels or delayer and invest in its existing hotels? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the hotels would add instant scale [k], because $9 million secures 4 hotels with 340 rooms, and horizontal integration could spread marketing and bulk-buying costs across 13 hotels [app], lifting revenue beyond $16 million and filling empty rooms quickly [an]. However, delayering fixes the disease, not the symptom [k], because removing 2 levels saves $650,000 a year and ends 8-week approvals before new hotels are added [app], improving satisfaction at the 9 existing hotels where it has already slipped to 71% [an]. Overall, I think Thornby should delayer and reinvest in its estate [eval], because slow decision-making would simply be amplified across a bigger group if it is not cured first [eval].
    Keywords: Kestreldon Hotels, $9 million, 4 hotels, 340 rooms, $650,000, 8 weeks, 71%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration gives instant scale and shared economies of scale; delayering saves costs and speeds up decisions at existing sites | application_max_2: $9 million for 4 Kestreldon hotels, 340 rooms / 9 existing hotels / $16 million revenue; removing 2 levels saving $650,000 a year / 8-week delays / 71% satisfaction | analysis_max_2: takeover lifts capacity and shared savings improve competitiveness fast; delayering cuts overheads and fixes approval delays, improving service at existing hotels | evaluation_max_2: reasoned judgement on takeover vs delayering, justified with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Calderridge Appliances Ltd is a private limited company in Country X assembling washing machines. The plant employs 300 workers and produced 50,000 machines last year, with total costs of $15 million and revenue of $18.5 million. Rapid growth has stretched 1 head office over 3 factories, and poor communication caused 4,200 warranty claims last year, double the previous year.

The managing director proposes dividing the business into 3 autonomous units, each with its own production and sales manager, to restore local decision-making. The finance director instead wants to add 2 regional managers to speed up approvals without changing the structure. Either option costs an estimated $700,000 to implement this year, and the board must choose at next week's meeting before volumes peak.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the average cost per washing machine. Show your working.
    Answer: Average cost = total costs / output = $15,000,000 / 50,000 machines = $300 per machine [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: correct method (total costs divided by output); $300 per machine

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems caused by poor communication between head office and the 3 factories.
    Answer: Problem 1: Rising warranty claims [k], because instructions and quality updates are delayed or misread across 1 head office and 3 factories, and claims doubled to 4,200 machines [app]. Problem 2: Slow responses to faults [k], because a stretched central structure cannot approve fixes quickly, leaving defective washing machines in production longer [app].
    Keywords: Calderridge Appliances Ltd, poor communication, 4,200 warranty claims, 3 factories, 1 head office
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delayed/distorted information raises error rates; slow decision-making leaves faults uncorrected | application_max_2: claims doubled to 4,200 last year; 1 head office stretched over 3 factories

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Calderridge of dividing into 3 autonomous units.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Local decisions are faster and better informed [k], because each unit's production and sales manager sees factory faults and local orders first-hand [app], cutting the delays blamed for the 4,200 warranty claims [an]. Benefit 2: Clear accountability for performance [k], because each autonomous unit can be measured separately on output, quality and the $18.5 million revenue [app], motivating managers to improve results [an].
    Keywords: 3 autonomous units, 4,200 warranty claims, $18.5 million, double the previous year, 300 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: faster/better local decision-making in autonomous units; clearer accountability/motivation of unit managers | application_max_2: 3 autonomous units with their own production and sales managers; 4,200 warranty claims / $18.5 million revenue | analysis_max_2: decisions closer to operations reduce errors and claims; measurable units focus managers on quality and profitability

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Calderridge should divide into 3 autonomous units or add 2 regional managers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Autonomous units restore speed and accountability [k], because each unit makes its own production and sales decisions locally [app], attacking the root cause of the 4,200 warranty claims at no extra cost beyond the $700,000 either option already needs [an]. However, 2 regional managers keep central control while speeding approvals [k], because they add decision-making capacity to the stretched 1 head office without the duplicated functions and disruption of 3 stand-alone units [app], which suits a business with $15 million of total costs managing 3 factories [an]. Overall, I think Calderridge should divide into 3 autonomous units [eval], because the evidence shows a structural rather than a staffing problem, and separation is the stronger cure for poor communication and slow decisions [eval].
    Keywords: 3 autonomous units, 2 regional managers, $700,000, 4,200 warranty claims, $15 million, 3 factories
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: autonomous units restore local decision-making and accountability; regional managers speed approvals while keeping central coordination | application_max_2: 3 autonomous units vs 2 regional managers, both costing $700,000; 4,200 warranty claims double the previous year / 1 head office over 3 factories / $15 million total costs | analysis_max_2: autonomous units remove central bottlenecks but duplicate functions and add risk; regional managers preserve single reporting lines and are cheaper to coordinate | evaluation_max_2: reasoned judgement on autonomous units vs regional managers, justified with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Redmoss Cider Co is a private limited company in Country X producing cider in an orchard region. The business buys 2,800 tonnes of apples a year from 24 growers at $900 per tonne, employs 70 staff and generated $3.6 million of revenue last year. After a poor harvest, apple prices jumped 25%, and 6 of its growers stopped supplying, forcing the mill to run at 70% of capacity.

The board is weighing backward vertical integration: buying 190 hectares of orchard for $3.8 million to secure its own apple supply. Alternatively, it could stay independent and sign 5-year supply contracts with 10 growers at fixed prices, keeping cash available for a planned production line upgrade next year. The harvest season begins in 5 months.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'productivity'.
    Answer: Productivity measures output per unit of input, such as output per worker or per hour, and rising productivity means the same resources produce more goods and services [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: output per input (e.g. per worker/hour); higher productivity means more output from the same resources

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems caused by the 25% jump in apple prices and lost growers.
    Answer: Problem 1: Margin squeeze [k], because a 25% rise lifts the apple cost from $900 to $1,125 per tonne, about an extra $630,000 a year at 2,800 tonnes [app]. Problem 2: Idle capacity [k], because 6 of its 24 growers stopped supplying, forcing the mill to run at 70% of capacity with the same fixed costs spread over fewer tonnes [app].
    Keywords: Redmoss Cider Co, 25%, $900 per tonne, 6 of its growers, 70%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: input cost rise squeezes profit margins; lost suppliers leave capacity underused with unchanged fixed costs | application_max_2: 25% price jump ($900 to $1,125 per tonne; about $630,000 a year extra); 6 of 24 growers stopped; mill at 70% of capacity

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Redmoss of buying the 190 hectares of orchard.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Guaranteed apple supply [k], because owning 190 hectares of orchard removes Redmoss's dependence on 24 outside growers who may stop supplying [app], ending the 70% capacity utilisation and restoring 2,800 tonnes of yearly throughput [an]. Benefit 2: Stable input costs [k], because integrated orchards are immune to the 25% price jumps seen this year [app], giving predictable production costs for the planned production line upgrade [an].
    Keywords: backward vertical integration, 190 hectares, $3.8 million, 70%, 24 growers, 2,800 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: secure/guaranteed supply of raw material (removes supplier risk); stable/lower input costs (no purchased-market price rises) | application_max_2: 190 hectares for $3.8 million / dependence on 24 growers reduced; 25% price jump removed / 70% of capacity restored towards 2,800 tonnes | analysis_max_2: secure supply restores full capacity, spreading fixed costs over more tonnes; predictable input costs improve planning and profitability

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redmoss should buy the 190 hectares of orchard or sign 5-year fixed-price contracts? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the orchard solves the supply problem at its root [k], because owning 190 hectares guarantees apples for the 2,800-tonne mill regardless of what the 24 growers decide [app], ending idle capacity for good and cutting exposure to 25% price spikes [an]. However, signing 5-year contracts with 10 growers at fixed prices is cheaper and faster [k], because $3.8 million stays in the business for the production line upgrade while supply risks are capped [app], keeping Redmoss focused on making cider rather than farming [an]. Overall, I think Redmoss should sign the 5-year contracts [eval], because the immediate crisis is supply availability and price, which the contracts solve without a $3.8 million commitment at 70% capacity [eval].
    Keywords: 5-year supply contracts, 10 growers, $3.8 million, 190 hectares, 70%, $900 per tonne, 2,800 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: backward vertical integration guarantees supply and removes market price risk; long-term fixed-price contracts secure supply cheaply while preserving cash | application_max_2: $3.8 million for 190 hectares / guarantees 2,800 tonnes regardless of growers; 5-year fixed-price contracts with 10 growers / 25% price spike / 70% capacity / $900 per tonne | analysis_max_2: orchard ownership restores full capacity and price stability long-term; contracts preserve capital for the production line and avoid farming risks | evaluation_max_2: reasoned judgement on orchard purchase vs contracts, justified with stem figures

Coraline Chocolate Co is a private limited company founded 6 years ago by Elena Marchetti in Country X. Elena's quality manager reports that final quality control inspections reject 4% of output, wasting $18,000 of chocolate a year. Elena is weighing two options: invest $60,000 in quality assurance, training staff to check ingredients and temperatures at every stage, or keep quality control but hire two extra inspectors at $2,000 each per month. The supermarket will review the contract in 6 months.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'quality control'.
    Answer: Quality control is checking finished products or samples during production to identify and remove faulty items before they reach customers [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: checking products during or after production; identifying and removing faulty items before customers receive them

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why high quality is important to Coraline Chocolate Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: High quality keeps customers satisfied [k], so shoppers who enjoyed the hand-finished truffles will keep buying from Coraline instead of rivals [app]. Reason 2: High quality protects the company's reputation [k], reducing the risk that the supermarket delists its products after the stale-centre complaints [app].
    Keywords: Coraline Chocolate Co, supermarket, stale centres, truffle, $18,000, 90,000, quality
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customer satisfaction and loyalty; brand reputation and image | application_max_2: customers keep buying the hand-finished truffles; risk of the supermarket delisting Coraline after stale-centre complaints

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Coraline Chocolate Co of replacing quality control with quality assurance.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Quality assurance prevents faults at the source [k], so ingredients and temperatures are checked at every production stage rather than after the 4% of output is wasted [app], cutting the $18,000 annual chocolate waste [an]. Benefit 2: Quality assurance makes every worker responsible for quality [k], so Elena's 22 confectioners catch stale centres before boxes are sealed [app], building trust with the supermarket customer [an].
    Keywords: quality assurance, quality control, $60,000, $18,000, 22 confectioners, stale centres, supermarket
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: prevents defects at the source / building quality into the process; makes all employees responsible for quality | application_max_2: checks ingredients and temperatures at every stage; 22 confectioners catching stale centres before sealing | analysis_max_2: cuts the $18,000 annual chocolate waste; builds trust with the supermarket customer

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Coraline Chocolate Co should invest $60,000 in quality assurance rather than hire two extra inspectors? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing in quality assurance builds quality into every stage of production [k], preventing the 4% defect rate that wastes $18,000 a year and satisfying the supermarket before its 6-month review [app], which should protect the $540,000 annual revenue long term [an]. However, quality assurance costs $60,000 up front plus staff training time [k], whereas two extra inspectors cost only $2,000 each per month and start catching faults immediately [app], which is safer if Elena's cash is tight [an]. Overall, quality assurance is the stronger choice because preventing faults is more reliable than catching them after they occur [eval], provided Elena can fund $60,000 without straining cash flow [eval].
    Keywords: quality assurance, $60,000, $18,000, $540,000, supermarket, 4%, two extra inspectors, 6 months
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quality assurance prevents defects at source; quality control / extra inspectors catch defects after production | application_max_2: $60,000 quality assurance investment and 6-month supermarket review; two extra inspectors at $2,000 each per month | analysis_max_2: protects the $540,000 annual revenue and the supermarket contract; inspectors start catching faults immediately but cost ongoing wages | evaluation_max_2: weighs prevention against inspection and gives a justified recommendation; conditional recommendation linked to Elena's cash position

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quality assurance prevents defects through process checks; inspection stations detect defects after production | application_max_2: $45,000 supervisor training to reach the 2% audit threshold; $30,000 inspection station saving $15,000 | analysis_max_2: protects the $900,000-a-year contract; end-of-line checks catch faults late, so rework still costs $14,400 a month | evaluation_max_2: weighs prevention against cheaper detection and gives a justified recommendation; conditional recommendation linked to passing next month's audit

--- STEM ---
Aster Court Hotel is an independent 45-bedroom hotel in Country X, owned by the Demir family for 11 years. It employs 38 staff and generated $1.1 million in room revenue last year. Online reviews averaged 3.6 out of 5, and 22% of the 380 reviews received mentioned slow breakfast service and worn room linen. Repeat guests have fallen from 40% to 31% of bookings.

Option one is a total quality management programme costing $25,000, involving all 38 staff in continuous improvement meetings and guest feedback systems.     Question: Define 'total quality management'.
    Answer: Total quality management is a company-wide approach in which every employee is responsible for quality and works to continuously improve processes and eliminate errors [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: company-wide approach involving all employees; focus on continuous improvement and eliminating defects/errors

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why high quality is important to Aster Court Hotel.
    Answer: Reason 1: Good service quality raises customer satisfaction [k], so guests who enjoyed their stay are more likely to book again [app]. Reason 2: Consistent quality builds a strong reputation [k], helping the hotel reverse its fall from 40% to 31% repeat bookings [app].
    Keywords: Aster Court Hotel, Repeat guests, 31%, 40%, 380 reviews, breakfast
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customer satisfaction in service businesses; reputation and repeat business | application_max_2: guests more likely to book again; repeat bookings already fell from 40% to 31%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Aster Court Hotel of introducing total quality management.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Total quality management involves all 38 staff in improving quality [k], so front-line teams can fix the slow breakfast service and worn room linen themselves [app], lifting online reviews above the current 3.6 out of 5 [an]. Benefit 2: Total quality management creates a culture of continuous improvement [k], so guest feedback systems and regular meetings keep service standards high all year [app], protecting $1.1 million in room revenue [an].
    Keywords: total quality management, 38 staff, breakfast, 3.6, $1.1 million, continuous improvement
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: all employees responsible for quality; culture of continuous improvement | application_max_2: 38 staff fixing slow breakfast service and worn room linen; guest feedback systems keeping standards high | analysis_max_2: raises the 3.6 out of 5 review average; protects $1.1 million in room revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Aster Court Hotel should introduce the $25,000 total quality management programme rather than targeted front-of-house training at $9,000? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Total quality management involves all 38 staff in continuous improvement [k], tackling both the slow breakfast service and room quality across the whole hotel [app], which should raise the 3.6 out of 5 review average and rebuild repeat bookings above 31% [an]. However, total quality management costs $25,000 against $9,000 for focused front-of-house training [k], and the family has only $60,000 in cash reserves [app], so an all-staff programme may strain cash before the busy summer [an].     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quality assurance prevents faults at source; quality control detects faults at the end of the line | application_max_2: $28,000 frame-gluing redesign and staff training; $12,000 final inspection bench with a two-person repair team | analysis_max_2: cuts the 3 out of 100 sofa returns and reverses the 35% complaint rise; quality control starts catching faults immediately against the six-month deadline | evaluation_max_2: weighs prevention against cheaper immediate detection and gives a justified recommendation; conditional recommendation linked to funding without halting production

--- STEM ---
Redvale Fruit Canners is a private limited company that has canned peaches and apricots for 6 years, employing 48 workers.   Qb [4 marks]

Overall, Westvale should stay in the vegetable district because the farm-access and rent savings protect shelf life and margins [eval], since chilled food quality depends more on raw-material freshness than on depot proximity [eval].

Overall, Site A is the better location because compliance certainty and the grant protect the firm's future [eval], even though rent is higher, since illegal discharge could close the business [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Site A meets legal controls/grant support; Site B cheaper but non-compliant risk | application_max_2: mains drainage; $50,000 green relocation grant; $11,000 a year in rent; $30,000 at Site A | analysis_max_2: avoids fines and keeps 40 trade customers supplied; without mains drainage the firm risks breaching environmental law again | evaluation_max_2: weighs compliance certainty and grant against rent saving in polluting-industry context

  Qb [4 marks]

    Question: Define the term 'relocation'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: moving operations from one place to another; may involve another country/site

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two features of Country Z that could attract Garrick Technical Textiles.
    Answer: Feature 1: Country Z offers wages 55% below Country X [app], substantially cutting the factory's labour bill [k]. Feature 2: Country Z offers a 10-year tax holiday and a rent-free state-built factory [app], lowering fixed costs and protecting profits in the early years [k].
    Keywords: Country Z, 55%, 10-year, state-built factory, tax holiday, zero rent

  Qc [6 marks]

Risk 2: Country Z levies an 8% duty on fabric exports [app], adding cost to every shipment bound for Country Y [k], which could erode the $5.2 million revenue base [an].
    Keywords: 1,900 km, 8%, Country Z, Country Y, duty, $5.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: longer supply lines increase cost/delay risk; export duty adds cost to shipments | application_max_2: yarn would travel 1,900 km; 8% duty on fabric exports; bound for Country Y | analysis_max_2: longer supply lines/higher transport costs; could erode the $5.2 million revenue base

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Garrick Technical Textiles should relocate to Country Z? Justify your answer.

However, freight to Country Y would rise from $38 to $52 per pallet and an 8% export duty applies [k], adding about $14 more per pallet plus duty on every shipment [app], and the 1,900 km supply line threatens delivery reliability [an]. Overall, Garrick should stay in Country X because the duty and freight increases erode the labour saving [eval], while supplier proximity and proven export routes protect customer service [eval].
    Keywords: Country Z, Country X, 55%, 8%, $52, $38, 1,900 km
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Country Z offers wage/tax/rent advantages; Country X offers lower freight/duty/supplier proximity | application_max_2: wages 55% below Country X; 10-year tax holiday; freight $38 to $52 per pallet; 8% export duty | analysis_max_2: could sharply reduce unit costs/free cash for growth; duty and freight increases threaten reliability and savings | evaluation_max_2: weighs labour/tax/rent savings against duty, freight and supply-line risks in textile context

--- STEM ---
Kelwick Knitwear Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making school jumpers and cardigans for 9 retail chains. It employs 180 machinists paid $1,150 a month and earned $9.6 million in revenue last year. Its wage bill reached $2.48 million, about 26% of revenue. A rival knitwear firm relocated to Country Y last year and now pays machinists the equivalent of $420 a month.

The directors must decide whether to open a $3.2 million factory in Country Y, where the same 180 machinists would cost $907,200 a year, or stay in Country X and upgrade 40 sewing machines. Orders from the 9 retail chains are steady at 620,000 garments a year, and two buyers insist that lead times stay under 6 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'variable cost'.

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why wage costs influence where Kelwick Knitwear locates production.
    Answer: Reason 1: Lower wages abroad cut production costs [k], because Country Y pays $420 a month compared with $1,150 in Country X, reducing the wage bill from $2.48 million to $907,200 [app]. Reason 2: Lower labour costs free up cash [k], because the $1.58 million annual saving could fund part of the $3.2 million factory [app].
    Keywords: $420 a month, $1,150, $2.48 million, $907,200, $3.2 million, Country Y, 180 machinists
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower wages abroad reduce production or wage costs; labour cost savings improve competitiveness or free cash | application_max_2: $420 a month in Country Y vs $1,150 in Country X; wage bill falls from $2.48 million to $907,200; $1.58 million annual saving contributing to the $3.2 million factory

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Kelwick Knitwear may face if it relocates to Country Y.
    Answer: Problem 1: The move demands heavy up-front spending [k], because the new factory costs $3.2 million before production begins [app], and recovering that money would take around 2 years of wage savings [an]. Problem 2: Distance threatens delivery times [k], because two buyers insist lead times stay under 6 weeks for orders from 9 retail chains [app], so freight delays could cost Kelwick contracts [an].
    Keywords: $3.2 million, 6 weeks, 9 retail chains, $907,200, Country Y, 620,000 garments
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relocation requires substantial up-front capital; greater distance risks slower delivery and lost orders | application_max_2: factory costs $3.2 million before production starts; lead times must stay under 6 weeks for 9 retail chains; 620,000 garments a year must still be delivered on time | analysis_max_2: $3.2 million cost would take around 2 years of the $1.58 million annual saving to recover; late deliveries risk breaching buyer terms and losing retail contracts

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kelwick Knitwear Ltd should relocate production to Country Y? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Relocating would cut running costs sharply [k], because the same 180 machinists would cost $907,200 a year instead of $2.48 million in Country X [app], releasing about $1.58 million a year to repay the $3.2 million factory in roughly 2 years [an]. However, staying in Country X protects delivery speed [k], because two buyers demand lead times under 6 weeks and the firm serves 9 retail chains with steady orders of 620,000 garments a year [app], and moving could disrupt production and quality while new staff settle [an]. Overall, Kelwick should relocate to Country Y [eval], because the $1.58 million annual wage saving is large relative to the $3.2 million factory cost and the steady 620,000-garment order book supports the move, provided the transfer is staged to protect the 6-week lead times [eval].
    Keywords: $907,200, $2.48 million, $3.2 million, 620,000 garments, 6 weeks, 9 retail chains, Country Y
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relocation lowers wage and production costs; relocation risks disruption and longer delivery times | application_max_2: $907,200 a year in Country Y vs $2.48 million in Country X; steady orders of 620,000 garments a year from 9 retail chains; buyers demand lead times under 6 weeks | analysis_max_2: $1.58 million annual saving repays the $3.2 million factory in roughly 2 years; disruption of production and quality during the move could breach buyer lead-time terms | evaluation_max_2: weighs $1.58 million annual wage saving against relocation cost and 6-week lead-time risk in a steady-order context

Marlowcrest Tableware Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing hand-decorated ceramic dinner plates and bowls. No other ceramic supplier in Country X currently exports to Country Z.

The directors are considering building a $5.5 million factory in Country Z employing 95 local workers, or keeping production in Country X and raising wholesale prices by 15%.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'tariff'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a tax or duty on imported goods; raises the price of imports and protects domestic producers

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the 22% tariff encourages Marlowcrest to produce tableware inside Country Z.
    Answer: Reason 1: Avoiding the tariff protects competitiveness [k], because exporting from Country X would add about $1.628 million a year in duty on $7.4 million of sales [app]. Reason 2: Local production reaches buyers without import restrictions [k], because plates made in Country Z sell freely through 340 stores [app].
    Keywords: $1.628 million, $7.4 million, 340 stores, 22% import tariff, Country Z, 15%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: avoiding the tariff keeps exports price-competitive; local production gains unrestricted access to the importing market | application_max_2: $1.628 million annual duty on $7.4 million of exports; plates made in Country Z sell freely through 340 stores

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Marlowcrest may face if it builds the Country Z factory.
    Answer: Problem 1: High capital cost [k], because the factory costs $5.5 million, most of the firm's $6.0 million retained profit [app], leaving little cash to absorb shocks if Country Z demand slows [an]. Problem 2: Training and quality risk [k], because 95 new local workers must learn Marlowcrest's hand-decoration standards [app], and faults would damage the brand in its 340 stores [an].
    Keywords: $5.5 million, $6.0 million, 95 local workers, 340 stores, Country Z, 8% annually
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high cost of setting up a new factory; quality and training risks with a new, untrained workforce | application_max_2: factory costs $5.5 million of the $6.0 million retained profit; 95 new local workers need hand-decoration training; quality failures would be visible across 340 stores | analysis_max_2: spending $5.5 million of $6.0 million retained profit weakens liquidity if demand slows; poorly trained workers risk faulty plates and brand damage in 340 stores

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marlowcrest Tableware Ltd should build the Country Z factory instead of continuing to export and raising prices by 15%? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Building the factory removes the tariff burden [k], because production in Country Z means the $1.628 million annual duty disappears while demand grows at 8% annually across 340 stores [app], protecting Marlowcrest's $7.4 million market more securely than a price rise would [an]. However, raising prices by 15% avoids the $5.5 million outlay [k], because it keeps all 120 workers in Country X and preserves the $6.0 million profit cushion [app], but higher prices could push buyers towards rival plates and sales may fall [an]. Overall, Marlowcrest should build the Country Z factory [eval], because avoiding $1.628 million of duty each year plus 8% annual market growth outweighs the $5.5 million set-up cost over time [eval].
    Keywords: $1.628 million, 8% annually, 340 stores, $5.5 million, 15%, Country Z, $7.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: local production avoids the import tariff; raising prices risks losing price-sensitive buyers | application_max_2: $1.628 million annual duty vs $5.5 million factory cost; 15% price rise alternative would keep 120 workers in Country X; demand growing 8% annually across 340 stores | analysis_max_2: avoiding duty plus growth protects the $7.4 million export market; a 15% price rise could cut sales volume and revenue | evaluation_max_2: weighs tariff avoidance ($1.628 million a year) and 8% annual growth against the $5.5 million set-up cost and the price-rise alternative

--- STEM ---
Steadham Speakers Ltd is a private limited company in Country X assembling 240,000 Bluetooth speakers a year. It imports $4.1 million of speaker components priced in dollars and employs 96 workers. Last year the Country X currency fell 18% against the dollar, so the imported components now cost about $4.84 million, roughly $740,000 more than before.

Steadham sells 60% of its output in Country X and exports 40%, worth $3.3 million, to Country R, with export invoices in dollars. The board is weighing two options: move component sourcing and final assembly to Country D, or keep assembly in Country X and raise local prices by 9%. A Country D factory would cost $2.7 million to build, and local wages are 25% lower.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'exchange rate'.
    Answer: The price of one currency in terms of another, for example how many local units equal one US dollar [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the price of one currency in terms of another; it determines how much local money is paid or received in foreign trade

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the 18% fall in the Country X currency affects Steadham Speakers.
    Answer: Reason 1: Imports become more expensive [k], because dollar-priced components rose from $4.1 million to about $4.84 million, an extra $740,000 [app]. Reason 2: Exports become more price-competitive [k], because the 40% of output worth $3.3 million is invoiced in dollars, so dollar receipts convert into more local currency [app].
    Keywords: $4.1 million, $4.84 million, $740,000, $3.3 million, 18% against the dollar, Country X
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a fall in the currency makes imports more expensive; a fall in the currency makes exports cheaper and more competitive abroad | application_max_2: components rose from $4.1 million to about $4.84 million, an extra $740,000; 40% of output worth $3.3 million is dollar-invoiced, so receipts buy more local currency

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why exchange rates influence Steadham's decision to locate production abroad.
    Answer: Reason 1: Relocation removes import-cost risk [k], because buying components in Country D's currency avoids another $740,000 of losses if the Country X currency falls again [app], giving stable, predictable costs [an]. Reason 2: Matching costs and revenue in dollars [k], because the $3.3 million export income is dollar-priced and Country D wages are 25% lower [app], so a natural hedge protects profit margins whichever way the rate moves [an].
    Keywords: $740,000, $3.3 million, 25% lower, Country D, $4.84 million, Country X
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: locating where inputs are bought removes exposure to import-cost swings; matching cost and revenue currencies creates a natural hedge | application_max_2: the 18% fall added $740,000 to component costs this year; $3.3 million of exports are dollar-priced while Country D wages are 25% lower | analysis_max_2: local currency sourcing would stabilise costs and ease planning; a dollar-based cost structure hedges the dollar revenue and defends margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Steadham Speakers Ltd should move assembly to Country D? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Moving to Country D would cut and stabilise costs [k], because components would be bought locally instead of importing at $4.84 million after the 18% fall, and wages there are 25% lower [app], which should recover the $740,000 margin lost to the currency in a few years [an]. However, relocating costs $2.7 million and disrupts skilled production [k], because 96 Country X workers would lose their jobs and new quality routines must be built in Country D [app], risking delayed orders for Country R buyers [an]. Overall, Steadham should move assembly to Country D [eval], because matching its export income with dollar costs and 25% lower wages protects both the $3.3 million export business and long-run profitability [eval].
    Keywords: $2.7 million, $4.84 million, 25% lower, $3.3 million, Country D, 96 workers, 18%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relocation can cut and stabilise production costs; relocation carries set-up cost and workforce disruption | application_max_2: $4.84 million component import bill after the 18% fall vs local sourcing; $2.7 million factory cost and 96 Country X workers displaced; $3.3 million dollar-priced export income to Country R | analysis_max_2: 25% lower wages plus local sourcing should recover the $740,000 currency loss within a few years; disruption of quality and delivery could damage orders from Country R buyers | evaluation_max_2: weighs stable dollar costs and 25% lower wages against the $2.7 million relocation cost and disruption to 96 workers and Country R orders

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: local production escapes quota limits and unlocks growth; building a factory is costly and must be justified financially | application_max_2: 1,900-tonne quota vs 2,300 tonnes exported; market growing 12% a year; $4.1 million factory and 60 workers to be funded; about $900,000 of annual export sales at risk under the quota | analysis_max_2: growth beyond the cap protects the $5.2 million export business; accepting the quota forfeits about $900,000 a year and caps growth | evaluation_max_2: weighs quota-free growth, 12% annual market growth and higher prices against the $4.1 million investment and $900,000 annual risk

--- STEM ---
Brinvale Toys Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing wooden railway sets and toy trains. It employs 88 workers and sells $6.3 million of toys a year, 70% in Country X and 30% exported to Country R. Country X has introduced strict toy safety rules requiring $380,000 of annual laboratory testing and batch certification before any toy can be sold. Brinvale is the only wooden-toy maker in Country X with its own paint workshop.

Country Q, where Brinvale could relocate, applies basic safety checks costing about $60,000 a year, and wages there are 35% lower. The move would cost $2.4 million. Country Q's legal system is slow at resolving contract disputes, and Country X import checks on toys stay equally strict wherever they are made.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'quality assurance'.
    Answer: A system of checking quality at every stage of production so that faults are prevented rather than found at the end [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quality is checked throughout the production process; aims to prevent faults rather than detect them at the end

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways legal controls influence where Brinvale locates its factory.
    Answer: Reason 1: Compliance costs differ between countries [k], because Country X requires $380,000 a year of laboratory testing and certification while Country Q checks cost about $60,000 [app]. Reason 2: Selling rules dictate market choice [k], because Country X import checks apply wherever toys are made, so relocation does not remove legal duties [app].
    Keywords: $380,000, $60,000, Country X, Country Q, 88 workers, $6.3 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: legal requirements raise or lower compliance costs; legal controls apply based on where the product is sold, not where it is made | application_max_2: Country X testing costs $380,000 a year vs $60,000 in Country Q; Country X import checks remain in force wherever the toys are manufactured

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Brinvale may face if it relocates to Country Q.
    Answer: Problem 1: Brand and safety risk [k], because Country X import checks remain strict, so any toy failing them would embarrass Brinvale in front of its $6.3 million customer base [app], destroying the trust its wooden railway sets rely on [an]. Problem 2: Legal uncertainty [k], because Country Q resolves contract disputes slowly, so suppliers may exploit weak enforcement [app], adding costs and risk to the relocated 88-worker operation [an].
    Keywords: $6.3 million, Country X, Country Q, $2.4 million, 35% lower, 88 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: products must still pass import checks where they are sold; a weak legal system makes contracts hard to enforce | application_max_2: Country X import checks stay strict despite relocation; Country Q's courts resolve disputes slowly; $6.3 million sales base would be exposed to brand damage | analysis_max_2: a failed check would destroy trust behind the $6.3 million sales base; slow dispute resolution raises risk and cost for the 88-worker relocated operation

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brinvale Toys Ltd should relocate to Country Q? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Relocating would cut legal and wage costs [k], because Country Q checks cost $60,000 a year instead of $380,000 and wages are 35% lower [app], saving around $320,000 a year plus payroll savings that could offset the $2.4 million move within a few years [an]. However, relocation would not relax Country X rules [k], because 70% of sales depend on passing strict import checks, and Country Q's slow legal system threatens contracts [app], so a quality or legal failure could cost far more than the $320,000 annual saving [an]. Overall, Brinvale should not relocate to Country Q simply to escape its legal duties [eval], because its $6.3 million reputation rests on safe, certified toys and Country X market access matters more than the compliance saving [eval].
    Keywords: $380,000, $60,000, 35% lower, $2.4 million, $6.3 million, 70%, Country Q
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relocation can reduce compliance and wage costs; relocation cannot remove legal controls where products are sold | application_max_2: $380,000 vs $60,000 annual checks; wages 35% lower; 70% of sales are in Country X under strict import checks; $2.4 million relocation cost against a $6.3 million sales base | analysis_max_2: $320,000 annual compliance saving plus wage savings could repay the $2.4 million move within a few years; a failed check or legal dispute could destroy far more value than $320,000 a year | evaluation_max_2: weighs compliance and wage savings ($320,000 a year, 35% lower wages) against brand risk, Country X import checks and Country Q's legal weakness — decides against relocating for cost reasons alone

--- STEM ---
Craymoor Flour Co is a private limited company in Country X milling flour for 60 independent bakeries. It employs 52 workers and produces 4,500 tonnes of flour a year, worth $3.1 million. Wheat is harvested in autumn, so the mill holds 700 tonnes of wheat, about 8 weeks of output, worth $260,000. Two of the bakeries buy only from Craymoor and would switch to other mills if supply failed.

Holding that stock costs about $105,000 a year in rent, insurance and interest, including $2,800 a month of warehouse rent. Last spring a supplier strike delayed deliveries for 3 weeks and the mill kept running only because of its wheat store. The directors are deciding whether to keep 700 tonnes or cut stock to 250 tonnes with weekly deliveries.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'inventory'.
    Answer: The stock of raw materials, work in progress and finished goods held by a business at a point in time [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: stock of raw materials, work in progress and finished goods; held to support production or customer orders

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Craymoor Flour holds 700 tonnes of wheat.
    Answer: Reason 1: To keep production running all year [k], because wheat is harvested only in autumn and 700 tonnes cover about 8 weeks of milling for 60 bakeries [app]. Reason 2: To survive supply disruption [k], because last spring's 3-week supplier strike was absorbed without stopping the mill [app].
    Keywords: 700 tonnes, 8 weeks, supplier strike, independent bakeries, $260,000, 4,500 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: inventory keeps production running between seasonal supplies; inventory protects against supply delays or disruption | application_max_2: wheat arrives only in autumn; 700 tonnes cover about 8 weeks of output; the 3-week supplier strike last spring was absorbed without stopping production; 60 independent bakeries rely on Craymoor's supply

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs of holding the wheat inventory.
    Answer: Cost 1: Storage and holding expenses [k], because rent of $2,800 a month and the total $105,000 a year for rent, insurance and interest on 700 tonnes [app], reduce the profit available for reinvestment [an]. Cost 2: Money tied up in stock [k], because the wheat is worth $260,000, cash that cannot be used elsewhere in the mill [app], so other opportunities such as equipment or debt repayment are postponed [an].
    Keywords: $105,000, $2,800, 700 tonnes, $260,000, 8 weeks, 250 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: holding inventory incurs storage, insurance and interest costs; cash tied up in stock cannot be used elsewhere (opportunity cost) | application_max_2: $2,800 a month warehouse rent; $105,000 a year total holding cost; the 700-tonne store is worth $260,000 | analysis_max_2: holding costs of $105,000 a year directly reduce profit; $260,000 tied up has an opportunity cost for the mill's other needs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Craymoor Flour Co should cut its wheat inventory from 700 tonnes to 250 tonnes? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cutting stock to 250 tonnes would save money [k], because holding costs of about $105,000 a year would fall by roughly $67,500 and less cash would sit in the store [app], freeing funds for the mill's other needs [an]. However, a 250-tonne store leaves only about 3 weeks of cover [k], because it supports far fewer days of milling for 60 bakeries than 700 tonnes [app], so the next supply strike could stop production and push bakeries to rival mills [an]. Overall, Craymoor should keep the 700-tonne inventory [eval], because the 3-week strike showed that stock protects uninterrupted production and the loyalty of 60 bakeries, outweighing the $67,500 annual saving [eval].
    Keywords: $105,000, $2,800, 250 tonnes, 700 tonnes, 3 weeks, independent bakeries, $260,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower inventory reduces holding costs and frees cash; lower inventory raises the risk of running out during disruption | application_max_2: $105,000 a year holding cost; about $67,500 potential saving; 700 tonnes vs 250 tonnes (about 8 vs about 3 weeks of cover); 60 bakeries rely on Craymoor, including two exclusive buyers | analysis_max_2: saving $67,500 a year improves cash flow and funds other needs; 3 weeks of cover risks stopping production during a strike and losing bakery customers | evaluation_max_2: weighs the $67,500 annual saving against supply continuity and loyalty of 60 bakeries, shown by the 3-week strike

--- STEM ---
Highgrove Garden Products Ltd is a family-owned company in Country X making metal garden arches and patio heaters. It employs 34 workers and sells through 110 garden centres. Annual revenue is $2.8 million, yet a single hot weekend in June brought $310,000 of orders, about 11% of the year, and 1,400 units were delivered within 9 days. The busiest season runs from April to August.

The company usually holds 2,600 finished units going into May, worth $480,000, in a rented warehouse costing $3,900 a month. Demand is unpredictable, and last year sales rose 60% in one month. If the summer is cold, unsold heaters would sit in the warehouse for months. The directors are debating whether to raise inventory to 3,500 units or switch to just-in-time supply with weekly deliveries.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'just-in-time'.
    Answer: A stock control system where supplies arrive only when they are needed, so almost no inventory is held [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: supplies arrive only when needed for production or sale; minimises or eliminates held inventory

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Highgrove Garden Products keeps finished units in stock.
    Answer: Reason 1: To meet sudden surges in demand [k], because a single hot June weekend brought $310,000 of orders and 1,400 units were needed within 9 days [app]. Reason 2: To avoid running out at peak season [k], because sales rose 60% in one month last year, and stock lets 110 garden centres restock immediately [app].
    Keywords: $310,000, 1,400 units, 9 days, 60%, 110 garden centres, $2.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: inventory meets unexpected or peak demand; inventory prevents stockouts and lost sales | application_max_2: $310,000 in one hot June weekend; 1,400 units in 9 days; sales rose 60% in a single month last year; 110 garden centres depend on immediate restocking

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs of holding 2,600 finished units.
    Answer: Cost 1: Warehouse expense [k], because rent of $3,900 a month is about $46,800 a year, a charge that continues even in a cold summer [app], squeezing margins on the $2.8 million revenue [an]. Cost 2: Capital tied up in stock [k], because the inventory is worth $480,000, cash unavailable for other uses [app], so the business cannot invest or repay debt quickly [an].
    Keywords: $3,900, $480,000, 2,600, 3,500 units, just-in-time, $310,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: storage incurs rent and related charges; cash tied up in inventory cannot be used elsewhere | application_max_2: $3,900 a month warehouse rent (about $46,800 a year); inventory of finished units worth $480,000; unsold heaters may sit for months after a cold summer | analysis_max_2: fixed storage cost continues regardless of demand, reducing profit; $480,000 tied up restricts liquidity and investment options

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Highgrove Garden Products Ltd should raise inventory to 3,500 units rather than switch to just-in-time? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Holding 3,500 units would protect peak-season sales [k], because one hot weekend generated $310,000 and 1,400 units were needed within 9 days, so extra stock prevents garden centres from switching to rivals [app], safeguarding the $2.8 million annual revenue stream [an]. However, just-in-time would cut costs [k], because the $3,900 monthly warehouse rent and the $480,000 of cash in stock would shrink, and unsold heaters would not pile up after a cold summer [app], freeing cash for marketing or new products [an]. Overall, Highgrove should raise inventory to 3,500 units rather than switch to just-in-time [eval], because demand swings of 60% in a month make stockouts more costly than storage charges in the April to August season [eval].
    Keywords: 3,500 units, $310,000, $3,900, $480,000, 60%, $2.8 million, 1,400 units
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: holding more stock protects against sudden demand surges; just-in-time reduces storage cost and capital tied up but risks stockouts | application_max_2: $310,000 hot June weekend and 1,400 units in 9 days; $3,900 monthly rent and $480,000 tied up in stock; sales rose 60% in a single month last year | analysis_max_2: extra stock protects $2.8 million revenue and 110 retailer relationships at peak; just-in-time would cut storage cost and free cash but invites stockouts in hot months | evaluation_max_2: weighs stockout risk in the April to August season (60% monthly swings) against storage cost and capital tied up — decides for the larger inventory

--- STEM ---
Pennywell Wholesale Co is a private limited company in Country X supplying rice, sugar and lentils to 240 corner shops. It employs 29 workers and buys 900 tonnes of rice a year at $640 a tonne. The supplier offers a 6% discount on orders above 250 tonnes, and Pennywell saves about $34,560 a year by buying quarterly in bulk. Rice is Pennywell's biggest line by volume. Two shops have already asked for weekly rice deliveries.

Its warehouse holds about 280 tonnes at peak, costing $5,200 a month in rent, insurance and handling, $62,400 a year. Last year a burst pipe damaged $38,000 of stored sugar. The directors are weighing half-yearly bulk buying for a 9% discount against monthly deliveries to cut storage costs.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'economies of scale'.
    Answer: The fall in average cost per unit as a business increases the scale of its operations, for example by buying in bulk [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: average cost per unit falls as scale increases; purchasing (bulk-buy) economies give discounts for large orders

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Pennywell buys 900 tonnes of rice in bulk.
    Answer: Reason 1: To earn bulk-buy discounts [k], because orders above 250 tonnes get a 6% discount, saving about $34,560 a year on rice at $640 a tonne [app]. Reason 2: To guarantee supply for shops [k], because 240 corner shops rely on rice deliveries and peak stock of about 280 tonnes prevents empty shelves [app].
    Keywords: 900 tonnes, $640, 6%, 250 tonnes, $34,560, 240 corner shops, 280 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bulk buying earns purchasing economies and lower unit costs; large inventory guarantees continuity of supply | application_max_2: 6% discount above 250 tonnes; about $34,560 saved a year on $640 a tonne rice; 240 corner shops rely on deliveries; peak stock of about 280 tonnes

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two costs of holding the larger inventory.
    Answer: Cost 1: Storage and handling charges [k], because rent, insurance and handling cost $5,200 a month, $62,400 a year [app], which eats into the $34,560 bulk-buy saving [an]. Cost 2: Risk of damage or spoilage [k], because a burst pipe destroyed $38,000 of stored sugar last year [app], showing that holding more stock raises the chance of losing goods and money [an].
    Keywords: $5,200, $62,400, $38,000, 280 tonnes, $34,560, 6%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: holding inventory incurs storage, insurance and handling costs; stored goods risk damage, spoilage or loss | application_max_2: $5,200 a month, $62,400 a year in rent, insurance and handling; a burst pipe damaged $38,000 of stored sugar last year | analysis_max_2: $62,400 a year of storage costs absorb much of the $34,560 saving; greater stored volume increases exposure to damage like the $38,000 sugar loss

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Pennywell Wholesale Co should switch to half-yearly bulk buying for the 9% discount? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Half-yearly bulk buying would deepen the discount [k], because raising the saving from 6% to 9% adds about $17,280 a year on rice at $640 a tonne, and two shops already want weekly deliveries [app], strengthening Pennywell's margins on its $34,560 existing saving [an]. However, larger half-yearly stocks would raise storage and risk [k], because rent and insurance already cost $5,200 a month, and a burst pipe once destroyed $38,000 of sugar [app], so doubled stock could raise holding costs and potential losses above the $17,280 gain [an]. Overall, Pennywell should keep its quarterly 6% bulk buying rather than switch to half-yearly orders [eval], because the extra $17,280 a year does not cover the added storage, insurance and damage risk on much larger stock [eval].
    Keywords: 9%, 6%, $5,200, $38,000, $34,560, $62,400, 280 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: larger bulk orders deepen purchasing discounts; larger stocks raise storage cost and damage risk | application_max_2: 9% vs 6% discount: about $17,280 extra a year on $640 a tonne rice; $5,200 a month for rent, insurance and handling; $62,400 a year; $38,000 of sugar lost to a burst pipe last year | analysis_max_2: extra $17,280 a year improves margins on rice sales; doubled stock raises $62,400 a year baseline storage and the chance of repeat losses above the saving | evaluation_max_2: weighs the extra $17,280 a year discount against higher storage cost and damage risk ($38,000 precedent) — decides to keep quarterly 6% buying

--- STEM ---
Harrowdale Electronics Ltd is a private limited company in Country X importing 180,000 electric kettles and toasters a year from Country M for resale to 350 retailers. It employs 21 office and warehouse staff and pays $9.5 million for the imports plus $1.9 million in import duties. Average wholesale price is $74 per unit. Competitors currently supply Country X from two other countries.

The directors are considering opening a $6.8 million assembly plant in Country Y, which shares a free trade area with Country X so finished units enter tariff-free, employing 130 workers at wages 40% below Country X levels. Alternatively, the company could keep importing from Country M and raise wholesale prices by 8%. Demand in Country X is steady at 180,000 units a year.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define the term 'import'.
    Answer: Goods or services bought by one country from a supplier in another country [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: goods or services bought from abroad; money flows out to the foreign supplier

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the Country Y assembly plant appeals to Harrowdale.
    Answer: Reason 1: It removes the import duty [k], because finished units from Country Y enter Country X tariff-free under the free trade area, saving the $1.9 million duty paid on current imports [app]. Reason 2: It cuts wage costs [k], because the 130 Country Y workers would be paid 40% below Country X levels [app].
    Keywords: $1.9 million, $9.5 million, Country Y, 130 workers, 40% below, $6.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: tariff-free entry under a free trade area removes import duties; lower wages abroad reduce production costs | application_max_2: $1.9 million duties saved each year on finished units; 130 Country Y workers paid 40% below Country X levels

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of opening the Country Y assembly plant.
    Answer: Problem 1: Large set-up cost [k], because the plant needs $6.8 million before it earns anything [app], leaving little headroom if sales of the 180,000 units slow [an]. Problem 2: New-workforce risk [k], because 130 Country Y workers need training to Country X quality standards [app], and faults would damage Harrowdale's name with its 350 retailers [an].
    Keywords: $6.8 million, 130 workers, 350 retailers, 180,000, Country Y, $74
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: setting up abroad requires major up-front investment; a new workforce needs training and quality control is harder to maintain | application_max_2: $6.8 million set-up cost before any revenue; 130 Country Y workers need training for Country X standards; faults would reach 350 retailers | analysis_max_2: $6.8 million of up-front spend strains cash if 180,000-unit demand slows; quality failures would harm relationships with 350 retailers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harrowdale Electronics Ltd should open the Country Y assembly plant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Opening the plant would cut landed costs sharply [k], because finished units enter Country X tariff-free, saving $1.9 million a year, and wages run 40% below Country X levels for 130 workers [app], which would widen the current margin of $1.92 million on $74 average prices considerably [an]. However, the plant risks a lot [k], because $6.8 million must be committed while demand is steady at 180,000 units and Harrowdale would rely on Country Y logistics and politics for every kettle sold [app], so a disruption would starve 350 retailers of stock [an]. Overall, Harrowdale should open the Country Y assembly plant [eval], because the $1.9 million annual duty saving and 40% wage advantage far outweigh the $6.8 million one-off cost given steady 180,000-unit demand [eval].
    Keywords: $6.8 million, $1.9 million, 40% below, 180,000, 350 retailers, Country Y, $74
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: local assembly under a free trade area removes duties and may cut wages; setting up a plant abroad carries cost and supply-chain risk | application_max_2: $1.9 million annual duty saved; wages 40% below Country X levels for 130 workers; $6.8 million set-up cost; steady demand at 180,000 units a year; $74 average price and $9.5 million import spend under the current arrangement | analysis_max_2: duty saving and wage cut would widen the $1.92 million margin substantially; a $6.8 million commitment with single-plant politics and logistics risk could disrupt supply to 350 retailers | evaluation_max_2: weighs $1.9 million annual saving and 40% lower wages against the $6.8 million cost and supply risk — decides for the plant given steady 180,000-unit demand

Willowfen Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Country X selling flat-pack wardrobes and bookcases through 95 Country X retailers. It employs 17 staff and imports 60,000 flat-pack units a year from a single Country G supplier at $118 each, paying $7.08 million a year. The supplier has just announced a 12% price rise, and quality complaints now affect 6% of units.

The directors are deciding between building a $3.9 million factory in Country G employing 85 local workers, or keeping the import arrangement and accepting the 12% rise, which would add about $850,000 a year. PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U5_SET_01
UNIT: Unit 5: Financial Information and Decisions
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
A retail apparel business operates as a Private Limited Company, managing 8 clothing stores across major shopping malls. Operating successfully for 6 years, the company reports annual sales revenue of $1,500,000, cost of sales of $900,000, and annual operating expenses of $450,000. Balance sheet data shows current assets of $350,000 (comprising $220,000 in inventory, $80,000 in trade receivables, and $50,000 cash balance) against current liabilities of $250,000 (comprising $170,000 in trade payables to clothing manufacturers and an $80,000 bank overdraft).

Non-current liabilities total $400,000 in long-term bank loans. To fund a major $200,000 winter stock expansion, the finance manager is preparing a comprehensive cash-flow forecast and evaluating potential sources of finance. The manager is comparing taking out an additional 5-year bank loan at 7% annual interest versus securing extended 90-day trade credit terms from fabric suppliers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the Gross Profit Margin for this business. Show your working.
    Answer: Gross Profit = Revenue ($1,500,000) - Cost of Sales ($900,000) = $600,000 [1]. Gross Profit Margin = ($600,000 / $1,500,000) x 100 = 40% [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: correct formula/working step; 40%

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the Acid-Test Ratio for this business and explain what this result indicates.
    Answer: Acid-Test Ratio = (Current Assets - Inventory) / Current Liabilities [k] = ($350,000 - $220,000) / $250,000 = 0.52 : 1. The business has only $0.52 of liquid assets for every $1.00 of short-term liabilities [app], meaning it would struggle to pay the $80,000 bank overdraft and trade payables immediately [app]. Such a very low ratio signals a serious short-term liquidity risk that the business must manage carefully [k].
    Keywords: $350,000, $250,000, $220,000, inventory, overdraft, receivables
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 0.52 : 1 calculation; explanation of liquid assets vs short-term debt | application_max_2: $0.52 liquid assets per $1 short-term debt; trade payables demand

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways this business could improve its cash flow position over the next 6 months.
    Answer: Way 1: Negotiate extended payment terms with fabric suppliers [k], delaying cash outflows for trade payables [app] and keeping cash in the bank for operational needs [an]. Way 2: Offer early payment discounts to retail trade receivables [k], encouraging faster cash inflows from credit customers [app] and reducing the reliance on the $80,000 bank overdraft [an].
    Keywords: payables, receivables, overdraft, fabric, cash
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delay payables / negotiate trade credit; encourage faster receivables payment / discounts | application_max_2: fabric suppliers / trade payables; retail trade receivables / $80,000 overdraft | analysis_max_2: keeps cash in bank for operational needs; reduces reliance on bank overdraft

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think taking out a 5-year bank loan is a better source of finance for the $200,000 winter stock expansion than securing extended trade credit? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A 5-year bank loan provides a structured long-term capital sum [k] to purchase the $200,000 winter stock upfront [app], spreading repayments over 5 years so current liquidity is not immediately drained [an]. However, the loan incurs 7% interest expenses [k], increasing annual overheads beyond the current $450,000 operating expenses [app] and creating long-term debt liabilities [an]. Extended 90-day trade credit avoids interest charges but requires fast-selling inventory to pay fabric suppliers within 90 days. Overall, the 5-year bank loan is better because purchasing seasonal stock requires long-term repayment stability [eval], whereas relying on 90-day trade credit with a low acid-test ratio of 0.52:1 risks severe insolvency if winter sales stall [eval].
    Keywords: stock, loan, interest, credit, $200,000, 90-day, trade credit, 7%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: spreads capital repayment over long term; incurs interest expenses / risk of default | application_max_2: $200,000 winter stock; 7% interest; $450,000 operating expenses; 0.52:1 acid-test ratio | analysis_max_2: protects immediate current liquidity; increases annual operating overheads | evaluation_max_2: weighs interest cost against insolvency risks given low 0.52:1 acid-test ratio in retail context

UNIT: Unit 5: Financial Information and Decisions
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
A commercial bakery operating as a Private Limited Company manufactures packaged artisan breads for regional supermarkets. The bakery employs 85 staff across two production sites. The business reports annual revenue of $2,400,000, cost of sales of $1,440,000, and annual operating overheads of $600,000. Current financial records indicate non-current assets of $1,200,000, current assets of $400,000 (including $150,000 inventory, $180,000 trade receivables, and $70,000 cash balance), and current liabilities of $300,000 (comprising $220,000 trade payables and $80,000 short-term bank borrowings).

Non-current liabilities stand at $500,000 in long-term bank loans. To fund a major capital expansion project involving $600,000 for automated baking ovens, management is evaluating whether to issue new ordinary share capital to existing shareholders or secure an additional 10-year bank loan at 6% annual interest.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two reasons why a business requires long-term finance.
    Answer: Reason 1: To purchase non-current assets such as machinery or premises [1]. Reason 2: To finance long-term business expansion or capital development projects [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: purchasing non-current assets; funding long-term growth/expansion

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the Working Capital for this commercial bakery and outline what this figure represents.
    Answer: Working Capital = Current Assets ($400,000) - Current Liabilities ($300,000) = $100,000 [k]. This positive working capital means the bakery's current assets comfortably exceed its current liabilities [app], suggesting it can settle its $220,000 trade payables and $80,000 short-term borrowings as they fall due [app]. It also indicates healthy short-term liquidity for day-to-day trading operations [k].
    Keywords: current assets, current liabilities, payables, borrowings, $400,000, $300,000, bakery
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: $100,000 calculation; definition/meaning of working capital | application_max_2: $400,000 current assets vs $300,000 current liabilities; $220,000 trade payables / $80,000 borrowings

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain one internal source and one external source of finance suitable for purchasing short-term raw material supplies.
    Answer: Internal Source: Retained profit from previous trading years [k] can be used without paying interest [an], drawing on the cash balance of $70,000 to buy ingredients for the artisan breads [app]. External Source: Trade credit from flour and ingredient suppliers [k] allows the bakery to delay payment while it awaits supermarket invoices being settled [an], easing pressure on its current liabilities of $300,000 [app].
    Keywords: breads, supermarkets, $70,000, $300,000, current liabilities, cash, bakery
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit; trade credit | application_max_2: $70,000 cash balance / retained profit; $300,000 current liabilities / supermarket sales | analysis_max_2: no interest costs incurred; improves short-term cash flow timing

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Consider whether issuing new ordinary shares or taking out a 10-year bank loan is the better source of finance for the $600,000 automated baking oven project. Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Issuing new ordinary shares brings permanent equity capital [k] for the $600,000 automated baking ovens [app], which never has to be repaid and incurs zero interest charges [an]. However, selling shares dilutes ownership control and requires paying dividends from profit for the year. A 10-year bank loan preserves ownership structure [k], but adds 6% annual interest expenses to existing overheads of $600,000 [app] and increases non-current liabilities beyond $500,000 [an]. Overall, issuing shares is recommended because adding a $600,000 loan to existing non-current liabilities of $500,000 significantly increases fixed-interest debt risk [eval], whereas equity finance provides safe funding for fixed capital without burdening monthly cash flow with interest repayments [eval].
    Keywords: loan, interest, ovens, liabilities, overheads, share capital, $600,000, 6%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: no repayment / no interest for equity; loan interest costs / increased financial risk | application_max_2: $600,000 automated baking ovens; 6% annual interest; $600,000 overheads; $500,000 non-current liabilities | analysis_max_2: avoids cash outflow debt pressure; increases annual financial interest overheads | evaluation_max_2: weighs fixed-interest financial risk against ownership dilution in capital expansion context
