PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U5_SET_46
UNIT: Unit 5: Financial Information and Decisions
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Baobab Sewing Cooperative is a rural start-up in Country X founded 8 months ago by 9 women making school uniforms. The cooperative sells 210 uniforms a month at $18 each and wants to buy an industrial sewing machine costing $5,400 to take a contract with a local school for 500 uniforms a term. Demand rises sharply before the autumn term, and the cooperative works from a donated room in the village clinic.

A government enterprise grant of $2,000 is available for rural start-ups that create at least 3 jobs. A micro-finance institution also offers $5,400 over 24 months at 12% annual interest. The cooperative's members have saved $900 so far and add about $300 a month from profits. Members work part-time around farming commitments.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'micro-finance'.
    Answer: Micro-finance is the provision of very small loans and financial services to people who cannot access traditional bank finance, typically to start or grow a very small business [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: very small loans for people excluded from bank finance; aimed at micro-businesses and start-ups

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of the government enterprise grant for the cooperative.
    Answer: Advantage 1: The $2,000 grant does not need to be repaid [k], so it directly reduces the amount the cooperative must borrow for the $5,400 machine [app]. Advantage 2: The grant supports rural start-ups that create jobs [k], helping the cooperative fund its plan to hire at least 3 local women when it signs the school contract [app].
    Keywords: government enterprise grant, $2,000, $5,400, local school, Baobab Sewing Cooperative, 500 uniforms, rural start-ups
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: grant is not repayable — free funding; grant encourages job creation in rural areas | application_max_2: $2,000 reduces the $5,400 machine cost needing finance; at least 3 local jobs requirement links to the school contract

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of relying only on the cooperative's own savings.
    Answer: Limitation 1: The members' savings total only $900 [k], exactly one sixth of the $5,400 machine [app], so saving alone cannot fund the school contract in time and the cooperative risks losing the 500-uniform order [an]. Limitation 2: Accumulating savings is slow [k]; even with the $2,000 grant, covering the remaining $3,400 at $300 a month would take about 11 months, and 18 months without the grant [app], by which time the school may have sourced its uniforms elsewhere [an].
    Keywords: $900, $5,400, $300, grant, 500 uniforms, local school, $2,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: savings accumulated are small relative to the requirement; slow accumulation delays the purchase and the contract | application_max_2: $900 saved vs $5,400 machine cost — one sixth of the requirement; $300 a month surplus: about 11 months with the grant, 18 months without | analysis_max_2: school may lose patience and source uniforms elsewhere; 500-uniform contract would be lost, undermining the whole plan

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the cooperative should take the micro-finance loan or wait and save from profits? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Taking the micro-finance loan of $5,400 [k] would let the cooperative buy the machine now and deliver the 500-uniform school contract, worth about $9,000 a term at $18 per uniform [app]; at 12% interest the cost is about $648 a year, manageable against sales of about $3,780 a month, and the machine pays for itself quickly [an]. Waiting to save $300 a month [k] avoids all interest and keeps the cooperative debt-free [app]; but saving the full amount would take 18 months, and even after the $2,000 grant about 11 months, risking the school contract entirely [an]. On balance, the cooperative should take the micro-finance loan and still apply for the $2,000 grant [eval], because the machine's revenue gain far outweighs roughly $1,296 of interest over 2 years [eval].
    Keywords: micro-finance, $5,400, 12%, $2,000, 500 uniforms, $18, $300, grant
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: loan buys the machine immediately and earns revenue sooner; saving is interest-free but slow and risky | application_max_2: $5,400 machine delivers the 500-uniform contract worth about $9,000 a term at $18 each; saving $300 a month takes 18 months (about 11 with the $2,000 grant) | analysis_max_2: $648 a year interest is absorbable against about $3,780 monthly sales; waiting risks losing the contract; interest over 2 years is only about $1,296 | evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation combining loan and grant application; judgement weighs contract revenue against interest cost

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U5_SET_47
UNIT: Unit 5: Financial Information and Decisions
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Elm & Iron Furniture is a new workshop in Country X founded 14 months ago by Rosa Marlowe making oak coffee tables. She invested $16,000 of her own savings and the workshop now sells 25 tables a month at $260 each. She wants to buy a $19,000 industrial sander to increase output. She employs 2 full-time carpenters, and her waiting list has grown to 40 tables. A home-decor magazine recently featured her best-selling oak coffee table.

A government training grant of $6,000 is available if the business employs and trains 5 apprentices for 2 years and submits quarterly progress reports. A micro-finance lender offers $19,000 over 3 years at 13% annual interest. Rosa worries the grant conditions will stretch her management time.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline two conditions attached to the government training grant.
    Answer: The business must employ and train 5 apprentices for 2 years [1] and must submit quarterly progress reports [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: employ and train 5 apprentices for 2 years; submit quarterly progress reports

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Elm & Iron Furniture of accepting the government training grant.
    Answer: Advantage 1: The $6,000 grant never needs to be repaid [k], so it covers nearly a third of the $19,000 sander with no interest to pay [app]. Advantage 2: The grant pays for apprenticeships [k], helping the workshop train workers who can later raise output above 25 tables a month and clear the waiting list of 40 tables [app].
    Keywords: government training grant, $6,000, $19,000, apprentices, 25 tables, Elm & Iron Furniture, industrial sander
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: grant is free, non-repayable funding; grant funds training, building workforce skills | application_max_2: $6,000 towards the $19,000 sander without interest; trained apprentices can help clear the 40-table waiting list beyond 25 tables a month

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of the grant for Elm & Iron Furniture.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: The grant conditions are demanding [k]; employing and training 5 apprentices for 2 years adds wage costs on top of the $16,000 Rosa already invested [app], stretching the workshop's cash before the sander even arrives [an]. Disadvantage 2: Quarterly progress reports add administrative work [k]; Rosa, who already manages sales of 25 tables a month and 2 carpenters, would lose time she cannot easily spare [app], reducing the hours available for production and supervision of the apprentices [an].
    Keywords: $6,000, $19,000, 5 apprentices, quarterly progress reports, $16,000, 25 tables, 2 full-time carpenters
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: conditions add significant ongoing obligations and costs; reporting requirements consume management time | application_max_2: 5 apprentices for 2 years on top of the $16,000 already invested; Rosa already runs 25 tables a month with 2 carpenters | analysis_max_2: cash strain before the $19,000 sander is even delivered; time lost to reports reduces production and supervision capacity

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rosa should accept the government training grant or take the micro-finance loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the grant [k] would give the workshop $6,000 that never needs repaying, cutting the borrowed amount for the $19,000 sander to $13,000 [app]; the 5 apprentices would also lift output beyond 25 tables a month and support the waiting list of 40 tables [an]. Taking the micro-finance loan alone at 13% [k] over 3 years costs about $2,470 a year, roughly $7,410 of interest, but avoids every grant condition and report [app]; Rosa keeps full control of her time and can focus on production [an]. On balance, Rosa should accept the grant [eval], because $6,000 of free money plus trained apprentices outweigh the administration, provided the extra wages fit the budget [eval]; if the conditions prove unmanageable, the loan remains the fallback.
    Keywords: government training grant, $6,000, $19,000, 13%, 5 apprentices, 25 tables, industrial sander, $16,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: grant is free funding but conditional and adds obligations; loan is flexible but adds interest cost | application_max_2: $6,000 grant cuts the $19,000 sander requirement to $13,000; 13% over 3 years costs about $2,470 a year (roughly $7,410 total) | analysis_max_2: apprentices could raise output and clear the 40-table waiting list; loan preserves Rosa's time but adds about $7,410 of interest | evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation weighing free money against conditions; judgement identifies the fallback if conditions become unmanageable

--- STEM ---
Redwood Retail Group runs 11 discount stores in Country X. It plans two moves this year: a $350,000 refit of its largest store over 18 months and an $80,000 bulk purchase of stock before the December trading season. The largest store employs 85 staff and anchors a regional shopping centre. The business made a profit after tax of $420,000 last year and holds retained profit of $260,000.

The directors must choose between using retained profit for the December stock and funding the refit with a long-term route, or using retained profit for the refit and covering the stock from short-term sources. Suppliers offer 60 days' trade credit on stock, and bank loans for refits are available at 8% annual interest over 6 years.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two factors a business should consider when choosing a source of finance.
    Answer: The factors include the cost of the finance, such as interest or dividend obligations [1], and the period over which the money is needed, short-term or long-term [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cost of finance (interest/dividends/fees); period required — short-term vs long-term

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why short-term finance suits the December stock purchase better than long-term finance.
    Answer: Reason 1: The December stock is needed for only a few weeks [k]; a short-term source such as 60 days' trade credit matches this, as the stock will sell before the refit finishes [app]. Reason 2: Short-term finance avoids paying 8% interest for 6 years on a purchase recovered within weeks [k]; the $80,000 stock will generate cash during December, making a 6-year loan wasteful [app].
    Keywords: December stock, $80,000, trade credit, 60 days, 8%, 6 years, Redwood Retail Group, December trading season
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: period of finance should match the life of the need; short-term finance avoids unnecessary long-term interest cost | application_max_2: 60 days' trade credit matches the December selling window; $80,000 stock recovered within weeks vs 8% for 6 years

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two factors the directors should weigh before using retained profit for the store refit.
    Answer: Factor 1: Amount required [k]; the $350,000 refit would absorb all $260,000 of retained profit and still leave $90,000 to find [app], so the December stock purchase could lose its planned funding source [an]. Factor 2: Control [k]; using retained profit keeps ownership fully with the existing shareholders [app], whereas outside long-term finance could dilute control or add conditions [an].
    Keywords: $350,000, $260,000, retained profit, largest store, December stock, Redwood Retail Group, $420,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: amount of finance required vs amount available; control — retained profit avoids dilution or conditions | application_max_2: $350,000 refit exceeds $260,000 retained profit leaving $90,000 to find; retained profit avoids dilution or conditions from outside lenders | analysis_max_2: December stock could lose retained-profit funding; outside finance risks control, ownership or lender conditions

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redwood Retail Group should use retained profit for the December stock or for the store refit? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Using retained profit for the $80,000 December stock [k] matches a short-term need with internal finance and leaves $180,000 of retained profit for other uses; the 60 days' trade credit could cover the stock anyway [app], freeing cash while the stock sells during the December trading season [an]. Using retained profit for the $350,000 refit [k] would exhaust the $260,000 and still leave $90,000 to find, leaving nothing for the stock [app]; the 18-month capital project also matches the long-term route offered by the 8%, 6-year bank loan instead [an]. On balance, retained profit should fund the $80,000 stock, not the refit [eval], because matching short-term finance to short-term needs keeps control and cash flexibility [eval].
    Keywords: retained profit, $80,000, December stock, $260,000, $350,000, 8%, 6 years, trade credit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: short-term needs match short-term internal sources; long-term capital projects suit long-term borrowing of matching period | application_max_2: $80,000 stock covered by retained profit leaving $180,000 or by 60 days' trade credit; $350,000 refit exhausts $260,000 retained profit leaving $90,000 to find | analysis_max_2: stock cash returns during December, quickly replenishing reserves; 8% over 6 years matches an 18-month refit's long-term benefit | evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation justified on period matching; judgement weighs preserving cash flexibility and control

--- STEM ---
Anchorline Hotel is a private limited company in Country X with 48 guest rooms. Last year the hotel reported revenue of $1,150,000 and a profit after tax of $230,000. Occupancy averaged 74% across the year, with weekend peaks. The board paid a dividend of $85,000 to shareholders. The hotel now wants to refurbish the restaurant kitchen costing $140,000 and replace its shuttle vans costing $54,000. The vans are used mainly for airport transfers.

The finance manager suggests funding the kitchen from retained profit and selling the 2 old shuttle vans for $14,000 towards the new ones. Shareholders are divided: some want a higher dividend, others prefer the investment. The hotel also holds $96,000 of retained profit brought forward from earlier years.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the retained profit Anchorline Hotel added this year. Show your working.
    Answer: Retained profit = Profit after tax − Dividends paid = $230,000 − $85,000 = $145,000 [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: correct formula: profit after tax − dividends; $145,000

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of using retained profit to fund the kitchen refurbishment.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Retained profit is an internal source of finance [k], so the hotel avoids interest charges on the $140,000 kitchen cost [app]. Advantage 2: Reinvesting retained profit keeps ownership unchanged [k]; no new shares need to be issued and existing shareholders retain full control [app].
    Keywords: retained profit, $140,000, Anchorline Hotel, profit after tax, 48 guest rooms, dividend, kitchen
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: internal source: no interest or repayment required; ownership and control remain unchanged | application_max_2: no interest on the $140,000 kitchen cost; no new shares issued; control stays with current shareholders

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of relying only on retained profit to fund both projects.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: The two projects total $194,000 [k], more than this year's $145,000 retained profit [app], so the hotel must draw on its $96,000 brought-forward balance, leaving nothing in reserve for next year [an]. Disadvantage 2: Retained profit is finite and may disappoint shareholders [k]; the board already paid $85,000 [app], and shareholders expecting an increase may resent an unchanged or lower dividend while funds are locked into the kitchen and vans [an].
    Keywords: $140,000, $54,000, $85,000, profit after tax, $230,000, $96,000, retained profit, shuttle vans
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit is limited in amount and may be insufficient; using retained profit may reduce or prevent a dividend | application_max_2: projects total $194,000 vs $145,000 retained profit this year; existing $85,000 dividend already paid and shareholders divided | analysis_max_2: drawing on the $96,000 brought-forward leaves no reserve for next year; shareholder dissatisfaction could damage relations with owners

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Anchorline Hotel should fund both projects from retained profit or pay a higher dividend? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Funding both projects from retained profit [k] gives the hotel a refurbished kitchen and new shuttle vans, protecting the $1,150,000 revenue from its 48 rooms [app]; the projects cost $194,000 and this year's retained profit is $145,000, so the $96,000 brought forward would comfortably cover the gap [an]. Paying a higher dividend [k] would reward shareholders who backed a 74% occupancy year and satisfy those shareholders wanting immediate returns [app]; however, it would leave the kitchen and vans unfunded, pushing the board towards borrowing or delaying investment that grows future profits [an]. On balance, the projects should be funded from retained profit [eval], because the refurbishment and vans should raise future earnings more than a one-off dividend rise would satisfy owners [eval].
    Keywords: retained profit, $96,000, kitchen, shuttle vans, $1,150,000, $85,000, dividend, 48 guest rooms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reinvestment strengthens future earning capacity; dividends reward shareholders in the short term | application_max_2: projects cost $194,000; $145,000 retained profit plus $96,000 brought forward covers it; dividend increase would reward 74%-occupancy performance but leaves kitchen and vans unfunded | analysis_max_2: $96,000 brought forward comfortably covers the shortfall on both projects; delaying or borrowing increases cost and slows investment for future profit | evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation balancing reinvestment against dividends; judgement weighs long-term earnings growth against immediate shareholder return

--- STEM ---
Foxglove Lodge is a guest house in Country X founded 3 years ago by Mark and Leanne Doyle, with 14 letting rooms. The lodge earned revenue of $310,000 last year and employs 6 part-time staff. Bookings peak in summer and the lodge advertises through travel websites. The owners want to add a self-catering annexe costing $120,000, which would add 8 family rooms, and repair the kitchen roof at $26,000.

They must keep enough cash to pay wages of $9,400 a month. The lodge holds $74,000 in retained profit, an unused minibus valued at $22,000, and the couple's personal savings of $30,000. Both owners work full-time in the business, and they are deciding which project to fund first and which source to use.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two needs for finance that Foxglove Lodge has.
    Answer: Capital expenditure for the annexe and the kitchen roof repair [1] and working capital to pay the monthly wages [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: capital expenditure (annexe / roof repair); working capital for day-to-day costs such as wages

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two internal sources of finance available to Foxglove Lodge.
    Answer: Source 1: Retained profit [k]; the lodge has accumulated $74,000 from past profits, which could pay the $26,000 roof repair in full and still leave $48,000 towards the annexe [app]. Source 2: Sale of the unused minibus [k] would raise $22,000 towards the project without borrowing or repaying interest [app].
    Keywords: retained profit, $74,000, minibus, $22,000, $26,000, Foxglove Lodge, annexe
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit — internal reinvestment of past earnings; sale of existing assets — selling unused property or equipment | application_max_2: $74,000 covers the $26,000 roof and leaves $48,000; minibus valued at $22,000 sold to fund part of the annexe

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the owners face when choosing between these sources.
    Answer: Problem 1: Each source is finite [k]; internal sources total $126,000 but the annexe and the roof cost $146,000 together, a shortfall of $20,000 [app], so something must be delayed, reduced or financed from outside the business [an]. Problem 2: Using personal savings carries a heavy opportunity cost [k]; the $30,000 is also the family's safety cushion [app], and spending it on the annexe would leave them exposed if bookings fell or another repair was needed [an].
    Keywords: $74,000, $22,000, $30,000, annexe, roof, personal savings, minibus, Mark and Leanne
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: internal sources combined may be insufficient for both needs; personal savings involve opportunity cost and lost security | application_max_2: $74,000 + $22,000 + $30,000 = $126,000 vs $120,000 + $26,000 = $146,000, a $20,000 gap; $30,000 personal savings double as the family safety cushion | analysis_max_2: projects cannot both be funded internally — delay, cut scope or borrow; spending savings leaves the family exposed to falling bookings or emergencies

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the Doyles should build the annexe now or delay it and repair only the roof? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Building the annexe now [k] would add 8 family rooms and could lift revenue beyond the $310,000 earned last year [app]; internal sources total $126,000, so after the $26,000 roof repair the couple could put $100,000 towards the $120,000 annexe, leaving only $20,000 to find [an]. Delaying the annexe and repairing only the roof [k] would protect the $30,000 personal savings and keep wages of $9,400 a month secure [app]; however, the lodge would forfeit a full summer of extra family-room income and might lose guests to rival guest houses [an]. On balance, the Doyles should build the annexe now [eval], using retained profit, the minibus sale and savings, and covering the $20,000 gap with a small short-term bank loan only if strictly needed [eval].
    Keywords: annexe, $120,000, $26,000, $74,000, $22,000, $30,000, $310,000, 14 letting rooms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: building now captures new revenue and growth; delaying protects personal security and cash stability | application_max_2: 8 new family rooms could lift revenue beyond $310,000; $126,000 internal sources; $100,000 available after the $26,000 roof, leaving a $20,000 gap | analysis_max_2: extra summer bookings would be forfeited by delaying; savings and $9,400 monthly wages stay protected if the annexe waits | evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation with a clear order of preference; judgement covers how the $20,000 gap would be handled

--- STEM ---
Silverbirch Aerospace Plc is a public limited company in Country X that manufactures small aircraft components, employing 240 workers and reporting revenue of $18 million last year. The company now wants to build a new $6.5 million production plant to meet rising orders from overseas customers and cut delivery times from 14 days to 10 days.

The Board is deciding between two external sources of finance. Option 1 is to issue 2.5 million new shares on the Country X stock exchange at $2.60 each. Option 2 is a bank loan of $6.5 million over 8 years at a fixed interest rate of 8.5% per year, costing $552,500 in interest every year. The Finance Director warns that the loan would add heavy fixed repayments, while existing shareholders own 40 million shares and fear control of the company would be diluted if new shares are issued.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'issue of shares' as a source of finance.
    Answer: An issue of shares is the sale of shares (small ownership stakes) in a company to investors in exchange for capital. It is a long-term source of external finance available to limited companies, and the money raised does not have to be repaid. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Sale of shares (ownership stakes) to investors for capital; Money raised does not have to be repaid; long-term external finance for limited companies

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of issuing new shares rather than taking a bank loan to finance the new plant.
    Answer: First advantage: issuing shares provides the $6.5 million of capital without adding fixed repayments, so $552,500 a year of interest is saved and cash flow is eased while the 240 workers are paid [k], which suits a company whose revenue is already $18 million and whose overseas orders are rising [app]. Second advantage: shares carry no obligation to repay the capital, unlike the 8-year bank loan at 8.5%, so the risk of insolvency is reduced if profits fall [k], and the $2.60 issue price means 2.5 million new shares raise exactly the $6.5 million needed without increasing the company's debt [app].
    Keywords: $6.5 million, $552,500, 2.5 million, $2.60, 8.5%, $18 million, 240 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: No repayment obligation and no interest to pay on share capital; Reduces insolvency risk compared with fixed loan repayments | application_max_2: $6.5 million raised matches the cost of the new plant; $552,500 per year of interest avoided; 2.5 million shares at $2.60 equals $6.5 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of issuing new shares for the existing shareholders of Silverbirch Aerospace Plc.
    Answer: First disadvantage: existing shareholders' ownership would be diluted, because issuing 2.5 million shares to new investors reduces the percentage held by the owners of the existing 40 million shares [k], meaning each share receives a smaller slice of any future dividends and has weaker voting power over how the new $6.5 million plant is run [app], so existing investors may resist the issue or demand a higher share price [an]. Second disadvantage: control of the company could change hands, because new shareholders voting at the AGM may outvote current holders on key decisions [k], for example whether the $6.5 million raised is reinvested to cut delivery times or paid out as dividends [app], so the original owners risk losing their ability to steer the company's long-term strategy [an].
    Keywords: 2.5 million, 40 million, $6.5 million, $2.60, $552,500, new shares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Dilution of existing shareholders' ownership percentage; Possible loss of control; weaker voting power over decisions | application_max_2: 2.5 million new shares compared with existing 40 million shares; Dividend per share and voting strength reduced for current holders; Decisions on spending the $6.5 million / cutting delivery times | analysis_max_2: Dilution leads to smaller dividends and weaker influence, causing shareholder resistance; Loss of control means original owners cannot direct company strategy

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Silverbirch Aerospace Plc should issue new shares rather than take the 8-year bank loan to finance the new plant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Issuing shares would raise the full $6.5 million needed for the plant without creating fixed repayments, saving $552,500 a year of interest and keeping cash flow healthy while orders grow [k], and because revenue is already $18 million with 240 workers, the company can afford to dilute the 40 million existing shares by issuing 2.5 million new ones at $2.60 [app], so the business avoids the risk of defaulting on the loan if overseas demand weakens [an]. However, the bank loan would keep ownership and control unchanged and protect the existing 40 million shares from dilution, costing only $552,500 per year of interest, which a business with $18 million revenue could comfortably cover [k], and loan interest is tax-deductible whereas share dividends are not, and unlike share issues the loan does not permanently reduce shareholders' claim on profits [app], so the loan is less damaging to owners in the long run [an]. Overall, I think the company should issue the new shares, because eliminating $552,500 of annual interest and avoiding 8 years of fixed repayments outweighs the dilution from a 2.5 million share issue when the plant will cut delivery times and win more overseas orders [eval]. The decision would change only if the current owners refused any loss of control, in which case the bank loan would be the safer choice [eval].
    Keywords: $6.5 million, $552,500, 2.5 million, $2.60, 40 million, $18 million, 240 workers, 8 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Share issue raises capital without repayment; loan adds fixed repayments and interest; Loan preserves existing ownership and control; interest is tax-deductible | application_max_2: $6.5 million required matches both options; $552,500 annual interest vs $18 million revenue and 240 workers; 2.5 million new shares at $2.60 vs existing 40 million shares | analysis_max_2: No fixed repayments reduce default risk during demand fluctuations; Dilution reduces owners' claim on profits and control | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing interest saving against dilution; Acknowledges the alternative view/conditions under which the choice would change

--- STEM ---
Bramblehurst Joinery Co is a private limited company in Country X that makes bespoke fitted kitchens and bedroom furniture, employing 45 workers across a workshop and a showroom. Revenue last year was $3.2 million and profit was $290,000. The business needs $850,000 to buy a CNC routing machine so that cutting times fall from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen.

The two founding families own all the shares and are deciding between two external sources of finance. Option 1 is a bank loan of $850,000 over 5 years at 9% interest, costing $76,500 per year and $382,500 in total interest. Option 2 is to issue new shares worth $850,000 to the two founding families, who would then own 60% of the company instead of 75%. Option 1 keeps ownership unchanged but adds fixed annual repayments; Option 2 brings in cash with no interest but dilutes control.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'bank loan' as a source of finance.
    Answer: A bank loan is a sum of money borrowed from a bank or other lender for an agreed period, to be repaid with interest in instalments. It is a long-term external source of finance commonly used to purchase fixed assets such as machinery. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Borrowing from a bank or lender for an agreed period; Repaid with interest, usually in regular instalments

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the bank loan may be attractive to Bramblehurst Joinery Co.
    Answer: First reason: the loan provides the full $850,000 needed to buy the CNC routing machine without giving up any ownership, because the two founding families keep their shares and control the business [k], which matters to them since Option 2 would cut their holding from 75% to 60% [app]. Second reason: although the $76,500 annual interest is a fixed cost, the machine should cut cutting times from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen and win more orders, lifting revenue above $3.2 million so the interest is comfortably covered [k], and the 5-year term spreads repayment instead of demanding one large up-front sum the business cannot fund from profit of $290,000 alone [app].
    Keywords: $850,000, 75%, 60%, $76,500, $3.2 million, $290,000, CNC routing machine
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large sum available immediately without losing ownership; Repayments spread over an agreed period; control retained by owners | application_max_2: $850,000 needed for the CNC routing machine; $76,500 per year interest versus $290,000 profit; Cutting time reduced from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks of taking the bank loan rather than issuing shares to the founding families.
    Answer: First risk: the loan creates fixed repayments of about $76,500 per year plus principal for 5 years, regardless of profits [k], so if revenue falls below $3.2 million or a major kitchen contract is lost, the business could fail to pay and the bank could demand repayment or seize the CNC routing machine offered as security [app], meaning the business faces a real risk of insolvency during a downturn [an]. Second risk: interest of $382,500 over the 5 years is a direct cost that reduces net profit [k], so profit of $290,000 last year would drop sharply once interest is paid, leaving little retained profit for dividends or expansion [app], which limits the business's ability to fund future growth from internal sources [an].
    Keywords: $76,500, $382,500, $290,000, $3.2 million, $850,000, 9 days, CNC routing machine
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed repayments must be made regardless of profit; default risk; Interest is a direct cost that reduces net profit and retained profit | application_max_2: $76,500 per year for 5 years plus $382,500 total interest; Profit of $290,000 would be heavily reduced by interest; CNC routing machine may be used as security | analysis_max_2: Fixed repayments in a downturn lead to insolvency risk; Higher interest charges leave less retained profit for future expansion

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Bramblehurst Joinery Co should take the bank loan rather than issue shares to the founding families? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Taking the bank loan keeps the founding families in complete control, with their holding at 75% instead of falling to 60% [k], and it provides the $850,000 for the CNC routing machine immediately so cutting times fall from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen and orders can rise [app], meaning the loan could pay for itself from extra revenue within a few years [an]. However, the loan adds fixed repayments of $76,500 a year plus interest totalling $382,500, which is heavy compared with profit of $290,000 last year [k], so a bad year could push the business into cash-flow difficulty, whereas issuing shares to the families would bring cash with no interest and no repayment deadline [app], although dilution to 60% would weaken the families' control over the business [an]. Overall, I think the business should take the bank loan, because keeping 100% family control and the prospect of faster production and higher revenue outweigh the $76,500 annual interest, provided the families are confident orders will grow [eval]. If sales were likely to fall, the share issue would be the safer option because it carries no repayment obligation [eval].
    Keywords: $850,000, 75%, 60%, $76,500, $382,500, $290,000, $3.2 million, CNC routing machine
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Loan keeps ownership/control unchanged; shares dilute existing holders; Loan adds fixed repayments and interest; shares carry no repayment obligation | application_max_2: Holding stays at 75% versus 60% under share issue; $76,500 per year and $382,500 total interest versus $290,000 profit; $850,000 needed for CNC routing machine; cutting time 9 days to 4 days | analysis_max_2: Loan could pay for itself through faster production and more orders; Fixed repayments create cash-flow risk in bad years versus dilution risk of shares | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation supported by stem figures; Acknowledges conditions under which the decision would change

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U5_SET_53
UNIT: Unit 5: Financial Information and Decisions
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Ashwick Garments Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing school uniforms for retail chains, employing 110 workers. Annual credit sales are $2.4 million and customers usually take 75 days to pay. At present $480,000 is owed by debtors, and the business is struggling to pay its own suppliers on time.

The Managing Director is choosing between two external sources of finance. Option 1 is to use a factoring company, which would advance 85% of the outstanding debts immediately, giving $408,000, and charges a fee of 3% of invoice value, about $14,400 a year. Option 2 is a bank loan of $350,000 over 3 years at 10% interest, costing $35,000 per year and $105,000 in total. Option 1 releases cash quickly but is more expensive; Option 2 is cheaper long term but adds a fixed monthly repayment.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'factoring of debts' as a source of finance.
    Answer: Factoring of debts is when a business sells its outstanding customer invoices (debtors) to a specialist factoring company for immediate cash, usually at a discount. It is a short-term external source of finance that improves cash flow without waiting for customers to pay. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Selling outstanding invoices/debts to a factoring company; Cash received immediately, usually at a discount; improves cash flow

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of factoring the $480,000 of debts rather than taking the bank loan.
    Answer: First advantage: factoring would release $408,000 immediately (85% of the $480,000 owed) [k], so the business can pay its suppliers on time and avoid running short of cash while customers take 75 days to settle [app]. Second advantage: the factor takes on the task of chasing and collecting payment from debtors [k], saving management time and letting the 110 workers focus on producing uniforms rather than debt collection [app].
    Keywords: $480,000, $408,000, 85%, 75 days, $2.4 million, 110 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Immediate access to cash tied up in debtors; improves liquidity; Factor handles credit control/collection, releasing management time | application_max_2: $408,000 = 85% of the $480,000 owed; Customers take 75 days to pay; Credit sales of $2.4 million per year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of factoring the $480,000 of debts.
    Answer: First disadvantage: factoring is expensive, with a fee of 3% of invoice value, about $14,400 a year, plus the 15% discount on the $480,000 of debts [k], so the business keeps only $408,000 of what it is owed, reducing profit from $2.4 million of credit sales [app], and this cost persists year after year while the factoring arrangement continues [an]. Second disadvantage: customers know their debt has been sold to a factor and may resent being chased by a third party [k], which could damage relationships with the uniform-chain buyers who place regular large orders [app], risking lost contracts and weakening Ashwick's reputation as a reliable supplier [an].
    Keywords: $480,000, $408,000, $14,400, 3%, $2.4 million, 75 days, 85%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Factoring is costly; fees and discounts reduce income received; Customer relationships and goodwill may be damaged by third-party collection | application_max_2: 3% fee = about $14,400 per year; Receives $408,000 of $480,000 owed (15% discount); Uniform-chain buyers place regular orders | analysis_max_2: Ongoing fees reduce profit year after year; Strained customer relationships lead to lost orders and weaker goodwill

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ashwick Garments Ltd should use factoring rather than a bank loan to solve its cash-flow problem? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Factoring would give the business $408,000 immediately without adding loan repayments, and the fee of about $14,400 a year is lower than the bank loan's $35,000 annual interest [k], and it would cover the gap created by customers taking 75 days to pay on $2.4 million of credit sales [app], relieving cash flow within weeks rather than after a lengthy loan application [an]. However, factoring costs 3% of every invoice ($14,400 a year) plus the 15% discount on the $480,000 debts, so over 3 years the total fees would exceed the $105,000 interest on a $350,000 bank loan [k], and the factor's control over debt collection could harm relationships with uniform-chain buyers who currently wait 75 days [app], which may matter more than the short-term saving on interest [an]. Overall, I think Ashwick should use factoring for its short-term cash-flow problem because the speed and lower annual cost outweigh the fee, provided customer relationships survive the handover to the factor [eval]. If the debt problem is long term, the bank loan at 10% would be cheaper over 3 years ($105,000) and would keep debt collection in-house [eval].
    Keywords: $408,000, $14,400, $35,000, $105,000, 75 days, $2.4 million, $480,000, $350,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Factoring provides immediate cash but charges fees and a discount; Bank loan adds fixed interest and repayments but is cheaper long term | application_max_2: $408,000 received immediately vs $350,000 loan option; $14,400 fee per year vs $35,000 interest per year and $105,000 total; Customers take 75 days to pay; $2.4 million credit sales | analysis_max_2: Factoring acts within weeks, closing the gap created by slow payers; Cumulative fees exceed loan interest over 3 years; collection handover harms relationships | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing speed and cost against fees; Acknowledges when the other option would be preferable

--- STEM ---
Aldermoor Engineering Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing precision metal castings for export, employing 320 workers with revenue of $24 million last year. The business needs $10 million to build a new export finishing facility and double overseas sales from 15% to 30% of output.

The Board is weighing two external-finance routes. Option 1 is to convert into a public limited company and issue new shares to the general public at $5.00 each, raising $10 million from 2 million shares, with listing costs of $400,000. Option 2 is to remain a private limited company and take a 7-year bank loan at 8% interest, costing $800,000 per year and $5.6 million in total interest. The twelve existing family shareholders fear losing control and their 80% combined holding if new public shares are issued.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'share capital' as a source of finance.
    Answer: Share capital is the money raised by a company through the issue of shares to shareholders, who become part-owners of the company. It is shown in the statement of financial position and is a long-term source of finance for limited companies. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Money raised by issuing shares to shareholders; Shareholders become part-owners; shown in statement of financial position

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of converting to a Plc and issuing shares rather than taking the bank loan.
    Answer: First advantage: issuing 2 million shares at $5.00 each raises the full $10 million needed for the export finishing facility without creating any repayment obligation [k], so unlike the 7-year bank loan costing $800,000 per year ($5.6 million in total), the company keeps more cash to fund the plan to double overseas sales from 15% to 30% of output [app]. Second advantage: a public listing raises the company's profile and makes future share issues and borrowing easier and cheaper [k], and the $400,000 listing cost is a one-off fee, far smaller than $5.6 million of interest over 7 years [app].
    Keywords: $10 million, $5.00, 2 million, $800,000, $5.6 million, $400,000, 15%, 30%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Share capital need not be repaid; no interest is payable; Public listing raises profile and eases future fundraising | application_max_2: 2 million shares at $5.00 raises $10 million; $5.6 million total interest avoided ($800,000 per year); $400,000 one-off listing cost compared with $5.6 million interest

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of issuing public shares for Aldermoor Engineering and its family shareholders.
    Answer: First disadvantage: the existing twelve family shareholders fear losing control, since selling 2 million new shares to the public could reduce the family's combined 80% holding below 50% [k], giving outside investors power to influence decisions on the new export finishing facility and on dividends [app], so the founding family could lose the final say over the company's direction just as overseas sales are set to double [an]. Second disadvantage: public companies face much heavier legal and reporting duties, including publishing audited accounts and informing the stock exchange [k], costing time and about $400,000 just to list, money a 320-worker company could otherwise spend on the $10 million facility [app], reducing the finance actually available for the expansion [an].
    Keywords: 2 million, 80%, $400,000, $10 million, 320 workers, twelve, $5.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Dilution of family control; possible loss of majority ownership; Heavier legal disclosure and reporting requirements for public companies | application_max_2: Family's 80% combined holding could fall below 50%; $400,000 listing cost reduces funds for the $10 million facility; 320 workers depending on export expansion | analysis_max_2: Loss of control means outside investors steer strategy at a critical moment; Listing and disclosure costs reduce capital available for the expansion

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Aldermoor Engineering should convert to a public limited company and issue shares rather than remain private and take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Converting to a Plc would raise the $10 million needed through 2 million shares at $5.00 each, with no interest to pay and no $800,000 annual charge for 7 years ($5.6 million saved) [k], and the issue would give the family easier access to large sums of capital for its plan to double overseas sales from 15% to 30% of output [app], removing the fixed repayment burden that a $24 million-revenue private company must carry even in weak trading years [an]. However, selling public shares could cut the family's 80% holding below 50%, so they would lose control of the company they built [k], and public status brings audit costs, listing fees of about $400,000 and ongoing disclosure duties that a 320-worker private limited company has so far avoided [app], which may outweigh the interest saving if the family values control above growth [an]. Overall, I think Aldermoor should remain a private limited company and take the 7-year bank loan, because preserving 80% family control and avoiding the disclosure burden matters more than saving $5.6 million of interest, provided profits can cover the $800,000 annual interest [eval]. If the family wanted to grow faster and share the risk with outside investors, the public share issue would be the bolder and cheaper long-term choice [eval].
    Keywords: $10 million, 2 million, $5.00, $800,000, $5.6 million, 80%, 15%, 30%, $400,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Plc share issue raises capital with no repayment or interest obligation; Public status brings disclosure duties; loan keeps company private and control intact | application_max_2: 2 million shares at $5.00 raises $10 million; $5.6 million interest avoided; Family's 80% holding could fall below 50%; $400,000 listing cost and disclosure burden for a 320-worker business | analysis_max_2: No fixed repayments protect cash flow in weak trading years; Loss of majority control gives outside investors influence over strategy | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing control against interest savings; Acknowledges conditions under which the public issue would be preferable

--- STEM ---
Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative is a small handloom weaving enterprise in Country X employing 18 artisan weavers. Members have saved $9,000 between them and sales reached $210,000 last year. The co-operative wants $45,000 to buy two new looms and train six members in modern weaving designs, which would lift output from 120 to 180 pieces a month.

The members are comparing two external sources of finance. Option 1 is a micro-finance loan of $45,000 from a rural micro-finance institution at 12% interest over 3 years, costing $5,400 per year and $16,200 in total interest. Option 2 is a rewards-based crowdfunding campaign aiming to raise $45,000 from online backers, with the platform charging a 6% fee and a target that may not be met. Micro-finance offers a guaranteed sum but adds fixed repayments; crowdfunding costs nothing if it fails but could leave the looms unbought.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'micro-finance' as a source of finance.
    Answer: Micro-finance is the provision of very small loans and other financial services to small businesses or individuals who cannot access traditional bank finance. It is usually delivered by specialist local institutions and supports micro-enterprises and start-ups. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Very small loans provided to those excluded from bank finance; Provided by specialist local institutions to micro-enterprises or start-ups

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of micro-finance for Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative.
    Answer: First advantage: micro-finance guarantees the full $45,000 the co-operative needs for the two new looms and training [k], unlike the crowdfunding option whose target may never be met [app]. Second advantage: the micro-finance institution specialises in rural enterprises and can offer financial advice and support [k], helping 18 artisan weavers run the co-operative professionally as output rises from 120 to 180 pieces a month [app].
    Keywords: $45,000, two new looms, 18 artisan weavers, 120 to 180 pieces, $9,000, $210,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Guaranteed access to the required funds if approved; Tailored to small/rural enterprises, often with business advice and support | application_max_2: $45,000 needed for two looms and training; Output to rise from 120 to 180 pieces a month; Members' savings of $9,000 are insufficient alone

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of micro-finance for Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative.
    Answer: First disadvantage: the micro-finance loan adds fixed repayments of $5,400 of interest per year for 3 years ($16,200 in total) [k], which is heavy for a business with sales of only $210,000 and members' savings of $9,000 [app], so a fall in orders could put the looms and the co-operative's future at risk [an]. Second disadvantage: $45,000 is still a small sum, so Mwangaza cannot use micro-finance to fund much larger expansion or exporting later [k], meaning that if the two looms succeed and output reaches 180 pieces a month, the co-operative will soon outgrow this source of finance [app], limiting its ability to scale up production [an].
    Keywords: $5,400, $16,200, $45,000, $210,000, $9,000, 180 pieces, 18 artisan weavers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interest and repayments burden small cash flows; Micro-finance provides only small sums, limiting expansion scope | application_max_2: $5,400 per year interest; $16,200 in total over 3 years; Sales of $210,000 and members' savings of $9,000; Output limited until looms arrive | analysis_max_2: Weak cash flow raises default and insolvency risk; Outgrowing the source forces refinancing and constrains growth

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative should use micro-finance rather than crowdfunding to raise the $45,000? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Micro-finance guarantees the $45,000 needed for the two looms and skills training, with a predictable cost of $5,400 of interest per year ($16,200 over 3 years) [k], so the 18 artisan weavers can plan output rising from 120 to 180 pieces a month with confidence [app], removing the risk of a crowdfunding campaign that might fail and leave the looms unbought [an]. However, crowdfunding would let the co-operative raise the $45,000 without any debt or interest, and with only a 6% platform fee it would be cheaper than $16,200 of interest [k], and a successful online campaign would also test demand and build a backer community who could become loyal customers of handmade woven products [app], turning the fundraising itself into free marketing [an]. Overall, I think Mwangaza should use micro-finance, because the guaranteed $45,000 and predictable repayments matter most to an 18-member rural co-operative that cannot afford a failed campaign [eval]. If the members are confident of reaching the $45,000 online target, crowdfunding would be cheaper and would build useful marketing buzz [eval].
    Keywords: $45,000, $5,400, $16,200, 120 to 180 pieces, 18 artisan weavers, 6%, $9,000, $210,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Micro-finance: guaranteed sum but fixed repayments and interest; Crowdfunding: no debt, only a platform fee, but target may not be met | application_max_2: $45,000 required for looms and training; 6% platform fee vs $16,200 interest; Output rising from 120 to 180 pieces a month; 18 artisan weavers and members' savings of only $9,000 | analysis_max_2: Guaranteed funds allow confident production planning; Crowdfunding provides marketing value and demand testing alongside funding | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing certainty against cost and marketing; Acknowledges when crowdfunding would be the better choice

--- STEM ---
Solway Green Energy Ltd is a private limited company in Country X installing commercial solar systems for farms and factories, employing 65 workers. Last year revenue was $7.8 million. The company needs $1.2 million to buy battery-storage equipment so it can store surplus power and offer clients a full day-and-night service.

The Board is considering two external-finance routes. Option 1 is to accept a government subsidy covering 30% of the equipment cost, $360,000, on condition that 60% of parts are sourced locally and progress is reported for 5 years; the remaining $840,000 would come from a bank loan at 7.5% over 6 years, costing $63,000 per year. Option 2 is a bank loan for the full $1.2 million at 7.5% over 6 years, costing $90,000 per year and $540,000 in total interest. Option 1 saves interest but brings conditions and paperwork; Option 2 is flexible but dearer.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'subsidy' as a source of finance.
    Answer: A subsidy is a payment or financial support given by the government to a business to encourage the production of certain goods and services. It reduces the business's costs and is a form of long-term external finance. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Payment or financial support from the government to a business; Reduces business costs; encourages desired goods or services

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of accepting the government subsidy rather than one large bank loan.
    Answer: First advantage: the subsidy covers $360,000 (30% of the $1.2 million equipment cost) [k], so the loan needed falls to $840,000, cutting annual interest from $90,000 to $63,000 and saving $162,000 over 6 years [app]. Second advantage: a government subsidy signals official support and strengthens Solway's reputation with farms and factories [k], potentially helping win more of the commercial solar contracts behind its $7.8 million revenue [app].
    Keywords: $360,000, 30%, $1.2 million, $840,000, $63,000, $90,000, $7.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Reduces the sum that must be borrowed; saves interest; Government backing enhances credibility and reputation | application_max_2: $360,000 = 30% of $1.2 million equipment cost; Loan needed falls to $840,000; interest $63,000 vs $90,000 per year; Revenue of $7.8 million from commercial solar contracts

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of accepting the government subsidy.
    Answer: First disadvantage: the subsidy comes with strict conditions, requiring 60% of parts to be sourced locally and progress reported for 5 years [k], which could force Solway to use more expensive local suppliers and add administration costs on top of managing the remaining $840,000 loan [app], reducing the real benefit of the $360,000 support [an]. Second disadvantage: subsidies are often slow to approve and can be withdrawn or changed by future governments [k], so if the 60% local-sourcing condition cannot be met or approval is delayed, the company may miss the installation season when farms want a day-and-night service [app], leaving the $1.2 million equipment order unfunded and the expansion stalled [an].
    Keywords: 60%, $840,000, $360,000, 5 years, $1.2 million, 7.5%, $63,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Conditions attached, such as local sourcing and reporting duties; Approval can be delayed and support withdrawn or changed | application_max_2: 60% of parts must be sourced locally; progress reported for 5 years; Remaining $840,000 still requires a bank loan at 7.5%; $1.2 million equipment order at risk if conditions fail | analysis_max_2: Local sourcing and reporting reduce the net benefit of the subsidy; Delay or withdrawal creates a funding gap and stalls the expansion

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Solway Green Energy Ltd should accept the subsidy rather than fund the equipment entirely through a bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the subsidy cuts the required borrowing to $840,000 and saves $27,000 of interest per year ($63,000 instead of $90,000), a saving of $162,000 over 6 years [k], on a project that lets Solway offer a day-and-night service to the farms and factories behind its $7.8 million revenue [app], so the subsidy route directly strengthens cash flow and margins while lowering loan risk [an]. However, the subsidy demands that 60% of parts are sourced locally and requires 5 years of progress reporting, which may push up costs and divert management time [k], and if local parts are much dearer or approval is delayed, the effective saving could be far smaller than $162,000 [app], whereas a single $1.2 million bank loan at 7.5% is flexible, quick to arrange and frees Solway from any government conditions [an]. Overall, I think Solway should accept the subsidy, because verified interest savings of $162,000 over 6 years and the marketing value of government-backed green credentials outweigh the reporting burden, provided local suppliers meet quality standards [eval]. If local sourcing proves impossible or much costlier, the single larger bank loan would be the more practical route [eval].
    Keywords: $840,000, $63,000, $90,000, $360,000, $1.2 million, 60%, 5 years, $7.8 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Subsidy reduces borrowing and interest but carries conditions; A single bank loan is flexible and fast but costs more interest in total | application_max_2: $360,000 subsidy; loan reduced to $840,000; interest $63,000 vs $90,000 per year; 60% local-parts condition and 5-year reporting; Revenue of $7.8 million from commercial solar clients | analysis_max_2: Interest savings strengthen cash flow and margins; Conditions and approval risk may erode or negate the saving | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing interest savings against conditions; Acknowledges when the larger bank loan would be preferable

--- STEM ---
Drummond Alloys Ltd is a well-established private limited company in Country X producing copper and aluminium alloys, employing 150 workers with revenue of $9 million last year. A new $2 million furnace is needed to replace ageing plant that breaks down about 12 times a year.

The Finance Manager has drawn up two external options. Option 1 is a bank loan of $2 million over 5 years at 8% interest, costing $160,000 per year in interest. Option 2 is to issue a $2 million debenture at 7.5% interest, redeemable after 10 years, with the debenture holders having no ownership but first claim on assets if the company fails. The debenture saves $10,000 in interest each year ($150,000 versus $160,000) but stays on the statement of financial position for twice as long.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the total interest payable on the bank loan over its 5-year term.
    Answer: Annual interest = $2,000,000 × 8% = $160,000 per year; total interest over 5 years = $160,000 × 5 = $800,000 [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Annual interest = principal × rate = $160,000 per year; Total interest over 5 years = $160,000 × 5 = $800,000

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of issuing a $2 million debenture rather than taking the bank loan.
    Answer: First advantage: the debenture carries 7.5% interest, only $150,000 per year against $160,000 on the bank loan, saving $10,000 per year [k], and debenture interest can be planned around the $2 million furnace project without the early-repayment pressure a bank might apply when plant breaks down 12 times a year [app]. Second advantage: debenture holders are not owners, so control of the company remains with the existing shareholders, and the 10-year repayment profile is gentler than repaying over 5 years [k], giving Drummond Alloys a longer, steadier repayment window for a $2 million furnace that will transform alloy output [app].
    Keywords: $150,000, $160,000, $10,000, $2 million, 10 years, 12 times a year, 7.5%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Debenture holders are creditors, not owners, so control is retained; Interest fixed and predictable; repayable over a longer term | application_max_2: 7.5% debenture = $150,000 per year vs $160,000 loan, saving $10,000 per year; 10-year debenture term vs 5-year bank loan; $2 million furnace needed to stop 12 breakdowns a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of issuing a $2 million debenture.
    Answer: First disadvantage: although debenture holders have no vote, they rank ahead of shareholders for repayment and have first claim on the company's assets if it fails [k], and with revenue of only $9 million and a $2 million furnace, assets pledged as security could leave the business with little cushion if alloy orders fall [app], discouraging banks and suppliers from offering further credit on good terms [an]. Second disadvantage: debenture interest of $150,000 per year must be paid even if profits fall, for 10 years, twice as long as the 5-year bank loan [k], so a prolonged downturn in copper and aluminium alloy orders would still leave the company paying $150,000 every year with no flexibility to pause [app], locking the business into high fixed costs for a decade [an].
    Keywords: $150,000, 10 years, 5 years, $9 million, $2 million, $160,000, 12 times a year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Debenture holders rank ahead of shareholders; first claim on assets if the company fails; Interest is a fixed charge payable in all years, for a long period | application_max_2: $2 million furnace against revenue of $9 million; $150,000 per year for 10 years versus $160,000 for 5 years; Statement of financial position carries the debenture for twice as long | analysis_max_2: Weak asset cushion increases insolvency risk and deters further credit; Decade-long fixed charge locks cash flow and limits flexibility

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Drummond Alloys Ltd should issue the debenture rather than take the bank loan to finance the furnace? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Issuing the debenture saves $10,000 of interest every year ($150,000 versus $160,000) and stretches repayment to 10 years instead of 5 [k], easing the burden on a company with $9 million revenue that needs the $2 million furnace to stop the roughly 12 breakdowns a year and stabilise output [app], so cash flow under the debenture is more predictable and safer in weak months [an]. However, the debenture ties the company up for 10 years and gives holders first claim on assets if it fails, unlike a 5-year bank loan that would be cleared in half the time [k], and total interest over 10 years ($1,500,000) far exceeds the bank loan's $800,000 [app], so the debenture is cheap per year but expensive overall [an]. Overall, I think Drummond Alloys should take the 8% bank loan, because clearing the debt in 5 years and saving $700,000 of total interest ($1,500,000 minus $800,000) outweighs the $10,000 annual saving [eval]. If preserving cash flow over the next 5 years is the priority, the debenture would be the better choice [eval].
    Keywords: $150,000, $160,000, $2 million, $9 million, 12, 10 years, 5 years, $10,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Debenture: lower annual interest but repaid over a longer term; Bank loan: higher annual interest but cleared sooner and cheaper overall | application_max_2: $150,000 vs $160,000 per year; $10,000 annual saving; 10-year debenture vs 5-year loan; $1,500,000 vs $800,000 total interest; $9 million revenue; furnace to stop 12 breakdowns a year | analysis_max_2: Debenture eases annual cash flow but raises total interest cost; Loan clears debt sooner and reduces long-term asset claims by creditors | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing annual saving against total interest; Acknowledges the alternative choice and when it would be preferable

--- STEM ---
Vantage Cold Storage Plc is a public limited company in Country X operating 8 refrigerated warehouses, employing 260 workers with revenue of $31 million last year. To win a contract to store imported medicines, it needs $12 million for 3 new automated cold rooms.

The Board is comparing two external sources of finance. Option 1 is to sell debentures of $12 million at 6% interest, redeemable in 12 years, costing $720,000 per year. Option 2 is to issue 3 million new shares at $4.00 each to the general public, with existing 25 million shares held by members of the public and institutions. Debenture holders would be owed a fixed payment every year regardless of profit; new shareholders would receive dividends only if the Board declares them and would dilute existing ownership from 100% to about 89%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'debenture' as a source of finance.
    Answer: A debenture is a long-term loan to a company, usually secured on the company's assets, paying fixed interest to debenture holders. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners, and are repaid on a set date. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Long-term loan to a company, usually secured on assets; Fixed interest; holders are creditors not owners; repaid on a set date

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of selling debentures rather than issuing new shares.
    Answer: First advantage: debenture holders are not owners, so existing shareholders keep 100% of the 25 million shares and full control of the company [k], avoiding the dilution to about 89% that would follow issuing 3 million new shares at $4.00 each [app]. Second advantage: debenture interest of $720,000 per year is fixed, predictable and tax-deductible, and may be cheaper than paying dividends to 3 million new shareholders [k], which suits a profitable medicines-storage contract where the Board knows the $12 million will be repaid over 12 years [app].
    Keywords: 25 million, 3 million, $4.00, $12 million, $720,000, 6%, 8 refrigerated warehouses
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Control is retained because debenture holders are creditors, not owners; Interest is fixed, predictable and tax-deductible; can be cheaper than dividends | application_max_2: 100% of the 25 million shares preserved versus dilution to about 89%; 3 million new shares at $4.00 each raises $12 million; $720,000 per year debenture interest

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of selling debentures to raise the $12 million.
    Answer: First disadvantage: the $720,000 fixed interest must be paid every year for 12 years, whatever profit the company earns [k], so if the medicines-storage contract underperforms, this fixed charge could push Vantage close to insolvency even though revenue was $31 million last year [app], and debenture holders could enforce their claim on the 8 refrigerated warehouses if payments are missed [an]. Second disadvantage: debentures add a long-term liability that stays on the statement of financial position for 12 years, limiting future share issues or loans [k], so when the $12 million medicines contract finishes or trade weakens, the company may struggle to raise further long-term finance for new cold rooms [app], constraining growth and financial flexibility [an].
    Keywords: $720,000, 12 years, $12 million, $31 million, 8 refrigerated warehouses, 6%, 260 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interest must be paid regardless of profit; fixed charge for many years; Added long-term liability limits future borrowing capacity | application_max_2: $720,000 per year for 12 years; Revenue of $31 million last year; medicines-storage contract; 8 refrigerated warehouses could be at risk of a security claim | analysis_max_2: Fixed charge in a weak year leads to insolvency risk and asset claims; Long-term liability reduces capacity for future finance and flexibility

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Vantage Cold Storage Plc should sell debentures rather than issue new shares? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Selling debentures would raise the $12 million needed for the 3 new automated cold rooms while keeping the existing 25 million shareholders in complete control (100% instead of about 89%) [k], and the fixed interest of $720,000 per year can be comfortably covered by a company with revenue of $31 million and 260 workers serving a new medicines-storage contract [app], avoiding the need to pay dividends to 3 million new shareholders who dilute ownership [an]. However, debenture interest of $720,000 must be paid for 12 years regardless of profit, and missing payments could put the 8 refrigerated warehouses used as security at risk [k], whereas new shares at $4.00 would bring in permanent capital with no repayment date or fixed charge [app], suiting a business taking on long-term medicines-storage work where financial flexibility is valuable [an]. Overall, I think Vantage should sell the $12 million debentures, because retaining 100% control and a predictable $720,000 annual cost is preferable while revenue and the medicines contract remain strong [eval]. If the Board fears trade could weaken or wants to remove the fixed charge entirely, issuing new shares would be the safer long-term choice [eval].
    Keywords: $12 million, 25 million, $720,000, $4.00, $31 million, 260 workers, 12 years, 3 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Debentures retain control but add a fixed charge for many years; Share issue brings permanent capital with no fixed repayment obligation | application_max_2: 100% control preserved versus dilution to about 89%; $720,000 per year for 12 years versus $31 million revenue; 3 million new shares at $4.00 raises $12 million | analysis_max_2: Fixed interest covered by strong revenue preserves control; Shares remove fixed-charge risk and add permanent capital if trade weakens | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing control against fixed-charge risk; Acknowledges when issuing shares would be preferable

--- STEM ---
Wrenfield Tablewares Ltd is a small private limited company in Country X handmaking ceramic tableware, employing 24 workers. Revenue reached $950,000 last year. It wants $120,000 to launch a new 'heritage' mug range aimed at tourist shops, which could lift sales by 20% within a year.

The owner is comparing two external sources of finance. Option 1 is a rewards-based crowdfunding campaign offering backers early mugs and 10% discounts, with the platform charging a 5% fee ($6,000) if the $120,000 target is met. Option 2 is a bank loan of $120,000 over 3 years at 11% interest, costing $13,200 per year and $39,600 in total. Crowdfunding could also test demand and build a customer list before production starts, but the target might not be reached.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two factors a business should consider when choosing a source of finance.
    Answer: Two factors are the cost of the finance (interest, fees or diluted ownership) and whether the provider requires control or conditions — for example, whether owners must give up shares or accept reporting duties. The amount needed and the time period of the finance also matter. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cost of finance (interest, fees or loss of ownership); Control and conditions required by the provider (or amount/time period)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of crowdfunding for Wrenfield Tablewares Ltd.
    Answer: First advantage: a rewards-based crowdfunding campaign could raise the full $120,000 needed for the 'heritage' mug range without any bank interest [k], and the 5% platform fee ($6,000) is far less than the $39,600 total interest on a bank loan [app]. Second advantage: the campaign doubles as marketing, letting backers pre-order the new mugs and spread the word online before production starts [k], which could help lift sales by 20% within a year and build a loyal tourist-shop customer base [app].
    Keywords: $120,000, $6,000, 5%, $39,600, heritage, 20%, $950,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: No bank interest; only a platform fee if the target is met; Campaign promotes the product and tests demand before launch | application_max_2: $6,000 platform fee versus $39,600 loan interest; $120,000 target funds the 'heritage' mug range; Goal of lifting sales by 20% within a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of crowdfunding for Wrenfield Tablewares Ltd.
    Answer: First disadvantage: the campaign might fail to reach the $120,000 target, in which case the mugs may never be produced and backers are repaid [k], leaving the business with unmet plans and its 24 workers with no new product to sell [app], delaying the range and letting competitors reach tourist shops first [an]. Second disadvantage: crowdfunding makes the business idea public, so competitors can copy the 'heritage' design before Wrenfield launches [k], and rewards such as 10% discounts and early mugs reduce the margin on every unit sold in the launch [app], squeezing profit in a business with revenue of only $950,000 [an].
    Keywords: $120,000, 24 workers, 10%, $950,000, heritage, 5%, $6,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: All-or-nothing funding; target may not be reached; Idea becomes public; rewards offered reduce margins | application_max_2: $120,000 target may not be met; mugs never produced; 10% discount rewards and early mugs cut launch margins; 24 workers; revenue of only $950,000 | analysis_max_2: Failed target delays launch and forfeits first-mover advantage; Rewards and design copying squeeze already-thin margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wrenfield Tablewares Ltd should use crowdfunding rather than a bank loan to raise the $120,000? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Crowdfunding would raise the $120,000 without bank interest, and the 5% fee ($6,000) is much cheaper than the $39,600 total interest on a 3-year bank loan at 11% [k], while the campaign could test demand and build a tourist-shop customer base before Wrenfield commits to producing the 'heritage' mugs [app], potentially helping sales rise 20% within a year and turning the new range into a profit centre [an]. However, the target might not be reached, leaving the mug range unlaunched, whereas a loan guarantees $120,000 upfront [k], and the bank loan's $13,200 annual interest is predictable and tax-deductible even if campaign buzz fizzles out [app], which is safer for a small business with only $950,000 revenue and 24 workers [an]. Overall, I think Wrenfield should use crowdfunding, because the saving of about $33,600 against loan interest ($39,600 minus $6,000) and the free marketing outweigh the risk of missing the target, provided the campaign is well promoted online [eval]. If the owner needs certainty of funds, the bank loan is the safer route [eval].
    Keywords: $120,000, $6,000, 5%, $39,600, $13,200, 11%, 20%, $950,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Crowdfunding: cheaper (platform fee only) but target may not be met; Bank loan: guaranteed sum, predictable interest but adds debt | application_max_2: $6,000 fee versus $39,600 total interest; $13,200 per year at 11%; $120,000 target for the 'heritage' mug range; 20% sales growth goal; Revenue of only $950,000 and 24 workers | analysis_max_2: Campaign builds demand and customer base before production; Loan guarantees funds but adds fixed annual interest | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing cost saving against campaign risk; Acknowledges when the bank loan would be preferable
