--- STEM ---
Highland Harvest Foods Plc is a public limited company in Country X producing dried pasta, sauces and canned vegetables, employing 480 workers. Revenue reached $42 million last year. It needs $8 million to build an automated sauce-bottling line and has already signed export contracts worth $5.5 million over 3 years with buyers in 3 countries.

The Board is weighing two external sources of finance. Option 1 is a bank loan of $8 million over 10 years at 8.25% interest, costing $660,000 per year in interest. Option 2 is to issue 4 million new shares at $2.00 each to the public, raising $8 million. Existing shareholders own 50 million shares; Option 2 would dilute their holding to just over 92%, while Option 1 keeps ownership unchanged but demands fixed repayments every year even if export profits disappoint.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two reasons why a business may choose external finance over internal finance.
    Answer: Two reasons are that internal sources such as retained profit may be insufficient to fund a large investment, and that external finance can provide the full sum needed more quickly than the business can build up reserves. External finance also lets the business keep internal funds for emergencies and day-to-day trading. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Internal finance may be insufficient for large investments; External finance provides the sum more quickly / keeps internal reserves for operations

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of the bank loan for Highland Harvest Foods Plc.
    Answer: First advantage: the loan provides the full $8 million immediately without any loss of ownership, so the existing 50 million shareholders keep all their rights and dividends [k], avoiding the dilution to just over 92% that a public issue of 4 million new shares at $2.00 would cause [app]. Second advantage: interest of $660,000 per year is tax-deductible and fixed, which aids financial planning, and the signed export contracts worth $5.5 million over 3 years give confidence that revenue will cover it [k], so the Board knows exactly the annual cost before committing [app].
    Keywords: $8 million, 50 million, 4 million, $2.00, $660,000, $5.5 million, 480 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: No dilution of ownership; control remains with existing shareholders; Interest is tax-deductible and fixed, aiding financial planning | application_max_2: $660,000 per year interest versus export contracts worth $5.5 million; 50 million shares retained versus dilution to just over 92%; $8 million loan provides the bottling-line finance

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of issuing new shares rather than taking the bank loan.
    Answer: First advantage: issuing 4 million new shares at $2.00 each raises the $8 million with no repayment date and no fixed interest, strengthening the statement of financial position [k], so Highland Harvest can fund the bottling line without $660,000 of interest every year in the early years when exports are still ramping up [app], preserving cash for operations and emergencies [an]. Second advantage: new public shareholders bring permanent capital and may support future rapid growth across the 3 countries [k], and dividends are paid only if the Board declares them, unlike mandatory loan interest of $660,000 every year even in weak years [app], giving the Plc flexibility if the $5.5 million export contracts deliver slowly [an].
    Keywords: 4 million, $2.00, $8 million, $660,000, $5.5 million, 3 countries, 480 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: No repayment obligation and no mandatory interest; strengthens equity; Permanent capital; dividends are discretionary, unlike loan interest | application_max_2: $660,000 annual interest avoided in early export years; 4 million shares at $2.00 raises $8 million; $5.5 million export contracts may deliver slowly | analysis_max_2: Cash preserved for operations while exports ramp up; Discretionary dividends give flexibility in weak years versus mandatory interest

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Highland Harvest Foods Plc should take the bank loan rather than issue new shares? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Taking the bank loan keeps the existing 50 million shareholders in full control and provides $8 million at $660,000 interest per year, which is easily covered by revenue of $42 million and the $5.5 million export contracts already signed [k], so the company avoids the dilution to just over 92% that issuing 4 million new shares at $2.00 would cause [app], and interest is tax-deductible, lowering the effective cost of the finance [an]. However, the $660,000 annual interest is mandatory for 10 years — $6,600,000 in total — even if exports disappoint, whereas the share issue would bring permanent capital with no repayments [k], and issuing shares would spread risk among more investors and strengthen equity for expansion into the 3 countries [app], making the Plc more resilient in a downturn [an]. Overall, I think Highland Harvest should take the bank loan, because retaining control and securing the cheapest form of finance matter most for a profitable Plc with contracted exports [eval]. If export profits prove volatile, or the Board wants maximum financial safety, issuing new shares at $2.00 would be the better route [eval].
    Keywords: $8 million, $660,000, 50 million, 4 million, $2.00, $5.5 million, $42 million, 10 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Loan keeps control intact; interest is mandatory but tax-deductible; Share issue brings permanent capital with no fixed repayment obligation | application_max_2: $660,000 per year for 10 years versus $42 million revenue; 50 million shareholders retained versus 4 million new shares diluting holding to just over 92%; $5.5 million export contracts already signed; $8 million required | analysis_max_2: Contracted exports and $42 million revenue cover the interest comfortably; Mandatory 10-year interest creates risk if exports disappoint | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing control and interest cost against flexibility; Acknowledges when issuing new shares would be preferable

--- STEM ---
Amberley Farm Shop is a private limited company opened 3 years ago by Jenny Marland in Country X, selling home-grown vegetables, eggs and preserves to about 210 customers each week and employs 6 staff. It has current assets of $48,000 and current liabilities of $31,500. In June it expects cash inflows of $9,400 and cash outflows of $11,200, a net cash flow of -$1,800.

July begins with an opening balance of $2,600, with inflows forecast at $12,750 against outflows of $8,900. Jenny plans a $26,000 cold-room purchase due in August but worries the shop cannot cover it. She is considering an overdraft from her bank or asking 60 debtors who owe money to pay sooner, and postponing the cold room by six months is the third option.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'net cash flow'.
    Answer: Net cash flow is the difference between a business's total cash inflows and its total cash outflows over a period of time (for Amberley Farm Shop, $12,750 inflows minus $8,900 outflows gives a net cash flow of +$3,850 in July). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Net cash flow is total inflows minus total outflows over a period; A positive net cash flow means more cash came in than went out during the period

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Amberley Farm Shop could overcome its short-term cash shortfall in June.
    Answer: Way 1: Amberley Farm Shop could arrange an overdraft with its bank [k]; the June forecast shows outflows of $11,200 against inflows of only $9,400, so a facility of roughly $2,000 would cover the gap until July, when inflows of $12,750 are forecast to exceed outflows of $8,900 [app]. Way 2: the shop could ask its 60 debtors to settle sooner [k]; pulling those payments forward would lift June inflows above $11,200, removing the -$1,800 deficit without borrowing [app].
    Keywords: $11,200, $9,400, 60 debtors, overdraft, $12,750, June
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: An overdraft lets a business spend more than its bank balance up to an agreed limit; Asking debtors to pay faster speeds up cash inflows | application_max_2: Applies the June figures: $11,200 outflows vs $9,400 inflows, roughly a $2,000 gap; Applies the 60 debtors and the -$1,800 June net cash flow to the faster-payment option

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Amberley Farm Shop of preparing a cash-flow forecast.
    Answer: Benefit 1: a forecast shows the shortfall before it happens [k]; because the June deficit of $1,800 would be visible in advance, Jenny can arrange an overdraft or chase the 60 debtors before wages and supplier bills fall due [app][an]. Benefit 2: it helps decide whether the $26,000 cold-room purchase in August is affordable [k]; the July closing balance will be about $6,450 (opening $2,600 plus net cash flow of +$3,850), far below the purchase price, so the forecast tells her extra finance or a postponement is essential [app][an].
    Keywords: $26,000, $2,600, 60 debtors, $1,800, June, August
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A cash-flow forecast highlights periods of expected shortage or surplus in advance; It supports decisions about large or irregular purchases | application_max_2: Applies the June deficit of $1,800 and the 60 debtors as early-warning use; Applies the July closing balance of about $6,450 against the $26,000 cold-room price | analysis_max_2: Explains that early warning allows action before the shortfall hits; Explains that a $26,000 purchase cannot be met from a $6,450 closing balance without new finance

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Jenny should buy the cold room now using an overdraft, or postpone it by six months? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Jenny could argue the cold room should be bought now so it is ready for the August vegetable peak [k]. However, the forecast shows only $2,600 opening in July and a +$3,850 net cash flow, so a $26,000 payment would swallow all available cash and push the shop deeper into overdraft while June is already forecast at -$1,800 [app][an]. Postponing six months protects the thin position and lets the shop build its balance from the stronger July forecast of $12,750 inflows, though it delays the extra capacity a growing shop with 210 customers may need [app][an]. Because postponement is reversible and cheap, whereas an overdraft is not guaranteed [k][eval], the sensible decision is to postpone the cold room until autumn sales are banked and only then confirm the purchase [eval].
    Keywords: $26,000, $2,600, overdraft, $12,750, 60 debtors, $48,000, August
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying now secures the equipment before the August peak; Postponement is a reversible, low-cost way to manage cash shortage | application_max_2: Applies the $2,600 July opening balance and +$3,850 net cash flow against the $26,000 price; Applies the June -$1,800 deficit and the $12,750 July inflows to the postponement option | analysis_max_2: Explains that a $26,000 payment cannot be funded from a $6,450 July closing balance; Explains that postponement lets cash rebuild from July inflows before committing | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to the reversibility of postponing and the risk of overdraft reliance; Recognises the trade-off with the August capacity need

--- STEM ---
Bluewater Surf School is a sole trader business run by Kai Delgado on the coast of Country X, teaching surf lessons to about 480 pupils each April-to-September season. Kai employs 4 instructors. His forecast shows July inflows of $18,600 against outflows of $13,400, August inflows of $15,200 against outflows of $14,750, and September inflows of only $6,800 against outflows of $9,900. He begins September with an opening balance of $7,900.

The school has current assets of $22,000 and current liabilities of $14,500, leaving working capital of $7,500. Kai wants to buy two new rescue boards costing $3,400 each in October, but the quiet winter months worry him. He is considering delaying the purchase until the spring term or taking out a small bank overdraft to cover the off-season shortfall.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'opening balance'.
    Answer: Opening balance is the cash a business has available at the start of a period, brought forward from the previous period's closing balance (Bluewater Surf School begins September with $7,900). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Opening balance is the cash held at the start of a period; The opening balance equals the previous closing balance

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why September is the hardest month of the season for Bluewater Surf School's cash flow.
    Answer: Reason 1: demand collapses once the season ends [k]; the forecast shows September inflows of only $6,800 against $18,600 in July and $15,200 in August [app]. Reason 2: outflows are slower to fall than inflows [k]; September outflows of $9,900 still exceed inflows, giving a net cash flow of -$3,100 and leaving a September closing balance of only $4,800 [app].
    Keywords: September, $6,800, $9,900, $18,600, $15,200, $14,750
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Seasonal businesses see demand fall sharply when the season ends; Fixed-style outflows (wages, storage) continue when revenue falls | application_max_2: Applies the fall in inflows from $18,600 (July) and $15,200 (August) to $6,800 (September); Applies September outflows of $9,900 vs inflows of $6,800, i.e. -$3,100 and closing $4,800

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Kai could overcome the cash-flow problem he expects in September.
    Answer: Way 1: Kai could ask his bank for an overdraft [k]; this covers the September shortfall of $3,100 so the school keeps paying instructors and boat maintenance while it waits for next season's deposits [app][an]. Way 2: he could delay buying the two new rescue boards costing $3,400 each until spring [k]; postponing this $6,800 capital item protects the $7,500 working capital and keeps September liquid [app][an].
    Keywords: $6,800, $9,900, two new rescue boards, $3,400, overdraft, $7,500, September, spring term
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: An overdraft or bank loan provides short-term finance for a cash-flow gap; Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure reduces cash outflow | application_max_2: Applies the $3,100 September shortfall ($9,900 outflows vs $6,800 inflows); Applies the $3,400 boards x 2 = $6,800 against the $7,500 working capital | analysis_max_2: Explains that an overdraft bridges the gap until next season's income arrives; Explains that delaying a discretionary purchase is a cheaper way to protect cash

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kai should buy the two rescue boards in October, or delay until the spring term? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Kai could argue the boards should be bought now, before the winter, because they are essential safety equipment for a school teaching 480 pupils and because October prices may rise [k]. The forecast offers little room: September closes at $4,800, already below the $6,800 cost of the boards, so both would be paid for out of a $7,500 working capital, cutting it to under $1,000 [app][an]. However, delaying to spring protects the cash position through the worst months, risks only a seven-month delay to the purchase and still lands in time for next season [app][an]. Because the boards are important but not needed until lessons restart [k], the evidence favours delaying to the spring term unless the bank confirms an overdraft in writing [eval]; overcommitting in the off-season would jeopardise instructor wages [eval].
    Keywords: two new rescue boards, $3,400, $9,900, $6,800, $7,500, overdraft, September, spring term
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Rescue boards are safety-critical equipment that cannot be postponed indefinitely; Delaying capital expenditure is a standard remedy for a short-term cash shortage | application_max_2: Applies the September closing balance of $4,800 vs the $6,800 board cost; Applies working capital of $7,500 falling to under $1,000 if both boards are bought | analysis_max_2: Explains that buying now would require (or dangerously assume) overdraft funding; Explains that delay costs reputation little but protects instructor wages and bills | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to the off-season cash constraint and the seasonal cycle; Weighs equipment safety against solvency and the overdraft condition

--- STEM ---
Redbank Construction Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago by Marta Okoro in Country X, employing 38 staff across two housing sites and a small joinery workshop. The business has current assets of $96,000 including $34,000 owed by debtors, against current liabilities of $58,000. Its largest client, a housing association, settles invoices 60 days late. March inflows are forecast at $21,500 against outflows of $29,300.

Redbank begins April with an opening balance of $5,100 and forecasts April inflows of $27,800 against outflows of $22,400. Marta is considering offering the housing association a 2% early-payment discount to bring the $34,000 in sooner, taking a $20,000 bank loan, or delaying the $32,000 cement mixer order until the association pays. She must decide before the April payroll.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'closing balance'.
    Answer: Closing balance is the cash a business has at the end of a period, found by adding the net cash flow to the opening balance (Redbank begins April with $5,100 and April's forecast net cash flow is +$5,400, giving a closing balance of $10,500). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Closing balance is the cash remaining at the end of a period; Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Redbank Construction of offering the 2% early-payment discount to the housing association.
    Answer: Benefit 1: the discount should pull cash in sooner [k]; the housing association is 60 days late and owes $34,000, so pulling even half into April would more than cover the $22,400 of April outflows [app]. Benefit 2: a 2% discount is cheap finance [k]; giving up $680 on $34,000 costs far less than the interest on a $20,000 bank loan and still lands before the April payroll [app].
    Keywords: $34,000, 2% early-payment discount, 60 days late, housing association, $27,800, $5,100
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount encourages debtors to pay faster, improving cash flow; A small discount can be cheaper than interest on borrowed finance | application_max_2: Applies the $34,000 owed and 60 days late payment by the housing association; Applies 2% of $34,000 = $680 against the $22,400 April outflows and $20,000 loan

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why delaying the $32,000 cement mixer order could help Redbank's cash flow.
    Answer: Reason 1: delaying postpones a very large capital outflow [k]; moving the $32,000 mixer out of April keeps April outflows at $22,400 and lets the forecast opening balance of $5,100 recover to about $10,500 without new borrowing [app][an]. Reason 2: it avoids committing before the association pays [k]; with the client 60 days late on $34,000, delaying the purchase means Redbank is not forced into a $20,000 loan before knowing when cash will actually arrive [app][an].
    Keywords: $32,000 cement mixer, $22,400, housing association, April payroll, $5,100, $34,000, debtors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure is a remedy for a short-term cash-flow problem; Avoiding new long-term borrowing reduces interest costs and insolvency risk | application_max_2: Applies the $32,000 mixer vs April outflows of $22,400 and opening balance of $5,100; Applies the association's 60-day lateness and the $34,000 owed to the loan alternative | analysis_max_2: Explains that delaying pushes the large outflow beyond the strained month; Explains that commitment before payment risks inability to fund the April payroll

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marta should offer the early-payment discount, or take the $20,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Marta could argue for the 2% early-payment discount because it tackles the root problem [k]. Costing only $680 on $34,000, it is cheaper than a $20,000 loan, avoids new debt and matches the fact that the housing association is already 60 days late [app][an]. However, the discount only helps if the association agrees and pays promptly, so if it still pays slowly the April payroll remains at risk and a loan - or the mixer delay - may still be needed [app][an]. Because the discount is cheap and non-binding while the mixer delay alone does not guarantee cash [k][eval], the evidence favours offering the discount first and taking the $20,000 loan only if the association refuses [eval]; the decision should be made before the April payroll, not after it.
    Keywords: 2% early-payment discount, $20,000 bank loan, $34,000, April payroll, $32,000 cement mixer, housing association, $5,100
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount is a cheap way to speed up debtors without new debt; A bank loan gives certain finance but adds interest and repayment obligations | application_max_2: Applies 2% of $34,000 = $680 vs interest on a $20,000 loan; Applies the payroll deadline and the association's 60-day lateness | analysis_max_2: Explains that the discount is cheap only if the association accepts and pays early; Explains that the loan guarantees funding but at extra cost and does nothing to fix late payment | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation sequencing discount first, loan as fallback; Weighs certainty of the loan against the cheapness and uncertainty of the discount

--- STEM ---
Saffron Spice Restaurant is an independent curry house in Country X opened 6 years ago by brothers Dev and Priya Nair, serving about 95 covers on a busy Saturday and 40 covers on weekdays, with both brothers working the stoves six nights a week. It rents rather than owns its kitchen equipment and turns over $38,000 a month. Current assets are $15,600 and current liabilities are $19,200.

After a roof leak in February, the Nairs face an unexpected $7,400 repair bill. The February forecast shows inflows of $31,800 against outflows of $34,600, while March forecasts $36,500 inflows against $33,100 outflows. They are deciding between a $9,000 bank overdraft and asking the spice wholesaler for a further 45 days credit before paying their February bill.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'overdraft'.
    Answer: An overdraft is a short-term bank facility allowing a business to withdraw more money than it holds in its account, up to an agreed limit, with interest charged on the amount borrowed. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: An overdraft is a short-term bank facility to spend more than the balance; Interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems caused by the restaurant's negative working capital position.
    Answer: Problem 1: current liabilities exceed current assets [k]; the restaurant holds only $15,600 of current assets against $19,200 of short-term debts, so working capital is negative at -$3,600 [app]. Problem 2: the business runs a cash deficit before the repair bill is paid [k]; February outflows of $34,600 already exceed inflows of $31,800, so the February net cash flow of -$2,800 plus the $7,400 roof bill means new finance is needed [app].
    Keywords: $15,600, $19,200, $31,800, $34,600, spice wholesaler, $7,400, February
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities; negative means short-term debts exceed short-term assets; Negative working capital risks inability to pay debts as they fall due | application_max_2: Applies $15,600 vs $19,200 giving working capital of -$3,600; Applies February inflows of $31,800 and outflows of $34,600 (-$2,800) plus the $7,400 repair

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the $9,000 overdraft compared with asking the spice wholesaler for 45 days credit.
    Answer: Benefit 1: the overdraft lets the repair proceed immediately without starving the kitchen [k]; the February gap of -$2,800 and the $7,400 bill mean a $9,000 facility covers both [app][an]. Benefit 2: it keeps the supplier relationship intact [k]; asking the spice wholesaler for 45 days credit risks delayed or refused spice deliveries exactly when the March forecast of $36,500 inflows depends on full service, while March outflows of $33,100 still fall due [app][an].
    Keywords: $9,000 bank overdraft, spice wholesaler, 45 days credit, $7,400, $36,500, $33,100, March
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: An overdraft is flexible short-term finance matched to the cash gap; Delaying supplier payments can damage the supplier relationship and supply of goods | application_max_2: Applies the -$2,800 February gap and the $7,400 repair vs the $9,000 overdraft; Applies March inflows of $36,500 and outflows of $33,100 to the delivery risk | analysis_max_2: Explains the overdraft covers both the deficit and the repair bill without affecting suppliers; Explains refused credit could disrupt supply in the strongest trading month

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the Nairs should take the $9,000 overdraft, or ask the spice wholesaler for 45 days credit? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The Nairs could argue for the overdraft because it keeps the wholesaler relationship safe while fixing the roof immediately [k]. A $9,000 facility would cover the -$2,800 February deficit and the $7,400 repair, and interest is paid only on what is drawn [app][an]. However, an overdraft is repayable on demand and adds a fixed monthly cost, so if March disappoints below the $36,500 inflow forecast the bank could call the facility in [app][an]. Because the wholesaler credit would cost nothing if granted but risks refusal and reputational damage [k][eval], the evidence favours taking the $9,000 overdraft now, agreed in writing, while honouring the March payment to the wholesaler in full [eval]; the decision should be reversed only if the bank refuses or prices the facility punitively.
    Keywords: $9,000 bank overdraft, spice wholesaler, 45 days credit, $7,400, February, $38,000, $15,600
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: An overdraft provides immediate short-term finance but is repayable on demand; Asking suppliers for more credit is free but damages the business relationship | application_max_2: Applies the $9,000 overdraft to the -$2,800 February deficit and $7,400 repair; Applies the March forecast of $36,500 inflows / $33,100 outflows to the overdraft risk | analysis_max_2: Explains the overdraft covers both the deficit and the repair without touching the supplier; Explains that a call-in risk exists if March underperforms | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to writing, cost comparison and relationship risk; Weighs overdraft certainty against supplier-credit cost and risk of refusal

--- STEM ---
Larkspur Florist is a partnership owned by Emma and Lucy Hartley in Country X, selling fresh flowers, wedding arrangements and weekly office subscriptions. It forecasts May inflows of $8,700 including $1,900 from two weddings against outflows of $10,300, and June inflows of $9,800 against outflows of $8,150; it also sells wedding corsages all year round. It begins May with an opening balance of $2,000 and employs 2 full-time florists.

The partnership has current assets of $12,400 and current liabilities of $7,900. Emma wants a refrigerated display cabinet costing $4,500 to cut flower wastage, but buying it now would use most of the remaining cash. The Hartleys are considering postponing the cabinet for three months, or switching office subscribers to weekly rather than monthly payment.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the forecast closing balance for May. Show your working.
    Answer: Closing balance for May = opening balance + net cash flow = $2,000 + ($8,700 - $10,300) = $2,000 - $1,600 = $400. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: May net cash flow = $8,700 inflows - $10,300 outflows = -$1,600; Closing balance = $2,000 opening + (-$1,600) = $400

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the May closing balance is forecast to be so low.
    Answer: Reason 1: May outflows exceed inflows [k]; the forecast shows $10,300 of outflows against $8,700 of inflows, a net cash flow of -$1,600 [app]. Reason 2: wedding takings are uneven and do not cover the month [k]; although May includes $1,900 from two weddings, office subscriptions are billed monthly, so cash received cannot absorb the flower, wage and delivery costs before the month closes [app].
    Keywords: $8,700, $10,300, $1,900, $2,000, May, office subscriptions, $8,150
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A cash-flow deficit month makes the closing balance low; Mismatch in timing between when money is owed and received lowers the closing balance | application_max_2: Applies $10,300 outflows vs $8,700 inflows = -$1,600 net cash flow; Applies the $1,900 wedding income and monthly-billed subscriptions to the timing gap

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the Hartleys could improve the florist's cash flow in June.
    Answer: Way 1: switching office subscribers to weekly rather than monthly payment pulls cash in sooner [k]; collecting subscriptions weekly instead of monthly smooths inflows and could lift May's and June's balances well above $400 and $2,050 respectively [app][an]. Way 2: postponing the refrigerated cabinet purchase cuts outflows [k]; holding the $4,500 cabinet spend out of May, a deficit month, keeps cash in the partnership until June's forecast net cash flow of +$1,650 arrives [app][an].
    Keywords: June, $9,800, $8,150, weekly rather than monthly, $1,900, two weddings, refrigerated display cabinet
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Reducing the time taken to collect receivables speeds up cash inflows; Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure reduces cash outflows | application_max_2: Applies weekly vs monthly subscriptions to inflow timing and closing balance; Applies the $4,500 cabinet against May's -$1,600 net cash flow and June's +$1,650 | analysis_max_2: Explains weekly billing accelerates cash without discounting; Explains delaying the cabinet avoids spending in the weakest month

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Emma and Lucy should buy the refrigerated display cabinet now, or postpone it for three months? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The Hartleys could argue for buying the cabinet now because it cuts wastage in a flower business where stock perishes quickly [k]. But the May forecast closing balance is only $400 after a -$1,600 net cash flow, so the $4,500 cabinet would consume more than the entire balance and leave nothing for weekly wages [app][an]. However, buying in June or July is feasible once June's +$1,650 net cash flow lifts the balance back above $2,000, and switching subscribers to weekly payment would help further [app][an]. Because the cabinet is an efficiency upgrade rather than a survival need [k][eval], the evidence favours postponing it for three months and revisiting the purchase once the weekly subscriptions are running [eval].
    Keywords: refrigerated display cabinet, $4,500, $12,400, $7,900, three months, weekly rather than monthly, $2,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying now reduces wastage but suits only businesses with spare cash; Postponement preserves cash during a deficit month | application_max_2: Applies the $400 May closing balance vs the $4,500 cabinet price; Applies June's +$1,650 and the switch to weekly subscriptions to the delay option | analysis_max_2: Explains the cabinet would drain the whole cash position immediately; Explains waiting restores affordability without abandoning the efficiency gain | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to postpone tied to the priority of wages over upgrades; Acknowledges the wastage benefit and the reassessment trigger

--- STEM ---
Northgate Veterinary Clinic is a private limited company opened 8 years ago by Dr Tom Whitfield in Country X, treating about 70 animals a week and vaccinating local farm herds. October inflows are forecast at $26,400 against outflows of $24,100, and November inflows at $24,900 against outflows of $27,600. The clinic begins October with an opening balance of $3,300 and is owed $9,800 by farm clients on 45-day terms.

The clinic has current assets of $34,500 against current liabilities of $17,000. Dr Whitfield wants to buy a digital X-ray machine for $28,000, which his supplier will sell on 60-day credit instead of for cash now. He is deciding whether to take the credit deal or wait a year and put the money towards a part-time nurse's wages instead.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'debtors'.
    Answer: Debtors are customers or clients who owe a business money because they have received goods or services on credit but have not yet paid (Northgate Veterinary Clinic is owed $9,800 by farm clients on 45-day terms). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Debtors owe money to a business for goods or services already supplied; Debtors appear as a current asset until payment is received

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to the clinic of asking farm clients to pay the $9,800 they owe more quickly.
    Answer: Benefit 1: asking debtors to pay faster brings cash forward [k]; Northgate is owed $9,800 on 45-day terms, and November needs it most because November inflows of $24,900 trail outflows of $27,600 [app]. Benefit 2: it reduces the need to borrow [k]; collecting even part of the $9,800 would more than cover the -$2,700 November net cash flow and protect the $3,300 opening balance [app].
    Keywords: $9,800, farm clients, 45-day terms, November, $24,900, $27,600, $24,100
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Asking debtors to pay faster speeds up cash inflows; Faster collection reduces reliance on borrowing or overdrafts | application_max_2: Applies the $9,800 owed on 45-day terms to November's gap ($24,900 vs $27,600); Applies -$2,700 November net cash flow and the $3,300 October opening balance

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Dr Whitfield might wait a year before buying the X-ray machine.
    Answer: Reason 1: the machine is unaffordable from current cash [k]; at $28,000 it is far beyond the October closing balance of about $5,600, so buying cash now would exhaust the $17,500 working capital [app][an]. Reason 2: waiting a year has a real opportunity cost he can weigh [k]; the $28,000 could fund a part-time nurse's wages in the meantime, lifting service quality while a smaller credit deal is negotiated again next year [app][an].
    Keywords: digital X-ray machine, $28,000, 60-day credit, part-time nurse's wages, $3,300, November, $17,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A large purchase may exceed available cash and working capital; Deferring a purchase frees resources for other priorities (opportunity cost) | application_max_2: Applies the $28,000 price vs October closing balance of about $5,600 and $17,500 working capital; Applies the $28,000 vs part-time nurse's wages alternative | analysis_max_2: Explains the purchase would leave the clinic dangerously under-funded; Explains the nurse alternative delivers value sooner and keeps options open

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Dr Whitfield should buy the X-ray machine now on 60-day credit, or wait a year? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Dr Whitfield could argue for the 60-day credit now because the machine improves diagnoses and could attract more farm clients [k]. The credit deal avoids an immediate $28,000 outflow, but the full price falls due 60 days later, when the November forecast shows a -$2,700 net cash flow and the $9,800 farm debt may not yet have landed [app][an]. However, borrowing $28,000 for one item against a $17,500 working capital leaves the clinic exposed if a farm client pays late, and delaying a year lets cash build from the October surplus of +$2,300 [app][an]. Because the farm vaccination income is seasonal and the machine is a discretionary purchase [k][eval], the evidence favours taking the credit deal only after confirming the $9,800 is collected early; otherwise waiting is safer [eval].
    Keywords: digital X-ray machine, $28,000, 60-day credit, part-time nurse's wages, $3,300, $9,800, November, $17,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Trade credit spreads a large purchase over time; A discretionary purchase can be deferred without breaking the business | application_max_2: Applies the $28,000 60-day credit falling due around November's -$2,700 net cash flow; Applies the $17,500 working capital and the $9,800 farm debt collection timing | analysis_max_2: Explains the machine benefit must be weighed against the crunch at payment date; Explains that collecting debtors first de-risks the credit deal | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditioned on collecting the $9,800 first; Weighs strategic benefit against seasonal cash risk and limited working capital

--- STEM ---
Willowbrook Children's Nursery is a social enterprise in Country X founded 5 years ago by Hannah Bhatt, providing affordable childcare for 64 children on a low-income estate. Parent fees cover most monthly costs and a community trust funds the shortfall. Current assets are $27,300 against current liabilities of $13,800. January inflows are forecast at $14,200 against outflows of $16,900, and February forecasts inflows of $18,500 against outflows of $16,200.

The nursery begins January with an opening balance of $4,700. Hannah wants to replace ageing outdoor play equipment for $9,000, but January's deficit leaves little spare cash. A local trust has offered a grant of $4,500 if she applies before 31 March; alternatively the bank will lend $5,000 repayable over 12 months at 8% interest.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'current assets'.
    Answer: Current assets are resources owned by a business that are expected to be converted into cash within one year, such as stock, debtors and money in the bank (Willowbrook Children's Nursery has $27,300 in current assets). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Current assets are expected to be turned into cash within one year; Examples include cash, debtors and stock

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Willowbrook's cash flow is weaker in January than in February.
    Answer: Reason 1: fees fall after the holiday period [k]; January inflows of $14,200 are well below February's $18,500, so children's fees simply do not cover the bills in a quiet month [app]. Reason 2: winter outflows are higher [k]; January outflows of $16,900 exceed both its inflows and February's outflows of $16,200, so the January deficit of $2,700 is driven by the gap between falling inflows and stubborn costs [app].
    Keywords: January, $14,200, $16,900, February, $18,500, $16,200
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Seasonal dips in income can create a deficit month; High fixed or winter costs keep outflows elevated when income falls | application_max_2: Applies January inflows of $14,200 vs February's $18,500; Applies January outflows of $16,900 vs February's $16,200 and the $2,700 deficit

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the grant compared with the bank loan.
    Answer: Benefit 1: the grant is not repayable [k]; unlike the $5,000 loan, the grant of $4,500 adds cash without creating a new outflow, protecting the end-of-January balance of $2,000 [app][an]. Benefit 2: it avoids interest and fixed repayments [k]; dodging the 8% interest on $5,000 ($400 a year) and twelve monthly repayments in a February deficit month keeps the nursery's tight working capital of $13,500 intact [app][an].
    Keywords: grant of $4,500, $5,000, 8% interest, 12 months, $16,900, $27,300, January
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A grant does not have to be repaid; A loan creates repayments and interest that worsen cash flow | application_max_2: Applies the $4,500 grant vs loan of $5,000 and the $2,000 January closing balance; Applies 8% interest on $5,000 = $400 and twelve repayments against $13,500 working capital | analysis_max_2: Explains the grant protects cash without new obligations; Explains loan repayments would worsen an already deficit month

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hannah should apply for the grant, or take the $5,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Hannah could argue for the grant because it is effectively free money and suits a social enterprise [k]. Applying before 31 March secures $4,500 with no interest and no repayments, which suits a nursery whose January deficit is forecast at $2,700 and whose January closing balance will be only $2,000 [app][an]. However, the grant is not guaranteed, takes time to process and may arrive after the equipment decision must be made, while the loan at 8% interest is certain and funds the $9,000 purchase immediately [app][an]. Because the equipment is not urgently required and the January deficit must be managed first [k][eval], the evidence favours applying for the grant while keeping the loan as a written fallback if the application fails [eval].
    Keywords: grant of $4,500, $5,000, 8% interest, $4,700, $9,000, February, $27,300, 31 March
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Grants are non-repayable finance well suited to social enterprises; A loan is certain but adds interest and repayment pressure | application_max_2: Applies the $4,500 grant, 31 March deadline and the $2,700 January deficit; Applies the $2,000 January closing balance and the $9,000 equipment cost | analysis_max_2: Explains the grant preserves cash but is slow and uncertain; Explains the loan is fast but increases the fixed outflow burden | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to apply for the grant with the loan as fallback; Weighs certainty vs cost in the context of the January deficit

Benefit 2: it strengthens February without giving away margin [k]; if the $19,000 arrives, the planned $8,500 February bulk buy could be funded from banked cash rather than an overdraft, instead of pairing a 20% discount with an already weak January closing balance of only $1,900 [app].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Spending cash before it is earned creates an unfunded outflow; Bulk buying ties up working capital in stock that sells slowly | application_max_2: Applies the $8,500 bulk buy vs the $1,900 January closing balance; Applies working capital of $17,000 (from $61,000 current assets and $44,000 current liabilities) | analysis_max_2: Explains the bulk buy would be funded by borrowing, adding cost and risk; Explains stock ties up cash needed for wages in the winter months

  Qd [8 marks]

--- STEM ---
Marigold Bakery & Patisserie is a private limited company founded 4 years ago in Country X by Samira Chaudhry, supplying 14 supermarkets with bread and celebration cakes. Its ovens run from 4 a.m. and supermarket invoices are paid 30 days late. Current assets are $52,000 and current liabilities are $29,000. March inflows are forecast at $41,200 against outflows of $46,700, and April at $48,900 against $43,300; the bakery begins March with an opening balance of $6,400.

Samira's two largest supermarket chains owe the bakery $23,500 between them. She is considering a 4% early-payment discount to bring the money in sooner, a $25,000 bank loan at 9% interest, and postponing the $11,000 mixer replacement by six months. She must decide before the March payroll is due.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'liquidity'.
    Answer: Liquidity is the ability of a business to convert its assets into cash quickly and to meet its short-term debts as they fall due (current liabilities of $29,000 must be payable out of current assets of $52,000). [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Liquidity is how quickly assets can be turned into cash; Liquidity measures the ability to pay short-term debts as they fall due

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to the bakery of offering the 4% early-payment discount.
    Answer: Benefit 1: cash arrives sooner [k]; instead of waiting 30 days late, the bakery collects part of the $23,500 owed before the March payroll, lifting the March closing balance above the forecast $900 [app]. Benefit 2: the discount is cheaper than the alternative finance [k]; a 4% discount costs $940, while a $25,000 bank loan at 9% interest costs $2,250 a year, so the discount saves about $1,310 [app].
    Keywords: 4% early-payment discount, $23,500, March, $41,200, $46,700, $6,400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount speeds up cash inflows from debtors; A small discount can cost less than interest on a loan | application_max_2: Applies $23,500 owed and the closing balance of only $900 vs the March payroll; Applies 4% of $23,500 = $940 vs 9% of $25,000 = $2,250 (about $1,310 saved)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of the 4% early-payment discount for the bakery.
    Answer: Drawback 1: the discount directly reduces profit [k]; giving up $940 of margin on $23,500 assumes both chains take the discount and pay on time, and the bakery still needs cash for the March payroll [app][an]. Drawback 2: it may set a precedent [k]; if the two largest supermarket chains expect a 4% discount every month, the $940 loss repeats while the April recovery of +$5,600 net cash flow is no guarantee that future invoices come in quickly [app][an].
    Keywords: 4% early-payment discount, $23,500, $25,000 bank loan, 9% interest, $52,000, $29,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount sacrifices profit to improve cash flow; Repeated discounts set a costly precedent with large customers | application_max_2: Applies $940 cost of the discount vs both chains taking it and the March payroll; Applies the repeat cost vs April's +$5,600 net cash flow forecast | analysis_max_2: Explains the saving is only real if chains accept and pay quickly; Explains repeated discounting compounds the margin loss

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Samira should offer the early-payment discount, or take the $25,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Samira could argue for the early-payment discount because it fixes the root cause - slow-paying supermarkets [k]. At 4% it costs $940, far below the $2,250 annual interest on the $25,000 loan, and every pound collected early improves the March closing balance forecast at only $900 [app][an]. However, the discount works only if the chains agree and pay promptly, so uptake may be weak and a loan could still be needed to bridge the $5,500 March deficit [app][an]. Because the discount is cheaper and strengthens the customer relationship [k][eval], the evidence favours offering the 4% discount now while arranging a standby overdraft in case uptake is slow, keeping the $25,000 loan, and the $11,000 mixer postponement, as back-up options [eval].
    Keywords: 4% early-payment discount, $25,000 bank loan, 9% interest, $23,500, $11,000 mixer, March payroll, $46,700, $6,400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Early discounting targets the cause of the shortfall rather than its symptoms; A standby facility is a cheaper form of contingency than an unconditional loan | application_max_2: Applies $940 cost vs $2,250 loan interest and the $900 March closing balance; Applies the $5,500 March deficit and the $11,000 mixer postponement as fallback | analysis_max_2: Explains the discount is cheaper only if chains actually take it; Explains keeping the loan as back-up covers the risk of weak uptake | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation sequencing discount first, backup finance second; Weighs certain saving vs uncertain uptake in the supermarket chain context

Thornfield Freight is a private limited company operating 9 HGVs in Country X, delivering to supermarkets and builders' merchants across two provinces. --- QUESTIONS ---

    Question: Calculate the working capital for Thornfield Freight. Show your working.
    Answer: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities = $74,000 - $41,000 = $33,000. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities; Working capital of $33,000 shows Thornfield's short-term resources exceed short-term debts

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons for the negative net cash flow forecast in January.
    Answer: Reason 1: January outflows exceed inflows [k]; the forecast shows $39,800 of outflows against $34,600 of inflows, a net cash flow of -$5,200 [app]. Reason 2: customers pay late and do not cover the gap [k]; customers owe $41,000, of which $19,000 is more than 60 days overdue, so January inflows barely reflect work already done [app].
    Keywords: January, $34,600, $39,800, $19,000, $41,000, 60 days overdue
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A net cash flow deficit occurs when outflows exceed inflows; Slow-paying debtors delay inflows even after work is done | application_max_2: Applies $34,600 inflows and $39,800 outflows = -$5,200 net cash flow; Applies $41,000 owed with $19,000 overdue over 60 days to the weak January inflows

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Thornfield could face if it delays the $28,000 diesel payment by 30 days.
    Answer: Problem 1: the supplier could refuse further deliveries [k]; delaying the $28,000 diesel payment by 30 days risks a stoppage, and without fuel the HGVs cannot complete the deliveries that generate February's $44,300 inflow [app][an]. Problem 2: postponement builds a larger bill [k]; the payment lands in February, when outflows already reach $38,200 against inflows of $44,300, so a late $28,000 payment on top could still strain the account despite the +$6,100 February net cash flow [app][an].
    Keywords: diesel supplier, $28,000, February, $38,200, $44,300, $41,000, 30 days
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delaying payments to suppliers risks refusal of future supplies; Postponing a payment does not remove the obligation, it just moves it | application_max_2: Applies the $28,000 diesel payment vs February's $44,300 inflow and the nine HGVs; Applies February outflows of $38,200 and the +$6,100 net cash flow to the extra $28,000 | analysis_max_2: Explains a fuel cut-off would stop deliveries and revenue entirely; Explains February cannot absorb both its own bills and a deferred $28,000 comfortably

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marcus should delay the diesel payment, or press customers to pay the overdue $19,000 first? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Marcus could argue for delaying the diesel payment because suppliers often accept 30 days more credit and fleet operations matter most [k]. But the diesel supplier can stop deliveries immediately, halting the nine HGVs and putting the $34,600 January workload at risk, whereas the $19,000 owed to Thornfield is legally due already [app][an]. Chasing the overdue debts first brings in cash without interest or reputational risk, and even partial collection would cover the January net cash flow of -$5,200 [app][an]. Because the overdue customer debts are the cheaper and more certain source of cash [k][eval], the evidence favours pressing customers to settle the $19,000 while negotiating a written 30-day extension with the diesel supplier in parallel and keeping the $16,000 tyre replacement for April [eval].
    Keywords: diesel supplier, $28,000, $19,000, $41,000, 30 days, $16,000 tyre replacement, January, April
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Delaying supplier payment is a common but risky remedy for a cash shortage; Collecting overdue debts is the safest way to raise cash without borrowing | application_max_2: Applies the nine HGVs and $34,600 January workload to the fuel cut-off risk; Applies the $19,000 overdue vs the -$5,200 January net cash flow | analysis_max_2: Explains unilateral non-payment risks the fleet halting entirely; Explains collecting the $19,000 closes the gap without new debt | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to chase debtors first with a parallel written supplier deal; Weighs supplier goodwill against debt collection certainty and cost

--- STEM ---
Fennick & Grey Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that mills oats into breakfast cereal for supermarket chains. The statement of financial position at 30 April 2026 shows non-current assets of $540,000, current assets of $210,000 and current liabilities of $90,000, giving working capital of $120,000 and capital employed of $660,000.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'Revenue'.
    Answer: Revenue is the total income a business earns from selling its goods or services during a trading period, before deducting any costs [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Total income earned from selling goods and/or services; Earned during a trading period, before any costs are deducted

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why profit is important to Fennick & Grey Foods Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Profit can be retained and reinvested, funding growth such as the new dehuller without extra borrowing [k], and the $48,000 Retained Profit shows that such funds are genuinely available [app]. Reason 2: Profit rewards shareholders for their risk, enabling the $30,000 dividend paid this year [k], which helps maintain investor confidence in the $500,000 of equity [app].
    Keywords: Fennick & Grey Foods Ltd, $48,000, dehuller, $30,000, Retained Profit, $500,000, supermarket chains
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Profit can be retained and reinvested to fund growth without borrowing; Profit rewards owners/shareholders and enables dividends to be paid | application_max_2: $48,000 Retained Profit is available towards the dehuller; $30,000 dividend paid, rewarding shareholders in a company with $500,000 equity

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the income statement is useful to the directors when choosing between the special dividend and the dehuller.
    Answer: Reason 1: The income statement confirms the company earned a Profit for the year of $78,000 after Expenses of $96,000, so the business is genuinely profitable and not just cash-rich [k], which tells directors that either option is genuinely affordable rather than a gamble on one good quarter [app][an]. Reason 2: It shows Retained Profit of $48,000 after the ordinary dividend of $30,000, indicating exactly how much could be committed towards the dehuller [k], so directors know Option 2 would use only two-fifths of the machine's cost and a further funding route would still be needed [app][an].
    Keywords: income statement, $78,000, $96,000, $48,000, $30,000, dehuller, Retained Profit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Confirms the business is profitable after deducting expenses; Shows retained profit available after dividends | application_max_2: $78,000 profit after $96,000 Expenses; $48,000 Retained Profit vs the dehuller's $120,000 cost | analysis_max_2: Sustainable profit means either option is affordable, not dependent on a windfall; $48,000 covers only two-fifths of the cost, so a further funding plan is required

  Qd [8 marks]

    Answer: Option 1 rewards shareholders for their risk and signals confidence in the company, returning part of the profit directly to investors [k], and it would be affordable given current assets of $210,000 and working capital of $120,000 [app], which should keep shareholders loyal ahead of the expansion [an]. Option 2 keeps the $48,000 inside the business and directs it towards the dehuller, protecting the future Gross Profit base rather than distributing it once [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the stronger choice because the dehuller should improve milling efficiency and lift future profits for every shareholder, whereas the special dividend is a one-off reward that shrinks the funds available for growth; the directors can revisit a dividend next year once the machine's returns are proven [eval][eval].
    Keywords: special dividend, $20,000, Option 2, dehuller, $48,000, working capital, $120,000, current assets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Dividends reward and retain shareholders; Retained profit can fund productive investment for long-term growth | application_max_2: Option 1 special dividend of $20,000 affordable from $210,000 current assets / $120,000 working capital; Option 2 keeps $48,000 retained towards the $120,000 dehuller | analysis_max_2: Dividend boosts loyalty now but leaves nothing for the machine; Dehuller should improve efficiency and protect/lift future Gross Profit | evaluation_max_2: For: immediate reward and signal of strength / option 2 costs shareholders cash; Against/Overall: Option 2 maximises long-term value; dividends can be paid once returns are proven

--- STEM ---
Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that services refrigeration units for supermarket and restaurant chains. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it earned Revenue of $1,150,000, with Cost of Sales of $690,000, Gross Profit of $460,000, Expenses of $350,000 and Profit for the year of $110,000. The company paid an ordinary dividend of $40,000 and retained the remaining $70,000.

The statement of financial position at 31 March 2026 shows non-current assets of $820,000, current assets of $300,000 (including inventories of $95,000) and current liabilities of $130,000. Working capital is $170,000 and capital employed is $990,000. Non-current liabilities comprise a $300,000 long-term bank loan, so shareholders' equity is $690,000. The bank will waive $6,000 of interest if $100,000 is repaid early (Option 1), or the business could buy a new delivery van for $92,000 (Option 2).

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'Current Assets'.
    Answer: Current assets are assets a business expects to convert into cash, sell or use within one year, such as inventories, trade receivables and cash at bank [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Assets expected to be sold, used or turned into cash within 12 months; Examples: inventories, trade receivables, cash at bank

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why positive working capital is important to Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Working capital pays the day-to-day running costs such as engineers' wages and supplier invoices, and Fenwick's $170,000 of working capital keeps its service visits operating smoothly [k][app]. Reason 2: Working capital shows whether current assets exceed current liabilities, and with $300,000 against $130,000 the company can meet its short-term debts on time [k][app].
    Keywords: Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd, $170,000, working capital, $300,000, $130,000, supermarket, restaurant chains, inventories
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Covers day-to-day operating outflows such as wages and supplier bills; Indicates ability to meet short-term debts as they fall due | application_max_2: $170,000 working capital funds the servicing operation; $300,000 current assets exceed $130,000 current liabilities

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the bank would study this statement of financial position before restructuring the loan.
    Answer: Reason 1: The bank checks whether current assets can absorb an early $100,000 repayment, and with $300,000 available (including $95,000 of inventories) the cover looks adequate [k][app][an]. Reason 2: The bank assesses how the $300,000 long-term loan sits against the $990,000 capital employed and the $690,000 of shareholders' equity backing it, judging whether rescheduling keeps the loan secure [k][app][an].
    Keywords: statement of financial position, $300,000, inventories, $95,000, $990,000, $690,000, bank loan, $100,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Bank assesses liquidity/capacity to absorb extra or early repayments; Bank checks solvency: loan size relative to capital employed and equity | application_max_2: $300,000 current assets including $95,000 inventories vs $100,000 repayment; $300,000 loan within $990,000 capital employed / $690,000 equity | analysis_max_2: After repayment, roughly $200,000 of current assets would remain, still ahead of $130,000 current liabilities; Equity of $690,000 gives the bank confidence restructuring adds no meaningful default risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd should repay $100,000 of the loan early (Option 1) or buy the delivery van (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option 1 would cut non-current liabilities from $300,000 and save $6,000 of interest, improving the balance sheet the bank assesses and freeing future cash flow for debt service [k][app][an]. Option 2's van would let the company reach more supermarket and restaurant contracts, protecting the $1,150,000 Revenue base and the servicing margin it generates [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the better decision because the guaranteed $6,000 saving is modest beside the Revenue the van could win, and with $300,000 of current assets covering $130,000 of current liabilities a $92,000 purchase still leaves working capital positive; the loan can be rebalanced next year once retained profits have rebuilt equity [eval][eval].
    Keywords: Option 1, Option 2, $100,000, $92,000, $6,000, delivery van, $1,150,000, working capital
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Early repayment cuts interest costs and improves the balance sheet; Investing in assets can generate additional revenue | application_max_2: Option 1 saves $6,000 on a $300,000 loan; Option 2 costs $92,000 and supports the $1,150,000 Revenue base | analysis_max_2: Lower debt improves future cash flow and bank relations; Van increases capacity to service more contracts; purchase still leaves working capital positive | evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: guaranteed $6,000 saving and lower risk / frees no new income; Overall: Option 2 wins on revenue generation; balance sheet remains healthy afterwards

--- STEM ---
Carrowmore Weavers Ltd is a private limited company in Country X weaving wool fabrics for made-to-measure tailoring businesses. In the year ended 31 January 2026 it recorded Revenue of $380,000, Cost of Sales of $228,000, Gross Profit of $152,000, Expenses of $87,000 and Profit for the year of $65,000. Despite this profit, the company held only $18,000 in its bank account.

Current assets total $208,000, including $120,000 owed by customers (one major customer settles around 60 days late) and inventories of $70,000. Current liabilities are $150,000, including $112,000 owed to suppliers, so working capital is $58,000. Non-current assets are valued at $410,000 and non-current liabilities at $150,000, giving capital employed of $468,000 and shareholders' equity of $318,000. Directors must choose between Option 1, an overdraft from the bank, and Option 2, asking suppliers to extend payment terms by 30 days.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline the difference between profit and cash.
    Answer: Profit is the surplus remaining after all costs are deducted from Revenue in the income statement, whereas cash is the money actually received and paid; a credit sale counts as profit before the cash arrives [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Profit = Revenue minus all costs, as reported in the income statement; Cash = money actually received and paid; timing differences make the two diverge

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Carrowmore Weavers Ltd is profitable but short of cash.
    Answer: Reason 1: Much of its earnings is tied up as $120,000 owed by customers, some of whom pay around 60 days late, so Revenue is recognised before the cash arrives [k][app]. Reason 2: The company must still pay Expenses of $87,000 and suppliers the $112,000 it owes, so cash goes out before the corresponding income is collected [k][app].
    Keywords: Carrowmore Weavers Ltd, $120,000, 60 days, $87,000, $112,000, $18,000, $65,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Credit sales create profit before cash is received; Costs must be paid when incurred, regardless of when cash arrives | application_max_2: $120,000 owed by customers, one pays about 60 days late; $87,000 expenses and $112,000 owed to suppliers still must be paid

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the statement of financial position shows how Carrowmore Weavers Ltd could improve its cash position.
    Answer: Reason 1: The $120,000 of receivables inside current assets could be collected faster with firmer payment terms, immediately lifting the $18,000 cash balance without any new finance [k][app][an]. Reason 2: Suppliers are owed $112,000, so Option 2's extra 30 days would defer cash outflow, protecting working capital of $58,000 while the receivables are collected [k][app][an].
    Keywords: current assets, $120,000, $18,000, $112,000, Option 2, working capital, $58,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Convert receivables to cash faster through stronger credit control; Defer payments to suppliers by negotiation | application_max_2: $120,000 receivables vs only $18,000 in the bank; $112,000 owed to suppliers could be stretched 30 days under Option 2 | analysis_max_2: Faster collection rebuilds the cash balance with no borrowing cost; Deferring outflow bridges the timing gap, keeping the business solvent month to month

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the directors should take the overdraft (Option 1) or ask suppliers to extend terms by 30 days (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: An overdraft would cover the immediate gap and is simple to arrange, but it is repayable on demand and its interest would eat into the $65,000 profit [k][app][an]. Option 2 defers the $112,000 supplier outflow at no direct cost and suits a profitable company with $58,000 of working capital waiting on $120,000 of receivables [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is preferable in the short term because Carrowmore is profitable and its problem is timing, not solvency; the directors should chase the $120,000 receivables firmly and keep the overdraft only as a backup if a major customer defaults [eval][eval].
    Keywords: Option 1, Option 2, overdraft, $112,000, $120,000, $58,000, $65,000, 30 days
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Overdrafts give immediate cash but are repayable on demand and carry interest; Extending supplier terms is cost-free short-term finance | application_max_2: Overdraft interest would reduce the $65,000 profit; Option 2 stretches the $112,000 supplier bill while awaiting $120,000 of receivables | analysis_max_2: Option 1 solves the gap quickly but increases financing cost and dependency; Option 2 aligns outflow with expected inflow, stabilising the $58,000 working capital | evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: certainty and immediacy / for Option 2: no cost but relies on supplier goodwill; Overall: Option 2, with the overdraft as backup — collect receivables and the cash crisis passes

Hollyhock Nurseries Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that grows ornamental plants and sells them to garden centres across the region. The statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $350,000, current assets of $160,000 (including cash of $55,000) and current liabilities of $70,000, giving working capital of $90,000 and capital employed of $440,000. Non-current liabilities are $120,000, so shareholders' equity is $320,000.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'Shareholders' Equity'.
    Answer: Shareholders' equity (shareholders' funds) is the owners' stake in the business, equal to capital employed minus non-current liabilities, made up of share capital plus retained profit and reserves [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: The owners'/shareholders' stake in the business; Equals share capital + retained profit, or capital employed − non-current liabilities

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why retained profit is an attractive way to fund the expansion.
    Answer: Reason 1: Retained profit is finance the business already owns, so it does not have to be repaid — keeping non-current liabilities at $120,000 unchanged [k][app]. Reason 2: Using retained profit avoids issuing new shares, so existing shareholders keep their proportional control of the $320,000 of equity [k][app].
    Keywords: Hollyhock Nurseries Ltd, retained profit, $120,000, $320,000, new shares, expansion, garden centres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Retained profit is permanent, internal finance — not repayable; Retained profit avoids diluting existing shareholders' control | application_max_2: Non-current liabilities stay at $120,000; Existing $320,000 equity remains in the same hands

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects on shareholders' equity and on the expansion if Option 1 is chosen rather than Option 2.
    Answer: Point 1: Issuing new shares for $200,000 would raise shareholders' equity immediately from $320,000 to $520,000, providing the whole expansion fund at once [k][app][an]. Point 2: Option 2 adds only about $43,000 to equity each year, so building a similar fund would take around five years of retained profits while the expansion waits [k][app][an].
    Keywords: Option 1, Option 2, $200,000, $320,000, shareholders' equity, retained profits, $43,000, new shares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A new share issue increases share capital and equity by the amount raised; Retained profit builds equity gradually through reserves | application_max_2: Equity would jump from $320,000 to $520,000 under Option 1; $43,000 a year means around five years to approach $200,000 under Option 2 | analysis_max_2: Option 1 lets the expansion proceed immediately and shares risk with new investors; Option 2 delays the project and keeps ownership unchanged, but growth is slow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the board should issue new shares (Option 1) or expand gradually from retained profits (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option 1 provides the full $200,000 immediately, letting Hollyhock respond to garden centre demand at once and lifting shareholders' equity to $520,000 without adding interest-bearing debt [k][app][an]. Option 2 avoids dilution and keeps every decision with the current owners, but at $43,000 a year the company would need roughly five years to match the fund, risking lost seasonal sales [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 1 is justified because Profit of $68,000 and Retained Profit of $43,000 prove trading strength, but not enough speed to seize the opportunity; new investors would enlarge the equity that backs the expansion and share the risk, so long as dividend expectations are negotiated carefully to protect existing owners [eval][eval].
    Keywords: Option 1, Option 2, $200,000, $43,000, $68,000, shareholders' equity, Retained Profit, new shares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: New share issues raise finance quickly and share risk with investors; Retained profit is the cheapest internal finance and preserves control | application_max_2: Option 1 raises $200,000 immediately; equity becomes $520,000; Option 2 yields about $43,000 a year — around five years to build a similar fund | analysis_max_2: Option 1 enables immediate expansion and faster growth in Revenue; Option 2 preserves control but loses the timing advantage of the opportunity | evaluation_max_2: Against Option 1: dilution and dividend expectations may pressure profits; Overall: Option 1, since retained profits alone are too slow to fund a time-sensitive expansion

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Gross Profit fell even though Revenue rose.
    Answer: Reason 1: Cost of Sales grew by about 52%, from $300,000 to $455,000, much faster than Revenue's 30% rise from $500,000 to $650,000, squeezing Gross Profit from $200,000 to $195,000 [k][app]. Reason 2: Higher yarn and material costs raised the cost of each metre of fabric, so although the company sold more, every sale contributed a lower margin [k][app].
    Keywords: Redhall Textiles Ltd, $455,000, $650,000, Gross Profit, $195,000, Cost of Sales, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: When cost of sales grows faster than revenue, gross profit is squeezed; Higher direct input costs reduce the surplus on each unit sold | application_max_2: Cost of Sales up from $300,000 to $455,000 (+52%) vs Revenue's 30% rise; Gross Profit fell from $200,000 to $195,000 despite higher sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the falling Gross Profit creates for the directors.

Reason 2: Less Gross Profit means less is available to retain from earnings, so while working capital is only $85,000 against $95,000 of current liabilities, funding growth or replacing looms becomes very difficult [k][app][an].
    Keywords: Gross Profit, $195,000, $140,000, $55,000, $85,000, $95,000, working capital, Expenses
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower gross profit leaves less to cover expenses and absorb shocks; Lower retained profit restricts internal funding for growth | application_max_2: $195,000 Gross Profit less $140,000 Expenses leaves only $55,000 Profit; Only $85,000 working capital against $95,000 of current liabilities | analysis_max_2: A further cost increase could push the business into losses; Without retained profit the business may need bank finance just to stand still

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the directors should raise the selling price by 8% (Option 1) or switch to the cheaper yarn supplier (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option 1 would lift Revenue to about $702,000 if sales volume holds, restoring Gross Profit to roughly $247,000 with no change in fabric quality [k][app][an]. Option 2 would cut Cost of Sales by about $45,500 a year (10% of $455,000), lifting Gross Profit to roughly $240,500 but risking the quality reputation that wins upholstery contracts [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 1 is the safer recommendation because Expenses of $140,000 and the falling $55,000 Profit leave no room for returns or complaints; working capital of $85,000 cannot absorb a quality dispute with a furniture manufacturer, so protecting the product matters more than the modest $6,500 difference in year-one Gross Profit [eval][eval].
    Keywords: Option 1, Option 2, 8%, 10%, Cost of Sales, $455,000, Revenue, working capital
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Raising prices increases revenue per unit but may reduce demand; Cheaper inputs cut cost of sales (raising margin) but may damage quality | application_max_2: Option 1: Revenue about $702,000 and Gross Profit about $247,000 (if volume holds); Option 2: about $45,500 saved, Gross Profit about $240,500 | analysis_max_2: Option 1 protects quality and brand, sustaining long-term contracts; Option 2 saves money but quality failures could cost more than the saving | evaluation_max_2: Against Option 1: higher prices may lose price-sensitive furniture manufacturers; Overall: Option 1 — quality protection outweighs the small year-one margin difference

--- STEM ---
Dunmore Cheese Co Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making farmhouse cheese from locally collected milk. In the year ended 30 September 2026 it recorded Revenue of $520,000, Cost of Sales of $286,000, Gross Profit of $234,000, Expenses of $164,000 and Profit for the year of $70,000. The statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $470,000, inventories of $85,000, trade receivables of $95,000 and cash of $10,000. Non-current liabilities are $180,000, so capital employed is $510,000 and shareholders' equity is $330,000. Directors are considering Option 1, cutting inventories to $55,000, or Option 2, asking the bank to convert a $60,000 overdraft into a long-term loan.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'Non-current Liabilities'.
    Answer: Non-current liabilities are long-term debts a business does not need to repay within the next 12 months, such as bank loans and debentures [2].
