UNIT: Unit 5: Financial Information and Decisions
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Fallowfield & Dean Licensed Grocers Ltd is a private limited company running 2 convenience stores in Country X, owned by cousins Priya and Danny Fallowfield. In the year to 30 April, revenue was $800,000, gross profit $304,000, expenses $232,000 and profit $72,000; capital employed was $960,000 and current assets of $288,000 included inventories of $128,000, against current liabilities of $160,000.

The cousins want a $350,000 bank loan at 9% interest to refit both stores, improve refrigeration and add a chilled food counter. Alternatively, they could refit slowly over 3 years from retained profit. The bank has asked for ratio analysis from their accountant before deciding whether to approve the loan for the full amount requested. The cousins must satisfy the bank's lending committee in December.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two uses of ratio analysis.
    Answer: Two uses of ratio analysis are firstly to compare a business's performance over time and against competitors, and secondly to support applications for finance such as bank loans by showing lenders the business's profitability and liquidity. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis compares performance over time or against competitors; Ratio analysis supports decisions and finance applications by quantifying profitability and liquidity

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways ratio analysis can support the bank loan application.
    Answer: Use 1: ratio analysis gives the bank a standardised view of creditworthiness [k]; the current ratio of 1.8:1 ($288,000 divided by $160,000) and an acid test ratio of 1.0:1 show the stores can cover short-term debts, supporting the $350,000 loan request [app]. Use 2: ratio analysis shows the owners understand their business numbers [k]; a gross profit margin of 38.0% ($304,000 divided by $800,000) and a 7.5% ROCE ($72,000 divided by $960,000) give the bank evidence the stores are profitable and professionally run [app].
    Keywords: $288,000, $160,000, $128,000, $304,000, $960,000, $350,000, ratio analysis
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis provides standardised evidence of creditworthiness; Ratio analysis demonstrates the owners understand their business performance | application_max_2: Applies the 1.8:1 current ratio and 1.0:1 acid test ratio ($288,000, $128,000, $160,000); Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin and 7.5% ROCE ($304,000 / $800,000; $72,000 / $960,000)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of ratio analysis the cousins should consider.
    Answer: Limitation 1: ratio analysis is based on historic accounts and cannot prove the refit will pay back [k]; a 9.0% profit margin ($72,000 divided by $800,000) would fall to about 5.1% after paying $31,500 of interest on the $350,000 loan (leaving $40,500 of profit), squeezing margins exactly when the stores need cash for the chilled counter [app][an]. Limitation 2: ratio analysis ignores qualitative factors and context [k]; neither the 38.0% gross profit margin nor the 1.8:1 current ratio captures customer loyalty, staffing stability or whether a chilled counter would actually lift sales, so the business plan matters as much as the figures [app][an].
    Keywords: $350,000, 9% interest, $72,000, $800,000, $304,000, chilled food counter
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis is historic and cannot prove future returns on investment; Ratio analysis ignores qualitative factors such as customers and staff | application_max_2: Applies the 9.0% margin falling to about 5.1% after $31,500 interest ($40,500 profit); Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin and 1.8:1 current ratio ignoring loyalty and the chilled counter | analysis_max_2: Explains interest costs sharply reduce final profit margin after borrowing; Explains figures alone cannot capture customer demand for the chilled counter

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the cousins should take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The cousins could take the loan because refitting both stores now, rather than over 3 years from retained profit, defends the 38.0% gross profit margin ($304,000) against rivals adding chilled counters and captures sales sooner [k][app]. Profit of $72,000 (9.0% margin) barely covers the $31,500 interest, leaving $40,500 (5.1%), so the refit must generate meaningful new sales to be worthwhile [an]. However, the acid test ratio of 1.0:1 leaves no slack for trading setbacks, and capital employed would rise to $1,310,000, cutting ROCE to about 3.1% ($40,500 divided by $1,310,000) unless profits recover quickly [app][an]. Conversely, refitting slowly from retained profit avoids interest entirely and keeps the 1.0:1 acid test intact, but it cedes competitive advantage for 3 years and may never deliver the chilled food counter at all [k][eval]. Overall, the cousins should take the loan only if the bank offers a grace period before full repayments begin, because a 5.1% post-interest margin leaves almost no room for error; otherwise they should refit from retained profit and accept the slower refit as the safer route [eval].
    Keywords: $350,000, retained profit, 9% interest, $72,000, $304,000, chilled food counter, $960,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Loan $350,000 at 9% = $31,500 interest; post-interest profit $40,500 (5.1% margin); ROCE falls to about 3.1% on $1,310,000 capital employed; acid test 1.0:1 | application_max_2: Applies the $31,500 interest and 5.1% post-interest margin to argue for caution; Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin defence and acid test 1.0:1 to argue for slow refit | analysis_max_2: Explains the refit must lift sales enough to cover the $31,500 annual interest; Explains capital employed rises to $1,310,000 diluting ROCE to about 3.1% | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to a bank grace period, otherwise slower retained-profit refit

--- STEM ---
Wexcombe Pottery Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 12 years ago and employing 58 workers at its Stokeham workshop. Staff belong to the Clay & Ceramics Union, which has tabled a 6% pay claim after the published final accounts showed revenue of $2.4 million, up from $2.1 million, and profit of $310,000, up from $185,000 a year earlier. The directors have countered with a 2% offer.

Union representatives want to inspect the full final accounts before talks, arguing the figures prove the claim is affordable. Managing Director Priya Nair must decide between granting 6%, costing the business an extra $96,000 a year, and holding to 2%, costing $32,000 and releasing funds for a kiln replacement. The annual wage bill is $1.6 million.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'final accounts'.
    Answer: Final accounts are the financial statements a business prepares at the end of an accounting period to show its profit, revenue and financial position, helping stakeholders judge performance [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Statements prepared at the end of the accounting period; Show profit, revenue and financial position to stakeholders

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the Clay & Ceramics Union would want to see Wexcombe Pottery Ltd's final accounts.
    Answer: First, the union wants to see whether the business can afford the 6% claim [k]. Profit rose to $310,000 on revenue of $2.4 million, so members argue the accounts prove the case for higher pay [app]. Second, the union uses the accounts to judge job security [k]. If profit fell back towards $185,000 or expenses spiked, jobs and future rises could be at risk, shaping whether to press for 6% or accept the $32,000 offer [app].
    Keywords: $310,000, $185,000, $2.4 million, 6%, 2%, $32,000, final accounts
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Judge whether the business can afford the pay claim; Assess job security and the basis for negotiating | application_max_2: Reference to profit $310,000 (up from $185,000) and revenue $2.4 million; Reference to the 6% claim versus the 2% offer ($32,000)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the directors might face if they agree to the 6% claim.
    Answer: First, agreeing the claim raises wage costs [k]. The extra $96,000 a year would come from profit of $310,000, leaving only about $214,000 before tax [app]. This squeezes the owners' return and could force price rises, risking orders from price-sensitive retailers [an]. Second, the claim absorbs funds for the kiln replacement [k]. The 2% offer costs $32,000, but 6% costs $96,000, a difference of $64,000 [app]. Without the new kiln, output and quality at Stokeham could deteriorate, hurting delivery reliability and customer trust [an].
    Keywords: $96,000, $310,000, $32,000, 6%, 2%, kiln replacement, Stokeham
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher wage costs reduce profit and flexibility; Removes funds earmarked for investment (kiln) | application_max_2: Reference to $96,000 a year against the $1.6 million wage bill; Reference to profit $310,000 and 2% offer costing $32,000 / kiln replacement | analysis_max_2: Chain from lower retained profit to price rises to lost orders; Chain from no kiln to lower output and quality to lost customers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wexcombe Pottery Ltd should accept the 6% pay claim? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Granting the 6% claim would reward workers after a strong year [k]. It costs $96,000 a year, and with profit of $310,000 the business could pay it while keeping about $214,000, improving morale across all 58 workers and cutting the risk of strikes [app]. Better motivation could lift output and reduce labour turnover at the workshop, protecting revenue of $2.4 million [an]. However, the 6% claim absorbs the funds needed for the kiln replacement, unlike the 2% offer costing $32,000 [k]. Accepting 6% would also set a precedent the business cannot afford if profit falls back towards $185,000 [app]. Sustained higher wages could force price rises that lose customers to rivals, eroding the very profit that makes the claim affordable [an]. Overall, I think Wexcombe Pottery Ltd should hold to the 2% offer plus a one-off profit-linked bonus [eval]. Profit did improve, but the full claim would commit about 31% of last year's profit to permanent extra wages when a cheaper deal funds both motivation and the kiln [eval].
    Keywords: 6%, 2%, $96,000, $32,000, $310,000, $185,000, $2.4 million, 58 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Granting improves morale / cuts risk of industrial action; 6% removes kiln investment funds and sets a precedent | application_max_2: Reference to $96,000 a year and profit $310,000 / about $214,000 remaining; Reference to 2% offer costing $32,000 and profit possibly falling back to $185,000 | analysis_max_2: Chain from morale to output and labour turnover to protected revenue; Chain from wage precedent to price rises to lost customers | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (2% plus bonus rather than full 6%); Weighs both options with stem figures ($96,000 vs $32,000; 31% of profit)

--- STEM ---
Aldergate Cycle Works Plc manufactures and sells bicycles across Country X from its Denham factory, employing 340 people, and is listed on the Country X Stock Exchange with about 420 shareholders. For the year just ended, revenue was $24 million and profit was $2.6 million on capital employed of $18.6 million, a return on capital employed of 14%, up from 11% two years ago.

The board plans a $2.2 million assembly hall. Under Option A, it pays an unchanged 6c dividend on the 10 million shares in issue, costing $600,000, leaving $2.0 million from profit; the $200,000 shortfall would be borrowed at 9% interest. Under Option B, the dividend is cut to 4c, costing $400,000, and the hall is funded entirely from retained profit.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'dividend'.
    Answer: A dividend is a payment made by a company to its shareholders out of profits, usually expressed per share held, as a return on their investment [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Payment made to shareholders out of profits; Usually expressed per share; a return on shareholders' investment

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why shareholders would use the final accounts of Aldergate Cycle Works Plc.
    Answer: First, shareholders use the accounts to judge whether the profit can support dividends [k]. Profit of $2.6 million covers the unchanged 6c dividend of $600,000, and ROCE of 14%, up from 11% two years ago, signals the business is using its capital well [app]. Second, shareholders use the accounts to assess the risk and growth prospects of their investment [k]. With revenue of $24 million and capital employed of $18.6 million, and the board planning a $2.2 million assembly hall, investors can judge future returns and decide between the 6c and 4c dividend options [app].
    Keywords: $2.6 million, 6c, $600,000, 14%, $24 million, $18.6 million, $2.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Judge ability to pay dividends / profitability of the business; Assess risk and growth prospects before investing | application_max_2: Reference to profit $2.6 million, 6c/$600,000 dividend and ROCE 14% vs 11%; Reference to revenue $24 million, capital employed $18.6 million, $2.2 million hall

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Aldergate of funding the assembly hall from retained profit rather than borrowing.
    Answer: First, funding from retained profit avoids interest charges [k]. Option B retains the full $2.2 million after a $400,000 dividend, whereas Option A leaves only $2.0 million and borrows $200,000 at 9%, costing about $18,000 a year in interest [app]. Avoiding that cost directly improves profit and frees up cash for tooling and maintenance in the new hall [an]. Second, retained profit avoids new debt and keeps control with existing shareholders [k]. Cutting the dividend to 4c funds the hall without loans or security, and shareholders keep ownership of a business whose ROCE is already 14% [app]. Lower debt levels reduce financial risk and protect independence, supporting the share price on the Country X Stock Exchange [an].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $400,000, $2.2 million, $2.0 million, $200,000, 9%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Avoids interest cost on borrowed funds; Avoids new debt / keeps control with existing shareholders | application_max_2: Reference to Option B retaining the full $2.2 million after a $400,000 dividend; Reference to Option A: $2.0 million left, $200,000 borrowed at 9% = about $18,000 a year | analysis_max_2: Chain from avoided interest to higher profit and freer cash; Chain from avoiding debt to lower financial risk and independence

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think shareholders should approve the 4c dividend? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Approving 4c would give the board $2.2 million to build the hall without borrowing [k]. Shareholders give up $200,000 of income, with the dividend falling from 6c to 4c on the 10 million shares in issue, but Aldergate avoids about $18,000 a year of interest and retains full independence [app]. A bigger, more efficient hall should lift output and revenue beyond $24 million, supporting future dividends and ROCE holding above 14% [an]. However, many shareholders rely on dividend income, and cutting the payout by a third may prompt some to sell, depressing the share price [k]. Others would prefer Option A's unchanged $600,000 payout with a modest $200,000 loan, accepting $18,000 annual interest to keep income stable [app]. Heavy selling could signal weak confidence and push the share price down, wiping out the income slowdown [an]. Overall, I think shareholders should approve the 4c dividend [eval]. It funds a $2.2 million hall, avoids debt, and reinvests profit when ROCE is rising, a price worth paying provided the board publishes clear targets for restoring dividends once the hall opens [eval].
    Keywords: 4c, 6c, $400,000, $600,000, $2.2 million, $200,000, 10 million shares, Option A
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Approving gives $2.2 million without borrowing; Some shareholders rely on income; a cut may press the share price down | application_max_2: Reference to $200,000 income loss and $18,000 a year interest avoided; Reference to Option A: 6c plus a $200,000 loan at 9%; 10 million shares | analysis_max_2: Chain from hall investment to output and revenue to future dividends; Chain from heavy shareholder selling to weaker share price | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified approval of the 4c dividend; Weighs both options with stem figures ($400,000 vs $600,000; $2.2 million hall)

--- STEM ---
Ternhill Dairy Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 9 years ago, which makes cheese and butter and supplies 14 regional supermarkets. It employs 46 staff and has applied to Country X Bank for a $400,000 loan to buy three refrigerated delivery vans. Last year it reported revenue of $5.1 million and profit of $420,000.

The statement of financial position shows current assets of $980,000, including inventories of $350,000 and debtors of $520,000, against current liabilities of $600,000. The current ratio has fallen to 1.63 from 1.9 two years ago, and the acid test ratio has fallen to 1.05 from 1.3. Cash at bank is $110,000 and the loan application is with the credit manager this week.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'liquidity'.
    Answer: Liquidity is the ability of a business to pay its short-term debts as they fall due, using cash or assets that can quickly be turned into cash [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Ability to pay short-term debts as they fall due; Using cash or assets quickly convertible to cash

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Country X Bank would examine Ternhill Dairy Ltd's statement of financial position before granting the loan.
    Answer: First, the bank wants to judge whether short-term debts can be paid [k]. Current assets of $980,000 against current liabilities of $600,000 give a current ratio of 1.63, down from 1.9 two years ago, which tells the bank Ternhill has some cushion but a weakening one [app]. Second, the bank wants to know what can be turned into cash quickly [k]. With inventories of $350,000 the acid test ratio is 1.05, down from 1.3, and cash is only $110,000, so the bank would probe the $520,000 of debtors to see whether supermarkets pay on time [app].
    Keywords: $980,000, $600,000, 1.63, 1.9, $350,000, 1.05, $520,000, $110,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Judge ability to pay short-term debts; Assess how much is quickly convertible to cash | application_max_2: Reference to current ratio 1.63 vs 1.9; current assets $980,000 vs current liabilities $600,000; Reference to acid test 1.05 vs 1.3; inventories $350,000, debtors $520,000, cash $110,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of using the current ratio and the acid test ratio to judge Ternhill's ability to repay the loan.
    Answer: First, ratios are a snapshot at one date [k]. Ternhill's current ratio of 1.63 and acid test ratio of 1.05 held at the year end, but a single late supermarket payment or a big stock delivery could change both quickly, so the figures may flatter the business on the day the $400,000 loan is decided [app]. Liquidity could be materially weaker exactly when the first instalments fall due [an]. Second, ratios ignore the quality of what the business owns [k]. Of the $980,000 of current assets, $350,000 is inventories and $520,000 is debtors; slow-paying or defaulting supermarkets, or damaged stocks, would shrink the real acid test well below 1.05 [app]. The bank could lend on the strength of figures that evaporate once debtors and inventories are properly valued [an].
    Keywords: 1.63, 1.05, $980,000, $350,000, $520,000, $400,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Ratios are a snapshot at one date; figures change quickly; Ratios ignore the quality of assets (stock and debtors may be impaired) | application_max_2: Reference to current ratio 1.63 and acid test 1.05 at year end; Reference to inventories $350,000 and debtors $520,000 of $980,000 current assets | analysis_max_2: Chain from year-end snapshot to weaker instalment-date liquidity; Chain from impaired stock or debtors to an overstated acid test

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Country X Bank should grant the $400,000 loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Ternhill is profitable, with profit of $420,000 almost covering the $400,000 loan in a single year [k]. Revenue of $5.1 million and supply deals with 14 regional supermarkets suggest steady cash generation, and three refrigerated vans would cut spoilage and secure deliveries, supporting future sales [app]. Stronger distribution could widen margins and lift profit further, improving the bank's repayment prospects across the term of the loan [an]. However, liquidity is weakening: the current ratio has fallen from 1.9 to 1.63, the acid test from 1.3 to 1.05, cash is only $110,000 and debtors are $520,000 — more than half of current assets [k]. Granting cash before debtors are collected could leave Ternhill unable to meet early instalments, especially if one supermarket pays late [app]. A rushed approval could turn a good customer into an overdraft problem, adding risk and cost to the bank with no extra margin [an]. Overall, I think Country X Bank should grant the loan, but in staged instalments linked to milestones, with vans delivered and debtors collected down to agreed limits [eval]. The profit and revenue justify supporting the business, yet the weakening acid test and $110,000 cash balance demand controls rather than one upfront payout [eval].
    Keywords: $400,000, $420,000, $5.1 million, 14 regional supermarkets, 1.63, 1.05, $110,000, $520,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Profitable business; loan is close to one year of profit; Weakening current ratio, acid test and cash position | application_max_2: Reference to revenue $5.1 million, profit $420,000 and 14 supermarkets; Reference to cash $110,000, debtors $520,000, current ratio 1.63, acid test 1.05 | analysis_max_2: Chain from new vans to lower spoilage and stronger sales to easier repayment; Chain from rushed approval to overdraft pressure and added risk | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to lend in stages; Weighs both sides with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Wicklow Builders Merchants Ltd is a family-run private limited company in Country X, founded 15 years ago, supplying roofing, insulation and timber to the construction trade. It employs 28 staff. A new customer, Hollowbrook Homes Ltd, a housing developer, wants to buy $180,000 of materials for a 24-house estate and asks for 60 days to pay.

Hollowbrook Homes' latest accounts show revenue of $6.4 million, profit of $250,000, current assets of $550,000 including inventories of $250,000, and current liabilities of $500,000, giving a current ratio of 1.1 and an acid test ratio of 0.6. Hollowbrook has also been slow to pay its existing suppliers. Wicklow must decide by Friday between granting 60-day credit or insisting on 30-day terms, risking the order to a rival merchant.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'trade credit'.
    Answer: Trade credit is an arrangement allowing a customer to receive goods immediately and pay the supplier after an agreed period, such as 30 or 60 days [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Goods received before payment; Payment made after an agreed period such as 30 or 60 days

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Wicklow Builders Merchants Ltd would want to see Hollowbrook Homes Ltd's accounts before offering trade credit.
    Answer: First, the accounts show whether Hollowbrook can pay [k]. Current assets of $550,000 against current liabilities of $500,000 give a current ratio of 1.1 and an acid test ratio of 0.6, so quick funds are thin for settling a $180,000 invoice [app]. Second, the accounts show whether the order is reasonable for the customer's size [k]. Revenue of $6.4 million and profit of $250,000 against a $180,000 order means the deal equals 72% of annual profit, so Wicklow must judge whether the margin justifies the exposure [app].
    Keywords: $550,000, $500,000, 1.1, 0.6, $180,000, $6.4 million, $250,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Assess ability to pay (liquidity); Assess order size relative to the customer's resources | application_max_2: Reference to current ratio 1.1, acid test 0.6, current assets $550,000 vs current liabilities $500,000; Reference to $180,000 order = 72% of $250,000 profit on revenue of $6.4 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks to Wicklow of granting 60-day credit.
    Answer: First, Wicklow faces late or non-payment [k]. Hollowbrook's acid test of 0.6 and inventories of $250,000, nearly half its current assets, show cash is tight and it is already slow paying existing suppliers, so the $180,000 could sit unpaid well beyond 60 days [app]. Wicklow would then lack cash for its own stock and wages, possibly needing costly overdraft borrowing [an]. Second, a single large customer raises dependence [k]. The $180,000 order equals 72% of Hollowbrook's $250,000 profit, so one default or insolvency would be a heavy blow to a 28-staff merchant [app]. Losing that sum could wipe out Wicklow's margin on the whole estate deal and strain relations with its own suppliers [an].
    Keywords: 0.6, $250,000, $180,000, inventories, 28 staff, 60-day
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Risk of late payment or default; Dependence on one large customer | application_max_2: Reference to acid test 0.6, inventories $250,000 (nearly half of current assets) and slow payment of suppliers; Reference to $180,000 = 72% of $250,000 profit; 28 staff | analysis_max_2: Chain from late payment to Wicklow cash strain and overdraft costs; Chain from one default to lost margin and supplier strain

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wicklow Builders Merchants Ltd should grant the 60-day credit? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Granting 60-day credit could win a $180,000 order for a 24-house estate and open a long-term relationship with a growing developer [k]. Hollowbrook is profitable at $250,000 on revenue of $6.4 million, and the deal equals 72% of its profit, so losing it to a rival merchant would hand over valuable future estate business [app]. Securing the account could bring regular orders and steady sales without new advertising spend [an]. However, Hollowbrook's liquidity is weak: acid test 0.6, current ratio 1.1, inventories of $250,000 and a record of slow payment to existing suppliers [k]. If payment slips beyond 60 days, Wicklow faces a cash gap of $180,000 on top of its own commitments, risking its ability to pay suppliers and staff [app]. One bad debt could erase months of Wicklow's margin, and repeated chasing strains the relationship the deal was meant to build [an]. Overall, I think Wicklow should not grant 60 days on the current terms [eval]; it should insist on 30-day terms, or staged payments with a deposit, because the acid test of 0.6 and the slow payment history do not justify open-ended 60-day credit, however attractive the order looks [eval].
    Keywords: 60-day, $180,000, 24-house, $250,000, inventories, 0.6, 1.1, $6.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Winning the order builds a relationship and future business; Weak liquidity and slow payment history make 60 days risky | application_max_2: Reference to $180,000 order, $250,000 profit, 72% of profit, 24-house estate; Reference to acid test 0.6, current ratio 1.1, inventories $250,000 | analysis_max_2: Chain from winning the account to regular future orders; Chain from late payment to a cash gap and bad-debt risk | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (30-day terms or staged payments instead); Weighs both options with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Stonemere Haulage Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, based at the Kinwell depot and the Northgate satellite yard, running 9 lorries for food and retail clients. It employs 34 drivers and warehouse staff. The government has announced grants covering 40% of the cost of electric trucks, provided applicants show two consecutive profitable years and create 3 new jobs per truck purchased.

Stonemere wants to buy 3 electric trucks at $160,000 each, totalling $480,000. Retained profit stands at $500,000 and the last two years produced profits of $175,000 and $210,000. The grant would contribute $192,000, leaving Stonemere to fund $288,000, but accepting it would oblige Stonemere to keep 9 new drivers for 3 years, publish its accounts annually and meet government reporting requirements.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'retained profit'.
    Answer: Retained profit is the profit left in the business after tax and shareholder dividends, kept in the business to reinvest in growth or fund future plans [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Profit remaining after tax and dividends; Kept in the business for reinvestment or future plans

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the government agency would want to see Stonemere Haulage Ltd's accounts before approving the grant.
    Answer: First, the agency must verify the two-year profit rule [k]. Stonemere's profits of $175,000 and $210,000 in consecutive years meet the eligibility test, and retained profit of $500,000 confirms the business is viable [app]. Second, the agency must judge whether the promised jobs will last [k]. Accounts showing steady profit and a $500,000 cushion help the agency assess whether Stonemere can pay nine drivers for three years, not just create paper jobs [app].
    Keywords: $175,000, $210,000, $500,000, 9 new drivers, 3 years, 40%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Verify two consecutive profitable years (eligibility); Assess ability to sustain the jobs for 3 years | application_max_2: Reference to profits of $175,000 and $210,000 in consecutive years; Reference to retained profit of $500,000 and nine drivers kept for three years

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks to Stonemere of accepting the grant.
    Answer: First, the grant binds Stonemere to keep 9 drivers for three years [k]. If demand falls, Stonemere must still pay nine wages although retained profit of $500,000 might otherwise fund maintenance or marketing [app]. This shrinks flexibility and could push the business into losses if a major client leaves [an]. Second, accepting means publishing accounts annually [k]. Clients and rivals would see that profit was $210,000 last year, weakening Stonemere's hand in price negotiations [app]. Visible margins invite tougher customer demands and higher wage claims, eroding much of the $192,000 benefit over three years [an].
    Keywords: 9 new drivers, 3 years, $500,000, $210,000, $192,000, publish its accounts
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Three-year, nine-job obligation reduces flexibility; Accounts must be published annually; loss of confidentiality | application_max_2: Reference to 9 drivers kept for 3 years against $500,000 retained profit; Reference to published profit of $210,000 and grant value of $192,000 | analysis_max_2: Chain from rigid wages to losses if demand falls; Chain from published margins to tougher client negotiations

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Stonemere Haulage Ltd should apply for the government grant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Applying secures $192,000 of the $480,000 truck cost, cutting Stonemere's own funding to $288,000 [k]. With retained profit of $500,000, the business keeps $212,000 in reserve for repairs and working capital, healthier than spending $480,000 outright, and three electric trucks fit the fleet's efficiency plans [app]. Lower operating costs per kilometre and contracts won on green credentials could lift profit beyond $210,000 a year, covering the grant obligations comfortably [an]. However, accepting ties Stonemere to keep 9 drivers for 3 years even through downturns, and its accounts must be published annually, exposing margins to clients and rivals [k]. Stonemere could instead fund $480,000 entirely from retained profit, leaving just $20,000, keeping full control and confidentiality with no government reporting [app]. Losing privacy could cost more than $192,000 over three years if clients demand price cuts on that evidence [an]. Overall, I think Stonemere should apply for the grant [eval], because $192,000 is 40% of the purchase price and preserving $212,000 of liquidity outweighs the publication risk, but only if it is confident of retaining the 9 drivers and handling the extra reporting for three years [eval].
    Keywords: $192,000, $480,000, $288,000, $500,000, $160,000, 3 electric trucks, 40%, 9 new drivers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Secures $192,000 (40%) of the truck cost; Binding obligations: 9 jobs, 3 years, published accounts | application_max_2: Reference to $288,000 own funding, $500,000 retained profit, $212,000 reserve; Reference to paying $480,000 outright leaving just $20,000 | analysis_max_2: Chain from a green fleet to lower costs and new contracts; Chain from published accounts to price pressure from clients | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to apply; Weighs both options with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Halcyon Reef Resorts Ltd runs three eco-resorts on the Country X coast and employs 210 staff. Comparing the last two years, revenue rose from $9.6 million to $10.4 million, but gross profit margin fell from 52% to 47% and profit fell from $840,000 to $720,000, a drop of $120,000. The current ratio held at 1.8 in both years and occupancy averaged 78%.

Managing Directors Aisha Bellocq and Tom Reyes disagree on the response. Option A raises room rates from $145 to $154, a rise of $9, to recover the margin. Option B keeps rates unchanged and cuts operating costs, mainly by re-tendering laundry and kitchen contracts, saving $120,000 a year but with some risk to service consistency. They have asked analysts to compare the accounts over the two years.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'ratio analysis'.
    Answer: Ratio analysis is the use of financial ratios, such as gross profit margin, return on capital employed and the current ratio, to assess a business's performance and financial position, often compared over time [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Using financial ratios to assess performance and financial position; Comparisons over time or against other businesses

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why comparing the accounts over two years is useful to managers.
    Answer: First, two years of ratios reveal trends that a single year cannot [k]. Revenue rising from $9.6 million to $10.4 million looks healthy on its own, but the gross profit margin falling from 52% to 47% shows growth is being bought with weaker pricing or higher input costs [app]. Second, trend analysis helps locate the problem precisely [k]. A current ratio steady at 1.8 alongside falling profit shows liquidity is fine, so managers should attack costs or pricing, and the profit drop of $120,000 matches the projected $120,000 saving exactly [app].
    Keywords: $9.6 million, $10.4 million, 52%, 47%, 1.8, $120,000, $840,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Reveals trends that a single year cannot; Locates whether problems are cost, price or liquidity | application_max_2: Reference to revenue $9.6 million to $10.4 million; gross profit margin 52% to 47%; Reference to current ratio steady at 1.8; profit fall of $120,000 matching the $120,000 saving

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of comparing Halcyon's ratios over just two years.
    Answer: First, two years is a short window and may catch one-off events [k]. Halcyon's profit fell from $840,000 to $720,000 partly because of higher laundry and kitchen costs, which the $120,000 saving would reverse, so the 47% margin may understate underlying performance [app]. Judging on a single cost shock could push directors into rushed rate rises or cuts that harm guests [an]. Second, ratios ignore qualitative factors [k]. Occupancy of 78% shows rooms are selling, but guest satisfaction, staff morale and brand reputation, all affected by Option B's service-consistency risk, sit outside the numbers [app]. Cutting the wrong contracts could save $120,000 yet damage the experience that drives occupancy and revenue of $10.4 million [an].
    Keywords: $840,000, $720,000, 47%, $120,000, 78%, $10.4 million, Option B
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Short window; one-off events distort the picture; Ratios ignore qualitative factors (service, morale, brand) | application_max_2: Reference to profit $840,000 to $720,000; 47% margin; $120,000 saving; Reference to occupancy 78% and revenue of $10.4 million | analysis_max_2: Chain from a short window to rushed, harmful decisions; Chain from blunt cost cuts to damaged occupancy and revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Halcyon Reef Resorts Ltd should choose Option B rather than Option A? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A raises rates from $145 to $154, a $9 increase, restoring revenue from existing guests without restructuring operations [k]. With occupancy at 78%, even a modest rise lifts revenue across three resorts, but it may deter price-sensitive holidaymakers already facing higher costs elsewhere [app]. If even 5% of guests defect, the lost contribution could erase the extra $9 a night and push occupancy below break-even [an]. Option B keeps rates at $145 and cuts costs by $120,000 a year, exactly the profit lost, by re-tendering laundry and kitchen contracts [k]. This attacks the problem directly and protects the $145 rate that keeps the resorts competitive, provided service standards are monitored closely [app]. Well-run contracts could restore profit towards $840,000 without touching price or occupancy [an]. Overall, I think Halcyon should choose Option B, with strict service-level monitoring [eval]; it exactly offsets the $120,000 profit fall and avoids demand risk at 78% occupancy, whereas Option A remains a useful fallback if service complaints rise after the switch [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $145, $154, $9, 78%, $120,000, $840,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A restores revenue but risks demand at 78% occupancy; Option B targets the cost cause and protects price and occupancy | application_max_2: Reference to $145 to $154 ($9) and occupancy 78% at three resorts; Reference to $120,000 saving equalling the profit lost; profit back towards $840,000 | analysis_max_2: Chain from a rate rise to guest defections and lower occupancy; Chain from cost re-tendering to protected price and margin recovery | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation for Option B with safeguards; Weighs both options with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Wrenfield Cider Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing apple cider, with revenue of $4.1 million, a gross profit margin of 39%, ROCE of 11% and a current ratio of 1.7. Its board is considering buying its smaller rival, Fenwick Orchards Ltd, whose accounts show revenue of $3.2 million, a gross profit margin of 44%, ROCE of 16% on capital employed of $1.6 million, helped by a one-off land sale contributing $90,000 of profit, and a current ratio of 1.4. Fenwick values inventories using a different method and its figures are already 12 months old.

Fenwick is asking $2.6 million. The board compares the two sets of accounts and debates whether the higher ratios prove Fenwick is the better business. Directors know ratio analysis has limitations and want wider evidence before committing to the purchase.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'current ratio'.
    Answer: The current ratio is a liquidity ratio that compares a business's current assets with its current liabilities, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Compares current assets with current liabilities; Calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Fenwick's higher ratios might not prove it is the better buy.
    Answer: First, one-off items can flatter a single year's ratios [k]. Fenwick's 16% ROCE was helped by a $90,000 one-off land sale, so underlying profit is nearer $166,000; $2.6 million is more than fifteen years of that recurring profit [app]. Second, different accounting policies distort comparisons [k]. Fenwick values inventories on a different basis and its figures are already 12 months old, so its 44% gross profit margin and 1.4 current ratio are not directly comparable with Wrenfield's 39% and 1.7 accounts [app].
    Keywords: 16%, $90,000, $2.6 million, 44%, 39%, 1.4, 1.7
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: One-off items can distort a single year's ratios; Different accounting policies undermine comparability | application_max_2: Reference to the $90,000 one-off land sale within the 16% ROCE; underlying profit nearer $166,000; Reference to Fenwick's inventory method and figures being 12 months old; 44% vs 39% gross profit margin; 1.4 vs 1.7 current ratio

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two other checks Wrenfield should make before buying Fenwick.
    Answer: First, Wrenfield should inspect Fenwick's physical assets and stock [k]. A current ratio of 1.4 tells nothing about condition; ageing cider, obsolete labels or tired bottling kit would force post-purchase write-downs, eroding the $2.6 million price [app]. Overstated assets would mean Wrenfield pays for value that no longer exists [an]. Second, Wrenfield should review Fenwick's customer contracts and forward orders [k]. Revenue of $3.2 million and a 44% gross profit margin mean little if pub and retail accounts are uncontracted, paying late, or reflecting a fading local cider trend captured in the 12-month-old figures [app]. Losing a key account after completion would cut the profit base that justified the price [an].
    Keywords: 1.4, $2.6 million, $3.2 million, 44%, 12 months old, Fenwick
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Inspect physical assets and stock quality; Review customer contracts and forward orders | application_max_2: Reference to the current ratio of 1.4 and the $2.6 million price; Reference to revenue of $3.2 million at a 44% gross profit margin and 12-month-old figures | analysis_max_2: Chain from overstated stock to post-purchase write-downs; Chain from lost accounts to a collapsed profit rationale

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wrenfield Cider Ltd should buy Fenwick Orchards Ltd for $2.6 million? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying would remove a rival and add $3.2 million of revenue at a 44% gross profit margin to Wrenfield's $4.1 million, 39% operation [k]. Even with the $90,000 one-off stripped out, leaving nearer $166,000 of recurring profit, synergies in buying apples, bottling and distribution could lift both margins and make the $2.6 million pay back faster [app]. If Wrenfield shares distribution routes and negotiates bulk supply, the deal could raise its own 39% margin towards Fenwick's 44% [an]. However, Fenwick's figures are 12 months old, inventories are valued differently, and its 16% ROCE rests partly on the $90,000 land sale [k]. Paying $2.6 million on unaudited, mismatched evidence risks overpaying by a wide margin, with limited recourse after completion [app]. A bad deal could tie up Wrenfield's cash for years, weaken its own current ratio of 1.7 and leave it exposed to poor harvests [an]. Overall, I think Wrenfield should not buy Fenwick at $2.6 million on the current evidence [eval]; it should renegotiate the price or commission updated, adjusted accounts and a stock audit first, since $2.6 million, more than fifteen years of recurring profit near $166,000, cannot be justified on a flattering single year [eval].
    Keywords: $2.6 million, $3.2 million, 44%, $4.1 million, 39%, $90,000, 12 months old, 1.7
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying removes a rival and adds revenue and margin; Stale, mismatched figures; reliance on a one-off profit | application_max_2: Reference to $3.2 million revenue at 44% vs $4.1 million at 39%; $90,000 one-off; underlying profit nearer $166,000; Reference to figures 12 months old, 16% ROCE, current ratio 1.7, $2.6 million price | analysis_max_2: Chain from merged distribution and bulk buying to margin improvement; Chain from overpayment to cash strain and exposure | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation not to buy at $2.6 million without updated accounts; Weighs both options with stem figures

UNIT: Unit 5: Financial Information and Decisions
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Garrow Fresh Fish Ltd is a private limited company in Country X supplying smoked and fresh fish to retail stores in the Northgate region. It employs 37 staff. Last year it reported revenue of $3.6 million and profit of $320,000, but cash at the bank is only $85,000 and debtors stand at $640,000 after several customers stretched their payment terms.

Its largest customer, Regional Stores Group, offers a 2-year exclusive contract worth $900,000 a year but demands payment after 90 days and a 4% price cut, worth $36,000 a year. Taking the order would add about $225,000 of unpaid invoices at any time, more than two and a half times the cash at bank. Garrow must decide by the end of this month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline the difference between profit and cash.
    Answer: Profit is the surplus of revenue over costs shown in the income statement, while cash is the actual money available in the bank to pay bills; a business can be profitable yet run out of cash [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Profit = revenue minus costs, shown in the income statement; Cash = money actually available; a profitable firm can still lack cash

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why profit and cash differ for Garrow Fresh Fish Ltd.
    Answer: First, sales on credit are booked as revenue before cash arrives [k]. Garrow's profit of $320,000 includes sales the income statement counts even though debtors already stand at $640,000, far above the $85,000 cash at bank [app]. Second, fish is bought, processed and delivered before customers pay [k]. Cash leaves the bank for suppliers and wages weeks before receipts arrive, and the $900,000 contract on 90-day terms would add about $225,000 of unpaid invoices at any time [app].
    Keywords: $320,000, $640,000, $85,000, $900,000, 90 days, $3.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Credit sales are recorded as revenue before cash arrives; Payments to suppliers and wages leave before customer receipts arrive | application_max_2: Reference to profit $320,000 vs debtors $640,000 vs cash $85,000; Reference to $900,000 contract at 90 days adding about $225,000 of unpaid invoices

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks to Garrow of accepting the 90-day payment terms.
    Answer: First, 90-day terms would strain working capital [k]. The contract adds about $225,000 of unpaid invoices, more than two and a half times the cash at bank of $85,000, while fish suppliers still need paying, so Garrow may need an overdraft whose interest eats into the $320,000 profit [app]. Sustained strain could force Garrow to delay its own payments and damage supplier trust [an]. Second, dependence on one dominant customer is risky [k]. Regional Stores Group demands 90-day payment plus a 4% price cut worth $36,000 a year, and an exclusive 2-year deal would concentrate Garrow's sales on a single buyer [app]. If that customer delisted Garrow or paid late, the $900,000 revenue stream could weaken suddenly, endangering the 37 jobs and margins across the wider business [an].
    Keywords: $225,000, $85,000, $320,000, $640,000, $36,000, 2-year, 4%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Working capital and cash-flow strain; Dependence on one dominant customer | application_max_2: Reference to about $225,000 added invoices vs $85,000 cash; $640,000 existing debtors; $320,000 profit; Reference to 4% cut worth $36,000 a year; exclusive 2-year deal; $900,000 revenue | analysis_max_2: Chain from cash strain to overdraft costs and delayed payments; Chain from customer concentration to sudden revenue risk and job losses

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Garrow Fresh Fish Ltd should accept the Regional Stores Group contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting would secure $900,000 a year of revenue for two years, a quarter of last year's $3.6 million, and guarantee shelf space in Regional Stores Group's outlets [k]. The 4% price cut costs $36,000 a year, but the exclusive deal should still lift total revenue and use of the 37 staff more fully, and repeat regional exposure builds the brand [app]. Steady two-year demand would support investment in packing and cold storage, widening Garrow's margin on all its sales [an]. However, 90-day terms add about $225,000 of unpaid invoices on top of existing debtors of $640,000, against cash of just $85,000 [k]. Accepting as drafted could leave Garrow cash-negative within months, unable to pay fish suppliers and risking the credit it needs to trade [app]. Contribution margins would also be capped for two years with no room to reprice [an]. Overall, I think Garrow should accept the contract only if the 90-day terms are renegotiated to 60 days or backed by a bank overdraft [eval]. At 90 days unamended the cash strain outweighs the revenue gain, but with credit secured the $36,000 concession is easily outweighed by two years of guaranteed demand [eval].
    Keywords: $900,000, $3.6 million, $36,000, $225,000, $640,000, $85,000, 2-year, 37 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Secures $900,000 a year for two years; guaranteed outlets; Adds about $225,000 of invoices on $640,000 of debtors against $85,000 cash | application_max_2: Reference to the 4% cut worth $36,000 a year; revenue equal to a quarter of $3.6 million; Reference to 37 staff, $640,000 debtors and $85,000 cash | analysis_max_2: Chain from steady demand to investment and wider margins; Chain from 90-day terms to cash-negative trading and credit risk | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (accept only with 60-day terms or an overdraft); Weighs both options with stem figures

--- STEM ---
Amberfield Fabrics Plc is listed on the Country X Stock Exchange and weaves shirting and suiting fabrics for fashion retailers from its Redmile mill, employing 480 staff. To fund $3 million of new weaving machinery, the board plans a share issue, and under Country X rules the accounts must be published so investors can judge the offer fairly.

Option A is to publish full accounts with a detailed prospectus, showing revenue of $12 million, profit of $1.5 million, a gross profit margin of 34% and a dividend of 5c per share on the 25 million shares in issue. Option B is to publish only the minimum required audited statements, keeping margin detail and customer information confidential, but risking a weak response from investors.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by 'published accounts'.
    Answer: Published accounts are the financial statements a limited company must make publicly available, showing its performance and financial position, so shareholders, lenders, employees, customers and the government can assess them [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Financial statements a limited company must make publicly available; Used by shareholders, lenders, employees, customers and the government

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Amberfield Fabrics Plc's accounts are published.
    Answer: First, publication is a legal requirement for a listed company [k]. Under Country X rules, a Plc on the Stock Exchange raising $3 million through a share issue must publish audited accounts so the offer is transparent to investors [app]. Second, publication lets stakeholders assess the business [k]. Investors can see revenue of $12 million, profit of $1.5 million, a 34% gross profit margin and a 5c dividend on 25 million shares ($1.25 million), judging whether the new machinery justifies subscribing [app].
    Keywords: $3 million, $12 million, $1.5 million, 34%, 5c, 25 million shares, share issue
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Legal requirement for a listed Plc; Transparency so stakeholders can assess the business | application_max_2: Reference to $3 million share issue and Country X Stock Exchange rules; Reference to revenue $12 million, profit $1.5 million, 34% margin, 5c on 25 million shares = $1.25 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two stakeholders, other than shareholders, who use Amberfield Fabrics Plc's published accounts and why.
    Answer: First, employees use published accounts to judge job security and pay prospects [k]. With 480 staff at the Redmile mill and profit of $1.5 million on revenue of $12 million, the workforce can see the business is profitable and funded for new machinery, shaping wage negotiations and retention of skilled weavers [app]. If the accounts instead showed falling profit, staff could anticipate restructuring and plan accordingly [an]. Second, the government uses published accounts to assess tax and approve support [k]. Corporation tax on the $1.5 million profit is computed from these figures, and agencies licensing the machinery or granting support rely on the same audited numbers [app]. Accurate reporting funds public services and keeps Amberfield compliant, avoiding penalties and reputational damage [an].
    Keywords: 480 staff, Redmile mill, $1.5 million, $12 million, new weaving machinery, published
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Employees use them to judge job security and pay; Government uses them to assess tax and approve grants or licences | application_max_2: Reference to 480 staff at the Redmile mill; profit $1.5 million on revenue of $12 million; Reference to corporation tax computed on $1.5 million profit and machinery licensing | analysis_max_2: Chain from visible profit to wage negotiations and retention; Chain from accurate reporting to compliance, public revenue and avoiding penalties

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Amberfield Fabrics Plc should publish full accounts as part of the share issue prospectus? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Publishing full accounts gives investors the evidence to subscribe for the $3 million issue [k]. Transparent figures, showing revenue of $12 million, profit of $1.5 million, a gross profit margin of 34% and a 5c dividend on 25 million shares worth $1.25 million, build trust, improving uptake and reducing the risk the issue fails [app]. Strong disclosure could attract institutional investors, securing the weaving machinery sooner and lifting output, sales and the share price [an]. However, full disclosure exposes margins and cost structures to rivals [k]. Rivals could undercut Amberfield or poach customers once the 34% margin and $1.5 million profit are public, and customers may press for lower prices on that evidence [app]. The competitive damage could exceed the financing benefit, making Option B's minimum publication tempting despite a weaker investor response [an]. Overall, I think Amberfield should publish the full accounts [eval]. As a listed Plc it already publishes audited statements, and the $3 million issue needs investor confidence; margins on shirting fabrics are hard to hide in a public offer anyway, and the certainty of funding outweighs the extra visibility, though customer lists should stay confidential [eval].
    Keywords: $3 million, $12 million, $1.5 million, 34%, 5c, share issue, 25 million shares, Option B
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Full accounts give investors evidence and build trust; Full disclosure exposes margins and cost structures to rivals | application_max_2: Reference to revenue $12 million, profit $1.5 million, 34% margin, 5c dividend on 25 million shares ($1.25 million); Reference to rivals or customers using published margins to undercut or renegotiate | analysis_max_2: Chain from disclosure to investor uptake to secured machinery and growth; Chain from visibility to price pressure and competitive damage | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to publish in full; Weighs both options with stem figures

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U5_SET_100
UNIT: Unit 5: Financial Information and Decisions
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Carrow Insulation Plc manufactures insulation boards for commercial buildings across Country X. Daljit Singh owns 40,000 of its 30 million shares. The accounts show revenue of $14 million, $15 million and $15.5 million over the last three years, while profit fell from $2.4 million to $1.9 million and then $1.2 million. ROCE fell from 17% to 12% and then 8%, and the dividend has been cut from 6c to 2c per share.

The current ratio held steady at 1.6 and gross profit margin slipped from 33% to 31% and then 24%. Daljit is deciding whether to sell his shares now, when they trade well below last year's price, or hold and hope the new chief executive's turnaround plan, including plant modernisation and tighter cost control, restores returns.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'acid test ratio'.
    Answer: The acid test ratio is a liquidity ratio measuring whether a business can pay its short-term debts from its most liquid assets, calculated as current assets minus inventories, divided by current liabilities [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A liquidity ratio using the most liquid assets; Formula: (current assets minus inventories) divided by current liabilities

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Daljit Singh would compare Carrow Insulation Plc's accounts over three years before deciding to sell.
    Answer: First, one year can flatter or alarm [k]. Profit of $1.2 million alone looks merely weak, but set against $2.4 million and $1.9 million in prior years it confirms a steady decline, with ROCE falling from 17% to 12% and then 8% over the same period [app]. Second, trends show whether the dividend is sustainable [k]. The dividend has been cut from 6c to 2c per share, so Daljit's income on 40,000 shares has fallen from $2,400 to $800 a year, and the three-year figures reveal whether this is a temporary dip or a structural decline [app].
    Keywords: $2.4 million, $1.9 million, $1.2 million, 17%, 12%, 8%, 6c, 2c
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A single year can mislead; the trend shows direction; Reveals whether the dividend is sustainable | application_max_2: Reference to profit $2.4 million to $1.9 million to $1.2 million; ROCE 17% to 12% to 8%; Reference to dividend cut from 6c to 2c; income falling from $2,400 to $800 on 40,000 shares

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of using ROCE alone to judge Carrow Insulation Plc's performance.
    Answer: First, ROCE ignores liquidity completely [k]. Carrow's current ratio held at 1.6 across all three years, genuinely stable, but ROCE of 8% says nothing about whether cash or debtors are under strain underneath that figure [app]. A shareholder judging by ROCE alone could miss early warning signs that a steady 1.6 can still conceal [an]. Second, ROCE does not show where the decline comes from [k]. Revenue actually grew from $14 million to $15.5 million, yet the gross profit margin slid from 33% to 24%, growth at worse pricing rather than weak demand [app]. Blind to margin detail, ROCE could mislabel Carrow's problem as a market dip rather than a cost or pricing failure, misleading sell decisions [an].
    Keywords: 1.6, 8%, $14 million, $15.5 million, 33%, 24%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ROCE ignores liquidity (current ratio steady at 1.6); ROCE hides the source of decline (margin compression vs demand) | application_max_2: Reference to the current ratio holding at 1.6 in all three years and ROCE of 8%; Reference to revenue rising $14 million to $15.5 million while gross profit margin slid 33% to 24% | analysis_max_2: Chain from a ROCE-only view to missed liquidity stress; Chain from margin detail to a misdiagnosed problem

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Daljit Singh should sell his 40,000 shares? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Selling now crystallises the reality of a three-year slide: profit fell from $2.4 million to $1.9 million and then $1.2 million, ROCE from 17% to 8%, and the dividend from 6c to 2c, cutting Daljit's income from $2,400 to $800 a year [k]. Waiting for the turnaround risks further losses if plant modernisation and cost control underperform, and the share price already trades well below last year's level [app]. Selling frees cash to redeploy into higher-yielding investments while the margin trend of 33% to 24% remains unproven [an]. However, holding has merit [k]. Carrow's current ratio has stayed at 1.6 for three years and revenue grew from $14 million to $15.5 million, showing demand is intact under a new chief executive with a modernisation plan [app]. If he restores the gross profit margin from 24% towards 33%, ROCE could recover towards double digits and the share price would reward patient holders [an]. Overall, I think Daljit should sell his 40,000 shares [eval]. Three consecutive years of falling profit, ROCE and dividend, with no turnaround evidence yet delivered, make holding speculation rather than investment; he can re-enter if the plan shows two quarters of margin recovery, but discipline says sell now at the current weak price [eval].
    Keywords: 40,000, $2.4 million, $1.2 million, 17%, 8%, 6c, 2c, $15.5 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Selling crystallises losses and cuts risk exposure; Holding has merit if the turnaround delivers | application_max_2: Reference to profit $2.4 million to $1.9 million to $1.2 million; ROCE 17% to 8%; dividend 6c to 2c; income $2,400 to $800; Reference to current ratio steady at 1.6, revenue $14 million to $15.5 million and margin 33% to 24% | analysis_max_2: Chain from an unproven margin trend to a weak share price; Chain from a successful turnaround to recovering ROCE and price | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to sell; Weighs both options with stem figures

Maya and Reuben are launching Copperfinch Roastery, a partnership planning to open a coffee roasting and tasting room in Country X. To launch, the business needs a $48,000 roasting machine, a $15,000 lease deposit and refurbishment for the shop, $7,000 of green coffee beans and $9,000 per month of working capital for the first 3 months before sales become steady.

In total, the start-up requires $97,000. Maya has $40,000 of owners' savings and Reuben has $35,000, giving $75,000 together. Reuben also owns an unused delivery van worth $25,000 that he could sell. Because the business is new it has no retained profit to use, so the partners must decide which internal sources of finance to rely on and whether to sell the van.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'start-up capital'.
    Answer: Start-up capital is the finance needed to set up and launch a new business, covering initial costs such as equipment, premises and stock before any sales revenue is received [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: finance needed to set up / launch a new business; covers initial costs before revenue is received

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Copperfinch Roastery needs $97,000 of start-up capital.
    Answer: Reason 1: To buy equipment and premises [k], including the $48,000 roasting machine and the $15,000 lease deposit and refurbishment [app]. Reason 2: To cover running costs before sales arrive [k], such as $9,000 per month of working capital for the first 3 months [app].
    Keywords: $48,000, $15,000, $9,000, roasting machine, working capital, $97,000, $7,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: capital needed to buy equipment/premises; capital needed to cover costs before revenue arrives | application_max_2: $48,000 roasting machine / $15,000 lease deposit; $9,000 per month working capital for the first 3 months

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using owners' savings to finance the start-up.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Owners' savings are immediately available [k], so Maya and Reuben can contribute $75,000 without waiting for outside lenders [app], letting the roastery open on schedule [an]. Benefit 2: Using savings carries no interest [k], so none of the $9,000 monthly working capital is absorbed by loan repayments [app], leaving more cash free for the first months of trading [an].
    Keywords: owners' savings, $75,000, Maya and Reuben, $9,000, roastery, internal sources
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: savings immediately available / no approval needed; no interest or repayment obligation | application_max_2: Maya and Reuben contribute $75,000; no repayments eating into the $9,000 monthly working capital | analysis_max_2: lets the roastery open on schedule; more cash free for the first months of trading

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Copperfinch Roastery should sell Reuben's delivery van to raise the remaining start-up capital? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Selling the van would raise $25,000 [k], covering the $22,000 gap between the $75,000 of owners' savings and the $97,000 required [app], so the partners keep the launch fully funded with internal sources [an]. However, the van may be needed once deliveries of beans and cafe supplies begin [k], and selling it now would remove a useful asset before the roastery proves its sales [app], leaving the business without transport just as it starts trading [an]. Overall, the van should be sold [eval], because it is unused and closes the gap exactly with $3,000 to spare, keeping the opening plan intact [eval].
    Keywords: $25,000, $75,000, $97,000, delivery van, start-up, retained profit, internal sources
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sale of unused asset raises internal finance; losing a still-useful asset before trading starts | application_max_2: $25,000 from the van versus the $22,000 gap; $75,000 of owners' savings against the $97,000 requirement | analysis_max_2: launch stays fully funded with internal sources; business loses transport just as it begins trading | evaluation_max_2: weighs sale proceeds against losing transport capacity; justified recommendation with spare $3,000 after covering the gap

Foulsham Joinery is a partnership owned by Elena and Marcus that has made bespoke oak furniture in Country X for 11 years. The firm employs 24 craftspeople making dining tables, wardrobes and cabinets, and last year generated sales revenue of $620,000. After all expenses, the partnership retained a profit of $60,000 for reinvestment. Cabinet orders have doubled this year, and the partners also hope to keep weekly wages stable.

Orders now exceed workshop capacity, so the partners want $110,000 of capital expenditure on an automated spray-finishing machine that would cut finishing time and reduce waste.     Question: Define 'capital expenditure'.
    Answer: Capital expenditure is money spent on non-current assets such as machinery, vehicles or premises that the business will use for more than one year [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: spending on non-current assets; assets used for more than one year

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Foulsham Joinery wants to invest $110,000 of capital expenditure in the spray-finishing machine.
    Answer: Reason 1: To increase efficiency [k], because the automated spray-finishing machine would cut finishing time and reduce waste on bespoke oak furniture [app]. Reason 2: To meet rising demand [k], since cabinet orders have doubled this year and orders now exceed workshop capacity [app].
    Keywords: automated spray-finishing machine, bespoke oak furniture, $110,000, workshop capacity, $620,000, capital expenditure, 24 craftspeople
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increased efficiency / faster production; ability to meet rising demand / take on more orders | application_max_2: machine cuts finishing time and reduces waste on oak furniture; cabinet orders doubled and now exceed workshop capacity

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of Foulsham Joinery using retained profit to fund the machine.
    Answer: Benefit 1: It carries no interest or repayment obligation [k], so the $60,000 reinvests money the firm itself earned, protecting monthly cash [app], which keeps the workshop running smoothly [an]. Benefit 2: It is immediately available [k], already in hand after last year's $620,000 revenue [app], letting the partners order the machine without outside approval [an].
    Keywords: retained profit, $60,000, $620,000, internal finance, spray-finishing machine, $110,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: no interest or repayments; immediately available internal finance | application_max_2: the $60,000 retained profit reinvested; in hand after the $620,000 revenue year | analysis_max_2: protects monthly cash flow / steady workshop running; machine can be ordered without outside approval

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Foulsham Joinery should fund the $110,000 spray-finishing machine mainly from retained profit rather than owners' savings? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Retained profit is long-term internal finance with no repayment obligation [k], so using the $60,000 to help fund the $110,000 machine reinvests money the business earned itself [app], strengthening the partnership without adding financial pressure [an]. However, owners' savings of $50,000 are also immediately available and carry no interest [k], so together the two sources exactly cover the $110,000 [app], letting the partners decide the split without any shortfall [an]. Overall, retained profit should be used as the main source [eval], because the $60,000 came from the firm's own $620,000 revenue and keeps personal risk low, with the $50,000 savings topping up the balance [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit is long-term internal finance with no repayment; owners' savings equally interest-free and available | application_max_2: $60,000 retained profit plus $50,000 savings equals $110,000; the $60,000 came from the firm's $620,000 revenue | analysis_max_2: strengthens the firm without financial pressure; split can be decided freely with no shortfall | evaluation_max_2: weighs reinvesting business earnings against committing personal funds; justified recommendation to use retained profit with savings top-up

--- STEM ---
Harriet Sloane runs Fernhill Orchard Farm, a sole trader growing apples and pears in Country X for 14 years. The farm employs 6 permanent workers and 20 seasonal pickers. Annual revenue is $240,000, but about 70% arrives between October and December after the harvest, while wages, fertiliser and packaging of $38,000 fall due between April and September. Most fruit is sold through supermarkets and a wholesale market in the nearest city.

Current assets total $95,000 against current liabilities of $60,000, leaving working capital of $35,000. From last year the farm has retained profit of $22,000, and Harriet has $16,000 of personal savings. She also owns an old tractor worth $14,000 that sees little use and prefers internal sources of finance to outside borrowing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'working capital'.
    Answer: Working capital is the money available to pay the day-to-day running of a business, calculated as current assets minus current liabilities [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: money for day-to-day running of the business; current assets minus current liabilities

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Fernhill Orchard Farm faces working capital pressure before the harvest.
    Answer: Reason 1: Costs fall due before revenue arrives [k], because wages, fertiliser and packaging of $38,000 are due between April and September [app]. Reason 2: Income is uneven across the year [k], with about 70% of the $240,000 annual revenue arriving between October and December [app].
    Keywords: $38,000, April and September, 70%, $240,000, October and December, working capital
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: costs due before revenue arrives; seasonal / uneven income pattern | application_max_2: $38,000 of wages, fertiliser and packaging due April to September; 70% of $240,000 revenue arriving October to December

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the farm using retained profit to ease its working capital need.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Retained profit is free and flexible internal finance [k], so the $22,000 can pay wages and suppliers without interest [app], preserving precious cash in the low-income months [an]. Benefit 2: It carries no repayment deadline [k], unlike an outside loan, so Harriet can rebuild reserves when the October and December income arrives [app], easing stress until the harvest revenue flows in [an].
    Keywords: retained profit, $22,000, internal sources of finance, October and December, working capital
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit is free / flexible internal finance; no repayment deadline attached | application_max_2: $22,000 used to pay wages and suppliers without interest; reserves rebuilt when October and December income arrives | analysis_max_2: preserves cash in the low-income months; eases stress until harvest revenue flows in

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fernhill Orchard Farm should sell the old tractor rather than use retained profit to cover its pre-harvest working capital need? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Selling the old tractor would raise $14,000 [k], turning an unused asset into cash for the $38,000 of pre-harvest costs [app], and would leave the $22,000 retained profit untouched for emergencies [an]. However, the tractor could still serve as a back-up during the busy picking season [k], and selling it now might force hire charges if the main tractor fails [app], cancelling out any gain [an]. Overall, the farm should use the retained profit first [eval], keeping the tractor as a working back-up, and sell it only if harvest revenue disappoints [eval].
    Keywords: $14,000, old tractor, $38,000, $22,000, retained profit, working capital, $16,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sale of unused asset raises internal finance; retained profit keeps an asset back-up available | application_max_2: $14,000 from the tractor against $38,000 of pre-harvest costs; selling now risks hire charges if the main tractor fails | analysis_max_2: preserves $22,000 retained profit for emergencies; loss of the back-up tractor could cancel the gain | evaluation_max_2: weighs asset sale against keeping the tractor back-up; justified recommendation to use retained profit first with sale as fallback

--- STEM ---
Denise Okafor owns Saltwell Laundry Co, a sole trader providing commercial laundry services to hotels and guesthouses in Country X. Operating for 8 years, the business employs 16 staff who collect and deliver laundry by van. Last year it earned sales revenue of $410,000 and recorded retained profit of $50,000. Hotels are charged a weekly collection fee for each laundry round. Guesthouse contracts are typically agreed for 12 months.

To keep up with demand, Denise must replace the delivery van at a cost of $68,000, which is capital expenditure. The old van could be sold for $18,000, and she has $25,000 of personal savings. Denise prefers internal finance where possible and is deciding how to combine retained profit and the old van sale to fund the $68,000 purchase.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'retained profit'.
    Answer: Retained profit is the profit a business keeps after paying all costs, expenses and owner drawings, held back for reinvestment as internal finance rather than withdrawn or distributed [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: profit kept after costs, expenses and drawings; held back / reinvested as internal finance

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why replacing the delivery van is capital expenditure rather than a day-to-day cost.
    Answer: Reason 1: The van is a long-term asset [k], used for several years to collect and deliver laundry for hotels and guesthouses [app]. Reason 2: It is a large one-off purchase [k], costing $68,000 rather than a regular expense such as wages [app].
    Keywords: delivery van, $68,000, hotels and guesthouses, capital expenditure, collect and deliver, $410,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: long-term asset used for more than one year; large one-off non-current asset purchase | application_max_2: van used for several years serving hotels and guesthouses; $68,000 one-off cost rather than regular wages

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using retained profit as the main source of finance for the van.
    Answer: Benefit 1: No interest or repayments are required [k], so using the $50,000 avoids adding loan repayments to monthly outgoings [app], protecting short-term cash flow [an]. Benefit 2: The decision can be made quickly by one person [k], since the $50,000 is already in hand after a $410,000 revenue year [app], so the van can be replaced without delay [an].
    Keywords: retained profit, $50,000, $410,000, internal finance, $68,000, delivery van
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: no interest or repayments required; decision can be made quickly / funds already in hand | application_max_2: $50,000 used directly without extra outgoings; $50,000 already in hand after the $410,000 revenue year | analysis_max_2: protects short-term cash flow; van replaced without delay

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Saltwell Laundry Co should sell its old van and use retained profit to fund the $68,000 replacement, rather than keep the old van and use owners' savings? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Selling the old van raises $18,000 [k], and together with the $50,000 retained profit it exactly funds the $68,000 replacement [app], leaving Denise's $25,000 savings untouched as a personal safety net [an]. However, the old van could remain useful as a back-up for busy hotel seasons [k], and using owners' savings instead would preserve two vehicles for collections and deliveries [app], at the cost of reducing Denise's personal reserves [an]. Overall, Saltwell Laundry Co should sell the old van and use the retained profit [eval], because the $50,000 plus the $18,000 sale is an exact fit for the $68,000 cost and keeps business and personal money separate [eval].
    Keywords: old van, $18,000, $50,000, $68,000, $25,000, retained profit, internal finance
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: sale of existing asset raises internal finance; old asset can remain as a back-up | application_max_2: $18,000 sale plus $50,000 retained profit exactly covers $68,000; owners' savings would preserve two vehicles for rounds | analysis_max_2: $25,000 savings preserved as a personal safety net; reducing personal reserves weakens the owner's position | evaluation_max_2: weighs exact funding fit against keeping a back-up vehicle; justified recommendation with clear personal/business separation
