--- STEM ---
Priya Raman owns Marram Hair & Beauty Studio, a hair and beauty salon in Country X trading for 6 years with 8 staff. The salon serves mainly walk-in clients and generates $185,000 of annual revenue. It offers cuts, colour treatments, manicures and facials. Monthly bills for rent, wages, utilities and products total about $11,000, and the salon holds $6,000 of stock.

A slow winter has left the studio with current assets of $28,000 and current liabilities of $19,000, giving working capital of $9,000. Three quiet months could see bills outrun takings. Last year the salon recorded retained profit of $8,500, and Priya has $10,000 of owners' savings. She wants internal sources of finance only and is choosing between the two for the winter months ahead.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by 'internal source of finance'.
    Answer: An internal source of finance is money raised from within the business itself, such as retained profit, owners' savings or proceeds from selling assets, rather than from outside investors or lenders [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: money raised from within the business itself; examples such as retained profit, owners' savings, asset sales

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the studio needs working capital during the winter months.
    Answer: Reason 1: To pay monthly bills on time [k], including rent, wages, utilities and products costing about $11,000 a month [app]. Reason 2: To keep services stocked [k], holding $6,000 of products for cuts, colour treatments, manicures and facials [app].
    Keywords: $11,000, $6,000, working capital, walk-in, $185,000, winter months, $9,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: to pay day-to-day bills on time; to hold stock for services | application_max_2: $11,000 a month for rent, wages, utilities and products; $6,000 of stock supporting cuts, colour, manicures and facials

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of using retained profit instead of owners' savings for the winter months.
    Answer: Advantage 1: It is the business's own reinvested money [k], so the $8,500 is available without Priya touching her $10,000 owners' savings [app], keeping business and personal money separate [an]. Advantage 2: It carries no repayment obligation [k], so the salon adds nothing to future outgoings [app], easing pressure until takings recover [an].
    Keywords: retained profit, $8,500, $10,000, owners' savings, internal sources of finance, $9,000, winter months
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: business's own reinvested money; no repayment obligation / no added outgoings | application_max_2: $8,500 available without touching Priya's $10,000 savings; nothing added to future outgoings for the winter | analysis_max_2: keeps business and personal money separate; eases pressure until takings recover

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marram Hair & Beauty Studio should use retained profit or owners' savings to fund its winter working capital need? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Retained profit of $8,500 covers most of the $9,000 gap [k], and using it first keeps Priya's $10,000 owners' savings intact [app], preserving a personal safety net for emergencies [an]. However, leaning only on $8,500 would empty the salon's profit reserve [k], whereas adding savings would bridge the small $500 difference wholly [app], which may be sensible if winter takings stay weak [an]. Overall, the studio should use retained profit first [eval], topping up with owners' savings only if the shortfall persists after takings recover [eval].
    Keywords: retained profit, $8,500, $9,000, $10,000, owners' savings, working capital, winter months
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit usable first as internal finance; drawing only retained profit empties the profit reserve | application_max_2: $8,500 against the $9,000 working capital gap; $10,000 owners' savings would bridge the $500 difference | analysis_max_2: preserves a personal safety net for emergencies; topping up may be sensible if winter takings stay weak | evaluation_max_2: weighs using business profit reserve against personal savings; justified recommendation to use retained profit with conditional top-up

In total the launch requires $40,000. Jack has $22,000 of savings and Lily has $13,000, totalling $35,000. Jack also owns an unused motorbike valued at $6,000.     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: personal money invested by the owners; into their own business for start-up or running costs

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Fernwell Pet Grooming needs start-up capital before it can begin trading.
    Answer: Reason 1: To buy the equipment needed to operate [k], including the $28,000 van conversion with bathing and drying equipment [app]. Reason 2: To cover costs incurred before revenue arrives [k], such as $2,000 of insurance and licences and $4,000 of working capital for the first 2 months [app].
    Keywords: start-up, $28,000, van conversion, $2,000, $4,000, working capital, $40,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: capital to buy equipment/premises to operate; capital to cover costs before revenue arrives | application_max_2: $28,000 van conversion with bathing and drying equipment; $2,000 insurance and licences plus $4,000 working capital

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the partners selling the motorbike to complete the funding.

Benefit 2: The motorbike is unused [k], so turning it into cash has no impact on grooming work [app], releasing money exactly when the first 2 months of working capital are needed [an].
    Keywords: motorbike, $6,000, $5,000, $35,000, $40,000, working capital, $22,000

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fernwell Pet Grooming should sell the motorbike rather than scale back the van conversion to fund the launch? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Selling the motorbike raises $6,000 [k], comfortably covering the $5,000 shortfall on the $40,000 launch [app], so the $28,000 van conversion can open fully equipped and win customers from day one [an]. However, Jack may rely on the motorbike for personal travel [k], and scaling back the conversion by about $5,000 would still leave a working grooming van [app], though with reduced capacity and a weaker first impression [an]. Overall, the partners should sell the motorbike [eval], because it is unused and preserves the professional conversion that the whole mobile business depends on [eval].
    Keywords: motorbike, $6,000, $5,000, $28,000, van conversion, $40,000, internal finance
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: selling an unused asset raises internal finance; scaling back reduces capacity/quality but keeps the asset | application_max_2: $6,000 sale covers the $5,000 shortfall on $40,000; scaling back leaves a working but reduced conversion | analysis_max_2: conversion opens fully equipped to win customers; reduced capacity weakens first impressions | evaluation_max_2: weighs selling personal transport against degrading the offer; justified recommendation that the unused motorbike should be sold

--- STEM ---
Oxenford Wholesale Grocers is a partnership supplying independent shops and cafes across Country X for 12 years. The firm employs 28 workers and buys food stock in bulk for $150,000 each month, paying suppliers within 30 days while customers often pay after 45 days. Weekly deliveries go to over 60 independent shops and cafes. Last year it earned revenue of $2,400,000 and retained profit of $95,000.

This has created a working capital gap of about $75,000. Current assets total $420,000 against current liabilities of $345,000, leaving working capital of $75,000. Storing stock is essential because bulk buying lowers unit costs. The firm owns an empty warehouse unit valued at $210,000 but is reluctant to sell. The partners want internal finance only and are weighing retained profit against selling the unit.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two internal sources of finance the partnership could use.
    Answer: Retained profit from last year's earnings [1]. Proceeds from selling existing assets, such as the empty warehouse unit [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit identified as internal source; sale of existing assets identified as internal source

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Oxenford Wholesale Grocers faces a working capital gap.
    Answer: Reason 1: It pays suppliers before customers pay [k], because suppliers require payment within 30 days while customers often pay after 45 days [app]. Reason 2: It buys stock in bulk each month [k], spending $150,000 on food stock every month [app].
    Keywords: 30 days, 45 days, $150,000, working capital, $75,000, bulk
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: suppliers paid before customers pay; bulk monthly stock purchases tie up cash | application_max_2: 30-day supplier terms versus 45-day customer payments; $150,000 monthly food stock purchases

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using the retained profit rather than selling the warehouse unit.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The $95,000 retained profit comfortably covers the $75,000 working capital gap [k], so the shortfall is met in one step [app], keeping the warehouse available for future expansion [an]. Benefit 2: Selling the unit would sacrifice a long-term asset [k], because rising revenue of $2,400,000 may soon need more storage space [app], whereas retained profit replenishes from future earnings [an].
    Keywords: $95,000, $75,000, warehouse unit, retained profit, $2,400,000, $210,000, working capital
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit can cover the gap directly; selling sacrifices a long-term asset | application_max_2: $95,000 covers the $75,000 working capital gap; $2,400,000 rising revenue may soon need more storage | analysis_max_2: warehouse kept available for future expansion; retained profit replenishes from future earnings

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Oxenford Wholesale Grocers should use retained profit rather than sell the empty warehouse unit to fund its working capital need? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Using retained profit of $95,000 avoids selling the $210,000 warehouse unit [k], fully covering the $75,000 working capital gap in a single step [app], and keeps a strategic asset for future growth and extra storage [an]. However, the $95,000 is finite, and holding it back leaves nothing in reserve if a quiet quarter cuts revenue [k], while selling the unit now would raise cash far beyond the gap [app], creating a buffer even if suppliers tighten the 30-day terms [an]. Overall, the partnership should use retained profit [eval], because the working capital need is recurring and temporary and is best met from earnings rather than by selling a long-term asset [eval].
    Keywords: retained profit, $95,000, $210,000, $75,000, warehouse unit, 30 days, internal finance
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit preserves the $210,000 warehouse asset; selling the unit raises a one-off large cash sum | application_max_2: $95,000 covers the $75,000 gap in one step; sale raises far beyond the gap as a buffer against tighter 30-day terms | analysis_max_2: strategic asset kept for future growth and storage; sale buffer protects against tighter supplier credit | evaluation_max_2: weighs preserving the asset against one-off cash buffer; justified recommendation to use retained profit for a recurring need

--- STEM ---
Gregory Nolan owns Hartley Vale Dairy Farm, a sole trader with 160 dairy cows in Country X run for 15 years. The farm employs 11 workers and produces 1,900,000 litres of milk a year, generating revenue of $730,000. Milk is supplied daily to a regional bottling plant and two cheese makers. Gregory retained a profit of $34,000 this year.

The farm needs a new $58,000 bulk milk cooler, which is capital expenditure, because the old cooler breaks down regularly. The old cooler could be sold for $8,000, and the farm owns an old tractor valued at $24,000 that sees little use. The new cooler arrives with a 5-year warranty. Gregory has $10,000 of personal savings and prefers internal finance, combining retained profit, the cooler sale and the tractor sale as needed.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'sale of existing assets'.
    Answer: Sale of existing assets is selling unwanted business assets, such as old machinery or vehicles, to raise cash that can be reinvested, and it is an internal source of finance [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: selling unwanted business assets; cash raised is reinvested as internal finance

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the bulk milk cooler is capital expenditure rather than a day-to-day cost.
    Answer: Reason 1: It is a long-term asset [k], used to chill the farm's 1,900,000 litres of milk for years [app]. Reason 2: It is a large one-off purchase [k], costing $58,000 rather than a regular expense like feed or wages [app].
    Keywords: bulk milk cooler, $58,000, capital expenditure, 1,900,000 litres, 160 dairy cows, $730,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: long-term asset used for more than one year; large one-off non-current asset purchase | application_max_2: cooler used for years on 1,900,000 litres of milk; $58,000 one-off cost rather than feed or wages

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of funding the cooler using retained profit and asset sales rather than owners' savings.
    Answer: Benefit 1: It keeps Gregory's $10,000 personal savings intact [k], and the $34,000 retained profit plus the $8,000 cooler sale raise $42,000 with no personal risk [app], leaving savings untouched for family emergencies [an]. Benefit 2: It turns idle assets into productive equipment [k], because the old cooler and the old tractor, valued at $8,000 and $24,000, are no longer needed [app], so money tied up in them works harder as a new cooler [an].
    Keywords: retained profit, $34,000, $8,000, $24,000, $10,000, bulk milk cooler, $58,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: keeps personal savings intact; converts idle assets into productive equipment | application_max_2: $34,000 retained profit plus $8,000 cooler sale raises $42,000; old cooler and old tractor valued at $8,000 and $24,000 | analysis_max_2: personal savings remain for family emergencies; money tied up in idle assets works harder as a new cooler

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hartley Vale Dairy Farm should sell the old tractor to help fund the new bulk milk cooler? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Selling the old tractor would raise $24,000 [k], and together with the $34,000 retained profit and the $8,000 cooler sale it would raise $66,000, exceeding the $58,000 cost [app], leaving the cooler fully funded by internal finance [an]. However, the tractor may still be needed at busy calving and haymaking times [k], and losing it could force the farm to hire machinery at short notice [app], which could cost more than the $24,000 raised [an]. Overall, the farm should sell the old tractor [eval], because it sees little use and the internal funds raised would exceed the $58,000 price with $8,000 to spare [eval].
    Keywords: old tractor, $24,000, $34,000, $8,000, $58,000, retained profit, internal finance
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: selling unused asset raises $24,000 internal finance; losing the tractor may force machinery hire | application_max_2: $24,000 plus $34,000 retained profit plus $8,000 cooler sale exceeds $58,000; hire costs at calving and haymaking could exceed $24,000 | analysis_max_2: cooler fully funded by internal finance; short-notice hire could be more expensive than the sale gain | evaluation_max_2: weighs raising internal finance against losing a back-up tractor; justified recommendation with $8,000 surplus after funding the cooler

--- STEM ---
Tanswell Design Studio Ltd is a private limited company in Country X operating for 5 years with 12 employees producing branding and packaging designs. The studio serves food producers and drink importers across the region. Annual revenue is $540,000, and the studio has retained profit of $28,000. The directors want to buy six workstations and new software costing $36,000, which is capital expenditure with a 4-year life.

The directors must decide whether this long-term need should be met by long-term internal finance or by short-term finance. Two owners are willing to inject $12,000 of owners' savings as a quick top-up, and a separate short-term cash need of $9,000 may arise next month. Directors meet monthly to review cash. The studio prefers internal finance and will avoid outside borrowing for now.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'long-term finance'.
    Answer: Long-term finance is finance provided for more than one year, used to fund major purchases such as non-current assets or expansion, and is not expected to be repaid within the year [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: finance provided for more than one year; used for major purchases / not repaid within the year

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two differences between short-term and long-term finance.
    Answer: Difference 1: Long-term finance is provided for more than one year [k], suiting the 4-year life of the $36,000 workstations [app]. Difference 2: Short-term finance is repaid or used within a year [k], matching the $9,000 cash need the studio expects next month [app].
    Keywords: long-term, short-term, 4-year, $36,000, $9,000, workstations, capital expenditure
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: long-term finance provided for more than one year; short-term finance repaid or used within a year | application_max_2: 4-year life of the $36,000 workstations; $9,000 cash need expected next month

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of using retained profit as long-term finance for the workstations.
    Answer: Advantage 1: It is permanent finance with no repayment date [k], so the $28,000 comes from the studio's own $540,000 revenue year [app], strengthening the balance sheet without outside claims [an]. Advantage 2: It avoids sharing ownership [k], because no new shares are issued to raise the money [app], keeping control with the existing owners [an].
    Keywords: retained profit, $28,000, $540,000, long-term internal finance, workstations, $36,000, private limited company
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: permanent finance with no repayment date; no new shares issued / ownership unchanged | application_max_2: $28,000 comes from the studio's $540,000 revenue year; money raised without issuing shares in the Ltd | analysis_max_2: strengthens the balance sheet without outside claims; control retained by the existing owners

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tanswell Design Studio Ltd should use retained profit rather than owners' savings to fund the $36,000 of workstations? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Retained profit of $28,000 is long-term internal finance [k], so it matches the 4-year life of the $36,000 capital expenditure [app], avoiding pressure to repay within the year [an]. However, $28,000 leaves an $8,000 gap, and the owners' $12,000 of savings could cover it immediately [k], completing the purchase now without outside borrowing [app], keeping the studio on schedule [an]. Overall, the studio should use retained profit as the main source [eval], because matching long-term assets with long-term internal finance is sound, with the savings meeting only the $8,000 balance [eval].
    Keywords: retained profit, $28,000, $36,000, owners' savings, internal finance, 4-year, $12,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: retained profit is long-term internal finance; owners' savings can fill the gap immediately | application_max_2: $28,000 retained profit against the 4-year life of $36,000 of workstations; owners' $12,000 savings cover the $8,000 gap | analysis_max_2: no pressure to repay within the year; purchase completed on schedule without outside borrowing | evaluation_max_2: weighs matching long-term assets with long-term finance against instant savings; justified recommendation to use retained profit with savings covering the $8,000 balance

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why The Salted Plum Delicatessen needs sufficient working capital.

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of using retained profit as the main source of finance for the second store.

Benefit 2: It is controlled entirely by Colette [k], using profits from the $390,000 revenue year rather than outside approval [app], so the expansion proceeds on her terms [an].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: no interest or repayments required; owner retains full control of the finance | application_max_2: $70,000 reinvested without added monthly costs; profits from the $390,000 revenue year used rather than outside approval | analysis_max_2: existing shop's cash flow stays stable; expansion proceeds on Colette's own terms

  Qd [8 marks]

However, using $25,000 of savings would complete the funding immediately [k], while preserving the retained profit as a cushion for the new store's first months [app], a prudent move given the $15,000 overdraft at the existing shop [an]. --- STEM ---
Thornfen Grain Milling Ltd is a private limited company in Country X founded 7 years ago by brothers Daniel and Owen Pryce. It mills wheat and maize at its Riverside mill, employing 26 workers and generating annual revenue of $2.4 million. The brothers own all 200,000 ordinary shares and want to install a new high-capacity roller mill costing $600,000 to meet rising bakery demand.

Thornfen can finance the purchase by issuing 400,000 new ordinary shares to existing family shareholders at $1.50 each, raising $600,000, or by taking a $600,000 bank loan at 6% annual interest over 8 years, costing $36,000 in interest each year. Daniel favours the loan to protect family control, while Owen prefers shares to avoid fixed interest payments. The board must decide by 31 March.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'issue of shares'.
    Answer: Selling new shares in the business to investors in return for capital, which the business does not have to repay [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: selling shares to investors raises capital for the business; share capital does not have to be repaid like a loan

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Thornfen of raising the $600,000 by issuing shares instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Reason 1: Issued share capital does not have to be repaid [k], so Thornfen avoids 8 years of fixed $36,000 annual interest payments the bank loan would require [app]. Reason 2: Share capital carries no mandatory interest cost [k], so Thornfen can keep more cash when revenue is only $2.4 million a year [app].
    Keywords: $600,000, $36,000, 8 years, $2.4 million, 200,000 ordinary shares, 400,000 new ordinary shares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: share capital is not a loan and does not have to be repaid; shares carry no compulsory interest charge | application_max_2: the loan would cost $36,000 interest every year for 8 years; Thornfen currently earns revenue of $2.4 million a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to the Pryce brothers of issuing 400,000 new ordinary shares.
    Answer: Problem 1: Issuing shares dilutes the existing owners' control [k], because 400,000 new shares at $1.50 each would be added to the brothers' existing 200,000 ordinary shares [app], so their percentage ownership and say in decisions at the Riverside mill would fall [an]. Problem 2: Shareholders commonly expect dividends [k], and with annual revenue of only $2.4 million the brothers may have to share profits with new shareholders each year [app], weakening the family's claim on future earnings [an].
    Keywords: 400,000 new ordinary shares, $1.50, 200,000 ordinary shares, $2.4 million, Riverside mill, family shareholders, 8 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: issuing new shares reduces existing shareholders' percentage of ownership; ordinary shareholders usually expect dividends from profits | application_max_2: 400,000 new shares at $1.50 each would take total shares from 200,000 to 600,000; Thornfen earns revenue of $2.4 million a year | analysis_max_2: the brothers lose voting power and influence over the business; profit is spread across more shareholders, reducing what the family keeps

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Thornfen Grain Milling Ltd should issue the new ordinary shares rather than take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Issuing shares would raise the full $600,000 without any fixed repayment [k], since 400,000 new ordinary shares at $1.50 each add $600,000 of permanent capital with no $36,000 interest every year for 8 years [app], so Thornfen's cash position stays flexible while bakery demand rises [an]. However, taking the loan keeps the business entirely in family hands [k]; the brothers avoid new shareholders expecting dividends even in lean years when revenue slips below $2.4 million [app], protecting their control of the Riverside mill [an]. Overall, Thornfen should take the bank loan [eval], because Daniel's wish to protect family control matters more to a 7-year-old family business than saving $36,000 of interest each year [eval].
    Keywords: 400,000 new ordinary shares, $1.50, $600,000, $36,000, $2.4 million, 8 years, Riverside mill
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: share issue avoids fixed interest repayments and adds permanent capital; bank loan preserves existing ownership and control | application_max_2: 400,000 shares at $1.50 each raises $600,000 against $36,000 annual loan interest for 8 years; current revenue is $2.4 million a year | analysis_max_2: cash flexibility versus ownership dilution trade-off; control of the family business weighed against the cost of interest | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the family-business context

--- STEM ---
Brackenridge Publishing Plc is a public limited company listed on the Country X Stock Exchange, publishing textbooks and trade paperbacks for 9 years. It employs 140 editorial, printing and sales staff, and reported annual revenue of $9.6 million last year. The board wants to build a $2 million regional distribution centre near the capital to cut delivery times. Trading was difficult last year after a weak Christmas sales season.

One option is a 10-year $2 million debenture issue at 7.5%, paying $150,000 interest each year. The alternative is a rights issue of 500,000 new shares at $4.00 each, raising the same $2 million in exchange for new ordinary shares. Debenture interest is tax-deductible, while shares carry no repayment obligation at all. Shareholders vote at an extraordinary general meeting on 18 June.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'debenture'.
    Answer: A long-term loan sold by a company to investors, paying a fixed rate of interest and repaid on an agreed future date [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a debenture is a long-term loan made to the company; debenture holders receive fixed interest and repayment at a set date

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Brackenridge Publishing Plc might prefer selling debentures to a rights issue.
    Answer: Reason 1: Debenture interest is tax-deductible [k], so Brackenridge can cut its tax bill while paying a predictable $150,000 each year on the $2 million raised [app]. Reason 2: Existing shareholders keep their full stake in the company [k], because no new shares are issued unlike the 500,000 new shares at $4.00 each under the rights issue [app].
    Keywords: $2 million, $150,000, 500,000, $4.00, 7.5%, 10-year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: debenture interest is tax-deductible; issuing shares dilutes existing shareholders' percentage of ownership | application_max_2: the 7.5% rate means $150,000 interest a year on $2 million; the rights issue would add 500,000 new shares at $4.00 each

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Brackenridge of a $2 million debenture issue at 7.5%.
    Answer: Problem 1: Debenture interest must be paid every year [k], and $150,000 a year reduces profit even while the new centre has not yet lifted revenue beyond $9.6 million after a weak Christmas [app], squeezing returns to existing shareholders [an]. Problem 2: The debenture must eventually be repaid [k], so $2 million falls due in a single payment after 10 years regardless of trading conditions [app], creating a huge cash demand in a year of weak sales [an].
    Keywords: $150,000, $2 million, 7.5%, $9.6 million, 10-year, weak Christmas
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: debenture interest is fixed and compulsory even in poor years; the principal must be repaid at the end of the debenture term | application_max_2: $150,000 a year of interest on $2 million at 7.5%; revenue last year was $9.6 million after a weak Christmas sales season | analysis_max_2: fixed interest reduces profits available to ordinary shareholders; a single $2 million repayment after 10 years strains future cash flow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brackenridge Publishing Plc should sell debentures rather than make a rights issue? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Debentures raise the full $2 million quickly and certainty of cost [k], carrying a known 7.5% charge of $150,000 a year that is tax-deductible [app], so the distribution centre can open sooner and cut delivery times across sales of $9.6 million a year [an]. However, a rights issue of 500,000 new shares at $4.00 raises the same $2 million with no repayment obligation [k], protecting a company that traded through a weak Christmas and cannot guarantee $150,000 cash in every future year [app], so shareholders avoid the risk of default on the debenture [an]. Overall, Brackenridge should make the rights issue [eval], because after a weak trading year avoiding a fixed $150,000 annual charge matters more than tax relief [eval].
    Keywords: $2 million, 7.5%, $150,000, 500,000, $4.00, $9.6 million, weak Christmas
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: debentures provide fast, known-cost finance with fixed annual interest; rights issue raises permanent capital with no repayment obligation | application_max_2: 7.5% on $2 million means $150,000 interest a year for 10 years; the rights issue of 500,000 shares at $4.00 raises the same $2 million | analysis_max_2: tax relief and speed weighed against weak recent trading; repayment risk and effect on shareholders of a failed debenture | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the stem figures and recent trading weakness

--- STEM ---
Caldervale Dairies Ltd is a private limited company in Country X founded 12 years ago, pasteurising and bottling milk for regional supermarkets. Its main supermarket contract was renewed for 3 years in January.

Caldervale can take a 5-year $250,000 bank loan at 8% annual interest, costing $20,000 a year and $100,000 in total, or ask its 9 shareholders to subscribe new shares at $12 each, raising $250,000 if all are taken up. Shareholders are willing to invest, but worry the dividend per share will fall. The board meets on 9 May.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'bank loan'.
    Answer: A sum of money borrowed from a bank and repaid with interest over an agreed period of time [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: money borrowed from a bank; repaid with interest over an agreed period

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Caldervale might choose the $250,000 bank loan over asking shareholders for more money.
    Answer: Reason 1: A bank loan does not change the ownership or control of the company [k], so the 9 shareholders keep exactly their current share of Caldervale [app]. Reason 2: The loan spreads the cost over time [k], costing $20,000 a year instead of demanding $250,000 from shareholders in one payment [app].
    Keywords: 9 shareholders, $250,000, $20,000, 5-year, $12, $100,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a bank loan does not affect ownership or control; loans are repaid in instalments over time rather than in one amount | application_max_2: Caldervale has only 9 shareholders whose holdings stay unchanged; interest would be $20,000 a year over 5 years

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Caldervale of taking the $250,000 bank loan at 8%.
    Answer: Problem 1: Loan interest is a fixed cost [k], adding $20,000 a year of interest to costs even when revenue growth from $2.7 million to $3.1 million stalls [app], squeezing profit in a bad season [an]. Problem 2: The loan must be repaid in full [k], so $100,000 of interest plus the $250,000 capital falls due within 5 years [app], leaving less cash for the Vale creamery's future needs [an].
    Keywords: $20,000, $100,000, $250,000, $2.7 million, $3.1 million, Vale creamery
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: loan interest is a fixed cost that reduces profit; loans are repayable with interest within an agreed period | application_max_2: $20,000 interest each year plus $100,000 total interest on the $250,000 loan; revenue grew from $2.7 million to $3.1 million | analysis_max_2: fixed interest squeezes profit in weak seasons; full repayment reduces cash available for other spending

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Caldervale Dairies Ltd should take the bank loan rather than issue new shares at $12 each? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The bank loan raises the money in one move [k], with interest of $20,000 a year for 5 years, so the plate pasteuriser can be replaced quickly while the 9 shareholders avoid subscribing $250,000 at $12 each [app], letting Caldervale keep its supermarket contracts [an]. However, new shares bring permanent capital [k], spreading the $250,000 between willing shareholders without the pressure of $100,000 total loan interest over 5 years [app], which suits a company whose revenue only recently passed $3.1 million [an]. Overall, Caldervale should take the bank loan [eval], because the shareholders' worry about the dividend per share makes borrowing the fastest route to a new pasteuriser [eval].
    Keywords: $250,000, $20,000, $100,000, 9 shareholders, $12, 5-year, $3.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bank loans provide quick fixed-term finance repaid with interest; share issue raises permanent capital without repayment obligation | application_max_2: loan costs $20,000 a year and $100,000 total over 5 years; shares at $12 each must raise $250,000 from 9 shareholders | analysis_max_2: speed and certainty of the loan versus dilution concerns about dividends; repayment burden weighed against permanent capital | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the stem figures and the shareholders' position

--- STEM ---
Dunsley Renewables Plc is a public limited company listed on the Country X Stock Exchange, building and operating wind farms for 6 years. Following a record year, the board wants to press ahead with a 12-turbine extension costing $4.5 million, the largest project in the company's history. It employs 95 engineers and technicians and reported revenue of $18.5 million last year.

Dunsley can fund the extension with a $4.5 million bank loan at 7% annual interest over 10 years, or by issuing $4.5 million of debentures at 6% annual interest over 10 years. The loan would be secured against the company's existing 30-turbine wind farm; the debentures would be unsecured. Dunsley has paid a 4 cent dividend per share for three straight years and plans to keep paying it.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the annual interest payable on the $4.5 million bank loan at 7% per year.
    Answer: $4.5 million Ã— 7% = $315,000 per year [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: interest = loan amount Ã— annual interest rate; $4.5 million Ã— 7% = $315,000 per year

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Dunsley of issuing $4.5 million of debentures at 6% instead of taking the bank loan at 7%.
    Answer: Reason 1: The debenture rate is 1 percentage point lower [k], saving $45,000 a year compared with the $315,000 charge on the 7% loan [app]. Reason 2: The debentures are unsecured [k], so the existing 30-turbine wind farm is not offered as security for the $4.5 million [app].
    Keywords: $4.5 million, 6%, 7%, 30-turbine, 10 years, 12-turbine
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a lower interest rate reduces the annual finance cost; unsecured debentures need no asset as security | application_max_2: 6% on $4.5 million is $270,000 a year versus $315,000 at 7%; the bank loan would be secured on the 30-turbine wind farm

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Dunsley of issuing $4.5 million of debentures.
    Answer: Problem 1: Debenture interest is fixed and compulsory [k], and $270,000 a year must be paid even if wind speeds cut output below revenue of $18.5 million [app], reducing profit left for dividends [an]. Problem 2: The debentures must be repaid after 10 years [k], so $4.5 million falls due in a single payment at the end of the term [app], a huge demand on cash for a company funding a 12-turbine extension [an].
    Keywords: $4.5 million, 6%, $18.5 million, 12-turbine, 10 years, wind farms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: debenture interest is fixed and compulsory even in poor years; the principal is repaid at the end of the debenture term | application_max_2: $270,000 a year of interest at 6% on $4.5 million; the extension is a 12-turbine project on top of an existing 30-turbine farm | analysis_max_2: fixed interest reduces profit available for dividends; a single $4.5 million repayment after 10 years strains cash flow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Dunsley Renewables Plc should issue debentures rather than take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Debentures are cheaper and unsecured [k]; at 6% the interest would be $270,000 a year instead of $315,000, and the existing 30-turbine wind farm stays safe [app], freeing cash for the 12-turbine extension [an]. However, the bank loan at 7% is quicker to arrange from one lender [k], with repayment terms negotiated over 10 years, whereas a failed payment on public debentures would damage Dunsley's Stock Exchange reputation and its streak of a 4 cent dividend per share [app], deterring future investors [an]. Overall, Dunsley should issue the debentures [eval], because a 1% saving of $45,000 a year and no charge on the wind farm outweigh the reputational risk for a company with $18.5 million revenue [eval].
    Keywords: $4.5 million, 6%, 7%, 30-turbine, 12-turbine, $18.5 million, 4 cent, 10 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: unsecured debentures at a lower rate cut finance cost and protect assets; bank loans are quicker to arrange but need security and may raise reputational stakes | application_max_2: 6% on $4.5 million is $270,000 a year versus $315,000 at 7%; existing 30-turbine farm would secure the loan; revenue last year was $18.5 million | analysis_max_2: cost saving and asset protection weighed against arrangement speed; reputational risk to dividends and future investor confidence | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the Stock Exchange context

    Question: Define 'external finance'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: finance obtained from outside the business; examples include loans, debentures, share issues and grants

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Southvale of issuing 4 million new ordinary shares at $2.50 each.
    Answer: Reason 1: Issued shares carry no fixed interest cost [k], so Southvale avoids the certain $650,000 charge a 6.5% debenture would add every year [app]. Reason 2: Shares are permanent capital [k], meaning the $10 million raised from 4 million shares at $2.50 never has to be repaid [app].
    Keywords: $650,000, 6.5%, 4 million, $2.50, $10 million, 8-year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: shares carry no compulsory interest payment; share capital is permanent and never has to be repaid | application_max_2: the 6.5% debenture would cost $650,000 a year; 4 million shares at $2.50 each raise $10 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to Southvale of the chairman's $10 million debenture issue at 6.5%.
    Answer: Problem 1: Debenture interest is fixed [k], and $650,000 a year must be paid even when seasonal demand makes yearly profits uneven [app], cutting the profit available to ordinary shareholders [an]. Problem 2: The debentures must be repaid after 8 years [k], so $10 million falls due in a single year even if antibiotic sales remain seasonal [app], creating refinancing pressure on the company [an].
    Keywords: $650,000, 6.5%, $10 million, 8-year, seasonal, 2028
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: debenture interest is fixed and compulsory even in weak years; the principal is repaid in full at the end of the term | application_max_2: $650,000 a year of interest at 6.5% on $10 million; demand for antibiotics is seasonal and yearly profits are uneven | analysis_max_2: fixed interest reduces profit available to shareholders; repaying $10 million in one year strains future cash flow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Southvale Pharma Plc should issue the new ordinary shares rather than the debenture? Justify your answer.
    Answer: New shares raise the $10 million without fixed interest [k]; 4 million shares at $2.50 each avoid the $650,000 a year debenture charge [app], keeping Southvale flexible when seasonal sales swing yearly profits [an]. However, a share issue dilutes existing shareholders [k], while the 8-year debenture at 6.5% is cheaper once the antibiotic research wing opens in 2028 and revenue climbs above $42 million [app], rewarding shareholders without issuing new stock [an]. Overall, Southvale should issue the new ordinary shares [eval], because avoiding a fixed $650,000 annual charge while yearly profits are uneven protects the company's cash flow better than tax-deductible interest [eval].
    Keywords: $10 million, 4 million, $2.50, $650,000, 6.5%, 2028, $42 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: share issue raises permanent capital with no fixed interest; debentures cost fixed, tax-deductible interest but require repayment | application_max_2: 4 million shares at $2.50 each raise $10 million, avoiding $650,000 a year; the research wing opens by 2028; revenue last year was $42 million | analysis_max_2: flexibility under seasonal profits weighed against dilution; tax-deductible interest versus the risk of fixed charges | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and seasonal demand

Falkenbrook can issue $1.2 million of 6% preference shares to institutional investors, paying a fixed $72,000 dividend each year but carrying no vote, or take a $1.2 million bank loan at 9% over 6 years, costing $108,000 interest annually but giving tax relief. The new furnaces would be installed during the July shutdown. Ordinary shareholders are divided and vote at the next general meeting in August.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'preference shares'.
    Answer: Shares that pay a fixed rate of dividend, paid before any dividend on ordinary shares, usually with no voting rights [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: preference shares pay a fixed rate of dividend; preference dividends are paid before ordinary dividends and usually carry no vote

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Falkenbrook of issuing the $1.2 million of 6% preference shares.
    Answer: Reason 1: Preference shareholders usually carry no vote [k], so the ordinary owners keep full control of Falkenbrook despite issuing $1.2 million of shares [app]. Reason 2: The dividend rate is fixed at 6% [k], costing $72,000 a year, which is less than the $108,000 annual interest on the bank loan [app].
    Keywords: 6%, $72,000, $108,000, no vote, $1.2 million, preference shares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: preference shares normally carry no voting rights; preference dividends are fixed in advance | application_max_2: the issue keeps $1.2 million raised while control stays with ordinary owners; 6% on $1.2 million is $72,000 a year versus $108,000 loan interest

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to Falkenbrook of issuing preference shares.
    Answer: Problem 1: The fixed preference dividend cannot be skipped [k], so $72,000 must be paid each year even when revenue stays at $7.8 million and gas bills stay high [app], reducing profit left for ordinary shareholders [an]. Problem 2: Preference dividends are not tax-deductible [k], unlike interest on the 9% bank loan which gives tax relief [app], so the effective annual cost of preference shares is higher than it first appears [an].
    Keywords: $72,000, $7.8 million, $108,000, 9%, 6%, Newton furnaces
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: preference dividends are fixed and must be paid before ordinary dividends; preference dividends are not tax-deductible | application_max_2: $72,000 a year of fixed dividend at 6% on $1.2 million; the bank loan at 9% would cost $108,000 but give tax relief | analysis_max_2: fixed payments reduce profit available to ordinary shareholders; lack of tax relief raises the true cost of preference shares

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Falkenbrook Glass Ltd should issue preference shares rather than take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Preference shares raise $1.2 million at a fixed 6% cost of $72,000 a year with no repayment deadline [k], preserving control because they carry no vote and saving gas bills of $90,000 a year once the furnaces are installed [app], so ordinary shareholders keep ownership while cash flow improves [an]. However, the 9% bank loan gives tax relief [k], and its $108,000 interest is deductible against profit, narrowing the real gap with the $72,000 dividend, and the loan disappears after 6 years while preference shares are never repaid [app], so Falkenbrook escapes the dividend burden sooner with the loan [an]. Overall, Falkenbrook should issue the 6% preference shares [eval], because no-vote control and a $36,000 a year lower headline cost outweigh the loan's tax relief for a 15-year-old glass maker [eval].
    Keywords: 6%, $72,000, $90,000, $108,000, 9%, $1.2 million, no vote, 6 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: preference shares preserve control and carry fixed, low dividends; bank loans are tax-deductible and finite but require security and fixed interest | application_max_2: 6% preference dividend is $72,000 a year against $108,000 loan interest at 9%; the furnaces would cut gas bills by $90,000 a year; loan runs 6 years | analysis_max_2: control and headline cost weighed against tax relief and loan term; permanent dividend burden versus finite loan repayments | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the July shutdown plan

Hartcliffe Aerospace Ltd is a private limited company in Country X founded 10 years ago, making precision components for light aircraft. It employs 63 machinists and reported revenue of $6.4 million last year. Two overseas buyers have already inspected the machines. Order books are full, and Hartcliffe needs $2 million for five new CNC machines to fulfil a $3.6 million aerospace contract.

Hartcliffe's bank will lend $2 million at 8.5% over 7 years ($170,000 interest a year), but only if Hartcliffe offers its factory building as security. The alternative is selling $2 million of 10-year debentures at 7%, costing $140,000 a year, with no charge on the factory. Payment for the contract milestone would arrive in March. The directors dislike risking the family-built building.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'collateral'.
    Answer: An asset offered as security for a loan, which the lender can claim if the borrower fails to repay [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an asset pledged as security for a loan; the lender may take the asset if repayments are missed

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Hartcliffe of selling $2 million of debentures instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Reason 1: Debentures need no security [k], so the family-built factory building is never at risk of the bank's claim [app]. Reason 2: The debenture rate is lower [k], at 7% costing $140,000 a year compared with $170,000 on the 8.5% loan [app].
    Keywords: $2 million, 7%, $140,000, 8.5%, $170,000, factory building
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: debentures can be issued without offering asset-backed security; a lower coupon rate reduces the annual cost of finance | application_max_2: the bank requires the factory building as security for $2 million; 7% costs $140,000 a year against $170,000 at 8.5%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Hartcliffe of offering its factory building as security for the bank loan.
    Answer: Problem 1: The building could be seized [k], because the bank can claim the family-built factory if Hartcliffe misses repayments on the $2 million [app], leaving 63 machinists without a workplace [an]. Problem 2: Security ties up the asset [k], preventing Hartcliffe from selling or remortgaging the factory during the 7-year loan at 8.5% costing $170,000 a year [app], limiting future flexibility [an].
    Keywords: $2 million, factory building, 63 machinists, 7 years, 8.5%, $170,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a secured lender can seize the pledged asset if repayments fail; a pledged asset cannot be freely sold or used as security elsewhere | application_max_2: the family-built factory is the security for the $2 million loan; Hartcliffe employs 63 machinists at the factory | analysis_max_2: loss of the factory threatens production and jobs; tied-up security limits options for future finance

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hartcliffe Aerospace Ltd should sell debentures rather than take the bank loan secured on the factory? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Debentures raise the $2 million with no charge on the factory [k], and at 7% cost $140,000 a year, $30,000 less than the $170,000 loan interest, to fulfil the $3.6 million aerospace contract [app], letting the directors protect family property [an]. However, the bank loan is likely quicker to arrange from a single known lender [k], while the 10-year debenture ties Hartcliffe to $140,000 a year and repayment of $2 million in year ten [app], which could strain cash flow if the aerospace contract milestones slip beyond March [an]. Overall, Hartcliffe should sell the debentures [eval], because protecting the family-built factory and saving $30,000 a year matter more than speed of arrangement [eval].
    Keywords: $2 million, 7%, $140,000, 8.5%, $170,000, factory building, $3.6 million, 10-year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: debentures raise finance without asset security; bank loans are quicker from one lender but need security and fixed repayments | application_max_2: debenture at 7% costs $140,000 a year versus $170,000 at 8.5%, saving $30,000; the contract is worth $3.6 million with a March milestone payment | analysis_max_2: asset protection and lower annual cost weighed against arrangement speed; long-term fixed obligation versus contract-milestone risk | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the family-built factory

--- STEM ---
Invermere Marine Plc is a public limited company listed on the Country X Stock Exchange, operating coastal freight and ferry services for 13 years. It employs 210 crew and staff and reported revenue of $21 million last year. Invermere wants $6 million for a 60-metre container vessel, expected to earn $1.5 million extra revenue a year. Ferry bookings have risen 12% since the new timetable began.

Invermere can raise the $6 million through a general issue of 3 million new ordinary shares at $2.00 each, or by borrowing $6 million for 10 years at a fixed 7.25%, costing $435,000 a year. The share issue would spread ownership across many new investors; the loan keeps ownership concentrated but fixes repayments for a decade. The shareholders vote on 25 October.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'long-term finance'.
    Answer: Finance used for a period longer than one year, usually to fund capital projects and expansion rather than short-term needs [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: finance used for more than one year; suited to capital projects and long-term expansion

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Calculate the total interest Invermere would pay over 10 years on the $6 million loan at 7.25% a year.
    Answer: Step 1: annual interest = $6,000,000 Ã— 7.25% [k] = $435,000 a year [app]. Step 2: total interest = $435,000 Ã— 10 years [k] = $4,350,000 [app].
    Keywords: $6 million, 7.25%, 10 years, $435,000, $2.00, 3 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: annual interest = principal Ã— annual rate; total interest = annual interest Ã— number of years | application_max_2: $6,000,000 Ã— 7.25% = $435,000 a year; $435,000 Ã— 10 years = $4,350,000 in total

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages to Invermere of borrowing $6 million at a fixed 7.25% for 10 years.
    Answer: Problem 1: Interest is fixed and compulsory [k], so $435,000 must be paid each of the 10 years even if freight demand dips below revenue of $21 million [app], reducing profit available for dividends [an]. Problem 2: The $6 million itself must be repaid [k], so a decade of annual $435,000 interest is followed by one large capital repayment [app], straining liquidity in the tenth year [an].
    Keywords: $6 million, 7.25%, $435,000, 10 years, $21 million, 60-metre
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fixed interest must be paid every year regardless of performance; loans must be repaid in full at the end of the term | application_max_2: $435,000 a year at 7.25% on $6 million for 10 years; last year's revenue was $21 million | analysis_max_2: fixed costs reduce dividend capacity in weak years; the final repayment creates a large cash strain

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Invermere Marine Plc should borrow the $6 million rather than issue new ordinary shares? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Borrowing keeps ownership concentrated [k], and at a fixed 7.25% the $435,000 yearly cost is covered by the vessel's expected $1.5 million extra revenue, leaving over $1 million of headroom a year [app], so a decade of repayments is affordable without diluting current investors [an]. However, the share issue of 3 million new shares at $2.00 raises the same $6 million with no repayment ever [k], protecting Invermere if freight demand turns, though it would spread ownership across many new investors expecting future dividends on $21 million revenue [app], cutting existing shareholders' share [an]. Overall, Invermere should borrow the $6 million [eval], because the vessel's $1.5 million extra annual revenue comfortably covers the $435,000 interest while ownership stays concentrated [eval].
    Keywords: $6 million, 7.25%, $435,000, $1.5 million, 3 million, $2.00, $21 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: borrowing preserves ownership but creates fixed repayments; share issue raises permanent capital but dilutes ownership | application_max_2: loan costs $435,000 a year at 7.25% versus $1.5 million expected extra revenue; 3 million shares at $2.00 raise the same $6 million | analysis_max_2: affordability of fixed interest weighed against dilution; risk of demand falling versus permanent capital safety | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the vessel investment

--- STEM ---
Keswickmoor Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company in Country X founded 9 years ago, making ceramic tiles for hotels and restaurants. It employs 52 workers at its Moorcroft kilns, earned $4.6 million revenue last year, and holds $1.1 million of retained profit. Two national hotel chains have asked for 300,000 extra tiles next year. Keswickmoor wants $750,000 for a new glaze laboratory and automated kiln line.

The directors can take a $750,000 bank loan at 5.5% over 6 years ($41,250 a year interest) or issue 500,000 new ordinary shares at $1.50 each to raise the same $750,000. The bank would give no further credit while the loan is outstanding. Keeping the glaze quality lead matters for its hotel clients. The board votes on 20 February.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'ordinary shares'.
    Answer: The standard voting shares of a company, giving holders ownership rights and a claim to dividends from profit [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ordinary shares carry ownership and voting rights; ordinary shareholders receive dividends from profit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Keswickmoor might take the bank loan rather than issue new shares.
    Answer: Reason 1: Existing shareholders keep full ownership [k], because no 500,000 new ordinary shares are added to the current holding [app]. Reason 2: Loan interest is certain and tax-deductible [k], at $41,250 a year for 6 years, reducing the tax payable on profits from $4.6 million revenue [app].
    Keywords: 500,000, $41,250, 6 years, $4.6 million, $750,000, 5.5%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a bank loan does not change ownership or control; loan interest is certain in advance and tax-deductible | application_max_2: the share option would add 500,000 new ordinary shares; the loan costs $41,250 a year at 5.5% over 6 years

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Keswickmoor of issuing the 500,000 new ordinary shares at $1.50 each.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Shares are permanent capital [k], so the $750,000 raised never has to be repaid, unlike the loan due in full after 6 years [app], protecting cash flow while the glaze laboratory is built [an]. Advantage 2: No fixed interest [k], so dividends can fall if hotel orders below $4.6 million disappoint, whereas $41,250 a year interest would still fall due [app], giving flexibility in weak seasons [an].
    Keywords: 500,000, $1.50, 6 years, $41,250, $750,000, glaze laboratory
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: share capital is permanent and never has to be repaid; ordinary dividends can be reduced when profit falls | application_max_2: 500,000 shares at $1.50 each raise $750,000; the loan at 5.5% costs $41,250 a year for 6 years | analysis_max_2: no repayment protects cash during the laboratory build; flexible dividends give room in weak seasons

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Keswickmoor Ceramics Ltd should take the bank loan rather than issue new ordinary shares? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The bank loan raises $750,000 quickly [k], preserves full ownership and costs a tax-deductible $41,250 a year, so Keswickmoor keeps control while hotel clients get their extra 300,000 tiles [app], and the 5.5% rate is affordable against $4.6 million revenue [an]. However, issuing 500,000 new shares at $1.50 brings $750,000 that never needs repaying [k], avoids the clause that the bank gives no further credit while the loan is outstanding and shields the glaze laboratory project if demand dips [app], reducing fixed obligations across the 6 years [an]. Overall, Keswickmoor should issue the new ordinary shares [eval], because the no-further-credit clause would cramp growth, making permanent share capital the safer route despite the $1.50 dilution [eval].
    Keywords: $750,000, 500,000, $1.50, $41,250, 5.5%, $4.6 million, 6 years, no further credit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: bank loans are quick, tax-deductible and preserve ownership; share issue raises permanent capital with no repayment obligation | application_max_2: loan costs $41,250 a year at 5.5% for 6 years; shares at $1.50 raise $750,000; two national hotel chains want 300,000 extra tiles; revenue was $4.6 million | analysis_max_2: speed and control weighed against the no-further-credit clause; permanent capital versus fixed annual obligations | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the hotel-chain order

====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Renwick Precision Ltd is a private limited company that manufactures metal brackets and gear housings for agricultural machinery in Country X. The business employs 18 workers and has supplied two tractor assemblers for the past 6 years. Sales revenue is $640,000, and margins have narrowed as steel costs rose by 12% this year. Owner Priya Raman wants to buy a CNC machining centre costing $80,000 to win a new contract worth $150,000 a year.

Priya is comparing two external sources of finance. She could use factoring of debts: her debtors currently owe Renwick $100,000, and a factor has offered an immediate advance of 80% of the invoices ($80,000) in return for a 3% fee of $3,000. Alternatively, she could launch a crowdfunding campaign on an online platform, targeting $85,000; the platform charges a 5% fee ($4,250) and she must film promotional videos and send rewards to backers. Renwick has no other finance available now.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'factoring of debts'.
    Answer: Factoring of debts is when a business sells its unpaid customer invoices (debtors) to a specialist finance company, which pays an immediate cash advance and then collects the money owed, usually in return for a fee. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Selling unpaid invoices/debtors to a specialist company (factor); Factor pays an advance and collects the debts for a fee

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of factoring of debts for Renwick Precision Ltd.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Factoring releases cash immediately [k], so Renwick receives the $80,000 advance now instead of waiting for debtors to pay the $100,000 they owe, allowing it to buy the CNC machining centre costing $80,000 [app]. Advantage 2: The factor takes over chasing and collecting the debts [k], saving Renwick's 18 workers time and effort so that Priya Raman can concentrate on the new contract worth $150,000 a year [app].
    Keywords: Renwick Precision Ltd, $100,000, $80,000, 18 workers, CNC machining centre, $150,000, debtors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Immediate cash advance against unpaid invoices; Factor handles collection/credit control of the debts | application_max_2: $80,000 advance received now (80% of $100,000 owed); CNC machining centre costing $80,000 / contract worth $150,000 a year; 18 workers employed

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of crowdfunding for Renwick Precision Ltd.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: The campaign may fail to reach its target [k]; Priya needs $85,000, and if pledges fall short the platform returns all the money, leaving Renwick unable to buy the CNC machining centre [app] and in no position to accept the new contract worth $150,000 a year [an]. Disadvantage 2: Running the campaign costs time and money [k]; Priya must film promotional videos, send rewards to backers and pay the 5% fee ($4,250) [app], distracting her from the core business and reducing the net cash raised [an].
    Keywords: crowdfunding, $85,000, $4,250, 5% fee, rewards, CNC machining centre, $150,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Funds returned if target not reached / no guarantee of raising the money; Platform fee and campaign effort/cost (videos, rewards) | application_max_2: $85,000 target / $4,250 fee (5%); CNC machining centre costing $80,000; New contract worth $150,000 a year | analysis_max_2: Insufficient funds mean the CNC purchase or the new contract is delayed/lost; Campaign effort and fees reduce the net cash or time available for the business

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Renwick Precision Ltd should use factoring of debts or crowdfunding? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Factoring has clear advantages: Renwick would receive the $80,000 advance immediately, the factor collects the $100,000 owed, and the fee is only $3,000 (3%) [k] [app]; the certainty suits a business that cannot wait for its debtors to pay [an]. However, Renwick loses some control over how customers are chased, and the advance leaves less margin on the invoices it sells [an]. Crowdfunding could raise the full $85,000 and build a public profile, but success is not guaranteed and the 5% fee costs $4,250 before rewards are sent to backers [k] [app]. Overall, I think Renwick should use factoring [eval], because the $3,000 fee is cheaper than the $4,250 crowdfunding fee and the $80,000 advance is far more certain; crowdfunding remains a useful fallback if Renwick cannot afford the immediate loss of margin [eval].
    Keywords: Renwick Precision Ltd, $80,000, $100,000, $3,000, $85,000, $4,250, factoring of debts, crowdfunding
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Factoring: immediate advance, factor collects the debts, fee payable; Crowdfunding: all-or-nothing target, platform fee, campaign effort/rewards | application_max_2: $80,000 advance / $100,000 owed / $3,000 fee (3%); $85,000 target / $4,250 fee (5%) | analysis_max_2: Certainty and speed of factoring vs uncertainty of crowdfunding; Effect on cash flow, profit margin and control of debtors | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing both sources with stem figures; Recognition of the condition under which crowdfunding might be preferable / justified overall judgement

--- STEM ---
Greyfin Fisheries Ltd is a fish-processing company based in a coastal port in Country X. It employs 26 workers who fillet, freeze and pack 9 tonnes of fish each week for supermarket chains, generating annual sales revenue of $520,000. The business's ageing cold-storage room failed twice last year, and the owner, Marco Dene, wants to replace it with a modern unit costing $60,000.

Marco is considering two external sources of finance. The government offers a non-repayable grant of $30,000 towards the project, but Greyfin must submit audited accounts, complete the work within 18 months and not use the money for wages. Alternatively, a local micro-finance institution offers a $45,000 loan at 11% annual interest over 4 years, costing $4,950 a year and $19,800 in total interest. Greyfin keeps $35,000 in cash reserves.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'grant'.
    Answer: A grant is a sum of money given to a business, often by a government, to support a specific purpose, which does not have to be repaid, normally subject to conditions. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Sum of money given to a business (often by government); Does not have to be repaid / usually has conditions and a specific purpose

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of the government grant for Greyfin Fisheries Ltd.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A grant does not have to be repaid [k], so Greyfin could fund half the $60,000 cold-storage room from the $30,000 grant and keep its $35,000 cash reserves intact [app]. Advantage 2: The grant pays towards a specific project the business wants to complete [k]; Greyfin can replace the cold-storage room that failed twice last year and protect its 26 jobs and $520,000 annual sales revenue [app].
    Keywords: Greyfin, $30,000, $60,000, $35,000, 26 workers, $520,000, grant
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: No repayment / non-repayable finance; Supports a specific purpose/project chosen by the business | application_max_2: $30,000 towards the $60,000 cold-storage unit; $35,000 reserves intact; 26 workers / $520,000 annual sales revenue / failed cold-storage room

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of micro-finance for Greyfin Fisheries Ltd.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: Interest and repayments must be made [k]; the $45,000 loan at 11% costs $4,950 a year and $19,800 in total interest [app], reducing the profit and cash available for other needs such as repairs or new equipment [an]. Disadvantage 2: Missing payments can damage the business [k]; with the cold-storage room unreliable, revenue could slip and Greyfin could struggle to meet the annual repayments of $4,950 [app], harming its credit record with lenders [an].
    Keywords: micro-finance, $45,000, 11%, $4,950, $19,800, 4 years, $520,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interest must be paid on the loan; Loan must be repaid on schedule / repayment risk | application_max_2: $45,000 loan / 11% / $4,950 a year / $19,800 total interest; 4 years repayment period / unreliable cold-storage room | analysis_max_2: Interest reduces profit and available working capital; Default risk damages credit record and future borrowing

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Greyfin Fisheries Ltd should accept the grant or take the micro-finance loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The grant is free money: $30,000 towards the $60,000 project, so with $35,000 of cash reserves Greyfin could fund the $30,000 balance without borrowing a penny [k] [app]; the project would cost nothing beyond the stated conditions [an]. However, the grant is not guaranteed until the audited accounts are assessed, the work must finish within 18 months, and the money cannot be used to pay wages [an]. Micro-finance is larger and faster ($45,000), giving Greyfin more headroom, but it costs $19,800 in total interest over 4 years and must be repaid even if fish sales dip [k] [app]. Overall, I think Greyfin should apply for the grant first [eval], using its $35,000 reserves to bridge any timing gap; it should take the micro-finance loan only if the grant is refused, delayed or insufficient [eval].
    Keywords: Greyfin, $30,000, $60,000, $35,000, $45,000, $19,800, grant, micro-finance
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Grant: non-repayable but conditional and not guaranteed; Micro-finance: smaller loans with interest and fixed repayment | application_max_2: $30,000 grant + $35,000 reserves vs the $60,000 cost; $45,000 loan / $19,800 total interest / 4 years | analysis_max_2: Grant: zero interest and cash preserved vs risk of delay/refusal/conditions; Micro-finance: certainty/speed/headroom vs interest burden and repayment risk | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing both sources with stem figures; Sensible fallback/sequencing argument or recognition of grant conditions / justified overall judgement

--- STEM ---
Loomfield Textiles Ltd is a garment workshop in Country X that cuts and sews workwear for hotels, employing 28 workers. Annual sales revenue is $780,000, and hotel clients buy on 60-day credit terms; they currently owe Loomfield $75,000. Rising energy bills have squeezed cash flow this year, and owner Daniel Okafor plans to install energy-efficient steam-dyeing and pressing equipment costing $36,000.

Daniel is weighing two external sources of finance. A factoring company will advance 85% of the outstanding invoices immediately ($63,750) for a fee of 2.5% ($1,875). Alternatively, the government offers a subsidy of $18,000 towards the upgrade, but Loomfield must retain all 28 jobs for at least 2 years and submit quarterly energy reports. The equipment supplier needs payment within 30 days.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'subsidy'.
    Answer: A subsidy is a payment made by a government to a business or organisation to encourage a particular activity, such as buying energy-efficient equipment; it does not have to be repaid. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Payment/financial support from government to a business/organisation; Intended to encourage a particular activity; not repayable

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of factoring of debts for Loomfield Textiles Ltd.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Immediate cash is received [k]; Loomfield gets $63,750 now (85% of the $75,000 owed) instead of waiting 60 days for its hotel clients to pay [app]. Advantage 2: The factor handles collection of the debts [k], taking the chasing burden off Daniel Okafor so he can meet the supplier's 30-day payment deadline for the $36,000 equipment [app].
    Keywords: factoring, $63,750, $75,000, 60-day credit, 30 days, Loomfield Textiles Ltd, $36,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Immediate advance of a percentage of outstanding invoices; Factor takes over collecting the debts | application_max_2: $63,750 = 85% of $75,000 owed; 60-day credit; 30-day supplier deadline / $36,000 equipment

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of the government subsidy for Loomfield Textiles Ltd.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: Conditions are attached to the money [k]; Loomfield must retain all 28 jobs for at least 2 years and submit quarterly energy reports [app], reducing flexibility and adding administrative work if hotel orders fall [an]. Disadvantage 2: Only half the cost is covered [k]; the subsidy pays $18,000 of the $36,000 price [app], so Loomfield must find the other $18,000 while its cash flow is already squeezed by energy bills [an].
    Keywords: subsidy, $18,000, $36,000, 28 jobs, quarterly energy reports, hotel clients, 2 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Conditions attached (job retention, reporting); Only part of the cost covered / balance must be self-funded | application_max_2: 28 jobs for at least 2 years / quarterly energy reports; $18,000 of $36,000 covered | analysis_max_2: Job-retention condition limits flexibility and adds admin cost; Unfunded balance strains already-squeezed cash flow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Loomfield Textiles Ltd should use factoring of debts or the government subsidy? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Factoring of debts is fast and certain [k]: $63,750 arrives immediately, which is more than enough to pay the $36,000 for the steam-dyeing equipment before the supplier's 30-day deadline, but the 2.5% fee costs $1,875 and the factor takes over chasing hotel clients, which may strain good relationships [app] [an]. The subsidy is cheaper in cash terms [k], at $18,000 of free money, but it covers only half the cost, depends on reports being approved and locks Loomfield into keeping 28 jobs for at least 2 years [app] [an]. Overall, I think Loomfield should use factoring of debts [eval], because the urgent 30-day deadline makes certainty more valuable than the $18,000 saving; once cash flow recovers, Loomfield could still claim future subsidies for other upgrades if the conditions then suit it [eval].
    Keywords: Loomfield Textiles Ltd, $63,750, $1,875, $36,000, 30 days, $18,000, factoring company, subsidy
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Factoring: immediate advance, fee payable, control of debts transferred; Subsidy: free money, partial coverage, conditions attached | application_max_2: $63,750 advance / $1,875 fee / $36,000 equipment / 30-day deadline; $18,000 subsidy covers half / 28 jobs for 2 years / quarterly energy reports | analysis_max_2: Certainty and speed vs cost saving of the subsidy; Effect on customer relationships, flexibility and cash flow | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing both sources with stem figures; Recognition of conditions/when the subsidy might be preferable / justified overall judgement
