--- STEM ---
Harewood Garden Centre is a partnership owned by Tom and Alice Harewood in Country X, employing 11 staff and selling plants, shrubs and garden furniture. Annual revenue is $540,000, with 60% earned between March and June. Monthly fixed costs are $14,000 all year, and the partners keep a cash reserve for the quiet winter months.

The partners are completing their cash-flow forecast for the spring peak. April: opening balance $7,200, inflows $38,500, outflows $41,900. May: inflows $44,000, outflows $39,200. June: inflows $29,500, outflows $33,800. They have also been offered two orders for the June delivery slot: a $25,000 order from a hotel group paying 90 days after delivery, or an $18,000 order from a garden club paying on delivery. Both orders must be accepted by 31 May.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the forecast closing balance for June. Show your working.
    Answer: April closing balance = $7,200 + ($38,500 - $41,900) = $3,800; May closing balance = $3,800 + ($44,000 - $39,200) = $8,600; June closing balance = $8,600 + ($29,500 - $33,800) = $4,300 [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow (inflows minus outflows); April net cash flow of -$3,400 carried into May, and May net of +$4,800 carried into June

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why preparing a cash-flow forecast helps Harewood Garden Centre manage its spring peak.
    Answer: Reason 1: A forecast shows the timing of inflows and outflows [k], so the partners can see April's outflows of $41,900 exceed inflows of $38,500 [app]. Reason 2: A forecast highlights the seasonal 60% surge between March and June [k], helping them plan stock, staffing and the June order decision before 31 May [app].
    Keywords: $41,900, $38,500, 60%, March and June, 31 May, $29,500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a forecast shows when cash enters and leaves the business; a forecast identifies peak and quiet periods in advance | application_max_2: April outflows of $41,900 exceed inflows of $38,500; 60% of revenue arrives March-June, so the June order must be decided by 31 May

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the partners could respond to a forecast June closing balance of only $4,300.
    Answer: Way 1: The partners could negotiate shorter payment terms with customers [k], because a hotel group paying 90 days after a $25,000 June delivery would push the balance well below $4,300 [app], leaving the business reliant on reserves or an overdraft in July and August [an]. Way 2: The partners could delay non-essential stock purchases [k], since June outflows of $33,800 already exceed inflows of $29,500 [app], which would protect the May balance of $8,600 and avoid using the winter cash reserve [an].
    Keywords: $25,000, 90 days, $33,800, $29,500, $44,000, garden club
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: asking debtors to pay faster improves inflow timing; delaying non-essential spending reduces outflows | application_max_2: hotel group pays 90 days after a $25,000 June delivery; June outflows of $33,800 exceed inflows of $29,500 | analysis_max_2: avoids dipping into reserves or needing an overdraft in July; protects the May balance of $8,600 entering the June deficit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harewood Garden Centre should accept the $25,000 hotel order rather than the $18,000 garden club order? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the $25,000 hotel order would maximise June revenue [k], adding $25,000 instead of $18,000 to the same delivery slot [app], and could open a long-term hotel client relationship worth more in future seasons [an]. However, the hotel pays 90 days after delivery [k], so the June forecast closing balance of $4,300 would be stretched further, while the garden club pays on delivery [app], protecting cash exactly when outflows already exceed inflows [an]. Overall, the partners should accept the $18,000 garden club order [eval], because certain immediate cash matters more than an extra $7,000 arriving 90 days late when June outflows of $33,800 already exceed inflows of $29,500 [eval].
    Keywords: $25,000, $18,000, 90 days, on delivery, $33,800, $29,500, garden club
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher-value orders raise revenue but may weaken immediate cash; payment timing matters more than order size when balances are thin | application_max_2: $25,000 hotel order paid 90 days after delivery vs $18,000 garden club paying on delivery; June closing balance of $4,300 against outflows of $33,800 exceeding inflows of $29,500 | analysis_max_2: longer payment terms strain a thin June balance further; immediate payment protects the position entering the quiet winter | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the $7,000 difference against 90-day delay and forecast deficit

Starbright Toys is a private limited company run by Marcus Webb in Country X, where it has traded for 6 years selling children's toys and games online and from one shop.     Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: overdraft allows spending beyond the current account balance; up to an agreed limit with interest on the amount used

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why festive toy retailers like Starbright prepare cash-flow forecasts before Christmas.
    Answer: Reason 1: A forecast shows the timing of cash movements [k], so Marcus can see that August inflows of $6,500 will not cover outflows of $15,800 [app]. Reason 2: A forecast identifies borrowing needs in advance [k], letting Marcus arrange the $20,000 overdraft before the balance falls below zero [app].
    Keywords: $6,500, $15,800, $20,000, $420,000, 55%, November and December
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: forecast shows timing of cash inflows and outflows; forecast reveals when borrowing will be needed | application_max_2: August inflows of $6,500 against outflows of $15,800; the overdraft must be arranged before the balance falls below zero

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Starbright could face if it delays paying toy suppliers until January.
    Answer: Problem 1: Delaying payment could damage supplier relationships [k], since suppliers expecting $14,000 in September would receive it only in January [app], so they may refuse to deliver festive stock next year [an]. Problem 2: Suppliers may charge late fees or withdraw credit terms [k], and Starbright's forecast already shows August inflows of only $6,500 against outflows of $15,800 [app], so extra costs would deepen the shortfall [an].
    Keywords: $14,000, January, $6,500, $15,800, $7,200, $15,100
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delaying payment risks losing supplier goodwill and credit terms; late payment may trigger fees or refusal to supply | application_max_2: $14,000 due to toy suppliers in September but deferred to January; August inflows of $6,500 against outflows of $15,800 | analysis_max_2: suppliers may refuse next year's festive deliveries; extra costs deepen the forecast cash shortfall

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marcus should arrange the $20,000 overdraft rather than delay paying toy suppliers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arranging the overdraft would protect supplier relationships ahead of the festive peak [k], because Starbright depends on suppliers delivering festive stock against $14,000 of September invoices [app], so keeping trust secures stock this year and next [an]. However, overdraft interest will add cost [k], and inflows of $6,500 and $7,200 in August and September sit well below outflows of $15,800 and $15,100 [app], so the balance could reach about -$8,200 by the end of September before festive sales arrive [an]. Overall, Marcus should arrange the $20,000 overdraft [eval], because the interest cost is lower than the risk of empty shelves in the two months that generate 55% of annual revenue [eval].
    Keywords: $20,000, $14,000, $6,500, $7,200, $15,800, $15,100, 55%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an overdraft bridges short-term gaps but carries interest; supplier goodwill is vital to secure festive stock | application_max_2: $14,000 September invoices and $20,000 overdraft option; inflows of $6,500 and $7,200 against outflows of $15,800 and $15,100 | analysis_max_2: supplier trust secures stock for the festive peak; interest adds cost while the balance approaches -$8,200 before December | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to 55% of annual revenue arriving in November-December

--- STEM ---
Bramble & Board Catering Co is a private limited company run by director Lena Ortiz in Country X with 14 staff, providing wedding and conference catering. Annual revenue is $680,000, and 65% of it arrives between May and September. Monthly fixed costs are $17,500. Wedding clients pay a 25% deposit at booking and the balance 14 days before the event.

Lena has forecast a quiet first quarter: inflows of $9,000 in January, $11,000 in February, $13,500 in March and $18,000 in April, against constant outflows of $21,000 a month. The opening balance on 1 January is $14,000. She is deciding between a $20,000 short-term bank loan at 9% interest, repayable in October, and asking her two largest suppliers to wait 60 days for payment.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'cash-flow forecast'.
    Answer: A cash-flow forecast is a document estimating a business's cash inflows, outflows, net cash flow and opening and closing balances for each future period [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: estimates future cash inflows and outflows; shows net cash flow and opening/closing balances per period

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why a catering company can be profitable yet still run out of cash.
    Answer: Reason 1: Profit is recognised when revenue is earned, not when cash is received [k], so wedding balances paid 14 days before events may still leave Bramble & Board short in January [app]. Reason 2: Deposits of 25% arrive months before work is done [k], making some months look strong while $17,500 of fixed costs falls due every month [app].
    Keywords: 25%, 14 days, $17,500, $680,000, $9,000, May and September
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: profit and cash differ because of timing differences; fixed costs must be paid even when inflows are weak | application_max_2: wedding balances paid 14 days before the event leave January short; 25% deposits arrive early while $17,500 costs fall due monthly

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Bramble & Board of taking the $20,000 short-term bank loan instead of delaying supplier payments.
    Answer: Advantage 1: The loan protects supplier relationships [k], so flour, meat and equipment suppliers keep delivering on normal terms through the quiet first quarter [app], avoiding stopped deliveries in the busy May to September season [an]. Advantage 2: The loan gives a known repayment schedule at 9% interest [k], and October wedding receipts, part of the 65% of revenue earned between May and September, can repay it [app], so the debt is cleared from peak-season cash [an].
    Keywords: $20,000, 9%, 65%, May and September, $17,500, $21,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a bank loan provides known, structured finance without straining suppliers; protecting supplier credit terms avoids supply disruption | application_max_2: $20,000 loan at 9% interest repayable in October; October receipts form part of the 65% of revenue earned May-September | analysis_max_2: avoids stopped deliveries heading into the peak season; debt cleared from peak-season cash rather than stretched into spring

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Lena should take the $20,000 short-term bank loan rather than ask suppliers to wait 60 days? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Taking the loan secures supplies and preserves goodwill with the two largest suppliers [k], at a known cost of 9% interest on $20,000 until October [app], so Lena keeps full reliability for the May to September peak [an]. However, asking suppliers to wait 60 days costs nothing in interest [k], and outflows of $21,000 a month against January inflows of $9,000 show a first-quarter gap that extra patience could bridge [app], so the loan could be unnecessary if suppliers agree [an]. Overall, Lena should take the loan [eval], because wedding clients book a year ahead and one failed delivery would cost more than the interest saved by stretching suppliers [eval].
    Keywords: $20,000, 9%, $21,000, $9,000, 60 days, May and September
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a short-term loan preserves supplier goodwill at a known interest cost; delaying payments to suppliers avoids interest but risks goodwill | application_max_2: $20,000 at 9% interest repayable in October; outflows of $21,000 a month against January inflows of $9,000 | analysis_max_2: reliance on suppliers without informing them risks hidden damage; the first-quarter gap could alternatively be bridged by 60-day patience | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing certain interest against vague supplier goodwill risk

--- STEM ---
Harvest Moon Pumpkin Farm is a partnership run by the Okoro family in Country X, employing 8 seasonal workers each October. It grows pumpkins for Halloween and keeps winter squash in storage for supermarket sales. Annual revenue is $230,000, with 80% earned in October and November. Monthly fixed costs are $6,200, and the family pays $34,000 for seeds, fertiliser and field preparation in March.

The family has forecast February to May: opening balance on 1 February of $11,500; inflows of $2,000 in February, $1,500 in March, $4,500 in April and $7,000 in May; outflows of $6,200 a month plus the $34,000 seed bill in March. The family must decide by 15 February whether to arrange a $35,000 overdraft or sell the older of their two tractors for $18,000 cash.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'liquidity'.
    Answer: Liquidity is how easily a business can turn its assets into cash in order to pay short-term debts as they fall due [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: liquidity measures ease of converting assets into cash; liquidity relates to paying short-term debts as they fall due

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Harvest Moon could be profitable overall yet very short of cash in spring.
    Answer: Reason 1: 80% of the $230,000 annual revenue arrives in October and November [k], so cash saved then must stretch across months like March when inflows are only $1,500 [app]. Reason 2: The $34,000 seed bill falls due in March before any pumpkins are sold [k], while fixed costs of $6,200 continue every month [app].
    Keywords: $230,000, October and November, $1,500, $34,000, $6,200, 80%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: profit and cash differ because of seasonal timing of inflows; large outflows may fall due before any sales revenue arrives | application_max_2: 80% of $230,000 arrives in October and November; March inflows of $1,500 against a $34,000 seed bill and $6,200 monthly costs

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of arranging the overdraft instead of selling the tractor.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Keeping both tractors protects the October harvest [k], so the 8 seasonal workers can still plant, cultivate and haul pumpkins at full speed [app], avoiding crop losses that would cost more than the overdraft interest [an]. Advantage 2: An overdraft is flexible [k], because the family draws only what it needs from February to April and repays it from the 80% of revenue earned in October and November [app], whereas a tractor sale is permanent and cannot be reversed [an].
    Keywords: $35,000, October, 8 seasonal workers, 80%, $18,000, $6,200
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: keeping productive assets protects output and revenue; overdrafts are flexible - draw only what is needed and repay from later inflows | application_max_2: both tractors needed for the October harvest with 8 seasonal workers; repayable from the 80% of revenue earned in October and November | analysis_max_2: avoids crop losses costing more than overdraft interest; tractor sale is permanent and reduces future capacity

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the Okoro family should arrange the overdraft rather than sell the tractor? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Arranging the overdraft keeps both tractors available for the October harvest [k], and the family can repay it from October and November sales worth 80% of $230,000 [app], so the seasonal cycle is funded and cleared within the year [an]. However, selling the tractor raises $18,000 immediately with no interest [k], and the forecast shows the balance falling to about -$33,100 by the end of April [app], so the $18,000 would only partly close the gap [an]. Overall, the family should arrange the overdraft [eval], because $35,000 covers the forecast April shortfall of about $33,100 while keeping the tractors needed to earn the sales that repay it [eval].
    Keywords: $35,000, 80%, $230,000, $18,000, October and November, $34,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an overdraft is flexible short-term finance repaid from later inflows; selling assets raises one-off cash but permanently reduces capacity | application_max_2: 80% of $230,000 arrives in October and November to repay an overdraft; forecast balance falls to about -$33,100 by end of April vs $18,000 tractor sale | analysis_max_2: the seasonal cycle is funded then cleared within one year; tractor proceeds only partly close the forecast gap | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the $35,000 overdraft vs a -$33,100 April trough

--- STEM ---
Bramshaw Wholesale Drinks Co is a private limited company distributing soft drinks and fruit juices to 140 corner shops across Country X. It is run by director Yusuf Demir with 18 staff and a fleet of 6 vans. Annual revenue is $1,900,000 on 60-day credit terms, and gross profit is $520,000. Monthly fixed costs are $38,000, and debtors currently owe $310,000.

Yusuf has prepared a cash-flow forecast for July and August showing an opening balance of $22,000 on 1 July, inflows of $95,000 in July and $88,000 in August, and outflows of $112,000 and $105,000. He must decide by 10 July between offering debtors a 2% early-payment discount and taking a $40,000 short-term loan at 10% interest, repayable in 6 months.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'debtors'.
    Answer: Debtors are customers who owe a business money for goods or services that have already been supplied to them on credit [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: debtors owe money to the business for goods/services supplied on credit; debtors are expected to pay within an agreed credit period

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways a 2% early-payment discount could improve Bramshaw's cash inflows.
    Answer: Reason 1: The 2% discount gives debtors an incentive to pay sooner [k], so some of the $310,000 owed could arrive before the usual 60-day terms [app]. Reason 2: Earlier payment raises each month's inflows [k], which would lift the forecast July inflow above $95,000 and stop the balance falling so sharply in August [app].
    Keywords: 2%, $310,000, 60-day, $95,000, $88,000, $22,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a cash discount encourages earlier payment from debtors; earlier receipts improve short-term cash inflows | application_max_2: some of the $310,000 owed could arrive before the 60-day terms; raising the July inflow above the forecast $95,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of taking the $40,000 short-term loan instead of offering the early-payment discount.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: The loan adds interest costs [k], roughly $2,000 over 6 months at 10% on $40,000 [app], which reduces cash available for wages, vans and stock [an]. Disadvantage 2: The loan must be repaid in 6 months [k], so $40,000 plus interest leaves the business again by January [app], while the discount is only paid on money actually collected early [an].
    Keywords: $40,000, 10%, 6 months, $520,000, $95,000, $310,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a loan carries certain interest charges; a loan creates a fixed repayment obligation | application_max_2: roughly $2,000 interest over 6 months at 10% on $40,000; the loan must be repaid in 6 months | analysis_max_2: interest reduces cash for other uses; repayment due by January while the discount only costs paid on receipts

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Yusuf should offer the 2% early-payment discount rather than take the $40,000 loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Offering the discount could convert part of the $310,000 debtors owe into cash within weeks [k], lifting July inflows above $95,000 and August above $88,000 [app], which could prevent the balance falling towards -$12,000 in August [an]. However, a 2% discount reduces revenue [k]; on a $95,000 month the discount costs about $1,900 [app], and not all debtors will pay faster, so the discount may not fully close the gap [an]. Overall, Yusuf should offer the discount [eval], because its cost is variable and only paid when cash arrives, unlike the certain $2,000 interest on the loan [eval].
    Keywords: $310,000, $95,000, $88,000, 2%, $40,000, 10%, 60-day
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an early-payment discount improves inflow timing at a variable cost; a loan provides certain cash at a fixed interest cost | application_max_2: $310,000 owed by debtors vs forecast inflows of $95,000 and $88,000; 2% on a $95,000 month costs about $1,900 | analysis_max_2: earlier cash could prevent the August balance dipping below zero; not every debtor pays early, so the gap may not close fully | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation comparing variable discount cost with certain loan interest

--- STEM ---
The Fig & Fiddle Café is a partnership run by Ana and Marco Silva in a Country X market town, employing 9 staff and serving all-day breakfasts, lunches and home baking. Weekend brunches are especially popular with visiting families. Annual revenue is $460,000, with 45% earned in December and during the summer tourist season. Last January revenue fell to $18,500 against fixed costs of $26,000.

The partners have forecast January and February: opening balance on 1 January of $5,400, January inflows of $18,500 and outflows of $30,200, and February inflows of $21,000 and outflows of $27,500. They must decide by 15 December whether to arrange a $15,000 overdraft or postpone the $12,000 kitchen equipment upgrade until April, when the spring tourist trade begins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'current assets'.
    Answer: Current assets are items owned by a business that are expected to be converted into cash or used up within one year, such as inventories, debtors and cash at bank [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: current assets are converted to cash or used within one year; examples include inventories, debtors and cash

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why The Fig & Fiddle Café can be profitable yet face a January cash shortfall.
    Answer: Reason 1: Profit is recognised when revenue is earned, not when cash arrives [k], so December's $460,000-a-year trading peak does not all land before January's $26,000 fixed costs fall due [app]. Reason 2: January revenue of $18,500 is far below the tourist peak [k], so inflows cannot cover the $30,200 of January outflows [app].
    Keywords: $26,000, $18,500, $460,000, 45%, $30,200, January
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: profit and cash differ because of timing differences; fixed costs continue regardless of monthly revenue swings | application_max_2: December income does not all arrive before January fixed costs of $26,000 are due; January revenue of $18,500 against outflows of $30,200

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of postponing the kitchen equipment upgrade instead of arranging an overdraft.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Postponing saves $12,000 of January outflows [k], which would more than close the forecast January gap of $11,700 between inflows of $18,500 and outflows of $30,200 [app], avoiding overdraft interest entirely [an]. Advantage 2: Upgrading in April lets the partners pay from spring tourist receipts [k], when revenue recovers towards the $460,000 annual level [app], so the equipment is funded from stronger inflows [an].
    Keywords: $12,000, $18,500, $30,200, April, $460,000, $15,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delaying capital expenditure removes a large outflow from the forecast; paying from stronger future inflows avoids borrowing costs | application_max_2: saving $12,000 of January outflows against an $11,700 gap; upgrading in April funded from the tourist recovery towards $460,000 | analysis_max_2: avoids overdraft interest entirely; equipment paid from stronger inflows rather than borrowed cash

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ana and Marco should postpone the equipment upgrade rather than arrange a $15,000 overdraft? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Postponing the upgrade avoids $12,000 of outflows in January [k], turning the forecast deficit into a near-break-even month and removing the need for overdraft borrowing [app], which keeps interest costs at zero [an]. However, without the upgrade the kitchen may struggle in the spring tourist season [k], and the partners would still face February outflows of $27,500 against inflows of $21,000 [app], so a smaller overdraft might still be needed [an]. Overall, the partners should postpone the upgrade [eval], because a four-month delay costs little goodwill compared with paying interest while the February shortfall approaches $12,800 [eval].
    Keywords: $12,000, $15,000, $27,500, $21,000, April, spring tourist
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delaying capital expenditure reduces the need for borrowed cash; an overdraft covers gaps but adds interest cost | application_max_2: saving $12,000 of January outflows; February outflows of $27,500 against inflows of $21,000 | analysis_max_2: immediate outflow removal turns January near break-even; February may still require a smaller overdraft | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing a four-month delay against interest and February's -$12,800 trough

--- STEM ---
Solace Fitness Studio is a private limited company in Country X run by director Hannah Lindqvist, offering personal training, group classes and a small gym. It employs 7 trainers and has 320 members paying $45 a month by direct debit. Annual revenue is $385,000. Monthly fixed costs are $19,800, and most income arrives reliably at the start of each month.

Hannah has forecast the first quarter: opening balance on 1 January of $9,300, January inflows of $24,500 against outflows of $21,000, February inflows of $22,000 against outflows of $20,400, and March inflows of $18,500 against outflows of $19,600. She is deciding whether to buy $16,000 of new gym equipment in January or spread the cost over 12 monthly payments of $1,450.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'creditors'.
    Answer: Creditors are suppliers or other organisations a business owes money to for goods or services received but not yet paid for [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: creditors are owed money by the business; for goods or services already received but unpaid

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Hannah should still prepare a monthly cash-flow forecast even though direct debits make inflows regular.
    Answer: Reason 1: Regular inflows can still fall below outflows [k], as March shows inflows of $18,500 against outflows of $19,600 [app]. Reason 2: One-off costs such as equipment purchases do not follow the monthly pattern [k], so a forecast tells Hannah whether $16,000 of equipment can be afforded in January [app].
    Keywords: $18,500, $19,600, $16,000, direct debit, $45 a month, 320 members
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: regular inflows do not guarantee every month stays positive; a forecast shows whether one-off items fit the budget | application_max_2: March inflows of $18,500 against outflows of $19,600; whether $16,000 of equipment can be afforded in January

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Solace Fitness Studio of spreading the equipment cost over 12 monthly payments instead of paying $16,000 up front.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Spreading the cost keeps the balance positive [k], since 12 payments of $1,450 avoid a one-off $16,000 hit in January [app], leaving the studio able to cover its $19,800 monthly fixed costs without borrowing [an]. Benefit 2: Spreading payments smooths cash through the quieter spring months [k], when March inflows of $18,500 already sit below outflows of $19,600 [app], so the studio is less likely to need an overdraft [an].
    Keywords: $1,450, $16,000, $19,800, $18,500, $19,600, January
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: spreading payments avoids a large one-off outflow; regular small payments are easier to budget around fixed costs | application_max_2: 12 payments of $1,450 instead of one $16,000 outflow; March inflows of $18,500 below outflows of $19,600 | analysis_max_2: fixed costs of $19,800 a month remain covered without borrowing; less reliance on an overdraft in the quiet spring

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hannah should buy the equipment in January by spreading the cost rather than paying $16,000 up front? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Spreading the cost keeps cash positive all through the first quarter [k], with the studio retaining its $9,300 opening balance and roughly $11,350 after January's payment [app], so $19,800 of fixed costs stay covered without an overdraft [an]. However, spreading the cost totals $17,400 [k], costing $1,400 more than the up-front price [app], and the studio may be locked into paying even if member numbers fall [an]. Overall, Hannah should spread the cost [eval], because the extra $1,400 is cheaper than overdraft interest and protects cash through the quiet March [eval].
    Keywords: $1,450, $16,000, $9,300, $19,800, 320 members, $45 a month
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: staged payments preserve short-term liquidity; spreading usually costs more in total than paying up front | application_max_2: 12 payments of $1,450 total $17,400, costing $1,400 extra; $9,300 opening balance with $19,800 monthly fixed costs | analysis_max_2: positive cash retained across the first quarter; fixed $1,450 payments bite if membership numbers fall | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation comparing $1,400 extra against overdraft interest and liquidity risk

--- STEM ---
Barley & Brioche Bakery Co is a private limited company in Country X run by directors Sam and Ruth Whitmore, employing 16 bakers and supplying fresh bread and pastries to 22 supermarkets. Annual revenue is $720,000 and supermarkets pay on 30-day credit terms. Monthly fixed costs are $24,000, and the bakery buys flour and butter for cash at the start of each month.

The October forecast shows inflows of $52,000 and outflows of $61,000, November inflows of $58,000 and outflows of $57,500, December inflows of $74,000 and outflows of $66,000, with an opening balance on 1 October of $13,600. A supermarket chain has offered a trial weekly order worth $9,600 a month from October if the bakery can hold $40,000 extra flour inventory.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'current liabilities'.
    Answer: Current liabilities are debts a business must repay within one year, such as trade payables, bank overdrafts and short-term loans [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: current liabilities are debts repayable within one year; examples include trade payables, overdrafts and short-term loans

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why rising sales to supermarkets could still leave Barley & Brioche short of cash.
    Answer: Reason 1: Supermarkets pay on 30-day credit terms [k], so the bakery buys flour and butter for cash now but receives payment for the $9,600 monthly order only weeks later [app]. Reason 2: Holding $40,000 of extra flour inventory locks cash up in stock [k], and October's forecast already shows outflows of $61,000 exceeding inflows of $52,000 [app].
    Keywords: 30-day, $9,600, $40,000, $61,000, $52,000, $24,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: credit sales delay cash receipts even when sales rise; extra inventory ties cash up in unsold goods | application_max_2: 30-day credit terms delay payment for the $9,600 monthly order; October outflows of $61,000 exceed inflows of $52,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the bakery could fund the supermarket trial order without harming its cash position.
    Answer: Way 1: The bakery could arrange an overdraft [k], sized to the forecast October drawdown after buying $40,000 of extra flour [app], which would smooth the gap until December's $74,000 inflows arrive [an]. Way 2: The bakery could ask the supermarket chain for shorter credit terms or a deposit [k], since the trial order is unproven and payment usually comes after 30 days [app], bringing cash in earlier and shrinking the borrowing needed [an].
    Keywords: $40,000, $74,000, $61,000, 30-day, $13,600, trial weekly order
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an overdraft funds short-term gaps and is repaid from later inflows; negotiating faster payment or deposits improves inflow timing | application_max_2: overdraft needed after buying $40,000 of extra flour in October; December inflows of $74,000 would repay the borrowing | analysis_max_2: smooths the gap until December's inflows arrive; earlier cash in shrinks the total borrowing required

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sam and Ruth should accept the supermarket trial order? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the order adds $9,600 a month of repeat revenue [k], building on December inflows of $74,000 [app], and a successful trial could open regular weekly supply across the chain [an]. However, accepting requires $40,000 of extra flour inventory in October [k], when the forecast closes October at only $4,600 and December at about $13,100 [app], so the bakery would need an overdraft until supermarket payments start arriving [an]. Overall, Sam and Ruth should accept the order [eval], because $9,600 a month of new revenue justifies a short-term overdraft that by December inflows can repay comfortably [eval].
    Keywords: $9,600, $74,000, $40,000, $13,600, 30-day, October
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: new recurring orders raise revenue but may require extra working capital; overdrafts bridge short gaps before larger inflows arrive | application_max_2: $9,600 a month of new revenue on top of December inflows of $74,000; $40,000 extra flour needed against October forecast close of $4,600 | analysis_max_2: trial could open a larger weekly supply relationship; overdraft required until supermarket cash receipts begin | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation comparing recurring $9,600 revenue with temporary overdraft need

--- STEM ---
Copperpipe Plumbing & Heating is a private limited company in Country X run by director Dan Kovac, employing 6 plumbers and 2 apprentices. annual revenue reached $390,000 last year. Boiler repairs and installations spike in winter, and most jobs are paid on completion; in summer, commercial contracts pay after 60 days. Monthly fixed costs are $15,500, and the older van has covered 140,000 miles.

Dan has forecast November inflows of $48,500 against outflows of $39,800, and December inflows of $56,000 against outflows of $52,300. The opening balance on 1 November is $17,200. He must decide by 31 October whether to buy a $30,000 van now for the winter rush or wait until the spring quiet period to replace the ageing van.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'cash flow'.
    Answer: Cash flow is the movement of money into and out of a business over a period, shown as inflows, outflows and the resulting net cash flow [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cash flow is the movement of money in and out of the business; measured as inflows minus outflows, giving net cash flow

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why winter is both the busiest and the riskiest season for Copperpipe's cash flow.
    Answer: Reason 1: Winter brings the highest job volumes [k], pushing inflows to $48,500 in November and $56,000 in December [app]. Reason 2: Winter jobs increase outflows for materials, parts and overtime [k], which explains November outflows of $39,800 and December outflows of $52,300 [app].
    Keywords: $48,500, $56,000, $39,800, $52,300, $390,000, 60 days
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: peak season means high job volumes and high receipts; peak season also drives higher outflows for parts and labour | application_max_2: inflows of $48,500 in November and $56,000 in December; outflows of $39,800 in November and $52,300 in December

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Dan could cover the November shortfall if he buys the van now.
    Answer: Way 1: Dan could arrange an overdraft with the bank [k], covering the forecast dip to about -$4,100 after paying $30,000 for the van [app], which lets the business complete winter jobs that would otherwise be turned away [an]. Way 2: Dan could delay non-essential equipment purchases [k], protecting the November balance of $25,900 before the van payment [app], so the cash gap stays smaller and interest costs are limited [an].
    Keywords: $30,000, $17,200, $48,500, $39,800, winter rush, 2 apprentices
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an overdraft covers short-term shortfalls up to an agreed limit; delaying non-essential spending reduces outflows | application_max_2: forecast dip to about -$4,100 after paying $30,000 for the van; protecting the November balance of $25,900 before the payment | analysis_max_2: keeps capacity to complete winter jobs that would be turned away; smaller gap means lower interest costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Dan should buy the van in November rather than wait until spring? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying now captures the winter rush [k], when inflows of $48,500 and $56,000 in November and December justify extra capacity [app], and the new van could generate enough extra jobs to pay for itself [an]. However, paying $30,000 in November drops the balance from $25,900 to about -$4,100 [k], forcing reliance on the bank through December [app], so the shortfall would need covering before spring work restarts [an]. Overall, Dan should buy the van now [eval], because missing the winter peak would lose more revenue than the modest overdraft needed to bridge two months [eval].
    Keywords: $30,000, $48,500, $56,000, $17,200, winter rush, spring
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: buying capacity ahead of peak season captures extra revenue; large one-off purchases can push cash negative in the short term | application_max_2: November and December inflows of $48,500 and $56,000 vs a $30,000 van; balance falls from $25,900 to about -$4,100 after purchase | analysis_max_2: extra capacity could pay for itself in the winter rush; reliance on the bank until spring receipts arrive | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation comparing lost winter revenue against two months of overdraft

--- STEM ---
Brackmere Paint & Decor is an independent paint and decorating-supplies shop in Country X, owned by Priya Raman for 6 years. It employs 9 staff and sells paint, tools and wallpaper to trade customers and homeowners, generating $680,000 in annual revenue. Current assets are $92,000, including $38,000 owed by trade debtors, while current liabilities are $74,000, including a $30,000 bank overdraft.

Priya has been offered a $150,000 contract to supply paint for a new office block in 4 months, but the client will pay 90 days after the work is completed. She is considering two options: ask existing debtors to pay 30 days sooner in exchange for a 2% discount, or arrange a bank overdraft of $40,000 to bridge the gap.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'working capital'.
    Answer: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. It measures the cash and other short-term assets available to fund day-to-day trading after short-term debts are accounted for [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working capital equals current assets minus current liabilities; it represents funds available for day-to-day operations / paying short-term debts

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Brackmere Paint & Decor needs sufficient working capital.
    Answer: Reason 1: Sufficient working capital allows a business to pay its short-term debts when they fall due [k], which matters because Brackmere's current liabilities are $74,000, including a $30,000 bank overdraft [app]. Reason 2: Working capital keeps a business trading while it waits for money it is owed to arrive [k], as $38,000 of Brackmere's $92,000 current assets is owed by trade debtors [app].
    Keywords: $92,000, $38,000, $74,000, $30,000 bank overdraft, trade debtors, $680,000, current assets, current liabilities
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working capital pays short-term debts / liabilities as they fall due; working capital funds day-to-day trading while awaiting payment from debtors | application_max_2: current liabilities are $74,000 including a $30,000 bank overdraft; $38,000 of current assets is owed by trade debtors

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Brackmere of asking existing debtors to pay sooner.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Getting cash in from debtors sooner brings money into the business faster [k], helping Priya fund the $150,000 office-block contract before the client pays 90 days after completion [app], which reduces the need to arrange the $40,000 bank overdraft [an]. Benefit 2: Converting $38,000 owed by trade debtors into cash more quickly would strengthen Brackmere's position [k], where current liabilities of $74,000 already exceed the cash balance and current assets of $92,000 leave only $18,000 of working capital [app], easing pressure on day-to-day payments such as wages and suppliers [an].
    Keywords: $150,000, 90 days, $40,000, $38,000, $92,000, 2% discount, current liabilities, trade debtors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: receiving debtor payments sooner speeds up cash inflows; faster collection improves the firm's cash / working capital position | application_max_2: the $150,000 office-block contract is paid 90 days after completion; $38,000 is owed by trade debtors while current liabilities are $74,000 | analysis_max_2: earlier collection reduces reliance on the $40,000 bank overdraft; stronger cash position eases payment of day-to-day expenses such as wages and suppliers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Priya should ask existing debtors to pay sooner or arrange the $40,000 bank overdraft? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Asking debtors to pay sooner would inject cash without further borrowing [k], and it directly tackles the $38,000 owed by trade debtors that is straining Brackmere's cash while current liabilities stand at $74,000 [app]. This would help fund the $150,000 contract sooner and reduce dependence on the $40,000 bank overdraft [an]. However, offering a 2% discount would cost money on every early-paying invoice [k], cutting into the $680,000 annual revenue Brackmere currently earns [app], and some debtors may still pay late despite the incentive, so the discount could be paid out without securing faster cash [an]. On balance, for a one-off gap of 4 months on a single contract, the bank overdraft is the more reliable option because it can be drawn down and repaid as soon as the contract client pays [eval]. Brackmere already uses a $30,000 bank overdraft within its current liabilities, so extending this arrangement is a familiar, flexible tool. Overall, Priya should arrange the $40,000 bank overdraft rather than discount debtors, since the 2% discount is a recurring cost while the overdraft is temporary and matches the 90-day payment gap [eval].
    Keywords: $150,000, 90 days, $40,000, $38,000, $74,000, $30,000 bank overdraft, 2% discount, $680,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: asking debtors to pay faster is an internal way to improve cash inflows; a bank overdraft provides flexible short-term borrowing repaid when cash arrives | application_max_2: $38,000 is owed by trade debtors and current liabilities are $74,000; the office-block contract is worth $150,000 with payment 90 days after completion | analysis_max_2: discount speeds up cash but permanently reduces margins on each early invoice; overdraft is repayable once the contract client pays, matching the short-term gap | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring one option with clear reasoning; weighs cost of discount against flexibility/temporary nature of overdraft

--- STEM ---
Darrowmere Marine Engines is a private limited company in Country X, repairing and servicing fishing-boat engines for 8 years. It employs 14 mechanics and turns over $540,000 a year. The workshop serves 30 regular fishing boats each month, with demand peaking before the autumn fishing season. At the end of May, current assets were $61,000 but current liabilities were $78,000, leaving negative working capital of $17,000. The workshop must pay $45,000 for engine parts within 10 days to keep its repair contract with the local fishing fleet.

Managing director Joss Darrow is considering two options: extend the existing $25,000 bank overdraft to $70,000, or take out a $45,000 bank loan at 9% interest per year, repayable over 3 years. Any borrowing would be paid from future repair income.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'bank overdraft'.
    Answer: A bank overdraft allows a business to withdraw more money than it holds in its current account, up to an agreed limit, with interest charged on the amount actually overdrawn [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: an overdraft lets the business spend more than its current account balance; interest is charged on the amount overdrawn, up to an agreed limit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Darrowmere Marine Engines needs sufficient working capital.
    Answer: Reason 1: Working capital allows a business to meet its short-term debts as they fall due [k], which is critical for Darrowmere as current liabilities of $78,000 exceed current assets of $61,000 [app]. Reason 2: Sufficient working capital keeps a workshop trading without interruption [k], as Darrowmere must pay $45,000 for engine parts within 10 days to keep its fishing-fleet repair contract [app].
    Keywords: $61,000, $78,000, $17,000, $45,000, 10 days, fishing fleet
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working capital pays short-term debts and obligations; working capital funds continuous day-to-day trading | application_max_2: current liabilities of $78,000 exceed current assets of $61,000; $45,000 for engine parts is due within 10 days to keep the fishing-fleet contract

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two differences between a bank overdraft and a bank loan as ways to overcome a short-term cash-flow problem.
    Answer: Difference 1: An overdraft is a flexible limit on the current account with interest charged only on the amount used [k], so Darrowmere could extend its $25,000 overdraft to cover the $45,000 parts bill and repay it as repair income arrives [app], which is ideal if the cash gap lasts only a few weeks [an]. Difference 2: A bank loan is a fixed sum borrowed for a set term with interest paid over the whole period [k], so the $45,000 loan at 9% interest repayable over 3 years spreads the cost predictably [app], but Darrowmere would keep paying interest even after the cash crisis has passed [an].
    Keywords: $25,000, $70,000, $45,000, 9% interest, 3 years, $540,000, fishing-boat engines
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: overdraft is flexible, interest only on amount used; loan is a fixed sum repaid over a set term with interest | application_max_2: the $25,000 overdraft could be extended to cover the $45,000 parts bill; the $45,000 loan at 9% interest is repayable over 3 years | analysis_max_2: overdraft suits a gap of only a few weeks as it is repaid quickly; loan interest continues over 3 years even after the cash crisis passes

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Joss should extend the overdraft to $70,000 or take the $45,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Extending the overdraft to $70,000 gives Darrowmere an immediate buffer with interest charged only on what is used [k], matching the $45,000 parts bill due within 10 days and the one-off nature of the gap [app]. If repair income recovers within weeks, total interest would be far below paying 9% on a $45,000 loan for 3 years [an]. However, the bank can demand repayment of an overdraft at short notice [k], which is risky for a firm whose current liabilities of $78,000 already exceed current assets of $61,000, leaving negative working capital of $17,000 [app]. The 3-year loan guarantees the $45,000 and cannot be withdrawn early, though it costs about $4,050 of interest each year plus the fixed repayments [an]. On balance, the bank loan is the safer choice because it cannot be recalled and fixes the repayment schedule while Darrowmere rebuilds its working capital [eval]. The loan also forces disciplined budgeting, whereas an extended overdraft could mask a deeper cash problem. Overall, Joss should take the $45,000 bank loan, since the predictable cost of about $4,050 a year is a fair price for security of funding [eval].
    Keywords: $25,000, $70,000, $45,000, 9%, $78,000, $61,000, $17,000, 10 days
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: overdraft is repayable on demand with interest on the amount used; loan is fixed for a term and cannot be withdrawn early | application_max_2: parts bill of $45,000 is due within 10 days to keep the fishing-fleet contract; current liabilities of $78,000 exceed current assets of $61,000, leaving negative working capital of $17,000 | analysis_max_2: loan guarantees funding but costs about $4,050 interest each year; overdraft is cheaper if repaid quickly but risky if called in | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring one option with clear reasoning; weighs security of loan funding against flexibility and cost of overdraft

--- STEM ---
Kettleworth Bakery is a family partnership in Country X, operating from a unit on the industrial estate and supplying bread and rolls to 45 cafes and grocery stores for 11 years. It employs 16 bakers and has annual sales of $720,000. The bakery pays flour and packaging suppliers within 30 days and is owed $52,000 by customers on 60-day terms. Current assets are $84,000 and current liabilities are $65,000.

A $120,000 industrial mixer has broken and the bakery urgently needs $30,000 to repair or replace it or lose its wholesale contract. Owner Marta Kettle is considering two options: ask suppliers for an extra 30 days of credit, delaying payment from 30 to 60 days, or arrange a $30,000 bank overdraft at 12% interest a year with the bakery's bank.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'creditors'.
    Answer: Creditors are people or businesses to whom money is owed, usually because goods or services have been bought on credit terms and have not yet been paid for [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: creditors are people or businesses the firm owes money to; the debt usually arises from goods or services bought on credit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Kettleworth Bakery needs sufficient working capital.
    Answer: Reason 1: Working capital allows a business to buy the materials it needs for daily trading [k], as Kettleworth must buy flour and packaging and pay its suppliers within 30 days [app]. Reason 2: Working capital allows a business to keep operating while awaiting payment from customers [k], since $52,000 of Kettleworth's money is owed by customers paying on 60-day terms [app].
    Keywords: $720,000, $52,000, $84,000, $65,000, 30 days, 60-day terms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working capital funds purchase of stock and daily running costs; working capital supports trading while awaiting debtor payments | application_max_2: the bakery pays flour and packaging suppliers within 30 days; $52,000 is owed by customers on 60-day terms

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Kettleworth may face if it delays payments to suppliers.
    Answer: Problem 1: Delaying payment breaks the trust that suppliers place in the business [k], so flour and packaging suppliers who currently wait 30 days may refuse the extra 30 days Marta requests, or stop deliveries to the bakery [app], threatening the wholesale contract with 45 cafes and grocery stores that depends on daily supply [an]. Problem 2: Late payment can increase the cost of buying on credit [k], for example through lost cash discounts or tighter terms on the $720,000 of annual sales [app], reducing the bakery's profit on each sale and cutting working capital further [an].
    Keywords: 30 days, $52,000, 45 cafes and grocery stores, $720,000, $30,000, current liabilities
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delaying creditors damages supplier trust and relationships; late payment can lead to lost discounts or tighter credit terms | application_max_2: suppliers currently wait 30 days and Marta asks for an extra 30 days; the bakery supplies 45 cafes and grocery stores on $720,000 of annual sales | analysis_max_2: stopping deliveries would threaten the wholesale contract and daily supply; tighter terms or lost discounts reduce profit and available working capital

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marta should ask suppliers for an extra 30 days of credit or arrange the $30,000 bank overdraft? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Asking suppliers for an extra 30 days of credit would preserve Kettleworth's cash without any interest cost [k], which is attractive because current assets of $84,000 and current liabilities of $65,000 leave only $19,000 of working capital [app]. Delaying payment from 30 to 60 days would free up cash to repair the equipment and protect the wholesale contract [an]. However, stretching suppliers risks deliveries being stopped or terms tightened [k], and the bakery depends on daily flour and packaging supplies to serve 45 cafes and grocery stores on $720,000 of annual sales [app]; a single missed delivery could lose customers to rivals [an]. A $30,000 bank overdraft at 12% interest would cost about $3,600 a year in interest , keeping suppliers happy and deliveries reliable, though it adds a permanent finance cost and the overdraft could be called in. On balance, the overdraft is the better choice because supplier goodwill is fragile and the interest of about $3,600 a year is modest compared with losing the wholesale contract [eval]. Overall, Marta should arrange the $30,000 bank overdraft rather than delay supplier payments, since reliable supply matters more than the interest saved [eval].
    Keywords: $84,000, $65,000, $30,000, 12% interest, 45 cafes and grocery stores, $720,000, 30 to 60 days, $120,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delaying payments to creditors is an internal way to ease cash-flow pressure; an overdraft is flexible short-term borrowing charged at interest | application_max_2: current assets $84,000 and current liabilities $65,000 leave working capital of $19,000; the bakery serves 45 cafes and grocery stores on $720,000 of annual sales | analysis_max_2: delayed payment risks deliveries stopping and losing the wholesale contract; overdraft interest of about $3,600 a year (12% of $30,000) is modest but ongoing | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring one option with clear reasoning; weighs supplier goodwill and supply reliability against interest cost

Rising timber prices have cut the cash balance to $18,000, and the firm owes $60,000 to suppliers within 3 weeks.   Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Aldermist Furniture Co needs sufficient working capital.

Reason 2: Working capital funds daily production and operating costs [k], which matters because Aldermist employs 26 workers to make wooden office furniture but its cash balance has fallen sharply with rising timber prices [app].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working capital pays immediate short-term debts; working capital funds day-to-day operating costs such as wages and materials | application_max_2: Aldermist owes $60,000 to suppliers within 3 weeks against a cash balance of $18,000; the company employs 26 workers amid rising timber prices

Benefit 2: Avoiding the $85,000 bank loan saves $6,800 of interest a year at 8% [k], reducing fixed finance costs that would otherwise eat into profits from the $1,150,000 of annual revenue [app], improving the working capital left after paying current liabilities of $95,000 [an].

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sofia should cancel the machine purchase or buy the machine now using the $85,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cancelling the machine purchase preserves Aldermist's cash [k], which is vital with only $18,000 in the bank and $60,000 owed to suppliers within 3 weeks [app], so wages and materials can be paid and production can continue without disruption [an]. However, delaying the sawing machine means the efficiency and output gains it offers arrive later [k], and 26 workers continue cutting timber manually while the firm generates $1,150,000 in annual revenue [app]; if a rival modernises first, Aldermist could lose orders [an]. Buying now with an $85,000 loan at 8% interest costs about $6,800 a year but spreads the cost while securing the machine's benefits immediately . On balance, cancelling is the safer option this year because survival and paying suppliers come before growth, and the loan's $6,800 annual interest would further strain working capital of only $45,000 [eval]. Sofia could revisit the purchase once the supplier debt is cleared and cash recovers. Overall, Sofia should cancel the machine purchase now and reconsider it later from healthier cash flow rather than take on an $85,000 loan [eval].
    Keywords: $85,000, $18,000, $60,000, 3 weeks, $1,150,000, 8% interest, $95,000, $140,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cancelling planned capital expenditure is a recognised way to ease short-term cash flow; delaying capital spending preserves cash for urgent obligations | application_max_2: cash balance is $18,000 against $60,000 owed within 3 weeks; the machine costs $85,000 and a loan at 8% costs about $6,800 a year | analysis_max_2: keeping cash avoids default and keeps production running; buying now spreads cost but adds about $6,800 yearly interest and strains working capital | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring one option with clear reasoning; weighs immediate survival/supplier payments against efficiency gains of the machine

Fenwhistle Farm Supplies is a wholesale agricultural supplier in Country X selling animal feed, seed and fertiliser for 14 years.     Question: Define 'current assets'.

  Qb [4 marks]

Reason 2: Working capital allows a business to cover the gap between outflows and inflows [k], as $64,000 of its current assets is owed by farm customers who now take 75 days to pay instead of the agreed 45 [app].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working capital funds stock purchases and daily running costs; working capital bridges the gap between making payments and receiving cash | application_max_2: the business must stock feed, seed and fertiliser for farms; $64,000 is owed by farm customers taking 75 days instead of the agreed 45

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Fenwhistle of offering a 3% discount for payment within 20 days.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The discount gives farm customers an incentive to settle bills quickly [k], targeting the $64,000 owed by customers who currently take 75 days instead of the agreed 45 [app], which turns slow debts into cash more quickly [an]. Benefit 2: Faster collection reduces the need to borrow [k], helping Fenwhistle avoid the $50,000 bank loan and its interest costs on current working capital of only $31,000 [app], easing the pressure on cash for wages and warehouse costs [an].
    Keywords: 3% discount, 20 days, $64,000, 75 days, agreed 45, $50,000, $31,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a cash discount incentivises debtors to pay earlier; earlier collection reduces reliance on external borrowing | application_max_2: $64,000 is owed by farm customers paying in 75 days instead of the agreed 45; current working capital is only $31,000 against a proposed $50,000 bank loan | analysis_max_2: earlier payment converts debtors into usable cash; avoiding the loan saves interest and eases cash pressure

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ben should offer the 3% discount or borrow $50,000 from the bank? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Offering a 3% discount within 20 days would encourage farms to pay the $64,000 owed much sooner [k], directly reducing the 75-day average payment period towards the agreed 45 days [app] and releasing working capital without any new debt [an]. On balance, the discount is the better option because it fixes the root cause of the cash shortfall rather than masking it with more borrowing [eval]. The cost of the discount is limited and only applies to early payers, while the loan's interest would be an ongoing burden. Overall, Ben should offer the 3% discount to collect the $64,000 faster, reserving a loan as a fallback if cash is still short [eval].
    Keywords: 3% discount, 20 days, $64,000, 75 days, agreed 45, $890,000, $50,000, $87,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a settlement discount motivates debtors to pay faster; a bank loan provides funds but increases liabilities and interest costs | application_max_2: $64,000 is owed by farm customers taking 75 days instead of the agreed 45; current liabilities are $87,000 and annual revenue is $890,000 | analysis_max_2: discount tackles the root cause of slow-paying debtors without new debt; loan protects revenue but adds ongoing interest on top of current liabilities | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring one option with clear reasoning; weighs discount cost against loan interest and liability increase

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delaying capital expenditure keeps cash in the business; delaying a purchase avoids borrowing and interest costs | application_max_2: current assets are $150,000 against current liabilities of $110,000; a $70,000 loan at 10% costs about $7,000 a year | analysis_max_2: cash is preserved for wages and materials during the 4-month wait; saving interest retains more of the $1,300,000 revenue as profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Leanne should delay the truck purchase or take the $70,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.

However, the ageing trucks may break down before the 4-month wait is over [k], disrupting site deliveries and risking delays on warehouse projects built by 32 workers [app], and any repair bills or lost time could cost more than the interest saved [an]. Taking the $70,000 loan gets reliable new trucks now and lets Colmworth complete jobs on schedule, though the interest adds to annual costs on top of existing obligations . On balance, delaying the purchase is the better option because the cash gap is clearly temporary and ends in 4 months, so interest would be pure extra cost [eval]. The trucks can be bought as soon as the $95,000 lands, keeping the firm debt-free. Overall, Leanne should delay the truck purchase rather than borrow, provided the old trucks remain serviceable for 4 months [eval].
    Keywords: $95,000, 4 months, $70,000, 10% interest, $150,000, $110,000, $1,300,000, 32 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delaying planned capital expenditure is a recognised way to ease short-term cash flow; a loan provides immediate funds at the cost of interest | application_max_2: current assets $150,000 and current liabilities $110,000 leave working capital of $40,000; the $95,000 is received in 4 months' time | analysis_max_2: delay avoids around $7,000 yearly interest and preserves cash; truck breakdown risk could delay projects and cost more than interest | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring one option with clear reasoning; weighs certain interest cost against risk of ageing trucks failing

--- STEM ---
Saltcove Harbour Hotel is a 28-room coastal hotel in Country X, owned by Renata Duarte for 7 years. It employs 19 staff and generates $760,000 in annual revenue, much of it earned during the busy summer season and growing each year. Current assets are $34,000, including $9,000 in cash, but current liabilities are $52,000, leaving negative working capital of $18,000. Staff wages of $15,000 are due at the end of this month, and a $25,000 loan repayment is due in 6 weeks.

Renata is considering two options: delay payments to suppliers by an extra 30 days to keep cash in the business, or negotiate a long-term loan of $40,000 from the bank to clear the shortfall before the summer bookings begin.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'current liabilities'.
    Answer: Current liabilities are amounts owed by a business that must be repaid within one year, such as trade creditors, bank overdrafts and short-term loans [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: current liabilities are debts repayable within one year; examples include trade creditors, overdrafts and short-term loans

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Saltcove Harbour Hotel needs sufficient working capital.
    Answer: Reason 1: Working capital allows a business to pay its most urgent short-term debts [k], which is critical for Saltcove with current liabilities of $52,000 exceeding current assets of $34,000 [app]. Reason 2: Sufficient working capital keeps a hotel operating day to day [k], as wages of $15,000 are due at the end of this month and 19 staff must be paid so guests can be served [app].
    Keywords: $34,000, $52,000, $9,000, $15,000, $25,000, 19 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working capital pays short-term debts and obligations; working capital funds day-to-day operations such as wages | application_max_2: current liabilities of $52,000 exceed current assets of $34,000; wages of $15,000 are due at the end of this month for 19 staff

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Saltcove may face if it delays payments to suppliers by an extra 30 days.
    Answer: Problem 1: Delaying payment to suppliers can damage the relationship with those suppliers [k], so the food and beverage suppliers delivering daily to a 28-room hotel may demand immediate payment or refuse further credit [app], disrupting the kitchen and the quality of guest service [an]. Problem 2: Late payment may increase costs for the hotel [k], for example through lost prompt-payment discounts on the $760,000 of annual revenue [app], squeezing profit margins on every room sold and shrinking working capital further [an].
    Keywords: 28-room, $760,000, $52,000, 30 days, $15,000, current liabilities
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delaying creditors damages supplier relationships and trust; late payment can raise costs through lost discounts or tighter terms | application_max_2: a 28-room hotel depends on daily food and beverage deliveries; the hotel generates $760,000 in annual revenue with current liabilities of $52,000 | analysis_max_2: suppliers refusing credit would disrupt guest service; lost discounts squeeze margins and shrink working capital further

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Renata should delay payments to suppliers or negotiate the $40,000 long-term loan? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Delaying payments to suppliers keeps cash in the hotel without extra borrowing [k], which matters when current assets are $34,000 against current liabilities of $52,000 [app], easing pressure on the $15,000 wages due this month [an]. However, delaying payments risks souring relations with suppliers [k], and a 28-room hotel depends on daily food and beverage deliveries to sustain $760,000 in annual revenue [app]; if suppliers refuse credit, service would collapse at the busiest time [an]. A $40,000 long-term loan would clear the shortfall and rebuild positive working capital, though it adds monthly repayments and interest. On balance, the long-term loan is the better option because it addresses the root deficit instead of borrowing goodwill from suppliers [eval]. Interest and repayments can be planned across the year, unlike supplier patience, which can run out at any time. Overall, Renata should negotiate the $40,000 long-term loan to stabilise the hotel's finances, treating delayed supplier payments as a last resort only [eval].
    Keywords: $34,000, $52,000, $15,000, 28-room, $760,000, $40,000, 30 days, $9,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: delaying creditors is an internal way to keep cash in the business; a long-term loan provides funds repaid over an extended period with interest | application_max_2: current assets are $34,000 against current liabilities of $52,000; the hotel generates $760,000 in annual revenue and wages of $15,000 are due soon | analysis_max_2: delayed payment risks suppliers refusing credit and service collapsing; the loan fixes the deficit but adds planned repayments and interest | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring one option with clear reasoning; weighs zero-cost delay against supplier-risk versus the structured loan

--- STEM ---
Fenmeadow Clothing is a menswear and womenswear retailer in Country X, trading through two high-street stores for 5 years. It employs 17 staff and has annual sales of $640,000, with a steady trade in school and work uniforms throughout the year. Current assets are $78,000, of which $45,000 is owed by employers on 60-day credit for staff uniforms, and current liabilities are $69,000.

The business urgently needs $35,000 for rent and insurance due in 3 weeks, and the refurbishment of the second store was planned for next spring. Owner Aisha Farouk is considering two options: offer uniform customers a 2.5% discount to settle invoices within 14 days, or postpone the $60,000 refurbishment of the second store for a year to preserve cash.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'debtors'.
    Answer: Debtors are customers or businesses that owe money to the business, usually for goods sold on credit, and they are recorded as current assets [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: debtors are customers or businesses owing the firm money; the debt usually arises from goods sold on credit

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Fenmeadow Clothing needs sufficient working capital.
    Answer: Reason 1: Working capital allows a business to meet short-term debts on time [k], as Fenmeadow urgently needs $35,000 for rent and insurance due in 3 weeks [app]. Reason 2: Working capital supports daily retail operations [k], and 17 staff across two high-street stores must be paid from the trading cash tied to $640,000 of annual sales [app].
    Keywords: $78,000, $45,000, $69,000, $35,000, 3 weeks, $640,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: working capital pays short-term debts and bills on time; working capital funds daily operations such as wages and stock | application_max_2: Fenmeadow urgently needs $35,000 for rent and insurance due in 3 weeks; 17 staff work across two stores on $640,000 of annual sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Fenmeadow of postponing the $60,000 refurbishment for a year.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Postponing the refurbishment keeps $60,000 in the business [k], so the urgent $35,000 rent and insurance bill due in 3 weeks can be paid without draining the $78,000 of current assets needed for stock [app], avoiding late-payment penalties [an]. Benefit 2: Delaying the spend avoids new borrowing [k], sparing the retailer interest and leaving the $9,000 of working capital available for wages and suppliers [app], which strengthens day-to-day stability while debtors still take 60 days to pay [an].
    Keywords: $60,000, $35,000, 3 weeks, $78,000, $45,000, 60-day credit, $640,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: postponing capital expenditure keeps cash in the business; delaying major spending avoids new borrowing and interest | application_max_2: the refurbishment costs $60,000 and $35,000 is due for rent and insurance in 3 weeks; current assets are $78,000 leaving working capital of $9,000 | analysis_max_2: keeping cash avoids penalties and protects stock levels; avoiding borrowing preserves the $9,000 of working capital

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Aisha should offer the 2.5% discount to debtors or postpone the refurbishment? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Offering a 2.5% discount to settle within 14 days turns slow debtors into fast cash [k], targeting the $45,000 owed by employers on 60-day credit [app], which would directly cover the $35,000 rent and insurance due in 3 weeks [an]. However, the discount costs money on every invoice settled early [k], trimming revenue below the $640,000 annual sales level on a margin-sensitive uniform trade [app], and employers who already pay within 14 days would receive a discount for nothing [an]. Postponing the $60,000 refurbishment preserves cash without discounting, though the second store stays dated for another year. On balance, postponing the refurbishment is the safer choice because it creates no direct cost, unlike the discount which eats directly into sales revenue [eval]. It also removes the $60,000 commitment from a business whose current liabilities of $69,000 already exceed what the $9,000 of working capital can comfortably cover. Overall, Aisha should postpone the refurbishment and keep the 2.5% discount as a reserve if debtors still pay too slowly [eval].
    Keywords: 2.5% discount, 14 days, $45,000, 60-day credit, $35,000, 3 weeks, $60,000, $640,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a settlement discount motivates debtors to pay earlier; postponing planned capital expenditure preserves cash at no direct cost | application_max_2: $45,000 is owed by employers on 60-day credit; $35,000 for rent and insurance is due in 3 weeks on $640,000 of annual sales | analysis_max_2: the discount directly reduces revenue and may reward early payers for nothing; postponing removes a $60,000 commitment and costs nothing upfront | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring one option with clear reasoning; weighs certain discount cost against the zero-cost delay of the refurbishment
