--- STEM ---
A private limited company manufactures budget-friendly wooden furniture items for residential homes. Operating for 8 years with a permanent workforce of 120 skilled carpenters, the business generates $2,800,000 in annual revenue, with 20% of sales derived from overseas exports. The national economy has recently entered a severe economic recession, characterized by two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth (-2.5%) and an increase in national unemployment rates from 4% to 9%.

In response to falling government tax receipts, the central authority increased personal income tax rates from 18% to 22%, drastically reducing household disposable income across the country. Additionally, national commercial banks have raised base interest rates to 6.5%. The company faces rising raw material storage costs, a 15% increase in industrial timber tariffs, and declining domestic orders for home furnishings.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'recession'.
    Answer: A period of negative Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth lasting for two or more consecutive quarters in an economy [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: negative GDP growth; two or more consecutive quarters

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two impacts on this business of an increase in national unemployment from 4% to 9%.
    Answer: Impact 1: Easier recruitment of staff [k], allowing the wooden furniture manufacturer to hire skilled carpenters from a larger labor pool [app]. Impact 2: Decreased consumer spending [k], as unemployed households reduce non-essential purchases, lowering domestic orders for home furnishings [app].
    Keywords: furniture, carpenters, furnishings, unemployment, recession, timber, GDP
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: easier recruitment / lower wage pressure; decreased consumer spending / lower demand | application_max_2: wooden furniture manufacturer; skilled carpenters; home furnishings; 9% unemployment

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways an increase in personal income tax from 18% to 22% affects this business.
    Answer: Way 1: Reduces consumer disposable income [k], leaving households with less money to spend on wooden furniture items [app], which leads to falling sales revenue across domestic retail markets [an]. Way 2: Workers may demand higher wage increases [k] to maintain their living standards after tax increases, raising operating costs for the 120 skilled carpenters [app] and reducing net profit margins [an].
    Keywords: tax, disposable, furniture, carpenters, income
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduces consumer disposable income; workers demand higher wages | application_max_2: wooden furniture items; 120 skilled carpenters; 22% income tax | analysis_max_2: leads to falling sales revenue; raises operating costs / reduces net profit margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think introducing a cheaper range of flat-pack furniture is a better strategy during a recession with -2.5% GDP growth than increasing export sales to overseas markets? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Introducing cheaper flat-pack furniture targets budget-conscious domestic consumers [k], appealing to households with falling disposable income during a -2.5% GDP recession [app] and maintaining sales volume [an]. However, developing flat-pack products requires new equipment and machinery investment [k], increasing capital costs when 6.5% interest rates make borrowing expensive [app]. Expanding export sales to overseas markets taps into foreign demand unaffected by the domestic slump, bringing in foreign currency revenue to support $2,800,000 total turnover and reducing reliance on the home market [an]. Overall, introducing flat-pack furniture is better because 80% of sales are domestic, and overcoming a 15% timber tariff on exports makes international expansion less profitable during a global downturn [eval], making local product adaptation crucial for business survival [eval].
    Keywords: recession, furniture, tariff, interest, export
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: targets budget consumers / maintains volume; taps into foreign demand / diversifies revenue | application_max_2: flat-pack furniture; -2.5% GDP recession; 6.5% interest rates; 15% timber tariff / $2,800,000 turnover | analysis_max_2: appeals to low-disposable-income buyers; reduces reliance on depressed home market | evaluation_max_2: weighs domestic focus against export expansion considering high tariffs and domestic sales share

--- STEM ---
A private limited company operates a commercial food processing plant specializing in packaged organic bakery goods. Trading for 15 years with 180 full-time factory workers, the business generates $5,200,000 in annual turnover, exporting 35% of output to neighboring countries. The domestic economy is currently experiencing rapid economic growth, with national annual GDP rising by 4.8%. However, this boom has caused severe labor shortages across industrial sectors, pushing national unemployment down to an all-time low of 1.8%.

To support low-income households amid 5% inflation, the government recently introduced legislation raising the statutory legal minimum wage by 12%, from $9.50 to $10.64 per hour. Simultaneously, the central bank raised commercial interest rates to 5.5% to prevent overheating. The firm faces higher wage costs, an annual carbon tax of $80,000 on baking ovens, and intense competition for factory operational staff.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'economic growth'.
    Answer: An increase in the total value of goods and services produced by an economy (real GDP) over a period of time [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increase in total value of goods and services; real GDP over time

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two impacts on this business of a 12% increase in the statutory legal minimum wage.
    Answer: Impact 1: Increased direct labor costs [k], directly raising wage expenses for the 180 full-time factory workers operating baking ovens [app]. Impact 2: Improved employee retention [k], reducing costly staff turnover in the organic bakery plant as hourly pay increases to $10.64 [app].
    Keywords: wage, bakery, workers, baking, minimum, inflation
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher labor costs / reduced profit margin; increased worker motivation / reduced turnover | application_max_2: organic bakery goods; 180 full-time factory workers; $10.64 per hour; baking ovens

  Qb [4 marks]

    Keywords: multinational, relocation, automotive, parts, wage, tax holiday

    Keywords: wage, relocation, multinational, gears, automotive

  Qd [8 marks]

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that demand/output rise in a boom; Identifies that labour is scarce / wages rise in a boom | application_max_2: References 9.5 million bricks and/or revenue of $14.2 million; References 180 workers, the full order book or the construction sector expansion

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of investing $3 million in a new third plant during the boom.
    Answer: Problem 1: Construction costs and wages are high in a boom, so the $3 million budget could overrun and the firm may need to borrow more. [k] With revenue of $14.2 million, extra borrowing at this point would still cut profit, especially if corporation tax rises from 24% to 28%. [app] Higher fixed costs from a third plant must be paid even if orders fall, so the break-even point rises and profit becomes more fragile. [an] Problem 2: When the boom ends, demand for bricks falls; a new plant built now may be underused, leaving excess capacity and heavy fixed costs. [k] Orders are full for the next 12 months, but the business cycle will eventually move into a slowdown, and the extra workers taken on cannot be avoided easily. [app] Underused capacity spreads fixed costs over fewer bricks, raising average costs and reducing competitiveness. [an]
    Keywords: $3 million, $14.2 million, 24% to 28%, 12 months, 180 workers, boom, third plant
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that costs are high in a boom / the budget may overrun; Identifies that demand will fall when the boom ends, leaving excess capacity | application_max_2: References the $3 million cost against $14.2 million revenue or the 24% to 28% tax rise; References the full 12-month order book or the boom eventually ending | analysis_max_2: Explains that higher fixed costs raise the break-even point and fragile profit; Explains that underused capacity raises average cost per brick (diseconomy/under-absorption)

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Coppermere Brick and Cement Co should invest $3 million in a third plant now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes: in a boom, demand is strong and delaying expansion means losing orders to rivals. [k] Revenue has already climbed from $11.8 million to $14.2 million and the order book is full for 12 months, so more capacity is needed urgently. [app] A third plant would let the firm serve all its housing-developer customers and raise profit despite the possible rise in corporation tax from 24% to 28%. [an] However, booms do not last forever; the business cycle will eventually turn to a downturn. [k] If the economy slows after the boom, the third plant's $3 million cost and the wages of extra workers would leave the firm with excess capacity and weaker cash to pay its 180 workers. [app] Delaying expansion until the boom ends would reduce this risk but would hand orders to competitors at the peak of demand. [an] Overall, the board should invest in the third plant now but phase the building over 18 to 24 months, keeping a cash reserve in case the cycle turns, because the revenue evidence strongly justifies expansion. [eval] This is justified by the $2.4 million revenue increase and the full order book; phasing the spend limits the damage if the boom ends sooner than expected. [eval]
    Keywords: $3 million, $11.8 million, $14.2 million, 24% to 28%, 180 workers, boom, order book, third plant
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies strong demand / capacity shortage in a boom; Identifies that the boom will end and demand will fall (cycle risk) | application_max_2: References revenue growth from $11.8 million to $14.2 million and the full order book; References the $3 million cost, 180 workers or the 24% to 28% corporation tax rise | analysis_max_2: Explains how extra capacity raises profit when demand is strong; Explains how excess capacity and fixed costs hurt the firm after the boom | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. invest now but phase it); Weighs opportunity cost of delay against the risk of over-expansion

--- STEM ---
Marlowe & Grey Fine Watches is a partnership in Country X selling luxury watches and jewellery from 2 boutiques. It employs 14 specialist sales staff. Average takings per boutique fell to $95,000 a month in the latest quarter, down from $130,000 a year earlier, as Country X entered a slump. Footfall has fallen by a third since the slump began, and two nearby luxury retailers have closed.

Consumer confidence is very low and sales of luxury goods have dropped sharply. To help the economy, the government has cut VAT from 20% to 15% for 12 months. The partners must decide whether to cut prices by 10% to attract cautious buyers, or keep prices unchanged to protect the exclusive image of the brand.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'slump'.
    Answer: A slump is the lowest point of the business cycle, when economic activity, output, incomes and employment are at their weakest and consumer spending is very low. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the slump as the lowest/weakest stage of the business cycle; Identifies very low output, incomes, employment and/or consumer spending

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why sales of luxury watches and jewellery fall during a slump.
    Answer: Reason 1: In a slump, consumer incomes and confidence are very low, so households postpone non-essential high-price purchases such as luxury watches. [k] This is shown by takings per boutique falling from $130,000 to $95,000 a month. [app] Reason 2: In a slump, people fear for their jobs, so they prioritise essentials over luxury goods. [k] Footfall has fallen by a third and two nearby luxury retailers have closed, confirming the collapse in demand. [app]
    Keywords: $130,000, $95,000, slump, 2 boutiques, 14 specialist sales staff, footfall, luxury watches
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies low consumer incomes/confidence as the cause of weak luxury demand; Identifies job insecurity/fear of unemployment causing postponement of big non-essential purchases | application_max_2: References takings falling from $130,000 to $95,000 per boutique a month; References footfall falling by a third / two nearby luxury retailers closing

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of cutting prices by 10%.
    Answer: Problem 1: A 10% price cut shrinks the profit margin on every watch sold, yet the boutiques still have to pay 14 specialist sales staff and rent. [k] Takings are already down to $95,000 per boutique a month, so lowering prices could erode profit further unless sales volume rises sharply. [app] Lower margins reduce the cash available to ride out the slump and could force staff hour cuts. [an] Problem 2: Heavy discounting can damage the exclusive brand image that convinces customers to pay high prices. [k] Keeping prices unchanged protects that exclusive image, but cutting prices by 10% may teach buyers to wait for discounts rather than pay full price. [app] If the exclusive image weakens, takings may never recover to $130,000 a month even when the slump ends. [an]
    Keywords: 10%, $95,000, $130,000, 14 specialist sales staff, 2 boutiques, slump, exclusive image
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that a price cut reduces profit margins per unit; Identifies that discounting damages an exclusive/premium brand image | application_max_2: References takings of $95,000 vs $130,000 or the 14 specialist sales staff; References the exclusive brand image / 10% discount | analysis_max_2: Explains the margin/volume trade-off and its effect on cash (staff cuts); Explains how a weakened brand image undermines long-term takingsRecovery

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marlowe & Grey Fine Watches should cut prices by 10%? Justify your answer.
    Answer: No: cutting prices by 10% would shrink margins on all watches and risk destroying the exclusive brand image. [k] Takings per boutique have fallen from $130,000 to $95,000, but a 10% discount would erode what profit remains and encourage buyers to delay purchases. [app] The VAT cut from 20% to 15% already lowers shelf prices by about 4% if passed on, which stimulates demand without the firm cutting its own prices. [an] Yes: a 10% cut could attract cautious buyers who feel they are getting value, especially during the 12 months the VAT cut lasts. [k] Takings of $95,000 a month per boutique show demand is weak; a well-advertised 10% discount could clear slow-moving stock and draw customers back into the 2 boutiques. [app] More sales at lower margin could raise total profit if enough extra customers are attracted, but it is uncertain whether a slump can be discounted away. [an] Overall, the partners should keep headline prices unchanged and pass on the VAT cut instead of cutting prices by a full 10%, because protecting the brand and margin matters most for luxury goods in a slump. [eval] This is justified by the collapse in takings from $130,000 to $95,000; discounting heavily rarely restores luxury demand, so a modest VAT-linked saving is the safer move. [eval]
    Keywords: $130,000, $95,000, 10%, 20% to 15%, 2 boutiques, 12 months, slump, exclusive image
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the margin/brand-image argument against a 10% price cut; Identifies the demand-stimulation argument in favour of a 10% price cut | application_max_2: References takings falling from $130,000 to $95,000 and the VAT cut from 20% to 15%; References the 2 boutiques, 12-month VAT window or footfall fall | analysis_max_2: Explains the VAT pass-on as a softer demand stimulus (roughly 4% shelf-price fall); Explains the margin/volume/brand trade-off and its effect on profit | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. keep prices, pass on VAT saving); Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

--- STEM ---
Harlan Building Materials Ltd is a private limited company in Country X supplying cement, sand and aggregates from 2 depots. It delivers to building firms, housing developers and public works contractors across the region. It employs 46 people and revenue was $6.8 million last year. In March the government announced a $250 million national road-building programme over 5 years.

Harlan has been invited to tender for a $4.5 million contract to supply cement to 3 road projects. Winning would require buying 2 new delivery trucks costing $380,000 each and hiring 12 more drivers, an investment of $760,000. The directors must decide whether to tender for the contract, or stay focused on their 140 regular small customers and avoid taking on debt.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'taxation'.
    Answer: Taxation is the compulsory payment of money to the government by individuals and businesses, used to fund public spending and services. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies taxation as compulsory payments to the government; Identifies that taxes are used to fund public spending/services

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Harlan Building Materials Ltd of government spending on road-building.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Public spending creates direct orders for building materials, so Harlan can win lucrative contracts such as the $4.5 million tender for 3 road projects. [k] The $250 million programme over 5 years guarantees demand far beyond what small customers alone would provide. [app] Benefit 2: Better roads improve distribution across the region, making deliveries from Harlan's 2 depots faster and cheaper and opening access to new customers. [k] [app]
    Keywords: $250 million, $4.5 million, 2 depots, 3 road projects, 5 years, road-building, Harlan Building Materials Ltd
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that government spending creates direct demand/contracts for materials; Identifies that better infrastructure lowers distribution costs or widens markets | application_max_2: References the $4.5 million tender / 3 road projects / $250 million, 5-year programme; References the 2 depots or the 140 regular customers context

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Harlan might face if it invests in the 2 new trucks and 12 drivers.
    Answer: Problem 1: Buying 2 trucks at $380,000 each costs $760,000, a large sum for a firm with $6.8 million revenue that could strain cash or require borrowing. [k] If the $4.5 million contract is lost or delayed, the trucks and 12 more drivers would sit underused, raising average costs per delivery. [app] High fixed costs from trucks and wages must be covered even in quiet months, so profit could fall sharply. [an] Problem 2: Relying on one big government programme makes the firm vulnerable if budget cuts or delays reduce the road-building. [k] The programme runs over 5 years, and public spending can change with a new budget or a downturn in the business cycle. [app] If the contract ends, Harlan would still have the trucks and drivers to pay, and selling trucks is hard in a weak market. [an]
    Keywords: $380,000, $760,000, $6.8 million, 2 new delivery trucks, 12 more drivers, $4.5 million, 5 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the capital cost/cash flow strain of buying trucks (or need to borrow); Identifies dependence on government spending / risk the programme ends or is cut | application_max_2: References $380,000 per truck / $760,000 total against $6.8 million revenue; References the 5-year programme, the $4.5 million contract or the 12 extra drivers | analysis_max_2: Explains how fixed costs raise average cost per delivery when demand is weak; Explains how dependence on a single government programme raises business risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harlan Building Materials Ltd should tender for the $4.5 million contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes: winning the contract would transform Harlan's scale and profitability. [k] Revenue is $6.8 million, so $4.5 million of work over 5 years is roughly two-thirds of a year's sales added steadily, backed by the $250 million national programme. [app] Spending $760,000 on 2 trucks and 12 drivers lets Harlan capture this growth and build a reputation for large public projects. [an] However, the investment is large relative to the business and depends on government spending continuing. [k] If the tender fails or the programme is delayed, the $760,000 spent on trucks would strain cash and leave extra drivers idle, while the 140 regular small customers could feel neglected. [app] Staying focused on small customers avoids this risk but means forgoing the fastest-growing source of revenue available. [an] Overall, Harlan should tender, but negotiate milestone payments and stage the truck purchases so cash flow is protected if work is delayed. [eval] This is justified by the scale of the $250 million programme; the opportunity outweighs the risk, provided contract terms are secured before spending. [eval]
    Keywords: $4.5 million, $6.8 million, $760,000, $250 million, 2 new delivery trucks, 12 more drivers, 5 years, 140 regular small customers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the growth/scale opportunity from the $4.5 million contract; Identifies the risk of dependence on government spending / a failed tender | application_max_2: References $6.8 million revenue vs $4.5 million contract (two-thirds of a year's sales); References the $760,000 investment, the $250 million programme or the 140 regular small customers | analysis_max_2: Explains how the contract spreads fixed costs and builds reputation/scale; Explains the cash-flow and neglect risk for existing customers if it fails | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. tender with milestone terms/staged spend); Weighs growth opportunity against dependence on government policy

--- STEM ---
Haver & Grey Electronics is a private limited company in Country X running 4 high-street shops selling TVs, laptops and washing machines. It has traded for 9 years and employs 52 staff. Revenue last year was $11.6 million, down from $12.9 million. The rise in tax was announced in the March budget.

To reduce a budget deficit, the government has raised income tax from 20% to 23% and VAT from 17.5% to 20%. The shops report fewer customers and average spend per transaction has fallen to $310 from $355. Footfall has been falling for 6 months. The directors must decide whether to cut prices by 5% to win sales back, or hold prices and wait for the government's promise of lower inflation.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two government economic objectives.
    Answer: Two government economic objectives are: (1) economic growth; and (2) stable prices (low inflation). Other acceptable answers include full employment, balance of payments stability and redistribution of income. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Names any two government economic objectives (e.g. economic growth, full employment, stable prices, balance of payments, redistribution of income); Accept equivalent wording, e.g. low unemployment or low prices/inflation

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Haver & Grey Electronics' revenue has fallen.
    Answer: Reason 1: Higher income tax from 20% to 23% reduces households' disposable income, so they cut back on big-ticket items such as TVs and washing machines. [k] This is shown by average spend per transaction falling from $355 to $310. [app] Reason 2: VAT has risen from 17.5% to 20%, pushing up prices in the shops and discouraging purchases; revenue has fallen from $12.9 million to $11.6 million across the 4 shops. [k] [app]
    Keywords: $12.9 million, $11.6 million, $355, $310, 20% to 23%, 17.5% to 20%, 4 high-street shops, Haver & Grey Electronics
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that higher income tax reduces disposable income and consumer spending; Identifies that higher VAT raises prices and reduces quantity demanded | application_max_2: References spend per transaction falling from $355 to $310 or the 20% to 23% income tax rise; References revenue falling from $12.9 million to $11.6 million or the 17.5% to 20% VAT rise / 4 shops

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of cutting prices by 5%.
    Answer: Problem 1: A 5% price cut reduces revenue per sale when spend per transaction has already fallen to $310, eroding retail margins. [k] On revenue of $11.6 million, a 5% cut removes about $580,000 of income unless volume rises sharply. [app] The fall is caused by higher taxes rather than high prices, so a price cut attacks the wrong problem and profit could fall below sustainable levels. [an] Problem 2: A price cut could start a price war; rivals may match the 5% cut, leaving all shops with lower margins and no extra market share. [k] With 4 shops and 52 staff to pay, Haver & Grey cannot absorb prolonged losses easily. [app] A price war risks damaging the shops' reputation and could force cost cuts that harm service and staff morale. [an]
    Keywords: 5%, $310, $11.6 million, $12.9 million, 4 high-street shops, 52 staff, 17.5% to 20%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that a price cut squeezes revenue/margins; Identifies the risk of a price war / rivals matching the cut | application_max_2: References $310 spend per transaction or $11.6 million revenue / the 5% cut; References the 4 shops and 52 staff or the wrong-diagnosis point (taxes, not prices) | analysis_max_2: Explains the arithmetic: a 5% cut on $11.6 million removes about $580,000 unless volume rises; Explains why a cut cannot fix a demand fall caused by taxation (wrong instrument)

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Haver & Grey Electronics should cut prices by 5%? Justify your answer.
    Answer: No: cutting prices by 5% would sacrifice margins without fixing the real problem, which is reduced disposable income caused by higher taxes. [k] Spend per transaction has already fallen from $355 to $310 and VAT is now 20%, so a 5% cut would lower revenue further when sales have dropped from $12.9 million to $11.6 million. [app] Holding prices preserves the cash needed to pay the 52 staff and keeps the shops stocked; targeted promotions on slow lines are safer than an across-the-board cut. [an] Yes: a 5% cut could pull cautious households back into the 4 shops and rebuild footfall while rivals hold prices. [k] If the government delivers its promise of lower inflation, spending power recovers, and a visible discount now could make Haver & Grey the value destination in town. [app] More transactions at slightly lower margins could stabilise total profit, and winning customers now builds loyalty for the recovery. [an] Overall, the directors should not cut prices across the board by 5%; they should use targeted discounts and promotions instead, protecting margins while tempting back customers. [eval] This is justified because the fall in sales is caused by higher taxes and lower spending power, not by price perception, so a blanket cut would sacrifice profit for uncertain gain. [eval]
    Keywords: $355, $310, $11.6 million, $12.9 million, 4 high-street shops, 52 staff, 5%, income tax
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the argument against a cut (margin loss, wrong diagnosis); Identifies the argument for a cut (stimulates demand, builds loyalty) | application_max_2: References spend falling from $355 to $310, VAT at 20% and revenue of $11.6 million/$12.9 million; References the 4 shops, 52 staff or the promise of lower inflation | analysis_max_2: Explains why a tax-driven demand fall is not cured by lowering prices (elasticity/diagnosis logic); Explains how a cut could raise volume and loyalty enough to stabilise profit | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. targeted promotions instead of a 5% cut); Weighs both sides using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

--- STEM ---
Penny & Thread is a private limited company in Country X running 3 discount clothing stores in low-income areas. The stores sell own-brand clothing, school uniforms and household basics at very low prices for cash-strapped families. It employs 27 staff and revenue last year was $4.9 million.

As part of redistributing income, the government has increased weekly benefits for low-income families by $30 per child and cut the income tax rate for low-income households to 10%. Footfall in the stores has risen 12% in the past 3 months, and shelves are emptying faster. The directors must decide whether to open a fourth store in a deprived estate at a cost of $600,000, or refurbish the existing 3 stores at a cost of $250,000.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'redistribution of income'.
    Answer: Redistribution of income is the transfer of income from higher-income groups to lower-income groups, for example through taxes and benefits, to make the distribution of income more equal. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the transfer of income from richer to poorer groups; Identifies the mechanism (taxes and benefits) or the aim (greater equality)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the government's redistribution of income on Penny & Thread.
    Answer: Effect 1: Low-income households have more money to spend, so demand for discount clothing rises; footfall in the stores has risen 12% in the past 3 months. [k] [app] Effect 2: Higher benefits of $30 per child per week and an income tax rate of just 10% raise disposable income, increasing sales of own-brand clothing and school uniforms at low prices. [k] [app]
    Keywords: 12%, $30 per child, 10%, 3 discount clothing stores, $4.9 million, low-income areas, Penny & Thread
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that benefits/lower tax raise disposable income of low-income households; Identifies that higher disposable income raises demand for goods and services | application_max_2: References the 12% rise in footfall / 3-month timeframe; References the $30 per child weekly benefit or the 10% income tax rate

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of refurbishing the existing 3 stores instead of opening a fourth.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Refurbishment at $250,000 costs less than half of the $600,000 needed for a new store, so the firm avoids heavy borrowing and keeps a cash cushion. [k] With revenue of only $4.9 million, committing $600,000 to an untested estate is a big financial risk. [app] Lower capital spending means lower financial risk and a quicker return on the investment, protecting profit and the 27 jobs. [an] Advantage 2: Upgrading the existing 3 stores keeps proven locations and customer bases while adding space and better displays to handle the 12% footfall rise. [k] The stores already sell own-brand clothing and uniforms that low-income families depend on, so improvements will directly serve current customers. [app] Refurbishment raises capacity where demand is already proven, so sales can rise with far less risk than opening in an untested estate. [an]
    Keywords: $250,000, $600,000, $4.9 million, 12%, existing 3 stores, 27 staff, low-income areas
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the lower capital cost/risk of $250,000 vs $600,000; Identifies that existing stores have proven demand/customers | application_max_2: References $250,000 vs $600,000 and $4.9 million revenue; References the 12% footfall rise or the existing 3 stores selling own-brand clothing | analysis_max_2: Explains how lower capital spending reduces financial risk and protects cash/jobs; Explains that improving proven locations adds capacity with less risk than an untested site

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Penny & Thread should open the fourth store in the deprived estate? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes: opening the fourth store puts Penny & Thread directly in front of the low-income families who have just gained from the redistribution of income. [k] Benefits up by $30 per child per week, an income tax rate of just 10% and a 12% rise in footfall all point to durable demand that the existing 3 stores cannot absorb. [app] A fourth store in a deprived estate would capture this demand, spread fixed costs across 4 stores and lift revenue beyond $4.9 million. [an] However, the new store costs $600,000, more than twice the $250,000 refurbishment, and the benefit increase could be reduced in a future budget. [k] If demand falls back, the fourth store's rent and wages would burden the business, whereas refurbishing the existing 3 stores copes with growth at lower cost and lower risk. [app] Staying small protects the 27 staff and the proven customer base, but shelves are already emptying faster and customers may switch to rivals. [an] Overall, the directors should open the fourth store, because the 12% rise in footfall and the ongoing benefit increase justify expanding into underserved areas. [eval] This is justified by the demonstrated rise in low-income spending; staging the opening over 12 months would manage the risk of a future policy reversal. [eval]
    Keywords: $600,000, $250,000, $4.9 million, 12%, $30 per child, 10%, 3 stores, low-income areas
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the demand opportunity created by redistribution of income; Identifies the capital cost and policy-reversal risk of a fourth store | application_max_2: References the $30 per child benefit, 10% tax rate and 12% footfall rise; References the $600,000 vs $250,000 costs and $4.9 million revenue | analysis_max_2: Explains how a new store spreads fixed costs and lifts revenue beyond $4.9 million; Explains the risk/return trade-off of refurbishing vs opening if policy reverses | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. open now, staged over 12 months); Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

--- STEM ---
Meadowgate Grocers is a private limited company in Country X operating 5 neighbourhood supermarkets. Each store carries about 6,000 product lines and trades 7 days a week. It employs 88 staff and revenue was $16.4 million last year. Fresh food prices rose sharply this year and inflation reached 6%, above the government's target of stable prices at 2%. Suppliers are demanding higher prices for milk, bread and fresh produce.

The government is committed to restoring stable prices and has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively. Meadowgate's costs have risen 8%. The 6% figure would be the first across-the-board rise in 3 years. The directors must decide whether to raise shelf prices by 6% in line with inflation, or absorb the cost increase by cutting staff hours and promotions.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'stable prices'.
    Answer: Stable prices means the general price level in the economy rises only slowly, i.e. inflation is low and predictable, so money keeps its value. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that the general price level rises only slowly (low inflation); Identifies that prices are predictable / money keeps its value

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects on Meadowgate Grocers of inflation rising to 6%.
    Answer: Effect 1: Supplier and wage costs rise — Meadowgate's costs have risen 8%, squeezing profit margins unless shelf prices go up; the firm is considering a 6% rise. [k] [app] Effect 2: Customers' purchasing power falls as prices rise, so shoppers become more price-sensitive and may switch to cheaper goods; with about 6,000 product lines to re-price, the workload and pressure on staff increase. [k] [app]
    Keywords: 8%, 6%, $16.4 million, 88 staff, 6,000 product lines, stable prices, Meadowgate Grocers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that inflation raises business costs/prices; Identifies that inflation erodes consumers' purchasing power and shifts demand | application_max_2: References the 8% rise in costs / the 6% price rise under consideration; References the 6,000 product lines or the 88 staff / $16.4 million revenue context

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of raising shelf prices by 6%.
    Answer: Problem 1: Higher prices may drive customers to discounters, reducing sales volume; with inflation already at 6%, a further rise could lose Meadowgate its price-sensitive shoppers. [k] Suppliers of milk, bread and fresh produce have raised prices by 8%, but passing on 6% of that still erodes margins while risking lower footfall across the 5 neighbourhood supermarkets. [app] Lower volumes would spread the 88 staff's wages over fewer sales, raising the average cost per transaction and squeezing profit. [an] Problem 2: Raising prices conflicts with the government's stable prices objective, and the government has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively; bad publicity could harm the brand. [k] The 6% rise would be the first across-the-board increase in 3 years, drawing customer attention to higher bills. [app] Reputational damage could outlast any short-term margin gain, especially if lower inflation arrives soon. [an]
    Keywords: 6%, 8%, 5 neighbourhood supermarkets, 88 staff, 3 years, stable prices, $16.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the risk of losing price-sensitive customers/sales volume; Identifies the conflict with the government's stable prices objective / reputational risk | application_max_2: References the 8% supplier cost rise vs the 6% proposed increase or the 5 supermarkets; References the 6,000 product lines, the 88 staff or the government's request | analysis_max_2: Explains the margin vs footfall trade-off (volume spread over fixed staff costs); Explains how reputational damage can outweigh short-term margin gains

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Meadowgate Grocers should raise prices by 6%? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes: with costs up 8%, not raising prices would wipe out margins and threaten the 88 jobs. [k] Revenue is $16.4 million and wages, rent and supplier costs are all rising with 6% inflation, so a 6% rise roughly tracks the market rather than exceeding it. [app] Raising prices protects the cash needed to stock about 6,000 product lines across 5 neighbourhood supermarkets, keeping service levels and staff hours intact. [an] However, the government wants stable prices at 2% and has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively, and customers already struggling with 6% inflation may shop elsewhere. [k] A 6% rise would be the first across-the-board increase in 3 years and could push price-sensitive shoppers to discounters, cutting volumes and revenue. [app] Absorbing costs by cutting staff hours and promotions protects headline prices but risks poorer service and lower morale among the 88 staff. [an] Overall, Meadowgate should raise prices by an average of 6% but keep staple items cheaper where possible, accepting slightly lower margins there to hold footfall. [eval] This is justified because fully absorbing an 8% cost rise would destroy profit, while a selective rise shares the burden fairly between the firm and its customers. [eval]
    Keywords: 6%, 8%, $16.4 million, 88 staff, 6,000 product lines, 3 years, stable prices, 5 neighbourhood supermarkets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the margin-protection case for a price rise; Identifies the customer-loss/reputation risk and the stable prices objective tension | application_max_2: References the 8% cost rise vs the 6% proposed increase, $16.4 million revenue; References the 6,000 product lines, the 88 staff or the first rise in 3 years | analysis_max_2: Explains why inaction destroys margins (cost-price squeeze); Explains the volume/margin trade-off across price-sensitive shoppers | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. selective 6% rise); Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

--- STEM ---
Larchmont Dairies is a private limited company in Country X producing butter and hard cheese. It buys milk from 38 local dairy farms and churns 6 days a week. It employs 96 workers at one creamery and sells mainly to supermarkets at home, and its main export is hard cheese. Last year it exported $2.1 million of cheese, double the $1.05 million exported the previous year.

The government wants to improve the balance of payments and is offering a 15% export grant for 3 years, and has imposed an 18% tariff on imported cheese. The directors must decide whether to build a second production line costing $2.8 million to expand exports, or focus on the domestic market, where the tariff on imports should lift their sales.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'balance of payments'.
    Answer: The balance of payments is a record of a country's economic transactions with the rest of the world over a period of time, including exports and imports of goods and services. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the balance of payments as a record of transactions with the rest of the world; Identifies that it includes exports and imports of goods and services

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Larchmont Dairies of exporting more cheese.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Export sales earn foreign currency for the country, directly supporting the government's balance of payments objective; Larchmont's exports rose to $2.1 million from $1.05 million. [k] [app] Benefit 2: Exporting spreads risk — selling abroad reduces reliance on the home market, so an economic downturn in Country X would not wipe out sales at the single creamery. [k] [app]
    Keywords: $2.1 million, $1.05 million, 96 workers, 38 local dairy farms, balance of payments, 6 days a week, Larchmont Dairies
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that exports earn foreign currency/support the balance of payments; Identifies that exporting spreads risk/reduces dependence on the home market | application_max_2: References exports doubling from $1.05 million to $2.1 million; References the single creamery / 96 workers / 38 local dairy farms context

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of building a second production line costing $2.8 million.
    Answer: Problem 1: The $2.8 million investment is large for one creamery employing 96 workers and may require borrowing, increasing financial risk. [k] If export demand disappoints, the new line may run below capacity, raising average costs and cutting profit. [app] High fixed costs would weigh on the firm even in quiet months, so the break-even point rises and profit becomes less secure. [an] Problem 2: Export markets are uncertain — exchange rate changes, transport costs and foreign competition can all squeeze margins. [k] The 15% export grant lasts only 3 years, and the 18% tariff on imported cheese could change in a future trade deal. [app] If the grant is withdrawn or the tariff is cut, the second line could become unprofitable and the firm would be left with surplus capacity. [an]
    Keywords: $2.8 million, 96 workers, $2.1 million, 15%, 3 years, 18% tariff, $1.05 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the capital cost/financial risk of a $2.8 million investment; Identifies export-market uncertainty (demand, exchange rates, foreign competition) | application_max_2: References the $2.8 million cost / 96 workers / one creamery; References the 15% grant ending after 3 years or the 18% tariff changing | analysis_max_2: Explains how underused capacity raises average costs and the break-even point; Explains how dependence on government policy (grant/tariff) threatens line profitability

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Larchmont Dairies should build the second production line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes: doubling exports to $2.1 million proves the overseas market and aligns with the government's balance of payments priority. [k] The 15% export grant for 3 years, plus the 18% tariff on imported cheese, gives Larchmont both an export boost and home-market protection. [app] A $2.8 million second line could double capacity at the single creamery, lifting export revenue and profit while helping the national economy. [an] However, $2.8 million is a major commitment for a firm employing 96 workers, and export demand can shift with exchange rates and foreign competition. [k] If the grant ends after 3 years or the 18% tariff is cut in a trade deal, export margins could shrink and the line could be underused. [app] Focusing on the home market would capture the tariff benefit immediately with no new borrowing, but would cap growth at current export levels. [an] Overall, Larchmont should build the second line, phased over 18 months with the grant secured first, because export momentum from $1.05 million to $2.1 million justifies expanding capacity. [eval] This is justified by the government's 15% grant and the proven doubling of exports; phasing construction protects cash if export growth slows. [eval]
    Keywords: $2.1 million, $1.05 million, $2.8 million, 15%, 3 years, 18% tariff, 96 workers, balance of payments
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the growth case for export expansion and the grant support; Identifies the risks of dependence on the grant/tariff and export-market volatility | application_max_2: References exports doubling from $1.05 million to $2.1 million, the 15% grant; References the $2.8 million cost, 96 workers, the 18% tariff or 3-year grant period | analysis_max_2: Explains how the grant and tariff improve export economics and home-market protection; Explains how policy changes or demand shifts would make the line unprofitable | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. build, phased, grant secured first); Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

--- STEM ---
Bluebell Catering Co is a private limited company in Country X providing school meals to 34 state schools in the capital. It cooks meals on-site and delivers to secondary schools. It employs 120 staff, including 45 kitchen assistants and 30 supervisors. Its school contract is worth $2.6 million a year, about 60% of revenue, which was $4.3 million last year. Staff costs are 65% of the contract price.

The government has announced cuts to education spending to reduce the budget deficit, cutting school catering budgets by 10% nationwide. The renewed contract would run for 3 years. Bluebell must decide whether to tender for the renewed contract at a 10% lower price, or move into corporate office catering, which would need $900,000 of new kitchen equipment.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'government spending'.
    Answer: Government spending is money spent by the government on public goods and services, such as schools, hospitals, roads, welfare benefits and defence. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies government spending as money spent by the state on goods and services; Gives examples such as education, health, infrastructure or welfare benefits

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects on Bluebell Catering Co of the 10% cut in school catering budgets.
    Answer: Effect 1: The renewed contract price falls — a 10% cut on $2.6 million is about $260,000 a year of lost revenue. [k] [app] Effect 2: Bluebell must cut costs, for example by reducing the hours of the 45 kitchen assistants, which could lower morale and the quality of meals served to the 34 state schools. [k] [app]
    Keywords: 10%, $2.6 million, $4.3 million, 120 staff, 45 kitchen assistants, 34 state schools, 60% of revenue
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that a 10% budget cut lowers government contract prices/revenue; Identifies that firms must reduce costs (staff, ingredients) to cope | application_max_2: References the 10% cut and/or the $2.6 million contract (about $260,000 a year); References the 45 kitchen assistants / 34 state schools / 120 staff

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of moving into corporate office catering.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Corporate clients are not affected by government education cuts, so revenue becomes more stable; Bluebell would be far less exposed if school budgets are cut again when the renewed 3-year contract ends. [k] Corporate meals would be sold at market rates, helping replace some of the $2.6 million school income. [app] Stable, higher-margin contracts would support the profit needed to pay the 120 staff and grow the business. [an] Benefit 2: Diversifying into offices and factories spreads risk and reduces dependence on a single government customer worth about 60% of revenue. [k] Winning new private clients would reduce reliance on political decisions made in each budget. [app] A broader customer base makes revenue more predictable and improves the firm's bargaining position with suppliers. [an]
    Keywords: $2.6 million, 60% of revenue, $900,000, 3 years, 120 staff, $4.3 million, corporate office catering
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that corporate clients are unaffected by government budget cuts (stable demand); Identifies that diversifying reduces dependence on one customer/sector | application_max_2: References the $2.6 million contract / 60% of revenue / $4.3 million revenue; References the 3-year contract, the 10% cut or the 120 staff | analysis_max_2: Explains how corporate income stabilises cash flow and supports wages/growth; Explains the risk-spreading benefit of a broader customer base

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Bluebell Catering Co should move into corporate office catering? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes: corporate catering frees Bluebell from budget cuts driven by government spending decisions, which have just fallen by 10%. [k] The school contract is worth $2.6 million, about 60% of revenue, so Bluebell is dangerously dependent on the government; diversifying spreads this risk. [app] Corporate clients would pay market rates instead of 10%-cut prices, lifting profit to support the 120 staff and the $4.3 million revenue base. [an] However, moving into corporate catering needs $900,000 of new kitchen equipment and Bluebell has no track record there. [k] Tendering for the renewed school contract at a 10% lower price keeps $2.6 million of income for 3 years and protects all 120 jobs, albeit at lower margins — a safer short-term option. [app] Corporate catering takes time to win, and if contracts are slow to arrive the firm could face a cash gap while paying for the new equipment. [an] Overall, Bluebell should move into corporate office catering in stages — keep the school contract and invest the $900,000 gradually as corporate orders grow. [eval] This is justified because it protects the existing 60% of revenue while reducing long-term dependence on government policy, balancing security with diversification. [eval]
    Keywords: $2.6 million, 60% of revenue, $4.3 million, 10%, $900,000, 120 staff, 3 years, 34 state schools
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the diversification/risk-reduction benefit of corporate catering; Identifies the cost and unproven-market risk ($900,000, no track record) | application_max_2: References the $2.6 million contract / 60% of revenue / $4.3 million revenue; References the 10% cut, the $900,000 equipment need, 3 years or 120 staff | analysis_max_2: Explains how corporate income replaces government-dependent revenue and stabilises profit; Explains the cash-flow risk of investing before corporate contracts are won | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. staged move keeping the school contract); Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

--- STEM ---
Harwick Appliances Ltd is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing washing machines and ovens. It sells to retailers, builders' merchants and export customers in 6 countries, and employs 210 workers at one factory. Revenue was $18.5 million last year, up from $16.1 million the year before. Wages have risen 7% this year.

The economy is close to full employment and the government has raised corporation tax from 21% to 25% to fund public spending. Harwick cannot recruit enough skilled assembly workers. The directors must decide whether to spend $1.5 million on automating 2 production lines, or keep the manual lines and accept slower output and rising labour costs. The 2 automated lines would cut the need for 30 assembly workers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'full employment'.
    Answer: Full employment is a situation in which everyone who is willing and able to work at the prevailing wage rate can find a job, i.e. unemployment is kept at a very low level. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies that everyone willing and able to work can find a job; Identifies that unemployment is kept very low

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects on Harwick Appliances Ltd of the economy being close to full employment.
    Answer: Effect 1: Skilled assembly workers are hard to find, so Harwick cannot recruit the workers it needs and output cannot grow; it already employs 210 workers at one factory. [k] [app] Effect 2: Wages across the economy are rising fast — Harwick's wages have risen 7% this year — pushing up costs and squeezing profit after the 25% corporation tax. [k] [app]
    Keywords: 210 workers, 30 assembly workers, 7%, $18.5 million, $16.1 million, 25%, full employment
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies labour shortages/recruitment difficulty near full employment; Identifies upward pressure on wages (and costs) | application_max_2: References 210 workers at one factory / inability to recruit assembly workers; References the 7% wage rise or the 25% corporation tax

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of automating the 2 production lines at a cost of $1.5 million.
    Answer: Problem 1: The $1.5 million investment must come from profit or borrowing, so cash is tied up and financial risk rises. [k] With corporation tax now at 25%, profit retained after tax is lower, making the $1.5 million harder to fund internally. [app] High upfront costs must be recovered through higher output, so the automated lines need to run at high capacity for years. [an] Problem 2: Automation would cut the need for 30 assembly workers, causing possible redundancies and lower morale among the remaining 210 workers. [k] Cutting jobs could damage Harwick's reputation as a stable employer in the 6 countries where it sells. [app] Low morale and industrial relations problems could disrupt production and offset the wage savings from automation. [an]
    Keywords: $1.5 million, 2 production lines, 30 assembly workers, 210 workers, 25%, 6 countries, $18.5 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies the capital cost/cash flow risk of $1.5 million or funding difficulty; Identifies redundancies/low morale/reputation risk from automation | application_max_2: References the $1.5 million cost or the 25% corporation tax (reduced retained profit); References the 30 assembly workers, 210 workers or 6 countries | analysis_max_2: Explains how upfront costs must be recovered through high utilisation; Explains how job losses/morale problems can offset automation savings

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harwick Appliances Ltd should automate the 2 production lines? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Yes: automating solves the underlying problem — near full employment means labour is scarce and Harwick's wages have risen 7% this year. [k] Harwick employs 210 workers, cannot recruit assembly staff and faces 25% corporation tax, so cutting unit labour costs protects profit. [app] The $1.5 million spent on 2 lines would stabilise output of washing machines and ovens and remove the 30 hard-to-fill vacancies. [an] However, $1.5 million is a major commitment and automating may cut jobs and lower morale among the workforce. [k] Keeping manual lines preserves all 210 jobs and avoids upfront debt, but slower output and rising wages would hold Harwick back while revenue grows from $16.1 million to $18.5 million. [app] Redundancies could also hurt the brand's reputation in 6 markets, though retraining affected workers onto the new lines would soften this. [an] Overall, Harwick should automate the 2 lines, because chronic labour shortages near full employment make the current approach unsustainable. [eval] This is justified by 7% wage growth and the recruitment gap; spending $1.5 million now is cheaper long-term than permanent wage inflation, provided some workers are retrained. [eval]
    Keywords: 210 workers, $18.5 million, $16.1 million, 7%, $1.5 million, 2 production lines, 25%, 30 assembly workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Identifies automation as the fix for labour scarcity/wage inflation; Identifies the job losses/morale/upfront cost risks of automation | application_max_2: References 210 workers, 7% wage rise, 25% corporation tax or the 30 assembly workers; References the $1.5 million cost, revenue growth from $16.1 million to $18.5 million or 2 production lines | analysis_max_2: Explains how automation cuts unit labour costs and stabilises output; Explains the morale/reputation risk and how retraining mitigates it | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. automate with retraining); Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

--- STEM ---
Coppermill Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Redbrook, Country X, manufacturing oak dining tables and chairs. It employs 34 workers and recorded sales revenue of $2.6 million last year. In 2023 it borrowed $400,000 from its bank at 5% annual interest to buy machinery. Two years of repayments have been made and the outstanding balance is $300,000.

The central bank has raised its base rate from 5% to 9%, so the rate on the outstanding balance will rise to 9% next month, adding $12,000 a year to interest costs. Owner Priya Raman wants to open a second workshop costing $180,000, funded by a further loan at 10% costing about $18,000 a year in interest. The order book is full for the next 6 months, but Priya fears customers may spend less if rates stay high. She must decide whether to expand now or wait until rates fall.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two effects of a rise in interest rates on a business with a bank loan.
    Answer: One effect is higher interest payments on the outstanding loan, which reduce profit. A second effect is less cash available to fund other spending or expansion, which may force the business to delay plans. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher interest payments on an existing loan reduce profit; Higher borrowing costs make new loans more expensive

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the interest rate rise on Coppermill Furniture Ltd.
    Answer: Higher interest costs: the rise from 5% to 9% on the $300,000 outstanding balance adds $12,000 a year, which will reduce Coppermill's profit [k], and this extra cost arrives while the machinery loan taken out in 2023 is still being repaid [app]. More expensive expansion finance: the proposed second workshop would need a further loan at 10%, costing about $18,000 a year in interest [k], which may make the $180,000 expansion hard to justify if customers spend less while rates stay high [app].
    Keywords: $300,000, $400,000, order book is full, $180,000, second workshop, $12,000, $2.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interest payments on an existing loan increase when rates rise; New borrowing becomes more expensive when rates rise | application_max_2: The outstanding balance is $300,000, so the rise from 5% to 9% adds $12,000 a year; The proposed $180,000 workshop loan at 10% would cost about $18,000 a year in interest

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why rising interest rates might reduce demand for Coppermill's furniture.
    Answer: Higher mortgage and loan payments: rising interest rates increase the cost of borrowing for households [k], so buyers of oak dining furniture already stretched by higher monthly repayments have less money to spend [app]. As buyers postpone big-ticket purchases, Coppermill's order book may shorten from its current 6 months, cutting future revenue [an]. Attractive savings returns: higher rates make saving more rewarding, so households save rather than spend [k], meaning demand for non-essential items like oak furniture falls [app], which would leave Coppermill with unsold stock and lower cash inflow [an].
    Keywords: order book, $2.6 million, oak dining, customers may spend less, rates stay high, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for consumers; Higher interest rates make saving more attractive than spending | application_max_2: Coppermill makes big-ticket items such as oak dining tables, which are often financed by borrowing; Coppermill fears customers may spend less if rates stay high | analysis_max_2: Higher mortgage and loan repayments reduce disposable income and big-ticket demand; More saving means less spending on non-essential furniture, cutting future sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Priya Raman should proceed with the $180,000 expansion now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Proceeding now would let Coppermill open the second workshop while its order book is full for the next 6 months [k], spreading the $18,000 a year interest on a $180,000 loan across higher sales [app], so profit could rise and the firm could win customers from rivals [an]. However, the rise from 5% to 9% already adds $12,000 a year to existing loan costs, and customers may spend less so demand could drop below the order book's promise [k], leaving the new loan hard to repay on only $2.6 million of sales [app], and serving two loans at once could push the business into debt it cannot service [an]. On balance, Priya should proceed but with caution, for example by confirming orders before signing the loan [eval], because the order book is full and waiting could mean missing the selling season when rates fall [eval].
    Keywords: $180,000, order book is full, $12,000, $18,000, $300,000, second workshop
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Expansion can increase output and sales while demand is strong; Higher interest rates increase repayment burdens and financial risk | application_max_2: The order book is full for the next 6 months at time the 9% rate takes effect; Existing loan balance of $300,000 now costs $12,000 a year extra; expansion loan would cost $18,000 a year | analysis_max_2: New capacity could lift output and win market share before demand falls; If sales fall, the business may be unable to service the additional loan | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation (proceed with caution or confirm orders first); Judgement weighs short-term opportunity against borrowing risk

--- STEM ---
Halden Motors is an independent car dealership in Dunmore, Country X, selling new and used family cars. It employs 12 sales staff and 6 service technicians, and sold 210 cars last year with revenue of $4.3 million. Around 70% of buyers use finance packages arranged through the dealership, and the average new car costs about $19,000.

The central bank has cut its base interest rate from 6% to 3% to encourage spending. Weekly finance applications at Halden Motors have risen from 18 to 29, and rival dealers are expanding their forecourts.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by the 'base rate' of interest.
    Answer: The base rate is the interest rate set by a country's central bank. It influences the rates commercial banks charge on loans and pay on savings, so a cut makes borrowing cheaper. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: The base rate is set by the central bank; The base rate influences commercial bank lending and saving rates

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the interest rate cut may increase Halden Motors' car sales.
    Answer: Cheaper borrowing for buyers: cutting the base rate from 6% to 3% reduces monthly finance payments on cars [k], and with 70% of Halden's buyers using finance packages, more customers can afford a new $19,000 car [app]. Borrowing is now more attractive than saving: lower rates make saving less rewarding and credit cheaper [k], which is why weekly finance applications have jumped from 18 to 29 [app].
    Keywords: finance packages, 70%, $19,000, 18 to 29, base interest rate, $4.3 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower interest rates reduce the cost of borrowing; Lower interest rates reduce the reward for saving | application_max_2: Around 70% of Halden's buyers use finance packages and the average new car costs about $19,000; Weekly finance applications have risen from 18 to 29 since the cut from 6% to 3%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Halden Motors of borrowing $250,000 to buy 40 additional new cars.
    Answer: Meeting rising demand: sales applications have risen from 18 to 29 a week and rival dealers are expanding their forecourts [k], so having 40 extra cars ready before the peak sales season would let Halden capture sales rather than lose buyers to competitors [app]. More cars in stock lifts potential revenue by roughly 40 x $19,000 = $760,000 [an]. Economies of bulk buying: ordering 40 cars at once may earn volume discounts from manufacturers [k], reducing the cost of each additional car [app], and with finance demand this strong the extra stock should sell quickly, protecting cash flow [an].
    Keywords: $250,000, peak sales season, finance applications, 18 to 29, $19,000, rival dealers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Having more stock lets a business meet demand and avoid lost sales; Buying in bulk can reduce the cost per unit | application_max_2: Finance applications have risen from 18 to 29 a week and rivals are expanding forecourts; The peak sales season is approaching and new cars average about $19,000 | analysis_max_2: Extra stock captures demand that would otherwise go to rivals; Higher sales volume raises revenue and cash inflow

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Mr Whitmore should borrow $250,000 to buy 40 additional new cars? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the cars would let Halden Motors exploit the surge in finance applications, from 18 to 29 a week, while rival dealers are already expanding [k], so acting now could capture sales worth roughly 40 x $19,000 = $760,000 [app], lifting profit and market share in Dunmore [an]. However, borrowing $250,000 adds interest costs and risk if the slowdown deepens [k]; used vehicles already cost nothing extra to finance and may be all that cautious customers need [app], and if rates rise again before the stock sells, margins could be squeezed [an]. On balance, Mr Whitmore should borrow to buy the cars, but order them in stages matched to confirmed orders [eval], because the evidence of demand (29 applications a week, up from 18) points to strong sales [eval].
    Keywords: $250,000, 18 to 29, $19,000, peak sales season, used vehicles, rival dealers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying more stock lets a business exploit rising demand; Borrowing increases costs and financial risk if sales disappoint | application_max_2: Finance applications have risen from 18 to 29 a week after the cut from 6% to 3%; The average new car costs about $19,000 and 70% of buyers use finance | analysis_max_2: Extra stock could secure substantial additional revenue and market share; If demand weakens, unsold cars create a heavy interest and storage burden | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation with a clear position on the $250,000 loan; Judgement weighs demand evidence against borrowing risk

--- STEM ---
Thistledown Home & Living is a private limited company operating 4 homewares stores across Country X, employing 58 staff and recording revenue of $3.4 million last year. It sells bedding, kitchenware and furniture to middle-income households. Since the central bank raised the base interest rate from 4% to 7%, customer visits have fallen by 18% and like-for-like sales dropped 12% in the first quarter. Savings accounts now pay 6% interest.

Owner Carla Ng must decide how to respond. One option is to cut prices by 15% on bedding and kitchenware to attract price-sensitive shoppers; at current volumes she estimates the margin on each $1 of sales would fall from 38 cents to around 27 cents. The other option is to reduce next season's stock orders by 25% and cut staff hours by 10% to protect cash flow. Store rents cost $9,000 per store per month regardless of sales.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State what is meant by 'consumer spending'.
    Answer: Consumer spending is the total amount of money households spend on goods and services. When consumers spend more, business sales and demand tend to rise. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Consumer spending is household expenditure on goods and services; Higher consumer spending increases demand for business products

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Thistledown's sales have fallen since interest rates rose.
    Answer: Borrowing is now more expensive: the rise from 4% to 7% increases mortgage, loan and credit costs for households [k], so customers on middle incomes have less money to spend on homewares [app]. Saving is now more attractive: with savings accounts paying 6% interest, households prefer to save rather than spend [k], which is why store visits have fallen 18% and like-for-like sales have dropped 12% in the first quarter [app].
    Keywords: $3.4 million, 4% to 7%, 18%, 12%, 6%, middle-income households
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive; Higher interest rates make saving more attractive | application_max_2: Thistledown sells to middle-income households across 4 stores generating $3.4 million last year; Customer visits have fallen 18% and like-for-like sales dropped 12% in the first quarter

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Thistledown of cutting prices by 15%.
    Answer: Lower profit per sale: a 15% price cut reduces the margin on each $1 of sales from 38 cents to around 27 cents [k], while rents of $9,000 per store per month still have to be paid [app], so sales volumes must rise just to stand still and profit could disappear [an]. Possible price war: competitors may match the cut, removing the sales gain [k], leaving Thistledown with thinner margins and no increase in volume [app], which could push the business towards cash-flow difficulties [an].
    Keywords: $9,000, 38 cents, 27 cents, 15%, 4 homewares stores, cash flow
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cutting prices reduces the profit earned per unit; Competitors may match a price cut, limiting any sales gain | application_max_2: The margin on each $1 of sales would fall from 38 cents to around 27 cents; Store rents cost $9,000 per store per month regardless of sales across 4 stores | analysis_max_2: Revenue must rise just to cover unchanged costs, squeezing profit; A price war could leave the business worse off with no volume gain

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Carla Ng should cut prices by 15% on bedding and kitchenware? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cutting prices could attract price-sensitive shoppers back into the 4 stores [k], and keeping some visitors spending beats empty stores paying $9,000 rent [app], which might rebuild visitor numbers and protect sales volumes [an]. However, the cut would reduce profit on existing sales while rents of $9,000 per store per month remain fixed [k], and if competitors match it, Thistledown gains nothing [app], pushing the business towards cash-flow problems while still needing to protect 58 jobs [an]. On balance, Carla should not cut prices across the board; she should use modest promotions together with the stock and staffing reductions [eval], because the margin fall from 38 cents to 27 cents makes a 15% cut too deep to sustain [eval].
    Keywords: 15%, 27 cents, $9,000, stock orders, price-sensitive shoppers, 38 cents
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower prices can stimulate demand and attract price-sensitive customers; Cutting prices reduces profit margins and may not increase revenue if demand is weak | application_max_2: Margin on each $1 of sales would fall from 38 cents to around 27 cents on a 15% cut; Rents of $9,000 per store per month over 4 stores are fixed, and sales fell 12% in the first quarter | analysis_max_2: A cut could rebuild traffic and protect sales volumes; If rivals match the cut, profit falls with no volume gain, worsening cash flow | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on whether to cut prices; Judgement weighs a margin of 38 to 27 cents against the need to keep customers

Saltwood Coffee Roasters is a private limited company in Country X, supplying roasted coffee beans to 240 independent cafés. It employs 16 staff and produced 320,000 bags of 1kg coffee last year with revenue of $2.9 million. Over the last 12 months, inflation in Country X has reached 9.5%. Green coffee bean costs are up 40%, roasting energy up 22%, and wages for packing staff up 8%.

Saltwood sells a 1kg wholesale bag for $24.00, but its production cost has risen from $17.50 to $21.00 per bag. Managing director Tomás Ibero must decide whether to raise the wholesale price to $27.50 next month, a 14.6% increase, or hold prices and accept a lower profit margin to keep loyal café customers. Two key café customers have already complained about the smaller price rises Saltwood made in 2025.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline two ways high inflation can affect a business.
    Answer: One way is that input costs such as raw materials, energy and wages rise, squeezing profit margins. A second way is that consumers' purchasing power falls, so demand may drop as customers spend less. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises the cost of inputs such as materials, energy and wages; Inflation reduces consumers' purchasing power, lowering demand

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Saltwood's profit margin has fallen.
    Answer: Rising input costs: inflation of 9.5% has pushed green coffee bean costs up 40% and roastery energy up 22% [k], so the cost of producing a 1kg bag has climbed from $17.50 to $21.00 [app]. Wage increases: packing staff wages have risen 8% [k], adding to costs that cannot be passed on while the wholesale price is held at $24.00 [app].
    Keywords: 9.5%, 40%, $17.50, $21.00, 22%, $24.00
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Rising input costs reduce profit margins; Rising wage costs increase production expenses | application_max_2: Green coffee bean costs are up 40% and roasting energy up 22%; Production cost per bag has risen from $17.50 to $21.00 with wages up 8%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks for Saltwood of raising the wholesale price to $27.50.
    Answer: Loss of café customers: raising prices by 14.6% may push price-sensitive cafés to cheaper suppliers [k], while two key café customers already complained about Saltwood's smaller 2025 price rises [app], so losing their weekly orders would cut volume across the 240 café network [an]. Reduced demand: higher wholesale prices may force cafés to raise their own prices, reducing café footfall [k], which passes inflation pressure onto end customers [app], shrinking Saltwood's sales and making the recovery of its 12.5% margin harder [an].
    Keywords: $27.50, 14.6%, two key café customers, 240 independent cafés, 2025, loyal café customers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher prices may push customers to cheaper suppliers; Higher prices can reduce demand | application_max_2: Two key café customers already complained about smaller price rises in 2025; Saltwood supplies 240 independent cafés and a 14.6% rise is proposed | analysis_max_2: Losing café customers cuts sales volume and revenue; Passing costs on to cafés may reduce end-consumer demand

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Saltwood should raise the wholesale price from $24.00 to $27.50? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising the price would restore Saltwood's margin: at $27.50 against a $21.00 cost, margin would rise from 12.5% to about 24% [k], and with bean costs up 40%, holding $24.00 would destroy profit on 320,000 bags a year [app], threatening the jobs of 16 staff [an]. However, a 14.6% increase may drive loyal café customers to rivals [k], and Saltwood has already faced complaints from two key customers in 2025 [app], so volume could fall and erase the benefit of the higher price [an]. On balance, Saltwood should raise the price, but by a smaller amount or with advance notice and quality assurances [eval], because the margin evidence shows it cannot absorb another year at 12.5% [eval].
    Keywords: $27.50, $24.00, $21.00, 240 independent cafés, 16 staff, 2025
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Raising price can restore profit margins when costs rise; Raising price risks losing customers to competitors | application_max_2: Production cost per bag rose from $17.50 to $21.00 while the price is held at $24.00; Two key café customers complained about the smaller 2025 price rises | analysis_max_2: A higher price protects profit and staff jobs; Volume loss from unhappy cafés could erase the margin gain | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the $27.50 price; Judgement weighs margin recovery against customer loyalty risk
