--- STEM ---
Eastmoor Budget Hotel is a private limited company in Millbrook, Country X, with 110 rooms near the Eastmoor industrial estate. It employs 42 staff and averages 55% occupancy, earning revenue of $2.4 million last year. In January the town's steel components factory closed with the loss of 900 jobs, pushing local unemployment from 3.5% to 7.2%. Inflation rose to 8% in the same period and consumer confidence fell sharply.

General manager Denise Whitaker has noticed business bookings are down 30%, while enquiries for weekly rates from job-seekers attending interviews have doubled. She must decide whether to cut the nightly room rate from $80 to $65 to stimulate demand, or introduce weekly rates of $400 for long-stay guests. The rate cut could fill 15 extra rooms a night, while weekly rates would give more predictable occupancy across the quiet summer months.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline two effects of rising local unemployment on a business.
    Answer: One effect is that consumers have less income to spend, so demand for products falls. A second effect is that more workers are available to hire, making recruitment easier and possibly cheaper. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher unemployment reduces consumer incomes and demand; Higher unemployment increases the supply of labour available to businesses

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the factory closure has affected Eastmoor Budget Hotel.
    Answer: Weaker demand from business travellers: the factory's closure with the loss of 900 jobs has cut local business activity and incomes [k], and Eastmoor has seen business bookings fall by 30% [app]. A new opportunity from long-stay guests: rising unemployment brings job-seekers needing affordable accommodation [k], shown by the doubling of enquiries for weekly rates [app].
    Keywords: 900, 3.5%, 7.2%, 30%, weekly rates, $2.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher unemployment reduces demand for business-related spending; Higher unemployment can increase demand for low-cost services from job-seekers | application_max_2: The steel components factory closed with the loss of 900 jobs and local unemployment rose from 3.5% to 7.2%; Business bookings are down 30% while enquiries for weekly rates have doubled

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Eastmoor of introducing weekly rates of $400 for long-stay guests.
    Answer: More predictable occupancy: weekly rates give a guaranteed share of the 110 rooms each week [k], which suits the hotel's need for steady occupancy in the quiet summer months [app], improving cash flow and making staffing easier to plan [an]. Better use of empty rooms: at $400 a week the effective nightly rate is about $57, below the standard $80 rate but above a $65 cut applied to every room [k], so the hotel fills rooms that would otherwise stay empty [app], raising total revenue without discounting all rooms [an].
    Keywords: 110 rooms, $400, 55%, $80, quiet summer months
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Weekly rates provide predictable, guaranteed occupancy; Weekly rates can fill otherwise empty rooms without discounting all sales | application_max_2: Eastmoor averages 55% occupancy with 110 rooms to fill; Enquiries for weekly rates from job-seekers have doubled | analysis_max_2: Predictable occupancy improves cash flow and staffing plans; Filling rooms at an effective rate above the proposed cut protects revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Denise Whitaker should cut the nightly room rate from $80 to $65? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cutting the nightly rate could attract price-conscious leisure guests [k], and filling 15 extra rooms a night at $65 would add about $975 of nightly revenue compared with empty rooms [app], lifting occupancy above 55% and spreading fixed costs over more guests [an]. However, the cut would reduce revenue on the rooms that would have been sold anyway [k], while weekly rates of $400 match the doubled demand from long-stay job-seekers without cutting standard prices [app], leaving the hotel worse off if existing guests simply switch from $80 to $65 [an]. On balance, the hotel should introduce the $400 weekly rate rather than cut the nightly price [eval], because it targets the proven demand, with enquiries doubled, at less risk to standard revenue [eval].
    Keywords: $80, $65, $400, 15 extra rooms, 55% occupancy, doubled
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cutting prices can stimulate demand and fill spare capacity; Cutting prices reduces revenue on sales that would have happened anyway | application_max_2: The nightly rate would fall from $80 to $65 with a possible gain of 15 extra rooms a night; Weekly rates of $400 match doubled enquiries from job-seekers | analysis_max_2: 15 extra rooms a night adds around $975 nightly revenue and spreads fixed costs; Existing guests switching to the cheaper rate would cut revenue with no extra occupancy | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the nightly rate cut; Judgement weighs extra occupancy against reduced revenue on existing sales

  Qb [4 marks]

Strong exports: food exports have risen 14%, and Drayton's customers need boxes to ship produce abroad [k], which is why its order book has grown 25% in 9 months [app].
    Keywords: 3.8%, 14%, 25%, order book, $6.8 million, food exporters
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Economic growth increases demand for goods and services; Rising exports increase demand for supporting domestic industries | application_max_2: Country X's economy grew by 3.8% last year, the fastest for a decade; Food exports have risen 14% and Drayton's order book has grown 25% in 9 months

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Drayton of recruiting 30 permanent workers.

Contract security: permanent staff would let Drayton extend supply for two key customers over 3 years [k], securing stable order volumes [app], and this stability supports revenue planning and investment in the 2 factories [an].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recruiting permanent staff raises sustainable capacity; Overtime is limited by law and cannot expand indefinitely | application_max_2: Overtime is already at 12 hours per worker per week, close to the legal limit; Two key customers want their supply contracts extended for 3 years | analysis_max_2: Recruitment avoids breaking legal overtime limits while meeting demand; Permanent capacity secures long-term contracts and stable revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Drayton should recruit 30 permanent workers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Recruitment would let Drayton meet the projected 20% rise in orders next year [k], with 130 existing workers already on 12 hours overtime near legal limits [app], and would help secure two 3-year supply contracts, protecting a large share of $6.8 million revenue [an]. However, $900,000 a year in wages is a heavy permanent cost [k]; overtime and subcontracting cost an extra $250,000 a year and avoid long-term commitments if demand falls [app], so a downturn could leave 30 extra workers idle and profit fragile [an]. On balance, Drayton should recruit the 30 workers [eval], because the evidence of sustained growth (25% order growth, GDP at 3.8%) makes long-term capacity cheaper and safer than overtime [eval].
    Keywords: $900,000, 12 hours, 3 years, 25%, 3.8%, $250,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recruiting permanent staff meets rising demand with sustainable capacity; Recruitment adds permanent wage costs and risk if demand falls | application_max_2: Projected orders rise another 20% over the next 12 months with overtime near legal limits at 12 hours; Recruitment costs $900,000 a year versus $250,000 extra for overtime and subcontracting | analysis_max_2: Permanent staff secure capacity for 3-year contracts and revenue growth; If demand disappoints, 30 extra workers become an expensive burden | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on recruiting the 30 workers; Judgement weighs sustained growth evidence against permanent wage risk

Option 1 is to cut standard membership from $42 to $35, which would reduce fee income by $26,600 a month before any new members join (3,800 x $7). Option 2 is to launch an off-peak membership at $25 for mornings only, aimed at retirees and job-seekers, without cutting standard prices. Renewals are due for 1,500 members next quarter.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'consumer confidence'.
    Answer: Consumer confidence is how optimistic consumers feel about the economy and their own finances. Higher confidence encourages spending; low confidence makes consumers save instead of spend. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Consumer confidence is how optimistic consumers feel; High confidence encourages spending; low confidence encourages saving

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why gym membership at Ainsworth has fallen recently.
    Answer: High inflation reduces real incomes: inflation of 8.5% means wages buy less, so consumers cut non-essential spending [k]; Ainsworth has lost 620 members in 6 months [app]. Low consumer confidence: the index has fallen from 105 to 88, so households feel pessimistic about their finances [k], and a $42 monthly leisure membership is an easy budget item to cancel [app].
    Keywords: 8.5%, 105 to 88, 620, 3,800, $42, $2.7 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: High inflation reduces consumers' purchasing power; Low consumer confidence reduces willingness to spend on non-essentials | application_max_2: Inflation is at 8.5% with interest rates at 7%; Some 620 members have cancelled or downgraded in 6 months

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Ainsworth of launching an off-peak membership at $25.
    Answer: Fills quiet morning capacity: gyms are often under-used before noon [k], and an off-peak $25 membership could attract retirees and job-seekers looking for affordable exercise [app], turning empty capacity into extra revenue without cutting standard prices [an]. Protects standard fees: standard members keep paying $42, avoiding the $26,600 monthly loss a full cut would cause [k], while the off-peak tier widens the market to price-sensitive groups [app], building the membership base to offset the 620 cancellations [an].
    Keywords: $25, off-peak, $26,600, retirees, mornings, 620
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Off-peak pricing monetises spare capacity at quiet times; A separate tier avoids discounting existing customers | application_max_2: The off-peak membership at $25 targets mornings, retirees and job-seekers; A full cut would reduce fee income by $26,600 a month before any new members join | analysis_max_2: Quiet morning capacity becomes revenue without diluting standard prices; A wider membership base offsets cancellations and protects total income

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Lucy Hammond should cut standard membership from $42 to $35? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A cut could win back some of the 620 cancelled or downgraded members [k], and at $35 Ainsworth might still keep more members paying something than losing $42 fees entirely [app], protecting footfall and class income across the 2 centres [an]. However, cutting the fee reduces income by $26,600 a month before any new members sign up [k], and an off-peak membership at $25 targets price-sensitive customers without discounting everyone [app], so a full cut may be unnecessarily deep while 1,500 renewals are due next quarter [an]. On balance, Ainsworth should launch the $25 off-peak membership rather than cut standard fees [eval], because the risk of losing $26,600 a month outweighs the uncertain gains from the cut [eval].
    Keywords: $42, $35, $26,600, 620, $25, 1,500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lowering price can stimulate demand and win back lapsed members; A price cut reduces revenue from existing members unless demand rises sharply | application_max_2: A cut from $42 to $35 would reduce fee income by $26,600 a month before any new members join; 620 members have cancelled or downgraded; 1,500 renewals are due next quarter | analysis_max_2: Retaining price-sensitive customers protects footfall and ancillary income; The fixed monthly loss applies immediately while new sign-ups are uncertain | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the membership price cut; Judgement weighs certain monthly revenue loss against uncertain demand recovery

Emmer & Oak Bakery is a family-run partnership in Country X, supplying fresh bread and rolls to 140 schools under a 12-month fixed-price contract worth $1.6 million.     Question: Outline what is meant by a 'fixed-price contract'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A fixed-price contract keeps the price unchanged for a set period; Fixed-price contracts give the buyer certainty but shift cost risk onto the supplier

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Emmer & Oak's costs have increased.
    Answer: Rising raw material costs: inflation of 10% has pushed flour prices up 35% and yeast and packaging up 18% [k], so every one of the 2.1 million loaves costs more to produce [app]. Higher energy bills: oven energy costs have risen 25% [k], which is significant for a bakery running ovens throughout the day [app].
    Keywords: 10%, 35%, 18%, 25%, 2.1 million loaves, $1.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises raw material costs; Inflation raises energy and utility costs | application_max_2: Flour costs are up 35% and yeast and packaging up 18%; Oven energy bills are up 25% for a bakery delivering 2.1 million loaves a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two risks for Emmer & Oak of asking the caterer to renegotiate now.

Damaged relationships: challenging a signed contract may make the caterer distrust future deals [k], and the schools' caterer may warn other public buyers about the bakery [app], making it harder to win the renewal or new contracts [an].
    Keywords: 3-month, $1.6 million, $90,000, rival bakery, 48 staff, 140 schools
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A buyer may cancel a contract under the notice period if asked to renegotiate; Challenging a contract can damage the supplier-buyer relationship | application_max_2: The caterer has written a 3-month notice period into the contract; The contract is worth $1.6 million a year supplying 140 schools, with 48 staff dependent on it | analysis_max_2: Cancellation removes roughly $133,000 of monthly revenue and threatens jobs; Reputation damage reduces the chance of winning the renewal or future bids

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Mira Castellanos should ask the caterer to renegotiate the contract now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Renegotiating now could stop the bakery losing $90,000 over its remaining 5 months [k], and with flour up 35% and oven energy up 25%, continuing at the agreed price is unsustainable for 48 staff [app], so an honest conversation backed by cost evidence might be accepted by the caterer [an]. On balance, Mira should wait until renewal and quote a higher price then, while absorbing a controlled loss now [eval], because protecting a 12-month customer relationship is worth more than $90,000 [eval].
    Keywords: $90,000, 5 months, 3-month notice, $1.6 million, 48 staff, renewal
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Renegotiating can recover rising costs on a fixed-price contract; Renegotiating risks cancellation and losing the customer | application_max_2: The contract will lose $90,000 over its remaining 5 months at current costs; The caterer has a 3-month notice period and could switch to a rival bakery | analysis_max_2: Successful renegotiation stops the $90,000 loss and stabilises margins; Cancellation removes $1.6 million of annual revenue and threatens jobs and capacity | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on renegotiating now; Judgement weighs the certain $90,000 loss against the risk of losing the whole contract

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Starting at a peak-demand moment maximises sales; Borrowing preserves internal finance for other needs | application_max_2: Phase 2 sold out in 8 months and mortgage approvals have risen 30%; The loan of $1.5 million at 5% costs about $75,000 a year, leaving $2.2 million retained profit intact | analysis_max_2: Early launch captures peak demand and raises revenue; Preserving retained profit protects cash flow against delays

  Qd [8 marks]

    Keywords: $1.5 million, $75,000 a year, 30%, 24 houses, Phase 2, spring

--- STEM ---
Clearbrook Logistics is a private limited company operating a distribution depot in Country X, employing 140 drivers, warehouse workers and office staff. It delivers 1,900 tonnes of goods a week for supermarket customers and recorded revenue of $5.2 million last year. Regional unemployment has fallen to 2.1%, the lowest on record, and Clearbrook has 25 unfilled driver vacancies despite advertising for 4 months.

Operations director Mr Ellison must decide how to respond. One option is to raise driver wages by 10%, adding $3,400 a year for each of its 96 drivers, a total of $326,400 a year. The other option is to launch an in-house training scheme costing $60,000 to recruit and licence 25 local people with no prior driving experience. Two rival firms have already raised wages by 8%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two problems a very low unemployment rate can cause a business.
    Answer: One problem is a shortage of available workers, making it hard to fill vacancies. A second problem is pressure to raise wages to attract and keep staff, increasing costs. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A shortage of available labour makes recruitment harder; Low unemployment creates upward pressure on wages

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Clearbrook is struggling to recruit drivers.
    Answer: Few unemployed workers: regional unemployment has fallen to 2.1%, the lowest on record, so almost all qualified drivers already have jobs [k], which is why Clearbrook has 25 unfilled vacancies after 4 months of advertising [app]. Rivals are competing for the same workers: two rival firms have already raised wages by 8% [k], so Clearbrook's current pay is no longer competitive [app].
    Keywords: 2.1%, 25 unfilled driver vacancies, $5.2 million, 8%, 4 months
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A shortage of labour makes filling vacancies difficult; Rival firms may outbid a business for scarce workers | application_max_2: Regional unemployment has fallen to 2.1%, the lowest on record; 25 driver vacancies remain unfilled after 4 months of advertising

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Clearbrook of launching the in-house training scheme costing $60,000.
    Answer: Cheaper than a 10% wage rise: the scheme costs $60,000 once, versus $326,400 a year extra for a wage rise across all 96 drivers [k], freeing cash for other needs such as vehicle maintenance [app], so profit is protected while vacancies are filled [an]. Grows a committed workforce: training 25 local people with no prior driving experience builds loyalty [k], and they arrive without holding rival offers created by the 8% wage rises elsewhere [app], reducing the risk of trained drivers simply leaving for competitors [an].
    Keywords: $60,000, $326,400, 96 drivers, 10%, $3,400, 8%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: In-house training can be cheaper than a general wage increase; Training internally can build loyalty and reduce turnover | application_max_2: The scheme costs $60,000 versus $326,400 a year for a 10% wage rise across 96 drivers; It would recruit and licence 25 local people with no prior driving experience | analysis_max_2: Lower one-off cost protects profit and cash flow; Loyal new drivers reduce the risk of poaching by rivals

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Mr Ellison should raise driver wages by 10%? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A 10% rise would match or beat rivals who have raised wages by 8% [k], adding $3,400 a year per driver and costing $326,400 a year across 96 drivers [app], which should stop current drivers leaving and make the 25 vacancies easier to fill [an]. However, $326,400 a year is a permanent increase to fixed costs [k], while the $60,000 training scheme creates 25 locally recruited drivers who may stay loyal for years [app], and it could deliver capacity faster than hoping the tight labour market frees up qualified drivers [an]. On balance, Clearbrook should launch the training scheme rather than raise all wages by 10% [eval], because $60,000 versus $326,400 a year is strongly better value for filling the vacancies [eval].
    Keywords: 10%, $326,400, $60,000, 8%, 96 drivers, 25 local people
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Raising wages helps attract and retain scarce labour; Raising wages permanently increases fixed costs | application_max_2: A 10% rise adds $3,400 a year per driver and $326,400 a year across 96 drivers; The alternative training scheme costs $60,000 once to licence 25 local people | analysis_max_2: Competitive wages stem turnover and fill vacancies; A permanent wage increase erodes profit if demand or margins weaken | evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the 10% wage rise; Judgement weighs $326,400 a year against a one-off $60,000 training cost

--- STEM ---
Harrington Paper Works is a private limited company operating a paper and cardboard mill in the town of Kestrel Vale for 14 years, employing 240 workers. The mill generates $9,500,000 in annual revenue but its older boilers emit sulphur dioxide and the plant discharges wastewater. A government inspection found emissions 30% above the legal limit, exposing the company to daily fines of $8,000 until it complies.

Management is considering a $1,200,000 emissions control system, including new boilers and water treatment, to meet the legal limit. A local pressure group, Clean Air Kestrel, is campaigning against the mill and has urged two retail clients worth $2,000,000 a year to boycott its packaging. The company could instead continue operating and pay the fines while searching for cheaper equipment.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'pollution'.
    Answer: The release of harmful substances, noise or energy into the environment in quantities that damage human health, wildlife or ecosystems [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: release of harmful substances, noise or energy into the environment; quantities that damage human health, wildlife or ecosystems

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems pollution from the paper mill creates for Harrington Paper Works.
    Answer: Problem 1: Heavy financial penalties [k], emissions 30% above the legal limit expose the mill to daily fines of $8,000 [app]. Problem 2: Reputational damage and lost orders [k], Clean Air Kestrel has urged two retail clients worth $2,000,000 a year to boycott its packaging [app].
    Keywords: Harrington Paper Works, $8,000, 30%, Clean Air Kestrel, boycott, $9,500,000, wastewater
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: heavy financial penalties / daily fines; reputational damage / lost orders from boycott | application_max_2: 30% above the legal limit; daily fines of $8,000; Clean Air Kestrel; $2,000,000 a year retail clients

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Harrington Paper Works of installing the $1,200,000 emissions control system.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Stops the daily fines [k], the system brings the Kestrel Vale mill back within the legal limit so the $8,000 daily fines end [app], protecting profit [an]. Benefit 2: Protects customer orders [k], calming Clean Air Kestrel and defending the $2,000,000 of retail clients from the boycott [app], securing future sales [an].
    Keywords: emissions control system, $1,200,000, $8,000, Clean Air Kestrel, $2,000,000, Kestrel Vale, boycott
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: stops daily fines / legal compliance; protects customer orders / reputation | application_max_2: $8,000 daily fines end; Kestrel Vale mill; Clean Air Kestrel; $2,000,000 of retail clients | analysis_max_2: protecting profit; securing future sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harrington Paper Works should invest in the $1,200,000 emissions control system or continue paying the daily fines? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing ends the fines permanently [k], bringing emissions 30% above the legal limit back within the law at Kestrel Vale so the $8,000 daily fines stop [app], saving up to $2,920,000 a year [an]. It also weakens the Clean Air Kestrel boycott threat and protects orders from retail clients worth $2,000,000 a year [app], securing future sales [an]. However, paying the fines avoids the immediate $1,200,000 outlay and preserves cash for 240 workers [k]. Overall, investing is the better option because the $2,920,000 annual saving far exceeds the one-off $1,200,000 cost within months [eval], and legal compliance also safeguards the mill's right to operate at Kestrel Vale long term [eval].
    Keywords: $1,200,000, $8,000, Kestrel Vale, Clean Air Kestrel, boycott, $2,000,000, emissions, legal limit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: ends the fines permanently / legal compliance; preserves short-term cash by paying fines | application_max_2: 30% above the legal limit; $8,000 daily fines; $2,920,000 a year saving; $2,000,000 a year retail clients; $1,200,000 outlay | analysis_max_2: saving up to $2,920,000 a year; securing future sales | evaluation_max_2: weighs one-off $1,200,000 cost against recurring fine savings; compliance safeguards long-term right to operate

UNIT: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
PalmCrest Estates is a private limited company operating 11,000 hectares of palm oil plantations in Country X, established 9 years ago by founder Renata Duarte. It employs 520 plantation workers and exports $6,800,000 of crude palm oil annually. To double output, the company plans to clear 1,500 hectares of remaining forest, expecting an extra $3,200,000 in annual sales.

Environmental groups claim the forest holds endangered primates and have organised a petition signed by 45,000 people. The government now requires an environmental impact assessment before any clearing, with fines of $500,000 for illegal logging. The board is weighing this against an alternative: buy 800 hectares of degraded, already-cleared land for $2,100,000, suited to replanting but with lower yields for the first 6 years of cultivation.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'deforestation'.
    Answer: The clearing and permanent removal of trees and forest cover from land, usually to make way for farming, logging or development [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: clearing and permanent removal of trees and forest cover; to make way for farming, logging or development

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems that clearing 1,500 hectares of forest could cause for PalmCrest Estates.
    Answer: Problem 1: Legal penalties [k], the government now requires an environmental impact assessment and illegal logging brings fines of $500,000 [app]. Problem 2: Reputational damage and lost sales [k], the petition signed by 45,000 people shows strong opposition to clearing the forest [app].
    Keywords: PalmCrest Estates, 1,500 hectares, $500,000, 45,000, environmental impact assessment, logging, forest
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: legal penalties / fines; reputational damage / lost sales | application_max_2: environmental impact assessment required; fines of $500,000 for illegal logging; petition signed by 45,000 people; 1,500 hectares of remaining forest

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for PalmCrest Estates of buying the 800 hectares of degraded land instead of clearing the forest.
    Answer: Advantage 1: No legal risk [k], already-cleared degraded land avoids the environmental impact assessment problem and the $500,000 illegal logging fine [app], removing the risk of losing the expansion programme [an]. Advantage 2: Protects reputation and exports [k], replanting degraded land keeps the $6,800,000 export business safe from the 45,000-signature petition [app], supporting continued sales growth [an].
    Keywords: 800 hectares, degraded, $500,000, $6,800,000, $2,100,000, petition, PalmCrest Estates
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: no legal risk / compliance; protects reputation and exports | application_max_2: already-cleared degraded land; $500,000 illegal logging fine; $6,800,000 export business; 45,000-signature petition | analysis_max_2: removing the risk of losing the expansion programme; supporting continued sales growth

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think PalmCrest Estates should buy the degraded land instead of clearing the 1,500 hectares of forest? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the degraded land avoids fines and rejection [k], because the government requires an environmental impact assessment and illegal logging brings fines of $500,000 [app], protecting the company's legal position and expansion plan [an]. It also safeguards the $6,800,000 export business, since buyers increasingly prefer sustainable palm oil while 45,000 people have signed the petition [app], securing long-term contracts [an]. However, clearing the forest could unlock $3,200,000 in extra sales quickly [k], boosting growth for 520 workers. Overall, buying the degraded land is wiser because the $2,100,000 price is outweighed by avoiding the $500,000 fine risk and reputational harm [eval], and sustainable replanting keeps the estates compliant and attractive to export buyers for years to come [eval].
    Keywords: degraded, $500,000, $6,800,000, $2,100,000, 45,000, 1,500 hectares, palm oil, 800 hectares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: avoids fines and rejection / legal compliance; clearing forest unlocks extra sales quickly | application_max_2: $500,000 illegal logging fine; $6,800,000 export business; 45,000 people signed the petition; $2,100,000 price | analysis_max_2: protecting the company's legal position and expansion plan; securing long-term contracts | evaluation_max_2: weighs $2,100,000 purchase price against $500,000 fine and reputational harm; sustainable replanting keeps estates compliant and attractive to buyers

--- STEM ---
BrightKiln Cement Works is a private limited company running a cement plant on the edge of the town of Alderney for 18 years, employing 150 workers and producing 90,000 tonnes of cement a year, with $11,000,000 in annual revenue. Local residents complain about night-time grinding noise of around 60 decibels, dust and lorry traffic passing up to 200 homes.

A residents' association has collected 1,200 signatures demanding action. A planned $750,000 noise barrier and enclosed conveyor would cut noise by 25 decibels, but shareholders want a $1,400,000 plant expansion next year that would double output. The local council has warned that continued breaches could bring an enforcement notice and possible closure. Alternatively, management could move night shifts to daytime, cutting capacity by 20%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'noise pollution'.
    Answer: Unwanted or excessive sound that harms the health and quality of life of people living or working near its source, such as machinery or lorry traffic [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: unwanted or excessive sound; harms the health and quality of life of people nearby

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two external costs the BrightKiln Cement Works plant creates for the local community.
    Answer: External cost 1: Noise disturbing homes [k], night-time grinding of around 60 decibels disturbs residents near the Alderney plant [app]. External cost 2: Dust and traffic pollution [k], lorries passing up to 200 homes and dust from the plant have driven 1,200 residents to sign the association's petition [app].
    Keywords: BrightKiln Cement Works, 60 decibels, Alderney, 200 homes, 1,200, dust, noise
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: noise disturbance to residents; dust and traffic pollution | application_max_2: 60 decibels night-time grinding; lorries passing up to 200 homes; 1,200 signatures; Alderney plant

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to BrightKiln Cement Works of installing the $750,000 noise barrier and enclosed conveyor.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Avoids closure [k], cutting noise by 25 decibels answers the council's warning over the 60 decibels night-time breaches [app], protecting $11,000,000 of annual revenue and 150 jobs [an]. Benefit 2: Repairs community relations [k], easing the complaints of the 1,200-signature residents' association [app], strengthening the plant's licence to operate and planning position [an].
    Keywords: $750,000, 25 decibels, 60 decibels, 1,200, noise barrier, Alderney, 150 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: avoids enforcement notice / closure; repairs community relations | application_max_2: cutting noise by 25 decibels; 60 decibels night-time breaches; 1,200-signature residents' association; $11,000,000 annual revenue | analysis_max_2: protecting $11,000,000 of annual revenue and 150 jobs; strengthening the plant's licence to operate and planning position

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think BrightKiln Cement Works should install the $750,000 noise barrier and enclosed conveyor or move night shifts to daytime? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The barrier permanently cuts noise by 25 decibels [k], removing the 60 decibels night-time breach that risks the council's enforcement notice and closure [app], safeguarding $11,000,000 annual revenue and 150 jobs [an]. It also defuses the 1,200-signature residents' petition, easing future planning consents [app], which supports the planned $1,400,000 expansion [an]. However, moving night shifts to daytime avoids the $750,000 cost entirely [k], preserving short-term cash, though cutting capacity by 20% reduces sales. Overall, installing the barrier is the stronger option because avoiding closure and the 20% capacity loss outweighs the one-off $750,000 [eval], and permanent noise control protects the $1,400,000 expansion and community support the plant needs [eval].
    Keywords: $750,000, $1,400,000, 25 decibels, 1,200, Alderney, 150 workers, 60 decibels
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: barrier permanently resolves the noise breach; moving night shifts avoids the cost / preserves short-term cash | application_max_2: 25 decibels reduction / 60 decibels breach; enforcement notice and possible closure; 1,200-signature residents' petition; $1,400,000 plant expansion; $750,000 cost | analysis_max_2: safeguarding $11,000,000 annual revenue and 150 jobs; supports the planned $1,400,000 expansion | evaluation_max_2: weighs closure risk and 20% capacity loss against one-off $750,000; permanent noise control protects expansion and community support

--- STEM ---
Eastmere Brickworks is a private limited company planning to build a new brick factory in the deprived town of Darnley Moor, creating 180 permanent jobs and a training academy expected to train 120 young people a year. Construction will cost $5,500,000 and take 18 months. The local council supports the scheme and has offered a 4-year business rates holiday worth $600,000.

The site sits beside 40 homes, and residents worry about lorry movements of up to 90 trucks a day, plus smoke from the kiln. The company could instead build on out-of-town land 12 kilometres away, avoiding complaints but adding $1,100,000 in transport costs and losing the rates holiday. Local unemployment in Darnley Moor is 9%, well above the national average.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'external benefits'.
    Answer: Benefits enjoyed by third parties who are not directly involved in a business decision, such as jobs, training or regeneration in the local community [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: benefits enjoyed by third parties; not directly involved in the decision, e.g. jobs, training, regeneration

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two external benefits the Eastmere Brickworks factory would create in Darnley Moor.
    Answer: External benefit 1: New jobs [k], 180 permanent jobs in a town where unemployment is 9% [app]. External benefit 2: Training and skills [k], the training academy is expected to train 120 young people a year [app].
    Keywords: Eastmere Brickworks, Darnley Moor, 180, 9%, 120, training academy, unemployment
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: new jobs for local people; training and skills development | application_max_2: 180 permanent jobs; unemployment is 9%; training academy; 120 young people a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Eastmere Brickworks of building on out-of-town land instead of in Darnley Moor.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Fewer complaints and delays [k], the out-of-town site avoids 90 trucks a day passing 40 homes [app], reducing the risk of objections [an]. Advantage 2: Lower environmental friction [k], no kiln smoke issues for neighbours eases pressure on planning and operations [app], protecting the 18-month construction timetable [an].
    Keywords: out-of-town, 90 trucks, 40 homes, $1,100,000, kiln, 12 kilometres, $600,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fewer complaints and delays; lower environmental friction / planning pressure | application_max_2: 90 trucks a day; 40 homes; kiln smoke; 12 kilometres away | analysis_max_2: reducing the risk of objections; protecting the 18-month construction timetable

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Eastmere Brickworks should build the factory in Darnley Moor or on out-of-town land 12 kilometres away? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The town site creates strong community support [k], bringing 180 jobs and training academy places for 120 young people a year to Darnley Moor where unemployment is 9% [app], while saving $1,100,000 in transport costs plus the $600,000 rates holiday [an]. However, the out-of-town site avoids 90 trucks a day passing 40 homes and kiln smoke complaints [app], reducing the risk of objections [k] and protecting the 18-month construction timetable [an]. Overall, the town site is the better option because the combined $1,700,000 saving outweighs the local complaint risk [eval], and regenerating a high-unemployment community strengthens the brickworks' reputation and future planning applications [eval].
    Keywords: Darnley Moor, 180, $600,000, $1,100,000, 40 homes, 90 trucks, $5,500,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: community support and regeneration from town site; out-of-town site avoids complaints and objection risk | application_max_2: 180 jobs / 120 young people a year; 9% unemployment; $1,100,000 transport saving / $600,000 rates holiday; 90 trucks a day / 40 homes; $1,700,000 combined saving | analysis_max_2: saving $1,100,000 in transport plus the $600,000 holiday boosts profit; out-of-town protects the 18-month construction timetable | evaluation_max_2: weighs the $1,700,000 combined saving against local complaint risk; regeneration strengthens reputation and future planning applications

--- STEM ---
Velvette Apparel is a private limited company designing fashion clothing sold through 25 stores, founded 7 years ago by Priya Raman, generating $18,000,000 in annual revenue. Its cheapest supplier in Country Y produces garments for $4 per unit compared with $9 from a certified ethical supplier, saving Velvette $1,250,000 a year at current volumes. An audit found the Country Y factory pays below the legal minimum wage and enforces excessive overtime.

The board must choose between renewing the Country Y contract for 3 years, switching fully to the ethical supplier and raising prices by 8%, or splitting orders 50/50. A survey showed 62% of 3,000 customers would pay more for ethically made clothes. The Country Y contract supports 900 factory workers in Country Y, who would lose their jobs if Velvette switched overnight.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two ethical issues businesses may face when choosing suppliers.
    Answer: Low pay and below the legal minimum wage for supplier workers [1]; excessive overtime and poor working conditions at supplier factories [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: low wages / below minimum wage; excessive overtime / poor working conditions

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the Country Y contract creates an ethical problem for Velvette Apparel.
    Answer: Reason 1: Exploitation of workers [k], the audit found the Country Y factory pays below the legal minimum wage for the $4 garments it supplies [app]. Reason 2: Unfair working conditions [k], enforcing excessive overtime at the factory producing Velvette's clothing [app].
    Keywords: Velvette Apparel, Country Y, $4, $9, minimum wage, excessive overtime, audit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exploitation of workers / below minimum wage; unfair working conditions / excessive overtime | application_max_2: Country Y factory; $4 garments; below the legal minimum wage; excessive overtime

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Velvette Apparel of switching fully to the certified ethical supplier.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Higher customer loyalty and sales [k], 62% of 3,000 customers would pay more for ethically made clothes [app], lifting revenue beyond the 8% price rise [an]. Benefit 2: Better reputation and lower risk [k], avoiding future scandals like the Country Y audit findings [app], protecting the $18,000,000 brand [an].
    Keywords: certified ethical supplier, 62%, 3,000, 8%, Country Y, $18,000,000, audit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher customer loyalty and sales; better reputation and lower risk | application_max_2: 62% of 3,000 customers; ethically made clothes; Country Y audit findings; $18,000,000 brand | analysis_max_2: lifting revenue beyond the 8% price rise; protecting the $18,000,000 brand

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Velvette Apparel should switch completely to the certified ethical supplier or keep the Country Y contract? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching completely protects Velvette from exploitation scandals [k], ending reliance on the below minimum wage Country Y factory supplying $4 garments [app], defending the $18,000,000 brand and 25 stores [an]. With 62% of 3,000 surveyed customers willing to pay more, the 8% price rise could hold sales [app], supporting profit despite higher unit costs [an]. However, keeping the Country Y contract saves $1,250,000 a year, avoids job losses for 900 workers and spares the 8% price rise [k]. Overall, switching is the better option because ethical sourcing matches the 62% customer preference and removes audit risk [eval], even though it trims short-term margin, as brand trust outlasts $1,250,000 of annual savings [eval].
    Keywords: Country Y, $4, 62%, 8%, $1,250,000, 900, ethical supplier, Velvette Apparel
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: switching protects against exploitation scandals; keeping the contract saves money and jobs | application_max_2: below minimum wage Country Y factory / $4 garments; $18,000,000 brand and 25 stores; 62% of 3,000 surveyed customers / 8% price rise; $1,250,000 a year saving / 900 workers | analysis_max_2: defending the brand and stores; the 8% price rise could hold sales despite higher costs | evaluation_max_2: weighs 62% customer preference and audit risk against $1,250,000 savings; brand trust outlasts short-term margin gains

--- STEM ---
Brookfield Supermarkets is a regional chain of 14 stores in Country X operating for 11 years, with 1,050 staff and $26,000,000 in annual sales. Electricity costs rose 28% last year, and refrigeration alone now costs $780,000 a year. Management is considering replacing open fridge units with doors and LED lighting across all stores for $2,300,000, saving an estimated $410,000 a year.

A loyalty survey of 9,000 customers found 58% prefer to shop with energy-efficient retailers, and a competitor chain recently launched an advertising campaign highlighting its green energy use. Brookfield could instead phase the change over 3 years to spread the cost, delaying most of the savings. Two banks have offered loans at 7.5% interest to fund the project immediately.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'green consumer'.
    Answer: A customer who deliberately chooses products and services that cause less environmental damage, sometimes willing to pay a premium for them [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customer who deliberately chooses environmentally-friendly products and services; sometimes willing to pay a premium

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Brookfield Supermarkets might want to reduce its energy use.
    Answer: Reason 1: Lower operating costs [k], electricity costs rose 28% last year and refrigeration alone now costs $780,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Attract green-minded customers [k], a loyalty survey of 9,000 customers showed 58% prefer energy-efficient retailers [app].
    Keywords: Brookfield Supermarkets, 28%, $780,000, 9,000, 58%, refrigeration, electricity
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower operating costs; attract green-minded customers | application_max_2: electricity costs rose 28%; refrigeration costs $780,000 a year; loyalty survey of 9,000 customers; 58% prefer energy-efficient retailers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Brookfield Supermarkets of installing fridge doors and LED lighting now.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Immediate energy savings [k], the $2,300,000 upgrade saves an estimated $410,000 a year across 14 stores [app], raising profit [an]. Advantage 2: Competitive advantage [k], acting now answers the 58% customer preference and the competitor's green energy campaign [app], strengthening customer loyalty and sales [an].
    Keywords: $2,300,000, $410,000, 14 stores, 58%, LED lighting, Brookfield, refrigeration
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: immediate energy savings; competitive advantage / customer loyalty | application_max_2: $2,300,000 upgrade; saves an estimated $410,000 a year; 14 stores; 58% customer preference; competitor's green energy campaign | analysis_max_2: raising profit; strengthening customer loyalty and sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brookfield Supermarkets should install the fridge doors and LED lighting now, or phase the change over 3 years? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Installing now captures savings immediately [k], delivering the estimated $410,000 a year across 14 stores from a $2,300,000 investment [app], recovering the cost in under 6 years and raising profit [an]. It also positions Brookfield ahead of the competitor's green campaign, matching the 58% of 9,000 surveyed shoppers who prefer energy-efficient retailers [app], building loyalty and repeat sales [an]. However, phasing over 3 years spreads the $2,300,000 and avoids a 7.5% loan [k], easing pressure on cash flow. Overall, installing now is the better option because delaying forfeits a large share of the $410,000 annual saving [eval], and the 28% electricity rise makes early action cheaper than waiting [eval].
    Keywords: $2,300,000, $410,000, 14 stores, 58%, 9,000, 7.5%, 28%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: installing now captures savings immediately; phasing spreads the cost and eases cash flow | application_max_2: $410,000 a year / $2,300,000 investment; 14 stores; 58% of 9,000 surveyed shoppers; 7.5% loan / 3 years | analysis_max_2: recovering the cost in under 6 years and raising profit; building loyalty and repeat sales | evaluation_max_2: weighs delay against forfeited savings; 28% electricity rise makes early action cheaper

--- STEM ---
Suncrest Soft Drinks is a private limited company producing bottled fruit juices and sodas, founded 12 years ago by Daniel and Ruth Okoro, with $13,000,000 in annual sales through 2,400 retail outlets. Its marketing team proposes a campaign claiming the new pure natural range contains zero additives and helps you live longer, although the range contains 9 additives and sugar equal to 10 teaspoons per bottle.

An honest campaign, taste the range responsibly, is expected to lift sales by 4% using $90,000 of adverts. The hyped campaign could lift sales by 18% but risks breaching advertising standards and a fine of up to $250,000, plus reputational harm if challenged. Posting the honest campaign on social media costs nothing extra, and the founders must approve by Friday.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'misleading advertising'.
    Answer: Promotion that gives consumers a false or exaggerated impression of a product, leading them to make buying decisions based on untrue claims [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: promotion giving a false or exaggerated impression; leading consumers to decide based on untrue claims

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the proposed pure natural campaign could be misleading.
    Answer: Reason 1: False additive claim [k], the new pure natural range claims to contain zero additives while actually containing 9 additives [app]. Reason 2: False health promise [k], claiming it helps you live longer despite sugar equal to 10 teaspoons per bottle [app].
    Keywords: pure natural, zero additives, 9 additives, 10 teaspoons, Suncrest Soft Drinks, 2,400, $13,000,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: false additive claim; false health promise | application_max_2: zero additives claim vs 9 additives; helps you live longer claim; 10 teaspoons per bottle; pure natural range

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Suncrest Soft Drinks of choosing the honest campaign instead of the hyped one.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Avoids legal breach and fines [k], the honest campaign does not risk advertising standards action or a fine of up to $250,000 [app], protecting profit [an]. Benefit 2: Protects brand trust [k], honest taste claims keep the 2,400 retail outlets confident in the brand [app], supporting long-term repeat purchases [an].
    Keywords: honest campaign, $250,000, advertising standards, 2,400, $90,000, $13,000,000, taste the range responsibly
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: avoids legal breach and fines; protects brand trust | application_max_2: honest campaign; advertising standards action; fine of up to $250,000; 2,400 retail outlets | analysis_max_2: protecting profit; supporting long-term repeat purchases

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Suncrest Soft Drinks should run the hyped pure natural campaign or the honest campaign? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The hyped campaign breaches advertising honesty [k], because zero additives is false for a range containing 9 additives and 10 teaspoons of sugar per bottle [app], risking a $250,000 fine and reputational harm [an]. The honest campaign lifts sales by 4% for $90,000 [app], protecting $13,000,000 of revenue across 2,400 retail outlets [an]. However, the hyped option could lift sales by 18% [k], tempting companies seeking fast growth. Overall, the honest campaign is the better option because it avoids the fine and preserves customer trust [eval], whereas an 18% spike built on false claims would collapse once challenged, costing more than it gains [eval].
    Keywords: honest campaign, $250,000, 18%, 4%, $90,000, 2,400, zero additives
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: hyped campaign is misleading / breaches advertising honesty; hyped option could lift sales by 18% | application_max_2: zero additives is false vs 9 additives and 10 teaspoons of sugar; $250,000 fine risk; honest campaign lifts sales by 4% for $90,000; $13,000,000 revenue / 2,400 outlets | analysis_max_2: risking a $250,000 fine and reputational harm; protecting revenue across retail outlets | evaluation_max_2: weighs fine avoidance and trust against a short-term 18% sales spike; false claims collapse once challenged

--- STEM ---
GoldenCrisp Foods is a private limited company processing potatoes into crisps at a plant near the town of Harbourne, employing 135 workers with $15,000,000 in annual revenue. The plant sends 850 tonnes of potato peelings and broken stock to landfill each year, at a cost of $120,000, and the landfill tax rises every year. Neighbours also report odour complaints, 26 in the last year.

A $950,000 anaerobic digestion unit would turn the waste into gas and fertiliser, saving $260,000 a year in energy and disposal and generating extra power for the plant. The government offers a 20% rebate on waste reduction equipment. Alternatively, the company could contract a local farm to collect waste free of charge, saving transport costs but not generating income.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'recycling'.
    Answer: Processing used materials and waste so they can be turned into new products or energy, instead of being sent to landfill [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: processing used materials and waste; turned into new products or energy instead of landfill

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems GoldenCrisp Foods faces from sending its waste to landfill.
    Answer: Problem 1: Rising disposal costs [k], 850 tonnes of potato peelings and broken stock go to landfill each year at a cost of $120,000 [app]. Problem 2: Community conflict [k], odour complaints from neighbours reached 26 in the last year near the Harbourne plant [app].
    Keywords: GoldenCrisp Foods, 850 tonnes, $120,000, 26, landfill, Harbourne, odour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rising disposal costs; community conflict / complaints | application_max_2: 850 tonnes to landfill each year; cost of $120,000; 26 odour complaints; Harbourne plant

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to GoldenCrisp Foods of installing the $950,000 anaerobic digestion unit.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Direct cost savings [k], the unit saves $260,000 a year in energy and disposal [app], improving profit [an]. Benefit 2: Cheaper investment through rebate [k], the 20% government rebate lowers the outlay by $190,000 on the $950,000 unit [app], freeing capital for other needs [an].
    Keywords: $950,000, $260,000, 20%, anaerobic digestion, 850 tonnes, landfill, GoldenCrisp
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: direct cost savings; cheaper investment through rebate | application_max_2: saves $260,000 a year in energy and disposal; 20% government rebate; $190,000 off the outlay; $950,000 unit | analysis_max_2: improving profit; freeing capital for other needs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think GoldenCrisp Foods should install the $950,000 anaerobic digestion unit or contract a local farm to collect the waste free of charge? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The anaerobic digestion unit turns waste into gas and fertiliser [k], saving $260,000 a year in energy and disposal, with a net cost of $760,000 after the 20% rebate [app], paying back in under 3 years [an]. It also reduces the 26 annual odour complaints and cuts reliance on the taxed landfill option [app], protecting neighbour relations [an]. The free farm collection avoids the $950,000 outlay entirely [k], safer for short-term cash. Overall, the digestion unit is the better option because it creates a permanent $260,000 annual saving and new energy supply [eval], whereas the farm contract merely shifts waste and leaves the rising landfill tax and odour issues unresolved [eval].
    Keywords: $950,000, $260,000, 20%, anaerobic digestion, landfill, 26, Harbourne
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: digester turns waste into gas and fertiliser / generates power; free farm collection avoids the outlay / safer short-term cash | application_max_2: saves $260,000 a year; net cost of $760,000 after the 20% rebate; 26 annual odour complaints; $950,000 outlay | analysis_max_2: paying back in under 3 years; protecting neighbour relations | evaluation_max_2: weighs permanent $260,000 annual saving and energy supply against avoiding outlay; farm contract shifts waste and leaves landfill tax and odour issues unresolved

--- STEM ---
Halloway Quarry Company is a private limited company operating a limestone quarry in the hill country of Marrowdale for 16 years, with 85 employees and $17,000,000 in annual revenue. Blasting at 7:30 am shakes homes up to 500 metres away, and 74 complaints were logged last year. The national regulator proposes new rules from 2027: blasting only after 9:00 am, dust limits of 50 micrograms per cubic metre, and fines of up to $400,000 per breach.

The company could install $680,000 of dust suppression and electric drills before the rules take effect in 2027, or continue current practices and lobby the regulator for lighter limits. Moving blasting to 9:30 am cuts output by 8% in the short term. Planning permission for the quarry is also due for renewal in 2 years.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two legal controls governments can impose on polluting businesses.
    Answer: Fines of up to $400,000 per breach [1]; limits on emissions, such as a dust concentration of 50 micrograms per cubic metre [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: fines per breach; emissions or dust concentration limits

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the proposed 2027 regulations could affect Halloway Quarry Company.
    Answer: Way 1: Higher compliance costs [k], blasting only after 9:00 am and dust limits of 50 micrograms per cubic metre require new equipment and monitoring at Marrowdale [app]. Way 2: Fine exposure [k], fines of up to $400,000 per breach apply if dust exceeds the limit or blasting runs before 9:00 am [app].
    Keywords: Halloway Quarry, 50 micrograms, $400,000, 9:00 am, blasting, Marrowdale, limestone
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher compliance costs; fine exposure / penalties | application_max_2: blasting only after 9:00 am; dust limits of 50 micrograms per cubic metre; $400,000 per breach; Marrowdale quarry

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Halloway Quarry Company of installing the $680,000 dust suppression and electric drills before 2027.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Avoids heavy fines [k], the system keeps dust within the 50 micrograms per cubic metre cap at the Marrowdale quarry [app], protecting profit from $400,000 penalties [an]. Benefit 2: Supports planning renewal [k], demonstrating compliance in 2 years strengthens the case to renew planning permission [app], safeguarding $17,000,000 of annual revenue [an].
    Keywords: $680,000, 50 micrograms, $400,000, planning permission, Marrowdale, $17,000,000, dust suppression
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: avoids heavy fines / compliance; supports planning permission renewal | application_max_2: 50 micrograms per cubic metre cap; Marrowdale quarry; $400,000 penalties; planning permission due for renewal in 2 years | analysis_max_2: protecting profit from penalties; safeguarding $17,000,000 of annual revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Halloway Quarry Company should install the $680,000 dust suppression and electric drills, or continue current practices and lobby the regulator for lighter limits? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Installing the equipment now avoids fines permanently [k], meeting the 50 micrograms dust cap and the 9:00 am blasting rule at Marrowdale [app], protecting $17,000,000 annual revenue and the 85-employee workforce [an]. It also strengthens the planning permission renewal due in 2 years [app], securing the quarry's long-term future [an]. However, continuing current practice preserves the $680,000 and avoids short-term output cuts from moving blasts to 9:30 am, which already reduce output by 8% [k]. Overall, installing now is the better option because two breaches would cost $800,000 in fines, more than the one-off $680,000 [eval], and visible compliance is the surest route to planning renewal and community acceptance [eval].
    Keywords: $680,000, $400,000, 50 micrograms, 9:00 am, planning permission, Marrowdale, 85
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: installing now avoids fines permanently; continuing practice preserves cash / avoids short-term cuts | application_max_2: 50 micrograms dust cap / 9:00 am blasting rule; $17,000,000 annual revenue / 85 employees; planning permission renewal due in 2 years; moving blasts to 9:30 am cuts output by 8% | analysis_max_2: protecting annual revenue and the workforce; securing the quarry's long-term future | evaluation_max_2: two breaches would cost $800,000, more than the one-off $680,000; visible compliance is the surest route to planning renewal and community acceptance

--- STEM ---
Velvet Hills Cocoa Company is a private limited company making premium chocolate in Country X, founded 5 years ago by Hannah Lindqvist, with $8,400,000 in annual sales through 600 shops. Switching would reduce annual profits by $420,000 at current volumes. However, 71% of the company's customers in a poll prefer ethically sourced chocolate, and two large supermarkets have offered premium shelf space for certified products worth $1,500,000 in extra sales. A publicised child labour scandal in Country Z last month threatens the whole sector's reputation.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'fair trade'.
    Answer: A certification and trading system guaranteeing producers in developing countries a fair, stable minimum price and decent working conditions [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guarantees a fair, stable minimum price; decent working conditions for producers in developing countries

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why sourcing cheap uncertified cocoa could damage Velvet Hills Cocoa Company.
    Answer: Reason 1: Reputation damage [k], the publicised child labour scandal in Country Z threatens the whole sector's reputation [app]. Reason 2: Lost supermarket listings [k], two supermarkets offer premium shelf space only for certified products, worth $1,500,000 in extra sales [app].
    Keywords: Velvet Hills Cocoa Company, Country Z, child labour, certified, $1,500,000, $2,100, $2,800
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reputation damage; lost supermarket listings | application_max_2: child labour scandal in Country Z; premium shelf space only for certified products; $1,500,000 in extra sales; uncertified cocoa

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Velvet Hills Cocoa Company of switching to the fair trade cooperative.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Access to premium shelf space [k], certified status unlocks $1,500,000 of extra sales offered by two supermarkets [app], raising revenue and market share [an]. Advantage 2: Stronger customer appeal [k], 71% of customers in a poll prefer ethically sourced chocolate [app], lifting loyalty and supporting the premium price [an].
    Keywords: fair trade, $1,500,000, 71%, cooperative, certified, $2,800, Velvet Hills
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: access to premium shelf space; stronger customer appeal | application_max_2: $1,500,000 of extra sales; two supermarkets; 71% of customers in a poll; ethically sourced chocolate | analysis_max_2: raising revenue and market share; lifting loyalty and supporting the premium price

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Velvet Hills Cocoa Company should switch to the fair trade cooperative or keep buying cocoa at $2,100 per tonne? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching guarantees a minimum price and no child labour [k], aligning with 71% of customers who prefer ethically sourced chocolate and the $1,500,000 of certified sales offered by two supermarkets [app], more than offsetting the $420,000 profit reduction [an]. It also shields the 5-year-old brand from Country Z scandal fallout [app], securing long-term growth [an]. However, keeping cheaper cocoa saves $700 per tonne, about $420,000 a year on $8,400,000 revenue [k], boosting short-term margin. Overall, switching is the better option because the extra certified sales exceed the $420,000 cost reduction [eval], and certification is the strongest defence against the reputational damage of the child labour scandal [eval].
    Keywords: fair trade, $2,100, $2,800, $420,000, $1,500,000, 71%, Country Z
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: switching guarantees minimum price and no child labour; keeping cheaper cocoa boosts short-term margin | application_max_2: 71% prefer ethically sourced chocolate; $1,500,000 of certified sales; $420,000 profit reduction; $700 per tonne saving on $8,400,000 revenue | analysis_max_2: offsetting the $420,000 profit reduction; securing long-term growth | evaluation_max_2: weighs $1,500,000 certified sales against $420,000 cost reduction; certification is the strongest defence against child labour scandal damage

--- STEM ---
Redmire Snack Foods is a private limited company in Country X that produces savoury snack packs. It sells 240,000 packs a year at $1.80 each, generating $432,000 in revenue, and employs 35 staff. Its founder, Priya Raman, started the firm 9 years ago and sales have been flat for 18 months. A multinational company from Country Z, Nordvik Foods, wants Redmire to become a dedicated supplier to its new Country X distribution centre.

Nordvik Foods proposes a 3-year contract for 300,000 packs a year at $1.45 per pack, requiring Redmire to invest $90,000 in a new packing line and pass quality audits four times a year. The Country X government offers firms in development regions a grant covering 20% of machinery costs. Redmire must decide whether to accept the contract or keep supplying domestic retailers at current prices.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'host country'.
    Answer: The country in which a multinational company locates production, offices or sales operations, which is different from the country where the multinational was originally based [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a multinational locates production/sales/operations in another country; that country is different from the multinational's home/origin country

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Redmire Snack Foods of accepting the Nordvik Foods contract.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A 3-year deal gives Redmire predictable, large-scale orders [k], with Nordvik wanting 300,000 packs a year, 60,000 more than the 240,000 packs Redmire currently sells [app]. Benefit 2: The government grant cuts the cost of the new packing line [k], covering 20% of the $90,000 investment, a saving of $18,000 [app].
    Keywords: 300,000 packs, 240,000, $90,000, 20%, $1.45, Nordvik Foods, 3-year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: guaranteed/regular large orders / stable demand from the multinational; government grants/support reduce the cost of investment | application_max_2: 300,000 packs a year vs 240,000 packs currently (60,000 more); 20% grant on $90,000 = $18,000 saving on the packing line

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Redmire Snack Foods could face if it accepts the Nordvik Foods contract.
    Answer: Problem 1: The contract price is much lower [k], at $1.45 per pack versus $1.80 for domestic retailers [app], so revenue per pack falls by about 19% and profits may shrink unless Redmire raises output efficiency [an]. Problem 2: Redmire could become too dependent on one buyer [k], because Nordvik's 300,000 packs would exceed Redmire's entire current output of 240,000 [app], leaving Redmire vulnerable if Nordvik ends the 3-year deal or demands price cuts later [an].
    Keywords: $1.45, $1.80, 300,000 packs, 240,000, $90,000, 20%, 3-year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower contract prices squeeze profit margins; over-dependence on a single customer/buyer | application_max_2: $1.45 per pack vs $1.80 domestic (about 19% lower); 300,000 packs would exceed all current output of 240,000 packs | analysis_max_2: profits shrink unless efficiency/output rises to offset lower prices; vulnerable if the 3-year contract ends or prices are renegotiated downward

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Redmire Snack Foods should accept the Nordvik Foods contract or keep supplying domestic retailers at current prices? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the contract gives Redmire predictable, high-volume sales [k], with 300,000 packs at $1.45 bringing in $435,000 a year, close to the $432,000 it earns domestically now [app], and the 20% grant saves $18,000 on the $90,000 packing line, so unit costs should fall as volume rises [an]. However, the price is well below the $1.80 domestic rate [k], so Redmire must check that higher volumes still cover costs and the four quality audits a year [app]; failing an audit could lose the 3-year deal after Redmire has committed $72,000 of its own money [an]. On balance, Redmire should accept the contract, because secured volume growth and the grant outweigh the margin risk for a firm whose sales have been flat for 18 months [eval]; it should also keep some domestic retail sales so no single buyer ever dominates [eval].
    Keywords: 300,000 packs, $1.45, $432,000, $1.80, 20%, $90,000, Nordvik Foods
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: multinational contracts offer large, predictable volumes and scale; lower prices and single-buyer dependence are risks of such deals | application_max_2: 300,000 packs at $1.45 = $435,000 vs $432,000 domestic; $18,000 grant on $90,000; $1.80 domestic vs $1.45 contract price; four quality audits a year; flat sales for 18 months | analysis_max_2: economies of scale and falling unit costs from higher output and the grant; margin risk and audit failure could strand the $72,000 investment | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on accepting the contract or not; recognises the continuing value of domestic retail sales as diversification

--- STEM ---
Wharfdale Cement Co is a private limited company in Country X, close to the northern quarry belt. It produced 180,000 tonnes of cement last year at a cost of $38 a tonne and sells at $52 a tonne, employing 64 workers. Domestic demand has grown slowly, at about 3% a year, and imports from Country Z have undercut its prices.

The directors are weighing two options: invest $2.4 million in a grinding plant in Country Y, where construction is booming and labour is 30% cheaper, or spend $1.1 million upgrading the Country X plant to export through the southern port. Country Y demand is projected at 400,000 tonnes a year, but the project needs a skilled expatriate team for the first 2 years and carries political and currency risks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline one benefit to a business of becoming a multinational company.
    Answer: It can access larger markets abroad, increasing sales and spreading risk across countries rather than relying on one domestic economy [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: access to larger/more foreign markets; spreads risk / less dependence on the home economy

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Wharfdale Cement Co of building the Country Y plant.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A Country Y plant would give Wharfdale access to a much bigger market [k], where projected demand is 400,000 tonnes a year, more than double its current 180,000 tonnes in Country X [app]. Benefit 2: Producing locally in Country Y would cut costs [k], because labour there is 30% cheaper, widening the $14 margin on each $52 tonne sold [app].
    Keywords: 400,000 tonnes, 180,000, $38, $52, 30%, Country Y, $2.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: access to larger foreign markets / more customers; lower operating costs from cheaper labour/inputs | application_max_2: 400,000 tonnes projected demand vs 180,000 tonnes produced now; labour 30% cheaper in Country Y; cost $38 vs price $52

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Wharfdale Cement Co could face if it builds the Country Y plant.
    Answer: Problem 1: The overseas plant demands heavy capital [k], at $2.4 million versus just $1.1 million for the export-upgrade option [app], so cash is tied up for years and any fall in Country Y demand would sharply reduce returns [an]. Problem 2: Operating abroad brings unfamiliar risks [k], including the 2 years of expatriate management and the political risks the board foresees [app], which could disrupt production and make budgeting very difficult [an].
    Keywords: $2.4 million, $1.1 million, Country Y, 2 years, 400,000 tonnes, 30%, $52
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: very high capital cost / large upfront investment; unfamiliar country risks (political, currency, management) | application_max_2: $2.4 million for Country Y vs $1.1 million for export upgrade; 2 years expatriate team; political and currency risks noted by the board | analysis_max_2: capital tied up; a fall in Country Y demand cuts returns; disruption risk and difficult budgeting in an unfamiliar country

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Wharfdale Cement Co should build the Country Y plant or upgrade the Country X plant for export? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Building in Country Y would let Wharfdale capture 400,000 tonnes of projected demand right at the customer [k], helped by 30% cheaper labour and the booming construction market [app], raising margins on each $52 tonne and spreading risk across two countries [an]. However, it costs $2.4 million, more than double the $1.1 million export upgrade [k], and needs 2 years of expatriate managers with political and currency risks [app], so a downturn in Country Y construction could leave an idle plant and stretched cash flow [an]. On balance, Wharfdale should upgrade the Country X plant and export through the southern port first [eval], because it is cheaper, reversible and tests overseas demand using existing strengths [eval].
    Keywords: 400,000 tonnes, 30%, $2.4 million, $1.1 million, $52, 180,000, Country Y
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: multinational location in growth markets brings scale and lower costs; overseas investment carries heavy capital and country risks | application_max_2: 400,000 tonnes projected demand; 30% cheaper labour; $52 per tonne; $2.4 million vs $1.1 million export option; 2 years expatriate team | analysis_max_2: higher margins and risk spreading via Country Y production; idle-plant/cash-flow risk if Country Y demand falters; export route is reversible | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (export first vs Y plant); recognises staged/conditional logic: revisit Country Y after export proves demand

--- STEM ---
Dunharrow Woollen Mills is a private limited company in Country X that weaves woollen cloth for suit makers. It produces 60,000 metres a month, employs 110 weavers and exports 25% of output. Country X has removed most trade barriers on textile imports and signed tariff-cutting deals with 9 countries, and improved container shipping has cut delivery times to overseas buyers from 6 weeks to 10 days.

A tailoring group in Country Y has offered to buy 1.2 million metres a year if Dunharrow can weave to its specification within 12 months. Dunharrow could either export from Country X or discuss a joint venture to weave in Country Y. The owner, Marcus Whitfield, fears the Country Y partner may copy designs, but keeping all production at home limits how fast the order can be served.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'trade barrier'.
    Answer: A government-imposed restriction on international trade, such as a tariff (tax on imports) or a quota (limit on the quantity of imports), used to protect domestic industry [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a government-imposed restriction on international trade; examples include tariffs (import taxes) and quotas

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two opportunities that the removal of trade barriers has created for Dunharrow Woollen Mills.
    Answer: Opportunity 1: Lower trade barriers open larger export markets [k], and the Country Y tailoring group alone wants 1.2 million metres a year, far more than the 60,000 metres Dunharrow makes each month [app]. Opportunity 2: Faster, cheaper shipping widens Dunharrow's reach [k], because delivery times have fallen from 6 weeks to 10 days, making overseas orders practical [app].
    Keywords: 1.2 million metres, 60,000 metres, 10 days, 6 weeks, 9 countries, 25%, Country Y
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: access to larger foreign markets after barriers removed; improved transport/communications make global trade faster and cheaper | application_max_2: 1.2 million metres a year wanted by Country Y vs 60,000 metres a month made; delivery times cut from 6 weeks to 10 days; deals with 9 countries

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Dunharrow Woollen Mills could face if it forms the joint venture with the Country Y partner.
    Answer: Problem 1: Dunharrow risks losing its designs [k], because the Country Y partner would see its specification and could copy it once the 12 months are up [app], damaging Dunharrow's competitive advantage in woven cloth [an]. Problem 2: A joint venture splits control [k], so decisions about quality, output and price must be agreed with the partner [app], which can slow responses to faults and disappoint the tailoring group [an].
    Keywords: 12 months, Country Y, 1.2 million metres, specification, 60,000 metres, 25%, 9 countries
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: risk of ideas/designs being copied by the partner; shared control slows decisions and creates friction | application_max_2: specification visible to partner; risk after the 12 months agreement; shared decisions on quality, output and price versus 1.2 million metres commitment | analysis_max_2: losing design secrecy destroys Dunharrow's competitive advantage; slower quality/fault responses risk breaching the order's standards

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Dunharrow Woollen Mills should serve the Country Y order by exporting from Country X or by forming the joint venture? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Exporting from Country X keeps Dunharrow in full control of its designs and quality [k], letting it earn the whole margin on 1.2 million metres a year through the 10-day container route [app], protecting the jobs of its 110 weavers and avoiding the risk of a partner copying its work [an]. Forming the joint venture would share the cost of weaving to specification and speed up the ramp-up within 12 months [k], giving local knowledge but splitting profits and ceding control of quality and price decisions [app], with the real danger of a future competitor armed with Dunharrow's specification [an]. On balance, Dunharrow should export from Country X [eval], because design protection and full margins outweigh shared setup costs, accepting a tight 12-month capacity challenge [eval].
    Keywords: 1.2 million metres, 10 days, 110 weavers, 12 months, Country Y, 60,000 metres, 25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exporting keeps full control and captures full profit; joint ventures share cost/resources but split control and profits | application_max_2: 1.2 million metres a year; 10-day container route; 110 weavers; 25% exports; 12-month deadline to weave to specification; Country Y partner demands | analysis_max_2: design secrecy and full margins vs partner copying and shared profits; capacity strain under 12-month deadline vs faster local ramp-up | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between exporting and the joint venture; weighs design protection/margin against speed and shared cost
