PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U6_SET_74
UNIT: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Stormont Electronics Ltd is a public limited company in Country X that assembles set-top boxes and routers. Its subsidiary in Country Z employs 480 workers and earned $6.2 million profit last year, of which $4.5 million was repatriated to Country X and $1.7 million was kept in Country Z as retained profit. The Country Z government has criticised foreign firms for moving profits home.

The board must decide whether to repatriate $5 million of this year's expected $6.8 million subsidiary profit to pay a special dividend in Country X, or reinvest it in a new assembly hall in Country Z costing $5.5 million. The Country X parent needs funds to upgrade its own factory, while the Country Z government hints that firms reinvesting locally may receive preferential tax treatment.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'repatriation of profits'.
    Answer: The transfer of profits earned by a multinational's subsidiary or branch in a foreign country back to the parent company in its home country [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: profits earned abroad are returned to the home/parent company; typically by a multinational's subsidiary or branch

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages for Country Z of Stormont repatriating $5 million of subsidiary profits.
    Answer: Problem 1: Country Z loses funds that could support local growth [k], because returning $5 million of the $6.8 million expected profit would leave only $1.8 million to reinvest or tax locally [app]. Problem 2: The host country gains less from foreign investment [k], so the planned assembly hall and its construction orders for local suppliers could be postponed [app].
    Keywords: $5 million, $6.8 million, 480 workers, $4.5 million, $1.7 million, $5.5 million, Country Z
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: less money remains in the host country for reinvestment; fewer local benefits (jobs, supplier orders, taxes) from the MNC's presence | application_max_2: $5 million repatriated out of $6.8 million expected profit leaves $1.8 million; assembly hall ($5.5 million) postponed / local construction orders lost

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Stormont Electronics Ltd might choose to repatriate the profits to Country X.
    Answer: Reason 1: Shareholders expect rewards from abroad [k], and paying a special dividend from repatriated profits boosts returns and may support the share price [app], which is why the board lists repatriation despite criticism from Country Z [an]. Reason 2: The parent company urgently needs funds at home [k], so repatriating $5 million could part-finance the Country X factory upgrade without new borrowing [app], improving productivity where head office and most owners are based [an].
    Keywords: $5 million, $6.8 million, $4.5 million, special dividend, 480 workers, $1.7 million, Country X
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reward shareholders / pay dividends; fund home-country investment without borrowing | application_max_2: special dividend planned to be paid in Country X; $5 million earmarked toward the Country X factory upgrade | analysis_max_2: shareholder approval and share-price support despite host-country criticism; improved home productivity / avoids interest on new loans

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Stormont Electronics Ltd should repatriate $5 million or reinvest it in the Country Z assembly hall? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Repatriating $5 million rewards shareholders and helps fund the Country X factory upgrade [k], continuing last year's pattern of sending $4.5 million home while keeping $1.7 million locally [app], though taking $5 million of the expected $6.8 million could worsen relations with the Country Z government and invite punitive taxes [an]. Reinvesting $5.5 million in the Country Z hall would secure the 480 workers' jobs, win the hinted preferential tax treatment and expand capacity near the market [k], but it leaves the Country X factory underfunded and Country X shareholders without their special dividend [app], tying scarce cash to one overseas site that faces political risk [an]. On balance, Stormont should reinvest in the assembly hall [eval], because the tax preference and host-country goodwill are worth more than this year's dividend, provided the board explains the decision clearly to shareholders [eval].
    Keywords: $5 million, $4.5 million, $1.7 million, $6.8 million, $5.5 million, 480 workers, special dividend
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: repatriation rewards shareholders and funds the parent company; reinvestment secures host-country relations, jobs and possible tax benefits | application_max_2: $4.5 million sent home vs $1.7 million retained in Country Z last year; $5 million vs $5.5 million hall; $6.8 million expected profit; special dividend | analysis_max_2: risk of punitive taxes and worsened host-country relations from heavy repatriation; shareholder disappointment/underfunded home factory vs tax preference and job security | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (reinvest vs repatriate); recognises need to manage shareholder expectations alongside the decision

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U6_SET_75
UNIT: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making brake discs and hub assemblies for domestic vehicle assemblers. It employs 88 workers, sells 500,000 discs a year and had revenue of $9.6 million last year, growing at about 8% a year. A foreign multinational, Kestrel Mobility Group, is opening a vehicle assembly plant in Country X and wants Trevelyan to supply 700,000 discs annually under a 4-year deal.

To win the contract Trevelyan must install automated grinding equipment costing $800,000 and meet Kestrel's quality standard, which Kestrel's engineers would help install. Trevelyan was founded by Diane Trevelyan 14 years ago and could instead stay with its domestic customers, who buy 300,000 discs a year at higher prices, but growth would remain slow.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'technology transfer'.
    Answer: The movement of technology, such as equipment, knowledge or skills, from one business or country to another, often from a multinational to a local business in the host country [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: technology/knowledge/skills move between businesses or countries; often flows from a multinational to a local firm or host country

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd of winning the Kestrel contract.
    Answer: Benefit 1: The contract would sharply increase Trevelyan's sales [k], with Kestrel wanting 700,000 discs a year against 500,000 currently made and 300,000 bought by domestic customers [app]. Benefit 2: Trevelyan gains new technology and skills [k], because Kestrel's engineers would help install the $800,000 automated grinding equipment, lifting quality and productivity [app].
    Keywords: 700,000 discs, 500,000, 300,000, $800,000, 4-year, 88 workers, Kestrel
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: much larger sales volume / access to a bigger customer; access to modern technology and skills (technology transfer) | application_max_2: 700,000 discs a year vs 500,000 current output / 300,000 domestic sales; Kestrel engineers help install the $800,000 automated grinding equipment

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd could face from the Kestrel deal.
    Answer: Problem 1: The deal demands heavy investment [k], with $800,000 of equipment against domestic sales of only 300,000 discs a year [app], so Trevelyan must borrow or use savings and risks losses if Kestrel cuts the order [an]. Problem 2: Trevelyan could become dependent on one customer [k], because 700,000 discs a year for 4 years would dominate its output [app], leaving it exposed if Kestrel switches supplier or closes the plant later [an].
    Keywords: $800,000, 700,000 discs, 300,000, 4-year, Trevelyan, Kestrel, $9.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high capital cost requiring loans or savings; over-dependence on a single large customer | application_max_2: $800,000 equipment vs domestic sales of 300,000 discs a year; 700,000 discs a year for 4 years would dominate output | analysis_max_2: debt/savings drain and losses if the order is cut or delayed; single-buyer exposure; plant closure or supplier switch would be devastating

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd should accept the Kestrel contract or keep supplying domestic customers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Accepting the Kestrel deal offers 700,000 discs a year of secured sales, well above Trevelyan's 500,000 output, plus technology transfer as Kestrel's engineers help install the grinding equipment [k]; the $800,000 cost is steep, but the 4-year contract spreads it and domestic demand of 300,000 discs cannot fill the line alone [app], so productivity and worker skills should jump [an]. Staying with domestic customers keeps higher prices and avoids $800,000 of debt [k], but growth stays slow and Trevelyan may lose competitiveness as rivals modernise [app], eventually shrinking its $9.6 million revenue [an]. On balance, Trevelyan should accept the contract [eval], because the scale, skills and technology gains outweigh the dependence risk, provided it keeps some domestic buyers for diversification [eval].
    Keywords: 700,000 discs, 500,000, 300,000, $800,000, 4-year, $9.6 million, Trevelyan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: MNC contracts bring volume, technology and skills to local firms; dependence and capital risk accompany a single large buyer | application_max_2: 700,000 discs vs 500,000 output and 300,000 domestic demand; $800,000 equipment; 4-year contract; $9.6 million revenue at stake | analysis_max_2: productivity and skills gains from technology transfer vs debt burden; domestic stability but falling competitiveness if rivals modernise first | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (accept vs stay domestic); recognises keeping some domestic buyers as a hedge/condition

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U6_SET_76
UNIT: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Brentmoor Steel Plc is a public limited company in Country X producing steel rods and sheet for construction firms. It employs 320 workers, makes 90,000 tonnes a year at a cost of $540 a tonne and sells at $610. Cheap imported steel from Country Z, priced about 18% below Brentmoor's price, has cut its domestic market share from 30% to 22% in 2 years.

Country X's government is consulting on a 15% import tariff on foreign steel, which would raise import prices and shield local mills. Brentmoor's largest customers, two construction groups, oppose the tariff because it raises their building costs. The board must decide whether to lobby for the tariff or compete without protection by cutting its $540 cost per tonne.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'protectionism'.
    Answer: Government policies that shield domestic industries from foreign competition, for example by imposing tariffs (import taxes) or quotas (limits on import quantities) [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: policies that shield domestic industries from imports; e.g. tariffs on imports or quotas

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Brentmoor Steel Plc of Country X imposing the 15% import tariff.
    Answer: Advantage 1: A tariff makes imported steel more expensive [k], narrowing the 18% price gap beneath Brentmoor's $610 and helping it win back market share from 22% [app]. Advantage 2: Protected demand would let Brentmoor use capacity fully [k], with its 90,000 tonnes a year and 320 workers better utilised rather than cutting shifts [app].
    Keywords: 15% import tariff, $610, 18%, 22%, 90,000 tonnes, 320 workers, $540
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: imports become pricier; domestic goods more price-competitive; protected demand raises capacity utilisation and protects jobs | application_max_2: 18% price gap closed vs $610; market share fell to 22%; 90,000 tonnes a year and 320 workers better utilised

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of the proposed tariff for Brentmoor Steel Plc's stakeholders.
    Answer: Problem 1: Construction customers would oppose Brentmoor [k], since the 15% import tariff raises their steel costs above the current $610 market price [app], risking lost orders to overseas contractors and damaged relationships [an]. Problem 2: Protection can reduce pressure to improve [k], so Brentmoor might delay cutting its $540 cost per tonne [app], leaving it weak if the tariff is later removed by trade deals [an].
    Keywords: 15% import tariff, $540, $610, 18%, two construction groups, 90,000 tonnes, 22%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customers/consumers face higher input costs and oppose protection; protection reduces the incentive to raise efficiency | application_max_2: two construction groups oppose; tariff lifts costs above $610; $540 cost per tonne pressure; 18% import price gap | analysis_max_2: lost orders to overseas contractors; strained customer relationships; complacency / vulnerable if the tariff is later removed

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brentmoor Steel Plc should lobby for the tariff or compete without protection by cutting costs? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Lobbying for the 15% tariff would narrow the 18% import gap, lifting Brentmoor's $610 competitiveness and defending its 22% market share and 320 workers [k], but it risks alienating the two construction groups that buy much of its 90,000 tonnes a year and invites retaliation against Country X exporters [app], while discouraging the efficiency drive needed on the $540 cost [an]. Cutting costs to compete freely keeps customers loyal and prepares Brentmoor for any removal of protection [k], but trimming $540 per tonne below import prices 18% under $610 is hard and may mean wage or job cuts [app], with no guarantee of success [an]. On balance, Brentmoor should lobby for the tariff in the short term while committing to an internal efficiency programme [eval], because defending 320 jobs now matters and protection cannot be permanent [eval].
    Keywords: 15% import tariff, 18%, $610, $540, 22%, 320 workers, two construction groups
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: tariffs protect domestic industry from cheaper imports; protection raises customer costs and breeds complacency | application_max_2: 15% tariff vs 18% import gap; $540 cost and $610 price; 22% share; two construction groups oppose; 90,000 tonnes a year; 320 workers | analysis_max_2: tariff defends jobs/share but risks losing customers and retaliation; efficiency focus keeps loyalty but is hard and may cut wages/jobs | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified position (short-term lobbying with long-term efficiency); recognises protection is temporary, not permanent

UNIT: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

--- STEM ---
Solway Preserves Co is a private limited company in Country X making jars of jam and chutney. It produces 800,000 jars a year, employs 46 staff and exports 15% of output. Jam accounts for 62% of jars sold. Improved container shipping and online ordering have opened markets abroad: Solway now receives enquiries from supermarkets in 6 countries and from customers via social media adverts reaching 2 million people.

The owners are weighing two options: invest $150,000 in a larger filling line to double output for export orders, or keep production at its current level and sell more in Country X, where two rivals have recently launched discount jams. Solway's cash reserves stand at $220,000 and the bank has offered a loan at 9% interest for expansion.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two reasons for globalisation.
    Answer: Improvements in transport and communications technology, making international trade faster and cheaper; the removal or reduction of trade barriers such as tariffs and quotas [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: improvements in transport/communications (e.g. container shipping, internet); removal/reduction of trade barriers such as tariffs or quotas

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why globalisation is creating opportunities for Solway Preserves Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: Cheaper, faster transport lets Solway reach distant buyers [k], and supermarkets in 6 countries have already enquired about importing its jars [app]. Reason 2: The internet and global media spread product awareness [k], with Solway's social media adverts reaching 2 million people and pulling in overseas interest [app].
    Keywords: 6 countries, 2 million, 800,000 jars, 15%, $150,000, $220,000, Solway
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: improved transport/communication opens export markets; global media/internet spread brand awareness worldwide | application_max_2: enquiries from supermarkets in 6 countries; social media adverts reaching 2 million people

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Solway Preserves Co could face if it doubles production for export.
    Answer: Problem 1: Doubling output needs heavy spending [k], with $150,000 for the bigger filling line on top of $220,000 reserves and a 9% loan [app], so interest and repayments strain cash if export orders lag [an]. Problem 2: Overseas buyers may demand changes [k], such as different labels, recipes or health regulations [app], raising costs and risking rejected shipments [an].
    Keywords: $150,000, $220,000, 9%, 6 countries, 800,000 jars, 15%, Solway
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high expansion cost financed by reserves or loans; foreign markets demand adaptation (labels, tastes, regulations) | application_max_2: $150,000 line vs $220,000 reserves and a 9% loan offer; enquiries from 6 countries with differing requirements | analysis_max_2: interest/repayment strain if export orders arrive slowly; higher adaptation costs and risk of rejected shipments

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Solway Preserves Co should invest in the new filling line to double output for export, or keep production the same and sell more in Country X? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing $150,000 would let Solway exploit enquiries from 6 countries and its reach to 2 million people on social media, doubling 800,000 jars of annual production [k]; with $220,000 reserves and a 9% loan, the line is affordable, and it would grow exports beyond the current 15% of output [app], spreading risk beyond a home market under attack from two discount rivals [an]. Keeping production steady avoids debt and the risk of unsold jars if overseas buyers prove slow [k], but it blocks growth and leaves Solway fighting discount jams at home with stagnant margins [app], likely losing share in Country X as well [an]. On balance, Solway should invest in the filling line [eval], taking the 9% loan only if confirmed export orders cover the repayments comfortably [eval].
    Keywords: $150,000, $220,000, 9%, 6 countries, 2 million, 15%, 800,000 jars
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: globalisation opens overseas demand through transport and media; expansion financed by reserves/loans carries repayment risk | application_max_2: $150,000 line; $220,000 reserves; 9% loan; 6 countries; 2 million reach; two discount rivals at home; exports at 15%; 800,000 jars a year | analysis_max_2: risk spreading beyond the embattled home market vs export order risk; domestic price war undermines the stand-still strategy | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (invest vs stay at current output); conditional logic: loan only when confirmed orders cover repayments

--- STEM ---
Fenwick Wind Components Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing steel towers and nacelles for wind turbines. It employs 74 workers, makes 120 towers a year and has revenue of $14 million. The Country X government has introduced local content rules requiring at least 45% of the value of every wind farm project to be made by Country X firms.

NordAero, a multinational turbine maker, plans a $30 million turbine plant in Country X and has asked Fenwick to become its local content supplier for 200 towers a year under a 5-year deal. Fenwick would need $3.2 million for new pressing equipment and would rely on NordAero for 80% of its revenue. Its alternative is to serve existing domestic customers, who order 90 towers a year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'local content rules'.
    Answer: Government rules requiring that a minimum share of a product's value or materials be made in the host country, used to boost domestic industry and jobs [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: rules requiring a minimum share of a product to be made locally; used to boost host-country industry/employment

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for Fenwick Wind Components Ltd of supplying the NordAero plant.
    Answer: Advantage 1: The deal would more than double Fenwick's output [k], with NordAero wanting 200 towers a year against 120 made now and only 90 ordered by domestic customers [app]. Advantage 2: Five years of contracted orders give Fenwick stable demand [k], supporting investment in the new pressing equipment and protecting the jobs of its 74 workers [app].
    Keywords: 200 towers, 120 towers, 90 towers, 5-year, $3.2 million, 74 workers, NordAero
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: much larger orders / rapid output growth; long-term stable contracts aid planning and investment | application_max_2: 200 towers a year wanted vs 120 made now and 90 domestic orders; 5-year deal; 74 workers; $3.2 million pressing equipment supported

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Fenwick Wind Components Ltd could face if it supplies NordAero.
    Answer: Problem 1: Fenwick would owe its survival to one buyer [k], because 80% of its revenue would come from NordAero under the 5-year deal [app], so any cancellation or price cut would threaten the whole business [an]. Problem 2: The $3.2 million pressing equipment strains finances [k], especially while relying on NordAero for 80% of revenue [app], so if NordAero's $30 million plant is delayed Fenwick still carries the debt [an].
    Keywords: 80%, 5-year, $3.2 million, $30 million, 45%, 200 towers, Fenwick
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: over-dependence on a single large customer; heavy capital investment required upfront | application_max_2: 80% of revenue from NordAero; 5-year deal; $3.2 million pressing equipment; NordAero's $30 million plant may be delayed | analysis_max_2: cancellation or price cut would threaten the whole business; debt burden even if the customer's plant is delayed

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fenwick Wind Components Ltd should sign the NordAero supply deal or stay with its domestic customers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Signing gives Fenwick 200 towers a year of contracted demand from a $30 million world-class plant, lifting output well beyond 120 towers, with valuable experience built under the 45% local content rule [k]; the $3.2 million equipment is affordable against $14 million revenue, especially spread over 5 years [app], and positions Fenwick as the leading local supplier [an]. However, 80% reliance on NordAero is dangerous [k]: if the plant is delayed or the deal is cancelled, Fenwick carries $3.2 million of debt with empty capacity [app], threatening its 74 workers and the firm's future [an]. On balance, Fenwick should sign the deal [eval], but only with safeguards such as staged payments and a minimum monthly order written into the contract [eval].
    Keywords: 200 towers, 120 towers, $3.2 million, 5-year, 80%, $14 million, 45%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: MNC supply contracts bring scale, experience and stability; dependence and capital risk come with a single large customer | application_max_2: 200 towers a year vs 120 made/90 domestic; $3.2 million over 5 years vs $14 million revenue; 80% reliance on NordAero; $30 million plant; 74 workers; 45% local content rule | analysis_max_2: scale and leadership gains vs single-buyer dependence; debt risk with empty capacity if the plant is delayed/cancelled | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (sign vs stay domestic); conditional safeguards such as staged payments/minimum orders

--- STEM ---
Marlowe Bicycles is a private limited company in Country X making steel-framed commuter bicycles. It employs 28 workers, sells 9,000 bicycles a year at $210 and has $1.9 million revenue. Two multinational retailers have entered Country X, selling imported bicycles at $150, and Marlowe's sales fell 20% last year while its market share dropped from 12% to 9%.

Marlowe's founder, Ellis Marlowe, opened the first workshop 14 years ago and the workforce is proud of its hand-built frames. The board must choose between two strategies: cut prices towards $160 and match the imports, or target a niche with hand-made premium touring bikes at $520, aimed at cycling tourists. The premium option needs $120,000 of retooling and specialist welders, but forecasts suggest sales of 800 premium bikes a year initially.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two threats of globalisation for businesses.
    Answer: Stronger competition from foreign firms and multinationals entering the home market; downward pressure on prices and loss of market share for domestic businesses [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: increased foreign competition / MNC entry into the domestic market; downward price pressure and loss of market share for local firms

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways globalisation is threatening Marlowe Bicycles.
    Answer: Threat 1: Multinational retailers sell imports far cheaper [k], at $150 per bicycle versus Marlowe's $210 [app], forcing painful discounting or lost sales. Threat 2: Globalisation has eroded Marlowe's position [k], with sales down 20% last year and market share falling from 12% to 9% [app].
    Keywords: $150, $210, 20%, 12%, 9%, $1.9 million, Marlowe
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: cheaper imports undercut domestic prices; foreign competition takes sales and market share | application_max_2: $150 imports vs Marlowe's $210 price; sales down 20% last year; market share 12% to 9%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two possible responses Marlowe Bicycles could take to the multinational threat.
    Answer: Response 1: Cut prices towards $160 [k], close to the $150 imports, which might win back price-sensitive buyers [app], restoring volume at the cost of much thinner margins and possible losses per bicycle [an]. Response 2: Differentiate with premium touring bikes at $520 [k], aimed at cycling tourists untouched by the $150 import flood [app], building loyalty in a niche where 800 bikes a year at higher margins could still profit [an].
    Keywords: $160, $150, $520, 800, $210, 9%, $1.9 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: competing on price / cost leadership against imports; differentiation / targeting a niche market | application_max_2: $160 close to $150 imports; margins squeezed on each bicycle; $520 premium touring bikes; cycling tourists; 800 bikes a year forecast | analysis_max_2: higher volume but much thinner or negative margins; niche loyalty and higher margins vs smaller total market

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marlowe Bicycles should cut prices towards $160 to match imports, or move into premium touring bikes at $520? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Matching imports at $160 might recover volume, but leaves almost no margin against $150 rivals [k], coming after sales already fell 20% and share dropped to 9% [app], so Marlowe could sell more bicycles yet still lose money, endangering its 28 jobs [an]. The premium route targets cycling tourists at $520 [k], needing $120,000 of retooling to sell an initial 800 bikes a year worth about $416,000 at healthy margins [app], avoiding a price war and building a defensible niche [an]. On balance, Marlowe should move into premium touring bikes [eval], because a 9%-share commuter range cannot beat global firms on price against $150 imports [eval].
    Keywords: $160, $150, $520, $120,000, 800, 9%, 28 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: price matching can win volume but destroys margin; differentiation avoids head-on price wars with global firms | application_max_2: $160 vs $150 imports; $520 touring bikes; $120,000 retooling; 800 bikes a year worth about $416,000; 28 jobs; share at 9%; sales fell 20% | analysis_max_2: volume recovery with no margin endangers the whole firm and jobs; niche strategy restores profitability and defensibility | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (premium vs price match); links the recommendation to the 9% market share reality

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U6_SET_80
UNIT: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Drummond Chocolates Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making handmade truffles and bars. It buys cocoa from Country Y and sells 1.5 million bars a year at $3.50, employing 57 staff with $5.25 million revenue. A new free trade agreement between Country X and its neighbours has removed the 8% tariff on cocoa and on chocolate exports.

Drummond's board must decide whether to build a $1.8 million export factory to sell 2.6 million bars a year across the free trade region, or keep the single factory and rely on premium domestic sales, where it already holds 18% market share. The new factory needs 25 extra workers and two years to reach full capacity, but regional sales could raise annual revenue to $9.1 million.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'free trade'.
    Answer: International trade between countries without tariffs, quotas or other restrictions, allowing goods and services to cross borders freely [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: trade between countries without tariffs/quotas/restrictions; goods and services move freely across borders

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two opportunities the free trade agreement creates for Drummond Chocolates Ltd.
    Answer: Opportunity 1: Removing the 8% export tariff makes Drummond's bars cheaper in neighbouring countries [k], supporting sales of up to 2.6 million bars a year across the region [app]. Opportunity 2: Removing the 8% tariff on cocoa cuts Drummond's input costs [k], improving margins on every bar sold at home and in the region [app].
    Keywords: 8%, 2.6 million bars, $3.50, $5.25 million, 57 staff, free trade, Drummond
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: export tariffs removed, so market access is cheaper/easier abroad; input tariffs removed, so production costs fall | application_max_2: 2.6 million bars a year possible under the regional plan; 8% tariff gone on cocoa bought from Country Y

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Drummond Chocolates Ltd could face if it builds the export factory.
    Answer: Problem 1: The $1.8 million factory strains finances [k], with only $5.25 million current revenue and two years before full capacity [app], so Drummond may need loans and face heavy interest during the ramp-up [an]. Problem 2: Regional competition is unfamiliar [k], with established local brands and price-sensitive shoppers [app], risking slow sales of the extra bars and wasted capacity [an].
    Keywords: $1.8 million, $5.25 million, two years, 2.6 million bars, 1.5 million bars, 18%, 25 extra workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high capital cost with a slow ramp-up creates financing risk; unfamiliar foreign competition and price sensitivity | application_max_2: $1.8 million factory; $5.25 million revenue; two years to full capacity; 2.6 million bars a year target vs 1.5 million bars now | analysis_max_2: loan/interest burden during the slow ramp-up period; slow uptake risks wasted capacity and weak returns

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Drummond Chocolates Ltd should build the export factory for the free trade region, or keep the single factory focused on domestic premium sales? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Building the export factory exploits free trade: with the 8% tariff gone, Drummond could sell 2.6 million bars a year and lift revenue from $5.25 million to $9.1 million [k], with cocoa also cheaper and 25 extra workers strengthening production [app], achieving larger scale and spreading risk beyond an 18%-share home market [an]. Keeping the single factory avoids $1.8 million of debt and protects the proven premium domestic position [k], but it ignores a revenue rise of about $3.85 million and leaves capacity trapped while regional rivals expand [app], risking long-term decline [an]. On balance, Drummond should build the export factory [eval], staged so the loan is only drawn once confirmed regional orders justify it [eval].
    Keywords: 8%, 2.6 million bars, $5.25 million, $9.1 million, $1.8 million, 18%, 25 extra workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: free trade removes tariffs, opening markets and cutting input costs; expansion carries heavy capital cost and ramp-up risk | application_max_2: 8% tariff gone; 2.6 million bars a year; revenue $5.25 million to $9.1 million; $1.8 million factory; two years to capacity; 18% domestic share; 25 extra workers | analysis_max_2: larger scale and risk spreading vs $1.8 million debt and ramp-up risk; ignoring a ~$3.85 million opportunity vs protecting the premium domestic niche | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (build vs stay single factory); staged/conditional approach tied to confirmed regional orders

--- STEM ---
Suncrest Olive Estate is a private limited company in Country X producing gourmet olive oil for export. It sells 400,000 bottles a year at $9 each, earning $3.6 million, and 60% of sales (240,000 bottles) go to buyers in Country W. The Country X dollar has appreciated by 12% against the Country W currency, so Suncrest's bottles now cost Country W buyers the equivalent of $10.08 each unless it cuts prices.

Managing Director Lena Ortiz must set the June price list before orders for the next season close. Option A is to cut the Country W price to $8.10 a bottle, taking 10% off, to keep order volumes steady. Option B is to hold the $9 price and accept that Country W orders may fall sharply, shifting marketing towards domestic supermarkets instead.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by 'appreciation'.
    Answer: Appreciation is a rise in the value of one currency compared with other currencies, so a currency buys more foreign currency than before [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A rise in the value of a currency; Compared with other currencies / buys more foreign currency than before

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the 12% appreciation on Suncrest Olive Estate.
    Answer: First, appreciation makes Suncrest's oil more expensive for buyers abroad [k]. Each $9 bottle now costs Country W customers the equivalent of $10.08, so demand for the 240,000 bottles a year they buy may fall [app]. Second, appreciation weakens Suncrest's competitiveness against rival suppliers [k]. Country W supermarkets may switch to locally bottled olive oil instead, so Suncrest risks losing listings and part of its $3.6 million revenue [app].
    Keywords: 12%, 240,000, $9, $10.08, Suncrest Olive Estate, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Appreciation makes exports more expensive abroad; Appreciation reduces export competitiveness versus foreign rivals | application_max_2: Reference to $10.08 equivalent / 12% / $9 price; Reference to Country W 240,000 bottles / $3.6 million revenue

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Suncrest Olive Estate might face if it chooses Option A.
    Answer: First, cutting the price by 10% reduces the revenue earned on every Country W bottle [k]. At $8.10 instead of $9, Suncrest loses 90 cents on each of its 240,000 Country W bottles, which is $216,000 a year less export revenue [app]. If volumes do not rise enough to replace this, profit falls and less money is available to reinvest in groves and bottling lines [an]. Second, a lower export price can trigger a price war with Country W rivals [k]. Rival producers may match the $8.10 offer to keep their supermarket listings, so Suncrest gains little extra shelf space [app]. Margins then stay permanently lower across a market that takes 60% of sales, making the business less able to absorb future cost rises [an].
    Keywords: Option A, $8.10, $9, 240,000, Country W, 10%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cutting price reduces revenue per unit; Lower prices risk competitor price matching / price war | application_max_2: Reference to $8.10 vs $9 / 90 cents x 240,000 = $216,000; Reference to Country W / 60% of sales / supermarket listings | analysis_max_2: Chain from lower price to lower revenue to reduced profit and less funds for reinvestment; Chain from rival price matching to no extra volume and permanently lower margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Suncrest Olive Estate should cut the Country W price to $8.10 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A cuts the Country W price by 10% to $8.10 to hold order volumes steady [k]. This keeps Suncrest competitive now that its bottles cost Country W buyers the equivalent of $10.08, helping to protect the 240,000-bottle order book that supplies 60% of its $3.6 million revenue [app]. Retaining shelf space prevents listings being lost to local Country W rivals, which would be hard and expensive to win back [an]. However, Option B holds the $9 price [k]. Refusing to discount protects the 90-cent margin on each bottle, so Suncrest avoids the $216,000 annual revenue loss built into Option A and keeps strong cash flow for the supermarkets [app]. The danger is that orders fall sharply as the 12% appreciation pushes Country W buyers towards cheaper local oil [an]. Overall, I think Suncrest should choose Option A [eval] because the appreciation was caused by currency markets rather than by Suncrest, and volume and shelf presence in Country W matter more than the margin; it can review the $8.10 price each season and raise it if the dollar weakens [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $8.10, $9, $10.08, 240,000, 60%, $3.6 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut price by 10% to $8.10 to defend volume; Option B: hold $9 and protect margin | application_max_2: Reference to $10.08 equivalent / 12% appreciation / 10% price cut; Reference to 240,000 bottles / 60% of sales / $3.6 million revenue / $216,000 | analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to retained competitiveness and protected Country W shelf space; Chain from holding price to preserved margin but risk of order losses to local rivals | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($8.10 vs $9, $216,000, 240,000 bottles)

--- STEM ---
Foxglove Denim Co is a private limited company in Country X weaving denim at its Glendale mill. It imports 30 tonnes of raw cotton a month from Country Z at $4,000 per tonne, costing $120,000 a month. The Country X dollar has depreciated by 15% against the Country Z currency, pushing the cotton price to $4,600 per tonne or $138,000 a month.

Managing Director Pavel Dvorak must decide on pricing by 1 August. Option A is to raise the wholesale price of jeans from $45 to $48 to protect profit margins, passing the $18,000 monthly increase to retailers. Option B is to keep prices at $45 and absorb the extra $216,000 a year, hoping cotton costs fall back or export sales to Country Z grow. 40% of Foxglove's jeans are exported.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by 'depreciation'.
    Answer: Depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency compared with other currencies, so the currency buys less foreign currency than before [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A fall in the value of a currency; Compared with other currencies / buys less foreign currency than before

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the 15% depreciation on Foxglove Denim Co.
    Answer: First, depreciation raises the cost of imported cotton [k]. Cotton now costs $4,600 per tonne, so the monthly bill has jumped from $120,000 to $138,000, an extra $18,000 a month [app]. Second, depreciation makes Foxglove's jeans cheaper for overseas buyers [k]. With 40% of jeans exported to Country Z, the finished garments cost Country Z retailers fewer Country Z units, so export orders may rise and partly offset the higher cotton bill [app].
    Keywords: 15%, $4,600, $138,000, $120,000, 40%, Country Z
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Depreciation raises the dollar cost of imports; Depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad | application_max_2: Reference to $4,600 per tonne / $138,000 vs $120,000 / $18,000; Reference to 40% exported to Country Z

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Foxglove Denim Co might face if it chooses Option B.
    Answer: First, absorbing the increase squeezes profit margins on every pair of jeans [k]. The extra $216,000 a year must come out of the margin on jeans sold at $45, leaving less for repairs, machinery or wages at the Glendale mill [app]. Lower retained profit means less money available for future investment, such as replacing weaving looms, which weakens competitiveness [an]. Second, Foxglove cannot know when cotton costs will fall back [k]. If the Country X dollar keeps depreciating beyond 15%, the $138,000 monthly cotton bill could rise further, so a fixed $45 price leaves the firm exposed to open-ended cost growth [app]. Continued absorption would eventually push certain lines into loss-making months, forcing emergency price changes or borrowing [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $45, $216,000, $138,000, $4,600, Glendale
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Absorbing costs squeezes profit margins; Currency costs may keep rising / future is uncertain | application_max_2: Reference to $216,000 a year / $138,000 monthly / $45 price; Reference to Glendale mill / further depreciation beyond 15% | analysis_max_2: Chain from absorbed costs to lower retained profit to weaker investment capacity; Chain from ongoing depreciation to open-ended cost growth to losses and forced price changes

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Foxglove Denim Co should raise its wholesale jean price from $45 to $48 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A raises the price by $3 to $48, passing the $18,000 monthly cotton increase on to retailers [k]. This restores margins without raising Foxglove's costs, which matters because depreciation lifted its bill from $120,000 to $138,000 a month [app]. Protecting $216,000 a year of margin lets Foxglove keep upgrading the Glendale mill and keeps its export pricing stable in Country Z terms [an]. However, Option B keeps prices at $45 [k]. Holding price may retain retailer loyalty and sales volume at home, and with 40% of jeans exported, stronger export volumes could offset the $216,000 absorbed [app]. The risk is that cotton costs keep rising if the dollar weakens further, so $45 may become unsustainable [an]. Overall, I think Foxglove should choose Option A [eval] because a $3 rise is only about 6.7% on a wholesale price and is caused by an external currency movement, so retailers are likely to accept it rather than lose supply; it should review the price each season in case cotton costs fall back [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $45, $48, $18,000, $216,000, 40%, Glendale
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: pass on cost via $3 rise to $48; Option B: hold $45 to protect loyalty and volume | application_max_2: Reference to $18,000 monthly increase / $216,000 a year / $45 to $48; Reference to 40% exports to Country Z / $120,000 to $138,000 | analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to restored margin to sustained investment; Chain from held price to volume retention but open-ended cost exposure | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($45 vs $48, $216,000, 40%)

--- STEM ---
Ridgemont Electronics Ltd is a private limited company in Country X assembling smartphone accessories at its Darnwell factory, employing 85 workers on two production lines. It imports circuit boards from Country W, paying €90,000 a month under a rolling supply agreement. The exchange rate has moved from $1.30 per euro to $1.45 per euro, so the dollar now buys fewer euros than six months ago.

Finance Director Mark Delgado must decide before the October supply contract is signed. Option A is to switch to a Country X circuit board supplier charging $135,000 a month, invoiced in dollars, with a 12-month fixed price. Option B is to keep importing from Country W at the current $130,500 a month and hope the rate swings back, accepting the uncertainty.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the dollar cost of the monthly €90,000 payment before and after the rate change.
    Answer: Before: €90,000 x $1.30 = $117,000. After: €90,000 x $1.45 = $130,500. The depreciation raises the monthly cost by $13,500 [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: €90,000 x $1.30 = $117,000; €90,000 x $1.45 = $130,500 (an increase of $13,500)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the exchange-rate movement on Ridgemont Electronics Ltd.
    Answer: First, the depreciation of the dollar raises the cost of imported circuit boards [k]. The monthly bill has increased from $117,000 to $130,500, an extra $13,500 a month that Ridgemont must absorb or pass on to customers [app]. Second, the movement reduces the reliability of Ridgemont's cost planning [k]. If the rate moves beyond $1.45 per euro, the $130,500 monthly import cost rises further, so the firm cannot confidently fix prices in its October supply contract [app].
    Keywords: $1.30, $1.45, €90,000, $130,500, $135,000, October
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A weaker dollar makes imports dearer; Rate uncertainty makes cost planning difficult | application_max_2: Reference to $117,000 to $130,500 / $13,500 a month / €90,000; Reference to October supply contract / $130,500 vs $135,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Ridgemont Electronics Ltd might face if it chooses Option B.
    Answer: First, the import cost is unpredictable month to month [k]. If the dollar weakens past $1.45 per euro, the €90,000 payment will exceed the current $130,500 and could approach the $135,000 charged by the Country X supplier [app]. Open-ended cost growth makes it hard to quote firm prices to customers, risking lost orders [an]. Second, continued importing keeps Ridgemont dependent on one foreign supplier and its lead times [k]. Any delay or disruption at the Country W factory would halt the Darnwell line that employs 85 workers [app]. A line stoppage would push up costs and damage reputation with accessory customers [an].
    Keywords: Option B, $130,500, $135,000, $1.45, Darnwell, 85 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Import costs can keep rising beyond current levels; Single foreign supplier creates dependency and lead-time risk | application_max_2: Reference to $1.45 per euro / $130,500 vs $135,000; Reference to Darnwell factory / 85 workers / October supply contract | analysis_max_2: Chain from further depreciation to import cost above $135,000 to eroded margin and lost orders; Chain from single-source dependency to line stoppage to costs and reputation damage

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ridgemont Electronics Ltd should switch to the Country X supplier (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A switches to a local supplier charging $135,000 a month with a 12-month fixed price in dollars [k]. For roughly $4,500 a month more than the current $130,500, Ridgemont buys certainty: its October supply contract can be priced firmly and its 85 Darnwell workers face no supply interruption [app]. Locking $135,000 removes the risk that the dollar weakens to $1.50 per euro, at which point €90,000 would cost $135,000 anyway [an]. However, Option B keeps the lower import price [k]. If the rate swings back towards $1.30 per euro, the import bill returns to $117,000, saving Ridgemont $13,500 a month, or $162,000 a year, against the fixed contract [app]. The saving is not guaranteed and costs remain unpredictable in the meantime [an]. Overall, I think Ridgemont should choose Option A [eval] because fixed costs remove the guesswork from the October contract and a domestic supplier also shortens lead times; it can revisit the decision when the 12-month contract expires [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $135,000, $130,500, $1.30, $1.45, October, Darnwell
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: fixed-price local supplier at $135,000; Option B: keep cheaper import at $130,500 / $117,000 if rate returns to $1.30 | application_max_2: Reference to €90,000 / October supply contract / 12-month fixed price; Reference to $130,500 vs $135,000 / Darnwell / 85 workers | analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed price to firm October pricing and no supply interruption; Chain from swinging rate to possible $162,000 annual saving forgone | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($135,000 vs $130,500, $1.30/$1.45)

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Depreciation raises the dollar cost of imports; Higher input costs squeeze margins / must recover through prices | application_max_2: Reference to $96,000 / $1.2 million / 8%; Reference to 40 homes / $2,400 per home / spring building season

    Question: Explain two problems Brannock Construction Ltd might face if it chooses Option A.
    Answer: First, domestic supplies cost $120,000 a year more than even the current import bill [k]. At $1.32 million against $1.2 million, Brannock pays a premium of $120,000, which is more than the $96,000 the depreciation added [app]. Millbrook builders all want local supplies at once, so lead times for domestic steel could run past the spring start, delaying the 40 homes [app]. Delays trigger penalty clauses in buyer contracts and raise site overhead, eroding the benefit of fixed prices [an].
    Keywords: Option A, $1.32 million, $1.2 million, $96,000, 40 homes, Millbrook
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Domestic suppliers charge more than imports; Local capacity and lead-time constraints | application_max_2: Reference to $1.32 million vs $1.2 million / $120,000 vs $96,000; Reference to 40 homes / spring building season / Millbrook | analysis_max_2: Chain from domestic premium to lower margin per home; Chain from local capacity limits to delays, penalties and overhead strain

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brannock Construction Ltd should source steel and timber from Country X suppliers (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A locks in Country X supplies at $1.32 million a year with no exchange-rate risk [k]. Because Brannock sells homes on fixed prices, a further depreciation beyond 8% would otherwise destroy its margin on 40 homes, and $1.32 million gives complete cost certainty for the spring programme [app]. Certain costs make cash flow and profit planning reliable, protecting the business from open-ended import bills [an]. However, Option B keeps the cheaper import route [k]. Overall, I think Brannock should choose Option A [eval] because its buyers have fixed-price contracts and cost certainty protects profit better than chasing a $24,000 saving that could vanish with one more rate move; it can return to imports if the dollar recovers [eval].

--- STEM ---
Thistledown Coffee Roasters is a private limited company in Country X importing 80 tonnes of green coffee a year from Country W at €2,800 a tonne, invoiced in euros, roasting them for independent cafe chains. The exchange rate has appreciated from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro, cutting the annual bean bill from $324,800 to $291,200 and saving $33,600.

Founder Marta Kowal must choose how to buy next year's beans before the new season arrives. Option A is to sign a 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne with the Country W supplier, locking costs regardless of rate movements. Option B is to keep buying monthly at spot rates and save even more if the dollar strengthens to $1.25 per euro, a bill of $280,000.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define what is meant by a 'stronger currency'.
    Answer: A stronger currency is one that has risen in value against other currencies, so it buys more foreign currency than before [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Currency has risen in value; Buys more foreign currency than before

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Thistledown Coffee Roasters.
    Answer: First, the appreciation cuts the annual green coffee bill [k]. At the new rate, 80 tonnes cost $291,200 rather than $324,800, saving $33,600 a year [app]. Second, the cheaper euros give Thistledown more room to compete and invest [k]. The $33,600 saving can be kept as extra profit or reinvested in roasting capacity without raising bean prices for cafe customers [app].
    Keywords: $291,200, $324,800, $33,600, 80 tonnes, €2,800, Thistledown Coffee Roasters
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Import bill falls in the home currency; Savings can be kept as profit or reinvested | application_max_2: Reference to $291,200 vs $324,800 / $33,600 saving; Reference to 80 tonnes / €2,800 a tonne / cafe customers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Thistledown Coffee Roasters might face if it chooses Option A.
    Answer: First, the contract locks the cost even if the dollar keeps strengthening [k]. If the rate reaches $1.25 per euro, spot buyers would pay only $280,000 a year, so Thistledown would overpay by $11,200 against spot purchases [app]. Overpaying weakens the margin on every bag of beans and wastes funds that could finance growth [an]. Second, a 12-month fixed contract removes flexibility to switch suppliers [k]. If the Country W supplier's quality or reliability slips, Thistledown cannot easily move its 80 tonnes to a rival roaster without renegotiating, and it is exposed for a full year [app]. Being locked in limits negotiating power on quality, delivery and payment terms during the peak season [an].
    Keywords: Option A, $280,000, $1.25, $33,600, $291,200, 80 tonnes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed contract overpays if the currency keeps strengthening; Long contracts reduce flexibility to switch suppliers | application_max_2: Reference to $280,000 at $1.25 / $11,200 gap vs $291,200; Reference to 80 tonnes / €2,800 a tonne / Country W supplier | analysis_max_2: Chain from locked price to overpaying vs spot to weaker margin and wasted funds; Chain from reduced flexibility to weaker negotiating power and supplier risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Thistledown Coffee Roasters should sign the 12-month fixed-price contract (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A signs a 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne [k]. This locks the bill at $291,200 equivalent regardless of rate movements, so planning, pricing and cash flow are predictable for the whole year [app]. Certainty matters because the bean bill is Thistledown's biggest cost, and locking it protects margin if the dollar weakens back towards $1.45, which would lift the bill to $324,800 [an]. However, Option B keeps monthly spot buying [k]. If the dollar strengthens to $1.25 per euro, the annual bill falls to $280,000, saving $11,200 more than the contract, and buying monthly avoids being locked into one supplier [app]. The trade-off is exposure to sudden reversals, which could add tens of thousands of dollars of cost overnight [an]. Overall, I think Thistledown should choose Option A [eval] because predictable input costs protect the business's narrow roaster margins and support firm pricing with cafe customers; the $11,200 possible extra saving is not worth the risk of a reversal [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $291,200, $280,000, $324,800, $1.25, $1.45, €2,800

--- STEM ---
Brinemare Fisheries is a private limited company fishing the cold waters off Country X's north coast, employing 60 crew and 12 factory staff. It exports 2,400 tonnes of frozen prawns a year, 70% of the catch to Country W supermarkets, at $4,000 a tonne, earning $9.6 million. The Country X dollar has depreciated by 10%, making its prawns cheaper in Country W shops.

Operations Director Sam Okoro must plan capacity for next year. Country W orders have risen by 25% to 3,000 tonnes, exceeding the 2,400-tonne freezing capacity. Option A is to invest $250,000 in a second blast freezer adding 800 tonnes of capacity. Option B is to hold output at 2,400 tonnes and quote new buyers higher prices and later delivery dates.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two types of business that benefit when a currency depreciates.
    Answer: Exporting businesses benefit because their goods become cheaper abroad; home businesses competing with imports benefit because imports become dearer [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Exporters benefit (goods cheaper abroad); Home businesses competing with imports benefit (imports dearer)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the depreciation for Brinemare Fisheries.
    Answer: First, depreciation makes Brinemare's prawns cheaper for Country W supermarkets [k]. Orders have already risen by 25% to 3,000 tonnes, worth up to $12 million a year if the extra volume is met [app]. Second, the weaker dollar strengthens Brinemare's competitiveness against Country W prawn suppliers [k]. Country X product now undercuts rivals in Country W shops, so Brinemare can win longer-term listings rather than one-off orders on its 70% export share [app].
    Keywords: 25%, 3,000, $4,000, $9.6 million, 70%, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Exports become cheaper abroad; Competitiveness against foreign rivals improves | application_max_2: Reference to orders up 25% to 3,000 tonnes / $4,000 a tonne / $12 million; Reference to 70% of catch to Country W supermarkets / $9.6 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Brinemare Fisheries might face if it chooses Option A.
    Answer: First, the $250,000 investment is a heavy up-front cash outlay [k]. Brinemare earns $9.6 million a year, so $250,000 is about 2.6% of revenue, and it must be financed before the extra 800 tonnes can be handled [app]. If the money is borrowed, interest payments raise costs until the freezer pays back [an]. Second, the extra capacity depends on export demand lasting [k]. The 10% depreciation could be reversed, and a 25% order surge might fade; an 800-tonne freezer running half empty would burden Brinemare with labour and running costs [app]. Idle capacity would eat the profit from core 2,400 tonnes and could leave the firm overstretched [an].
    Keywords: Option A, $250,000, $9.6 million, 800 tonnes, 2,400-tonne, 10%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large up-front investment must be financed; Demand surge may not last if the rate reverses | application_max_2: Reference to $250,000 / $9.6 million / 800 tonnes; Reference to 25% order rise / 10% depreciation / 2,400-tonne capacity | analysis_max_2: Chain from investment to finance costs and payback pressure; Chain from rate reversal to idle capacity and wasted running costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brinemare Fisheries should invest in a second blast freezer (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A invests $250,000 in a second blast freezer adding 800 tonnes of capacity [k]. Demand has already risen 25% to 3,000 tonnes, so the investment would let Brinemare capture up to $12 million a year of prawn sales instead of turning customers away [app]. Extra volume spreads the fixed costs of 60 crew and the factory over more tonnes, improving profit per tonne [an]. However, Option B holds capacity at 2,400 tonnes and manages scarcity with higher prices and later delivery dates [k]. This protects margins on current sales without new finance, and higher prices could lift revenue per tonne from the fixed 2,400 tonnes [app]. The risk is that Country W buyers turned away now sign with rival suppliers and do not return when the capacity arrives [an]. Overall, I think Brinemare should choose Option A [eval] because refusing orders above capacity risks the permanent loss of Country W listings, while $250,000 is recoverable through the margin on extra tonnes; it can phase the investment over two fishing seasons to limit the cash risk [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $250,000, 800 tonnes, 2,400-tonne, 3,000, $9.6 million, $4,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: invest $250,000 in 800 tonnes extra capacity; Option B: hold 2,400 tonnes, use higher prices and later deliveries | application_max_2: Reference to 3,000 tonnes vs 2,400 / $12 million potential; Reference to $250,000 / $4,000 a tonne / 70% Country W | analysis_max_2: Chain from new capacity to captured volume and spread fixed costs; Chain from refusing orders to permanent loss of listings | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($250,000, 3,000 vs 2,400 tonnes)

--- STEM ---
Alderney Motors is a private limited company selling cars in Country X's capital city from a showroom near the ring road. It imports 18 cars a month from Country W at €26,000 each, invoiced in euros. The Country X dollar has appreciated from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro, so each car now costs $33,800 instead of $37,700, a saving of $3,900 per car or $842,400 a year.

Sales Director Ruth Adler must set showroom prices for the new plate month. Option A is to cut prices by $2,000 per car to attract buyers and increase monthly sales volume. Option B is to keep prices unchanged and keep the extra $70,200 a month in profit, using it to expand the service department instead.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two ways consumers benefit when their country's currency appreciates.
    Answer: Imported goods become cheaper in home-currency terms; foreign holidays and imported products become more affordable [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Imported goods become cheaper; Foreign travel and imported products become more affordable

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Alderney Motors.
    Answer: First, each imported car costs $3,900 less [k]. The monthly saving on 18 cars is $70,200, equal to $842,400 a year at the new rate [app]. Second, Alderney can choose how to use the saving [k]. A modest price cut of $2,000 a car would still leave most of the $3,900 saving intact while winning price-sensitive buyers from rival showrooms [app].
    Keywords: $3,900, $70,200, $842,400, 18 cars, €26,000, $33,800
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower import costs in home currency; Flexibility to cut prices or keep margin | application_max_2: Reference to $3,900 a car / $70,200 a month / $842,400; Reference to 18 cars / €26,000 / $33,800 vs $37,700

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Alderney Motors might face if it chooses Option A.
    Answer: First, the price cut gives back $36,000 a month of the $70,200 saving immediately [k]. The margin per car falls from $3,900 to $1,900, so Alderney keeps only half the windfall and volumes may not rise enough to compensate [app]. Weaker margins squeeze the cash available for staff, stock and the showroom, risking losses if sales stay flat [an]. Second, rival dealers will also see the appreciation lift their margins [k]. If they match a $2,000 cut, no showroom gains share, and Alderney's prices fall with no extra cars sold [app]. Market-wide discounting lowers revenue across the whole market and trains customers to wait for promotions rather than buy [an].
    Keywords: Option A, $2,000, $70,200, $3,900, 18 cars, $33,800
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cutting prices sacrifices margin without guaranteed volume; Rivals likely to match the cut | application_max_2: Reference to $2,000 / $36,000 of the $70,200 / $1,900 remaining margin; Reference to 18 cars / rival showrooms / the capital city | analysis_max_2: Chain from margin sacrifice to weaker cash flow if volumes stay flat; Chain from price matching to market-wide discounting and customers waiting for deals

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Alderney Motors should cut showroom prices by $2,000 per car (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A cuts showroom prices by $2,000 a car to win buyers [k]. Because import costs fell to $33,800 from $37,700, this still leaves $1,900 of extra margin per car, and lower sticker prices should increase footfall and sales of the 18-car monthly quota [app]. More volume spreads overheads such as showroom staff and service bays, improving overall profit if sales respond [an]. However, Option B keeps prices unchanged and keeps the extra $70,200 a month [k]. Alderney banks a full $842,400 a year with zero risk to margin, which can expand the service department and deepen customer relationships after the sale [app]. The danger is that price-sensitive buyers drift to rivals who advertise lower prices, costing Alderney volume and long-term service work [an]. Overall, I think Alderney should choose Option B [eval] because the $70,200 monthly saving is certain while the volume gain from a $2,000 cut is not guaranteed; funding the service department strengthens the whole business, and selective promotions can target fence-sitters without a blanket cut [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $2,000, $70,200, $842,400, $33,800, $37,700, 18 cars
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut prices by $2,000 to boost volume; Option B: hold prices and keep $70,200 a month | application_max_2: Reference to $37,700 to $33,800 / $3,900 saving / $1,900 cushion; Reference to $842,400 a year / 18 cars / service department | analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to uncertain volume response and spread overheads; Chain from held prices to certain $842,400 margin funding service expansion | evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures ($2,000, $70,200, $842,400)

  Qb [4 marks]

Second, the swing makes it hard to set prices and budgets [k]. Its costs in Country X, such as wages and materials, stay in dollars, so a $1.35 million revenue swing lands straight on profit, making the next year's plan unreliable [app].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Most revenue is in foreign currency; Dollar costs against euro revenue create planning uncertainty | application_max_2: Reference to €9 million / 70% of revenue / $1.30 vs $1.45; Reference to 500,000 boxes / $13.05 million vs $11.7 million / $1.35 million swing

Losing tendered contracts would damage Tarnmoor's market share precisely when it needs stable export income [an]. Second, re-quoting every quarter creates administrative work and disputes [k].     Keywords: Option B, $1.30, $1.45, €9 million, 500,000, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Customers dislike unpredictable prices / risk of losing contracts; Admin burden and disputes from frequent re-quoting | application_max_2: Reference to quarterly re-quotes / Option B / Country W buyers; Reference to $1.30 to $1.45 / 500,000 boxes / hospital supply contracts | analysis_max_2: Chain from quarterly price changes to lost fixed-price tenders and export share; Chain from repeated renegotiation to admin strain and disputed payments

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Tarnmoor Medical Supplies should sign the 12-month fixed-price contract (Option A)? Justify your answer.

Overall, I think Tarnmoor should choose Option A [eval] because certainty wins long-term medical contracts and protects 70% of its revenue; $1.40 sits comfortably inside the $1.30-$1.45 band, so the deal is fair to both sides across a full year [eval].

  Qb [4 marks]

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two disadvantages of the import quota for construction firms in Country X.

However, protection depends on the ministry's final decision [k]; if imports are relaxed to 60,000 tonnes, the mill loses that advantage [app], squeezing profit and putting those jobs at risk [an]. A $1.2 million rolling line would make the business more efficient whether or not the quota is tightened. Overall, Ironhart should invest in the rolling line because being cost-competitive is safer than relying on government protection [eval], although lobbying for the tighter quota remains sensible as a short-term back-up while output is rising [eval].

--- STEM ---
CaneValley Foods Ltd is a manufacturer of sauces and jams in Country X, operating for 7 years with 120 employees. It imports 3,000 tonnes of cane sugar a year at $480 per tonne. The government introduced an import quota of 1,800 tonnes a year plus a 20% tariff on sugar above the quota, so the extra 1,200 tonnes now cost $576 per tonne, adding $115,200 a year to costs.

The managing director can switch the shortfall to domestic beet sugar at $545 per tonne, adding $78,000 a year to costs, or lobby the ministry to raise the quota. Lobbying could take 18 months with no guarantee of success. The beet sugar supply is reliable. The board must decide which option best protects profit margins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'import licence'.
    Answer: An import licence is a permit issued by a government allowing a business to import certain goods, used to control the quantity or value of imports [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a permit issued by a government; allows certain goods to be imported / used to control import quantity or value

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why CaneValley Foods might lobby the ministry to raise the sugar quota instead of switching to domestic beet sugar.
    Answer: Reason 1: Switching to beet sugar at $545 per tonne adds $78,000 a year to costs [k], which successful lobbying would avoid by restoring more cane sugar imports beyond the 1,800-tonne quota [app]. Reason 2: Successful lobbying would let the business buy all 3,000 tonnes at $480 per tonne [k], avoiding the $115,200 a year tariff paid on the 1,200-tonne shortfall [app].
    Keywords: $545, $78,000, 1,800, $480, $115,200, beet sugar, 20% tariff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: switching to beet sugar raises costs; a larger quota restores cheaper imported supply | application_max_2: $545 per tonne / $78,000 a year extra cost; 3,000 tonnes at $480 / $115,200 a year tariff on the 1,200-tonne shortfall

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the sugar import quota creates for CaneValley Foods.
    Answer: Problem 1: The 1,800-tonne quota forces the business to pay a 20% tariff on the extra 1,200 tonnes at $576 per tonne [k], adding $115,200 a year to costs [app] and squeezing profit margins on its sauces and jams [an]. Problem 2: Cane sugar supply is capped [k], so CaneValley may not secure its full 3,000-tonne yearly need [app], risking production delays and lost sales to retail buyers [an].
    Keywords: 1,800, $576, $115,200, 3,000 tonnes, import quota, $480, 120 employees
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: quota restricts import quantity / forces tariff on the overflow; capped supply may disrupt production | application_max_2: $576 per tonne / 1,200 tonnes above the quota / 20% tariff; 3,000-tonne yearly need / $115,200 a year added cost | analysis_max_2: squeezes profit margins on sauces and jams; production delays / lost sales to retail buyers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think CaneValley Foods should switch to domestic beet sugar or lobby the ministry for a larger quota? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching to beet sugar guarantees a reliable supply [k]; at $545 per tonne the 1,200-tonne shortfall adds $78,000 a year, less than the $115,200 tariff bill on imported sugar above the quota [app], so margins are protected immediately [an].   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'member state'.
    Answer: A member state is a country that has joined a trade bloc and agreed to follow its rules, such as trading without tariffs with other member countries [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a country that has joined a trade bloc; agreed to follow the bloc's rules / trades on agreed terms with other members

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to Rosewood Fashion of Country X joining the Aster Trade Bloc.
    Answer: Advantage 1: The 18% import tariff on clothing from the other 6 member countries is removed [k], so the imported garments that make up 70% of its $4.8 million stock become cheaper to buy [app]. Advantage 2: Bloc-based suppliers offered prices 15% below its current supplier [k], saving about $504,000 a year on the $3.36 million of imported garments [app].
    Keywords: 18%, Aster Trade Bloc, 6 member countries, $3.36 million, $504,000, 70%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: tariff removal lowers import costs; cheaper bloc-based suppliers | application_max_2: 18% tariff / 6 member countries / 70% of $4.8 million stock; $504,000 a year saving on $3.36 million of imports

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Rosewood Fashion could face if it switches to these bloc-based suppliers.

Problem 2: Switching after 8 years means unproven quality and reliability [k]; faulty garments would damage Rosewood's brand image [app], leading to lost customers and lower repeat sales [an].
    Keywords: 60 days, 14 stores, 8 years, Rosewood, $504,000, $3.36 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: new suppliers may end 60 days' credit terms; switching risks unproven quality and reliability | application_max_2: 60 days' credit / 14 stores stocking seasonal lines; 8 years with the current supplier / Rosewood's brand image | analysis_max_2: cash-flow strain across the stores; brand damage / lost customers and lower repeat sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rosewood Fashion should switch to the bloc-based suppliers when Country X joins the Aster Trade Bloc, or keep its existing supplier? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching removes the 18% tariff and saves about $504,000 a year on $3.36 million of imports [k], lifting profit across its 14 stores [app] without raising prices for middle-income families [an]. However, keeping the current supplier preserves 60 days' credit and 8 years of trust [k]; unknown suppliers risk quality and cash-flow problems [app], which could hurt the brand more than the saving is worth [an]. Overall, Rosewood should switch to the bloc-based suppliers because $504,000 a year is a major saving and bloc membership gives lasting tariff-free access [eval], although it should negotiate credit terms close to the existing 60 days before committing [eval].
    Keywords: $504,000, 18%, 14 stores, 60 days, 8 years, Aster Trade Bloc, $3.36 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: switching cuts import costs / tariff removed; keeping the supplier preserves credit and trust | application_max_2: $504,000 a year saving on $3.36 million of imports / 14 stores; 60 days' credit / 8 years with current supplier / 18% tariff | analysis_max_2: higher profit without raising prices; risk to brand and cash flow from unknown suppliers | evaluation_max_2: weighs switching for the saving against keeping the trusted supplier; justified recommendation with figures

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a group of countries trading goods without tariffs between members; each member keeps its own tariff on goods from outside the area

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Kibale Tea Co might enter the new member market.
    Answer: Reason 1: Tea exported to another Tzara Free Trade Area member country faces no tariff [k], unlike sales to non-member countries [app]. Reason 2: Demand for premium loose-leaf tea in the new market is growing at 9% a year [k], with projected first-year sales of $750,000 against a $300,000 entry cost [app].
    Keywords: Tzara Free Trade Area, 9%, $750,000, $300,000, 60%, loose-leaf tea
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: no tariff on exports to member countries; rising demand in the new market | application_max_2: member of the Tzara Free Trade Area; 9% a year growth / $750,000 first-year sales / $300,000 entry cost

  Qc [6 marks]

Problem 2: Established member-country tea growers already know their home market [k], so Kibale may have to cut prices or spend heavily on promotion [app], reducing profit per kg on its premium teas [an].
    Keywords: $300,000, 60%, $750,000, premium loose-leaf tea, member country, 3 tea estates
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: upfront launch costs strain cash flow; competition from established local producers | application_max_2: $300,000 launch cost / 60% export share / 20 kg sacks; new member market where local growers know the market | analysis_max_2: delays other investments / cash shortfall; lower profit per kg / heavy promotion spend

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kibale Tea Co should spend $300,000 to enter the new member market, or focus on existing non-member markets? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Entering the new member market gives tariff-free access and demand growing at 9% a year [k], with projected first-year sales of $750,000, far above the $300,000 entry cost [app], so the investment could be recovered within the first year [an]. However, non-member markets need no entry spend [k]; demand is flat rather than falling, so focusing there protects cash flow [app], although the business misses a growing tariff-free market and long-term revenue [an]. Overall, Kibale should enter the member market because tariff-free trading and 9% annual demand growth make $300,000 a sound investment [eval], provided management tracks the $750,000 sales forecast against actual results [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: tariff-free access to a growing member market; non-member markets need no entry spend / demand flat | application_max_2: 9% a year demand growth / $750,000 projected first-year sales; $300,000 entry cost / 60% export share | analysis_max_2: investment recoverable within first year; staying protects cash flow but misses growth and long-term revenue | evaluation_max_2: weighs entering the member market against focusing on non-member markets; justified recommendation with figures

--- STEM ---
Copperton Appliances Ltd manufactures washing machines in Country X, operating for 13 years with 260 employees. On 1 March the bloc raised its common external tariff on washing machines from 10% to 28%, adding about $85 to the landed cost of each machine.

Copperton could build an assembly plant inside the bloc for $2.5 million, employing 60 workers and making bloc sales tariff-free.
