--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'customs union'.
    Answer: A customs union is a trade bloc in which member countries remove tariffs on trade between themselves and agree a common external tariff on goods coming from outside the bloc [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: member countries remove tariffs between themselves; members agree a common external tariff on goods from outside the bloc

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Copperton Appliances might build an assembly plant inside the Meridian Trade Bloc.
    Answer: Reason 1: Bloc sales of $4.9 million a year would avoid the common external tariff after it rose from 10% to 28% [k], keeping its washing machines competitively priced [app]. Reason 2: A plant inside the bloc keeps tariff-free access permanently [k], securing bloc revenue of $4.9 million a year even if the tariff rises again [app].
    Keywords: $4.9 million, Meridian Trade Bloc, 28%, 10%, $85, 260 employees
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: avoids the higher common external tariff; secures permanent tariff-free access / keeps prices competitive | application_max_2: $4.9 million bloc revenue / sold through 9 electrical retailers; tariff rose from 10% to 28% / about $85 added per machine

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Copperton Appliances could face if it builds the assembly plant inside the bloc.
    Answer: Problem 1: The $2.5 million build cost is a large upfront outlay [k], which drains liquidity for a business with $14 million revenue [app], increasing financial risk if bloc sales disappoint [an]. Problem 2: Running an overseas site adds management complexity [k]; coordinating 60 new workers and shipping parts across the border [app] stretches existing management and may slow decisions [an].
    Keywords: $2.5 million, 60 workers, $14 million, $4.9 million, Country X, 28%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: large upfront investment / cash-flow strain; extra management complexity abroad | application_max_2: $2.5 million build cost / $14 million revenue; 60 new workers / shipping parts across the border | analysis_max_2: financial risk if bloc sales disappoint; stretched management / slower decisions

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Copperton Appliances should build the assembly plant inside the bloc, or keep production in Country X and raise bloc prices? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Building the plant protects $4.9 million of annual bloc revenue [k]; avoiding the 28% tariff that adds $85 per machine keeps Copperton competitive [app], letting steady sales repay the $2.5 million cost [an]. However, staying in Country X avoids that outlay and keeps $14 million revenue undisturbed [k]; a 10% price rise risks losing 15% of bloc sales, about $320,000 of revenue [app], but keeps production simple and local [an]. Overall, Copperton should build the plant, because tariff-free access secures the bloc market for the long term, whereas paying 28% or raising prices erodes bloc demand [eval], even though the $2.5 million cost must be carefully financed [eval].
    Keywords: $2.5 million, $4.9 million, 28%, 10%, 15%, $85, Country X
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: building inside the bloc avoids the common external tariff; staying avoids the large upfront outlay / keeps production simple | application_max_2: $4.9 million bloc revenue / $85 added per machine / $2.5 million plant; 10% price rise risks 15% sales fall / $14 million revenue | analysis_max_2: steady sales repay the plant cost / long-term security; higher prices erode bloc demand / about $320,000 revenue risk | evaluation_max_2: weighs building inside the bloc against staying in Country X and raising prices; justified recommendation with figures

    Question: Explain two disadvantages of the import quota for consumers in Country X.
    Answer: Disadvantage 1: With imports capped at 6,000 tonnes a year [k], apple supply is restricted and prices rose from $1.40 to $1.85 per kg [app], so households spend more on fruit [an]. Disadvantage 2: Quotas reduce consumer choice [k]; shops stock fewer foreign apple varieties [app], leaving shoppers with less variety outside the season [an].
    Keywords: 6,000 tonnes, $1.40, $1.85, 9,000 tonnes, import quota, 45 hectares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: supply is restricted by the quota; consumer choice is reduced | application_max_2: 6,000 tonnes cap / prices rose from $1.40 to $1.85 per kg; fewer foreign apple varieties in shops | analysis_max_2: households spend more on fruit; less variety outside the season

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Elmsgrove Apples should support the ministry's proposal to raise the apple import quota from 6,000 to 9,000 tonnes? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Supporting the higher quota would raise import competition and push prices down [k]; raising the cap to 9,000 tonnes could cut prices back from $1.85 towards $1.40 per kg [app], eroding Elmsgrove's $1.1 million revenue [an]. Opposing the rise protects Elmsgrove's prices and its 30 seasonal pickers [k], keeping the quota at 6,000 tonnes as it stands today [app], but it looks self-interested while consumers pay more and get less choice [an]. Overall, Elmsgrove should oppose the quota increase, because its business depends on the $1.85 per kg price and $1.1 million revenue, and the 9,000-tonne cap could cost 10 pickers their jobs [eval], although the owner could offer to support a smaller increase in exchange for a phased rise [eval].
    Keywords: 9,000 tonnes, 6,000 tonnes, $1.85, $1.40, $1.1 million, 30
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher quota increases import competition / pushes prices down; opposing the rise protects the grower's prices and pickers | application_max_2: raising the cap to 9,000 tonnes / prices back from $1.85 towards $1.40 per kg; $1.1 million revenue / 30 seasonal pickers / 10 pickers at risk / 6,000 tonnes today | analysis_max_2: revenue erodes if prices fall; looks self-interested / consumers pay more with the quota kept | evaluation_max_2: weighs supporting against opposing the quota rise; justified recommendation with figures

The board must decide whether to invest in exporting or stay domestic.

--- QUESTIONS ---

    Question: Define 'market access'.
    Answer: Market access is the ability of a business to sell its goods or services in a foreign market, for example selling dining furniture to member countries of a trade bloc [2].

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Salterns Furniture should export to the new bloc markets.
    Answer: Reason 1: The two new member countries create a combined tariff-free market of 160 million consumers [k], far bigger than domestic growth of 2% a year [app]. Reason 2: First-year bloc sales are projected at $2 million, rising to $3.5 million in year three [k], outstripping domestic expansion [app].
    Keywords: 160 million, $2 million, $3.5 million, 2%, $900,000, Meridian Trade Bloc
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: large new tariff-free market for its products; projected sales growth in the new markets | application_max_2: 160 million consumers / 2% a year domestic growth; $2 million first-year bloc sales / $3.5 million by year three

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Salterns Furniture could face exporting to the new bloc markets.
    Answer: Problem 1: The $900,000 cost of distribution and safety standards must be paid up front [k], which is large for a business with $5.5 million revenue [app], reducing cash available for other needs [an]. Problem 2: Salterns must learn different customer tastes and rules in two new countries [k], so early promotion could fail to win buyers [app], delaying the $2 million first-year sales target [an].
    Keywords: $900,000, $5.5 million, $2 million, 75 employees, Meridian Trade Bloc, 160 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: large upfront distribution and compliance cost; unfamiliar markets and different rules | application_max_2: $900,000 up-front cost / $5.5 million revenue / 75 employees; $2 million first-year sales target / two new member countries | analysis_max_2: reduced cash for other needs; delayed sales target / weak launch

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Salterns Furniture should invest $900,000 to export to the new bloc markets, or expand in the domestic market? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Exporting gives tariff-free access to 160 million consumers in the new member countries [k], with sales projected at $2 million in year one and $3.5 million in year three [app], so the $900,000 investment is recovered within the first year [an]. Expanding domestically is cheaper [k], and the team knows its customers, but the market grows at only 2% a year [app], so growth stays limited [an]. Overall, Salterns should invest in exporting, because $3.5 million of year-three sales in a tariff-free market dwarfs 2% domestic growth [eval], provided it secures the $900,000 finance without risking existing operations [eval].
    Keywords: $900,000, 160 million, $2 million, $3.5 million, 2%, Meridian Trade Bloc
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: exporting gives tariff-free access to 160 million consumers; expanding domestically is cheaper but growth is limited | application_max_2: $2 million year one / $3.5 million year three / 160 million consumers; $900,000 investment / 2% a year domestic growth | analysis_max_2: investment recovered within the first year; domestic expansion stays limited at 2% a year | evaluation_max_2: weighs investing $900,000 to export against expanding domestically; justified recommendation with figures

--- STEM ---
Kestrelview Kitchens makes fitted kitchen cabinets in Country X and has traded for 5 years. It employs 14 carpenters and sold 260 kitchens last year at an average price of $3,800, generating revenue of $988,000. Fixed costs are $6,500 a month and materials cost $2,100 per kitchen.

Country X is in the growth stage of the business cycle and gross domestic product rose by 3.4% last year. Orders have risen 18% since January and the order book is full for the next 4 months. The owner, Priya Raman, is deciding whether to open a second workshop with 6 more carpenters at a cost of $180,000, or keep one workshop and operate a waiting list. She must decide before the end of the quarter.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'the business cycle'.
    Answer: The regular pattern of ups and downs in economic activity and growth that economies experience over time, moving through stages such as growth, boom, recession and slump [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the business cycle is the regular pattern of fluctuations in economic activity over time; the cycle moves through stages such as growth, boom, recession and slump

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the growth stage of the business cycle affects Kestrelview Kitchens.
    Answer: Reason 1: Growth means rising output, incomes and consumer spending [k]; Kestrelview's orders have risen 18% since January and gross domestic product rose by 3.4% last year [app]. Reason 2: Growth encourages firms to expand [k], so Priya is considering a second workshop with 6 more carpenters at a cost of $180,000 [app].
    Keywords: 18%, 3.4%, 4 months, second workshop, $180,000, growth stage, 260 kitchens
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: growth stage means rising GDP, incomes and consumer spending; growth encourages firms to expand output and invest | application_max_2: orders risen 18% since January with GDP growth of 3.4%; second workshop with 6 more carpenters at a cost of $180,000 under consideration

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Kestrelview Kitchens might face if it opens the second workshop too quickly.
    Answer: Problem 1: Rapid expansion raises fixed costs [k]; with fixed costs already $6,500 a month, a second workshop would push these higher before revenue from extra kitchens arrives [app], so cash reserves could be strained if demand slows [an]. Problem 2: Hiring 6 more carpenters quickly risks quality and control [k]; the 14 existing carpenters could struggle to produce 260 kitchens a year while training newcomers [app], so the reputation built over 5 years could be damaged [an].
    Keywords: $6,500 a month, 6 more carpenters, 14 carpenters, 260 kitchens, 5 years, second workshop, $180,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: expansion increases fixed costs and overheads; rapid hiring creates quality and control problems | application_max_2: fixed costs already $6,500 a month before expansion; 14 carpenters produce 260 kitchens; 6 new hires must be trained | analysis_max_2: cash-flow strain if growth cools before the new workshop pays for itself; quality slip could damage a reputation built over 5 years

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kestrelview Kitchens should open the second workshop now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Opening the second workshop now would capture the high demand [k]; orders are up 18% since January, the book is full for the next 4 months and revenue has reached $988,000, so added capacity with 6 more carpenters could lift sales further [app], strengthening market share while the growth stage lasts [an]. However, expansion is risky and costly [k]; the workshop costs $180,000, fixed costs are already $6,500 a month, and the surge may not last beyond the growth stage [app], so idle capacity and strained quality could hurt the business in a downturn [an]. Overall, Kestrelview should open the second workshop now [eval], because 3.4% GDP growth and a full 4-month order book give strong evidence that demand will keep the new workshop busy [eval].
    Keywords: 18%, 4 months, $988,000, $180,000, $6,500 a month, 3.4%, second workshop
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: expansion during growth captures rising demand and raises revenue; expansion carries cost and demand risk if the cycle turns | application_max_2: orders up 18% since January, book full for 4 months, revenue $988,000; $180,000 cost with fixed costs of $6,500 a month and 3.4% GDP growth | analysis_max_2: extra capacity converts waiting-list demand into sales; idle capacity and quality strain if the economy leaves growth | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing strong current demand against cycle risk

Its main ingredient costs rose by 12% this year, fixed costs are $9,000 a month and it employs 74 staff across the summer peak.

Country X is in a boom, with consumer spending up 6.1% and unemployment at just 2.8%. Parlour footfall is up 25% and staff are struggling to meet demand, especially on hot weekends. The owner, Lena Costa, is deciding whether to raise prices by 6% across all parlours or absorb the higher ingredient costs and keep prices unchanged. She wants a decision before the peak summer season begins on 1 June.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'a boom'.
    Answer: The peak stage of the business cycle, when the economy is strongest, with very high demand and output, low unemployment and rising incomes [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a boom is the peak stage of the business cycle with very high output; a boom brings high demand, high incomes and very low unemployment

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the boom benefits Sorrento Gelato Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: A boom means very high consumer spending [k]; spending across Country X rose by 6.1% and Sorrento's parlour footfall is up 25% [app]. Reason 2: In a boom incomes are high [k], so customers can afford $4.50 tubs and Sorrento sold 420,000 tubs and made $1,890,000 of revenue last year [app].
    Keywords: 6.1%, 25%, $4.50, 420,000 tubs, $1,890,000, 2.8%, boom
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a boom brings very high consumer spending and demand; a boom brings high incomes and low unemployment | application_max_2: consumer spending up 6.1% and footfall up 25%; 420,000 tubs sold at $4.50 generating $1,890,000 of revenue

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Sorrento Gelato Co faces during the boom.
    Answer: Problem 1: A boom creates cost pressure as demand competes for scarce resources [k]; Sorrento's ingredient costs have risen by 12% this year [app], squeezing margins if tub prices stay at $4.50 [an]. Problem 2: Low unemployment makes hiring difficult [k]; with unemployment at just 2.8%, Sorrento's staff are struggling to serve 25% more footfall through its 9 parlours [app], so poor service could cost sales in the peak season [an].
    Keywords: 12%, 2.8%, $4.50, 9 parlours, 25%, $9,000 a month, peak summer season
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a boom pushes up business costs through resource competition; a boom makes recruiting and retaining staff difficult | application_max_2: ingredient costs risen 12% this year; unemployment at just 2.8% with staff struggling to meet demand | analysis_max_2: margins squeezed if tub prices are held at $4.50; understaffing risks lost sales and slower service during the peak season

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Sorrento Gelato Co should raise prices by 6% for the summer season? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising prices by 6% would protect margins [k]; ingredient costs are up 12% and demand is strong with footfall up 25% while consumer spending rose 6.1% [app], so $1,890,000 of revenue can be defended and profits increased [an]. However, higher prices may test customer loyalty [k]; customers already face higher costs, and a rise from $4.50 may deter price-conscious buyers outside the summer peak [app], so sales volumes could fall and undo the gain [an]. Overall, Sorrento should raise prices by 6% [eval], because boom conditions with 6.1% spending growth and 2.8% unemployment mean demand is strong enough to absorb a modest rise [eval].
    Keywords: 6%, 12%, 25%, 6.1%, 2.8%, $4.50, $1,890,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: raising prices in a boom protects profit margins; price rises risk losing price-sensitive customers | application_max_2: ingredient costs up 12% with footfall up 25%; consumer spending up 6.1% and unemployment at 2.8% | analysis_max_2: margin recovery and extra profit to fund staffing; volume risk if the 6% rise deters customers outside the peak | evaluation_max_2: justified decision linked to boom conditions and cost pressure

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'a recession'.
    Answer: A period in which the economy shrinks for at least two consecutive quarters, with falling output and rising unemployment [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a recession is a fall in GDP/output for two or more consecutive quarters; a recession brings rising unemployment and falling consumer spending

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects the recession is having on Lindenbrook Clothing Co.
    Answer: Reason 1: A recession cuts consumer demand [k]; Lindenbrook's revenue fell from $2.4 million to $1.9 million, a fall of almost 21% [app]. Reason 2: Falling confidence hits high-street retailers [k]; footfall has dropped 22% across Lindenbrook's 8 high-street clothing stores [app].
    Keywords: $2.4 million, $1.9 million, 21%, 22%, 8 high-street, 6.5%, recession
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a recession cuts consumer demand and spending; a recession reduces retail sales and revenues | application_max_2: revenue fell from $2.4 million to $1.9 million, almost 21%; footfall dropped 22% across the 8 stores

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of making 12 sales assistants redundant.
    Answer: Problem 1: Redundancies cut capacity to serve customers [k]; removing 12 sales assistants leaves 48 staff for 8 stores needing at least 5 each [app], so any absence could force closures or lost sales [an]. Problem 2: Redundancies damage morale and public image [k]; with unemployment already rising to 6.5% in a recession, further job losses would be unpopular with staff and the public [app], lowering effort and driving customers to rivals [an].
    Keywords: 12 sales assistants, 60 sales assistants, $28,000 a month, 5 staff, 6.5%, 8 high-street, 10%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: redundancy reduces staffing and service capacity; redundancy damages staff morale and the firm's reputation | application_max_2: cutting 12 leaves 48 staff for 8 stores needing at least 5 each; unemployment already rising to 6.5% in a recession | analysis_max_2: understaffing risks forcing closures or lost sales during peak trading; low morale and bad publicity could further cut the 22%-down footfall

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Lindenbrook Clothing Co should make 12 sales assistants redundant rather than cut wages by 10%? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Redundancy would cut payroll costs immediately [k]; removing 12 of 60 sales assistants saves their wages in a business whose revenue fell almost 21% to $1.9 million [app], protecting cash flow while fixed costs of $28,000 a month continue [an]. However, a 10% wage cut spreads the pain across all 60 sales assistants [k], keeping experienced staff on the 8 high-street stores rather than paying redundancy costs and harming morale while unemployment is 6.5% [app], so service quality is preserved for the recovery [an]. Overall, Lindenbrook should cut wages by 10% rather than make redundancies [eval], because retaining the experienced team protects its 8 stores better while the recession lasts [eval].
    Keywords: $1.9 million, $28,000 a month, 10%, 6.5%, 60 sales assistants, 8 high-street, 21%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: redundancy lowers wage costs quickly; a wage cut retains skills and morale at lower risk | application_max_2: revenue down almost 21% to $1.9 million with fixed costs of $28,000 a month; 60 sales assistants across 8 stores with unemployment at 6.5% | analysis_max_2: immediate payroll relief against lost experience and redundancy costs; skills retention aids recovery when demand returns | evaluation_max_2: justified preference with stem evidence and a clear final choice

  Qb [4 marks]

  Qd [8 marks]

--- STEM ---
Northfen Contact Services runs a call centre in Country X employing 120 staff over two shifts at its offices in the market town of Jessop. It handles customer queries for 3 utilities companies and earns $5.1 million a year. Wages average $16,800 per worker per year, staff turnover is 28% and absence runs at 9%.

The government's economic objective of full employment has led it to offer a $3,000 grant plus free training for every long-term unemployed person hired. Northfen is deciding whether to hire 40 unemployed workers using the grants, worth $120,000, or to spend $250,000 on automation software that would reduce the need for 25 posts and lower average call times.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'full employment'.
    Answer: A situation in which virtually everyone who is able and willing to work can find a job, with only very low levels of unemployment remaining [2].

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the government's full employment objective benefits Northfen Contact Services.

Reason 2: Reducing unemployment widens the available labour pool [k]; with 28% staff turnover, free trained recruits would help Northfen replace staff at its 120-seat call centre for 3 utilities companies [app].
    Keywords: $3,000, $120,000, 40 unemployed workers, free training, 28%, 120 staff, full employment
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: full employment policies back job creation with grants and training; reducing unemployment widens the effective labour pool | application_max_2: $3,000 grant plus free training per hire; $120,000 for 40 hires; 28% turnover among 120 staff serving 3 utilities companies

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Northfen Contact Services might face if it hires the 40 unemployed workers.
    Answer: Problem 1: New hires may need close supervision [k]; although training is free, long-term unemployed staff handling queries for 3 utilities companies may need experienced agents beside them [app], diverting staff from live calls [an]. Problem 2: Retention could be poor [k]; with staff turnover already 28%, some of the 40 hires may not stay beyond their first year [app], so the $120,000 grant benefit could be eroded by repeat recruitment [an].
    Keywords: 3 utilities companies, 28%, 120 staff, $120,000, $3,000, 40 unemployed workers, free training
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: inexperienced or long-term unemployed staff need supervision and training; high staff turnover wastes recruitment and training investment | application_max_2: free training but close supervision still needed for 3 utilities companies; turnover already 28% among the existing 120 staff | analysis_max_2: supervision burden diverts experienced staff from revenue-earning calls; repeat recruitment could cancel out the $120,000 grant benefit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Consider whether Northfen Contact Services should hire 40 unemployed workers using the government grants or invest in $250,000 of automation software. Recommend one option and justify your answer.
    Answer: Hiring 40 workers with the grants would keep capacity high [k]; $120,000 of grants plus free training cuts the cost of 40 recruits whose wages would otherwise total $672,000 a year at $16,800 per worker [app], protecting service for the 3 utilities companies [an]. However, automation would remove 25 posts [k]; $250,000 is a one-off cost that could cut long-run labour costs and ease the 28% turnover problem [app], raising productivity beyond what extra hiring achieves [an]. Overall, Northfen should hire the 40 unemployed workers using the grants [eval], because $120,000 of support plus free training meets its staffing needs and aids the government's full employment aim before the scheme closes on 31 August [eval].
    Keywords: $120,000, $250,000, 40 unemployed workers, $16,800 per worker, 28%, 3 utilities companies, 31 August
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: government grants and training reduce the net cost of hiring; automation lowers long-run labour costs and raises productivity | application_max_2: $120,000 grants plus free training; wages would total $672,000 a year; $250,000 software removing 25 posts; turnover 28% and $16,800 per worker | analysis_max_2: grants protect service quality and capacity at low net cost; automation saves recurring wages but cuts posts and morale | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the grant deadline and the figures

--- STEM ---
Fennimore Tea Rooms runs 6 tea rooms in Country X serving 92,000 customers a year, with revenue of $1.4 million. A slice of cake costs $4.00 before tax and cakes make up 15% of total sales. The government has raised VAT from 17.5% to 20% on 1 April as part of its drive for stable prices and lower public debt, although the change is expected to push up the general price level.

The owner, Amara Osei, must decide whether to pass the full VAT increase on to customers by raising prices or absorb it and keep menu prices unchanged. At a $4.00 cake slice, the tax rises from 70 cents to 80 cents. She must decide before printing new menus this month.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'inflation'.
    Answer: A sustained rise in the general price level of an economy over time, which reduces the purchasing power of money [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level; inflation reduces the purchasing power of money

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the VAT rise on Fennimore Tea Rooms.
    Answer: Reason 1: VAT is an indirect tax on spending [k]; with VAT at 20% the tax on a $4.00 cake rises from 70 cents to 80 cents [app]. Reason 2: The VAT rise increases the price customers pay [k]; passing it on would raise menu prices for Fennimore's 92,000 customers a year across 6 tea rooms [app].
    Keywords: 17.5%, 20%, 70 cents, 80 cents, 92,000 customers, $4.00, 6 tea rooms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: VAT is an indirect tax on consumer spending collected by businesses; a VAT increase raises the prices consumers pay | application_max_2: tax on a $4.00 cake rises from 70 cents to 80 cents; 92,000 customers a year across 6 tea rooms; revenue $1.4 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of absorbing the VAT rise rather than raising prices.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Absorbing the rise keeps prices stable [k]; holding the cake slice at $4.00 plus the old tax keeps menu prices attractive while the government pursues stable prices [app], protecting customer goodwill [an]. Benefit 2: Stable prices protect sales volume [k]; avoiding even a 10-cent rise on each cake slice could prevent a fall in footfall among 92,000 customers a year [app], keeping the $1.4 million revenue steadier through the change [an].
    Keywords: $4.00, 92,000 customers, $1.4 million, stable prices, 70 cents, 80 cents, 6 tea rooms
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: absorbing indirect tax rises keeps prices stable or competitive; stable prices protect demand and customer goodwill | application_max_2: cake slice held at $4.00 plus the old tax during the government's stable prices drive; 92,000 customers a year and $1.4 million revenue at stake | analysis_max_2: goodwill and competitive edge from not raising prices; avoids a demand fall, protecting annual revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fennimore Tea Rooms should pass the VAT rise on to customers through higher prices? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Passing on the rise would protect profit [k]; covering the extra tax from 70 cents to 80 cents on each $4.00 cake across 92,000 customers a year keeps margins intact on $1.4 million of sales [app], so Fennimore does not subsidise the government's tax rise itself [an]. However, raising prices conflicts with the stable prices objective [k]; a rise from $4.70 to $4.80 is small, but across 6 tea rooms even a modest increase could deter price-conscious customers [app], cutting footfall when rivals face the same change [an]. Overall, Fennimore should raise prices [eval], because a 10-cent rise on a $4.00 cake is small enough to keep most customers while protecting the margin needed to trade profitably [eval].
    Keywords: 70 cents, 80 cents, $4.00, 92,000 customers, $1.4 million, 17.5%, 20%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: passing indirect tax rises to customers protects profit margins; raising prices risks losing price-sensitive customers | application_max_2: tax on cake rises from 70 cents to 80 cents on a $4.00 slice; 92,000 customers a year across 6 tea rooms with $1.4 million revenue | analysis_max_2: margin protection across the whole sales base; footfall risk if the rise deters customers | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the figures and the stable prices context

  Qb [4 marks]

Reason 2: Lower disposable income pushes shoppers towards cheaper goods [k]; average transactions of $240 across 36,000 sales may shrink as wealthy customers trade down [app].
    Keywords: 70%, 40%, 45%, 36,000 transactions, $240, $8.64 million, high-income customers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher income tax reduces disposable income; lower disposable income can reduce discretionary spending | application_max_2: 70% of revenue comes from high-income customers; top rate from 40% to 45%; 36,000 transactions averaging $240; revenue $8.64 million

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Argent & Vale Department Store should launch 'Argent Value' aimed at lower-income shoppers? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Launching 'Argent Value' would open a new market [k]; with the top income tax rate rising from 40% to 45%, lower-income shoppers keep relatively more spending power and the range could win new customers [app], spreading risk beyond the 70% of revenue from high-income customers [an].     Keywords: Argent Value, 45%, 40%, $8.64 million, $240, 70%, 12 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a budget range accesses price-sensitive customer segments; a premium focus protects established brand equity | application_max_2: top income tax rate rises from 40% to 45% to redistribute income; $8.64 million revenue from 36,000 transactions at $240; 70% from high-income customers | analysis_max_2: a new segment diversifies revenue away from tax-hit high earners; brand dilution could cut premium sales built over 12 years | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing diversification against brand risk

--- STEM ---
Veloce Cycles Ltd imports 5,000 bicycles a year from Country Z and sells them in Country X at $320 each, earning $1.6 million in revenue and a margin of $170 per bike. Each bike costs $150 to import. The government, aiming to improve the balance of payments, has imposed a 25% import tariff on finished bicycles, raising the import cost to $187.50.

The owner, Tomás Rivera, must decide whether to raise the selling price above $320 or open a small assembly plant in Country X using imported parts, which are not tariffed, costing $175 per bike plus $300,000 of equipment and saving $12.50 per bike, or $62,500 a year. He must decide before the tariff takes effect on 1 October.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'import tariffs'.
    Answer: Taxes placed on goods brought into a country, used to raise revenue, protect domestic producers or improve the balance of payments [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: tariffs are taxes on imported goods; tariffs raise revenue, protect domestic industry or improve the balance of payments

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the 25% import tariff on Veloce Cycles Ltd.
    Answer: Reason 1: Tariffs raise the cost of imports [k]; each $150 bike now costs $187.50, cutting the margin on every one of the 5,000 bicycles [app]. Reason 2: Tariffs squeeze margins or force price rises [k]; holding the price at $320 would cut the unit margin from $170 to $132.50 [app].
    Keywords: 25%, $150, $187.50, $320, 5,000 bicycles, $1.6 million, $170
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: tariffs increase the cost of imported goods; tariffs squeeze importer margins or push up retail prices | application_max_2: import cost rises from $150 to $187.50; margin falls from $170 to $132.50; 5,000 bicycles a year sold at $320; revenue $1.6 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of assembling bicycles in Country X rather than importing finished bikes.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Local assembly avoids the finished-bike tariff [k]; imported parts are not tariffed, so building bikes at $175 each undercuts the $187.50 tariffed import cost [app], protecting the margin on 5,000 bicycles a year [an]. Benefit 2: Local assembly gives Veloce more control over supply [k]; building to order in Country X cuts the lead time and shipping risk of supplies from Country Z [app], so stockouts and lost sales on the $1.6 million pipeline are less likely [an].
    Keywords: $175, $187.50, $320, 5,000 bicycles, Country Z, $300,000, import tariff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: local assembly avoids tariffs on finished goods; local assembly improves control and reliability of supply | application_max_2: parts not tariffed; assembled cost $175 vs $187.50 tariffed import cost; 5,000 bicycles a year imported from Country Z to sell at $320 | analysis_max_2: margin restored on 5,000 units a year; less shipping risk protects sales and revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Veloce Cycles Ltd should set up the assembly plant in Country X? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Setting up assembly would avoid the 25% tariff [k]; parts are not tariffed and building at $175 per bike beats the $187.50 tariffed import cost, saving $12.50 per bike or $62,500 a year on 5,000 bicycles [app], recovering most of the lost margin and independence from the tariff [an]. However, the plant needs $300,000 of equipment [k]; with margins already squeezed and no certainty the tariff will last, the outlay may take years to recover if sales fall [app], straining cash flow in the first year [an]. Overall, Veloce should set up the assembly plant [eval], because $62,500 a year of savings plus freedom from the 25% tariff outweighs the $300,000 one-off cost given steady demand [eval].
    Keywords: $175, $187.50, $62,500, $300,000, $320, 5,000 bicycles, 25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: local assembly avoids tariffs and protects margins; new plants require significant upfront capital investment | application_max_2: $175 assembled cost vs $187.50 tariffed import; $62,500 a year saved; $300,000 equipment against sales of 5,000 bicycles at $320 | analysis_max_2: margin recovery on 5,000 units a year; upfront strain before savings accumulate | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation balancing savings against the one-off cost

Brackendale is deciding whether to buy a $900,000 CNC machine that would cut full cost per valve from $31 to $24, saving $7 per valve, or $420,000 a year. Profit would rise even after the higher tax.   Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the corporation tax rise on Brackendale Precision Ltd.

Reason 2: Higher tax makes boards more cautious about investment [k]; with $95,000 a month of fixed costs, the board may delay the $900,000 machine to preserve cash [app].
    Keywords: 19%, 25%, $95,000 a month, $900,000, $2.64 million, 60,000 valves, $31
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher corporation tax reduces retained profit; higher tax makes investment decisions more cautious | application_max_2: rate rises from 19% to 25% on profits; $95,000 monthly fixed costs and a $900,000 machine under consideration

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of buying the new CNC machine despite the tax rise.

Benefit 2: Lower costs strengthen competitiveness [k]; at $24 full cost Brackendale can defend its $44 selling price against rivals [app] or absorb future cost shocks, protecting its place with industrial buyers [an].
    Keywords: $31, $24, $420,000, 60,000 valves, $44, 25%, $900,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: automation cuts unit costs; lower costs raise profit and competitiveness | application_max_2: full cost falls from $31 to $24, saving $420,000 a year across 60,000 valves; valves sell at $44 generating $2.64 million of revenue | analysis_max_2: the $420,000 saving outweighs the extra 6 percentage points of tax on profit; a cost edge supports pricing against rivals and wins orders

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brackendale Precision Ltd should buy the $900,000 CNC machine? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the machine raises profit despite the tax rise [k]; cutting full cost from $31 to $24 saves $420,000 a year on 60,000 valves, so profit after 25% corporation tax would exceed profit after 19% tax without it, by roughly $268,200 a year [app], creating real value for shareholders [an]. However, the $900,000 price is a heavy strain [k]; with fixed costs of $95,000 a month and only 48 staff, financing the purchase could stretch cash flow if orders soften [app], so the board must be sure of future demand before committing [an]. Overall, Brackendale should buy the machine [eval], because the $420,000 annual saving comfortably outweighs the extra 6 percentage points of corporation tax and secures long-term competitiveness [eval].
    Keywords: $900,000, $420,000, $31, $24, 60,000 valves, 25%, $95,000 a month
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: capital investment can raise profit even after higher corporation tax; large purchases strain cash flow and may need external finance | application_max_2: $420,000 saving from $31 to $24 on 60,000 valves vs $900,000 cost; fixed costs $95,000 a month; profit taxed at 25% instead of 19% | analysis_max_2: after-tax profit comparison favours buying ($900,000 vs $631,800 retained a year); cash-flow risk if orders soften before savings accumulate | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the tax change and the figures

Management is debating whether to cut prices to stimulate demand or to hold prices steady and accept lower sales volumes in the coming trading year.

    Question: Define 'income tax'.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: tax paid by individuals on income/wages/salaries; amount rises as income increases / deducted by the government

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two likely effects of the rise in income tax on Bramble & Rowan Outfitters.
    Answer: Effect 1: Lower disposable income for customers [k], so shoppers at the 5 stores keep less of their pay after tax and buy fewer mid-range casual clothes [app]. Effect 2: Falling sales revenue [k], adding to the 8% drop in footfall already seen this year across the company's stores [app].
    Keywords: Bramble & Rowan, income tax, disposable income, 2,400,000, footfall, 25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: customers have less disposable income / reduced spending power; sales revenue falls / demand declines | application_max_2: 5 stores / mid-range casual clothing; 8% fall in footfall

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways in which the rise in income tax could affect Bramble & Rowan's customers.
    Answer: Way 1: Customers have reduced disposable income [k], so after the basic rate of income tax rises to 25% they keep less of their wages [app], which means non-essential purchases like casual clothing are cut first [an]. Way 2: Customers become more price-sensitive [k], so shoppers compare Bramble & Rowan's mid-range prices against discounters [app], leading some to switch to cheaper stores and reducing the company's sales volumes [an].

  Qd [8 marks]

Overall, cutting prices moderately is the stronger option because footfall has already dropped 8% and the business needs traffic through its stores to protect total profit, even though margins will narrow.
    Keywords: income tax, footfall, 8%, 2,400,000, 42%, 25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: price cut stimulates demand / attracts shoppers; holding prices protects margin / profit per item | application_max_2: 8% fall in footfall; 42% gross profit margin / revenue $2,400,000 | analysis_max_2: lower prices lift volume using the margin cushion; holding prices risks further traffic decline and no volume recovery | evaluation_max_2: weighs price cut against price hold in light of the tax rise; justified recommendation referencing footfall and margin

Kettle & Rye Café is a private limited company operating 3 cafés in Country X. It employs 26 staff and serves around 3,200 customers a week, selling breakfasts, lunches and coffee to commuters and nearby office workers. Management is deciding whether to absorb the extra tax, cutting its profit margin, or to increase menu prices by 4% across the board.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'value added tax'.
    Answer: A tax charged on goods and services at the point of sale, collected by the business and passed on to the government [2].

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two likely effects of the VAT rise on Kettle & Rye Café.

Effect 2: A choice between absorbing or passing on the tax [k], because absorbing it cuts the 55% gross profit margin while raising prices risks losing trade to the two competing cafés [app].
    Keywords: value added tax, 10%, 14%, 3,200, Kettle & Rye, 55%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher tax per sale / VAT collected increases; must absorb the tax or raise prices | application_max_2: VAT rises from 10% to 14%; 3,200 customers a week / 55% gross profit margin

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways in which the VAT rise could affect the café's customers.
    Answer: Way 1: Higher menu prices [k], so if the café adds 4% to prices customers pay more for their average $9 meal [app], reducing real spending power and possibly how often they eat out [an]. Way 2: Switching to competitors [k], as customers may choose the two nearest competing cafés that have not raised prices [app], leaving the café with fewer customers and lower sales [an].
    Keywords: menu prices, average meal, competing cafés, VAT, customers, 14%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher prices / real spending power falls; customers switch to cheaper alternatives | application_max_2: menu prices increased by 4% / average $9 meal; two nearest competing cafés have not raised prices | analysis_max_2: customers cut spending on eating out; café loses customers to rivals, reducing sales

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kettle & Rye Café should absorb the VAT rise rather than increase menu prices? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Absorbing the rise protects customer loyalty [k] because prices stay the same for the 3,200 customers served weekly [app], helping the café avoid losing trade to the two competing cafés that have not raised prices [an]. However, absorbing the tax cuts the 55% gross profit margin [k] and squeezes profit on every meal sold at an average of $9 [app], which could weaken cash flow for the business [an]. On one hand, holding prices steady may win market share while rivals raise prices [eval]; on the other hand, the 4% menu price increase would restore margins if demand stays buoyant [eval]. Overall, absorbing the VAT rise in the short term is the better option, because the café risks losing commuters to rivals and must defend $1,500,000 of annual sales.
    Keywords: absorb, VAT, competing cafés, 55%, 3,200, 1,500,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: absorbing tax protects customer loyalty / prices stable; absorbing tax squeezes profit margin | application_max_2: 3,200 customers a week; 55% gross profit margin / average $9 meal | analysis_max_2: avoids losing trade to competing cafés; weakens cash flow if margins fall | evaluation_max_2: weighs price-hold market share gain against margin loss; justified recommendation referencing competitor behaviour

--- STEM ---
Greyfen Textiles Ltd is a private limited company weaving polyester fabric for garment makers in Country X. It employs 64 weavers on 3 production lines and reported revenue of $2,900,000 last year, supplying fabric to 22 clothing factories across the country and abroad.

The Country X government has introduced a 15% import tariff on fabric imports from abroad. Greyfen imports 70% of its raw fabric and its annual imported fabric bill is $800,000, so the tariff will add $120,000 a year to its production costs. A domestic fabric supplier charges 20% more than the imported price but can deliver within 2 weeks of ordering. Management must decide whether to switch to the domestic supplier or to absorb the tariff cost and keep importing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'import tariff'.
    Answer: A tax placed on goods imported from other countries, paid by the importing business when the goods cross the border [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: tax on imports / imported goods; paid by the importer at the border

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two likely effects of the import tariff on Greyfen Textiles Ltd.
    Answer: Effect 1: Higher production costs [k], as the 15% tariff adds $120,000 a year on top of the $800,000 imported fabric bill [app]. Effect 2: Lower profit margin or higher prices [k], because Greyfen must either absorb the extra $120,000 cost from revenue of $2,900,000 or raise prices for its 22 clothing factory customers [app].
    Keywords: import tariff, 120,000, 800,000, 2,900,000, 70%, Greyfen
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher costs / higher import bill; lower profit margin or higher prices | application_max_2: 15% tariff adds $120,000 a year to the $800,000 fabric bill; revenue of $2,900,000 / 22 clothing factories

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why a government might impose import tariffs.
    Answer: Reason 1: To protect domestic producers [k], for example a Country X fabric supplier would benefit if Greyfen switched from 70% imported fabric to local sources [app], helping domestic firms compete and keeping jobs in the country [an]. Reason 2: To raise government revenue [k], collecting the 15% tariff on Greyfen's $800,000 fabric imports would yield $120,000 a year [app], which the government can spend on public services [an].
    Keywords: import tariff, 15%, 120,000, 800,000, 70%, domestic fabric supplier
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: protect domestic industry / domestic jobs; raise government revenue / public spending | application_max_2: Greyfen switched from 70% imported fabric to local sources; 15% tariff on $800,000 imports yields $120,000 | analysis_max_2: domestic firms become more competitive; tariff revenue funds public services

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Greyfen Textiles should switch to the domestic fabric supplier rather than absorb the tariff? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching to the domestic supplier avoids the $120,000 tariff [k], because domestic fabric priced 20% above imports removes the border tax on $800,000 of fabric [app], and deliveries within 2 weeks improve reliability for its 22 clothing factory customers [an]. However, the domestic price is 20% higher than imports [k], adding around $160,000 a year to the fabric bill [app], which exceeds the $120,000 cost of the tariff [an]. On one hand, absorbing the tariff keeps annual costs $40,000 lower [eval]; on the other hand, domestic sourcing supports Country X jobs and removes import risk [eval]. Overall, absorbing the tariff is the stronger short-term option, because $120,000 a year is cheaper than the domestic premium, but Greyfen should renegotiate with the domestic supplier and review its sourcing next year.
    Keywords: domestic fabric supplier, import tariff, 120,000, 20%, 800,000, 70%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: switching avoids the tariff / domestic delivery is faster; domestic price is 20% higher / tariff is cheaper | application_max_2: $120,000 tariff vs $160,000 domestic premium (20% of $800,000); deliveries within 2 weeks / 22 clothing factories | analysis_max_2: absorbing keeps costs lower by $40,000 a year; domestic sourcing removes import risk and supports local jobs | evaluation_max_2: weighs tariff cost against domestic premium; justified recommendation with review next year

Benefit 2: Increased demand for its services [k], as government infrastructure spending raises orders for civil engineering firms like Coppergate, which already reported $9,000,000 of revenue [app].

However, the bid requires $800,000 of new heavy equipment financed by a bank loan [k], adding repayments that strain cash flow before the contract pays out [app], and execution risk is high if costs overrun or the bid is lost [an]. From next year the subsidy will be cut by half to $45,000, as government spending will shift towards renewable energy projects elsewhere. The owner must decide whether to continue organic production with lower support or to switch to conventional dairy farming instead, which could earn $700,000 a year but requires $150,000 of new milking equipment and fewer staff.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: payment by government to producers; reduces costs / encourages production

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two likely effects of the subsidy cut on Sunhollow Dairy Farm.
    Answer: Effect 1: Reduced income [k], as the subsidy falls by half from $90,000 to $45,000, removing $45,000 of support each year [app]. Effect 2: Lower profitability or pressure to change production [k], because the farm's $620,000 revenue must now cover more of its costs itself [app].
    Keywords: subsidy, 90,000, 45,000, 620,000, Sunhollow, organic milk
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: reduced income / less government support; lower profitability / pressure to change production | application_max_2: subsidy falls from $90,000 to $45,000; $620,000 revenue / 220 dairy cows

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why a government provides subsidies to farmers.
    Answer: Reason 1: To keep food affordable [k], because supporting organic milk production like Sunhollow's helps maintain supply and restrains price rises for consumers [app], stabilising the cost of living [an]. Reason 2: To protect rural employment and the environment [k], since the $90,000 subsidy supports 14 farm workers on Sunhollow and encourages organic, welfare-friendly methods [app], preserving local jobs and sustainable farming [an].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: keep food affordable / secure food supply; protect rural employment / encourage sustainable farming | application_max_2: organic milk production like Sunhollow's; $90,000 subsidy / 14 farm workers | analysis_max_2: stabilises the cost of living; preserves local jobs and sustainable methods

  Qd [8 marks]

    Answer: Continuing organic production preserves the farm's identity [k], keeping the organic milk that generated $620,000 of revenue and maintaining animal welfare standards [app], and retaining loyal customers who pay a premium for organic produce [an]. However, switching to conventional farming could earn $700,000 a year [k], $80,000 more than current organic revenue [app], but it requires $150,000 of new milking equipment and loses the remaining $45,000 subsidy [an]. On one hand, the subsidy cut makes organic production marginal [eval]; on the other hand, switching costs and losing organic buyers create their own risks [eval]. Overall, Sunhollow should continue organic production for now, because the revenue difference is modest relative to $150,000 of new equipment, but it should review the decision if subsidies fall further.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: organic preserves identity / loyal premium customers; switching earns more but needs investment | application_max_2: organic milk generated $620,000 / switching could earn $700,000; $150,000 new milking equipment / $45,000 remaining subsidy | analysis_max_2: loyal customers pay a premium, protecting demand; switching forfeits subsidy and organic buyers | evaluation_max_2: weighs organic margin loss against switching gains; justified recommendation with conditional review

Pennybrook Discount Stores is a private limited company operating 9 discount supermarkets in Country X. Most of its customers have low incomes and live within walking distance of the stores.

The Country X government has announced cuts of 12% to means-tested welfare payments from January, reducing the disposable income of many households on low incomes. The director believes shoppers will trade down from full-price supermarkets to discounters like Pennybrook over the next year. The board is debating whether to open a tenth store in a nearby town or to improve the layout and capacity of its existing nine stores locally.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'disposable income'.
    Answer: The income individuals have left to spend or save after income tax and other deductions have been paid [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: income left after tax/deductions; available to spend or save

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two likely effects of the welfare payment cuts on Pennybrook's customers.
    Answer: Effect 1: Lower disposable income [k], because the 12% cut to means-tested welfare payments leaves low-income households with less money to spend each week [app]. Effect 2: Reduced spending on non-essentials [k], so customers using the $18 average basket focus on essentials and cheaper own-label goods [app].
    Keywords: disposable income, means-tested welfare payments, 18, 12%, Pennybrook, basket value
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: lower disposable income; reduced spending on non-essentials / essentials prioritised | application_max_2: 12% cut to means-tested welfare payments; average basket value of $18

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways in which the benefits cut could affect Pennybrook Discount Stores.
    Answer: Way 1: Increased demand for discount groceries [k], as cash-strapped shoppers trade down from full-price supermarkets to Pennybrook's stores [app], potentially increasing footfall and sales revenue [an]. Way 2: Smaller average basket size [k], because customers with less disposable income may buy fewer items per visit even at discount prices [app], so revenue gains depend on attracting many more customers [an].
    Keywords: trade down, discount, basket value, disposable income, supermarkets, revenue
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: demand for discount groceries rises; average basket size may shrink | application_max_2: shoppers trade down from full-price supermarkets; average basket value of $18 | analysis_max_2: footfall and sales revenue may rise; revenue gains depend on attracting more customers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Pennybrook should open a tenth store rather than improve its existing nine stores? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Opening a tenth store captures the expected wave of trade-down shoppers [k], expanding Pennybrook's reach beyond its current 9 stores and 85 staff [app], and building long-term revenue if the welfare cuts persist [an]. However, a new store requires heavy capital spending [k], and sales per store may fall if the trade-down boom is modest or short-lived [app], while the existing nine stores already serve local low-income communities well [an]. On one hand, improving the nine existing stores costs less and lifts capacity where demand is proven [eval]; on the other hand, a tenth store locks in market share before rivals respond [eval]. Overall, improving the existing nine stores first is the safer option, because demand uplift from the welfare cuts is uncertain, and Pennybrook can invest later once the trading-down trend is clearly visible in the $7,200,000 revenue figures.
    Keywords: tenth store, existing nine stores, 85 staff, 7,200,000, trade down, welfare
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: opening a new store captures trade-down demand; new store requires heavy capital spending | application_max_2: current 9 stores and 85 staff; $7,200,000 revenue / average basket $18 | analysis_max_2: locks in long-term revenue if welfare cuts persist; improving existing stores costs less with proven demand | evaluation_max_2: weighs expansion risk against low-cost capacity upgrade; justified recommendation to improve existing stores first

--- STEM ---
Alderford Kitchens Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 9 years ago, selling and installing fitted kitchens from a showroom and workshop in Redby. It employs 28 staff and generated sales of $3.9 million last year. The business also holds around $1.1 million of showroom stock and unsold fitted units. The average installed kitchen costs $9,400, and around 65% of customers spread the payment over three years using a finance plan arranged by the showroom.

Over the past 12 months, Country X's central bank raised its base rate from 3% to 6% to control inflation of 5.2%. Monthly finance applications fell from 160 to 92, and showroom orders dropped from 200 to 156 last quarter, a fall of 22%. Owner Daniel Reyes must decide how to respond to weakening demand for high-value kitchens.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'interest rate'.
    Answer: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing money or the reward for saving, expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed or saved per year. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interest rate is the cost of borrowing or the reward for saving, expressed as a percentage; Measured on the amount borrowed or saved, usually on an annual basis

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the rise in interest rates has reduced demand for Alderford Kitchens.
    Answer: Reason 1: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive [k]. With the base rate up at 6%, monthly payments on a finance plan for an average $9,400 kitchen have risen, so some customers can no longer afford the repayments and postpone buying [app]. Reason 2: Higher rates increase the reward for saving [k]. With savings now earning more interest, customers prefer to keep their money in the bank rather than commit to a three-year finance plan [app].
    Keywords: $9,400, 3% to 6%, 160 to 92, 65%, $3.9 million, finance plan, $1.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, reducing demand for financed purchases; Higher interest rates increase the incentive to save rather than spend | application_max_2: Base rate raised from 3% to 6%; finance plan for an average $9,400 kitchen; Monthly finance applications fell from 160 to 92

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the fall in orders from 200 to 156 causes for Alderford Kitchens.
    Answer: Problem 1: Lower sales revenue and profit [k]. Orders dropped from 200 to 156 last quarter, a fall of 22%, so fewer kitchens are being sold and income from sales and fitting work has fallen [app], threatening the business's ability to cover fixed costs such as rent and the workshop [an]. Problem 2: Idle staff and wasted capacity [k]. With fewer kitchens to install, the 28 staff across the showroom and workshop in Redby have less work each week [app], so labour costs are spread over fewer jobs and may force the owner to cut hours or make redundancies [an].
    Keywords: 200 to 156, 22%, 28 staff, Redby, $3.9 million, $9,400, $1.1 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower revenue and profit threaten the ability to cover fixed costs; Falling output leaves staff and capacity underused | application_max_2: Orders dropped from 200 to 156 last quarter, a fall of 22%; 28 staff across the showroom and workshop in Redby; $1.1 million of stock | analysis_max_2: Fixed costs spread over fewer kitchens reduce the profit margin and cash flow; Underused labour raises the average cost per kitchen and may force redundancies or shorter hours

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Alderford Kitchens should cut the price of an average kitchen to boost demand? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cutting the price could help win back price-sensitive buyers [k]: showroom orders dropped from 200 to 156 after the base rate rose from 3% to 6% [app], so a 10% price cut might lift volume enough to spread fixed costs over more kitchens and protect the workshop's workload [an]. However, a broad price cut would squeeze profit per kitchen [k]: the average installed kitchen already costs $9,400 and the real barrier is the higher 6% interest on finance plans used by 65% of customers [app], so cheaper prices alone may not restore demand while borrowing stays expensive [an]. Overall [eval], Alderford should avoid a permanent across-the-board price cut and instead offer a time-limited discount or contribution to finance costs [eval], because the fall in orders was driven by borrowing costs rather than the kitchen price itself.
    Keywords: $9,400, 200 to 156, 3% to 6%, 65%, $3.9 million, base rate, finance plan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Price cuts can stimulate demand by improving value for money; Cutting prices reduces the profit margin earned on each unit sold | application_max_2: Orders fell from 200 to 156 after the base rate rose from 3% to 6%; Average installed kitchen costs $9,400; 65% of customers use a finance plan | analysis_max_2: Higher volume after a cut spreads fixed costs over more kitchens, lifting margin per period; If the barrier is finance cost, a price cut does not remove it and margins simply fall | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures before reaching a justified position; Conditional, justified recommendation (time-limited offer, not a permanent cut)

SET ID: P1_U6_SET_122

--- STEM ---
Marne Valley Dairies is a family-run dairy farm in Country X, trading for 14 years. It keeps 85 cows, employs 11 workers and sells milk to a regional processing plant under a supply agreement, earning revenue of $820,000 and a profit of $46,000 last year.

Two years ago the farm borrowed $400,000 from its bank at a variable interest rate of 4% to replace its milking parlour. Since then the central bank has raised the base rate to 7%, so annual interest on the loan has risen from $16,000 to $28,000, an extra $12,000 a year. Milk prices have stayed flat while feed and energy costs have risen. Owner Marta Ellison must decide how to manage the loan now that interest rates are much higher.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate how much more interest the farm pays each year at 7% compared with 4% on its $400,000 loan.
    Answer: At 4% the annual interest is $16,000 and at 7% it is $28,000 [1]; the difference is $28,000 - $16,000 = $12,000 extra a year [1]. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 4% of $400,000 = $16,000 and 7% of $400,000 = $28,000; Difference = $12,000 additional interest per year

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why a rise in interest rates increases the financial pressure on businesses with loans.
    Answer: Reason 1: Higher rates directly raise the cost of borrowing [k]. Marne Valley's annual interest on its $400,000 loan has risen from $16,000 to $28,000, an extra $12,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Higher interest payments reduce profit and cash flow [k]. The farm's profit was only $46,000 last year, so the extra $12,000 removes over a quarter of its profit before tax or reinvestment [app].
    Keywords: $400,000, $16,000, $28,000, $12,000, $46,000, variable interest rate, $820,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interest costs rise when variable rates rise, increasing fixed financial commitments; Higher interest payments reduce profit and cash available for investment | application_max_2: Interest risen from $16,000 to $28,000 on the $400,000 variable-rate loan; Profit of $46,000; the extra $12,000 is over a quarter of annual profit

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Marne Valley Dairies could respond to the extra $12,000 annual interest cost.
    Answer: Way 1: Cut production costs [k]. Feed and energy costs have already risen even though milk prices have stayed flat [app], so the farm could trim waste and renegotiate supplier prices to restore the margin [an]. Way 2: Renegotiate the loan with its bank [k]. The $400,000 outstanding loan could be stretched over a longer repayment period or converted to a fixed rate [app], which spreads the cost more evenly and removes the risk of rates rising again [an].
    Keywords: $400,000, $12,000, $46,000, $820,000, milking parlour, feed and energy, $28,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Reducing costs offsets higher interest without cutting sales; Refinancing or renegotiating can spread repayments or fix the rate | application_max_2: Feed and energy costs have risen while milk prices have stayed flat; Variable-rate loan of $400,000; base rate raised to 7%; interest now $28,000 a year | analysis_max_2: Lower costs rebuild the profit margin absorbed by the extra $12,000; A longer term or fixed rate smooths cash flow and caps future repayments

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Marne Valley Dairies should switch its loan to a fixed rate now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching to a fixed rate would give the farm certainty [k]: at 7.5% the annual interest would be $30,000, only $2,000 more than the $28,000 it pays now [app], so the business can budget with confidence if the base rate rises again [an]. However, a fixed rate removes the benefit if rates fall [k]: if the base rate returns to 4%, the farm would still pay $30,000 instead of $16,000, an extra $14,000 a year [app], which would hurt a farm whose profit is only $46,000 [an]. Overall [eval], with profit so thin and rates already well above the 4% at which the loan was taken, the farm should fix the rate to protect cash flow [eval], accepting a small premium for certainty.
    Keywords: $400,000, $28,000, $16,000, $46,000, variable interest rate, $12,000, milking parlour
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed rate gives certainty of repayments regardless of rate movements; Fixed rate removes the benefit if market interest rates fall | application_max_2: Fixed at 7.5% = $30,000 a year vs $28,000 now, only $2,000 more; If the rate fell back to 4% the farm would pay $14,000 a year extra; profit only $46,000 | analysis_max_2: Certainty helps budgeting and protects against further rises; Being locked into a high fixed rate wastes money if rates fall | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures before deciding; Reaches a justified, qualified recommendation (fix to protect thin profit and cash flow)

UNIT: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

--- STEM ---
Harbury Carpets is an independent carpet and flooring retailer in Country X, trading for 11 years from two high-street stores. It employs 19 trained staff, and last year it sold carpets worth $2.7 million, up from $2.35 million the year before. The average fitted carpet costs $1,850, including underlay and fitting.

Nine months ago the central bank cut its base rate from 6% to 4% to boost consumer spending, and the government hopes the cut will restore confidence after a slow year. Since then, applications from customers wanting to spread the cost with finance have risen by 35%, and Harbury's weekly takings have increased by 15%. Owner Sophie Aldana is considering hiring five more sales assistants and increasing stock levels to meet expected demand.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'base rate'.
    Answer: The base rate is the interest rate set by a country's central bank, which influences the cost of borrowing and the return on savings across the whole economy. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interest rate set by the central bank; Influences other borrowing and saving interest rates in the economy

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the cut in interest rates has increased demand for Harbury Carpets.
    Answer: Reason 1: Cheaper finance makes spreading the cost more affordable [k]. Applications from customers wanting to spread the cost with finance have risen by 35% since the base rate was cut from 6% to 4% [app]. Reason 2: Lower borrowing costs leave households with more disposable income [k]. Weekly takings have increased by 15% and sales rose to $2.7 million from $2.35 million [app].
    Keywords: 6% to 4%, 35%, 15%, $2.7 million, $2.35 million, $1,850, base rate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower interest rates reduce the cost of finance and loans; Lower borrowing costs increase households' disposable income | application_max_2: Finance applications up 35% after the base rate cut from 6% to 4%; Weekly takings up 15%; sales of $2.7 million vs $2.35 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Harbury Carpets of the recent rise in demand.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Higher sales revenue [k]. Sales rose from $2.35 million to $2.7 million last year, an increase of about $350,000 [app], which gives the business more cash to reinvest, stock up or hire staff [an]. Benefit 2: Fixed costs are spread over more output [k]. Selling carpets costing $1,850 each from two high-street stores spreads rent, wages and display costs over more units [app], so the profit margin on each carpet rises as volume grows [an].
    Keywords: $2.7 million, $2.35 million, $1,850, two high-street stores, 19 trained staff, 35%, Harbury Carpets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher sales revenue improves cash flow and profit; Higher output spreads fixed costs, raising the profit margin | application_max_2: Sales rose from $2.35 million to $2.7 million, about $350,000 more; Two high-street stores; average fitted carpet $1,850; 19 trained staff | analysis_max_2: Extra revenue can be reinvested in stock or hiring to sustain growth; Fixed costs shared over more carpets raise the profit earned per sale

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Harbury Carpets should hire five more sales assistants now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Hiring five more sales assistants would help the business cope with buoyant demand [k]: takings rose 15% and finance applications jumped 35% after the base rate was cut from 6% to 4% [app], so extra staff can serve the two stores properly, protect service quality and convert more enquiries into sales [an]. However, the recovery may not last [k]: takings grew from $2.35 million to $2.7 million, but demand could fall back if the central bank reverses the cut, leaving the business paying five more salaries [app], so costs would rise faster than sales and profit would fall [an]. Overall [eval], with demand up 15% and two busy stores, hiring part-time assistants first is justified [eval], but Sophie Aldana should review staffing monthly in case the base rate is raised again.
    Keywords: $2.7 million, 6% to 4%, 35%, 15%, $1,850, two high-street stores, $2.35 million, five more sales assistants
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Matching labour capacity to demand supports service and sales conversion; Adding fixed wages raises costs if demand falls back | application_max_2: Takings up 15% and finance applications up 35% after the base rate cut from 6% to 4%; Sales rose from $2.35 million to $2.7 million; two high-street stores; $1,850 average carpet | analysis_max_2: Extra staff convert enquiries into sales and maintain customer service; If rates rise again, idle staff inflate wage costs and erode profit | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures and reaches a justified position; Conditional recommendation (hire, ideally part-time first, review monthly)

SET ID: P1_U6_SET_124
UNIT: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

--- STEM ---
Caldermoor Crane Hire Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, operating for 8 years hiring tower cranes and mobile cranes to building firms. It employs 24 staff, including 6 crane operators, and earned $3.1 million in revenue last year.

The company needs to borrow $600,000 to buy two new tower cranes. Its bank offers either a fixed rate of 7.5% for five years, costing $45,000 interest each year, or a variable rate, currently 6% ($36,000 a year), which could rise or fall. The base rate has moved from 5% to 6.5% over the past year, and the central bank has warned that further increases remain possible. Directors must choose between the fixed and variable loans before signing the crane purchase order.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'fixed rate'.
    Answer: A fixed rate is an interest rate that stays the same for an agreed period of time, so the borrower's repayments do not change even if other interest rates move. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Interest rate held constant for an agreed period; Repayments remain unchanged regardless of market rate movements

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons Caldermoor Crane Hire Ltd may prefer the fixed-rate loan.
    Answer: Reason 1: Certainty of repayments [k]. At 7.5% the company would pay $45,000 interest each year for five years, a known cost it can budget for regardless of rate movements [app]. Reason 2: Protection against further rate rises [k]. The base rate has moved from 5% to 6.5% over the past year, and the central bank has warned more increases are possible, so fixing now caps the company's exposure [app].
    Keywords: fixed rate of 7.5%, $45,000, $600,000, 5% to 6.5%, $36,000, $3.1 million, two new tower cranes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed rate gives certainty of interest costs for planning; Fixed rate protects against future rises in market interest rates | application_max_2: $45,000 interest each year for five years at a fixed rate of 7.5%; Base rate moved from 5% to 6.5% this year; further increases possible

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Caldermoor Crane Hire Ltd could reduce the financial risk of the $600,000 loan.
    Answer: Way 1: Choose the fixed option [k]. Paying $45,000 a year is $9,000 more than the current variable cost of $36,000, but it caps the maximum the company will pay [app], removing the risk of repayments climbing if the base rate rises again [an]. Way 2: Fund part of the purchase from retained profit [k]. Revenue last year was $3.1 million, so saving a deposit towards the two cranes would shrink the amount borrowed [app], which lowers the total interest bill whatever rate is charged [an].
    Keywords: $600,000, $45,000, $36,000, $3.1 million, two new tower cranes, fixed rate, variable rate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed rate caps exposure to future interest rate rises; Part-funding from retained profit reduces the amount borrowed | application_max_2: $45,000 fixed vs $36,000 variable now, a $9,000 annual premium; Revenue of $3.1 million last year; two new tower cranes needing $600,000 | analysis_max_2: Paying a small premium eliminates the risk of much higher repayments later; A smaller principal means lower total interest paid and lower risk

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Caldermoor Crane Hire Ltd should choose the fixed-rate loan at 7.5% rather than the variable-rate loan at 6%? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Choosing the fixed rate gives Caldermoor certainty [k]: the company would pay $45,000 each year regardless of movements, and the base rate has already climbed from 5% to 6.5% with more increases warned [app], so fixing protects a business with $3.1 million revenue from surprise repayment rises on the $600,000 loan [an]. However, the fixed option costs $9,000 more each year right now [k]: at 6% the variable loan costs just $36,000, and if the base rate stabilises or falls the company would overpay for five years [app], draining cash that could fund crane maintenance or marketing [an]. Overall [eval], with rates rising and the central bank warning of further increases, the fixed loan is the safer choice [eval], provided the extra $9,000 a year does not push cash flow below the level needed to run 24 staff and service the cranes.
    Keywords: $600,000, fixed rate of 7.5%, $45,000, $36,000, 5% to 6.5%, $3.1 million, variable rate, two new tower cranes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixed rate removes repayment uncertainty; Variable rate is cheaper initially but can rise unpredictably | application_max_2: $45,000 per year fixed vs $36,000 per year variable (a $9,000 difference); Base rate moved from 5% to 6.5% with further increases possible; loan of $600,000 | analysis_max_2: Certainty protects cash flow and supports budgeting and planning; Overpaying $9,000 a year if rates fall wastes money that could fund operations | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures; Justified recommendation with a cash-flow proviso, not a one-sided answer
