--- STEM ---
Alcott Windows Ltd is a double-glazing and window installer based in Country X, operating for 12 years. It employs 22 staff and generated $2.6 million in revenue last year, installing windows, doors and roofline products for homes and small offices across the region. The business holds $400,000 of window and door stock in its warehouse.

The central bank has raised its base rate from 3.5% to 6.5% over 9 months. Around 75% of Alcott's customers pay by finance plan, and installations have fallen from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%. The workshop is running at half its usual capacity. Staff fear job losses, and owner Luis Cabrera must decide how to respond to falling orders and rising finance costs before the summer peak.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'mortgage'.
    Answer: A mortgage is a long-term loan used to buy property such as a house or flat, repaid with interest over many years and usually secured against the property itself. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Long-term loan used to purchase property; Repaid with interest over many years, typically secured on the property

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why higher interest rates have reduced demand for Alcott Windows.
    Answer: Reason 1: Finance to spread the cost of windows is now more expensive [k]. Around 75% of Alcott's customers pay by finance plan, and with the base rate up at 6.5% the monthly repayments on new orders have risen [app]. Reason 2: Higher rates leave households with less disposable income [k]. Homeowners face bigger mortgage repayments, so installations have fallen from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30% [app].
    Keywords: 3.5% to 6.5%, 75%, 120 to 84, 30%, $2.6 million, $400,000, finance plan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates increase the cost of finance plans; Higher rates raise mortgage costs, reducing disposable income | application_max_2: 75% of customers pay by finance plan; base rate raised to 6.5%; Installations fell from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the fall from 120 to 84 installations a quarter causes Alcott Windows.
    Answer: Problem 1: Lower revenue and profit [k]. A drop of 30% means far fewer windows sold each quarter [app], so fixed costs such as warehouse rent and the interest on $400,000 of stock are spread over fewer jobs, squeezing margins [an]. Problem 2: Under-used labour and capacity [k]. The workshop is running at half its usual capacity, with 22 staff and much of the $400,000 stock sitting unsold [app], so the business may be forced to cut hours or make installers redundant [an].
    Keywords: 120 to 84, 30%, $400,000, 22 staff, half its usual capacity, $2.6 million, finance plan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Falling orders reduce revenue and profit; Falling output leaves labour and stock underutilised | application_max_2: Installations fell from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%; $400,000 of stock; workshop at half its usual capacity; 22 staff | analysis_max_2: Fewer sales spread fixed costs over less output, squeezing the profit margin; Idle capacity pressures the business into wage cuts or redundancy

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Alcott Windows should cut prices by 10% to win back orders? Justify your answer.
    Answer: A 10% price cut could win back price-sensitive customers [k]: installations have fallen from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%, so a discount might persuade cautious homeowners to proceed before the summer peak [app], lifting volume enough to cover fixed warehouse costs on $400,000 of stock [an]. However, the real barrier is the 6.5% base rate, not the price [k]: around 75% of Alcott's customers pay by finance plan, so higher monthly repayments are stopping purchases, not the quoted price [app], meaning a blanket 10% cut would simply reduce margin on the 84 orders still coming in [an]. Overall [eval], Alcott should offer a targeted discount or contribution to finance costs on finance-plan sales rather than a blanket 10% cut [eval], because the demand fall is driven by borrowing costs rather than the headline price.
    Keywords: 120 to 84, 30%, 75%, 3.5% to 6.5%, $2.6 million, $400,000, finance plan, half its usual capacity
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Price cuts can attract price-sensitive customers; Demand driven by borrowing cost is not resolved by price cuts | application_max_2: Installations fell from 120 to 84 per quarter, a drop of 30%; 75% of customers pay by finance plan; base rate raised from 3.5% to 6.5% | analysis_max_2: A discount could lift volume enough to cover fixed costs; Margins on remaining orders fall without fixing the real barrier | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures; Justified, conditional recommendation (targeted offer, not a blanket cut)

--- STEM ---
Elmcrest Farm Machinery is a tractor and combine dealer in rural Country X, trading for 15 years and supplying an area of about 4,000 square kilometres. It employs 17 staff, sells new and used machines and provides servicing, parts and breakdown cover, earning revenue of $5.4 million last year.

New tractor sales, usually around 120 a year at an average price of $48,000, have fallen to 66 this year after the central bank raised its base rate from 4% to 7%. Most farmers finance purchases with bank loans. To fund showroom stock the dealer uses a $500,000 overdraft, and overdraft interest has risen from 6% to 9%, costing an extra $15,000 a year. Several farmers have asked to defer orders until rates fall.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'overdraft'.
    Answer: An overdraft is a bank facility that lets a business withdraw more money from its current account than it holds, up to an agreed limit and repaid with interest. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Facility allowing withdrawal beyond the account balance up to an agreed limit; Repayable with interest, often on demand

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why farmers may postpone buying new tractors when interest rates rise.
    Answer: Reason 1: Loans to buy tractors become more expensive [k]. Most farmers finance purchases with bank loans, and with the base rate up from 4% to 7% the interest on financing a $48,000 tractor has jumped sharply [app]. Reason 2: Farmers are uncertain about future income while rates are high [k]. Tractor sales fell from 120 a year to 66 this year, showing farmers are delaying major capital purchases [app].
    Keywords: 4% to 7%, $48,000, 120 a year, 66 this year, $5.4 million, bank loans, $500,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher interest increases the cost of finance for capital purchases; Uncertainty and low confidence make buyers delay major investments | application_max_2: Base rate raised from 4% to 7%; average tractor price $48,000; New tractor sales fell from 120 a year to 66 this year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Elmcrest Farm Machinery could reduce the cost of holding stock.
    Answer: Way 1: Reduce showroom stock and order to demand [k]. With sales down to 66 from 120 a year, fewer machines are needed on the forecourt [app], so the dealer can shrink its $500,000 overdraft and cut the interest it pays [an]. Way 2: Renegotiate the overdraft with its bank [k]. Overdraft interest has risen from 6% to 9%, costing an extra $15,000 a year [app], so even a 1% reduction in the margin would save $5,000 a year [an].
    Keywords: $500,000, 6% to 9%, $15,000, 66 this year, $5.4 million, overdraft, 120 a year
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower stock levels reduce financing needs and interest costs; Renegotiating bank facilities can cut interest margins | application_max_2: Sales fell from 120 a year to 66; overdraft of $500,000; Overdraft interest rose from 6% to 9%, an extra $15,000 a year ($30,000 to $45,000) | analysis_max_2: Less stock directly reduces the overdraft and its interest charge; Even a 1% lower margin yields $5,000 a year and frees working capital

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Elmcrest Farm Machinery should offer a promotional discount on new tractors to clear stock? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Offering a time-limited discount could clear slow-moving stock [k]: sales fell from 120 a year to 66 this year after the base rate was raised from 4% to 7% [app], so discounting machines would reduce the $500,000 overdraft and the extra $15,000 a year of interest now being paid [an]. However, discounting cuts the margin on each $48,000 tractor and may train buyers to wait for promotions [k]: farmers have already asked to defer orders until rates fall, so a discount might simply shift sales forward rather than create new demand [app], reducing revenue of $5.4 million and further eroding profit [an]. Overall [eval], a modest, time-limited promotional discount is justified [eval], because cutting stock and overdraft interest is worth more than defending the full margin while interest rates remain high.
    Keywords: 120 a year, 66 this year, 4% to 7%, $500,000, $15,000, $48,000, $5.4 million, 6% to 9%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Promotions stimulate demand and clear excess stock; Discounting reduces margin and can train customers to wait for deals | application_max_2: Sales fell from 120 a year to 66 after the base rate was raised from 4% to 7%; $500,000 overdraft; interest rose from 6% to 9%, an extra $15,000 a year | analysis_max_2: Lower stock cuts overdraft interest and frees working capital; Lower margins and wait-for-discount behaviour reduce profit | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures; Justified recommendation (modest, time-limited promotional discount)

PAPER: Paper 1
SET ID: P1_U6_SET_127
UNIT: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
====================================================================================================

--- STEM ---
Rowanbrook Ice Cream Co is a private limited company in Country X producing premium ice cream, founded 6 years ago. It employs 34 staff and generated $2.8 million in sales last year, exporting some of its output to two neighbouring countries. Demand has been strong as the economy grows by 4.5% a year.

Inflation has reached 6.5%, well above the government target of 2%, so the central bank raised its base rate from 3% to 6% to cool spending. The company is profitable and carries no debt apart from the planned loan. Rowanbrook wants to build a $900,000 factory extension funded by a bank loan, costing $54,000 in annual interest at 6% and creating 26 new production jobs. Owner Elena Marsh must decide whether to proceed now or wait until rates fall.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'boom'.
    Answer: A boom is a phase of the business cycle in which the economy is growing rapidly, with high consumer spending, low unemployment and rising incomes and output. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Phase of the business cycle with rapid economic growth; High spending, low unemployment and rising incomes/output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the central bank may raise interest rates during a boom.
    Answer: Reason 1: To control inflation [k]. Inflation has reached 6.5%, well above the government target of 2%, so higher interest rates should cool spending and slow price rises [app]. Reason 2: To reduce excessive borrowing [k]. The economy is growing at 4.5% a year and the base rate was raised from 3% to 6%, so higher rates discourage households and businesses from taking on more debt [app].
    Keywords: 6.5%, 2%, 4.5%, 3% to 6%, $2.8 million, $900,000, base rate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Raise rates to bring inflation back towards its target; Raise rates to curb excessive borrowing and credit growth | application_max_2: Inflation at 6.5% compared with the 2% target; Economy growing at 4.5% a year; base rate raised from 3% to 6%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Rowanbrook Ice Cream Co of the current boom.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Strong sales demand supports growth [k]. The economy is growing by 4.5% a year and Rowanbrook generated $2.8 million in sales last year, exporting some of its output to two neighbouring countries [app], so demand may support the planned factory extension [an]. Benefit 2: Profits can partly fund expansion [k]. The company is profitable and carries no debt apart from the planned loan [app], so it can use retained profit to cover part of the $900,000 cost and borrow less [an].
    Keywords: 4.5%, $2.8 million, $900,000, $54,000, two neighbouring countries, 6%, 26 new production jobs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Strong consumer demand lifts sales and output; Healthy profits and cash flow enable self-financing of investment | application_max_2: Economy growing at 4.5% a year; sales of $2.8 million; exports to two neighbouring countries; Profitable business with no debt apart from the planned loan for the $900,000 extension | analysis_max_2: Strong demand supports the case for extra capacity; Retained profit cuts the amount borrowed and the interest bill

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rowanbrook Ice Cream Co should proceed with the $900,000 factory extension now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Proceeding would capture strong demand at the right time [k]: the economy is growing at 4.5% a year and Rowanbrook sold $2.8 million of ice cream last year [app], so extra capacity would lift output and spread fixed costs, raising the profit on each tub [an]. However, borrowing now is expensive [k]: the base rate was raised from 3% to 6% to cool inflation of 6.5%, and the loan would cost $54,000 a year in interest [app], so if the boom cools the new factory may run below capacity while the interest still has to be paid [an]. Overall [eval], the extension is justified if Rowanbrook fixes the loan rate before it rises further [eval], since strong demand, profitability and no existing debt give the business scope to service the repayments; it should delay only if orders soften before the 26 new jobs are hired.
    Keywords: 4.5%, $2.8 million, $900,000, $54,000, 3% to 6%, 6.5%, 26 new production jobs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Investing in capacity during strong demand maximises returns; Borrowing at higher rates increases fixed financial commitments | application_max_2: Economy growing at 4.5% a year; sales of $2.8 million; extension costing $900,000; Base rate raised from 3% to 6%; loan costing $54,000 a year in interest at 6% | analysis_max_2: Extra capacity spreads fixed costs and lifts output and profit; If demand cools, fixed interest must still be paid on below-capacity output | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures; Conditional, justified recommendation (proceed with a fixed rate, delay if orders soften)

--- STEM ---
Fernwood Café Ltd is a small café in Marrowgate, Country X, trading for 7 years. It employs 12 staff and serves office workers, market shoppers and families, and it is busiest at lunchtimes and weekends. Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over the last 18 months after two local factories closed with the loss of 240 jobs.

Local unemployment has risen from 4% to 9%, and the central bank cut its base rate from 6% to 3.5% to encourage spending and borrowing. Footfall remains weak despite cheaper credit, and the meal deals introduced in January had little effect. Owner Priya Nandakumar is considering a $150,000 second outlet in a neighbouring town, or staying with one site and trimming staff hours, and she fears opening now could magnify losses.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'recession'.
    Answer: A recession is a phase of the business cycle in which economic activity falls, usually shown by two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth, with rising unemployment and falling consumer spending. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Period of falling economic output/negative GDP growth; Rising unemployment and weak consumer spending

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the cut in interest rates from 6% to 3.5% could help Fernwood Café.
    Answer: Reason 1: Customers can afford to borrow and spend more [k]. Lower rates reduce the cost of personal loans and overdrafts, so office workers and families may return to the café at lunchtimes and weekends [app]. Reason 2: The café could finance a second outlet more cheaply [k]. With the base rate cut to 3.5%, a loan for the $150,000 neighbouring-town outlet would carry much lower interest [app].
    Keywords: 6% to 3.5%, $150,000, $420,000, $330,000, 240 jobs, Marrowgate, 12 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower rates increase disposable income and the incentive to spend; Lower rates reduce the cost of business borrowing | application_max_2: Base rate cut from 6% to 3.5%; café serves office workers and families; A second outlet costing $150,000 in a neighbouring town

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Fernwood Café may still struggle despite cheaper credit.
    Answer: Reason 1: Consumer confidence is low and unemployment is high [k]. Local unemployment has risen from 4% to 9% after two local factories closed with the loss of 240 jobs [app], so even cheap credit may not persuade cautious households to eat out [an]. Reason 2: The café's revenue has already collapsed [k]. Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over the last 18 months [app], so fixed costs such as rent and the wages of 12 staff are spread over far fewer customers, squeezing profit [an].
    Keywords: 4% to 9%, 240 jobs, $420,000, $330,000, 12 staff, 6% to 3.5%, Marrowgate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Low confidence and high unemployment suppress spending regardless of rates; Falling revenue against unchanged fixed costs erodes profit | application_max_2: Unemployment rose from 4% to 9%; two factories closed with 240 jobs lost; Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over 18 months; 12 staff | analysis_max_2: Fearful households save rather than spend, so the rate cut has limited effect; Fixed costs spread over fewer sales reduce margin and risk losses

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fernwood Café should open the second outlet now? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Opening now would give Fernwood a foothold in a neighbouring town before the market recovers [k]: a loan at the cut base rate of 3.5% would be relatively cheap for the $150,000 cost [app], and capturing customers early could help rebuild revenue towards the $420,000 it earned before the closures [an]. However, the café is already weakened by the recession [k]: revenue has fallen from $420,000 to $330,000 and local unemployment has risen to 9% with 240 jobs lost in two factory closures [app], so taking on $150,000 of new commitments while one site struggles could magnify losses and threaten the original café [an]. Overall [eval], Fernwood should wait rather than open now [eval], because opening in a recession with weak footfall and collapsed revenue risks compounding losses; it should hold the $150,000 and focus on restoring sales at the existing site.
    Keywords: $150,000, 6% to 3.5%, $420,000, $330,000, 240 jobs, 9%, Marrowgate
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Early expansion can secure a new market when credit is cheap; Expanding while loss-making multiplies financial risk | application_max_2: Base rate cut from 6% to 3.5%; second outlet costing $150,000; Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000; unemployment rose to 9%; 240 jobs lost | analysis_max_2: Early mover advantage could rebuild revenue towards pre-closure levels; New fixed commitments in a downturn magnify losses at the existing site | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures; Clear, justified recommendation (wait; restore the existing site first)

--- STEM ---
Corvale Deliveries Ltd is a regional parcel and grocery delivery firm in Country X, trading for 10 years. It employs 29 staff and serves over 300 business customers, running a fleet of 8 diesel vans bought three years ago with a $240,000 bank loan secured against the vehicles. Revenue was $1.9 million last year.

The base rate has risen from 3% to 6%, so annual interest on the van loan has risen from $7,200 to $14,400, an extra $7,200 a year. Inflation has reached 7%, pushing diesel and wage costs higher, and the fuel bill rose by $38,000 last year. Customers resist surcharges. Owner Aaron Bell must decide whether to raise delivery prices by 8% across all contracts or absorb the extra costs and cut other expenses.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'inflation'.
    Answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services, which reduces the purchasing power of money over time. [2]
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in the general price level; Reduces the purchasing power of money (each unit buys less)

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems rising inflation causes for Corvale Deliveries.
    Answer: Reason 1: Diesel and wage costs rise faster than revenue [k]. Inflation has reached 7%, the fuel bill rose by $38,000 last year, and wages must keep pace to retain the firm's 29 staff [app]. Reason 2: Pressure on margins because customers resist surcharges [k]. Interest on the $240,000 van loan is also up $7,200 a year after the base rate rose from 3% to 6%, so the gap between costs and revenue keeps widening [app].
    Keywords: 7%, $38,000, $7,200, 3% to 6%, $240,000, $1.9 million, $14,400
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises input costs such as fuel and wages; Inflation forces higher prices or squeezes profit margins | application_max_2: Inflation at 7%; fuel bill rose by $38,000; 29 staff; Interest on the $240,000 van loan up $7,200 a year after the base rate rose from 3% to 6%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways Corvale Deliveries could respond to its rising costs.
    Answer: Way 1: Raise delivery prices to customers [k]. An 8% increase across all contracts would recover some of the extra $7,200 a year of interest and the $38,000 fuel increase [app], though the firm risks losing rounds to cheaper rivals [an]. Way 2: Improve route efficiency and cut empty miles [k]. Combining parcel routes across its 300-plus business customers would cut diesel use per drop [app], lowering costs without raising prices [an].
    Keywords: 8%, $7,200, $38,000, $240,000, 300 business customers, 8 diesel vans, 29 staff
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Passing costs on through higher prices restores margin; Efficiency improvements reduce cost per unit delivered | application_max_2: Proposed 8% increase across all contracts; extra $7,200 interest; $38,000 fuel rise; 300-plus business customers; 8 diesel vans; 29 staff | analysis_max_2: Higher prices recover costs but risk losing contracts to rivals; Better route planning cuts fuel burn, protecting margin without price rises

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Corvale Deliveries should raise its delivery prices by 8% across all contracts? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising prices would protect the firm's margin [k]: inflation has reached 7%, the fuel bill rose by $38,000 last year and interest on the $240,000 van loan is up $7,200 a year [app], so an 8% rise across all contracts would broadly recover these quantified extra costs [an]. However, a flat 8% rise risks losing price-sensitive contracts [k]: customers resist surcharges and rivals that hold prices could win the firm's rounds [app], so Corvale could lose more revenue than it recovers [an]. Overall [eval], Corvale should raise prices by a smaller, cost-linked amount rather than a flat 8%, or add a transparent fuel surcharge [eval], because recovering proven cost increases is fairer and less likely to drive away the 300-plus business customers it serves.
    Keywords: 7%, $38,000, $7,200, $240,000, $1.9 million, $14,400, 8 diesel vans
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher prices recover rising input costs; Flat across-the-board rises risk driving customers to rivals | application_max_2: Inflation at 7%; fuel bill up $38,000; interest up $7,200 on the $240,000 loan; Customers resist surcharges; 8% proposed across all contracts | analysis_max_2: An 8% rise broadly offsets the quantified cost increases; Losing contracts could outweigh the recovered costs | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures; Justified, qualified recommendation (smaller cost-linked rise or fuel surcharge)

  Qb [4 marks]

Eldercombe's sales fell from $3.4 million in the boom year to $2.6 million in the slump, so producing at full capacity would create unsold stock and waste [app]. Reason 2: Falling profits force cost-cutting [k]. Profit dropped to $120,000 in the slump, so reducing staff hours and output was necessary to avoid losses [app].

Benefit 2: Cheaper borrowing for expansion [k]. The base rate was cut from 6% to 3% [app], so financing even part of the $350,000 moulding-line expansion would cost less interest than before [an].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Recovery increases consumer and retailer demand; Lower base rates reduce the cost of borrowing | application_max_2: Economy growing at 2.8% a year; Christmas accounts for 55% of sales; retailers rebuilding stock; Base rate cut from 6% to 3%; expansion costing $350,000 | analysis_max_2: Higher demand spreads fixed costs and lifts output and profit; Cheaper credit reduces the interest cost of the expansion and improves returns

  Qd [8 marks]

Brackenbury Fashions Ltd is a private limited company in Country X employing 46 staff across 3 high-street stores, selling mid-priced womenswear. Last year Country X's economy shrank by 2.1%, unemployment rose from 5.2% to 8.6% and the consumer confidence index fell from 105 to 78. Brackenbury's annual sales dropped 18% to $1.86 million as fewer shoppers entered its stores and average basket values fell. Footfall fell 22% over the same 12 months.

The directors are choosing between launching a budget 'Essentials' range priced 30% below current lines to win cautious shoppers, or holding prices and trimming 8 staff through redundancy to protect margins.   Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'recession'.
    Answer: A period of at least two consecutive quarters of falling GDP, when economic output and spending decline [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: falling GDP for two or more consecutive quarters; a period of declining economic activity and output

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Brackenbury's sales fell when Country X's economy shrank.

Reason 2: Falling consumer confidence makes people delay non-essential purchases [k], and with the confidence index down from 105 to 78, shoppers cut basket values and footfall fell 22% [app].
    Keywords: 18% to $1.86 million, 5.2% to 8.6%, 105 to 78, 22%, mid-priced womenswear, $1.86 million, high-street stores
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: unemployment reduces disposable income and spending power; falling consumer confidence makes households delay non-essential purchases | application_max_2: sales dropped 18% to $1.86 million at the 3 high-street stores; confidence index fell from 105 to 78 and footfall fell 22%

  Qc [6 marks]

    Keywords: Essentials, 30% below current lines, 8.6%, 105 to 78, 22%, 3 high-street stores, $1.86 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a budget range attracts price-sensitive customers and widens the customer base; lower prices can lift sales volume and capacity use | application_max_2: unemployment rose to 8.6% and confidence fell to 78, so shoppers traded down; Essentials priced 30% below current lines targets the 22% footfall lost | analysis_max_2: recovering lost footfall restores revenue towards previous levels; higher volume per store improves capacity utilisation and spreads fixed costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brackenbury Fashions should launch the 'Essentials' range rather than trim 8 staff through redundancy? Justify your answer.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a budget range targets price-sensitive shoppers when confidence falls; redundancy cuts wage costs quickly but removes capacity and can harm morale | application_max_2: Essentials priced 30% below current lines, ready in 4 months, targets the post-2.1%-shrinkage market; sales already down 18% to $1.86 million; 8 staff cut to 38 protects margins | analysis_max_2: range option recovers revenue but risks cannibalising mid-priced lines; redundancy option limits losses but weakens the ability to serve recovering demand | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the confidence index of 78 and the 22% footfall loss; recommendation consistent with protecting long-term brand strength over short-term cost cuts

Pennyroyal Café is an independent café in Country X employing 14 staff and serving breakfast, brunch and lunch, founded 5 years ago. Country X's GDP grew by 4.2% last year, unemployment fell to 3.8% and restaurant spending has risen 11% over 2 years.   Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why Pennyroyal's revenue grew during the economic boom.

Benefit 2: Two venues share customer goodwill and catering costs [k], and with 55 customers seated the $240,000 build cost can be spread across higher combined volume [app], improving overall profit margins [an].
    Keywords: retail park, $240,000, 55 customers, 3 km, $86,000, 40 seats, 25 minutes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a new location reaches new customers and widens the catchment; expansion spreads fixed costs and shared resources across sites | application_max_2: retail park near a growing industrial estate, 3 km from the current site; new site seating 55 customers for $240,000 versus refitting 40 seats | analysis_max_2: higher combined volume lifts total revenue above $86,000 a month; fixed costs spread over two sites improve margins if demand holds

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Pennyroyal Café should open the retail park café rather than extend the current site? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Opening the retail park site would capture the boom at its peak [k]; with GDP up 4.2%, unemployment at 3.8% and restaurant spending up 11%, a café seating 55 customers near the industrial estate could reach a new market while the original site keeps the loyal crowd causing 25-minute weekend waits [app], so revenue could grow well past $86,000 a month [an]. However, extending the current site by refitting 40 seats is cheaper and less risky [k]; it costs far less than $240,000 and keeps one 14-person team focused on one location [app], so profit per café rises without duplicated management or split oversight while the boom lasts [an]. Overall, Pennyroyal should open the retail park café [eval], because demand fundamentals (GDP +4.2%, confidence at its highest for a decade) support two locations, and waiting 8 weeks risks losing the lease to a rival [eval].
    Keywords: retail park, $240,000, 55 customers, 4.2%, 3.8%, 11%, $86,000, 25 minutes, 40 seats
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: opening a second site captures new markets during rapid growth; extending the existing site is cheaper and keeps management simple | application_max_2: $240,000 new site seating 55 customers near a growing industrial estate; current site refit of 40 seats; weekend waits of 25 minutes at $86,000 monthly revenue | analysis_max_2: two-site revenue growth and capacity relief versus $240,000 outlay and execution risk; single-site efficiency and lower risk versus missing the retail park lease deadline | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the 8-week lease deadline and boom-stage demand; recommendation links back to confidence at its highest for a decade

Calder Vale Motors is a franchised car dealership in Country X employing 38 staff at a ring-road site. Country X's economy has contracted for 3 consecutive quarters, unemployment has risen to 9.4% and consumer confidence has fallen to its lowest in 12 years. Car sales at Calder Vale dropped 24% last year to 610 vehicles, and the used-car forecourt is ageing, with 140 cars unsold for over 60 days. New-car showroom visits are down 30% year on year.

The dealer principal must choose between a 'Sale Days' promotion offering 8% discounts and free 2-year servicing to clear stock, or cutting forecourt costs by making 5 sales staff redundant and reducing marketing spend by 40%. Rivals have cut prices by up to 10%. The decision is due before quarter end, in 5 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'consumer confidence'.
    Answer: A measure of how optimistic households feel about the economy, influencing their willingness to spend, especially on big-ticket items [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a measure of household optimism about the economy; confidence influences willingness to spend, especially on major purchases

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why car sales fell at Calder Vale.
    Answer: Reason 1: Low consumer confidence makes buyers postpone major purchases [k], and with confidence at its lowest in 12 years, new-car showroom visits fell 30% and sales dropped 24% to 610 vehicles [app]. Reason 2: Rising unemployment reduces disposable income [k], and at 9.4% unemployment many households delay replacing cars, leaving 140 cars unsold for over 60 days [app].
    Keywords: 9.4%, 12 years, 24%, 610 vehicles, 140 cars, 30%, 60 days, 3 consecutive quarters
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: low confidence makes households delay big-ticket purchases; rising unemployment reduces disposable income available for car purchases | application_max_2: confidence at its lowest in 12 years; showroom visits down 30% and sales down 24% to 610; unemployment at 9.4%; 140 used cars unsold for over 60 days

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Calder Vale of making 5 sales staff redundant.
    Answer: Problem 1: Redundancy cuts sales capacity [k], and with 38 staff already stretched and 610 vehicles to shift, losing 5 experienced salespeople leaves fewer people to close deals [app], so any demand upturn would be harder to capture [an]. Problem 2: Redundancy damages morale among remaining staff [k], leaving 33 employees facing the pressure of clearing 140 aged cars with 9.4% unemployment weighing on buyers [app], so motivation and customer service may decline [an].
    Keywords: 5 sales staff, 38 staff, 610 vehicles, 140 cars, 9.4%, 40%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: redundancies reduce the workforce and sales capacity; redundancy harms morale and service quality among remaining staff | application_max_2: losing 5 of 38 staff leaves 33 to shift 610 vehicles and 140 aged cars; buyers already hesitant at 9.4% unemployment need more, not fewer, sales staff | analysis_max_2: reduced capacity weakens the response when confidence recovers; low morale among 33 remaining staff risks weaker service and lost deals

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Calder Vale Motors should run the 'Sale Days' promotion rather than make 5 sales staff redundant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The Sale Days promotion attacks the real problem [k]; sales fell 24% to 610 vehicles because confidence is at its lowest in 12 years, so 8% discounts and free 2-year servicing directly lower the cost of buying now [app], which could clear the 140 aged cars and revive showroom footfall [an]. However, redundancy would cut overheads immediately [k]; with marketing spend reduced by 40% and 5 fewer salaries, Calder Vale preserves cash while sales run 24% below last year [app], but it sells into a falling market with a weaker team and 140 cars still ageing on the forecourt [an]. Overall, Calder Vale should run the Sale Days promotion [eval], because the slump is cyclical and confidence can recover, while 140 unsold cars and showroom visits down 30% demand action to move vehicles, not a smaller sales force [eval].
    Keywords: Sale Days, 8%, 610 vehicles, 12 years, 140 cars, 40%, 30%, free 2-year servicing, 9.4%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: discounting stimulates demand when confidence is low; redundancy cuts fixed labour costs but removes capacity and may harm morale | application_max_2: Sales Days with 8% discounts and free 2-year servicing vs 140 unsold cars; marketing spend cut by 40% and 5 of 38 staff made redundant | analysis_max_2: promotion clears stock and revives footfall versus margin erosion on each deal; redundancy saves cash now but leaves the dealer weak when demand recovers | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to confidence at its lowest in 12 years; recommendation favours revenue action over cost cuts for aged stock

The directors are deciding whether to raise wages by 10% across the 78 workers to attract staff from rivals, or to subcontract the 2 new contracts at rates that cut profit margins from 9% to 5%.   Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of low unemployment on Rillwater.

Effect 2: Recruiting from rivals costs more [k], and with GDP growth of 3.6% and three new housing estates due to start, keeping the 78 workers it has is harder [app].
    Keywords: 4.1%, $2.8 million, 12%, 78 construction workers, 3.6%, 2 contracts, 17%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: low unemployment creates skills shortages; low unemployment pushes wages up and intensifies competition for staff | application_max_2: unemployment fell to 4.1% and site wages rose 12%; 2 contracts worth $2.8 million turned down for lack of skilled trades

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Rillwater of raising wages by 10%.

Benefit 2: Better pay improves retention and morale [k], so the 78 workers are less likely to leave for rivals whose site wages already rose 12% [app], protecting site productivity and delivery dates [an].
    Keywords: $2.8 million, 2 contracts, 12%, 78 workers, 10%, $9.4 million, 4.1%

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Rillwater Construction should raise wages by 10% rather than subcontract the 2 contracts? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Raising wages by 10% retains and attracts the skilled trades Rillwater needs [k]; with unemployment at 4.1%, GDP growth of 3.6% and wages already up 12% in the region, higher pay is the realistic way to win the 2 contracts worth $2.8 million while keeping the $9.4 million order book on schedule [app], so revenue and reputation both benefit despite higher payroll costs [an]. However, subcontracting avoids permanent wage inflation [k]; paying 25% deposits upfront and accepting margins cut from 9% to 5% on the 2 contracts would still clear the workload if recruiting fails [app], so subcontracting protects cash while the labour market stays tight [an]. Overall, Rillwater should raise wages by 10% [eval], because subcontracting at 5% margin sacrifices profit on $2.8 million of work, whereas higher wages keep control of quality, schedules and the full 9% margin on the strongest order book in 6 years [eval].
    Keywords: 4.1%, 3.6%, 12%, $2.8 million, $9.4 million, 10%, 9%, 5%, 25% deposits upfront
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: raising wages attracts and retains scarce skilled workers in a boom; subcontracting avoids permanent wage increases but erodes margins | application_max_2: 10% wage rise vs 2 contracts worth $2.8 million and a $9.4 million order book; subcontract margins cut from 9% to 5% with 25% deposits upfront | analysis_max_2: winning the contracts with permanent staff protects quality and schedule control; subcontracting clears workload but halves the margin and demands cash deposits | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the 6-year-high order book of $9.4 million; recommendation weighs long-term capability against short-term cash protection

Skerry Bay Hotel is a 3-star hotel in Country X with 120 rooms and 64 employees.   Qb [4 marks]

Reason 2: Weak confidence and incomes reduce business tourism [k], and with GDP down 1.4% and corporate bookings dried up completely, international tourist numbers also fell 9% [app].
    Keywords: 10.2%, fell 16%, 71% to 58%, 1.4%, fell 9%, $3.1 million, $2.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: high unemployment reduces disposable income for leisure travel; weak growth and confidence reduce business and overseas travel | application_max_2: unemployment at 10.2% and holiday spending down 16%; occupancy fell from 71% to 58%; GDP down 1.4%, corporate bookings dried up completely and international visitors fell 9%

  Qc [6 marks]

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Skerry Bay Hotel should cut room rates by 15% rather than close the leisure wing and make 9 staff redundant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Cutting room rates by 15% would win price-sensitive domestic business [k]; with unemployment at 10.2% and holiday spending down 16%, families switching from overseas trips are the realistic growth segment, and rivals have already cut rates by 12% [app], so matching the market could lift occupancy from 58% and protect the $2.4 million revenue base [an]. Overall, Skerry Bay should cut room rates by 15% [eval], because closing the leisure wing removes the facilities that differentiate the hotel, whereas a targeted discount rebuilds occupancy from 58%, keeps 64 staff in work and preserves the 3-star offer for the recovery [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: discounting attracts domestic demand when household budgets are squeezed; closing underused facilities and redundancy cut fixed costs but remove value-adding capacity | application_max_2: 15% rate cut vs rivals already at 12% off and 10.2% unemployment; closing the leisure wing and 9 of 64 staff redundant vs $700,000 revenue shortfall | analysis_max_2: rate cut restores volume and add-on revenue versus deeper margin per room; closure saves costs now but weakens the hotel's offer when demand recovers | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to occupancy of 58% versus 71% before the slump; recommendation keeps facilities and staff for the recovery

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]

  Qb [4 marks]

Reason 2: Falling unemployment raises household incomes [k], and with unemployment down from 9.6% to 9.1%, orders climbed from $1.9 million to $2.4 million [app].
    Keywords: 0.8%, 9.6% to 9.1%, $1.9 million, $2.4 million, 3 consecutive months, 2 quarters, 11 weeks
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: recovery raises confidence, encouraging big-ticket spending; falling unemployment increases household disposable income | application_max_2: GDP rose 0.8% and confidence improved for 3 consecutive months; unemployment edged down from 9.6% to 9.1%; orders climbed from $1.9 million to $2.4 million

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Bramwell Furniture of hiring 8 extra production staff and building inventory.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Extra staff shorten delivery times [k], letting Bramwell cut lead times from 11 weeks further and satisfy the two national retailers wanting larger ranges for spring [app], winning repeat orders [an]. Benefit 2: Holding inventory ahead of demand captures the early recovery [k], and with the order book already climbing from $1.9 million to $2.4 million, Bramwell can fulfil demand without delays [app], protecting its reputation with national buyers [an].
    Keywords: 8 extra production staff, 11 weeks, $2.4 million, $1.9 million, two national retailers, spring retail catalogue, 52 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: additional staff reduce lead times and enable larger order fulfilment; holding inventory ahead of demand captures upswing orders | application_max_2: 8 extra staff needed to serve the two national retailers' spring ranges; lead times already shortened from 14 weeks to 11 weeks with orders at $2.4 million | analysis_max_2: shorter lead times win repeat spring orders and strengthen retailer relationships; inventory readiness avoids stockouts and protects revenue during the upswing

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Bramwell Furniture should hire 8 extra production staff rather than keep staffing at 52? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Hiring 8 extra production staff matches output to the recovery [k]; with GDP up 0.8%, unemployment down to 9.1% and the order book climbing $500,000 to $2.4 million, Bramwell can only cut its 11-week lead times and supply the two national retailers' spring ranges if it lifts capacity [app], so revenue and market share should grow through spring [an]. However, waiting is safer if the recovery stalls [k]; recovery is only early, timber prices are 13% higher than two years ago, and if confidence slips again the extra 8 wages and unsold sofas would squeeze a margin already hit by input costs [app], so keeping staffing at 52 protects cash until orders keep rising [an]. Overall, Bramwell should hire the 8 extra staff [eval], because lead times must fall from 11 weeks to win the two national retailers' spring ranges, and the downside of a modest, reversible staffing increase is smaller than the cost of turning away growing orders [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: hiring ahead of recovery wins early market share and retailer listings; holding staffing fixed protects cash if the recovery stalls | application_max_2: 8 extra staff vs keeping 52; order book up $500,000 to $2.4 million; timber prices 13% higher; lead times need to fall from 11 weeks | analysis_max_2: capacity gain versus risk of excess wages if demand softens; winning two national retailers' spring ranges versus cash protection in a fragile recovery | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the spring retail catalogue deadline in 3 weeks; recommendation weighs the fragile 0.8% GDP recovery against order momentum

Reason 2: Growing consumer and business demand raises deliveries [k], which is why Cormorant's own deliveries rose 14% to 38,000 pallets a year [app].
    Keywords: 3.1%, 9%, 14%, 38,000 pallets, 24 trucks, 51 staff, $1.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: economic growth raises production and distribution volumes; rising demand from businesses and consumers increases goods movement | application_max_2: GDP grew 3.1% and national freight volumes rose 9%; Cormorant's deliveries rose 14% to 38,000 pallets a year

  Qc [6 marks]

    Keywords: $9,200, $780,000, 5 years, 25%, 6 new trucks, 24 trucks, $1.2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: buying avoids large cumulative lease payments over time; owned assets can be resold and give full operational control | application_max_2: 6 trucks at $9,200 per month per truck = $55,200 a month over 5 years; purchase $780,000 vs lease total $3,312,000; capacity lifts 25% | analysis_max_2: purchase saves roughly $2.53 million over the lease term; ownership enables fast deployment and resale value retention

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Cormorant Freight should buy the 6 trucks rather than lease them? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Buying the 6 trucks for $780,000 is far cheaper than leasing [k]; leasing at $9,200 per month per truck totals $3,312,000 over 5 years, so buying saves about $2.53 million while lifting capacity 25% to serve $1.2 million in annual contracts [app], directly converting GDP-driven freight growth of 9% into profit [an]. Overall, Cormorant should buy the 6 trucks [eval], because the 3 customers signing $1.2 million a year and GDP growth of 3.1% make demand reliable, and owning avoids paying over four times the purchase price in lease charges [eval].
    Keywords: $780,000, $9,200, 5 years, $900,000, $1.2 million, 25%, 3.1%, 9%, 38,000 pallets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: buying is cheaper than leasing over long periods if cash allows; leasing preserves cash and includes maintenance but costs more in total | application_max_2: $780,000 purchase vs lease $9,200 per month per truck over 5 years ($3,312,000); $900,000 reserves; $1.2 million annual contracts; 25% capacity lift | analysis_max_2: purchase saves about $2.53 million and converts growth into profit; leasing spreads cash outflow but triples long-run cost and depends on demand holding | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to reliable $1.2 million annual contracts; recommendation accepts reserve depletion for long-run saving

--- STEM ---
Bluefin Leisure Centres Ltd is a private limited company in Country X operating 4 fitness clubs with 21,000 members and 96 staff. After 3 years of growth, Country X's GDP rose just 0.4% last quarter, unemployment crept up from 4.9% to 5.3% and consumer confidence slipped from 112 to 104. Gym visits are down 7% since January.

Membership has plateaued; annual revenue is $8.9 million and costs are rising. Two rival chains have discounted memberships by 20%. The board is deciding whether to press ahead with a 5th premium club in the northern suburbs costing $3.6 million, signed this quarter, or to freeze expansion, cut costs by $600,000 a year and prepare for a possible downturn. The 5th club would create 30 jobs. The decision is due within 4 weeks.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'business cycle'.
    Answer: The recurring pattern of growth and decline in an economy, moving through boom, recession, slump and recovery [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: the recurring pattern of economic expansion and contraction; moves through boom, recession, slump and recovery

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two signs that Country X is near the top of the business cycle.
    Answer: Sign 1: GDP growth has slowed sharply [k], and after 3 years of growth output rose just 0.4% last quarter, signalling that momentum is fading [app]. Sign 2: Confidence and unemployment are turning [k], with confidence slipping from 112 to 104 and unemployment creeping up from 4.9% to 5.3%, both classic late-cycle warnings [app].
    Keywords: 0.4%, 112 to 104, 4.9% to 5.3%, 3 years of growth, 21,000, $8.9 million, 7%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: slowing GDP growth signals the top of the cycle; falling confidence and rising unemployment are late-cycle signals | application_max_2: GDP rose just 0.4% last quarter after 3 years of growth; confidence slipped from 112 to 104 and unemployment rose from 4.9% to 5.3%

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Bluefin of pressing ahead with the 5th premium club.
    Answer: Benefit 1: A first mover captures the northern suburbs [k], winning demand before rivals react as the premium club creates 30 jobs and lifts capacity beyond 21,000 members [app], securing revenue through the plateau [an]. Benefit 2: Fitness demand often holds up early in a slowdown [k], and with revenue at $8.9 million across 4 clubs, a premium site could lift yield per member [app], diversifying income across locations [an].
    Keywords: 5th premium club, northern suburbs, 30 jobs, 21,000, $8.9 million, 20%, 4 fitness clubs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: first-mover advantage captures new market demand before rivals; premium positioning can raise revenue per member | application_max_2: 5th premium club in the northern suburbs creating 30 jobs, beyond 21,000 members; revenue of $8.9 million across 4 existing clubs | analysis_max_2: early capture of northern suburbs secures revenue during the plateau; higher yield per member diversifies and stabilises income across more sites

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Bluefin Leisure Centres should press ahead with the 5th premium club rather than freeze expansion? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Pressing ahead captures remaining growth before the cycle turns [k]; GDP rose 0.4% last quarter and confidence still stands at 104, so northern-suburb demand may absorb a premium club creating 30 jobs, lifting capacity beyond 21,000 members and revenue above $8.9 million [app], so Bluefin would enter any downturn as the larger, stronger operator [an]. However, freezing expansion is the prudent response to clear late-cycle signals [k]; with growth of just 0.4%, unemployment rising to 5.3%, confidence slipping from 112 to 104 and two rivals discounting memberships by 20%, a $3.6 million commitment could strain Bluefin if member numbers fall [app], whereas cutting costs by $600,000 a year shields margins through a downturn [an]. Overall, Bluefin should freeze expansion for now [eval], because the late-cycle data (0.4% GDP, confidence 104, rivals discounting 20%) outweigh the case for a $3.6 million club, and the northern suburbs can be entered once confidence stabilises [eval].
    Keywords: 0.4%, 104, 112 to 104, 5.3%, 20%, $3.6 million, $600,000, $8.9 million, 21,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: pressing ahead captures late-cycle demand at the cost of balance-sheet risk; freezing expansion and cutting costs protects the business through a downturn | application_max_2: 5th premium club costing $3.6 million creating 30 jobs vs $600,000 annual cost cuts; GDP +0.4%, confidence 104, unemployment 5.3%, rivals discounting 20% | analysis_max_2: larger scale versus late-cycle risk to a $3.6 million commitment; cost cutting preserves margins but sacrifices first-mover gains | evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to late-cycle indicators (0.4% GDP, confidence 104); recommendation favours financial resilience over expansion now

--- STEM ---
Calderrow Tannery Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that has operated for 9 years. It employs 36 workers and produces 420,000 square metres of finished leather each year, with sales revenue of $2.4 million. Tanning uses 1,850 tonnes of salt, lime and chromium compounds annually, and the waste effluent is discharged into the River Senn after basic settling only.

Downstream of the tannery, 14 licensed fishermen report catches down 40% since the plant opened, blaming chromium pollution for fish kills and tainted water. The Environment Agency warns that discharges exceed the legal limit by 35%, with daily fines of $3,000 from 1 March unless the firm installs a $480,000 effluent treatment plant. The directors must choose between treating the waste, relocating upriver, or appealing the ruling.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'pollution'.
    Answer: Pollution is the release of harmful substances or waste into the natural environment, such as chemical effluent entering rivers or fumes entering the air, damaging ecosystems and human health. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Release of harmful substances or waste into the environment; Causes damage to ecosystems, people or the environment

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two external costs created by Calderrow Tannery.
    Answer: Reason 1: The effluent damages the river's fish stocks [k], because pollution from the tannery is blamed for catches falling 40% for 14 licensed fishermen who gain no benefit from the factory [app]. Reason 2: The discharges impose costs on the wider community [k], as they exceed the legal limit by 35%, risking daily fines of $3,000 and tainted water for riverside households [app].
    Keywords: Calderrow Tannery, River Senn, 14 licensed fishermen, 40%, 35%, $3,000, $480,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: External costs fall on third parties not involved in production; Pollution imposes costs beyond the polluting business | application_max_2: Catches down 40% for 14 licensed fishermen downstream; Discharges 35% above the legal limit; $3,000 daily fines

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Calderrow Tannery if it installs the effluent treatment plant.
    Answer: Problem 1: The plant requires a large immediate outlay [k], costing $480,000 which must be funded from cash reserves or borrowing, straining the company's finances [app], so less money remains for wages, hides and repairs in the short term [an]. Problem 2: Running the plant adds ongoing costs [k], since treating 1,850 tonnes of salt, lime and chromium waste each year means buying chemicals, power and monitoring equipment [app], pushing up the cost per square metre of leather and squeezing profit margins [an].
    Keywords: Calderrow Tannery, $480,000, 1,850 tonnes, River Senn, chromium, $2.4 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Large capital outlay strains business finances; Running costs raise average production costs | application_max_2: $480,000 installation cost for the treatment plant; 1,850 tonnes of salt, lime and chromium compounds treated each year | analysis_max_2: Less cash available for other spending in the short term; Higher unit costs squeeze profit margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Calderrow Tannery should install the $480,000 effluent treatment plant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for installing the plant is that it brings the firm into legal compliance immediately [k], avoiding $3,000 daily fines from 1 March while protecting the $2.4 million annual revenue and the jobs of 36 workers [app], so the firm can keep trading while restoring its reputation with the 14 licensed fishermen affected by chromium pollution [an]. However, one argument against is the strain on cash flow [k], as a $480,000 cost is one-fifth of a year's revenue and must be paid before any benefit is seen [app], so appealing could delay payment, but the firm would keep risking fines and eventual closure of the River Senn site [an]. Overall, Calderrow Tannery should install the effluent treatment plant [eval], because fines of $3,000 a day would exceed $1 million in a year of breach, more than double the $480,000 capital cost, and compliance permanently eliminates the pollution problem [eval].
    Keywords: Calderrow Tannery, $480,000, River Senn, $3,000, 14 licensed fishermen, $2.4 million, 36 workers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Compliance avoids fines and protects trading; Large capital outlay strains cash flow | application_max_2: $480,000 cost equals one-fifth of $2.4 million annual revenue; $3,000 daily fines from 1 March; 36 workers and 14 licensed fishermen affected | analysis_max_2: Continued trading protects revenue, jobs and reputation; Appealing keeps fines and closure risk hanging over the business | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both installing the plant and appealing or delaying; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

--- STEM ---
Bramblefold Poultry Farm is a family partnership in Country X keeping 17,000 laying hens across two barns for 6 years. It sells 5.1 million eggs a year to regional supermarkets, earning $890,000 in sales revenue with 9 full-time employees. The farm sits just 400 metres from Lower Ashby village, home to 1,150 residents.

Over the past 18 months the district council has received 26 written complaints about ammonia smells and flies in hot weather. Its survey found boundary ammonia levels averaging 0.09 parts per million, twice the recommended figure for homes. Bramblefold can install covered manure storage and a bio-filter system costing $65,000, or cut its flock to 12,000 hens, lowering output by 30% but reducing odour and improving bird welfare.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'external costs'.
    Answer: External costs are the costs of a business or economic activity that fall on third parties not involved in the production or consumption of the good, such as pollution, noise or odour affecting people living nearby. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Costs falling on third parties not involved in the activity; Examples include pollution, noise or odour affecting residents

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two external costs created by Bramblefold Poultry Farm.
    Answer: Reason 1: Odour from the barns harms villagers' quality of life [k], because boundary ammonia levels average 0.09 parts per million, twice the recommended figure for homes 400 metres away [app]. Reason 2: The farm imposes disruption on the community [k], as shown by 26 written complaints about flies and smells received over the past 18 months [app].
    Keywords: Bramblefold, 17,000, Lower Ashby, 0.09, 26 written complaints, 400 metres, 1,150 residents
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: External costs affect third parties, such as residents, not the producer; Odour, ammonia and flies are examples of external costs | application_max_2: Boundary ammonia averaging 0.09 parts per million, twice the recommended figure; 26 written complaints received over the past 18 months

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Bramblefold would face if it cut its flock to 12,000 hens.
    Answer: Problem 1: Egg output and income would fall [k], as removing about 5,000 hens cuts production by roughly 30% from 5.1 million eggs, reducing supermarket supply and revenue from $890,000 [app], so the partners' drawings and cash flow would shrink [an]. Problem 2: Staffing becomes less efficient [k], because the same two barns and 9 employees would serve a flock 30% smaller [app], raising the average cost per egg and squeezing profit margins [an].
    Keywords: Bramblefold, 12,000, 17,000, 5.1 million, $890,000, 9 full-time employees, 30%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cutting output reduces revenue; Fixed resources spread over fewer units raise unit costs | application_max_2: Flock cut from 17,000 to 12,000 hens, lowering output by 30% from 5.1 million eggs; Two barns and 9 employees working for a smaller flock | analysis_max_2: Partners' income and cash flow fall; Average cost per egg rises, squeezing profit margins

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Bramblefold should install the $65,000 bio-filter system instead of reducing its flock to 12,000 hens? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for the bio-filter is that it removes the odour problem while keeping full production [k], so Bramblefold keeps 17,000 hens and its $890,000 revenue with its 9 employees [app], protecting contracts with regional supermarkets and farm profits [an]. However, one argument against is the cost [k], as $65,000 is a large outlay for a farm earning $890,000 a year, and the system needs regular maintenance to stay effective [app], and ammonia could still drift if wind spreads it beyond the bio-filters, so 26 complaints may not stop immediately [an]. Overall, Bramblefold should install the $65,000 bio-filter system [eval], because keeping production at 5.1 million eggs preserves revenue far above the installation cost, whereas cutting the flock by 30% would permanently shrink the business and risk supermarket contracts [eval].
    Keywords: Bramblefold, $65,000, 17,000, $890,000, 5.1 million, 12,000, Lower Ashby
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Bio-filter removes odour while retaining output; Large outlay plus maintenance burden for the farm | application_max_2: $65,000 cost versus $890,000 annual revenue and 5.1 million eggs; Cutting to 12,000 hens would lower output by 30% | analysis_max_2: Full output protects supermarket contracts and profits; Residual ammonia drift may not stop all complaints | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both installing the bio-filter and cutting the flock; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

--- STEM ---
Estwick Brick Co is a private limited company in Country X producing 9 million clay bricks a year for housebuilders. It employs 74 workers, operates two kilns around the clock and has annual turnover of $3.7 million. The town of Estwick, 500 metres away, is home to 9,000 residents, many in homes downwind of the chimneys.

Local doctors have recorded 34 cases of childhood asthma near the plant in the last year, and Environment Agency tests show chimney particulates 45% above the legal limit. The Agency may fine the company $1,500 per day of breach, or order the oldest kiln shut down. The board can fit electrostatic filters for $210,000, switch to low-sulphur gas at an extra $28,000 a year, or appeal against the ruling.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'externalities'.
    Answer: Externalities are the effects of producing or consuming a good on third parties not involved in the transaction; they may be negative, such as pollution, or positive, such as jobs created for the local community. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Effects on third parties not involved in the transaction; Can be negative external costs or positive external benefits

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the Environment Agency intervenes in Estwick Brick Co's operations.
    Answer: Reason 1: To protect public health [k], since 34 cases of childhood asthma were recorded near the plant in the last year, linked to dust drifting over 500 metres into a town of 9,000 residents [app]. Reason 2: To enforce the law against pollution [k], because chimney particulates measured 45% above the legal limit, so fines of $1,500 per day are needed to force compliance [app].
    Keywords: Estwick Brick Co, 34 cases of childhood asthma, 45%, $1,500, 9,000 residents, 500 metres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: To protect public health from pollution; To enforce legal limits and standards | application_max_2: 34 cases of childhood asthma near the plant last year; Particulates 45% above the legal limit; fines of $1,500 per day

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects on Estwick Brick Co of fitting the electrostatic filters costing $210,000.
    Answer: Effect 1: Emissions fall and fines stop [k], as filters capture particulates so the output stays legal and the $1,500 daily fines are avoided [app], preventing penalties that could total over $540,000 a year [an]. Effect 2: A large short-term cost [k], as $210,000 must be spent immediately, equal to about 5.7% of annual turnover of $3.7 million [app], squeezing short-term cash flow and reducing profit for the year [an].
    Keywords: Estwick Brick Co, $210,000, $1,500, two kilns, $3.7 million, 9 million, 500 metres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Filters reduce emissions and end fines; Filters are a large one-off capital cost | application_max_2: Filters cost $210,000 and avoid $1,500 daily fines; $210,000 equals about 5.7% of $3.7 million turnover | analysis_max_2: Avoided fines could save over $540,000 a year; Short-term cash flow and profit are squeezed

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Estwick Brick Co should fit the $210,000 electrostatic filters? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for fitting the filters is that they solve the legal problem permanently [k], removing the 45% excess particulates and stopping $1,500 daily fines while keeping both kilns running for its 9 million bricks [app], protecting turnover of $3.7 million, the jobs of 74 workers and relations with Estwick's 9,000 residents [an]. However, one argument against is the immediate cost [k], since $210,000 equals roughly 5.7% of annual turnover and the firm could instead switch to low-sulphur gas at just $28,000 a year extra, preserving cash for expansion [app], although switching fuel may not capture the heavier particulates and would delay compliance [an]. Overall, Estwick Brick Co should fit the electrostatic filters [eval], because fines of $1,500 a day would exceed the $210,000 installation cost in 5 months of breach, making compliance cheaper and safer for its licence to operate [eval].
    Keywords: Estwick Brick Co, $210,000, $1,500, 45%, $3.7 million, 74 workers, $28,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Filters deliver permanent legal compliance; Upfront cost versus cheaper but partial gas switching | application_max_2: $210,000 filter cost versus $28,000 extra per year for gas; 45% excess particulates; fines of $1,500 per day | analysis_max_2: Compliance protects turnover, jobs and community relations; Gas switching is cheaper but may not capture heavier particulates | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both fitting filters and switching fuel or appealing; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

--- STEM ---
Kongwe Plantations Ltd is a private limited company in Country X growing oil palm across 2,600 hectares for 11 years. It employs 190 workers, produces 7,400 tonnes of crude palm oil a year and exports 80% of its output to food manufacturers, earning $4.6 million in export revenue. Palm oil appears in 3,000 everyday supermarket products across the region.

Satellite surveys by Earthwatch Alliance, an environmental pressure group, show 640 hectares of irreplaceable native forest were cleared in the last 4 years, releasing stored carbon and destroying habitat. Buyers in Country Y now demand certified sustainable palm oil; certification costs $85,000 a year, plus a $140,000 upgrade to a traceable mill. Kongwe risks losing two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year if it cannot prove sustainability.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'deforestation'.
    Answer: Deforestation is the clearing or removal of forests and trees from land, usually so the land can be used for agriculture, logging, mining or settlement. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Clearing or removal of forests or trees; For agriculture, logging, mining or settlement

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why clearing native forest harms the environment.
    Answer: Reason 1: Habitats and biodiversity are destroyed [k], as clearing 640 hectares of native forest in the last 4 years removes homes for wildlife and reduces species diversity [app]. Reason 2: Forests store carbon, so their removal worsens climate change [k], and clearing on this scale across the 2,600-hectare plantation adds to greenhouse gas emissions [app].
    Keywords: Kongwe Plantations Ltd, 640 hectares, native forest, 2,600 hectares, oil palm, 4 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Destroys habitats and reduces biodiversity; Releases stored carbon, worsening climate change | application_max_2: 640 hectares of native forest cleared in the last 4 years; Clearing across the 2,600-hectare plantation

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Kongwe of gaining sustainable palm oil certification.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Continued access to export markets [k], because buyers in Country Y now demand certified sustainable palm oil, and certification protects two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year [app], safeguarding the export revenue stream the business depends on [an]. Benefit 2: A stronger public image [k], as certification shows Kongwe takes environmental responsibility seriously after the Earthwatch Alliance report [app], attracting buyers who value sustainability and reducing the risk of consumer boycotts [an].
    Keywords: Kongwe, certified sustainable palm oil, $1.9 million, $85,000, $140,000, Country Y, Earthwatch Alliance
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Certification keeps export market access open; Certification improves public image and reputation | application_max_2: Country Y buyers now demand certified sustainable palm oil; Two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year at risk | analysis_max_2: Export revenue stream is safeguarded; Lower risk of boycotts from sustainability-minded buyers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kongwe should pay for sustainable palm oil certification? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for certification is that it secures the company's markets [k], protecting two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year by meeting Country Y buyers' demands, at a cost of $85,000 a year plus a $140,000 one-off mill upgrade [app], so annual certification fees absorb only about 4.5% of the protected revenue [an]. However, one argument against is the ongoing cost [k], since certification costs $85,000 a year indefinitely and $140,000 for traceable mills, reducing profit for a business earning $4.6 million in exports [app], and Kongwe could instead plant only on degraded land to rebuild trust without the audit burden [an]. Overall, Kongwe should pay for the certification [eval], because preserving $1.9 million of export contracts far outweighs $225,000 of first-year costs and protects its position in the 3,000 supermarket products that rely on its palm oil [eval].
    Keywords: Kongwe, $85,000, $140,000, $1.9 million, $4.6 million, Country Y, 3,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Certification secures export markets; Certification carries ongoing costs and audits | application_max_2: $85,000 a year plus $140,000 one-off mill upgrade; first year $225,000; Two export contracts worth $1.9 million a year at stake | analysis_max_2: Annual fees are only about 4.5% of protected revenue; Degraded-land replanting rebuilds trust without audit costs | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both certifying and avoiding certification costs; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

--- STEM ---
Stonemill Precision Ltd is a maker of wind-turbine gearboxes based in the capital city of Country X. It wants to build a $6.5 million factory in Ravenfield, a former mining town where the last coal mine closed in 2019 after seven decades of coal extraction. The new plant would employ 240 workers at average wages of $34,000, with a further 110 jobs expected at local suppliers.

Ravenfield's unemployment rate is 13% and its high street has 27 empty shops. The government has offered a $900,000 training grant and 5 years without business rates if Stonemill proceeds. However, residents fear 600 lorry movements a week near the Ravenfield Levels, a protected wetland, and the board prefers expanding the existing site 120 kilometres away.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'external benefits'.
    Answer: External benefits are the positive effects of a business activity that accrue to third parties not involved in the transaction, such as job creation, training opportunities and the regeneration of local areas. [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Positive effects on third parties not involved in the activity; Examples include jobs, training and local regeneration

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two external benefits the Stonemill factory would bring to Ravenfield.
    Answer: Reason 1: New jobs would cut unemployment [k], as 240 jobs at average wages of $34,000 plus 110 supplier jobs would lift a town with a 13% unemployment rate [app]. Reason 2: Skills and regeneration would improve [k], since the government's $900,000 training grant would raise local skills and spending would help revive 27 empty shops [app].
    Keywords: Stonemill Precision Ltd, $6.5 million, 240 workers, $34,000, 110 jobs, 13%, Ravenfield
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Job creation reduces local unemployment; Training and regeneration raise local skills and spending | application_max_2: 240 jobs at average wages of $34,000 plus 110 supplier jobs; $900,000 training grant and 27 empty shops on the high street

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two reasons why the government offers Stonemill a $900,000 training grant and 5 years without business rates.
    Answer: Reason 1: To regenerate a deprived area [k], because Ravenfield's 13% unemployment and 27 empty shops show the town needs private investment after the coal mine closed in 2019 [app], so public money leverages far more private spending than it costs [an]. Reason 2: To build a skilled industrial workforce [k], as training 240 workers with a $900,000 grant creates transferable manufacturing skills [app], raising local productivity and helping attract further employers [an].
    Keywords: Stonemill, $900,000, 13%, 27 empty shops, Ravenfield, 2019
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Public money levers private investment and regeneration; Grants create transferable skills in the local workforce | application_max_2: Ravenfield has 13% unemployment and 27 empty shops after the 2019 mine closure; $900,000 grant to train 240 workers with 5 years free of business rates | analysis_max_2: Leveraged private spending exceeds the public cost; Skills raise productivity and attract further employers

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Stonemill Precision Ltd should build its new factory in Ravenfield? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One argument for building in Ravenfield is the strong support package [k], with $900,000 of training grants and 5 years free of business rates cutting the cost of a $6.5 million project [app], while 240 jobs at $34,000 and 110 supplier jobs would transform a town with 13% unemployment [an]. However, one argument against is the environmental and logistical risk [k], as 600 lorry movements a week near the protected Ravenfield Levels could trigger legal action and delays [app], whereas expanding the capital site 120 kilometres away reuses existing infrastructure and avoids the wetland [an]. Overall, Stonemill Precision Ltd should build in Ravenfield [eval], because the public subsidy and available labour outweigh the traffic concerns, and routing lorries away from the Levels on agreed timetables would protect the wetland while keeping regeneration on track [eval].
    Keywords: Stonemill, Ravenfield, $900,000, $6.5 million, 240, 600 lorry movements, Ravenfield Levels, 120 kilometres
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Support package cuts project costs; Environmental and logistical risks at the wetland site | application_max_2: $900,000 training grant and 5 years of waived business rates on a $6.5 million project; 600 lorry movements a week near the Ravenfield Levels; 120 kilometres to capital site | analysis_max_2: Jobs and suppliers transform a 13% unemployment town; Capital site reuses infrastructure and avoids legal action | evaluation_max_2: Weighs both Ravenfield construction and capital-site expansion; Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures
