--- STEM ---
Halvoren Foods Plc is a Country X manufacturer of breakfast cereals and snack bars. It employs 380 workers at one factory and has no overseas operations. Last year it generated $24 million in revenue, 75% of it from Country X. Country X's economy is forecast to grow by only 1% this year, while Country Y and Country Z are expected to grow by 5% and 6% respectively.

The board must choose between spending $5 million launching Halvoren's products in Country Y and Country Z, or investing $2 million in a new Country X product line. Expansion abroad would spread sales across three economies and reduce dependence on the slow-growing Country X market, but unfamiliar competitors, higher marketing costs and currency changes make the returns uncertain.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'globalisation'.
    Answer: The increasing integration of economies and markets around the world, so that businesses trade, invest and operate across national borders [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: economies and markets around the world becoming increasingly connected; businesses trading, investing and operating across national borders

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Halvoren Foods Plc of expanding into Country Y and Country Z.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Halvoren would gain access to faster-growing markets [k], as Country Y and Country Z are forecast to grow by 5% and 6% versus only 1% in Country X [app]. Benefit 2: Sales would be spread across three economies [k], so Halvoren would no longer rely on Country X for 75% of its revenue [app].
    Keywords: 5% and 6%, 1%, 75%, $24 million, Country Y and Country Z, Halvoren Foods, $5 million, $2 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: access to larger or faster-growing overseas markets; spreading risk by diversifying across several economies | application_max_2: Country Y and Country Z growing at 5% and 6% vs 1% in Country X; 75% of revenue currently from Country X; sales spread across three economies

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Halvoren Foods Plc could face if it expands into Country Y and Country Z.
    Answer: Problem 1: The launch would cost far more than the home option [k], at $5 million it is two and a half times the $2 million needed for the new Country X line [app], so Halvoren may need loans or share issues, increasing its financial risk [an]. Problem 2: Success abroad is uncertain [k], because unfamiliar competitors, higher marketing costs and currency changes could erode its margins [app], so Halvoren could spend heavily on marketing and still win too few customers to break even [an].
    Keywords: $5 million, $2 million, Country Y, Country Z, Halvoren, 75%, $24 million
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: overseas expansion requires large funds and increases financial risk; unfamiliar markets, competitors and currency changes make returns uncertain | application_max_2: $5 million launch vs $2 million for the domestic product line; unfamiliar competitors, higher marketing costs and currency changes | analysis_max_2: borrowing or new share issues raise financial risk if the launch fails; heavy marketing spend may not recover if too few customers are won

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Halvoren Foods Plc should expand into Country Y and Country Z or invest in the new Country X product line? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Expanding abroad would let Halvoren tap two faster-growing economies [k], with growth of 5% and 6% against 1% at home, while reducing dependence on Country X for 75% of the $24 million revenue [app], spreading risk and opening a much larger customer base [an]. However, the $5 million launch is two and a half times the $2 million domestic alternative [k], and returns are uncertain given unfamiliar competitors and currency changes [app], so failure would leave Halvoren with high debt and little to show for the outlay [an]. Overall, Halvoren should expand into Country Y and Country Z, because diversifying away from a single slow-growing market protects long-term revenue better than one domestic product line [eval], provided it launches in one country first to test demand before committing the full $5 million [eval].
    Keywords: 5% and 6%, 1%, 75%, $24 million, $5 million, $2 million, Country Y and Country Z, Halvoren
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: overseas expansion opens faster-growing markets and spreads risk; overseas expansion is costly and the returns are uncertain | application_max_2: 5% and 6% growth vs 1% in Country X; 75% of $24 million revenue from Country X; $5 million launch vs $2 million domestic; unfamiliar competitors and currency changes | analysis_max_2: diversification protects long-term revenue across three economies; failure would leave high debt and wasted outlay | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on expanding abroad; suggests a phased entry, testing one country first, showing balanced judgement

--- STEM ---
Nordmere Mining Plc is a Country X multinational that extracts copper ore at a mine in Country Y, where it has operated for 8 years. The mine employs 520 local workers and produced ore worth $50 million last year. After taxes and wages, Nordmere made $7.5 million profit in Country Y, equal to 15% of the ore's value.

The board must decide what to do with the $7.5 million. Option one is to repatriate it to Country X headquarters to pay a larger dividend to shareholders, who have complained about low dividends for two years. Option two is to reinvest it in a new Country Y processing plant costing $7 million, which would create 90 skilled jobs. Country Y's government offers a 5-year tax rebate to firms that reinvest profits locally.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'repatriation of profits'.
    Answer: The practice of a multinational sending profits earned in a host country back to its home country [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: profits earned in the host country are sent abroad; back to the multinational's home country

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Nordmere Mining Plc of repatriating the $7.5 million to Country X.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Shareholders would receive a larger dividend [k], as the $7.5 million could be paid out rather than tied up in Country Y [app]. Benefit 2: Nordmere would centralise cash in Country X [k], giving head office $7.5 million to fund other projects without needing a loan [app].
    Keywords: $7.5 million, Country X, Country Y, Nordmere, $50 million, 520, 15%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: higher dividends for shareholders; cash central to head office, avoiding the need to borrow | application_max_2: $7.5 million could be paid out as a dividend; $7.5 million available at Country X headquarters

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Nordmere Mining Plc could face if it repatriates the $7.5 million to Country X.
    Answer: Problem 1: Nordmere would lose the 5-year tax rebate [k], which Country Y grants only to profits reinvested locally, so repatriating the $7.5 million raises its tax bill [app], leaving less net profit than reinvesting would [an]. Problem 2: Country Y's government may view repatriation badly [k], as the $7.5 million would leave instead of funding a $7 million processing plant with 90 skilled jobs [app], risking tougher treatment when the mining licence is renewed [an].
    Keywords: 5-year, $7.5 million, $7 million, 90, Country Y, Nordmere, 520
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: host government tax rebates are lost when profits are repatriated; repatriation can damage relations with the host government | application_max_2: 5-year tax rebate only for profits reinvested locally; $7 million plant with 90 skilled jobs left unfunded | analysis_max_2: higher tax bill reduces net profit compared with reinvesting; poor government relations could endanger the mining licence

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Nordmere Mining Plc should repatriate the $7.5 million to Country X or reinvest it in the new Country Y processing plant? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Repatriating the $7.5 million would let Nordmere pay the larger dividend shareholders want [k], distributing the full $7.5 million rather than holding it in Country Y [app], which would improve short-term returns and financial flexibility for head office [an]. However, reinvesting would earn the 5-year tax rebate [k] and create a $7 million processing plant with 90 skilled jobs [app], which should lift the mine's long-run profit and protect Nordmere's standing with the Country Y government [an]. Overall, Nordmere should reinvest the money in the processing plant, because the tax rebate and future processing profit outweigh a one-off dividend [eval], while shareholders can still be rewarded once the plant generates cash [eval].
    Keywords: $7.5 million, 5-year, $7 million, 90, Country X, Country Y, 15%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: repatriation rewards shareholders and centralises cash; reinvestment can earn host country tax rebates and build long-term capacity | application_max_2: full $7.5 million distributed vs tied up in Country Y; 5-year tax rebate; $7 million plant with 90 skilled jobs | analysis_max_2: repatriation improves short-term returns and financial flexibility; reinvestment lifts long-run profit and protects the mining licence and government relations | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on repatriation or reinvestment; recognises shareholders can be rewarded once the plant generates cash

--- STEM ---
Aldric Metals Plc, a Country X steel multinational, runs a foundry in Country Y employing 260 workers and has operated there for 11 years. The Country Y government has pressured Aldric to install modern computer-controlled casting equipment, which would cost $4 million, replace worn machines and train 120 Country Y workers in the new technology.

Aldric's board is split. Replacing the equipment would transfer new casting technology to Country Y and cut reject rates from 9% to 3%, but would require two senior Country X engineers to relocate. The alternative is to keep the old machines and pay Country X experts to fly in for three weeks each quarter, at a cost of $120,000 a year. The board must reach a decision by 30 June.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'technology transfer'.
    Answer: The process by which a multinational brings its technology, skills and working methods into the host country, spreading knowledge to local firms and workers [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: movement of technology, skills and methods from one country to another; from the multinational into the host country, benefiting local workers and firms

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Aldric Metals Plc of installing the new casting equipment.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Defects and waste would fall sharply [k], with the reject rate dropping from 9% to 3% [app]. Benefit 2: Aldric would gain a more skilled local workforce [k], as the investment would train 120 Country Y workers rather than rely on flying in experts at $120,000 a year [app].
    Keywords: 9% to 3%, $4 million, 120, 260, Aldric, Country Y, $120,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: improved quality and lower reject rates raise efficiency; training the host country workforce builds local skills and capacity | application_max_2: reject rate from 9% to 3%; 120 Country Y workers trained vs $120,000 a year on flying in experts

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Aldric Metals Plc could face if it installs the new casting equipment.
    Answer: Problem 1: The investment is a large cash outflow [k], at $4 million it dwarfs the $120,000 a year cost of expert visits [app], so Aldric may need loans and its short-term profit will fall [an]. Problem 2: Installing new technology spreads Aldric's knowledge [k], as 120 trained workers and modern methods become part of the Country Y economy [app], meaning local firms could copy Aldric's techniques and undercut it later [an].
    Keywords: $4 million, $120,000 a year, 120, 9% to 3%, Country Y, 260, 11 years
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: large capital outlay increases financial risk and cuts short-term profit; technology and skills can leak to local competitors once transferred | application_max_2: $4 million cost vs $120,000 a year for expert visits; 120 Country Y workers trained in the new technology | analysis_max_2: borrowing to fund the equipment raises interest payments and lowers short-term profit; local competitors could learn the methods and undercut Aldric

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Aldric Metals Plc should install the new casting equipment or keep the old machines? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Installing the equipment would cut the reject rate from 9% to 3% [k], saving on wasted metal and rework after a $4 million outlay [app], which lowers unit costs and raises quality over the machines' life [an]. However, keeping the old machines costs only $120,000 a year in expert visits [k], yet it keeps reject rates at 9% and ignores the host government's pressure and the training potential of 120 workers [app], which could sour relations and invite stricter treatment later [an]. Overall, Aldric should install the new equipment, because long-term quality gains and government goodwill outweigh the high upfront cost [eval], particularly as 120 trained Country Y workers can run it without permanent expatriate support [eval].
    Keywords: 9% to 3%, $4 million, $120,000 a year, 120, 260, Country Y, Aldric
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: new equipment improves quality and efficiency; keeping obsolete equipment preserves cash but leaves inefficiency in place | application_max_2: reject rate from 9% to 3%; $4 million outlay; $120,000 a year on expert visits vs government pressure and 120 workers to train | analysis_max_2: lower unit costs and better quality improve competitiveness over the equipment's life; ignoring the host government risks tougher treatment; old machines keep reject rates high | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on installing the equipment; recognises a trained local workforce removes the need for permanent expatriate support

--- STEM ---
Kelvarn Dyes Ltd is a garment-dyeing factory in the Country X town of Millbrook, owned by a European multinational. It employs 300 local workers, mostly on the dyeing line, and discharges waste water into the River Calder. Tests show dye levels 4 times the legal limit downstream of the factory.

The Country X environmental agency proposes new legal controls forcing all dye works to install closed-loop effluent treatment by next year, or face fines of $250,000 and closure. Kelvarn can spend $2.2 million on a treatment plant, or relocate production to Country Z, where controls are weaker. Closing Millbrook would remove 300 jobs from a town with 500 unemployed adults. The town council wants the factory to stay, but farmers complain the polluted river harms their crops.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'external cost'.
    Answer: A cost of a business activity that falls on people not directly involved in the transaction, such as pollution suffered by the local community [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a cost paid by third parties, not those in the transaction; for example, pollution suffered by the local community

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Kelvarn Dyes Ltd of installing the treatment plant.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Kelvarn would avoid fines and closure [k], eliminating the risk of $250,000 fines and being shut down under the new legal controls [app]. Benefit 2: Kelvarn would protect its reputation and licence to operate [k], as complying stops pollution of the River Calder and keeps 300 Millbrook jobs, satisfying the town council and farmers [app].
    Keywords: $2.2 million, $250,000, 300, Millbrook, River Calder, 500
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: compliance avoids fines and closure; compliance protects reputation and relations with the community | application_max_2: $250,000 fines and closure under the new controls; River Calder pollution ended; 300 Millbrook jobs kept; town council and farmers satisfied

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Kelvarn Dyes Ltd would face if it relocates production to Country Z.
    Answer: Problem 1: Relocation would make 300 Millbrook workers redundant [k], cutting jobs from a town with 500 unemployed adults [app], meaning large redundancy payments and serious reputational damage for Kelvarn [an]. Problem 2: Moving to a country with weaker controls only helps short term [k], as the River Calder tests show how strictly Country X polices pollution [app], so if Country Z adopts similar laws Kelvarn faces the same compliance costs plus lost trust from customers and the public [an].
    Keywords: 300, 500, Millbrook, Country Z, River Calder, $2.2 million, $250,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: closing a factory makes workers redundant and damages reputation; operating where regulation is weak may not be sustainable as laws tighten everywhere | application_max_2: 300 Millbrook workers redundant; town already has 500 unemployed adults; River Calder dye levels 4 times the legal limit show strict Country X enforcement | analysis_max_2: redundancy payments and bad publicity would harm Kelvarn's profit and image; future regulation in Country Z would strand the investment and customers may lose trust

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kelvarn Dyes Ltd should install the treatment plant or relocate production to Country Z? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Installing the plant keeps Kelvarn operating [k], avoiding $250,000 fines and closure under the new legal controls while protecting 300 Millbrook jobs [app], so production continues with a safer reputation and the River Calder recovers [an]. However, the $2.2 million outlay is significant [k], and Country Z has weaker controls and possibly lower operating costs [app], yet relocation abandons Millbrook, its workers and community relationships, and risks Kelvarn being seen as polluting wherever rules are weakest [an]. Overall, Kelvarn should install the treatment plant, because compliance protects its licence, its 300 workers and its reputation for far less than the damage of fleeing [eval], and the investment secures the factory's future beyond next year's deadline [eval].
    Keywords: $2.2 million, $250,000, 300, 500, Millbrook, Country Z, River Calder
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: compliance avoids fines and closure and protects reputation; relocation avoids upfront compliance costs but abandons assets and community ties | application_max_2: $250,000 fines and closure vs $2.2 million treatment plant; 300 jobs kept; Country Z has weaker controls; Millbrook town with 500 unemployed adults | analysis_max_2: compliance keeps production and community relations intact and river recovers; relocation severs community ties and damages Kelvarn's image as a responsible multinational | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on installing the plant; recognises the long-term security the investment brings beyond the deadline

--- STEM ---
Baltica Mart Plc is a European multinational supermarket chain with 210 stores across 9 countries. It plans to enter Country X, where the retail grocery market is worth $900 million a year. A Country X chain, Castleton Retail Co, has offered Baltica a joint venture using its 25 stores and distribution depot.

Baltica's board is deciding between the joint venture and opening 12 stand-alone megastores. Castleton would hold a 40% stake, and Country X competition authorities are reviewing the plans. The megastores would undercut Castleton and many small Country X retailers on price, and estimates suggest 40 local shops could close, while the joint venture would keep Castleton's 480 staff and local purchasing. However, the joint venture would halve Baltica's expected market share gains.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'ethical issue'.
    Answer: A situation in which a decision involves a conflict between making profit and doing what is considered morally right [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a conflict between profit and what is morally right; for example, fairness to workers, rivals, suppliers or communities

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Baltica Mart Plc of choosing the joint venture with Castleton Retail Co.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Baltica would gain immediate access to Country X [k], entering through Castleton's 25 stores and distribution depot rather than building stores from scratch [app]. Benefit 2: Baltica would protect its reputation [k], as the joint venture would keep Castleton's 480 staff and local purchasing, avoiding accusations that it forces 40 local shops to close [app].
    Keywords: 25 stores, Castleton Retail Co, 480 staff, 40 local shops, 40%, $900 million, Baltica Mart, 12
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: faster, cheaper market entry using an established partner; protects reputation and stakeholder relationships | application_max_2: 25 stores and distribution depot already in place; 480 staff kept and 40 local shops not forced to close

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Baltica Mart Plc could face if it opens the 12 stand-alone megastores.
    Answer: Problem 1: Baltica could face serious opposition [k], as estimates suggest 40 local shops could close and many small Country X retailers would be undercut on price [app], damaging Baltica's reputation and inviting boycotts or criticism in Country X [an]. Problem 2: Competition authorities may block or restrict the stores [k], because the plans are being reviewed by Country X competition authorities [app], so Baltica could waste money on a launch that is delayed or not allowed [an].
    Keywords: 12, 40 local shops, 480, competition authorities, Castleton, $900 million, Baltica
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: crowding out local firms damages reputation and provokes opposition; competition authorities can restrict or block large market entries | application_max_2: estimates suggest 40 local shops could close; plans are being reviewed by Country X competition authorities | analysis_max_2: public backlash and boycotts reduce sales and harm the brand; delays or a blocked launch would waste the cost of opening 12 megastores

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Baltica Mart Plc should enter the joint venture with Castleton Retail Co or open the 12 stand-alone megastores? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The megastores would let Baltica set its own prices, layouts and range [k], giving it full control of a share of Country X's $900 million grocery market [app], which could maximise long-term profit if the stores win customers quickly [an]. However, opening 12 megastores could force 40 local shops to close [k] and puts the plans under review by competition authorities [app], risking conditions, delays or a blocked launch, plus reputational damage that slows sales [an]. Overall, Baltica should take the joint venture, because sharing ownership with Castleton still opens Country X's market while protecting jobs, local supply chains and regulatory goodwill [eval], even though it halves Baltica's expected market share gains [eval].
    Keywords: $900 million, 12, 40 local shops, 480, 25 stores, Castleton, Baltica, 40%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: stand-alone stores give full control but provoke opposition and regulatory risk; joint ventures give market access with shared ownership and goodwill | application_max_2: $900 million Country X grocery market; full control of 12 megastores; 40 local shops could close; plans reviewed by competition authorities; 40% Castleton stake | analysis_max_2: full control could maximise long-term profit if rapid customer wins; opposition and regulatory conditions could damage reputation and slow the launch | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on joint venture or stand-alone stores; recognises the trade-off of halving expected market share gains for goodwill and jobs

--- STEM ---
Varello Steel Plc is a multinational steel producer based in Country Y.     Question: Define 'import tariff'.

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Varello Steel Plc of building the mini-mill in Country X.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Varello would avoid the proposed tariff entirely [k], as steel made inside Country X pays no 22% import duty on $40 million of sales [app]. Benefit 2: Varello would gain secure, low-cost local production [k], with 150 workers on wages 20% below the industry average and no risk of being shut out of the market [app].
    Keywords: 22%, $40 million, $12 million, 150, 20%, 90,000, Country X, 1,150
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: avoiding tariffs by producing inside the market; secure market access with lower local costs | application_max_2: 22% import duty on $40 million of sales avoided; 150 workers on wages 20% below the industry average

  Qc [6 marks]

    Keywords: $12 million, 1,150, $40 million, 22%, 150, 90,000, Country X
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: large capital investment increases financial risk; new foreign plants may provoke backlash from protected local firms | application_max_2: $12 million outlay for the mini-mill; 3 remaining Country X mills employ 1,150 workers | analysis_max_2: a demand fall would leave the $12 million investment underperforming; lobbying by local mills could bring tougher rules or taxes on Varello

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Varello Steel Plc should absorb the tariff or build the mini-mill in Country X? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Absorbing the tariff keeps Varello's options open [k], requiring no $12 million outlay on a market it has served for 6 years [app], which protects short-term cash flow if Country X demand is uncertain [an]. However, the 22% tariff would cut the margin on $40 million of sales [k], costing Varello roughly $8.8 million a year [app], so profits would be heavily squeezed every year the tariff remains [an]. Overall, Varello should build the mini-mill, because avoiding about $8.8 million a year of tariff costs soon recovers the $12 million investment and secures its Country X position [eval], while creating 150 local jobs would please the trade minister and reduce political risk [eval].
    Keywords: 22%, $40 million, $12 million, 150, 20%, 90,000, Country X
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: absorbing the tariff avoids upfront investment but erodes margins; local production avoids the tariff and secures market access | application_max_2: no $12 million outlay; 6 years supplying Country X; 22% on $40 million of sales costs about $8.8 million a year | analysis_max_2: absorbing the tariff protects short-term cash flow; tariff costs compound every year and outweigh the one-off investment | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on building the mini-mill; political goodwill from 150 local jobs strengthens the recommendation

--- STEM ---
Veyr Cement Plc, a Turkish multinational, exports 200,000 tonnes of cement a year to Country X, generating $26 million in revenue. It has sold there for 5 years. Country X has introduced an import quota of 120,000 tonnes a year, starting in 3 months, to protect its national cement firms and cut dependence on imports.

Veyr's board must decide how to respond to the quota. It could build a $9 million cement plant in Country X, which would let it keep selling the full 200,000 tonnes, 80,000 of them produced locally, or reduce Country X sales to the 120,000-tonne quota and serve other markets instead. The new plant would employ 110 workers, and Country X's industry minister says the quota will last at least 4 years.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'import quota'.
    Answer: A physical limit on the quantity of a product that may be imported into a country over a period of time [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: a limit on the quantity of a product that can be imported; set by government, often to protect domestic industry

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Veyr Cement Plc of building the Country X plant.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Veyr could keep its Country X volumes [k], producing 80,000 tonnes locally to top up the 120,000-tonne import quota and still sell the full 200,000 tonnes [app]. Benefit 2: Veyr would show its commitment to Country X [k], creating 110 local jobs, which may win government support and smoother approvals in future [app].
    Keywords: $9 million, 200,000 tonnes, 120,000, 80,000, $26 million, 110, Veyr Cement Plc
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: local production bypasses the import quota volume limit; investment in local jobs builds goodwill with the host government | application_max_2: 80,000 tonnes produced locally plus 120,000-tonne quota = 200,000 tonnes; 110 workers would be employed at the new plant

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Veyr Cement Plc could face if it builds the Country X plant.
    Answer: Problem 1: The $9 million outlay is a big commitment [k], compared with simply redirecting sales to other markets instead of Country X [app], so if local production costs are higher than expected the investment could take many years to justify [an]. Problem 2: Veyr could become dependent on a rule-changing market [k], as the industry minister says the quota will last at least 4 years [app], so Veyr may face tougher restrictions later and struggle to leave the market once the plant is built [an].
    Keywords: $9 million, 4 years, 200,000, 120,000, 80,000, $26 million, 110
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: large upfront investment may not be justified if returns are weak; dependence on a market whose rules can change increases long-term risk | application_max_2: $9 million cost of the new Country X plant; industry minister says the quota will last at least 4 years | analysis_max_2: higher-than-expected local costs would make the investment hard to justify; once built, the plant makes Veyr vulnerable to further rule changes

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Veyr Cement Plc should build the Country X plant or reduce sales to the 120,000-tonne quota and serve other markets instead? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Building the plant would let Veyr keep selling 200,000 tonnes [k], holding on to $26 million of Country X revenue despite the 120,000-tonne quota [app], so turnover and market presence are protected [an]. However, the $9 million plant is a heavy outlay [k] and Country X could tighten its rules again after the current 4-year quota period [app], leaving Veyr exposed to a market it cannot leave easily [an]. Overall, Veyr should build the plant, because local production neutralises the quota and secures a key market for the long term [eval], while the 110 jobs created may improve relations with the ministry and ease future negotiations [eval].
    Keywords: $9 million, 200,000 tonnes, 120,000, 80,000, $26 million, 110, 4 years, Country X
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: local production bypasses quota limits and protects revenue; large investments in rule-heavy markets carry dependency risk | application_max_2: 200,000 tonnes still sold with 80,000 produced locally vs 120,000-tonne quota; $9 million plant; quota to last at least 4 years; $26 million revenue | analysis_max_2: keeping full volumes protects turnover and market presence; dependency on Country X leaves Veyr exposed if rules tighten | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on building the plant; recognises the goodwill from 110 jobs may ease future ministry negotiations

Zalvara Mining Plc is a Country X-based multinational that operates an open-cast bauxite mine in Country Z. The mine employs 850 workers and generated $300 million in exports last year. Zalvara's board must respond. It could spend $15 million on land restoration and cleaner haul trucks to comply, or relocate operations to Country Y, which has weaker environmental rules. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'sustainable development'.
    Answer: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: meets the needs of the present generation; does not compromise the ability of future generations to meet their own needs

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to Zalvara Mining Plc of complying with the new law.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Zalvara would keep its licence to operate [k], securing the mine for the next 15 years and avoiding a $10 million fine [app]. Benefit 2: Complying would protect Zalvara's reputation [k], as 850 workers and the local community would see it meeting the 30% emissions cut [app].
    Keywords: $10 million, 850, 30%, 15 years, $15 million, $300 million, Country Z
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: compliance secures the licence to operate and avoids fines; compliance protects reputation with workers and the community | application_max_2: mine secured for the next 15 years; $10 million fine avoided; 850 workers; 30% emissions cut shows commitment

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Zalvara Mining Plc would face if it relocates to Country Y.
    Answer: Problem 1: Relocation would strand huge past investment [k], abandoning $40 million of infrastructure at the Country Z mine [app], so Zalvara would lose capital that cannot be recovered [an]. Problem 2: Operating where environmental rules are weak is a short-term tactic [k], as Country Y has weaker environmental rules today [app], and if Country Y later adopts similar laws Zalvara faces the same compliance costs plus damage to its image as a responsible multinational [an].
    Keywords: $40 million, Country Y, weaker environmental rules, $15 million, 850, Country Z, Zalvara
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: relocation strands capital already invested in the site; weak regulation is a temporary advantage as laws tighten globally | application_max_2: $40 million of infrastructure already invested would be abandoned; Country Y has weaker environmental rules | analysis_max_2: the lost $40 million cannot be recovered and would weigh on profit for years; future Country Y laws would impose the same costs plus reputational damage

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Zalvara Mining Plc should comply with the new law or relocate to Country Y? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Complying would secure the mine's future [k], keeping the licence for 15 years and avoiding $10 million fines after a $15 million investment [app], which protects a $300 million annual export operation [an]. However, relocating to Country Y avoids the 30% emissions cut and the $15 million outlay in the short run [k], though it abandons $40 million of installed infrastructure and relies on rules that may tighten later [app], damaging Zalvara's standing with governments and communities [an]. Overall, Zalvara should comply with the law, because keeping the mine operating over 15 years is worth far more than the $15 million cost [eval], and showing responsible practice may win it government support and community trust across Country Z [eval].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: compliance secures the licence and avoids fines but costs cash upfront; relocation defers compliance costs but strands assets and risks future regulation | application_max_2: licence for 15 years; $10 million fines; $15 million investment; $300 million exports; 30% emissions cut avoided; $40 million infrastructure abandoned; weaker rules in Country Y | analysis_max_2: compliance protects a $300 million annual export operation for 15 years; relocation loses $40 million of installed infrastructure and damages standing | evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on complying with the law; recognises reputational gains and community trust from responsible practice

--- STEM ---
Ravensworth Creamery is a private limited company in Country X producing mature cheddar in two maturing rooms. It exports 420,000 kilograms a year to Country W supermarkets, invoiced in dollars at $15 a kilogram, earning $6,300,000, about 60% of its $10,500,000 annual sales revenue. The Country X dollar has appreciated from $1.50 per euro to $1.25 per euro since March. Currency movements are the single biggest external influence on profits this year.

Managing Director Carla Jimenez must set export prices for next season. Option A is to cut the dollar price to $12 a kilogram, so Country W buyers pay €9.60, to hold orders steady. Option B is to keep the $15 price, accept that Country W orders may fall, and instead win delicatessen listings in Country X. The creamery employs 38 workers and carries $500,000 of bank loans repayable this year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'appreciation'.
    Answer: Appreciation is an increase in the value of one currency against other currencies, so the currency buys more of a foreign currency than it did before [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A rise in the value of one currency; Compared with other currencies / buys more foreign currency than before

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the appreciation on Ravensworth Creamery.
    Answer: First, appreciation makes exports more expensive for buyers abroad [k]. At $1.25 per euro, the same $15 kilogram now costs Country W supermarkets €12 instead of €10, so they may baulk at renewing the contract or demand discounts [app]. Second, demand for exports may fall as buyers switch to cheaper locally produced cheddar [k]. The 420,000 kg Country W order book, worth $6,300,000 a year, could shrink if supermarkets delist Ravensworth in favour of domestic suppliers [app].
    Keywords: $15, $1.25, $1.50, $6,300,000, 420,000, Country W, Ravensworth Creamery
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Appreciation makes exports more expensive abroad; Demand for exports may fall as buyers switch to cheaper alternatives | application_max_2: €12 at $1.25 per euro vs €10 at $1.50 per euro for the $15 kilogram; 420,000 kg / $6,300,000 Country W order book at risk of delisting

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems Ravensworth Creamery might face if it chooses Option A.
    Answer: First, cutting the price shrinks the revenue earned on every kilogram [k]. At $12 instead of $15, Ravensworth forgoes $3 per kilogram across 420,000 kilograms, about $1,260,000 a year of lost revenue [app]. That leaves less cash to repay the $500,000 bank loans this year, raising the risk of refinancing at worse terms or missing repayments [an]. Second, a sharp price cut can provoke rival suppliers into cutting prices too [k]. Country W rivals may match the €9.60 shelf price to defend their own listings [app]. Margins then stay permanently lower across the category, so Ravensworth struggles to fund the two maturing rooms and its 38 workers even after winning orders back [an].
    Keywords: Option A, $12, $15, 420,000, Country W, €9.60
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cutting price reduces revenue earned per unit; Lower prices can trigger a price war with rival suppliers | application_max_2: $3 per kilogram x 420,000 kg is about $1,260,000 of lost revenue; Reference to €9.60 shelf price being matched by Country W rivals | analysis_max_2: Chain from lower price to lower revenue to difficulty repaying $500,000 bank loans; Chain from price war to permanently lower margins and funding pressure on maturing rooms and staff

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ravensworth Creamery should cut the export price to $12 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A cuts the price by 20% to $12 a kilogram [k]. At the new rate Country W buyers pay €9.60, below the €10 they paid before the appreciation, so the 420,000 kg order book worth $6,300,000 is far more likely to hold [app]. Keeping the Country W contract fills both maturing rooms, protects the jobs of 38 workers, and avoids the slow, risky push into delicatessens in Country X where volumes are much smaller [an]. However, Option B holds the $15 price [k]. Refusing to discount avoids forgoing $1,260,000 a year, keeping cash flow stronger for the $500,000 bank loan repayments, and it bets on higher-margin delicatessen listings instead [app]. The danger is that Country W supermarkets, now facing €12 per kilogram, delist Ravensworth altogether and leave it with idle capacity and falling sales [an]. Overall, I think Ravensworth should choose Option A [eval]. The appreciation was driven by currency markets, not by anything Ravensworth failed to do, so protecting volume and shelf space in Country W matters more than squeezing the margin per kilogram, and the price can be reviewed if the dollar weakens next season [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $12, $15, €9.60, Country W, $6,300,000, 420,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut the dollar price to $12 (€9.60) to defend export volume; Option B: hold the $15 price and pursue Country X delicatessen listings | application_max_2: €9.60 at $1.25 per euro vs €12 at the held $15 price / €10 before the appreciation; Reference to 420,000 kg / $6,300,000 of Country W sales / $1,260,000 / $500,000 loans | analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to retained Country W volume and filled maturing rooms; Chain from holding the price to preserved margin but risk of delisting and idle capacity | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and notes the exchange-rate cause of the problem

--- STEM ---
Netherfield Glassworks is a private limited company in Country X producing toughened glass panels for office towers. It imports 500 tonnes of glass blanks a year from Country W, invoiced in euros at €4,000 a tonne. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.30 per euro to $1.56 per euro, so the $2,600,000 annual bill is now $3,120,000, an extra $520,000 a year.

Finance Director Priya Nair must decide how to cover the increase. Option A is to absorb it from the $380,000 retained-profit reserve. Option B is to raise prices by 12% across its $4,400,000 annual sales, adding $528,000. The firm employs 26 glass technicians and three big customers hold fixed-price contracts worth $1,900,000. The tempering oven due in June is already paid for.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the dollar cost of 500 tonnes of glass blanks before and after the rate change.
    Answer: 500 × €4,000 = €2,000,000 a year. Before at $1.30 per euro: €2,000,000 × 1.30 = $2,600,000 [1]. After at $1.56 per euro: €2,000,000 × 1.56 = $3,120,000 [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Correct calculation before the change: $2,600,000; Correct calculation after the change: $3,120,000

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Netherfield Glassworks.
    Answer: First, imports become more expensive when the currency weakens [k]. The annual glass blank bill rises from $2,600,000 to $3,120,000, an extra $520,000 a year for exactly the same 500 tonnes of inputs [app]. Second, higher input costs squeeze the profit margin [k]. The $380,000 retained-profit reserve is not enough to absorb a $520,000 rise, so Netherfield must cut costs, raise prices or eat into the reserve [app].
    Keywords: $2,600,000, $3,120,000, $520,000, $380,000, Country W, Netherfield Glassworks, $1.56
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes imports more expensive in local currency; Higher costs squeeze profit margins | application_max_2: Import bill rises from $2,600,000 to $3,120,000 (extra $520,000); $380,000 reserve is insufficient to cover the extra $520,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of choosing Option B, to raise prices by 12%.
    Answer: First, customers may resist a double-digit price rise and switch to cheaper rivals [k]. The three big customers' contracts are fixed-price worth $1,900,000, so the 12% rise cannot touch them; the full $528,000 must come from smaller and new customers, who are the most price-sensitive [app]. If they defer or cancel orders, sales fall below $4,400,000 and the expected $528,000 gain shrinks fast [an]. Second, raising prices may trigger wider price competition in the office-tower market [k]. Rival glassworks may hold prices to grab Netherfield's share, leaving it with fewer orders to spread fixed costs across [app]. Falling volumes raise unit costs, cutting profit at a time when the $380,000 reserve is already stretched by the $520,000 import rise [an].
    Keywords: Option B, 12%, $528,000, $1,900,000, $4,400,000, $520,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher prices risk losing customers to cheaper rivals; Price rises can trigger competitive price cuts / lost volume | application_max_2: Fixed-price contracts worth $1,900,000 cannot be repriced, so the rise falls on smaller customers; Reference to $528,000 expected gain vs $4,400,000 sales and the $380,000 reserve | analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to lost orders to sales below $4,400,000 and a shrinking gain; Chain from competition on price to lower volume to higher unit costs and lower profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Netherfield Glassworks should raise prices by 12% (Option B)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option B raises prices by 12% across $4,400,000 of annual sales, adding $528,000 a year [k]. That more than covers the extra $520,000 import bill and leaves $8,000 spare, restoring the $380,000 reserve for genuine emergencies such as a machine breakdown [app]. Holding real prices up protects the margin needed to keep the 26 technicians busy and avoids eating into reserves that took years to build [an]. However, Option A absorbs the $520,000 from the $380,000 reserve [k]. This keeps Netherfield fully competitive on price and protects relationships with the three fixed-price customers while their contracts run, which may win follow-on work after next summer [app]. The danger is that the reserve is wiped out entirely and still leaves $140,000 unfunded, so the firm enters winter with no cushion if the dollar weakens further or if repairs arise [an]. Overall, I think Netherfield should choose Option B [eval], because absorbing a $520,000 rise it cannot afford is riskier than the possible loss of price-sensitive orders; the firm should apply the rise to new work first and soften it if order volumes fall sharply [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $528,000, $520,000, $380,000, $1,900,000, 12%, $4,400,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option B: 12% price rise adding $528,000 a year; Option A: absorb the extra $520,000 from the $380,000 reserve | application_max_2: $528,000 gain vs $520,000 extra cost / $8,000 surplus; $380,000 reserve cannot cover $520,000 (shortfall $140,000) / $1,900,000 fixed contracts | analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to covered import bill to restored reserve and financial safety; Chain from absorbing the cost to exhausted reserve and no cushion for further depreciation | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and notes linking the rise to new work first

--- STEM ---
Whinmoor Wool Exports is a partnership in Country X combing and dyeing wool tops on two lines in a converted mill. It sells 70% of its 120,000 kg annual output to garment factories in Country W, invoiced in euros at €18 a kilogram — 84,000 kg worth €1,512,000. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.25 per euro to $1.50 per euro, lifting dollar receipts from $1,890,000 to $2,268,000.

Partners Dana Whitmore and Ruth Iyer must decide how to respond. Option A is to chase 25 new Country W accounts while wool tops are cheap abroad. Option B is to sign a three-year domestic supply contract with knitwear mills in Country X at a fixed dollar price. The partnership employs 19 dyers and expects sheep prices to climb 10% next year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'depreciation'.
    Answer: Depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency against other currencies, so the currency buys less of a foreign currency than it did before [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A fall in the value of one currency; Compared with other currencies / buys less foreign currency than before

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the weaker currency for Whinmoor Wool Exports.
    Answer: First, a weaker currency means each euro of Country W sales converts into more dollars [k]. The 84,000 kg exported at €18 per kilogram bring in €1,512,000, worth $2,268,000 now instead of $1,890,000 at the old rate — an extra $378,000 for no extra output [app]. Second, a weaker currency makes Whinmoor's wool tops cheaper for overseas buyers [k]. Country W garment factories can now buy the same combed, dyed yarn for fewer euros, which should help Whinmoor win the 25 new accounts it is chasing [app].
    Keywords: $1.25, $1.50, $1,890,000, $2,268,000, 84,000, Country W, €18
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A depreciation raises the local currency value of foreign earnings; A depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad / more competitive | application_max_2: 84,000 kg x €18 = €1,512,000 now worth $2,268,000 instead of $1,890,000; Reference to 70% of output exported to Country W / chasing 25 new accounts

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to chase 25 new Country W accounts.
    Answer: First, adding new export accounts raises output volumes and revenue [k]. Selling into 25 additional Country W factories could lift the current 84,000 kg export run-rate well beyond 70% of the 120,000 kg annual output [app]. Higher volume keeps both lines near capacity, spreading fixed mill costs over more kilograms and lifting profit per kilogram [an]. Second, the weaker currency gives Whinmoor room to win share without cutting its €18 price [k]. Country W buyers see the same yarn effectively cheaper to their shareholders at $1.50 per euro, even while Whinmoor still receives $27 a kilogram [app]. Winning the accounts now locks in revenue before sheep prices climb 10% next year, protecting margins while the currency advantage lasts [an].
    Keywords: Option A, 25, Country W, 84,000, 120,000, €18
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: New accounts raise export sales volume and revenue; A weaker currency allows winning share without cutting the foreign price | application_max_2: Reference to 84,000 kg current exports / 70% of 120,000 kg output; Reference to €18 price / $1.50 per euro / 25 new Country W accounts | analysis_max_2: Chain from more accounts to fuller capacity to lower unit costs and higher profit; Chain from currency advantage to locked-in revenue before sheep prices climb 10%

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Whinmoor Wool Exports should chase 25 new Country W accounts (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A commits the partnership to chasing 25 new Country W accounts while the currency favours exporters [k]. At $1.50 per euro, euro invoices at €18 a kilogram bring $27 a kilogram, so extra orders add directly to the $2,268,000 already expected, and spreading output across more customers reduces reliance on the existing 84,000 kg order book [app]. If the two lines run closer to capacity, fixed mill costs spread further, although chasing accounts costs sales time and extra working capital for dyeing and shipping the additional tops [an]. However, Option B signs a three-year domestic supply contract with Country X knitwear mills at a fixed dollar price [k]. It gives the partnership certainty over volume and price, insulating it from a rebound in the dollar and from the expected 10% rise in sheep prices, making cash flow easy to plan for its 19 dyers [app]. The risk is that it locks in fixed dollar prices just as the currency advantage is paying out, and domestic mills may demand keen prices because they know exporters need volume, capping margins for three years [an]. Overall, I think Whinmoor should choose Option A [eval], because the depreciation window is temporary and export demand is already proven by 70% of output going to Country W, so capturing new accounts now builds lasting positions; the domestic contract remains a sensible fallback if sheep costs rise 10% as feared [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $2,268,000, 84,000, 70%, €18, Country W, 10%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: chase 25 new Country W accounts while the currency is favourable; Option B: three-year domestic contract at a fixed dollar price | application_max_2: Reference to $27 per kg at $1.50 per euro vs €18 price and the $2,268,000 export revenue; Reference to 84,000 kg / 70% of output / 19 dyers / expected 10% sheep price rise | analysis_max_2: Chain from new accounts to fuller capacity to better spread of fixed costs and profits; Chain from fixed domestic contract to cost certainty but capped margins and lost currency upside | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and the expected sheep price rise

--- STEM ---
Quillbeck Leather Co is a private limited company in Country X cutting and stitching leather shoulder bags for high-street shops. It imports 25,000 square metres of calfskin a year from Country W at €60 a square metre, a bill of $2,250,000 at $1.50 per euro. The Country X dollar has appreciated from $1.50 per euro to $1.20 per euro, cutting the bill to $1,800,000, a saving of $450,000.

Owner Beatriz Quintero must decide what to do with the saving. Option A is to cut retail prices by 5% across its $3,600,000 of annual shop sales, giving up $180,000 to win market share. Option B is to hold prices and bank the extra margin. The company employs 22 cutters and sewers and sells through 60 shops in Country X.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two effects of a stronger currency on consumers.
    Answer: Imported goods and foreign products become cheaper, so consumers can buy more for their money [1]. Holidays and goods bought abroad cost less in local currency, stretching consumers' purchasing power further [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Imported goods become cheaper for consumers; Consumer purchasing power rises / foreign travel and imports cost less

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Quillbeck Leather Co.
    Answer: First, imports become cheaper for the business [k]. The 25,000 square metres of calfskin now cost $1,800,000 a year instead of $2,250,000, saving $450,000 on its single biggest input [app]. Second, lower input costs improve profit margins without raising prices [k]. Even if only part of the saving is banked, margins on bags sold through its 60 shops improve, leaving more profit available for wages, materials and future investment [app].
    Keywords: $1.50, $1.20, $2,250,000, $1,800,000, $450,000, 60 shops, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A stronger currency makes imports cheaper for the business; Lower import costs improve profit margins | application_max_2: Calfskin bill falls from $2,250,000 to $1,800,000 (saving $450,000); Reference to sales through 60 shops / 25,000 square metres of calfskin

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of choosing Option A, to cut retail prices by 5%.
    Answer: First, lower shelf prices attract price-sensitive shoppers and lift sales volume [k]. Giving up $180,000 across $3,600,000 of annual shop sales is affordable because the import saving is $450,000, leaving $270,000 of the saving to bank [app]. Extra footfall should raise sales of bags and accessories together, lifting total revenue beyond the $180,000 given up [an]. Second, passing on part of the saving builds goodwill and loyalty among regular customers [k]. Shoppers at the 60 shops see leather goods become more affordable, which encourages repeat visits and word-of-mouth recommendations [app]. Stronger loyalty consolidates Quillbeck's position before rivals match the cut, making future price rises or new range launches easier to accept [an].
    Keywords: Option A, 5%, $3,600,000, $180,000, $450,000, 60 shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower prices attract customers and increase sales volume; Passing on savings builds goodwill and customer loyalty | application_max_2: $180,000 cost of the 5% cut is affordable from the $450,000 saving (leaving $270,000); Reference to $3,600,000 shop sales / 60 shops | analysis_max_2: Chain from lower prices to higher footfall to more than offsetting the $180,000 given up; Chain from passed-on savings to loyalty to defending share against rival matching

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Quillbeck Leather Co should cut retail prices by 5% (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A cuts retail prices by 5% across its $3,600,000 of annual shop sales, giving up $180,000 of revenue [k]. The import saving is larger at $450,000, so after funding the cut Quillbeck still retains $270,000 of extra margin, and cheaper bags can win new shoppers across its 60 Country X shops [app]. Attracting price-sensitive customers now builds loyalty and shelf presence ahead of peak seasons, and higher footfall may lift accessory sales as well as bags [an]. However, Option B holds prices and banks the full $450,000 margin [k]. That strengthens retained profit for investment, cushions the business if the dollar slips back against the euro, and avoids the risk that the 5% cut fails to lift volumes — $180,000 is a real cost even if shoppers barely notice [app]. Holding prices also protects the existing margin if wages or transport costs rise later, though rivals may undercut it if they pass on their own savings [an]. Overall, I think Quillbeck should choose Option A [eval], because a 5% cut is affordable from a $450,000 saving and the loyalty and share gains in its home market are worth more than banking the margin now; it should review the cut after two months and restore prices if footfall does not rise [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $450,000, $180,000, $3,600,000, 5%, 60 shops, $1,800,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: 5% price cut costing $180,000 to win market share; Option B: hold prices and bank the $450,000 margin saving | application_max_2: $180,000 of the $450,000 saving returned to shoppers, leaving $270,000; Reference to $3,600,000 shop sales / 60 shops / $1,800,000 calfskin bill | analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to higher footfall and loyalty to long-term share gains; Chain from holding prices to banked margin but loss of competitive goodwill if rivals pass on savings | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes monitoring the cut

--- STEM ---
Holmfirth Surgical Instruments is a private limited company in Country X producing bone drills for export to hospitals in Country W. It sells 320 sets a year at €2,400 each, about €768,000. The dollar-euro rate swung between $1.20 and $1.50 over the past 12 months, so dollar receipts move between $921,600 and $1,152,000, a gap of $230,400.

Managing Director Yusuf Rahman must set the price list for next year's contracts. Option A is to invoice in Country X dollars at $3,000 a set, shifting currency risk to buyers. Option B is to invoice in euros at €2,400 a set and carry the dollar uncertainty. The firm employs 17 machinists and banks through a Country X clearing bank. Each 0.10 move in the rate shifts annual cash by about $76,800.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Outline what is meant by 'exchange-rate fluctuation'.
    Answer: Exchange-rate fluctuation is when the value of one currency against another rises and falls over time rather than staying fixed, so the price of foreign currencies changes frequently [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: The value of one currency against another changes over time; Rates are not fixed / they move up and down frequently

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the fluctuation creates for Holmfirth Surgical Instruments.
    Answer: First, export earnings in dollars become unpredictable [k]. The 320 sets sold each year at €2,400, worth €768,000, can yield $921,600 at the low point of the range or $1,152,000 at the high point, a swing of $230,400 on identical orders [app]. Second, the firm finds budgeting and cash-flow planning difficult [k]. It cannot fix monthly dollar inflows, making it hard to schedule wages for 17 machinists or to plan equipment purchases with confidence [app].
    Keywords: $921,600, $1,152,000, $230,400, $1.20, $1.50, 320, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fluctuations make foreign-currency earnings unpredictable; Fluctuations make budgeting and cash-flow planning difficult | application_max_2: Reference to $921,600 at the low point and $1,152,000 at the high point; Reference to the $230,400 gap / 320 sets / €768,000 a year

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to invoice in Country X dollars at $3,000 a set.
    Answer: First, dollar invoicing removes the exchange-rate risk from Holmfirth entirely [k]. At $3,000 a set the firm knows it will receive about $960,000 a year for 320 sets, whatever happens between $1.20 and $1.50 [app]. Predictable receipts let it budget wages, materials and the clearing-bank account without guessing each month's conversion, cutting financial stress and borrowing costs [an]. Second, invoicing in the home currency simplifies bookkeeping and management reports [k]. All 320 export invoices are written and collected in dollars, so no conversion work or foreign-currency bank charges apply to each deal [app]. Management can compare monthly performance directly against equivalent euro figures, improving control and the speed of decision-making [an].
    Keywords: Option A, $3,000, $1.20, $1.50, 320, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Invoicing in the home currency removes exchange-rate risk for the seller; Invoicing in the home currency simplifies bookkeeping and administration | application_max_2: $3,000 x 320 sets is about $960,000 a year regardless of the rate between $1.20 and $1.50; Reference to 320 sets a year / Country X clearing bank | analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed dollar receipts to reliable budgeting to lower stress and borrowing costs; Chain from dollar invoicing to simpler administration to faster, better-informed decisions

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Holmfirth Surgical Instruments should invoice 2027 orders in dollars at $3,000 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A invoices in Country X dollars at $3,000 per set, fixing annual revenue at about $960,000 for 320 sets [k]. It removes the $230,400 swing between the low and high points of the dollar-euro range, making wages for 17 machinists and loan repayments easy to plan, and it spares the firm conversion fees and extra paperwork [app]. The trade-off is that Country W hospitals face a euro price that moves with the rate — at $1.50 the price is €2,000 and at $1.20 it is €2,500 — so buyers may push back or compare rival quotes, which could cost Holmfirth orders [an]. However, Option B invoices in euros at €2,400 per set [k]. Buyers see a stable euro price, which they prefer, and it may help Holmfirth win and keep hospital contracts against rival suppliers whose quotes also move with the rate [app]. The cost is that Holmfirth carries the full currency risk itself, so a year of adverse rates could cost $230,400 of margin, out of earnings of between $921,600 and $1,152,000 [an]. Overall, I think Holmfirth should choose Option A [eval], because the swing is worth about $230,400 a year — too large to gamble on hospital loyalty, and the firm can discount individual deals if a buyer complains, whereas it cannot recover euro invoices already written; it should review the $3,000 price each quarter as the rate moves [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $3,000, €2,400, $921,600, $1,152,000, $230,400, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: dollar invoicing at $3,000 fixes revenue at about $960,000; Option B: euro invoicing at €2,400 gives buyers price stability but Holmfirth carries the risk | application_max_2: Reference to $921,600–$1,152,000 range and the $230,400 gap; Reference to 320 sets / €2,400 / $3,000 / 17 machinists / Country W hospitals | analysis_max_2: Chain from dollar invoicing to revenue certainty to easier wages and loan planning; Chain from euro invoicing to buyer price stability but $230,400 of currency risk for Holmfirth | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes quarterly price review

--- STEM ---
Brayford Marine Engines is a private limited company in Country X importing outboard motors from Country W, invoiced in euros at €3,100 each. It sells 240 motors a year at an average retail price of $5,400, earning $1,296,000. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.25 per euro to $1.50 per euro, so the import bill rose from $930,000 to $1,116,000, an extra $186,000 a year.

Managing Director Mark Davison must set the spring price list. Option A is to raise retail prices by 20% to $6,480, adding $259,200 a year. Option B is to hold $5,400 and absorb the $186,000 rise from the $260,000 profit reserve. The company employs 9 fitters and a workshop service manager and sells through 4 dealer partners.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the dollar cost of 240 outboard motors at €3,100 each before and after the rate change.
    Answer: 240 × €3,100 = €744,000 a year. Before at $1.25 per euro: €744,000 × 1.25 = $930,000 [1]. After at $1.50 per euro: €744,000 × 1.50 = $1,116,000 [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Correct calculation before the change: $930,000; Correct calculation after the change: $1,116,000

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Brayford Marine Engines.
    Answer: First, imported motors become more expensive in local currency [k]. The 240 motors a year rise from a $930,000 to a $1,116,000 import bill, an extra $186,000 a year for the same stock [app]. Second, margins are squeezed if prices are held at $5,400 [k]. Holding price absorbs $186,000 of the $260,000 profit reserve, leaving just $74,000 of cover for the whole year [app].
    Keywords: $1.25, $1.50, $930,000, $1,116,000, $186,000, $260,000, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes imports more expensive in local currency; Holding prices squeezes profit margins / cash reserves | application_max_2: Import bill rises from $930,000 to $1,116,000 (extra $186,000); $260,000 reserve left with only about $74,000 after absorbing $186,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems of choosing Option A, to raise prices by 20% to $6,480.
    Answer: First, a 20% price rise may drive fishing crews to rival importers or the used-motor market [k]. Moving from $5,400 to $6,480 adds $1,080 to each motor, and crews working on tight margins may simply delay replacing engines [app]. Every ten motors lost cuts $64,800 of revenue, so losing more than forty motors a year would wipe out the $259,200 gain from the rise [an]. Second, the rise may trigger retaliatory discounting across the small-engine market [k]. Brayford's nine fitters could be left with idle workshop hours if demand falls away [app]. Idle capacity spreads fixed workshop costs over fewer units, pushing up unit costs and eroding the very margin the price rise was meant to protect [an].
    Keywords: Option A, $6,480, $5,400, $259,200, 240, $1,296,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Higher prices risk losing price-sensitive customers to rivals; Price rises can trigger competitor discounting and lower volume | application_max_2: Reference to $1,080 increase per motor / 240 motors a year / $259,200 expected gain; Reference to fishing crews being price-sensitive and 9 fitters facing idle hours | analysis_max_2: Chain from lost sales to revenue falling to the point that $259,200 gain is erased; Chain from lower volume to fixed costs spread over fewer units to higher unit costs

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Brayford Marine Engines should raise retail prices by 20% (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A raises the retail price by 20% to $6,480, adding $1,080 per motor and about $259,200 a year at 240 motors [k]. That more than covers the extra $186,000 import cost and would rebuild the profit reserve, a strong position if the dollar falls further [app]. The margin of safety is also comfortable: Brayford can lose about forty motor sales a year, roughly one sixth of volume, before the rise loses its benefit [an]. However, Option B holds the $5,400 price and absorbs the $186,000 rise from the $260,000 profit reserve [k]. Holding prices protects goodwill with fishing crews and ferry operators who buy on reputation and aftercare, keeping the order book and workshop utilisation stable [app]. The risk is that the reserve falls to about $74,000, leaving almost no cover if the rate weakens again or if warranty claims arrive, which could force an emergency loan at painful interest [an]. Overall, I think Brayford should choose Option A [eval], because the price rise stays well ahead of the reserve cushion even after realistic customer losses, and absorbing a permanent $186,000 cost into a $74,000 reserve would be reckless; it should monitor weekly orders and soften the rise if sales collapse [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $6,480, $5,400, $259,200, $186,000, $260,000, 240
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: 20% rise to $6,480, about $259,200 extra a year; Option B: hold $5,400 and absorb $186,000 from the $260,000 reserve | application_max_2: $259,200 gain vs $186,000 extra cost / margin of safety of about forty motors; Reference to $260,000 reserve falling to about $74,000 under Option B / 240 motors / $1,296,000 sales | analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to covered import bill to rebuilt reserve and resilience; Chain from holding price to exhausted reserve to risk of emergency borrowing | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes monitoring weekly orders

--- STEM ---
Ossett Digital Stores is a regional electronics retailer in Country X with 6 shops across the midlands. It imports 20,000 tablets a year from Country W at €150 each, invoiced in euros. The Country X dollar has appreciated from $1.60 per euro to $1.28 per euro, so the cost of each tablet fell from $240 to $192, saving $48 each.

Owner Nadia Hussain must decide the autumn promotion. Option A is to cut shelf prices by 8% across $6,000,000 of tablet sales, giving up $480,000 to advertise record value. Option B is to hold prices and use the saving to fund a 7th shop in the northern suburbs. The chain employs 34 staff and made $410,000 profit last year. Competition from online rivals is intensifying.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two ways consumers benefit when their country's currency appreciates.
    Answer: Imported goods and foreign products become cheaper, so consumers get more for their money [1]. Holidays and purchases abroad cost less in local currency, stretching consumers' budgets further [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Imported goods become cheaper for consumers; Purchasing power rises / foreign spending costs less in local currency

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Ossett Digital Stores.
    Answer: First, the imported tablets it sells cost less to buy in [k]. Each of the 20,000 tablets falls from $240 to $192, saving $48 each — about $960,000 across the year's purchases [app]. Second, Ossett's margins improve if it holds prices while costs fall [k]. The $48 saving on every unit drops straight to profit on $6,000,000 of tablet sales, comfortably lifting profit beyond the $410,000 made last year [app].
    Keywords: $1.60, $1.28, $240, $192, $48, 20,000, $6,000,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A stronger currency makes imports cheaper to buy; Lower import costs improve profit margins | application_max_2: Tablet cost falls from $240 to $192 (saving $48 each); Reference to $6,000,000 of tablet sales / $410,000 profit last year / 20,000 tablets

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to cut shelf prices by 8%.
    Answer: First, lower prices attract value-hungry shoppers away from rivals [k]. Cutting 8% off $6,000,000 of sales returns $480,000 to customers as savings, a strong headline claim for in-store and local advertising [app]. If footfall and basket sizes rise even modestly, tablet and accessory sales together could far outweigh the $480,000 given up [an]. Second, passing on part of the saving builds goodwill and defends market share [k]. Consumers benefit directly from cheaper tablets, strengthening Ossett's value image across the midlands [app]. A reputation for passing on savings makes future promotions more trusted, supporting volume ahead of the 7th shop and spreading fixed costs over more sales [an].
    Keywords: Option A, 8%, $6,000,000, $480,000, $48, 6 shops
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Lower prices attract customers and grow sales volume; Passing on savings builds goodwill and loyalty | application_max_2: Reference to 8% off $6,000,000 = $480,000 returned to shoppers; Reference to the $48 per-tablet import saving / 6 shops across the midlands | analysis_max_2: Chain from lower prices to higher footfall to sales outweighing the $480,000 given up; Chain from passed-on savings to goodwill to defending share ahead of the 7th shop

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ossett Digital Stores should cut shelf prices by 8% (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A cuts shelf prices by 8% across $6,000,000 of tablet sales, giving up $480,000 of revenue [k]. The import saving is larger, at about $960,000 a year, so even after the price cut Ossett keeps roughly half the benefit, and lower shelf prices can lift volume and footfall in all 6 shops ahead of opening a 7th store [app]. Winning midlands shoppers now — before rivals respond — builds loyalty, and accessory sales typically follow tablet purchases, compounding the gain [an]. However, Option B holds prices and uses the saving to fund a 7th shop in the northern suburbs [k]. Retaining the full margin grows profit comfortably beyond last year's $410,000 and funds expansion without borrowing, the bigger long-term prize [app]. The danger is that rivals cut prices first, and Ossett, holding price, loses volume and carries excess tablet stock through the crucial winter season [an]. Overall, I think Ossett should choose Option A [eval], because the $480,000 cut is affordable from a $960,000 saving and the extra share and loyalty are what the northern expansion will live or die by; it should run the promotion for the autumn only, review sales weekly, and bank the surplus toward the 7th shop if the uplift is weak [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $480,000, 8%, $6,000,000, $48, 20,000, $410,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: 8% price cut costing $480,000 to drive volume and share; Option B: hold prices and use the saving to fund a 7th shop | application_max_2: $480,000 of the about $960,000 annual saving returned to shoppers; Reference to $6,000,000 tablet sales / $410,000 profit / 6 shops / 20,000 tablets | analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to higher footfall and loyalty to compounding accessory sales; Chain from holding prices to banked margin but lost volume if rivals cut first | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes a time-limited promotion
