--- STEM ---
Garrowby Grain Co is a partnership in Country X growing wheat and milling flour for export to Country W, while importing all its fertiliser and tractor parts from Country W. It exports 9,000 tonnes of flour a year at $420 a tonne, worth $3,780,000, and imports €700,000 of fertiliser. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.30 per euro to $1.56 per euro.

Partner Edward Garrowby must decide on next season's export pricing. Option A is to sign a two-year export deal at $420 a tonne, fixing dollar revenue. Option B is to quote Country W buyers in euros and let revenue move with the rate. The partnership employs 23 staff and farms 2,600 hectares. The partnership's banker asked for a forecast by Friday.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Identify two effects of a weaker currency on a business that both imports and exports.
    Answer: Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, so export orders and sales may rise [1]. Imports become more expensive in local currency, so the cost of raw materials and parts rises [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers / export demand may rise; Imports become more expensive in local currency / input costs rise

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Garrowby Grain Co.
    Answer: First, its flour exports become cheaper for Country W buyers [k]. At $420 a tonne, flour now costs buyers about €269 per tonne instead of €323, so the 9,000-tonne offer becomes more attractive against Country W domestic mills [app]. Second, imported inputs become more expensive for the partnership [k]. The €700,000 fertiliser and tractor parts bill rises from $910,000 to $1,092,000, an extra $182,000 a year [app].
    Keywords: $1.30, $1.56, $420, €700,000, 9,000, $3,780,000, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers; A depreciation makes imports more expensive in local currency | application_max_2: Reference to €269 vs €323 per tonne at $420 a tonne / 9,000 tonnes of flour; Reference to the €700,000 fertiliser bill rising from $910,000 to $1,092,000

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to sign a two-year export deal at $420.
    Answer: First, a two-year deal at $420 a tonne fixes dollar revenue [k]. With 9,000 tonnes a year, the partnership is guaranteed $3,780,000 in each of the two years, regardless of how the rate moves [app]. Predictable inflows make it far easier to plan cash for the higher fertiliser bills and tractor-part purchases, cutting the risk of short-term borrowing [an]. Second, it removes the risk of an unfavourable move in the exchange rate against the partnership [k]. If the dollar rebounds towards $1.30, euro-quoted revenue under Option B would shrink, but Option A pays out the agreed $420 per tonne in dollars [app]. Certainty also strengthens the partnership's case for credit with suppliers and its bank, easing investment across its 2,600 hectares [an].
    Keywords: Option A, $420, 9,000, $3,780,000, two-year, $1.30, 2,600 hectares
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Fixing the price gives revenue certainty over two years; Fixing the price removes exposure to adverse exchange-rate moves | application_max_2: Reference to $420 x 9,000 tonnes = $3,780,000 a year guaranteed; Reference to $1.30 rebound scenario / 2,600 hectares / fertiliser bills | analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed revenue to reliable cash planning to avoiding short-term borrowing; Chain from removed rate risk to stronger credit standing to easier investment

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Garrowby Grain Co should sign the two-year export deal at $420 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A fixes export revenue at $420 a tonne — $3,780,000 a year for two years on 9,000 tonnes [k]. It guarantees cash far above the extra $182,000 fertiliser cost and lets management plan drilling, buying and 23 staff wages with confidence through 2027 and 2028 [app]. The trade-off is giving up the upside: if the dollar weakens further beyond $1.56, an euro-quoted deal would have paid more dollars, so signing now caps the benefit just when the currency is most favourable [an]. However, Option B quotes Country W buyers in euros and lets revenue float with the rate [k]. If the dollar stays weak or weakens further, euro-invoiced sales could bring in well over $3,780,000, but if it strengthens back towards $1.30, dollar revenue falls and margins compress exactly when input costs stay high [app]. The partnership would carry the full currency risk with no certainty, which is uncomfortable for a 23-staff business farming 2,600 hectares with thin cash cover [an]. Overall, I think Garrowby should choose Option A [eval], because certainty on $3,780,000 a year matters more to a partnership facing a certain $182,000 rise in import costs than speculative gains from further depreciation; it can revisit currency terms when the two-year deal expires [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, $420, $3,780,000, $1.56, $1.30, 9,000, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: two-year deal fixes $420 per tonne ($3,780,000 a year); Option B: euro-quoted pricing lets revenue float with the exchange rate | application_max_2: Reference to $3,780,000 annual revenue / 9,000 tonnes / $420 a tonne; Reference to $1.56 and $1.30 per euro / $182,000 extra fertiliser cost / 23 staff / 2,600 hectares | analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed deal to predictable cash to confident planning of wages and inputs; Chain from euro quoting to either gains above $3,780,000 or falling dollar revenue and squeezed margins | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and the extra fertiliser cost

--- STEM ---
Amberfell Instruments is a private limited company in Country X building laser levels for construction firms in Country W. It exports 1,500 units a year at $380 each, worth $570,000. The dollar has swung between $1.25 and $1.60 per euro over the past year, so profit is hard to predict at budget time.

Director Lena Kovac must decide how to invoice 2027 orders. Option A is to invoice in Country X dollars at $380 a unit and shift the risk to buyers. Option B is to invoice in euros at €304 a unit, giving $570,000 at $1.25 per euro or $729,600 at $1.60 per euro. The firm employs 24 specialists and buys imported lenses costing €96,000 a year. The firm plans to exhibit at the trade fair in March.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Calculate the dollar revenue at $1.25 and $1.60 per euro if 1,500 units are invoiced at €304 each.
    Answer: 1,500 × €304 = €456,000 a year. At $1.25 per euro: €456,000 × 1.25 = $570,000 [1]. At $1.60 per euro: €456,000 × 1.60 = $729,600 [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Correct calculation at $1.25 per euro: $570,000; Correct calculation at $1.60 per euro: $729,600

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems the exchange-rate swing creates for Amberfell Instruments.
    Answer: First, it makes annual revenue unpredictable [k]. Invoicing in euros could yield $570,000 at $1.25 per euro or $729,600 at $1.60 per euro — a difference of $159,600 on exactly the same sales of 1,500 units [app]. Second, the firm finds costing and pricing very difficult [k]. It cannot set firm budgets for wages for 24 specialists or for imported lenses when the payout for identical orders can swing by six figures in a single year [app].
    Keywords: $1.25, $1.60, $570,000, $729,600, €304, 1,500, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Exchange-rate swings make revenue unpredictable; Exchange-rate swings make budgeting and pricing decisions difficult | application_max_2: Reference to $570,000 at $1.25 vs $729,600 at $1.60 per euro; Reference to the $159,600 swing / 1,500 units / 24 specialists

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of choosing Option B, to invoice in euros at €304.
    Answer: First, euro invoicing appeals strongly to Country W buyers [k]. A fixed €304 per unit removes currency risk for the construction firms, so their purchasing departments can approve orders without worrying about monthly rate moves [app]. Lower buyer risk should win repeat orders against rivals who quote in volatile currencies, keeping the workshop fuller [an]. Second, if the dollar weakens further, euro invoices convert to more dollars [k]. At $1.60, 1,500 units at €304 yield $729,600 — $159,600 above the $570,000 floor — while the imported lenses at €96,000 a year also cost more dollars at the same time [app]. This partial natural offset protects margin without any special financial instruments [an].
    Keywords: Option B, €304, $1.60, $729,600, $570,000, €96,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Invoicing in the buyer's currency removes buyer risk and can win orders; A weaker dollar raises the local-currency value of foreign earnings | application_max_2: Reference to €304 fixed unit price appealing to Country W construction firms; Reference to $729,600 at $1.60 vs $570,000 at $1.25 and €96,000 lenses rising in dollar terms | analysis_max_2: Chain from buyer price certainty to more repeat orders and fuller capacity; Chain from euro invoicing to revenue and lens costs moving together to protected margin

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Amberfell Instruments should invoice 2027 orders in euros at €304 (Option B)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option B invoices in euros at €304 per unit, so Country W buyers face a stable price and no currency risk [k]. That should help Amberfell win and keep contracts in a market where buyers prefer simplicity, and at $1.60 the same invoices yield $729,600, comfortably covering the €96,000 lens cost and lifting margin well above the $570,000 floor [app]. The trade-off is that if the dollar strengthens towards $1.25, Amberfell receives only $570,000 from the same orders, with zero upside if the dollar weakens further [an]. However, Option A invoices in dollars at $380, fixing Amberfell's annual revenue at $570,000 whatever happens to the rate [k]. That gives complete certainty for budgeting 24 specialists' wages and removes the $159,600 swing, but it pushes all currency risk onto buyers: at $1.60 they would pay just €237.50, while at $1.25 they pay €304, which buyers will resist [app]. The risk is losing price-sensitive orders to suppliers who quote in euros [an]. Overall, I think Amberfell should choose Option B [eval], because revenue and lens costs are both priced in euros, so euro invoicing creates a natural balance that a dollar invoice cannot match; it should monitor the rate monthly and raise the €304 price if the dollar strengthens persistently [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, €304, $380, $570,000, $729,600, €96,000, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option B: euro invoicing at €304 gives buyers price certainty; Option A: dollar invoicing at $380 fixes revenue but shifts risk onto buyers | application_max_2: Reference to $570,000 at $1.25 and $729,600 at $1.60 per euro; Reference to $380 dollar price / €96,000 lenses / 24 specialists / Country W buyers | analysis_max_2: Chain from euro invoicing to buyer certainty to more orders and natural offset of euro costs; Chain from dollar invoicing to fixed $570,000 but buyers resisting a swinging euro price | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes monitoring the rate monthly

--- STEM ---
Larkhill Brewery Co is a private limited company in Country X brewing craft ale for pubs and bottle shops. It exports 30% of its 480,000 litres a year to Country W at $6 a litre — 144,000 litres worth $864,000 — and imports hops from Country W at €320,000 a year. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.30 per euro to $1.56 per euro.

Founder Sofia Almeida must decide the 2027 strategy. Option A is to expand exports, since the ale is now cheaper for Country W buyers at about €3.85 a litre instead of €4.62. Option B is to raise domestic pub prices by 4% on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640 to offset pricier hops. The brewery employs 14 staff and made $290,000 profit last year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: State two effects of a depreciation on a business that imports its raw materials.
    Answer: Imports become more expensive in the local currency, so raw material costs rise [1]. Profit margins are squeezed because prices cannot always be raised to cover the higher input costs [1].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Imports become more expensive in local currency; Profit margins are squeezed / input costs rise

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Larkhill Brewery Co.
    Answer: First, its ale exports become cheaper for Country W buyers [k]. At $6 a litre, the 144,000 litres exported now cost buyers about €3.85 a litre instead of €4.62, making the push into Country W more competitive without cutting the dollar price [app]. Second, imported hops become more expensive for the brewery [k]. The €320,000 hop bill rises from $416,000 to $499,200 a year, an extra $83,200 of cost [app].
    Keywords: $1.30, $1.56, €320,000, $864,000, €3.85, €4.62, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers; A depreciation makes imported raw materials more expensive | application_max_2: Reference to €3.85 vs €4.62 per litre / 144,000 litres / $864,000 export revenue; Reference to the €320,000 hop bill rising from $416,000 to $499,200 (extra $83,200)

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to expand exports.
    Answer: First, expanding exports exploits the weaker currency immediately [k]. With ale effectively cheaper at €3.85 a litre, Larkhill can pitch to new Country W pubs and bottle shops without cutting its $6 price [app]. Winning accounts now locks in demand before rivals adjust, spreading fixed brewhouse costs over more litres and lifting profit beyond the $290,000 of last year [an]. Second, growing beyond the 30% export share reduces reliance on Country X pubs [k]. Increasing output past the 144,000 litres now shipped abroad diversifies the customer base across two countries [app]. Diversification protects revenue if domestic pub closures or duty changes hurt the home market, and export success can later support stronger negotiating positions with distributors [an].
    Keywords: Option A, €3.85, 144,000, 30%, $6, $290,000, Country W
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A weaker currency lets the business expand exports without cutting price; Export growth reduces dependence on the domestic market / diversifies risk | application_max_2: Reference to €3.85 a litre / $6 price / pitching to new Country W pubs; Reference to 30% export share / 144,000 litres / $290,000 profit last year | analysis_max_2: Chain from cheaper ale abroad to locked-in demand to fuller capacity and higher profit; Chain from diversification to protected revenue if the home market weakens

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Larkhill Brewery Co should expand exports (Option A)? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Option A expands exports while ale is cheap for Country W buyers at about €3.85 a litre [k]. The existing 144,000 litres already earn $864,000, and each extra litre sold at $6 adds margin while the dollar stays weak, so expanding now is the highest-return use of the brewery's capacity [app]. Success would spread fixed costs further and could lift profit well above the $290,000 achieved last year [an]. However, Option B raises domestic pub prices by 4% on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640 [k]. That almost covers the $83,200 extra cost of imported hops, protecting margins with no overseas risk, no new working capital and no sales effort in a foreign market, and pubs usually accept modest rises more easily than large ones [app]. The danger is that 4% may still put some price-sensitive drinkers off, and it does nothing to capture the cheap-ale window or to cut dependence on the 70% domestic share [an]. Overall, I think Larkhill should choose Option A [eval], because the depreciation is temporary and only Option A converts it into lasting market position and profit growth; the brewery should keep domestic prices under review and apply Option B if export orders disappoint or the dollar rebounds [eval].
    Keywords: Option A, Option B, €3.85, €4.62, $80,640, $290,000, 144,000, $864,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Option A: expand exports while the ale is cheap for Country W buyers; Option B: 4% domestic price rise on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640 | application_max_2: Reference to €3.85 vs €4.62 a litre / $6 price / $864,000 export revenue; Reference to $80,640 vs $83,200 extra hop cost / $290,000 profit / 144,000 litres / 70% domestic share | analysis_max_2: Chain from cheaper ale abroad to growing export volume to spread fixed costs and higher profit; Chain from 4% domestic rise to covered hop costs but lost share and untapped export opportunity | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B; Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes keeping Option B under review

--- STEM ---
Ashvale Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company that imports and wholesales glazed wall tiles across Country X. The business has traded for 9 years, employs 26 staff and generates $3,400,000 in annual revenue. Around 60% of its stock, worth $400,000 each year, is bought from Country Z, which lies outside the Celestra Trade Bloc of which Country X is a member.

From next quarter, the Country X government will raise the import tariff on wall tiles from Country Z from 10% to 25%. Domestic tile makers, who already supply 40% of Ashvale's stock, welcome the protection. Management must now decide whether to switch entirely to domestic suppliers or keep importing from Country Z and pass the extra $60,000 annual cost on to retail customers, who currently pay $45 per box.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'import tariff'.
    Answer: A tax placed on goods or services brought into a country, increasing their price to buyers [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A tax on imports / goods brought into a country; Raises the price of the imported good / protects domestic industry

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two impacts on Ashvale Ceramics Ltd of the tariff rising from 10% to 25%.
    Answer: Impact 1: Raised import costs [k], adding about $60,000 a year to the $400,000 of Country Z stock Ashvale buys annually [app]. Impact 2: Improved price competitiveness of domestic tiles [k], allowing Ashvale to sell more of the 40% domestic stock it already handles [app].
    Keywords: Ashvale Ceramics Ltd, import tariff, Country Z, $400,000, $60,000, Celestra Trade Bloc, $45, glazed wall tiles
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Tariff raises the cost/price of imports; Tariff makes domestic goods relatively more competitive | application_max_2: $400,000 of Country Z stock; the 15 percentage point rise adds about $60,000 a year; Domestic tiles already supply 40% of stock so this share can grow

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the higher tariff could affect Ashvale Ceramics' retail customers.
    Answer: Way 1: Higher retail prices for imported tiles [k], as Ashvale passes on the extra $60,000 a year to shoppers paying $45 per box [app], leaving customers with less disposable income for other purchases [an]. Way 2: Reduced choice on the shelves [k], because fewer Country Z tile lines will be stocked from next quarter [app], so customers may not find the exact style or size they want [an].
    Keywords: retail customers, $45, Country Z, $60,000, Ashvale Ceramics Ltd, 10%, 25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Prices of imported goods rise when a tariff is charged; Range/stock of imported goods falls | application_max_2: Extra $60,000 a year passed on; customers pay $45 per box; Country Z lines will be restocked less often from next quarter | analysis_max_2: Households have less disposable income / switch spending elsewhere; Customers cannot find desired styles and may shop elsewhere

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Ashvale Ceramics Ltd should switch entirely to domestic suppliers or continue importing tiles from Country Z? Justify your answer.
    Answer: One option is to switch entirely to domestic suppliers, which would remove the $60,000 yearly tariff cost [k]; with domestic tiles already supplying 40% of stock, Ashvale could expand buying from proven local makers and protect its $3,400,000 revenue [app]. This would cut delivery lead times and reduce exposure to further tariff changes [an]. The alternative is to keep importing from Country Z, preserving the wide glazed wall tile range that customers pay $45 per box for [app]; margins would shrink as the duty rises to 25%, so prices may need to rise [an]. Imported goods face higher costs when governments use tariffs to protect local industry [k]. Overall, switching entirely to domestic suppliers is better because the 25% tariff is confirmed for next quarter and saving $60,000 a year directly improves profit [eval], although keeping a small premium import line could retain choice-conscious customers [eval].
    Keywords: $60,000, Country Z, $3,400,000, $45, glazed wall tiles, 25%, domestic suppliers
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Domestic suppliers avoid the import tariff cost; Tariffs raise the cost of imported goods above domestic alternatives | application_max_2: $60,000 yearly cost removed; domestic tiles already 40% of stock; Country Z range preserved; $45 per box; 25% duty from next quarter | analysis_max_2: Shorter lead times and lower risk of further tariff rises; Margins shrink and shop prices may have to rise for imported styles | evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement using stem figures; Weighs the trade-off and qualifies the recommendation

--- STEM ---
Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd is a family-owned chicken farm and processing business in rural Country X. It has operated for 11 years, employs 45 workers and sells 9,000 chickens every week at an average of $4.50 per kilogram, generating $6,000,000 in annual revenue. The farm is running at 85% of its housing capacity and already supplies several national supermarket chains with fresh chicken each week.

The Country X government has announced that the import quota for chicken meat will fall from 8,000 tonnes to 3,000 tonnes a year, to protect domestic producers. Imported frozen chicken, previously cheaper at $3.20 per kilogram, will become scarcer in supermarkets. Hollinbrook could invest $1,200,000 in two new sheds to house 2,500 more birds a week, or continue at its current output.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'import quota'.
    Answer: A physical limit on the quantity of a good that a country allows to be imported [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A limit on the quantity/amount of an import; Restricts how much of the good may enter the country

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd of the government cutting the chicken import quota from 8,000 to 3,000 tonnes.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Reduced competition from imports [k], so supermarkets seeking chicken at around $4.50 per kilogram are more likely to contract Hollinbrook's 9,000 weekly birds [app]. Benefit 2: Opportunity to raise price or output [k], as scarce supply lets the farm push up margins or fill its 85% capacity with extra orders [app].
    Keywords: Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd, import quota, 8,000, 3,000, 9,000, $4.50, supermarket
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Limiting import supply reduces foreign competition for domestic firms; Domestic firms can sell more and/or charge higher prices when imports are capped | application_max_2: 9,000 chickens a week at $4.50 offered to supermarkets; Farm only at 85% capacity so room to raise sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of relying on the import quota for Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd's success.
    Answer: Limitation 1: The quota could be relaxed later [k], so demand for Hollinbrook's chicken could fall back to supermarkets' previous import mix [app], leaving the farm with half-empty sheds and falling capacity utilisation [an]. Limitation 2: Protection reduces pressure to improve efficiency [k], so the farm may not tackle its $6,000,000 cost base as it would under import competition [app], meaning it struggles on price if the 3,000-tonne protection ends [an].
    Keywords: import quota, Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd, 3,000, $6,000,000, 85%, $3.20
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Quotas can be temporary and removed later; Protection removes the incentive to improve efficiency / cut costs | application_max_2: If imports return to 8,000 tonnes, supermarket demand for domestic chicken falls; Revenue of $6,000,000 without cost pressure from cheaper $3.20 imports | analysis_max_2: Idle sheds / falling capacity utilisation if demand slips; Uncompetitive prices once protection ends / lower long-term profit

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd should invest $1,200,000 in two new sheds to increase output or maintain its current output? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing $1,200,000 in two new sheds would raise capacity by 2,500 birds a week [k]; with imported chicken capped at 3,000 tonnes a year, supermarket demand is likely to shift to domestic suppliers such as Hollinbrook's 9,000-bird weekly output [app], lifting revenue above $6,000,000 and pushing capacity past 85% [an]. However, maintaining current output avoids the $1,200,000 cost and any debt risk [k]; if the quota is relaxed or demand softens, the extra sheds would sit empty and cut profit [app], leaving the farm with weak cash flow [an]. Overall, investing in the sheds is the better option because the quota cut from 8,000 to 3,000 tonnes is a confirmed government policy and the gain comes through sales of 2,500 extra birds a week [eval], although the board should secure supermarket contracts before building begins [eval].
    Keywords: $1,200,000, 2,500, 3,000 tonnes, 9,000, $6,000,000, 85%, import quota, Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Expansion increases capacity/output; Maintaining output avoids large capital spending / debt | application_max_2: 2,500 extra birds a week; quota capped at 3,000 tonnes; $1,200,000 cost; quota could be relaxed | analysis_max_2: Revenue rises above $6,000,000; capacity utilisation improves beyond 85%; Idle sheds and weak cash flow if demand falls back | evaluation_max_2: Overall justified judgement tied to the confirmed quota cut; Acknowledges condition/uncertainty before recommending

--- STEM ---

About 70% of stock comes from outside the Orin Trade Bloc. The government has confirmed an 18% import tariff plus an annual quota of 200,000 toy units on non-bloc imports, down from unlimited entry. Bloc-made toys enter tariff-free but cost about 12% more at wholesale and come in a narrower range. Management expects the average shelf price of an imported toy to rise from $50 to $59, while overall choice on the shelves will shrink.

  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'trade bloc'.
    Answer: A group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers between members to encourage trade [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A group of countries trading together; Trade barriers between members are reduced or removed

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the 18% import tariff on Willow & Whistle Toys.
    Answer: Effect 1: Higher cost of imported stock [k], since the average shelf price of an imported toy rises from $50 to $59 under the 18% tariff [app]. Effect 2: Greater appeal of bloc-made toys [k], which enter the Orin Trade Bloc tariff-free and so become more price-competitive in the shop's range [app].
    Keywords: Willow & Whistle Toys, 18%, $50, $59, Orin Trade Bloc, 70%, trade bloc
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A tariff raises the price of imported goods; Tariffs improve the competitiveness of goods from inside the bloc | application_max_2: Average imported toy price rises from $50 to $59; Bloc-made toys enter tariff-free and become comparatively cheaper

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two ways the import quota of 200,000 toy units could affect the shop's customers.
    Answer: Way 1: Fewer toys available on the shelves [k], as only 200,000 non-bloc units may enter Country X each year [app], so popular imported lines may sell out as families shop for birthdays [an]. Way 2: Less product choice for shoppers [k], because the shop cannot restock its usual import-heavy range and must narrow the 70% of stock sourced from outside the Orin Trade Bloc [app], leaving customers with fewer styles and brands [an].
    Keywords: 200,000, Country X, Orin Trade Bloc, 70%, imported toy, Willow & Whistle Toys
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A quota caps the volume of imports available; Reduced import supply reduces customer choice / availability | application_max_2: Only 200,000 non-bloc toy units may enter each year; 70% of stock comes from outside the Orin Trade Bloc | analysis_max_2: Popular lines sell out / customers cannot buy wanted toys; Narrower range means shoppers switch to other shops

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Willow & Whistle Toys should switch to mainly bloc-made toys or keep its current import-heavy range? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching to mainly bloc-made toys removes the 18% tariff cost [k]; since tariff-free bloc toys are only about 12% more expensive at wholesale, the shop's shelf prices would stay closer to $50 levels while protecting margins [app]. This also strengthens ties with bloc suppliers and guarantees supply under the quota [an]. However, keeping the import-heavy range preserves the variety customers value, with 70% of stock from outside the Orin Trade Bloc [app]; the 200,000-unit quota and the $59 price point will squeeze sales and margins [an]. Import duties raise consumer prices and reduce choice when stocked goods come from outside a trade bloc [k]. Overall, switching to mainly bloc-made toys is better because the quota and 18% tariff are confirmed, whereas the 12% wholesale premium is modest against avoiding a $9 price rise per toy [eval], although the shop should keep a small import range for loyal customers [eval].
    Keywords: 18%, 12%, Orin Trade Bloc, 70%, $59, 200,000, bloc-made toys
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Bloc-made goods enter tariff-free inside the bloc; Tariffs raise consumer prices and reduce choice | application_max_2: Tariff-free toys only 12% dearer at wholesale vs $59 price point; 70% of stock from outside bloc; 200,000-unit quota confirmed | analysis_max_2: Secures supply and protects margins within the quota; Import range squeezes sales and margins as prices rise to $59 | evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified overall recommendation with figures; Recognises conditions under which keeping some imports still works

    Keywords: Vesper Electronics Assembly Ltd, Meridia Free Trade Area, 16%, $7,700,000, $1,232,000, 190 million, Country W

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Vesper Electronics Assembly Ltd of relocating to Country W.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Relocating requires major capital investment / set-up costs; Relocation can cause redundancies and disruption for the workforce | application_max_2: $6,500,000 to build the Country W plant; 210 Country X workers face redundancy or relocation | analysis_max_2: Stretched cash flow / higher financial risk; Low morale and disrupted output during transition

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Vesper Electronics Assembly Ltd should build the new assembly plant in Country W or keep producing in Country X? Justify your answer.

--- STEM ---
Dunfell Steel Rolling Co is a public limited company operating a rolling mill in northern Country X. The mill has run for 17 years, employs 340 workers and produces reinforcing bar for construction firms, with annual revenue of $12,000,000. Capacity utilisation stands at 60%, leaving room to expand output. Around 20% of sales, worth $2,400,000, go to Country Y.

The Country X government is considering a 30% tariff on imported steel to protect domestic producers. Supporters claim the tariff would shield the industry and its jobs, but critics note it may raise prices for construction firms and prompt Country Y to retaliate against Country X exports. Dunfell's directors must decide whether to back the proposal, covering a steel import market worth $90,000,000 a year, or oppose it openly.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'protectionism'.
    Answer: Government action, such as tariffs or quotas, to restrict imports and shelter domestic producers from foreign competition [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Government action to restrict imports (tariffs, quotas); Aims to shelter domestic producers from foreign competition

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Dunfell Steel Rolling Co of the proposed 30% tariff on imported steel.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Reduced foreign competition [k], making Dunfell's reinforcing bar more competitive than imported steel, which would cost 30% more [app]. Benefit 2: Higher sales volumes [k], with the mill at 60% capacity, construction firms could shift rebar orders to Dunfell, raising output and its $12,000,000 revenue [app].
    Keywords: Dunfell Steel Rolling Co, 30%, reinforcing bar, 60%, $12,000,000, imported steel
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Tariff raises import prices so domestic goods undercut them; Domestic producers can increase sales volumes | application_max_2: Imported steel costs 30% more than Dunfell's reinforcing bar; Mill only at 60% capacity so room to lift output and $12,000,000 revenue

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two limitations of the proposed 30% tariff for Dunfell Steel Rolling Co.
    Answer: Limitation 1: Risk of retaliation by Country Y [k], which buys $2,400,000 of Dunfell's steel each year and could impose its own tariff in response [app], costing Dunfell part of its export business and forcing the mill to find new buyers [an]. Limitation 2: Higher steel prices for construction firms [k], which could dampen building activity in Country X [app], cutting demand for Dunfell's reinforcing bar and leaving the mill short of orders [an].
    Keywords: Country Y, $2,400,000, 30%, Dunfell Steel Rolling Co, construction firms, reinforcing bar
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Tariffs can provoke retaliation from trading partners; Tariffs raise input/output prices and can reduce demand | application_max_2: Country Y buys $2,400,000 of exports; could retaliate; Construction firms pay more for reinforcing bar | analysis_max_2: Export sales lost / need new markets; Demand for the mill's output falls / under-utilised capacity

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the government should introduce the 30% tariff on imported steel, considering Dunfell Steel Rolling Co? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The 30% tariff would shelter Dunfell Steel Rolling Co from cheaper foreign steel [k], allowing its reinforcing bar to win orders at a mill running at only 60% capacity, supporting 340 workers and part of its $12,000,000 revenue [app]; protecting home industry should lift domestic output and employment [an]. However, protecting an industry can breed complacency, letting inefficient firms survive without cutting costs [k]. Country Y, which buys $2,400,000 of Dunfell's output, could retaliate with its own tariff [app], costing Dunfell export sales and profits [an]. Overall, on balance the tariff is more likely to harm Dunfell in the long run because retaliation would wipe out the $2,400,000 export stream and customer prices would rise across a $90,000,000 market [eval], although in the short term the mill would gain orders and capacity use [eval].
    Keywords: 30%, 60%, 340, Country Y, $2,400,000, $12,000,000, reinforcing bar, $90,000,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Tariffs protect domestic producers from foreign competition; Protection can reduce the incentive to improve efficiency | application_max_2: 60% capacity; 340 workers; $12,000,000 revenue; Country Y buys $2,400,000 of exports; $90,000,000 steel market | analysis_max_2: Short-run boost to output, jobs and domestic capacity use; Retaliation and higher prices cut demand and export profit | evaluation_max_2: Balanced judgement reaching a clear conclusion; Weighs short-term gain against long-term harm using figures

--- STEM ---
Kingsley Motor Group Plc is a multinational company with assembly plants in 5 countries. Its Country X plant has operated for 14 years, employs 1,800 workers and builds 24,000 vehicles a year, generating $480,000,000 in revenue. Country X sits inside the Valdonia Customs Union, whose members charge a 12% tariff on vehicle parts imported from outside the union.

Kingsley imports engines and gearboxes from Country F, outside the union, at a cost of $60,000,000 a year, paying $7,200,000 in tariffs. A union-based supplier has quoted a price 15% higher, about $69,000,000 a year, but with tariff-free delivery and faster lead times. The government has warned the tariff could rise to 20% within 2 years. The board must decide whether to switch suppliers or stay with the Country F parts.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'multinational company (MNC)'.
    Answer: A company that has operations or facilities in two or more countries [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A company operating in more than one country; Has facilities/operations across national borders

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for Kingsley Motor Group Plc of switching to union-based parts suppliers.
    Answer: Benefit 1: No tariff on parts [k], avoiding the $7,200,000 a year the 12% tariff costs on $60,000,000 of imports [app]. Benefit 2: Faster, more reliable delivery [k], as union-based suppliers quoted tariff-free delivery with shorter lead times, reducing stock needs for the 24,000 vehicles built each year [app].
    Keywords: Kingsley Motor Group Plc, $7,200,000, 12%, $60,000,000, 24,000, Valdonia Customs Union
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying inside a customs union avoids the import tariff; Local/bloc sourcing shortens delivery times and improves reliability | application_max_2: Saves $7,200,000 a year (12% on $60,000,000); 24,000 vehicles a year; union suppliers quote faster lead times

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems for Kingsley Motor Group Plc of switching to union-based suppliers.
    Answer: Problem 1: Higher parts prices [k], with union-based suppliers quoting about $69,000,000 a year, roughly $9,000,000 more than Country F imports [app], squeezing margins unless vehicle prices rise [an]. Problem 2: Limited supplier choice and quality risk [k], as the union has few qualified engine and gearbox makers [app], creating dependence on a small number of suppliers and possible delivery delays [an].
    Keywords: union-based supplier, $69,000,000, 24,000, Country F, Kingsley Motor Group Plc, engines and gearboxes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Bloc-based inputs may cost more than non-bloc imports; Fewer qualified suppliers raises dependence and supply risk | application_max_2: $69,000,000 quote vs $60,000,000; about $9,000,000 more a year; Engines and gearboxes; few union-based manufacturers | analysis_max_2: Margins squeezed unless vehicle prices increase; Supply delays / over-reliance on a few suppliers hurt output

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Kingsley Motor Group Plc should switch parts sourcing to union-based suppliers inside the Valdonia Customs Union? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Switching removes the 12% tariff [k], saving $7,200,000 a year on parts worth $60,000,000 and shielding the plant if the tariff rises to 20% within 2 years, when the duty would cost $12,000,000 [app]; this would improve margins and protect the 1,800 jobs at the Country X plant [an]. However, staying with Country F keeps the lowest quoted price but relies on imports facing $7,200,000 to $12,000,000 of tariff costs [app], weakening competitiveness over time [an]. Free trade within a customs union lowers the cost of member-based sourcing [k]. Overall, Kingsley should switch to union-based suppliers because the saving beats the 15% price premium if the tariff rises to 20% [eval], although it should negotiate phased contracts to manage quality risk [eval].
    Keywords: $7,200,000, 12%, 20%, 2 years, $60,000,000, 1,800, Valdonia Customs Union, $69,000,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Sourcing inside a customs union avoids the common external tariff; Free trade agreements lower the cost of trade between members | application_max_2: $7,200,000 now rising to $12,000,000 if tariff hits 20%; Union quote $69,000,000 vs Country F $60,000,000; tariff-free delivery | analysis_max_2: Margins improve and 1,800 jobs are protected; Staying with Country F weakens competitiveness as tariffs rise | evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement with quantitative reasoning; Qualifies the switch with a risk-management condition

Advantage 2: New customer base [k], adding Country B's 300 stores to income alongside its $2,750,000 home-market sales [app].
    Keywords: Fernhollow Biscuit Co, Country B, Orin Trade Bloc, 40,000 cases, $9.00, $360,000, $2,750,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Exports to bloc members enter without tariffs; Exporting adds a new customer base / diversifies sales | application_max_2: 40,000 cases a year at $9.00; tariff-free within the Orin Trade Bloc; 300 Country B stores to add to $2,750,000 home sales

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two challenges for Fernhollow Biscuit Co of serving Country B.
    Answer: Challenge 1: Strong local competition [k], as three established biscuit makers already supply Country B [app], forcing Fernhollow to spend heavily on promotion or undercut on price to win shelf space [an]. Challenge 2: Extra logistics costs [k], with transport and insurance adding $18,000 a year to the contract [app], cutting into the net gain from the $360,000 deal [an].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Foreign markets have established local competitors; Exporting adds transport and insurance costs | application_max_2: Three established biscuit makers already supply Country B; $18,000 a year transport and insurance cost | analysis_max_2: Higher promotion spend or lower prices needed to win distribution; Net revenue from the $360,000 deal is reduced

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Fernhollow Biscuit Co should accept the Country B export contract or expand domestic distribution into 400 more outlets? Justify your answer.

However, domestic expansion into 400 more outlets reaches familiar shoppers with none of the $18,000 transport and insurance costs [app], protecting margins while the firm learns foreign trade [an]. Successful exporting widens markets and can lift output and profit [k]. Overall, Fernhollow should accept the Country B contract because bloc membership makes the trade tariff-free and the chain is committed to 300 stores [eval], although it should pilot the stores before any wider export push [eval].
    Keywords: $360,000, 40,000 cases, $9.00, Country B, $18,000, 80%, 1,200, Orin Trade Bloc
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Export contracts can secure foreign revenue and diversify markets; Exporting widens markets and can raise output and profit | application_max_2: $360,000; 40,000 cases at $9.00; 300 stores; 80% home sales; Domestic push adds 400 outlets; avoids $18,000 logistics cost | analysis_max_2: Diversification and brand building overseas; Lower-risk margins from domestic growth before exporting widely | evaluation_max_2: Clear justified choice with evidence from the stem; Qualifies recommendation with a cautious first step

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Buying goods or services from abroad; Goods or services come from another/foreign country

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two effects of the import quota cut on Varrow Bay Fisheries Ltd.
    Answer: Effect 1: Reduced cod supply [k], as the quota falls from 6,000 to 2,000 tonnes a year while Varrow Bay currently imports 5,500 tonnes [app]. Effect 2: Higher input costs [k], with domestic cod at $1,150 per tonne replacing Country D supplies at $900 [app].
    Keywords: Varrow Bay Fisheries Ltd, import quota, 6,000, 2,000, 5,500, $900, $1,150
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A lower quota restricts the volume of imports available; Scarcer domestic supply costs more than imports | application_max_2: Quota falls from 6,000 to 2,000 tonnes vs 5,500 tonnes imported now; Domestic cod $1,150 vs $900 per tonne from Country D

  Qc [6 marks]

Effect 2: Higher prices [k], as cod rises to $1,150 per tonne with only 1,800 tonnes of spare catch available [app], lifting revenue for domestic fishermen [an].

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Cutting imports raises demand for domestic producers; Scarcity of domestic supply pushes prices up | application_max_2: Processors must source up to 2,000 tonnes domestically; Only 1,800 tonnes spare catch; $1,150 per tonne | analysis_max_2: Fuller order books / higher utilisation for fishing boats; Higher prices raise fishermen's revenue

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think Varrow Bay Fisheries Ltd should invest $850,000 in its own trawler or sign long-term contracts with domestic fishing boats? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Investing $850,000 in a trawler would secure cod supplies when imports are capped at 2,000 tonnes [k], letting Varrow Bay catch its own fish instead of paying $1,150 per tonne for scarce domestic landings and protecting its $7,500,000 revenue [app]; reliable supply supports supermarket listings and avoids stockouts [an]. Signing contracts with domestic boats needs no $850,000 upfront cost [k], but only about 1,800 tonnes of spare catch exists, so prices may stay firm and volumes limited [app], risking supply disputes [an]. Overall, Varrow Bay should sign contracts with domestic boats now because it avoids the $850,000 commitment while the quota's long-term future is unclear [eval], although it should revisit the trawler purchase if the quota becomes permanent [eval].

--- STEM ---
Aldercombe Footwear Ltd is a private limited company that manufactures leather shoes in Country X. The factory has operated for 15 years, employs 75 workers and produces 85,000 pairs a year, generating $5,200,000 in annual revenue. Its best-selling shoe retails at $65, slightly above the $58 price of imported rivals from Country F.

The government has introduced a 22% tariff on imported footwear to protect domestic manufacturers. Imported rival shoes will now cost about $71 at the border, above Aldercombe's price. However, the tariff is temporary, with a review after 3 years, and some ministers warn protection breeds inefficiency. Directors are weighing whether to invest $1,100,000 in new lasting machines to cut production costs before the review, or to enjoy the shelter the tariff provides.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Qa [2 marks]
    Question: Define 'trade barrier'.
    Answer: Any government measure that restricts international trade, such as a tariff or quota [2].
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: A government measure restricting international trade; Examples include tariffs and quotas

  Qb [4 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits of the 22% tariff for Aldercombe Footwear Ltd.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Removes price undercutting [k], as imported rivals from Country F will now retail at about $71, above Aldercombe's $65 price [app]. Benefit 2: Higher sales volumes [k], as price-sensitive shoppers shift to the domestic 85,000 pairs Aldercombe can supply with 75 workers [app].
    Keywords: Aldercombe Footwear Ltd, 22%, $71, $65, Country F, 85,000, 75
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Tariff raises import prices so domestic goods win on price; Domestic firms gain market share / higher sales volumes | application_max_2: Country F imports now about $71 vs Aldercombe's $65; Capacity of 85,000 pairs a year with 75 workers

  Qc [6 marks]
    Question: Explain two drawbacks of relying on the tariff for Aldercombe Footwear Ltd's success.
    Answer: Drawback 1: Complacency risk [k], as shelter from competition may let inefficient working practices persist [app], weakening the firm before the government reviews the tariff after 3 years [an]. Drawback 2: Reduced consumer choice may shrink the market [k], as shoppers face higher prices and fewer imported styles [app], cutting total footwear demand in Country X and Aldercombe's own sales [an].
    Keywords: Aldercombe Footwear Ltd, 22%, 3 years, $65, Country F, $5,200,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Protection reduces the incentive to improve efficiency; Tariffs raise consumer prices and reduce choice | application_max_2: Tariff review after 3 years; inefficient practices may persist; Imported styles cost about $71, above Aldercombe's $65 | analysis_max_2: Firm weakened / uncompetitive once the review happens; Total footwear demand falls / firm's own sales reduced

  Qd [8 marks]
    Question: Do you think the 22% import tariff is likely to benefit Aldercombe Footwear Ltd in the long run? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The 22% tariff lifts Aldercombe Footwear Ltd above Country F imports, which now retail at about $71 against Aldercombe's $65 [app], lifting orders and protecting $5,200,000 revenue and 75 jobs in the short term [an]; tariffs are designed to protect domestic producers from cheaper foreign competition [k]. However, shelter can breed inefficiency, letting firms delay cutting costs [k]; the tariff is temporary, facing a review after 3 years [app], so Aldercombe could struggle if protection ends while its costs stay high [an]. Overall, the tariff will benefit Aldercombe in the long run only if it invests the $1,100,000 in new lasting machines during the 3-year protection [eval], because protection will expire and competition from Country F imports will return [eval].
    Keywords: 22%, $71, $65, Country F, 3 years, $1,100,000, $5,200,000, Aldercombe Footwear Ltd
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: Tariffs protect domestic producers from foreign competition; Protection can breed inefficiency / delay cost-cutting | application_max_2: $71 Country F imports vs $65 price; $5,200,000 revenue; 75 jobs; Tariff temporary with review after 3 years; $1,100,000 machine investment | analysis_max_2: Short-term protection of orders, revenue and employment; Competitiveness lost after the review if costs stay high | evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement on long-term benefit; Recognises conditions (investment) for tariff to bring lasting gains

--- STEM ---
Tasty Treats (TT) was established 10 years ago as a private limited company in Country X. TT currently operates a retail chain of 50 cafes specializing in premium handcrafted luxury desserts, including gourmet cakes and artisan gelato. To expand market reach, the board plans to open a new flag-ship cafe at an estimated capital expenditure of $500,000. Managing Director Frances must decide whether to finance this project using accumulated retained profits or by securing an additional 5-year bank loan. The expansion involves hiring 1 store manager and 10 full-time employees who require specialized training in dessert assembly, customer service, and inventory control. Weekly operations at each cafe incur fixed overheads of $1,000 and total variable costs of $20,000 while serving 5,000 desserts. TT aims to maintain an environmentally sustainable brand image by utilizing 100% recyclable packaging for take-home orders.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages to TT of operating as a private limited company.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Limited liability protects owners' personal assets if the 50 cafes incur major debts. Application: Shareholders only risk capital invested in the $500,000 expansion.
Advantage 2: Ability to raise capital by selling shares to friends and family. Application: Provides finance towards the $500,000 expansion budget without public flotation.
Disadvantage 1: Shares cannot be sold to the general public on a stock exchange. Application: Restricts access to large equity capital when funding 50 cafes.
Disadvantage 2: Financial accounts must be published annually. Application: Competitors selling luxury desserts can view TT's cost metrics and profit margins.
    Keywords: 50 cafes, $500,000, luxury desserts, 10 employees, 5,000 desserts, gelato, cakes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage/disadvantage identified (max 2 advantages, max 2 disadvantages). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to business context.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider the following three market research methods TT could use before opening the new cafe: Competitors' websites, Focus groups, and Observation in rival cafes. Which method should TT use? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Competitors' websites allow TT to quickly view prices of luxury desserts and menu choices at minimal cost, though online data may not reflect local customer preferences near the new cafe site. Focus groups gather detailed qualitative feedback on gelato flavors and packaging from potential customers in the targeted location, though organizing them is expensive and time-consuming. Observation in rival cafes provides accurate behavioral data on customer order frequency and dessert selections without direct questioning bias, though it fails to explain the underlying reasons behind customer choices. Recommendation: Focus groups should be used because gathering direct qualitative feedback on specific luxury dessert preferences of local residents in the new area is vital to ensure high demand for the 5,000 weekly desserts target, outweighing higher initial research costs.
    Keywords: 5,000 desserts, gelato, $500,000, luxury desserts, 10 employees, 50 cafes, recyclable packaging
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outline of research methods with limited context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages/disadvantages of at least two methods in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three methods in context with a fully supported recommendation.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to TT of providing formal employment contracts to the 10 new cafe employees.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Clearly defines job duties and working hours, minimizing misunderstandings. Application: Ensures the 10 employees clearly understand expectations regarding customer service and making luxury desserts.
Benefit 2: Provides legal security and specifies notice periods. Application: Prevents sudden staff turnover among cafe workers, ensuring operational continuity across the 50 cafes.
    Keywords: 10 employees, 50 cafes, luxury desserts, 5,000 desserts, store manager
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each relevant benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider the following two motivation methods TT could use for its cafe staff: 'Employee of the Month' award with a $20 voucher, or Job Enrichment. Which method should TT choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: An 'Employee of the Month' award offering a $20 dessert voucher creates low-cost competition among the 10 employees to deliver excellent customer service, but it may demotivate the remaining staff who feel their hard work is unrewarded. Job enrichment involves giving employees added responsibilities such as choosing ingredient suppliers or designing new artisan cake recipes, which satisfies higher-level esteem needs under Herzberg's theory and boosts productivity, though it requires extra training expenses. Recommendation: Job enrichment is preferred because giving staff genuine responsibility over dessert creation builds long-term commitment and maintains high service standards across the 50 cafes, whereas a $20 voucher offers negligible long-term motivation.
    Keywords: $20 voucher, 10 employees, 50 cafes, luxury desserts, ingredient suppliers, 5,000 desserts
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of motivation techniques. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits/drawbacks of one or both methods in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in context with a justified recommendation.

    Answer: Calculations: 2024 Current Ratio = ($10m + $3m + $2m) / $5m = $15m / $5m = 3.0:1. 2024 Acid Test Ratio = ($15m - $10m) / $5m = 1.0:1.

--- STEM ---
VeloCraft Bikes (VB) is a private limited company operating a single manufacturing factory with 40 skilled production workers. VB produces premium custom carbon-fiber bicycles for competitive cyclists. Management plans to expand operations by introducing a new line of mass-produced commuter electric bikes (e-bikes) costing $1,200,000 in capital machinery. The factory currently operates under batch production, incurring fixed costs of $12,000 per month and total variable costs of $48,000 while producing 200 custom bicycles monthly. Directors are debating whether to maintain batch assembly or transition to an automated flow line. Additionally, VB faces quality control challenges, as 5% of custom frames currently fail stress testing, incurring expensive rework costs.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to VB of maintaining its current business legal structure as a private limited company during expansion.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Limited liability protects shareholders' personal assets if the $1,200,000 e-bike expansion project fails. Application: Investors only lose capital equity invested in the factory.
Advantage 2: Maintenance of operational control without risk of hostile takeover. Application: The original founders retain majority ownership while managing 40 production workers.
    Keywords: $1,200,000, 40 workers, carbon-fiber bicycles, e-bikes, 200 custom bicycles, batch production
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for applied contextual explanation.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider three growth strategies VB could use for the new commuter e-bike line: Internal growth (expanding existing factory), Horizontal integration (merging with a rival bike maker), or Joint Venture with a battery manufacturer. Which strategy should VB choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Internal growth allows VB to retain complete control over carbon-fiber quality standards, though building line capacity takes considerable time and requires financing the full $1,200,000 expenditure. Horizontal integration provides immediate access to established retail channels and manufacturing capacity, though integrating corporate cultures across 40 skilled workers creates conflict risks. A Joint Venture spreads investment risks and combines battery technology expertise directly with bike frame assembly, though profits must be shared. Recommendation: A Joint Venture is the best strategy because sharing the financial burden mitigates risk when entering the unfamiliar commuter e-bike market while accessing specialized battery tech.
    Keywords: $1,200,000, 40 workers, commuter e-bike, carbon-fiber, 200 custom bicycles
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies growth methods with general explanation. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes pros and cons of two or three growth options in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three growth strategies with a well-justified recommendation.

SET ID: P2_SET_06
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- STEM ---
Starlight Hotels (SH) is a private limited company that operates a regional chain of 4 luxury boutique hotels. To capture rising business travel demand, SH plans to build a 5th hotel featuring extensive conference facilities at an investment cost of $4,000,000. Managing Director Sophia must decide whether to finance this project by issuing corporate debentures or securing a 15-year commercial mortgage loan. Each hotel employs 50 staff across house-keeping, front desk, and catering services under a tall hierarchical structure. Monthly fixed overheads per hotel average $80,000, with variable operating costs totaling $120,000 while hosting 2,000 booked room nights. SH faces high staff absenteeism (10%) among house-keeping workers and receives customer complaints regarding delayed room check-ins.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to SH of using long-term debentures rather than a bank loan to finance the $4,000,000 hotel expansion.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Debentures carry fixed interest rates over long loan tenures. Application: Protects SH from rising interest charges on the $4,000,000 capital outlay over 15 years.
Advantage 2: Debenture holders do not acquire voting rights or equity control. Application: Ensures existing shareholders retain decision-making control across the 4 boutique hotels.
    Keywords: $4,000,000, 4 boutique hotels, debentures, 5th hotel, 2,000 booked room nights
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid advantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for applied context.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider three methods SH could use to conduct market research for the new conference hotel: Online corporate customer surveys, Professional hotel industry market reports, or Pilot testing conference packages at existing hotels. Which method should SH choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Online corporate surveys gather direct feedback from corporate event planners regarding facility requirements and budget pricing, though response rates may be low. Professional industry market reports provide comprehensive macro data on regional occupancy rates and rival hotel pricing, though reports are expensive and lack customized feedback. Pilot testing conference packages at existing hotels provides realistic booking data and operational feedback from corporate guests, though facility constraints limit test accuracy. Recommendation: Pilot testing at existing hotels is best because live trial bookings validate guest demand and operational capacity before committing $4,000,000 in construction capital.
    Keywords: $4,000,000, 4 boutique hotels, conference packages, room night tariff $150, 2,000 room nights
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outlines market research methods simply. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes pros and cons of two or three research methods in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of all three methods with a fully supported recommendation.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits to SH of delayering its tall organizational hierarchy across its hotels.
    Answer: Benefit 1: Speeds up communication channels between hotel managers and front desk staff. Application: Resolves check-in delays faster, raising customer satisfaction ratings above 3.8/5.0.
Benefit 2: Reduces management overhead salary expenses. Application: Cuts fixed overhead costs below $80,000 per month per hotel branch.
    Keywords: 3.8/5.0 rating, $80,000 fixed costs, 50 staff, tall hierarchy, check-in delays
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid benefit (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider the following two methods SH could use to reduce high (10%) house-keeping staff absenteeism: Introducing flexible working hours, or Implementing Herzberg-based job enrichment. Which method should SH choose? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Flexible working hours allow house-keeping staff to balance personal commitments, directly reducing absenteeism (currently 10%) and staff turnover, though scheduling coverage for morning room cleaning becomes complex. Job enrichment gives house-keeping staff added responsibility for room quality inspections and guest amenity restocking, satisfying Herzberg hygiene and motivator factors, though it requires extra staff training. Recommendation: Flexible working hours should be chosen because non-standard work shifts directly address the root cause of house-keeping absenteeism, ensuring rooms are cleaned promptly for check-in.
    Keywords: 10% absenteeism, house-keeping staff, 50 staff, 4 boutique hotels, room check-ins
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies motivation theories/methods simply. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of flexible hours vs job enrichment in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Thorough comparative evaluation leading to a well-supported recommendation.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SH's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SH's financial position improved?
    Answer: Calculations: 2024 Current Ratio = ($100k + $200k + $200k) / ($200k + $50k) = $500k / $250k = 2.0:1. 2024 Acid Test Ratio = ($500k - $100k) / $250k = 1.6:1.
2025 Current Ratio = ($150k + $150k + $150k) / ($300k + $150k) = $450k / $450k = 1.0:1. 2025 Acid Test Ratio = ($450k - $150k) / $450k = 0.67:1.
Evaluation: Liquidity severely deteriorated in 2025. The current ratio dropped from a healthy 2.0:1 to a vulnerable 1.0:1, while the acid test ratio plunged from 1.6:1 to 0.67:1 due to trade payables expanding to $300k and bank overdrafts reaching $150k alongside $2,500k in mortgage debt. Conclusion: Financial position did not improve; tight liquidity restricts SH's ability to fund the $4,000,000 expansion without securing long-term borrowing.
    Keywords: 2.0:1, 1.0:1, 1.6:1, 0.67:1, $150k overdraft, $2,500k mortgage, $4,000,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Describes financial line items without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates liquidity ratios for both years with contextual analysis. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of liquidity trends across both years with a supported judgment.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to SH of introducing sustainable energy practices (such as solar water heating) across its hotels.
    Answer: Advantage: Reduces ongoing utility overhead costs and builds green reputation. Application: Lowers electricity expenses below current levels, offsetting the 10% utility tariff hike across the 4 hotels.
Disadvantage: High initial capital expenditure required for equipment installation. Application: Increases capital outlays when financial resources are concentrated on the $4,000,000 expansion.
    Keywords: solar water heating, 4 hotels, 10% utility tariff, $4,000,000 expansion
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid advantage/disadvantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for applied context.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how a 15% aviation tax cut, an 8% municipal hotel tax, and a 10% electricity tariff hike will affect SH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your choice.
    Answer: A 15% aviation tax cut lowers flight costs, boosting international tourist arrivals and increasing room occupancy above 70% across SH's 4 hotels. An 8% municipal hotel tax increases total room booking costs for guests, potentially dampening room demand unless absorbed by SH. A 10% electricity tariff hike directly increases fixed monthly operating costs above $80,000 per hotel. Conclusion: The 15% aviation tax cut will have the greatest impact because boosting tourist arrivals increases overall room occupancy and conference venue bookings, generating revenue that outweighs higher electricity bills.
    Keywords: 15% aviation tax, 8% hotel tax, 10% electricity tariff, 70% occupancy, $80,000 fixed costs, 4 hotels
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outlines external environment changes simply. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes the business impact of two or three external changes in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of all three factors in context with a well-reasoned judgment on greatest impact.

--- STEM ---
Apex Garments (AG) is a private limited company operating a textile manufacturing plant employing 80 sewing machine operators. AG produces denim jackets and workwear apparel for wholesale clothing distributors. To meet growing export orders, AG plans to automate cutting processes by purchasing Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) fabric cutting equipment costing $600,000. Managing Director Marcus must decide whether to finance this purchase via a 3-year hire purchase contract or a bank loan. Monthly operations under batch production generate fixed costs of $30,000 and total variable costs of $90,000 while producing 15,000 denim jackets. AG struggles with high fabric material waste (6%) due to manual cutting errors and faces severe price competition from low-cost overseas textile factories.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages to AG of using hire purchase to acquire the $600,000 fabric cutting machinery.
    Answer: Advantage 1: Spreads machinery costs over time without massive cash outlays. Application: Preserves cash reserves when liquidity is tight, avoiding an immediate $600,000 cash drain.
Advantage 2: Ownership transfers to AG upon final installment payment. Application: Adds the CAM cutting equipment to non-current assets on the statement of financial position.
    Keywords: $600,000 machinery, denim jackets, fabric cutting, hire purchase, 15,000 jackets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid advantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider three extension strategies AG could use for its denim jacket line: Designing eco-friendly recycled denim lines, Selling directly to online retail consumers, or Lowering wholesale selling prices. Which strategy should AG choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Designing eco-friendly recycled denim lines creates a unique selling point (USP) that appeals to sustainable fashion buyers, commanding higher selling prices above $10.00, though sourcing certified recycled denim elevates raw material costs. Selling directly to consumers via e-commerce captures full retail margins, bypassing wholesalers, though building an online retail infrastructure and managing individual shipping is costly. Lowering wholesale prices increases order volume from distributors, though thin gross profit margins are further eroded. Recommendation: Recycled denim lines are best because developing an eco-friendly USP allows AG to command premium prices and stand out against low-cost overseas competitors.
    Keywords: denim jackets, $10.00 price, recycled denim, 15,000 jackets, wholesalers
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outlines extension strategies simply. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes pros and cons of two or three extension strategies in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of all three options leading to a well-supported recommendation.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two problems AG may experience due to poor communication between factory supervisors and sewing machine operators.
    Answer: Problem 1: Increases garment sewing errors and rework. Application: Contributes to the current 3.5% defect rate among sewing machine operators during batch assembly.
Problem 2: Slows down line setup changes between garment batches. Application: Delays batch production schedules across the 80 machine operators, reducing monthly output below 15,000 jackets.
    Keywords: 3.5% defect rate, 80 machine operators, denim jackets, 15,000 jackets, batch production
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid problem (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for applied context.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider the consequences for AG of downsizing its workforce by replacing 20 manual cutting workers with the $600,000 automated CAM machinery. Should AG proceed with redundancy? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Proceeding with redundancy by replacing 20 manual cutting staff with CAM machinery eliminates 6% fabric waste ($12,000 monthly scrap loss) and significantly reduces monthly wage costs, helping offset legal minimum wage increases. However, compulsory redundancies incur substantial statutory severance payout costs, demotivate the remaining 60 sewing machine operators who fear further job losses, and risk trade union industrial action. Recommendation: AG should proceed with redundancy because eliminating $12,000 in monthly fabric scrap and securing automated cutting precision is essential to survive low-cost overseas competition.
    Keywords: 20 cutting workers, $600,000 CAM machinery, 6% fabric waste, $12,000 scrap loss, 60 sewing operators
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies redundancy/downsizing concepts simply. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes financial and human resource impacts of redundancy in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Thorough evaluation of redundancy consequences leading to a well-supported judgment.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]

    Answer: 
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct method, 1 mark for correct final output ($8.00 and $6.00). 1 mark per valid management application.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AG's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has AG's financial position improved?
    Answer: Calculations: 2024 Current Ratio = ($0.9m + $0.6m + $0.3m) / ($0.4m + $0.2m) = $1.8m / $0.6m = 3.0:1. 2024 Acid Test Ratio = ($1.8m - $0.9m) / $0.6m = 1.5:1.
2025 Current Ratio = ($0.9m + $0.4m + $0.2m) / ($0.6m + $0.4m) = $1.5m / $1.0m = 1.5:1. 2025 Acid Test Ratio = ($1.5m - $0.9m) / $1.0m = 0.6:1.
Evaluation: AG's liquidity deteriorated significantly in 2025. The current ratio halved from 3.0:1 to 1.5:1, while the acid test ratio plunged from 1.5:1 to an illiquid 0.6:1 due to bank overdrafts doubling to $0.4m and trade payables rising to $0.6m. AG holds $0.9m tied up in inventory relative to liquid cash ($0.2m). Conclusion: Financial position did not improve; poor liquidity restricts AG's ability to fund the $600,000 CAM equipment without external debt.
    Keywords: 3.0:1, 1.5:1, 0.6:1, $0.4m overdraft, $0.9m inventory, $600,000 CAM, denim jackets
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Describes balance sheet line items without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates liquidity ratios for both years with contextual analysis. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of liquidity trends across both years with a supported conclusion.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to AG of installing Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) fabric cutting equipment.
    Answer: Advantage: Maximizes fabric cutting precision and speed. Application: Eliminates 6% fabric wastage ($12,000 monthly scrap loss) when cutting denim rolls.
Disadvantage: High initial setup costs and operator retraining expenses. Application: Requires $600,000 capital outlay and training for remaining machine operators.
    Keywords: CAM cutting equipment, 6% fabric waste, $12,000 scrap loss, $600,000, denim rolls
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark per valid advantage/disadvantage (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for applied context.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how an 8% tariff on imported garments, a 5% minimum wage increase, and a corporate tax rise to 22% will affect AG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your choice.
    Answer: An 8% tariff on imported finished garments makes foreign competitor apparel more expensive in Country X, driving domestic wholesale buyers toward AG's denim jackets. A 5% minimum wage increase elevates direct labor expenses across 80 sewing machine operators, increasing variable costs above $6.00 per jacket. Corporate profit tax rising from 20% to 22% reduces retained net profit available for internal reinvestment. Conclusion: The 8% import tariff will have the greatest impact because protecting AG from low-cost overseas garment competition boosts domestic order volume significantly, offsetting higher wage costs.
    Keywords: 8% tariff, 5% minimum wage, 20% to 22%, 80 sewing operators, $6.00 variable cost, denim jackets
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Outlines external factors with simple explanation. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyzes the business impact of two or three external changes in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of all three factors in context with a well-reasoned judgment on greatest impact.
