Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $12.40 per hour): The insert gives a 6.9% rise from $11.60 to $12.40 — a derived delta of $0.80 per hour ($12.40 − $11.60; check: 6.9% × $11.60 ≈ $0.80). Harvest pluckers and rolling operators anchored to the floor become more expensive from April 2026, and bands above the floor typically shift as well. The insert does not state hours worked, so the annual cash impact cannot be computed precisely; however, for an 85-strong workforce the effect would be a clearly material annual cash strain, landing precisely when 11% absenteeism already inflates effective labour cost per kilo plucked and the new $480,000 line depends on full, consistent plucking input.

Input cost inflation (8.7% fertilizer and shipping containers): Fertilizer supports yield per hectare and container rates govern export economics, but the insert never decomposes the $21.00 variable cost, so no per-unit input figure can be derived honestly. What can be shown is the percentage effect: applying the insert's 8.7% rise to the entire variable cost gives an explicit upper bound of 8.7% × $21.00 = about $1.83 per unit (8.7% × $21.00 = $1.83, derivation shown; an upper bound since not all of the $21.00 is fertilizer and freight). Even a fraction of that bound squeezes the $5.00 contribution and erodes premium pricing power, though compostable-sachet positioning and direct-to-consumer sales let VPTE pass some of the rise to loyal subscribers.

Conclusion: The 6.9% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It is a mechanical $0.80-per-hour ($12.40 − $11.60) rise on the estate's scarcest resource — plucking labour — exactly when 11% absenteeism already strains harvest capacity and the new $480,000 line needs full, consistent input. It is a larger and more immediate threat than the 8.7% input-cost rise (an explicit upper bound of about $1.83 per unit if applied to the entire variable cost; the true effect is far smaller in practice) and than the interest-rate rise, which VPTE largely avoids through retained profit and fixed lease payments. VPTE should respond with higher labour productivity targets, completion of the orthodox-rolling certification to unlock mechanisation, careful pay-band redesign and modest premium price rises for subscriptions, while hedging fertilizer and container contracts as secondary measures.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 6.9%, 8.7%, $12.40, $11.60, 4.6%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VPTE. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VPTE's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VPTE with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Harwick Precision Engineering (HPE) is a private limited company in the precision engineering sector, manufacturing industrial flow-control valves for oil and gas clients, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2004 by Marcus Whitfield, HPE operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. HPE plans to invest $1,450,000 in a robotic CNC machining cell to fulfil a five-year export order, financed by an $800,000 bank loan and $650,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.50 a unit and a selling price of $32.00, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. HPE faces an operational problem: its defect rate has risen to 4.6% and rework costs are increasing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HPE plans to finance part of its robotic CNC machining cell expansion with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for HPE of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs HPE nothing in interest or repayments, protecting cash flow and profit margin while it already carries fixed costs of $540,000 a year alongside an $800,000 bank loan. Money not paid as interest can absorb the 9.6% rise in steel and component input costs without pushing the $32.00 selling price above what oil and gas clients will accept.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral risk attached to a bank loan, so the $650,000 does not put the new $1,450,000 CNC machining cell at risk of repossession if the export order ramps up more slowly than expected. It also keeps Marcus Whitfield's ownership and control intact, with no lender able to impose conditions on how the CNC cell is operated, expanded or staffed. This suits HPE's hierarchical structure, where the founder prefers to direct investment decisively while tackling the 4.6% defect rate and stabilising output of 48,000 units a year.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $650,000, $800,000, $1,450,000, private limited company
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Harwick Precision Engineering and its expansion decision.

    Answer: Trade exhibition: Exhibiting at a major international oil and gas or water-treatment exhibition puts HPE's valves directly in front of procurement engineers, allows live demonstrations of the new CNC machining cell and builds credibility for a five-year export order. However, stand space, travel and staffing can cost tens of thousands of dollars, enquiries may be slow to convert, and one exhibition alone cannot fill an order book aimed at 48,000 units a year.

Trade journal advertising: Advertising in specialist engineering journals is far cheaper than broadcast media and reaches exactly the industrial buyers HPE wants, with repetition across monthly issues building brand familiarity. Readership is passive - buyers may never see the advert while evaluating rivals - and print lead times are long, dulling the launch of a time-sensitive export opportunity.

LinkedIn and digital marketing: A campaign aimed at procurement managers in the 80 export distributors HPE surveyed targets the 68% requiring ISO 9001 certification and the 57% willing to switch suppliers, with measurable clicks, demo requests and cost per lead. It is far cheaper than exhibitions, scales internationally and suits the 5.4% growth in export demand, though it needs consistent content and rapid follow-up, and some traditional oil and gas buyers prefer face-to-face relationships.

Recommendation: HPE should choose LinkedIn and targeted digital marketing, reinforced by a single well-chosen exhibition each year. It reaches the exact segments identified in HPE's research at a fraction of exhibition cost, suits national distribution to oil and gas regions, and supports the export order quickly. Journal advertising is rejected as too passive to shift buyers, and exhibiting alone is rejected as too expensive and infrequent for a 120-person manufacturer funding a $1,450,000 cell with an $800,000 bank loan.

    Question: HPE's defect rate has risen to 4.6% and rework costs are increasing. Explain two benefits for HPE of using autocratic leadership to address quality problems in its production team.

With 24 of 120 staff untrained on the CNC cell, strict direction on who operates which machine protects output of 48,000 units a year and reinforces the chain of command in HPE's hierarchical structure. Although some employees may feel less consulted, speed and consistency matter more while the defect rate is being brought under control and the $1,450,000 investment beds in.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HPE must train 24 production staff to operate the new CNC machining cell. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at a specialist centre. Which should HPE choose? Justify your decision.

Decision: HPE should choose on-the-job training for the first twelve months, supplemented by off-the-job certification for two senior operators who can then cascade training to the rest. This keeps output of 48,000 units stable while the defect rate is investigated, costs far less than $27,600 and fixes the immediate quality problem. Full off-the-job training is rejected for now because withdrawing 24 staff from a 120-person workforce during a quality crisis and export ramp-up would risk late deliveries, penalties and further rework on top of the $38,000 already lost last quarter.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HPE's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HPE's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.93 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.25 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $340,000 trade receivables + $80,000 cash = $630,000; 2025 current assets = $150,000 + $420,000 + $110,000 = $680,000. Conclusion: HPE's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures rose (1.40 to 1.60 and 0.93 to 1.25), and the improvement does not depend on stock.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.6%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in input costs will affect AAC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.9% to 5.6%): A 0.7% rise on AAC's $1,200,000 variable-rate loan adds about $8,400 a year to interest costs and slightly raises the burden above its $570,000 fixed costs. Higher rates may also make car manufacturers more cautious about committing to large contracts, and could increase the cost of future borrowing for the $2,300,000 relocation. The impact is real but modest and can be capped by fixing the rate for part of the loan.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $11.80 per hour): AAC employs 340 staff; if the lowest-paid 45 operatives move from $11.12 to $11.80, each gains about $1,360 a year, or roughly $61,200 across the group. Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in aluminium and steel input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeatedly reduces contribution on every unit sold, totalling roughly $100,800 a year, the largest single cash exposure of the three. The wage increase is the second concern at roughly $61,200 a year, compounded by morale risk, while the interest-rate rise costs only about $8,400 a year and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three still require AAC to negotiate price recovery with car manufacturers and drive down the 2.2% defect rate to protect margins.

--- STEM ---
Aldermere Packaging Cooperative (APC) is a cooperative in the packaging sector, manufacturing corrugated and eco-friendly cardboard boxes at high volume for e-commerce and retail fulfilment clients across the country, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Rosa Jiménez, APC operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. APC plans to invest $980,000 in an automated die-cutting and folding line, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $310,000 a year, a variable cost of $1.10 a unit and a selling price of $4.20, and currently produces 160,000 units a year. APC faces an operational problem: offcut waste has risen to 11% of output.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: APC plans to finance part of its automated die-cutting and folding line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for APC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs APC nothing in interest or repayments, which matters for a cooperative whose members share any surplus and who want stable returns. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 13.8% rise in recycled paper and pulp input costs, helping APC hold the $4.20 price for e-commerce clients and protect the $3.10 contribution per box earned on 160,000 units a year.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral risk attached to a bank loan, so the $380,000 does not put the new $980,000 die-cutting line at risk of repossession if demand from distribution centres falters. It also preserves the members' democratic ownership and control, since no lender can impose conditions on how the line is staffed, scheduled or priced. It also signals financial discipline to members who vote on major commitments, reinforcing trust in Rosa Jiménez's judgement. This suits APC's flat structure, where members expect a voice in big decisions and are already engaged in tackling the 11% offcut waste problem.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $380,000, $600,000, $980,000, cooperative
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Aldermere Packaging Cooperative and its expansion decision.

    Answer: Social media campaign: A targeted social media campaign aimed at e-commerce brands and fulfilment buyers is cheap, measurable and fast. APC can showcase the 71% of surveyed customers who specify 100% recyclable boxes and the 49% willing to pay $0.15 more, reach procurement staff precisely, and direct them to samples within days. It suits a 60-member cooperative with limited marketing budget, though results compound slowly and require consistent content and follow-up.

Packaging trade journals: Journal advertising builds credibility among packaging engineers and print buyers with repetition across issues at low cost, and it reaches an exactly relevant audience. Readership is passive, response is difficult to measure, and print lead times blunt the launch of a range tied to a 6.2% growth in e-commerce packaging demand.

Trade fair exhibition: Exhibiting puts APC's die-cut samples directly into the hands of distribution-centre buyers, supports live demonstrations of the new automated line and can win multi-year contracts on the spot. Stand space, travel and staffing are expensive, however, and one event provides only a brief window to reach the 250 e-commerce customers already surveyed.

Recommendation: APC should choose a social media campaign aimed at e-commerce brands, supported by one trade fair each year for relationship building. It delivers the widest reach per dollar, speaks directly to the 71% sustainability-first segment and reinforces APC's eco-friendly positioning at the 97% on-time fulfilment that e-commerce buyers demand. Journal advertising is rejected as too passive and slow, and exhibiting alone is rejected as too expensive and infrequent for a cooperative funding a $980,000 automated line with a $600,000 bank loan.

    Question: APC must upskill 18 members to operate the new die-cutting line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at an external centre. Which should APC choose? Justify your decision.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate APC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has APC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.74 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.34 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $285,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $150,000 + $85,000 = $305,000. However, trade receivables rose from $130,000 to $150,000, tying up member funds; if e-commerce clients pay late, the margin for error narrows, and inventories of $70,000 must still support timely delivery against 2.4 days lead time.

Conclusion: APC's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures rose (1.50 to 1.74 and 1.00 to 1.34), and the gain does not rest on stock. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so APC should tighten credit terms with distribution centres and keep monitoring the 97% on-time fulfilment rate while the new line beds in.

It differentiates MTT in a commoditised textiles market, supports the demand for certified sustainable fabrics growing at 7.1% and helps win specification on workwear and transport contracts, including the three new export clients worth $180,000 in a quarter.

Disadvantage: Recycled fibres can cost more and behave less predictably in spinning and dyeing, raising the $7.60 variable cost and risking a return of dye-consistency complaints before the new finishing process stabilises. Certification audits and recycled-content documentation add cost and admin to an 85-person business with 12% absenteeism, and if flame-retardant performance is compromised, the decisive certification advantage for 61% of buyers would be destroyed, damaging orders and MTT's technical reputation.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.1%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in input costs will affect MTT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.2% to 6.1%): MTT's $450,000 bank loan, if variable-rate, rises by 0.9%, adding about $4,050 a year to interest costs and slightly lifting the fixed-cost burden above $432,000. Conclusion: The 10.5% rise in cotton and polyester input costs will have the greatest impact. The wage increase is the second concern at roughly $39,000 a year, while the interest-rate rise costs only about $4,050 a year and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three reinforce the case for the recycled-fibre premium strategy and tighter cost control in the weaving hall.

--- STEM ---
Vantor Electronics (VEL) is a private limited company in the electronics assembly sector, assembling printed circuit board control panels for domestic appliance makers, employing a workforce of 210. Founded in 2008 by Marcus Whitfield, VEL operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $784,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.20 a unit and a selling price of $24.00, and currently produces 130,000 units a year.     Question: VEL plans to finance part of its surface-mount technology assembly lines with a share issue. Explain two advantages for VEL of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit avoids diluting Marcus Whitfield's ownership and control, keeping strategic direction firmly in the founder's hands under VEL's autocratic flat structure. Money generated by the existing 130,000-unit operation can be reinvested without creating pressure for dividends or returns that new shareholders would expect, protecting the $784,000 fixed-cost base from additional financial strain. It also keeps cash available for wages and components already under 14.6% input-cost pressure.

Point 2: Retained profit is the cheapest finance available: it involves no issue costs, no legal prospectus or shareholder approvals, and no interest or repayment schedule, so the $450,000 is deployed directly into the $1,100,000 surface-mount technology lines, without lender consent or delay. Unlike a share issue, it does not signal to the market that VEL needs external capital, and it avoids the administrative burden of managing a larger shareholder register while the business is already stretched by 28 staff lacking certification and a 14.6% rise in component costs.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VEL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VEL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.54 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.14 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $260,000 inventories + $380,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $730,000; 2025 current assets = $200,000 + $440,000 + $130,000 = $770,000. Conclusion: VEL's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures rose (1.40 to 1.54 and 0.90 to 1.14), and the improvement does not rest on stock. The main residual risk is rising receivables, so VEL should tighten credit control with appliance makers while the SMT lines reach full output.

--- STEM ---
Velvet Finch (VF) is a private limited company in the independent fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2013 by Isla Marchetti, the business runs a single boutique in the market town of Wexley and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. VF plans to invest $780,000 in a second boutique and a new e-commerce channel, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $330,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $24 a unit and a selling price of $42, and currently produces 19,000 units a year. VF faces a serious operational problem: inventory shrinkage has reached 4.6% of stock purchases through shoplifting and till errors.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VF intends to fund part of the second boutique and e-commerce launch from retained profit. Explain two advantages for VF of using retained profit rather than the $450,000 ten-year bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs VF nothing in interest or repayments, which protects cash flow and the $42 selling price at a time when fixed costs are $216,000 a year. Every dollar of profit not paid as loan interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in cotton and linen input costs, so VF can hold its $58-$95 dress price points and defend the $74 average transaction value without a bank dictating repayment dates or lender conditions on the new store fit-out.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and recovery risk attached to the $450,000 bank loan, so the second boutique and e-commerce channel are not at risk of repossession if footfall disappoints or the 9% returns rate drags on margins. It also preserves full ownership and the freedom of laissez-faire leadership, letting Isla Marchetti deploy the $330,000 immediately, without bank consent for hiring the 28-person team or for later expansion decisions — important when the boutique trades on personal service and the second store must feel like the original, not a replica. VF can also time the retained-profit drawdown around seasonal peaks rather than serving a rigid monthly repayment.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $330,000, $450,000, second boutique, $216,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Velvet Finch, its expansion decision and its costs.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VF is launching its second boutique and online store. Consider a social media influencer campaign, a local radio sponsorship, or print advertising in a regional fashion magazine. Which should VF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Social media influencer campaign: Fashion and lifestyle influencers with strong regional reach would put VF's dresses directly in front of the 47% of Wexley shoppers who already use rival boutiques and the 58% who said they would buy VF clothing online. Costs are modest, results are measurable in clicks and promo-code redemptions, and sustainable-fabric messaging can be woven into content for the 34% of respondents who prefer responsible sourcing. The risk is that influencer credibility varies and results compound over weeks rather than instantly.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio reaches a broad local audience during commuting hours and suits time-limited launch messages for the Wexley catchment. However, it is one-way communication with no visual merchandising of the dresses, wastes spend on listeners outside the trading area, and offers no click-through to the online store, limiting its power to drive both boutique footfall and e-commerce orders.

Print advertising in a regional fashion magazine: Print offers prestige and full-page visuals of the new range, but circulation is declining, readership cannot be matched to the shopper segments VF's own research identifies, and there is no measurable click-through, making it hard to attribute the $74 basket uplift to the spend. Cost per reached shopper is high for a 28-person business funding a $780,000 expansion.

Recommendation: VF should choose a social media influencer campaign. It targets the exact shopper segments identified in its research, costs a fraction of print or radio, delivers measurable online and boutique conversion, and reinforces the sustainability story valued by 34% of respondents. Radio is rejected as one-way and untargeted for fashion visuals, and print is rejected for declining, unmeasurable reach; VF can add posters in its existing storefront to support opening weekend.

    Question: VF operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for VF of laissez-faire leadership in motivating its boutique and e-commerce team.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives VF's experienced stylists and online merchandisers genuine freedom to curate collections, set window displays and reply to customer queries in their own voice. This satisfies esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow), raising job satisfaction and loyalty so the 28-person team stays rather than costing VF recruitment fees and lost local knowledge, and it empowers staff to create the in-store theatre that draws the 1,850 weekly visitors past the till.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VF wants to cut its 4.6% inventory shrinkage and lift staff effort. Consider introducing a commission on sales or a profit-sharing scheme. Which should VF choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Commission on sales: A percentage of each sale would directly reward selling effort, raise average basket value above $74, and suit the boutique's competitive service culture. It is simple to calculate and visible to staff every week. However, commission rewards revenue rather than loss prevention: staff would have no incentive to confront shoplifters, audit stock or report till errors, so the 4.6% shrinkage could worsen even as sales rise. It could also encourage overselling at busy periods, pushing customers toward returns, which already run at 9% of units sold.

Profit-sharing scheme: Sharing a portion of annual profit, with the distribution linked partly to a stock-loss target, aligns every member of the 28-person team behind protecting inventory. Staff gain a direct financial reason to watch the shop floor, challenge suspicious behaviour and keep tills accurate, and it reinforces the trust laissez-faire leadership depends on. Drawbacks are that the reward arrives once a year, weakening its motivational pull for short-term effort, and that staff may see payouts as small or unequal if measured loosely; it also needs transparent profit reporting in a private limited company.

Decision: VF should choose a profit-sharing scheme with a shrinkage-reduction condition attached to the annual payment. It targets the real problem (4.6% of stock purchases lost), rewards collective vigilance rather than individual selling pressure, and costs only when profit is actually made, protecting cash during the $780,000 expansion. Commission is rejected because it incentivises sales volume while ignoring the loss problem, risks clashing with the low-pressure styling service VF prides itself on, and could inflate the 9% returns rate further; VF can review commission for top stylists next year if conversion rates lag.
    Keywords: 4.6%, inventory shrinkage, workforce of 28, laissez-faire, $74, flat organisational structure
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation methods with limited application to VF. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of one or both schemes in the context of VF. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both schemes in the context of VF with a well-justified decision explaining why a sales commission is rejected and profit-sharing with a loss condition is preferred.

    Keywords: 12,000, $18.00, $216,000, $24, $42, $450,000, 7,000

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.91 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.17 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.81 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.04 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $260,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $100,000 cash = $450,000; 2025 current assets = $295,000 + $120,000 + $150,000 = $565,000. 2024 cover = $450,000 ÷ $235,000 current liabilities = 1.91; 2025 cover = $565,000 ÷ $260,000 = 2.17. 2024 liquid cover = ($450,000 − $260,000) ÷ $235,000 = $190,000 ÷ $235,000 = 0.81; 2025 liquid cover = ($565,000 − $295,000) ÷ $260,000 = $270,000 ÷ $260,000 = 1.04.

The improvement is genuine, not cosmetic; VF should scrutinise whatever is driving the extra $30,000 of trade receivables and keep shrinkage at 4.6% or below so the stronger liquidity converts into sustainable profit for the second boutique.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether VF's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VF of launching the e-commerce channel alongside the second boutique.
    Answer: Advantage: The e-commerce channel lets VF sell beyond the Wexley catchment to the 58% of surveyed shoppers who said they would buy online with next-day delivery, and to younger buyers drawn by sustainable-fabric messaging that 34% of respondents value. It spreads fixed costs of $216,000 across more units sold, lifts the $74 average basket value through online exclusives, and generates direct customer data for promotions without paying for further leases.

It also needs website build, photography and stock integration within the $330,000 retained profit earmarked for the launch, and may cannibalise core boutique sales if the two channels are not priced and promoted coherently under VF's laissez-faire structure.
    Keywords: e-commerce, 58%, 9%, 34%, $330,000, second boutique
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VF's research data, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in input costs will affect VF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (from 4.25% to 5.0%): VF's $450,000 ten-year bank loan, if variable-rate, costs roughly 0.75% more a year, about $3,375 extra annual interest, marginally lifting the $216,000 fixed-cost burden. Higher rates also make consumers more cautious with discretionary clothing spending, though clothing spending still grew 2.8%, and raise the cost of any top-up borrowing for the second boutique fit-out. The direct cash impact is real but small, and VF can reduce it by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.9% rise to $12.81 per hour from April 2026): Every hourly-paid staff member at VF moves from $12.10 to $12.81 — shown arithmetic, $0.71 more per hour, a 5.9% rise recurring on every shift of all 28 staff across the boutique floor, e-commerce fulfilment and tills. The insert gives no payroll-hours figure, so the exact annual cash cost cannot be computed, but this rise recurs every hour VF trades and cannot be removed by one refinancing or one supplier negotiation. Because laissez-faire leadership keeps staffing flexible rather than automated, offsets must come from productivity gains, cross-training and modest price adjustments on $58-$95 dresses.

Input-cost inflation (9.8% rise in cotton and linen): Wholesale garment costs feed directly into VF's $24 variable cost per unit. The insert does not split the $24 between materials and labour, so the exact cash impact cannot be computed; even so, a full 9.8% on the entire variable cost is a shown-arithmetic upper bound of $2.35 a unit (9.8% × $24 = $2.352), about $44,688 a year on 19,000 units ($2.352 × 19,000), squeezing the $18.00 contribution per unit well below budget. In reality only the cotton-and-linen component is exposed, so the true impact sits below that bound — but it is still recurring and unavoidable without renegotiation or selective price rises.

Conclusion: The 5.9% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact on VF. It recurs permanently on every hour worked by all 28 staff, cannot be fixed, renegotiated away or hedged, and lands on the shop floor that drives the $74 average basket value — whereas the interest-rate rise costs only $3,375 a year (0.75% × $450,000, computed) and the input-cost rise, though up to an upper bound of about $44,688 a year on the whole $24 variable cost, in practice applies only to the exposed cotton-and-linen component and can partly be recovered in price. VF should respond with flexible rostering, multiskilling and a small, targeted price rise on best-selling dresses, while fixing its loan rate and pressing suppliers to blunt the next-biggest threat.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 5.9%, 9.8%, $450,000, interest rate, $12.81
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VF's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VF with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Sole Ledger (SL) is a private limited company operating an online sneaker resale marketplace in the capital city of Dunmoor, employing a workforce of 62. Founded in 2016 by DeShawn Carter, the business authenticates and resells limited-edition trainers through a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. SL plans to invest $950,000 in a national authentication hub and a verified-seller onboarding programme for 300 new sellers, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $350,000 from a share issue. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $21.00, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. SL faces a serious operational problem: returns abuse has reached 6.8% of orders, driven by worn or switched pairs sent back for refunds.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SL must choose how to fund the national authentication hub. Explain two advantages for SL of using a share issue to raise $350,000 instead of increasing the $600,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue carries no repayment schedule and no interest charge, so SL avoids adding further fixed obligations while it absorbs a 10.6% rise in logistics and authentication input costs and a 4.9% minimum wage increase. This protects cash for the $950,000 hub build, when Appendix 2 already shows cash fell from $150,000 to $60,000 and current liabilities rose to $505,000 during expansion.

Point 2: Equity funding does not require the hub itself as collateral, so if launch yields slower seller sign-ups than the 300-seller target, the authentication hub is not at risk of repossession. It also strengthens SL's balance sheet and lender confidence, making the remaining $600,000 bank loan easier to service and assuring consigned sellers that a well-capitalised platform will honour their stock and payouts.
    Keywords: share issue, $600,000, bank loan, $950,000, workforce of 62, returns abuse

    Question: SL is onboarding 300 new verified sellers to its marketplace. Consider a social media influencer campaign, advertising in sneaker culture magazines, or sponsorship of a sneaker trade convention. Which should SL choose to promote seller onboarding? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Social media influencer campaign: Sneaker and streetwear creators could showcase the authentication process to both buyers and aspiring sellers. With 61% of buyers already discovering SL through social media and 78% willing to pay a $19 authentication fee, the channel directly reaches the exact audience and can onboard sellers with referral codes, live authentication demos and seller-spotlight series. It is measurable, inexpensive per reach, and compounds virally; its risk is follower vanity metrics and inconsistent seller-quality enquiries.

Sneaker culture magazine advertising: Print ads carry prestige and suit long-form storytelling about counterfeit detection, appealing to serious collectors who value authentication. However, print circulation is shrinking, ads cannot be clicked to sign up, and measuring response requires QR-code campaigns with soft conversion; spending would have narrow impact for reaching 300 new verified sellers nationally.

Sponsorship of a sneaker trade convention: A booth at a national convention would put SL face-to-face with bulk sellers, restorers and graders, ideal for the 300-seller target, and permits live grading demonstrations. But it is a one-off, geographically concentrated spend with high booth and staffing costs, limited to attendees, and cannot sustain onboarding momentum across the following quarters.

Recommendation: SL should choose a social media influencer campaign. It matches how the sneaker community already discovers the platform, scales nationally for a fraction of print or convention costs, and directly supports the 300-verified-seller drive with trackable sign-ups. Magazine print is rejected as unmeasurable and declining, and convention sponsorship is rejected as episodic and location-bound; SL can layer a single flagship convention appearance on top of the influencer programme rather than anchor the whole launch to it.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to SL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SL with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazine print and convention sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SL wants to cut fraudulent returns running at 6.8% of orders. Consider retraining its authentication staff on-the-job or hiring temporary auditors during peak releases. Which should SL choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job retraining: Senior authenticators train every packer and grader on the exact checks used in the Dunmoor hub — stitching, box labels, SKU matching and weight checks — so learning maps directly onto live consignments. Decision: SL should choose on-the-job retraining as its core response, reserving temporary auditors only for the two biggest release weekends. Retraining is cheaper, machine- and process-specific, raises long-term accuracy rather than patching peaks, and supports Carter's autocratic standard-setting with a skilled internal team. Hiring temps as the main solution is rejected because it treats symptoms, never builds internal capability, and erodes margins on every $210 sale while the 480 switched-item cases keep growing; permanent upskilling plus spot audits is the sustainable route.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 2.02 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.77 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.07 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.87 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $410,000 inventories + $310,000 trade receivables + $150,000 cash = $870,000; 2025 current assets = $455,000 + $380,000 + $60,000 = $895,000. 2024 cover = $870,000 ÷ $430,000 current liabilities = 2.02; 2025 cover = $895,000 ÷ $505,000 = 1.77. 2024 liquid cover = ($870,000 − $410,000) ÷ $430,000 = $460,000 ÷ $430,000 = 1.07; 2025 liquid cover = ($895,000 − $455,000) ÷ $505,000 = $440,000 ÷ $505,000 = 0.87.

Evaluation: SL's liquidity has deteriorated even though the business is growing. Non-current assets rose from $2,600,000 to $3,150,000 as the authentication hub and onboarding programme were built, but cash fell from $150,000 to $60,000 and current liabilities climbed from $430,000 to $505,000, so overall cover slipped from 2.02 to 1.77. The liquid cover slid from 1.07 to 0.87, meaning SL can no longer meet short-term debts without realising stock, an uncomfortable position for a platform holding $455,000 of unsold consigned inventory and $380,000 of trade receivables from sellers on settlement terms. Growing receivables suggest some sellers are slow to remit, and if the 300-seller onboarding accelerates cash absorption further, SL could face a squeeze precisely when the $600,000 bank loan repayments bite and interest costs rise with the base rate.

Conclusion: SL's financial position has not improved. Both measures fell — cover from 2.02 to 1.77 and liquid cover from 1.07 to 0.87 — because expansion consumed working capital faster than it generated it. SL should tighten seller settlement terms, stage the onboarding of the 300 sellers in cohorts, and pause further borrowing until cash recovers, even though the hub will strengthen long-term competitiveness and support premium authentication fees.
    Keywords: 2.02, 1.77, 1.07, 0.87, $870,000, $895,000, $950,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of the deterioration caused by expansion and a justified conclusion that SL's financial position has not improved.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.6% rise in resale input costs will affect SL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (from 4.5% to 5.25%): The 0.75% increase adds roughly $4,500 a year to repayments on a $600,000 variable-rate bank loan, and raises any top-up funding for the authentication hub. Conclusion: The 4.9% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact on SL, adding roughly $78,000 a year against about $37,000 for input costs and only around $4,500 for interest. --- STEM ---
Greenbasket Organics (GBO) is a cooperative in the organic food retail sector, employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2010 by Hannah Okafor, the members' cooperative runs two organic shops and a farm-box scheme in Riverton, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. GBO plans to invest $640,000 in a third organic store with a home-delivery depot, financed by $400,000 member share capital and $240,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $198,000 a year, a variable cost of $2.20 a unit and a selling price of $5.50, and currently produces 78,000 units a year. GBO faces twin operational problems: seasonal staffing shortages run 28% above roster in the December peak and organic waste is running at 7.5% of stock.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GBO must finance part of the third store and home-delivery depot. Explain two advantages for GBO of using member share capital instead of the $240,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Member share capital carries no fixed interest or repayment, which matters when GBO's margins are tight — variable cost is $2.20 against a $5.50 selling price and organic waste already costs $36,000 a year. Avoiding loan repayments protects the cash needed for the $640,000 depot build and keeps the price of weekly farm boxes stable for price-sensitive member households.

Point 2: Raising money from members deepens the cooperative's democratic ethos and loyalty: the same members who invest are the 71% who prefer local farms within 50 km and the 66% who would join an expanded home-delivery scheme. Members who hold share capital are more likely to stay, shop and volunteer at the depot, strengthening GBO's local roots and making the launch less dependent on bank goodwill than the $240,000 bank loan alone would allow.
    Keywords: member share capital, bank loan, $240,000, $640,000, cooperative, farm-box
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Greenbasket Organics, its cooperative structure and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GBO is opening its third organic store with a home-delivery depot. Consider in-store tastings and farm open days, a local radio campaign, or social media food-blogger promotion. Which should GBO choose to promote the opening? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: In-store tastings and farm open days: Face-to-face events let Riverton members taste organic produce, meet the 50 km-radius farmers GBO buys from, and sign up for the expanded home-delivery scheme on the spot, directly converting the 71% local-farm preference and the 66% who would join delivery into sales. Events build the cooperative community spirit that differentiates GBO from supermarkets, and costs are mainly staff time and free samples; the limit is reach — only those who attend are persuaded, so coverage is slower and more manual than media.

Local radio campaign: Radio reaches car commuters and farm-box households across Riverton quickly and repeatedly, suits opening-week announcements and delivery-route launches, and a cooperative message about local sourcing can feel authentic on air. However, it is one-way, cannot demonstrate freshness or taste, and spend is wasted on non-organic households; measuring response beyond a generic mention is difficult.

Social media food-blogger promotion: Food and farm bloggers could show recipes, box contents and farm visits to health-conscious followers, with trackable links to sign up for delivery. It is inexpensive and measurable, but GBO's members skew toward families and older buyers who may not follow bloggers daily, and blogger endorsement can backfire if a post overlooks the 7.5% waste problem GBO is trying to fix.

Recommendation: GBO should choose in-store tastings and farm open days as the anchor promotion, supported by a light social media schedule. It converts local trust into subscriptions exactly where the 71% and 66% research points, costs little beyond produce already in store, and embodies cooperative values better than broadcast or influencer marketing. Radio is rejected as one-way and wasteful outside the organic segment, and blogger-first promotion is rejected as too narrow and fragile for a weekly grocery habit; a small influencer budget can amplify the open days rather than replace them.
    Keywords: home-delivery, 71%, 66%, farm-box, $28.40, cooperative
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to GBO. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GBO with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GBO with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and blogger-first promotion are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GBO operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for GBO of democratic leadership when tackling its seasonal staffing shortage in the December peak.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives GBO's 34 staff and returning seasonal workers a genuine voice in building December rosters, so the people who know peak demand can flag gaps early rather than GBO discovering 28% under-staffing on the shop floor. Staff who help design rotas feel ownership, reducing absenteeism and no-shows in the exact weeks when basket sizes and footfall peak, protecting the 6,800 boxes a quarter delivered at 98.2% on-time.

Point 2: Participation satisfies social and esteem needs (Maslow), so seasonal hires are more likely to return next year, cutting the annual cost of re-recruiting and re-briefing. A flat structure also means Hannah Okafor hears directly from packers and drivers about damaged stock and breakage, feeding the quality loop that has already cut breakage complaints from 24 to 11 per month and the 7.5% waste figure.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GBO wants to motivate seasonal checkout and packing staff for the December peak. Consider a seasonal attendance bonus or a profit-sharing scheme for all staff. Which should GBO choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Seasonal attendance bonus: A fixed cash bonus for any seasonal worker achieving near-perfect attendance across the four-week peak directly attacks the roster crisis, since the December shortfall of 28 hires is partly driven by unpredictable absences. However, the reward is delayed until accounts close, weak for casuals on four-week contracts, may feel unfair if a bad weather week erases the surplus, and requires transparent surplus reporting GBO must prepare for every member.

Decision: GBO should choose a seasonal attendance bonus for the December cohort, keeping its existing profit-sharing for permanent members. The bonus targets the exact failure point — no-shows at peak when 28 extra hires are needed — is affordable, instant and easy to communicate to casuals, and can include a quality hurdle (breakage below a set rate) to blunt the careless-attendance weakness. A profit-sharing rollout now is rejected because it cannot motivate four-week seasonal staff whose contract may end before any payout, and because its administration cost outweighs gains in a peak crisis; GBO can extend it to high-performing seasonal staff next year once the depot opens.
    Keywords: seasonal, December, workforce of 34, 7.5%, $28.40, cooperative
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation schemes with limited application to GBO. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both schemes in the context of GBO. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both schemes in the context of GBO with a well-justified decision explaining why profit-sharing is rejected for the December cohort and an attendance bonus with a quality hurdle is preferred.

    Keywords: 60,000, 18,000, $3.30, $198,000, 78,000, $2.20, $5.50
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GBO's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GBO's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.76 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.96 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.95 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $85,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $185,000; 2025 current assets = $105,000 + $75,000 + $95,000 = $275,000. 2024 cover = $185,000 ÷ $105,000 current liabilities = 1.76; 2025 cover = $275,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.96. 2024 liquid cover = ($185,000 − $85,000) ÷ $105,000 = $100,000 ÷ $105,000 = 0.95; 2025 liquid cover = ($275,000 − $105,000) ÷ $140,000 = $170,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.21.

Cash rose sharply from $40,000 to $95,000, reflecting member share capital flowing in ahead of the depot, while inventories grew only modestly from $85,000 to $105,000 and trade receivables from $60,000 to $75,000 (local farm invoices and cooperative wholesale accounts). Non-current assets climbed from $1,150,000 to $1,540,000, and capital employed from $1,235,000 to $1,600,000, consistent with near-complete preparation for the new store. One caution: 7.5% waste worth $36,000 means some 2025 inventory is at risk of never converting to sales, so healthy liquid cover depends on maintaining donation and markdown disciplines.

Conclusion: GBO's financial position has improved. Overall cover strengthened from 1.76 to 1.96 and the liquid cover from 0.95 to 1.21, meaning short-term debts are now comfortably covered without forced selling of perishable stock. GBO should still tighten terms with slower wholesale buyers and keep waste below 7.5% so liquidity converts into sustainable surplus for members and the new depot's launch.
    Keywords: 1.76, 1.96, 0.95, 1.21, $185,000, $275,000, $640,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of cash, inventory and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether GBO's financial position improved.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GBO of introducing a home-delivery box scheme for its farm-box members.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in organic input costs will affect GBO. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (from 4.0% to 4.75%): GBO's $240,000 bank loan, if variable-rate, costs roughly $1,800 more a year, a negligible sum next to the $640,000 depot build and well within cooperative cash of $95,000. Minimum wage increase (5.2% rise to $13.41 per hour from April 2026): GBO's workforce is deliberately part-time and seasonal; the 34 permanent members plus 28 December seasonal hires work limited weekly hours. The annual wage bill is therefore modest (roughly $5,000–$10,000 extra a year, heavier in December), and can be partly offset by productivity rostering, multiskilling between till and packing, and the attendance bonus rather than blanket pay rises.

Input-cost inflation (11.2% rise in grain, dairy and fresh vegetables): produce is the dominant component of GBO's $2.20 variable cost per unit, around $1.85–$2.00 of it. Organic food inflation is 7.4%, so full pass-through would push GBO's prices ahead of the market and risk member churn at the 66% delivery-scheme sign-up stage.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in organic input costs will have the greatest impact on GBO. It attacks GBO on two fronts — procurement cost and waste value — every single week, against a sector where consumer tolerance for price rises is capped by 7.4% inflation and where cooperative members are exceptionally price-aware. The wage rise is second (a few thousand dollars, peak-weighted), and the interest-rate move is trivial and fixable. GBO should respond by locking annual supply contracts with its 50 km farms, expanding donation and markdown processes to cut the 7.5% waste, and negotiating a small basket-fee increase rather than headline price rises.

--- STEM ---
Hartwell Homewares (HHW) is a public limited company in the homeware retail sector, employing a workforce of 210. Founded in 1994 by Gregory Hartwell, the chain operates twelve out-of-town stores across the Alderney region under a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HHW plans to invest $1,850,000 in three new out-of-town homeware stores, financed by a $1,200,000 share issue and $650,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,050,000 a year, a variable cost of $13 a unit and a selling price of $25.50, and currently produces 108,000 units a year. HHW faces a serious human resources problem: labour turnover has reached 41% a year across its stores and seasonal shelf-stacking gaps widen every Christmas.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HHW intends to fund part of the three-store expansion by share issue. Explain two advantages for HHW of financing the expansion with a $1,200,000 share issue instead of the $650,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue carries no interest and no fixed repayment dates, which is vital when HHW already faces fixed costs of $1,050,000 a year and a variable-rate bank loan element rising with the base rate. Avoiding further debt service protects HHW's cash headroom — important with labour turnover at 41% and wage inflation approaching — and leaves the $650,000 bank loan manageable alongside the share-issue proceeds.

Point 2: Selling shares spreads the ownership risk of three unproven out-of-town sites across many public investors rather than loading it onto HHW's property assets as security. It also strengthens the balance sheet and makes HHW more credible to landlords, suppliers and local authorities during catchment negotiations, supporting the 8.1 out of 10 catchment scores the three sites achieved, and preserving the freedom to stage openings rather than commit to aggressive early repayments.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $1,200,000, $650,000, $1,850,000, labour turnover
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Hartwell Homewares, its expansion decision and its finances.

    Question: HHW is opening three new out-of-town homeware stores. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship in the three catchment areas, or social media marketing with home-lifestyle influencers. Which should HHW choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: Television would reach millions across the whole Alderney region and build instant national awareness of the new stores, reinforcing HHW's twelve-store reputation. However, production and airtime are extremely expensive, much of the audience lives far outside the three catchments, and for a public limited company raising $1,200,000 in new equity, the wastage is hard to justify when only three stores open, and television cannot tell viewers exactly where to park or what opening offers apply locally.

Local radio sponsorship in the three catchment areas: Radio reaches commuters and local householders precisely where the stores will trade, suits opening-weekend messaging, price announcements and loyalty-card drives, and is far cheaper than television. Its weakness is audio-only communication — homewares is visual, so sofa styles and kitchen ranges cannot be shown — and frequency of spots is needed before recall builds, with no interactive click-through to HHW's website.

Social media marketing with home-lifestyle influencers: Influencers could tour showroom kitchens, style living rooms with HHW furniture and post discount codes, measurable through clicks and redemptions, suiting the 57% of shoppers willing to buy online. It is inexpensive and visual, but skew toward younger audiences under-represents HHW's core family furniture buyers, and quality control across many influencers is harder for a hierarchical, democratically governed chain.

Recommendation: HHW should choose local radio sponsorship anchored in the three catchment areas. It concentrates spend exactly where stores open, suits price-led homeware messages for family buyers, and costs a fraction of television and more targeting than untargeted social reach. National television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for three stores, and influencer-first social marketing is rejected as too young-skewing and hard to police for a 210-person chain; HHW should add in-store events and local press leaflets to convert radio listeners into opening-weekend footfall.

Point 2: Defined chains of command speed up escalation when problems arise, for example stock shortages or the 12% of shoppers complaining about checkout queues over 10 minutes; democratic leadership then lets employees contribute ideas through team briefings and worker forums before decisions are finalised, combining tight control with genuine staff buy-in from departments that understand homewares operations best.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HHW wants to reduce its 41% annual labour turnover. Consider performance-related bonuses or job enrichment for store staff. Which should HHW choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Performance-related bonuses: Linking a monthly bonus to individual or team sales targets, mystery-shop scores and queue times would reward results directly — the $46 average basket value and 66% satisfaction with in-store service are measurable, and bonuses are easy to understand. Enrichment costs little in cash, builds skills HHW needs for three new stores, and directly addresses boredom-driven quitting among younger shelf teams. Its limits are slower to show results, requires careful training and supervision, and cannot satisfy staff purely motivated by take-home pay.

Decision: HHW should choose job enrichment as its primary remedy, wrapped in targeted team bonuses only for new-store opening teams. Enrichment attacks the root cause of the 41% turnover — monotony and lack of progression in shelf and till roles — costs far less than adding bonus pay on top of a 6.1% minimum-wage rise, and builds the versatile staff the expansion needs. Performance-related bonuses alone are rejected because they pay more for output without fixing why people leave, risk worsening stock shrinkage and corner-cutting at busy periods, and would be repeated indefinitely; enrichment with recognition is the sustainable fix.
    Keywords: labour turnover, 41%, $46, workforce of 210, democratic leadership, minimum wage

--- STEM ---
Velvette Beauty (VB) is a private limited company in the beauty and cosmetics retail sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2019 by Amara Osei, the pure-player brand sells skincare and cosmetics online from its Norwood fulfilment centre under a flat structure with autocratic leadership. VB plans to invest $920,000 in its first physical flagship store in the Norwood shopping district, financed by $480,000 venture capital and $440,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 44,000 units a year. VB faces a growing operational problem: returns abuse has reached 13% of online orders, with buyers ordering multiple shades and sending almost all of them back.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VB intends to fund part of the flagship store launch with venture capital. Explain two advantages for VB of using venture capital instead of its $440,000 retained profit to fund the store.
    Answer: Point 1: Venture capital brings more than money: VB gains an investor with beauty and retail expertise, supplier contacts and board-level guidance on site selection in Norwood, lease negotiation and store design — knowledge a 38-person pure-player brand may lack as it opens its first physical shop. The money arrives without interest or repayment dates, protecting VB's cash while the $920,000 build is on site.

Point 2: Keeping the $440,000 retained profit inside the business preserves a working-capital buffer for the online operation that still drives 31,500 units a quarter, absorbing the 10.8% rise in botanical and packaging input costs and the 13% returns abuse before the store pays for itself. VB's backers also back the brand publicly, boosting credibility with landlords and landlords' lenders, and patient venture capital is more flexible than a bank if opening weekends underperform targets. It also strengthens the balance sheet with new equity, making VB more credible to the Norwood shopping district's letting agents and their lenders.
    Keywords: venture capital, retained profit, $440,000, $920,000, $480,000, flagship store

An in-store event with skincare demos, shade-matching and limited edition bundles would fill the 900 first-month visitor target, generate genuine user content from the venue itself, and convert online fans into walk-in buyers for the price of appearances and samples rather than airtime.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio would speak directly to Norwood listeners with opening offers, parking directions and loyalty-card sign-ups, cheap and frequent. However, VB's core 18-34 audience streams rather than listens to radio, beauty is visual, and radio cannot demonstrate texture, shade and scent — the very attributes that close beauty sales in store.

Decision: VB should choose a picking-accuracy bonus for fulfilment staff, reviewed quarterly, rather than across-the-board profit sharing. The returns problem is specific and measurable; a targeted bonus hits it directly, costs less than splitting profits, and fits the flat, autocratically led culture with clear targets and instant feedback. Profit sharing is rejected as the primary lever because it rewards diffuse outcomes, pays out for drivers VB cannot attribute to individuals, and weakens the urgent focus needed before the flagship store doubles order volume; VB can add a modest annual profit-sharing payout later, once the returns rate falls below 8%.

Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.02 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $45,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $285,000; 2025 current assets = $210,000 + $60,000 + $175,000 = $445,000. 2024 cover = $285,000 ÷ $180,000 current liabilities = 1.58; 2025 cover = $445,000 ÷ $230,000 = 1.93. 2024 liquid cover = ($285,000 − $150,000) ÷ $180,000 = $135,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.75; 2025 liquid cover = ($445,000 − $210,000) ÷ $230,000 = $235,000 ÷ $230,000 = 1.02.

Evaluation: VB's liquidity has strengthened substantially. Cash jumped from $90,000 to $175,000 as venture capital and retained profit were banked ahead of the store build, inventories rose only moderately from $150,000 to $210,000 (sensible for launch stock without over-ordering shades), and trade receivables, although small, rose from $45,000 to $60,000 as some influencer and wholesale partners pay on terms. Current liabilities climbed from $180,000 to $230,000, but current assets grew far faster. Non-current assets increased from $1,300,000 to $1,720,000 and capital employed from $1,405,000 to $1,725,000, consistent with fit-out spend on the flagship store. The strongest signal is that the liquid cover crossed 1.00 (1.02), meaning VB no longer relies on selling stock to meet short-term obligations — valuable while the store is generating its first customers and before its cash position is proven.

Conclusion: VB's financial position has improved. Both cover measures rose, and the liquid measure moved above 1.00, giving VB genuine headroom into its first physical year. VB should still cap launch-stock depth to avoid shade obsolescence discounting, watch receivables from any retail partners, and preserve cash until the flagship hits its 900 first-month daily-visitor target and order volumes scale.
    Keywords: 1.58, 1.93, 0.75, 1.02, $285,000, $445,000, $920,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of cash, inventory and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether VB's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VB of introducing refillable skincare packaging for its core moisturiser range.
    Answer: Advantage: Refillable packaging would let VB charge a premium on its best-selling moisturiser while giving the 54% of buyers aged 18-34 — the most sustainability-conscious cohort in its campaign data — a visible reason to stay loyal. Refills lock customers into repeat purchasing, lowering customer-acquisition costs below the $21,000 quarterly campaign spend, differentiating VB on Norwood's shopping strip, and cutting packaging weight and cost per refill, partially offsetting the 10.8% rise in botanical input costs.

Disadvantage: Refill systems require new moulds, sealing line changeovers and consumer education on how to return or refill pods, upfront spending that competes with the $920,000 store budget. If refills are messy or hygiene perceptions fail, VB risks damaging the exact product whose shade and texture drive its $34.60 average order, and refill returns could worsen the 13% returns abuse if tracking does not identify whether empty pods came back with genuine refill intent or abusive free-merchandise claims.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.9%, the 6.3% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in botanical input costs will affect VB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (from 4.1% to 4.9%): VB carries no variable-rate bank debt — the $480,000 venture capital is equity and the $440,000 retained profit is free — so the direct interest impact is negligible. The rise instead makes later borrowing (for stock lines or store expansion) pricier and may cool consumers' willingness to use credit for premium beauty, though online beauty spending still grew 9.3%. This is the smallest of the three threats for VB, and it can be managed entirely by avoiding variable-rate borrowing.

Minimum wage increase (6.3% rise to $13.87 per hour from April 2026): VB's 38 staff span fulfilment packers, customer service and, from opening day, store advisors and till staff on hourly contracts. Only a minority of the team is salaried; the fulfilment and store floor is largely hourly. On an hourly wage base of roughly $260,000 a year, the 6.3% rise adds about $16,400 a year — noticeable but absorbable, especially if VB lifts shift productivity, multiskilling and the 900 first-month daily-visitor target converts to sales.

Input-cost inflation (10.8% rise in botanicals and packaging): botanical extracts and active ingredients dominate VB's $7.00 variable cost per unit — roughly $4.60 of it is spent on raw ingredients and jars. A 10.8% rise adds close to $0.50 per unit, or about $22,000 a year on 44,000 units, and squeezes the $9.00 contribution per unit toward $8.50. Worse, cosmetics-price inflation is 6.6%, so VB cannot fully pass the increase on without breaking its mid-market positioning against cheaper supermarket skincare.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in botanical input costs will have the greatest impact on VB. At roughly $22,000 a year it exceeds the $16,400 wage rise and the negligible interest effect, it is inseparable from product quality (the core of VB's reputation), and it compounds with every unit sold online and in-store. VB should respond by locking 12-month botanical supply contracts, introducing a small, phased price increase concentrated on hero products, launching a refill programme where consumers accept higher value per pump, and expanding margin-accretive accessories — while fixing store rosters efficiently so the wage increase stays a manageable second threat.
    Keywords: 4.9%, 6.3%, 10.8%, interest rate, $13.87, $480,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VB's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VB with a well-justified judgement that the input-cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
