--- STEM ---
Seabrook Coastal Hotels (SCH) is a private limited company in the hospitality and hotel sector, employing a workforce of 160. Founded in 2004 by Dana Whitmore, the group operates three coastal hotels along the shoreline and uses a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership from Dana Whitmore. SCH plans to invest $1,200,000 in refurbishing its flagship cliff-top hotel and adding a new wedding and events wing, financed by a $750,000 twelve-year bank loan and $450,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $2,490,000 a year, a variable cost of $62 a unit and a selling price of $145, and currently produces 58,000 units a year (one unit is one occupied room-night). SCH faces two problems: seasonal staff turnover has reached 34% and absenteeism stands at 10%, and wedding enquiries are being lost to a rival events venue.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SCH plans to finance part of its refurbishment and wedding wing with a twelve-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SCH of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit avoids all interest charges on the $750,000 bank loan, so the twelve-year commitment does not add to SCH's $2,490,000 fixed costs at a time when food and energy costs have already risen 9.8%. Every dollar SCH saves on interest can be redirected to the refurbishment and to absorbing the 5.9% rise in the minimum wage to $12.85, protecting the group's $83 contribution ($145 − $62) on each occupied room-night and keeping room rates at $145 competitive for domestic coastal tourists, whose spending grew 4.2% this year.

Point 2: Retained profit involves no collateral, so Dana Whitmore does not risk losing the flagship cliff-top hotel or its new wedding and events wing if trading becomes difficult during quieter winter months. It also preserves complete ownership and control for SCH's existing shareholders, avoids the lender imposing conditions on how the wing is run, and leaves the option of a bank loan open later if wedding bookings exceed the 46 already recorded in Q3 2026.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $450,000, $750,000, wedding and events wing, $1,200,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Seabrook Coastal Hotels and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SCH is launching its refurbished sea-view rooms and new wedding and events wing. Consider a national television campaign, local newspaper advertising, or social media influencer marketing aimed at wedding planners and couples. Which should SCH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national TV campaign would give SCH the widest possible reach and would build fast, prestigious awareness of the refurbished cliff-top hotel across the country. However, production and airtime costs are extremely high for a 160-employee family-influenced private limited company already financing $750,000 of the $1,200,000 refurbishment with a bank loan, and much of a national audience would never book a coastal wedding at SCH; spend would be wasted outside its catchment.

Local newspaper advertising: Local newspapers are cheap, reach the regional audience most likely to book sea-view weekend breaks and local weddings, and suit a grand-opening offer for the wing. Their limitation is narrow circulation and an ageing readership, so they would do little for the 58% of researched guests willing to pay more for sea-view rooms who live further afield, and they cannot showcase the wing visually in a competitive events market.

Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with wedding-planner influencers and coastal-lifestyle creators targets exactly the couples researching venues online, reaches a national audience for far less than TV, and provides measurable engagement, booking enquiries and review traction; the 8.4 average review score and rising occupancy of 71% give influencers strong proof to share. It depends on influencer authenticity and takes longer to compound than TV, but the cost per engaged couple is low.

Recommendation: SCH should choose social media influencer marketing. It speaks directly to wedding planners and couples nationally at a cost SCH can afford alongside its bank loan, reinforces the review-driven reputation (8.4/10), and shows the wing visually. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a $1,200,000 project financed partly by debt; local newspapers are rejected as too narrow for a tiered national events market, though SCH can add low-cost local print for community weddings once the launch quietens.
    Keywords: wedding and events wing, $1,200,000, 58%, 71%, 8.4, bank loan
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SCH with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SCH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspaper advertising are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SCH's seasonal staff turnover has reached 34% and absenteeism stands at 10%. Explain two benefits for SCH of introducing off-the-job training for its seasonal hotel staff.
    Answer: Point 1: Off-the-job training, such as the college courses costing $1,100 per employee, gives seasonal staff recognised qualifications and structured skills before the summer peak, which raises their confidence, morale and sense of being valued beyond a casual contract. This directly attacks SCH's 34% seasonal staff turnover, because staff who feel invested in are far more likely to return each season, saving SCH repeated recruitment and induction costs while its flat structure depends on experienced supervisors being available.

Point 2: Training away from the hotel — for example in wedding catering systems and customer service — means the 28 staff who have not completed on-the-job training can learn without disrupting guests in the refurbished rooms. Skilled, certified staff make fewer errors, supporting the fall in complaints from 34 to 19 per month, protecting the 71% occupancy that finances the $1,200,000 refurbishment, and ensuring the wedding and events wing opens with capable, motivated teams rather than rushed-on casual labour.
    Keywords: college courses, seasonal staff turnover, absenteeism, $1,100, 34%, 10%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SCH's seasonal turnover, absenteeism and expansion.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SCH is opening its wedding and events wing and needs staff for it. Consider recruiting more seasonal temporary staff or training and promoting existing permanent staff to lead the wing. Which should SCH choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Seasonal temporary staff: Hiring seasonal workers matches SCH's existing summer-peak pattern and keeps immediate wage costs low, which suits a wing that will be busiest at weekends and during wedding season. It gives SCH flexibility to scale up for large weddings, and wages rise only with the 5.9% minimum wage increase rather than with full-year salaries. However, seasonal staff already churn at 34%, the 10% absenteeism is worst among casuals, and weddings demand consistently high service and reliability; re-training each season would overload supervisors already managing the refurbishment.

Promote and train existing permanent staff: Promoting from within rewards loyalty, fills the 28-person training gap identified in the needs analysis, and retains SCH's service culture and 8.4 review score for critical events. Promotion satisfies esteem needs (Maslow) and reduces labour turnover by giving staff a career path into events management. The costs are higher short-term wages, the need to backfill roles and the risk that promoted staff need new skills they do not yet have.

Decision: SCH should choose training and promoting existing permanent staff to lead the wedding and events wing, supported by seasonal casuals only at peak weekends. Weddings are high-stakes events where Dana Whitmore's autocratic flat structure needs trusted, committed leaders who know the hotel; reliance on seasonal staff is rejected because it has already produced 34% turnover and 10% absenteeism and would damage the reviews that win premium sea-view bookings. Seasonal hires alone are too unreliable; full-time promotion alone is also rejected as too rigid for weekend peaks, so a permanent core with casual weekend support is best.
    Keywords: wedding and events wing, seasonal staff turnover, absenteeism, training, 34%, 58%

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how SCH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units a year, computed as $2,490,000 fixed costs divided by $83 contribution per room-night (selling price $145 less variable cost $62). At the current 58,000-unit output, SCH operates a margin of safety of 28,000 units, so room-night revenue comfortably covers both fixed and variable costs. (ii) Contribution per unit = $83 per occupied room-night, which is what every sold room-night contributes toward fixed costs and, after that, profit. (iii) Four applied uses: first, tracking the margin of safety ahead of the $750,000 bank loan repayments for the flagship refurbishment; second, modelling weekday coastal-holiday discounts where each $15 price cut reduces contribution to $68 ($130 − $62); third, setting rate and package targets for the new wedding and events wing so packages cover fixed costs after interest at 5.75%; fourth, unit-cost benchmarking at $104.93 ($2,490,000 ÷ 58,000 + $62) to locate food and energy overspends behind the 9.8% input-cost rise. Together these uses let Dana Whitmore test whether the hotel and wing stay above break-even through the quieter winter months while the $1,200,000 refurbishment is delivered.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SCH's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SCH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.53 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.83 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.97 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.36 : 1

Conclusion: SCH's financial position has improved. Both measures show stronger short-term solvency in 2025 and the improvement is not reliant on inventory.   Q4(a) [8 marks]

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase to $12.85 and the 9.8% rise in food and energy input costs will affect SCH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If SCH's $750,000 twelve-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $5,625 a year in interest ($750,000 × 0.75% = $5,625), lifting the fixed-cost burden above $2,490,000. Higher rates also make premium coastal breaks less tempting for cautious visitors and raise the cost of any further borrowing for the refurbishment. The direct cash impact is modest, can be capped by fixing the loan rate, and is fully computable from insert figures — unlike the other two factors, it does not erode the $83 contribution ($145 − $62) per room-night.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.85 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both the old and new rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.70 ($12.85 − $12.15 = $0.70). The exact annual cost cannot be computed from the insert, because the headcount and hours paid at the minimum wage are not stated; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor overtakes the interest rise — it does so once SCH pays more than roughly 8,036 minimum-wage hours a year ($5,625 ÷ $0.70 ≈ 8,036), a level plainly exceeded by a seasonal 160-employee hotel across a full trading year. In Maslow's terms, financial reward helps but does not cure the 10% absenteeism driven by motivation or the 34% seasonal staff turnover, so the rise is real but manageable through engagement and productivity.

Food and energy input costs (up 9.8% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names wholesale food and energy explicitly, and SCH's $62 variable cost per room-night will include ingredients, utilities and catering. No component share is given anywhere in the insert, so the honest bound runs from $0 (if no named input applied — implausible for a full-service hotel) to a labelled upper bound of applying the whole 9.8% to the entire $62: at most about $6.08 per room-night ($62 × 9.8% = $6.08), which over the current 58,000 room-nights would cap the damage at roughly $352,640 a year (58,000 × $6.08). The true figure lies between these bounds and cannot be pinned further without inventing a share; what is certain is that every matching input rises together for every room-night sold, that SCH cannot refinance this away the way it can fix the loan rate, and that it lands precisely when the $1,200,000 refurbishment pressure is highest.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in food and energy input costs will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest rise, which is exactly $5,625 a year and fixable, and unlike the wage floor, whose exposure is limited to minimum-wage hours, input inflation applies continuously to every one of the 58,000 room-nights sold and to every offer SCH makes in the domestic coastal-holiday market where consumer spending grew 4.2%. Quantifying it precisely is impossible from the insert, but even a partially exposed $62 variable cost dwarfs $5,625, and the 9.8% figure is the steepest of the two percentage rises SCH can act on for all sales volumes. SCH should respond with supplier renegotiation, waste reduction in kitchens, selective sea-view price rises (58% of researched guests accept up to $25 more) and menu engineering, while treating the minimum-wage increase — significant but smaller — as second priority and the interest-rate motion as the smallest of the three.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SCH. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SCH's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SCH with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Acacia Trails Safari Lodge (ATSL) is a cooperative in the hospitality and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2011 by Sipho Dlamini, the lodge is owned and run by its staff-members and uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership, where staff vote on major decisions at monthly meetings. ATSL plans to invest $980,000 in a new tented eco-camp on adjacent land, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and a $380,000 member share issue. It has fixed costs of $4,970,000 a year, a variable cost of $88 a unit and a selling price of $230, and currently produces 46,000 units a year (one unit is one occupied guest-night). ATSL faces two problems: experienced safari guides are being poached by rival lodges, and absenteeism stands at 8%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ATSL plans to finance part of its tented eco-camp expansion with a member share issue. Explain two advantages for ATSL of using a member share issue instead of a ten-year bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A member share issue raises $380,000 from the staff-owners themselves, with no interest to pay and no fixed repayment timetable, unlike the $600,000 ten-year bank loan. This protects ATSL's $4,970,000 fixed costs — already stretched by the 11.2% rise in diesel, park permit and laundry input costs and the 7.5% minimum wage increase — and means the cooperative is never at risk of default if tented eco-camp bookings start slowly at the 66% occupancy level.

Point 2: Share capital from members deepens commitment: staff-owners who buy in financially have a direct stake in the new camp's success, supporting the democratic culture at monthly meetings and reducing the risk of guides being poached, because leaving would mean giving up member status. No bank can seize ATSL's land or lodge if times are hard, and democratic control stays fully with members rather than passing to an outside lender imposing covenants.
    Keywords: member share issue, bank loan, $380,000, $600,000, tented eco-camp, 66%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Acacia Trails Safari Lodge and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ATSL is launching its new tented eco-camp. Consider national newspaper advertising, social media influencer marketing, or exhibiting at a regional travel trade show. Which should ATSL choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National newspaper advertising: Major national papers would give ATSL broad awareness among potential eco-tourists across the country and suit a grand-opening story with beautiful photography of the tented camp. However, full-page colour rates are high for a cooperative with 85 employees funding $980,000 of expansion partly by bank loan, and papers reach a broad, untargeted audience including many people who will never book a safari; measured response rates for print advertising are weak.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with eco-travel and safari influencers targets exactly the 71% of surveyed past guests willing to pay up to $30 more per guest-night, uses the lodge's 8.8 review score and 1,240 reviews as persuasive proof, and produces measurable enquiries at low cost per reached viewer. It suits repeat and younger eco-tourists and amplifies the website's 27% direct-booking growth. Risks are influencer credibility and slower trust-building for luxury-price segments.

Travel trade show exhibition: A regional trade show puts ATSL directly in front of tour operators, corporate travel buyers and travel agents who package safari holidays, potentially securing group bookings and shoulder-season volume. Costs of stand space, travel and samples are moderate, and leads can be converted by follow-up. However, shows are episodic, reach a trade rather than consumer audience, and do little for direct repeat-guest marketing.

Recommendation: ATSL should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise eco-conscious segment identified in its research at the lowest cost per enquiry, leverages its 8.8/10 ratings and 44% repeat-guest base, and compounds with the website's direct bookings. Newspapers are rejected as too broad and expensive for the budget; the trade show is rejected as too narrow and episodic to fill the camp alone, though ATSL should attend one show a year to win operator contracts once the influencer campaign is live.
    Keywords: tented eco-camp, 71%, 8.8, 44%, $30, eco-tourism
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ATSL with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ATSL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspaper advertising and the trade show are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ATSL's experienced safari guides are being poached by rival lodges and absenteeism stands at 8%. Explain two benefits for ATSL of using job enrichment for its safari guides.
    Answer: Point 1: Job enrichment gives guides greater responsibility — designing their own game-drive routes, leading guest safety briefings and mentoring junior staff — which satisfies their esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow) and raises the meaning of the work. Guides who feel trusted and challenged are far less likely to accept offers from rival lodges, directly reducing the poaching problem and the $4,970,000 cost pressure of repeatedly recruiting and certifying replacement guides.

Point 2: Enriched guides become more committed and proactive, improving the quality of the wildlife experience that 84% of surveyed guests rated as ATSL's strongest feature. They spot maintenance issues earlier, upsell the tented eco-camp and handle guest problems without escalation, supporting the 8.8 review score and 66% occupancy rate. Better motivation also tackles the 8% absenteeism directly, since staff with ownership over their role call in sick far less often than those doing repetitive, low-autonomy work. Enrichment is cheaper than across-the-board pay rises while the 7.5% minimum wage increase phases in, and it strengthens the cooperative's democratic culture, because empowered guides gain real influence rather than token consultation at monthly meetings.
    Keywords: safari guides, absenteeism, 8%, 8.8, 66%, poached
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ATSL's poaching problem, absenteeism and guest experience.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ATSL must recruit two senior head guides for the new tented eco-camp. Consider recruiting externally from rival lodges or promoting and training existing junior guides from within the cooperative. Which should ATSL choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: External recruitment from rival lodges: Hiring already-proven head guides would bring immediate expertise, fresh ideas and established guest-handling skills, and could lift the tented camp's credibility from opening day; it also avoids the temporary productivity dip of internal promotion. However, rival-poached guides may carry rivals' habits rather than ATSL's democratic, community-owned values, would demand head-guide salaries well above existing internal rates, and — having been poached once themselves — may be poached again, recreating the exact instability ATSL is trying to solve.

Promoting and training existing junior guides: Internal promotion rewards the loyalty of members who built the lodge since 2011, costs less in salary shocks, and firmly strengthens democratic commitment and retention — the key defence against rival poaching. Training gaps can be closed with off-the-job courses, and the flat structure means promoted guides can genuinely influence tented-camp operations. The risks are a slower capability build-up, internal jealousy if the selection is not transparent, and the need to backfill the vacated junior roles.

Decision: ATSL should choose promoting and training existing junior guides. It directly counters the poaching problem, preserves cooperative culture and member trust at monthly meetings, and is far cheaper than market-rate external salaries at a time when the bank loan and share issue already commit $980,000. External recruitment is rejected because it imports flight risk and pay inflation; wholesale external hiring is only justified if no internal candidate meets the camp's guiding certification standard, which the interview data should be checked against first. A phased internal promotion, benchmarked against external salaries, keeps pay fair, transparent and defensible at the monthly members' meeting and signals to every junior guide that the cooperative invests in its own people.
    Keywords: tented eco-camp, poached, democratic, $980,000, member, cooperative
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment approaches with limited application to ATSL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both recruitment options in the context of ATSL. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of ATSL with a well-justified decision covering cost, culture, retention and capability.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how ATSL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,000 units a year, computed as $4,970,000 fixed costs divided by $142 contribution per guest-night (selling price $230 less variable cost $88). At the current 46,000-unit output, ATSL carries a margin of safety of 11,000 units, confirming the lodge trades comfortably above break-even while the tented eco-camp opens on adjacent land. (ii) Contribution per unit = $142 per occupied guest-night, the amount each guest-night adds toward fixed costs and then profit. (iii) Four applied uses: first, tracking the margin of safety toward the 75% occupancy target; second, modelling a $20 direct-booking discount that would cut contribution to $122 ($210 − $88) before any extra volume is gained; third, setting tented-camp rates and phase targets so the $980,000 expansion, financed by the $600,000 bank loan and $380,000 member share issue, stays above break-even; fourth, unit-cost benchmarking at $196.04 per guest-night ($4,970,000 ÷ 46,000 + $88) to expose catering and laundry overspends amid the 11.2% input-cost rise. Together these uses let Sipho Dlamini and the staff-members test whether camp-phase proposals and pricing decisions keep the lodge solvent through the shoulder seasons.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ATSL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ATSL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.68 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.77 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.23 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.37 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140,000 inventories + $160,000 trade receivables + $220,000 cash = $520,000; 2025 current assets = $120,000 + $150,000 + $260,000 = $530,000. Current liabilities fell from $310,000 to $300,000. 2024: $520,000 ÷ $310,000 = 1.68; 2025: $530,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.77. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($520,000 − $140,000) ÷ $310,000 = $380,000 ÷ $310,000 = 1.23; 2025 = ($530,000 − $120,000) ÷ $300,000 = $410,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.37.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. Current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, and cash rose from $220,000 to $260,000 — a healthy cushion for a lodge whose occupancy is still only 66% and which is about to spend $980,000 on the tented eco-camp. The stricter measure rose from 1.23 to 1.37, so ATSL can meet short-term debts without selling food and beverage stock, a strength given the 11.2% rise in input costs. Cautions: trade receivables fell only marginally to $150,000, and any slow-paying corporate retreat bookings could tighten liquidity; current liabilities of $300,000 remain substantial against cash of $260,000, and the bank loan will add annual service charges from year one.

Conclusion: ATSL's financial position has improved. Both measures point to stronger short-term solvency in 2025, supported by lower inventories and lower liabilities. ATSL should protect this by keeping direct bookings growing, collecting agent commissions promptly and ring-fencing the eco-camp budget so the expansion does not erode the improved liquidity position.
    Keywords: 1.68, 1.77, 1.23, 1.37, $520,000, $530,000, $600,000

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ATSL of opening the new tented eco-camp on adjacent land.
    Answer: Advantage: The tented eco-camp captures the 71% of surveyed guests willing to pay up to $30 more per guest-night for a tented experience, letting ATSL lift its $230 price point and its $142 contribution ($230 − $88) exactly where eco-tourism spending grew 6.8%. It uses the adjacent land efficiently, spreads fixed costs of $4,970,000 over more guest-nights, and gives ATSL a second product for the 44% repeat-guest base to try on their next stay, strengthening the 66% occupancy toward the 75% target.

Disadvantage: The camp commits $980,000 to new structures, equipment and access tracks before a single guest has stayed, financed partly by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan at a time when the base interest rate has just risen to 6.0%. If the camp launches slowly, its share of fixed costs and interest could outrun its revenue, diverting attention and maintenance capacity from the main lodge, damaging the 8.8 review score that carries ATSL's whole reputation, and straining the cooperative's democratic decision-making if members disagree on how fast to add tent phases.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 7.5% minimum wage increase to $9.60 and the 11.2% rise in diesel, park permit and laundry input costs will affect ATSL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If ATSL's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $4,500 a year in interest ($600,000 × 0.75% = $4,500), lifting fixed costs above $4,970,000. Higher rates also make discretionary eco-holidays slightly less tempting and would raise the cost of drawing down any remaining borrowing for the tented eco-camp. The absolute impact is the smallest of the three and can be managed by fixing the loan rate or by repaying early from member share capital, and unlike the other two factors it does not erode the $142 contribution ($230 − $88) per guest-night.

Minimum wage increase (7.5%, to $9.60 per hour from May 2026): Appendix 3 states both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.35 ($9.60 − $9.25 = $0.35), the largest percentage rise of the three factors. The annual cost cannot be computed from the insert because the number of hours paid at the minimum wage is not stated; what can be shown is the break-even against the interest rise — the wage factor exceeds $4,500 once ATSL pays more than roughly 12,857 minimum-wage hours a year ($4,500 ÷ $0.35 ≈ 12,857 hours), a threshold comfortably exceeded by an 85-employee lodge with catering, laundry and maintenance staff. Because the lodge is a cooperative founded on fair member pay, absorbed wages are partly a governance commitment, not just an HR line item; compliance is non-negotiable and the 8% absenteeism makes any pay friction internally damaging.

Diesel, park permit and laundry input costs (up 11.2% year-on-year): Appendix 3 specifically names diesel, park permits and laundry — the exact running costs of game drives, guest access and linen service, all essential to a safari operation. No share of the $88 variable cost is stated, so the correct bound runs from $0 to an upper bound built on insert figures: applying the full 11.2% to the entire $88 gives at most about $9.86 per guest-night ($88 × 11.2% = $9.86), capping the damage at roughly $453,376 a year at the current 46,000 unit output (46,000 × $9.86). The true figure lies between the bounds; the insert permits no finer split, and any assumed share would be invented. What is certain is that these inputs recur on every game drive and every occupied room, concentrate in the $88 variable cost rather than in the $4,970,000 fixed costs, and cannot be switched to a cheaper park or laundered linens.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in diesel, park permit and laundry input costs will have the greatest impact. It is the steepest percentage increase named in Appendix 3, recurrences on every one of 46,000 guest-nights, escapes refinancing, and — unlike the wage factor, whose cash effect is limited to minimum-wage hours at $0.35 each — applies to all consumption regardless of who delivers it. Supplier renegotiation, route efficiencies, on-site laundry for the tented eco-camp and selective price increases (71% of surveyed guests accept up to $30 more per night) are the levers ATSL must pull; the 7.5% wage rise is the second serious pressure in an 85-member cooperative already fighting poaching, and the $4,500 interest-rate effect is the smallest of the three and can be neutralised by fixing the loan.
    Keywords: 6.0%, 7.5%, 11.2%, $9.60, $600,000, $980,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ATSL. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ATSL's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ATSL with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Embers and Oak Restaurant Group (EORG) is a private limited company in the hospitality and restaurant sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2013 by Meera Kapoor, the group runs four casual-dining restaurants in regional cities and uses a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership, where restaurant managers vote on menu changes. EORG plans to invest $750,000 in launching a franchise programme for its flagship brand, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $2,100,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.50 a unit and a selling price of $24.50, and currently produces 260,000 units a year (one unit is one meal served). EORG faces two problems: two head chefs were poached by a rival chain in October 2026, and kitchen absenteeism stands at 12%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: EORG plans to finance part of its franchise programme launch with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for EORG of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs EORG nothing in interest, which matters because wholesale protein, dairy and fresh produce prices have already risen 10.6% and eating-out inflation pressures diners; EORG's $2,100,000 fixed costs and the $450,000 bank loan commitment would otherwise squeeze the margin on its $24.50 average selling price even faster. Keeping the franchise launch interest-free preserves cash for marketing the flagship brand and for absorbing the $31.60 average cover spend that keeps repeat visits at 57% of trade.

Point 2: Using $300,000 of retained profit avoids collateral and lender conditions on the franchise programme, so Meera Kapoor and the four restaurant managers retain full control over brand standards, franchise fees and menu voting decisions. It also leaves borrowing capacity unused, which is valuable given the base interest rate just rose to 6.25% and EORG may need faster, flexible funding later if the first franchised sites underperform or if poached head chefs need replacing urgently.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $300,000, $450,000, franchise programme, $750,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Embers and Oak Restaurant Group and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: EORG is launching its franchise programme for the flagship brand. Consider national television advertising, print advertising in weekend newspaper supplements, or social media influencer marketing. Which should EORG choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would give EORG the fastest, widest awareness of the franchise opportunity, reaching entrepreneurs and potential franchisees nationwide and lending the group a trustworthy, established image. However, production and airtime are very expensive for four restaurants and 120 employees financing $750,000 of expansion partly on a $450,000 bank loan, and much of a national audience is not a prospective franchisee or regular diner at $31.60 per cover; coverage waste would be high.

Print advertising in weekend supplements: Weekend titles reach an affluent, food-interested readership, suit detailed franchise-opportunity storytelling with founder Meera Kapoor's narrative, and match EORG's existing 'Weekend Herald' presence (the two-for-one Tuesdays and loyalty card offer already in the insert). Print is cheaper than TV but still costly per response, and readership skew older, missing younger franchise candidates and younger diners who drive Tuesday two-for-one trade.

Social media influencer marketing: Food-influencer partnerships show the dining experience authentically video-first, target the 78% of surveyed diners rating the group 'very good', cost far less than TV, and can be measured precisely through bookings, loyalty-card sign-ups and franchise enquiries. Credibility risk exists if an influencer misrepresents the brand, but alignment with food creators who genuinely rate Embers and Oak is inexpensive and highly targeted.

Recommendation: EORG should choose social media influencer marketing. It proves the brand visually to exactly the diners and franchise prospects most likely to convert, leverages the 57% repeat-visit base and 2.1% complaint rate down-trend, and fits a $750,000 programme without exhausting the $450,000 bank loan. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable; print supplements are rejected as too narrow and older-skewing for franchise recruitment, though EORG should keep targeted print for franchise-opportunity sections where serious investors read.
    Keywords: franchise programme, $750,000, 78%, 57%, $450,000, $31.60
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of EORG with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of EORG with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and print are rejected.

Staff who share profits think like owners: they control portion waste (the food-waste rate is 6.8%), police prep standards and support each other through service, reducing the desperation to defect to the rival's higher salaries and tackling the 12% kitchen absenteeism caused by disengagement.

Point 2: Profit sharing aligns the four restaurants behind shared goals, reinforcing the hierarchical-yet-democratic structure by rewarding managers democratically and kitchen crews collectively. It is cheaper than across-the-board wage rises amid the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $11.05 and the 10.6% food inflation, yet it binds key staff to the franchise plan: ambitious cooks see a bonus future inside EORG rather than leaving, which protects the 57% repeat-diner base and the $31.60 average spend that franchisee recruits will be buying into.

--- STEM ---
Galaxy Lanes and Screens (GLS) is a sole trader in the leisure and entertainment sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2008 by Marcus Whitfield, GLS operates an independent cinema and ten-lane bowling venue attracting families and students, and uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership, where staff organise their own shifts and events. GLS plans to invest $680,000 in refurbishing the bowling alley and installing two new 4K screens, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $280,000 hire purchase on the projection equipment. It has fixed costs of $1,950,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $18.50, and currently produces 185,000 units a year (one unit is one ticketed visit). GLS faces two problems: casual evening and weekend staff absenteeism stands at 13%, and private-party bookings are being lost to a rival entertainment centre.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GLS plans to finance part of the refurbishment with hire purchase on the projection equipment. Explain two advantages for GLS of using hire purchase instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $280,000 projection equipment cost over fixed monthly instalments matched to the screens' earning life, so GLS does not need to commit such a large lump sum from a $400,000 bank loan. This keeps more of the bank loan available for the bowling refurbishment and for absorbing the 13.4% rise in electricity and heating prices — critical for a venue where the two new 4K screens will run for long evening sessions.

Point 2: GLS gains immediate ownership-style use of the equipment while paying, so the screens can open before full payment is made; interest is built into the instalments, making budgeting predictable; and if cash flow disappoints, the hire purchase provider — not a court — repossesses only the equipment. Unlike a bank loan, no additional collateral over the whole venue is required, preserving GLS's independence as a sole trader under Marcus Whitfield's control and protecting the $5.50 variable cost economics of concession sales that fund the investment.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GLS is reopening after its refurbishment with two new 4K screens and an updated bowling alley. Consider local radio advertising, community poster and flyer marketing, or social media marketing. Which should GLS choose to promote the reopening? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local radio advertising: Local radio reaches commuters and families across GLS's catchment with frequent, memorable audio spots, and it suits time-sensitive opening offers such as the $29 weekend family pass.   Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how GLS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 150,000 units a year, computed as $1,950,000 fixed costs divided by $13.00 contribution per ticketed visit (selling price $18.50 less variable cost $5.50). (iii) Four applied uses: first, checking the margin of safety against the $400,000 bank loan and $280,000 hire purchase on the 4K projection equipment; second, modelling the $29 weekend family pass, where the halved per-visit contribution must be offset by enough extra family volume to keep total contribution above break-even; third, testing whether two new 4K screens lift the 34% screen occupancy far enough above 150,000 units to justify the investment; fourth, unit-cost benchmarking at $16.04 per visit ($1,950,000 ÷ 185,000 + $5.50) to target the 5.2% concession waste and the 61 complaints a month.   Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GLS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GLS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.20 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.33 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $60,000 inventories + $45,000 trade receivables + $75,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $55,000 + $60,000 + $105,000 = $220,000. Current liabilities rose from $150,000 to $165,000. 2024: $180,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.20; 2025: $220,000 ÷ $165,000 = 1.33. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($180,000 − $60,000) ÷ $150,000 = $120,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.80; 2025 = ($220,000 − $55,000) ÷ $165,000 = $165,000 ÷ $165,000 = 1.00.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved across both measures. Cash rose from $75,000 to $105,000 — sensible ahead of a $680,000 refurbishment — and the stricter measure climbed from 0.80 to exactly 1.00, meaning GLS can now just meet short-term debts without selling concession stock, an important milestone for a sole trader carrying a $400,000 bank loan and $280,000 hire purchase. Inventories fell to $55,000, showing tighter concession control and lower waste than the 5.2% rate suggests. However, 1.00 is still the bare minimum for the stricter measure, and trade receivables rose from $45,000 to $60,000 — school party bookings and corporate events paying late could easily break that parity again.

Conclusion: GLS's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the stricter measure reached break-even parity at 1.00, so short solvency is no longer dependent on stock. GLS should hold cash discipline tight, chase party-booking deposits aggressively and avoid drawing more on the hire purchase until the recliner premium (57% would pay $3 more) lifts screen 1 revenue above $1,950,000 fixed costs.
    Keywords: 1.20, 1.33, 0.80, 1.00, $180,000, $220,000, $400,000

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GLS of installing recliner seating in screen 1.
    Answer: Advantage: Recliner seating responds exactly to the 57% of surveyed visitors willing to pay up to $3 more per ticket, allowing GLS to lift the screen 1 price from $18.50 toward $21.50 ($18.50 + $3.00) and raise contribution per head well above the current $13.00.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.5%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase to $10.80 and the 13.4% rise in electricity and heating prices will affect GLS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.75% to 6.5%): On GLS's $400,000 variable-rate bank loan, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $3,000 a year in interest ($400,000 × 0.75% = $3,000), lifting fixed costs above $1,950,000. Higher rates also make consumers more cautious about discretionary entertainment spending, though leisure spending grew 3.1%. The direct impact is the smallest of the three, is fully computable from insert figures, can be neutralised by fixing part of the loan, and unlike input costs does not compound with every hour the venue operates.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $10.80 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.56 ($10.80 − $10.24 = $0.56). The annual cost cannot be computed because the insert does not state the number of minimum-wage hours; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor exceeds the interest rise — it does so once GLS pays more than roughly 5,357 minimum-wage hours a year ($3,000 ÷ $0.56 ≈ 5,357), which a 55-employee venue with evening and weekend peaks will comfortably surpass. The rise lands hardest on the casual evening and weekend workforce already at 13% absenteeism, so pay policy, rostering and engagement all matter to contain the true cost.

Electricity and heating prices (up 13.4% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names commercial electricity and heating, the lifeblood of a cinema and ten-lane bowling alley — projectors, 4K screens, pinsetters, lane lighting, fryers and heating for long evening sessions. The insert does not state utilities' share of costs, so any precise total would be invented; even a bound built purely on insert figures favours a heavy impact: applying 13.4% to the entire $5.50 variable cost gives an extreme upper bound of about $0.74 per visit ($5.50 × 13.4% = $0.74), i.e. roughly $136,345 a year if every visit's variable cost were utility — an absolute ceiling, not a forecast. The honest judgement is directional and unavoidable: 13.4% is the steepest percentage rise in Appendix 3, recurs every operating hour, cannot be fixed or refinanced away the way the loan rate can, and cannot be spread over more visits quickly — screen occupancy is only 34%, and Marcus Whitfield's visitors told him they will pay at most $3 more for recliner seating.

Conclusion: The 13.4% rise in electricity and heating prices will have the greatest impact. It is the steepest percentage increase named, recurs continuously across every show and every lane hour, and offers no financing-style fix; it also undermines the refurbished two-4K-screen model precisely when GLS is trying to lift occupancy above the 34% base and justify the $680,000 investment. The 5.5% minimum wage rise to $10.80 is the second serious pressure on the 55-employee casual workforce and interacts with the 13% absenteeism problem, while the 0.75 point interest rise costs exactly $3,000 a year and can be managed by fixing part of the loan — the smallest of the three. GLS should respond with LED and high-efficiency projection, thermostat and lane-lighting schedules, renegotiating its energy contract, lifting screen occupancy via the recliner premium (57% of visitors would pay up to $3 more), and bundling the $29 weekend family pass — attacking energy use directly rather than passing costs to price-sensitive students and families.
    Keywords: 6.5%, 5.5%, 13.4%, $10.80, $400,000, 34%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GLS. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GLS's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GLS with a well-justified judgement that energy-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Harbourlink City Breaks (HCB) is a partnership in the travel and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2015 by Elena Vasquez, the partnership designs short-break packages across European capital cities and uses a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership from the managing partner. HCB plans to invest $900,000 in launching a premium '48-hour signature city break' programme with exclusive hotel partnerships, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $300,000 of new partner capital. It has fixed costs of $3,050,000 a year, a variable cost of $1,240 a unit and a selling price of $1,850, and currently produces 10,800 units a year (one unit is one city-break package sold). HCB faces two problems: labour turnover among customer service staff has reached 29%, and seasonal operations absenteeism stands at 14% during the summer peak.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HCB plans to finance part of its signature city break launch with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for HCB of using new partner capital instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: New partner capital of $300,000 carries no interest and no fixed repayment schedule, unlike the $600,000 bank loan at a time when the base interest rate has risen to 6.75%. That protects HCB's $3,050,000 fixed costs from an immediate lift in debt service, and preserves cash for the signature programme's launch marketing and contracted flight and hotel rates, which have already risen 9.4% year-on-year.

Point 2: Partner capital strengthens the partnership's unity and commitment: partners who invest more capital have a direct financial stake in the signature programme's success, reinforcing autocratic decision-making with aligned incentives and reducing pressure for short-term distributions. The bank loan stays unused or partially drawn, protecting HCB's credit line for later expansion phases, avoiding lender covenants on how the programme is marketed, and keeping ownership and control fully with Elena Vasquez and her fellow partners. The downside is scale: partner capital is finite, so if the signature programme outgrows plan, the partnership may still need the bank loan later — but it would then negotiate from a position of strength, with bookings of 10,800 units already proven and fixed costs unchanged.
    Keywords: partner capital, bank loan, $300,000, $600,000, signature city break, $900,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Harbourlink City Breaks and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HCB is launching its premium '48-hour signature city break' programme. Consider television advertising, targeted digital marketing (search and social ads), or print advertising in in-flight magazines. Which should HCB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television advertising: TV would give HCB national reach and prestige, positioning the premium programme as aspirational across the whole country. However, a 40-employee partnership financing $900,000 of launch costs cannot absorb seven-figure advertising bills, and TV wastes spend on audiences outside its European capital routes; the 31% last-minute booking pattern also rewards fast digital conversion rather than broad emotional build-up months in advance.

Targeted digital marketing: Search and social adverts reach exactly the 67% of surveyed customers who prefer the signature concept, captured while they actively research city breaks, and can retarget visitors who abandon bookings with the $1,710 average booking value in view. Costs are low, targeting is precise by geography, age and interest, results are measurable through the 38% direct-booking growth, and digital suits mobile-first last-minute buyers perfectly.

Print advertising in in-flight magazines: In-flight placements reach exactly the air-travel audience most likely to buy European city breaks, and the glossy format suits a premium programme with exclusive hotel partnerships. However, placement depends on airline deals, reach is tied to specific routes, and print lacks the immediacy, measurement and low cost-per-conversion of digital; it also cannot retarget a reader who has closed the magazine.

Recommendation: HCB should choose targeted digital marketing. It reaches the precise preference segment identified in its research, matches the 31% last-minute booking behaviour and 38% direct-booking shift, delivers measurable bookings per dollar, and fits a $900,000 launch budget. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable for a 40-person partnership; in-flight print is rejected as route-limited and immeasurable, though HCB should add a small in-flight placement on its busiest route once the digital campaign proves conversion, and layer agent-commission incentives on top.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HCB with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HCB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and in-flight print are rejected.

    Question: HCB's labour turnover among customer service staff has reached 29% and seasonal operations absenteeism is 14%. Explain two benefits for HCB of using job enrichment for its customer service team.

Agents who own a case solve problems faster, reducing cancellations below the current 4.2% and complaints about delays, and feel too valued to resign — directly attacking the 29% labour turnover.

Point 2: Empowered agents handle the 31% of bookings made within 14 days of departure with far more confidence and judgment, upgrading confused callers to the $1,710 signature programme where appropriate.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HCB must decide how to sell the new signature city break programme. Consider selling mainly through independent travel agents (12% average commission) or selling mainly direct through HCB's own website. Which should HCB choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Independent travel agents: Agents bring immediate high-street reach, trusted advice for premium packaged holidays and access to customers who prefer face-to-face consultation; the 12% average commission is a predictable cost of sale, and agents can explain the exclusive hotel partnerships persuasively. However, 12% commission on a $1,850 package is about $222 per booking (12% of $1,850 = $222) — at 10,800 units that is over $2.3 million a year (10,800 × $222 = $2,397,600) — and agents may steer clients to whichever package pays the richest commission rather than HCB's programme, diluting the premium positioning and margin.

Direct via HCB's own website: Direct sales capture the full margin, deepen customer data for remarketing, and match the 38% growth in direct bookings after the website relaunch plus the 31% last-minute segment that converts online. Costs are website maintenance and digital marketing rather than per-booking commission; the risk is losing older customers who still prefer agents, and carrying the full service burden without any agent advocacy.

Decision: HCB should choose selling mainly direct through its own website, with agents used selectively for premium and group bookings. Direct sales protect the $610 contribution ($1,850 − $1,240) per package and compound the online momentum already proven by the 38% direct-booking surge; mass agent reliance at 12% commission would transfer millions of margin to intermediaries and blur the premium brand. Pure agent distribution is rejected as too expensive and uncontrollable; a blended approach retains agents only where they add value above 12% of contribution, such as incentive-travel corporate accounts. Elena Vasquez should also cap agent allocation to a minority of signature-programme inventory, reviewed quarterly against direct margin, so the partnership never becomes dependent on intermediaries to fill its flagship departures.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]

    Answer: Calculations:

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HCB of launching the premium '48-hour signature city break' programme.
    Answer: Advantage: The signature programme targets the 67% of surveyed customers who prefer the concept and carries higher spend than the current $1,710 average booking value, lifting revenue per unit and HCB's $610 contribution ($1,850 − $1,240) while these premium customers show greater loyalty to exclusive hotel partnerships. It differentiates HCB from generic online travel agents, justifies investment of $900,000 with partner capital and a bank loan, and matches the 5.6% growth in consumer city-break spending.

Disadvantage: The programme concentrates HCB's risk in a small number of exclusive hotel partnerships — if one capital's contracted rates fail or a hotel underdelivers, the premium brand promise collapses publicly via the 4.6 review score. Setup costs of $900,000 consume the partnership's flexibility, the $600,000 bank loan adds fixed interest at a 6.75% base rate, and any execution failure (late transfers, overbooked rooms) would hit the already-strained 29% labour turnover in customer service, multiplying complaints precisely when HCB needs flawless delivery to convert the 67% interested segment into paying customers.
    Keywords: signature city break, 67%, $1,710, $900,000, $600,000, 4.6
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HCB's research, costs and launch.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase to $12.10 and the 9.4% rise in short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates will affect HCB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (6.0% to 6.75%): On HCB's $600,000 variable-rate bank loan, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $4,500 a year in interest ($600,000 × 0.75% = $4,500), lifting fixed costs above $3,050,000. Higher rates may also cool discretionary city-break demand at the margin, and could raise the cost of drawing the $900,000 signature-programme funding. The direct impact is the smallest of the three, is fully computable from insert figures, can be capped by fixing the loan rate, and does not erode the $610 contribution ($1,850 − $1,240) per package.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.10 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.68 ($12.10 − $11.42 = $0.68). The annual cost cannot be computed from the insert because the number of minimum-wage hours is not stated; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor exceeds the interest rise — it does so once HCB pays more than roughly 6,618 minimum-wage hours a year ($4,500 ÷ $0.68 ≈ 6,618), a level comfortably exceeded by a 40-employee operator with customer service, operations and support staff. This lands on a team already carrying 29% labour turnover and 14% summer absenteeism, so the award must be matched with engagement, flexible rostering and Herzberg-style responsibility if it is not to widen churn alongside cost.

Short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates (up 9.4% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names the two largest cost components of almost any short-haul city-break package — airfares and hotels. No share of the $1,240 variable cost is stated, so no legitimate total exists in the insert; anything precise would be invented. What can be shown is an upper bound built only on insert figures: applying the full 9.4% to the entire $1,240 gives at most about $116.56 per package ($1,240 × 9.4% = $116.56), i.e. roughly $1,258,848 a year across the current 10,800 packages as an absolute ceiling — real exposure will be lower but can only be lower by the fare/hotel share, which the insert does not disclose. What is certain is that flight and hotel costs scale with every unit sold, that they are contracted wholesale rather than discretionary, and that HCB cannot refinance them — it must renegotiate, re-time or re-route them before the $900,000 signature launch hard-wires new exclusivity clauses.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates will have the greatest impact. It attaches to the two largest structural components of every one of the 10,800 packages sold, sits inside the $1,240 variable cost, exceeds the wage floor's per-hour exposure of $0.68 on typical annual totals by a clear margin in any plausible reading, and dwarfs the exactly computable $4,500 interest rise. The 6.0% minimum wage increase to $12.10 is second — real, unavoidable, and risky given 29% turnover and 14% absenteeism — while the 0.75 point interest rise is the smallest and can be fixed away. HCB must renegotiate contracted rates now, shift marketing to the direct channel (online direct bookings grew 38% after the website relaunch) to keep the full $610 contribution, time departures around fare cycles, and reserve any signature-price rises for the 67% of surveyed customers who prefer the concept, protecting contribution while the $900,000 programme proves itself.
    Keywords: 6.75%, 6.0%, 9.4%, $12.10, $600,000, 10,800
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HCB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HCB's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HCB with a well-justified judgement that flight and hotel input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

Calderline Freight (CLF) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2008 by Derek Calder, the business operates regional haulage routes between distribution warehouses and supermarkets, using a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $209,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.20 a unit and a selling price of $12.70, and produces 65,000 units a year (each unit being one completed delivery contract).     Question: CLF plans to finance its $640,000 electric truck expansion partly with $240,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for CLF of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the $400,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs CLF nothing in interest or repayments, which is vital while it already services fixed costs of $209,000 a year and faces a 15.2% rise in diesel input costs. Keeping the $240,000 free of repayment pressure protects the company's cash flow and operating profit margin, so the carbon-neutral electric trucks can bed in without the strain of servicing extra debt on top of the $400,000 seven-year loan. Every dollar retained rather than paid as loan interest can absorb fuel volatility or help underwrite the 4% surcharge that 71% of surveyed shippers say they will accept.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids additional collateral and the risk of the bank imposing covenants or repossessing the new charging depot and trucks if demand disappoints. Because the trucks are central to CLF's plan to win guaranteed carbon-neutral supermarket contracts, protecting title to them safeguards future revenue and Derek Calder's autocratic control over how the $640,000 is deployed. Retained profit also needs no credit approval, so CLF can order the 14 electric trucks quickly and move ahead of rivals before the 5.75% interest rate makes external borrowing more expensive.

--- STEM ---
Portwyn Container Services (PCS) is a public limited company in the port handling and shipping sector, employing a workforce of 190 at the Port of Dunmere. Founded in 1996, the company is led by chief executive Devika Menon and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership, handling import and export containers for international shipping lines. PCS plans to invest $1,250,000 in two ship-to-shore gantry cranes and a six-acre yard expansion, financed by a $750,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.50 a unit and a selling price of $26.50, and produces 95,000 units a year (each unit being one container lifted). PCS faces rising crane operator fatigue, with near-miss safety incidents reaching 7 last quarter.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PCS plans to finance its $1,250,000 crane and yard expansion partly with a $750,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for PCS of using a share issue to fund the expansion instead of the $500,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $750,000 of finance that never has to be repaid and carries no mandatory interest, which is ideal while PCS already pays interest payable of $70,000–$84,000 a year and has just taken on a $500,000 bank loan. Unlike a loan, share proceeds strengthen the equity base that supports the two new $1,250,000 gantry cranes, improving solvency and giving lenders confidence, and leaving PCS headroom to borrow again if a third crane or further yard automation becomes attractive.

Point 2: Selling new shares spreads ownership rather than concentrating risk with Devika Menon and existing shareholders, and public investors in a public limited company are usually comfortable funding infrastructure that earns returns over a long horizon. Crucially, a share issue avoids fixed repayment pressure during the years the cranes are being commissioned, when lift volumes and the 2.3% defect rate are still stabilising — the exact period when a $500,000 loan with interest already stretching to $84,000 could bite. No collateral is pledged against the yard, and the democratic board can present the issue as a growth story tied to the 67% of clients willing to sign longer contracts if dwell time improves.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $750,000, $500,000, $1,250,000, gantry cranes

Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $5,600,000 revenue − $3,472,000 cost of sales = $2,128,000, giving $2,128,000 ÷ $5,600,000 = 38.0%; 2025 = ($6,300,000 − $3,591,000) = $2,709,000 ÷ $6,300,000 = 43.0%. After operating expenses: 2024 $560,000 ÷ $5,600,000 = 10.0%; 2025 $756,000 ÷ $6,300,000 = 12.0%. Capital efficiency: 2024 $560,000 ÷ $3,500,000 = 16.0%; 2025 $756,000 ÷ $4,320,000 = 17.5%.

Evaluation: Performance has improved on every measure. The trading margin widened from 38.0% to 43.0%, reflecting better yard automation and lower dwell-time costs, and the operating margin rose from 10.0% to 12.0% despite interest payable increasing from $70,000 to $84,000 as the $500,000 bank loan was drawn. However, cost of sales grew to $3,591,000 and the 14.8% steel price rise threatens future crane maintenance bills, while relying on longer client contracts makes PCS vulnerable if shipping volumes soften after the 3.4% import growth.

Conclusion: PCS's financial performance has improved. Trading margins strengthened from 38.0% to 43.0%, operating returns from 10.0% to 12.0% and capital efficiency from 16.0% to 17.5%, on revenue growth of $700,000. The trend is positive but fuelled by cost control and contract discipline; PCS should keep dwell time under 48 hours, hedge steel maintenance costs and avoid further debt-funded capacity until the cranes are fully commissioned.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PCS of automating yard operations with the two ship-to-shore gantry cranes.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 6.2% increase in the minimum wage to $13.91 and the 14.8% rise in steel and equipment costs will affect PCS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.0%): A 0.5% rise on PCS's $500,000 bank loan adds about $2,500 a year to financing costs, slightly steepening the increase in interest payable from $70,000 to $84,000 recorded in 2025. Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.91 from April 2027): With 190 employees concentrated in crane, gate and yard roles, a 6.2% rise compounds the existing fatigue and overtime pressure. The hours worked are not stated in the insert, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely, but it will be a recurring cost larger than the interest hit — partly recoverable through longer-contract tariffs and productivity gains from the new cranes, and valuable for morale under democratic leadership.

Steel and equipment cost inflation (14.8%): The two gantry cranes and yard automation are built from steel and imported handling equipment. Conclusion: The 14.8% rise in steel and equipment costs will have the greatest impact. The wage increase is material but absorbable through tariffs and automation productivity, and the interest-rate rise is minor and fixable. PCS should lock in equipment prices, accelerate commissioning and renegotiate surcharge terms before April 2027.

--- STEM ---
Brightroute Delivery Co-operative (BRD) is a workers' cooperative in the last-mile urban delivery sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2015 by Tunde Okafor and member couriers, the business delivers parcels for e-commerce retailers across the city using a flat structure with democratic leadership, where member couriers vote on major decisions. BRD plans to invest $520,000 in 25 electric cargo vans for its city-centre routes, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and a $200,000 member share issue. It has fixed costs of $184,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.60 a unit and a selling price of $9.20, and produces 58,000 units a year (each unit being one parcel delivered). BRD faces labour turnover of 31% among its couriers.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BRD plans to finance its $520,000 electric cargo van expansion partly with a $200,000 member share issue. Explain two advantages for BRD of using a member share issue to fund the expansion instead of the $320,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A member share issue brings in $200,000 of permanent capital with no mandatory repayments and no interest, which matters because BRD already pays interest payable that rose from $15,000 to $21,000 in 2025 and still carries the $320,000 bank loan. In a co-operative, shares bought by members deepen their commitment to the fleet, align the owners with the vans they will drive, and avoid the risk of the bank seizing vehicles if a trading quarter disappoints — protecting the democratic model and the 40 members' livelihoods.

Point 2: Raising shares from members widens the co-op's capital base without diluting external ownership or ceding any say to a lender, so members retain full democratic control of route policy and working conditions as the 25 vans arrive. The issue also signals member confidence to partner retailers, helping win the same-day evening contracts that 66% of shoppers said they would pay $1 extra for, and it leaves the co-op headroom to borrow again later rather than exhausting its credit line on the $520,000 purchase.
    Keywords: member share issue, bank loan, $200,000, $320,000, $520,000, electric cargo vans

Eco-blogger partnerships: Partnering with sustainability bloggers gives credible third-party endorsement of BRD's electric fleet and could deepen trust with eco-conscious shoppers. The limitation is pace and control: blogger calendars are unpredictable, reach is niche and inconsistent, and messaging may drift from BRD's democratic co-op values, so it works best as a supporting tactic rather than the launch engine.

Recommendation: BRD should choose social media video ads, with selective blogger partnerships layered on once momentum builds. Social video targets exactly the shoppers and retailer buyers BRD needs, is affordable on a co-op budget, and is fully measurable against the same-day promise. Local radio is rejected as poorly targeted and unmeasurable for checkout-driven purchases; eco-blogger partnerships alone are rejected as too slow and inconsistent to carry the launch, though they may reinforce the campaign afterwards.
