  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RRC's absenteeism has reached 11% and contamination of incoming sorted waste has averaged 6.4%. Explain two benefits for RRC of its democratic leadership and flat structure.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 member-employees a genuine voice in how the sorting line is organised — shift patterns, contamination checks and safety briefings — which satisfies social and esteem needs (Maslow) and strengthens Herzberg's motivation factors of involvement and recognition. Workers who helped design the new contamination-flagging routine are more likely to follow it consistently, directly attacking the 6.4% average that forces reject loads, rework cost and extra $650 refresher training for 18 uncertified staff.

Point 2: A flat structure shortens the chain of command, so an absence spike reaches Ana Whitmore's management group the same shift and cover can be rearranged without a management layer; informal peer communication also means safety near-misses are flagged quickly. It reinforces cooperative values of equality and shared responsibility, lowering the turnover and disengagement that typically drive 11% absenteeism, and it keeps overhead inside the $640,000 fixed costs while the $980,000 second pelletizing line beds in.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, absenteeism, 11%, 6.4%, 60, flat organisational structure

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RRC wants to improve productivity on the sorting line without raising contamination. Consider performance-related piece-rate pay or team working for its sorters. Which should RRC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Piece-rate pay: Paying sorters per tonne processed would directly reward output, suiting Taylor-style scientific management, and could lift volumes toward what the new $980,000 pelletizing line needs to run at capacity. It is simple to administer and feels immediately rewarding. However, sorters rushing for money will miss contaminants, the 6.4% contamination rate would likely rise, reject loads would cost councils' trust (complaints fell from 17 to 9 per month), and safety near-misses (14 were logged) would increase as speed trumps care. It also conflicts with RRC's cooperative ethos of equal sharing.

Team working: Grouping sorters into small teams with shared quality and safety targets builds social belonging and shared ownership — the very motivators that sit behind RRC's democratic leadership and cooperative ethos — satisfying esteem needs and tapping Herzberg's motivators of teamwork and responsibility. Teams can run quality circles to attack contamination at its source, watch each other's near-misses and cover absences mutually — crucial with absenteeism at 11%. Drawbacks: pay is not immediately tied to output, some strong performers may resent free-riders, and team bonus administration is more complex.

Decision: RRC should choose team working. It directly supports the two problems identified — 6.4% contamination (through shared quality ownership and peer checking of loads) and 11% absenteeism (through peer support and belonging) — while fitting cooperative culture and protecting the council contracts that took years to win; team meetings can be slotted into shift changeovers so output is protected. Piece-rate pay is rejected because it incentivises raw speed over quality and safety, would likely push contamination and injuries upward, disadvantages newer sorters, and conflicts with the cooperative's equal-share principles; crucially, it does nothing to address why people are absent.
    Keywords: council, $650, 6.4%, 11%, democratic leadership, 17 to 9

Landfill tax rise (14.0%, to $126 a tonne from April 2027): This is market-shaping rather than cost-side. It also enables RRC to renegotiate multi-year council contracts at better prices. The risk is contamination rising with volumes.

Conclusion: The landfill tax rise will have the greatest impact. It is the only one of the three that expands RRC's market and revenue, not merely its costs; it reshapes council behaviour in RRC's favour for years, outweighing the ~$96,000 wage award and the negligible rate effect. The wage increase is second in cash terms, the interest rise is smallest and can be managed by fixing HP terms; all three still require RRC to invest in contamination control and mechanisation.

--- STEM ---
ThermaWool Industries (TWI) is a private limited company in the insulation and eco-materials manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2016 by Lena Pettersson, the business makes recycled-denim and sheep's-wool insulation boards for the construction industry, and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership at senior level. TWI plans to invest $1,100,000 in a second automated recycled-denim line, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $500,000 hire purchase of machinery. It has fixed costs of $1,150,000 a year, a variable cost of $13.50 a unit and a selling price of $25.00, and currently produces 166,000 units a year. TWI faces two problems: a skills gap, with 28 of 85 staff not certified for the new line, and a defect rate of 2.9%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TWI plans to finance part of the second recycled-denim line with a $600,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TWI of using a bank loan rather than hiring the machinery for the full $1,100,000.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan gives TWI immediate ownership of the $600,000 machinery with no hire-purchase premium or hidden interest embedded in instalments, so total financing cost is transparent and usually cheaper than machinery hire over the same term, and TWI can claim the line as its own asset for its whole life. The fixed monthly repayment also simplifies budgeting against the $1,150,000 fixed costs, useful while 28 of 85 staff await certification.

Point 2: Unlike hire, a bank loan can be renegotiated or refinanced if interest rates ease, rather than locking TWI into a fixed hire contract at a rate set today. Ownership also lets TWI modify the line and use it as collateral for future borrowing — valuable given the defect rate (2.9%, down from 4.1%) still has room to fall as output scales toward 166,000 units a year, and given energy costs rose 15.3% year-on-year.
    Keywords: bank loan, $600,000, $1,100,000, hire purchase, $1,150,000, 166,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ThermaWool Industries and its expansion decision.

    Question: TWI's skills gap means 28 of 85 staff are not certified for the new line, and the defect rate is 2.9%. Explain two benefits for TWI of laissez-faire leadership at senior level.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership empowers TWI's senior engineers and production leads to design the new recycled-denim line, set certification curricula and solve defects autonomously, playing directly to the expertise TWI hired them for. With 28 staff awaiting certification, autonomous leads can tailor shop-floor coaching to each person's pace and knowledge gaps rather than forcing everyone through an identical script — something rigid top-down sign-off would slow dramatically.

    Question: TWI must reduce its 2.9% defect rate on the new recycled-denim line. Consider quality control or quality assurance for the new line. Which should TWI choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality control: QC inspects finished boards at the end of the line, catching defects before dispatch — straightforward, familiar, and requires only the existing inspection station. It would hold the current 2.9% rate or push it marginally lower by weeding failures. But it matches the premium positioning TWI is selling to the 63% of merchants who will pay up to 8% more for defect-free boards, and it dovetails with the certification programme.

Decision: TWI should choose quality assurance. Prevention beats detection when variable cost is $13.50 and boards are reworked at full material cost; QA addresses why defects occur, supports the certification rollout laissez-faire engineers can lead, and protects the eco-brand that wins the 71% stocking commitment. Quality control alone is rejected because it weeds out defects after value is destroyed, permits drift back above 2.9%, and cannot support a premium-price strategy on its own; a final inspection layer should complement, not replace, QA.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TWI of using recycled denim and sheep's-wool as feedstock for its insulation boards.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 15.3% rise in gas and electricity costs will affect TWI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): On the $600,000 bank loan, 0.75 points adds about $4,500 a year, and the $175,000 interest payable will edge higher still on renewal. Greater is the demand-side signal: at 5.75%, builders and housing associations face costlier development finance, which can delay specification decisions and the 6.2% eco-materials demand growth TWI is counting on. Modest direct cost, noticeable strategic risk; TWI can fix the loan at renewal.

Minimum wage rise (5.9%, to $12.97 per hour from April 2027): With 85 staff, mainly line operators and packers on hourly pay, the award adds roughly $0.72 per hour; at around 2,000 hours a year that is about $1,440 per worker or roughly $122,000 a year — around 13% of operating profit. Combined with the certification programme ($800 each for 28 staff), payroll pressure is real but mechanisation on the new automated line will offset part of it through labour productivity.

Gas and electricity costs (+15.3% year-on-year): Insulation manufacture is energy-intensive — drying ovens, die heating and compressed systems run continuously. If energy is even one-quarter of the $13.50 variable cost (about $3.38), a 15.3% rise adds about $0.52 per unit; across 166,000 units that is roughly $86,000 a year, compounding every quarter with no volume offset. TWI can hedge with fixed-term contracts and solar but must renegotiate before margins erode further.

Conclusion: The 15.3% gas and electricity rise will have the greatest impact. Unlike the rate rise, it scales with every unit produced, exceeds the rate rise in annual cash terms and — critically — outruns the 6.2% demand growth that was meant to absorb it, squeezing both contribution and the energy-hungry commissioning of the new line. The wage increase is second (large but mechanisable); the interest-rate rise is smallest. TWI must lock in energy contracts, fit sub-metering on the new line and reprice contracts with an energy surcharge.

--- STEM ---
VerdeMix Concrete (VMC) is a public limited company in the green concrete sector, employing a workforce of 110. Founded in 2014 by Maria Doyle, the business produces low-carbon precast blocks made with GGBS and recycled aggregates for infrastructure and housing projects, and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. VMC plans to invest $1,750,000 in acquiring a recycled aggregate washing and batching facility, financed by a $1,000,000 share issue and $750,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,350,000 a year, a variable cost of $45.00 a unit and a selling price of $75.00, and currently produces 104,000 units a year.   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VMC plans to finance the recycled aggregate facility with a $1,000,000 share issue and $750,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for VMC of using retained profit rather than enlarging the share issue further.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit funds the $750,000 portion with no new shares, so existing shareholders' ownership, dividend rights and control are diluted as little as possible; every extra diluted share cedes both earnings and voting influence that Maria Doyle and the founding team worked to keep when VMC went public. It also avoids underwriting fees and the placing discount typically demanded by institutional buyers, stretching the $1,000,000 issue further and keeping the acquisition fully funded.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no interest, dividend or repayment obligation of any kind, unlike the $1,000,000 share issue alternative of deeper equity or any loan, so VMC keeps flexibility to fund the recycled aggregate washing facility's silica-dust safety upgrades for 34 uncertified staff or additional batching capacity if the $2.1 million rail-depot contract extends. It also signals genuine cash generation to the market, supporting the share price that enabled the issue and reassuring infrastructure clients of VMC's financial stability.

Pure off-the-job training is rejected because generic classroom content cannot certify competence on VMC's actual machines and would stop the line against a live order book.

--- STEM ---
Wexford Vale Creamery Cooperative (WVC) is a cooperative in the dairy processing and farming sector, owned by 64 member farms and employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2004 and led by general manager Celia Brannigan, the business supplies farmhouse cheese and butter to regional and national supermarket chains, and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. WVC plans to invest $720,000 in a new cheese maturation and packing facility, financed by $300,000 member capital contributions, $280,000 retained profit and $140,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 64,000 units a year. WVC faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 7% and a skills gap has opened in cheese grading, with 14 of 38 staff not yet trained on the new grading line.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WVC plans to finance part of its new cheese maturation and packing facility through $300,000 of member capital contributions rather than relying entirely on a bank loan. Explain two advantages for WVC of using member capital contributions instead of a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Member capital contributions cost WVC nothing in interest or arrangement fees, which protects the cooperative's cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $225,000 a year and a $140,000 bank loan commitment on the new $720,000 facility. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in dairy feed and energy input costs, helping WVC keep its $14.00 selling price stable for supermarket contracts rather than passing increases on to shoppers who are already cautious about food-price inflation at 7.2%.

Point 2: Because WVC is a cooperative owned by 64 member farms, raising $300,000 from members deepens their financial stake and loyalty, reducing the risk that they sell milk elsewhere when prices are tight. It also preserves the democratic control of the cooperative, since no external lender can attach covenants over how the maturation facility is run or veto the hiring of the 14 untrained graders. Contributions strengthen the balance sheet without forcing members to surrender ownership, unlike a share issue by an investor-owned firm, and they signal commitment to the 4.1% growth in locally produced cheese that the members' milk depends on.
    Keywords: member capital contributions, bank loan, $300,000, $720,000, cooperative, $140,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wexford Vale Creamery Cooperative, its cooperative ownership and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WVC is launching its locally produced farmhouse cheese range to national supermarkets. Consider a national television campaign, regional press and farmers' market sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should WVC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A national TV campaign would reach millions of viewers very quickly and would build awareness of the WVC brand in the supermarket chains it supplies. However, production and airtime costs run into hundreds of thousands of dollars, and much of the audience sits outside WVC's supermarket distribution or does not buy premium locally produced cheese, so the spend would be poorly targeted for a 38-person cooperative carrying a $720,000 expansion and a $140,000 bank loan.

Regional press and farmers' market sponsorship: This is far cheaper and reaches the exact regional catchment where the 58% of surveyed shoppers willing to pay up to $0.60 more for eco-packaging and locally produced cheese live. Sampling at farmers' markets builds trust and direct feedback at low cost. Its limitation is reach: the new national supermarket listings need national awareness, so regional press alone cannot generate the volume required to fill the maturation facility or justify the $720,000 investment.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can demonstrate the eco-packaging story to the 47% of shoppers who read origin labels, generate measurable engagement, and scale cheaply from regional to national coverage. Cost per reached shopper is low, and campaigns can be timed to supermarket launch windows. Results compound more slowly than television and depend on influencer credibility, but WVC can test messages with the 500 surveyed shoppers before committing.

Recommendation: WVC should choose social media influencer marketing, layered with small regional press adverts rather than a stand-alone buy. It is affordable, targeted at the eco-conscious segment, and nationally scalable. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a cooperative funding an expansion largely with member money; regional press and farmers' markets are rejected as the sole launch channel because its reach is regional only, insufficient for national supermarket listings.
    Keywords: locally produced cheese, eco-packaging, $0.60, 58%, 47%, supermarket, $720,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WVC with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WVC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the national television campaign and regional press sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WVC operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. Explain two ways for WVC to apply Maslow's hierarchy of needs to motivate its 38 employees on the maturation and grading lines.
    Answer: Point 1: WVC can satisfy esteem and self-actualisation needs by giving grading-line staff responsibility for cheese quality sign-off and involving them in democratic decisions about maturation routines and shift patterns. Workers whose judgement is trusted, and who chair the quality circles that cut the defect rate from 3.6% to 2.4%, feel respected and fulfilled, which raises commitment and directly attacks the 7% absenteeism rate on the grading line.

Point 2: WVC can satisfy social needs by building team working between member-farm liaison staff and packing crews, for example celebrating member visits with shared tastings of the farmhouse cheese. Visible cooperation with the 64 member farms gives employees a sense of belonging to the cooperative's shared purpose, which is especially motivating for a members' business where profit is distributed according to each farm's milk supply. Recognising strong attendance with team rewards, rather than punishing absence, should reduce labour turnover, protect the 64,000-unit annual output and help the 14 untrained graders feel supported through the $750 agricultural college course.
    Keywords: 64 member farms, workforce of 38, democratic leadership, absenteeism, flat organisational structure, $750
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid motivational application of Maslow's hierarchy identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WVC's flat democratic structure, its cooperative identity and its 7% absenteeism.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WVC must improve motivation on the maturation line. Consider introducing performance-related bonus payments or a profit-sharing scheme for its 38 employees. Which should WVC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Performance-related bonus payments: Bonuses tied to individual or team output targets give immediate, visible rewards for above-standard effort, for example hitting packing targets as the facility ramps up to serve national supermarket orders. They are simple to administer and can be targeted at the 14 untrained graders who complete the on-the-job grading certification. The drawbacks are that individual bonuses can encourage corner-cutting on quality — risking a rise from the current 2.4% defect rate — and they can create resentment between elected democratic team leaders and other staff in a cooperative that prides itself on equality among 64 member farms and 38 employees.

Profit-sharing scheme: Profit sharing distributes a share of the cooperative's surplus to all 38 employees, reinforcing the democratic, collective ethos of a member-owned business. It rewards overall performance, aligns everyone with the supermarket growth that funds the $720,000 facility, and costs nothing in lean years — the scheme simply pays less. However, payouts are annual and distant from daily effort, individual contribution is invisible, and weak individual performers free-ride on team effort, which can frustrate high performers on the grading line.

Decision: WVC should choose profit sharing, possibly with a small recognition element rather than a pure performance bonus. Profit sharing matches the cooperative identity, rewards everyone for the supermarket growth that makes the $720,000 expansion viable, and avoids the quality risks and internal divisions that individual bonuses can create — critical while absenteeism is 7% and grading skills are being rebuilt. Performance-related bonuses are rejected as the main scheme because they can undermine quality culture and equality in a member-owned flat structure, though WVC can layer spot recognition for safety and quality suggestions on top of the profit-sharing pot.
    Keywords: cooperative, workforce of 38, democratic leadership, $720,000, absenteeism, 64 member farms
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of bonus payments and profit sharing with limited application to WVC. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of WVC and its cooperative structure. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of WVC with a well-justified decision explaining why performance-related bonus payments are rejected as the main scheme.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how WVC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units. Working: contribution per unit is $14.00 − $9.50 = $4.50, and $225,000 ÷ $4.50 = 50,000 units. (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50. This is the revenue each unit of farmhouse cheese and butter contributes toward fixed costs after variable costs are covered. (iii) Four contextual uses explained: First, WVC's managers can set the supermarket sales budget with confidence because current output of 64,000 units clears the 50,000-unit break-even with a margin of safety of 14,000 units, so the maturation facility can absorb softer demand before losses begin. Second, the $4.50 contribution lets managers test any price negotiated with supermarket chains molecule by molecule: a $0.60 price cut would still leave $3.90 per unit, so a volume uplift above 58,000 units would keep total contribution above the $225,000 fixed costs. Third, break-even knowledge supports the $720,000 expansion appraisal: the second phase only proceeds once contracted volumes push output comfortably beyond 50,000 units, protecting the $140,000 bank loan repayment and the interests of the 64 member farms. Fourth, unit-cost analysis ($225,000 ÷ 64,000 units + $9.50 = $13.02) gives WVC a benchmark to attack the 4.7% trimmings waste, identify whether the $9.50 variable cost should be renegotiated against the 9.8% input-cost inflation, and decide whether to keep grading in-house or outsource during the 14-person skills gap.
    Keywords: 50,000, $4.50, 64,000, $225,000, $9.50, $14.00, 13.02
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WVC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has WVC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.56 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.66 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.91 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $160,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $325,000; 2025 current assets = $145,000 + $155,000 + $50,000 = $350,000. 2024 = $325,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.30; 2025 = $350,000 ÷ $225,000 = 1.56. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($325,000 − $160,000) ÷ $250,000 = $165,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.66; 2025 = ($350,000 − $145,000) ÷ $225,000 = $205,000 ÷ $225,000 = 0.91.

Evaluation: WVC's liquidity has strengthened. The improvement in coverage of short-term obligations is helped by current liabilities falling from $250,000 to $225,000 while current assets rose from $325,000 to $350,000, partly reflecting the $50,000 cash build-up as supermarket contracts converted to receivables. The acid test, which strips out inventories of cheese wheels in maturation, moved from 0.66 to 0.91, so WVC now almost covers short-term debts without selling stock — essential while it services the $140,000 bank loan and stages the $720,000 facility. However, trade receivables rose from $130,000 to $155,000, meaning more cash is tied up with supermarket customers; if they stretch payment terms, the stronger position could deteriorate. Inventories fell from $160,000 to $145,000, so stock availability for peak Christmas cheese demand should be monitored rather than assumed.

Conclusion: WVC's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures show clearer coverage of current liabilities, and the improvement does not rely on inventories, which actually fell. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so WVC should tighten supermarket credit terms and monitor collection while proceeding with the facility build-out and continuing to serve its 64 member farms.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WVC of introducing paper-based eco-packaging for its farmhouse cheese range.
    Answer: Advantage: Paper-based eco-packaging matches the values of the 58% of shoppers in WVC's market research who would pay up to $0.60 more for such packaging, allowing WVC to hold or raise its $14.00 selling price and protect its $4.50 contribution per unit while input costs rise 9.8%. It also appeals to the 47% of shoppers who read origin labels, strengthening the local, member-farm story that wins national supermarket listings for the new $720,000 maturation facility and supporting the 4.1% growth in locally produced cheese spending.

Disadvantage: Sustainable paper and coatings typically cost more than conventional plastic or wax wrap, raising the $9.50 variable cost per unit and squeezing the contribution margin unless the $0.60 premium is accepted across the whole range. Paper can also offer a shorter shelf life or weaker moisture barrier for maturing cheese; any rise in damage or mould would push the current 2.4% defect rate upward and increase trimmings waste above 4.7%, eroding the gains the new facility is meant to deliver — especially before the 14 untrained graders complete their on-the-job certification.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in dairy feed and energy input costs will affect WVC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): With a $140,000 bank loan attached to the $720,000 facility, if WVC's loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by 0.75%, adding roughly $1,050 a year to financing costs — real but modest against fixed costs of $225,000. Higher rates also cool consumer appetite for premium locally produced cheese and raise the cost of any future borrowing to complete the facility. The direct cash impact is the smallest of the three changes and can be partly managed by fixing the loan rate or accelerating member contributions.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $12.66 per hour from April 2026): WVC's workforce of 38, weighted toward grading, maturation and packing, faces a materially higher wage bill. If average hourly pay moves from about $12.00 to $12.66, the annual cost of one full-time employee rises by roughly $1,400, adding perhaps $53,000 a year across 38 staff — a significant burden for a cooperative whose member farms also face rising feed costs, though higher productivity on the new grading line (64,000 units ÷ 38 employees ≈ 1,684 units per worker) can offset part of it.

Input cost inflation (9.8% dairy feed and energy): WVC's $9.50 variable cost is dominated by milk, feed and energy. A 9.8% rise on even the feed-and-energy component adds roughly $0.55–$0.93 per unit; at 64,000 units that is about $35,000–$60,000 a year, cutting contribution from $4.50 toward $3.60–$3.95 and undermining the margin that justifies the maturation facility — though WVC can recover part through the $0.60 eco-packaging premium and supermarket price negotiations.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in dairy feed and energy input costs will have the greatest impact. It compresses the $4.50 contribution on every one of the 64,000 units WVC sells and feeds straight into member farmers' own costs, threatening the whole cooperative model. The wage rise is the second most serious pressure, while the interest rate increase is the smallest in cash terms and can be managed by fixing rates — but WVC must act on all three, prioritising input-cost control, premium pricing and productivity gains.

--- STEM ---
Rio Sol Fruit Juices (RSFJ) is a public limited company in the fruit juice manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 240. Founded in 1991 by brothers Luis and Marco Herrera, the business bottles premium cold-pressed juice for national supermarkets and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership at head office. RSFJ plans to invest $1,850,000 in a new aseptic bottling plant, financed by a $1,100,000 share issue and $750,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $510,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.10 a unit and a selling price of $7.50, and currently produces 210,000 units a year. RSFJ faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 16% among production staff and its warehouse reports a rising defect rate on capped bottles.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RSFJ plans to finance part of its new aseptic bottling plant through a $1,100,000 share issue rather than bank borrowing. Explain two advantages for RSFJ of a share issue instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises $1,100,000 with no obligation to repay or to pay fixed interest, which protects RSFJ's cash flow while it carries fixed costs of $510,000 a year and absorbs the 14.2% rise in orange, mango and guava costs. Debt service on an equivalent bank loan would add to the annual interest burden after the central bank's move to 6.25%, squeezing the margin above the $510,000 fixed base at exactly the moment RSFJ needs headroom to commission a $1,850,000 plant.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads ownership and risk across new shareholders rather than concentrating it with a lender, and the $750,000 retained profit plus fresh equity avoids pledging the new aseptic line or existing plant as collateral. For a public limited company whose shares are already traded, accessing equity capital is a normal growth tool; it signals confidence to existing shareholders while leaving the board free to decide whether to pay dividends from future premium-juice profits rather than being locked into contractual interest. It also positions RSFJ to fund any later stage of the plant without renegotiating loan terms if premium-beverage demand, growing at 5.2%, accelerates.
    Keywords: share issue, $1,100,000, aseptic bottling plant, $750,000, public limited company, $1,850,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Rio Sol Fruit Juices, its public limited status and its bottling plant expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RSFJ is launching its premium cold-pressed juice in new regions. Consider a national television campaign, in-store supermarket promotions, or social media influencer marketing. Which should RSFJ choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: Television would give RSFJ mass national reach very quickly, building awareness of the Rio Sol brand across every region it now supplies. It suits a public limited company with access to capital markets. However, production and airtime are extremely expensive, much of the audience neither drinks cold-pressed juice nor shops in RSFJ's supermarket partners, and the dilution of spend across hundreds of millions of non-target viewers would be hard for the board to justify while funding a $1,850,000 plant and absorbing 14.2% input-cost inflation.

In-store supermarket promotions: Point-of-sale tastings, shelf-edge pricing and loyalty card offers place the product directly in front of the buyers who already shop for juice. They are relatively cheap, measurable in units sold per store, and can push the 61% of shoppers who prefer cold-pressed to from-concentrate toward a first trial. Limitations are that promotions reach only existing footfall in listed stores, build little brand story beyond the aisle, and depend entirely on supermarket partners agreeing to display space and margin.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and health influencers can demonstrate freshness, premium quality and the $0.80 premium the 55% of surveyed shoppers will pay, targeting exactly the five regions in the market research with measurable engagement. It scales nationally at low cost per reached shopper, supports the 18% already buying via e-commerce, and lets RSFJ test creative before the full launch. Effectiveness is slower to compound and depends on influencer credibility, but the cost profile fits a company mid-expansion.

Recommendation: RSFJ should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by targeted in-store supermarket promotions at launch. Influencers reach the research-identified premium segment nationally and affordably, reinforcing freshness and justifying the $0.80 premium; television is rejected as wasteful and unaffordable against the plant investment and 14.2% input costs; in-store promotions alone are rejected as the primary strategy because they cannot build the brand story beyond existing shoppers or drive national trial quickly enough.
    Keywords: cold-pressed juice, $0.80, 55%, 61%, e-commerce, $1,850,000, supermarket
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RSFJ with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RSFJ with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the television campaign and stand-alone in-store promotions are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RSFJ operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. Explain two advantages for RSFJ of this structure and leadership style as it expands nationally.
    Answer: Point 1: A hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership gives RSFJ a clear chain of command from head office to regional bottling and distribution teams, which speeds up decisions such as supermarket allocation, quality hold-ups on the capping line and responses to the 16% labour turnover problem. Senior leaders can impose uniform safety and hygiene standards across all sites without lengthy consultation, protecting national delivery lead times of 2.5 days and customer satisfaction with the declining complaint rate (45 to 28 per month).

Point 2: Autocratic direction is valuable during the commissioning of the new aseptic bottling plant, when RSFJ needs disciplined execution of capital works, staffing and supplier contracts across a 240-person workforce. Clear accountability and defined roles reduce confusion at shift handovers on the 4,300-unit weekly line, and experienced foremen can enforce the capping-machine training programme (34 staff outstanding) consistently. Predictable decision-making also reassures supermarket customers and the banks and shareholders funding the $1,850,000 plant that national expansion is being managed tightly rather than improvised.
    Keywords: hierarchical, autocratic, workforce of 240, labour turnover, $1,850,000, 240
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RSFJ's national expansion, its 240-person workforce and its new plant.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RSFJ needs 30 additional supervisors for the new aseptic bottling plant. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment for these positions. Which should RSFJ choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal recruitment: Appointing supervisors from within RSFJ's 240 employees promotes experienced capping- and filling-line staff who already know the quality standards, the 1.5% defect rate target and the supermarket service culture. It motivates existing staff by showing career progression, shortens induction because internal candidates know RSFJ's systems, and is cheaper than advertising externally — important while funding a $1,850,000 plant. Drawbacks: internal promotion empties the skilled operator pool on the line, can entrench old habits that sit oddly with a new aseptic process, and may spark rivalry between equally experienced candidates, especially where hierarchy is rigid and leadership is autocratic.

External recruitment: Hiring 30 supervisors from outside brings fresh aseptic-process expertise from the wider food industry, wider talent choice, and new ideas on cutting the rising defect rate on capped bottles. It also avoids stripping experienced operators from the production floor during a sensitive ramp-up. However, external searches cost more in advertising, agency fees and longer induction, newcomers face cultural adjustment to RSFJ's hierarchical, autocratic style, and local labour turnover at 16% suggests onboarding must be strong to retain them.

Decision: RSFJ should choose internal recruitment for at least half the supervisor posts and external hires only for the specialised aseptic specialisms, then train the rest. Internal promotion is faster, cheaper and motivational during expansion, protects the line's existing quality culture, and fits the funds available after the share issue and retained profit commitment. External recruitment is rejected as the primary route because it costs more, learns more slowly against supermarket lead times of 2.5 days, and risks weakening RSFJ's proven 1.5% defect performance; where genuine aseptic expertise is absent in-house, a small number of external hires is justified as a complement, not a substitute.
    Keywords: workforce of 240, labour turnover, autocratic, hierarchical, $1,850,000, 1.5%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of internal and external recruitment with limited application to RSFJ. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both recruitment options in the context of RSFJ's expansion. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both recruitment options in the context of RSFJ with a well-justified decision explaining why external recruitment is rejected as the primary route.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how RSFJ's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 150,000 units. Working: contribution per unit is $7.50 − $4.10 = $3.40, and $510,000 ÷ $3.40 = 150,000 units. (ii) Contribution per unit = $3.40. This is what each premium bottle contributes toward covering fixed costs after the fruit, bottle and cap costs are paid. (iii) Four contextual uses explained: First, RSFJ's managers can compare current output of 210,000 units with the 150,000-unit break-even to confirm a margin of safety of 60,000 units, giving the board confidence to commit to the new aseptic bottling plant without jeopardising the $750,000 retained profit cushion. Second, the $3.40 contribution lets managers model supermarket promotions precisely: a $0.40 promotional cut would leave $3.00 per unit, so RSFJ needs volumes above 170,000 units to keep total contribution above the $510,000 fixed costs — a concrete test of any promotion RSFJ is offered. Third, break-even analysis disciplines the regional rollout: each new supermarket region must commit to order volumes that push group output beyond 150,000 units before launch advertising is signed off, protecting the $1,850,000 plant investment. Fourth, unit-cost benchmarking ($510,000 ÷ 210,000 units + $4.10 = $6.53 a unit) lets RSFJ track the effect of the 14.2% orange, mango and guava inflation, judge whether the rising defect rate on capped bottles is inflating rework costs, and decide when to pass costs into the $0.80 premium shoppers already accept.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RSFJ's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RSFJ's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Conclusion: RSFJ's financial position has improved — but modestly and with concentration risk.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.25%, the 7.0% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in orange, mango and guava input costs will affect RSFJ. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.

--- STEM ---
Copper Kettle Bakery (CKB) is a sole trader business in the artisan baking sector, employing a workforce of 12. Founded in 2011 by Rosa Jiménez, the bakery supplies wholesale pies, pastries and breads to 34 cafés across the city region, and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. CKB plans to invest $145,000 in a new wholesale pie and pastry line, financed by a $70,000 five-year bank loan and $75,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $90,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.75 a unit and a selling price of $8.50, and currently produces 34,000 units a year. CKB faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 22% among weekend staff and its delivery van fleet is ageing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CKB plans to invest $145,000 in a wholesale pie and pastry line rather than opening a second retail shop. Explain two advantages for CKB of the wholesale expansion rather than the second shop.
    Answer: Point 1: The wholesale line leverages CKB's existing production capability and reputation with its 34 café customers, multiplying sales without the overheads of a second retail shop — lease deposits, refurbishment, shopfitting, till equipment and two extra retail staff. CKB can reach more outlets from one kitchen, spreading its $90,000 fixed costs across more units and pushing annual output toward the new line's potential while protecting the $4.75 variable cost through bulk flour and butter purchasing.

Point 2: Wholesale revenue is recurring and predictable: café owners reorder weekly boxes, smoothing cash flow against a $70,000 five-year bank loan and letting CKB plan production and van routes efficiently. A second retail shop would add location risk — footfall, parking, local competition — before loyalty is proven, whereas the wholesale trade is already validated by 68% of 180 surveyed café owners wanting same-day delivery. The wholesale route also compounds CKB's artisan brand story across the city region and keeps Rosa Jiménez's flat, autocratic structure workable, since one production lead can manage the line without diluting the personal oversight that defines a sole trader's quality guarantee.
    Keywords: wholesale, $145,000, 34, fixed costs, $90,000, sole trader
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Copper Kettle Bakery, its café customer base and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CKB is launching its wholesale pie and pastry range to new cafés. Consider a local radio sponsorship, a food-festival stall with free tastings, or a printed catalogue with introductory discounts. Which should CKB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local radio sponsorship: A weekly morning-show sponsorship around artisan breakfast time would reach city-region listeners, many of whom are café customers, and is far cheaper than television. It builds broad local awareness of the launch. Its weakness is that radio is a passive, audio-only medium — listeners cannot taste the pastry — and the audience includes many people outside the 34-café trade area, so wastage is significant for a 12-person sole trader whose marketing capacity and budget are limited by the $70,000 loan commitment.

Food-festival stall with free tastings: A stall at the city food festival puts the pies and pastries directly into the mouths of café owners and their customers, generating instant feedback, trial orders and word-of-mouth in exactly the target segment. Sampling converts sceptics quickly and photographs well for social media. The drawback is a one-off spike of attention with no guarantee of repeat wholesale orders after the festival ends, and the labour cost of manning the stall falls on the same 12-person team already stretched by weekend shifts.

Printed catalogue with introductory discounts: A professional catalogue mailed to the 180 surveyed café owners (44% of whom would pay up to $0.50 more per box for organic flour) directly drives wholesale enquiries, showcases the full new line with prices, and the introductory discount de-risks the first order. Catalogues can sit on café counters for weeks as a reminder. However, print reaches only existing prospects, conversion is slow and unmeasurable without follow-up calls, and printing and postage costs bite if response is below roughly 20%.

Recommendation: CKB should choose the printed catalogue with introductory discounts, supported by one food-festival tasting at launch rather than a full stall programme. The catalogue is the only option that reaches all 180 respondent cafés directly at low cost, matches the data-driven segmentation already in the operations log, and pushes the 68% wanting same-day delivery to try the line; it is rejected only as a stand-alone tool. Radio is rejected as untargeted and unmeasurable for a $70,000-loan-financed sole trader; the festival stall alone is rejected as a one-off spike that cannot sustain the weekly reorder volume the new line needs.
    Keywords: wholesale, 68%, 44%, $0.50, organic flour, $70,000, café

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CKB's labour turnover has reached 22% among weekend staff. Explain two problems for CKB of this labour turnover.
    Answer: Point 1: High weekend labour turnover means CKB constantly loses trained hands on its busiest days, forcing Rosa Jiménez to re-recruit and re-train weekend bakers repeatedly. Each leaver takes tacit knowledge of the laminated-pastry process, so defect rates edge upward (they are already 2.9%), rework and flour waste rise above the 6.1% benchmark, and the bakery misses the same-day delivery expectations of the 68% of café owners who want it — risking lost wholesale accounts worth far more than the cost of a weekend wage.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CKB must train its remaining 3 staff on the new laminated-pastry process. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the bakery college. Which should CKB choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training inside the bakery is directly relevant to CKB's own ovens, flour suppliers and pastry techniques, costs nothing in fees, and keeps the 3 staff producing boxes during the busiest laminated-pastry season. Mistakes are made on real orders where feedback is immediate, and Rosa can coach flaws out of the process in person — critical for a sole trader who knows every batch. Drawbacks: if Rosa teaches while producing, her own output falls, bad habits can be passed on uncorrected, and there is no formal certification, which matters if café auditors or insurers ask for documented competency on the new line.

Off-the-job training: The bakery college course at $600 per employee — $1,800 for 3 staff — gives structured, up-to-date tuition, a recognised certificate and exposure to techniques beyond Rosa's own kitchen, such as waste reduction toward the 6.1% benchmark and food-safety hygiene. Time away from the bakery removes 3 staff for the course duration, however, pressuring weekend cover that is already failing at 22% turnover, and content is generic rather than CKB-specific, so fine-tuning on return would still be needed.

Decision: CKB should choose on-the-job training with a short college visit for certification only, rather than full off-the-job courses. It is nearly free, preserves weekend capacity CKB cannot spare, and matches the urgent need to stabilise the new line while the $70,000 loan is serviced. Full off-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because removing 25% of the workforce (3 of 12) from production during launch would strain same-day delivery promises and Rosa's supervision load; the $1,800 fee is affordable, but the output loss and generic content make it a poor substitute — though retaining a college certificate as a weekend-staff retention incentive is worth doing once the line stabilises.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job, $600, 22%, laminated-pastry, $70,000

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how CKB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 24,000 units. Working: contribution per unit is $8.50 − $4.75 = $3.75, and $90,000 ÷ $3.75 = 24,000 units. (ii) Contribution per unit = $3.75. This is what each wholesale box of pies, pastries and breads contributes toward covering fixed costs after flour, butter and packaging are paid. (iii) Four contextual uses explained: First, Rosa can compare current output of 34,000 units with the 24,000-unit break-even to confirm a margin of safety of 10,000 units, reassuring herself and her bank that the wholesale line can absorb seasonal café dips without breaching the $70,000 loan schedule. Second, the $3.75 contribution lets Rosa test launch incentives: a $0.50 introductory cut would leave $3.25 per unit, so she knows any introductory offer needs volumes above roughly 27,700 units to keep the business beyond break-even for the year. Third, knowing the 24,000-unit break-even lets Rosa set minimum weekly café orders and van route density, ensuring every dispatched route recovers its fuel, the 6.1% flour and butter waste and its labour before the schedule is committed. Fourth, unit-cost benchmarking ($90,000 ÷ 34,000 units + $4.75 = $7.40 a unit) gives Rosa a yardstick for the 2.9% defect rate: she can trace rework cost per box, decide whether the 44% of cafés wanting organic flour justify a price premium, and renegotiate the $4.75 variable cost with suppliers amid the 13.5% wheat flour and butter inflation.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CKB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CKB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.29 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.37 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.02 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $28,000 inventories + $35,000 trade receivables + $8,000 cash = $71,000; 2025 current assets = $22,000 + $48,000 + $15,000 = $85,000. 2024 = $71,000 ÷ $55,000 = 1.29; 2025 = $85,000 ÷ $62,000 = 1.37. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($71,000 − $28,000) ÷ $55,000 = $43,000 ÷ $55,000 = 0.78; 2025 = ($85,000 − $22,000) ÷ $62,000 = $63,000 ÷ $62,000 = 1.02.

Evaluation: CKB's liquidity has clearly improved in quality, not just quantity. The stock-independent measure crossed the 1.00 threshold — CKB can now pay all current liabilities without selling a single pie — which 2024's 0.78 could not claim. Inventories fell from $28,000 to $22,000 (an efficient 6.1%-waste improvement), reducing write-off risk for fresh pastry. The caveat is trade receivables, which rose from $35,000 to $48,000 as more café accounts bought on weekly credit terms; if those café owners stretch payment, the stronger position could reverse, and current liabilities still rose from $55,000 to $62,000, so discipline is needed on the loan and supplier terms.

Conclusion: CKB's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures strengthened, and critically the improvement survives stripping out inventories, which fell anyway. For a sole trader carrying a new five-year bank loan, this is genuine progress rather than cosmetic stock build-up. The main risk is rising trade receivables, so Rosa should enforce café payment terms and review credit limits while the new wholesale line beds in.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CKB of installing a computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) proving oven for its pastry line.
    Answer: Advantage: A CAM-controlled proving oven holds temperature, humidity and timing far more precisely than manual checking, cutting the 2.9% defect rate further and reducing rejected wholesale boxes. Precision baking also lowers the 6.1% flour and butter waste, and automation steadies output on weekend shifts where the 22% labour turnover makes manual quality assurance fragile. Consistent laminated pastry strengthens CKB's reputation for same-day delivery to the 68% of café owners who want it, supporting the new wholesale line and the repayment of the $70,000 bank loan from higher, more reliable margins.

Disadvantage: The CAM oven is a capital commitment on top of the $145,000 wholesale line investment and the $70,000 loan, so CKB takes on heavier fixed capacity and maintenance obligations, including software licences, sensor calibration and specialist repair call-outs that a 12-person sole trader cannot absorb easily. If demand dips in the city region — or café orders grow slower than forecast — the oven's fixed cost per box rises, eroding the $3.75 contribution. Staff also need retraining on the new controls, and any electronic failure during a peak Saturday bake could halt the whole wholesale line until a technician arrives, threatening the same-day delivery promise the range depends on.
    Keywords: 2.9%, 6.1%, 22%, 68%, $145,000, $70,000

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate cut to 4.5%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 13.5% rise in wheat flour and butter costs will affect CKB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate cut (5.0% to 4.5%): For a sole trader carrying a $70,000 five-year bank loan on the new wholesale line, a 0.5% cut saves roughly $350 a year in interest — helpful but small. Lower rates also ease overdraft pressure on the $48,000 trade receivables balance and make any future van purchase (relevant given the ageing fleet) cheaper. The cut genuinely supports small businesses, as the bulletin intends, but its cash benefit to CKB is marginal next to weekly ingredient invoices.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.72 per hour from April 2026): With 12 employees, mainly production and weekend delivery staff, the wage bill rises by about $1,500 a year per full-time worker at the floor rate — roughly $10,000–$18,000 a year across the team, before differentials for skilled pastry staff. For a $90,000 fixed-cost operation this is meaningful, but CKB can partly offset it with the automation of the new line, reduced overtime from better batch planning, and productivity benchmarks (34,000 units ÷ 12 staff ≈ 2,833 boxes per worker).

Input cost inflation (13.5% wheat flour and butter): These two ingredients dominate the $4.75 variable cost per unit. A 13.5% rise adds roughly $0.40–$0.64 per unit; at 34,000 units that is about $13,600–$21,800 a year, direct and unavoidable, hitting every box sold. CKB must either raise prices to its 34 cafés — risking volume — or absorb the hit against the $3.75 contribution, unless the 44% of cafés willing to pay $0.50 more for organic flour can fund the gap.

Conclusion: The 13.5% rise in wheat flour and butter costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit CKB sells, unlike the interest saving which is fixed and small, and unlike the wage rise which can be partially offset by automation and productivity; ingredient inflation is recurring, front-of-mind, and directly reaches cafés' willingness to pay. The wage rise is second; the rate cut is welcome but minor — but CKB must act on all three, renegotiating supplier contracts and pricing the organic premium carefully to protect its $3.75 contribution.
    Keywords: 4.5%, 6.0%, 13.5%, $12.72, 7.8%, 2.8%, $4.75

--- STEM ---
Ironhill Coffee Roasters (ICR) is a partnership between three partners in the speciality coffee roasting sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2015 by Petra Lindqvist and Sam Okafor, the business roasts single-origin beans for independent cafés and sells branded retail bags online and in store, and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ICR plans to invest $260,000 in a second roastery unit, financed by a $120,000 bank loan and $140,000 partners' capital contributions. It has fixed costs of $141,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.80 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. ICR faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8% on packing shifts, and its roasting defect rate has risen to 2.1%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ICR plans to finance its second roastery unit with a $120,000 bank loan and $140,000 partners' capital contributions. Explain two advantages for ICR of using partners' capital contributions instead of a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Partners' capital contributions cost ICR no interest and no arrangement fees, which protects the partnership's cash flow at a time when it carries fixed costs of $141,000 a year and must absorb the 15.6% rise in green coffee bean costs. Every dollar of interest avoided shields the $16.50 selling price of the single-origin bags, helping ICR stay competitive with supermarket own-label speciality coffee while food-price and coffee inflation sit at 10.5%.

Point 2: Bringing in $140,000 from the three partners deepens their personal commitment to the second roastery unit and avoids pledging partners' homes or the roasting equipment as collateral for a bigger bank loan. In a partnership, unlimited personal liability already exists, but using retained partner funds preserves flexibility if the 15.6% bean-cost shock persists: the bank is not in a position to impose repayment terms or covenant breaches, and profit distribution can be adjusted by agreement among Petra Lindqvist, Sam Okafor and the third partner rather than to satisfy a lender's timetable — keeping democratic leadership workable during the build-out.
    Keywords: partners' capital contributions, bank loan, $140,000, $260,000, partnership, $120,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Ironhill Coffee Roasters, its partnership structure and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ICR is launching its branded single-origin coffee bags. Consider café sampling roadshows, social media influencer marketing, or a loyalty card scheme with partner cafés. Which should ICR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Café sampling roadshows: Travelling roasters and tasting sessions inside independent cafés let ICR demonstrate traceable, single-origin quality directly to the 63% of 400 surveyed café owners who would stock the bags, building owner advocacy at the point of sale. Costs are modest — a van, samples, a roaster and staff time — and tastings convert sceptical owners fast. Limitations: roadshows reach only the cafés visited, scale slowly across the country, and interrupt normal production with the same 16 staff, while travel and labour costs accumulate quickly per account signed.

Social media influencer marketing: Speciality-coffee influencers can reach thousands of home-brewing enthusiasts at low cost per engagement, driving online and in-store bag sales and explaining the $1.00 traceability premium the 48% of surveyed café owners would pay. It scales nationally, suits ICR's flat democratic marketing style, and content compounds over time. Downsides: conversion to wholesale café listings is indirect, influencer credibility varies, results are slower and harder to attribute, and creative demands time ICR's small team may lack.

Loyalty card scheme with partner cafés: A joint loyalty card giving regulars their ninth bag free (or partnered café points) drives repeat purchase, rewards the partner cafés that back ICR, and generates first-party data on drinking preferences. It is relatively cheap, measurable, and encourages weekly delivery patterns the 57% of café owners want. However, it only retains customers after first trial — it does not create awareness — and managing card logistics across dozens of independent cafés adds administrative load for a 16-person business.

Recommendation: ICR should choose social media influencer marketing, amplified by café sampling at two or three flagship accounts. Influencers create the national awareness and brand story that the $260,000 roastery launch needs, reaching both café owners and home drinkers affordably; sampling builds proof at the counter, but as a launch driver it is too slow and local to carry the campaign. Loyalty cards are rejected as a launch tool because retention mechanics matter only after awareness and trial exist — they should follow influencer-driven first sales, not precede them.
    Keywords: single-origin, 63%, 48%, $1.00, traceable, $260,000, café
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ICR with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ICR with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the sampling roadshows and loyalty scheme are rejected as the lead strategy.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ICR operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for ICR of democratic leadership for its roasting and packing teams.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives ICR's 16 employees a voice in roast profiles, packing rotas and green-bean sourcing decisions, which raises motivation and ownership in a partnership business where staff see themselves as part of the craft. Employees who help set roast curves flag scorching or under-development early, attacking the 2.1% defect rate at source rather than through after-the-fact inspection — exactly what the planned quality assurance pilot with the two largest café accounts requires.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions builds commitment and reduces absenteeism on packing shifts, where it has reached 8%. When operatives help design shift patterns around peak café delivery days (57% of owners want weekly delivery), attendance improves and cover gaps shrink without costly agency labour. Democratic consultation also strengthens the flat structure: fewer management layers means faster feedback from the roasting log to the partners, supporting the 2-day order fulfilment and keeping the 5 untrained staff engaged through the $800 coffee institute course rather than feeling imposed-upon.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, workforce of 16, 2.1%, absenteeism, flat organisational structure, $800
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ICR's democratic leadership, defect rate, absenteeism and cooperative-style partner culture.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ICR is launching branded single-origin retail bags at scale. Consider batch production or flow production for the new bags. Which should ICR choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Batch production: Roasting and packing in batches preserves the single-origin, small-lot identity that independent cafés and home drinkers pay a premium for, allows ICR to switch origins (e.g. Ethiopian, Colombian) between batches, and limits unsold roasted stock in a volatile bean market. It supports traceability for the 48% of café owners willing to pay $1.00 more per bag for fully traceable lots, and quality control per batch is straightforward. The drawbacks are higher average unit setup costs, more cleaning/changeover downtime, and slower throughput — batch scheduling is stretched across 1,900 kg a week with 5 of 16 staff still untrained on the new drum roaster.

Flow production: A continuous roast-and-pack flow would maximise throughput, minimise handling between roaster and bagger, and lower unit costs through automation — appealing for winning national listings and supermarket own-label trials. Unit costs fall and consistency rises, important for the 2.1% defect target. However, flow production demands sustained high volume of one or two blends, large capital spend (impossible alongside the $260,000 second unit already financed by a $120,000 loan and $140,000 partner capital), rigid sequencing for any origin change, and would sacrifice the freshness window and the small-lot brand story that justify ICR's $16.50 price point.

Decision: ICR should choose batch production, at least for the launch phase. Batch fits the single-origin, traceable, premium brand the 63% of café owners already want to stock, matches the modest capital remaining after the second unit investment, and absorbs the 8% packing absenteeism with flexible scheduling. Flow production is rejected as the launch method because it forces volume before demand is proven, dilutes the craft positioning that underpins ICR's pricing power, and would over-commit the partnership's finances — though ICR can move one hero blend to a flow line later, once daily orders from the loyalty scheme and café contracts justify it.
    Keywords: single-origin, 63%, 48%, $1.00, traceable, 2.1%, $260,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of batch and flow production with limited application to ICR. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both production options in the context of ICR's premium positioning. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both production methods in the context of ICR with a well-justified decision explaining why flow production is rejected for the launch.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how ICR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units. Working: contribution per unit is $16.50 − $11.80 = $4.70, and $141,000 ÷ $4.70 = 30,000 units. (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.70. This is what each single-origin retail bag contributes toward covering fixed costs after green beans, bags and roasting energy are paid.   Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ICR of introducing a quality assurance (QA) system for its roasting process.
    Answer: Advantage: A QA system builds quality into each stage — green bean intake, roast curve monitoring, resting and bagging — rather than inspecting bags after they are sealed, driving the 2.1% defect rate down toward the levels the two largest café accounts (on the January 2027 pilot) will demand. Prevention is cheaper than rework and waste, protects flavour consistency for the 400 surveyed café owners, and supports the $1.00 traceability premium the 48% would pay, strengthening ICR's claim to fully traceable single-origin lots and the supermarket listings the $260,000 roastery is designed to win.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 15.6% rise in green coffee bean costs will affect ICR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.5%): ICR carries a $120,000 bank loan on the $260,000 second roastery. A 0.5% rise adds about $600 a year to interest — trivial in cash terms, though it raises the cost of any top-up borrowing and signals tighter money markets for the partnership. Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.42 per hour from April 2026): With 16 staff weighted to roasting, packing and delivery, the annual wage bill rises by roughly $1,400 per full-time worker at the floor rate, about $22,000–$25,000 across the team — meaningful for a partnership drawing profit distributions, but partial offsets exist: automation in the second unit, cross-training (reducing the 5 untrained), and productivity benchmarks (40,000 units ÷ 16 staff = 2,500 bags per worker per year). The wage rise is second; the interest rise is third and containable — but ICR must act on all three: forward-buy green bean contracts, lock the loan rate, and automate the second unit to hold unit costs and protect its $4.70 contribution.
