  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SAW of switching the new metal farm to certified aerospace-grade recycled titanium powder.
    Answer: Advantage: Certified recycled titanium powder unlocks the exact segment the market research points to — 62% of the 130 marine and aerospace buyers surveyed would pay a 15% premium for certified aerospace-grade parts, and 55% require ISO 9001 supplier certification. Recycled powder also cuts embodied carbon per part, a genuine differentiator in defence and sustainability-sensitive tenders, and typically costs less than virgin powder once scaled, partially offsetting the 15.6% year-on-year alloy inflation already hitting SAW's $17 variable cost. Qualification data from previous runs should shorten the certification timeline on the new farm.

Disadvantage: Recycled powder varies more in particle size and chemistry than virgin stock, and any batch drift directly feeds the 6.5% defect rate and the $58,000 quarterly rework bill — a single failed build on a $40 part erases its margin. Certification and batch testing add cost and lead time (powder must be quarantined, sampled and logged), supply of certified recycled powder is thin in Southeast Asia, and if SAW certifies against one feedstock then must re-qualify whenever the supplier changes blend, creating a recurring compliance burden that 24 members and the current 84% uptime cannot easily absorb alongside the metal-farm ramp-up.
    Keywords: 15% premium, 55%, 62%, 6.5%, $58,000, $17
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SAW's quality, certification and costs.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 4.6% lending rate, the 8.0% rise in the Employment Pass qualifying salary to $5,600 and the 15.6% rise in alloy powder costs will affect SAW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Lending rate rise from 4.1% to 4.6%: SAW financed the metal farm internally ($260,000 retained profit plus $220,000 from selling older equipment) with no new bank borrowing, so the direct interest effect is close to zero. Indirectly, higher rates raise the cost of any future machinery finance, compress clients' capital budgets (marine yards delaying refits), and cool 7.5% order-book growth if financing dries up across the region. Because SAW is deliberately debt-light, it is better insulated than leveraged rivals — a real competitive edge that should be preserved rather than spent. Notably it also makes the cooperative's no-external-finance choice look wise in hindsight.

Employment Pass qualifying salary rise of 8.0% to $5,600 per month: SAW hires whichever skilled technicians it cannot source locally — perhaps 6 of its 24 staff — so the extra $448 per month each is about $32,300 a year of additional wage cost, roughly $2.80 per employee per month of margin across the team. Morale and fairness issues arise if local members' wages are not reviewed in step, and the tighter qualifying salary may squeeze mid-tier technicians out of Singapore entirely, worsening the skills pool for the metal farm. Mitigation: multi-skilling locals, retention bonuses below the EP threshold effect, and automation of powder handling.

Alloy powder inflation of 15.6%: This is a direct, recurring hit on the dominant input in SAW's $17 variable cost — titanium and nickel feeds for certified parts. If powder is two-thirds of variable cost (~$11.30), a 15.6% rise adds about $1.76 per unit; across 28,000 units that is roughly $49,300 a year, or 4.4% of revenue, before any recovery through price. It also raises the stakes of the 6.5% defect rate — every scrapped batch wastes more expensive powder — and of the 11% throughput waste. Locking 12-month supply contracts, qualifying a second powder source and pursuing the certified 15% premium tier all recover part of this, but nothing fully offsets it.

Conclusion: The 15.6% rise in titanium and nickel alloy powder costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every unit SAW produces, compounds with rework and waste at the new farm, and cannot be hedged away like debt costs. The EP salary rise is second — material (~$32,300 a year) but targetable through contracts and multi-skilling — while the 4.6% lending rate is smallest because SAW deliberately expanded without new debt. SAW should lock powder pricing, accelerate certification to defend the 15% premium, and keep its debt-light discipline.
    Keywords: 4.1%, 4.6%, 8.0%, $5,600, 15.6%, 7.5%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SAW. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SAW's costs, demand or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SAW with a well-justified judgment that alloy cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Brightcart Digital (BCD) is a partnership in the digital-services sector, building and hosting e-commerce stores and online marketplaces for Gulf retailers from Dubai. Founded in 2019 by Omar Haddad and Sara Nasser, BCD employs a workforce of 30 and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership under managing partner Omar Haddad. BCD plans to invest $320,000 in a headless commerce platform and fulfilment dashboard, financed by a $200,000 bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. The business has fixed costs of $312,000 a year, a variable cost of $150 a unit and a selling price of $540, and currently produces 6,500 units a year of store retainer packages. BCD faces an HR problem: its support team is understaffed, absenteeism is 7% and response times are slipping.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BCD plans to finance its headless commerce platform with a $200,000 bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for BCD of using a bank loan instead of bringing in a new partner.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan leaves BCD's ownership, profit share and decision rights entirely with Omar Haddad and Sara Nasser. Bringing in a new partner would dilute the two founders' authority — critical for a flat structure with autocratic leadership under Omar — and permanently hand over a slice of the profits from the 6,500 store retainer packages the partnership produces. The loan is repaid on a fixed schedule and ends; a partner's profit share lasts as long as the partnership does, so the loan is far cheaper in the long run if BCD hits its targets.

Point 2: The loan is a known, finite cost — plausible repayments over five years on $200,000 are budgetable against 68% client renewal income and a 10.0% operating margin, and success releases all retained profit back to the partners afterwards. A new partner chosen in haste to secure $200,000 could deadlock decisions on the SellEverywhere roadmap, client selection or pricing, conflict with BCD's execution discipline, and be extremely costly to exit. The loan also builds BCD's credit history with UAE banks for future expansion, whereas equity never gets 'paid off' and negotiation with incoming partners would consume management time BCD cannot spare while support response times slip.
    Keywords: bank loan, retained profit, $200,000, $120,000, $320,000, $312,000

Mall kiosk advertising: Kiosks inside flagship malls could demo a live store on the spot and hand out QR codes to retail chains with physical presence — vivid for the 41% of owners frustrated by unreliable payment gateways. Drawbacks: premium mall rents (already up 8.7%) make kiosks expensive, reach is limited to footfall in selected malls, staffing costs for demos, and scaling beyond Dubai into the wider Gulf requires duplicating physical presence everywhere.

Recommendation: BCD should choose bilingual social media advertising. It alone combines precise targeting of the surveyed 74% rebuild-intent segment, full measurability (already $45 per lead), bilingual reach across the Gulf, and a natural bridge to the 59% hosted-subscription preference with instant-demo landing pages. Radio is rejected as untargeted, English-only and unmeasurable for B2B services; kiosks are rejected as high-cost, mall-bound and unscalable beyond Dubai.     Question: BCD must motivate its delivery and support teams during the SellEverywhere push. Consider commission on every new retainer signed, or a profit-sharing scheme for all staff. Which should BCD choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Commission on every new retainer: Commission gives individual salespeople a direct, immediate payout for each retained store signed, directly feeding the 290-leads-in-30-days pipeline and the 74% rebuild-intent segment. In a flat partnership with 30 staff it rewards collaboration, encourages support quality that lifts renewals, aids retention, and satisfies equity-sensitivity in Dubai's labour market. Its weakness is the effort-reward link: a junior support agent may see little personal gain from one extra renewal, the pot varies (hurting planning in a variable-cost $150/unit model), and partners must disclose business performance openly — uncomfortable in an autocratic-led partnership.

Decision: BCD should choose profit-sharing for all staff. Growth without quality delivery would hollow out the 68% renewal engine that justifies the $320,000 platform investment, and the crisis is in support staffing and absenteeism — frontline colleagues will not accept a growth tool that rewards only closers. Commission is rejected as the lead mechanism because it would deepen the build-versus-support divide and likely degrade client satisfaction (4.3 out of 5) before the launch even lands. BCD should, however, layer a small team bonus for the support pod tied to renewal milestones, keeping some individual accountability inside the collective scheme.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 4.90% base rate, the 3.4% Dubai inflation with 8.7% rent rises, and the 11.2% rise in payment gateway and logistics fees will affect BCD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base rate rise from 4.40% to 4.90%: BCD carries a $200,000 bank loan financing the headless commerce platform; a 0.50-percentage-point rise adds about $1,000 a year to interest — trivial against $386,000 operating profit and the 18.2% return on capital. Dubai inflation at 3.4% and prime rents up 8.7%: Inflation lifts BCD's own cost base — office rent in a prime location, salaries it must offer to hold developers against better-paid regional rivals, and the general cost of client acquisition. Rents up 8.7% directly inflate the fixed costs already at $312,000; even a $2,000/month increase adds $24,000 a year, equivalent to roughly $3.70 per retainer package. Clients squeezed by inflation and rent will negotiate harder on fees, and the 74% rebuild-intent segment may stretch timelines from 12 months to 18. Mitigation: shift some roles remote, renegotiate lease before the 2027 review, and pre-raise prices modestly with the next renewal cycle.

Gateway and logistics fees up 11.2%: This recurs on every transaction flowing through every store BCD hosts. For a hosted-subscription model where the platform clips or passes through fees, an 11.2% rise either compresses BCD's take or is pushed onto merchants, who — already at the 41% gateway-frustration pain point — may churn toward rivals or demand discounts. It directly threatens the hosted-subscription preference of the 59% segment, the 68% renewal engine and BCD's entire SellEverywhere economics. Logistics inflation also weakens the fulfilment-dashboard value proposition for omnichannel retailers. BCD should counter by renegotiating bulk gateway rates across its client book, consolidating volumes onto one provider, making fee transparency a selling point, and absorbing selectively for anchor clients.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in payment gateway and logistics fees will have the greatest impact. It is the only change that multiplies across every order on every hosted store BCD operates, corrodes the 59% hosted-preference economics and the 68% renewal income on which the $320,000 platform investment depends, and lands directly on the 41% gateway-frustration pain point BCD must cure — not create. The 3.4% inflation with 8.7% rent rises is second (meaningful fixed-cost creep, mitigable by lease action and pricing), while the 4.90% base rate is smallest (~$1,000 a year, fixable by contract). BCD should make fee renegotiation and transparent pass-through pricing its first 2026 priority.

Avoiding that interest helps DAC absorb the 11.5% rise in consumables without breaching the premium pricing its clients expect, protecting its $42.00 contribution per treatment and keeping the $620,000 investment affordable while the new suite ramps up.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership and control fully with Dr Sofia Duarte and existing shareholders, with no bank covenants or security charges hanging over the laser-rejuvenation suite if demand disappoints. There is no repossession risk and no lender interference in clinic operations, which matters for a private limited company positioning itself as premium. Operating profit rose from $270,000 (270 ÷ 1,800 = 15.0% of revenue) to $396,000 (396 ÷ 2,200 = 18.0% of revenue). With capital employed of $1,500,000 in 2024 and $1,760,000 in 2025, the return on capital moved from 270 ÷ 1,500 = 18.0% to 396 ÷ 1,760 = 22.5%. Revenue grew $400,000 (22.2%) while cost of sales grew only $130,000, evidence of premium pricing power in the anti-ageing range.

Evaluation: Performance has improved decisively. Margins widened because the $400,000 revenue gain outran cost growth, and the return on capital now comfortably exceeds any bank deposit rate, validating the expansion logic behind the second suite. However, interest payable climbed from $45,000 to $60,000 as borrowing rose, the 11.5% consumables inflation threatens next year's margin, and the 5.8% minimum wage rise from April 2026 will lift the wage bill further. DAC should also watch treatment waiting times, as lost appointments quietly erode revenue per room.

Conclusion: DAC's financial performance has improved across all three measures — profitability (40.0% to 45.0%), operating margin (15.0% to 18.0%) and return on capital employed (18.0% to 22.5%). The improvement is broad-based rather than a one-off, but DAC must protect it by managing consumables inflation and wage costs while the second suite ramps up to full utilisation.
    Keywords: 40.0%, 45.0%, 15.0%, 18.0%, 22.5%, 990, 1,760

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: DAC is trialling recyclable, eco-friendly packaging for single-use treatment consumables. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for DAC of introducing this packaging.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 11.5% rise in consumables costs will affect DAC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): DAC's $400,000 ten-year variable-rate loan costs about 0.75% more a year — roughly $3,000 extra interest — small against $396,000 of operating profit. Conclusion: The 11.5% consumables inflation will have the greatest impact. It adds about $83,500 to annual costs — more than double the wage rise (roughly $37,000) and nearly twenty-eight times the interest increase (roughly $3,000) — and it hits every one of the 11,000 treatments sold each year, threatening the exact margin that justifies the $620,000 expansion. DAC should renegotiate supplier terms and nudge prices upward with the anti-ageing premium, while managing the wage and rate rises through rosters and loan-rate fixing.

--- STEM ---
Wayline Driving School (WDS) is a private limited company in the education and training sector, operating eight franchised driving schools and employing a workforce of 24. Founded in 2011 by Tomas Byrne, the business operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. WDS plans to invest $300,000 in eight dual-control vehicles and a digital booking platform for three new franchise locations, financed by a $180,000 hire purchase agreement and $120,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $128,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 13,500 units a year, measured in one-to-one lessons. WDS faces rising lesson-cancellation rates and a shortage of certified instructors.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WDS plans to finance part of its fleet expansion with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for WDS of using hire purchase to fund the eight dual-control vehicles instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the cost of the eight dual-control vehicles over their working lives, matching monthly instalments to the lesson revenue the fleet generates. WDS keeps its cash for fuel, insurance and the new booking platform rather than paying out $180,000 upfront, which protects working capital while fixed costs already stand at $128,000 a year.

Point 2: The vehicles themselves act as security for the hire purchase agreement, so WDS avoids pledging all its business assets as collateral, unlike a bank loan secured across the whole company. Ownership transfers automatically once the final instalment is paid, the agreement is straightforward to arrange at the point of vehicle purchase, and there is no large balloon repayment — suiting a private limited company funding a $300,000 expansion with $120,000 retained profit and limited spare cash.
    Keywords: hire purchase, retained profit, $180,000, $120,000, $300,000, $128,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wayline Driving School and its fleet expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WDS is launching its winter intensive-course promotion. Consider national television advertising, local newspaper advertising, or door-to-door flyer drops across nearby estates. Which should WDS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: Television would put the winter intensive course in front of millions and build instant brand recognition across all eight franchise catchments. However, production and airtime costs are prohibitive for a 24-employee business funding a $300,000 expansion largely through hire purchase, and most national viewers live outside the school's teaching areas, so the spend-to-enrolment ratio would be very poor for a local service.

Local newspaper advertising: Regional papers are read by parents of prospective learners in exactly the neighbourhoods WDS serves, carry strong local trust, and cost a fraction of television. They suit timed offers such as the winter promotion and can be repeated weekly through January. The limitation is modest reach — circulation is declining and younger learners increasingly discover services online rather than in print.

Door-to-door flyer drops: Flyers are extremely cheap per household, hyper-local around each of the eight schools, and ideal for households with 17-year-olds. However, they are easy to ignore, unmeasurable, create litter and waste, and cannot carry the detailed course information learners want — and much of each estate includes households with no learner driver.

Recommendation: WDS should choose local newspaper advertising. It balances reach and cost across all eight catchments, carries trust with parents of young learners, and supports the timed winter offer better than scattergun television or easily-binned flyers. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a regional driving school; door-to-door flyers are rejected as too narrow, wasteful and unmeasurable, though a small flyer run around the three new locations could reinforce the newspaper campaign.
    Keywords: driving school, 3,240, 71%, 58%, 6 days, $4
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WDS with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WDS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and flyers are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WDS's flat structure and autocratic leadership shape how its front-line instructors work. Explain two benefits for WDS of using autocratic leadership when managing its driving instructors.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives WDS's 24 instructors clear, non-negotiable standards — for safety, vehicle checks, punctuality and pupil conduct — which is essential when mistakes can kill. Decisive direction from Tomas Byrne's management team means every school applies the same rules, the 61% first-time pass rate stays consistent across franchises, and complaint counts like the punctuality complaints that fell from 17 to 9 per month keep falling.

Point 2: Autocratic leadership enables fast decisions when operational problems hit: for example, re-allocating instructors immediately when cancellations (now averaging 14%) spike, authorising cover for sickness or pushing a winter promotion live within days. In a flat structure with a wide span of control there is little middle-management friction, so urgent calls are made without committee delays — protecting the 13,500 lessons delivered a year and the digital booking platform's promise of 6-day booking turnaround.
    Keywords: autocratic leadership, flat structure, workforce of 24, 13,500, 61%, 14%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WDS's safety needs, cancellations and franchise consistency.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WDS faces a shortage of certified instructors for its three new franchise locations. Consider recruiting experienced instructors externally or retraining existing part-time instructors internally. Which should WDS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: External recruitment: Bringing in experienced, certified instructors fills the gap immediately, unlocks the three new locations on schedule, brings fresh teaching techniques and competitor insight, and keeps the digital booking platform's 6-day promise intact. --- STEM ---
Brightpath Home Tutors (BHT) is a private limited company in the education services sector, delivering one-to-one home and online tutoring and employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2015 by Dr Nadia Rahman, the business operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. It has fixed costs of $70,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.50 a unit and a selling price of $22.50 a unit, and currently produces 12,500 units a year, measured in one-to-one sessions.   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BHT plans to finance part of its virtual classroom platform with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for BHT of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs BHT nothing in interest or repayments at a time when the base rate has just risen from 4.50% to 5.25%, lifting the cost of any variable-rate borrowing. It protects cash flow against a backdrop of weak household education spending growth of only 3.1%, and lets BHT fund about 42% of the $240,000 platform investment ($100,000) without committing future tuition income to a lender.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps full ownership and control with Dr Nadia Rahman and existing shareholders, with no bank covenants restricting how BHT prices STEM coaching or hires tutors. It avoids interest charges against an already thin 12.0% operating margin, preserves loan capacity for contingencies, and signals financial health to parents and exam boards — a significant trust factor for a home-tutoring business entering online one-to-one tuition, where 66% of surveyed parents already want to move.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $100,000, $140,000, $240,000, $70,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Brightpath Home Tutors and its platform expansion decision.

Results build within weeks and costs are controllable, though success depends on consistent content quality and credible tutor profiles.

Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a regional tutoring business; school events are rejected as too slow for a platform launch, though BHT should keep them as a secondary channel to deepen local trust after launch.

--- STEM ---
Hartwell Community Pharmacy (HCP) is a private limited company in the healthcare retail sector, dispensing prescriptions and delivering medicines to local care homes across the city, and employing a workforce of 27. Founded in 2008 by Margaret Ellison, the business operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HCP plans to invest $450,000 in an automated dispensing robot and a home-delivery hub, financed by a $250,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $168,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 34,000 units a year, measured in items dispensed. HCP faces stubbornly high dispensing errors and lengthy customer-waiting times at its counter.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HCP plans to finance part of its dispensing robot with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for HCP of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs HCP nothing in interest or repayments at a time when the base rate has risen from 4.75% to 5.5%, making new variable-rate borrowing markedly dearer. It protects cash flow against the 10.5% rise in wholesale medicine prices, which is already straining working capital, and avoids committing the pharmacy's steady but regulated prescription income to a lender.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership and control with Margaret Ellison and existing shareholders, with no bank covenants over stock levels, margins or the home-delivery hub. It avoids interest on top of fixed costs already standing at $168,000 a year, preserves loan capacity for future regulatory or equipment changes, and signals to the local community and care-home partners that HCP is a financially resilient independent — valuable reputation capital for winning delivery contracts.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $200,000, $250,000, $450,000, $168,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Hartwell Community Pharmacy and its dispensing expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HCP is launching its new home-delivery service for medicines. Consider local radio sponsorship, community health-fair sponsorship, or a social media campaign. Which should HCP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local radio sponsorship: Local radio would reach a broad cross-section of HCP's catchment — commuters, retired listeners and care staff — repeatedly and cheaply. It suits reminder-style messages such as the 73% who want a repeat-prescription reminder service. However, airtime is untargeted, half the audience will never order a delivery, and younger decision-makers who arrange care for elderly relatives are poorly reached by local AM/FM formats.

Community health-fair sponsorship: Health fairs put HCP directly in front of exactly the people the home-delivery service serves — elderly patients, unpaid carers, care-home managers and GP surgery staff. Trust transfers from the event to the pharmacy, demonstrations of the delivery process reassure nervous patients, and partnerships with care homes can produce bulk contracts. The weakness is limited scale: one event per month touches only a few hundred people.

Social media campaign: A targeted campaign reaches the adult children and carers who usually arrange medicines for elderly relatives, pushes the home-delivery message to thousands, and drives measurable sign-ups at low cost. However, HCP's core patients are older and less active on social platforms, so conversion relies on family intermediaries and creative execution.

Recommendation: HCP should choose community health-fair sponsorship. It reaches the highest-intent audience with the greatest trust, directly previewing the service for care-home decision-makers and the 61% of customers who said they would use home delivery. Local radio is rejected as too broad and weakly targeted for a niche service; social media alone is rejected as a primary channel because HCP's end users are older and sceptical online, though a small paid campaign aimed at carers should support the fairs.

On-the-job coaching is rejected as the sole solution, though it remains essential afterwards for the final clinical safety check on every robot-prepared prescription.

Clearview Optometry & Eyewear (CVO) is a private limited company in the healthcare retail sector, providing sight tests and designer eyewear from one flagship store, and employing a workforce of 41. CVO avoids committing its consultation income to a lender, keeps cash for fit-out and stock at the second branch, and pays dividends only if profits allow — a flexible cost of capital while the boutique ramps up.

Point 2: Because existing shareholders subscribe, ownership and control stay within the founding Whitmore family and loyal existing shareholders, with no outsider board seats or lender covenants dictating how the retinal-scanning suite is used. There is no repossession risk over the flagship store or diagnostics kit, the issue signals confidence to staff and suppliers, and it preserves bank loan capacity for contingencies — strengthening the case for a $780,000 organic expansion without bank dependence.

--- STEM ---
Greywater Slate Quarry (GSQ) is a private limited company in the primary extraction and construction-materials sector, quarrying and dressing roofing slate for builders, roofers and heritage restoration contractors. Founded in 2013 by Mared Llewelyn, it employs a workforce of 46 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. GSQ plans to invest $700,000 in a diamond-wire sawing and computerised sorting line to cut waste and lift output, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.10 a unit and a selling price of $9.60, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. Its cutting-section defect rate has reached 6.3%, sending valuable slate to low-value aggregate.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GSQ plans to finance part of its diamond-wire sawing and computerised sorting line with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for GSQ of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs GSQ no interest or arrangement fees, protecting cash at a time when fixed costs already run at $225,000 a year. The central bank has raised its base rate from 4.5% to 5.0%, so every variable-rate dollar borrowed becomes more expensive; funding $250,000 internally avoids that exposure, preserves the $5.10 variable-cost cushion on 75,000 units, and avoids weakening the $9.60 selling price that roofers and heritage contractors currently accept for certified matched-size slate. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 8.6% rise in diesel, blasting and haulage costs without cutting the 57% of contractors who would pay a 6% premium.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps full ownership and control with Mared Llewelyn and the existing shareholders. No lender can impose covenants on how the sawing line is operated, on staffing levels across the flat democratic structure, or on future investment; GSQ can time installation around the 3.8% growth in public-building repair spending. It also avoids collateral risk against the $700,000 plant itself, which could be repossessed under the bank loan if 6.3% defect rates persisted and heritage orders slipped past the expected monthly delivery guarantee.

Quality of finance: Using $250,000 retained profit for part of the $700,000 line means the bank loan covers only $450,000, keeping repayments well inside the cash flow generated at the current 75,000 units of output and matched against the premium-pricing upside identified in the market research.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $250,000, $450,000, diamond-wire, $225,000, 5.0%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Greywater Slate Quarry and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GSQ is marketing its certified matched-size roofing slate to roofers and heritage contractors. Consider architectural magazine print advertising, roofing-trade exhibitions, or targeted email marketing to contractors. Which should GSQ choose to promote the slate? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Architectural magazine print advertising: Advertising in the magazines read by architects and heritage specifiers gives GSQ credible exposure to the people who write slate into restoration and new-build specifications. Print suits a high-value, durable product: colour photography of the new sawing line, certified matched-size slate and its chain-of-custody paperwork can be shown in detail, and the 57% of surveyed contractors willing to pay a 6% premium for matched-size slate are precisely the type to notice certificates. Drawbacks: response is slow, readership among younger specifiers is falling, and GSQ cannot easily prove who enquired after the advertisement appeared.

Roofing-trade exhibitions: Exhibiting at roofing and heritage shows puts GSQ face-to-face with the 350 roofing contractors and architects surveyed, lets buyers handle matched-size samples, and builds relationships where the 68% who rank guaranteed monthly deliveries as decisive can be reassured about the new computerised sorting line. However, stands, travel and sample freight are expensive, there are only a few shows a year, and most visitors are unrelated or browsing — cost per qualified lead is high for a 46-employee private company financing a $450,000 bank loan.

Targeted email marketing: A direct email campaign to the 350-contractor and architect mailbox lists costs little, can carry data sheets, delivery calendars and the matched-size certification, and produces measurable open, reply and quote-request rates tied to the 4 days order fulfilment promise. It demands clean data and regular, readable content, risks being ignored as spam, and cannot replace the tactile proof of slate samples.

Recommendation: GSQ should choose targeted email marketing, supported by sample-box mailings to the highest-value heritage specifiers identified in the research. It is the cheapest option per qualified lead, directly reaches the exact buyers identified in its market research, is measurable in a way print is not, and fits a 46-employee quarrier financing a bank-loan expansion better than the high-cost, infrequent exhibition circuit. Magazine print advertising is rejected as slow, falling in reach and impossible to tie to quote requests; roofing-trade exhibitions are rejected as too costly and too episodic to sustain order momentum. Email alone also cannot close large heritage contracts, so GSQ should reserve a small exhibition budget only for one flagship show per year.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GSQ's cutting-section defect rate has reached 6.3%. Explain two benefits for GSQ of using democratic leadership to motivate its quarry and dressing crews.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Fourteen of GSQ's 46 staff lack diamond-wire saw refresher certification. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at $780 per employee. Which should GSQ choose? Justify your decision.

It removes staff from bad habits and provides the certificate GSQ's insurers and heritage clients want; however, it takes 14 people off production, the generic syllabus may not match GSQ's specific grading gauges, and travel plus backfill cover adds hidden cost during the busiest dispatch weeks.

Decision: GSQ should choose on-the-job training, supplemented by one external safety audit day for the whole saw crew. On-the-job training costs nothing in fees, keeps dressing output stable while the new sorting line beds in, and passes on machine-specific fault detection faster than a generic college syllabus; the single external audit day satisfies insurers without the $10,920 fee. Full off-the-job training is rejected because pulling 14 of 46 staff off the wire saws for a college week during peak heritage-order season would jeopardise the 68% of customers who rank guaranteed monthly deliveries as decisive, and the certificate alone does not fix the thickness faults causing the 6.3% reject rate — those are corrected at the machine, not in a classroom.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.0%): If GSQ's $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, a 0.5 percentage-point rise adds about $2,250 a year of interest — modest against fixed costs of $225,000 — though it also discourages new construction borrowing and could slow the 3.8% growth in public-building repair spending that drives roofing-slate demand. Minimum wage increase (5.5% to $12.10): Quarry dressing is labour-intensive. Democratic leadership and the new sorting line should absorb part of this through fewer rejections and rehandling, but the cash hit is material.

Input-cost inflation (8.6% diesel, blasting and haulage): Fuel, explosives and haulage sit inside the $5.10 variable cost of every unit GSQ produces. Even if they represent about 45% of that cost (≈ $2.30), an 8.6% rise adds about $0.20 per unit, or roughly $14,900 a year on 75,000 units, compounding with the 6.3% defect rate that already forces expensive reprocessing.

Conclusion: The 5.5% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest-rate rise (about $2,250 a year and fixable through the loan terms) and the fuel increase (roughly $14,900 a year, partly recoverable through the 6% matched-size premium), the wage bill lands directly on GSQ's core dressing workforce — its scarcest resource — adding nearly $38,000–$40,000 a year before any productivity offset, and squeezing the $5.10 variable-cost cushion from day one. GSQ must raise dressing-crew productivity through the new sorting line, renegotiate merchant price lists to pass on part of the increase, and prioritise hiring retentions over expansion until the margin recovers.

--- STEM ---
Caldbeck Lime Works (CLW) is a partnership in the eco-materials and construction-materials sector, burning high-calcium lime for conservation mortars, plasters and limewash used by restoration contractors. Founded in 2009 by Harriet and Joe Callis, it employs a workforce of 33 and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership that trusts its experienced kiln burners. CLW plans to invest $520,000 in a new kiln with waste-heat recovery to cut fuel use and emissions, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $168,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.40 a unit and a selling price of $14.40, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. Its kiln batch defect rate has reached 4.7%, wasting fuel and forcing expensive reburning.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CLW plans to finance part of its waste-heat recovery kiln with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CLW of using retained profit to fund the kiln instead of the bank loan.

The central bank has raised its base rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, so variable-rate borrowing keeps getting more expensive; funding $200,000 internally avoids that exposure and preserves the $8.40 variable-cost cushion on 40,000 units of lime. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices without weakening the $14.40 selling price that conservation contractors accept for certified high-calcium lime.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps full ownership and control with Harriet and Joe Callis as the two partners. No lender can impose covenants on kiln scheduling, staffing across the flat laissez-faire structure, or how the new kiln is commissioned. It also avoids collateral risk against the kiln itself if the 4.7% batch defect rate persisted and reburning kept consuming an extra 61 tonnes of gas, and it avoids diluting the partnership's simple structure — no share issue, no community investors, no outside shareholder expectations for dividends if a quarter's profits are retained to weather fuel-price volatility.

Quality of finance: Using $200,000 retained profit for part of the $520,000 package means the bank loan covers only $320,000, keeping annual repayments well within the cash generated at 40,000 units of output and matched against the 5% premium the 62% of surveyed contractors already signal.

Capital employed grew from $2,800,000 to $3,520,000 as the kiln project was funded, and interest payable rose from $140,000 to $165,000.

Evaluation: Performance strengthened across every measure. Caution is warranted: capital employed grew by $720,000, reburning still consumed an extra 61 tonnes of gas, and interest payable rose to $165,000 alongside the $320,000 loan — so any slip in the 4.7% defect rate would compress returns quickly in a year of 14.9% gas inflation.

Trading margins and returns on the capital base all moved favourably, and the improvement is rooted in genuine premium pricing and waste reduction rather than accounting effects.   Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CLW of adopting the waste-heat recovery kiln to produce lower-carbon lime.
    Answer: Advantage: Waste-heat recovery recaptures exhaust heat to pre-dry and pre-heat incoming limestone, cutting the fuel burned per unit of lime and directly reducing exposure to the 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices. It also cuts CLW's emissions per unit, letting the partners claim verified lower-carbon lime — a claim the 62% of surveyed contractors willing to pay a 5% premium for certified product would value, and one that strengthens chain-of-custody paperwork demanded by heritage bodies specifying for listed buildings.

During installation, average order fulfilment slips beyond the current 6 days, jeopardising the 54% of contractors who rank consistent supply as decisive and risking contract penalties on scheduled restoration scaffolding. If the heat-recovery system underperforms, fuel savings may be lower than modelled, squeezing the $8.40 variable cost exactly when gas prices have risen 14.9%.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices and the 1.5% minimum wage increase will affect CLW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): If CLW's $320,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.5 percentage-point rise adds about $1,600 a year of interest — modest against fixed costs of $168,000. Higher rates also cool construction lending, which could slow the wider restoration pipeline that drives demand for conservation lime, and raise the cost of refinancing when the loan is renewed. CLW can fix or hedge; the direct cash impact is small.

Minimum wage increase (1.5% to $11.70): With 33 staff, mainly kiln burners, loader drivers and mill crew, a 1.5% rise adds roughly $11,400 a year if all staff earn near the current rate (33 × $23,050 × 1.5% ≈ $11,400) — meaningful but absorbable through batch discipline gains and the 5% certified premium. It ranks behind the fuel problem in urgency.

Industrial gas price rise (14.9%): The kiln is CLW's biggest cost engine. Gas already forced reburning of an extra 61 tonnes last quarter at a 4.7% defect rate. If fuel is roughly 30% of the $8.40 variable cost (≈ $2.52), a 14.9% rise adds about $0.38 per unit — roughly $15,100 a year on 40,000 units, before any reburning multiplier on faulty batches. Unlike wages and interest, this cost scales with every unit produced and cannot be renegotiated away without the waste-heat recovery kiln.

Conclusion: The 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices will have the greatest impact. It is the largest percentage increase on CLW's biggest production cost, it compounds with the 4.7% defect rate into reburning waste, and it applies to every one of the 40,000 units sold — totalling roughly $15,000 a year before reburning, several times the interest-rate impact ($1,600) and comfortably above the 1.5% wage rise (around $11,400). CLW must commission the waste-heat recovery kiln quickly, lock fuel contracts with suppliers, and pass part of the increase into the certified 5% premium before taking on new restoration orders.

--- STEM ---
Montagu Cork Flooring Co-operative (MCFC) is a cooperative in the eco-materials and construction-materials sector, laminating cork-bark granules into floating floor tiles and acoustic underlay for low-energy housing. Founded in 2016 by 21 members led by general manager Rosa Inglis, it employs a workforce of 29 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic, member-elected leadership. MCFC plans to invest $480,000 in an automated lamination and edge-sealing press, financed by a $280,000 bank loan and a $200,000 community share issue. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. Its offcut dust contamination rate has reached 5.8%, wasting premium cork and slowing lines.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MCFC plans to finance part of its lamination and edge-sealing press with a community share issue. Explain two advantages for MCFC of using a community share issue to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A community share issue spreads ownership across the 21 founding members and local supporters instead of concentrating risk with one lender, which fits the co-operative constitution and means the $200,000 raised typically carries no fixed repayment schedule or collateral call on the press itself. With the base rate raised to 5.25%, every variable-rate dollar of the alternative $280,000 bank loan adds interest MCFC cannot pass on easily; community shares instead carry flexible, patient capital that members understand and rarely rush.

Point 2: Member investors are customers too — likely builders, homeowners and housing co-ops — so the issue strengthens the local market for certified renewable-bark flooring exactly where the 64% of surveyed buyers willing to pay a 7% premium live. They campaign for MCFC, recommend it in community groups, and stay patient on returns. It also avoids the bank's covenants over the flat democratic structure, preserving member control of pressing schedules, hires and the eco-housing tender pipeline rather than subordinating the co-op to lender conditions.

Quality of finance: Using a $200,000 community issue for part of the $480,000 package means the bank loan covers only $280,000, keeping annual repayments within cash flow at 45,000 units of output and matched against the 7% premium opportunity.

--- STEM ---
Vulcan Structural Steel (VSS) is a public limited company in the construction-materials and fabrication sector, cutting, drilling and welding structural steel portal frames for commercial buildings and stadiums. Founded in 1998 by engineers Marcus and Lena Vale, it employs a workforce of 120 and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. VSS plans to invest $1,500,000 in a computer-controlled plasma-cutting and robotic welding cell, financed by a $900,000 bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $840,000 a year, a variable cost of $28.50 a unit and a selling price of $38.50, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. Its weld defect rate has reached 3.1%, causing rework and delivery delays for major contractors.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VSS plans to finance part of its plasma-cutting and robotic welding cell with a share issue. Explain two advantages for VSS of using a share issue to fund the cell instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital with no repayment schedule and no interest. VSS has already committed to a $900,000 bank loan, the central bank has just pushed its base rate to 5.25%, and interest payable reached $420,000 last year. Financing the $600,000 balance with shares instead of a larger loan keeps annual debt service fixed, protects the cash buffer against the 10.2% steel-price shock, and removes any risk that the lender calls in collateral — the $1,500,000 cell — if welding defects of 3.1% delay the contractor payments it was bought to win.

Point 2: Share capital is permanent and uninsured in maturity — it never falls due for repayment, unlike the ten-year loan tenor staring down the income statement. That lets VSS plan for the slow ramp of the plasma-cutting cell and the robotic line, build the 9 certified robotic-welding leads, absorb the $38,000 bridge-beam rework without covenant stress, and fund further certification without scrambling for overdraft headroom. Dividends remain discretionary, so in a weak quarter VSS can retain cash for loan paydown instead of being forced to service fixed interest.

Quality of finance: Using the $600,000 share issue for part of the $1,500,000 cell means the $900,000 bank loan remains a fixed, knowable liability — permanent capital now covers the long-life half of the asset while the loan funds the quick-returning half.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $600,000, $900,000, $1,500,000, 3.1%, 5.25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Vulcan Structural Steel and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VSS is promoting its certified zero-defect structural steel to commercial contractors. Consider construction awards sponsorship, trade journal case-study advertising, or targeted LinkedIn marketing. Which should VSS choose to promote the steel? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Construction awards sponsorship: Sponsoring a regional construction or engineering awards dinner buys gala-night visibility, trophy-table networking with chief estimators and developers, and halo credibility when VSS wins or sponsors the zero-defect prize. Drawbacks: costs are high (table, branding, tickets) relative to a 120-person fabricator mid-investment; the audience is hundreds, not the thousands of contractors who specify steel nationwide; and attribution back to qualified quote requests is almost impossible to prove.

Trade journal case-study advertising: Detailed case studies in fabricated-metals and construction trade journals carry technical weight with the 280 contractors surveyed — showing how the plasma-cutting and robotic welding cell delivered two bridge beams, zero rework and 7 days fulfilment — and suits buyers who research before tendering. Drawbacks: print readership is shrinking, lead times are long, copy cannot be tested or rotated quickly, and the format reaches only existing journal subscribers rather than the full contractor market.

Targeted LinkedIn marketing: LinkedIn allows VSS to target by job title and company — procurement managers, project directors and chief estimators at the exact contractors surveyed — with short project-completion videos, weld-quality metrics and certified zero-defect certificates, then measure every click, connection and quote request. Cost per qualified enquiry is low, creative can be rotated weekly, and the 69% premium-acceptors can be re-targeted with the 3% premium justification. Drawbacks: it demands consistent content, sales follow-through and is powerless against buyers who ignore social media entirely.

Recommendation: VSS should choose targeted LinkedIn marketing. Trade journal case studies are rejected as too slow and too quiet to shift a 120-person order book; construction awards sponsorship is rejected as costly, unmeasurable and too narrow in reach for a national fabrication launch. VSS should keep a modest case-study placement inside one journal issue per quarter to reinforce the LinkedIn story rather than replace it.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VSS's weld defect rate has reached 3.1%. Explain two benefits for VSS of its hierarchical structure with a clear chain of command for meeting contractor deadlines.
    Answer: Point 1: A hierarchical structure with a clear chain of command lets VSS route every weld-defect decision — rework authorisation, beam release, or hold-point inspection — upward in minutes instead of hours, which is decisive when on-time delivery is the decisive factor for 57% of the 280 contractors surveyed.     Question: Nine of VSS's 120 staff hold robotic-welding tickets. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at $1,100 per employee. Which should VSS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training 111 uncertified staff at the cell keeps them producing bridge beams and portal frames while they learn VSS's own machine paths and weld schedules at no course-fee cost, and pairs them with the 9 ticketed veterans for supervised practice. Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $1,100 per employee gives robotic-welding certification covering procedure qualification records, parameter verification and non-destructive testing awareness, costing $122,100 for all 111 staff — or $9,900 for just the 9 leads initially, focused spending against a $1,500,000 cell investment. Drawbacks: weeks away from the cutting cell, generic syllabus vs VSS's specific jigs and beams, and backfill cost during peak tender season.

Decision: VSS should choose off-the-job training for the 9 robotic-cell leads first, with on-the-job mentoring for the remaining staff built around those certificates. Certified leads satisfy contractors' audits immediately, anchor the quality system the 3% premium depends on, and can then train the rest internally against recognised procedure-qualification records. Full on-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because it produces no certification for the auditors of the 280 contractors surveyed, and certification is the precondition of VSS's zero-defect marketing claim — without it, neither the premium nor the tender pipeline is real. The contained $9,900 lead-programme cost makes the decision easy to defend to the board.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $1,100, robotic-welding, 69%, 3.1%

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VSS of introducing a scrap-steel recycling loop inside its new robotic welding cell.

Disadvantage: Scrap handling needs dedicated skip space, segregation discipline and transport slots, raising fixed costs above $840,000 and adding admin for a 120-person hierarchy whose supervisory layers already slow decisions. The wage increase (≈ $82,000) ranks second and needs productivity offset from the new cell; the interest-rate rise (≈ $4,500) is trivial by comparison. VSS must negotiate mill contracts in bulk, qualify a second scrap source, enforce the certification programme to cut rework, and pass the smallest viable increase into contract price lists before taking on further infrastructure tenders.

--- STEM ---
Bower Formwork Systems (BFS) is a sole trader in the construction-materials and building-services sector, manufacturing reusable steel formwork panels and support props for concrete contractors and formwork hire firms. Founded in 2018 by Rosa Bower, it employs a workforce of 21 and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. BFS plans to invest $240,000 in a CNC press-brake and robotic welding bay to cut panel distortion, financed by a $150,000 hire purchase agreement and $90,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $160,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.50 a unit and a selling price of $15.50, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. Absenteeism in the fabrication workshop has reached 6%, stretching delivery deadlines on fixed-price contracts.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BFS plans to finance part of its CNC press-brake and robotic welding bay with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for BFS of using retained profit to fund the bay instead of hire purchase.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit buys the press-brake outright, so BFS owns it from day one and never faces hire-purchase interest or arrangement fees. A $150,000 hire purchase agreement typically adds thousands of dollars in charges over its life and, crucially, the HP company retains legal ownership until the final instalment — if BFS missed payments during a slow quarter, the machine would be repossessed and the fabrication workshop, and its delivery of 10,000 units a quarter, would stop immediately.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps Rosa Bower completely free to modify, resell or relocate the CNC asset — no HP restrictions on usage, no mileage-style conditions on operation hours, and no consent needed for a spindle upgrade at $2,800. It also keeps the workshop's credit lines clean: a young sole trader with fixed-price contracts cannot afford to have finance houses rejecting a materials overdraft application because HP instalments are consuming the headroom.

Quality of finance: Using $90,000 retained profit for part of the $240,000 bay means the hire purchase agreement underwrites only $150,000, trimming total interest charges and keeping ownership risk minimal while the machine pays for itself through certified 500-use panel demand.
    Keywords: retained profit, hire purchase, $90,000, $150,000, $240,000, CNC press-brake, 5.5%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bower Formwork Systems and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BFS is promoting its certified 500-use formwork panels to concrete contractors. Consider design-build expo sponsorship, a referral and reward scheme for contractors, or industry magazine print advertising. Which should BFS choose to promote the panels? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Design-build expo sponsorship: A regional expo puts BFS's panels, props and walers in front of commercial contractors and formwork hire firms in one weekend, with live bend-quality demonstrations on a CNC-accurate sample rack. It suits the 61% of the 300 surveyed contractors who rank local lead time as decisive, and builds face-to-face relationships. Drawbacks: one-off events, costs of a branded stand and demo material, and limited reach beyond one city — the strongest leads still need months of follow-up quoting.

Referral and reward scheme: A structured scheme paying existing contractors a reward for every qualified referral turned into a panel order converts BFS's strongest asset — its on-time, complaint-free delivery record — into a marketing channel. Contractors trust peer recommendations, the cost is paid only on results, and the 58% willing to pay a 5% premium for certified 500-use panels can be rewarded in material credit. Drawbacks: rewards must be funded, tracking referrals honestly takes admin discipline, and rewards can be abused if loosely policed.

Industry magazine print advertising: Print in construction magazines reaches quantity surveyors and project managers who specify formwork, and suits a considered, specification-led purchase. Drawbacks: slow response, shrinking readership among younger buyers, and no guarantee the phone rings — measuring return is nearly impossible for a sole trader spending $240,000 capital on new equipment.

Recommendation: BFS should choose the referral and reward scheme. It converts existing customer trust into measurable, low-cost orders at a moment when BFS's HP instalments already squeeze cash; cost is payable only on signed business; and it reinforces the 5 days lead-time advantage that 61% of contractors rank decisive. The design-build expo is rejected as a single weekend spike with weak follow-through; magazine print advertising is rejected as passive, slow and unmeasurable for a 21-person sole trader. BFS can revisit expo sponsorship later, funded from scheme-generated margin.
    Keywords: formwork panels, 58%, 61%, 300, 500-use, $240,000, 5 days

    Question: BFS's absenteeism in the cutting bay has reached 6%. Explain two benefits for BFS of its flat organisational structure for communicating with its fabrication crew.

Problems surface in minutes, not through a chain of supervisors: a worker struggling with a CNC programme or a difficult bend pattern gets an immediate answer, morale rises because people feel heard, and absenteeism of 6% can be discussed face-to-face — shift root causes (fatigue, machine faults, transport) rather than guessed at.

Point 2: Flat communication cuts distortion between what the workshop decides and what actually happens. When the new press-brake arrives, Bower can brief all 21 staff herself, demo the bend quality targets and the 500-use certification goal in one sitting, and collect instant feedback on guarding and workflow. Fewer layers also mean fewer meetings, faster decisions and lower overhead — vital for a sole trader holding fixed costs at $160,000 a year while maximising margin on 40,000 units.

--- STEM ---
Valle Dorado Olive Oil (VDO) is a private limited company in the olive oil production and bottling sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2007 by Catalina Reyes, the business presses and bottles single-estate extra virgin olive oil for supermarket supply across three export markets and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VDO plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated bottling and filtration line with eco-friendly glass packaging, financed by a $650,000 share issue and $550,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.20 a unit and a selling price of $14.60, and currently produces 95,000 units a year. VDO faces two problems: quality complaints about sediment in unfiltered bottles have reached 26 per month, and its warehouse has reported rising spillage waste.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VDO plans to fund part of its bottling-line expansion with a $650,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for VDO of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs VDO nothing in interest or dividend payments, protecting cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $288,000 a year and is committing $1,200,000 to the automated bottling and filtration line. Every dollar not paid to new shareholders stays inside the company to absorb the 9.8% rise in olive harvest and bottle-glass costs, so VDO can hold its $14.60 selling price instead of raising it for supermarket customers.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids issuing new shares, so Catalina Reyes keeps full ownership and control of VDO and no external shareholder can influence how the automated line is run or demand higher dividends. It also signals financial strength to supermarkets considering the three export contracts, and preserves the $650,000 share issue as a standby funding source if the filtration unit costs overrun or the spillage waste problem proves more expensive to fix than budgeted, and it avoids revealing commercial terms to new shareholders while VDO is still negotiating its third export market.
    Keywords: retained profit, share issue, $650,000, $550,000, $1,200,000, single-estate, $288,000, filtration unit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Valle Dorado Olive Oil and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VDO is launching its certified single-estate range to supermarket shoppers. Consider a national television campaign, food-magazine advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VDO choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A national TV slot would reach millions of viewers quickly and give the new single-estate range mass brand awareness across all three export markets. However, production and airtime costs would absorb a large share of the $1,200,000 expansion budget, and much of the audience buys value vegetable oil rather than premium extra virgin products, so wastage would be very high for a 64-employee business financing the line through a share issue and retained profit.

Food-magazine advertising: Specialist food and lifestyle magazines reach readers who actively seek premium cooking oils, and full-page features can explain single-estate origin and certification in depth, matching the 47% of 750 surveyed shoppers who check origin traceability. The drawbacks are narrow circulation, monthly frequency, and no direct way to show younger supermarket buyers the packaging story at the point of purchase, so awareness builds slowly against well-funded rival brands.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with cookery and family lifestyle influencers targets exactly the 58% of surveyed shoppers willing to pay up to $0.50 more for certified single-estate oil, delivers measurable engagement, and shows the eco-friendly glass packaging story directly to younger buyers with high video quality. Results depend on influencer credibility and are slower to compound than TV, and a share of spend is lost to follower fraud, but cost per genuinely interested shopper is far lower than television.

Recommendation: VDO should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise premium segment already proven in its research, costs a fraction of television, scales across all three export markets unlike local print editions, and reinforces the origin story that 47% of shoppers check. Television is rejected as unaffordable and wasteful for a $1,200,000 expansion funded partly by retained profit; food-magazine advertising is rejected as too narrow and slow to support a 95,000-unit national launch; influencers should be layered with in-store supermarket tastings to convert reach into sales.
    Keywords: single-estate, $1,200,000, 95,000, 58%, 47%, supermarket
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VDO with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VDO with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and food-magazine advertising are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VDO's quality complaints have reached 26 per month. Explain two benefits for VDO of using autocratic leadership to enforce consistent bottling standards in its production team.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets VDO's Catalina Reyes set exact bottling, filtration and sealing procedures and enforce them immediately, which is valuable when defect rates of 2.4% still produce 26 complaints a month. Clear instructions remove ambiguity on the line, so every operator follows the same sediment-removal standard, protecting the supermarket export contracts that the $1,200,000 automated line depends on.

The flat status commands also underline urgency to the 64 employees, and because the structure is hierarchical, supervisors can monitor compliance closely and report upward, giving VDO the tight control it needs while 18 staff still lack filtration training and the warehouse spillage waste keeps climbing. --- STEM ---
Bramblewick Free-Range Eggs (BRE) is a partnership between siblings Dan and Meg Bramble in the free-range egg farming and packing sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2013, the business runs two free-range laying units and a grading and packing shed supplying cafés, farm shops and independent grocers across the region, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. BRE plans to invest $600,000 in a second 12,000-bird free-range laying barn and upgraded packing shed, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $180,000 hire purchase for the grading machinery. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.70 a unit and a selling price of $9.50, and currently produces 105,000 units a year. BRE faces two problems: the rejection rate for cracked or blood-spot eggs has reached 6.5%, and labour turnover among weekend packers is rising.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BRE plans to fund the grading machinery with $180,000 hire purchase. Explain two advantages for BRE of hire purchase instead of funding the machinery entirely with the $420,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $180,000 cost of the grading machinery over fixed monthly instalments, so BRE keeps more of its $420,000 bank loan free for the laying barn, feed stores and wage costs during the expensive construction phase. The machinery secures its own finance, useful for a partnership whose combined borrowing is already stretched by the $600,000 expansion.

Point 2: Payments under hire purchase are matched to the useful life of the grading machinery, which is exactly how the asset generates revenue — graded boxes of 27,300 per quarter at a 6.5% rejection rate BRE badly needs to cut. BRE gets immediate use of the machine without a single large outflow, protects working capital while feed costs rise 11.6%, and gains ownership outright once the final instalment is paid, unlike an overdraft that could be called in at short notice; it also keeps the partners' personal credit untouched ahead of any future barn refinancing, and avoids pressure from the bank to shorten the $420,000 loan term once the new shed is trading.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $180,000, $420,000, $600,000, grading machinery, 27,300
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bramblewick Free-Range Eggs and its expansion decision.

    Answer: National television advertising: A national TV campaign would give BRE's free-range boxes instant mass awareness and could shift national attitudes toward free-range certification. However, production and airtime costs would consume a large part of the $600,000 expansion budget, and most viewers live outside BRE's delivery region, where cafés and farm shops cannot receive boxes; for a 35-employee partnership funded by a bank loan and hire purchase, the wasted reach would be unaffordable and unmeasurable.

Sponsorship of a regional food festival: A weekend festival stall with egg cookery demonstrations reaches exactly BRE's farm-shop and café customer base face to face, lets buyers taste egg dishes, and builds the personal relationships that independent grocers value; the 61% of 500 surveyed buyers willing to pay up to $0.30 more per box can be converted on the spot with samples and QR sign-ups for traceability. The drawback is very short exposure — one weekend a year — and no scale beyond the regional catchment, so sales lift fades quickly without follow-up.

Social media marketing aimed at local buyers: Targeted posts and short videos aimed at local cafés, farm shops and conscious consumers cost little, can showcase the 6.5%-to-4.9% quality drive, the QR-code traceability that 44% of buyers want, and the $0.30 price premium story, and they reach exactly the regional catchment BRE serves, with measurable clicks to an order form. Its weakness is that reach builds slowly and depends on consistent content, and some café owners still prefer print tasting notes over social feeds.

Recommendation: BRE should choose social media marketing aimed at local buyers. It is the only option that is low-cost, targeted to the exact regional customer base, aligned with the 61% premium-willing segment and the 44% wanting QR traceability, and measurable weekly; television is rejected as too costly and geographically wasteful for a regional supplier, and festival sponsorship is rejected as a one-weekend tactic with no lasting reach, though BRE should keep a single festival stall as a complement rather than the lead promotion.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BRE must cut the 6.5% rejection rate. Consider quality control (end-of-line inspection) or quality assurance (prevention built into the grading process). Which should BRE choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality control: End-of-line inspection means trained graders checking every box after packing and downgrading cracked or blood-spot eggs before dispatch. It is simple to introduce, needs no process redesign, and matches BRE's existing routine, so stale-complaint numbers can keep falling from the current 11 per month. Quality assurance: Quality assurance builds prevention into each stage — calibrated grading machines, on-the-job coaching for the 9 untrained staff at $320 each, gentler conveyors, tray audits at the feeder and egg-quality sampling at the laying barn. It costs more up front in training, machine settings and documentation time, but it attacks root causes, so rejections fall before eggs reach the box, waste and rework disappear, and café and farm-shop customers receive consistent graded product that protects the $9.50 price and the $0.30 certification premium that 61% of buyers would pay.

Decision: BRE should adopt quality assurance as its primary approach, keeping a light end-of-line quality control check as a safety net. Prevention is the only route to reversing the 6.5% rejection rate rather than merely containing it, it fits the democratic flat structure where staff propose fixes, and its up-front cost is repaid through less waste, fewer complaints than the peak of 24 per month and stronger certification credibility for the new barn. Quality control alone is rejected because it leaves root causes untouched, locks in avoidable waste on every box packed, and would force BRE to hire more weekend graders at rising wage rates instead of solving the problem once.
    Keywords: quality control, quality assurance, 6.5%, 4.9%, 27,300, $4.70

--- STEM ---
Stonebarrow Vineyard & Wine Co-operative (SBV) is a cooperative owned by 31 member grape-growing families in the wine production sector, employing a workforce of 58. Founded in 1994 and led by chairperson Tessa Vidal, the cooperative vinifies member grapes into single-vineyard still and sparkling wines sold to independent wine merchants and its cellar door, operating a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership among member growers. SBV plans to invest $950,000 in a temperature-controlled fermentation and barrel-maturation hall with an extended cellar door and online shop, financed by a $400,000 community share issue and $550,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.60 a unit and a selling price of $16.80, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. SBV faces two problems: labour turnover among casual harvest pickers reached 28% this season, and barrel-fault defect rates are rising.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SBV plans to fund the fermentation hall with $550,000 retained profit and a $400,000 community share issue. Explain two advantages for SBV of using retained profit instead of relying entirely on the community share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs SBV nothing in dividends, interest or issue administration, protecting the cash flow of a cooperative whose 31 member families already expect stable grape payments while it funds a $950,000 hall. Avoiding sole reliance on the community share issue reduces the risk that member appetite for shares falls short of the target, which would leave the fermentation hall underfunded or push SBV toward expensive unplanned borrowing from a bank that knows nothing of wine cycles — damaging member confidence in the cooperative model itself.

Point 2: Using retained profit first signals to members and wine merchants that SBV is financially disciplined and self-reliant, strengthening confidence in the single-vineyard expansion and in the 59% premium-willing segment identified in its research. It also preserves the $400,000 community share issue as a buffer for cost overruns on the temperature-controlled hall — significant because barrel-fault defects and 13.2% bottle-glass inflation could both squeeze the project's budget before the 2027 vintage, and because member appetites for further share calls would fade if the hall overran its cost.
    Keywords: retained profit, community share issue, $400,000, $550,000, $950,000, single-vineyard

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
