  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in bottle glass and cork costs will affect SBV. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): SBV's $950,000 expansion is funded by a $400,000 community share issue and $550,000 retained profit, not new variable-rate debt, so the direct hit is small — it applies mainly to any equipment finance and overdraft margins; a 0.75-point rise on modest borrowing adds at most a few thousand dollars a year. It could, however, temper consumer premium spending if households trade down from $16.80 bottles, and it raises the minimum return the board expects when it tests future purchases such as replacement barrels or the online shop build-out.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $14.38 per hour): SBV employs 58 staff plus casual harvest pickers on 34-hour weeks. A 6.9% rise adds roughly $1,900 per full-time worker and increases the cost of the proposed $0.40-per-tonne harvest bonus scheme; for the casual picker cohort the extra 34-week bill could reach tens of thousands of dollars across the season. Democratic member involvement helps absorb this through shared efficiency gains, but the wage floor now rises faster than the premium wine market is guaranteed to pass on, pressuring SBV's per-bottle economics on 120,000 units.

Input cost inflation (13.2% bottle glass and cork): Bottles and closures are a direct per-unit cost within the $9.60 variable cost. A 13.2% rise on glass and corks adds roughly $0.35–$0.50 per bottle — at 120,000 bottles that is about $42,000 to $60,000 a year, eroding the $7.20 contribution before any of the $1.20 single-vineyard premium is passed on, and arriving exactly as the barrel-maturation hall comes online and volumes rise.

Conclusion: The 13.2% rise in bottle glass and cork costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every bottle SBV fills — roughly $42,000 to $60,000 a year at 120,000 units — directly reducing the $7.20 contribution and colliding with a 13.2%-fuelled packaging budget for the hall launch; unlike the wage rise it cannot be offset by productivity, and unlike the interest rise it scales with every bottle sold. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious pressure and can be partly absorbed by the harvest-bonus retention saving on re-recruitment, while the interest-rate change is minor given SBV's equity-funded expansion; SBV should nevertheless lock in a bottle and cork supply contract or forward purchase before April 2027 to defend its margin.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 6.9%, 13.2%, $14.38, interest rate, $9.60

--- STEM ---
Goldensheaf Milling Company (GSM) is a public limited company in the flour milling and baking-mix sector, employing a workforce of 260. Founded in 1988 by Arthur Bellingham, GSM is led by chief executive Duncan Pryce and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and elected staff councils. The company plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new wholegrain flour and baking-mix production plant, financed by a $900,000 share issue and a $600,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.30 a unit and a selling price of $18.50, and currently produces 150,000 units a year. GSM faces two problems: spillage and dust waste is running at 4.8% of throughput, and the business faces a skills gap in certified mill operatives.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GSM plans to fund the wholegrain plant partly with a $900,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for GSM of using the share issue instead of increasing the $600,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $900,000 without creating any repayment obligation or interest charge, so GSM's fixed costs do not rise on top of the existing $540,000 a year. This protects the profit margin and cash flow of a public company whose $1,500,000 plant must also bear a rising interest-rate environment, and keeps headroom with the bank for working capital such as wheat purchases amid 10.7% input inflation.

Point 2: Equity finance spreads ownership risk and strengthens the Statement of Financial Position for future negotiations with wholesale bakery clients and ISO 22000 auditors, since capital employed rises without extra debt. Dividend payments can be varied or passed in a difficult year, unlike loan interest, giving GSM flexibility through wheat-price cycles; and the share issue deepens the public shareholder base, potentially raising GSM's profile before it supplies national baking-mix contracts — and keeping the balance sheet clean at exactly the moment auditors will scrutinise the expansion funding.
    Keywords: share issue, $900,000, $600,000, $1,500,000, wholegrain, $540,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Goldensheaf Milling Company and its expansion decision.

LinkedIn business-to-business campaign: Targeted LinkedIn adverts and Duncan Pryce's company-page content can reach bakery owners, production directors and procurement managers by job title, sector and region, showcase the 49% of buyers wanting ISO 22000 certification, link directly to a sample-request form, and deliver measurable click-through and cost-per-lead within weeks. It complements the trade exhibition's reach at a fraction of the cost, though it requires disciplined content and cannot replace human relationship-building with the largest national bakery accounts.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GSM faces a skills gap on its new wholegrain line. Consider training its existing workforce with external assessors or recruiting certified mill operatives externally. Which should GSM choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Training existing workforce with external assessors: Developing current staff costs $1,100 per employee with external assessors certifying competencies; for a cohort of, say, 20 operatives that is $22,000 — modest against $1,500,000. Internal candidates already know GSM's hygiene culture, the 25 kg bagging line, and the ISO 22000 audit environment, so disruption is minimal, morale rises, and the elected staff councils can help schedule around production of 36,500 bags a quarter. Drawbacks are that some current staff may lack aptitude for the more technical wholegrain process, training takes time away from shifts, and assessed competency is individual, so a failed assessment wastes part of the $22,000.

Recruiting certified mill operatives externally: External hires bring immediate certified competence, fresh techniques from other mills and machinery experience from day one, ideal when the wholegrain line starts up and the 4.8% waste problem cannot wait. However, certified operatives are scarce regionally, salaries command a premium, induction into GSM's culture and ISO standards takes weeks, and poaching risks resentment among long-serving staff passed over for certification, undermining the democratic staff-council compact that keeps turnover low.

Decision: GSM should train its existing workforce with external assessors as the primary route, supplemented by recruiting two or three certified operatives externally as line leads and mentors. Training builds a home-grown certified cohort, preserves morale and process knowledge, and costs far less; pure external recruitment is rejected because the scarce regional talent could idle the new line at launch, add salary inflation, and weaken the internal pipeline GSM needs for ISO 22000 recertification — while recruiting only internally is rejected too, because line leads accelerate everyone's competence and bring outside best practice to the 1.2% off-spec target immediately.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.7% rise in wheat costs will affect GSM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): GSM carries a $600,000 bank loan attached to the $1,500,000 plant; on a variable or repricing facility a 0.50-point rise adds roughly $3,000 a year in interest, modest against $540,000 fixed costs and $18.50 pricing. Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.17 per hour): GSM employs 260 staff; if most earn near the current $13.32 minimum, a 6.4% rise adds roughly $1,700 per worker, or about $440,000 a year across the full workforce — a major payroll pressure, though many mill operatives and engineers earn above minimum, so the true figure is somewhat lower. Wheat cost inflation (10.7% year-on-year): Wheat dominates the $11.30 variable cost. A 10.7% rise on the wheat component adds roughly $0.90–$1.10 per 25 kg bag; at 150,000 units that is about $135,000–$165,000 a year, cutting contribution from $7.20 toward $6.10–$6.30 before price rises, exactly as GSM launches flour off the new wholegrain plant and tries to hold $18.50 with a promised $0.75 premium for certified low-waste product.

Conclusion: The 10.7% rise in wheat costs will have the greatest impact. It is the largest single raw material cost, it compounds with every unit milled — roughly $135,000–$165,000 a year at current volumes and far more once the plant ramps — and it attacks the contribution margin that funds the $600,000 bank loan. The minimum-wage increase is the second-biggest pressure and can be mitigated through automation on the new line and through democratic staff councils raising labour productivity, while the interest-rate rise is the smallest in cash terms at a few thousand dollars and can be capped by fixing loan pricing; GSM should nevertheless hedge wheat purchases and renegotiate wholesale bakery contracts to pass through part of the cost before the April 2027 wage change compounds it.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.4%, 10.7%, $14.17, interest rate, $11.30
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GSM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GSM's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GSM with a well-justified judgement that wheat-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Amberline Honey Farm (AHF) is a sole trader in the raw honey production and bottling sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2015 by Jessamine Cole, the business harvests and bottles raw unfiltered honey from 480 managed hives, selling through farmers' markets and its online honey club, operating a flat structure with autocratic leadership. AHF plans to invest $450,000 in a solar-powered extraction and bottling shed to supply its online honey club, financed by a $270,000 personal savings injection and a $180,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.60 a unit and a selling price of $8.40, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. AHF faces two problems: absenteeism during the late-summer harvest has reached 11%, and complaints about leaking caps are rising.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AHF plans to fund the new solar-powered extraction and bottling shed with $270,000 personal savings and a $180,000 overdraft. Explain two advantages for AHF of using personal savings instead of relying on the overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: Personal savings carry no interest charge, whereas the $180,000 overdraft would accrue interest from day one — and with the base interest rate now at 5.0%, overdraft costs are rising across the board. Every dollar saved on interest protects AHF's $4.80 contribution per unit and keeps the $450,000 expansion affordable for a sole trader whose entire livelihood rides on the harvest and the bottling shed paying for itself.

Point 2: Personal savings have no repayment deadline or withdrawal clause, unlike an overdraft that the bank can demand repaid or reduce at short notice — a serious risk while AHF's receivables have grown to $55,000 and its cash balance is only $38,000. Using $270,000 of savings keeps the overdraft undrawn for genuine emergencies such as a hive-collapse winter or a bottling-machine breakdown, and demonstrates to the bank that Jessamine Cole has committed her own funds, which strengthens any future negotiation for a longer-term loan to refinance the overdraft after March 2027.
    Keywords: personal savings, $270,000, $180,000, overdraft, $450,000, harvest
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Amberline Honey Farm and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AHF is launching its raw unfiltered local honey through new channels. Consider expanding farmers' market stalls, the online honey club subscription, or supermarket in-store tastings. Which should AHF choose to grow sales? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Expanding farmers' market stalls: Farmers' market stalls suit raw honey's artisan image, let Jessamine meet the 63% of 400 surveyed buyers willing to pay $0.60 more, and generate impulse purchases from Saturday shoppers. Each stall, however, costs pitch fees, transport and — critically — staff time: with harvest absenteeism at 11% and three helpers gone since May, AHF cannot reliably staff three more weekend stalls, and sales are weather-dependent and capped by stall-day traffic rather than the 80,000-unit annual output AHF wants to sell.

Online honey club subscription: The honey club converts the 46% of surveyed buyers who said they would subscribe to a monthly club into recurring, predictable revenue with no pitch fees, and boxes can ship direct at a 2.9-day fulfilment time with the flat structure autocratically managed for tight dispatch. Subscriptions smooth seasonality between harvests, build a first-party customer list for new varietals, and fit the $450,000 shed's role as an online-fulfilment hub; the risks are packaging and postage costs, subscription fatigue, and needing reliable dispatch staffing during harvest.

Supermarket in-store tastings: Tastings in national supermarkets would put raw honey in front of mass shoppers and could win permanent listings that absorb large volumes fast — attractive given 80,000 units of capacity. However, supermarkets demand margins, slotting fees, strict delivery windows and often private-label pricing that conflicts with raw unfiltered premium positioning, and they would squeeze the $8.40 price and $4.80 contribution; AHF would also compete on shelf with mass honey brands capitalised for national advertising, which a 16-person sole trader cannot match.

Recommendation: AHF should choose the online honey club subscription. It aligns with the 46% subscription-willing segment and the 63% premium-willing buyers, creates recurring revenue that smooths the harvest cycle, costs far less than supermarket slotting fees or three extra staffed stalls, and fits the shed investment and the 2.9-day fulfilment operation; farmers' markets are rejected as the growth engine because absenteeism and helper losses make new stalls unstaffable and weather-dependent, and supermarket tastings are rejected because the listing margin and compliance burden would destroy the premium positioning and $4.80 contribution that fund the expansion.
    Keywords: online honey club, 46%, 63%, $0.60, $450,000, raw unfiltered
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the channel options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AHF with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AHF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why farmers' markets and supermarkets are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AHF's absenteeism during the late-summer harvest reached 11%. Explain two benefits for AHF of using non-financial motivators such as job rotation to improve attendance in its harvest team.
    Answer: Point 1: Job rotation between hive work and the bottling shed breaks up repetitive, hot, sting-risk tasks that cause harvest workers to skip shifts; alternating roles satisfies workers' variety and esteem needs (Maslow) and makes each role feel fairer, which lifts attendance during the critical six-week crush when every absent picker directly reduces jars bottled of the 80,000-unit annual target.

Point 2: Rotation builds a flexible team that can cover capping, filling and labelling when someone is ill, reducing the disruption that 11% absenteeism causes to the 2.9-day fulfilment promise made to online honey club members. Because AHF is autocratic and flat, job rotation also gives Jessamine Cole a low-cost way to show she trusts and values the 16 staff, lowering turnover among the part-time helpers she has struggled to keep since May, without raising wages she cannot yet afford against a $3.60 variable cost. It also gives permanent staff a structured way to pass on cap-seal and fulfilment know-how to new helpers, embedding the quality push into the team rather than into Jessamine alone.
    Keywords: absenteeism, 11%, job rotation, part-time, 80,000, flat structure
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AHF's absenteeism, workforce and fulfilment performance.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AHF is short of harvest hands. Consider paying overtime to the existing part-time team or recruiting two additional part-time harvest helpers. Which should AHF choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Paying overtime to the existing part-time team: Overtime rewards loyal part-time staff who already know the hives, the extraction room and the cap-seal standard, avoiding recruitment, induction and the $260 food-handler certification per new helper; it can start this weekend and directly covers the absentees. However, overtime pay usually runs at a premium, quickly breaching AHF's $144,000 fixed-cost base, tired workers make more cap-seal mistakes (cap-seal complaints already fell from 26 to only 14 per month), and pushing the same sixteen staff harder at harvest risks deepening the 11% absenteeism problem rather than curing it, since fatigue is often why staff stay away in August.

Recruiting two additional part-time harvest helpers: Two extra helpers spread the harvest load, cut overtime premiums, give AHF cover for the 11% absence rate, and fresh capacity supports the cap-seal quality push and the online club's fulfilment promise; at $260 each the certification cost is only $520 and they can be trained via the owner's autocratic supervision and job rotation alongside the core team. Disadvantages are that two unknown recruits may not stay — three helpers have left since May — and supervision, equipment and insurance costs rise, while inexperienced hands can slow the extraction room during the critical six weeks.

Decision: AHF should recruit the two additional part-time harvest helpers and reserve modest overtime for the peak fortnight only. Recruitment spreads the physical load, protects cap-seal quality, keeps the online honey club dispatching on time, and costs just $520 in certification plus wages, whereas overtime-only reliance would overload the tired core team, worsen the 11% absenteeism and cap quality precisely when the $450,000 shed is launching; pure recruitment without any overtime is rejected too, because one helper will inevitably fall ill during harvest and a small premium-rate safety valve keeps the line moving without permanent headcount growth.
    Keywords: overtime, part-time, 11%, $260, absenteeism, online honey club
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two staffing options with limited application to AHF. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of both options in the context of AHF's absenteeism and harvest workload. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of AHF with a well-justified decision covering cost, quality, fatigue and certification.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AHF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Which judgement do the figures support — has AHF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.47 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.94 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.68 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.16 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $75,000 inventories + $40,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $140,000; 2025 current assets = $62,000 + $55,000 + $38,000 = $155,000. Short-term coverage 2024 = $140,000 ÷ $95,000 = 1.47; 2025 = $155,000 ÷ $80,000 = 1.94. Quick coverage excluding inventories 2024 = ($140,000 − $75,000) ÷ $95,000 = $65,000 ÷ $95,000 = 0.68; 2025 = ($155,000 − $62,000) ÷ $80,000 = $93,000 ÷ $80,000 = 1.16.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved markedly. The coverage of immediate debts rose from 1.47 to 1.94, helped by current liabilities falling from $95,000 to $80,000 and cash rising to $38,000. The quick coverage improved from 0.68 to 1.16 — a move from dangerous reliance on selling honey to meet debts, to comfortable coverage without touching stock, which is vital while a $180,000 overdraft is partly funding the shed. However, receivables rose from $40,000 to $55,000, suggesting wholesale or club customers are paying later and tying up cash just as the overdraft lingers; and inventories fell from $75,000 to $62,000, an efficient cut but one to watch if the harvest underdelivers or online orders spike after the club launch. Relying on an overdraft at a 5.0% base rate remains the weakest part of the funding mix, and refinancing to a term loan post-expansion would strengthen the position further.

Conclusion: AHF's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.47 to 1.94) and the acid test ratio (0.68 to 1.16) show stronger short-term solvency without depending on inventory sales, and the improvement is backed by falling liabilities. The residual risks are the rising receivables and overdraft-funded expansion, so AHF should tighten club and wholesale payment terms, refinance the $180,000 overdraft into a secured loan once the shed is operational, and set a target to keep quick coverage above 1.0 through the April 2027 wage change.
    Keywords: 1.47, 1.94, 0.68, 1.16, $140,000, $155,000, $450,000

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for AHF of launching the online honey club subscription.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in sugar and bee-feed costs will affect AHF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): AHF funds the $450,000 shed partly through a $180,000 overdraft, so a 0.75-point rise adds roughly $1,350 a year in interest directly, and any refinanced overdraft will also price higher. The bigger risk is strategic: with only $38,000 cash and $55,000 receivables, AHF cannot afford prolonged reliance on expensive overdraft funding, so the rate rise accelerates the need to convert the overdraft to a fixed-rate term loan backed by Jessamine Cole's personal guarantee once the shed is operational. Cash impact is real but small relative to payroll.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.73 per hour): AHF employs 16 staff including a part-time harvest team already needing overtime rota cover. A 6.0% rise adds roughly $1,600 per full-time worker — across the 16-strong workforce, roughly $25,000 to $30,000 a year in extra wages including harvest overtime premiums. This lands directly on the thin $3.60 variable cost and the $144,000 fixed-cost base, and it coincides with the shed launch, when Jessamine needs harvest productivity most to meet online honey club dispatch slots; absenteeism at 11% could worsen if pay fails to keep pace with the April 2027 rate.

Input cost inflation (9.4% sugar and bee-feed): Bee feed is used to sustain weak colonies through dearth periods and winter, and sugar syrup supplements late-season flows; a 9.4% rise adds real but bounded cost — on an apiary budget plausibly $25,000 to $35,000 a year, roughly $2,400 to $3,300 extra — far smaller than payroll, though it compounds if weak hives increase after a poor season and coincides with food inflation of 7.4%, pressuring price points.

Conclusion: The 6.0% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It adds roughly $25,000 to $30,000 a year to AHF's payroll across 16 staff, it is unavoidable, it lands during the shed launch and honey club ramp-up, and it hits the same harvest team whose 11% absenteeism already strains output. The 9.4% bee-feed rise is the second most serious pressure but is bounded by scale and can be partly offset by reformulating feed and colony management; the interest-rate rise is the smallest at roughly $1,350 a year on the overdraft and can be eliminated by converting to a term loan — so AHF should reprice its subscription plan modestly, push for the $0.60 premium, and refinance the overdraft before April 2027.

--- STEM ---
Kingsbarrow Ceramics (KBC) is a private limited company in the technical ceramics sector, supplying high-voltage electrical insulators to national grid contractors, employing a workforce of 68. Founded in 2008 by Priya Raman, the business operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and is based in Gujarat, India. KBC plans to invest $1,150,000 in a new automated isostatic pressing line and high-efficiency electric kiln, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $450,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.50 a unit and a selling price of $18.50, and currently produces 75,000 units a year.   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KBC plans to finance part of its pressing-line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KBC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs KBC no interest charges or repayment obligations, protecting cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $700,000 ten-year bank loan commitment. Money not paid to a lender can be kept inside the business to absorb the 9.6% rise in alumina and feldspar input costs, helping KBC hold its $18.50 selling price against rival insulator suppliers while the new automated line beds in.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids the security and covenant requirements attached to a bank loan, so the $450,000 can be committed without putting the new $1,150,000 isostatic pressing line at risk of repossession if grid contractor demand softens. It also preserves Priya Raman's full ownership and control of the private limited company — no external lender can impose conditions on how the line is staffed, operated or expanded next — which suits a founder accustomed to directing the business single-handedly.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $450,000, $700,000, $1,150,000, $360,000

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KBC of switching its new kiln to renewable electric firing as part of the expansion.

A renewable-fired kiln would let KBC market verified low-carbon insulators to the 71% of procurement officers demanding type-tested certification and the 49% willing to pay a 4% premium, strengthening bids for grid framework contracts and reinforcing its positioning ahead of the 10,000-hour guaranteed range. Lower firing emissions also help KBC pre-qualify for tenders that now score suppliers on carbon intensity alongside unit price.

Disadvantage: Renewable electricity and grid connection upgrades typically carry higher upfront tariffs and installation costs than conventional fuel, which would strain the $1,150,000 budget and could push the effective variable cost above the $9.50 it uses today, squeezing the $9.00 contribution per unit unless the 4% premium is accepted across the range. Any shortfall in contracted renewable supply would also disrupt kiln scheduling, threatening the 94.2% on-time delivery record that KBC's contractors rely on during the commissioning year.
    Keywords: renewable, electric kiln, $1,150,000, 9.6%, 10,000-hour, 71%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KBC's research data, costs, expansion and delivery record.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in input costs will affect KBC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.00% to 5.75%): The 0.75 percentage point rise applies to $700,000 of KBC's variable-rate exposure if its ten-year bank loan is variable, adding 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250 a year in interest — small against fixed costs of $360,000 a year, and zero if the loan was fixed at signing. KBC is only partly geared in practice because $450,000 of the $1,150,000 expansion is retained profit. Higher base rates may also cool grid-contractor spending and make any future borrowing for a phase-two kiln more expensive, so KBC should fix rates or prepay while cash allows.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $12.27 per hour from April 2026): KBC employs 68 staff, most of them hourly pressing, glazing and packing roles, so the rise is unavoidable and feeds directly into the wage bill. The insert gives no hours worked and no pay decomposition, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest benchmark is productivity: 75,000 units ÷ 68 staff ≈ 1,103 units per worker a year, so the rise is absorbable only if output and productivity hold or improve, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $9.00 contribution per unit erodes. It also raises the bar for the on-the-job training programme, since higher wages make every lost or disengaged worker costlier.

Input cost inflation (9.6% alumina and feldspar): KBC's $9.50 variable cost is dominated by raw materials, but the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 9.6% it would add 9.6% × $9.50 = $0.91 per unit (0.096 × $9.50 = $0.912); at 75,000 units a year that is about $68,400 a year (0.912 × 75,000). Even a milder illustrative $0.50 per unit would remove about $37,500 a year. KBC can offset part of this through the 4% premium that 49% of surveyed buyers accept and through price negotiations with grid contractors, but the squeeze lands immediately and compounds on every unit sold.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 75,000 units, directly eroding the $9.00 contribution that justifies the $1,150,000 expansion, and unlike interest it cannot be hedged by fixing a rate; unlike wages it hits every unit of material, not just labour minutes. The minimum wage rise is second, managed through productivity at roughly 1,103 units per worker; the interest rate rise is smallest at about $5,250 a year on a variable $700,000 loan, and close to zero if KBC fixed its terms. KBC should respond with supplier renegotiation, the certified-range premium and tighter glaze-waste control before seeking price rises.
    Keywords: 5.75%, 5.8%, 9.6%, $12.27, interest rate, $9.50
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to KBC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KBC's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of KBC with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

Redmoor Abrasives (RMA) is a public limited company in the industrial abrasives sector, manufacturing resin-bond grinding wheels and cutting discs for steel fabrication plants, employing a workforce of 140. This matters while RMA carries fixed costs of $528,000 a year: every dollar of profit reinvested rather than paid out can absorb the 10.7% rise in aluminium oxide and resin input costs without diluting headline earnings for the 2027 reporting year.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids issuing new shares, which would dilute the control and voting power of Marek Nowak and the founding shareholder group in the public limited company. Using retained profit instead of selling $600,000 of equity keeps decision-making with current owners, avoids the effort and expense of a prospectus and shareholder meetings, and signals to the market that the board is confident the new line will generate its own returns without fresh capital. It also reassures investors that RMA's growth story is equity-financed rather than debt-driven, protecting the share price that funded the other $1,000,000 of the programme.

It targets the measurable 8.4% absenteeism that is disrupting commissioning of the new line, delivers fast, legible rewards on the shop floor, and is affordable while fixed costs of $528,000 a year and the share issue must be safeguarded. Profit sharing is rejected as too diffuse and too dependent on whole-company profit to change operator behaviour in the short term; once attendance normalises, RMA can layer a modest profit-sharing pool on top to sustain engagement beyond the commissioning phase.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.05 : 1

Conclusion: RMA's financial position has broadly improved in quality even though the headline short-term cover dipped from 1.70 to 1.60. Quick cover (1.05 to 1.09) and a lower inventory burden show stronger, more dependable liquidity, and cash grew by $50,000. The rise in trade receivables and the heavier liability base mean the position is not fully comfortable, so RMA should tighten credit control and keep the curing line at high utilisation to ensure the $600,000 retained profit portion of the expansion continues to reward shareholders.

--- STEM ---
Clearspire Filtration (CSF) is a partnership in the industrial filtration sector, producing pleated air and coolant filter cartridges for manufacturing plants, employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2013 by Sofia Almeida and Rafael Duarte, the partnership operates a flat structure with shared democratic decision-making and is based in Joinville, Brazil. CSF plans to invest $780,000 in a new automated pleating and welding line, financed by hire purchase of $480,000 on the machinery and a $300,000 overdraft facility. It has fixed costs of $312,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. CSF faces a serious quality problem: the defect rate on pleated cartridges has risen to 3.4%, driving 12 complaints this quarter.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CSF plans to finance its pleating-line expansion partly with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for CSF of using hire purchase instead of the overdraft facility.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $480,000 machinery cost over fixed instalments matched to the productive life of the new pleating and welding line, so CSF keeps more short-term cash available for wages and materials while the 12 current complaints are cleared. Fixed instalments are also easier to budget than an overdraft, whose interest rate can move with every base-rate rise and whose full balance can be demanded at any time.

Point 2: Under hire purchase the machinery secures itself — CSF gains use of a productive asset immediately with ownership passing on the final payment — whereas an overdraft is unsecured short-term debt best suited to working-capital gaps, not a $780,000 expansion. Using hire purchase for the line preserves the $300,000 overdraft as a flexible buffer for seasonal demand and unexpected repairs, rather than being fully absorbed by the purchase and leaving the partnership with no liquidity headroom. Fixed instalments also make month-by-month cash planning far more reliable for a two-partner business without a specialist finance team.
    Keywords: hire purchase, overdraft, $480,000, $300,000, $780,000, $312,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Clearspire Filtration and its expansion decision.

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $145,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $280,000; 2025 current assets = $100,000 + $165,000 + $65,000 = $330,000. 2024 = $280,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.40; 2025 = $330,000 ÷ $220,000 = 1.50. Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened sensibly. Short-term cover improved from 1.40 to 1.50 and quick cover from 0.95 to 1.05, meaning CSF no longer has to sell its pleated cartridges to pay short-term debts — important while hire purchase instalments on the $480,000 machinery and reliance on a $300,000 overdraft both tighten monthly cash commitments. Cash rose from $45,000 to $65,000 and inventories only edged up $10,000, showing tight stock control. The warning sign is trade receivables rising from $145,000 to $165,000: if plant managers stretch payment terms, quick cover could slide back below 1.0, and the partnership's modest capital base (capital employed of $1,700,000 against non-current assets of $1,550,000) leaves limited room for comfort.

Conclusion: CSF's financial position has improved. Short-term cover (1.40 to 1.50) and quick cover (0.95 to 1.05) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory build-up. The main residual risk is the $20,000 rise in receivables layered on a relatively small capital base, so CSF should tighten credit terms for new filter accounts and reserve part of the overdraft for commissioning contingencies rather than day-to-day trading.
    Keywords: 1.40, 1.50, 0.95, 1.05, $280,000, $330,000, $780,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether CSF's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CSF of shifting from Quality Control final inspection to Quality Assurance built into the pleating line.
    Answer: Advantage: Quality Assurance prevents defects at source rather than catching them at the end, which directly attacks the 3.4% defect rate and the 12 complaints recorded this quarter. With in-process checks on each stage — checking 1 in 20 cartridges as planned — CSF can prove consistent efficiency to the 74% of plant managers demanding guaranteed 99% filtration, win the 5% premium, and cut the scrap and rework that currently consumes margin on 11,500 units a quarter.

Disadvantage: Building Quality Assurance into the pleating and welding process requires upfront investment in gauges, staff training and revised sampling routines — real money for a partnership already stretching to hire purchase of $480,000 and an overdraft facility. If the in-process checks slow cycle time or flag false rejects, unit output falls and the 4.1-day fulfilment promise slips; and if monitoring lapses once the new line is running steadily, inspection discipline fades, letting defects reach customers who were promised a guarantee rather than a hope.
    Keywords: Quality Assurance, Quality Control, 3.4%, 99%, 1 in 20, $480,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CSF's quality data, research, costs and fulfilment record.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in input costs will affect CSF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The 0.75 percentage point rise lifts the cost of CSF's variable-rate exposures: hire purchase of $480,000 would add 0.75% × $480,000 = $3,600 a year if variable, and a fully drawn $300,000 overdraft would add 0.75% × $300,000 = $2,250 a year — an illustrative $5,850 a year altogether. That is significant against fixed costs of $312,000, and higher base rates also make any future borrowing for expansion costlier, though the new line is already largely secured through hire purchase rather than an unsecured loan.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $15.10 per hour from April 2026): CSF's 34 staff are mostly hourly press and packing operatives, so the rise is unavoidable. The insert gives no hours worked or pay split, so no annual wage total can be invented; the honest benchmark is productivity: 48,000 units ÷ 34 staff ≈ 1,412 units per worker a year. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if pleating-line disruption during commissioning lowers output per worker, unit labour cost climbs and the $12.00 contribution per unit erodes quickly.

Input cost inflation (13.2% polypropylene media and aluminium frames): CSF's $18.00 variable cost is dominated by media and frames, though the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 13.2% it would add 13.2% × $18.00 = $2.38 per unit (0.132 × $18.00 = $2.376); at 48,000 units a year that is about $114,048 (0.132 × $18.00 × 48,000). Even a gentler illustrative $1.50 per unit would strip about $72,000 a year. Recovery depends on holding the 5% premium the 74% of managers will pay — now roughly $1.50 per unit at $30.00 — so the margin gain from quality may be consumed entirely by input inflation.

Conclusion: The 13.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit of the 48,000 CSF sells, can wipe out in one swoop the entire $12.00 contribution gain from the 99% efficiency guarantee programme, and cannot be fixed by choosing a different finance product. The minimum wage rise is second, significant but manageable through productivity near 1,412 units per worker if commissioning goes smoothly; the interest rate rise is third, at an illustrative $5,850 a year. CSF should lock supplier contracts now, push the 5% premium hard with guaranteed-efficiency customers, and keep the overdraft for contingencies only.
    Keywords: 5.00%, 7.1%, 13.2%, $15.10, interest rate, $18.00

--- STEM ---
Thorncombe Belting (THB) is a cooperative in the conveyor belting sector, manufacturing steel-cord conveyor belts and power transmission belts for mining and agriculture, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2002 by Thandi Mokoena, the cooperative operates a flat structure with democratic leadership and is based in Rustenburg, South Africa. THB plans to invest $920,000 in a new calendering line for steel-cord belts, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and a $320,000 share issue to members. It has fixed costs of $405,000 a year, a variable cost of $27.00 a unit and a selling price of $45.00, and currently produces 36,000 units a year. THB faces a serious skills problem: a wave of retirements has left a shortage of qualified rubber calendering technicians across the shop floor.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: THB plans to finance part of its calendering-line expansion with a share issue to members. Explain two advantages for THB of using a member share issue instead of relying entirely on the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A member share issue keeps capital inside the cooperative and reduces THB's dependence on the $600,000 bank loan, lowering fixed interest commitments while fixed costs already total $405,000 a year. Member capital also strengthens the cooperative's balance sheet at a time when input costs for natural rubber and steel cord are rising 14.6%, giving THB more room to negotiate without breaching loan covenants.

Point 2: Shares issued to members bind the workforce to the cooperative's long-term success — members who hold equity are more likely to stay, train and invest effort, which directly supports closing the calendering skills gap. It also spreads the $920,000 expansion risk across the membership rather than concentrating it with one lender, preserving democratic control: no bank acquires decision rights over THB's strategy, so Thandi Mokoena and the members remain in charge of how the new line is staffed and prioritised.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $320,000, $600,000, $920,000, $405,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Thorncombe Belting and its expansion decision.

    Question: THB is launching its locally reinforced steel-cord belt range. Consider sponsoring the national mining summit, advertising in a mining trade magazine, or producing case-study videos for social media. Which should THB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Mining summit sponsorship: Sponsoring the national mining summit puts THB directly in front of mine engineers, procurement officers and farm-machinery managers in one venue, ideal for showcasing 10-year wear-warranty belts and the local reinforcing angle that 77% of the 180 surveyed managers prefer. The drawbacks are sponsorship fees, staffing and logistics for an event several hundred kilometres from Rustenburg, no guarantee that the right decision-makers stop at the stand, and a single day of visibility that cannot sustain awareness between events.

Mining trade magazine advertising: A full-page advert with technical wear data reaches professional readers across South Africa and neighbouring mines, building credibility over a long 12-month shelf life. However, print lead times are slow, effectiveness is hard to measure, and the premium for full-page colour is steep for a cooperative whose fixed costs already run at $405,000 a year; coverage also includes readers who will never specify conveyor belts.

Case-study videos for social media: Short films showing the calendering line, a mine's uptime gains and the solar array trial (22% daylight electricity saving) can run on LinkedIn and YouTube, targeting the 53% willing to pay a 5% premium and the 77% preferring locally reinforced belts. Production is inexpensive for industrial storytelling, measurable through views and enquiries, and reusable across sales proposals — though reach depends on disciplined posting and paid boosting to mine-specific audiences.

Recommendation: THB should choose case-study videos for social media. It showcases the local reinforcement and solar story authentically, costs far less than the summit, scales beyond any single venue, and measurably targets the premium-accepting managers in its research. The summit sponsorship is rejected as too expensive and one-off for a $920,000 expansion; the trade magazine advertisement is rejected as slow and unmeasurable for an industrial audience now living on digital channels; THB should cut three videos — uptime, warranty and member craftsmanship — and follow every enquiry with a site visit offer.

    Question: THB's retirement wave has left 17 of 52 staff without certified rubber-calendering qualifications. Explain two benefits for THB of introducing profit sharing for its members.

When calendering technicians see that efficiency gains flow into a shared distribution, they are more likely to flag machine drift, tighten seam tolerances and mentor apprentices — protecting output of 36,000 units and supporting the business case for the $920,000 calendering line.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: THB's coordination is straining as the calendering line prepares to start. Consider keeping its flat democratic structure or appointing a full-time operations manager with authority over shifts. Which should THB choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Keeping the flat democratic structure: Retaining member-elected, democratic shift leadership preserves the cooperative's identity, keeps decision-making close to the work, and holds member engagement high while 17 of 52 staff retrain. Decision: THB should keep its flat democratic structure for now and appoint a member coordinator pair — two elected technicians with defined shift-authority — rather than an outside hierarchical manager. This strengthens coordination without breaking the cooperative constitution, costs far less than an external appointment, and directly accelerates skills transfer while 17 members retrain. A full-time operations manager is rejected at this stage because it risks member disengagement and added fixed cost before the new calender proves its output; THB should review the decision in 12 months, and if on-time delivery and waste targets are still failing after full certification, a member vote can then consider a dedicated manager with clearly bounded authority.

--- STEM ---
Dunmore Plastics (DMP) is a private limited company in the agricultural plastics sector, extruding uPVC irrigation pipes and fittings for farm suppliers, employing a workforce of 81. Founded in 2010 by Daniel Soriano, the business operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership and is based in Cebu, the Philippines. DMP plans to invest $1,350,000 in a second uPVC extrusion line with in-line wall-thickness testing, financed by a $800,000 bank loan and $550,000 from the sale of its old delivery fleet. It has fixed costs of $315,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.10 a unit and a selling price of $12.60, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. DMP faces a serious quality problem: customer complaints about inconsistent pipe wall thickness rose for two consecutive quarters.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: DMP plans to finance part of its extrusion-line expansion from the sale of its old delivery fleet. Explain two advantages for DMP of using the sale of assets instead of relying entirely on the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Selling the old delivery fleet converts idle capital into $550,000 of usable funds without adding a single dollar of new debt to the $800,000 bank loan, so DMP's total obligations stay lower and its fixed charges of $315,000 a year are not inflated by extra interest. The fleet had reached the end of its economic life, so the sale releases trapped value at little operational cost while the new line is commissioned.

Point 2: Using asset sale proceeds avoids diluting ownership and avoids additional loan conditions or security demands on the new in-line wall-thickness testing equipment. It also simplifies the balance sheet ahead of any future audit of pipe consistency certificates for farm suppliers, demonstrates to lenders that DMP funds expansion from its own resources, and preserves headroom on the $1,350,000 programme should dealerships for the extrusion line run over budget.
    Keywords: delivery fleet, bank loan, $550,000, $800,000, $1,350,000, $315,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Dunmore Plastics and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: DMP is launching its certified wall-thickness consistent uPVC pipe range. Consider advertising in farm trade magazines, a presence at national agricultural shows, or Facebook and YouTube marketing aimed at farm suppliers. Which should DMP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Farm trade magazine advertising: Full-page adverts in irrigation and farm-supply magazines reach professional buyers with long shelf life, technicians and owners can keep the certification details beside the catalogue, and the audience is directly the 280 farm supply managers DMP surveyed. Drawbacks are slow lead times, modest measurability, and wastage where circulation extends well beyond DMP's distributor patch in Cebu and the central Visayas.

National agricultural shows: A stand at the flagship farm show would let DMP demonstrate actual pipe cross-sections, wall-thickness certificates and the 4% UV-stabilised premium story face to face, and could sign up whole supplier networks in two days. The downsides are heavy fees, freight and staffing costs, a single-event impact window, and disruption to a lean 81-employee team during harvest-season demand peaks.

Facebook and YouTube marketing: Video demos of the in-line testing rig, customer testimonials from Cebu farm suppliers and reinforced UV-stabilised messaging target exactly the 69% who would switch for certified consistency and the 45% paying a 4% premium. Production is modest in cost, click-through and enquiry metrics are immediate, and content can be boosted to province-level farm-supply audiences — though creative quality drives results and younger followers may not match the buyer profile of every supply shop.

Recommendation: DMP should choose Facebook and YouTube marketing aimed at farm suppliers. It is cheap, measurable and precisely matched to the 69% switching segment and the 45% premium-accepting segment in its research, and it scales beyond any single show. Farm trade magazines are rejected as too slow and hard to measure for a first-mover range; the agricultural show is rejected as high fixed cost and short-lived for a small private limited company; social video should be supported by sending QR-linked certificate samples to every enquiring supplier to convert attention into trials.
    Keywords: 69%, 45%, 280, $1,350,000, workforce of 81, wall-thickness
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of DMP with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of DMP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade magazines and the agricultural show are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: DMP's pipe wall-thickness complaints rose for two consecutive quarters. Explain two benefits for DMP of introducing job enrichment for its extrusion-line operators.
    Answer: Point 1: Job enrichment gives operators ownership of the full extrusion task — from resin feed through in-line wall-thickness checks to end-of-line certification — rather than minding a single machine. Operators who see the pipe leave the line certified are more invested in consistency, which directly attacks the two quarters of rising complaints and supports the 2.8% defect rate that has already improved from 4.2% a year ago.

Point 2: Enriched roles stretch skills and create the pipeline of certified in-line testers DMP needs for the new line, reducing dependence on Daniel Soriano's personal oversight. Higher responsibility satisfies the esteem needs (Maslow) and motivators (Herzberg) that pay alone cannot, raising attendance and lowering the monotony that long extrusion shifts create — protecting the 2.6-day fulfilment promise and helping DMP meet the 69% of farm supply managers ready to switch for certified consistency.
    Keywords: wall-thickness testing, wall-thickness, 2.8%, 4.2%, 2.6 days, 69%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to DMP's quality problem, certification appeal and fulfilment record.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: DMP must fix rising wall-thickness complaints on the extrusion line. Consider installing the in-line CAM wall-thickness scanner operated by existing staff or hiring two full-time quality inspectors. Which should DMP choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: In-line CAM wall-thickness scanner: Computer-aided manufacturing scanning within the extruder feedback loop would measure every metre of pipe continuously, catch deviations before scrap is cut, and generate certificates farm suppliers can file. CAM is squarely within proven manufacturing technology and matches the $1,350,000 expansion's in-line theme. Limits: it needs calibration discipline, operators trained to respond to alarms (not just watch dashboards), and a real investment beyond the base line — plus residual dependence on the system vendor for maintenance.

Two full-time quality inspectors: Two inspectors would provide independent eyes, immediate physical checks at the end of line, and human judgement on borderline pipes. They also give DMP a visible commitment to farm suppliers who visit the works. The drawbacks are ongoing wages on top of a workforce of 81 and fixed costs of $315,000 a year, subjectivity and sampling gaps (however good, they cannot measure every metre), slower root-cause feedback because inspectors find defects after extrusion rather than during it, and no automatic certificate generation.

Decision: DMP should install the in-line CAM wall-thickness scanner and train existing operators to run it, backed by one senior inspector for periodic audits rather than two. The scanner prevents defects at the point of manufacture — exactly what the two consecutive quarters of complaints demand — certifies every metre for the 69% of managers ready to switch, and scales with the new line without growing payroll. Two full-time inspectors are rejected as a slower, costlier, sampling-based patch that finds rather than prevents wall-thickness drift; the single senior auditor keeps human judgement in the system while the scanner does the continuous measuring.
    Keywords: in-line wall-thickness testing, wall-thickness, $1,350,000, 69%, $315,000, workforce of 81

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate DMP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has DMP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.94 : 1

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for DMP of using 30% recycled uPVC regrind in its irrigation pipes.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.50%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in input costs will affect DMP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.50%): If DMP's $800,000 ten-year bank loan is variable, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.75% × $800,000 = $6,000 a year (0.0075 × $800,000) to interest costs — noticeable against fixed costs of $315,000 a year, and zero if the loan was fixed at signing. The risk extends to any future borrowing for the remaining kit on the $1,350,000 programme and to farm suppliers slowing their own capital spending, though higher rates can also cool rival imports. DMP should confirm its loan rate and consider partial early repayment from operating cash before expansion peak.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $11.60 per hour from April 2026): With 81 staff mostly on hourly extrusion and packing rates, the rise is unavoidable. The insert gives no hours or pay split, so no annual wage total can be honestly invented; the honest benchmark is productivity: 110,000 units ÷ 81 staff ≈ 1,358 units per worker a year. If the new line lifts this figure, the rise is absorbable; if commissioning drags, unit labour cost climbs, the $4.50 contribution shrinks, and DMP's ability to service the $550,000 of asset-sale-funded expansion weakens precisely when overtime demand is peaking.

Input cost inflation (11.2% uPVC resin and stabilisers): DMP's $8.10 variable cost is dominated by raw resin, but the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 11.2% it would add 11.2% × $8.10 = $0.91 per unit (0.112 × $8.10 = $0.907); at 110,000 units a year that is about $99,792 (0.112 × $8.10 × 110,000). Even a milder illustrative $0.60 per unit strips roughly $66,000 a year. The 30% recycled regrind trial (15% lower resin cost per metre) helps, but stabiliser costs also rise 11.2%, and stabiliser performance is exactly what the UV-stabilised premium depends on.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 110,000 units, compresses the $4.50 contribution from both ends, and cannot be fixed by refinancing — only by pricing, renegotiation and the regrind programme. The minimum wage rise is second, absorbable if the new line raises productivity beyond roughly 1,358 units per worker; the interest rate rise is third at about $6,000 a year on a variable $800,000 loan. DMP should lock resin and stabiliser contracts through 2027, hold the 4% premium fiercely, and use agricultural output growth of 3.1% to win certified-pipe share before inflation compounds further.
    Keywords: 5.50%, 6.4%, 11.2%, $11.60, interest rate, $8.10

--- STEM ---
Hallam & Grey Electrical (HGE) is a private limited company in the consumer electronics and home appliance retail sector, employing a workforce of 132 across nine superstores in the Norwick region and an online shop. Founded in 2009 by Nadia Rahman, the business operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. HGE plans to invest $980,000 in a next-day home-delivery fulfilment centre with an in-house repair workshop, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $500,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $55, and currently produces 32,000 units a year. HGE faces a growing operational problem: labour turnover among shop-floor sales staff has climbed sharply, and customer complaints about late deliveries are increasing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HGE plans to finance its $980,000 home-delivery fulfilment centre with a $600,000 bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for HGE of using retained profit rather than borrowing the full amount.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $380,000 of its own retained profit costs HGE nothing in repayments or interest, which eases cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $500,000 a year and is about to service a $600,000 ten-year loan. The retained-profit route also protects HGE from interest-rate risk: the central bank has just raised the base rate to 5.0%, so each further 0.25% rise would add $1,500 a year to a variable-rate $600,000 loan (0.0025 x $600,000), and retained profit avoids that exposure entirely for this portion of the funding.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps decision-making with Nadia Rahman and HGE's directors, with no lender covenants dictating how the fulfilment centre, delivery schedule or pricing are run. It also signals financial strength to suppliers, helping HGE negotiate better terms as it scales the nine superstores plus the online shop, which processed 9,600 orders last quarter, into next-day fulfilment. Using internal funds also avoids security being pledged against the new $980,000 centre, keeping the expansion fully under HGE's control while labour turnover among shop-floor staff is being fixed.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $380,000, $600,000, $980,000, $500,000

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HGE is launching its next-day home-delivery service. Consider a national television advertising campaign, a regional newspaper advertising campaign, or social media advertising. Which should HGE choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A national TV campaign would give the launch huge reach very quickly and could put HGE's next-day delivery promise in front of millions of viewers across the country. However, production and airtime costs for national slots are extremely high for a nine-superstore regional retailer, and a large share of the audience would live far beyond the Norwick region HGE actually serves. With complaints about late deliveries still fresh and labour turnover climbing, tying up capital in wasteful national coverage is hard to justify when the expansion already absorbs $980,000.

Regional newspaper campaign: Local and regional newspapers are far cheaper than national television and reach the Norwick catchment where HGE's nine superstores and online customers are concentrated. Newspaper advertising suits price-led, time-bound messages such as launch offers. Its weaknesses are a shrinking and older readership, limited space for visual demonstrations of the new fulfilment promise, and poor measurability compared with digital channels, given that 71% of HGE customers check online reviews before buying.

Social media advertising: Social campaigns let HGE target its exact 46% of surveyed shoppers who said free next-day delivery would decide where they buy, plus the 71% who research online. Spend is measurable click by click, creative can be adjusted quickly, and it keeps the cost far below television. Reach among younger appliance buyers is strong, though it demands consistent content production and some spend on paid promotion to stand out.

Recommendation: HGE should choose social media advertising. It is the cheapest of the three per relevant customer reached, it is measurable, and it targets precisely the online-review-checking segment identified in HGE's own research, reinforcing the 9,600-order online channel. National television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a regional nine-superstore chain funding an $980,000 expansion from retained profit and a $600,000 loan; the regional newspaper is rejected as too narrow in reach and weak for younger buyers. Social media should be supported by in-store posters, but it should carry the launch.

--- STEM ---
Wren & Quill Booksellers (WQB) is a partnership in the independent book retail sector, employing a workforce of 34 across three bookshops in Elmsworth and an online store. Founded in 2016 by sisters Ada and Rosa Quill, the business operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. WQB plans to invest $425,000 in a second flagship shop with a reading cafe and click-and-collect hub, financed by a $270,000 bank loan and $155,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $187,500 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $15, and currently produces 42,000 units a year. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WQB plans to finance its $425,000 second flagship shop with a $270,000 bank loan and $155,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for WQB of using retained profit rather than increasing the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs WQB nothing in interest or fees, which matters because the partnership already faces warehouse absenteeism of 8% and rising delivery pressure: the $155,000 portion of the $425,000 expansion funded internally carries no repayment duty at a time when cash is needed to keep the online hub dispatching 11,300 orders a quarter on a 1.9-day average delivery. Avoiding extra debt also insulates WQB from the central bank's latest base-rate rise to 5.25%, which would lift the cost of any variable-rate borrowing taken instead of retained profit.

Point 2: Keeping funding internal preserves the sisters' ownership and autonomy over the new shop, its reading cafe and its click-and-collect hub; no bank can impose trading covenants or demand security over personal assets. For a 34-person partnership in a sector where 4.1% growth in book spending is decent but not spectacular, lower fixed interest burdens protect the $15 selling price and the contribution each unit earns, leaving room to invest in member-focused offers such as the proposed $8-a-month reading club and to manage stock shrinkage of 1.6% without external pressure.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $155,000, $270,000, $425,000, 5.25%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wren & Quill Booksellers and its flagship expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WQB is launching its second flagship shop with a reading cafe. Consider a loyalty-member email campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should WQB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Loyalty-member email campaign: Emailing WQB's 450 loyalty members is almost free, instantly measurable, and perfect for announcing the new shop, cafe opening hours and click-and-collect slots to customers who already buy an average basket of $34. Its ceiling is obvious, however: it reaches only existing members, so it cannot pull in new shoppers for a launch event designed to broaden local awareness in Elmsworth, and repeated emails risk unsubscribes if overused.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is relatively cheap, reaches a broad Elmsworth audience at breakfast and drive time, and can carry repeated memorable messages about the cafe and in-store events, suiting the launch's family audience. Its drawbacks are limited targeting, no direct clickable call to action, and fading reach among younger readers who increasingly discover books through social media, which 63% of WQB's own survey respondents said they use.

Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with local bookstagram and booktok creators matches the 63% of members who discover new titles through social media, showcases the cafe visually, and creates shareable launch content. Engagement is measurable and the cost per young customer reached is low, though results depend on choosing authentic creators and sustaining posts beyond launch week.

Recommendation: WQB should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact discovery channel its research identifies, combines reach with measurability, and is affordable for a partnership funding a $425,000 expansion. Local radio is rejected as too broad and untargeted for a shop-plus-cafe opening that needs measurable footfall; the email campaign, while cheap and useful for existing members, is rejected as the lead channel because it cannot grow awareness beyond the 450-member base; WQB should still email members first as a low-cost warmup to the influencer launch.
    Keywords: 450, $34, 63%, $425,000, loyalty members, reading cafe
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to WQB. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WQB with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WQB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio sponsorship and the email-only approach are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WQB's warehouse absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for WQB of using democratic leadership to reduce it.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership involves the 34 employees in scheduling, workload and picking workflows rather than imposing them, which raises ownership and job satisfaction among warehouse staff. Workers who help design shift patterns and rest breaks face less fatigue and are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking the 8% absenteeism rate that delays online orders and forces costly overtime at the Elmsworth hub.

Lower absenteeism protects the 1.9-day delivery promise that underpins WQB's $34 average online basket, and it reduces disruption to the cafe and shop teams. Because WQB already operates a flat structure with democratic leadership, extending it costs nothing and supports retention of the 34-strong team while the partnership asks more of everyone ahead of the second flagship opening and its $8-a-month reading club launch.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If WQB's $270,000 expansion loan is variable-rate, the additional annual cost is 0.75% x $270,000 = $2,025 a year (0.0075 x $270,000). Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $12.90 per hour): WQB's warehouse, cafe and shop teams include hourly-paid workers, so the rise flows straight into payroll and is unavoidable. No hours or pay rates are stated in the insert, so a firm total cannot be invented; judged against productivity, 42,000 units / 34 employees = 1,235.3 units per employee, the wage cost per unit stays manageable only if the 97.4% picking accuracy holds and absenteeism falls below 8%. Paper and printing cost rise (9.8% year-on-year): Publisher input inflation is the change that scales across everything WQB sells. As an explicit upper bound built from insert figures, if the whole $9 variable cost reflected publisher paper inflation it would add 9.8% x $9 = $0.88 per unit; at 42,000 units a year that is about $37,000 a year (42,000 x $0.88 = $36,960), cutting contribution from $6 toward $5.12. Cover prices rarely move by 9.8%, so margins will likely absorb part of it; 3.9% inflation and 4.1% growth in book and leisure spending help demand, but WQB cannot fully recover the gap without pricing itself off competitors.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in paper and printing costs will have the greatest impact. It applies across every one of the 42,000 units sold, unlike the fixed $2,025 annual interest effect or the bounded wage rise, which depends on hours not stated; and unlike the wage rise, it directly attacks the $6 contribution that funds the flagship and reading cafe. WQB should widen its mix toward higher-margin sidelines such as the $8 reading club and gift lines to offset it.

--- STEM ---
Kettlewell Furniture (KWF) is a cooperative in the flat-pack and upholstered furniture retail sector, employing a workforce of 58 across its Brandleford workshop, showroom and delivery team. Founded in 2004 by Margaret Ellison, the member-owned cooperative operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. KWF plans to invest $640,000 in a large Brandleford showroom with a click-and-collect warehouse, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $34, and currently produces 30,000 units a year. KWF faces a growing operational problem: material waste in the cutting workshop has risen to 9.4% and damaged-stock write-offs are increasing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KWF plans to finance its $640,000 Brandleford showroom with a $400,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for KWF of using retained profit rather than increasing the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs KWF no interest or arrangement fees, which matters because the cooperative already carries a 4.7% assembly defect rate and must fund waste-cutting work in the cutting workshop. KWF's control of its own cash becomes more precious now that the central bank has lifted the base rate to 5.0%: a variable-rate $400,000 loan already costs $2,000 a year for each 0.5% rise (0.005 x $400,000), so the 1.0% rise this year adds $4,000 a year, and borrowing any more would deepen that burden.

Point 2: Internal funding keeps the cooperative's member ownership undiluted and avoids lender covenants that could restrict showroom merchandising, pricing or member benefits. It also preserves KWF's standing with its 520 surveyed members, 66% of whom prefer locally made furniture: demonstrating that the $640,000 expansion is funded without overstretching debt reassures members, supports the membership drive behind the showroom, and protects the $34 price point while furniture spending grows only 1.3% and input costs inflate 14.6%.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $240,000, $400,000, $640,000, 5.0%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Kettlewell Furniture and its showroom expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KWF is opening its Brandleford showroom. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media marketing. Which should KWF choose to promote the opening? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would deliver massive brand reach and could showcase KWF's upholstered furniture to a national audience in seconds, dramatising the local-made story at scale. For a single Brandleford showroom whose delivery range covers only the surrounding region, however, the wastage of national airtime is enormous, and the production and slot costs would dwarf KWF's $240,000 retained-profit contribution to the $640,000 budget at a time when input costs are rising 14.6%.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is affordable, trusted and geographically precise for the Brandleford catchment, and sponsoring home and garden or weekend shows fits KWF's local-made story told to the 66% of members who prefer it. Its reach is limited to listeners, it lacks visual impact for furniture buyers, and younger purchasers increasingly ignore radio entirely, so attendance at the opening would depend on repeat slots and promotions rather than a single broadcast.

Social media marketing: Social media lets KWF show sofa-building reels, before-and-after cutting-workshop clips, and member testimonials, targeting exactly the 41% of members who would pay 8% more for locally made furniture. It is measurable, interactive and cheap, drives showroom footfall and click-and-collect pre-orders, and suits a flat-organisation founder brand like Margaret Ellison's; it does require consistent creative effort and at least a modest paid boost around launch week.

Recommendation: KWF should choose social media marketing. It aligns with KWF's member research, costs far less than television, reaches beyond radio's listener base with story-led owned media, and is measurable against showroom footfall and the 30,000-unit production plan. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable for one regional showroom; local radio is rejected as audio-only with weaker appeal to younger buyers, so it should only support the launch as a short sponsorship burst rather than lead the campaign.
