In a cutting workshop where 640 frames were processed last quarter, quick, uniform decisions matter; a slow consultative process would let waste creep back above the improved 7.1% achieved after nesting software was introduced.

Point 2: Clear top-down accountability makes it obvious who owns each quality outcome, the cut, the assembly bench and the dispatch bay, so defective frames are caught before delivery rather than after. This directly attacks the 4.7% assembly defect rate and the complaint count about damaged deliveries, which has already fallen from 27 to 15 per month. The flat structure means supervisors sit close to the work, and autocratic clarity suits safety-critical cutting-machinery rules; KWF should pair directives with briefings so all 58 employees understand the reasons, or motivation and the co-op culture may suffer.

--- STEM ---
Foxglove Pet Supplies (FPS) is a private limited company in the online pet food and supplies retail sector, employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2019 by Priya Nandakumar in Dunmarrow, the business sells pet food, toys and accessories online with two stores and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. FPS plans to invest $535,000 in an automated subscription fulfilment kitchen and a second store, financed by $310,000 hire purchase for the packing line and $225,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $96,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $20, and currently produces 24,500 units a year. FPS faces a growing operational problem: packing staff turnover has reached 18% and short or incorrect shipments persist.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: FPS plans to finance its $535,000 expansion partly with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for FPS of using hire purchase for the packing line rather than a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $310,000 cost of the packing line across its working life, matching payments to the revenue the line will generate from the 14,200 orders it helps pack each quarter. FPS keeps its cash buffer intact, vital when 4.4% of shipments are still short or incorrect and complaints, though down from 61 to 40 per month, keep arriving; the $225,000 of retained profit can then stay available to stabilise operations rather than being swallowed by one asset purchase.

Point 2: Hire purchase agreements usually secure onto the equipment itself, so it can be simpler to arrange than a further bank loan when the base rate sits at 5.25%. Interest is fixed in the agreement, giving FPS certainty for budgeting the automated kitchen and second store, no surprises if rates rise again, and full ownership of the line at the end of the term, after which maintenance and staffing savings can be redirected into the subscription growth its members support, 57% of whom want a wider grain-free range and 49% of whom would bundle toys with food deliveries.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $310,000, $535,000, $225,000, 5.25%, 14,200
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of hire purchase identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Foxglove Pet Supplies and its subscription expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: FPS is launching its subscription bundle. Consider paid social media advertising, influencer marketing with pet creators, or local radio sponsorship. Which should FPS choose to promote the subscription? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Paid social media advertising: Paid social lets FPS target lookalike audiences built from its 700 surveyed subscribers, retarget abandoned baskets, and push the bundle (food plus toy bundling appeals to 49% of subscribers) at low cost per click. It is measurable and fast to set up, but feeds are competitive, creative must be refreshed constantly, and subscription intent is hard to read from a cold ad alone.

Influencer marketing with pet creators: Partnering with pet creators reaches exactly the 57% of subscribers wanting a wider grain-free range and the 49% interested in toy bundles, with trusted, authentic content; unboxing videos of the fulfilment kitchen convert strongly in pet communities, and creators can demonstrate the actual box contents and next-day feel. Results depend on creator fit, disclosure and consistency beyond launch week.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheap and local to Dunmarrow and reinforces brand familiarity for the two stores, and it can repeat a memorable subscription offer to commuters. But it cannot visualise the product, skews toward older listeners, and lacks a direct, trackable path to online subscription sign-up, which is FPS's growth engine and where 92% next-day coverage already applies.

Decision: FPS should choose on-the-job coaching as the primary route, sending shift leads to the college to standardise their coaching. It is specific, immediate and fee-free, directly attacking the 4.4% error rate without stripping the packing line during peak subscription weeks. Full off-the-job training for the whole workforce is rejected because $29,250 plus cover costs strain cash precisely when liquidity has tightened, and generic modules would need customising to FPS's SOPs anyway; leads can then cascade the same checklist back to their crews.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $12.40 per hour): FPS's packing and delivery teams include hourly-paid staff, so the rise is compulsory and recurring. It applies to every one of the 24,500 units sold, unlike the capped $2,325 annual interest effect or the productivity-contingent wage rise. FPS should re-price the grain-free premium range, lock in annual supplier contracts, keep the $225,000 retained-profit buffer intact, and monitor liquidity before committing to any further expansion.

--- STEM ---
Auric & Sons Jewellers (ASJ) is a partnership in the high-street jewellery retail sector, employing a workforce of 26. Founded in 1987 by Yusuf and Leila Auric in Saltmere, and now managed by their son Darius, the firm operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. ASJ plans to invest $700,000 in a bridal suite and certified watch workshop inside its Saltmere flagship, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $275,000 a year, a variable cost of $180 a unit and a selling price of $230, and currently produces 11,000 units a year. ASJ faces a growing operational problem: a shortage of qualified watchmakers and goldsmiths, so the repair queue is lengthening.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ASJ plans to fund its $700,000 flagship expansion with a $450,000 bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for ASJ of using retained profit rather than an overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge at all, whereas an overdraft is typically variable-rate and repayable on demand, which is dangerous now the central bank has lifted the base rate to 5.0% and ASJ's $450,000 loan already commits it to ten years of repayments. Keeping the $250,000 portion internal protects the partnership's $275,000 fixed-cost base and leaves headroom if bridal demand disappoints or gold pushes the $180 variable cost higher still.

Point 2: Funding the bridal suite and certified watch workshop from retained profit keeps the expansion entirely under the Auric family's control, with no bank able to renegotiate facilities if luxury spending grows only 1.8% or if gold keeps climbing. For a partnership about to market certified watch servicing, which 54% of loyal clients already asked about, covenant-free funding reassures staff and clients that the workshop, apprentice pipeline and new bridal collection can be delivered on schedule, without the administrative burden and personal-asset exposure an overdraft would add to a family firm.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $250,000, $450,000, $700,000, 5.0%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Auric & Sons Jewellers and its flagship expansion.

But a single-flagship jeweller making 11,000 units a year would be buying national reach it cannot fulfil from one store, and the production and airtime costs are unjustifiable against a $700,000 project funded partly from retained profit with gold prices rising 17.8% year-on-year.

Print jewellery catalogue for loyal clients: A posted catalogue targets clients with proven wealth, lists the $1,850-average valuation service beautifully, and suits older buyers who have bought wedding jewellery from the family for decades. However it costs print and postage per client, is slow to update once gold prices move, and younger engaged couples increasingly begin their search on Instagram and Google rather than reading posted catalogues.

Social media advertising: ASJ can target couples in Saltmere and nearby towns searching engagement content, showcase the suite and certified pieces visually, and retarget website visitors; 61% of its enquiry traffic is already on mobile after a campaign that lifted enquiries 44%, and 33% of loyal clients follow ASJ on social channels, so the seed audience already exists for lookalike targeting.

Recommendation: ASJ should choose social media advertising. It converts the 44% enquiry momentum and mobile-first traffic into booked suite appointments, reaches younger engaged couples at a fraction of TV's cost, and fits the existing 33% social following. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable for a single Saltmere flagship; the print catalogue is rejected as the lead channel because it reaches only existing clients too slowly to build launch buzz, though a small mailer to the valuation list would complement the digital push rather than replace it.

--- STEM ---
Valbruna Ski Chalets (VSC) is a private limited company in the alpine hospitality sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2012 by Elena Marchetti, the business operates six timber chalets offering guided ski holidays, with a flat organisational structure and democratic leadership. VSC plans to invest $720,000 in six new eco-chalets with snowmaking equipment, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $222,000 a year, a variable cost of $48 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently produces 12,000 units a year. VSC faces two operational problems: seasonal absenteeism has reached 8% and customer complaints about slow room turnaround are rising.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VSC plans to finance its eco-chalet expansion partly with retained profit. Explain two advantages for VSC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the $450,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or repayment schedule, which protects VSC's cash flow at a time when it already faces fixed costs of $222,000 a year and a $450,000 ten-year loan commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 11.8% rise in heating fuel and timber input costs, helping VSC defend its $85 selling price and its margin on 12,000 units a year while the six eco-chalets bed in.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk attached to the bank loan, so the $270,000 from retained profit is available without putting the new $720,000 eco-chalet site at risk if snowfall or bookings disappoint. It also preserves Elena Marchetti's ownership and control — no external lender can impose conditions on how the snowmaking equipment or eco-chalets are operated, and VSC's flat structure with democratic leadership keeps decision-making with the founder and staff.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VSC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VSC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.44 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.56 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.04 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $55,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 = $65,000 + $75,000 + $55,000 = $195,000. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($180,000 − $90,000) ÷ $125,000 = $90,000 ÷ $125,000 = 0.72; 2025 = ($195,000 − $65,000) ÷ $125,000 = $130,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.04.

The 2025 liquidity figure improved from 1.44 to 1.56, meaning current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $35,000 to $55,000 and inventories falling from $90,000 to $65,000. The stricter liquidity measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.72 to 1.04, so VSC no longer relies on selling stock to meet short-term debts — critical while it services a $450,000 bank loan and funds a $720,000 eco-chalet expansion. However, trade receivables rose from $55,000 to $75,000, tying up cash; if tour operators pay late, the stronger ratios could deteriorate quickly, and inventories fell sharply, so chalet stock availability for peak weeks should be monitored.

Conclusion: VSC's financial position has improved. Both the 2024-to-2025 liquidity measures (1.44 to 1.56, and 0.72 to 1.04) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so VSC should tighten deposit and credit terms with travel partners while proceeding with the eco-chalet expansion.

Conclusion: The 11.8% rise in heating fuel and timber input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeatedly erodes the $37.00 contribution on every one of the 12,000 units sold, totalling roughly $36,800 a year and threatening the margin that justifies the $720,000 eco-chalet expansion. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious risk at roughly $20,000 a year, while the interest-rate rise is the smallest in cash terms at about $3,375 and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three still require VSC to prioritise cost control and premium pricing.

Southswell Surf School (SWS) is a sole trader in the surf school and beach resort sector, employing a workforce of 24. Founded in 2014 by Riley Tanaka, the business runs lessons, board hire and a small beach café at Flagstaff Beach, with a flat structure and laissez-faire leadership. SWS plans to invest $340,000 in a new beachfront learn-to-surf centre with solar showers and a board repair workshop, financed by a $200,000 ten-year bank loan and a $140,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $52,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $22, and currently produces 9,600 units a year. SWS faces two operational problems: labour turnover among instructors has reached 22% and complaints about lesson safety briefings are rising.

    Question: SWS plans to finance its new learn-to-surf centre with a bank loan rather than extending its overdraft. Explain two advantages for SWS of using a $200,000 ten-year bank loan instead of a $140,000 overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: A ten-year bank loan gives SWS a known, fixed repayment schedule, which makes budgeting and break-even planning far easier than an overdraft that can be withdrawn or repriced at short notice. With fixed costs of $52,000 a year and $22 prices, Riley Tanaka can forecast monthly repayments against 9,600 units of annual lesson output and avoid being caught short during quiet winter weeks.

Point 2: The bank loan is designed for long-term investment, so the $200,000 is cheaper and more stable than rolling an overdraft indefinitely; overdraft interest is typically higher and unsecured limits are reviewed frequently. Using the loan for the $340,000 centre also frees the overdraft for genuine working-capital swings, such as buying wetsuits before the 5.4% rise in coastal leisure demand, and reduces the risk of the bank cancelling short-term funding mid-expansion.

--- STEM ---
Harrowgate Riverside Inns (HRI) is a public limited company in the hospitality and riverside dining sector, employing a workforce of 230. Founded in 1987 by Margaret Harrowgate, the group operates nine riverside inns across the county, with a hierarchical structure and autocratic leadership. HRI plans to invest $1,800,000 in refurbishing six inns with riverside dining terraces and boutique rooms, financed by a $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $1,140,000 a year, a variable cost of $38 a unit and a selling price of $95, and currently produces 26,000 units a year. HRI faces two operational problems: labour turnover has reached 28% in its kitchens and food-waste complaints at two inns are rising.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HRI plans to finance its six-inn refurbishment partly with a $600,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for HRI of using a share issue instead of a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises capital without creating a repayment obligation, so HRI's cash flow is not strained by fixed monthly repayments while the refurbishment disrupts six inns. Unlike the $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan, new equity carries no interest charge, protecting fixed costs of $1,140,000 a year and freeing cash to absorb the 13.1% rise in food and beverage input costs without raising menu prices above the $95 room-night benchmark.

Point 2: Equity funding strengthens HRI's statement of financial position, lowering the burden on its current ratio and leaving capacity to borrow again if terrace costs overrun. It also spreads ownership and risk across more shareholders rather than concentrating debt with one bank, which suits a public limited company refurbishing $1,800,000 of assets, and avoids covenants that could restrict how the inns are operated during the refit.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HRI's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HRI's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.60 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.08 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.16 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $320,000 trade receivables + $110,000 cash = $640,000; 2025 = $235,000 + $345,000 + $150,000 = $730,000. Liquidity 2024 = $640,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.60; 2025 = $730,000 ÷ $425,000 = 1.72. The 2025 liquidity figure rose from 1.60 to 1.72, meaning current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $110,000 to $150,000 and current liabilities rising only from $400,000 to $425,000. The rise in liabilities also shows HRI is leaning more on short-term credit, so working capital discipline matters during the six-inn refit.

Conclusion: HRI's financial position has improved, though only gradually. Both the 2024-to-2025 liquidity measures (1.60 to 1.72, and 1.08 to 1.16) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not rest on inventory. The main residual risks are rising receivables and growing current liabilities, so HRI should tighten deposit terms on events and functions while the terraces open, and keep kitchen waste at or below 9.5% of prep weight to free cash for the expansion.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If HRI's $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by about 0.75%, adding roughly $9,000 a year to financing costs and slightly raising fixed costs above $1,140,000. Roughly 45 kitchen porters and cleaners at or near minimum wage, each working about 1,800 hours a year, would see about $13.09 × 1,800 × 6.4% ≈ $1,510 extra a year per worker, or roughly $68,000 across those roles — though HRI can offset part through productivity gains of 113 units per worker (26,000 units ÷ 230 staff).

A 13.1% rise on that portion adds about $3.14 per unit; at 26,000 units that is roughly $81,600 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $57.00 toward $53.86 and reducing profit, though HRI can partially recover through the $8 locally sourced premium menu and tighter waste control below the current 9.5% of prep weight.

Conclusion: The 13.1% rise in food and beverage input costs will have the greatest impact. It directly and repeatedly erodes the $57.00 contribution on every one of the 26,000 units sold, totalling roughly $81,600 a year, comfortably above the minimum-wage effect of roughly $68,000 across the lowest-paid cohort, and far above the $9,000 interest-rate increase. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious risk, while the interest-rate rise is smallest and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three still require HRI to review menu pricing before the April wage change.

--- STEM ---
Caldera Springs Spa Resort (CSSR) is a cooperative in the wellness and spa tourism sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 2016 by Priya Raman, the resort operates geothermal baths and a treatment wing in the highlands, with a flat structure and democratic leadership. Retained profit requires no buyer to be found, no negotiation over price, and no disruption to guest services during the build.

Point 2: Retained profit costs CSSR nothing in interest, repayments or disposal losses, protecting cash flow at a time when it already faces fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $600,000 ten-year bank loan commitment. Every dollar of retained profit used preserves margin against the 14.2% rise in energy prices, helping CSSR hold the $52 price point and keep the cooperative's members' returns healthy without diluting member ownership the way an external capital raise would.

--- STEM ---
Marlowe Meadows Glamping (MMG) is a partnership in the leisure and glamping sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2019 by Sam and Priya Whitmore, the business operates a meadow site with safari tents, a communal kitchen and guided nature walks, with a flat structure and democratic leadership. MMG plans to invest $480,000 in 12 new safari tents and a meadow kitchen, financed by a $330,000 ten-year bank loan and a $150,000 hire purchase agreement. It has fixed costs of $90,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $32, and currently produces 12,000 units a year. MMG faces two operational problems: labour turnover among cleaners has reached 25% and customer complaints about Wi-Fi and noise after dark are rising.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MMG plans to finance its 12 new safari tents partly with a $150,000 hire purchase agreement. Explain two advantages for MMG of using hire purchase to acquire the safari tents instead of financing them from the $330,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the cost of the 12 safari tents over their working life, so MMG keeps more of the $330,000 bank loan for the meadow kitchen build and other cash needs. Repayments are predictable, ownership passes to the partnership at the end of the term, and the tents start generating revenue during the 82% peak-weekend occupancy season rather than waiting for cash to accumulate.

Point 2: Hire purchase is secured on the tents themselves, so MMG avoids over-burdening the bank loan with assets that lose value quickly. It preserves working capital for the rising 15.4% canvas, timber and energy input costs and protects the partners' ownership structure without new external investors, while the fixed repayment schedule keeps the flat structure's budgeting discipline simple for a 16-person team.
    Keywords: hire purchase, bank loan, $150,000, $330,000, safari tents, 82%

Current Ratio 2024 = 1.47 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.43 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.69 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $18,000 inventories + $12,000 trade receivables + $14,000 cash = $44,000; 2025 = $26,000 + $15,000 + $9,000 = $50,000. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($44,000 − $18,000) ÷ $30,000 = $26,000 ÷ $30,000 = 0.87; 2025 = ($50,000 − $26,000) ÷ $35,000 = $24,000 ÷ $35,000 = 0.69.

Inventories rose from $18,000 to $26,000, tying up cash that could have funded the meadow kitchen, and trade receivables rose from $12,000 to $15,000; if agency and platform partners pay late, short-term pressure will intensify.

Conclusion: MMG's financial position has not improved. --- STEM ---
Bluecrest Airport Shuttle (BAS) is a private limited company in the passenger transport sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Priya Nandakumar, the business runs a fleet of coaches and minibuses carrying passengers between Westmoor International Airport and the surrounding towns, operating a flat structure with democratic leadership. BAS plans to invest $720,000 in six electric shuttle buses and charging infrastructure, financed by a $450,000 seven-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.60 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. BAS faces rising driver absenteeism, which reached 8% last quarter, and two new competitors have started undercutting its airport fares.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BAS plans to finance the expansion with a $450,000 seven-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for BAS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of relying solely on the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs BAS nothing in interest or repayments, which protects cash flow while it already services the $450,000 bank loan and carries fixed costs of $270,000 a year. Every dollar not paid out as interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in grid electricity costs, helping BAS hold the $9.00 selling price against two new competitors undercutting its airport fares and defending its $5.40 contribution per unit.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so if passenger numbers at Westmoor International Airport dip, BAS would not be forced to sell coaches to meet loan repayments. Funding $270,000 this way also preserves the democratic, flat structure that Priya Nandakumar created: no external lender can impose conditions on how the six electric shuttle buses are routed, priced or timetabled, and ownership remains entirely with existing shareholders, avoiding dilution or lender interference as the business invests $720,000 in its future.
    Keywords: retained profit, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, bank loan, fixed costs
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bluecrest Airport Shuttle and its expansion decision.

    Answer: Airport terminal advertising boards: Advertising inside Westmoor International Airport reaches arriving and departing passengers at the exact point of need, building instant awareness of the new electric shuttle. High footfall and captive dwell times give strong visibility, and the format suits a service whose entire market is airport passengers. However, airport media contracts are expensive for a 38-employee business funding a $720,000 expansion, and they reach only passengers already at the airport, not residents or workers who could use the service for commuting or hotel transfers.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is far cheaper than airport media, supports time-sensitive launch messages such as 'new electric shuttle now running', and reaches the towns BAS serves, matching its fixed route network. Its limitation is that many listeners will never use an airport shuttle, so wastage is high, and coverage stops at the regional boundary, capping the volume of passengers BAS can attract for its 100,000 units a year.

Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with local travel, family and sustainability influencers targets the 58% of 500 surveyed passengers willing to pay up to $0.30 more for guaranteed-seat bookings and the 46% who prefer electric vehicles, telling the electric story directly to engaged audiences with measurable likes, clicks and bookings at low cost per reached customer. Influencer trust builds more slowly than airport boards and depends on influencer fit, but spend can be scaled, paused or redirected quickly.

Recommendation: BAS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches precisely the passengers BAS's research shows will pay a premium, costs far less than airport terminal contracts, scales beyond the local radio audience, and reinforces the eco-friendly positioning that city commuters increasingly expect. Airport terminal advertising is rejected as too costly and captive-market only; local radio is rejected as too narrow for routes serving hotels, towns and the airport itself; influencer campaigns should be supported with modest stands at the terminal during peak summer months.

--- STEM ---
Redbark Timber Haulage (RBH) is a partnership in the bulk timber road transport sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2008 by cousins Daniela and Rory Whitmore, the business operates a fleet of road trains hauling logs from Highfen forestry estates to sawmills across the north region, with a hierarchical structure led by senior partner Daniela. RBH plans to invest $960,000 in four double-trailer road trains, financed by $600,000 hire purchase and $360,000 partners' capital contributions. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $55 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. RBH faces a skills gap: only 9 of its 52 drivers hold the double-trailer licence needed for the new road trains.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RBH plans to finance the $960,000 road train purchase with $600,000 hire purchase and $360,000 partners' capital contributions. Explain two advantages for RBH of using hire purchase instead of relying solely on partners' capital.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase lets RBH spread the $600,000 cost over several years while the four road trains generate revenue immediately, preserving Daniela and Rory Whitmore's partners' capital of $360,000 for working capital such as diesel, driver wages and maintenance across a workforce of 52. Tying up all partner funds in vehicles would leave the business exposed to the 14.7% diesel price rise and any sawmill payment delays without a cash buffer.

Point 2: Hire purchase treats the road trains as security for the finance, so RBH does not need to pledge private partner assets or dilute ownership. Because the vehicles are productive assets earning an $85 selling price on every unit hauled, the repayments can be matched against the income they create, easing cash flow and keeping the $360,000 capital contribution available as a safety cushion while the double-trailer licence bottleneck is cleared and the new fleet beds in.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RBH is launching its guaranteed 24-hour double-trailer delivery service. Consider advertising in a national forestry trade magazine, direct mail to sawmill customers, or exhibiting at a forestry and logistics trade exhibition. Which should RBH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National forestry trade magazine advertising: A placement in the sector's main title would reach hundreds of forestry estates, sawmills and timber buyers nationwide, building credibility for RBH's new double-trailer service and its carbon-report capability. It is cost-effective per reader, and 61% of sawmill customers already ask for carbon-report data with every load, so a well-placed advert can lead with that differentiator. However, print readership among actual decision-makers is limited, ads are easy to ignore, and measuring enquiry rates is weak, so many impressions will never convert to load contracts.

Direct mail to sawmill customers: RBH can mail its own base of 18 surveyed sawmill customers plus prospects, offering guaranteed 24-hour delivery — the single most cited switching trigger, named by 72% of survey respondents. Personalised, evidence-led mail is cheap, targeted and easy to track through follow-up calls, and it suits a small partnership without a marketing department. Its drawback is scale: it cannot efficiently reach new forestry regions outside RBH's existing Highfen-to-sawmill corridor, and poorly designed mailers risk being filed away unread.

Forestry and logistics trade exhibition: Exhibiting puts RBH face-to-face with estates, sawmills and timber buyers in one venue, enabling live demonstrations of road train payloads (26 tonnes average) and on-the-spot contract talks. Exhibitions build trust fast in a relationship-driven industry. However, stand fees, travel and staff time cost thousands of dollars for a partnership whose cash is committed to $960,000 of vehicles, and a single event delivers only one-off, geographically random exposure.

Recommendation: RBH should choose direct mail to sawmill customers. It speaks directly to the 72% who would switch for guaranteed 24-hour delivery, targets the exact buyers who control volume, costs a fraction of exhibition space, and produces measurable enquiry data within weeks. The trade magazine advert is rejected as untargeted and slow to convert; the exhibition is rejected as expensive and infrequent for a business that must fill four new road trains quickly; RBH can add a small magazine presence later, funded from first-contract revenues.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RBH must close its double-trailer licence gap. Consider internal recruitment and promotion of existing drivers or external recruitment of licensed double-trailer drivers. Which should RBH choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal recruitment and promotion: Promoting from within rewards loyal Highfen drivers, lifts morale and reinforces the hierarchical structure Daniela Whitmore runs, and internal candidates already understand RBH's routes, sawmill customers and safety culture. It is quicker and cheaper than external search, and the $1,150 licensing fee per driver is far less than external salary uplift. However, only drivers without licences are available to promote in volume (43 of 52 hold none), coaching capacity is constrained because on-the-job mentoring depends on the 9 existing licence holders, and internal promotion alone cannot widen the talent pool if demand for road trains outruns licence completion.

External recruitment of licensed drivers: Hiring certified double-trailer drivers delivers immediate capacity for the four new road trains, brings fresh techniques from other fleets, and relieves pressure on the 9 in-house mentors. Advertising, agency fees and higher starting salaries raise costs, and new hires still need route-specific induction on Highfen estates and sawmill drop-off protocols; cultural fit with a family partnership also cannot be guaranteed.

Decision: RBH should choose internal recruitment combined with targeted external hires only for stubborn gaps — prioritising existing drivers for licence training with bonuses. Internal development is cheaper, morale-boosting, and aligns with the $1,150 per driver certification budget already identified; RBH can certify its 43 unlicensed drivers in waves and cover peaks with one or two external hires. External-first recruitment is rejected as too costly, culturally risky and unnecessary given how quickly the licence courses can be completed, though RBH should revisit it if sawmill demand outstrips the licensing pipeline or absenteeism in the mentor group rises.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RBH of introducing GPS fleet tracking technology across its road train fleet.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 14.7% diesel price rise, the 6.5% minimum wage increase to $13.00 and the base interest rate rise to 6.0% will affect RBH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Diesel price rise (14.7% year-on-year): Diesel is RBH's single largest variable cost inside the $55 a unit figure. A 14.7% rise adds roughly $5–$6 to the variable cost of every unit hauled; across 40,000 units a year that is $200,000–$240,000 a year, dragging contribution per unit from $30 toward $24–$25 and seriously weakening the case for $960,000 of new road trains unless surcharges or fuel hedging are agreed with sawmills.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.00 per hour): With 52 staff, mainly drivers and depot crew, a 6.5% rise adds roughly $1,700 per full-time employee a year, or about $88,000 across the workforce — significant but smaller than the diesel exposure, and partly offsettable through route productivity (40,000 units ÷ 52 staff ≈ 769 units per worker) and the bonus scheme tied to licence completion and delivery reliability.

Base interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If RBH's hire purchase or any loan is variable-rate, a 0.75 percentage point rise adds roughly $4,500 a year on $600,000 of financing, plus extra cost on the $360,000 partners' capital if it is effectively invested at opportunity cost. Interest payable is already $88,000 in 2025 per Appendix 2; a further rise has the mildest direct cash impact of the three and can be managed by fixing rates.

Conclusion: The 14.7% diesel price rise will have the greatest impact. It flows straight into every unit RBH hauls, totalling roughly $200,000–$240,000 a year, compressing the $30 contribution and the 45.0% gross figure that justifies the expansion. The minimum wage rise is second, adding around $88,000, while the interest rate rise is smallest in cash terms and manageable by fixing finance; RBH should respond with diesel hedging, fuel-linked customer surcharges and aggressive idle-time reduction in the tracked fleet.
    Keywords: 14.7%, 6.5%, 6.0%, $13.00, $55, diesel

--- STEM ---
Caldera Geothermal Heat (CGH) is a cooperative in the renewable energy sector, employing a workforce of 34. Established in 2014 by community investors led by heat engineer Tomas Verhoeven, the cooperative operates the deep-borehole Caldera geothermal heat network, supplying district heating to 1,200 homes and St Anselm's Hospital. It works a flat structure governed democratically by an elected member board. CGH plans to invest $1,250,000 in a second heat exchanger station and 4 km of insulated pipework, financed by an $800,000 member share issue and $450,000 retained reserves. It has fixed costs of $630,000 a year, a variable cost of $78 a unit and a selling price of $120, and currently produces 27,000 units a year. CGH faces rising quality complaints about heat outages across its older connections.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CGH plans to finance the heat network expansion with an $800,000 member share issue and $450,000 retained reserves. Explain two advantages for CGH of using the member share issue instead of relying solely on retained reserves.
    Answer: Point 1: An $800,000 member share issue raises far more expansion capital than the $450,000 of retained reserves alone, letting CGH fund the second heat exchanger station and 4 km of insulated pipework in full rather than scaling the project back. Deep-borehole geothermal assets are long-lived; member investors buying shares are essentially funding the community network that supplies 1,200 homes and St Anselm's Hospital, aligning their stake with the cooperative's mission.

Point 2: Share issues spread the financing burden across the membership instead of draining reserves earmarked for repairs and the rising outage complaints (7% of connections still fail). Instead of paying interest on a bank loan, CGH shares profits or surplus dividends with the households that own it, preserving the $630,000 a year fixed-cost cover and keeping tariffs affordable — the survey shows 84% of members would even accept a $0.06 per unit rise, giving the board room to price the service sustainably.
    Keywords: member share issue, $800,000, $450,000, $1,250,000, retained reserves, 1,200 homes
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Caldera Geothermal Heat and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CGH is launching its expanded heat network to St Anselm's Hospital and the homes along the 4 km pipework route. Consider community open days, local newspaper advertising, or targeted social media marketing to member households. Which should CGH choose to promote the expansion? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Community open days: Hosting site visits at the borehole and heat exchanger lets member households, St Anselm's Hospital estates staff and local councillors see geothermal engineering first-hand, building trust in a technology many people do not understand. Open days suit a cooperative's democratic culture — 59% of members already chose CGH for environmental reasons — and can convert sceptics into vocal advocates. However, they cost staff time and venue logistics for modest reach, and they attract mostly the already-engaged rather than new households in the 4 km extension zone.

Local newspaper advertising: Print adverts in the town's weekly paper would publicise lower bills and carbon-free heating to the extension area, reaching homeowners who do not follow CGH's channels. It is cheap per insertion and simple to book, but circulation has fallen, younger households rarely read print, response rates are hard to measure, and complex geothermal benefits cannot be explained well in a small advert.

Targeted social media marketing: Geo-targeted posts, videos of the heat exchanger and member testimonials can reach precisely the households inside the 4 km pipework route and the hospital's community, at low cost with measurable clicks, survey sign-ups and consultation attendance. They suit the 84% who would support a $0.06 per unit tariff rise and the environmentally motivated 59%, and allow CGH to run pre-launch consultations and FAQ sessions online. Risks include excluding less digitally connected elderly members and reliance on platform algorithms.

Recommendation: CGH should choose targeted social media marketing, supported by one well-publicised annual open day. Social media is the only option that reaches the right households at scale for a small workforce of 34, while honouring the cooperative's democratic consultation duty around the tariff rise. Community open days are rejected as the primary channel because of their limited reach beyond the already committed; local newspaper advertising is rejected as expensive per engaged household and weak for explaining geothermal benefits; the open day is retained as a trust-building complement, not the lead strategy.
    Keywords: geothermal, 84%, 59%, $0.06, 1,200 homes, workforce of 34
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CGH with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CGH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why community open days and newspaper advertising are rejected as lead channels.

    Question: CGH faces rising quality complaints about heat outages, with 7% of connections still affected. Explain two benefits for CGH of using quality circles to involve its technicians in solving the outage problem.
    Answer: Point 1: Quality circles give CGH's 34 employees — especially the 6 technicians lacking weld recertification — a structured, voluntary forum to analyse outage causes and fault histories, using their hands-on knowledge of the network. Engaging the people who repair faults in under 4.6 hours surfaces root causes that managers miss, such as weld micro-fractures in older connections, directly attacking the 22 complaints per month and the $630,000 fixed-cost pressure.

Point 2: When technicians propose and pilot solutions themselves, they gain pride, ownership and skill development, satisfying esteem needs within the cooperative's flat, democratic structure. Successful quality circles lower the 7% outage rate, protect supply to St Anselm's Hospital, reduce emergency call-outs, and free staff for the $1,250,000 expansion project — improving reliability at a time when 84% of members already judge tariffs acceptable enough to back growth. Dependable repairs also strengthen the hospital's continuity planning confidence, which will matter when CGH negotiates the 2027 government grant towards the second heat exchanger station.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CGH must recertify the 6 technicians whose high-pressure weld qualifications have lapsed. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional training centre. Which should CGH choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching beside the network's most experienced welders keeps repairs on the older connections moving while qualifications lapse, costs nothing in fees, and passes on CGH-specific knowledge of its borehole and pipework layouts. It protects output of 27,000 units a year and the 4.6-hour average repair time. However, CGH has no surplus senior welders while outages run at 7%, practice on live pressurised lines risks safety and further failures, and no recognised certificate is issued, which could breach insurer and hospital supply conditions.

Off-the-job training: The regional training centre course at $1,400 per technician costs $8,400 in total, gives structured high-pressure welding theory, safety drilling and a recognised certificate for all 6 technicians. Staff are away from the network during training, stretching the remaining crew, and course content may not match CGH's exact 4 km pipework alloys, so supervised on-site verification welds would still be required on return.

Decision: CGH should choose off-the-job training at the regional training centre, followed by supervised verification welds back on the network. High-pressure weld integrity is a safety and hospital-supply issue where an accredited certificate is non-negotiable; $8,400 is trivial against a $1,250,000 expansion, and the cooperative can absorb short absences by re-scheduling planned maintenance. On-the-job-only training is rejected because certifying welds practiced only on live, aging connections exposes residents and St Anselm's Hospital to failure and cannot produce the paperwork insurers demand; however, purely college-based delivery without on-site sign-off would leave CGH still uncertain about pipework-specific defects, so the combined approach is required.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $1,400, $1,250,000, 7%, workforce of 34

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase to $13.60 and the 11.3% construction materials inflation will affect CGH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): CGH's $1,250,000 expansion is funded by a member share issue and retained reserves rather than a conventional bank loan, so direct interest exposure is limited to interest payable, which already rose from $72,000 to $96,000 in Appendix 2 — a 5.25% rate environment adds modestly to financing costs if any component is loan-based. Higher rates do make the alternative of bank finance less attractive, strengthening the case for the member issue, but the cash impact is small relative to a utility-scale project.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.60 per hour): With a workforce of 34 technicians and support staff, a 7.1% rise adds roughly $1,900 per employee a year, or about $65,000 across the cooperative — meaningful against $486,000 of 2025 operating profit, and one that CGH can partly offset through the quality-circle productivity drive, the 4.6-hour repair-time gains and automation of metering.

Construction materials inflation (11.3%): Pipework, heat exchangers, insulation and trenching dominate the $1,250,000 expansion budget. An 11.3% rise on materials adds roughly $110,000–$130,000 to the project cost; even if the 2027 government grant covers 30% of eligible costs, the unfunded balance still rises, and pressure lands on the $800,000 member share issue and the $0.06 per unit tariff rise. Materials inflation also squeezes the $78 variable cost per unit of ongoing operations and maintenance.

Conclusion: The 11.3% construction materials inflation will have the greatest impact. It adds six figures directly to the expansion CGH is about to start, threatens to breach the member share issue envelope, and forces either a deeper tariff rise or delayed works on the 4 km pipework — striking the cooperative's core strategy rather than just its cost line. The minimum wage rise costs around $65,000 a year and is manageable through productivity; the interest rate rise is smallest in cash terms because CGH is largely member-funded; all three reinforce the need for early procurement and fixed-price contracts with suppliers.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 7.1%, $13.60, 11.3%, minimum wage, $1,250,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CGH. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CGH's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CGH with a well-justified judgment that construction materials inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Brightvolt EV Charging (BEC) is a public limited company in the electric vehicle charging sector, employing a workforce of 210. Founded in 2016 by Ada Mensah, the company operates 340 fast-charging bays across motorway service areas and retail parks, with a hierarchical structure and delegated regional management teams. BEC plans to invest $2,400,000 in nine 350 kW ultra-fast charging hubs along the M4 corridor, financed by a $1,500,000 share issue and a $900,000 five-year bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,575,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $18, and currently produces 260,000 units a year. BEC faces a skills gap: its field technicians lack the high-voltage certification needed to commission the new hubs.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BEC plans to finance the M4 charging hubs with a $1,500,000 share issue and a $900,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for BEC of using the share issue instead of relying solely on bank borrowing.
    Answer: Point 1: A $1,500,000 share issue raises permanent capital with no compulsory repayment schedule or interest, strengthening BEC's balance sheet while it carries fixed costs of $1,575,000 a year and a new $900,000 bank loan. The $2,400,000 hub programme can therefore proceed without over-stretching cash flow, and shareholders rather than lenders absorb the construction-phase risk before the nine 350 kW hubs open. Avoiding further lender covenants also keeps BEC free to direct operating cash into 350 kW hardware and software rather than accelerated repayments.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads ownership risk across many investors and avoids the restrictive covenants and asset charges that a pure bank loan would attach to the charging estate. For a public limited company, a well-received share issue can also lift BEC's profile with the investment community, supporting the 18.2% growth in electric-vehicle registrations behind its market, and keeps Ada Mensah's strategy free from lender interference when choosing hub locations, pricing and rollout pace along the M4 corridor.
    Keywords: share issue, $1,500,000, $900,000, $2,400,000, bank loan, $1,575,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Brightvolt EV Charging and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BEC is launching its nine ultra-fast M4 charging hubs. Consider motorway service-area advertising, a national television campaign, or an EV-manufacturer partnership marketing programme. Which should BEC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Motorway service-area advertising: Advertising inside services on the M4 places BEC directly in front of drivers just as they approach range anxiety, with dwell time to absorb the message. It targets the 57% of 800 surveyed drivers who prefer 350 kW speeds and the 63% who would pay $3 more per session for guaranteed bay availability. Costs are far below national TV, and site-specific offers can be tracked. However, reach is limited to M4 users, other motorway corridors see nothing, and competitor hubs sit in the same services, so share of voice is contested.

National television campaign: TV would build mass brand awareness for Brightvolt across the UK driving public, positioning the nine hubs as a national fast-charging standard and supporting the share issue story. However, production and airtime costs run into hundreds of thousands of dollars — hard to justify while $2,400,000 is committed to hubs and $900,000 of bank debt is outstanding — and much of the audience will never drive the M4 corridor, wasting spend for marginal incremental sessions.

EV-manufacturer partnership marketing: Co-marketing with EV makers — in-car navigation prompts, onboarding packs and dealer referrals — reaches BEC's exact target at the moment of vehicle purchase, when charging habits are formed. It locks in high-value 350 kW users with manufacturer endorsement and measurable referral volumes, and the revenue from guaranteed $3 premium sessions improves the economics. Drawbacks are dependence on partner priorities, revenue-share negotiations, and slower brand independence.

Recommendation: BEC should choose EV-manufacturer partnership marketing. It reaches qualified ultra-fast drivers at the cheapest effective cost, converts the 57% who want 350 kW speeds into hub users, and builds durable volume that underwrites the share issue and loan. Motorway service-area advertising is rejected as the sole strategy because reach ends at one corridor and competition for attention is fierce; the national television campaign is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted while $2,400,000 is locked in hubs. BEC should layer low-cost service-area signage onto the manufacturer programme to catch corridor traffic.
    Keywords: $2,400,000, $900,000, 57%, 63%, $3, 350 kW
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BEC with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BEC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why service-area advertising and television are rejected as lead strategies.

    Question: BEC faces a skills gap, with 9 of 210 field technicians lacking high-voltage certification. Explain two benefits for BEC of using performance-related bonuses to motivate technicians to complete the certification.

Linking bonuses to commissioning the nine M4 hubs on schedule focuses effort on the exact bottleneck delaying hub openings, so BEC converts its $2,400,000 investment into revenue faster.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BEC must appoint managers for the nine new M4 hubs. Consider internal promotion of existing operations staff or external recruitment of hub managers. Which should BEC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal promotion: Promoting BEC's own operations staff into hub manager roles rewards loyalty, strengthens morale and signals a clear career path in a 210-person workforce, supporting retention when high-voltage skills are scarce. External recruitment of hub managers: External hires bring high-voltage commissioning experience, fresh network-operator contacts and relieve internal bottlenecks immediately; salaries and agency fees are higher, and new managers still need cultural induction into BEC's delegated regional model and Ada Mensah's customer-experience standards. Poorly chosen external hires could clash with service-area hosts or demotivate internal candidates who expected promotion.

Decision: BEC should choose internal promotion for most hub manager posts, with one or two external hires only where no certified internal candidate exists. Internal promotion is faster, cheaper and motivating across the 210-person workforce, leverages existing service-area relationships, and keeps Ada Mensah's standards consistent across the M4; it also complements the bonus scheme driving certification. External-first recruitment is rejected as costlier and culturally riskier as a general approach, though BEC should use external search selectively if certified internal candidates cannot cover all nine hubs. In all cases every hub manager, promoted or hired, must hold current high-voltage certification before commissioning, and external hires should still complete BEC's high-voltage audit before solo supervision.

    Answer: Minimum wage increase (6.7%, to $13.23 per hour): With a workforce of 210, mainly field technicians and site staff, a 6.7% rise adds roughly $1,750 per employee a year, or about $367,000 across the workforce — very significant against 2025 operating profit of $702,000. The minimum wage rise is the second-largest, at around $367,000 across 210 staff, while the interest rate rise is smallest in cash terms and can be hedged by fixing the $900,000 loan; BEC should respond with off-peak PPAs, dynamic pricing, the $3 guaranteed-bay premium and rigorous site productivity.

--- STEM ---
Saltmarsh Harbour Ferries (SHF) is a sole trader in the coastal passenger transport sector, employing a workforce of 12. Founded in 2012 by Captain Owen Pryce, the business runs two vessels on 14-minute crossings between Saltmarsh quay and the island of St Bride, with an autocratic leadership style and a hands-on, close-knit team. SHF plans to invest $480,000 in a new 60-seat hybrid ferry, financed by the sale of the older vessel for $150,000 and a $330,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.40 a unit and a selling price of $16, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. SHF faces rising labour turnover, which reached 21% among seasonal deck crew last summer.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SHF plans to finance the new hybrid ferry with the $150,000 sale of the older vessel and a $330,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for SHF of using the sale of the older vessel instead of relying solely on the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Selling the older vessel raises $150,000 without any interest or repayment obligation, cutting the amount SHF must borrow from $480,000 to $330,000 and reducing the strain of loan repayments while fixed costs already stand at $216,000 a year. Lower borrowing also means interest payable — $34,000 in 2025 — will rise less when the 5.5% base rate feeds through, directly protecting Owen Pryce's profit.

Point 2: The older vessel is ageing and costly to maintain, so selling it removes rising repair bills and safety risk while funding the $480,000 hybrid replacement. Retaining full control matters to a sole trader: by using the sale proceeds, Owen Pryce avoids extra lender conditions on how the 60-seat hybrid is deployed, keeps fare-setting freedom at $16, and shows good asset management to any future lender assessing the loan application.
    Keywords: sale of the older vessel, $150,000, $330,000, $480,000, bank loan, $216,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Saltmarsh Harbour Ferries and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SHF is launching the new hybrid ferry service to St Bride. Consider local radio advertising, summer brochure leaflet drops, or social media fare-deal campaigns. Which should SHF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local radio advertising: A spot on the regional station would reach commuters and holidaymakers planning St Bride trips, building awareness of the hybrid ferry with 14-minute crossings and family tickets 25% off. Radio suits the drive-then-sail audience on Saltmarsh quay routes and is more affordable than national media for a 12-person business. However, listener attention is fragmented, recall of fare details is low without repetition, and coverage beyond the Saltmarsh catchment is weak — many island-bound visitors come from much further afield.

Summer brochure leaflet drops: Dropping the Summer 2027 brochure (already read by 420 surveyed passengers) through regional hotels, holiday parks and tourist information centres reaches high-intent travellers with full fare tables, the hybrid-electric message and the family discount. Print is trusted by older island visitors and cheap to produce; wastage occurs on households with no travel plans, and print cannot create urgency or capture last-minute bookings.

Social media fare-deal campaigns: Geo-targeted social posts offering weekend fare deals, hybrid-ferry features and guaranteed-seat upsells speak directly to the 66% willing to pay up to $4 more for a guaranteed seat and the 71% who rate hybrid ferries important. Deals can be switched on for peak weekends, tracked through booking codes, and shared by island community groups — ideal for a 12-person team with limited time, and measurable end-to-end. Risks are reliance on platform reach and weaker penetration of older, non-digital islanders.

Recommendation: SHF should choose social media fare-deal campaigns. They reach exactly the passengers its research identifies, deliver measurable bookings at the lowest cost, and suit the sole trader's limited hours; the guaranteed-seat and hybrid messages differentiate SHF from competing transport. Local radio is rejected as too broad and costly per actual booking for a single-route ferry; brochure drops are rejected as the lead channel because they lack urgency and tracking, though a small print run in hotels should remain to reach older visitors; social campaigns should run continuously through the season.
    Keywords: $16, 25% off, 66%, 71%, $4, hybrid
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SHF with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SHF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why local radio and brochure drops are rejected as lead channels.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SHF's seasonal deck crew labour turnover reached 21% last summer. Explain two benefits for SHF of using job enrichment to reduce this labour turnover.
    Answer: Point 1: Job enrichment gives deck crew upgraded responsibilities — cross-training as mates, running passenger safety briefings and overseeing hybrid charging checks — making the role more varied and satisfying, which lifts esteem and reduces the boredom that drives summer deckhands to quit. With seasonal bookings up 12%, keeping trained crew able to supervise the new 60-seat hybrid protects service levels at peak.

Point 2: Enriched roles build loyalty and skill depth in a 12-person team, reducing recruitment and re-induction costs, since every departure forces Owen Pryce personally to recruit and brief replacements. --- STEM ---
Carrick Shelf Analytics (CSA) is a private limited company in the retail technology (IoT) sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2017 by Matteo Ricci, the business supplies smart-shelf sensor systems to national supermarket chains and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. CSA plans to invest $950,000 in a new computer-vision smart-shelf platform with recyclable sensor housings, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $340,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.50 a unit and a selling price of $26.50, and currently produces 60,000 units a year.     Answer: Point 1: A ten-year bank loan spreads the cost of the $950,000 expansion across the working life of the computer-vision smart-shelf platform instead of draining CSA's cash reserves at once. Keeping part of the $350,000 retained profit inside the business preserves a liquidity buffer to absorb the 9.8% rise in semiconductor and shelf-sensor component costs without breaching supermarket supply agreements or delaying the 140-store rollout.

Point 2: Fixed equal repayments make the $600,000 debt predictable, so CSA can budget its cash flow precisely alongside fixed costs of $340,000 a year and interest payable, which rose from $55,000 to $78,000. Because the loan is external debt rather than new share capital, Matteo Ricci retains full ownership and control of the private limited company; no outside investor gains voting rights, and the flat laissez-faire structure can continue without shareholder interference in day-to-day decisions about the 38 employees and the sensor platform.

--- STEM ---
Bramblewick Civic Software (BCS) is a public limited company in the public-sector software (govtech) sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2013 by Yusuf Rahman, the business supplies council management and permit-processing software to local authorities across the country and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $520,000 a year, a variable cost of $95 a unit and a selling price of $135, and currently produces 22,000 units a year.   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BCS plans to raise $700,000 of its $1,100,000 expansion through a share issue. Explain two advantages for BCS of using a share issue rather than a bank loan.

The AI permit-processing platform will take time to generate revenue from the 66% of 320 surveyed council procurement officers willing to upgrade within 18 months; equity financing lets BCS fund that ramp-up without breaching cash reserves or missing council service-level commitments.

Point 2: Selling shares to a wider investor base spreads the risk of an ambitious $1,100,000 public-sector technology project across many shareholders rather than concentrating it on BCS and its retained profit alone. As a public limited company, BCS can also use the issue to raise its profile with council clients and future investors, and the permanent capital strengthens the balance sheet — reflected in capital employed of $11,400,000 — supporting further contracts without granting any lender security over the platform or diluting control in the same way debt covenants might restrict autocratic decision-making.

Cost of sales rose proportionally from $3,840,000 to $4,560,000, holding gross profit growth in line with revenue and lifting gross profit from $5,760,000 to $6,840,000. Operating profit increased from $1,920,000 to $2,508,000, up 30.6%, a faster rate than revenue — evidence of genuine scale efficiency and tight control of fixed costs at $520,000 a year. Capital employed rose from $9,600,000 to $11,400,000, exactly in line with revenue growth, while interest payable climbed from $140,000 to $165,000.

Evaluation: Operating performance has improved even though the top-line conversion of revenue into gross profit stayed flat at 60.0%. The operating improvement from 20.0% to 22.0% shows BCS converting extra revenue into profit efficiently, and the return on capital employed confirms the larger asset base is working harder, not idle. The unchanged 60.0% gross figure suggests limited scope to raise licence prices further given council IT budgets are capped at a 2.0% increase; future margin gains must come from AI automation reducing delivery cost per permit. Residual risks: interest payable is rising, quality complaints cost engineer time, and the 2.0% council budget cap could stall upgrade deals.

Conclusion: BCS's financial performance has improved. Operating profit grew faster than revenue and capital employed, the flat gross conversion was held at a healthy 60.0%, and the return on capital employed rose from 20.0% to 22.0%. The improvement is real but narrow — BCS must now deliver AI-driven cost savings to protect margins against the budget cap.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 4.25% to 4.75%, the 4.8% minimum wage increase and the cap of 2.0% on council IT budgets will affect BCS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 4.75%): BCS is financing its $1,100,000 expansion through a $700,000 share issue and $400,000 retained profit, so it has no new variable-rate loan and the direct extra interest cost is limited to the modest interest payable of $140,000 to $165,000 on existing borrowing. The indirect effect is that councils themselves face higher borrowing costs and may delay capital projects, and BCS's own future loan capacity for phase two narrows. Manageable, but worth watching.

Minimum wage increase (4.8%, from $13.30 to $13.94 per hour): With 64 staff, mainly developers, liaison officers and support staff, BCS will feel the 4.8% rise mainly among junior and support roles near the minimum wage. If 24 staff sit near $13.30 an hour, the annual base is roughly 24 staff × 2,000 hours × $13.30 = $638,400, so the rise adds roughly $30,600 a year — meaningful but not decisive against $2,508,000 of operating profit, and partly offset by productivity from the AI platform.

Council IT budget cap (2.0% maximum increase next year): This is a demand-side shock aimed directly at BCS's customer base. With council pay and energy costs forecast to rise 6.5%, discretionary software spend is the squeeze target: new AI permit-processing licences risk being deferred or shrunk even though 66% of 320 surveyed officers want to upgrade. The cap also pressures renewal pricing across the 27 live council contracts, threatening BCS's 18.75% revenue growth and the case for its $700,000 share issue.

Conclusion: The 2.0% cap on council IT budgets will have the greatest impact. BCS sells almost entirely into councils, so capping their discretionary technology spend directly suppresses BCS's sales pipeline, renewal uplift and expansion case, whereas the wage rise adds only about $30,600 a year and the interest-rate move barely touches an equity-financed balance sheet. BCS must respond with hard ROI evidence — the 14-day to 6-day permit turnaround and measurable savings — to win scarce budget within the cap.

--- STEM ---
Aldermont Route Optimisation (ARO) is a private limited company in the logistics technology (SaaS) sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2016 by Helena Duarte, the business supplies route-optimization software to national freight and delivery fleets and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ARO plans to invest $1,000,000 in a new live-traffic AI route-optimization engine, financed by $700,000 of venture capital and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $630,000 a year, a variable cost of $140 a unit and a selling price of $210, and currently produces 20,000 units a year. ARO faces two operational problems: customer onboarding is taking 6 weeks instead of the 4-week target, and labour turnover among customer-support staff has reached 17%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ARO plans to raise $700,000 of the $1,000,000 expansion through venture capital. Explain two advantages for ARO of venture capital rather than a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Venture capital carries no fixed repayment schedule and no monthly interest, so ARO avoids straining cash flow while fixed costs are already $630,000 a year. The live-traffic AI engine will take months to generate new subscription revenue from the 68% of 500 surveyed fleet managers willing to switch for a fuel-saving guarantee; equity financing lets ARO fund that ramp-up without breaching covenants or repossession risk on the platform.

Point 2: Venture capitalists typically bring logistics-sector expertise, introductions to national fleets and board credibility that accelerate enterprise sales — worth far more than cash to a 52-person private limited company competing against larger incumbents. Unlike a bank, a venture investor shares the downside if the engine launch slips beyond the 4-week onboarding target recovery, and Helena Duarte keeps control of daily operations while gaining a partner motivated to see the $1,000,000 investment succeed.
    Keywords: venture capital, route-optimization, $700,000, $1,000,000, $630,000, retained profit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Aldermont Route Optimisation and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ARO is launching its live-traffic AI route-optimization engine to national freight and delivery fleets. Consider a weekly webinar and demo series with live traffic simulations, advertising in Fleet Management Weekly trade magazine, or sponsoring a national logistics conference. Which should ARO choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Webinar and demo series with live traffic simulations: A weekly webinar lets ARO prove its strongest asset — 96% of 18,400 routes generated in under 3 minutes, delivering 11.5% average fuel savings — in front of exactly the 68% of the 500 surveyed fleet managers willing to switch for a 15% fuel-saving guarantee. Demonstrations are interactive, capture leads automatically, and cost little compared with a conference stand. Drawbacks are that some senior managers avoid webinars and attendance can fade after the first sessions, so ARO must keep content sharp and follow up personally within 48 hours.

Fleet Management Weekly advertising: A trade-magazine campaign reaches a targeted logistics readership and builds brand credibility cheaply over several months. However, print advertising is passive and hard to measure; fleet managers rarely switch SaaS providers on the strength of an advert, and the 11.5% fuel-saving proof is far more persuasive shown live than described on paper.

National logistics conference sponsorship: Sponsoring a headline national conference puts ARO in front of hundreds of fleet decision-makers and anchors its brand beside industry leaders. The cost is high for a 52-person business already carrying a $1,000,000 build, attendance includes non-buyers, and a one-off event generates leads unevenly rather than a dependable weekly pipeline.

Recommendation: ARO should choose the webinar and demo series. It is the only option that demonstrates live performance to the 68% of switch-ready fleet managers at low cost, generates measurable weekly leads, and lets ARO quantify 11.5% fuel savings in front of each prospect. The magazine advert is rejected as too passive to convert, and the conference sponsorship is rejected as a single, expensive burst of exposure unsuited to a long enterprise sales cycle and an expansion already absorbing venture capital.
    Keywords: route-optimization, $1,000,000, 68%, 500, 11.5%, 96%

Higher retention saves replacement and retraining costs, protects the 11.5% fuel-saving commitments clients expect, and makes ARO's flat structure genuinely agile — democratic participation keeps the whole 52-person workforce aligned behind the $1,000,000 engine launch without adding expensive management layers.

--- STEM ---
Harborne Vision Institute (HVI) is a private limited company in the private healthcare sector, specialising in ophthalmology, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Dr Lena Harborne, HVI operates two eye clinics in the Harborne district and uses a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $306,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.50 a unit and a selling price of $40.00, and currently produces 78,000 units a year (treatment episodes).   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HVI plans to finance part of its laser expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HVI of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.

Every dollar not paid to a lender can absorb the 8.8% rise in ophthalmic lens and consumable costs, helping HVI hold its $40.00 selling price and protect the $25.50 contribution per treatment unit without squeezing patients or margins.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $320,000 is available without putting the new $920,000 laser eye-surgery suite at risk of repossession if demand disappoints. It also preserves Dr Lena Harborne's ownership and control, since no external lender can impose conditions on how the second suite is staffed or run. Retained profit is also flexible — it carries no fixed monthly repayment schedule, unlike the loan, which matters while the 16% nursing-staff turnover is being addressed and waiting times stabilise.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $320,000, $600,000, $306,000, laser

Cost per reached patient is low, engagement is measurable, and the eco-conscious, health-focused positioning of the new suite with solar panels can be shown directly. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, so content must be medically accurate.

Recommendation: HVI should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment already identified in its research (59% and 44%), costs far less than television for a 38-person business, scales better than local radio, and reinforces the clinic's modern, patient-centred image. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a two-site clinic; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is too narrow for county-wide laser referrals, though short local bursts could support the launch. Influencers alone lack mass reach, so HVI should pair them with its own patient-referral programme and in-clinic leaflets.
