    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 8.8% rise in input costs will affect HVI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If HVI's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $4,500 a year to financing costs — real but modest next to $306,000 of fixed costs. Higher rates also make further borrowing for clinic number three more expensive, could raise renewal quotes on the hire-purchase-style equipment leases, and may make patients more cautious about elective procedures, softening the 4.6% growth in private eye-care spending. HVI can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.56 per hour): HVI employs 38 staff, mostly nurses, technicians and reception alongside clinical leadership; clinical pay sits well above minimum wage, but support, cleaning and administrative roles are affected. If even 15 of the 38 staff sit near the minimum wage on roughly 40-hour weeks, the 5.9% rise adds roughly $1,250 per affected worker per year — around $19,000 a year — on top of the 16% turnover already inflating recruitment and the $820-per-head retraining bill. The impact is material but concentrated on the support-staff budget.

Input cost inflation (8.8% ophthalmic lens and consumables): HVI's variable cost of $14.50 a unit is dominated by lenses, viscoelastics and sterile consumables. An 8.8% rise on the consumable share (say 60% of the variable cost, $8.70) adds roughly $0.77 per treatment unit; at 78,000 units a year that is about $60,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $25.50 toward $24.73 and eroding roughly 3% of margin. The private eye-care market grew 4.6%, so passing on only part of the increase risks a competitive backlash while absorbing it all bites directly into ROCE.

Conclusion: The 8.8% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 78,000 units sold, totalling roughly $60,000 a year and steadily eroding the $25.50 contribution margin that justifies the $920,000 laser suite. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious risk, concentrated in support roles and amplified by 16% turnover, while the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms (about $4,500 a year on the drawn loan) and can be managed by fixing the rate. Even so, HVI must address all three — negotiate consumable contracts, redesign support-role rosters productively, and review the loan structure — or the improved cost-of-sales performance shown in Appendix 2 will unwind.

--- STEM ---
Hexfield Code Academy (HCA) is a private limited company in the education sector, specialising in digital-skills training, employing a workforce of 26. Founded in 2018 by Rhea Calloway, HCA runs coding bootcamps for career-changers and uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. HCA plans to invest $650,000 in a second campus in Leeds with expanded data-analytics labs and solar panels, financed by a $400,000 five-year bank loan and a $250,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $715,000 a year, a variable cost of $450 a unit and a selling price of $1,000, and currently produces 6,800 units a year (course enrolments). HCA faces two problems: an instructor skills gap in cloud computing and rising learner complaints about outdated course materials.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HCA plans to finance part of its Leeds expansion with a bank loan and a share issue. Explain two advantages for HCA of using a share issue instead of a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $250,000 with no repayments and no interest, protecting HCA's cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $715,000 a year and a $400,000 five-year bank loan. Every dollar not paid to a lender can absorb the 10.8% rise in cloud licensing and laptop costs, helping HCA hold its $1,000 course price and protect the $550 contribution per enrolment rather than passing costs straight on to learners.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads the ownership of HCA across more shareholders, so the expansion risk is shared rather than borne by Rhea Calloway alone, and no extra collateral is required over the Leeds campus assets. It also avoids the repayment-pressure and covenant risk of a larger loan at a time when the base interest rate has just risen from 4.25% to 5.0% — interest payable already rose from $30,000 to $41,000, and a bigger loan would compound that burden just as the Leeds site ramps up enrolments.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $250,000, $400,000, $715,000, $1,000

However, HCA is a 26-person academy funding a $650,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most viewers neither want to change careers into data analytics nor live near Leeds, so most spend would be wasted on the wrong audience. Television is also hard to measure beyond broad reach, which a private training business needs to justify its marketing budget.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is cheap, reaches Leeds and surrounding commuter belt repeatedly, and suits time-boxed messages such as enrolment deadlines for the new intake. Its weakness is reach — HCA's bootcamps already serve career-changers online nationally, producing 6,800 course enrolments a year, so a purely local station cannot drive the volume needed for the Leeds campus's capacity or build brand outside the Yorkshire region.

Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with data-career YouTubers and LinkedIn creators targets exactly the 57% of surveyed learners who would enrol on a data-analytics bootcamp and the 46% who would pay up to $150 more per month for evening and weekend classes. Content can demonstrate real student outcomes, cost per reached learner is low, engagement is measurable, and the solar-powered Leeds campus and completion-rate story (87%, up from 79%) give influencers credible material. Results take time to compound and depend on influencer credibility, but the audience match is far better than TV or radio.

Recommendation: HCA should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment already identified in its research (57% and 46%), costs far less than television for a 26-person business, scales nationally where local radio cannot, and lets prospects see the campus and graduate outcomes directly. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is too narrow for a national online bootcamp, though short Leeds radio bursts could support the launch affordably. Influencers alone lack broadcast reach, so HCA should pair them with open days and referral incentives for alumni.

--- STEM ---
Vital Roots Meal Prep (VRM) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, specialising in plant-based meal-prep delivery, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2020 by Sofia Marin, VRM prepares and delivers weekly plant-based meal boxes across the Bristol region and uses a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VRM plans to invest $780,000 in a second kitchen with a refrigerated delivery fleet, financed by a $450,000 hire purchase agreement on the vans and $330,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $247,500 a year, a variable cost of $7.25 a unit and a selling price of $12.75, and currently produces 96,000 units a year (meal boxes). VRM faces two problems: food waste of 7.4% in the kitchen and labour turnover of 19% among delivery drivers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VRM plans to finance part of its second kitchen with a $450,000 hire purchase agreement on the vans. Explain two advantages for VRM of using retained profit to fund part of the expansion instead of relying on hire purchase.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $330,000 of retained profit instead of extending hire purchase costs VRM nothing in interest or finance charges, protecting the $5.50 contribution per meal box at a time when input costs have risen 11.2% and fixed costs already stand at $247,500 a year. Every dollar not paid as hire-purchase interest can absorb the plant-protein and compostable-packaging inflation or fund the new kitchen's launch marketing, helping VRM keep its $12.75 price competitive against other meal-prep firms.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no repossession risk on the refrigerated vans if weekly payments are missed or demand dips over winter, so VRM keeps full ownership and control of the delivery fleet from day one. It also avoids adding to the hire-purchase burden at a time when the base interest rate has risen from 3.75% to 4.5% — interest payable already rose from $15,000 to $24,000 — and unlike external finance it imposes no usage mileage or maintenance conditions on how the second kitchen and its vans are operated.
    Keywords: retained profit, hire purchase, $330,000, $450,000, $247,500, $12.75
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Vital Roots Meal Prep and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VRM is launching its second kitchen and expanded delivery zone. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VRM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national television campaign would put the Vital Roots brand in front of millions of viewers quickly and could build strong awareness of the plant-based subscription offer. However, VRM is a 52-employee regional business funding a $780,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most viewers live far outside the Bristol delivery zone, where delivery time averages 1.8 days — distant customers cannot receive fresh boxes, so spend would be largely wasted. Television also suits mass FMCG brands, not subscription meal services that need targeted sign-ups.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper, reaches Bristol-area commuters repeatedly at breakfast and drive-time, and suits messages such as subscription discounts for new postcodes. Its limitation is narrow and aging reach; the health-conscious plant-based audience skews younger, and local radio cannot build the national brand reputation VRM needs for wholesale or multi-site growth, nor target by diet or delivery postcode.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with Bristol-based nutritionists, chefs and fitness creators targets exactly the 63% of surveyed subscribers interested in fully compostable packaging and the 49% who cite plant-based health benefits, with measurable sign-ups and strong storytelling potential around defect-rate improvements (3.6% to 2.2%) and food waste falling from 9.1% to 7.4%. Results are slower to compound than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but cost per acquired subscriber is low and conversion can be tracked directly through discount codes.

Recommendation: VRM should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment identified in its research (63% packaging interest, 49% health motivation), costs far less than television for a 52-employee regional operator, scales across all new postcodes faster than local radio, and lets VRM show the second kitchen's quality improvements. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted beyond the delivery zone; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its audience skews older and cannot be geo-targeted to new routes, though short drive-time bursts could support the launch. Influencers alone lack broadcast reach, so VRM should pair them with introductory subscriber offers and referral discounts.
    Keywords: compostable packaging, 63%, 49%, 96,000, meal boxes, $780,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VRM with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VRM with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VRM's labour turnover is 19% among delivery drivers and food waste of 7.4% persists in the kitchen. Explain two benefits for VRM of autocratic leadership in this context.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives VRM fast, clear decisions on route planning, load-out and fridge temperature protocols — essential when drivers leave the kitchen on tight 1.8-day delivery windows and when food-safety (food-safety) breaches could destroy the whole brand. A single decisive manager can re-plan deliveries mid-week without committee delay, directly protecting delivery reliability and the fall in complaints from 41 to 23 per month.

Point 2: Autocratic direction keeps kitchen routines disciplined and uniform, which is exactly what VRM needs to push food waste below the 7.4% level and toward the 5% target: one standard for portioning, stock rotation and labelling, enforced consistently across pickers and packers. In a 52-person operation with 16 of 52 staff still untrained in food-safety, clear instruction reduces errors quickly, contains the 2.2% mislabel defect rate and tightens portion control, while turnover of 19% is addressed through induction and pay review rather than diluted decision-making.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VRM's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has VRM's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.

Disadvantage: Compostable materials cost more than conventional plastic, increasing the $7.25 variable cost per box and squeezing margins unless the $1.50 premium is accepted by enough subscribers or backed by the new second-kitchen scale. Any failure in the new packaging — weaker seals, shorter chill life or leaks in transit — would also raise the 2.2% mislabel/defect rate, increase food waste above the 7.4% level and destroy the 1.8-day delivery promise that underpins VRM's reputation with retail and corporate customers.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in input costs will affect VRM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If the $450,000 hire purchase agreement on the vans is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $3,400 a year to finance costs — real but modest next to $247,500 of fixed costs. Higher rates also make further borrowing for a third kitchen more expensive, could raise the cost of renewing the fleet, and may temper consumer appetite for subscription meal services, slowing the 6.1% growth in plant-based spending. VRM can fix the hire-purchase rate or accelerate retained-profit repayments to limit exposure.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.30 per hour): VRM employs 52 staff, many drivers, pickers and kitchen operatives near or below middle-band wages. If roughly 30 of the 52 staff sit close to the minimum wage on 40-hour weeks, the 6.4% rise adds roughly $1,660 per affected worker a year — around $50,000 a year — on top of 19% driver turnover already inflating recruitment and onboarding costs. This is materially larger than the rate impact and lands directly on VRM's largest cost line, wages, though many Bristol drivers are paid above minimum.

Input cost inflation (11.2% plant-protein and compostable packaging): VRM's variable cost of $7.25 a unit is dominated by plant proteins, grains, fresh produce and packaging. An 11.2% rise on, say, 70% of the variable cost ($5.08) adds roughly $0.57 per box; at 96,000 boxes a year that is about $55,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $5.50 toward $4.93 and eroding roughly 10% of margin. With 6.1% growth in plant-based spending intact, VRM can pass through part of the increase via the $1.50 compostable premium, but full pass-through would surrender its price edge against own-label supermarket ready meals.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 96,000 boxes, totalling roughly $55,000 a year and steadily eroding the $5.50 contribution margin that justifies the $780,000 second-kitchen expansion. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious risk, around $50,000 a year on support and delivery roles and amplified by 19% turnover, while the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms (roughly $3,400 a year) and can be managed by fixing the hire-purchase rate. VRM should therefore renegotiate protein supply contracts, push the compostable premium and optimise routes — or the gross-margin gains in Appendix 2 will be reversed within a year.
    Keywords: 4.5%, 6.4%, 11.2%, $13.30, $7.25, $450,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VRM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VRM's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VRM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic (RPS) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, specialising in physiotherapy and sports rehabilitation, employing a workforce of 31. Founded in 2015 by Dr Natalie Rowan, RPS uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership from its Guildford clinic. RPS plans to invest $540,000 in a second clinic in Woking with a hydrotherapy pool and water-recycling technology, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $342,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.00 a unit and a selling price of $60.00, and currently produces 42,000 units a year (treatment sessions). RPS faces two problems: a skills gap in qualified sports physiotherapists and rising patient complaints about waiting times.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RPS plans to finance part of its Woking expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for RPS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $240,000 of retained profit instead of borrowing more costs RPS nothing in interest or repayment charges, protecting cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $342,000 a year and a $300,000 five-year bank loan. Every dollar not paid to a lender can absorb the 9.2% rise in medical equipment and consumable costs, helping RPS hold its $60.00 session price and protect the $38.00 contribution per session without squeezing patients or referring clinicians.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $240,000 is available without putting the new $540,000 Woking clinic or its hydrotherapy pool at risk of repossession if demand disappoints. It also preserves Dr Natalie Rowan's ownership and control, since no external lender can impose conditions on how Woking is staffed, marketed or equipped. At a time when the base interest rate has risen from 4.0% to 4.75%, keeping borrowings low also shields RPS's variable-rate loan from further cost increases and keeps the 12-day waiting list affordable to run down.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $240,000, $300,000, $540,000, $342,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RPS is launching its second clinic in Woking with a hydrotherapy pool. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should RPS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national television campaign would put the Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic brand in front of millions of viewers quickly and could build awareness of the hydrotherapy offer. However, RPS is a 31-employee clinic funding a $540,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most viewers live far outside the Guildford–Woking catchment or have no need for private physiotherapy, so most spend would be wasted. Television also suits mass consumer brands rather than appointment-led healthcare, where local trust and clinician reputation drive bookings.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper, reaches Guildford and Woking commuters repeatedly, and suits appointment-led messages such as early-morning sessions and waiting-time reductions. Its limitation is reach beyond the catchment — patients travel from across Surrey and Hampshire for specialist sports rehabilitation, so a purely local station cannot fill the Woking hydrotherapy pool or build county-wide referral relationships with clubs and gyms.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with local sports clubs, fitness creators and post-injury recovery bloggers targets exactly the 61% of surveyed patients who would use the Woking clinic and the 47% willing to pay up to $20 more per session for early-morning appointments. Content can show real recoveries, cost per reached patient is low, engagement is measurable through booking codes, and the water-recycling and sustainability story of the hydrotherapy pool gives influencers distinctive material. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but the audience match is far better.

Recommendation: RPS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment identified in its research (61% Woking interest, 47% early-morning premium), costs far less than television for a 31-person clinic, scales across the county where local radio cannot, and showcases the hydrotherapy pool effectively. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is too narrow for county-wide sports-referral growth, though short Woking drive-time bursts could support the launch. Influencers alone lack broadcast reach, so RPS should pair them with club partnerships and GP referral letters.

--- STEM ---
Halcyon Montessori Preschool (HMP) is a private limited company in the education and childcare sector, specialising in early-years education, employing a workforce of 22. Founded in 2013 by Clara Whitmore, HMP operates a preschool in Teddington and uses a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. HMP plans to invest $380,000 in a purpose-built second preschool with a nature garden, financed by a $250,000 ten-year bank loan and a $130,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $155,000 a year, a variable cost of $2.30 a unit and a selling price of $8.50, and currently produces 96,000 units a year (child sessions). HMP faces two problems: staff turnover of 21% among nursery practitioners and rising parent complaints about waiting lists for places.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HMP plans to finance part of its second preschool with a $250,000 bank loan and a $130,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for HMP of using a share issue instead of a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $130,000 with no repayments and no interest, protecting HMP's flat cash-flow profile at a time when fixed costs already stand at $155,000 a year. Every dollar not paid to a lender can absorb the 8.4% rise in toys, learning materials and food costs or fund nature-garden maintenance, helping HMP keep its $8.50 session price stable for parents while the waiting list averages 6 weeks.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads ownership and risk across more than one shareholder rather than loading everything onto the $250,000 bank loan, and no collateral is required over the Teddington property or the new purpose-built site. It also avoids deeper repayment pressure at a time when the base interest rate has risen from 5.00% to 5.75% — interest payable already rose from $9,000 to $17,000 — and unlike borrowing it imposes no covenants on staffing ratios, fees or how the second preschool and nature garden are run.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $130,000, $250,000, $155,000, nature garden
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Halcyon Montessori Preschool and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HMP is opening its second preschool with a nature garden. Consider a local newspaper campaign, local radio sponsorship, or parenting influencer marketing on social media. Which should HMP choose to promote the opening? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local newspaper campaign: A full-page feature or regular adverts in the Teddington Gazette would put the nature-garden Montessori offer directly in front of local families, and newspapers remain trusted by parents researching childcare. However, readership is declining, younger parents increasingly skip print, and a one-off feature generates a short burst of enquiries that fades before the 6-week waiting list can be converted into enrolments at the second site.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio reaches commuting parents at breakfast and drive-time repeatedly and is cheap, suiting time-boxed messages such as open-day invitations and limited places for the autumn term. Its limitation is undifferentiated reach — most listeners are not local parents of preschool-age children, messaging cannot show the nature garden or the calm Montessori environment, and radio cannot capture registrations directly, so conversion must happen through a phone number or web link with no proof of fit.

Parenting influencer marketing on social media: Working with local parenting bloggers, Montessori educators and family-lifestyle creators targets exactly the 58% of surveyed parents who would choose a Montessori setting with a nature garden and the 45% willing to pay up to $1.20 more per session for extended hours. Content can tour the garden, testimonial-led posts can address waiting-list anxieties, and discount/referral codes make enrolments measurable. Results build more slowly than broadcast media and depend on influencer authenticity, but cost per registered family is low and alignment with HMP's values is high.

Recommendation: HMP should choose parenting influencer marketing on social media. It reaches the precise segment identified in its research (58% nature-garden preference, 45% extended-hours interest), costs far less than repeating national advertising, targets local parents better than either newspaper or radio, and lets prospective families see the nature garden directly. A newspaper campaign is rejected as short-lived and increasingly unread by target parents; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its audience is undifferentiated and cannot showcase the garden, though occasional 10-second pre-open drive-time spots could supplement it. Influencers alone lack broadcast reach, so HMP should pair them with open days and an alumni-parent referral scheme.
    Keywords: nature garden, 58%, 45%, $1.20, 6 weeks, $380,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HMP with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HMP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspaper and radio are rejected.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 6.8% minimum wage increase and the 8.4% rise in input costs will affect HMP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.00% to 5.75%): If HMP's $250,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $1,875 a year to financing costs — real but small next to $155,000 of fixed costs. Higher rates also make further borrowing for the second site more expensive, may dampen consumer confidence in discretionary early-years spending, and raise the cost of servicing the loan ahead of the new preschool's opening. HMP can partly shield itself by fixing the rate or issuing more shares.

Minimum wage increase (6.8%, to $13.14 per hour): Early-years education is labour-intensive — wages dominate HMP's cost structure, and many nursery practitioners sit near the minimum wage. If roughly 18 of the 22 staff are near it on 40-hour weeks, the 6.8% rise adds roughly $1,840 per affected worker a year — around $33,000 a year — on top of 21% practitioner turnover already inflating recruitment and induction costs, and the 7 of 22 staff still awaiting safeguarding certification. This lands directly on HMP's largest cost line and is compounded by the April 2026 timing, mid-expansion.

Input cost inflation (8.4% toys, learning materials and food): HMP's variable cost of $2.30 a unit includes play materials, food for extended hours and garden supplies. An 8.4% rise on the materials-and-food share (say 60% of variable cost, $1.38) adds roughly $0.12 per session; at 96,000 sessions a year that is about $11,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $6.20 toward $6.08 — under 2% of margin. With 4.9% growth in private early-years spending, HMP can absorb or modestly pass this on through the $1.20 extended-hours premium (the 45% willing to pay more), but parents remain price-sensitive given waiting-list-driven scarcity pricing power is limited.

Conclusion: The 6.8% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Early-years preschools are people-heavy businesses, and roughly $33,000 a year on near-minimum wages lands on top of a 21% turnover crisis HMP is already managing badly — it threatens the 96% satisfaction rating and the second-site launch directly. The input-cost rise is the next risk, about $11,000 a year and manageable through pricing; the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms (roughly $1,875 a year) and can be managed by fixing the loan rate. HMP should therefore restructure rosters, seek efficiency in extended-hours delivery, consider a modest fee review justified by nature-garden quality, and complete safeguarding training promptly — or the Appendix 2 profit gains will be unwound by the April 2026 wage bill.
    Keywords: 5.75%, 6.8%, 8.4%, $13.14, $2.30, $250,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HMP. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HMP's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HMP with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Wexley Plasterboard (WPB) is a private limited company in the building materials sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2011 by Priya Wexley, the business manufactures gypsum plasterboard with recycled-paper facings for the construction industry and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. WPB plans to invest $1,400,000 in a new automated drying and cutting line, financed by a $900,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.50, and currently produces 170,000 units a year. WPB faces two operational problems: a board defect rate of 2.6% with rising cutting-line waste, and labour turnover among machine operators has reached 14%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WPB plans to finance part of its automated drying and cutting line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for WPB of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs WPB nothing in interest or repayment charges, which protects cash flow at a time when the company already carries fixed costs of $600,000 a year and has committed to a $900,000 ten-year bank loan for the $1,400,000 automated drying and cutting line. Avoiding interest on the retained $500,000 leaves more operating cash to absorb the 9.8% rise in gypsum and recycled paper input costs, so WPB can defend its $12.50 selling price against cheaper imports and keep the 2.6% defect-reduction programme funded without straining merchant order books.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $500,000 is available without putting the new $1,400,000 line at risk of repossession if construction demand disappoints. It also preserves Priya Wexley's ownership and control of the private limited company, since no lender can impose covenants or conditions on how the automated line is operated, priced or expanded in later phases — particularly valuable while housing starts are only growing 3.2% a year.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $500,000, $900,000, $1,400,000, $600,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wexley Plasterboard and its expansion decision.

However, colour space is expensive, the readership is broad — much of it is architects or DIY readers outside WPB's merchant coverage — and a single insertion gives no measurable response data, making it hard to judge against a tight launch budget on top of an $900,000 loan commitment.

Regional radio sponsorship: Sponsoring a drive-time building programme is far cheaper than national print and would reach site managers and merchant staff commuting across WPB's Derbyshire catchment with high frequency. Its weakness is narrow geographic reach: WPB supplies merchant chains nationally and wants the 71% of surveyed merchants who would stock certified low-carbon plasterboard to hear the message everywhere, not just regionally. Radio also struggles to convey technical performance such as facing strength and defect rates.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with builders, joiners and sustainable-construction influencers targets exactly the 58% of 480 surveyed merchants willing to pay $0.60 more per sheet and the 71% planning to stock low-carbon board. Cost per reached buyer is low, engagement and click-throughs are measurable, and influencers can demonstrate the recycled-paper facing story on real sites — ideal for a technical B2B product. Credibility depends on honest, experienced voices rather than celebrities.

Recommendation: WPB should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segments already identified in its research, scales nationally, produces measurable results and costs far less than trade press or radio, fitting a company servicing debt on a $900,000 loan. National trade-press advertising is rejected as too expensive and insufficiently targeted for launch; regional radio is rejected as too narrow for national merchant listings. WPB should nevertheless support influencers with modest in-store merchant promotions to capture older buyers who do not use social media.

--- STEM ---
Wrenford Limestone Walling (WLW) is a partnership in the stone quarrying and building materials sector, employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2004 by Tom Wrenford, the business extracts and dresses limestone walling stone for landscapers and builders and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. WLW plans to invest $750,000 in a new diamond-wire cutting and dressing shed, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $375,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.50 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. WLW faces two operational problems: labour turnover among quarry operatives has reached 16% and a skills gap in diamond-wire sawing, alongside rising cutting waste.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WLW plans to expand with its new diamond-wire cutting and dressing shed. Explain two advantages for WLW of growing organically by opening the shed instead of taking over a rival quarry.
    Answer: Point 1: Organic expansion through the new dressing shed lets WLW grow at a pace its 32 workers and Tom Wrenford's democratic decision-making can absorb, keeping the flat structure and the culture that brought complaints down from 17 to 9 per month. A takeover of a rival quarry would fuse two workforces overnight, create clashes over pay and rostering, and risk losing the very operatives WLW needs to close its diamond-wire sawing skills gap — with turnover already at 16%, cultural disruption could prove expensive and slow.

Point 2: Organic growth avoids the premium price, lawyers' fees and hidden liabilities a takeover would carry, keeping the $750,000 investment within reach of a $450,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. WLW also keeps full control over quality — the breakage rate already fell from 5.2% to 3.4% under its own supervision — whereas an acquired site would arrive with unknown stock, equipment and contracts, and weak integration could hit the certified low-carbon stone programme that 54% of surveyed architects and landscapers would pay $1.20 more per unit for.
    Keywords: diamond-wire, dressing shed, workforce of 32, retained profit, $750,000, $450,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wrenford Limestone Walling and its expansion decision.

    Answer: Print advertising in landscaping and architecture magazines: Specialist print would place WLW's certified low-carbon stone in front of exactly the 68% of surveyed architects and landscapers who specify natural limestone, with technical credibility and a lasting physical copy. However, glossy space is expensive per enquiry, magazines circulate monthly rather than at the moment a buyer specifies stone, and response is hard to measure — risky for a partnership still funding a $750,000 shed with a bank loan.

Sponsoring a heritage-buildings exhibition: A single-day presence at a heritage and conservation exhibition would concentrate high-quality, decision-making buyers — conservation officers, heritage contractors and architects — and WLW could demonstrate dressed samples and cutting precision in person. Social media marketing aimed at architects: Architect-focused content (case studies, carbon figures, installation details) reaches the 54% willing to pay $1.20 more per unit for certified low-carbon stone at low cost, is measurable through enquiries and downloads, and can be sustained all year rather than on one exhibition day. It demands consistent quality content and may miss less digitally active small landscaping firms.

Recommendation: WLW should choose social media marketing aimed at architects. It reaches the exact premium-paying segment identified in research, costs least per qualified enquiry, and keeps the pipeline flowing beyond any single event — important while servicing the $450,000 loan. Print advertising is rejected as too slow and difficult to measure; the heritage exhibition is rejected as high-cost and narrowly attended, though a small stand could be a later addition once the certified range is fully launched.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WLW's labour turnover among quarry operatives has reached 16%. Explain two benefits for WLW of using induction training for its new quarry operatives.

For a workforce of only 32, one serious accident would remove a trained operative for months and disrupt the 18,500-unit quarterly processing target; induction also slows the churn feeding the 16% turnover because new starters feel supported rather than thrown onto the face to learn unsupervised.

Point 2: A structured induction sets quality expectations around breakage and waste from day one — explaining why 12 operatives lack wire-saw certification and why cutting waste is 9.0% of output. New recruits who understand the 3.4% breakage target and the certified low-carbon standard from the start make fewer costly mistakes, complement the $600 college certification route, and let democratic team meetings focus on improvement rather than re-teaching basics.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: WLW's breakage rate is 3.4%. Consider introducing quality control (inspection of finished stone) or quality assurance (prevention through process checks). Which should WLW choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality control (inspection of finished stone): Inspecting dressed walling units at the end of the shed would catch breakage and sub-standard cuts before they reach the 68% of buyers specifying natural limestone, protecting WLW's complaint count (already down from 17 to 9 per month) and its certified low-carbon reputation. It is relatively cheap and quick to start — hire or nominate an inspector, set tolerances, tick and reject. However, it detects defects after money has been spent cutting the stone, so waste and rework are already sunk costs, and it adds nothing to why breakage happens.

Quality assurance (prevention through process checks): Building quality checks into extraction, sawing, dressing and handling — blade maintenance schedules, moisture monitoring, verified low-carbon sourcing — attacks the causes of the 3.4% breakage rate and the 9.0% cutting waste at source. It raises consistency for the premium $1.20 certified range and cuts long-run costs, but requires training, documented procedures and cultural change, and benefits arrive slowly; the partnership must keep delivering 72,000 units a year while it is introduced.

Decision: WLW should choose quality assurance as its primary approach, supported by basic end-of-line inspection. With turnover at 16% and a skills gap in wire-sawing, fixing process discipline and operator competence is the only way to bring breakage sustainably below 3% and protect margins on the certified range; pure inspection is rejected because it accepts waste as inevitable and cannot differentiate WLW on carbon certification. Modest inspection remains as a safety net, but prevention must come first, backed by the $600 college certification for the 12 uncertified operatives.
    Keywords: 3.4%, cutting waste, certified low-carbon, $600, 72,000, workforce of 32
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of quality control and quality assurance with limited application to WLW. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches in the context of WLW. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of WLW with a well-justified decision covering waste, cost, certification and operator skills.

Revenue rose $700,000 while cost of sales rose just $140,000, so gross profit rose $560,000.

Evaluation: Profitability has improved, though returns on capital are rising only slowly. The move towards certified low-carbon stone lifted gross profit from $1,890,000 to $2,450,000 and the gross margin from 45.0% to 50.0% — clear evidence the $1.20 premium is sticking. Operating profit rose 40% to $735,000, but capital employed grew $875,000 to fund the dressing shed, so the return on capital edged up only one percentage point to 21.0%. Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.91 per hour): Quarry operatives are WLW's largest cost block; most of the 32 staff are on or near the minimum wage. Democratic leadership and re-rostering could share the burden, but wage-driven turnover could accelerate, worsening the existing 16% rate.

Input cost inflation (8.4% diesel and quarrying costs): Diesel powers quarry plant and delivery; say fuel and consumables represent around 40% of the $10.50 variable cost ($4.20). An 8.4% rise adds about $0.35 per unit; at 72,000 units that is roughly $25,000–$30,000 a year. WLW can partially offset via the $1.20 certified premium, but passing on the full rise risks losing price-sensitive landscaping accounts.

Conclusion: The 6.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It compounds across the entire workforce regardless of volume, adding roughly $54,000 a year — approaching a tenth of operating profit — and lands on top of a 16% turnover problem WLW is already trying to fix. The diesel rise (~$25,000–$30,000) is serious but controllable through price reviews, and the interest rise (~$3,400) is trivial; even so, WLW must combine premium pricing with retention policies and energy-efficient machinery to protect margins from all three.

--- STEM ---
Ferndale Green Steel (FGS) is a public limited company in the steel recycling sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2016 by Raya Ferndale, the business melts scrap steel in electric arc furnaces to produce certified low-carbon steel for construction and manufacturing and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. FGS plans to invest $2,400,000 in a new automated scrap-sorting line and baghouse filter, financed by a $1,300,000 share issue and $1,100,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $3,600,000 a year, a variable cost of $440 a unit and a selling price of $620, and currently produces 34,000 units a year. FGS faces two operational problems: absenteeism has reached 10% and scrap contamination is driving rework in the melt shop.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: FGS plans to finance part of its $2,400,000 expansion with a share issue. Explain two advantages for FGS of using a share issue instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises finance without creating interest or repayment obligations, protecting FGS's cash flow at a time when the company already carries fixed costs of $3,600,000 a year and services $240,000–$310,000 of annual interest. Avoiding extra debt repayments on the $2,400,000 automated scrap-sorting line leaves more operating cash to absorb the 11.2% rise in scrap costs and the 9.5% rise in industrial electricity prices — critical for a furnaces business whose variable cost is already $440 a unit.

Point 2: New equity strengthens FGS's balance sheet and credit rating, making later borrowing cheaper if the line outperforms. There is also no collateral at risk: if low-carbon steel demand disappoints, shareholders bear the loss rather than the melt shop being repossessed. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders' control and future dividends, but Raya Ferndale judged this worthwhile to fund the certified low-carbon programme that 74% of 250 surveyed industrial buyers would pay 8% more for.
    Keywords: share issue, retained profit, $1,300,000, $1,100,000, $2,400,000, $3,600,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Ferndale Green Steel and its expansion decision.

Consider advertising in national business newspapers, a targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement managers, or sponsorship of the Green Manufacturing Expo. Which should FGS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National business newspaper advertising: Full-page adverts in national papers would reach a broad business audience and raise FGS's profile among institutional investors as well as buyers, signalling the permanence of a public limited company. However, national print is very expensive, much of the readership is irrelevant to steel specification, response is hard to measure, and a single issue barely dents the procurement habits of the 74% of buyers willing to pay 8% more for certified low-carbon steel.

Sponsorship of the Green Manufacturing Expo: Exhibiting and speaking at a green-manufacturing expo would put FGS face-to-face with sustainability officers, specifiers and major contractors, with strong credibility from the 92% scrap recovery and certified low-carbon positioning. The weaknesses are high one-off fees, attendance limited to event days, and poor reach for the hundreds of regional fabricators and distributors who also buy steel; it builds depth, not breadth.

A targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement managers: Precise targeting by industry, role and company size lets FGS deliver technical carbon-footprint content directly to the people who specify steel — at low cost per reached decision-maker, with measurable enquiries, and sustained all year. It suits a B2B technical product perfectly, though it requires continuous quality content and may under-reach less digitally active small buyers.

Recommendation: FGS should choose the targeted LinkedIn campaign. It reaches the precise procurement audience identified in research, costs least per qualified lead, runs year-round beyond one expo, and produces the measurable enquiry data a public limited company needs to justify the $2,400,000 investment to shareholders. Business-newspaper advertising is rejected as too expensive and too broad; the expo is rejected as too narrow and event-limited, though FGS could add a small stand later once the certified range wins its first major framing contract.

    Answer: Point 1: Team working pools the furnace crew's practical knowledge of why scrap contamination happens, generating joint fixes such as better pre-sort checks and clearer signals between cranes and furnace operators. Teams also cover for each other during absences, keeping the melt shop running at 8,600 tonnes a quarter instead of losing output when one of the 120 staff is off — directly relieving the 10% absenteeism and the rework driven by contaminated charges.

Point 2: Teams build peer accountability and social support, satisfying Maslow's social needs and reversing the isolation behind high absence. Operators who help each other also learn faster on the new shredder, support the 22 staff awaiting training, and sustain the improvement from a 3.4% to 2.2% rework rate. Lower absenteeism and rework cut overtime, scrap-disposal and quality-failure costs, protecting the $620 selling price and the margins FGS needs to justify the $2,400,000 expansion.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: FGS must upskill 22 scrap-sorting operators for the new automated line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college at $1,100 per employee. Which should FGS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training beside the shredder and furnace is directly relevant to FGS's own scrap grades, recovery targets and safety regime, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 22 operators productive — protecting throughput of 8,600 tonnes a quarter and the drop in rework from 3.4% to 2.2%. Weaknesses: trainers are production staff whose own duties suffer, informal bad habits spread, and no external certificate is issued to demonstrate competence to clients auditing FGS's certified low-carbon claims.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $1,100 per employee would cost $24,200 for all 22 — easily affordable against a $2,400,000 investment. It provides structured, up-to-date theory (metallurgy, sorting standards, safety regulation) and recognised certification, strengthening FGS's certified credentials with buyers willing to pay 8% more. However, it removes over 18% of the workforce from the melt shop for course days, risks delivery delays, and the generic syllabus may not match FGS's exact shredder settings, so site coaching would still be required.

Decision: FGS should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, reserving college certification for two lead operators and the quality supervisor. This is the cheapest and most machine-specific route, keeps the furnaces fed, and avoids withdrawing 22 of 120 staff while absenteeism is already 10%. Full off-the-job training is rejected as too disruptive to the delivery schedule and poor value for operators who need hands-on sorting practice; the $24,200 would be better spent on a follow-up QA audit once the line is stable and rework falls toward 1.5%.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.6% living wage increase and the 11.2% rise in steel scrap costs will affect FGS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.

Scrap cost inflation (11.2% year-on-year, plus 9.5% electricity): Scrap likely represents 60–70% of the $440 variable cost (about $270–$300). An 11.2% rise adds roughly $30–$34 per unit; at 34,000 units that is $1,020,000–$1,156,000 a year — potentially wiping out half of operating profit before price recovery. --- STEM ---
Aldervan Engineered Timber (AET) is a cooperative in the engineered timber sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2013 by Jonas and Petra Aldervan, the business presses cross-laminated timber panels and glulam beams from certified Scandinavian spruce for sustainable construction and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. AET plans to invest $1,850,000 in a new CLT press and finger-jointing line, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $1,150,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,640,000 a year, a variable cost of $128 a unit and a selling price of $210, and currently produces 26,500 units a year. AET faces two operational problems: offcut waste is running at 8% of input timber and labour turnover among press operators has reached 13%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AET plans to finance part of its CLT press expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for AET of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs AET nothing in interest or repayment charges, protecting cash flow while the cooperative already carries fixed costs of $1,640,000 a year and has committed to a $700,000 ten-year bank loan for the $1,850,000 press. Avoiding interest on the $1,150,000 retained portion leaves more operating cash to absorb the 8.8% rise in spruce and pine input costs, so AET can defend its $210 selling price and keep the certified CLT programme funded without raising member prices or compromising the 2.9% reject-rate drive.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids collateral and repayment risk, so the $1,150,000 is available without putting the new press at risk of repossession if mass-timber demand disappoints. It also preserves the cooperative's member ownership and democratic control — no external lender can impose covenants over how the press is scheduled, priced or staffed, which matters while green-building demand is growing 9.3% but overall construction output only 2.1%, and while members vote on reinvestment.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $1,150,000, $700,000, $1,850,000, $1,640,000

Sponsoring a televised eco-home series: A sponsorship slot would give AET the widest possible reach and powerful emotional association with sustainable homes — ideal for the public-facing story of timber replacing concrete and steel. It demonstrates carbon credentials and real building case studies directly to the 380 architects and contractors in AET's research, though it depends on influencer credibility and consistent quality content.

Recommendation: AET should choose social media marketing with sustainability influencers. It reaches the precise dual-audience of professional specifiers and engaged self-builders identified in research, costs least per qualified lead, runs continuously rather than around one series or monthly issue, and reinforces the certified low-carbon positioning behind the 6% premium. --- STEM ---
Ashcombe Eco Bricks (AEB) is a private limited company in the building materials sector, employing a workforce of 140. Founded in 1998 by Marta Ashcombe, the business manufactures recycled-content eco blocks and facing blocks for the housebuilding market and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. AEB plans to invest $980,000 in a new recycled-aggregate batching plant and vibro-compaction press, financed by hire purchase, a $550,000 bank loan and $430,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $888,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.80 a unit and a selling price of $8.50, and currently produces 305,000 units a year. AEB faces two operational problems: absenteeism has reached 11% and recycled-aggregate inconsistency is causing occasional sub-standard batches.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AEB plans to acquire its new vibro-compaction press by hire purchase. Explain two advantages for AEB of using hire purchase for the press instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $980,000 cost of the batching plant and vibro-compaction press into fixed instalments without an immediate capital outlay, easing cash flow while AEB already carries fixed costs of $888,000 a year and services a $550,000 bank loan. Crucially, ownership passes to AEB once the final payment is made, so the press becomes a long-term asset producing 305,000 units a year without the flat structure straining to raise or secure a larger unsecured facility.

Point 2: Hire purchase keeps the specific press asset as security for the finance provider rather than general charges over AEB's premises or other equipment, protecting Marta Ashcombe's flexibility to mortgage land later if the eco-block range expands. It also matches payments to output: as the recycled-content blocks generate revenue at $8.50 a unit, instalments track productive use, and AEB keeps $430,000 of retained profit in reserve for the $35,000 dust-control upgrades and for materials during aggregate-price spikes.

Social media campaign targeting self-build homeowners: Content on recycled aggregate, carbon savings and strength tests reaches a fast-growing DIY audience directly, at low cost, with measurable engagement — ideal for driving them into merchants asking for AEB blocks. Decision: AEB should choose flow production for its core eco block, with a small batch-production cell retained for specialist products. A 7.6% rise adds about $0.24 per unit; at 305,000 units that is roughly $73,000 a year. AEB can recover much of this through the $0.80 certified premium and housebuilder price reviews, and has aggregate contracts to renegotiate — but partial recovery is the realistic ceiling this year.

Conclusion: The 6.7% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 140 employees whatever happens to sales volume, adding roughly $245,000 a year — more than three times the input-cost rise and nearly ninety times the loan interest increase — and it strikes the labour-heavy part of the process hardest. Input costs (~$73,000) are the second-greatest threat and are partly recoverable through price reviews; the rate rise is the smallest and most easily hedged, though all three demand AEB prioritise attendance, productivity and premium pricing to defend its margins through 2027.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.7%, 7.6%, interest rate, $13.44, $4.80
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to AEB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AEB's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AEB with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Mistral Coffee Roasters (MCR) is a private limited company in the beverage sector, specialising in specialty coffee roasting, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Mistral, the business supplies independent cafes across the region and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. MCR plans to invest $540,000 in a new automated roasting and packing line, financed by a $320,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $189,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.20 a unit and a selling price of $10.50, and produces 80,000 units a year. MCR faces two problems: quality complaints about inconsistent roast colour have risen sharply and absenteeism has reached 7% among packing staff.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MCR is funding its $540,000 expansion with a $320,000 bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. Explain two benefits for MCR of using retained profit rather than increasing the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payment and no capital repayment, so using the $220,000 keeps MCR's cash flow free while it services the $320,000 bank loan and meets fixed costs of $189,000 a year. Every dollar of the $540,000 funded internally is a dollar that does not add to the loan commitment, protecting the $10.50 selling price from having to cover extra interest at a time when 7% absenteeism and quality complaints are already disrupting output.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves Sofia Mistral's ownership and control untouched, since no lender can impose conditions on how the new roasting and packing line is run or demand collateral. It is also immediately available and avoids arrangement fees and approval delays, letting MCR respond quickly to cafe demand and to the 68% of 500 surveyed buyers who would pay $0.50 more for certified sustainable beans. Keeping borrowing lower also reduces exposure if rates rise, making the expansion safer for a 36-person roaster.
    Keywords: retained profit, $320,000, $220,000, $540,000, $189,000, democratic leadership
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MCR is launching a new single-origin coffee range. Consider cafe trade exhibitions, a social media campaign, or free in-cafe sampling. Which should MCR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Cafe trade exhibitions: A trade show puts MCR's single-origin range in front of many cafe owners at once and lets buyers taste the product, which helps answer the quality complaints about inconsistent roast colour. It also builds personal contacts with the independent cafes MCR supplies. However, stand fees, travel and staffing are costly for a business funding a $540,000 expansion with a $320,000 loan, and many visitors are competitors or non-buyers, so cost per genuine order can be high.

Social media campaign: A campaign can reach thousands of buyers at low cost per contact and can tell the origin story that 47% of surveyed buyers check. It is measurable and scalable nationally. Its weakness is that coffee is a taste product: an online advert cannot prove roast consistency, and engagement does not reliably convert into cafe orders, especially with a 36-person team and only 19,500 units roasted last quarter.

Free in-cafe sampling: Placing samples in the cafes that already stock MCR lets buyers taste the improvement at the point of purchase, directly tackling the quality complaints. It uses existing distribution, so cost is limited to product giveaway and staff time, and it targets the 68% willing to pay $0.50 more for certified sustainable beans. The drawback is slow reach and reliance on cafe staff.

Recommendation: MCR should choose free in-cafe sampling. It neutralises the quality complaints, uses the existing cafe network instead of costly new channels, and converts the 68% premium preference into trial. Trade exhibitions are rejected as too expensive and untargeted for a 36-employee roaster carrying a $320,000 loan; social media is rejected because it cannot demonstrate taste and is less certain to win cafe orders. MCR can add low-cost social posts later to support the sampling.
    Keywords: $540,000, 68%, 500, quality complaints, $0.50, 19,500
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to MCR. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two options with advantages and disadvantages applied to MCR. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of MCR with a justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

    Question: MCR's absenteeism has reached 7% and quality complaints about roast colour are rising. Explain two benefits for MCR of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its packing team.

Workers who help set packing routines are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking the 7% absenteeism that disrupts the 19,500 units roasted each quarter and the effort to cut the 2.4% defect rate.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MCR must upskill 14 of its 36 staff on the new roasting controls. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should MCR choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training the 14 of 36 staff at the roasting controls is directly relevant to MCR's own machines and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps staff productive while they learn, protecting the 19,500 units packed last quarter and the fall in defects to 2.4%. Decision: MCR should choose on-the-job training first, with short college courses later for senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while absenteeism is 7% and quality complaints are already a problem. Full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $10,500 and releasing 14 staff at once would disrupt the 80,000-unit target; the college route can be added once the new line is stable.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MCR's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MCR's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.29 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.49 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.83 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.10 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $140,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $270,000; 2025 current assets = $78,000 + $165,000 + $52,000 = $295,000. Cover of the 2024 current liabilities of $210,000 was $270,000 / $210,000 = 1.29; cover of the 2025 liabilities of $198,000 was $295,000 / $198,000 = 1.49. Liquid assets excluding inventories were $270,000 - $95,000 = $175,000 in 2024, giving $175,000 / $210,000 = 0.83, and $295,000 - $78,000 = $217,000 in 2025, giving $217,000 / $198,000 = 1.10.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. Cover rose from 1.29 to 1.49, helped by current liabilities falling from $210,000 to $198,000 while current assets rose from $270,000 to $295,000. More importantly, liquid-asset cover improved from 0.83 to 1.10, so MCR no longer depends on selling coffee inventories to meet short-term debts. That matters while it services a $320,000 bank loan and funds a $540,000 expansion. However, trade receivables grew from $140,000 to $165,000, tying up cash; if cafe customers pay late the improvement could reverse. Inventories fell from $95,000 to $78,000, so stock availability for the 80,000-unit target should be watched.

Conclusion: MCR's liquidity has improved. Both cover measures rose and the liquid-asset measure crossed 1.0, so the stronger position does not rest on stock. The residual risk is slower receivable collection, so tighter credit control is advised before further borrowing.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in green coffee bean import prices will affect MCR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.54): MCR has a workforce of 36, but the insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so no annual wage bill can be invented. The defensible benchmark is productivity: 80,000 units / 36 staff = about 2,222 units per worker. If output per worker holds, the rise is absorbable within the $4.20 variable cost and $6.30 contribution; if 7% absenteeism reduces output, unit labour cost rises. Input cost inflation (9.6% green coffee): The insert does not decompose the $4.20 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is honest: if the whole $4.20 rose 9.6%, that is 9.6% x $4.20 = about $0.40 per unit, or roughly $32,000 a year at 80,000 units. That directly erodes the $6.30 contribution that justifies the $540,000 line. MCR can recover part through the $0.50 premium accepted by 68% of buyers.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in green coffee import prices will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit sold and hits contribution directly, unlike the one-off $2,400 interest effect; the wage rise matters but is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity, whereas ingredient costs strike at the margin that funds the expansion.

--- STEM ---
Golden Acre Cereals (GAC) is an agricultural cooperative in the cereal milling industry, employing a workforce of 42. Founded in 2008 by Rowan Golden, the business supplies breakfast cereal to regional grocers and independent shops and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. GAC plans to invest $460,000 in a new automated flaking and packing line to cut waste, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $60,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and produces 70,000 units a year. GAC faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and packaging waste has reached 6.1% of output.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GAC has financed its $460,000 expansion with a $400,000 bank loan and $60,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for GAC of using the bank loan rather than relying only on retained profit.
    Answer: Point 1: A $400,000 bank loan gives GAC the full capital immediately, so the $460,000 flaking and packing line can be installed in one stage rather than waiting years to accumulate retained profit. For a cooperative with only $60,000 retained, waiting would delay the automation needed to cut the 6.1% packaging waste and the 2.9% defect rate, risking the trust of the regional grocers it supplies.

Point 2: Using the loan preserves GAC's limited retained profit for day-to-day working capital and for the $680 per employee short courses needed by 16 of 42 operatives. Repayments are spread over ten years, so the cost is matched to the years of benefit from the new line and does not consume the $12.00 selling price all at once. Interest is also tax-deductible in many systems, and the loan leaves member funds untouched, which suits a cooperative accountable to its members, unlike a share issue which a cooperative cannot use.
    Keywords: $400,000, $60,000, $460,000, cooperative, retained profit, $210,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

They generate engagement quickly but may attract entrants who never buy cereal, and a cooperative with hierarchical, autocratic leadership may find it hard to respond fast to online feedback.

Recommendation: GAC should choose in-store demonstrations. They convert the 61% carton preference into actual trial at the point of sale, fit the regional grocer channel, and need no expensive media buy. Television is rejected as unaffordable and too broad for a $460,000 expansion with a $400,000 loan; social competitions are rejected because engagement does not equal sales and the 39% price-focused shoppers need a direct reason to switch.

--- STEM ---
Bellwether Dairy (BWD) is a dairy processing partnership in the food industry rather than a sole trader, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2013 by Aoife Bellwether, the business supplies supermarket chains with locally sourced cheese and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. BWD plans to invest $330,000 in a new automated cheese packing line to cut waste, financed by a $210,000 bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $156,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.80 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and produces 65,000 units a year. BWD faces two problems: absenteeism is high among packing staff and milk waste has reached 4.7% of input.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BWD is a partnership funding a $330,000 expansion with a $210,000 bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. Explain two benefits for BWD of operating as a partnership rather than a sole trader.
    Answer: Point 1: A partnership allows Aoife Bellwether to share the $330,000 investment risk and the management workload with other partners, rather than carrying all of the $210,000 loan liability alone as a sole trader would. With a workforce of 28 and 4.7% milk waste to control, shared decision-making under laissez-faire leadership brings different skills to quality and packing problems, improving the $9.00 product without overburdening one owner.

Point 2: Partners can contribute extra capital and creditworthiness, making the $210,000 bank loan easier to secure than for a single owner, and profits can be retained as $120,000 for the new cheese packing line. Unlike a sole trader, the business survives if one partner leaves, which reassures supermarket chains about continuity of locally sourced supply. Shares of profit are agreed in advance in the partnership deed, reducing disputes while the 65,000-unit output is maintained, and the shared management load lets Aoife Bellwether focus on the 4.7% milk waste problem rather than handling every decision alone.
    Keywords: partnership, sole trader, $330,000, $210,000, $120,000, Bellwether Dairy
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BWD is promoting a new locally sourced cheese range. Consider farmers' market tastings, local radio advertising, or local newspaper coupons. Which should BWD choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Farmers' market tastings: Tastings let shoppers try the cheese and speak to Aoife Bellwether about the farm origin, directly using the 57% of 380 buyers who would pay $0.35 more for locally sourced dairy and the 44% who check farm-origin labels. It builds loyalty and gives immediate feedback on quality. The limit is scale: a market reaches only local visitors, and with a workforce of 28 and high absenteeism, staffing several events could strain the 15,600-unit packing schedule.

Local radio advertising: Radio is relatively cheap and can reach the whole regional catchment quickly, repeating the local-source message to drivers and shoppers. It suits a perishable product with a 2.6-day delivery lead time. Its weakness is that adverts cannot show or taste the cheese, and the message is easily forgotten; 44% of buyers check labels in store, so radio alone may not convert to purchases of the $9.00 product.

Local newspaper coupons: Coupons give a measurable, price-led reason to try the range and can be clipped by exactly the shoppers already buying supermarket cheese. They are low cost per unit and traceable. However, discounting undercuts the $0.35 premium that 57% of buyers will pay and can train customers to wait for offers, squeezing the $3.80 contribution per unit needed to justify the $330,000 line.

Recommendation: BWD should choose farmers' market tastings. They convert the 57% premium preference into trial and prove origin to the 44% who check labels, without discounting. Radio is rejected because it cannot demonstrate quality and is forgettable; coupons are rejected because they erode the premium and the contribution funding the $210,000 loan. BWD can support tastings with cheap social posts later.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BWD's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has BWD's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.24 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.72 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $88,000 inventories + $72,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $200,000; 2025 current assets = $96,000 + $104,000 + $30,000 = $230,000. Cover of the 2024 current liabilities of $160,000 was $200,000 / $160,000 = 1.25; cover of the 2025 liabilities of $185,000 was $230,000 / $185,000 = 1.24. Liquid assets excluding inventories were $200,000 - $88,000 = $112,000 in 2024, giving $112,000 / $160,000 = 0.70, and $230,000 - $96,000 = $134,000 in 2025, giving $134,000 / $185,000 = 0.72.

Evaluation: Liquidity is broadly flat but the mix has weakened. Cover edged down from 1.25 to 1.24 because current liabilities rose from $160,000 to $185,000 almost as fast as current assets grew from $200,000 to $230,000. The liquid-asset measure rose slightly from 0.70 to 0.72, which looks better, but this was achieved while cash fell from $40,000 to $30,000 and inventories rose from $88,000 to $96,000. Trade receivables jumped from $72,000 to $104,000, tying up cash with supermarket chains; if those customers pay late, the small improvement in liquid cover could quickly unwind. Servicing the $210,000 loan while funding a $330,000 packing line leaves little spare cash, and the 4.7% milk waste adds pressure.

Conclusion: BWD's liquidity has not clearly improved. Overall cover slipped and the modest rise in the liquid-asset measure is offset by lower cash and much higher receivables, so the position is more dependent on collection. Tighter credit control is needed before further borrowing.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in feed and dairy input costs will affect BWD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If BWD's $210,000 loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $210,000 = $1,575, which is small against fixed costs of $156,000 and a $330,000 expansion. Higher rates may make supermarket chains cautious and raise future borrowing costs, but the direct annual hit is modest and can be capped by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.41): BWD has a workforce of 28, yet the insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The honest measure is productivity: 65,000 units / 28 staff = about 2,321 units per worker.
