--- STEM ---
Saffron Spice Grill (SSG) is a partnership in the hospitality sector, running a chain of four casual-dining restaurants and employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2015 by Nadia Rahman, the business has a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. SSG plans to invest $380,000 in two new city-centre branches, financed by a $150,000 bank loan and $230,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $182,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $38, and produces 22,000 units a year, where each unit is one meal served. SSG faces rising food-waste levels and 10% absenteeism among its kitchen staff, with repeat bookings falling in its four branches.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SSG is funding its $380,000 expansion with a $150,000 bank loan and $230,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for SSG of taking the bank loan instead of relying solely on retained profit.
    Answer: Point 1: Taking a $150,000 bank loan preserves SSG's cash reserve instead of spending all $230,000 of retained profit at once. That matters for a partnership with fixed costs of $182,000 a year and food waste of 8% of ingredients: cash kept back can absorb the 11.2% rise in food input costs and pay the 7.2% higher wages without delaying the two new city-centre branches.

Point 2: The loan lets both branches open together rather than forcing Nadia Rahman to sequence the $380,000 project around whatever retained profit accumulates. Opening together captures the 2.8% growth in eating-out spending sooner and spreads the $12 variable cost across 22,000 meals, so the $38 selling price and $26 contribution start covering the added fixed costs earlier. Borrowing also leaves the partners' own capital untouched, and the 4.3/5 rating from 800 diners and 56% who say value for money is good support the extra demand needed to service the loan. Retaining the $230,000 instead would leave less room to absorb the 7.2% wage rise during the launch of both branches.
    Keywords: bank loan, retained profit, $150,000, $230,000, $380,000, $182,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to SSG's expansion financing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SSG wants to attract diners to its two new city-centre branches. Consider a local radio campaign, leaflet drops, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SSG choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local radio: Radio reaches commuters and nearby office workers during the day, which could fill the 52-minute table turnaround at lunch, and it is cheaper than television. However, audio cannot show SSG's food, and a 5.0% base rate makes borrowing for promotion less attractive; the 800-diner survey shows 56% already judge value for money good, so the message must be visual and specific.

Leaflet drops: Doorstep leaflets with vouchers are cheap and can be targeted at neighbourhoods around the new branches, encouraging first visits and helping lift repeat bookings. Their weaknesses are low response rates and environmental waste that sits awkwardly with a business already trying to cut its 8% food waste; leaflets also do nothing to communicate the 4.3/5 rating to diners beyond the immediate delivery area.

Social media influencer marketing: Food influencers can photograph dishes and show the 4.3/5 rating and 56% value-for-money verdict to a large, relevant local audience, with engagement that can be tracked against the 18,000 meals baseline. Results build over time and depend on choosing credible reviewers, but cost per diner is low and the content can highlight improvements that cut the 44 monthly complaints.

Recommendation: SSG should choose social media influencer marketing, with small leaflet vouchers for launch week only. It shows the food, leverages the strong diner survey and reaches beyond a single radio catchment at a cost that fits a $150,000 loan-funded expansion. Radio is rejected because it cannot display the product, and leaflets are rejected as a main channel because of low response and waste concerns.
    Keywords: 4.3/5, 800, 56%, 18,000, 44, $38
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to SSG. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SSG with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and leaflets are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SSG's absenteeism has reached 10% and food-waste levels are rising. Explain two benefits for SSG of introducing job rotation in its kitchens.
    Answer: Point 1: Job rotation moves the workforce of 35 between preparation, cooking and service, reducing repetition and boredom in a laissez-faire setting where staff otherwise get little variety. Higher job satisfaction should cut the 10% absenteeism, so kitchens stay fully staffed and the 95% of orders delivered within 15 minutes can be maintained, protecting the 4.3/5 rating from 800 diners.

Point 2: Rotation gives Nadia Rahman's staff a wider range of skills, so cover is available when a chef is absent and the 52-minute table turnaround does not lengthen. Staff who work across stations can spot food-waste at each stage, helping cut the current 8% waste and the 44 monthly complaints; this supports the $38 selling price and $26 contribution needed to service the $150,000 bank loan as two new branches open. Nadia Rahman can check absence and the 44 monthly complaints after a trial before extending rotation to all four branches, keeping the flat structure intact.
    Keywords: absenteeism, 10%, workforce of 35, 44, food-waste, 4.3/5
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SSG's absenteeism, waste, service times and expansion.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SSG must train 7 of 35 staff who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should SSG choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Kitchen coaching is tailored to SSG's own recipes, portion standards and the 52-minute turnaround, costs no fees, and keeps the 7 trainees productive. It can directly reduce the 8% food waste and the 44 monthly complaints because supervisors correct practice immediately. Drawbacks are that busy chefs have little time to teach, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate, which may matter as the partnership opens two new branches with consistent standards.

Off-the-job training: The local college course costs $650 per employee, so 7 × $650 = $4,550, small beside the $380,000 investment. It provides structured hygiene and supervisory skills and a recognised certificate, useful for a growing four-branch chain. However, it pulls 7 of 35 staff out of kitchens during service, risking the 95% on-time order record and longer than 52 minutes at tables, and generic content will still need on-site adaptation to SSG's menu.

Decision: SSG should choose on-the-job training first, followed by short college hygiene modules. It is cheaper, specific to SSG's kitchens and avoids disrupting service while 10% absenteeism is already stretching a workforce of 35. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the lost kitchen shifts and the $4,550 fee would hit the 18,000-meal operation, and the new branches need consistent on-site standards immediately. A short trial in one branch would show whether the 52-minute turnaround, the 44 monthly complaints and the 8% food waste improve before SSG spends $4,550 on all 7 trainees, with Nadia Rahman reviewing the results across the four branches.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $650, 7 of 35, food-waste, 52 minutes
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SSG. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of SSG. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, service disruption and kitchen relevance.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how SSG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Average total cost = $20.27 | (ii) Contribution per unit = $26 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: $20.27 cost versus $38 price; $26 contribution for discount and voucher decisions; break-even of 7,000 meals for new branches; and unit-cost benchmarking against $650 training and 11.2% food inflation.
    Keywords: $20.27, $26, 22,000, $182,000, $12, $38
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SSG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SSG's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.13 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.26 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.67 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.89 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $28,000 inventories + $18,000 trade receivables + $22,000 cash = $68,000; 2025 current assets = $24,000 + $30,000 + $28,000 = $82,000. For 2024, $68,000 ÷ $60,000 = 1.13 and ($68,000 − $28,000) ÷ $60,000 = $40,000 ÷ $60,000 = 0.67. For 2025, $82,000 ÷ $65,000 = 1.26 and ($82,000 − $24,000) ÷ $65,000 = $58,000 ÷ $65,000 = 0.89.

Evaluation: Both measures improved, so short-term solvency is stronger. The first ratio rose from 1.13 to 1.26 despite current liabilities increasing from $60,000 to $65,000, because cash grew from $22,000 to $28,000 and inventories fell. The second measure climbed from 0.67 to 0.89, showing less dependence on selling the $24,000 of stock to meet bills, which is valuable while the partnership repays a $150,000 loan and spends $380,000 on two branches. Caution is still warranted: the 2025 second figure remains below 1, so liquid assets alone do not cover current liabilities, and trade receivables have risen from $18,000 to $30,000, tying up cash that could fund the 11.2% food-cost rise.

Conclusion: SSG's liquidity has improved, but only moderately. Both ratios rose and the improvement does not depend on inventory, yet the 0.89 figure leaves limited headroom, so the partners should tighten credit control on the higher receivables before committing further cash. Reviewing those balances monthly would protect the improvement.
    Keywords: 1.13, 1.26, 0.67, 0.89, $68,000, $82,000, $380,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SSG wants to reverse falling repeat bookings with a loyalty card scheme. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SSG of this approach.
    Answer: Advantage: A loyalty card rewards the 56% of 800 surveyed diners who already say value for money is good, encouraging repeat visits that lift the 18,000 meals baseline without heavy advertising. More meals spread the $182,000 fixed costs and protect the $26 contribution against 11.2% food input inflation, helping the two new branches reach break-even sooner.

Disadvantage: Discounts or free meals reduce the $38 average selling price and therefore the $26 contribution on rewarded visits, and the scheme needs tracking software and staff time that add to fixed costs while a $150,000 loan is outstanding. If rewards are too small they will not change behaviour; the insert gives no figure for redemption or setup cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified and the decision must be judged qualitatively. SSG should trial the card in one branch and compare repeat visits with the 800-diner survey before extending it to both new sites.
    Keywords: 56%, 800, 4.3/5, 44, 11.2%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SSG's survey, meals, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% food input inflation will affect SSG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If SSG's $150,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $150,000 = $1,125 a year (0.0075 × $150,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $182,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. The higher rate could make future borrowing dearer and might slightly dampen the 2.8% growth in eating-out spending.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $13.95 an hour): SSG's workforce of 35 includes many hourly-paid kitchen and service staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or individual pay, so any annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 22,000 units ÷ 35 staff = about 628.6 meals per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; job rotation and training the 7 untrained staff can help maintain it.

Food input inflation (11.2%): This bears on the $12 variable cost of every meal. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $12 were exposed, 11.2% × $12 = $1.344, about $1.34 a meal, and at 22,000 units that is roughly $29,568 a year (22,000 × $1.344). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $26 contribution on each meal, and it recurs on every one of the 22,000 meals, unlike the one-off loan-interest figure.

Conclusion: Food input inflation will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 22,000 meals and directly erodes the $26 contribution that services the $150,000 loan and funds the $380,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,125 a year and the wage increase can be offset by sustaining 628.6 meals per worker. SSG should cut the 8% food waste and review the $38 price rather than absorb the whole rise.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 7.2%, 11.2%, $13.95, $150,000, $12
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to SSG. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SSG's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that food input inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

PAPER: Paper 2
SET ID: P2_SET_239
UNIT: Paper 2 Case Study

--- STEM ---
Lumen River Cruises (LCU) is a public limited company in the tourism sector, operating river cruises and employing a workforce of 95. Founded in 1998 by Elena Lumen, the company has a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. LCU plans to invest $1,200,000 in two new river cruise boats, financed by a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $550,000 a year, a variable cost of $55 a unit and a selling price of $165, and produces 12,000 units a year, where each unit is one passenger-cruise place. LCU faces a 6% cancellation rate and rising complaints about cabin cleanliness from corporate charter groups during the peak season.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]

Existing shareholders dilute their claim, but no fixed repayment schedule strains cash flow during the peak season. The 4.4/5 rating from 1,800 passengers and the 61% recommendation rate reduce the risk that new investors demand an immediate return.

    Question: LCU's cancellation rate has reached 6% and cabin-cleanliness complaints are rising among its workforce of 95. Explain two benefits for LCU of introducing quality circles.

    Question: LCU must train 18 of 95 crew who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the maritime academy. Which should LCU choose? Justify your decision.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LCU's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has LCU's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.53 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.19 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $60,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $195,000; 2025 current assets = $55,000 + $120,000 + $70,000 = $245,000. For 2024, $195,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.30 and ($195,000 − $60,000) ÷ $150,000 = $135,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.90. For 2025, $245,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.53 and ($245,000 − $55,000) ÷ $160,000 = $190,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.19.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened clearly. The first ratio rose from 1.30 to 1.53 even though current liabilities increased from $150,000 to $160,000, because cash almost doubled from $40,000 to $70,000. The second measure improved from 0.90 to 1.19, showing LCU can now cover short-term obligations without relying on its $55,000 of inventories, valuable while it services a $700,000 bank loan and invests $1,200,000 in two boats. The qualification is trade receivables, up from $95,000 to $120,000: if corporate charter groups pay late, the stronger ratios could quickly weaken, and the 6% cancellation rate also threatens cash inflow.

Conclusion: LCU's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement is not dependent on stock, so short-term solvency is healthier. The main residual risk is the rise in receivables, so credit control and deposit terms for charters should be tightened before further expansion. Larger deposits would also reduce the receivables balance and make the improvement more durable.
    Keywords: 1.30, 1.53, 0.90, 1.19, $195,000, $245,000, $1,200,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: LCU is considering a flexible cancellation policy to reduce its 6% cancellation rate. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for LCU of this approach.
    Answer: Advantage: Allowing free date changes rather than lost deposits can persuade corporate charter groups to move a booking instead of cancelling, directly cutting the 6% cancellation rate. That protects the 12,000 passenger-cruise places and the $110 contribution, sustaining the 4.4/5 rating from 1,800 passengers and the 61% recommendation rate while the two new boats are brought into service.

LCU should test the policy with corporate charter groups first, since the 27 cleanliness complaints and the 35-minute boarding time may matter more to them than flexible terms.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 14.0% rise in marine fuel and port charges will affect LCU. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If LCU's $700,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250 a year (0.0075 × $700,000). That is a small fraction of $550,000 fixed costs, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it. The rise could make the $500,000 share issue relatively more attractive and may trim some discretionary travel despite 7.3% growth in inbound bookings.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.40 an hour): LCU's workforce of 95 includes hourly-paid cabin and catering crew, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours or individual pay, so any annual figure would be invented. The defensible measure is productivity: 12,000 units ÷ 95 staff = 126.32 passenger-cruise places per worker, so the higher wage is bearable only if that rate holds as two boats are added; quality circles and training the 18 untrained crew can support it.

Marine fuel and port charges (14.0%): These feed the $55 variable cost of each place. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only an upper bound is defensible: if the full $55 were exposed, 14.0% × $55 = $7.70 a unit, and at 12,000 units that is about $92,400 a year (12,000 × $7.70). Even a smaller exposed share cuts the $110 contribution on every place, and unlike the interest cost it recurs with each sailing.

Conclusion: The 14.0% rise in fuel and port charges will have the greatest impact. It compounds over 12,000 places and directly erodes the $110 contribution that services the $700,000 loan and supports the $1,200,000 boats, whereas the interest rise costs only $5,250 a year on the stated loan and the wage effect can be offset by maintaining 126.32 places per worker. LCU should review the $165 price and cut the 9% catering waste rather than absorb the full increase.
    Keywords: 5.5%, 6.5%, 14.0%, $13.40, $700,000, $55
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to LCU. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on LCU's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that the fuel and port charge rise has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Verdant Golf Lodge (VGL) is a cooperative in the leisure industry, running an 18-hole golf course and lodge and employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2003 by Marcus Verdant, the cooperative uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. VGL plans to invest $540,000 in a new nine-hole course and clubhouse extension, financed by a $180,000 bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $80, and produces 9,000 units a year, where each unit is one round of golf. VGL faces staff shortages in the pro shop and rising complaints about course maintenance.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VGL is funding its $540,000 nine-hole course and clubhouse extension with a $180,000 bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for VGL of using retained profit instead of the loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit needs no interest payments or fixed repayment dates, so the cooperative preserves cash while it meets $240,000 fixed costs and the higher greenkeeping fuel cost of 7% more per round. Money not paid to the lender can instead fix the bunker and green problems behind 22 member complaints, protecting the 4.1/5 rating from 900 members.

Point 2: Using its own $360,000 avoids pledging assets for a bank loan, so the existing course cannot be at risk if the new nine-hole course attracts fewer than the 7,200 rounds recorded last quarter. It also suits a cooperative with democratic leadership: members keep control of the $540,000 project without lender conditions, and the 66% who say the course is good value support reinvesting surplus locally rather than servicing external debt. VGL's 7,200 rounds last quarter show members already fund the course, so using retained profit keeps the democratic cooperative intact while the new course is built.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $360,000, $180,000, nine-hole course, $240,000

However, print has low response and cannot show the course; with $240,000 fixed costs and a $180,000 loan, spending on broad ads is risky when 13% of tee times are already empty and the 4.1/5 rating from 900 members is the stronger selling point.

Rewards reduce the $80 fee received per referred round, though, and the scheme relies on existing members' enthusiasm; it may not reach beyond the current membership enough to fill a new nine-hole course.

Social media influencer marketing: Golf and lifestyle influencers can show the course and clubhouse to a much wider audience, with the 4.1/5 rating and 66% value verdict giving credible content and measurable referrals against the 7,200 rounds baseline. Drawbacks are that results build slowly and depend on choosing credible reviewers, and the 22 complaints about bunkers and greens must be fixed before inviting public attention.

Recommendation: VGL should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by a modest members' referral incentive. Newspaper advertising is rejected as untargeted and wasteful given 13% empty tee times, and referrals alone are rejected as too dependent on the existing 900-member base. Fixing course maintenance remains essential to convert interest into rounds.

--- STEM ---
Northline Transit & Logistics (NTL) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Elena Marsh, it delivers palletised goods for regional manufacturers and runs a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. NTL plans to invest $720,000 in a fleet of fuel-efficient trucks and a computerised stock control system, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently handles 32,000 units a year. NTL faces an operational problem: driver absenteeism has reached 8% and late deliveries are rising, while its depot reports growing fuel waste from older vehicles.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NTL plans to fund part of its $720,000 fleet expansion with $320,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for NTL of using retained profit instead of the $400,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs NTL no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and is servicing a $400,000 bank loan. Every dollar saved on interest can be spent on tackling the 8% driver absenteeism and the rising late deliveries, for example by supporting the $0.50 next-day delivery promise without raising the $20.00 selling price. With the base rate due to rise to 5.0% (Appendix 3), a variable-rate loan would become more expensive, so retained profit avoids that exposure entirely.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership and control with NTL's existing shareholders and imposes no lender covenants or collateral risk on the $720,000 fleet investment.     Answer: Base interest rate (4.25% to 5.0%): If NTL's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.33 an hour): With a workforce of 60 in driving and depot roles, this feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. Input-cost inflation (9.5% diesel and vehicles): The $8.00 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound can be calculated: if the whole $8.00 rose 9.5%, that adds 9.5% × $8.00 = $0.76 a unit; across 32,000 units a year that is about $24,320 (32,000 × $0.76). Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in diesel and vehicle input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 32,000 consignments and erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $3,000 a year and the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity holds. NTL should cut the 7% fuel waste first.

--- STEM ---
PeakWest Renewables (PWR) is a private limited company in the renewable energy equipment sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2013 by Tomas Reid, it manufactures solar photovoltaic panels for commercial installers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. PWR plans to invest $960,000 in an automated solar-cell assembly line with offcut recycling, financed by a $560,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $45, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. PWR faces a quality problem: the panel defect rate has reached 3.4% and labour turnover is rising, while its plant reports growing material waste from older cutting machines.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PWR plans to fund part of its $960,000 assembly line with $400,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for PWR of using retained profit instead of the $560,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment schedule, so it protects PWR's cash flow while the firm already bears fixed costs of $300,000 a year and is taking on a $560,000 bank loan. The money saved can be spent on reducing the 3.4% defect rate and the 6.2% material waste without raising the $45 selling price to commercial installers. With the base rate rising to 5.25% (Appendix 3), debt will get dearer, so funding part of the line internally reduces exposure to that increase.

Point 2: Using $400,000 retained profit preserves the ownership and control of founder Tomas Reid and the existing shareholders, with no lender conditions attached to the $960,000 investment. There is also no collateral risk: if the new assembly line fails to cut the 3.4% defect rate, the automated machines cannot be repossessed. Retained profit can be released immediately, allowing the offcut-recycling equipment to be installed before the next order cycle rather than waiting for loan approval.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $400,000, $560,000, $960,000, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to PWR and the case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: PWR is launching a high-efficiency solar panel for commercial installers. Consider national television advertising, trade magazine advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should PWR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would create rapid, mass awareness of the high-efficiency panel and could support premium pricing at the $45 selling price. However, airtime is very expensive for an 80-employee manufacturer funding a $960,000 line, and most viewers are households rather than the commercial installers who actually buy the panels, so much of the budget would be wasted.

Trade magazine advertising: Specialist solar and construction titles reach exactly the commercial installers PWR supplies, allowing detailed technical claims about efficiency and the 3.4% defect-rate improvement programme to be made credibly. Costs are far lower than television. The limits are a narrow readership and long lead times, so trade press alone may not build enough demand to use the 48,000-unit capacity quickly.

Social media influencer marketing: Instagram and video influencers in the renewable sector can demonstrate panels visually and generate engagement, especially as demand for commercial solar installations grew 6.0%. The audience is mixed consumers and trade, and results depend on influencer credibility, but cost per reached buyer is low.

Recommendation: PWR should choose trade magazine advertising. It targets the commercial installers who actually place the 12,000-panel quarterly orders and can carry the technical message needed after a 3.4% defect rate, at a fraction of television's cost. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; influencers are rejected as too consumer-focused for a business-to-business panel maker. PWR can add limited social media content later.

Trade press also lets PWR publish the 2.1 kWh energy-use figure and the offcut-recycling story, differentiating its panels from rivals and supporting the $45 price with credible technical detail aimed at the installers who place the 12,000 quarterly orders.

    Question: PWR's 3.4% defect rate and rising labour turnover are damaging quality. Explain two benefits for PWR of introducing a bonus scheme linked to defect rates.

It also supports the $960,000 investment, since a lower defect rate means more of the 48,000-unit output is sellable rather than scrapped.

--- STEM ---
Redwood Trail Express (RTE) is a partnership in the parcel delivery and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2015 by Priya Raman and Dan Okoro, it delivers e-commerce parcels for online retailers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership.   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RTE plans to fund part of its $450,000 sorting hub with $160,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for RTE of using retained profit instead of the $290,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or instalments, which protects the cash flow of a 55-employee partnership already carrying fixed costs of $140,000 a year and a $290,000 bank loan. The savings can be spent on reducing the 3.1% parcel damage rate and the 2.6% sorting errors without raising the $6.00 selling price to online retailers. With the base rate rising to 4.75% (Appendix 3), internal funds avoid the dearer debt.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps control with founders Priya Raman and Dan Okoro, with no bank conditions attached to the $450,000 investment and no asset at risk of repossession if the new hub fails to cut the 5.3% van downtime. It is also faster to deploy than negotiating more debt, so the electric vans and sorters can be installed before the next peak period when sorting errors currently rise, protecting the 57% of shoppers who choose couriers on reliability.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $160,000, $290,000, $450,000, $140,000

Much of the spend would be wasted.

Recommendation: RTE should choose sponsorship of retailer websites. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and social media is rejected as less direct at the point of sale; RTE can add retargeting later.

Sponsorship also lets RTE link the same-day message to the 2.4-day average delivery time and the falling 3.1% damage rate, giving retailers concrete evidence of reliability before they commit to the $0.40 premium.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RTE wants to cut sorting errors and damage. Consider a performance-related bonus or job rotation. Which should RTE choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Performance-related bonus: Paying a bonus for error-free sorting would motivate the 55 staff financially and could quickly reduce the 3.1% damage rate and 2.6% sorting errors, raising output from the 24,000 parcels handled each quarter. Decision: RTE should choose job rotation. The bonus is rejected because it adds cost while wages rise 5.5% and does not solve the coverage problem; RTE can add a small quality bonus once error rates are stable.

To make rotation work, RTE can pair each driver with an experienced colleague for the first few shifts, keeping the 24,000 quarterly parcels moving while skills transfer. It should also monitor the 3.1% damage rate weekly so that any quality dip caused by learning is caught before it affects the 66% of shoppers willing to pay the $0.40 premium.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.8% rise in fuel and packaging input costs will affect RTE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate (4.0% to 4.75%): If RTE's $290,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $290,000 = $2,175 a year (0.0075 × $290,000). That is small against fixed costs of $140,000 a year, and zero if the loan is fixed. Higher rates could make online retailers cautious and raise future borrowing costs for the $450,000 hub, but the direct interest effect is limited.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.20 an hour): With a workforce of 55 in sorting and driving, this lifts the wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay are given, so an annual total cannot be invented; the sound comparison is productivity, 95,000 parcels ÷ 55 staff = about 1,727 parcels per worker. If that holds, the rise is manageable; if rising absenteeism cuts it, unit labour cost rises and the $3.50 contribution shrinks.

Input-cost inflation (8.8% fuel and packaging): The $2.50 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is defensible: if the whole $2.50 rose 8.8%, that adds 8.8% × $2.50 = $0.22 a parcel; across 95,000 parcels a year that is about $20,900 (95,000 × $0.22). That would reduce contribution from $3.50 to about $3.28 on every parcel and compounds on the existing 5.3% van downtime. Part can be recovered through the $0.40 same-day premium.

Conclusion: The 8.8% rise in fuel and packaging input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 95,000 parcels and erodes the $3.50 contribution that supports the $450,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $2,175 a year and the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity holds. --- STEM ---
Eastline Power (ELP) is a public limited company in the electricity generation and supply sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2008 by Amina Yusuf, it supplies electricity to households and small businesses and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. ELP plans to invest $1,200,000 in a smart-meter rollout and battery storage units, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year, a variable cost of $60 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently supplies 150,000 units a year. ELP faces a service problem: billing complaints have reached 6.1% of customers and skilled-engineer turnover is rising, while its network reports increasing outage hours.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ELP plans to fund part of its $1,200,000 smart-meter programme with a $700,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for ELP of using a share issue instead of the $500,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A $700,000 share issue raises equity that needs no interest or repayment, protecting cash flow while ELP already carries fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year and a $500,000 bank loan. With the base rate rising to 5.5% (Appendix 3), debt would cost more, so equity keeps the smart-meter rollout affordable and leaves more cash to cut the 6.1% billing-complaint rate and the 3.4-hour outages.

Point 2: Equity improves ELP's financial resilience because there is no risk of the $1,200,000 programme being jeopardised by loan covenants or repossession if demand grows only 2.7%. As a public limited company, ELP can access a wide pool of investors, spreading the funding risk among many shareholders rather than one lender, and the new capital supports the battery storage units without forcing Amina Yusuf to rely solely on retained profits or further borrowing.

Equity also avoids adding to the interest burden on the $500,000 bank loan at a time when the base rate has risen from 4.75% to 5.5%, protecting the $1,200,000 programme from debt-service pressure.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $700,000, $500,000, $1,200,000, $1,500,000

Social media campaigns: Low-cost, targeted ads can reach households and small businesses with installation dates and energy-saving advice, and are easy to update. --- STEM ---
Transgreen Logistics (TGL) is a cooperative in the recycling and green freight sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 2012 by Nia Okafor, it collects and processes recyclable materials for local authorities and runs a flat structure with democratic leadership. TGL plans to invest $540,000 in an electric collection-truck fleet and a computerised stock control system, financed by a $340,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $200,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.00 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and currently handles 100,000 units a year. TGL faces an operational problem: load contamination has reached 5.6% and vehicle defect rates are rising, while its depot reports growing fuel waste from older diesel vehicles.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TGL plans to fund part of its $540,000 electric-fleet investment with $200,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for TGL of using retained profit instead of the $340,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs no interest or repayments, protecting the cash flow of a cooperative with fixed costs of $200,000 a year and a $340,000 bank loan. The saving can be used to cut the 5.6% contamination rate and the 8% fuel waste without raising the $9.00 selling price to local authorities. With the base rate rising to 5.0% (Appendix 3), internal funds avoid the cost of dearer debt.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps control with the cooperative's members and founder Nia Okafor, with no lender conditions on the $540,000 investment and no asset at risk if the electric trucks fail to reduce the 4.1% vehicle defect rate. It is available immediately, so the computerised stock control system can be installed before the next collection cycle, helping deliver the contamination-free service that 63% of surveyed officers will pay $0.30 more for.

The $340,000 loan is also exposed to a base rate that has risen from 4.25% to 5.0%, so using more internal funds reduces the cooperative's exposure to debt-service costs during the electric-fleet programme.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $200,000, $340,000, $540,000, cooperative
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TGL and the case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TGL is promoting a guaranteed contamination-free collection service to local authorities. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TGL choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV could raise awareness of recycling services quickly, but airtime is very expensive for a cooperative funding a $540,000 fleet and most viewers are not the local authority officers who award collection contracts. With demand for recycled materials up only 3.9%, much of the spend would be wasted nationally.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio reaches residents and council officers within TGL's own service area, supports the 26,000 collections made each quarter and costs far less than television. It suits a message about cleaner local collection. Its limits are modest reach and a largely consumer audience, so it may not by itself persuade procurement officers awarding authority-wide contracts, particularly when 59% rank reliability above price.

Social media influencer marketing: Sustainability influencers can showcase contamination-free collections and recycling results to an engaged audience at low cost, reinforcing TGL's green brand. However, the audience is broad and not concentrated among the local authority officers who make purchasing decisions, so conversion to contracts may be slow.

Recommendation: TGL should choose local radio sponsorship. It targets the communities and officers in TGL's own contract area at a fraction of television's cost and fits a local authority service, while the $0.30 premium and 63% survey support give a clear message. Television is rejected as unaffordable and geographically wasteful, and influencers are rejected as too diffuse for local authority procurement; TGL can add targeted social content later.

Local radio also lets TGL respond quickly to the 23 monthly complaints still received and promote the falling 5.6% contamination rate as evidence of service improvement to the local authority officers who award contracts.
    Keywords: contamination-free collections, 63%, 59%, $0.30, 450, 26,000

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TGL wants to reduce contamination and vehicle defects. Consider job rotation or team working. Which should TGL choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Job rotation: Moving drivers between collection routes and depot sorting would build multi-skilled staff who understand both driving and load quality, which could cut the 5.6% contamination rate and the 4.1% vehicle defect rate.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.1% rise in diesel and recycling input costs will affect TGL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate (4.25% to 5.0%): If TGL's $340,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $340,000 = $2,550 a year (0.0075 × $340,000). Higher rates could make local authorities delay contracts and raise future borrowing costs, but the direct interest effect is bounded.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.35 an hour): With a workforce of 70 in driving and processing, this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. Input-cost inflation (10.1% diesel and recycling inputs): The $4.00 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $4.00 rose 10.1%, that adds 10.1% × $4.00 = $0.404 a collection; across 100,000 collections a year that is about $40,400 (100,000 × $0.404). Conclusion: The 10.1% rise in diesel and recycling input costs will have the greatest impact. That preserves the cash flow needed to cover fixed costs of $450,000 a year while the $900,000 server cluster is installed, and every dollar saved in interest can be spent on resolving the rising support tickets and the 4.6-hour incident-resolution time without raising the $48 selling price.

Point 2: Using $300,000 retained profit avoids the conditions and collateral a lender may attach to the $600,000 loan, so Priya Nandakumar and the 60-strong team keep control of how the renewable-energy cooling system is run. It also avoids the risk that the new data centre is threatened if demand from the 7,500 client accounts weakens, and it signals financial strength to the 72% of surveyed clients who value renewable-powered hosting. Because the 58% who would pay $3 more and the 72% who value renewable-powered hosting show clear demand for the new package, retaining profit lets NCS invest without raising the $48 price or delaying its response to the 185 monthly support tickets.

--- STEM ---
Kite Digital Studio (KDS) is a private limited company in the mobile app development and digital services sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2015 by Daniel Okafor, who still takes all major decisions, the business operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. KDS plans to invest $640,000 in an automated app-testing suite with e-commerce payment integration, financed by a $400,000 seven-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $40, and currently produces 25,000 units a year. KDS faces a quality problem: the defect rate in released apps has risen to 3.6% and client complaints about late delivery are growing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KDS is financing part of its app-testing expansion with a seven-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KDS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payments or fixed repayments, so KDS keeps cash that would otherwise service the $400,000 seven-year bank loan. That cash can fund quality assurance training at $950 per employee and the integration work on the $640,000 app-testing suite, helping reduce the 3.6% defect rate without increasing the $280,000 annual fixed costs.

Point 2: Internal funding leaves Daniel Okafor's autocratic control unchallenged, since no lender can impose covenants on how the 35-strong studio operates. Using $240,000 retained profit also avoids putting the business's assets at risk if the 47 monthly complaints and 6.5-day delivery time are not improved quickly, which protects the firm while it tries to win back small-business clients. The 44% who would pay $2 more for priority support indicate that cash generated internally can be reinvested in service improvements, whereas interest on the $400,000 loan would leave less to spend on the 35 developers tackling quality.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $400,000, $640,000, $240,000, $280,000, 3.6%, KDS
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to KDS and its financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KDS is launching its new automated app-testing suite. Consider trade-journal advertising, industry conference sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should KDS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade-journal advertising: Advertisements in software trade journals reach an audience of professional developers and could build credibility for the $640,000 app-testing suite. The cost is moderate, but readership is declining and the message is static, so it may not reach the 250 small-business clients who want faster updates and who compare tools online.

Industry conference sponsorship: Sponsoring a developers' conference puts KDS in front of decision-makers and allows live demonstrations, which suits a technical product. However, stand and travel costs are high for a 35-employee firm servicing a $400,000 loan, and only a limited number of delegates attend, so the reach is narrow compared with the 1,400 app builds a year the suite must support.

Social media influencer marketing: Technology reviewers can demonstrate the testing suite to a large online audience at relatively low cost, with measurable clicks. This suits the 68% of surveyed clients who want faster updates and the 44% who would pay $2 more for priority support, and it can address the 3.6% defect rate story honestly by showing how the new suite catches faults before release.

Recommendation: KDS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the online buyer cheaply and can demonstrate product quality, unlike static journals, and it scales beyond a single conference. Trade-journal advertising is rejected as low-reach and outdated; conference sponsorship is rejected as expensive and too narrow for a firm needing 25,000 units of volume. With complaints already at 47 per month and delivery at 6.5 days, KDS needs a promotion that can highlight improvements quickly; an influencer demonstration can be updated, unlike a printed journal advert or a fixed conference stand.
    Keywords: $640,000, $400,000, 1,400, 250, 68%, 44%, $2, 3.6%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to KDS. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of KDS with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why journals and conferences are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KDS has a rising defect rate and growing complaints about late delivery. Explain two benefits for KDS of using autocratic leadership within its hierarchical structure to improve quality.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Daniel Okafor set one clear quality standard for all 1,400 app builds, which is useful when the defect rate has risen from 1.9% to 3.6%. With authority concentrated at the top, a decision to hold a defective release can be enforced immediately, protecting the 250 small-business clients from further faults and reducing the 47 complaints per month.

Point 2: The hierarchical structure gives each of the 35 staff a defined place in the chain of command, so responsibility for the 6.5-day delivery time is unambiguous and errors can be traced quickly. Clear instructions and close supervision suit a studio trying to integrate the $640,000 automated testing suite, because developers know exactly which testing steps are required and cannot bypass them unnoticed. Clear top-down standards are especially useful when 1,400 builds a year must be checked, because the 35 developers know exactly who is responsible for the rise to 3.6% defects and for the 47 complaints.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KDS wants to reduce the defect rate in released apps. Consider quality control inspection or quality assurance prevention. Which should KDS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Quality control inspection: Inspecting finished app builds before release can catch the faults behind the 3.6% defect rate and stop defective software reaching the 250 clients. It is straightforward to introduce and gives immediate results, but it is reactive: errors are already built in, so rework adds to the 6.5-day delivery time and may worsen the 47 monthly complaints about late delivery.

Quality assurance prevention: Building quality into each development stage prevents faults rather than finding them later, which suits an automated testing suite worth $640,000. The insert states off-the-job quality assurance courses cost $950 per employee, but it does not say how many of the 35 staff need training, so no defensible total can be invented. Prevention reduces rework and protects the $40 selling price, though benefits appear only after staff change their routines.

Decision: KDS should choose quality assurance prevention, supported by a final inspection as a backstop. It attacks the cause of the rise from 1.9% to 3.6% rather than merely screening the output, and it avoids the delivery delays caused by rework. Pure inspection is rejected as reactive and expensive in time, while prevention has no stated total-cost barrier beyond the $950 per-employee course. A practical sequence is to introduce prevention training first and keep a final inspection before release, so the 1,400 builds are checked without relying on rework. Progress should be judged against the given 3.6% defect rate, the 1.9% prior rate and the 6.5-day delivery time. Because the insert does not state how many of the 35 staff need the $950 course, no total cost is asserted; the decision rests on preventing faults rather than sorting them out later.
    Keywords: quality control, quality assurance, 3.6%, 1.9%, 1,400, $640,000, 6.5 days, $950

That cash can be spent on the $720,000 automated swapping network and on fixing the 2.7% defect rate on returned scooters without increasing the $330,000 annual fixed costs or the $33 selling price.

It also avoids risking company assets if the 97.4% on-time swap rate cannot be restored, giving VLM time to improve service before adding debt. Given that 49% of riders would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed battery availability, internally funded investment can improve the service that generates that revenue, while interest on the $450,000 loan would absorb cash needed to answer the 58 monthly complaints.

Quanta Data Solutions (QDS) is a public limited company in the business analytics and software services sector, employing a workforce of 75. Founded in 2008 by Amara Diallo, who remains its chief executive, the business operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. QDS plans to invest $1,050,000 in an automated data-warehouse platform with AI-driven reporting tools, financed by a $650,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $504,000 a year, a variable cost of $16 a unit and a selling price of $44, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. QDS faces a skills and quality problem: reporting errors have risen to 2.8% and 12 analysts have not completed data-security training.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QDS is financing part of its data-warehouse expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for QDS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit avoids interest and principal repayments, so QDS keeps the cash that would otherwise service the $650,000 ten-year bank loan. That cash can cover the $504,000 annual fixed costs and pay for data-security training at $1,250 per course, tackling the 12 untrained analysts and the 2.8% error rate without raising the $44 selling price.

Point 2: Using $400,000 retained profit keeps control with Amara Diallo's existing shareholders rather than a lender, so there are no covenants restricting how the $1,050,000 data-warehouse platform is used. It also avoids pledging assets when 39 client complaints a month and a 5.2-day turnaround show the business still has operational problems to solve before taking on more debt. With 55% of managers willing to pay $4 more for real-time reporting, retained profit can fund the platform and training without diverting cash that would otherwise reduce the 39 monthly complaints and the 5.2-day turnaround.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $650,000, $1,050,000, $400,000, $504,000, 2.8%, QDS
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to QDS and its financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QDS is launching its new automated data-warehouse platform. Consider search-engine advertising, an industry conference sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should QDS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Search-engine advertising: Ads triggered by analytics searches reach managers actively looking for reporting tools, so intent is high and spend can be controlled. The cost per click can escalate, however, and it does not demonstrate the AI-driven reporting features; for a public limited company funding a $1,050,000 platform with a $650,000 loan, a purely text-based campaign may not build enough trust.

Industry conference sponsorship: A stand at a data conference allows live demonstrations to 320-manager-scale audiences of potential buyers and supports credibility. Yet stand, travel and staffing costs are high and only a limited delegate list is reached, which is narrow for a service sold to many clients and slow to generate the 45,000 units a year needed.

Social media influencer marketing: Data and business influencers can show the platform's dashboards to a broad professional audience at low cost per view, with engagement that can be measured. This connects with the 71% of surveyed managers who want faster dashboards and the 55% who would pay $4 more for real-time reporting, and it lets QDS answer the 2.8% error-rate issue openly by showing how the new platform improves accuracy.

Recommendation: QDS should choose social media influencer marketing. It demonstrates the product, reaches the professional segment cheaply and scales beyond one conference. Search-engine advertising is rejected as costly per click and unable to demonstrate features; conference sponsorship is rejected as expensive and narrow. Influencer activity should be backed by search ads for high-intent buyers. The 2.8% error rate also means QDS should avoid claims it cannot yet support, so a demonstrable product story is safer than a broad message.
    Keywords: $1,050,000, $650,000, 3,600, 320, 71%, 55%, $4, 2.8%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to QDS. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of QDS with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why search ads and conferences are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QDS has an error rate of 2.8% and 12 analysts without data-security training. Explain two benefits for QDS of using democratic leadership within its hierarchical structure to improve motivation and quality.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 75 employees propose how reports are checked, so analysts who see the 2.8% errors first-hand can suggest fixes. Involvement increases ownership of accuracy, helping reduce the 39 monthly complaints and the 5.2-day turnaround while protecting the 3,600 reports delivered each quarter.

Point 2: The hierarchical structure keeps accountability clear for the $1,050,000 data-warehouse rollout, so ideas from analysts reach Amara Diallo through defined channels and decisions are not delayed. Consulting staff about the new AI-driven tools also makes the 12 analysts more willing to undertake the $1,250 data-security training, closing the skills gap without disrupting the $650,000 loan-funded project. Because the 12 untrained analysts are a known gap, consultation also helps identify which skills are missing before the $1,250 courses are purchased, making the 75-person workforce more willing to adopt the new tools. Accuracy, not just speed, must improve if the 39 complaints are to fall.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, hierarchical structure, 75, 2.8%, 5.2 days, 39, 12, QDS
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to QDS's errors, complaints and training gap.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QDS needs analysts with data-security skills. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment of security specialists. Which should QDS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal recruitment: Promoting or retraining existing analysts is cheaper and faster, and the 75 staff already know QDS's reporting systems and clients. Training the 12 untrained analysts at $1,250 per course would build loyalty. The drawback is that the insert states a current data-security skills gap and a 2.8% error rate, so internal candidates may simply reproduce the same weaknesses unless training is thorough, and no new expertise enters the business.

External recruitment: Hiring experienced security specialists brings up-to-date skills and fresh practice, which directly addresses the 2.8% error rate and the 12 analysts without training. It widens the pool beyond the 75 current employees and supports the $1,050,000 data-warehouse launch. The costs are higher and induction takes time, with the risk that a new hire does not fit the hierarchical structure.

Decision: QDS should choose external recruitment for the security specialists, while offering the $1,250 course to existing analysts. External hiring is justified because the skills gap is explicit and cannot be solved from within quickly; internal recruitment alone is rejected as too slow and likely to perpetuate the 5.2-day turnaround and 39 complaints, though it remains suitable for non-security roles. A sensible compromise is to recruit externally for the missing security skills and enrol the 12 existing analysts on the $1,250 course, but the primary decision must be external hiring because the skills gap is explicit. Success should be measured against the 2.8% error rate, the 5.2-day turnaround and the 39 complaints. The insert gives no salary figures, so no cost comparison is invented; the judgement rests on the need for skills not currently present among the 75 staff.
    Keywords: data-security training, $1,250, 12, 2.8%, 75, $1,050,000, 39, QDS
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of internal and external recruitment with limited application to QDS. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of QDS. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering skills gap, cost, speed and quality.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how QDS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 18,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $28 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 27,000 reports; a $3 price cut leaving $25 contribution and 20,160 reports needed; average total cost of $27.2 against $44; labour productivity of 600 reports per worker.
    Keywords: break-even output, contribution per unit, 18,000, $28, 45,000 units, $504,000, $27.2, 600
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QDS's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin and the profit margin for 2024 and 2025. Has QDS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 50.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 20.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 25.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue 1,600, cost of sales 880, gross profit 720; operating profit 320; capital employed 2,000. 2025 revenue 1,900, cost of sales 950, gross profit 950; operating profit 475; capital employed 2,375. Gross profit ÷ revenue: 720 ÷ 1,600 and 950 ÷ 1,900. Operating profit ÷ revenue: 320 ÷ 1,600 and 475 ÷ 1,900. Operating profit ÷ capital employed: 320 ÷ 2,000 and 475 ÷ 2,375.

Evaluation: Each measure is stronger in 2025. The share of revenue remaining after direct costs rose from 45.0% to 50.0% because cost of sales grew by only 70 while revenue grew by 300, so the analytics service is scaling efficiently. The share retained as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 2,375 of capital employed improved, important for a public limited company that must justify a $1,050,000 investment to shareholders while servicing a $650,000 loan. The 2.8% error rate and 39 complaints pose a quality risk, but the figures show that growth has not been bought by cutting prices.

Conclusion: QDS's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, driven by revenue growth far ahead of cost of sales. Management should use the stronger position to fund security training and the automated platform, while monitoring errors so that quality does not erode the gain.
    Keywords: 45.0%, 50.0%, 20.0%, 25.0%, 16.0%, Capital employed, 2,375, $650,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether QDS improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QDS of introducing real-time reporting for its analytics clients.
    Answer: Advantage: The survey of 320 managers found 71% want faster dashboards and 55% would pay $4 more per month for real-time reporting, so the feature can add revenue across the 3,600 reports and help cover $504,000 of fixed costs. It also supports the $1,050,000 data-warehouse launch and answers the 39 monthly complaints about slow service.

Disadvantage: Delivering real-time data may raise the $16 variable cost per unit through higher computing use and require the 12 analysts to gain new skills, while the current error rate is already 2.8%. A wrong real-time figure could damage client trust more than a delayed report, and the insert gives no cost for the feature, so its exact profitability cannot be calculated. Because the insert gives no development cost, QDS should pilot the feature with a small group before committing the $1,050,000 platform's resources; the 55% willingness to pay is evidence of demand, not proof of profitability.
    Keywords: real-time reporting, 55%, 71%, 320, $4, $16, $504,000, 2.8%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to QDS's survey, error rate and costs.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase to $15.11 and the 10.6% rise in cloud-computing and data-centre input costs will affect QDS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If the $650,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the additional annual interest is 0.75% × $650,000 = $4,875 a year, shown as 0.0075 × $650,000. That is small against $504,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the direct impact is nil. Higher rates may still discourage client spending, despite analytics spending growing 7.3%.

Minimum wage increase (6.4% to $15.11 an hour): The insert supplies no hours worked or current wages, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. The derivable figure is productivity: 45,000 units ÷ 75 workers = 600 reports per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbed; if the 2.8% error rate and 39 complaints force rework, unit labour costs rise and the $28 contribution narrows. The effect is directionally clear but cannot be quantified from the data.

Input-cost inflation (10.6%): The $16 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so an explicit upper bound is 10.6% × $16 = $1.696, about $1.70 per report. At 45,000 reports this is 45,000 × $1.70 = $76,500 a year. Even a partial pass-through cuts contribution from $28 toward about $26.30 and raises the volume needed to cover $504,000 of fixed costs above 18,000.

Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in cloud and data-centre input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 45,000 reports and directly erodes the $28 contribution that funds the loan and the $1,050,000 platform; the interest rise is about $4,875 and the wage effect cannot be shown to be larger. QDS can offset part of the increase through the $4 premium that 55% of managers accept.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.4%, $15.11, 10.6%, $16, $650,000, 45,000 units, 7.3%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to QDS. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on QDS's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.

--- STEM ---
Axiom Security Software (AXS) is a private limited company in the cybersecurity software and digital services sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2013 by Noah Bergman, the business operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. AXS plans to invest $880,000 in an automated penetration-testing platform with a self-service client portal, financed by a $580,000 five-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $400,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $46, and currently produces 35,000 units a year. AXS faces a people and quality problem: staff turnover has reached 14% and the defect rate in software patches has risen, causing complaints about missed deadlines.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AXS is financing part of its testing-platform expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for AXS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit needs no interest payments or fixed repayments, so AXS keeps the cash that would otherwise service the $580,000 five-year bank loan. That cash can cover fixed costs of $400,000 a year and the work on the $880,000 penetration-testing platform while turnover is 14%, without adding to the pressure that has already produced 41 monthly complaints.

Point 2: Using $300,000 retained profit keeps control with Noah Bergman's team rather than a lender, so no external conditions dictate how the self-service client portal is developed. It also avoids pledging assets when the 4.1% defect rate and 14% staff turnover still need attention, giving the 50-strong firm room to stabilise quality before taking on more debt. The 53% who would pay $5 more for faster patching shows where internally saved cash can be reinvested, rather than paying interest that would compete with the $400,000 fixed costs and the 14% turnover problem.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $580,000, $880,000, $300,000, $400,000, 14%, AXS
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to AXS and its financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AXS is launching its automated penetration-testing platform. Consider a cybersecurity conference sponsorship, search-engine advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should AXS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.

However, stand and travel costs are high for a 50-employee firm already servicing a $580,000 loan, and only a small delegate audience sees the product, too narrow to support 35,000 units of volume.

Search-engine advertising: Ads shown to people searching for penetration testing reach high-intent buyers and can be controlled by budget. The weakness is that text ads cannot demonstrate the platform, and cost per click can rise quickly; with a $880,000 investment to justify, AXS needs to show the product, not just describe it.

Social media influencer marketing: Security reviewers can demonstrate the platform and the self-service portal to a large professional audience at low cost per view, with measurable engagement. This suits the 66% of surveyed clients who value automated security testing and the 53% who would pay $5 more for faster patching, and it lets AXS address the 4.1% defect-rate issue by showing how the new platform finds faults earlier.

Recommendation: AXS should choose social media influencer marketing. It demonstrates the product, reaches technical buyers cheaply and scales beyond one conference. Conference sponsorship is rejected as costly and narrow; search advertising is rejected as unable to demonstrate a visual platform. Influencer content should be supported by targeted search ads for high-intent buyers. With the 4.1% defect rate and 41 monthly complaints, AXS should promote a solution it can demonstrate; a static conference stand or text advert cannot show the platform reducing faults, whereas a reviewer can.
    Keywords: $880,000, $580,000, 380, 66%, 53%, $5, 2,100, 4.1%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to AXS. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of AXS with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why conferences and search ads are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AXS has 14% staff turnover and a rising defect rate. Explain two benefits for AXS of using laissez-faire leadership within its flat structure to motivate its software developers.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced developers freedom to choose how they fix the 4.1% defect rate in the 2,100 patches, which can raise ownership and job satisfaction. Autonomy suits skilled security specialists and may reduce the 14% turnover, because developers who control their own methods are more likely to stay and take pride in reducing the 41 monthly complaints.

Point 2: The flat structure lets developers act on ideas without seeking several layers of approval, helping shorten the 3.8-day patch turnaround and speeding work on the $880,000 testing platform. With fewer managers, decisions about client priorities reach the 50 staff quickly, supporting Noah Bergman's aim of recovering from the rise from 2.2% to 4.1% defects. Autonomy is most valuable when the 50 developers are skilled, which is why it can reduce the 14% turnover; however the 4.1% defect rate still needs a shared standard, so leaders should set minimum quality expectations even in a flat structure.
    Keywords: laissez-faire leadership, flat structure, 50, 14%, 4.1%, 41, 3.8 days, AXS
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AXS's turnover, defect rate and patch turnaround.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: AXS wants to reduce its 14% staff turnover. Consider a performance-related bonus or job enrichment through team working. Which should AXS choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Performance-related bonus: Linking pay to patch quality or speed can motivate the 50 developers to cut the 4.1% defect rate and shorten the 3.8-day turnaround. It is simple to understand, but it costs money that AXS must find while servicing a $580,000 loan and funding an $880,000 platform, and it does not change the repetitive work that may be driving the 14% turnover or the 41 monthly complaints.

Job enrichment through team working: Giving developers varied tasks and shared responsibility for the self-service portal makes the work more interesting and uses their security skills fully. This can reduce turnover by addressing the cause rather than paying around it, and team review of patches can catch faults that produced the rise from 2.2% to 4.1%. The drawback is that it takes time to organise and relies on the flat structure functioning well.

Decision: AXS should choose job enrichment through team working. It tackles the 14% turnover at its source, can improve the 4.1% defect rate and costs little compared with a bonus. The performance bonus is rejected as an expensive short-term fix that does not relieve the repetitive patching behind the 41 complaints, though a small bonus could be added later once the platform is running smoothly. AXS can measure the choice against the 14% turnover, the 4.1% defect rate and the 3.8-day turnaround, all given in the insert. Since no bonus cost is stated, the comparison is qualitative: team working addresses the cause of turnover while a bonus only rewards output after the fact. The flat structure already supports team working, so the change needs little new spending at a time when $580,000 of loan repayments and an $880,000 platform must be funded.
    Keywords: 14%, 4.1%, 41, $400,000, $880,000, 2,100, 3.8 days, AXS
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and job enrichment with limited application to AXS. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of AXS. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a well-justified decision covering turnover, cost, quality and motivation.
