--- STEM ---
Meadowlands Poultry (MPP) is a sole trader business in the poultry farming and meat processing sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2007 by farmer Aisha Meadowlands, it supplies packaged chicken to regional supermarkets and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. MPP plans to invest $880,000 in a new automated poultry processing and packaging line, financed by a $480,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 from the sale of unused farmland. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 95,000 units a year. The proceeds can go directly into the $880,000 packaging line and help absorb the 9.8% rise in feed grain and packaging costs without raising the $13.00 selling price charged to regional supermarkets.

Point 2: Asset sale finance needs no collateral on the trading business and carries no repossession risk, so the new processing line cannot be seized if demand for packaged chicken falls. It also keeps control firmly with Aisha Meadowlands as sole trader, since no lender can impose conditions on how the farm is run. Because the land was unused, the sale releases idle value rather than taking on new debt, and it avoids the variable-rate exposure created when the base rate rose from 4.10% to 4.85%. Overall, the sale is cheaper and less risky than borrowing more.
    Keywords: sale of unused farmland, bank loan, $400,000, $480,000, $280,000, $880,000, $6.00

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MPP's research data, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.85%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in input costs will affect MPP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.10% to 4.85%): If MPP's $480,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points × $480,000 = $3,600 a year (0.0075 × $480,000). That is modest against $280,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also make consumers cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $880,000 line, but MPP can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $13.95 an hour): MPP employs a workforce of 30 in processing and packing, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay figures are given, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented; the honest test is productivity: 95,000 units ÷ 30 staff = 3,166.67 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $7.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.8% feed grain and packaging): MPP's $6.00 variable cost per unit contains feed and packaging, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.8% that adds about 9.8% × $6.00 = $0.59 per unit, and at 95,000 units that is roughly $56,000 a year. Even a smaller rise erodes contribution, but the $0.70 free-range premium and supermarket price talks can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 95,000 units and directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that justifies the $880,000 line, and unlike the loan it cannot be neutralised by fixing a rate. The wage rise is real but manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only about $3,600, so both are smaller.
    Keywords: 4.85%, 6.9%, 9.8%, interest rate, $13.95, $6.00
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to MPP. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MPP's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MPP with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Kestrel Precision Components (KPC) is a private limited company in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Freya Kestrel, it machines aerospace engine components for civil aircraft manufacturers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KPC plans to invest $720,000 in a new CNC machining cell with automated inspection, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $24.00, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. KPC faces two problems: its defect rate has reached 4.2% with rising quality complaints, and labour turnover is increasing among CNC programmers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KPC plans to fund part of its $720,000 CNC expansion with a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KPC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $270,000 of retained profit costs KPC no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the company already carries fixed costs of $300,000 a year and is servicing a $450,000 bank loan. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on tackling the 4.2% defect rate, for example by cutting the $28-per-unit rework burden or funding the $1,100 CNC courses, helping KPC hold its $24.00 selling price for aerospace buyers who rank on-time delivery first.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk of a bank loan, so the $720,000 machining cell is not endangered if the 68% of surveyed buyers who demand on-time delivery are disappointed and orders slip. It also preserves the ownership and control of founder Freya Kestrel: no lender can impose conditions on how the flat, democratically led team runs the new CNC cell, letting KPC react quickly to the 57% of buyers who say they would switch supplier after two late deliveries. Retained profit therefore speeds the decision and keeps control local.
    Keywords: retained profit, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, bank loan, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KPC's costs, defect rate, finance and ownership.

Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National trade-press campaign: Advertisements in aerospace magazines would build wide awareness of KPC's new CNC-machined components across the whole industry, reinforcing the 8,400 components inspected monthly and the fall from 6.5% to 4.2% in defects. However, print is costly, has a long lead time and reaches many firms outside KPC's civil-aircraft niche; with a $720,000 expansion and fixed costs of $300,000 a year, much of the spend would be wasted on readers who never buy engine components.

Exhibition sponsorship: Sponsoring an aerospace trade exhibition gives face-to-face credibility and direct access to procurement teams, valuable because 68% of 250 surveyed buyers rank on-time delivery first and 57% would switch after two late deliveries, so trust must be built personally. The drawbacks are high stand fees, staff time away from the 40,000-unit production target and results that depend on a single event; for a 60-employee firm with a $450,000 loan this is a large, lumpy risk.

Targeted email marketing: Sending focused technical messages to KPC's known OEM buyer list is cheap, immediate and measurable, and can carry the 12-day delivery lead time and quality data straight to the engineers who decide. It lacks the brand reach of print and the personal trust of an exhibition, and works only where contact data is accurate, but its cost per qualified enquiry is far lower than either alternative.

Recommendation: KPC should choose targeted email marketing, supported later by a small exhibition presence. It reaches exactly the civil-aircraft buyers who matter, can be justified against $300,000 fixed costs and a $450,000 loan, and directly communicates the reliability message the survey identifies. National trade-press advertising is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and full exhibition sponsorship is rejected as too costly and disruptive for a 60-staff firm; email can be scaled up once the machining cell proves its 4.2% defect improvement.

Conclusion: KPC's financial position has improved. Both cover measures are higher and the improvement does not rely on stock. The residual risk is higher inventories and slow receivables, so management should tighten credit control before further expansion.

    Answer: Advantage: Heat-recovery equipment would reuse waste heat from the press, cutting the electricity element of the 11.3% rise in input costs and lowering the $22.00 variable cost per unit. This supports the 62% of 180 surveyed plant managers who would pay 3% more for lower-carbon forged parts, helping DFM win orders and defend the $38.00 selling price while reducing the $41-per-tonne rework burden associated with the 7.4% scrap rate.

Disadvantage: The equipment adds to the $1,100,000 capital already committed on top of a $600,000 bank loan and fixed costs of $540,000 a year, so it raises financial risk if the 2.8% growth in construction output proves weak. It also needs specialist maintenance that DFM may lack, since 26 of 120 workers are not yet press-certified; a breakdown could interrupt the 18-day delivery lead time and worsen the 31 monthly quality complaints if temperatures drift during forging. The 180 plant managers surveyed also expect documented quality, which the equipment alone cannot guarantee.
    Keywords: 7.4%, $41, 15,000, 62%, 180, $1,100,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to DFM's waste data, survey and investment.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in steel scrap and electricity input costs will affect DFM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If DFM's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000), which is small against fixed costs of $540,000, and zero if the loan is fixed. The larger risk is that higher rates deter construction investment beyond the modest 2.8% output growth. DFM can reduce this by fixing the rate or repaying part of the loan from the $500,000 share issue.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.87 per hour): With a workforce of 120, many pressing and packing roles are hourly paid, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can honestly be invented; the defensible comparison is with given productivity, 60,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 500 units per worker. If productivity stays at 500 units the $16.00 contribution can absorb the rise; if it falls, unit labour cost pushes up the $31.00 average total cost.

Input cost inflation (11.3% steel scrap and electricity): The $22.00 variable cost includes these inputs, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3% that would add 11.3% × $22.00 = $2.49 per unit, or about $149,000 a year at 60,000 units (60,000 × $2.49). A portion can be recovered through the 3% premium that 62% of buyers would pay, but not all.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 60,000 units, directly erodes the $16.00 contribution that funds the $1,100,000 press and cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate. The interest rise is small and manageable; the wage rise depends on productivity that DFM can influence. Input inflation is therefore the deepest threat.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 6.2%, 11.3%, $14.87, $22.00, 2.8%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to DFM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on DFM's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to DFM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Tarrant Rubber Mouldings (TRM) is a partnership in the rubber-products sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2013 by Dev Tarrant, it makes moulded rubber seals and gaskets for car manufacturers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. TRM plans to invest $480,000 in a new injection-moulding machine with a recycled-rubber feed system, financed by a $180,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $175,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. TRM faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and waste from rubber off-cuts on the line is rising steadily.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TRM is financing its $480,000 moulding machine with a $180,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for TRM of using the bank loan rather than relying only on retained profit.
    Answer: Point 1: The $180,000 bank loan lets TRM keep the $300,000 of retained profit as a cash buffer against the problems in the case, namely off-cut waste costing $16 per kilogram and a defect rate that has risen to 3.6%. With fixed costs of $175,000 a year and car production growing only 3.2%, holding that reserve protects the 7-day delivery lead time and avoids a cash crisis if a batch of gaskets has to be remade.

Point 2: Borrowing the $180,000 spreads the cost of the $480,000 machine over time instead of draining the partnership's own funds at once, preserving working capital for raw rubber and wages. It also leaves the partners' personal capital untouched, so the business can fund the 12 staff requiring injection-moulding certification from revenue rather than asking the partners for more money. Used alongside the $300,000 retained profit, the loan keeps the 45,000-unit operation liquid while it adjusts to the new machine.
    Keywords: bank loan, $180,000, $300,000, $480,000, $175,000, retained profit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TRM's waste, costs, liquidity and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TRM is promoting its new recycled-rubber seals. Consider sponsorship of a motorsport team, advertising in automotive supplier magazines, or listings on industrial e-commerce marketplaces. Which should TRM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Motorsport sponsorship: Associating TRM with a racing team would raise brand recognition quickly among car enthusiasts and could suggest high-performance rubber, but it is extremely expensive for a 38-staff partnership and reaches the general public rather than the procurement engineers who buy 45,000 gaskets. With fixed costs of $175,000 and a $180,000 loan, such spend would be hard to justify against the 3.6% defect problem.

Automotive supplier magazines: Print advertisements would reach a specialist readership and could explain the recycled-rubber feed message, which 71% of 200 surveyed buyers prefer. However, magazines have long lead times, high costs and no immediate response mechanism, and only 48% of buyers check environmental credentials, so much of the spend would not convert into orders for a small firm with a 7-day lead time.

Industrial e-commerce listings: Listing the seals on established B2B marketplaces puts TRM in front of buyers actively searching for gaskets, is relatively low-cost and gives measurable enquiries and orders. The recycled-rubber story can be shown in the product description, appealing directly to the 71% who prefer such suppliers. Listings alone do not build deep brand loyalty and depend on good product data and prompt fulfilment, but they suit a small partnership.

Recommendation: TRM should choose industrial e-commerce listings, supported by modest magazine advertising later. Marketplaces reach active buyers cheaply and measurably, which matters against $175,000 fixed costs and a $180,000 loan. Motorsport sponsorship is rejected as unaffordable and aimed at the wrong audience, and magazine advertising alone is rejected as slow and hard to measure; online listings can generate the volume that makes later print worthwhile.
    Keywords: $480,000, 45,000, 71%, 200, 7 days
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional options with minimal application to TRM. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with advantages and disadvantages in the context of TRM and some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to TRM with a justified recommendation explaining why motorsport sponsorship and magazine-only advertising are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TRM's labour turnover has reached 14%. Explain two benefits for TRM of its flat structure with laissez-faire leadership in motivating its production team.
    Answer: Point 1: A flat structure with laissez-faire leadership gives TRM's 38 experienced moulding operators real autonomy over how they set up their machines and solve problems, which can satisfy esteem needs and raise job satisfaction. In a small partnership there are few layers, so skilled staff are trusted rather than closely supervised; that freedom can reduce the 14% labour turnover by making operators want to stay, avoiding repeated recruitment and the $780-per-employee cost of replacing certified staff.

Point 2: Delegating decisions speeds problem-solving on the factory floor, which matters with off-cut waste costing $16 per kilogram and a defect rate that has risen from 2.4% to 3.6%. Operators who can adjust a mould immediately prevent waste and keep the 7-day delivery lead time, supporting the 71% of 200 surveyed buyers who prefer recycled-rubber suppliers. Dev Tarrant can then focus on the $480,000 investment and the 45,000-unit target instead of approving routine choices, while the 12 staff needing certification can learn by doing.
    Keywords: laissez-faire leadership, 14%, workforce of 38, 12, $780, labour turnover
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified, max 2. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to TRM's turnover, waste, delivery and structure.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TRM must upskill 12 staff to operate the new injection-moulding machine. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job courses at the local college. Which should TRM choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training beside the moulding machine is tailored to TRM's own equipment, costs no fees and keeps all 12 staff producing gaskets while they learn, protecting the 11,250 units made each quarter and the 7-day delivery lead time. It also lets experienced partners coach workers on reducing the 3.6% defect rate and the $16-per-kilogram off-cut waste. Off-the-job courses: The local college course at $780 per employee gives structured skills and a recognised qualification for all 12 staff, costing $9,360 in total, affordable beside the $480,000 machine. Formal certification supports the 71% of 200 surveyed buyers who prefer recycled-rubber suppliers and helps cut waste through better machine settings. However, it takes 12 of a workforce of 38 away from production, risking the 45,000-unit target and the 7-day lead time, and the generic content may need site-specific follow-up. With labour turnover at 14%, newly qualified staff could also leave.

Decision: TRM should choose on-the-job training, with short college modules for the most senior operators. It is cheap, machine-specific and protects output and delivery while the partnership absorbs a $180,000 loan. Full off-the-job training is rejected because removing 12 of 38 staff would disrupt the 7-day lead time and the 45,000-unit target, and the $9,360 fee can be spent later once the machine is stable and the 3.6% defect rate is understood.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TRM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of TRM. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods applied to TRM with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and certification.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TRM's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TRM's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.59 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.81 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.02 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.10 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $38,000 cash = $263,000; 2025 current assets = $110,000 + $118,000 + $52,000 = $280,000. Evaluation: Liquidity has improved clearly. Current assets rose from $263,000 to $280,000 while current liabilities fell from $165,000 to $155,000, lifting short-term cover from 1.59 to 1.81. The partnership has also moved cash from $38,000 to $52,000 while funding the $480,000 machine, so it has kept a usable buffer for the 7-day delivery promise and the $180,000 loan.

Conclusion: TRM's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the improvement does not rest on inventory alone, since the acid-test rise confirms it. Management should keep control of the rising stock and the 14% labour turnover, but the balance sheet can support the expansion.

--- STEM ---
Westmore Kiln & Ceramics (WKM) is a cooperative in the industrial ceramics sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 1987 by Elaine Westmore, it makes refractory bricks and kiln furniture for foundries and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. WKM plans to invest $640,000 in an energy-efficient kiln with waste-heat recovery, financed by a $340,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $260,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.50 a unit and a selling price of $22.50, and currently produces 50,000 units a year.   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WKM plans to fund part of its $640,000 kiln project with a $340,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for WKM of using retained profit rather than the bank loan for this part of the investment.

Money not paid to the bank can be spent on reducing the 5.3% defect rate and the $23-per-unit remake cost, or on the $860 kiln-control courses, helping the cooperative hold its $22.50 selling price and answer the 29 monthly complaints.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no collateral, so the $640,000 kiln is not at risk of repossession if foundry output, which grew only 2.4%, disappoints and the 50,000-unit plan is missed. It also suits WKM's cooperative structure: member-control is preserved because no lender can impose conditions on how the democratic leadership runs the business or reinvests surplus. Using internal funds therefore speeds the decision and keeps control with the members while the $340,000 loan remains available for other needs.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to WKM's energy waste, defects, finance and ownership.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WKM of installing waste-heat recovery on its new kiln.
    Answer: Advantage: Waste-heat recovery would cut the energy that is currently 14% of kiln costs, directly reducing the pressure from the 10.8% rise in gas and clay input costs and lowering the $17.70 average total cost. It supports the 66% of 220 surveyed buyers who would pay 2% more for low-energy ceramics and the 54% who check sustainability credentials, helping WKM sell the 50,000 units at $22.50 and defend the $640,000 investment.

Disadvantage: The recovery system adds capital cost and technical complexity to a project already funded by a $340,000 loan and fixed costs of $260,000 a year, raising risk if foundry output grows only 2.4%. With 15 of 70 workers lacking kiln-control certification and a defect rate of 5.3%, poor operation could cause temperature faults that raise the $23 remake cost and the 29 monthly complaints, while maintenance downtime could threaten the 15-day delivery time. WKM's members would also need training on the new controls, and 15 of 70 workers are not yet kiln-certified.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to WKM's energy, survey and investment data.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in natural gas and clay input costs will affect WKM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If WKM's $340,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $340,000 = $2,550 a year (0.0075 × $340,000), modest next to fixed costs of $260,000, and zero if the loan is fixed. Dearer credit may also discourage foundry investment beyond the forecast 2.4% output growth, but WKM can largely remove this risk by fixing the loan rate at outset.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.79 per hour): With a workforce of 70, many kiln and packing roles are hourly paid, so the wage bill rises unavoidably. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual figure can honestly be calculated; the defensible check is productivity of 50,000 units ÷ 70 staff = 714 units per worker. If that holds, the $10.00 contribution can absorb the rise; if defects of 5.3% reduce effective output, unit labour cost will push up the $17.70 average total cost.

Input cost inflation (10.8% gas and clay): The $12.50 variable cost includes these inputs, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8% that adds 10.8% × $12.50 = $1.35 per unit, about $67,500 a year at 50,000 units (50,000 × $1.35). Waste-heat recovery and the 2% price premium accepted by 66% of buyers can offset part of this, but not all of a broad rise.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in gas and clay input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 50,000 units and directly erodes the $10.00 contribution that must cover $260,000 fixed costs and service the $340,000 loan. The interest rise is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be managed through productivity; input inflation is the change WKM can least control and therefore bites deepest.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.4%, 10.8%, $14.79, $12.50, 2.4%

--- STEM ---
Pinnion Gear Manufacturing (PGM) is a private limited company in the engineering sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 2008 by Anika Pinnion, it produces precision gears for agricultural machinery and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. PGM plans to invest $560,000 in a new gear-grinding line with automated oil recycling, financed by a $260,000 bank loan, $200,000 retained profit and a $100,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $19.00, and currently produces 52,000 units a year. PGM faces two problems: a skills gap in gear grinding and a defect rate of 4.8%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PGM is funding part of its $560,000 grinding line with a $260,000 bank loan and a $100,000 overdraft. Explain two advantages for PGM of using retained profit instead of the overdraft for the $200,000 it contributes.
    Answer: Point 1: The $200,000 of retained profit costs no interest and has no repayment deadline, unlike the $100,000 overdraft, protecting cash flow while PGM already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $260,000 bank loan. Because an overdraft can be withdrawn on demand, using internal funds for the $560,000 grinding line removes the risk that the line stalls mid-installation, which would worsen the 4.8% defect rate and the $32-per-gear rework cost.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no security over the company's assets, so the new grinding line is not exposed if agricultural machinery sales, which grew 3.6%, fall below the 52,000-unit plan. It also preserves founder Anika Pinnion's control, since no bank can impose conditions on the flat, autocratically led team through an overdraft facility. Using the $200,000 keeps the overdraft free for genuine short-term cash needs such as the $1,050 grinding courses, while the 10-day delivery promise stays protected.
    Keywords: retained profit, $200,000, $100,000, $260,000, overdraft, $240,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PGM's defects, costs, finance and control.

Social-media video demonstrations: Short videos showing the grinding process and measurement checks can prove precision visually, are cheap to produce, can be targeted at agricultural-equipment engineers and give measurable views and enquiries. They can also address the 61% who would switch after quality failures by showing inspection in action. Their limits are that they reach buyers only where contact data or targeting is accurate and cannot replace a technical conversation, but they demonstrate the product far better than print.

Recommendation: PGM should choose social-media video demonstrations, supported later by a small exhibition presence. Current Ratio 2025 = 1.89 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.09 : 1

Every dollar not paid as loan interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in packaging and courier inputs, helping QRF hold its $38.00 selling price and stay competitive in online fashion without raising prices.

Point 2: Using internal funds avoids the collateral and default risk of the $400,000 bank loan, so the new $620,000 fulfilment centre cannot be repossessed if the launch disappoints or the return rate stays at 14%. It also preserves Priya Quill's ownership and control: no lender can impose conditions on how the automated sorting operation is run, which suits QRF's flat structure and democratic leadership and leaves the founder free to redirect the $220,000 if customer demand shifts.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QRF of offering free returns to its online womenswear customers.

It also differentiates QRF from rivals and may help reduce the 14% return rate by encouraging customers to order their usual size with confidence rather than over-ordering.

Disadvantage: Free returns shift the cost of reverse shipping and restocking onto QRF, raising the effective cost of each sale beyond the $14.00 variable cost per unit and squeezing the $24.00 contribution if the 14% return rate persists. Handling returned garments also adds picking work at a time when parcel-picking errors are already rising, and returned womenswear may lose seasonal value, tying up the $120,000 of inventories shown in 2025 and worsening cash flow. Refunds also reduce the cash available to service the $400,000 loan and weaken the 1.85 current ratio shown in Appendix 2.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 3.75% to 4.25%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in packaging and courier input costs will affect QRF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.25%): If QRF's $400,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.50% of $400,000 = $2,000 a year (0.005 × $400,000). That is small next to fixed costs of $180,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates may also make consumers more cautious about discretionary fashion and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but QRF can largely neutralise this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $14.20 per hour): With a workforce of 50, this rise feeds directly into the wage bill of the fulfilment centre and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The honest benchmark is the given productivity data: 20,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 400 units per worker. Only if productivity holds at 400 units or output grows can QRF absorb the wage rise without pushing unit labour cost up and eroding the $24.00 contribution per unit.

Input cost inflation (9.8% packaging and courier): The insert does not decompose the $14.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 9.8% that adds 9.8% × $14.00 = $1.37 per unit; at 20,000 units that is about $27,400 a year. Even a smaller effect on packaging alone would cut the $24.00 contribution, and QRF has only a limited ability to recover it because consumer spending on fashion grew just 1.2% and the sector return rate is 16%.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 20,000 units and directly erodes the $24.00 contribution that justifies the $620,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only about $2,000 and the wage rise can be offset if 400-unit productivity holds. Input inflation is rejected as smaller only if packaging is a tiny share of cost, which the insert does not state, so it must be treated as the largest risk.
    Keywords: 3.75%, 4.25%, 5.5%, $14.20, 9.8%, $400,000

--- STEM ---
Tidewater Surfwear (TSW) is a private limited company in the coastal apparel retail sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2016 by Elena Marlow, the business sells surfwear through its website and a small chain of seaside stores, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $162,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $39.00, and currently produces 15,000 units a year.     Question: TSW plans to finance part of its $540,000 cutting-facility investment with a $240,000 share issue rather than a larger bank loan. Explain two advantages for TSW of using this share issue.

Unlike the $300,000 bank loan, the share money does not add to interest charges if the base rate rises, leaving more of the $39.00 selling price to cover the 11.3% rise in fabric input costs and keeping cash available for the $540,000 facility.

Point 2: Because the $240,000 is equity rather than debt, no lender can repossess the new $540,000 facility if demand for surfwear disappoints, reducing financial risk for a 40-employee coastal retailer dependent on seasonal trade. The $240,000 also enlarges the shareholder base, bringing fresh capital and potentially new contacts or retail experience, which can support Elena Marlow's plans to grow the seaside stores and website alongside the automated cutting line.
    Keywords: share issue, $240,000, $300,000, $540,000, fixed costs of $162,000

    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.57 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.81 : 1

Conclusion: TSW's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the improvement is not just an inventory effect, since inventories actually fell from $150,000 to $130,000. The main residual risk is higher receivables, so TSW should tighten credit control while proceeding with the cutting facility.

--- STEM ---
Nova Vale Leather (NVL) is a private limited company in the leather goods retail and e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Vale, the business sells handmade bags and wallets through its flagship website, and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. NVL plans to invest $780,000 in a new eco-tannery and online fulfilment hub, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and $330,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $20.00 a unit and a selling price of $62.00, and currently produces 14,000 units a year.     Question: NVL is funding its $780,000 eco-tannery with a $450,000 bank loan and $330,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for NVL of using the bank loan rather than relying only on retained profit.
    Answer: Point 1: A $450,000 bank loan lets NVL keep its $330,000 retained profit as a cash buffer against fixed costs of $210,000 a year and an 18% labour turnover that forces repeated hiring and retraining. Preserving that internal reserve is valuable when the eco-tannery may overrun and when customer returns already run at 4.5% of orders, so the business can meet short-term commitments without running out of cash.

Point 2: Borrowing the $450,000 allows the full $780,000 project to go ahead immediately, capturing the 38% of surveyed customers who would pay a $15 premium for traceable leather, rather than delaying until enough profit is accumulated. Faster completion lets NVL start earning from the new capacity sooner, and a predictable bank loan repayment plan is easier to budget for than an uncertain stream of future retained profit in a market where accessory spending fell 0.8%, rather than waiting for profits that may not appear if demand stays weak.
    Keywords: bank loan, $450,000, $330,000, $780,000, retained profit, fixed costs of $210,000

Engagement is measurable and cost can be controlled. With accessory spending already down 0.8%, NVL cannot assume buyers will accept a higher price.
    Keywords: traceable leather, eco-tannery, 38%, $15, 55%, 18%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to NVL's survey, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 3.5% to 4.25%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 13.6% rise in raw hide and freight costs will affect NVL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.5% to 4.25%): If NVL's $450,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is significant next to fixed costs of $210,000 a year, and it would also raise the cost of financing the remaining $780,000 eco-tannery. If the loan is fixed, the immediate effect is zero, so NVL can reduce this risk by fixing the rate, and the fall in accessory spending of 0.8% is a separate demand concern.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $13.90 per hour): With a workforce of 35 and 18% labour turnover, this rise feeds directly into wage costs for cutting, finishing and fulfilment and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The correct benchmark is the given productivity figure: 14,000 units ÷ 35 staff = 400 units per worker. If productivity holds at 400 units and turnover falls, the rise is absorbable; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $42.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Raw hide and freight inflation (13.6%): The insert does not decompose the $20.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole variable cost rose 13.6%, that adds 13.6% × $20.00 = $2.72 per unit, or about $38,080 a year at 14,000 units. Even a partial increase would erode the contribution that funds the $780,000 project, and with spending on luxury accessories down 0.8% and fashion returns averaging 17%, NVL has limited scope to raise the $62.00 price.

Conclusion: The 13.6% rise in hide and freight costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit, is larger than the $3,375 interest increment and the absorbable wage rise, and directly attacks the $42.00 contribution on which the $780,000 expansion depends. The interest rise is smaller and manageable by fixing the rate; the wage rise can be offset by 400-unit productivity, so input inflation is the dominant threat.
    Keywords: 3.5%, 4.25%, 7.2%, $13.90, 13.6%, $450,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to NVL. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on NVL's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of NVL with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Zaara Eyewear (ZAE) is a public limited company in the eyewear e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by Zaara Nasser, the business sells prescription frames and sunglasses online, and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. ZAE plans to invest $960,000 in an automated lens-fitting line and a new mobile shopping platform, financed by a $600,000 share issue and a $360,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $222,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $55.00, and currently produces 18,500 units a year. ZAE faces two problems: the lens-fitting defect rate has reached 4.2% and online returns are rising as sales grow.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ZAE is funding its $960,000 lens-fitting line with a $600,000 share issue and a $360,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for ZAE of using the share issue rather than a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Share issue money does not require interest or repayment, so it protects ZAE's cash flow while the public limited company carries fixed costs of $222,000 a year and a 4.2% defect rate that forces remakes. With the base rate rising to 5.0%, a larger loan would add interest expense; equity avoids this, leaving more of the $55.00 selling price available to cover the 10.5% rise in lens and frame costs.

Point 2: Issuing $600,000 of shares strengthens the capital base for a public limited company without creating a lender who could threaten the $960,000 investment if cash flow weakens. It gives ZAE more financial flexibility to fund the new mobile platform and to weather the 4.2% return rate, and new shareholders may bring useful retail or technology expertise that supports growth in online eyewear without adding fixed-interest commitments, and the stronger equity base leaves room to borrow further if the $960,000 line needs extra funding.
    Keywords: share issue, $600,000, $360,000, $960,000, bank loan, public limited company
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to ZAE's costs, defects, financing mix and legal structure.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ZAE wants to increase repeat orders for its frames and sunglasses. Consider a seasonal price discount, a free-delivery offer, or a loyalty scheme. Which should ZAE choose to build repeat custom? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Seasonal price discount: Cutting the $55.00 price would stimulate short-term demand and help fill the new automated line's capacity, clearing the 18,500-unit target. However, a discount comes straight out of the $37.00 contribution per unit, and with lens costs up 10.5% and a 4.2% defect rate, ZAE can ill afford to give away margin. Discounts also train customers to wait for sales rather than buy at full price.

Free-delivery offer: Removing delivery charges reduces a common barrier for the 63% of 750 surveyed shoppers who buy eyewear online and can lift conversion against a 2.9% click-through rate. It is simple to promote and supports the 3.1-day delivery promise. The weakness is that carriage is a real cost that would further squeeze the $37.00 contribution, and it does not by itself encourage a second purchase.

Loyalty scheme: A points or repeat-purchase scheme directly targets repeat custom, rewarding the 49% of shoppers who would pay $20 more for custom-fitted frames and encouraging them to return. It builds a customer database for targeted marketing and, because rewards can be capped, the cost is more controllable than a blanket discount.

Recommendation: ZAE should choose the loyalty scheme. It is designed for repeat orders, fits the premium custom-fitted positioning that 49% of buyers value, and controls cost better than a discount that erodes $37.00 contribution. Free delivery is rejected as a costly short-term conversion tool that does not create loyalty; seasonal discounts are rejected because they damage margin when input costs are already rising 10.5%, and ZAE should track the 4.2% return rate to confirm the scheme is not encouraging more orders than the line can fit accurately.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]

Profit sharing is rejected as the main tool because profit is affected by the 10.5% cost rise; team working alone is rejected because it lacks the financial incentive needed to change behaviour on the line, so ZAE should review the 4.2% defect rate monthly against the 6.8% return figure of a year ago.

    Answer: Calculations:

Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.03 : 1

--- STEM ---
Kirsi Home Stores (KHS) is a private limited company in the home furnishings e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2014 by Kirsi Salo, the business sells flat-pack furniture and decor through its website, and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. KHS plans to invest $700,000 in an automated furniture warehouse and a new dropshipping platform, financed by a $350,000 bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $192,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $48.00, and currently produces 16,000 units a year.     Question: KHS is funding its $700,000 warehouse with a $350,000 bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for KHS of using the bank loan rather than only retained profit.

Keeping that reserve is prudent while stock-outs are rising and inventories stand at $205,000, giving Kirsi Salo flexibility to buy stock or handle a delayed launch without exhausting internal cash.

Point 2: Borrowing lets the whole $700,000 automated warehouse and dropshipping platform proceed at once rather than waiting to accumulate profit, so KHS can capture the 42% of surveyed customers who would pay $25 more for flat-pack sustainable furniture. With the base rate cut from 5.0% to 4.5%, loan interest is cheaper than it was, making debt an attractive way to fund the project while the 1.6% growth in home-furnishing spending offers a chance to win new demand. A lower interest burden also supports the $28.00 average total cost and leaves more cash for the 5.6-day delivery operation.
    Keywords: bank loan, $350,000, $700,000, retained profit, $192,000, $48.00
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KHS's costs, reserves, complaints and expansion.

    Answer: Own delivery fleet: Controlling delivery in-house lets KHS set careful handling standards, directly attacking the 7% damage-related complaint rate and protecting the $48.00 selling price from refunds. It also supports the 57% of 650 surveyed customers who choose free delivery over speed. However, buying vehicles and employing drivers adds fixed costs on top of $192,000 a year and the $700,000 warehouse plan, and a fleet may be underused, so it is expensive for a 40-employee retailer.

Third-party courier: A specialist courier offers national reach, established logistics and variable costs that rise only with orders, which suits the new dropshipping platform and avoids heavy capital spending. The drawback is less control over how fragile flat-pack furniture is handled, which could keep the 7% damage rate high, and courier input costs have risen 8.9%, so charges may increase just as volume grows.

Dropshipping: Suppliers dispatch directly to customers, removing warehouse handling and much of KHS's stock risk, which eases the stock-out problem and cuts the need for the $700,000 facility. In practice KHS loses control of packing and timing, and a 5.6-day average delivery plus 7% damage suggests fragile items need close oversight; margins are also thinner, squeezing the $32.00 contribution per unit.

Recommendation: KHS should use a third-party courier with strict handling agreements and its own quality checks. It gives national scale without the fixed cost of a fleet and more control than dropshipping, which is rejected because it removes control of packing when damage is already 7%. An in-house fleet is rejected as too capital-intensive alongside a $700,000 investment and 5.6-day delivery targets.

Flat packs can also arrive damaged or incomplete, and with a 7% damage-related complaint rate and 2.7% conversion, any quality slip would raise refunds and weaken the 29% repeat-purchase rate, so the 4.5% base rate is welcome as cheaper credit to fund the transition.
    Keywords: flat-pack sustainable furniture, 42%, $25, 57%, 29%, 7%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KHS's survey, costs and damage rate.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate cut from 5.0% to 4.5%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 8.9% rise in timber and courier input costs will affect KHS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate cut (5.0% to 4.5%): This is a favourable change. If KHS's $350,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost falls by 0.5% of $350,000 = $1,750 a year (0.005 × $350,000), easing the burden of fixed costs of $192,000 a year and freeing cash for the $700,000 warehouse. If the loan is fixed, the saving is delayed until refinancing. Lower rates may also support the 1.6% growth in home-furnishing spending, though the benefit is a modest, one-off gain rather than a change to unit costs.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.40 per hour): With a workforce of 40, this rise pushes up wage costs in warehousing and packing and is unavoidable. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The correct benchmark is the given productivity figure: 16,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 400 units per worker. If productivity holds at 400 units, the rise is absorbable; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $32.00 contribution per unit is squeezed at a time when the 7% damage rate already adds cost.

Timber and courier input inflation (8.9%): The insert does not decompose the $16.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole variable cost rose 8.9%, that adds 8.9% × $16.00 = about $1.42 per unit, or roughly $22,784 a year at 16,000 units. Courier inflation also makes the 7% damage problem more expensive to fix through returns, and with home-furnishing spending up only 1.6% and fuel surcharges adding 3.2% to delivery, KHS has limited power to pass costs on through its $48.00 price.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in timber and courier costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit, is far larger than the $1,750 interest saving, and directly threatens the $32.00 contribution that funds the $700,000 expansion. The wage rise can be offset if 400-unit productivity holds, and the rate cut is a benefit rather than a threat, so input inflation is clearly the dominant external change.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 4.5%, 5.8%, $13.40, 8.9%, $350,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KHS. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KHS's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of KHS with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Harbour Bay Poultry (HBP) is a private limited company in the food processing sector, converting fresh chicken into frozen ready-to-cook meals sold through national supermarket chains. Founded in 2012 by Jernej Munoz, the business employs a workforce of 42. It operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. HBP plans to invest $720,000 in a new frozen-line grading and packaging plant with contactless automation, financed by a ten-year bank loan and retained profit. It has fixed costs of $620,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.50 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and currently produces 180,000 units a year. HBP faces a worsening defect rate record on sealing and rising quality complaint levels from retail buyers.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for HBP of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs HBP nothing in repayments or interest on the $720,000 expansion, so every dollar not paid as loan interest can absorb the 6.9% rise in agricultural input costs, keeping the $16.50 meals affordable to supermarket buyers and defending the $4.00 contribution ($16.50 − $12.50) during the $620,000 plant build. It also avoids the collateral and default risk attached to the ten-year bank loan, so the whole frozen-line grading and packaging plant is not at risk of repossession.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership with the management team, so no lender can impose conditions on how HBP runs the freezing automation or sets prices; HBP keeps full flexibility to reinvest surplus into further capacity or quality improvements once the plant stabilises.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $720,000, $16.50, $12.50, $620,000, 6.9%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to HBP's expansion, contribution and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider a national frozen-meals marketing campaign, local TV sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should HBP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: 1. National frozen-meals marketing campaign: a national TV campaign reaches millions of buyers quickly, but airtime and production costs are extremely high, so much of the spend would be wasted on viewers outside HBP's supermarket footprint or buyers of unfrozen meals.

2. Local TV sponsorship: cheaper than national TV, suits time-sensitive launch messages near supermarkets, but local reach alone cannot generate the volume needed to justify the 180,000-unit output plan across national supermarket chains.

3. Social media influencer marketing: food and family lifestyle influencers show the frozen meals being cooked, sliced and delivered, targeting the retail buyers described in appendix 1 who pay up to $16.50 per meal; cost per reached shopper is low and results are measurable in pre-orders.

Recommendation: HBP should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets retail buyers described in the appendix, fits the $720,000 plant better than national TV, and supports the launch; national TV is rejected as too costly for the $4.00 contribution margins, and local TV as too narrow for national supermarket listings; HBP should add modest in-store tasting sessions with supermarkets as a support to the influencer campaign.
    Keywords: 180,000, $16.50, $720,000, $800, 62%, 48%, ready-to-cook
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HBP with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HBP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why national TV and local TV are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for HBP of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its kitchen and freezing teams.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives HBP's 42 staff a genuine voice in rota planning, oven schedules and equipment maintenance, which satisfies their social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help decide shift patterns and press sealing are more likely to attend reliably, directly attacking the rising quality complaint levels from retail buyers.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions surfaces practical ideas from the people who handle frozen meals daily, improving sealing quality and pushing the 3.9% defect rate down further. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, saving HBP's $800 per employee off-the-job recertification cost while protecting the 180,000-unit output plan during the plant build.
    Keywords: worsening defect rate, 3.9%, $800, 180,000, 42, quality complaint levels, frozen ready-to-cook meals
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to HBP's attendance, quality and output.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HBP must upskill 12 production staff on the new freezing equipment before the new plant opens. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should HBP choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Training on HBP's own freezing equipment is directly relevant, costs nothing in course fees and keeps the 12 staff productive during the run-up to the plant opening, protecting the 180,000-unit output plan. Drawbacks are that trainers are production staff whose own work suffers, and bad habits can be passed on informally.

Off-the-job training: The $800 per employee course at the regional college gives structured, certified hygiene training.

Decision: HBP should choose on-the-job training for the 12 staff, with short college sessions for lead operators added after launch. On-the-job training is cheapest and machine-specific while capacity is needed; the $800 college course is used later for broader skills. HBP will still need the $800 per employee recertification to satisfy auditors — off-the-job training is rejected because removing 12 staff from the line during the launch period hurts output.
    Keywords: off-the-job training, $800, 3.9%, freezing equipment, $620,000, 12 of the 42 staff
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HBP. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the training methods in the context of HBP. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how HBP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 155,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 1. Margin of safety: HBP produces 180,000 units against break-even 155,000, leaving about 25,000 units of buffer before profit turns negative. 2.   Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HBP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HBP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.49 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.47 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.83 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.91 : 1

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved slightly. The acid test improved from 0.83 to 0.91, so HBP no longer relies on selling stock to meet short-term debts; the margin of safety for retail buyers grew. Trade receivables rose from $42,000 to $47,000, and inventories fell, so cash should be monitored while the $620,000 plant is built.

Conclusion: HBP's financial position has improved, as shown by the stronger acid test ratio (0.83 to 0.91).
    Keywords: 1.49, 1.47, 0.83, 0.91, $131,000, $140,000, 88,000, 58,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether HBP's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HBP of introducing eco-packaging with extended shelf life for its frozen ready-to-cook meals.
    Answer: Advantage: Eco-packaging matches the preferences of the 62% of 320 surveyed processors who would pay a $2.10 premium per meal for it, allowing HBP to charge a premium that protects the $16.50 selling price and the $4.00 contribution ($16.50 − $12.50) during the $620,000 plant build. It also strengthens HBP's brand image with the 48% of buyers who check shelf life, helping win or retain supermarket listings.

Disadvantage: Sustainable materials typically cost more than conventional plastic, which would increase HBP's $12.50 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $2.10 premium is accepted on the whole range. Any failure in eco-materials (for example, shorter shelf life for frozen meals) would raise the current 3.9% defect rate and increase waste before the plant stabilises.
    Keywords: eco-packaging, $2.10, 62%, 48%, $12.50, $16.50, 320 processors
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HBP's research data, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 7.5% minimum wage rise to $14.51 per hour, the 14.2% agricultural-input cost inflation and the 2.1% fall in ready-to-cook frozen-meal consumer spending will affect HBP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: The 7.5% minimum wage rise to $14.51 per hour: with a workforce of 42, most of which is hourly-paid, this feeds directly into HBP's wage bill. The insert does not give hours worked, so the honest judgement is against productivity data: 180,000 units ÷ 42 staff = about 4,286 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds at that level or output grows.

The 14.2% agricultural-input inflation: this compounds on every one of HBP's 180,000 units and directly erodes the $4.00 contribution ($16.50 − $12.50). If the entire $12.50 variable cost rose 14.2%, that would be $1.78 per unit, and at the 180,000 units HBP produces a year that is about $320,000 of extra cost; a realistic share of ingredient costs rose, so the true impact lies between $45,000 and $60,000 of extra cost per year. HBP can recover part of it through the $2.10 eco-packaging premium and supermarket price negotiations, both given in appendix 1.

The 2.1% fall in frozen-meal consumer spending: weak demand softens HBP's 180,000-unit plan, though spending on fresh chilled meals grew 4.7%, so the fall is partially offset by the rising fresh-meal segment.

Conclusion: the 14.2% input-cost inflation will have the greatest impact on HBP, because it is charged on every unit of the 180,000-unit output and directly erodes the $4.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 expansion. HBP should negotiate ingredient prices or lock in supply contracts now and lean on the $2.10 premium to claw back margin.
    Keywords: 7.5%, $14.51, 14.2%, 2.1%, $13.50, 6.9%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HBP. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HBP's costs or demand in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.

--- STEM ---
Azure Coast Resorts (ACR) is a private limited company in the hospitality sector, running a seaside resort of villas and suites on the southern coast. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Marchetti, it employs a workforce of 160 and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. ACR plans to invest $900,000 in a new villa wing with contactless check-in and solar-powered housekeeping automation, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $55 a unit and a selling price of $175, and currently produces 24,000 units a year. ACR faces rising labour turnover and increasing guest complaints about room readiness, with housekeeping rework now affecting 6% of stays.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for ACR of using retained profit to fund the $900,000 villa-wing expansion instead of the bank loan.

That protects the $120 contribution per unit ($175 − $55) and keeps the new villas competitive at the $175 selling price even while the workforce faces a 6.5% minimum wage rise. It also removes the risk that the lender could repossess the new wing if guest demand disappoints.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership and control with Sofia Marchetti's management team rather than a bank, so no lender can impose conditions on how the contactless check-in and solar-powered housekeeping automation are operated. The $300,000 retained profit can be redirected quickly to reduce the 6% housekeeping rework rate and answer the rising guest complaints, protecting the resort's reputation without adding debt to a business already carrying $480,000 of fixed costs a year.
    Keywords: retained profit, $900,000, $600,000, $300,000, $175, $55, 6.5%, 11.6%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ACR's expansion, contribution and ownership.

Television is rejected as unaffordable and geographically wasteful; regional radio is rejected as too narrow to generate the 24,000 room-nights needed. ACR should add modest in-resort signage to support the influencer campaign.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to ACR. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ACR with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ACR with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.
