--- STEM ---
Treetop Canopy Lodges (TCL) is a private limited company in the leisure and tourism sector, operating forest eco-pods and canopy walkways in a northern rainforest reserve. Founded in 2015 by Nathan Oyelaran, it employs a workforce of 90 and uses a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. TCL plans to invest $750,000 in twelve new treehouse pods with automated eco-sensors, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and a $350,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $40 a unit and a selling price of $140, and currently produces 15,000 units a year. TCL faces rising labour turnover among its guides and a worsening guest complaint rate about pod maintenance.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for TCL of using a share issue rather than the bank loan to help fund the $750,000 treehouse-pod expansion.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $350,000 of equity that carries no interest and no fixed repayment dates, unlike the $400,000 ten-year bank loan. With $360,000 of annual fixed costs already committed, TCL avoids the 0.75% rise in borrowing cost and preserves cash to absorb the 9.4% increase in fuel and timber inputs, protecting the $100 contribution per unit ($140 − $40) on its 15,000 guest-nights.

Point 2: The new shareholders share the risk of the twelve pods with automated eco-sensors, so Nathan Oyelaran's business is not solely exposed if the 5.8% minimum wage rise pushes costs up or the worsening guest complaints delay bookings. Equity also strengthens the statement of financial position shown in appendix 2, giving TCL more headroom than piling another loan onto existing debt before the $750,000 programme is complete.
    Keywords: share issue, $350,000, $400,000, $750,000, $140, $40, 9.4%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TCL's financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider national eco-travel magazine advertising, local radio sponsorship, or partnerships with specialist outdoor tourism websites. Which should TCL choose to promote its new canopy-view pods? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National eco-travel magazine advertising: A full-page campaign in national magazines would build prestige for TCL's forest reserve and reach educated travellers who might pay the $25 premium for canopy-view pods. The downside is high production and media cost against $360,000 of fixed costs, long lead times, and waste: most readers will never visit a northern rainforest reserve, and a static photograph cannot show the automated eco-sensors.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is inexpensive and reaches listeners near the reserve, which suits last-minute stays, but TCL's 15,000 guest-nights are drawn from a much wider catchment than one local area. A short audio message also cannot demonstrate the pods or capture the 58% of surveyed guests who prefer to book through the app, so bookings would be limited.

Partnerships with specialist outdoor tourism websites: Listing the pods on sites used by hikers and eco-travellers targets exactly the guests described in appendix 1 — the 71% of 420 surveyed guests who would pay a $25 premium — and links straight to online booking. Costs are largely performance-based, results are measurable, and the site can display the canopy views and eco-sensor features. Reach is narrower than a national magazine, but the audience is far better qualified.

Recommendation: TCL should choose partnerships with specialist outdoor tourism websites. They reach the precise segment willing to pay the premium, support the app booking channel and cost less than print. National magazine advertising is rejected as costly and geographically wasteful, and local radio is rejected as too narrow to sustain 15,000 guest-nights; TCL can add small in-resort signage as a support.
    Keywords: 15,000, $750,000, $25, 71%, 58%, 420 guests, canopy-view pods
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to TCL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TCL with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TCL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazine advertising and local radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for TCL of using team working to improve motivation among its guides and pod-maintenance staff.
    Answer: Point 1: Team working suits TCL's flat structure and gives its 90 employees shared responsibility for the canopy walkways and pod maintenance, satisfying social needs and raising job satisfaction. Guides and maintenance staff who plan rotas together are more likely to attend reliably, directly tackling the rising labour turnover and the worsening guest complaint rate about pod upkeep.

Point 2: Small teams can swap practical knowledge about the automated eco-sensors, so faults are spotted earlier and the 5.8% pod maintenance rework rate can fall further from its 8.1% level. Stronger team commitment also reduces the need to replace leavers, saving part of the $620 per employee course cost for the 14 of the 90 staff needing recertification while protecting the 15,000 guest-nights sold each year.
    Keywords: team working, labour turnover, 5.8%, 8.1%, $620, 14 of the 90 staff, workforce of 90
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TCL's turnover, rework and output.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TCL must upskill 14 of its 90 staff on the new automated eco-sensors. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional centre. Which should TCL choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Senior guides can coach the 14 staff beside the actual pods and canopy walkways, so the training is specific to TCL's own monitoring systems, costs no course fees and keeps everyone available for the 15,000 guest-nights. It also lets teams immediately apply fixes that push the 5.8% rework rate down. The drawback is that coaching guides have less time for their own duties, and without a formal certificate the skills may be hard to verify if guests question safety procedures.

Off-the-job training: The regional centre course at $620 per employee, $8,680 in total for 14 people, offers structured teaching and a recognised certificate, which is modest next to the $750,000 pod programme. It takes staff away from the reserve during busy periods, however, and generic content may not match TCL's exact eco-sensors, so site coaching would still be required afterwards.

Decision: TCL should choose on-the-job training led by experienced guides, followed later by short certified modules for lead technicians. This is cheaper, specific to the pods and avoids losing capacity while labour turnover is a concern. Full off-the-job training is rejected because removing 14 of 90 staff would disrupt the guest-complaint improvement and the $620 fee can be spent later on the formal recertification the new systems need.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $620, 14 of the 90 staff, 5.8%, $750,000, automated eco-sensors
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TCL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the training methods in the context of TCL. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of TCL with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how TCL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 3,600 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $100 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 11,400 units against 15,000 sold; pricing discipline at $140 with $100 contribution; covering the $400,000 loan and $750,000 expansion; and benchmarking at $64 a unit with labour productivity of about 167 units per employee to tackle the 5.8% rework.
    Keywords: 3,600, $100, $140, $40, $360,000, 15,000, $64, 167
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TCL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TCL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.12 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.16 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.82 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.85 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $45,000 inventories + $85,000 trade receivables + $38,000 cash = $168,000; against $150,000 of short-term obligations this gives 1.12, and excluding inventories $123,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.82. In 2025 current assets = $52,000 + $96,000 + $44,000 = $192,000 against $165,000 owed, giving 1.16; without stock, $140,000 ÷ $165,000 = 0.85.

Evaluation: Liquidity improved only slightly. The broad measure moved from 1.12 to 1.16 because current assets rose by $24,000 while current liabilities rose by $15,000, helped by cash climbing from $38,000 to $44,000. The stricter measure, which removes inventories, rose from 0.82 to 0.85 but remains below 1, so TCL still cannot cover near-term debts without relying on stock — a concern while it services a $400,000 loan and funds the $750,000 pod programme. Trade receivables also grew from $85,000 to $96,000, tying up cash; if guests and tour operators pay late, these thin margins could disappear.

Conclusion: TCL's financial position has improved, but only marginally. Both measures are higher and the stricter measure is less stock-dependent, yet with cover still under 1 on that measure the improvement is modest, so managers should tighten credit control before committing further to the expansion.
    Keywords: 1.12, 1.16, 0.82, 0.85, $168,000, $192,000, $750,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether TCL's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TCL of offering canopy-view pods at a $25 premium.
    Answer: Advantage: The $25 premium is supported by appendix 1, where 71% of 420 surveyed guests would pay more for canopy-view pods and 58% already book through the app. It lifts revenue above the $140 base price and defends the $100 contribution per unit as fuel and timber input costs rise 9.4% and the 5.8% wage increase takes effect, helping TCL justify the $750,000 investment in twelve new pods.

Disadvantage: Building and maintaining canopy-view pods with automated eco-sensors is likely to raise the $40 variable cost per unit and add to the $360,000 fixed costs, so margins could be squeezed if fewer than the surveyed 71% actually pay the premium. The 5.8% pod maintenance rework rate could also worsen if the new structures need specialist attention, deepening the guest complaints about pod upkeep just as the new pods open.
    Keywords: $25, 71%, 420 guests, 58%, $40, $140, $750,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TCL's research data, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in input costs will affect TCL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate rise from 4.25% to 5.0%: If TCL's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75-point rise adds 0.75% × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). That is modest against $360,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no extra charge. Higher rates may still reduce guests' discretionary spending on forest breaks, but TCL can cap this exposure by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage rise of 5.8% from $14.00 to $14.81 per hour: With a workforce of 90 this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 15,000 units ÷ 90 staff = about 167 units per employee, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or guest-nights grow; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $100 contribution falls.

Input-cost inflation of 9.4%: The insert never decomposes the $40 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if all $40 were exposed, 9.4% × $40 = $3.76 a unit, which at 15,000 guest-nights is $56,400 a year. A smaller exposed share would cost proportionally less. TCL can recover part through the $25 canopy-view premium that 71% of 420 surveyed guests said they would pay.

Conclusion: The 9.4% input-cost inflation has the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 15,000 guest-nights and directly erodes the $100 contribution that underpins the $750,000 pod programme, while the interest effect is only $3,000 and the wage effect depends on unknown hours. TCL should seek fixed-price supply deals and promote the $25 premium.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 5.8%, 9.4%, $14.81, $400,000, $40, 4.25%, $14.00
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TCL. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TCL's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TCL with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Summit Ridge Tours (SRT) is a public limited company in the tourism sector, organising guided mountain treks and alpine base-camp stays. Founded in 2008 by Priya Raghunathan, it employs a workforce of 120 and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership for safety. SRT plans to invest $1,100,000 in a new alpine base camp with automated safety-monitoring equipment, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $400,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $85 a unit and a selling price of $205, and currently produces 22,000 units a year. SRT faces rising labour turnover among guides and a worsening equipment defect rate found during safety inspection.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for SRT of financing the $1,100,000 base camp with a share issue rather than a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: The $700,000 share issue brings equity that requires no interest and no fixed repayments, unlike the $400,000 bank loan. With $540,000 of fixed costs already committed, SRT avoids extra debt service as the base rate climbs from 5.0% to 5.75%, leaving cash to absorb the 10.8% rise in fuel and climbing-equipment costs and protecting the $120 contribution per unit ($205 − $85) on 22,000 trek places.

Point 2: Equity shares the risk of the new alpine base camp and automated safety-monitoring equipment with shareholders, so Priya Raghunathan's company is not solely exposed if the 7.2% minimum wage rise pushes costs up or the worsening equipment defect rate delays departures. A stronger equity base also supports the public limited company's statement of financial position in appendix 2, making future borrowing for the $1,100,000 programme easier.
    Keywords: share issue, $700,000, $400,000, $1,100,000, $205, $85, 10.8%

--- STEM ---
Meridian Leisure Group (MLG) is a partnership in the leisure sector, running an indoor theme park and family attractions in a large city. Founded in 2003 by Elena Vasquez, it employs a workforce of 200 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MLG plans to invest $750,000 in a new indoor leisure dome with automated ride-monitoring and contactless ticketing, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $720,000 a year, a variable cost of $28 a unit and a selling price of $88, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. MLG faces rising labour turnover among ride operators and increasing visitor complaints about queue times.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for MLG of using a ten-year bank loan rather than an overdraft to fund the $750,000 leisure-dome expansion.
    Answer: Point 1: A ten-year bank loan gives MLG a fixed repayment schedule matched to the long life of the $750,000 indoor dome, whereas an overdraft is repayable on demand and could be withdrawn just as the $500,000 is needed. With $720,000 of fixed costs a year, predictable instalments make budgeting far easier, especially as the base rate has risen from 4.75% to 5.5%.

Point 2: The loan provides a large, committed $500,000 alongside $250,000 retained profit, so MLG can complete the automated ride-monitoring project without draining the cash needed to run 40,000 admissions and ease the 24-minute queue time. An overdraft would leave the partnership exposed to sudden calls on its cash and could undermine the 3.4% defect-rate improvements just as the new dome opens.
    Keywords: $500,000, $750,000, $250,000, $88, $28, 12.3%, $720,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MLG's financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider city-wide billboard advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should MLG choose to promote its new indoor leisure dome? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: City-wide billboard advertising: Large billboards would create high visibility for the new dome across the city and support a premium family brand. However, production and site rentals are costly against $720,000 of fixed costs, the message cannot show the automated ride-monitoring, and exposure cannot be measured or tied to the 49% of surveyed visitors who book online.

Social media influencer marketing: Family influencers can film the rides and fast-track entry, reaching exactly the visitors in appendix 1 — the 63% of 700 surveyed visitors who would pay a $12 premium. Engagement is measurable and cheap per view, but much of the audience may live outside the city catchment, and a youth-focused following may convert poorly into the 40,000 admissions needed to fill the dome.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is inexpensive, reaches listeners in MLG's immediate city catchment and suits urgent messages about opening days and shorter queues. Billboards are rejected as expensive and unmeasurable, and influencers are rejected as too geographically diffuse to guarantee 40,000 admissions; MLG should reinforce radio with in-park signage and its online booking channel.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MLG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MLG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.20 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.93 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $55,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $220,000; against $220,000 of short-term obligations this gives 1.00, and without inventories $165,000 ÷ $220,000 = 0.75. Receivables grew by $25,000, tying up cash; if corporate customers pay late, the gain could erode quickly.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.5%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 12.3% rise in input costs will affect MLG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate rise from 4.75% to 5.5%: If MLG's $500,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75-point rise adds 0.75% × $500,000 = $3,750 a year (0.0075 × $500,000). That is small compared with $720,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates may still trim family spending on leisure, although spending on attractions grew 4.8%, and MLG can limit the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage rise of 6.4% from $13.60 to $14.47 per hour: With a workforce of 200 this feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual total can be calculated honestly. The defensible comparison is productivity: 40,000 units ÷ 200 staff = 200 units per employee, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or admissions grow; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $60 contribution shrinks.

Input-cost inflation of 12.3%: The insert does not decompose the $28 variable cost, so only an upper bound can be shown: if all $28 were exposed, 12.3% × $28 = $3.444 a unit, and at 40,000 admissions that is $137,760 a year. A smaller exposed share would cost proportionally less. MLG can recover part through the $12 fast-track premium that 63% of 700 surveyed visitors said they would pay.

Conclusion: The 12.3% input-cost inflation has the greatest impact. It is charged across all 40,000 admissions and directly erodes the $60 contribution that supports the $750,000 dome, whereas the interest effect is only $3,750 and the wage effect depends on unknown hours. MLG should negotiate fixed-price energy deals and promote the $12 premium.

--- STEM ---
Trailpine Freight (TPF) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2011 by Nelia Brooks, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. TPF plans to invest $480,000 in an electric delivery truck fleet and depot charging hub, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and produces 45,000 units a year. TPF faces a rising consignment damage rate of 3.2% and driver absenteeism of 7%, which are slowing depot turnaround and worrying retail clients. The founder still chairs the board and sets delivery targets personally.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for TPF of funding the $480,000 electric fleet from retained profit rather than the $300,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment obligation, so TPF keeps the cash needed to run 45,000 consignments a year. The base rate has moved from 4.5% to 5.25%, making the $300,000 five-year bank loan more expensive, whereas the $180,000 retained profit is free. With a $14.00 selling price and an $8.00 variable cost, every consignment earns $6.00 contribution, or $270,000 a year at current volume, and that cash can absorb the 11.3% rise in diesel and depot electricity without pushing the $14.00 price up to business clients.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids collateral and repossession risk on the $480,000 truck fleet and charging hub. If the 3.2% damage rate and 7% driver absenteeism delay the return from the new vehicles, no lender can seize the trucks or impose conditions on Nelia Brooks's delivery targets. Ownership and control stay with the founder, which suits a private limited company that wants to reinvest surplus in further depot capacity once the electric fleet is working.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $480,000, $180,000, $14.00, $8.00, 45,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Trailpine Freight (TPF), its fleet investment and its cost structure.

However, airtime and production are very expensive for a 40-employee private limited company funding a $480,000 electric fleet, and most viewers are not business buyers of road freight, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper and suits a time-limited message about a new depot service. It reaches listeners near TPF's hub, but the survey identifies buyers of logistics services rather than local listeners, and region-only coverage cannot help TPF fill the 45,000 consignments a year needed to cover $180,000 of fixed costs.

Targeted social-media advertising: Advertising on professional and industry platforms lets TPF aim at logistics and purchasing managers, the same kind of respondents as the 250 business clients surveyed. It is measurable, far cheaper than television, and can demonstrate the 91% on-time delivery record and the guaranteed next-day service bought by the 68% who would pay $0.60 more. Its weakness is slower mass-brand recognition than television.

Recommendation: TPF should choose targeted social-media advertising. It reaches the decision-makers in the survey, costs a fraction of television, and supports the $0.60 premium that protects the $6.00 contribution ($14.00 − $8.00). National television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a business servicing a $300,000 loan; local radio is rejected as too narrow and aimed at consumers rather than business freight buyers. --- STEM ---
Solstice Solar Systems (SSS) is a private limited company in the renewable energy sector, installing rooftop solar panels and battery storage, with a workforce of 28. Founded in 2016 by Rohan Mehta, it operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. SSS plans to invest $600,000 in a solar-panel assembly and battery-storage line, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and produces 36,000 units a year. SSS faces a panel rework rate of 4.1% and rising installation-quality complaints from households. Experienced installation teams set their own schedules.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for SSS of funding the $600,000 assembly line through a share issue rather than the $300,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Share capital does not require interest or capital repayments, so SSS keeps cash to cover $144,000 of fixed costs while the assembly line is commissioned. The base rate has risen from 4.25% to 5.0%, making the $300,000 five-year bank loan more expensive; equity avoids that interest entirely. With a $16.50 selling price and a $9.00 variable cost, each system contributes $7.50, or $270,000 at 36,000 units, and keeping that cash helps absorb the 13.6% rise in lithium and silicon prices.

Point 2: Equity is permanent capital suited to a long-lived solar and battery facility, so no lender can repossess the line if the 4.1% rework rate delays output. A share issue also spreads risk among investors instead of leaving Rohan Mehta's firm solely exposed to debt. The trade-off is some dilution of ownership, but SSS retains the $300,000 bank loan for flexibility and can use the extra headroom to improve the 86% on-time installation record.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $300,000, $600,000, $16.50, $9.00, 36,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Solstice Solar Systems (SSS), its line investment and its cost structure.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider national newspaper advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social-media advertising to householders. Which should SSS choose to promote its battery-ready systems? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National newspaper advertising: Newspaper campaigns could reach many householders and give SSS credibility for solar installations. However, national print space is costly for a 28-person private limited company funding a $600,000 line, and most readers are outside SSS's installation area, so the spend would be poorly targeted.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper, reaches listeners near SSS's service area and can carry a short message about battery-ready systems. Its limit is reach and recall: with only 86% of installations completed on the booked date, a narrow local audience cannot deliver the 36,000-unit volume needed to cover $144,000 of fixed costs.

Social-media advertising: Paid social campaigns can target householders by location and interest in renewable energy, show installation photographs and measure enquiries directly. The survey of 300 households found 71% would pay $0.80 more for a battery-ready system and 47% compare installers by warranty length, both messages that can be tested cheaply online. The drawback is that online leads need quick follow-up to convert.

Recommendation: SSS should choose social-media advertising. It targets the households in the survey, is affordable alongside a $300,000 loan, and supports the $0.80 premium. National newspapers are rejected as expensive and untargeted; local radio is rejected as too narrow to fill the 36,000-unit plan. SSS should pair the campaign with prompt quoting to improve on the 86% booked-date record. SSS can measure enquiry quality against the 300-household survey before expanding the campaign.
    Keywords: battery-ready system, 71%, $0.80, 300, 86%, $600,000, 36,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to SSS. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SSS with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of SSS with a justified recommendation explaining why newspapers and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for SSS of using laissez-faire leadership with its 28 installation technicians.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced technicians freedom to decide how they fit solar panels and battery units on each roof. Because teams already set their own schedules, autonomy can speed up job allocation and improve the 86% of installations completed on the booked date. Technicians who control their own methods feel trusted, which supports motivation among the 28 staff while the $600,000 assembly line is being introduced.

    Answer: Base interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): The rise is 0.75 percentage points. Lithium and silicon prices (up 13.6%): This attacks the $9.00 variable cost on every one of 36,000 systems. SSS can recover part through the $0.80 battery-ready premium supported by 71% of surveyed households.

Minimum wage rise (6.1%, $12.40 to $13.16 an hour): Installation wage bills rise, but the insert states neither hours worked nor technician pay, so no annual total can be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 36,000 systems ÷ 28 technicians = about 1,286 systems per technician, so the rise is affordable only if that rate is maintained or the 4.1% rework rate falls.

Conclusion: The 13.6% component-price rise will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 36,000 systems and directly reduces the $7.50 contribution that funds the line, unlike the conditional $2,250 interest effect and the wage rise, which cannot be quantified from the insert.

--- STEM ---
Northgate Logistics (NGL) is a private limited company in the distribution and courier sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2005 by Priya Raman, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NGL plans to invest $840,000 in an automated warehouse sorting system and an electric van fleet, financed by a $480,000 five-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $17.50, and produces 75,000 units a year. NGL faces a parcel mis-sorting rate of 2.8% and rising damage complaints from online retailers. Priya Raman personally approves all capital spending, and the depot runs two shifts a day.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for NGL of funding the $840,000 sorting system from retained profit rather than the $480,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charge or instalments, preserving cash while the automated sorter is installed. The base rate has moved from 4.6% to 5.35%, so the $480,000 five-year bank loan is becoming dearer; the $360,000 retained profit is free. Each consignment earns $7.50 ($17.50 − $10.00), giving $562,500 of contribution at 75,000 consignments, which NGL can use to absorb the 2.8% mis-sorting cost without raising the $17.50 price.

Point 2: Equity funding avoids collateral and the risk of repossession if the new sorter fails to cut the 33 monthly complaints. No lender can impose conditions on Priya Raman's capital decisions, which suits her centralised, autocratic control of spending. Using retained profit also keeps the bank's credit headroom intact for a later van-fleet purchase, giving NGL flexibility if the 7.8% fall in online retail spending reduces the volume passing through the warehouse. The 12% growth in consignment volume recorded in Appendix 1 makes that internal cash especially valuable if the sorter needs further adjustment.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $480,000, $360,000, $840,000, $17.50, $10.00, 75,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Northgate Logistics (NGL), its sorting investment and its cost structure.

Most viewers do not buy courier contracts, so the campaign would reach few of the 350 retailers in the survey.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and quick to book, and it could cover NGL's depot catchment. However, e-commerce retailers buy nationally, and local listeners are largely consumers rather than business decision-makers; the reach is too narrow to fill the 75,000-consignment plan needed against $300,000 of fixed costs.

Trade-magazine advertising: Advertising in logistics and e-commerce publications reaches the purchasing managers who decide on carriers, matching the 350 retailers surveyed. It is far cheaper than television, can show the 93.5% on-time delivery record and the $0.55 same-day premium, and can be repeated in issues timed to peak seasons. Its weakness is long lead time and limited reach outside the trade.

Recommendation: NGL should choose trade-magazine advertising. National television is rejected as costly and untargeted; local radio is rejected as too narrow and consumer-focused. NGL should follow up magazine leads with direct sales visits, since the 7.8% fall in online spending means contracts must be won actively. NGL can measure lead quality against the 350-retailer survey before renewing the campaign.

--- STEM ---
Voltway Charging (VWC) is a private limited company in the electric-vehicle charging and energy retail sector, employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2018 by Sofia Alvarez, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. VWC plans to invest $720,000 in a rapid-charging hub network with solar canopies, financed by a $450,000 five-year bank loan and a $270,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.20 a unit and a selling price of $15.60, and produces 60,000 units a year. VWC faces a charger fault rate of 6.4% and rising billing complaints from fleet drivers. Sofia Alvarez consults her technicians before changing prices.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for VWC of funding the $720,000 charging hub through a share issue rather than the $450,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Share capital requires no interest or repayment, keeping cash to run 60,000 charging sessions a year. The base rate has moved from 4.9% to 5.65%, so the $450,000 five-year bank loan is getting dearer, while the $270,000 share issue has no finance charge. Each session earns $8.40 ($15.60 − $7.20), or $504,000 at current volume, and that cash can absorb the 15.2% wholesale electricity rise without raising the $15.60 price to fleet drivers.

Point 2: Equity is permanent funding for long-life charging hardware and solar canopies, so no lender can repossess the hubs if the 6.4% charger fault rate delays the expected usage. Investors share the risk of the $720,000 network with the founder, and Sofia Alvarez keeps the bank's credit line free for later hub sites. The cost is some dilution of control, but it is preferable to tying the whole programme to a variable-rate loan in a rising-rate environment.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $450,000, $270,000, $720,000, $15.60, $7.20, 60,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Voltway Charging (VWC), its hub investment and its cost structure.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two benefits for VWC of using democratic leadership to reduce its 6.4% charger fault rate and billing complaints.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Consider on-the-job coaching for the ten technicians or funded high-voltage certification at $1,250 each. Which should VWC choose? Justify your decision.

Funded certification: The $1,250 course gives the ten technicians formal high-voltage certification, directly closing the stated skills gap and supporting the reliability message to the 61% of fleet managers who choose networks on reliability. Ten places cost $12,500 (10 × $1,250), a defined sum within the $720,000 programme. A further consideration is the 14% rise in sessions: as the network grows, informal coaching by a few experts will not scale, so formal certification is the better foundation. --- STEM ---
Harbourline Ferries (HLF) is a private limited company in the coastal ferry and tourism transport sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 1998 by Eamon Doyle, it operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. HLF plans to invest $560,000 in a hybrid-electric ferry and online booking system, financed by a $320,000 five-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $220,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and produces 60,000 units a year. HLF faces a 4.6% passenger complaint rate and rising crew absenteeism. Eamon Doyle approves every timetable change himself, and all sailings still use the old port terminal.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for HLF of funding the $560,000 hybrid ferry from retained profit rather than the $320,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment, so HLF keeps cash to run 60,000 passenger trips a year. The base rate has risen from 4.4% to 5.1%, making the $320,000 five-year bank loan more costly, while the $240,000 retained profit is free. Each trip earns $5.50 ($13.50 − $8.00), or $330,000 at current volume, and that cash can absorb the 8.5% fall in coastal day-trip spending without raising the $13.50 fare.

Point 2: Funding from internal reserves avoids collateral and repossession risk on the $560,000 ferry if the 4.6% complaint rate delays the return from the new vessel. No lender can impose terms on Eamon Doyle's timetable decisions, which suits his direct control, and HLF keeps bank headroom for later booking-system upgrades. The retained profit also signals that the existing service generates enough surplus to support expansion without diluting ownership. The 5% growth in trips recorded in Appendix 1 makes that reserve useful if the new ferry needs early adjustment.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $320,000, $240,000, $560,000, $13.50, $8.00, 60,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Harbourline Ferries (HLF), its ferry investment and its cost structure.

    Answer: National television advertising: A television campaign would show the hybrid ferry to a wide audience and build awareness of coastal travel. However, airtime is expensive for a 48-employee firm funding a $560,000 vessel, and most viewers live far from the route, so the spend would reach few of the 420 tourists in the survey.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and can target listeners near the port, which suits a time-sensitive message about sailings. Yet radio does not reach tourists planning a trip in advance, and the 89% on-time record needs a credibility message rather than a short jingle; coverage is too narrow to fill 60,000 trips against $220,000 of fixed costs.

Partnerships with coastal hotels and tour operators: Hotel and tour partnerships put HLF's premium offer in front of visitors already near the port, matching the 70% who would pay $1.20 more for a guaranteed seat. Partners can bundle tickets with stays, address the 55% who book on price with a package deal, and cost far less than television. The drawback is dependence on partners' willingness and slower reach than a media campaign.

Recommendation: HLF should choose partnerships with coastal hotels and tour operators. They reach the surveyed tourists, support the $1.20 premium and fit a $320,000 loan budget. National television is rejected as costly and geographically wasteful; local radio is rejected as too short-term. HLF should improve the 89% punctuality before promoting a guaranteed-seat product. HLF can measure bookings against the 420-tourist survey before renewing the campaign.

--- STEM ---
Pinecrest Analytics (PCA) is a private limited company in the software and cloud-computing sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Asha Nair, the firm supplies cloud inventory software to independent retailers across the country and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. Pinecrest plans to invest $720,000 in a new cloud analytics platform, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. The firm faces two problems: client quality complaints have risen and developer absenteeism has reached 8%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PCA plans to fund part of its $720,000 cloud analytics platform with a $400,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for PCA of using the $320,000 retained profit instead of borrowing the full amount.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment obligation, so PCA keeps the cash it would otherwise pay on the $400,000 ten-year bank loan. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year and a $720,000 platform to fund, preserving cash strengthens liquidity and lets Asha Nair absorb the 9.6% rise in cloud hosting input costs without raising the $16.00 selling price. Every dollar of interest avoided directly protects the $7.00 contribution per unit and gives the 60-employee firm more room to respond to client quality complaints.

Point 2: Using the $320,000 retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk attached to a bank loan, so the new cloud analytics platform cannot be repossessed if sales of the 60,000 units disappoint. It also keeps control with the existing owners, since no lender can impose conditions on how the platform is run, and it avoids the 4.5% base-rate environment that makes further borrowing more expensive for a software business.
    Keywords: retained profit, $400,000, $320,000, $720,000, democratic leadership, 60,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: PCA is launching its new cloud analytics platform. Consider a national trade-press advertising campaign, sponsorship of an industry conference, or targeted email and social-media marketing. Which should PCA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National trade-press advertising: A campaign in software and cloud journals would build credibility with PCA's retailer audience and reach many buyers at once, which suits a $720,000 platform launch. However, print costs are high and much of the readership will not buy inventory software, so a 60-employee firm would waste a large share of its budget; results are also hard to measure against the 60,000-unit target.

Industry conference sponsorship: Sponsoring a retail-technology conference puts PCA in front of a highly relevant, decision-making audience and allows live demonstrations of the analytics platform. The drawbacks are a narrow reach limited to delegates who attend, high event fees, and the long lead time before any sales appear, which delays recovery of the $400,000 loan.

Targeted email and social-media marketing: Using the survey insight that 68% of 450 clients would pay $0.50 more for priority support and 57% rank security as their top criterion, PCA can segment outreach precisely, measure clicks and conversions, and scale nationally at low cost per contact. Results compound more slowly than a big print campaign, but the budget goes only to interested retailers. Measurement is a further advantage: unlike print or events, email clicks can be tracked against the 15,000 licence units shipped last quarter, letting Asha Nair redirect spend quickly if response is weak.

Recommendation: PCA should choose targeted email and social-media marketing. It is the most cost-effective and measurable option for a firm with fixed costs of $280,000, reaches the exact retailers identified in the survey, and can scale as the platform grows. Trade-press advertising is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and conference sponsorship is rejected as too narrow and slow to justify the $720,000 investment on its own.
    Keywords: cloud analytics platform, $720,000, 68%, $0.50, 57%, 450
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of promotional options with minimal application to PCA. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in PCA's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in PCA's context with a justified recommendation explaining why trade-press advertising and conference sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Developer absenteeism at PCA has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for PCA of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its development team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives PCA's developers a real say in how the new analytics platform is built, which helps satisfy esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow) and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help set coding standards and release schedules are more likely to attend consistently, directly tackling the 8% absenteeism rate and protecting output of 60,000 units while the $720,000 platform beds in.

Point 2: Involving developers in decisions draws on the expertise of the people who know the software best, generating ideas that reduce the client quality complaints recorded in the Operations report and the 2.2% defect rate. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers the risk of losing skilled staff, protecting the $1,100-per-employee certification investment and keeping the flat structure effective as Pinecrest grows beyond its current 60 staff. These benefits are especially valuable because Pinecrest is a flat, 60-person organisation where democratic participation is practical to implement, and the $720,000 platform makes stability of the development team essential to meeting the 60,000-unit plan.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, 8%, 60,000, 2.2%, $1,100, 18
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: PCA must upskill 18 of its 60 staff on the new analytics tools. Consider on-the-job training or the external certification courses costing $1,100 per employee. Which should PCA choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching the 18 staff on PCA's own analytics tools is directly relevant, costs no course fees, and keeps staff productive while they learn, protecting the 15,000 licence units shipped last quarter and the fall in the defect rate to 2.2%. The downside is that mentors are developers whose own work suffers, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no external certificate, which may matter if retailer clients demand proof of competence.

External certification courses: Paying $1,100 per employee gives all 18 staff structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification, costing $19,800 in total — small beside the $720,000 investment. Brightwell Digital Media (BDM) is a partnership in the digital marketing and web-design sector, employing a workforce of 40.     Question: BDM plans to fund its $450,000 app-development studio with a $250,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for BDM of using the $250,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: The $250,000 bank loan lets Brightwell fund the full $450,000 app-development studio without draining the partnership's limited reserves, which matters for a 40-person agency with fixed costs of $175,000 a year. Retaining the $200,000 profit as working capital protects cash flow while the new studio is built and helps absorb the 11.3% rise in freelance developer day rates.

Point 2: Repaying the loan over time spreads the cost, so the agency does not have to wait until profits are large enough to self-fund. With a selling price of $15.00 and contribution of $7.00 a unit, the 45,000-unit output can service the loan gradually, letting Liam Okafor keep the partnership's own capital intact and pursue the studio immediately rather than delaying the launch. The agency's flat, 40-person structure and the 11.3% rise in freelance day rates make preserving the $200,000 reserve particularly sensible, because it gives Liam Okafor room to hire or subcontract when the new studio is at full capacity.

Vertex Apps (VAP) is a private limited company in the mobile-app and fintech sector, employing a workforce of 55. With 70,000 units to sell and app-crash complaints to fix, the $300,000 lets Tomas Reyes invest fully in the $660,000 platform without squeezing the $7.00 contribution per unit to service debt.

Point 2: Venture capitalists bring sector expertise and contacts that a bank cannot, which can help a 55-person fintech improve its 1.9% crash rate and reach the 700 surveyed users. Unlike a larger loan, there is no repossession risk if launch volumes disappoint, although the investors will expect a share of ownership and a return on exit. The arrangement also spreads risk for a 55-person fintech with a 1.9% crash rate to fix: investor support can fund additional testing and the $1,050 training courses without forcing Vertex to cut the 70,000-unit plan or raise the $14.00 price prematurely.

It also leaves borrowing capacity for future renewable-energy investment, though heavy use of reserves reduces the cushion available if energy waste pushes costs above plan. For a 90-person cooperative with democratic leadership, keeping $600,000 of reserves under member control also avoids the covenants a larger lender might impose on the green data centre, and leaves room to fund the $1,300 renewable-energy courses for the 25 technicians who need them.

Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings (all figures $'000): 2024 gross margin = 525 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 35.0%; 2025 = 720 ÷ 1,800 × 100 = 40.0%. Operating return on sales 2024 = 180 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 12.0%; 2025 = 270 ÷ 1,800 × 100 = 15.0%. Return on capital 2024 = 180 ÷ 1,125 × 100 = 16.0%; 2025 = 270 ÷ 1,350 × 100 = 20.0%. Cost of sales rose from 975 to 1,080 while revenue grew from 1,500 to 1,800.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, so HCC's financial position has strengthened. The gross margin rising from 35.0% to 40.0% shows better control of direct costs despite 14.2% electricity and hardware inflation, and the operating return on sales climbing from 12.0% to 15.0% indicates the flat 90-person cooperative is absorbing overheads more effectively as revenue grows. Return on capital improved from 16.0% to 20.0%, so the 1,125 to 1,350 of capital employed is being used more productively, supporting the $1,500,000 centre. The strongest evidence is the 20.0% return on capital, because it shows the larger capital base is generating higher returns rather than profit merely tracking sales. A caveat is interest payable rising from 24 to 30 as the $900,000 loan is serviced.

Conclusion: HCC's financial position has improved on every measure, with the rise in return on capital from 16.0% to 20.0% the clearest sign of value creation; the growing interest burden from the $900,000 loan is the main risk to monitor.

--- STEM ---
Kestrel Medical Supplies (KMS) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2011 by Priya Kestrel, it manufactures sterile wound-care dressings for hospital groups and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. KMS plans to invest $720,000 in an automated sterile-dressing line, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $10.50, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. Its main hospital contracts require delivery within 48 hours, and it prides itself on a strong sterility record. KMS faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8% and complaints about torn sterile packaging are rising.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KMS plans to fund part of its $720,000 sterile-dressing line with a $420,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KMS of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or compulsory repayments, so the $300,000 KMS sets aside from past profits protects its cash flow while it services fixed costs of $240,000 a year. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.6% rise in fabric and packaging input costs without pushing the $10.50 selling price above what hospital groups will accept, preserving the $5.00 contribution per unit on 110,000 units.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids the security and default risk of the $420,000 loan, so the new automated line cannot be repossessed if hospital orders fall short. It also leaves Priya Kestrel's ownership and control intact, since no lender can attach conditions to how the sterile-dressing line is run. Retained profit is immediately available with no application delay, letting KMS respond quickly to the torn-packaging complaints and begin the 48-hour delivery improvements its hospital contracts demand. Together these advantages let KMS direct scarce cash toward the 8% absenteeism problem and the torn-packaging complaints rather than toward a lender.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $420,000, $720,000, $240,000, $10.50
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KMS, its $720,000 line, costs and hospital contracts.

    Answer: National trade-journal advertising: A campaign in hospital-supply journals would reach procurement departments across the country and lend KMS credibility as a sterile-dressing supplier. Print production and placement costs are high, however, and much of the readership will not be in a position to switch supplier, so the spend is largely wasted for a 50-employee firm committing $720,000 to a new line. Results are also slow to arrive and hard to measure.

Hospital conference sponsorship: Sponsoring a major clinical conference puts KMS in front of the exact sterile-pack decision-makers and allows live demonstration of the tamper-evident seal, which directly answers the 68% of surveyed procurement staff who would pay $0.30 more and the 57% who check sterility certification. The drawbacks are a very high one-off cost and a single event with limited reach; with 500 staff surveyed and only 27,500 units packed last quarter, one conference cannot on its own sustain the 110,000-unit output target.

Targeted email and social media marketing: Direct digital marketing to procurement staff lets KMS show the tamper-evident design and certification to precisely the segment its research identified, at low cost per contact and with measurable responses. Messages can be updated quickly to reflect the falling 2.4% defect rate. Its weakness is that procurement decisions are relationship-driven and digital messages can be ignored, so it works best alongside personal follow-up.

Recommendation: KMS should choose targeted email and social media marketing, supported by a small conference presence. It reaches the 68% willing to pay $0.30 more and the 57% checking certification far more cheaply than national print, and unlike a single conference it can run continuously to support 110,000 units of output. National journals are rejected as expensive and untargeted; full conference sponsorship is rejected as too costly and one-off for a business already funding a $420,000 loan.
    Keywords: tamper-evident, 68%, $0.30, 57%, 500, 27,500

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LMA's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has LMA's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 13.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 19.5%
ROCE 2025 = 21.5%

Operating profit of $234,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 13.0% in 2024 and $322,000 ÷ $2,150,000 = 15.0% in 2025. The return on capital employed divides operating profit by capital employed: $234,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 19.5% and $322,000 ÷ $1,500,000 = 21.5%.   Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for LMA of producing regularly updated digital resources.
    Answer: Advantage: Updated digital resources match the survey finding that 71% of parents would pay up to $0.50 more and that 63% check accreditation before enrolling.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in input costs will affect LMA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If LMA's $300,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% x $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 x $300,000), small against fixed costs of $180,000. If the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Parents may also cut discretionary tuition spending when borrowing is dearer, but LMA can largely remove this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (4.9%, to $13.22 an hour): With a workforce of 40 and output of 80,000 units, labour productivity is 80,000 ÷ 40 = 2,000 units per worker. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented; the defensible test is whether each tutor maintains around 2,000 units. With absenteeism at 7%, any fall in productivity would raise unit labour costs and shrink the $5.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (11.3% in paper, broadband and energy): The insert states a variable cost of $4.00 per unit without decomposing it, so only an illustrative bound is possible. If the entire $4.00 rose 11.3%, that is 11.3% x $4.00 = $0.452, about $0.45 per unit; over 80,000 units that is roughly $36,000 a year (80,000 x $0.45). Even a $0.35 rise would cost $28,000 a year (80,000 x $0.35), pulling contribution from $5.00 to about $4.65.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It hits all 80,000 units and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that underpins the $540,000 studio, and at up to about $36,000 a year it far exceeds the conditional $2,250 interest cost. The wage rise is real but cannot be quantified from the insert and depends on the 2,000-unit productivity holding, while interest risk can be fixed. LMA should renegotiate supplier contracts and recover part of the increase through the $0.50 premium.
    Keywords: 4.5%, 4.9%, 11.3%, $13.22, $4.00, $300,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to LMA. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on LMA's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller, with arithmetic shown from insert figures.

--- STEM ---
Pinecrest Health Centre (PHC) is a partnership in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2008 by Dr Sofia Pinecrest, it provides private outpatient consultations and diagnostic scans and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. PHC plans to invest $680,000 in a new minor-operations suite and scanner, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year, each a patient visit. Demand from local employers has grown steadily. PHC faces two problems: patient waiting times have risen and nursing absenteeism has reached 10%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PHC plans to fund part of its $680,000 minor-operations suite with a $400,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for PHC of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit brings no interest bill or fixed repayment schedule, so the $280,000 drawn from past profits protects the partnership's cash flow while it meets fixed costs of $300,000 a year. Cash saved can absorb the 10.5% rise in medical consumables and energy costs without raising the $14.00 price, preserving the $6.00 contribution on 90,000 patient visits.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk of the $400,000 loan, so the new scanner suite cannot be threatened if patient numbers disappoint. It also keeps decision-making with Dr Sofia Pinecrest and the partners, since no lender can impose conditions. Because it is already in the business, it can be released at once to cut the 38-minute waiting time and address the 10% nursing absenteeism. Its hierarchical structure can then direct the cash saved specifically to cutting the 38-minute waiting time that patients complain about while the new scanner suite beds in.
    Keywords: retained profit, $280,000, $400,000, $680,000, $300,000, $14.00
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PHC, its suite, costs and services.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: PHC is promoting its new minor-operations suite. Consider advertising in local newspapers, sponsoring a regional healthcare conference, or targeted social media and email marketing to existing patients. Which should PHC choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local newspaper advertising: Newspaper adverts would reach the local community and build awareness of the new suite. Costs are moderate but readership is ageing and falling, and a general audience includes many who will never need private scans, so much of the spend is wasted for a 60-staff partnership committing $680,000. The message is also static and hard to measure.

Regional healthcare conference sponsorship: This would put PHC in front of GPs and employers who refer patients, and allows demonstration of the scanner, supporting the 59% of surveyed patients who check waiting-time ratings. It is prestigious but a costly one-off event with limited reach; with 700 patients surveyed and 21,000 visits last quarter, one conference alone cannot fill 90,000 visits a year.

Targeted social media and email marketing: Digital messages to existing patients can promote same-day scans directly to the 66% who would pay $0.80 more, show current waiting times and be tracked cheaply. Content can be updated as the 38-minute waiting time falls. The weakness is that some patients ignore email and word-of-mouth still drives clinic choice, so personal reminders from reception staff would help.

Recommendation: PHC should choose targeted social media and email marketing, supported by a small conference presence. It reaches the 66% willing to pay $0.80 more at low cost and can run continuously to sustain 90,000 visits, unlike a single event. Newspapers are rejected as wasteful and declining; major conference sponsorship is rejected as too expensive and one-off for a partnership already servicing a $400,000 loan.
    Keywords: 66%, $0.80, 59%, 700, 21,000, waiting
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to PHC's survey or services. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of PHC with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options with a justified recommendation that explains why newspapers and conference sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PHC's nursing absenteeism has reached 10% and waiting times have risen. Explain two benefits for PHC of introducing a performance-related bonus for its nursing staff.
    Answer: Point 1: A performance-related bonus links part of pay to measurable targets such as reducing the 38-minute waiting time and keeping the 2.7% re-scan rate low, giving the 60 staff a clear financial incentive (Herzberg's motivator) to improve service quality. Faster appointments would strengthen the appeal of same-day scans to the 66% of surveyed patients willing to pay $0.80 more.

Linking part of pay to punctuality also gives supervisors an objective appraisal measure within the hierarchical structure, satisfying the 59% of patients who check waiting-time ratings and giving fair evidence for bonus payments.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]

Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 43.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 14.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 21.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $600,000 on revenue of $1,500,000 in 2024 gives 600 ÷ 1,500 = 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $774,000 on $1,800,000 gives 774 ÷ 1,800 = 43.0%. Interest payable fell from $24,000 to $20,000, reducing the drag on surpluses.

Cash kept can absorb the 12.7% rise in eco-product and vehicle-energy costs without raising the $12.00 price, preserving the $6.00 contribution on 100,000 jobs.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids pledging security for the $320,000 loan, so the new plant and van fleet cannot be repossessed if demand slows. Internal funds are available at once, letting SSC replace the machines behind the 2.9% re-clean rate and reduce the 11% absenteeism disrupting appointments. Fixed costs of $264,000 a year are a real burden for a company founded only in 2017, so avoiding interest on the $320,000 loan protects its early growth; the electric vans also need capital, and preserving cash protects the 100,000-job target.

--- STEM ---
Norwood Valley Preserves (NVP) is a private limited company in the food processing sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Ines Norwood, the business makes fruit preserves and chutneys for regional grocery chains and independent supermarkets, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NVP plans to invest $720,000 in an automated glass-jar filling line with recyclable eco-packaging, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.80 a unit and a selling price of $10.80, and currently produces 96,000 units a year.     Question: Explain two advantages for NVP of using retained profit to fund the glass-jar filling line instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $270,000 of retained profit costs NVP nothing in interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when it already carries $240,000 of fixed costs a year. With the base interest rate at 5.75%, servicing a $450,000 bank loan would add a substantial interest burden, whereas internally funded money lets every dollar of the $5.00 contribution on each jar stay in the business to absorb the 9.5% rise in glass and packaging costs. This matters for a preserves maker selling at $10.80 to regional grocery chains that resist price increases.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk attached to a bank loan, so Ines Norwood's $720,000 automated filling line is not jeopardised if demand for chutneys disappoints. It also keeps ownership and control inside the founder's private limited company: no lender can impose conditions on how the recyclable eco-packaging line is run, and no outside party gains a claim on future profits, which suits NVP's hierarchical, autocratic style where the founder retains tight control of strategy and of the warehouse waste problem.

Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 24.0%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $1,470,000 came from revenue $4,200,000 less cost of sales $2,730,000; $1,470,000 ÷ $4,200,000 = 35.0%. In 2025 gross profit of $2,016,000 = revenue $5,040,000 − cost of sales $3,024,000; $2,016,000 ÷ $5,040,000 = 40.0%. Stronger evidence: the profit margin, because it gained five percentage points and directly reflects operating efficiency from the given revenue and cost figures, whereas the return on capital is also influenced by the enlarged capital base.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NVP of introducing recyclable eco-packaging for its preserves range.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in glass and packaging input costs will affect NVP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate (5.0% to 5.75%): If NVP's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $450,000 = $3,375 a year. That is modest against $240,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher base rates could also make future borrowing for the $720,000 line dearer and make consumers more cautious about premium preserves, but NVP can cap this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage (5.5%, to $14.14 from $13.40 per hour): With a workforce of 60 in packing and warehouse roles, this feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no honest annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity of 96,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 1,600 units per worker. If output per worker holds, the rise is absorbable; if it slips, unit labour cost rises and the $5.00 contribution shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.5% glass and packaging): The insert does not decompose the $5.80 variable cost, so only a bound can be computed: if all of it rose 9.5%, that adds 9.5% × $5.80 = $0.55 per unit; across 96,000 units that is about $52,800 a year (96,000 × $0.55). Only part can be recovered through the $0.50 eco-packaging premium, while spending on preserves grew just 2.8%.

Conclusion: The 9.5% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 96,000 jars and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that underpins the $720,000 investment. The interest effect is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation strikes the core unit economics with little pricing room.

--- STEM ---
Kestrel Ridge Footwear (KRF) is a public limited company in the footwear manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2008 by Ravi Kestrel, the business supplies durable work boots to national retailers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KRF plans to invest $960,000 in an automated stitching line using recycled leather alternatives, financed by a $560,000 share issue and a $400,000 five-year bank loan. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. KRF faces a rising defect rate on stitching and growing labour turnover in its cutting room.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for KRF of financing the stitching line with a share issue rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A $560,000 share issue brings in equity that carries no interest or compulsory repayment, protecting KRF's cash flow while it carries $360,000 of fixed costs a year. With the base interest rate at 5.0%, a $400,000 bank loan would create an annual interest commitment; share capital instead lets the full $8.00 contribution on each boot remain available to absorb the 8.4% rise in upper-material costs without squeezing the $20.00 selling price to national retailers.

Point 2: Equity does not have to be secured against KRF's assets, so the automated stitching line cannot be repossessed if demand for work boots falls, which matters given the current 2.2% defect rate and labour turnover. As a public limited company, KRF can access a wide pool of investors for the $960,000 project without depending on one lender's conditions or covenants. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders, but for a large capital scheme this spreads risk more widely than concentrating it in a single bank loan.
    Keywords: share issue, $560,000, $400,000, $960,000, bank loan, $360,000

Trade shows are rejected as expensive and short-lived for a business servicing a $400,000 loan; print is rejected as passive and unable to demonstrate the $1.20 recycled-material premium. Operating profit rose from $540,000 to $729,000; $540,000 ÷ $3,600,000 = 15.0% and $729,000 ÷ $4,050,000 = 18.0%. Capital employed moved from $3,000,000 to $3,645,000; $540,000 ÷ $3,000,000 = 18.0% and $729,000 ÷ $3,645,000 = 20.0%. Interest payable was $60,000 then $75,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, so TMB's profitability strengthened. Gross profitability rose from 30.0% to 34.0%, consistent with better control of flour and dairy costs as the 4.6% waste rate fell. The operating return on sales improved from 15.0% to 18.0%, showing the $180,000 fixed costs are being spread across more output of 72,000 units. Return on capital rose from 18.0% to 20.0% despite capital employed reaching $3,645,000 to fund the $540,000 ovens, so the new assets are earning their keep.

Stronger evidence: the profit margin, because it gained three percentage points directly from the given revenue and operating profit and is not distorted by the larger asset base that also affects the return on capital figure.

Conclusion: TMB's financial performance has improved on every measure. The operating return on sales is the clearest sign of efficiency; the residual caution is the $300,000 loan and rising interest payable, which still need to be met from the improved margins.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements, and a justified conclusion naming the stronger evidence.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TMB of adopting recyclable packaging for its bread range.
    Answer: Advantage: Recyclable packaging matches the 66% of 400 surveyed customers who would pay $0.30 more, helping TMB protect its $5.00 contribution per unit while flour and dairy input costs climb 11.2%.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in flour and dairy input costs will affect TMB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base interest rate (3.75% to 4.5%): If TMB's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250 a year. That is small beside $180,000 of fixed costs, and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates may make future borrowing dearer, but the direct annual cost is modest and TMB can reduce it by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage (7.1%, to $13.49 from $12.60 per hour): With a workforce of 50 in baking and delivery, this feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it slips, unit labour costs rise and the $5.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (11.2% flour and dairy): The insert does not decompose the $4.20 variable cost, so only a bound can be stated: if all of it rose 11.2%, that adds 11.2% × $4.20 = $0.47 per unit; across 72,000 units that is about $33,800 a year (72,000 × $0.47). The $0.30 recyclable-packaging premium recovers only part of this, while bakery spending grew just 1.9%.

Conclusion: The 11.2% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 72,000 units and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that supports the $540,000 investment. The interest effect is minor and fixable, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation hits unit economics with almost no pricing room.
