--- STEM ---
Kestrel Ridge Aggregates (KRA) is a private limited company in the quarrying and construction aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2007 by Bryn Kestrel, the business supplies crushed stone to regional building contractors and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. KRA plans to invest $720,000 in a recycled-aggregate crushing plant with stormwater recycling, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and produces 96,000 units of crushed aggregate a year. KRA faces two operational problems: stone-dust complaints from nearby residents are rising, and labour turnover is increasing among crusher operators.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KRA plans to fund part of its recycled-aggregate crushing plant with retained profit rather than the $450,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for KRA of using the $270,000 retained profit instead of the loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $270,000 of retained profit costs KRA no interest charges or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the business already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Every dollar not paid as interest can instead absorb the 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs, helping KRA hold its $14.00 selling price for crushed stone and stay competitive against other quarries supplying regional building contractors. Retained profit also has no fixed repayment timetable, so the $720,000 recycling plant can be commissioned at the quarry's own pace.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk. If demand for recycled aggregate disappoints, the bank cannot seize the new crusher or the quarry site, so Bryn Kestrel's owner-managed company keeps control of its core asset. The bank loan, by contrast, would require security and regular servicing whatever the level of stone-dust complaints or output. Using internal funds also preserves the company's borrowing headroom for later investment in stormwater recycling, and it avoids the lender conditions that could restrict how the 96,000-unit operation is run or expanded.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $450,000, $270,000, $720,000, $240,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to KRA's cash flow, costs and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KRA is promoting its new recycled aggregate to building contractors. Consider advertising in trade magazines, sponsoring a local building show, or a targeted social media campaign. Which should KRA choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade magazine advertising: A trade magazine reaches building contractors directly and gives KRA space to explain the recycled content and stormwater recycling of the new plant, which matters to the 47% of surveyed builders who check environmental credentials. It is a credible, permanent medium for technical claims. However, a full-page campaign is expensive for a 52-employee quarry already servicing a $450,000 loan, the audience is narrower than the regional contractor base KRA supplies, and print cannot demonstrate the product or respond to the 61% of builders who would pay $0.50 more until long after the $720,000 plant is running.

Local building show sponsorship: A stand at a local show lets KRA meet contractors face to face, hand over samples of recycled aggregate and answer questions about quality, directly tackling the stone-dust complaints by showing the stormwater system. It is cheaper than national print and builds relationships in KRA's own region. Its weakness is reach: a three-day event touches only the contractors who attend, so it cannot by itself sell enough of the 96,000 units the quarry produces, and the cost per order can be high.

Targeted social media campaign: Paid social ads can be aimed at regional contractors and sustainability-focused builders, showing short videos of the crushing line and linking the 61% premium finding to a clear $0.50 message. It is measurable, scalable and cheap per contact, and can be adjusted quickly if the 2.4% defect rate or delivery times of 4.5 days need explaining. It depends on builders actually using the platforms and on sustained spend to keep visibility.

Recommendation: KRA should choose the targeted social media campaign. It reaches the exact segment identified in the 500-builder survey, costs far less than trade print, and scales regionally in a way a single local show cannot. The building show is rejected as too limited in reach; trade magazines are rejected as costly and slow. KRA should use the show only as a low-cost supporting opportunity.
    Keywords: 61%, 47%, 500, $0.50, recycled aggregate, 24,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to KRA. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KRA with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of KRA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade magazines and the building show are rejected.

Under the present autocratic, hierarchical approach, operators simply follow instructions and disengage; involving them raises job satisfaction and commitment, which directly addresses the rising labour turnover and protects the 96,000-unit output needed to justify the $720,000 plant.

Point 2: Consulting operators draws on their experience of the new crusher and the 14 staff still without on-the-job training, generating ideas that reduce the current 2.4% defect rate and the complaints that fell from 34 to 19 per month. --- STEM ---
Thornbury Timber & Board (TTB) is a cooperative in the sustainable forestry and recycled board sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Fiona Thorn, the business supplies low-energy fibreboard to furniture makers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TTB plans to invest $640,000 in a low-energy board-pressing line using recycled wood fibre, financed by a $300,000 bank overdraft and $340,000 of new member share capital. It has fixed costs of $198,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and produces 84,000 units of board a year. TTB faces two operational problems: wood-fibre waste is above target, and defects on the new press are frequent.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TTB plans to fund its low-energy pressing line with new member share capital rather than the $300,000 bank overdraft. Explain two advantages for TTB of using the $340,000 share capital instead of the overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: The $340,000 of new member share capital does not have to be repaid and carries no interest, so TTB avoids the volatile financing cost of a $300,000 overdraft whose rate rises with the base rate to 4.50%. For a cooperative running fixed costs of $198,000 a year, that saving protects the $5.50 contribution on each board and helps absorb the 11.3% rise in fibre and resin costs without increasing the $11.00 selling price to furniture makers.

Point 2: Share capital does not require the security or daily repayment pressure of an overdraft, so the $640,000 pressing line cannot be withdrawn by a bank at short notice if member withdrawals or a dip in orders occur. It also keeps decision-making in the hands of the cooperative's members, including founder Fiona Thorn, rather than giving a lender influence over how the recycled wood fibre is sourced. With the right to share in future profits, members have a direct incentive to reduce the 8.6% wood-fibre waste and improve the 3.4% defect rate, aligning financing with the 84,000-unit output target.
    Keywords: share capital, overdraft, $340,000, $300,000, $640,000, $198,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TTB's cooperative structure, costs and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TTB is launching its low-energy recycled board to furniture manufacturers. Consider advertising in a woodworking trade magazine, sponsoring a furniture trade fair, or a targeted digital campaign. Which should TTB choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Woodworking trade magazine advertising: A trade magazine reaches furniture manufacturers directly and can carry the technical detail behind TTB's low-energy board and recycled wood fibre, which is relevant to the 44% who require environmental certification. It is a credible and lasting medium for a cooperative. However, a national campaign is costly for a 38-member business with a $300,000 overdraft, much of the readership lies outside TTB's regional customer base, and print cannot prove certification or demonstrate the board's quality as effectively as face-to-face contact.

Furniture trade fair sponsorship: A sponsored stand lets TTB show samples of the recycled board, explain the pressing process and hand over certification documents to the very manufacturers who buy the 21,000 boards produced last quarter. It directly answers the 44% certification requirement and builds personal relationships. The limits are cost, limited reach to those who attend, and the fact that a single event cannot generate the orders needed for 84,000 units a year on its own.

Targeted digital campaign: Paid digital ads and emails can be aimed at furniture makers and specifiers, showing the 58% premium finding and the 5.5-day delivery record with measurable responses.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in recycled fibre and resin costs will affect TTB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): The $300,000 bank overdraft is explicitly variable-rate in effect, so a 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250 a year if the full overdraft is drawn. The main wider effect is that future borrowing for the $640,000 programme becomes dearer.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.59 an hour): TTB employs a workforce of 38 at the mill, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. Fibre and resin costs (11.3%): These are direct inputs into the board. Even a partial pass-through cuts contribution from $5.50 toward roughly $4.90, and the 58% of buyers willing to pay $0.45 more can offset only part of it.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in fibre and resin costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every board, directly reduces the contribution that funds the $300,000 overdraft and the $640,000 line, and cannot be removed by a single financing decision. The interest rise is small and reducible at $2,250, while the wage effect depends on hours not supplied in the insert and can be offset by productivity, so both are lesser threats.

Marlowe Hill Furniture (MHF) is a family partnership in the reclaimed furniture and eco-materials sector, employing a workforce of 26. The money saved can be spent on tackling the 2.9% finish defect rate and the $0.60 per unit rework cost, or absorbed if reclaimed timber and low-VOC finish costs rise 10.6%, allowing MHF to hold its $16.50 selling price for interior designers.

Point 2: Retained profit gives no lender the right to repossess the new workshop machinery if orders slip, so Callum Marlowe and the other partners keep control of the $540,000 investment and the reclaimed furniture range. Hire purchase would tie the partners to fixed payments and security regardless of the shortage of skilled joiners or the 1.4% fall in furniture spending. Internal funds also preserve the partnership's borrowing capacity for later phases of the workshop and avoid committing future profits to finance charges at a time when contribution per unit is under pressure.

--- STEM ---
Grange Lane Bricks (GLB) is a public limited company in the construction materials and recycled bricks sector, employing a workforce of 74. Founded in 1998 by Aoife Grange, the business supplies bricks to housebuilders and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. GLB plans to invest $880,000 in a recycled-content brick kiln with waste-heat recovery, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and a $380,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.00 a unit and a selling price of $10.00, and produces 110,000 units of brick a year. GLB faces two operational problems: kiln temperature variation is raising the defect rate, and off-spec rejection is wasting output.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GLB plans to fund part of its recycled-content kiln with a share issue rather than the $500,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for GLB of using the $380,000 share issue instead of the loan.
    Answer: Point 1: The $380,000 raised by the share issue does not require interest or capital repayment, so GLB avoids adding to the interest payable that already rose to $30,000 while carrying a $500,000 bank loan. The saving helps cover fixed costs of $300,000 a year and protects the $6.00 contribution on each brick as clay and energy costs rise 13.2%, allowing the $10.00 price to hold for housebuilders.

Point 2: Equity has no fixed maturity and no security over the kiln, so the $880,000 waste-heat recovery plant cannot be at risk of repossession if the 4.2% defect rate persists or housing starts fall 2.3%. As a public limited company, GLB can also reach a wide pool of investors without surrendering control to a single lender, keeping founder Aoife Grange's strategy intact. The new shareholders share the risk of the recycled-content venture, and the capital strengthens the balance sheet for future borrowing while the 110,000-unit output is established.
    Keywords: share issue, $380,000, $500,000, $880,000, $300,000, bank loan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to GLB's financing, costs and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: GLB is promoting its recycled-content bricks to housebuilders. Consider advertising in construction trade journals, sponsoring a housebuilders' association award, or a targeted email and digital campaign. Which should GLB choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Construction trade journal advertising: A trade journal reaches housebuilders and can carry technical data on recycled-content bricks and waste-heat recovery, relevant to the 49% who check environmental credentials when tendering. It lends credibility to a public company. However, full-page advertising is costly for a business with a $500,000 loan, much of the readership is outside GLB's regional market, and print cannot demonstrate brick quality or respond quickly to the 4.2% defect rate concerns.

Housebuilders' association award sponsorship: Sponsoring an award builds prestige and puts GLB in front of senior buyers at one event, supporting the 63% who would pay $0.35 more and the 49% checking credentials. It is a strong relationship-building tool. Its limits are a narrow audience confined to attendees, high sponsorship fees, and the fact that one award cannot by itself secure orders for the 110,000 bricks the kiln produces.

Targeted email and digital campaign: Emails and digital ads can be aimed at regional housebuilders and procurement managers, showing the $0.35 premium message and the 3.8-day delivery record with measurable responses. It is cheap per contact, fast to adjust if kiln defects need explaining, and can be segmented by the 49% who care about credentials.   Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: GLB uses autocratic leadership in a hierarchical structure, and kiln variation is raising the defect rate to 4.2%. Explain two benefits for GLB of this approach in responding to the problem.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership allows founder Aoife Grange to take a quick, decisive response when kiln temperature variation pushes the defect rate to 4.2% and 7.4% of output is rejected.     Question: GLB must train 18 of its 74 workers on the new kiln controls. Consider on-the-job training at the plant or off-the-job courses at the technical centre at $910 per worker. Which should GLB choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching at the kiln teaches the 18 workers the exact control settings behind the recycled-content process, at no course fee, while keeping the 27,500 bricks per quarter flowing.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GLB's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has performance improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in clay, recycled aggregate and energy costs will affect GLB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If the $500,000 ten-year bank loan carries a variable rate, a 0.75 percentage point increase adds 0.0075 × $500,000 = $3,750 a year. This is modest against fixed costs of $300,000 and could be removed by fixing the rate, while the $380,000 share issue reduces the need for further debt. A higher rate could nevertheless weaken housebuilder demand at a time when housing starts already fell 2.3%.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $14.03 an hour): GLB has a workforce of 74 in kiln operations and packing, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert supplies neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 110,000 units ÷ 74 workers ≈ 1,486 bricks per worker. The rise is sustainable only if that output holds and the 4.2% defect rate is reduced, otherwise unit labour costs erode the $6.00 contribution.

Clay, aggregate and energy costs (13.2%): These are the core material and fuel inputs of brick making. The $4.00 variable cost is not broken down, so only a labelled upper bound is possible: if all of it rose 13.2%, that adds 0.132 × $4.00 = $0.53 per brick (rounded); over 110,000 units that is $58,300 a year (110,000 × $0.53). Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution from $6.00 toward about $5.47, and the $0.35 premium available to 63% of builders covers only part of it.

Conclusion: The 13.2% rise in clay, recycled aggregate and energy costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every brick, directly erodes the contribution that services the $500,000 loan and justifies the $880,000 kiln, and cannot be neutralised by a refinancing decision. The interest rise is quantifiably small at $3,750 and can be fixed, while the wage effect depends on hours not given and can be offset by productivity, so both are subordinate.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to GLB. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GLB's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GLB with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Westmoor Eco Panels (WEP) is a private limited company in the construction materials and recycled panel sector, employing a workforce of 31. Founded in 2015 by Rhys Westmoor, the business supplies composite wall panels to builders and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. WEP plans to invest $690,000 in a recycled-composite panel line using agricultural waste fibre, financed by a $260,000 lease and $430,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $186,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and produces 72,000 units of panel a year. WEP faces two problems: a shortage of trained machine operators and rising panel waste.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: WEP plans to fund its recycled-composite panel line with retained profit rather than the $260,000 lease. Explain two advantages for WEP of using the $430,000 retained profit instead of the lease.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $430,000 of retained profit avoids the regular rental payments and finance charges attached to the $260,000 lease, protecting cash flow while WEP already carries fixed costs of $186,000 a year. The saving can be used to reduce the 2.2% defect rate and the 9.1% waste fibre level, or absorbed if recycled fibre, resin and transport costs keep rising 12.1%, allowing the $13.50 selling price to hold for builders.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership of the new panel line with Rhys Westmoor and the company, so there is no risk of the leased equipment being repossessed if the shortage of trained machine operators delays commissioning or panel waste stays high. The lease would lock WEP into fixed payments irrespective of the 35 monthly complaints. Internal funds also keep the $690,000 investment free of lender conditions and preserve borrowing capacity for later expansion of the recycled-composite range.

--- STEM ---
Marrowvale Organic Farms (MOF) is a private limited company in the agribusiness sector, growing and packing organic vegetables for regional supermarkets and veg-box subscribers. The business has a workforce of 42 and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership, with founder Priya Nandra consulting growers at weekly planning meetings. MOF plans to invest $720,000 in a new wash-and-grade packhouse with cold storage, financed by a $450,000 five-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.20 a unit and a selling price of $12.20, and currently produces 82,000 units a year, where each unit is a packed carton. MOF faces two problems: 9.5% of harvested crates are rejected at grading for blemishing, and absenteeism among packing staff has reached 8%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MOF plans to fund part of its $720,000 packhouse with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MOF of using retained profit instead of the bank loan to finance the investment.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no fixed repayment schedule, which matters because MOF must cover fixed costs of $252,000 a year from a contribution of only $7.00 a carton ($12.20 − $5.20). Interest on a $450,000 loan would be a commitment in every month, including months when a poor harvest pushes the 9.5% rejection rate higher; keeping that cash inside the business protects the seasonal wage bill and the spending needed to cut rejected crates.

Point 2: Using MOF's own $270,000 removes the lender's security and conditions, so no bank can claim rights over the new wash-and-grade packhouse or veto the cropping plans that Priya Nandra agrees with growers at weekly meetings. Control stays with the existing owners, which suits the flat, democratic structure. The cost is that $270,000 of reserves can no longer act as a buffer if 8% absenteeism disrupts packing or if organic input costs keep rising.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, $252,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MOF's costs, reserves and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MOF wants to build demand for its certified organic veg boxes. Consider advertising in organic trade magazines, hosting farmers' market tastings, or running a social media campaign for subscribers. Which should MOF choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Organic trade magazines: A technical advert reaches supermarket produce buyers and wholesale decision-makers, and it can carry the evidence buyers now demand, such as the wash-line trial that cut rejected crates from 9.5% to 4.2%. Readership is small, and the message does not reach the 500 subscribers among whom 68% would pay $0.50 more.

Farmers' market tastings: Sampling at markets lets shoppers taste the vegetables and builds local loyalty, which supports the 57% who choose farms with waste-reduction plans. It is cheap and gives instant feedback, but each event reaches only a few hundred people, lasts a day, and is slow to grow the 19,600 cartons packed each quarter, so the link to the $720,000 packhouse is weak.

Social media campaign: A subscriber-facing campaign can show harvests, the wash line and recyclable cardboard boxes at low cost per view, with results measured click by click. It converts the 68% willing to pay $0.50 more into actual premium sales and reinforces the 2.8-day delivery story. It demands constant content and cannot present detailed quality evidence to supermarket buyers.

Recommendation: MOF should choose the social media campaign, supported by occasional market tastings. It targets the subscribers already identified in the survey, scales beyond a single market and costs far less than magazine advertising while the $450,000 loan is being serviced. Trade magazines are rejected because they miss the subscribers who will pay the premium, and market tastings are rejected as too small and short-lived to fill a packhouse built for 82,000 cartons a year.

    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If the $450,000 five-year loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.75% × $450,000 = $3,375 a year to interest. --- STEM ---
Kestrel Creek Creamery (KCC) is a public limited company in the dairy processing sector, making milk, butter and soft cheese for supermarkets and food-service wholesalers. The company employs a workforce of 37 and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and narrowly defined jobs. Founder Niamh Kestrel plans to invest $560,000 in a cheese maturation cellar and an automated bottling line, financed by a $360,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $198,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.40 a unit and a selling price of $10.40, and produces 74,000 units a year, where each unit is a one-litre carton. KCC faces two problems: 7.4% of cartons fail quality checks for curdling or leaking seals, and labour turnover among production staff has reached 18%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KCC plans to fund part of its $560,000 maturation cellar and bottling line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for KCC of using retained profit instead of the loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payment and no fixed repayment date, which is valuable because KCC must cover fixed costs of $198,000 a year from a contribution of $6.00 a carton ($10.40 − $4.40). Interest on a $360,000 loan would be due even in months when the 7.4% failure rate spikes; using the $200,000 already generated keeps cash in the company and protects the 18%-turnover-hit production team from cutbacks.

Point 2: Funding from internal reserves avoids the collateral and covenants a bank would attach to a public limited company, so Niamh Kestrel's board can operate the new bottling line without lender interference. No external claim is created over the maturation cellar. The trade-off is that $200,000 of reserves is no longer available as a cushion if cheese demand weakens or the 10.4% feed-cost rise persists, leaving KCC more exposed than with a spread of funding sources. A phased approach, using retained profit first and borrowing later only if cheese demand grows in line with the 3.6% spending trend, would keep that reserve intact.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $200,000, $360,000, $560,000, $198,000

--- STEM ---
Harbourleaf Tea Company (HTC) is a partnership in the hot-beverage sector, blending and packing loose-leaf and bagged teas for cafes and supermarkets. The partnership has a workforce of 26 and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership under founder Mei Treasury. HTC plans to invest $430,000 in a new blending and automated packing line, financed by a $250,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $154,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.10 a unit and a selling price of $8.10, and produces 58,000 units a year, where each unit is a tea caddy. HTC faces two problems: 12% labour turnover among packing staff and rising complaints about inconsistent blends.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HTC plans to fund part of its $430,000 packing line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for HTC of using retained profit instead of the loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charge and no fixed repayment date, which matters because HTC must cover fixed costs of $154,000 a year with only $5.00 contribution per caddy ($8.10 − $3.10). Servicing a $250,000 loan would absorb cash even in months when the 6.3% rejection rate rises; keeping the $180,000 inside the partnership protects wages and lets Mei Treasury spend on fixing the inconsistent blends.

Point 2: Internal funding avoids the security and conditions a bank would impose, so the partners keep full control of blending recipes and the flat structure, with no lender able to veto decisions taken by the team. This suits a partnership where laissez-faire leadership relies on trusted staff. The drawback is that $180,000 of reserves can no longer cushion a bad quarter, leaving HTC dependent on the 12%-turnover-hit packing team to sustain the 58,000-caddy output. A phased approach, using the $180,000 first and borrowing only if the 4.2% speciality-tea demand growth persists, would preserve flexibility for the partners.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $180,000, $250,000, $430,000, $154,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to HTC's costs, reserves and ownership.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HTC wants to launch a single-origin certified tea range. Consider sponsoring a barista competition, handing out free samples in cafes, or a social media campaign for tea drinkers. Which should HTC choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Barista competition sponsorship: A competition puts HTC's tea in front of professional buyers and baristas whose opinions influence cafe listings, and it can carry the ethical-sourcing message that 53% of surveyed cafe buyers check. It is costly and short-lived, however, and reaches few of the 420 surveyed buyers directly while a $250,000 loan is being repaid.

Free samples in cafes: Sampling lets buyers taste the blend and reduces the risk of a listing, which is valuable after complaints about inconsistent blends and a 6.3% rejection rate. It is cheap per tasting and gives instant feedback, but coverage is limited to a handful of cafes and cannot quickly build the 14,200-caddy quarterly base, so the link to the $430,000 line is slow.

It can convert the 66% who would pay $0.40 more into premium sales, though it needs steady content and cannot give buyers the tactile tasting evidence a café contract requires.

Recommendation: HTC should choose the social media campaign, backed by limited cafe sampling for trade buyers. It reaches the 66% willing to pay the premium, scales beyond a few cafes and costs far less than a competition while the $250,000 loan is outstanding.   Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HTC's labour turnover is 12% and 6.3% of batches are rejected for inconsistent blends. Explain two benefits for HTC of introducing team working in its packing area.

    Question: HTC must train 8 of 26 staff on the new packing line. Consider on-the-job training on the line or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should HTC choose? Justify your decision.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HTC's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HTC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.51 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.79 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.94 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.26 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $74,000 inventories + $96,000 trade receivables + $26,000 cash = $196,000, and 2025 current assets = $66,000 + $112,000 + $44,000 = $222,000. Excluding inventories: ($196,000 − $74,000) ÷ $130,000 = $122,000 ÷ $130,000 = 0.94, and ($222,000 − $66,000) ÷ $124,000 = $156,000 ÷ $124,000 = 1.26.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 8.6% rise in tea leaf and packaging costs will affect HTC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If the $250,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.75% × $250,000 = $1,875 a year. That is modest against $154,000 of fixed costs, and the partners could fix the rate, so the direct impact is limited. The indirect impact is that dearer credit makes the $430,000 line harder to finance later and reduces the value of the $180,000 retained profit kept for contingencies.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, from $12.50 to $13.24): Each packing hour costs $0.74 more (5.9% × $12.50 = $0.7375). The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay, so an annual total cannot be calculated honestly; the sound judgement is that 12% labour turnover forces repeated hiring at the higher rate, and unless productivity holds near 58,000 caddies from a workforce of 26, unit labour cost rises and the $5.00 contribution falls.

Tea leaf and packaging costs (up 8.6%): These feed the $3.10 variable cost on every caddy. Even a smaller share cuts the $5.00 contribution on every unit, and retail tea prices rose only 1.8%, so little of the rise can be passed on.

Conclusion: The 8.6% rise in tea leaf and packaging costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs across all 58,000 caddies and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that must repay the $250,000 loan and justify the $430,000 line, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,875 a year and can be capped by fixing the rate. The wage rise is second because it recurs with each new hire, but team working can offset part of it. HTC should cut the 6.3% rejection rate and seek the $0.40 premium instead of absorbing every increase.

--- STEM ---
Sunhill Citrus Packers (SCP) is a private limited company in the agribusiness sector, grading, waxing and exporting citrus fruit for overseas supermarket chains. The company has a workforce of 54 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership, with founder Rafael Sunhill consulting shift leaders each week. SCP plans to invest $880,000 in an automated grading and waxing line with a cold store, financed by a $520,000 five-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $286,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.20 a unit and a selling price of $14.20, and produces 96,000 units a year, where each unit is a graded crate. SCP faces two problems: 8.6% of fruit is rejected for blemishing and absenteeism among graders has reached 11%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SCP plans to fund part of its $880,000 grading line and cold store with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SCP of using retained profit instead of the loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no fixed repayment date, which matters because SCP must cover fixed costs of $286,000 a year from $8.00 contribution per crate ($14.20 − $6.20). Interest on a $520,000 loan would be payable even when the 8.6% rejection rate rises; using the $360,000 already earned keeps cash available to pay the 11%-absence-hit grading team and to fund quality improvements.

Point 2: Internal funds avoid the security and covenants a bank would require, so Rafael Sunhill and the shift leaders can run the new line without lender conditions attached to the cold store. Control stays with the company rather than a creditor. The cost is that $360,000 of reserves is no longer a buffer if export rejection notices keep climbing from 36 a month or freight costs keep rising, leaving SCP reliant on its 96,000-crate output to absorb shocks. Rafael Sunhill could phase the $880,000 project so retained profit funds the grader first and the $520,000 loan is drawn only when the 3.8% export demand growth justifies the cold store.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $360,000, $520,000, $880,000, $286,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to SCP's costs, reserves and financing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SCP wants to win more overseas listings for its graded citrus. Consider hosting buyer visits to the packing house, advertising in an export trade journal, or a social media campaign for consumers. Which should SCP choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Buyer visits to the packing house: Inviting supermarket buyers to see the optical grader lets them witness the fall in rejections from 8.6% to 3.8% and inspect the residue-testing process that 49% of buyers require. This builds trust and can secure listings directly, but it is time-consuming, only reaches a few buyers at a time, and diverts managers while the $880,000 line is being commissioned.

Export trade journal advertising: An advert in a specialist journal reaches many produce buyers at once and can carry the 3.8% trial result and the 3.4-day dispatch promise. It is cheaper than hosting visits, but print cannot demonstrate the fruit's quality, and readership may include buyers outside SCP's export markets, so part of the spend is wasted while a $520,000 loan is outstanding.

Social media campaign: A campaign can show the groves, grading and waxing to consumers in importing countries, supporting the 61% who would pay $0.60 more for waxed grade-A fruit and building pull-through for supermarket buyers. Engagement is measurable against the 24,600 crates graded last quarter, but results build slowly and consumer interest does not itself sign an export contract.

Recommendation: SCP should choose buyer visits to the packing house, supported by a small trade journal advert. Visits directly convert the 3.8% trial evidence and residue-testing proof into listings, which is what sells 96,000 crates a year. Journal advertising alone is rejected because print cannot demonstrate quality, and social media is rejected as an indirect consumer channel that cannot close an overseas order while the $520,000 loan must be serviced.

Better attendance and fewer rejections protect the $14.20 price and $8.00 contribution needed to service the $520,000 loan. SCP should pilot the bonus on one shift and compare rejection and absence figures with the current baselines before extending it across all 54 staff. The scheme should be reviewed against the 36 monthly rejection notices as well, because a bonus that lifts output without improving quality would waste the $880,000 investment.

--- STEM ---
Quarryfield Ale Brewers (QAB) is a cooperative in the beverage sector, brewing craft ale for independent retailers and taprooms. The cooperative has a workforce of 33 and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership, with founder Elin Quarryfield putting major decisions to member votes. QAB plans to invest $680,000 in new fermentation tanks and a canning line, financed by a $420,000 bank overdraft and $260,000 retained surplus. It has fixed costs of $245,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.10 a unit and a selling price of $12.10, and produces 80,000 units a year, where each unit is a can of ale. QAB faces two problems: 6.8% of cans are rejected for leaking seals and absenteeism among brewing staff has reached 9.5%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QAB plans to fund part of its $680,000 fermentation and canning project with a bank overdraft. Explain two advantages for QAB of using retained surplus instead of the overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained surplus carries no interest charge and no variable-rate exposure, which matters because QAB must cover fixed costs of $245,000 a year from $7.00 contribution per can ($12.10 − $5.10). Interest on a $420,000 overdraft would rise whenever the base rate moves, especially with the rise to 5.25%; using the $260,000 already accumulated keeps cash inside the cooperative and protects the wages of a workforce of 33.

Point 2: Internal funding avoids the daily repayment pressure and security of an overdraft, so the fermentation tanks cannot be threatened by a bank recall if ale sales dip below the 17,800 cans filled last quarter. Control stays with the members who vote on decisions under Elin Quarryfield. The cost is that $260,000 of surplus is no longer a reserve for the 6.8% rejection problem, so QAB relies more on its own trading cash flow. Elin Quarryfield should put the choice to a member vote, weighing the 5.2% growth in local-ale spending against the risk of holding no reserve if seal failures persist.
    Keywords: retained surplus, bank overdraft, $260,000, $420,000, $680,000, $245,000

--- STEM ---
Marden Industrial Pumpworks (MIPW) is a private limited company in the industrial machinery sector, manufacturing precision pumps for water-treatment plants and supplying municipal contracts across two regions, with a workforce of 60. Founded in 2007 by Anja Marden, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MIPW plans to invest $720,000 in a CNC machining cell for pump impellers, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and produces 40,000 units a year. MIPW faces a 5.5% defect rate on impeller castings and rising scrap levels that threaten distributor deliveries under tight customer windows.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MIPW plans to fund part of its CNC machining cell with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MIPW of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $270,000 retained profit costs MIPW no interest or scheduled repayments, protecting cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a $450,000 bank loan. Every dollar saved can absorb the 9.6% rise in steel and cast-iron input costs, helping Anja Marden keep the $30.00 selling price competitive on municipal water-treatment contracts without borrowing more.

Point 2: Retained profit does not require collateral or give a lender power to repossess the new CNC cell if demand slips, so the $720,000 investment is safer. It also preserves the existing owners' control: no bank can impose conditions on how the 60-worker site is run, which matters when a 5.5% defect rate is already straining output and management needs freedom to re organise production quickly.

For a firm of 60 employees producing 40,000 units, the choice also affects risk: retained profit is internal and already earned, so it cannot be withdrawn by a lender if the 5.5% defect rate pushes rework above the $6,800 spent last quarter. Founder Anja Marden keeps control of the $720,000 cell and can redirect the $270,000 if municipal orders slip. By contrast, servicing the $450,000 loan on top of $360,000 fixed costs would consume contribution from the 30,000 units needed to break even, so internal funding protects the 10,000-unit margin of safety.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, $360,000

Technical visits give engineers the certification evidence behind the 68% premium acceptance, and results from the 9,800 inspected units can be shown directly. A campaign that merely builds awareness would not fix the 5.5% defect rate that caused 26 monthly complaints, so spending on broad reach before quality is consistent would waste cash needed for the $450,000 loan.

Decision: MIPW should choose prevention through quality assurance and operator training, retaining only light final sampling. Pure inspection is rejected because it finds faults after the cost is incurred, and training alone without process checks would not give the consistent tolerances water-treatment buyers demand.

--- STEM ---
Norhaven Technical Fasteners (NTF) is a public limited company in the metal components sector, producing threaded fasteners for construction equipment and exporting to three continents, with a workforce of 85. Founded in 1998 by Soren Norhaven, it uses a flat organisational structure and laissez-faire leadership. NTF will invest $1,080,000 in an automated thread-rolling line, financed by a $600,000 share issue, a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and produces 60,000 units a year. NTF suffers labour turnover of 14% and a 3.4% defect rate on threaded components, delaying shipments to distributors.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NTF plans to finance part of its thread-rolling line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for NTF of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A $600,000 share issue brings equity that needs no interest and no fixed repayment dates, leaving the $300,000 bank loan as the only debt commitment. With fixed costs of $420,000 a year and output of 60,000 units, that protects cash flow and lets Soren Norhaven direct funds to reducing the 3.4% defect rate rather than servicing debt.

Point 2: Equity widens NTF's shareholder base and spreads the risk of the $1,080,000 investment across investors instead of pledging company assets. As a public limited company it can access many shareholders, so the automated line can be funded without pushing the 85-worker business further into borrowing, though existing shareholders would be diluted.

For a public limited company with 85 workers and $420,000 fixed costs, equity also avoids the risk that a 5.25% base rate raises the $300,000 loan cost further. Shareholders share the risk of the $1,080,000 line in return for dividends, whereas a lender must be paid whether or not the 3.4% defect rate is fixed, so the $600,000 issue protects the 25,000-unit margin of safety.

Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1

Minimum wage up 4.9% to $13.80: With a workforce of 85, this raises the wage bill on every production hour and cannot be avoided. 11.2% alloy steel and nickel input costs: The insert does not decompose the $14.00 variable cost per unit, so only a labelled upper-bound illustration is honest: if the entire $14.00 were exposed, the rise would add 0.112 × $14.00 = $1.568 a unit, or $94,080 a year at 60,000 units. This bound is well above the $2,250 interest effect and shows why supplier negotiation matters more than loan terms.

Conclusion: the 11.2% rise in alloy steel and nickel input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 60,000 units, directly erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $1,080,000 plan, and dwarfs the $2,250 interest effect; the wage rise is material but cannot be quantified from the insert. Preston Gearbox Assemblies (PGB) is a worker cooperative in the automotive components sector, assembling gearboxes for commercial vehicles and supplying two domestic fleet operators, with a workforce of 42. Founded in 2011 by Isabel Preston, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and produces 36,000 units a year. PGB faces absenteeism of 8% and a 2.7% defect rate in final gear assembly, which is straining its delivery schedule.

    Answer: Point 1: Leasing the $200,000 of equipment spreads payment over the asset's life and avoids a large immediate cash outflow, which matters when PGB's fixed costs are $240,000 a year and absenteeism is 8%. Cash is preserved for the 42-worker cooperative to tackle the 2.7% defect rate while the $340,000 loan is serviced.

Point 2: With leasing, the lessor normally maintains the robotic cell, shifting technical risk away from a small cooperative with no specialist engineering team. Isabel Preston can therefore adopt the $540,000 investment without tying up the cooperative's reserves, though the asset is not owned at the end and total payments may exceed a loan.

Leasing also suits a cooperative with 42 members because it avoids asking members for more capital while 19 complaints and 8% absenteeism must be solved. The $340,000 loan and fixed costs of $240,000 already require 26,666.67 units to break even, so preserving cash matters more than owning the asset at the end of the term.

--- STEM ---
Ridgeway Quality Castings (RQC) is a private limited company in the foundry sector, making iron castings for agricultural machinery and serving four regional equipment makers, with a workforce of 110. Founded in 2003 by Tomas Ridgeway, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. RQC plans to invest $960,000 in a sand-casting moulding line using recycled metal feedstock, financed by a $560,000 bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and produces 50,000 units a year. RQC reports waste of 6.8% and labour turnover of 12%, raising unit costs across the foundry.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RQC plans to fund its sand-casting line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for RQC of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $400,000 retained profit avoids interest on that part of the $960,000 scheme, easing cash flow while RQC already carries fixed costs of $480,000 a year and a $560,000 loan. The saving can be spent on reducing the 6.8% waste rate and the $13.90 wage pressure, protecting the $12.00 contribution on 50,000 castings.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no security and leaves control with Tomas Ridgeway, so the hierarchical structure can act quickly on the 12% labour turnover problem without lender conditions. It also avoids piling more debt onto a foundry already exposed to the 4.75% base rate.

For a foundry with 110 workers and $480,000 fixed costs, retained profit also avoids the 4.75% rate environment on $400,000 of the scheme. --- STEM ---
Thistle & Loom Retail (TLR) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2016 by Fiona Thistlewaite, the business sells knitwear and lifestyle clothing through its own e-commerce website and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TLR plans to invest $420,000 in a new automated e-commerce fulfilment centre with computer stock control, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and currently produces 24,000 units a year. TLR faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 16% and its online return rate is 14%, with picking errors rising.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TLR plans to finance part of its $420,000 expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TLR of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $120,000 of retained profit costs TLR no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the firm already carries fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $300,000 bank loan. Every dollar not paid to the lender can absorb the 9.5% rise in cotton and fabric input costs, letting TLR hold its $30.00 selling price and protect the $12.00 contribution per unit on each of its 24,000 units. This matters when the online return rate is already 14% and each returned parcel costs an average $22.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the security and repayment risk of the bank loan, so the automated fulfilment centre is not exposed to repossession if demand for the new range disappoints. It also preserves Fiona Thistlewaite's ownership and control: no lender can impose covenants on how the e-commerce operation is run, which fits the flat, democratic structure and lets TLR react quickly to the 16% labour turnover problem without seeking external approval.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $120,000, $300,000, $420,000, $180,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TLR's retained profit, bank loan, costs and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TLR is launching a new knitwear range through its e-commerce website. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social-media influencer marketing. Which should TLR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A national TV advert would build mass awareness of the new knitwear range quickly across the whole country, which could drive traffic to the e-commerce website. However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 60-person retailer funding a $420,000 fulfilment centre, and most viewers are outside TLR's target online fashion segment, so spend wastage would be severe. TV also gives poor tracking of clicks and sales.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper, reaches a defined regional audience and suits time-limited launch messages. Its weakness is narrow geographic reach: TLR sells through a national e-commerce website, so local listeners cannot deliver the order volumes needed to utilise 24,000 units of capacity, and there is no direct route from hearing an ad to buying online.

Social-media influencer marketing: Fashion and lifestyle influencers reach precisely the online fashion shoppers TLR surveyed, where 71% value fast delivery and 58% would switch brand after a returns problem. Influencer posts link straight to the website, are measurable, cost far less than television, scale nationally unlike radio, and can demonstrate the new range visually. Credibility risk exists if an influencer is poorly matched, and results build more slowly than a TV burst.

Recommendation: TLR should choose social-media influencer marketing. It targets the exact online segment at low cost, is measurable, and can showcase knitwear visually while reinforcing the reliable-delivery message the survey demands. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm with $180,000 fixed costs and a $300,000 loan; local radio is rejected because its regional reach cannot serve a national website. TLR should pair influencers with modest on-site promotions rather than either rejected mass medium.
    Keywords: e-commerce, $420,000, 24,000, 71%, 58%, workforce of 60
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to TLR. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to TLR with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to TLR with a justified recommendation that explains why television and local radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TLR's labour turnover has reached 16% and its online return rate is 14%. Explain two benefits for TLR of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its fulfilment team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 employees a real voice in how the new fulfilment centre is organised, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help design picking routines are more likely to stay, directly tackling the 16% labour turnover and reducing the disruption that contributes to the 2.1% picking error rate.

Point 2: Consulting the people who handle returns daily generates practical ideas for cutting the 14% return rate, for example clearer size guidance or better packing, which lowers the average $22 cost per returned parcel. Higher involvement also builds commitment and reduces absence, protecting output of 24,000 units while the $420,000 automated centre beds in, and it fits TLR's flat structure because decisions do not have to pass through many layers.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, labour turnover, 16%, 14%, flat organisational structure, workforce of 60
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TLR's turnover, return rate and output.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TLR must train 18 of its 60 staff on the new computer stock-control system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should TLR choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching at the fulfilment line is directly relevant to TLR's own computer stock-control system and packing standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn. That protects the 2.1% picking error rate and the effort needed to cut the 14% return rate during the $420,000 centre rollout. The drawbacks are that trainers are themselves operators whose work slows, bad habits may be passed on, and there is no external certificate if customers ever ask for formal records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $750 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 18 staff, costing $13,500 in total (18 × $750) — small against the $420,000 investment. It removes staff from the line, however, reducing short-term capacity when labour turnover is already 16%, and the generic content may not match TLR's exact stock-control settings, so follow-up coaching would still be required.

Decision: TLR should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with short college top-ups later for the most senior operators. It is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while the return rate is high; full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $13,500 and withdrawing 18 of 60 staff would disrupt the design and packing schedule, and TLR can add college visits once the new centre stabilises.
    Keywords: stock control, 18 of 60, $750, 2.1%, workforce of 60, $420,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TLR. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to TLR. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods applied to TLR with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to the stock-control system.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how TLR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 9,000 units versus 24,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $180,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $300,000 bank loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $25.50 to tackle the 14% return rate.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TLR's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TLR's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.25 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $75,000 + $80,000 + $45,000 = $200,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $180,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.50; for 2025 it is $200,000 ÷ $100,000 = 2.00. The stricter 2024 measure is ($180,000 − $90,000) ÷ $120,000 = $90,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.75; for 2025 it is ($200,000 − $75,000) ÷ $100,000 = $125,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.25.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has clearly strengthened. The broader measure rose from 1.50 to 2.00 as current liabilities fell from $120,000 to $100,000 while current assets rose from $180,000 to $200,000. The stricter measure, which strips out inventories, improved from 0.75 to 1.25, so TLR no longer depends on selling stock to meet short-term debts — important while it services a $300,000 bank loan and funds a $420,000 fulfilment centre. The stronger of the two signals is the stricter measure, because it still exceeds 1.0 without relying on inventory that may be slow to sell given the 14% return rate. The main residual risk is trade receivables rising from $60,000 to $80,000, tying up cash; if online shoppers or wholesale customers pay late, the improvement could unravel, and inventories fell from $90,000 to $75,000, which may limit stock available for peak fashion demand.

Conclusion: TLR's liquidity has improved. Both the broader measure (1.50 to 2.00) and the stricter measure (0.75 to 1.25) show stronger short-term solvency, and the gain does not rest on inventory. The outstanding concern is rising trade receivables, so TLR should tighten credit control while proceeding with the expansion.
    Keywords: 1.50, 2.00, 0.75, 1.25, $180,000, $200,000, $420,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TLR of introducing an automated computer stock-control system in its new fulfilment centre.
    Answer: Advantage: Computer stock control gives real-time inventory counts, which directly attacks the 2.1% picking error rate and the 14% return rate by ensuring the correct item and size is dispatched. Faster, more accurate fulfilment supports the 71% of surveyed shoppers who value fast delivery and the 58% who would switch brand after a returns problem, protecting the $30.00 selling price and the 24,000-unit output that underpins the $420,000 centre.

Disadvantage: The software and scanners add to the $180,000 fixed costs and must be integrated with the e-commerce website, requiring staff training — the insert shows 18 of 60 staff still need training and college courses cost $750 each.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.25%, the 5.0% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in fabric input costs will affect TLR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.25%): If TLR's $300,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.5% of $300,000 = $1,500 a year (0.005 × $300,000). That is modest next to $180,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct effect is zero. Higher base rates may still make consumers more cautious about discretionary fashion spending and raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $420,000 centre, but TLR can largely neutralise this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.0%, to $13.65 per hour): With a workforce of 60 in packing and fulfilment, this feeds into the wage bill and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 24,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 400 units per worker. A wage rise is affordable only if productivity holds at that level or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $12.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Fabric input-cost inflation (9.5%): The insert never decomposes the $18.00 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 9.5%, that adds 9.5% × $18.00 = $1.71 a unit; at 24,000 units a year this is about $41,040 a year (24,000 × $1.71). Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution per unit materially, and the 14% return rate means some of this cost is wasted. TLR can recover part through price negotiations and better stock control, but the pressure is continuous.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in fabric input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 24,000 units and directly erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $420,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise is around $1,500 a year on a fixed-sum loan and can be hedged, and the wage effect depends on 400-unit productivity that management can influence through training.
    Keywords: 4.25%, 5.0%, 9.5%, $13.65, $18.00, $300,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TLR. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TLR's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to TLR with a well-justified judgement that fabric input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Nimbus Online Outfitters (NOO) is a public limited company in the urban streetwear e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2013 by Dev Raman, the business sells hoodies and trainer-compatible clothing through its own website and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. NOO plans to invest $560,000 in an automated returns-processing line with computer stock control, financed by a $200,000 share issue and a $360,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 30,000 units a year. NOO faces two problems: labour turnover is high and its online return rate has reached 13.5%, with refund processing slowing.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NOO is funding part of its $560,000 expansion through a $200,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for NOO of using a share issue rather than a further bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Share capital carries no interest or repayment obligation, so the $200,000 raised does not add to the $360,000 bank loan or the $240,000 annual fixed costs. Cash that would have serviced debt can instead absorb the 7.8% rise in fabric prices, helping NOO hold its $38.00 selling price and protect the $16.00 contribution on each of 30,000 units. This matters when 13.5% of orders are returned and refund processing takes 6.3 days.

Point 2: Equity is permanent capital with no collateral or repossession risk, so the automated returns-processing line is secure if online demand falls short. As a public limited company, NOO can access shareholders for further funds if the expansion needs topping up, and with a hierarchical structure and 120 staff the board can plan long-term without a lender imposing short-term repayment conditions that might force cuts in the returns team.
    Keywords: share issue, $200,000, bank loan, $360,000, $560,000, public limited company
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NOO's share issue, bank loan, costs and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NOO is launching a new hoodie collection online. Consider print advertising in fashion magazines, sponsorship of a music festival, or social-media influencer marketing. Which should NOO choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Print advertising in fashion magazines: A magazine campaign reaches fashion-interested readers and gives a durable, credible impression for a premium hoodie collection. However, print has long lead times, no direct link to the e-commerce website and weak measurement, which is a poor fit for a 120-staff business funding a $560,000 returns line and needing quick sales of 30,000 units.

Music festival sponsorship: Sponsorship would put the brand in front of large crowds of young streetwear buyers and could generate strong social media content and instant credibility. It is expensive, however, with much of the audience not necessarily online buyers, and the impact is concentrated in a few days rather than sustained. For a firm with $240,000 fixed costs and a $360,000 bank loan, a one-off festival fee is hard to justify on reach alone.

Social-media influencer marketing: The insert shows 68% of surveyed streetwear shoppers buy mainly on mobile and 61% check the return policy before ordering. Influencers reach exactly these mobile-first buyers, posts link straight to the website, and results are measurable. Content can explicitly address the 13.5% return rate by showing sizing and quality, reducing the 6.3-day refund problem. Risks include influencer credibility and slower compounding than a big event, but cost per engaged buyer is low.

Recommendation: NOO should choose social-media influencer marketing. It targets the mobile-first, return-conscious segment identified in the research, is measurable and scales nationally, and can be tied directly to online sales. Magazine print is rejected as slow and unmeasurable for an e-commerce retailer, and festival sponsorship is rejected as an expensive short burst that does not reliably convert to online orders. NOO should complement influencers with on-site sizing guides rather than either rejected option.
    Keywords: e-commerce, $560,000, 30,000, 68%, 61%, workforce of 120
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to NOO. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to NOO with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to NOO with a justified recommendation explaining why print and festival sponsorship are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]

More stable, experienced staff make fewer mistakes, supporting the 97.2% picking accuracy and protecting output of 30,000 units while the $560,000 automated returns line is introduced.

Rotation is low-cost, immediately attacks monotony and high labour turnover, and provides cover while the automated line beds in; full job enrichment is rejected at once because the 120 staff would need substantial training and the insert gives evidence of a 24-person skills gap, so responsibility should be phased in once accuracy is stable.

--- STEM ---
Coral Bay Swimwear (CBS) is a partnership in the coastal swimwear retail sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2011 by Isla Corbin, the business sells swimwear through a Cornwall shop and a growing e-commerce channel and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. CBS plans to invest $180,000 in a new e-commerce website and photography studio, financed by $90,000 of trade credit from fabric suppliers and $90,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $98,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and currently produces 14,000 units a year. CBS faces two problems: fabric waste has reached 11.2% and delivery times are lengthening.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CBS is funding part of its $180,000 expansion with $90,000 of trade credit from fabric suppliers. Explain two advantages for CBS of using trade credit rather than spending its retained profit.
    Answer: Point 1: Trade credit lets CBS obtain fabric now and pay later, preserving the $90,000 of retained profit as a cash buffer against fixed costs of $98,000 a year. That liquidity is valuable when delivery times are lengthening and 11.2% of fabric is wasted, because the partnership can still buy replacement materials without immediately drawing down its own funds.

Point 2: Supplier credit is flexible and usually interest-free in the short term, unlike a bank loan, so it does not add a fixed repayment commitment alongside the $180,000 website and studio investment. Keeping the $90,000 retained profit untouched also gives Isla Corbin's partnership room to fund quality-control training at $640 per person, helping reduce the 2.8% defect rate without seeking outside finance.
    Keywords: trade credit, $90,000, $180,000, $98,000, retained profit, 11.2%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to CBS's trade credit, retained profit and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CBS is launching a new sustainable swimwear range. Consider sponsorship of a local surf competition, print advertising in a holiday magazine, or social-media influencer marketing. Which should CBS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local surf competition sponsorship: Sponsoring a surf event puts the brand directly in front of coastal swimwear buyers and builds local credibility for a Cornwall-based partnership. It is relatively low-cost and generates photographs for the new e-commerce website. However, its reach is geographically narrow; a website can sell nationally, so a single local event may not generate enough orders to utilise 14,000 units of capacity, and impact is concentrated in one weekend.

Holiday magazine print advertising: Print reaches holidaymakers planning beach trips and suits a seasonal product, with a tangible, credible presence. Lead times are long, however, and there is no direct link from the page to the website, so conversion is hard to measure. For a small 30-staff firm investing $180,000 in a new website, a magazine campaign that cannot be tracked is difficult to justify against fixed costs of $98,000.

Social-media influencer marketing: The insert shows 66% of surveyed beachwear customers prefer sustainably made swimwear and 57% would pay $3 more for it. Influencers can demonstrate the sustainable range visually, link straight to the e-commerce site, and are measurable. They reach a national audience far beyond a local event and can be selected for beach and lifestyle credibility, though results depend on choosing credible partners and can take time to build.

Recommendation: CBS should choose social-media influencer marketing. It targets the sustainability-conscious segment revealed by the survey, is measurable, and drives traffic to the new website nationally.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CBS's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CBS's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.25 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $54,000 inventories + $36,000 trade receivables + $18,000 cash = $108,000; 2025 current assets = $45,000 + $48,000 + $27,000 = $120,000. The stronger evidence is the stricter measure, since its rise is not dependent on inventory that may not sell quickly out of season. Trade receivables did rise from $36,000 to $48,000, however, which could strains cash if shop or online customers pay late, and the partnership should monitor this as the $180,000 website investment begins.

Conclusion: CBS's liquidity has improved. Both the broader measure (1.50 to 2.00) and the stricter measure (0.75 to 1.25) show stronger short-term solvency without depending on stock.     Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CBS of switching to sustainable fabric for its swimwear range.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.00%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in fabric input costs will affect CBS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.50% to 4.00%): CBS has no bank loan in the insert — its $180,000 expansion is funded by $90,000 trade credit and $90,000 retained profit — so there is no direct interest charge to recalculate. The effect is indirect: suppliers offering credit may face higher borrowing costs, and the 3.9% growth in seaside tourism spending could slow if households face dearer credit. Because the impact is second-order and the partnership has no loan exposure, this is the least damaging of the three changes.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.23 per hour): The insert states a workforce of 30 but no hours worked or pay rates, so a defensible annual wage total cannot be invented. The appropriate comparison is productivity — 14,000 units ÷ 30 staff = about 467 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is manageable; if the 5.4-day delivery time and 11.2% fabric waste absorb staff time, unit labour cost rises and the $14.00 contribution per unit is squeezed. Training the two staff lacking quality-control skills at $640 each would help protect productivity.

Fabric input-cost inflation (11.3%): The insert does not decompose the $12.00 variable cost, so only a labelled bound is honest: if the entire variable cost rose 11.3%, that adds 11.3% × $12.00 = $1.36 a unit; at 14,000 units this is about $19,040 a year (14,000 × $1.36). Even a partial increase cuts contribution on every unit, and the 11.2% waste rate means some fabric is discarded entirely. The $3 sustainable premium and 57% of customers willing to pay it offer a partial offset, but not enough to remove the threat.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in fabric input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every unit produced and directly erodes the $14.00 contribution that funds the $180,000 expansion, while the interest rise is indirect because CBS has no bank loan, and the wage effect can be mitigated if 467-unit productivity is maintained through training and waste reduction.

--- STEM ---
Vela Vintage Fashion (VVF) is a private limited company in the second-hand fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 25. Founded in 2018 by Priya Vela, the business reconditions and sells vintage clothing through its e-commerce website and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. VVF plans to invest $240,000 in a new photography studio and packing area, financed by $150,000 hire purchase and $90,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $126,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and currently produces 18,000 units a year. VVF faces two problems: damage in transit has reached 3.4% and return requests in its online orders are rising.
