  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VVF is financing part of its $240,000 expansion through $150,000 of hire purchase. Explain two advantages for VVF of using hire purchase rather than a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $150,000 cost of the photography studio and packing equipment into regular instalments, so VVF does not need the full sum upfront and can keep the $90,000 retained profit as working capital. That preserves cash against fixed costs of $126,000 a year while the business deals with 3.4% damage in transit and 12.6% return requests.

Point 2: The asset is used immediately while it is being paid for, so the studio can start producing the detailed photographs that 63% of surveyed vintage shoppers trust, supporting sales of 18,000 units. Unlike a bank loan, hire purchase does not require a separate lump-sum deposit or the same level of collateral negotiation, which suits a small 25-staff firm whose founder Priya Vela wants to keep control.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $150,000, $240,000, $126,000, $90,000, retained profit

    Answer: Lifestyle magazine print advertising: Print can showcase high-quality photographs of the vintage collection and reach readers interested in style, giving a credible, tangible impression. However, magazines have long lead times, high upfront costs and no direct link to the e-commerce website, so conversion cannot be measured. For a 25-staff firm funding a $240,000 studio with $126,000 fixed costs, untrackable print spend is hard to justify.

Social-media influencer marketing: The insert shows 74% of vintage shoppers worry about item condition and 63% trust detailed photographs. Influencers can demonstrate condition and styling honestly, link directly to the e-commerce site, and provide measurable engagement at low cost. They reach a national audience that a local event cannot, though results depend on choosing credible, style-matched partners and may build more slowly than a one-off event.

Recommendation: VVF should choose social-media influencer marketing. It addresses the exact concerns in the survey, drives measurable traffic to the website and scales nationally at a fraction of print or event costs. Magazine advertising is rejected as slow and unmeasurable, and fashion-event sponsorship is rejected as expensive and geographically limited for an online business with $126,000 fixed costs. VVF should pair influencers with the new studio photographs rather than either rejected option.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to VVF. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to VVF with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to VVF with a justified recommendation explaining why print and event sponsorship are rejected.

--- STEM ---
Quarry Lane E-Commerce (QLE) is a cooperative based in Leeds in the online fashion marketplace sector, employing a workforce of 40. Led by Marcus Bell, the business connects independent designers with shoppers through its own website and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. QLE plans to invest $320,000 in a cloud stock-control and packing hub, financed by a $200,000 bank loan and a $120,000 member share issue. It has fixed costs of $160,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $32.00, and currently produces 20,000 units a year. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QLE is funding part of its $320,000 expansion with a $120,000 member share issue. Explain two advantages for QLE of using a share issue rather than a larger bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Member shares bring in $120,000 with no interest or fixed repayment, so QLE can keep the $200,000 bank loan smaller and protect cash against fixed costs of $160,000 a year. That matters while packing errors run at 2.6% and late deliveries still reach 28 a month, because funds are not diverted to debt service when they are needed to improve service.

Point 2: Equity is permanent capital with no repossession risk, so the cloud stock-control and packing hub is secure even if the marketplace grows more slowly than expected. As a cooperative, a member share issue also spreads ownership among the people involved in the business, reinforcing the democratic structure and avoiding a lender's conditions that might restrict how Marcus Bell and the members run the platform.
    Keywords: share issue, $120,000, bank loan, $200,000, $320,000, cooperative
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to QLE's share issue, bank loan and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QLE is promoting its marketplace to new shoppers. Consider online display advertising, sponsorship of a design fair, or social-media influencer marketing. Which should QLE choose to promote the platform? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Online display advertising: Banner and paid display ads can generate large volumes of impressions quickly and can be targeted by interest, driving traffic to the marketplace. However, display ads are often ignored and click-through rates are low, so much of the spend is wasted. Design fair sponsorship: Sponsoring a fair puts QLE in front of independent designers and fashion buyers, helping recruit sellers as well as shoppers and building credibility. It is a focused but geographically limited and short-lived channel; the costs of a stand and sponsorship can be high, and attendees may already be designers rather than the 73% of shoppers who value fast, reliable delivery that the platform needs to reach.

Social-media influencer marketing: The insert shows 73% of surveyed marketplace shoppers value fast, reliable delivery and 59% compare seller ratings before buying. Influencers can demonstrate reliable dispatch and explain seller ratings, link directly to the website and provide measurable engagement at modest cost. They reach a national audience beyond a single fair, though results depend on selecting credible, fashion-relevant partners.

    Keywords: e-commerce, $320,000, 20,000, 73%, 59%, workforce of 40
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to QLE. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to QLE with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to QLE with a justified recommendation explaining why display ads and design fair sponsorship are rejected.

    Question: QLE has a flat structure with democratic leadership and packing errors of 2.6%. Explain two benefits for QLE of this leadership style in the new packing hub.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 40 members to suggest improvements to packing routines, so practical ideas for cutting the 2.6% error rate and the 4.6-day dispatch time come from the people doing the work. A flat structure means these suggestions reach Marcus Bell quickly without passing through many management layers, speeding up problem-solving.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QLE's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has QLE's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.20 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $72,000 inventories + $36,000 trade receivables + $27,000 cash = $135,000; 2025 current assets = $60,000 + $54,000 + $36,000 = $150,000.     Answer: Interest rate rise (3.25% to 3.90%): If QLE's $200,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost increases by 0.65% of $200,000 = $1,300 a year (0.0065 × $200,000). Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $14.03 per hour): The insert gives 40 staff but no hours worked or pay rates, so a defensible annual wage bill cannot be invented. Conclusion: The 6.6% rise in packing and cloud-storage input costs will have the greatest impact. --- STEM ---
Harborview Hotel Group (HHG) is a private limited company in the hospitality and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2001 by Elena Vasquez, it runs a chain of coastal boutique hotels and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. HHG plans to invest $900,000 in refurbishing its flagship property with energy-efficient systems, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,200,000 a year, a variable cost of $60 per room-night and a selling price of $180 per room-night, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. HHG faces two problems: guest complaints about room cleanliness are rising and annual staff turnover has reached 18%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HHG plans to finance part of its $900,000 refurbishment with retained profit. Explain two advantages for HHG of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit of $300,000 requires no interest payments or capital repayment, so HHG avoids adding to the interest burden created by its $600,000 ten-year bank loan at a time when the base rate has risen to 5.0%. The cash saved can help absorb the 9.2% rise in energy and linen costs and protect the $120 contribution per room-night without raising the $180 selling price, which matters because surveyed guests are already sensitive to price and cleanliness. Every dollar of interest avoided improves the operating profit available to tackle the 18% staff-turnover problem.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps control with the existing owners, since no lender can impose conditions on how the flagship hotel is refurbished or how the 60-strong workforce is organised. It also avoids the repossession risk that would put HHG's $3,800,000 of non-current assets at stake if refurbished rooms failed to lift the 71% occupancy rate. Because the money is already inside the business, the energy-efficient refurbishment can start immediately rather than waiting for loan approval.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $600,000, $900,000, 5.0%, 9.2%, energy and linen
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to HHG's refurbishment, costs and financing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HHG is choosing how to promote its refurbished flagship hotel. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HHG choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A national TV campaign would build awareness of the refurbished rooms across the country and could attract inbound tourists, which matters as tourism spending grows. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a business carrying a $600,000 bank loan and $1,200,000 fixed costs, and most viewers will never book a coastal boutique hotel, so much of the spend is wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is far cheaper and reaches the domestic market that makes up much of HHG's 71% occupancy, and it can carry a time-limited refurbishment message. Its weakness is narrow reach: it cannot reach the 68% of 500 surveyed guests who would pay $15 more if they live outside the broadcast area, so it cannot fill 40,000 room-nights by itself.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and lifestyle influencers can show the energy-efficient refurbished rooms directly to the 68% of surveyed guests willing to pay $15 more and the 55% who choose on cleanliness reviews. It is measurable, much cheaper than television, and its reach is national, though results build slowly and depend on influencer credibility.

Recommendation: HHG should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets precisely the segment the survey identified, costs far less than television, and reaches beyond radio's local catchment while reinforcing the cleanliness message needed to cut the 47 monthly complaints. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted given the $900,000 refurbishment and loan commitments; radio is rejected as too narrow to lift occupancy back toward the 78% level of a year earlier.
    Keywords: $900,000, $600,000, 68%, $15, 55%, 40,000, 71%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to HHG. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in HHG's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in HHG's context with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HHG's cleanliness complaints have risen to 47 per month and staff turnover is 18%. Explain two benefits for HHG of introducing team working among its housekeeping staff.
    Answer: Point 1: Team working lets housekeeping staff share a common cleaning checklist for the refurbished rooms, so the 47 monthly complaints can be tackled collectively rather than by isolated individuals. Under a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership, formal teams give staff a route to report pinch points and standardise room preparation, improving the guest experience that drives the 55% of surveyed guests who choose a hotel on cleanliness reviews. Teams also spread the workload when occupancy is high, so the 71% occupancy rate does not lead to rushed cleaning.

Experienced room attendants can coach new recruits on the new energy-efficient systems, cutting the induction burden on the 60-strong workforce and protecting the 40,000 room-nights target while the flagship property is being refurbished. Because the $900,000 refurbishment changes room layouts, teams can share the updated checklist quickly, cutting the time new recruits take to reach the required standard.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to HHG's complaints, turnover and workforce.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HHG must reduce its 18% housekeeping staff turnover. Consider paying a financial bonus or introducing job enrichment. Which should HHG choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Financial bonus: A cash bonus tied to cleanliness scores would directly reward staff for cutting the 47 monthly complaints, and because it is a variable payment it need not permanently raise the $1,200,000 fixed costs. It uses little cash, but it consumes management time, may be resisted in a hierarchical/autocratic culture, and works gradually.

Decision: HHG should choose job enrichment, adding a small bonus only after complaints fall. Job enrichment tackles the 18% turnover directly, costs little while loan repayments and the refurbishment absorb cash, and suits a 60-strong workforce. A large universal bonus is rejected because it raises costs during a 5.5% wage rise and treats symptoms only, whereas the 47 complaints need genuine ownership. A bonus would also need a fair cleanliness measure, which the current 47 complaints show is inconsistent. --- STEM ---
Redpine Ski Resorts (RSR) is a public limited company in the tourism and leisure sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 1994 by Anika Berg, it operates three alpine ski lodges and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership. RSR plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new high-speed cable car, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 from a share issue. It has fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year, a variable cost of $90 per visitor-day and a selling price of $240 per visitor-day, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. RSR faces two problems: lift downtime is rising and ski-equipment defect rates have climbed to 3.4%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RSR plans to fund part of its $1,200,000 cable car through a share issue. Explain two advantages for RSR of using this share issue rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: The $500,000 raised from a share issue does not have to be repaid and carries no mandatory interest, unlike the $700,000 ten-year bank loan whose cost rises with the base rate now at 5.25%. This strengthens RSR's cash flow while it already carries $1,500,000 fixed costs, so more of the $150 contribution per visitor-day can be spent on cutting the 14 hours of monthly lift downtime rather than on debt service.

Point 2: Equity widens RSR's shareholder base without putting its $5,600,000 of non-current assets at risk of repossession if the new cable car fails to attract the 61% of surveyed visitors who would pay $20 more for reliability. As a public limited company, RSR can access many investors, and the fresh capital also improves the equity cushion shown in its financial position, making future borrowing for the lodges easier. Existing shareholders dilute their control, but the democratic leadership style can manage that trade-off.
    Keywords: share issue, $500,000, $700,000, $1,200,000, 5.25%, democratic
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to RSR's financing and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RSR wants to attract skiers to its new cable car. Consider sponsoring a national ski champion, targeted email marketing to past guests, or winter sports magazine advertising. Which should RSR choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Sponsoring a national ski champion: Association with a champion would build credibility and excitement around the high-speed cable car and reach the winter-sports community quickly. It is expensive, however, and the endorsement lasts only while the athlete stays prominent; for a business servicing a $700,000 loan and spending $1,200,000 on the cable car, the fee could be hard to justify, and it does not directly target past guests who already know RSR's three lodges.

Targeted email marketing: Emailing the past guests who make up much of the 12,400 visitor-days is cheap, measurable and personal, and can promote the 61% of surveyed visitors willing to pay $20 more for reliability. Its limit is reach: it cannot attract new skiers beyond the existing database, so it cannot by itself lift the 45,000 visitor-day target or counter the 49% who rebook only when queues are short.

Winter sports magazine advertising: Print adverts reach committed skiers across the country and suit a premium, reliability-focused message. Yet readership is falling, the lead time is long, and there is no measurable response, which is a problem when lift downtime is already 14 hours a month and guests must be convinced quickly.

Recommendation: RSR should choose targeted email marketing, supported by small social posts. It is low-cost, precisely reaches the guests behind 45,000 visitor-days, and can highlight the new cable car to the 61% who value reliability. Champion sponsorship is rejected as costly and transient given the $700,000 loan; magazine advertising is rejected as slow and unmeasurable compared with the 5.2% growth in inbound tourism.
    Keywords: $20, 61%, 49%, 45,000, $1,200,000, 5.2%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to RSR. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in RSR's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in RSR's context with a justified recommendation explaining why the other two are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RSR's lift downtime is rising and equipment defects have reached 3.4%. Explain two benefits for RSR of its democratic leadership style in addressing these problems.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 85 employees, especially lift technicians, to share ideas about why downtime averages 14 hours a month. In a flat structure, their practical suggestions can be acted on quickly, reducing breakdowns and helping deliver the 61% of surveyed visitors who would pay $20 more for guaranteed lift reliability, while protecting the 12,400 visitor-days recorded last winter. Fewer breakdowns also protect the $240 price because fewer refunds are needed.

Point 2: Consulting staff about the 3.4% ski-equipment defect rate gives them ownership of quality checks, so faults are reported early rather than hidden. Greater involvement raises motivation and commitment, which can reduce the 52 monthly complaint cards and lower the $700-per-employee retraining cost on the new cable-car system, as experienced technicians pass on their knowledge willingly. With 85 staff across three lodges, that local ownership reduces the need for head-office intervention. Reliable lifts also support the 5.2% growth in inbound tourism that RSR is trying to capture.
    Keywords: 3.4%, 14 hours, democratic leadership, 12,400, $700, 52
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to RSR downtime, defects and staff.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RSR must upskill technicians to maintain the new cable car. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should RSR choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Learning beside the existing lifts is directly relevant to RSR's own equipment and keeps technicians productive, which helps cut the 14 hours of monthly downtime and the 3.4% defect rate without losing operating days. It costs no course fees and suits the flat structure. However, trainers pass on their own habits, formal certification is limited, and a safety-critical cable car may require documented qualifications that on-the-job coaching cannot provide.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $700 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for the technicians, which matters for a public limited company operating a new high-speed cable car. It also brings outside expertise on fault diagnosis that can tackle the 52 monthly complaints. The costs include fees and time away from the lifts, and the generic content may not cover RSR's exact machines, so follow-up coaching is still needed, and 14 hours of monthly downtime is costly in lost visitor-days, so training speed matters.

--- STEM ---
Suncoast Travel Tours (STT) is a partnership in the travel and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2011 by Marcus Hale, it sells coastal coach holidays to regional travellers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. STT plans to invest $450,000 in a fleet of newer coaches, financed by hire purchase and $150,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $200 per tour package and a selling price of $320 per tour package, and currently produces 30,000 units a year. STT faces two problems: coach breakdowns have cancelled tours and complaints about late documentation have risen sharply, threatening repeat bookings.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: STT is acquiring its $450,000 coach fleet. Explain two advantages for STT of using hire purchase instead of a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $450,000 cost into regular instalments, so STT does not need the full sum upfront and can preserve cash for the $600,000 fixed costs and the 6 days currently needed to send documents. Because the loan is secured on the coaches themselves, the lender has less need for other collateral, protecting the partnership's other assets while the new fleet cuts the 4.6% cancellation rate.

Point 2: STT gains use of the newer coaches immediately and can start winning the 72% of surveyed clients who prefer an operator with newer vehicles, generating the $320 per tour needed to meet instalments. This is valuable while the base rate has risen to 5.5% and domestic holiday spending is up only 3.8%, since hire-purchase payments are fixed and easier to budget than a variable-rate bank loan, so the 72% of clients who prefer newer coaches can be won without taking on more debt.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $450,000, $600,000, $320, 5.5%, 4.6%, 3.8%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to STT's fleet decision and finances.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: STT wants to promote its newer coach holidays. Consider bus-stop posters, partnerships with travel agents, or short video adverts on social media. Which should STT choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Bus-stop posters: Posters are cheap and can be placed in coastal towns near STT's routes, giving repeated local exposure. However, they cannot show the comfort of the new coaches, reach is limited to passers-by, and there is no way to measure bookings, which is a problem when 4.6% of tours are already cancelled and the $450,000 fleet must be filled.

Partnerships with travel agents: Agents already meet holidaymakers at the moment they book and can recommend STT's newer coaches to the 72% of 400 surveyed clients who prefer modern vehicles, while explaining the flexible booking valued by 58%. Commission is paid only on sales, so cost is linked to revenue, which suits a partnership with $600,000 fixed costs. The drawback is that agents take a share of the $320 price and may favour larger competitors.

Short video adverts on social media: Video can show the new coaches and flexible booking to a wide audience at modest cost and can be tracked. Yet results depend on algorithms and constant content, and viewers outside the coastal market may never buy a package, so spend can be wasted.

Recommendation: STT should choose travel-agent partnerships. They reach buyers at the point of purchase, convert the 72% preference for newer coaches into bookings, and keep costs tied to sales, unlike untargeted posters or unmeasurable video ads. Posters are rejected for narrow, unmeasurable reach and video advertising for uncertain conversion; agent commission is affordable against the $320 price and the 3.8% growth in domestic holidays, and agent feedback can guide service improvements.
    Keywords: 72%, 58%, 7,200, 4.6%, $320, $450,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to STT. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in STT's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in STT's context with a justified recommendation explaining why posters and video adverts are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: STT's coach cancellations have reached 4.6% and complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for STT of its laissez-faire leadership style.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives STT's 40 experienced drivers freedom to choose the quickest routes and to arrange replacements when a coach breaks down, which can reduce the 4.6% cancellation rate without waiting for head-office approval. In a flat structure this speeds decisions and helps deliver the 7,200 package tours sold last quarter on time, protecting the $320 revenue per package.

Point 2: Trusting capable drivers to solve problems raises their motivation and ownership of service quality, which can cut the 34 monthly complaints about documents because drivers can chase paperwork locally. Autonomy also reduces the need for supervisors, saving on the $380-per-employee retraining budget and letting STT focus resources on the $450,000 coach fleet. In a 40-person partnership, autonomy also cuts supervision costs and lets drivers work to the 2-day document target locally; the flat structure keeps decisions close to the action. That protects the 58% of clients who value flexible booking and depend on timely confirmations.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: STT must prepare new drivers for the coach fleet. Consider formal induction training or on-the-job training. Which should STT choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Formal induction training: A structured induction explains STT's booking system, safety procedures and the 2-day document target, which directly addresses the 6 days currently taken to send confirmations and the 34 monthly complaints; consistent paperwork would also appeal to the 72% of clients who want professionally run operators. It gives every driver the same standards and a record of competence. The induction fixes the document delays and sets consistent safety standards, which protects the $450,000 fleet investment, while route coaching keeps the training practical. Pure on-the-job training is rejected because it would leave the 6-day documentation problem and the 34 complaints unsolved, even though it is cheaper and less disruptive. Formal induction sets the standard the $450,000 fleet deserves, and with 6.7% wage inflation a well-trained driver is cheaper than repeated mistakes. --- STEM ---
Golden Gate Leisure (GGL) is a private limited company in the leisure and entertainment sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1988 by Priya Raman, it runs an indoor entertainment complex with arcades and a food court, and combines democratic leadership with a hierarchical structure. With $1,800,000 fixed costs and a food-waste rate of 7.8%, avoiding interest protects the $60 contribution per guest visit and leaves more cash to tackle the 63 monthly cleanliness complaints without raising the $95 price. With 63 complaints a month, protecting quality spending matters more than avoiding interest.

Point 2: Internal funding keeps decision-making with the existing owners and avoids pledging GGL's $4,700,000 of non-current assets as loan collateral. It is also quick: the new dining floor can open without waiting for lender approval, which matters while consumer spending on leisure grows only 2.9% and food and beverage inputs cost 10.1% more — early opening captures demand before conditions tighten further, helping GGL take a share of the limited 2.9% growth in leisure spending.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.49 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.61 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $300,000 inventories + $200,000 trade receivables + $100,000 cash = $600,000; 2025 current assets = $360,000 + $170,000 + $80,000 = $610,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $600,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.50; 2025 = $610,000 ÷ $410,000 = 1.49. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($600,000 − $300,000) ÷ $400,000 = $300,000 ÷ $400,000 = 0.75; 2025 = ($610,000 − $360,000) ÷ $410,000 = $250,000 ÷ $410,000 = 0.61.

Evaluation: Liquidity has deteriorated, especially on the stricter measure. Current assets rose only from $600,000 to $610,000 while current liabilities increased from $400,000 to $410,000, leaving short-term cover almost unchanged and slightly lower. More seriously, inventories grew from $300,000 to $360,000 and cash fell from $100,000 to $80,000, so the business holds more stock and less money; excluding that stock, near-term cover fell from 0.75 to 0.61. Trade receivables did fall from $200,000 to $170,000, which helps, but not enough to offset the weaker cash and higher liabilities while GGL plans to spend $1,500,000 and owes $900,000 on loan with only $80,000 in cash.

Conclusion: GGL's financial position has not improved. Both measures fell, and the sharper fall in the stricter ratio shows the business is more dependent on selling inventories to meet short-term debts. GGL should reduce stock and rebuild cash before drawing further on debt for the new floor.
    Keywords: 1.50, 1.49, 0.75, 0.61, $600,000, $610,000, $1,500,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on GGL's financial position.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GGL of introducing a waste-reduction programme in its food court.

Disadvantage: Introducing recycling and training 120 staff costs $320 per employee and management time, adding to $1,800,000 fixed costs while a $900,000 loan is outstanding. With $1,800,000 fixed costs already high, payback may be slow, and if waste falls only gradually from 7.8% the 53% who value it may barely notice.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 10.1% rise in food and beverage input costs will affect GGL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If GGL's $900,000 loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.75% × $900,000 = $6,750 a year, which is small against $1,800,000 fixed costs; a fixed-rate loan would see no direct change. Higher rates may also make the $1,500,000 floor harder to finance and discourage the 2.9% growth in leisure spending, but fixing the rate limits this.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.12 per hour): With a workforce of 120, wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. No hours or individual pay are given, so a defensible annual wage total cannot be invented; the test is productivity — 55,000 guest visits ÷ 120 staff = about 458 visits per employee. If the new dining floor lifts visits, the extra pay is absorbed; if complaints and 7.8% waste persist, the $60 contribution per visit is squeezed.

Food and beverage costs (+10.1%): These feed the $35 variable cost per guest visit. As an illustrative upper bound, if the whole $35 rose 10.1% that is $3.54 per visit (10.1% × $35), or roughly $194,000 a year at 55,000 visits. Even a partial rise cuts the $60 contribution, and the $8 premium wanted by 66% of guests offsets only part of it, especially with only 2.9% leisure-spending growth.

Conclusion: The 10.1% rise in food and beverage costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every guest visit and directly erodes the $60 contribution that must cover $1,800,000 fixed costs and the $900,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is small and fixable and the wage effect depends on productivity from the new floor.

--- STEM ---
Bluewater Cruises (BWC) is a cooperative in the tourism and leisure sector, employing a workforce of 95. Founded in 2007 by Sofia Marino, it operates river cruises on scenic routes through the valley and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership among its member-crew. BWC plans to invest $2,000,000 in a new passenger vessel, financed by member share subscriptions and a $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan. It has fixed costs of $2,700,000 a year, a variable cost of $270 per cruise berth and a selling price of $450 per cruise berth, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. BWC faces two problems: cabin-service complaints are rising and crew absenteeism has reached 11%, disrupting sailings.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BWC is funding its $2,000,000 vessel partly through member share subscriptions. Explain two advantages for BWC of this source of finance rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Member share subscriptions bring in ownership money that does not require interest or repayment, unlike the $1,200,000 bank loan whose cost rises with the base rate now at 5.0%. As a cooperative, BWC can draw on its member-crew and community, keeping more of the $180 contribution per berth to meet $2,700,000 fixed costs instead of paying a lender while marine fuel costs rise 12.6%; tackling the 49 cabin complaints also needs cash that interest would otherwise absorb.

Point 2: Member ownership strengthens commitment to the cooperative and gives members a voice in how the new vessel is run, which supports the flat structure and democratic leadership. It also avoids pledging BWC's $7,200,000 of non-current assets as collateral, so a downturn in the 4.4% growth of cruise bookings would not put the vessel at risk of repossession as it would with loan finance, and members are more likely to back a vessel they have helped fund.
    Keywords: member share subscriptions, $2,000,000, $1,200,000, 5.0%, 12.6%, cooperative
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to BWC's financing and cooperative structure.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BWC wants to fill berths on its new vessel. Consider river-port leaflets, email campaigns to past passengers, or short video adverts on social media. Which should BWC choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: River-port leaflets: Leaflets handed out at ports are cheap and reach people already near the departure points. However, their reach is tiny compared with the 40,000 berths BWC must sell, they cannot show the new vessel, and response cannot be measured, which is a problem when the $2,000,000 vessel must be covered.

Email campaigns to past passengers: Emailing previous guests is low-cost and can offer repeat bookers the $450 berth directly, using the database behind 9,600 passenger-berths last quarter. It is measurable and personal. Its weakness is reach: it cannot attract the 70% of 650 surveyed passengers willing to pay $25 more for a newer vessel if they have never cruised with BWC, so it cannot expand demand much beyond 4.4% growth.

Short video adverts on social media: Video can show the newer vessel and the cleanliness that 57% of passengers rank first, reaching far beyond past guests at controlled cost, with click-through tracking. The risk is that views do not convert into bookings and constant content is needed, so early spend may be slow to pay back.

Recommendation: BWC should choose short video adverts on social media. They showcase the newer vessel to the 70% who would pay $25 more and the 57% who prioritise cleanliness, reaching new passengers that emails miss. Leaflets are rejected for negligible, unmeasurable reach and emails for failing to attract new cruisers; video gives the scale needed to fill 40,000 berths against the $1,200,000 loan, and the adverts can be changed quickly if the 4.4% booking growth stalls.
    Keywords: 70%, $25, 57%, 9,600, $2,000,000, 4.4%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to BWC. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in BWC's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in BWC's context with a justified recommendation explaining why leaflets and emails are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: BWC's cabin-service complaints have risen to 49 a month and absenteeism is 11%. Explain two benefits for BWC of its democratic leadership style.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 95 crew to suggest how to cut the 49 monthly cabin-service complaints, and because the structure is flat their ideas about boarding and cabin checks can be tried quickly. Member-crew who help set standards are more likely to meet the 57% of surveyed passengers who rank cleanliness first, protecting the 9,600 berths sailed last quarter; fewer complaints also protect the 70% who would pay $25 more for a newer vessel.

Point 2: Giving the crew a real voice raises commitment and can reduce the 11% absenteeism that disrupts cabin service and lengthens the 35-minute boarding time. Higher involvement also makes the $520-per-employee service training more effective, as members apply ideas themselves rather than obeying instructions, which suits a cooperative with shared ownership. The 9,600 berths sailed last quarter depend on reliable crews, so cutting 11% absence matters, and in a cooperative members have a direct stake in that reputation.
    Keywords: 11%, 49, democratic, 95, $520, 9,600
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to BWC's complaints, absence and crew.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: BWC must improve cabin service. Consider job enrichment or team working for the cabin crew. Which should BWC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Job enrichment: Giving each crew member responsibility for a whole cabin area, with a say in cleanliness checks, makes the work more meaningful and can raise the standards wanted by 57% of surveyed passengers. It suits the cooperative's democratic leadership and may reduce the 11% absenteeism. However, it depends on motivated individuals, takes time to design, and one weak member could leave the 49 monthly complaints unresolved on their section, although the 35-minute boarding time could improve if crew members take charge of their own area.

Team working: Organising cabin crews into teams with shared checklists lets members cover for the 11% absenteeism, standardise service across the vessel and jointly tackle the 49 complaints. Teams support the flat structure and allow experienced crew to coach newcomers on the new vessel, making the $520 training stick; teams can also rotate tasks when the 2.9% fitting defects create extra cleaning work. The risks are group conflict, slower decisions and blurred responsibility if no team leader is clear.

Decision: BWC should choose team working, adding elements of job enrichment within each team. Teams directly cover absences and raise consistent standards on the $2,000,000 vessel, while the 6.2% wage rise makes paid individual enrichment harder to afford. Job enrichment alone is rejected because it cannot shield service when 11% of crew are absent, whereas teams redistribute work and protect the 40,000-berth target. With $2,700,000 fixed costs to cover and 6.2% wage inflation, this is a low-cost way to raise standards. Stronger service also protects the 70% who would pay $25 more.

--- STEM ---
Trailmark Northern Logistics (TNL) is a private limited company in the road freight and parcel logistics sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Freya Marsh, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TNL plans to invest $720,000 in a fleet of GPS-tracked electric delivery vans and a depot charging hub, financed by a $450,000 five-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8 a unit and a selling price of $20, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. TNL also faces driver absenteeism of 8% and a rising parcel-damage rate at the depot, and aims to cut delivery emissions while protecting its supermarket contracts.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TNL is funding part of its electric-van expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TNL of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or fixed repayments, so TNL keeps the cash that would otherwise service the $450,000 five-year bank loan. That cash can absorb fixed costs of $300,000 a year and fund the running of the new $720,000 electric-van fleet while driver absenteeism of 8% is still lifting costs. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on the depot charging hub or on reducing the 2.4% parcel-damage rate, helping TNL protect its supermarket contracts without raising the $20 selling price.

Point 2: Using $270,000 retained profit leaves control with Freya Marsh's management team instead of a lender, so no bank can impose conditions on how the GPS-tracked vans or the charging hub are operated. It also avoids pledging company assets when the 8% absenteeism and 2.4% damage rate still need attention, giving the 60-strong workforce room to stabilise service before taking on more debt. The survey evidence that 68% of clients value GPS tracking and 55% would pay $1.50 more shows where internally saved cash can be reinvested, rather than being paid to a bank as interest that competes directly with the $300,000 fixed costs and the cost of the fleet expansion.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $270,000, $450,000, $720,000, $300,000, 8%, TNL
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to TNL and its financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TNL is promoting its new low-emission van fleet. Consider a national television campaign, regional radio sponsorship, or targeted social media and van-livery promotion. Which should TNL choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A TV advert would build awareness of TNL's low-emission van fleet across the whole country very quickly, which could help win new supermarket contracts. However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 60-employee logistics firm already servicing a $450,000 loan and investing $720,000, and most viewers do not buy freight or parcel services. Much of the spend would be wasted, and television cannot demonstrate the GPS tracking that 68% of surveyed clients value.

Regional radio sponsorship: Sponsorship of local radio is much cheaper and reaches TNL's regional catchment where its 15,000 quarterly parcels are collected, so it suits a time-sensitive message about a new electric fleet. Its weakness is narrow reach: radio listeners are not necessarily the 450 business clients in the survey, and a 2.4% parcel-damage rate is better addressed by showing service quality than by buying airtime.

Targeted social media and van-livery promotion: Posts aimed at logistics managers, combined with branding on the GPS-tracked vans themselves, reach exactly the buyers who place freight contracts and can demonstrate the tracking and lower emissions. This is low cost per contact, measurable, and reinforces the 55% who would pay $1.50 more for greener delivery; it also lets TNL answer complaints directly and show how the charging hub cuts damage and downtime.

Recommendation: TNL should choose targeted social media and van livery. It reaches the precise decision-makers, costs far less than television, and works nationally unlike local radio. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 60-person operator funding a $450,000 loan; radio is rejected as too narrow for clients spread across supermarket supply chains. Social media lacks television's mass reach, so TNL should support it with a small regional radio top-up during the launch weeks only.
    Keywords: $720,000, $450,000, 450, 68%, 55%, $1.50, 15,000, 2.4%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to TNL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of TNL with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TNL's driver absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for TNL of using autocratic leadership within its hierarchical structure to improve reliability.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Freya Marsh set clear, uniform delivery and vehicle-check procedures for all 60 drivers, so everyone follows the same routine regardless of the 8% absenteeism rate. In a hierarchical structure, instructions pass down a defined chain of command, which reduces confusion when drivers are swapped between routes at short notice and helps hold the 2.4% parcel-damage rate steady.

Point 2: Quick, central decisions speed up responses to problems on the new $720,000 electric-van fleet: managers can immediately reassign routes or order a replacement van when charging or breakdown issues arise, protecting the 15,000 quarterly parcels and the 2.6-day fulfilment target. Clear expectations also make it easier to identify who needs the $750 certification course, so the 18 uncertified drivers are trained in a controlled way. This decisiveness suits an operation servicing a $450,000 loan, where delay costs money; the 68% of clients valuing GPS tracking can be assured that standards are enforced consistently. Autocratic leadership is most effective here because the work is rule-based and time-critical, allowing TNL to stabilise reliability before considering more participative methods.
    Keywords: autocratic leadership, hierarchical structure, 8%, workforce of 60, 2.4%, $750, 60,000 units, TNL
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TNL's absenteeism, damage rate and fleet investment.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TNL wants to cut its 8% absenteeism and 2.4% parcel-damage rate. Consider a performance-related bonus or job enrichment through team working. Which should TNL choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Performance-related bonus: Paying drivers for low damage and full attendance could motivate the 60 staff to reduce the 8% absenteeism rate and the 2.4% parcel-damage rate, and it is easy to measure against the 15,000 quarterly parcels. However, the insert gives no bonus cost, so its expense cannot be quantified; it would add to fixed costs of $300,000 a year at a time when TNL is servicing a $450,000 loan and funding a $720,000 fleet. A bonus also rewards outcomes after the event and does not change the routine that causes damage.

Job enrichment through team working: Giving drivers varied routes, shared responsibility for vehicle checks and a say in depot layout makes the work less repetitive and uses their local knowledge, which can cut the 2.4% damage rate at source. Team checks can also spot the faults behind the 34 monthly complaints, and shared ownership can reduce the 8% absenteeism by raising commitment. The drawback is the time needed to organise teams in a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership, and results may be slower than a bonus.

Decision: TNL should choose job enrichment through team working. It addresses the causes of absenteeism and damage rather than paying around them, costs little compared with a bonus, and fits the 18 drivers needing $750 certification by pairing them with experienced colleagues. The bonus is rejected as an expensive short-term payment whose size is unstated and which does not change working methods, though a small bonus could be added later once teams are established. With no stated bonus rate, the comparison is qualitative: team working changes how the 60 drivers work, while a bonus only rewards them after damage has occurred.
    Keywords: 8%, 2.4%, $750, 18, $300,000, $720,000, 15,000, TNL
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and job enrichment with limited application to TNL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of TNL. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a well-justified decision covering absenteeism, damage, cost and motivation.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TNL's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin and the profit margin for 2024 and 2025. Has TNL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

The share of revenue left after direct costs rose from 40.0% to 45.0% because revenue grew by 180 while cost of sales rose by only 54, so the electric-fleet operation is becoming more efficient. The share retained as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 1,080 of capital employed improved, which matters because TNL must service a $450,000 loan while funding a $720,000 expansion. The 8% absenteeism and 2.4% damage rate remain risks, but they have not prevented stronger profitability. Interest payable of 24 in 2025 is modest beside operating profit of 189, so financing costs are not eroding the gain.

Conclusion: TNL's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, with revenue growing much faster than cost of sales. Management should use the stronger margins to fund driver certification and damage reduction so that absenteeism does not reverse the improvement.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether TNL improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TNL of introducing GPS-tracked electric vans with a depot charging hub.
    Answer: Advantage: The survey of 450 business clients found that 68% value real-time GPS tracking and 55% would pay $1.50 more for carbon-neutral delivery, so the new vans can win contracts and add contribution above the $8 variable cost per unit. Better tracking also lets managers tackle the 2.4% parcel-damage rate and the 19 remaining monthly complaints, protecting the $20 selling price and the 60,000-unit output.

Disadvantage: The $720,000 fleet and charging hub add to the capital TNL must finance with a $450,000 loan, and charging downtime could reduce the 15,000 parcels handled each quarter if recharging is not managed.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase to $14.60 and the 9.5% rise in diesel and battery costs will affect TNL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If TNL's $450,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% × $450,000 = $3,375 a year, shown as 0.0075 × $450,000. That is small against $300,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may still slow the 4.2% growth in low-emission logistics demand.

Minimum wage increase (5.8% to $14.60 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or current pay, so an annual wage cost cannot be invented. The derived measure is productivity: 60,000 units ÷ 60 workers = 1,000 units per worker. If that holds, the wage rise can be absorbed; if the 8% absenteeism and 2.4% damage rate reduce effective output, unit labour costs rise and the $12 contribution falls. The direction is clear but the size cannot be quantified here.

Input-cost inflation (9.5%): The $8 variable cost is not split into components, so an explicit upper bound is 9.5% × $8 = $0.76 per unit. Across 60,000 units that is 60,000 × $0.76 = $45,600 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution from $12 toward about $11.24 and pushes the break-even output above 25,000 units.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in diesel and battery costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 60,000 units and directly erodes the $12 contribution that must cover $300,000 fixed costs and service the $450,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is about $3,375 and the wage effect is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity. TNL can recover part of it through the $1.50 premium that 55% of clients accept.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 5.8%, $14.60, 9.5%, $8, $450,000, 60,000 units, 4.2%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TNL. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TNL's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.

--- STEM ---
Evernorth Renewable Energy (ENR) is a public limited company in the renewable energy and battery-storage sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2015 by Imogen Kaur, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. ENR plans to invest $960,000 in an automated battery-storage assembly line with robotic cell welding, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and a $360,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $42, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. ENR also faces labour turnover of 12% and a rising defect rate in battery cells, and aims to win more residential storage contracts next year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ENR is funding part of its assembly-line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for ENR of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payments or fixed repayments, so ENR keeps the cash that would otherwise service the $600,000 ten-year bank loan. That cash can cover fixed costs of $420,000 a year and the running of the new $960,000 battery-storage line, giving room to reduce the 3.3% defect rate and the 34 monthly complaints before they damage the 70,000-unit output. Every dollar not paid as interest can be spent on the robotic welders or on training the 22 untrained staff.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps ownership and control with Imogen Kaur's shareholders rather than with a lender, so no bank can impose covenants on how the automated line is run. It also avoids pledging company assets while labour turnover of 12% and a $360,000 share issue already dilute and stretch the business. The survey evidence that 72% of installers value long-life batteries and 61% would pay $3 more shows where internally saved cash can be reinvested, instead of paying interest that competes with the $420,000 fixed costs and the cost of fixing the rising defect rate.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $360,000, $600,000, $960,000, $420,000, 12%, ENR
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to ENR and its financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ENR is launching its automated battery-storage line. Consider an energy-industry trade exhibition, search-engine advertising, or installer-focused social media and training webinars. Which should ENR choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Energy-industry trade exhibition: A stand at a trade exhibition lets ENR demonstrate the new battery line to specialist installers and distributors and build credibility in a technical market. However, stand, travel and staffing costs are high for an 80-employee firm already servicing a $600,000 loan and investing $960,000, and only a limited delegate audience attends, too narrow to support 70,000 units of output. It also does little to address the 3.3% defect rate directly.

Search-engine advertising: Ads shown to people searching for home battery storage reach high-intent buyers and can be tightly budget-controlled, which suits the 72% of surveyed installers who value long-life batteries. The weakness is that text ads cannot demonstrate the faster-charging cells that 61% would pay $3 more for, and cost per click can rise quickly when a $960,000 investment must be justified.

Installer-focused social media and training webinars: Technical posts and live webinars can show the robotic welding process and the improved cell quality to installers directly, answering the 34 monthly complaints about early failures. This is low cost per contact, measurable, and can teach correct installation, which matters because faults may come from the 22 staff still untrained on the welders and from the 12% labour turnover.

Recommendation: ENR should choose installer-focused social media and training webinars. They demonstrate quality, reach the exact buyer and cost far less than a trade stand. The exhibition is rejected as expensive and narrow for a firm servicing a $600,000 loan; search advertising is rejected because it cannot demonstrate a technical product or reduce complaints. Webinars lack exhibition face-to-face contact, so ENR should add a small presence at one regional exhibition once the 3.3% defect rate is under control.
    Keywords: $960,000, $600,000, 520, 72%, 61%, $3, 3,500, 3.3%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to ENR. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of ENR with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the exhibition and search ads are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ENR has labour turnover of 12% and a rising defect rate. Explain two benefits for ENR of using democratic leadership within its flat structure to motivate its production staff.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 80 employees a real voice in how the 3,500 battery units are assembled, so staff can suggest fixes for the rise from 2.0% to 3.3% defects. In a flat structure, their ideas reach Imogen Kaur quickly without passing through several management layers, raising ownership and job satisfaction and helping to reduce the 12% labour turnover that disrupts the automated line.

Point 2: Consulting staff on shift patterns and welder routines uses the practical knowledge of the 22 workers still to be trained on the robotic welders, so training can be scheduled around production and the $1,100 course is better targeted. Involvement also helps tackle the 34 monthly complaints because assemblers who help set quality checks are more likely to catch faulty cells early. With a $960,000 line to run and a $600,000 loan to service, motivation that lowers turnover protects the 70,000-unit output and keeps the 4.5-day installation promise. Democratic leadership suits a skilled workforce whose ideas improve quality, though final quality standards must still be enforced to bring defects down.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, flat structure, 12%, workforce of 80, 3.3%, $1,100, 3,500, ENR
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ENR's turnover, defect rate and training needs.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ENR wants to cut its 12% labour turnover and 3.3% defect rate. Consider a performance-related bonus or job enrichment through team working. Which should ENR choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Performance-related bonus: Linking pay to cell quality or output could motivate the 80 staff to push the defect rate back from 3.3% toward 2.0% and shorten the 4.5-day installation time. The drawback is the time needed to organise teams and the need for clear standards in a flat structure.

Decision: ENR should choose job enrichment through team working. It attacks the 12% turnover at source, can lower the 3.3% defect rate and costs little next to a bonus whose size is unstated. Fairway Road Freight (FRG) is a partnership in the road haulage and freight transport sector, employing a workforce of 40. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $6 a unit and a selling price of $16, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. The share retained as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 850 of capital employed improved, which matters because FRG must service a $300,000 loan while investing $500,000 in new lorries. Interest payable of 20 in 2025 is modest beside operating profit of 153, so financing costs are not undermining the gain. The 7% absenteeism and 31 monthly damage claims remain risks that could reverse the trend if service quality slips.

Conclusion: FRG's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, with revenue growing faster than cost of sales. The partners should use the stronger margins to fund telematics training and vehicle maintenance so that absenteeism and breakdowns do not erase the improvement.
    Keywords: 37.5%, 40.0%, 15.0%, 17.0%, Capital employed, 850, $300,000, 360
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether FRG improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FRG of introducing low-emission articulated lorries with telematics.
    Answer: Advantage: The survey of 300 haulage customers found that 64% value a low-emission fleet and 58% would pay $0.80 more for greener freight, so the new lorries can help FRG win contracts and add contribution above the $6 variable cost per unit. Telematics data can also tackle the 31 monthly damage claims and the fall to 91.5% on-time delivery, protecting the $16 selling price and the 45,000-unit output.

Disadvantage: The $500,000 fleet must be financed alongside a $300,000 loan, and the 14 drivers needing $600 telematics training cannot use the system fully until trained, which is difficult with 7% absenteeism. The insert gives no figure for low-emission fuel, maintenance or charging, so the exact running-cost saving cannot be calculated; only a qualitative judgement is possible. If telematics data is not acted on, the 11,000 quarterly deliveries and 2.8-day delivery promise may not improve, so the benefit depends on management using the information and on the 58% premium being accepted across contracts.
    Keywords: telematics, 64%, 58%, $0.80, $6, $500,000, 91.5%, FRG
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FRG's survey, service quality and costs.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.6%, the 5.4% minimum wage increase to $13.91 and the 10.2% rise in diesel and tyre costs will affect FRG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.8% to 4.6%): If FRG's $300,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.8% × $300,000 = $2,400 a year, shown as 0.008 × $300,000. That is small against $180,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may still slow the 3.3% growth in road-freight volumes.

Minimum wage increase (5.4% to $13.91 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or current pay, so an annual wage cost cannot be invented. The derived measure is productivity: 45,000 units ÷ 40 workers = 1,125 units per worker. If that holds, the wage rise can be absorbed; if the 7% absenteeism and falling 91.5% on-time rate reduce effective output, unit labour costs rise and the $10 contribution falls. The direction is clear but the size cannot be quantified here.

Input-cost inflation (10.2%): The $6 variable cost is not split into components, so an explicit upper bound is 10.2% × $6 = $0.612, about $0.61 per unit. Across 45,000 units that is 45,000 × $0.61 = $27,450 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution from $10 toward about $9.39 and pushes the break-even output above 18,000 units.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in diesel and tyre costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 45,000 units and directly erodes the $10 contribution that must cover $180,000 fixed costs and service the $300,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is about $2,400 and the wage effect is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity. FRG can recover part of it through the $0.80 premium that 58% of customers accept, but breakdowns and downtime already threaten the 91.5% on-time rate.
    Keywords: 4.6%, 5.4%, $13.91, 10.2%, $6, $300,000, 45,000 units, 3.3%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to FRG. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FRG's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.

--- STEM ---
Keystone Haulage Link (KHL) is a cooperative in the freight forwarding and warehouse logistics sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2012 by Priya Nair, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. KHL plans to invest $640,000 in an automated warehouse sorting system with barcode scanners, financed by a $400,000 seven-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $23, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. KHL also faces staff turnover of 11% and a rising parcel mis-sort rate, and aims to improve sorting accuracy and cut complaints from its retail members.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KHL is funding part of its sorting-system expansion with a seven-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KHL of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or fixed repayments, so KHL keeps the cash that would otherwise service the $400,000 seven-year bank loan. That cash can cover fixed costs of $252,000 a year and the running of the new $640,000 sorting system while staff turnover of 11% and a 2.9% mis-sort rate are adding cost. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on scanner training or on reducing the 41 monthly complaints, helping the cooperative keep its retail members without raising the $23 selling price.

Point 2: Using $240,000 retained profit keeps control with the cooperative's members and Priya Nair's team rather than a lender, so no bank can impose conditions on how the barcode scanners are used. It also avoids pledging cooperative assets while the 16 staff still need $820 training and mis-sorts are rising. The survey evidence that 70% of retail clients value next-day sorting and 56% would pay $1.20 more shows where internally saved cash can be reinvested, rather than paid as interest that competes with the $252,000 fixed costs and the cost of the expansion.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $240,000, $400,000, $640,000, $252,000, 11%, KHL
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to KHL and its financing decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KHL is promoting its automated sorting service to retail clients. Consider a national trade exhibition, direct mail to retailers, or targeted social media and member referrals. Which should KHL choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National trade exhibition: A stand at a logistics exhibition could introduce KHL's automated sorting to retailers from many regions and build credibility for the cooperative. However, stand, travel and staffing costs are high for a 55-employee cooperative already servicing a $400,000 loan and investing $640,000, and only a small delegate audience attends, too narrow to support 55,000 units of output. It also does not directly address the 2.9% mis-sort rate.

Direct mail to retailers: Sending details to a targeted list of retail clients can reach the exact firms that buy sorting services and can include proof of guaranteed accuracy, which 56% of the 410 surveyed clients would pay $1.20 more for. The weakness is low response rates and printing and postage costs; a leaflet cannot demonstrate the barcode scanners or explain how the 41 monthly complaints will fall.

Targeted social media and member referrals: Posts aimed at retail logistics managers, combined with referrals from KHL's own cooperative members, reach buyers who already trust the brand and can show the sorting system working. This is low cost per contact and measurable, and it lets KHL demonstrate accuracy improvements that answer the 41 complaints and the 2.2-day dispatch time, while the 70% who value next-day sorting provide a clear message.

Recommendation: KHL should choose targeted social media and member referrals. They reach the precise decision-makers, cost far less than a trade stand and convert trust in the cooperative into new contracts. The exhibition is rejected as costly and broad for a cooperative funding a $400,000 loan; direct mail is rejected as low-response and unable to demonstrate accuracy. Social media lacks the face-to-face credibility of an exhibition, so KHL should add a small presence at one regional event once the mis-sort rate is below control.
    Keywords: $640,000, $400,000, 410, 70%, 56%, $1.20, 13,500, 2.9%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to KHL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of KHL with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the exhibition and direct mail are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KHL has staff turnover of 11% and a rising mis-sort rate. Explain two benefits for KHL of using democratic leadership within its flat structure to motivate its warehouse staff.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 55 employees a voice in how the 13,500 consignments are sorted, so staff can suggest practical fixes for the rise in mis-sorts from 2.1% to 2.9%. In a flat structure their ideas reach Priya Nair directly, raising ownership and job satisfaction and helping to reduce the 11% staff turnover that disrupts the new barcode system.

Point 2: Consulting staff on shift patterns and scanner routines makes the 16 workers still needing training more willing to take the $820 course, because they help shape how it is used. Involvement also helps tackle the 41 monthly complaints, as sorters who help set accuracy checks are more likely to catch errors before dispatch, protecting the 2.2-day turnaround. With a $640,000 system to run and a $400,000 loan to service, motivation that lowers turnover protects the 55,000-unit output and the 70% of clients who value next-day sorting. Democratic leadership suits a cooperative whose members expect to be consulted, though clear accuracy standards must still be enforced to bring mis-sorts down.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, flat structure, 11%, workforce of 55, 2.9%, $820, 13,500, KHL
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KHL's turnover, mis-sort rate and training needs.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KHL wants to cut its 11% staff turnover and 2.9% mis-sort rate. Consider a performance-related bonus or job enrichment through team working. Which should KHL choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Performance-related bonus: Linking pay to sorting accuracy or attendance could motivate the 55 staff to push the mis-sort rate back from 2.9% toward 2.1% and improve the 2.2-day dispatch time. Pairing the 16 untrained staff with experienced colleagues also spreads the $820 training more effectively. The drawback is the time needed to organise teams and agree standards in a flat structure.

Decision: KHL should choose job enrichment through team working. It attacks the 11% turnover at source, can lower the 2.9% mis-sort rate and costs little next to a bonus whose size is unstated. With no stated bonus rate the comparison is qualitative: team working changes the work itself and builds skills, while a bonus only rewards output after the event and competes with $252,000 of fixed costs and the $400,000 loan.     Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and job enrichment with limited application to KHL. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of KHL. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a well-justified decision covering turnover, cost, quality and motivation.

The share of revenue left after direct costs rose from 40.0% to 45.0% because revenue grew by 220 while cost of sales rose by only 66, so the refurbishment service is becoming more efficient despite the 3.7% rework rate. The share retained as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 1,650 of capital employed improved, which matters because WFR must service a $750,000 loan while investing $1,150,000 in the new plant. Interest payable of 42 in 2025 is modest beside operating profit of 297, so financing costs are not undermining the gain. The 10% absenteeism and 38 monthly complaints remain risks that could reverse the trend if quality slips.

Conclusion: WFR's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, with revenue growing much faster than cost of sales. Management should use the stronger margins to fund composite training and quality checks so that absenteeism and defects do not erase the improvement.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether WFR improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WFR of introducing composite repair robotics at its refurbishment plant.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase to $15.89 and the 12.1% rise in composite resin and carbon-fibre costs will affect WFR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.2% to 5.0%): If WFR's $750,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.8% × $750,000 = $6,000 a year, shown as 0.008 × $750,000. Minimum wage increase (5.9% to $15.89 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or current pay, so an annual wage cost cannot be invented. Input-cost inflation (12.1%): The $22 variable cost is not split into components, so an explicit upper bound is 12.1% × $22 = $2.662, about $2.66 per unit. Across 64,000 units that is 64,000 × $2.66 = $170,240 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution from $28 toward about $25.34 and pushes the break-even output above 17,000 units.

Conclusion: The 12.1% rise in composite resin and carbon-fibre costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 64,000 units and directly erodes the $28 contribution that must cover $476,000 fixed costs and service the $750,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is about $6,000 and the wage effect is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity.
