  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: AGN plans to fund part of its shelling-facility expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for AGN of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit costs AGN no interest or capital repayments, protecting the cash flow of a cooperative that already carries fixed costs of $225,000 a year and a variable cost of $4.80 a unit. The $300,000 of retained profit is generated by the grower members themselves, so money that would have gone to the $390,000 bank loan can instead be used to cut the 3.6% reject rate on the new optical sorters or to absorb the 8.7% rise in nut and packaging costs.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps control with the grower members led by Tomas Bergström, since no lender can impose conditions on how the $690,000 shelling and packing facility is run. This matters for a cooperative with democratic leadership where members expect a say in decisions. It also avoids the collateral and default risk of the bank loan: if health-food wholesalers cut orders, the facility cannot be repossessed, and the project can start at once without waiting for loan approval while the 26,400-unit quarterly throughput is maintained.

--- STEM ---
Kelpwave Seaweed Farms (KSF) is a private limited company in the seaweed aquaculture sector, based off the northern Atlantic coast and employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2016 by Fiona O'Donnell, it supplies dried seaweed to health-food manufacturers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. KSF plans to invest $780,000 in a new drying and packaging plant, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.10 a unit and a selling price of $11.60, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. KSF faces a quality problem: the defect rate in dried packs has reached 3.9% and labour turnover is rising.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KSF plans to fund part of its drying-plant expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KSF of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payments or capital repayments, protecting cash flow for a company with fixed costs of $330,000 a year and a variable cost of $6.10 a unit. The $300,000 of retained profit is already inside KSF, so money that would have serviced the $480,000 bank loan can instead be spent on the 3.9% defect rate in dried packs or on absorbing the 10.2% rise in packaging and energy costs while defending the $11.60 selling price.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk of the bank loan, so the $780,000 drying and packaging plant is not exposed to repossession if health-food manufacturers reduce orders. It also preserves the control of founder Fiona O'Donnell and existing shareholders without lender covenants, which suits a hierarchical structure. Because no loan approval is needed, the plant can be commissioned quickly, helping KSF reverse the rise in complaints from 21 to 34 per month and protect the 28,600-unit quarterly run rate.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $480,000, $780,000, $330,000, $6.10
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to KSF and its expansion decision.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KSF is launching a new organic-certified seaweed range. Consider national television advertising, coastal radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should KSF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: TV would create rapid awareness of organic-certified seaweed among consumers nationwide and could support a premium price. However, airtime is extremely costly for a company committing $780,000 to a drying plant and already servicing a $480,000 loan, and most TV viewers are not buyers of dried seaweed for health-food manufacturers, so spend would be heavily wasted. TV also cannot display the organic certification that 66% of surveyed buyers value.

Coastal radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and can reach listeners around the northern Atlantic coast where KSF's brand has local recognition, with frequent low-cost reminders. Its weakness is limited reach: KSF supplies health-food manufacturers beyond the coastal region, and audio cannot show the 51% of buyers who check sustainability claims the certification itself.

Social media influencer marketing: Health and cooking influencers can demonstrate the dried seaweed and organic certification visually to a targeted national audience, with measurable engagement and low cost per lead. Credibility must be managed and results build gradually, but the 66% premium segment and the 51% who check sustainability claims can be reached directly.

Recommendation: KSF should choose social media influencer marketing, with modest coastal radio support for local brand goodwill. It targets the researched segment, costs far less than TV and reaches beyond the local catchment. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted given the $330,000 fixed costs and $480,000 loan; radio alone is rejected as too narrow for supplying health-food manufacturers nationally.
    Keywords: 66%, 51%, $0.55, 380, health-food manufacturers, 28,600
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KSF with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of KSF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KSF's defect rate in dried packs has reached 3.9% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for KSF of using autocratic leadership to enforce food-safety standards.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Fiona O'Donnell impose clear, uniform food-safety rules the moment the defect rate in dried packs reaches 3.9%, which is effective in a hierarchical structure where fast, consistent decisions limit risk. With 17 of 55 staff still untrained on the new dryers, workers need precise instructions rather than discussion, so faulty packs can be isolated before the rate rises from 2.7% to 3.9% further and the $780,000 plant's reputation with health-food manufacturers is protected.

Point 2: Top-down control can also stabilise staffing by setting firm shift rotas and expectations, reducing disruption from rising labour turnover on a line with fixed costs of $330,000 a year. Because the leader allocates tasks directly, trained operators can be redeployed immediately to cover absences, protecting output of 110,000 units and the $11.60 selling price while the $480,000 bank loan is serviced.
    Keywords: autocratic leadership, hierarchical, 3.9%, labour turnover, 55, 17
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KSF's quality, staffing and output.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KSF must upskill 17 staff to operate the new dryers. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the coastal college. Which should KSF choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching the 17 untrained staff beside the new dryers is directly relevant to KSF's own drying standards and costs no course fees, unlike the $1,050 per employee charged by the coastal college. It keeps all 17 workers productive while they learn, protecting the 28,600 units packed last quarter and the food-safety effort behind the 2.7%-to-3.9% defect problem. The drawbacks are that trainers have their own output to maintain and bad habits can spread without formal assessment.

Off-the-job training: The $1,050 per employee college course gives structured teaching and a recognised certificate for all 17 staff, costing $17,850 in total — small against the $780,000 investment. It removes 17 of 55 workers from the line, cutting short-term capacity when the defect rate is deteriorating, and generic content may not match KSF's dryer settings without follow-up coaching.

Decision: KSF should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, adding short college modules later for senior operators. It is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids losing output while quality is fragile; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing $17,850 and 17 of 55 staff would disrupt supply to health-food manufacturers when the $480,000 loan must be serviced.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $1,050, 17, 55, $780,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KSF. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of KSF. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of KSF with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how KSF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 50,000 units vs 110,000 output; the $0.55 organic premium against $330,000 fixed costs; loan servicing on the $480,000 bank loan; and unit cost of $9.10 with labour productivity of 2,000 units per worker.
    Keywords: 60,000, $5.50, $330,000, $11.60, $6.10, $9.10, 2,000
    Mark scheme: working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KSF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KSF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.35 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.10 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $105,000 inventories + $150,000 trade receivables + $42,000 cash = $297,000; 2025 current assets = $84,000 + $168,000 + $63,000 = $315,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $297,000 ÷ $220,000 = 1.35 and 2025 = $315,000 ÷ $210,000 = 1.50. Excluding inventories gives 2024 = ($297,000 − $105,000) ÷ $220,000 = $192,000 ÷ $220,000 = 0.87 and 2025 = ($315,000 − $84,000) ÷ $210,000 = $231,000 ÷ $210,000 = 1.10.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The 2024 figure of 1.35 rose to 1.50 as current liabilities fell from $220,000 to $210,000 and current assets rose to $315,000, helped by cash increasing from $42,000 to $63,000. The inventory-excluding measure improved from 0.87 to 1.10, so KSF is less reliant on selling dried-stock to meet short-term debts while servicing a $480,000 loan and funding a $780,000 plant. There is a caveat: receivables rose from $150,000 to $168,000, so cash could be tied up if health-food manufacturers pay late, and the 3.9% defect rate may leave some stock difficult to sell even though inventories fell to $84,000.

Conclusion: KSF's financial position has improved. Both measures show stronger short-term solvency and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The main residual risk is higher receivables, so credit control should be tightened as the new plant operates.
    Keywords: 1.35, 1.50, 0.87, 1.10, $297,000, $315,000, $780,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether KSF's financial position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KSF of introducing organic certification for its dried seaweed.
    Answer: Advantage: Organic certification addresses the 66% of 380 surveyed buyers who would pay up to $0.55 more, protecting the $5.50 contribution per unit while packaging and energy costs rise 10.2%. It also answers the 51% who check sustainability claims, strengthening KSF's position with health-food manufacturers and the $780,000 drying plant.

Disadvantage: Certification involves inspection and compliance costs that could increase the $6.10 variable cost per unit unless the $0.55 premium is accepted throughout the range. A certification failure or poor harvest could add to the 3.9% defect rate and cut the 28,600 units packed each quarter, while fixed costs of $330,000 continue regardless of output.
    Keywords: 66%, 51%, $0.55, 10.2%, 3.9%, $6.10
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage. | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KSF's research data, costs and expansion.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in packaging and energy costs will affect KSF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): The base rate goes up by 0.75 percentage points. If the $480,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.0075 × $480,000 = $3,600 a year, modest beside fixed costs of $330,000 a year and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates could make consumers cautious about seaweed snacks, but KSF can largely remove the direct cost by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, from $12.00 to $12.77 per hour): This raises the wage bill for a 55-person workforce and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The comparison that can be derived is productivity: 110,000 units ÷ 55 staff = 2,000 units per worker. If that holds the rise is absorbable; if rising labour turnover cuts throughput, unit labour cost rises and the $5.50 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Input cost inflation (10.2% on packaging and energy): The insert does not decompose the $6.10 variable cost, so only a labelled bound is honest: if the entire variable cost rose 10.2%, the addition is 0.102 × $6.10 = $0.62 per unit, and at 110,000 units a year that is about $68,420. This is an upper bound, not a forecast; the real addition depends on the packaging-and-energy share, which is not stated. KSF can recover part through the $0.55 organic premium accepted by 66% of surveyed buyers.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in packaging and energy costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit and attacks the $5.50 contribution that supports the $780,000 plant, whereas the interest effect of $3,600 is small and fixable and the wage effect can be offset if 2,000-units-per-worker productivity holds. Input-cost inflation therefore deserves the strongest response.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 6.4%, 10.2%, $12.77, $480,000, $6.10
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to KSF. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KSF's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of KSF with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Gingerfield Craft Beverages (GCB) is a partnership in the craft soft-drinks sector, based near the Great Lakes and employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2013 by brothers Daniel and Samuel Okafor, it supplies ginger beer to independent retailers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. GCB plans to invest $540,000 in a new bottling and canning line, financed by a $340,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.90 a unit and a selling price of $8.40, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. GCB faces rising waste: 2.8% of cans fail the fill-level check and labour turnover is increasing.

    Question: GCB plans to fund part of its canning-line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for GCB of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.

The $200,000 of retained profit is already in the business, so cash that would have gone to the $340,000 bank loan can be spent on reducing the 2.8% waste rate at the filler or on absorbing the 11.5% rise in ginger, sugar and aluminium can costs without raising the $8.40 selling price.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps decision-making with Daniel and Samuel Okafor, with no lender covenants restricting how the $540,000 bottling and canning line is run — important for a flat structure with democratic leadership. It also avoids the collateral and default risk of the bank loan: if independent retailers cut orders, the equipment cannot be repossessed, and the project can begin immediately without the delay of loan approval while the 23,400-unit quarterly run rate is maintained.

--- STEM ---
Mendip Gasket & Fasteners (MGF) is a private limited company in the industrial components sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Priya Mendip, it supplies precision gaskets and fasteners to commercial vehicle assemblers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MGF plans to invest $720,000 in a new CNC machining cell, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and produces 75,000 units a year. MGF faces two operational problems: the defect rate on machined seals has reached 2.4% and labour turnover is rising among skilled machinists.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MGF plans to fund part of its $720,000 CNC machining cell from retained profit. Explain two advantages for MGF of using retained profit rather than increasing its $450,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no compulsory repayment. MGF must already meet fixed costs of $300,000 a year and service a $450,000 ten-year bank loan, so funding $270,000 of the $720,000 CNC cell internally avoids adding another fixed interest commitment. With the base rate raised to 5.25%, any further variable-rate borrowing would increase costs again, whereas retained profit leaves cash flow free to absorb the rework caused by the 2.4% defect rate on machined seals.

Point 2: Using $270,000 of retained profit keeps control with founder Priya Mendip and avoids the collateral and lender conditions attached to more debt. Because MGF is already committed to a $450,000 loan, a smaller debt burden reduces the risk that a fall in orders from commercial vehicle assemblers leaves the firm unable to meet repayments. Internal funding also shows that the business can support part of its own expansion, which strengthens its position if it seeks finance later.
    Keywords: retained profit, $270,000, $720,000, $450,000, bank loan, $300,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to MGF.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MGF is launching a new alloy fastener range. Consider trade press advertising, an industry exhibition, or direct sales visits to assemblers. Which should MGF choose to win new contracts? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade press advertising: A campaign in a commercial-vehicle engineering magazine would reach assemblers' technical managers nationally at a low cost per reader. However, print cannot demonstrate the dimensional accuracy that 58% of the 400 surveyed buyers rank as the main purchase criterion, and it does nothing to answer concerns about the 6.5-day delivery lead time against a 5-day promise. For a business carrying $300,000 of fixed costs, spending that does not prove tolerances is difficult to justify.

Industry exhibition: A stand would let MGF show machined samples and meet several assemblers in one place, giving technical credibility. Yet stand fees, travel and staff time are expensive, and results depend on who visits. With a workforce of 60, the machinists manning the stand would be away from the CNC cell while the defect rate is already 2.4%, so output of 75,000 units could suffer.

Direct sales visits: An engineer can visit procurement teams with test certificates, answer questions on accuracy and negotiate delivery personally. This directly addresses the 47% of surveyed buyers who would switch supplier after two late deliveries, because MGF can explain how it will shorten the 6.5-day lead time. The cost per contract is higher in travel time, but each buyer approached is already qualified, so conversion is more likely than with print.

Recommendation: MGF should choose direct sales visits. They convert the 58% who buy on accuracy and reassure the 47% at risk from late delivery, which neither print advertising nor a passive exhibition stand achieves as reliably. Trade press is rejected as too indirect and unable to prove tolerances; the exhibition is rejected because its high fixed cost and staffing demands pull scarce machinists away from the $720,000 CNC cell. MGF should follow up visits with brief emails containing dimensional data.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MGF's defect rate on machined seals has reached 2.4% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for MGF of using democratic leadership instead of its current autocratic style.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives MGF's 60 employees a voice in how the new CNC machining cell is organised, tackling the rising labour turnover among skilled machinists. Under the current autocratic style, decisions come from Priya Mendip alone, so the machinists who handle the seals daily have no route to flag problems. Point 2: Consultation produces practical suggestions that an autocratic manager may miss. Machinists closest to the 2.4% defect rate can propose fixture or cutting-speed changes, improving quality without further capital beyond the $720,000 cell. Fewer defects mean less rework and less demand for agency cover at $280 a day, protecting the $300,000 fixed-cost base.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MGF wants to reduce the 2.4% defect rate and the absence among 11 of 60 machinists. Consider a productivity bonus or team working. Which should MGF choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Productivity bonus: Paying machinists for output above a target would raise effort and could spread the $300,000 fixed costs over more of the 75,000 units. It is easy to understand and links pay to results. However, a volume-based bonus rewards speed at precisely the wrong time: the defect rate on machined seals is already 2.4%, and 58% of surveyed buyers rank dimensional accuracy first, so faster working could create more rejected parts and more returns, undoing the benefit of extra output.

Team working: Organising machinists into small teams responsible for a whole batch means members check one another's work, so defects are caught before parts leave the cell. Teams can rotate tasks, reducing the boredom behind 11 of 60 workers taking more than ten days of unplanned leave, and peer support eases the pressure that drives labour turnover. This uses the skilled staff MGF already employs, avoiding further agency cover at $280 a day while the $720,000 cell beds in. The weaknesses are that group norms can shield slow members and that targets must be explicit.

Decision: MGF should choose team working. It attacks both problems at source — the 2.4% defect rate and the absence among 11 of 60 machinists — while a productivity bonus risks trading quality for volume when 58% of customers buy on accuracy and 47% would change supplier after late deliveries. A bonus could be added only after the defect rate falls; it should not be introduced now. Across 75,000 units a year, fewer rejected parts protect the $14.00 selling price and the cash available to meet the $300,000 fixed costs.
    Keywords: 2.4%, 11 of 60, $280, 58%, workforce of 60, $300,000

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MGF's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MGF's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.85 : 1

Inventories also rose to $165,000, and with a 2.4% defect rate some of that stock may be slow-moving.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.0% rise in wholesale steel prices will affect MGF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If the $450,000 ten-year loan carries a variable rate, the extra annual cost is 0.75% × $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $300,000, and if the loan is fixed the direct effect is zero. Higher rates could still make future borrowing for the $720,000 cell more expensive.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, from $12.50 to $13.40): Each paid hour rises by $13.40 − $12.50 = $0.90. MGF has a workforce of 60 and the insert gives no hours worked, so no annual wage total can be claimed honestly. The useful comparison is productivity: 75,000 units ÷ 60 workers = 1,250 units per worker. If that holds, the higher wage is absorbed by the $14.00 selling price; if absence among 11 of 60 machinists cuts output, unit labour cost rises. Wholesale steel and alloy inflation (9.0%): The insert does not split the $8.00 variable cost into materials, so only an explicit bound is defensible. If the whole $8.00 were steel-linked, 9.0% × $8.00 = $0.72 a unit; across 75,000 units that is $72,000 a year (75,000 × $0.72). Even a quarter of that, $18,000, would cut into the $6.00 contribution on every part and compound the rework from the 2.4% defect rate.

Conclusion: The 9.0% rise in steel prices will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit sold, cannot be avoided by fixing a loan rate, and directly erodes the contribution that justifies the $720,000 investment. The interest rise is small and conditional, while the wage rise can be offset if productivity stays at 1,250 units per worker.

Kelvin Valve and Pump (KVP) is a public limited company in the industrial equipment sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by Danica Kelvin, it supplies control valves to water utilities and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. KVP plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated valve-testing line, financed by a $700,000 five-year bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and produces 100,000 units a year.     Question: KVP is funding its $1,200,000 valve-testing line with a $700,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for KVP of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Share capital does not have to be repaid and dividends can be paid only when profits allow, unlike the fixed interest and instalments on a $700,000 five-year bank loan. As a public limited company KVP can issue shares to investors, so the $500,000 raised strengthens the balance sheet without adding to the $450,000 annual fixed costs. This matters while the defect rate on cast bodies is still 3.1% and output of 100,000 units has to be maintained.

Point 2: Equity finance avoids the collateral and covenants a lender would demand, leaving KVP's existing assets free and its flat structure of democratic leadership unencumbered by lender conditions. With a workforce of 120 and absenteeism at 8%, the firm needs flexibility to spend on agency cover at $230 a day rather than commit cash to debt service. A share issue also spreads the risk of the $1,200,000 testing line across shareholders instead of leaving Danica Kelvin's management exposed to a single bank.
    Keywords: share issue, $500,000, $700,000, $1,200,000, $450,000, absenteeism

Trade-directory advertising is rejected as too passive to prove certification; the exhibition is rejected because it is expensive and pulls staff from the testing line at a time when 12 of 120 workers are already absent. --- STEM ---
Redwood Gear Works (RGW) is a partnership in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2005 by Callum Redwood and Imani Redwood, it makes custom gearboxes for renewable-energy converters and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. RGW plans to invest $640,000 in a gear-grinding cell, financed by $240,000 partners' capital, a $250,000 bank loan and $150,000 of hire purchase. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and produces 60,000 units a year. RGW faces a rising scrap rate of 3.6% on gear blanks and a shortage of skilled grinders in its Bristol workshop.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RGW is financing its $640,000 grinding cell with $240,000 partners' capital, a $250,000 bank loan and $150,000 of hire purchase. Explain two advantages for RGW of using hire purchase rather than the bank loan for the equipment.
    Answer: Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $150,000 cost of the grinding equipment into regular payments, so RGW keeps its $250,000 bank loan available as working capital. That matters when 17 of 94 delivery promises were missed and 39% of surveyed firms had changed supplier after a late order; the partnership needs cash to improve deliveries rather than tying it all up in machinery.

Point 2: With hire purchase RGW can use the asset immediately while paying for it, and the gear-grinding cell starts reducing the 3.6% scrap rate and 58 weekly rework hours right away. The $210,000 fixed-cost base is not increased by a second full loan, so the partners, Callum and Imani Redwood, retain more control and the $640,000 expansion can proceed even with only 7 of 35 workers certified. Hire purchase also matches payment to the life of the asset, so the partnership is not still paying for the cell once it is obsolete; with 17 of 94 orders late and 39% of surveyed firms having changed supplier, keeping the $250,000 loan free for delivery improvements is more valuable than extra equipment debt.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $150,000, $250,000, $640,000, $210,000

--- STEM ---
Tarn Polymer Works (TPW) is a private limited company in the polymer components sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2014 by Sofia Tarn, it moulds technical plastic parts for domestic appliance makers and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. TPW plans to invest $880,000 in a new injection-moulding press, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $350,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.50, and produces 120,000 units a year. TPW faces a waste rate of 4.2% in moulding and a rising number of quality complaints from appliance assemblers in its Newton plant.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TPW is funding its $880,000 press with a $600,000 bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for TPW of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or repayment, so TPW avoids increasing the fixed commitment on its $600,000 loan while it already carries $350,000 of fixed costs. The $280,000 saved in interest can be spent on retraining at $650 per operator, addressing the 4.2% waste rate and 41 monthly complaints, or on absorbing the 8.7% resin price rise without raising the $12.50 selling price.

Point 2: Internal finance keeps Sofia Tarn's control intact and avoids the security a lender would demand over the new press. A smaller loan also leaves TPW better placed if appliance sales fall by the forecast 1.5% and output drops below the 120,000 units needed to cover costs. Using $280,000 of profit demonstrates that the business generates enough cash to support part of the $880,000 investment, which could help if further finance is needed. Avoiding extra loan interest also leaves more of the $12.50 selling price available to meet the $650 retraining cost for the remaining 66 operators (80 − 14) who have not completed it.
    Keywords: retained profit, $280,000, $600,000, $880,000, $350,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to TPW.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TPW is trying to cut its 4.2% waste rate and 41 monthly complaints. Consider end-of-line inspection, quality circles, or a total quality management programme. Which should TPW choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: End-of-line inspection: Checking finished parts before dispatch is straightforward and would stop the 35% of buyers who rejected batches for visible defects from receiving faulty goods. It gives immediate feedback to the 80-strong workforce. However, inspection catches waste only after resin, machine time and labour have been used, so the 4.2% waste rate and the rise from 2.8% remain. With $350,000 fixed costs and a $600,000 loan, paying inspectors to sort scrap is less useful than preventing it, and the 4.4-day lead time against a 3-day target would lengthen.

Quality circles: Small groups of operators meet to find and fix the causes of moulding defects. This tackles waste at source, uses the knowledge of the operators, and suits a firm where only 14 of 80 have completed retraining. Circles can target the 41 complaints and 2.6% rejection rate directly, and they cost little beyond meeting time. Results depend on management acting on suggestions, and improvements may take weeks.

Total quality management: TQM embeds quality in every process and could transform the 4.2% waste rate and lift the 57% of buyers who would pay more for consistency. It is powerful but demands culture change, training across all 80 workers and sustained leadership — expensive and slow for a company servicing $600,000 of debt and a $880,000 press.

Recommendation: TPW should choose quality circles. They attack the causes of the 4.2% waste and 41 complaints at a cost the firm can afford while only 14 of 80 operators are trained. Inspection is rejected because it detects defects after the material is wasted, and TQM is rejected as too broad and slow given the loan burden. TPW can move toward TQM once circles have delivered results.
    Keywords: 4.2%, 41, 35%, 14 of 80, $650
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Names the three quality approaches with little reference to TPW. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two approaches with applied reference to TPW's waste, complaints and training data. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three approaches in TPW's context, recommends quality circles and explains why inspection and TQM are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TPW's waste rate is 4.2% and only 14 of 80 operators are trained on the new press. Explain two benefits for TPW of on-the-job training for the remaining operators.
    Answer: Point 1: On-the-job training takes place at the press itself, so the 66 untrained operators learn on the machine settings that are causing the 4.2% waste rate. Learning is immediately relevant and can start cutting the 41 monthly complaints without the $650-per-person course fees, which would be expensive across a workforce of 80 while $350,000 of fixed costs must be met.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]

TPW should keep decision rights clear so democracy does not delay urgent line stops. --- STEM ---
Zenith Nut and Coupling (ZNC) is a workers' cooperative in the industrial fastener sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2007 by Ravi Zenith, it supplies stainless couplings to marine-engine builders and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership.   Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ZNC is financing its $800,000 thread-rolling machine with $200,000 of member share capital, a $400,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for ZNC of using member share capital instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Member share capital does not require interest or fixed repayments, so ZNC can keep its $400,000 loan for working capital while meeting $270,000 of fixed costs. The $200,000 raised from members can fund training at $720 per person to cut the 2.9% defect rate, without adding to the debt burden that would be expensive at the higher base rate.

Point 2: Share capital from members reinforces the cooperative's democratic ownership and keeps decision-making with the 50 workers rather than a lender. With 8 of 50 machinists having left in six months, member commitment helps stabilise the workforce, and the $800,000 machine can be installed without new collateral. A bank loan would impose covenants and interest that could strain cash if marine orders grow only 2.2%. Member capital also signals commitment to Ravi Zenith's cooperative, which helps when recruiting machinists after 8 of 50 left, whereas added borrowing would have to be serviced from the $6.00 contribution per unit.
    Keywords: member share capital, $200,000, $400,000, $800,000, $270,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZNC.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ZNC is seeking marine-engine contracts. Consider a marine trade exhibition, a search-engine advertising campaign, or a direct sales team. Which should ZNC choose to win business? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Marine trade exhibition: A stand lets ZNC show certified stainless couplings and discuss corrosion resistance with engine builders face to face, which suits the 63% who rank it first. Exhibitions gather many buyers in one place. Costs stand fees, travel and staff time, however, and with a workforce of 50 and 8 of 50 machinists already having left, pulling people away from the 22,500-coupling line could worsen the 5.8-day delivery time.

Search-engine advertising: Paid ads reach builders actively looking for couplings and can be measured by clicks and enquiries. It is cheaper than a stand and can target marine-engine terms precisely. The drawback is that clicks are not contracts; the 49% who would pay a premium for certification need proof, and an ad cannot answer technical questions or reassure buyers about the 16 rejected batches a month as well as a person can.

Direct sales team: A sales engineer can visit marine-engine builders, present corrosion-test data and agree delivery dates. This directly addresses the 63% who put corrosion resistance first and the 49% seeking certified couplings, while allowing ZNC to explain how it will cut rejected batches. The cost is salaries and travel, and one small team cannot cover every port.

Recommendation: ZNC should choose a direct sales team. Certified technical selling converts the 63% and 49% identified in the survey and lets the cooperative defend the premium price, which neither a passive stand nor search ads can match consistently. The exhibition is rejected because of its cost and the strain on 50 staff; search advertising is rejected because it generates enquiries rather than the technical trust marine buyers require. ZNC should support the team with a simple website.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZNC's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ZNC's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.38 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.89 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $100,000 inventories + $125,000 trade receivables + $50,000 cash = $275,000; 2025 current assets = $115,000 + $140,000 + $30,000 = $285,000. The broader liquidity measure is $275,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.375, about 1.38, in 2024 and $285,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.50 in 2025. Excluding inventories, the stricter measure is ($275,000 − $100,000) ÷ $200,000 = $175,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.875, about 0.88, in 2024 and ($285,000 − $115,000) ÷ $190,000 = $170,000 ÷ $190,000 = 0.89 in 2025.

Evaluation: The headline picture looks better but the improvement is weak. The broader measure rose from 1.38 to 1.50 mainly because current liabilities fell from $200,000 to $190,000, while current assets grew only $10,000. The stricter measure barely moved, from 0.88 to 0.89, and remains below 1.0, so ZNC still depends on selling inventories to meet short-term obligations. Cash actually fell from $50,000 to $30,000, which is concerning while the cooperative services a $400,000 loan and commits $800,000 to a new machine. Inventories rose to $115,000 despite a 2.9% defect rate and 16 rejected batches a month, so some stock may be slow to sell, and receivables climbed to $140,000.

Conclusion: ZNC's liquidity has not meaningfully improved. The broader measure is higher, but the stricter measure at 0.89 and the fall in cash show the gain relies on inventory rather than liquid funds. Management should rebuild cash and tighten credit control before expanding further.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 7.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in stainless-steel prices will affect ZNC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): The rise is 0.75 percentage points. If the $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, extra interest is 0.75% × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000), manageable against $270,000 fixed costs but a drain on funds for the $800,000 machine. If the loan is fixed, the direct effect is deferred.

Minimum wage increase (7.5%, from $12.70 to $13.65): Each hour rises by $13.65 − $12.70 = $0.95. ZNC has a workforce of 50 but the insert gives no hours worked, so no annual total may be assumed. Productivity is 90,000 units ÷ 50 = 1,800 units per worker; if that is maintained, the $13.20 price can absorb the rise. Stainless-steel inflation (9.4%): The insert does not split the $7.20 variable cost, so an explicit bound is the honest method: if all of it were steel-linked, 9.4% × $7.20 = $0.6768, about $0.68 a unit; over 90,000 units that is roughly $60,912 a year. Even one sixth of that, about $10,000, exceeds the loan interest increase and would cut the $6.00 contribution while the 2.9% defect rate already wastes material.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in stainless-steel prices will have the greatest impact. It touches every coupling, cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate and directly erodes the contribution needed for the $800,000 investment. The interest rise is small and conditional; the wage rise is absorbable while productivity holds near 1,800 units per worker.

--- STEM ---
Tanner & Rowe Boutique (TNR) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2013 by Imogen Tanner in Manchester, the business sells women's clothing through its own website and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TNR plans to invest $620,000 in a new e-commerce fulfilment warehouse and click-and-collect hub, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and sells 30,000 units a year. TNR faces two operational problems: the online return rate has risen to 8.5% and customers have complained about sizing errors.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TNR plans to fund part of its $620,000 e-commerce fulfilment warehouse with a $400,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TNR of using $220,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $220,000 of retained profit avoids interest payments and capital repayments on that portion of the $620,000 warehouse, protecting TNR's cash flow while it already services a $400,000 ten-year bank loan. With fixed costs of $180,000 a year and an 8.5% return rate that creates reworking costs, every dollar saved in interest can be spent on reducing sizing errors rather than paid to lenders, and the $26.00 selling price does not have to be raised to cover finance charges.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the new click-and-collect hub is not endangered if online demand falls short of the 30,000-unit target. It also preserves Imogen Tanner's control of the private limited company: no lender can impose conditions on how the fulfilment operation is run, allowing the democratic leadership team to redirect spending quickly towards the 71% of shoppers who want free returns. Retaining the $220,000 also signals financial strength to suppliers when TNR negotiates delivery terms amid 9.3% parcel-cost inflation.
    Keywords: retained profit, $220,000, $400,000, $620,000, $180,000, 8.5%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TNR's funding decision, costs and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TNR is promoting the launch of its click-and-collect hub. Consider local radio advertising, social media advertising, or a fashion influencer partnership. Which should TNR choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local radio advertising: Radio is cheap and can reach Manchester shoppers near the new click-and-collect hub, with quick turnaround for a launch message. However, TNR sells through its own website to a national audience, so a local audience is too narrow to drive the 30,000 units a year needed, and radio cannot show the garments that generate the 8.5% sizing-related returns.

Social media advertising: Paid social campaigns can target lookalike audiences of online fashion shoppers, show products visually to cut sizing confusion, and direct buyers straight to the website or click-and-collect hub. Results are measurable and scalable within the $620,000 expansion budget, but costs per click can rise sharply with fashion competition, and ads may be ignored without credible content.

Fashion influencer partnership: Influencers demonstrate fit and styling on real bodies, directly tackling the sizing complaints behind the 8.5% return rate, and their credibility appeals to the 58% of surveyed shoppers who check delivery speed and the 71% who want free returns. Reach can be national without the wastage of radio, though fees are less predictable and depend on the influencer's reputation.

Recommendation: TNR should choose social media advertising, with a small influencer test layered on top. Social advertising gives the widest measurable national reach at controllable cost and can carry the free-returns message that 71% of shoppers want; influencers alone are less predictable and slower to scale, while local radio is rejected as too narrow for a web-based business aiming at 30,000 units. Radio can be used later only for the Manchester click-and-collect catchment.
    Keywords: click-and-collect, 30,000, 8.5%, 71%, 58%, $620,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TNR with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TNR with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and influencers lose.

--- STEM ---
Rowan & Jade Cooperative (RJC) is a fashion retail cooperative in the ethical clothing sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2011 by Aoife Rowan in Galway, the business sells recycled-fabric garments online and through two outlets, and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.00 a unit and a selling price of $25.00, and sells 28,000 units a year. RJC faces two operational problems: fabric offcut waste has reached 7.4% and supplier deliveries are arriving late.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RJC plans to finance its $480,000 recycled-fabric range with a $300,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for RJC of using $180,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Applying $180,000 of retained profit to the $480,000 range means RJC borrows less and avoids interest and capital repayments on that portion, protecting cash flow alongside fixed costs of $210,000 a year. The money saved can be spent on tackling the 7.4% offcut waste or on the $6,000 quality assurance programme, rather than being paid to a lender, and the $25.00 selling price need not be raised to cover finance costs.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no security or repossession risk, so the new e-commerce returns hub is safe even if demand for recycled fabric disappoints. It also preserves member control of the cooperative: no bank can attach conditions to how the $300,000 is used, so the democratic leadership can respond to the 67% of members who value recycled fabric and the 62% who would pay $2.00 more. Retaining the $180,000 also demonstrates financial strength when negotiating with suppliers whose deliveries currently take 12 days.
    Keywords: retained profit, $180,000, $300,000, $480,000, $210,000, 7.4%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to RJC's funding decision and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RJC is launching its new recycled-fabric clothing range. Consider local newspaper advertising, social media advertising, or in-store demonstrations at its two outlets. Which should RJC choose to promote the range? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Local newspaper advertising: Print ads can reach Galway shoppers cheaply and suit a cooperative's community image, with simple delivery before the launch. However, RJC sells online as well as through two outlets and needs volume close to 28,000 units a year, so a regional newspaper has limited reach and cannot show the texture and colour of recycled fabric that 67% of members value.

Social media advertising: Visual platforms can demonstrate recycled garments, target ethical-fashion audiences nationally, and link directly to the website and the new e-commerce returns hub. Spend is measurable within the $480,000 budget and can highlight the premium that 62% of members would pay. The drawback is that feeds are crowded, costs can rise, and results depend on creating strong images of the fabric.

In-store demonstrations: Demonstrations at the two outlets let customers touch the fabric and ask staff questions, which could reduce the 4.6% complaint rate and the 640 returns. They also build member loyalty. However, they reach only shoppers near the outlets, are labour-intensive for a workforce of 52, and do little to drive the online sales that the returns hub is meant to serve.

Recommendation: RJC should choose social media advertising, supported by small in-store demonstrations. Social media gives national, measurable reach at controllable cost and can carry the recycled-fabric and $2.00-premium message to the 62% of members willing to pay more; in-store events alone are too local and costly per customer, and newspapers are rejected as static and regionally limited. Demonstrations can be retained as a low-cost supplement at the two outlets once online demand is established.
    Keywords: 67%, 62%, $2.00, 28,000, $480,000, e-commerce

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RJC's fabric offcut waste has reached 7.4% and supplier deliveries are late. Explain two benefits for RJC of using democratic leadership in its flat structure.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the workforce of 52 to propose ways of cutting the 7.4% offcut waste, and the flat structure means a cutter's suggestion reaches Aoife Rowan without passing through several management layers. This is practical knowledge from the Galway cutting room, where 18 garments failed inspection out of 1,200, so small changes suggested by operators can quickly reduce the gap from the earlier 9.1% waste figure.

Point 2: Consultation increases commitment to quality, which supports the $6,000 quality assurance programme and makes staff more willing to accept retraining at $450 per cutter. Lower waste protects the $25.00 selling price and the contribution earned on 28,000 units, helping RJC cover fixed costs of $210,000 a year and the $480,000 range investment. Democratic discussion with members also builds trust when the cooperative must decide how to handle supplier lead times that have stretched from 8 to 12 days.   Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RJC wants to reduce its 7.4% fabric waste and late supplier deliveries. Consider retraining cutters in quality control or introducing a supplier quality assurance programme. Which should RJC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Retraining cutters in quality control: At $450 per cutter this is cheap against the $480,000 investment, and it addresses waste directly in the Galway cutting room where 7.4% of fabric is currently lost and 18 of 1,200 garments failed inspection. Staff learn to spot faults before cloth is cut, and training can be spread across the workforce of 52. Its limit is that it cannot fix late deliveries or poor fabric arriving from suppliers, so the 12-day lead time would remain.

Supplier quality assurance programme: Costing $6,000 a year, this sets standards with suppliers and checks material before it reaches the cutting room, so it tackles both the incoming cause of the 7.4% waste and the late deliveries that have stretched lead times from 8 to 12 days. It may need staff time to audit suppliers and will not immediately improve the 18 failed garments if cutting skills are weak, but it prevents problems earlier in the chain.

Decision: RJC should introduce the supplier quality assurance programme first, with limited cutter retraining alongside it. The $6,000 annual cost is small beside fixed costs of $210,000 and the $480,000 range, and it attacks the external causes — late and variable fabric — that training alone cannot reach; retraining is therefore rejected as the sole response because it leaves the 12-day lead time untouched. A few $450 training places should still be funded so the 18 inspection failures fall, combining the two approaches rather than relying only on in-house fixes. The cooperative should review the 7.4% waste figure and the 12-day lead time each quarter so it can judge whether the $6,000 annual spend is delivering value.
    Keywords: quality control, quality assurance, $450, $6,000, 7.4%, 9.1%

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RJC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RJC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.40 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1

    Question: RJC is considering charging a $2.00 premium for its recycled-fabric range. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RJC of this decision.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 4.8% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in organic cotton and recycled-fabric costs will affect RJC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If RJC's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost increases by 0.75% of $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). This is small next to fixed costs of $210,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed there is no immediate extra charge. The cooperative can limit the risk by fixing the rate, so this is the least pressing of the three changes.

Minimum wage rise (4.8%, to $13.60 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 52 but no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. Qualitatively, the rise increases the cost of running the two outlets and the returns hub and cannot be avoided. Because 7.4% of fabric is wasted and a $450 cutter retraining place is budgeted, any wage increase that is not matched by productivity will raise unit cost and narrow the $14.00 contribution, but the effect is spread across the cooperative rather than concentrated on one input.

Input cost inflation (11.2%): The insert gives a $11.00 variable cost per unit but does not decompose it. If all of it rose by 11.2%, the increase would be 0.112 × $11.00 = $1.23 per unit, and at 28,000 units that is $34,440 a year (28,000 × $1.23). Even a smaller rise would erode the $14.00 contribution on every garment sold; the $2.00 premium that 62% of members would accept can offset only part of it.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in fabric costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 28,000 units, reaches a larger annual sum than the $2,250 interest change, and directly threatens the contribution that funds the $480,000 range. The interest rise is modest and can be fixed, and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert, so both rank lower; RJC should negotiate bulk fabric prices and introduce the premium gradually while monitoring the 7.4% waste figure.
    Keywords: 6.0%, 4.8%, 11.2%, $13.60, $300,000, 7.4%

--- STEM ---
Quill & Muse Boutique (QMB) is a sole trader business in the luxury online accessories sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2016 by Seraphina Quill in Paris, the business sells handmade scarves and bags through its own website and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. QMB plans to invest $260,000 in a digital photography studio and an automated stock-control system, financed by a $150,000 bank loan and $110,000 of the owner's savings. It has fixed costs of $96,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $42.00, and sells 8,000 units a year. QMB faces two operational problems: the return rate has reached 12.1% because of sizing complaints and stock-outs are losing sales.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QMB plans to fund part of its $260,000 photography studio with a $150,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for QMB of using $110,000 of the owner's savings instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $110,000 of the owner's savings avoids extra interest and repayment obligations, which protects QMB's cash flow while fixed costs already stand at $96,000 a year. The money not borrowed can instead fund the automated stock-control system, tackling the 9% of scarves affected by stock-outs, without increasing the burden of the $150,000 bank loan or forcing the $42.00 selling price higher.

Point 2: Owner savings carry no collateral or repossession risk, so Seraphina Quill's luxury accessories business is not exposed if the studio fails to reduce the 12.1% return rate. As a sole trader she also keeps full control: no lender can set conditions on how the website or photography is run, so decisions can be made quickly under the hierarchical structure. Committing her own savings also demonstrates personal commitment to suppliers and to the 16-strong workforce when the business invests $260,000 in new capacity. Keeping $110,000 of savings invested also reduces the risk that a fall in sales below the 4,000-unit break-even point leaves her unable to meet loan instalments.
    Keywords: owner's savings, $110,000, $150,000, $260,000, $96,000, 12.1%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to QMB's funding decision and costs.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QMB is relaunching its scarf and bag range online. Consider fashion magazine print advertising, social media influencer marketing, or search engine advertising. Which should QMB choose to promote the relaunch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Fashion magazine print advertising: A glossy magazine suits a Paris luxury brand and can convey status through high-quality images. However, print is expensive, slow to book and hard to measure, and a national readership would include few of the 300 surveyed online accessories buyers; it also cannot respond quickly to the 9% stock-out problem.

Social media influencer marketing: Influencers can show scarves and bags in many angles and outfits, which matters because 73% of buyers consult photographs and 68% said more angles would increase purchases. Content can target luxury accessories audiences and link straight to the website. The disadvantages are that influencer fees vary, results take time, and a poorly matched partner could damage the brand image behind the $42.00 price.

Search engine advertising: Paid search reaches shoppers already looking for handmade accessories, so it converts strongly and can be switched on or off as stock allows, which helps when 9% of scarves are out of stock. It is measurable within the $260,000 investment, but it depends on text rather than the photography that 73% of buyers consult, and popular keywords can be costly.

Recommendation: QMB should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by limited search advertising. Influencer content best exploits the new photography studio and answers the 68% who want more angles, potentially lowering the 12.1% return rate driven by sizing complaints. Search ads alone show too little of the product, while magazine advertising is rejected as slow, expensive and unmeasurable for a 16-person online business; search can be used as a low-cost supplement for high-intent buyers.
    Keywords: 73%, 68%, 300, $42.00, $260,000, website
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of QMB with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of QMB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazines and search-only advertising lose.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QMB's return rate is 12.1% and stock-outs are losing sales. Explain two benefits for QMB of its autocratic leadership style within a hierarchical structure.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Seraphina Quill decide quickly how to fix the 12.1% return rate, for example by ordering clearer size guides without waiting for committee approval. In a hierarchical structure the instruction passes down a short chain to the workforce of 16, so the 52 complaints about unclear images can be acted on immediately, protecting the $42.00 selling price and the luxury image.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QMB wants clearer product images to cut its 12.1% return rate. Consider hiring a freelance photographer or training an existing employee in product photography. Which should QMB choose? Justify your decision.

--- STEM ---
Vale & Wren Xpress (VWX) is a public limited company in the fast-fashion e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 240. Founded in 2007 by Dominic Vale in Singapore, the business sells low-cost clothing through mobile apps and 30 stores and operates a hierarchical structure with centralised, autocratic leadership. VWX plans to invest $1.8 million in an automated e-commerce distribution centre, financed by a $1.0 million share issue and an $800,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $660,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $19.50, and sells 120,000 units a year. VWX faces two operational problems: a 3.6% garment defect rate and labour turnover of 18%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VWX plans to finance its $1.8 million automated e-commerce distribution centre with a $1.0 million share issue. Explain two advantages for VWX of using the share issue rather than borrowing an extra $1.0 million.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings $1.0 million of permanent capital with no interest or repayment schedule, easing pressure on the existing $800,000 bank loan and on fixed costs of $660,000 a year. The cash can be directed at the automated e-commerce distribution centre instead of servicing debt, helping VWX handle the 3.6% defect rate and the 5.6-day delivery time without raising the $19.50 selling price.

Point 2: Issuing shares strengthens the balance sheet and lowers reliance on lenders, so the public limited company is less exposed if interest rates rise or consumer spending on fast fashion falls 3.2%. Unlike another loan, equity does not require collateral over the $1.8 million centre. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders and possible dividend pressure, but given a 18% labour turnover problem and 412 complaints, VWX needs cash flexibility more than the preservation of every existing shareholding percentage. Equity also absorbs losses if the 3.6% defect rate is not fixed quickly, whereas loan interest would still be due; this protects the $1.8 million centre in its first year.
    Keywords: share issue, $1.0 million, $800,000, $1.8 million, $660,000, 3.6%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to VWX's funding decision and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VWX is promoting its low-cost clothing range. Consider mobile app notifications, celebrity endorsement, or national television advertising. Which should VWX choose to promote the range? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Mobile app notifications: VWX already sells through mobile apps, so push messages and in-app offers can reach existing buyers instantly and drive repeat orders towards the 120,000-unit target. The cost is low and offers can be targeted by past purchases, which helps when 3.2% less is being spent on fast fashion. The limitation is that notifications only reach people who have installed the app, so they cannot easily attract new customers.

Celebrity endorsement: A well-chosen celebrity could generate rapid awareness and social media coverage for low-cost fashion, helping VWX compete for attention and supporting the $1.8 million distribution centre's volume. However, fees are high and unpredictable, and if the celebrity's image clashes with the brand or a scandal occurs, the $19.50 range loses credibility; it also says little about quality when 3.6% of garments fail inspection.

National television advertising: TV gives the widest reach and can build mass awareness across the 30 stores and the apps, which suits a public limited company with 240 staff. Yet airtime and production are very expensive relative to a $660,000 annual fixed-cost base, and much of the audience will not buy online fashion, so wastage would be high.

Recommendation: VWX should choose mobile app notifications, backed by small social promotions. They are cheap, measurable and use the existing app channel to protect contribution on 120,000 units; celebrity endorsement is rejected as costly and risky when a 3.6% defect rate needs fixing first, and television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted. VWX can add wider advertising once the 18% labour turnover and complaint levels are under control.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VWX's labour turnover has reached 18% and 61% of leavers cited repetitive work. Explain two benefits for VWX of introducing job rotation.
    Answer: Point 1: Job rotation moves the workforce of 240 between packing, inspection and stock-recording tasks, which directly addresses the 61% of leavers who cited repetitive work. Greater variety should raise motivation and reduce the 18% labour turnover, cutting the disruption caused by 34 staff leaving in one quarter and lowering recruitment and induction costs for a business with fixed costs of $660,000 a year.

Point 2: Rotation also builds multi-skilled staff who can cover the automated e-commerce distribution centre when demand spikes, improving the 5.6-day delivery time and helping maintain output of 120,000 units. Workers who have performed inspection are more likely to spot the 3.6% garment defects, while the $180 per worker training cost is small beside the $1.8 million investment. Under the hierarchical structure, managers can schedule rotation to keep the centralised autocratic leadership's standards consistent across the 30 stores and the packing line. Management must still schedule rotation so that inspection remains independent, otherwise the 3.6% defect rate and the 1.9% stock-record errors could be missed.
    Keywords: job rotation, labour turnover, 18%, 61%, $180, workforce of 240

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VWX wants to cut its 3.6% garment defect rate. Consider installing an inspection station or introducing a supplier quality assurance programme. Which should VWX choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Installing an inspection station: At $24,000 this is a one-off cost that catches faulty garments before they are packed, directly reducing the 3.6% failure rate recorded across 31,000 orders and limiting the 412 customer complaints. Inspectors can give immediate feedback on the packing line and the cost is small against the $1.8 million distribution centre. Its weakness is that it detects defects after production, so waste has already occurred, and it does nothing to address the 1.9% stock-record error rate or supplier quality.

Supplier quality assurance programme: Costing $90,000 a year, this sets standards with suppliers and prevents poor material entering production, which can tackle the source of the 3.6% defects and reduce rework. Because 5.1% of garments previously failed inspection, prevention could produce a lasting fall. The recurring $90,000 is larger than the inspection station's $24,000, however, and it will not catch packing mistakes inside VWX itself.

Decision: VWX should install the inspection station first and add a limited supplier quality assurance programme once defect data identifies which suppliers are at fault. The $24,000 one-off cost gives immediate control over the 3.6% defects and 412 complaints, whereas committing $90,000 a year before diagnosing the cause is rejected as premature. Supplier assurance is not abandoned: it is deferred until inspection records show whether defects originate with suppliers, at which point prevention becomes the better long-term tool. VWX should set a target for the 3.6% defect rate and review the 31,000-order log monthly, judging the $24,000 purchase on whether complaints fall from the current 412.
    Keywords: inspection station, quality assurance, $24,000, $90,000, 3.6%, 5.1%
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two quality approaches with limited application to VWX. | level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of VWX. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of VWX with a well-justified decision covering cost, timing and defect prevention.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.5% rise in cotton and synthetic fabric costs will affect VWX. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.25%): Because the bulletin specifies a variable-rate $800,000 loan, the extra interest is 0.75% of $800,000 = $6,000 a year (0.0075 × $800,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $660,000 a year, and VWX can cap it by fixing the rate, so this is the smallest direct cost change even though higher rates may add to the 3.2% fall in fast-fashion spending.

Minimum wage rise (7.1%, to $14.80 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 240 but no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual wage bill cannot honestly be invented. Qualitatively the rise increases distribution and store costs and is unavoidable. Its effect depends on the 120,000 units sold: with labour turnover already 18% and 61% of leavers citing repetitive work, a wage rise is only affordable if job rotation holds productivity, otherwise unit labour cost climbs and narrows the $11.00 contribution.

Fabric cost inflation (13.5%): The insert states a $8.50 variable cost per unit but does not break it into materials and other elements. The honest upper bound is 0.135 × $8.50 = $1.1475 per unit, which across 120,000 units is $137,700 a year (120,000 × $1.1475). Even if only part of variable cost is fabric, the increase recurs on every garment and directly attacks the $11.00 contribution that must cover $660,000 fixed costs and service the $1.8 million centre.

Conclusion: The 13.5% fabric cost rise will have the greatest impact. It can reach roughly $137,700 a year, far above the $6,000 interest change, and unlike the wage rise it can be bounded from the insert and hits every unit sold. The interest rise is small and fixable, while the wage effect cannot be quantified and depends on productivity, so both rank below input inflation. VWX should renegotiate fabric contracts and use the $24,000 inspection station to avoid wasting expensive material on the 3.6% of faulty garments.

--- STEM ---
Zephyr & Loom Fabrics (ZLF) is a partnership in the sustainable home-textile and fashion-fabric e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2018 by partners Priya Loomis and Daniel Zephyr in Copenhagen, the business sells dyed fabrics online to craft and fashion makers through its own website and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. ZLF plans to invest $540,000 in a digital fabric-printing and online fulfilment hub, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $21.00, and sells 36,000 units a year. ZLF faces two operational problems: dye waste has reached 6.8% and customer deliveries are running late.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ZLF plans to fund its $540,000 digital fabric-printing hub with a $320,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for ZLF of using $220,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: Using $220,000 of retained profit reduces the amount borrowed and avoids interest and capital repayments on that portion, protecting cash flow alongside fixed costs of $240,000 a year. The saving can be spent on the $28,000 colour-matching system or on tackling the 6.8% dye waste, rather than paid to a lender, and the $21.00 selling price need not rise to cover extra finance costs.

Point 2: Retained profit has no security or repossession risk, so the printing and fulfilment hub is safe even if demand from craft makers disappoints. It also protects the partners' control of the business: no bank can impose conditions on how the website or printing is run, which suits the flat structure and laissez-faire leadership. Committing $220,000 of profit signals confidence to suppliers while the partnership negotiates around 12.8% dye-cost inflation and 38 complaints about late delivery. Avoiding extra borrowing also leaves room to fund the $28,000 colour-matching system if the 6.8% dye waste fails to fall, without returning to the bank.
    Keywords: retained profit, $220,000, $320,000, $540,000, $240,000, 6.8%
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZLF's funding decision and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: ZLF is launching its digitally printed fabrics. Consider craft trade fairs, social media video advertising, or email marketing to existing makers. Which should ZLF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Craft trade fairs: Fairs let makers see and touch printed fabric, which builds trust and can generate immediate orders for a Copenhagen-based partnership. Staff can explain the sustainable printing process directly. However, stands, travel and staff time are costly for a workforce of 34, and the audience is geographically limited, so fairs cannot easily deliver the 36,000 units a year needed to justify the $540,000 hub.

Social media video advertising: Video can show colour and print quality online, which matters because 64% of surveyed makers would pay $1.50 more for digitally printed fabric and 57% value faster delivery. Platforms allow precise targeting of craft and fashion audiences and can link straight to the website, with measurable spend within the $540,000 budget. The drawbacks are crowded feeds, rising costs and the need for regular new creative content.

Email marketing to existing makers: This is cheap, fast and uses the customer list ZLF already has, so it can announce the launch at almost no extra cost and encourage repeat orders. It is measurable and easy to tailor. Its weakness is reach: it cannot attract new makers, and if the 38 late-delivery complaints are not resolved, repeated emails may annoy existing customers rather than win sales.

Recommendation: ZLF should choose social media video advertising, supported by a low-cost email announcement to existing makers. Video reaches new customers nationally and demonstrates the printed fabric that 64% of makers value, while email cannot grow the customer base; trade fairs are rejected as expensive and too local for a business selling mainly through its website. A small fair presence can be reconsidered once the 6.8% dye waste and delivery times are under control.
    Keywords: 64%, 57%, $1.50, 350, 36,000, website
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal context. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ZLF with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ZLF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade fairs and email-only marketing lose.
