    Question: ZLF's dye waste is 6.8% and 38 customers complained about late delivery. Explain two benefits for ZLF of its laissez-faire leadership style in a flat structure.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets the experienced dye technicians decide how to reduce the 6.8% waste themselves, using their practical knowledge of the vats. Because the flat structure has few managerial layers, a technician can adjust a dye run without waiting for Priya Loomis or Daniel Zephyr, which matters when 27 rolls out of 1,500 were rejected for colour inconsistency and the earlier waste figure was 8.3%.

Point 2: Delegation can speed up responses to the 38 late-delivery complaints and the 6.2-day dispatch time against a 4-day promise, because the workforce of 34 closest to dispatch can rearrange work without seeking approval. Autonomy may raise job satisfaction and reduce the risk of mistakes in a business with fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $540,000 investment. The partners keep overall control of the $28,000 colour-matching purchase, so freedom operates within agreed limits rather than becoming a lack of direction.

    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZLF's waste, complaints and structure.

    Question: ZLF wants to reduce the 27 rejected fabric rolls and its 6.8% dye waste. Consider retraining a dye technician in colour control or buying a computer colour-matching system. Which should ZLF choose? Justify your decision.

The $28,000 cost is small relative to fixed costs of $240,000 and the $540,000 hub, and it gives consistent results across the whole workforce, so retraining alone is rejected as too dependent on one person and unlikely to eliminate all 27 rejects. They should set a target for the 27 rejected rolls and review the 6.8% waste monthly, so the $28,000 spend is judged against the 12.8% rise in dye costs.

--- STEM ---
Thorncliff Bay Resort (TBR) is a private limited company in the seaside hospitality and tourism sector on the south coast, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 2011 by Priya Rathore, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and sells 18,000 units a year, one unit being an occupied room-night at an average selling price of $160. TBR plans to invest $900,000 in a new sea-view wing and spa, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year and a variable cost of $60 a unit. TBR faces rising labour turnover among housekeeping staff and guest complaints about slow check-in at peak weekends.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TBR plans to fund part of its new sea-view wing and spa with a $600,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TBR of using the $300,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $300,000 retained profit avoids all interest and repayment charges on that portion of the $900,000 sea-view wing and spa, protecting TBR's cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $420,000 a year and faces a base-rate rise to 4.5%. Every dollar not paid to the lender can instead cover the 9.6% increase in hotel energy and food inputs or fund the new spa's launch, so the resort can hold its $160 selling price rather than passing costs to guests. Retained profit is also immediately available, with no loan-approval delay before the building work starts.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no collateral and no fixed monthly instalments, so Priya Rathore's resort is not exposed to repossession risk if the new wing attracts fewer bookings than forecast, which matters given the rising labour turnover among housekeeping staff. It also keeps ownership and control within the existing company: a larger loan would let the lender impose conditions on how the sea-view wing is run. Using the $300,000 first therefore reduces the $600,000 bank loan actually needed, cutting TBR's debt commitment while it tackles slow peak-weekend check-in and a 5.2% wage rise.
    Keywords: retained profit, $300,000, $600,000, $900,000, $420,000, sea-view
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TBR's wing investment, costs and borrowing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TBR is promoting its new sea-view wing and spa. Consider a national television campaign, regional radio advertising, and social media travel influencers. Which should TBR choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A television advertisement would build awareness of the new sea-view wing and spa quickly across the south coast and beyond, reaching the 68% of surveyed guests who would pay $12 more for such a room and helping justify the $900,000 investment. However, airtime and production are expensive for a 90-employee resort already servicing a $600,000 bank loan, and much of the audience lives outside TBR's drive-to catchment, so a large share of the spend would be wasted.

Regional radio advertising: Local radio is far cheaper and can target drive-to weekend guests within the resort's catchment, with flexible short-notice messages about spa breaks. Its weakness is reach and format: radio cannot show the sea views or the refurbished spa, and it will not reach the corporate and tour guests who make up much of the 18,000 room-nights, so it is unlikely to fill a whole new wing on its own.

Social media travel influencers: Travel and wellness influencers can show the sea-view spa visually to exactly the segment identified in TBR's research — the 57% of 750 guests who choose hotels on sustainability credentials and the 68% willing to pay $12 more. Engagement is measurable, cost per reached guest is low, and user-generated content keeps promoting the wing after launch. Results build more slowly than television and depend on choosing credible influencers.

Recommendation: TBR should choose social media travel influencers, backed by modest local radio for last-minute weekend availability. Influencers give visual reach at a fraction of television's cost and directly target the guests whose stated preferences justify the $900,000 wing. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted while TBR carries a $600,000 loan and $420,000 fixed costs; radio alone is rejected because it cannot display the spa or reach enough guests to fill 18,000 room-nights.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TBR's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TBR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.56 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.97 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $85,000 inventories + $120,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $240,000; 2025 current assets = $60,000 + $150,000 + $55,000 = $265,000. Excluding stock: 2024 = ($240,000 − $85,000) ÷ $160,000 = $155,000 ÷ $160,000 = 0.97; 2025 = ($265,000 − $60,000) ÷ $170,000 = $205,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.21.

The concern is trade receivables rising from $120,000 to $150,000; if corporate guests and tour operators pay late, cash could tighten quickly. Inventories fell to $60,000, so stock availability for peak weekends should be monitored.

Conclusion: TBR's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher in 2025 and the improvement does not rely on inventory, with the 0.97 to 1.21 move the clearest evidence of stronger underlying liquidity.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in energy and food input costs will affect TBR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If TBR's $600,000 bank loan tracks the base rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is small against fixed costs of $420,000 and can be largely removed by fixing the loan rate. Minimum wage increase (5.2%, to $14.80 an hour): Housekeeping and front-of-house roles at TBR are hourly paid, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and is not optional. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the defensible judgement is qualitative against the given data of 200 room-nights per employee and $100 contribution per unit. If productivity holds, a wage rise is absorbable through the $12 room premium; if labour turnover disrupts service, unit labour costs rise and contribution is squeezed.

Energy and food input costs (9.6%): These apply to every one of the 18,000 room-nights. The insert does not decompose the $60 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated honestly: if the whole variable cost rose 9.6%, that adds 9.6% × $60 = $5.76 a unit, or about $103,680 a year (18,000 × $5.76). Even a narrower increase would materially cut the $100 contribution that justifies the spa investment. TBR can recover part through the $12 premium and supplier renegotiation.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in energy and food inputs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 18,000 units and directly erodes the $100 contribution underpinning the $900,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise is small and fixable by fixing the loan rate, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity and the $12 premium. Input-cost inflation therefore deserves the most urgent management response.

--- STEM ---
Marlowe City Hotels (MBH) is a public limited company in the boutique hospitality sector, employing a workforce of 160 across six city-centre properties. Founded in 2008 by Daniel Okafor, it has a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership and sells 24,000 units a year, one unit being an occupied apartment-night at an average selling price of $170. MBH plans to invest $1,200,000 in refurbishing and rebranding its properties, financed by a $500,000 share issue and a $700,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year and a variable cost of $70 a unit. MBH's guest satisfaction score has fallen to 3.9 out of 5 and absence among reception staff has reached 7%.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MBH plans to fund part of its refurbishment with a $700,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for MBH of using the $500,000 share issue instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital that carries no interest and no fixed repayment dates, so MBH can commit the $500,000 to refurbishing six city-centre properties without adding to the interest burden on its $700,000 bank loan, especially as the base rate has risen to 4.75%. With fixed costs already at $600,000 a year and energy costs up 11.3%, avoiding debt service protects the $100 contribution earned on each of the 24,000 apartment-nights and leaves more cash to reverse the falling 3.9 guest satisfaction score.

Point 2: Share capital does not require collateral, so the properties themselves are not put at risk if the rebrand fails to attract bookings — a real concern while 7% of reception shifts are uncovered. As a public limited company, MBH can access equity investors more easily than a smaller firm, and the extra capital strengthens the balance sheet before the $1,200,000 programme. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders including founder Daniel Okafor, but the avoided interest and repayment obligations make the share issue attractive for a long-life refurbishment that will earn returns over many years.
    Keywords: share issue, $500,000, $700,000, $1,200,000, refurbishing, $600,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to MBH's funding and refurbishment.

However, print has no direct booking link, its reach is hard to measure, and the cost of full-page colour adverts in national titles would be high for a business already funding a $1,200,000 refurbishment with a $700,000 bank loan. Much of the readership will not be in MBH's six cities, so wastage is significant.

Sponsorship on hotel-booking platforms: Paid placement on the sites where 54% of surveyed guests say they book boutique hotels would intercept customers at the moment of decision and drive measurable bookings for the refurbished suites. The downside is cost per click on competitive city keywords and dependence on a third-party platform that also lists rivals; MBH would be renting visibility rather than owning a direct relationship with guests, which weakens the brand it is trying to rebuild.

Social media travel influencers: Design, food and city-break influencers can showcase the refurbished suites visually to the 54% who book via review sites and the 61% who would pay $15 more for a refurbished suite. Content is shareable, targeting is precise and cost per engagement is lower than print, though results take time to build and depend on credible, well-matched influencers.

Recommendation: MBH should choose sponsorship on hotel-booking platforms as the primary channel, reinforced by a smaller influencer campaign. Platform sponsorship converts the 54% who already book through review sites at the decision point, which is what the $1,200,000 refurbishment needs to fill 24,000 apartment-nights. Print is rejected as unmeasurable and costly while MBH services a $700,000 loan and $600,000 fixed costs; influencers alone are rejected because they build awareness more slowly than booking-platform placement. The $500,000 share issue can fund the launch without more debt.

--- STEM ---
Kestrel River Expeditions (KRE) is a partnership in the adventure tourism and outdoor leisure sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 2013 by Sofia Almeida and two partners, it runs a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and sells 14,000 units a year, one unit being a paid rafting place at an average selling price of $120. KRE plans to invest $640,000 in new rafts and a riverside activity centre, financed by a $240,000 hire-purchase agreement and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year and a variable cost of $40 a unit. A recent gear inspection found a 4.2% defect rate in safety equipment and guide absence has reached 8%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KRE plans to fund part of its new rafts and activity centre with a $240,000 hire-purchase agreement. Explain two advantages for KRE of using the $400,000 retained profit instead of more hire purchase.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $400,000 retained profit avoids the interest charges and fixed periodic instalments attached to the $240,000 hire-purchase agreement, which matters for a seasonal rafting business whose cash inflows are concentrated in summer. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year already committed and the base rate rising to 4.25%, every dollar of retained profit spent now is a dollar of finance cost avoided, protecting the $80 contribution earned on each of the 14,000 expedition places.

Point 2: Retained profit gives KRE immediate ownership of the new rafts and centre without a hire-purchase lender holding title until the final payment, so the partnership is not exposed to repossession if a poor season reduces bookings. It also preserves the partners' control: no finance company can impose conditions on how Sofia Almeida and her partners run the riverside operation. Drawing on the $400,000 first reduces the hire-purchase balance actually required, cutting KRE's fixed commitments while it deals with a 4.2% defect rate in safety gear and 8% guide absence.
    Keywords: retained profit, $400,000, $240,000, hire-purchase, $640,000, $280,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KRE's seasonal cash flow and expansion funding.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KRE is launching its new riverside activity centre. Consider local radio advertising, leaflets in tourist offices, and social media adventure influencers. Which should KRE choose? Justify your recommendation.

Social media adventure influencers: Outdoor and travel influencers can show the rafting experience on video to precisely the audience identified in KRE's feedback — the 72% of 640 participants who value clear safety briefings and the 66% who would pay $9 more for upgraded wetsuit hire. Content is shareable and results are measurable, though it takes time to build and depends on choosing influencers with genuine credibility in adventure tourism.

Influencers demonstrate the experience visually and reach the safety-conscious, experience-seeking segment that underpins the $640,000 centre, at a cost controllable from the $400,000 retained profit.     Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KRE's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KRE's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.45 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.14 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $30,000 inventories + $45,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $100,000; 2025 current assets = $35,000 + $60,000 + $65,000 = $160,000. Excluding stock: 2024 = ($100,000 − $30,000) ÷ $100,000 = $70,000 ÷ $100,000 = 0.70; 2025 = ($160,000 − $35,000) ÷ $110,000 = $125,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.14.

The improvement is driven mainly by cash rising from $25,000 to $65,000 and receivables from $45,000 to $60,000. Trade receivables are still higher, so slower-paying tour operators could weaken the position, but the larger cash balance gives a real cushion for the $640,000 centre plan.

Conclusion: KRE's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher in 2025, and the 0.70 to 1.14 move in the stock-excluding measure is the clearest evidence that underlying liquidity is stronger. KRE should keep monitoring receivables but can proceed with the activity centre from a sounder short-term position.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.25%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.4% rise in diesel and equipment input costs will affect KRE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (3.50% to 4.25%): If KRE's $240,000 hire-purchase cost tracks the base rate, the extra annual finance charge is 0.75% of $240,000 = $1,800 (0.0075 × $240,000). Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $14.35 an hour): Guides are hourly paid, so this rise increases KRE's wage bill and cannot be avoided. Conclusion: The 13.4% rise in diesel and equipment costs will have the greatest impact. --- STEM ---
Pinecrest Leisure Parks (PLP) is a public limited company in the leisure and visitor-attraction sector, employing a workforce of 225. Founded in 1996 by Grace Oyelaran, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and sells 45,000 units a year, one unit being a park admission at an average selling price of $75. PLP plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new water-slide complex and splash zone, financed by a $900,000 bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $750,000 a year and a variable cost of $25 a unit. Average queue times at three popular rides have reached 42 minutes and food-outlet waste has risen to 6.4% of purchases.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PLP plans to fund part of its water-slide complex with a $900,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for PLP of using the $600,000 share issue instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue provides permanent capital with no interest charges and no fixed repayment dates, so PLP can commit the $600,000 to the water-slide complex without increasing the burden of its $900,000 bank loan at a time when the base rate has risen to 5.0%. With fixed costs of $750,000 a year and energy costs up 10.8%, avoiding extra debt service protects the $50 contribution earned on each of the 45,000 admissions and leaves cash to tackle the 42-minute queues.

Point 2: Equity does not require the park's land and rides to be offered as collateral, so the $1,500,000 development does not put existing assets at risk if the new attraction underperforms — a genuine concern while complaints have risen to 63 and 6.4% of food purchases are wasted. As a public limited company, PLP can raise the $600,000 from investors and strengthen its balance sheet before borrowing the remaining $900,000. The cost is dilution of shareholders including founder Grace Oyelaran, but for a long-life attraction that will earn revenue for years, permanent share capital is better matched than short-term debt.
    Keywords: share issue, $600,000, $900,000, $1,500,000, water-slide, $750,000

--- STEM ---
Cedar Grove Catering (CGC) is a cooperative in the hospitality and contract-catering sector, employing a workforce of 100. Founded in 2015 by Habiba Yusuf, it operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership and produces 20,000 units a year, one unit being a catered meal sold at an average selling price of $90. CGC plans to invest $520,000 in a new central production kitchen and chilled-delivery vans, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year and a variable cost of $30 a unit. Food waste has reached 6.8% of meals prepared and client complaints have risen to 18 a month, up from 11 a month last year.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CGC plans to fund part of its new central kitchen with a $320,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for CGC of using the $200,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
    Answer: Point 1: Applying the $200,000 retained profit means CGC pays no interest or instalments on that part of the $520,000 kitchen and van project, which protects its cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $300,000 a year and faces a base-rate rise to 4.0%. Every dollar of interest avoided can instead absorb the 12.8% food input-cost inflation or fund waste-reduction measures, protecting the $60 contribution earned on each of the 20,000 catered meals.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no collateral, so the cooperative's existing assets are not exposed to repossession if the new kitchen fails to win enough contracts — relevant while food waste is 6.8% and complaints have risen to 18 a month. It also preserves member control: no lender can impose operating conditions on how Habiba Yusuf and the members run CGC. Using the $200,000 first reduces the $320,000 bank loan actually required, lowering CGC's fixed debt commitment at a time when delivery punctuality is only 91%.
    Keywords: retained profit, $200,000, $320,000, $520,000, cooperative, $300,000

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CGC's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CGC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.19 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1

Excluding stock: 2024 = ($145,000 − $40,000) ÷ $145,000 = $105,000 ÷ $145,000 = 0.72; 2025 = ($178,000 − $62,000) ÷ $150,000 = $116,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.77.

If clients pay late or stock cannot be used, the stronger headline position could quickly weaken.

Conclusion: CGC's financial position has improved slightly, but only just. The 1.00 to 1.19 rise in the broad measure is the more favourable evidence; the small 0.72 to 0.77 move in the stock-excluding measure shows the gain is not based on liquid assets.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.0%, the 7.4% minimum wage increase and the 12.8% rise in food input costs will affect CGC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.

Dearer credit could make future borrowing for the $520,000 kitchen more expensive, but the direct annual effect on CGC is limited.

Minimum wage increase (7.4%, to $14.95 an hour): Kitchen and delivery staff are hourly paid, so this rise increases the wage bill across the workforce of 100 and cannot be avoided. The insert provides no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be invented; the correct judgement is qualitative against the given 200 meals per employee and $60 contribution per meal. Food input costs (12.8%): These apply to every one of the 20,000 catered meals. The insert does not decompose the $30 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated honestly: if the whole variable cost rose 12.8%, that adds 12.8% × $30 = $3.84 a meal, or about $76,800 a year (20,000 × $3.84). Even a narrower rise would reduce the $60 contribution needed to fund the $520,000 kitchen. The $6 low-waste premium recovers only part of this, so supplier negotiation and menu design matter.

Conclusion: The 12.8% rise in food input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 20,000 meals and directly erodes the $60 contribution underpinning the $520,000 investment, whereas the interest rise is small and hedgeable by fixing the loan rate, and the wage rise can be partly offset through productivity and the $6 premium. --- STEM ---
Northern Rails Freight (NRF) is a private limited company in the rail freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2011 by Anika Northern, the business hauls bulk containers for manufacturers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NRF plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new diesel-electric shunting fleet and a regional depot, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $28, and handles 40,000 units of freight a year. NRF faces two problems: wagon turnaround delays have pushed late deliveries to 14%, and a diesel-maintenance skills gap is raising repair costs.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for NRF of financing its $1,200,000 depot expansion with retained profit instead of the $700,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $500,000 retained profit costs NRF no interest or capital repayment, which protects cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $320,000 a year and a $700,000 loan commitment. With late deliveries at 14% and repair costs rising because of the diesel-maintenance skills gap, keeping interest charges low leaves more cash to fund training and shunting-fleet reliability. Every dollar not paid to the lender supports the $28 selling price and the $10 contribution without passing costs on to the 400 manufacturing clients.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk attached to the ten-year bank loan, so the $1,200,000 depot and new shunting fleet are not jeopardised if freight demand falls short of the 40,000-unit target. It also preserves Anika Northern's ownership and control: no external lender can impose conditions on how the regional depot is run or on the guaranteed overnight-slot strategy. That freedom lets NRF respond quickly to the 71% of surveyed clients who would pay a premium for guaranteed slots, which a lender imposing repayment milestones might restrict.
    Keywords: retained profit, $500,000, $700,000, $1,200,000, $320,000, bank loan

It is measurable through opens and replies, and can be personalised by depot. Its limits are that it cannot win entirely new customers and inboxes are crowded, so the message must be sharp.

Recommendation: NRF should choose the direct email campaign. It targets the precise segment in its own research, costs far less than trade press, and reaches the 71% willing to pay a premium, while radio and press are rejected as untargeted and expensive for a business funding an $1,200,000 expansion. --- STEM ---
Harbourline Logistics (HLG) is a private limited company in the port and container logistics sector, employing a workforce of 95. Founded in 2007 by Ravi Harbour, the business unloads and forwards shipping containers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. HLG plans to invest $950,000 in an automated container-stacking yard and a new warehouse, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $21, and handles 60,000 units a year. HLG faces two problems: a 6.2% container damage rate at the quay and rising labour turnover among crane operators.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for HLG of financing its $950,000 stacking-yard expansion with a bank loan rather than a share issue.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan leaves ownership and control with Ravi Harbour and the existing shareholders. A share issue would bring in new shareholders who would vote at meetings and share future profits, whereas the $600,000 loan has no voting rights. For a private limited company with a flat structure and democratic leadership, keeping decision-making inside the existing team is especially valuable when handling a 6.2% container damage rate that needs quick, coordinated action.

Point 2: Borrowing does not permanently give away a slice of profit. Once the loan is repaid, HLG keeps all the earnings from the new yard, while equity holders would share those earnings every year. The loan also lets HLG preserve its $350,000 retained profit as working capital to pay the 44 damage claims a month and fund crane-operator training, rather than surrendering cash to investors. With fixed costs of $450,000 a year, retaining that buffer reduces the risk of a cash shortfall while the automated yard beds in.
    Keywords: $950,000, $600,000, bank loan, $350,000, $450,000, retained profit
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to HLG's financing choice and case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HLG is deciding how to expand its container handling capacity. Consider owning a new stacking yard, leasing yard space, or using a third-party depot. Which should HLG choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Owning a new stacking yard: Building and owning the facility gives HLG full control over layout, equipment and service standards, which matters because 55% of surveyed shipping clients rank damage-free handling above price and the current damage rate is 6.2%. Owning also builds an asset for the long term. The drawbacks are the large $950,000 commitment, the need to service a $600,000 loan out of fixed costs already at $450,000 a year, and the risk that demand falls short of the 60,000-unit volume.

Leasing yard space: Leasing avoids the huge upfront outlay and keeps debt lower, giving flexibility if container volumes change. It can be negotiated with maintenance included and frees the $350,000 retained profit for other uses. However, lease payments are a continuing fixed commitment without building an asset, the landlord controls improvements, and HLG may struggle to install the automated stacking equipment it plans if the site is not its own.

Using a third-party depot: Outsourcing needs almost no capital and converts fixed costs into variable payments, which is attractive while labour turnover among crane operators is a problem. Control of quality is weaker, though, so the 6.2% damage rate could worsen, and margins would be shared with the depot operator, reducing the $9 contribution on each of 60,000 units.

Recommendation: HLG should own the new stacking yard. Control of handling quality is essential to cut the 6.2% damage rate and meet the 68% of clients willing to pay a 4% premium for reliable two-day clearance, and the $9 contribution on 60,000 units can service the $600,000 loan. Leasing is rejected because it blocks the automated investment, and outsourcing is rejected because it sacrifices quality control and margin.
    Keywords: 6.2%, 350, 68%, 4%, two-day clearance, 60,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies capacity options with limited application to HLG. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in HLG's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options using case figures and gives a justified recommendation explaining why leasing and outsourcing are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: HLG's container damage rate is 6.2% and labour turnover among crane operators is rising. Explain two benefits for HLG of using democratic leadership to improve performance at the quay.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 95 employees, especially crane operators, to suggest safer handling methods. Because the flat structure has few layers, their ideas about why 6.2% of containers are damaged can reach Ravi Harbour quickly and be tested in practice. Staff who help design the new stacking procedures are more likely to follow them, reducing the 44 monthly damage claims and protecting the $21 service price.

Point 2: Involvement raises job satisfaction and can reduce the rising labour turnover among crane operators. The audit shows 22 of 95 operators lack stacking certification, and consulting them about the $1,250 external courses makes training feel supportive rather than punitive. Lower turnover preserves experience at the quay, shortens the 3.4-day turnaround and protects the $9 contribution per unit from the extra recruitment and induction costs that high turnover would create. The same consultation helps HLG direct its $350,000 retained profit effectively, because operators who understand the new yard procedures waste less time and cause fewer damage claims.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, 6.2%, 22, $1,250, flat, 95
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to HLG's damage, turnover and training data.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: HLG needs 22 crane operators to gain stacking certification. Consider promoting experienced internal staff or recruiting certified operators externally. Which should HLG choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal promotion: Promoting existing crane operators rewards loyalty and uses workers who already know HLG's quay routines, which helps cut the 6.2% damage rate without a long induction. It supports the flat, democratic culture and can be combined with the $1,250 external courses to certify 22 staff at a cost of 22 × $1,250 = $27,500, far below the $950,000 yard investment. The limitation is that internal candidates may lack formal stacking qualifications and need time to train, during which the 3.4-day turnaround could suffer, and the pool of willing staff may be small.

External recruitment: Hiring already certified operators brings proven skills immediately and could reduce the 44 monthly damage claims quickly. New recruits also bring practice from other ports. However, external hiring is expensive in advertising and selection, risks clashing with the existing team, and raises labour turnover if the newcomers leave; it also does nothing to motivate the 22 current staff who remain uncertified, and the insert gives no evidence that external candidates are available locally.

Decision: HLG should promote internal staff and fund the $1,250 courses for all 22. The $27,500 cost is modest against the $600,000 loan, and internal promotion preserves experience and morale at a time when turnover is rising. External recruitment is rejected because its costs and integration risk are not justified when the skills gap can be closed with training, though HLG should recruit externally later if 22 internal candidates cannot be found. Spreading the $1,250 courses over several intakes would keep the 3.4-day quay turnaround stable while all 22 operators qualify.
    Keywords: $1,250, 22, 95, 6.2%, crane operators, certification

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HLG's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HLG's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 35.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $2,250,000 divided by revenue of $7,500,000 gives 30.0%; 2025 gross profit of $2,940,000 divided by $8,400,000 gives 35.0%. Operating profit of $900,000 divided by 2024 revenue gives 12.0%; 2025 operating profit of $1,260,000 divided by $8,400,000 gives 15.0%. Return on capital employed of $900,000 on $5,000,000 capital gives 18.0%; 2025 return of $1,260,000 on $6,000,000 gives 21.0%. Revenue rose 12.0% while cost of sales rose only 4.0%, and operating profit grew 40% against a 20% rise in capital employed.

Evaluation: The trend is positive on every measure. The gross margin improved from 30.0% to 35.0% because revenue grew much faster than cost of sales, suggesting HLG controlled quay and handling costs even with a 6.2% damage rate. Operating return rose from 12.0% to 15.0%, showing overheads were absorbed better as volumes approached 60,000 units. Returns on capital improved from 18.0% to 21.0%, important because the $950,000 stacking yard raises the capital base and the $600,000 loan must be serviced. Interest payable increased from $150,000 to $180,000, but operating profit rose far more, so the extra debt has not weakened returns. A limitation is that these are historic figures and do not yet reflect the 7.3% rise in equipment and diesel costs in Appendix 3.

Conclusion: HLG's profitability has improved, and the improvement is broad-based rather than a one-off: both trading margins and the return on the enlarged capital base rose together. The key risk is that the 35.0% gross margin could be squeezed by rising input costs, so management should protect the $9 contribution per unit and monitor the damage rate.

    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or trends with little or no accurate ratio calculation. | level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with some relevant analysis of the trends. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, capital and interest movements, and a justified conclusion on profitability.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HLG of offering guaranteed two-day container clearance to shipping clients.
    Answer: Advantage: The survey of 350 shipping clients found that 68% would pay a 4% premium for guaranteed two-day clearance and that 55% rank damage-free handling above price. HLG can therefore raise its effective price above the $21 unit price and increase the $9 contribution, while giving clients a clear reason to choose HLG over other ports. Faster clearance also reduces the 3.4-day quay turnaround, easing the congestion that contributes to the 6.2% container damage rate.

Disadvantage: A two-day guarantee requires more crane capacity and tighter scheduling, which pushes up the $450,000 fixed costs and may increase the $12 variable cost per unit through overtime or expedited handling. With a $600,000 bank loan to repay, any extra cost could absorb the 4% premium before the new $950,000 yard is fully productive.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 4.75%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 7.3% rise in handling-equipment and diesel costs will affect HLG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If HLG's $600,000 loan is variable-rate, the increase is 0.75 percentage points, so 0.0075 × $600,000 = $4,500 a year. That is small against fixed costs of $450,000 and interest payable of $180,000, and it could be removed by fixing the rate. Higher rates might also make future borrowing for the $950,000 yard dearer, but the direct effect is limited and one-dimensional.

Minimum wage increase (4.9% to $14.20): HLG has 95 staff and handles 60,000 units, so productivity is 60,000 ÷ 95 = 631.6 units per worker. Hours and individual pay are not stated, so an exact wage-bill increase cannot be invented; the proper test is whether productivity stays near 632 units or volumes rise, otherwise unit labour cost grows and the $9 contribution narrows. The effect is recurring and unavoidable, but training the 22 uncertified crane operators could offset it.

Equipment and diesel cost rise (7.3%): The insert does not break down the $12 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is valid: if all of it were affected, 7.3% × $12 = $0.876 per unit, and at 60,000 units that is 60,000 × $0.876 = $52,560 a year. Even a smaller share cuts the $9 contribution, and with warehouse rents up 6.1% and logistics inflation at 3.6%, HLG has limited scope to pass costs on.

Conclusion: The 7.3% rise in handling-equipment and diesel costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 60,000 containers, directly erodes the contribution that services the $600,000 loan and funds the $950,000 yard, and is harder to hedge than a $4,500 interest change or a wage rise that higher productivity can absorb. The wage rise ranks second and the interest rise third.
    Keywords: 4.75%, 4.9%, 7.3%, $12, 4.0%, $600,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to HLG. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on HLG's costs or financing using case figures. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown arithmetic, a justified greatest-impact judgement on input costs, and reasons why the other two are smaller.

--- STEM ---
Voltwave Energy (VWE) is a public limited company in the renewable energy sector, installing rooftop solar systems, and employs a workforce of 80. Founded in 2013 by Priya Volt, the business serves commercial buildings and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VWE plans to invest $1,500,000 in a battery-storage assembly line, financed by an $800,000 bank loan and a $700,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $40 a unit and a selling price of $70, and produces 26,000 units a year. VWE faces two problems: a 4.5% defect rate in battery packs and a shortage of qualified electricians delaying new commercial installations.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for VWE of financing its $1,500,000 battery-storage line with a share issue rather than extra bank borrowing.
    Answer: Point 1: Money raised from the $700,000 share issue does not have to be repaid and carries no interest, so VWE can devote its cash to the $600,000 fixed costs and to reducing the 4.5% battery-pack defect rate without adding to the interest payable already on the $800,000 loan. For a public limited company, equity is a natural source of long-term capital for a $1,500,000 assembly line whose returns may take several years to arrive.

Point 2: Equity requires no collateral and cannot be repossessed if installation delays persist, so the new line and the commercial installations are not put at risk. It also spreads the financing risk between shareholders and lenders. Although existing shareholders are diluted, no cash leaves the business to service the capital, leaving more of the $30 contribution per unit to reinvest in training the 18 technicians who lack certification and in cutting the 5.6-day installation time that clients care about.
    Keywords: $1,500,000, $700,000, share issue, bank loan, $800,000, $600,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to VWE's financing choice and case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VWE is launching its certified battery-storage systems. Consider trade exhibitions, social media campaigns, or partnerships with commercial property developers. Which should VWE choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Trade exhibitions: Industry exhibitions let VWE demonstrate the certified battery packs to technical buyers and network with installers, which suits a product with a 4.5% defect rate that buyers will want to inspect. However, stand costs and staff time are high, attendance is infrequent, and the audience is broad rather than the 280 commercial property clients already surveyed, so conversion may be slow for a business carrying $600,000 of fixed costs.

Social media campaigns: Social platforms can build awareness cheaply and target ads by job title or location, and short videos can show quick installation, which 61% of surveyed clients value most. The weakness is that complex technical claims about certification are hard to convey in a short post, and clicks do not necessarily become the large commercial orders needed to justify the $1,500,000 assembly line.

Partnerships with commercial property developers: Working directly with developers puts VWE in front of the exact buyers commissioning rooftop solar, and can be tied to the 73% of surveyed clients who would pay a 6% premium for certified storage. Joint bids make the 5.6-day installation promise credible and generate repeat projects. The drawback is dependence on a few partners and possible pressure on price, but the fit with the product and market is strong.

Recommendation: VWE should choose partnerships with commercial property developers. They reach the precise market in the survey, support a 6% premium and turn certification into a selling point, while exhibitions are rejected as costly and episodic and social media as too diffuse for large commercial contracts. VWE can use small social campaigns to support the partner-led sales effort.
    Keywords: 73%, 6%, 61%, 280, commercial, $1,500,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to VWE. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VWE with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context with a justified recommendation explaining why exhibitions and social media are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VWE's battery-pack defect rate is 4.5% and a shortage of qualified electricians is delaying installations. Explain two benefits for VWE of using autocratic leadership to improve performance.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership allows Priya Volt to impose one strict assembly checklist across the hierarchical structure, so all 80 staff follow the same testing routine. With the defect rate at 4.5% and rework jobs still at 18 a month, firm instructions and close inspection can cut faults fast, protecting the $70 selling price and the 73% of surveyed clients who will pay more for certified storage.

Point 2: Top-down decisions speed up the response to the electrician shortage. The audit shows 18 technicians without certification, and an autocratic leader can immediately allocate the $1,400 accredited courses and set deadlines without delay. Faster decisions also let VWE resequence the 5.6-day installations so skilled electricians work where they are most needed, reducing delays and defending the $30 contribution per unit. A consultative approach would take longer to agree testing routines, which suits neither the 4.5% defect target nor the 280 commercial clients demanding certified systems.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: VWE must train 18 technicians who lack electrical certification. Consider in-house on-the-job coaching or accredited external courses costing $1,400 per employee. Which should VWE choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: In-house on-the-job coaching: Coaching on VWE's own assembly line teaches the exact battery-pack routines linked to the 4.5% defect rate, and the 18 technicians keep producing while they learn. On-the-job coaching is rejected because it cannot confer certification and relies on the scarce electricians VWE is trying to replace with skilled staff. --- STEM ---
Swiftroute Couriers (SRC) is a private limited company in the parcel delivery and express logistics sector, employing a workforce of 140. Founded in 2015 by Daniel Swift, the business delivers same-day parcels for retailers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. SRC plans to invest $780,000 in an electric van fleet and a sorting hub, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $5 a unit and a selling price of $12, and delivers 50,000 units a year. SRC faces two problems: 8% of parcels arrive late and absenteeism among van drivers is rising during peak periods.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for SRC of financing its $780,000 sorting-hub expansion with retained profit instead of the $480,000 bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit of $300,000 needs no interest or repayment, which protects cash flow while SRC already meets fixed costs of $280,000 a year and has a $480,000 loan commitment. With 8% of parcels late and absenteeism rising among van drivers, the cash saved from interest charges can fund the $750 training courses and extra sorting capacity, helping protect the $12 price and the 69% of shoppers who will pay $1.50 more for reliable same-day delivery.

Point 2: Using internal funds avoids collateral and repossession risk, so the $780,000 electric vans and sorting hub are safe even if parcel volumes fall short of the 50,000-unit target. It also keeps control with Daniel Swift and the existing team: no lender can attach conditions to how the flat, democratic business runs its routes. That freedom matters when responding quickly to the 57% of shoppers who choose a courier on reliability, since service improvements can be made without seeking a lender's approval.
    Keywords: $780,000, $480,000, $300,000, retained profit, bank loan, $280,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to SRC's financing choice and case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SRC is promoting its guaranteed same-day delivery service. Consider sponsoring a city delivery event, local radio advertising, or a targeted email campaign to online retailers. Which should SRC choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Sponsoring a city delivery event: A high-profile event builds brand visibility and lets SRC demonstrate vans and speed directly to the public. It suits a same-day service and can generate word of mouth. However, sponsorship is expensive for a business with fixed costs of $280,000 and a $480,000 loan, and the audience includes many people who never buy parcel delivery, so the spend is poorly targeted and results are hard to measure.

Local radio advertising: Radio is cheaper than sponsorship and can repeat a simple reliability message, which matters because 57% of the 500 surveyed shoppers choose a courier on reliability. Its weakness is that listeners are a broad local audience while SRC's customers are online retailers, and radio cannot convey the $1.50 same-day premium clearly or prove that parcels arrive on time.

Targeted email campaign: An email to SRC's retailer contacts reaches the exact businesses that buy same-day delivery, can quote the 69% finding that shoppers will pay $1.50 more, and is cheap and measurable through replies and conversions. It can be personalised by retailer and adjusted quickly. The limits are that it will not build broad consumer awareness and inboxes are crowded, so the offer must be clear and timely.

Recommendation: SRC should choose the targeted email campaign.     Question: SRC wants to reduce rising absenteeism among van drivers. Consider an attendance bonus or job rotation between driving and sorting tasks. Which should SRC choose? Justify your decision.

Job rotation: Moving drivers between driving and sorting tasks reduces boredom and stretches skills, addressing the root of absenteeism and the 30 drivers lacking electric-van training by giving them varied experience. It supports the flat, democratic culture and can be introduced without a new wage bill. The weaknesses are that rotation needs training time, may initially slow the 1.4-day delivery average, and sorting staff may resist extra driving duties.

Decision: SRC should choose job rotation, supported by the $750 electric-van courses. It tackles the cause of disengagement rather than paying workers to attend, needs no new payment the insert cannot quantify, and builds flexibility that helps the 50,000-unit target. The attendance bonus is rejected because it would mask the problem and add unquantified cost, though a small bonus could be reconsidered if absence remains high after rotation is established.     Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 8.6% rise in electric-van battery and charging costs will affect SRC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Base rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If SRC's $480,000 loan is variable-rate, the interest increase is 0.75 percentage points, so 0.0075 × $480,000 = $3,600 a year. Electric-van charging cost rise (8.6%): The insert does not split the $5 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is valid: if all of it were energy, 8.6% × $5 = $0.43 per parcel, and at 50,000 parcels that is 50,000 × $0.43 = $21,500 a year. Any real effect is smaller because the variable cost also covers other items, and fuel duty up 3.2% partly offsets the switch to electric vans. The $7 contribution would shrink only modestly.

Minimum wage increase (6.4% to $13.94): SRC has 140 drivers and sorters and delivers 50,000 parcels, so productivity is 50,000 ÷ 140 = 357.1 parcels per worker. Hours and individual pay are not given, so an exact wage-bill total cannot be invented; the correct test is whether productivity holds near 357 parcels per worker. Unlike the interest change, this rise cannot be hedged, and unlike the energy upper bound it is not confined to the $5 variable cost: it applies to the whole workforce of a labour-intensive courier.

Conclusion: The 6.4% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It affects all 140 staff, cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate, and is not limited to a fraction of the $5 variable cost as the 8.6% energy rise is; on the evidence available it poses the largest recurring cost pressure. The energy rise ranks second at up to $21,500, and the $3,600 interest rise ranks third.

--- STEM ---
Coldchain Haulage (CHX) is a private limited company in the refrigerated road transport sector, employing a workforce of 110. Founded in 2010 by Elena Cold, the business carries chilled and frozen food for supermarkets and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. CHX plans to invest $1,100,000 in a fleet of refrigerated trucks and a temperature-monitoring system, financed by a $650,000 bank loan and $450,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $15 a unit and a selling price of $27, and carries 54,000 units a year. CHX faces two problems: a 3.8% spoilage rate from temperature excursions and high driver turnover on long routes.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain two advantages for CHX of financing its $1,100,000 fleet expansion with a bank loan rather than a short-term overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan gives CHX a fixed repayment schedule spread over years, matched to the working life of the new refrigerated trucks. An overdraft can be withdrawn on demand, which would be dangerous when the 3.8% spoilage rate and temperature-alarm incidents already disrupt cash flow. With fixed costs of $540,000 a year, predictable loan repayments let Elena Cold plan the $1,100,000 fleet investment without fearing a sudden call on funds.

Point 2: The $650,000 loan leaves the $450,000 retained profit free for the temperature-monitoring system and for training the 24 drivers without refrigerant-handling certification. It also avoids giving away ownership: control stays with Elena Cold rather than being diluted by a share issue. Because the loan is long-term, CHX can spread the cost across the 54,000 units carried each year instead of funding capital equipment from volatile short-term credit. The temperature-monitoring system also protects the 66% of suppliers who value verified transport, strengthening the case for long-term finance.
    Keywords: $1,100,000, $650,000, $450,000, bank loan, retained profit, $540,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to CHX's financing choice and case data.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CHX is deciding how to win more chilled-transport work. Consider long-term supermarket contracts, spot-market haulage, or an online logistics platform. Which should CHX choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Long-term supermarket contracts: Agreeing regular contracts with supermarket suppliers gives CHX predictable volumes toward the 54,000-unit target and a stable base for the $1,100,000 fleet investment. It supports the 66% of surveyed suppliers who would pay a 3.5% premium for verified temperature-controlled transport and rewards the fall in spoilage to 3.8%. The downside is dependence on a few large buyers, which can squeeze rates and expose CHX if a contract is lost.

Spot-market haulage: Taking ad-hoc loads keeps CHX flexible and fills spare capacity when demand changes, with no long commitment. Rates can be high at peak times. However, income is unpredictable, making it hard to service a $650,000 loan against fixed costs of $540,000, and constant route changes can undermine the temperature control that 59% of surveyed suppliers rank above price, risking spoilage.

Online logistics platform: Listing capacity on a digital platform can quickly find loads and reduce empty running, and it needs little sales investment. Yet CHX would pay platform fees that reduce the $12 contribution per unit, and it would have little control over service standards or customer relationships, which matters when selling verified temperature-controlled transport.

Recommendation: CHX should prioritise long-term supermarket contracts. They give the volume certainty needed to justify the refrigerated fleet and allow the 3.5% premium to be earned, while spot haulage is rejected as too volatile for loan servicing and the online platform as margin-eroding and weak on service control. Spot loads can still fill genuine spare capacity. CHX should review contract rates each year so the 3.5% premium is not eroded by dependence on a single dominant buyer.
    Keywords: 66%, 3.5%, 59%, 320, supermarket, $1,100,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the options with limited reference to CHX. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in CHX's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options with case figures and a justified recommendation explaining why spot haulage and the platform are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CHX's spoilage rate is 3.8% and driver turnover on long routes is high. Explain two benefits for CHX of using autocratic leadership to improve performance.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Elena Cold impose one strict temperature-check procedure across the hierarchical structure, so all 110 drivers follow identical refrigeration settings and recording. With spoilage at 3.8% and 14 temperature-alarm incidents a month, firm rules and close monitoring can cut losses quickly, protecting the $27 price and the 66% of surveyed suppliers who will pay more for verified transport.

Point 2: Decisive top-down action can address high driver turnover on long routes. The audit shows 24 of 110 drivers without refrigerant-handling certification, and an autocratic leader can immediately assign the $1,050 courses and set route standards without lengthy consultation. Clear instructions and faster decisions reduce the 2.8-day journey time variability that causes temperature excursions, defending the $12 contribution per unit. --- STEM ---
Northstar Software (NSD) is a private limited company in the software sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Priya Raman, it develops cloud accounting software for small firms and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. NSD plans to invest $900,000 in a new cloud data centre with automated testing tools, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $29.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. NSD faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and a skills gap in cloud engineering is slowing product releases.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NSD plans to fund part of its $900,000 cloud data centre with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for NSD of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using retained profit costs NSD no interest charges or repayments, protecting cash flow while it services a $600,000 bank loan and funds the $900,000 cloud data centre. Every dollar saved on interest can be spent on specialist training at $1,200 per employee to close the skills gap and reduce 14% labour turnover, or absorbed if cloud-server input costs rise 11.0%. Keeping the $300,000 in-house also means the 80,000-unit software licence output does not have to carry extra debt service.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral risk. If the new data centre failed to attract customers, a lender could call in the $600,000 loan, whereas $300,000 of internal funds puts no company asset at risk and preserves Priya Raman's control. It also avoids lender conditions on how the automated testing tools are introduced, letting NSD respond flexibly to the 2.4% defect rate and the 68% of surveyed clients who want guaranteed uptime. Retained profit is therefore cheaper, safer and leaves decisions with the founder.
    Keywords: retained profit, $900,000, $600,000, $300,000, $420,000, bank loan
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to NSD's financing decision, costs and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: NSD is launching a new cloud accounting package. Consider advertising in the national business press, paid search and social media advertising, or sponsoring a technology trade conference. Which should NSD choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National business press advertising: Full-page ads in national business newspapers would build credibility and reach owners of small firms, the target market for NSD's cloud accounting software. However, airtime and design costs are high, much of the readership is outside the small-firm segment, and the message is one-way with no click-through data. For a 60-person company already committing $900,000 to a data centre and servicing a $600,000 loan, this broad, expensive reach would waste scarce cash.

Paid search and social media advertising: These channels reach people actively searching for accounting software and can be targeted at small-firm decision-makers, with measurable clicks and low entry cost. They suit a product whose 68% of surveyed clients already want 99.9% uptime and 57% rank data security first, because copy can highlight those features directly and be adjusted quickly using ticket data (310 down to 185 per month). The drawback is that costs rise with competition for keywords and results need skilled management NSD currently lacks given its cloud-engineering skills gap.

Technology trade conference sponsorship: This puts NSD in front of an audience of IT professionals and partners, generating high-quality leads and demonstration opportunities for automated testing. It is far cheaper than a national press campaign but reaches few small-firm buyers directly, so the 80,000-unit sales target would not be supported, and one event gives only a short-lived spike.

Recommendation: NSD should choose paid search and social media advertising. It is measurable, affordable and targets the exact clients in its 450-person research who value security and uptime. National press is rejected as expensive and untargeted; conference sponsorship is rejected as too narrow to drive 80,000 units. NSD should fund it from the $300,000 retained profit rather than adding debt.
    Keywords: $900,000, 80,000, 68%, 57%, 450, workforce of 60

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 8.5% rise in developer salaries and the 11.0% rise in cloud-server input costs will affect NSD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If NSD's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). Developer salary rise (8.5%): NSD employs a workforce of 60 and the insert does not state how many are developers or their hours, so no annual wage total can be invented. Even a partial pass-through would materially shrink the surplus covering $420,000 fixed costs.

Conclusion: The 11.0% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit, can add up to $123,200 a year on the stated assumptions and directly erodes the contribution that services the loan; the interest rise is only $4,500 at most and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity.

Cash that would have serviced debt can instead fund certification at $950 per employee for the 18 untrained staff, helping cut the 3.2% error rate, and can absorb a rise in processing costs.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral, so DLT's payment-platform assets are not at risk of repossession if the launch disappoints, unlike a bank loan. It also spreads ownership rather than concentrating debt risk with one lender, giving Daniel Okafor more room to invest in the 70,000-unit transaction base while fixed costs of $350,000 a year are covered. A bank loan would add interest payable, already $70 in 2025; the share issue avoids that burden entirely. The 7.2% salary inflation expected in the sector makes avoiding extra interest especially valuable to a 55-person firm.

--- STEM ---
Crestline Technology Group (CTG) is a public limited company in the digital services sector, employing a workforce of 72 across its regional operations. Founded in 2008 by Sofia Marchetti, it provides managed web hosting to small businesses and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership that delegates decisions to experienced engineers. CTG plans to invest $750,000 in a green data centre with automated server monitoring, financed by a $500,000 share issue and a $250,000 bank overdraft. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $32.00, and currently produces 85,000 units a year. CTG faces two problems: recurring server downtime during peak evening hours and 30 of 72 staff lacking cloud-security training.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CTG plans to fund part of its $750,000 green data centre with a bank overdraft. Explain two advantages for CTG of using a share issue rather than the overdraft.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue provides permanent capital with no compulsory monthly repayment or interest charge, so CTG can commit the $500,000 raised to the $750,000 green data centre without increasing the $250,000 bank overdraft. Money saved can be spent on certification at $1,050 per employee for the 30 untrained staff, helping address the downtime problem, and on absorbing a 10.3% rise in electricity costs.

Point 2: Equity requires no collateral, so CTG's hosting assets are not exposed to seizure if the data centre underperforms, whereas an overdraft is repayable on demand and could be withdrawn when 99.2% uptime slips. The share issue also spreads funding across shareholders rather than one bank, protecting Sofia Marchetti's ability to serve 85,000 units and the 66% of clients who demand 99.9% uptime without a lender dictating terms. With 10.3% electricity cost inflation expected, keeping cash uncommitted to overdraft interest is particularly useful for a 72-person firm.
    Keywords: share issue, $750,000, $500,000, $250,000, $480,000, bank overdraft
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to CTG's financing mix, hosting operations and expansion.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: CTG is promoting its new green hosting package. Consider print advertising in technology magazines, search-engine marketing, or partnerships with web-design agencies. Which should CTG choose? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Print advertising in technology magazines: Ads can explain the green data centre and build brand prestige with IT professionals, and print is tangible for a technical audience. However, costs are high, circulation is slow to convert and results cannot be measured. With $750,000 already earmarked and a $250,000 overdraft to manage, heavy magazine spend would divert cash from fixing the downtime behind 99.2% uptime.

Search-engine marketing: Paid search reaches firms actively looking for hosting, is measurable and can highlight 99.9% uptime and green hosting to the 66% and 58% of the 720 surveyed clients who value them. Partnerships with web-design agencies: Agencies already advise firms choosing hosting, so referral deals put CTG in front of qualified buyers at low cost and can offer 99.9% uptime as a joint selling point. This suits a 72-person firm and can be managed through a small partner team. The drawback is slower reach than paid search and sharing margin on a $32.00 price.

    Keywords: $750,000, 85,000, 66%, 58%, 720, workforce of 72
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Lists or describes promotional options with limited application to CTG. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in CTG's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in CTG's context and gives a justified recommendation explaining why magazine advertising and search marketing are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: CTG's uptime is 99.2% and 30 of its 72 staff lack cloud-security training. Explain two benefits for CTG of using laissez-faire leadership in its technical teams.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced engineers the freedom to diagnose and fix server downtime immediately, without waiting for approval from Sofia Marchetti. --- STEM ---
Apex Mobile Applications (APX) is a partnership in the mobile app development sector, employing a workforce of 40 across its product teams. Founded in 2015 by Marcus Bell, it designs productivity apps for small businesses and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership that consults developers before each release. APX plans to invest $680,000 in a new app-testing laboratory with automated crash-reporting, financed by $400,000 hire purchase and $280,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $27.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. APX faces two problems: a 1.9% app crash rate after updates and 12 of 40 staff lacking mobile-security training.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: APX plans to acquire part of its $680,000 app-testing laboratory through hire purchase. Explain two advantages for APX of using retained profit instead of hire purchase.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no hire-purchase interest or instalments, so APX can commit the $280,000 to the $680,000 laboratory without adding to fixed costs of $300,000 a year or to the $400,000 hire-purchase commitment. Cash saved can fund certification at $880 per employee for the 12 untrained staff and help reduce the 1.9% crash rate, protecting the $27.00 price.

Point 2: Using internal funds avoids the risk that the lab equipment is repossessed if repayments are missed, unlike hire purchase where ownership passes only at the end. It also preserves the partnership's decision-making independence, letting Marcus Bell change testing priorities as the 500-user survey (71% wanting offline access) evolves, without a finance company's conditions. Retained profit is therefore cheaper and lower-risk than hire purchase. With consumer app spending growing 4.8%, that freed cash can fund features the 71% of surveyed users want, such as offline access, rather than payments to a finance company.
    Keywords: retained profit, $680,000, $400,000, $280,000, $300,000, hire purchase
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to APX's financing decision, costs and laboratory investment.

Costs vary widely and results depend on influencer credibility, with little control over the message; for a 40-person partnership spending $680,000 on a testing lab, a large campaign would be risky.

Recommendation: APX should choose in-app referral rewards. They harness the 63% willing to recommend among 500 surveyed users and the 42,000-to-58,000 growth in active users, at low cost that can be funded from $280,000 retained profit rather than more hire purchase. Influencer campaigns are rejected as unpredictable and costly; paid search is rejected because competitive keywords and a skills gap would waste cash that is needed to cover $300,000 fixed costs. --- STEM ---
Vantage Digital Platforms (VDP) is a cooperative in the e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 2012 by Aisha Bello, it runs an online marketplace for small retailers and operates a flat structure with autocratic leadership. VDP plans to invest $600,000 in a new automated fulfilment warehouse with digital stock control, financed by a $350,000 bank loan and $250,000 from the sale of assets. It has fixed costs of $390,000 a year, a variable cost of $13.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VDP plans to fund part of its $600,000 automated warehouse with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for VDP of using the bank loan rather than the sale of assets.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan lets VDP keep the assets it would otherwise sell, so the cooperative retains the resources needed to run its marketplace while investing $350,000 of the $600,000 in the automated warehouse. Selling assets would reduce the capacity serving 75,000 units, whereas the loan preserves the asset base that supports the 2.7% pick-error improvement programme.

Point 2: A loan provides the full sum immediately and can be repaid over time, while a sale of assets may take months and fetch less than expected in a downturn. This certainty helps Aisha Bello commit to digital stock control and training at $980 per employee for 24 staff without delaying the project. It leaves the 65-member cooperative in control of operations, provided the $390,000 fixed costs and interest can be met. With packaging and delivery costs expected to rise 9.4%, avoiding an asset sale also keeps the cooperative's earning assets in place to absorb that pressure.
    Keywords: bank loan, $600,000, $350,000, $250,000, $390,000, sale of assets
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to VDP's financing choice, operations and warehouse investment.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]

    Answer: Paid social media advertising: Social ads can reach many shoppers quickly and can target the 55% of the 640 surveyed who buy mainly on mobile. They are measurable but costs rise with competition and results depend on creative quality; for a cooperative committing $600,000 to a warehouse and servicing a $350,000 loan, unmeasured spend would be risky.

Email marketing to existing shoppers: Email is cheap, directly reaches known customers and can highlight the free returns wanted by 62% of respondents and faster delivery from the new warehouse. It is readily measurable through open and click rates. Its limitation is that it cannot reach new shoppers beyond the existing list, so it may not grow the 75,000-unit base on its own.

Discount vouchers with influencers: Influencer vouchers can create buzz and attract new, younger shoppers, and can be tied to 62% preferring free returns. However, discounts cut the $28.00 price and $15.00 contribution, influencer fees are uncertain, and a 65-person cooperative has little experience managing such campaigns.

Recommendation: VDP should choose email marketing to existing shoppers. It is low-cost, measurable and matches the research insight that 62% want free returns and 55% buy on mobile, with funds better kept for the $600,000 warehouse. Paid social is rejected as competitive and costly; influencer vouchers are rejected because discounts would erode contribution needed to cover $390,000 fixed costs and the bank loan.     Keywords: $600,000, 75,000, 62%, 55%, 640, workforce of 65
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Lists or describes promotional options with limited application to VDP. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in VDP's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in VDP's context and gives a justified recommendation explaining why social advertising and influencer vouchers are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: VDP has a 2.7% pick-error rate and 24 of its 65 staff lack digital stock-control training. Explain two benefits for VDP of using autocratic leadership in the warehouse.
    Answer: Point 1: Autocratic leadership sets one clear picking procedure for all staff, directly targeting the 2.7% pick-error rate, down from 4.1% a year earlier, and helping complaints stay below 88 per month.     Question: VDP must train 24 staff in digital stock control. Consider on-the-job coaching or external training at $980 per employee. Which should VDP choose? Justify your decision.

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VDP's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed for 2024 and 2025. Has VDP's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
