--- STEM ---
Kestrel Brook Vineyards (KBV) is a private limited company in the wine and beverage sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2007 by Rowan Kestrel, it now supplies bottled wine to national supermarket chains and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KBV plans to invest $720,000 in a new irrigation system and automated bottling line, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $245,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.20 a unit and a selling price of $16.20, and currently produces 60,000 units a year for its retail customers. KBV faces two operational problems: bottling-line defects of 2.4% and labour turnover of 9%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KBV plans to fund part of its bottling-line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KBV of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit is internally generated, so KBV pays no interest or capital repayments on the $270,000 used for the new irrigation system and automated bottling line. With fixed costs of $245,000 a year and a $450,000 bank loan already outstanding, avoiding another debt-service charge protects cash flow and the $7.00 contribution earned on each of 60,000 bottles. Every dollar saved in interest can instead absorb the 9.3% rise in glass and cork input costs, helping KBV hold its $16.20 selling price for national supermarket chains.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps ownership and control with founder Rowan Kestrel and the existing shareholders. A further bank loan could impose covenants and, if the 2.4% bottling defects persisted and sales slipped, the lender could demand repayment or secure company assets, putting the whole $720,000 investment at risk. Retained profit carries no such condition, so the flat, democratic management team can decide how to run the new line without external pressure, while the existing $450,000 facility stays available for working capital and the 9% labour-turnover problem can be addressed with training.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $270,000, $450,000, $245,000, bottling
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KBV's $270,000 retained profit, $450,000 loan, costs and defects.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KBV is launching its new sustainably bottled wine range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should KBV choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A nationwide TV campaign would build brand awareness quickly across all the supermarket chains stocking KBV's wine and could reach millions of buyers in one flight. The drawbacks are decisive for a 40-employee vineyard: airtime and production costs are very high relative to $245,000 fixed costs, and much of the audience drinks no premium wine or lives outside the distribution network, so spend is wasted. Funding it would also compete with the $450,000 bank loan repayments on the $720,000 bottling investment.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is much cheaper, targets KBV's core local catchment and suits time-sensitive messages about a new launch. Its reach is narrow, however; KBV supplies national supermarket chains and needs volume to sell 60,000 units a year, so regional listeners alone cannot create the demand required. It also cannot showcase the visual story of sustainable bottling as well as digital media.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can demonstrate the sustainable bottles directly to the 68% of 500 surveyed shoppers willing to pay up to $0.50 more and the 47% who check recycling, with measurable engagement at low cost per reached shopper and national reach. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but this option precisely matches the research evidence.

Recommendation: KBV should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact identified segment, costs far less than television, scales nationally unlike radio, and supports the premium price needed for a $7.00 contribution per unit. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; radio is rejected as too narrow for national supermarket distribution.
    Keywords: sustainably bottled, 68%, 47%, $0.50, 500, 60,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to KBV. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in KBV's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context and recommends influencer marketing, explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KBV's bottling-line defects are 2.4% and its labour turnover is 9%. Explain two benefits for KBV of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its production team.
    Answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 40 employees a real voice in how the new automated bottling line is run, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help set sealing routines and shift patterns are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking KBV's 9% labour turnover and reducing disruption to the 60,000-unit output plan. This suits the flat organisational structure and keeps decision-making close to the people handling the bottles.

Point 2: Consulting operators produces practical ideas for reducing the 2.4% defect rate, because those staff see the sealing machines daily. Involvement builds commitment, so fewer skilled workers leave and KBV avoids repeatedly spending $800 per employee on off-the-job courses for the 12 of 40 staff still needing training. Higher commitment also protects the $7.00 contribution per unit and the $720,000 investment by keeping quality stable while the new line beds in, rather than relying on autocratic instructions that can breed resentment.
    Keywords: democratic leadership, 2.4%, 9%, workforce of 40, 12 of 40, $800
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to KBV's 2.4% defects, 9% turnover and training costs.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: KBV must upskill 12 production staff to operate the new bottling machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should KBV choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching at the bottling line is directly relevant to KBV's own machines and quality standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 12 staff productive while they learn. This protects the 15,000 units packed last quarter and the effort already made to cut defects from 3.6% to 2.4%. The weaknesses are that trainers are themselves production workers whose output suffers, bad habits may be passed on, and there is little formal certification, which could matter if supermarket auditors request records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $800 per employee costs $9,600 for all 12 staff — small beside the $720,000 investment — and provides structured, up-to-date skills with a recognised certificate. It also removes 12 of 40 workers from the line for a period, cutting short-term capacity and risking the 9% labour-turnover situation worsening; the generic content may not match KBV's exact machine settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: KBV should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with short college top-ups later for senior operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids further output loss while defects are still 2.4%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $9,600 and withdrawing 12 staff from a 40-person workforce would disrupt supermarket deliveries; college sessions can be added once the line is stable.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $800, $720,000, 12 of 40, 2.4%

    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KBV's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KBV's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.58 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.92 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $110,000 trade receivables + $38,000 cash = $298,000; 2025 current assets = $132,000 + $128,000 + $55,000 = $315,000. Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. However, trade receivables increased from $110,000 to $128,000, tying up cash with supermarket customers, and cash of $55,000 is still small relative to $200,000 liabilities, so a late payment could weaken the position quickly.

Conclusion: KBV's liquidity has improved. Both measures are higher and the improvement does not rely on inventories, though rising receivables mean management should tighten credit control before further borrowing.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KBV of offering sustainably bottled wine.

    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.3% rise in glass and cork input costs will affect KBV. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.

--- STEM ---
Thornfield Dairy Produce (TDP) is a cooperative in the dairy-processing sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 1998 by Marta Thornfield, it supplies cheese and yoghurt to regional supermarket chains and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TDP plans to invest $960,000 in a new cheese-making and cold-storage facility on its existing site, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year for its retail customers. TDP faces two operational problems: milk-spoilage waste of 4.1% and absenteeism of 8% among production staff.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TDP plans to fund part of its cold-storage expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TDP of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit of $360,000 needs no interest payments or capital repayments, so TDP avoids adding debt-service costs to fixed costs of $360,000 a year while it already carries a $600,000 bank loan. The cash saved can be spent on reducing the 4.1% milk-spoilage waste or on training the 18 of 65 staff still needing induction on the pasteuriser, protecting the $6.00 contribution earned on each of 90,000 units.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps decision-making inside the cooperative and avoids conditions a lender might attach to a $600,000 facility, such as limits on further borrowing or security over the new cold store. Because TDP has autocratic leadership in a hierarchical structure, using internally generated funds lets Marta Thornfield and the committee control the $960,000 project without external interference, and no extra interest exposure arises if the 8% absenteeism rate temporarily reduces output. Retaining profit also avoids the risk that a lender calls in the loan if sales dip.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $360,000, $600,000, $960,000, cooperative
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TDP's $360,000 retained profit, loan, waste and staffing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: TDP is launching a new farm-assured cheese range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TDP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: A TV advert could reach millions and quickly build awareness of the farm-assured label across the country. For a 65-member cooperative with $360,000 fixed costs, however, production and airtime charges are high and much of the audience buys no cheese or lies outside the regional supermarket catchment, so a large share of the spend is wasted. It would also compete with repayments on the $600,000 loan funding the $960,000 cold store.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is affordable, reaches the core shoppers near TDP's supermarkets and works well for a time-limited launch message. Its clear limitation is reach: TDP needs to sell 90,000 units a year, and local listeners alone cannot generate that volume; radio also cannot show the farm-assured and animal-welfare story visually.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can explain animal-welfare credentials to the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.35 more and the 55% who check welfare labels, at low cost per person reached and with measurable engagement. Results build gradually and depend on influencer credibility, but the targeting matches the research precisely.

    Keywords: farm-assured, 61%, 55%, $0.35, 750, 90,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited TDP context. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in TDP's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options and recommends influencer marketing, explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: TDP's milk-spoilage waste is 4.1% and absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for TDP of using team working to address these problems.
    Answer: Point 1: Team working lets the 65 employees share responsibility for spoilage, so workers can check each other's handling of milk and immediately spot practices that cause the 4.1% waste rate. Because staff closest to the pasteuriser understand the causes, group problem-solving can protect the $6.00 contribution on each of 90,000 units more effectively than hierarchical instructions alone, reducing waste without spending more on the $960,000 facility.

Point 2: Working in teams gives members social support and a sense of belonging, which can improve morale and reduce the 8% absenteeism rate. Lower absence means fewer disruptions to the 24,000 units packed each quarter and less need to retrain staff; with 18 of 65 workers still to complete on-the-job training at $950 a head for college courses, stability lowers training costs and helps maintain the cooperative's delivery schedule to regional supermarkets.
    Keywords: 4.1%, 8%, workforce of 65, 18 of 65, $950, $960,000

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TDP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TDP's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.38 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.58 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.88 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $42,000 cash = $317,000; 2025 current assets = $150,000 + $120,000 + $70,000 = $340,000. Dividing by $230,000 and $215,000 current liabilities gives 1.38 and 1.58. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($317,000 − $180,000) ÷ $230,000 = 0.60; 2025 = ($340,000 − $150,000) ÷ $215,000 = 0.88.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. The current ratio rose from 1.38 to 1.58 as current assets increased by $23,000 and current liabilities fell by $15,000, giving a stronger cushion for paying suppliers. The acid test rose from 0.60 to 0.88, and this is the stronger evidence of genuine improvement because it removes $180,000 of stock in 2024 and $150,000 in 2025; with milk-spoilage waste at 4.1%, some inventories may be slow to sell. Cash rose from $42,000 to $70,000, which helps the cooperative meet bills while servicing a $600,000 loan. The concern is that trade receivables climbed from $95,000 to $120,000, so cash is tied up with supermarkets, and the acid test below 1 means TDP still cannot cover all current liabilities without stock.

Conclusion: TDP's liquidity has improved, since both ratios are higher and the gain does not come from holding more inventory. However, the acid test of 0.88 shows the improvement is incomplete, so the cooperative should chase outstanding receivables before borrowing further for the $960,000 facility.

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.5% rise in feed and milk input costs will affect TDP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): On a variable-rate $600,000 ten-year loan the extra charge is 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). This is small compared with $360,000 fixed costs, and zero if the rate is fixed. The rise may make consumers more cautious and dearer future borrowing, but TDP can limit the effect by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.02 an hour): With a workforce of 65 this affects many pay packets and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours or individual wages, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. The defensible check is labour productivity: 90,000 units ÷ 65 staff = roughly 1,385 units each, so the increase is sustainable only if that productivity is maintained or output rises, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $6.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (11.5% feed and milk): The $8.00 variable cost is not broken down in the insert, so only an illustrative bound is honest: if the whole $8.00 rose 11.5%, that is $0.92 a unit (0.115 × $8.00), or $82,800 a year across 90,000 units. Even a partial pass-through would sharply cut contribution, though the $0.35 farm-assured premium and 4.0% demand growth can offset some of it.

Conclusion: The 11.5% rise in feed and milk costs will have the greatest impact because it hits every unit produced and directly threatens the $6.00 contribution backing the $960,000 investment. The interest effect is a known $4,500 and the wage effect depends on unstated hours, whereas input inflation is large, continuous and harder to pass on quickly.

--- STEM ---
Sunridge Citrus Ranch (SCR) is a partnership in the citrus-growing and fresh-produce sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2011 by Elena Sunridge, it supplies fresh citrus to national fruit wholesalers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. SCR plans to invest $540,000 in a new packing and cold-storage shed, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and currently produces 50,000 units a year for its wholesalers. SCR faces two problems: a blemish defect rate of 3.3% and labour turnover of 11%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SCR plans to fund part of its packing-shed expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SCR of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit of $240,000 requires no interest or repayment, so the partnership avoids increasing debt service on top of the $300,000 bank loan while meeting fixed costs of $180,000 a year. The saving can fund better grading to tackle the 3.3% blemish rate and protects the $6.00 contribution on each of 50,000 units sold to wholesalers.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids lender conditions and keeps control with founder Elena Sunridge and the partners. If the 11% labour turnover held back the harvest, a bank could seek repayment or security over the new shed, endangering the $540,000 project; internally generated cash has no such risk. Retained profit can also be deployed immediately for the 9 of 30 staff needing training, unlike a loan whose drawdown depends on approval, and it leaves the existing $300,000 facility untouched for seasonal working capital.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $240,000, $300,000, $540,000, partnership
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to SCR's $240,000 retained profit, loan, defects and turnover.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: SCR is promoting its new locally grown citrus range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SCR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: Television could rapidly create awareness of locally grown citrus among millions of shoppers nation-wide. For a 30-worker partnership facing $180,000 fixed costs, however, airtime and production are expensive and a large fraction of viewers buy no fresh citrus or are beyond the wholesaler network, making much of the spend wasteful. It would also compete with repayments on the $300,000 loan used for the $540,000 shed.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is cheap and reaches the communities near SCR's orchards, and it suits a short seasonal campaign. Its weakness is coverage: SCR supplies national fruit wholesalers and must move 50,000 units a year, so local listeners alone cannot drive enough volume, and radio cannot show the fruit's appearance or origin labels.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can show the origin story to the 72% of 400 surveyed buyers who would pay $0.30 more for locally grown citrus and the 58% checking origin labels, at low cost per reached buyer with measurable responses. Results take time to build and depend on influencer trust, but the match to the research is strong.

Recommendation: SCR should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the identified buyers nationally, costs far less than television and supports the premium underpinning the $6.00 contribution per unit. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; radio is rejected because its reach is too narrow for national wholesale contracts.
    Keywords: locally grown, 72%, 58%, $0.30, 400, 50,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited SCR context. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in SCR's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options and recommends influencer marketing, explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q3(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HSP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HSP's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.62 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.97 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $160,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $425,000; 2025 current assets = $185,000 + $195,000 + $82,000 = $462,000. Dividing by $300,000 and $285,000 current liabilities gives 1.42 and 1.62. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($425,000 − $210,000) ÷ $300,000 = 0.72; 2025 = ($462,000 − $185,000) ÷ $285,000 = 0.97.

Evaluation: Liquidity is stronger in both measures. The current ratio rose from 1.42 to 1.62 as current assets grew by $37,000 and current liabilities fell by $15,000, giving more cover for short-term obligations while HSP services a $700,000 loan. The acid test rising from 0.72 to 0.97 is the stronger evidence of genuine improvement because it excludes $210,000 of stock in 2024 and $185,000 in 2025, which for frozen seafood could be slow to realise if the 3.8% defect rate persists. Cash increased from $55,000 to $82,000, adding flexibility. The reservation is that trade receivables rose from $160,000 to $195,000 with supermarkets, tying up cash, and the acid test still remains below 1, so HSP is not yet able to cover all current debts without inventory.

Conclusion: HSP's liquidity has improved, since both ratios are higher and the progress is not dependent on building stock. However, receivables growth and an acid test of 0.97 mean the company should tighten credit control before further borrowing for the $1,200,000 plant.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]

  Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.35%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 13.1% rise in fish and energy input costs will affect HSP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.6% to 5.35%): On a variable-rate $700,000 ten-year loan the extra annual cost is 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250 (0.0075 × $700,000), modest beside $480,000 fixed costs and zero if the loan is fixed. Higher rates may also cool consumer spending on frozen seafood and make future finance dearer, but fixing the rate can mostly neutralise this.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $14.27 an hour): The workforce of 120 means this feeds directly into the wage bill and cannot be refused. Because the insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, a valid annual wage total cannot be invented. The sound comparison is productivity: 120,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 1,000 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if that productivity is maintained or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost reduces the $6.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (13.1% fish and energy): The $7.50 variable cost is not decomposed, so only an illustrative bound is honest: if the whole $7.50 rose 13.1%, that adds $0.98 a unit (0.131 × $7.50), about $117,600 a year at 120,000 units. Even partial pass-through would materially reduce contribution, though the $0.45 sustainability premium and 2.6% demand growth recover some.

Conclusion: The 13.1% rise in fish and energy input costs will have the greatest impact: it applies to every unit and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution supporting the $1,200,000 investment. The interest effect is a known $5,250 and the wage effect depends on unstated hours, whereas input inflation is large, continuous and difficult to offset quickly.

--- STEM ---
Millgrove Grain Kitchens (MGK) is a sole trader in the cereal and grain-milling sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2003 by Owen Millgrove, it supplies breakfast cereals to regional food retailers and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MGK plans to invest $840,000 in a new grain mill and packaging line, financed by a $520,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.25 a unit and a selling price of $12.25, and currently produces 75,000 units a year for its regional retail customers. MGK faces two problems: waste of 4.6% and absenteeism of 7%.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MGK plans to fund part of its mill expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MGK of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit of $320,000 requires no interest or instalments, so the sole trader avoids piling debt service on fixed costs of $300,000 a year while already owing $520,000 to the bank. The cash saved can attack the 4.6% waste rate and protect the $6.00 contribution earned on each of 75,000 cereal units, improving the return on the $840,000 mill investment.

Point 2: Internal funding keeps ownership and decisions with founder Owen Millgrove and avoids bank covenants or security over the new mill. If the 7% absence rate held back output, a lender might demand repayment, whereas retained profit carries no such threat. Because MGK has democratic leadership in a hierarchical structure, the owner can consult staff on how to use the $320,000 immediately for the 14 of 55 workers needing training, while leaving the $520,000 loan available for seasonal working capital rather than increasing borrowing.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $320,000, $520,000, $840,000, sole trader
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to MGK's $320,000 retained profit, loan, waste and staffing.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: MGK is launching its new wholegrain cereal range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should MGK choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television campaign: Television could build quick, mass awareness of wholegrain cereals across all regional retailers. The cost is high and a substantial share of viewers buys no cereal or lives outside the delivery area, so much of the spend is wasted. For a 55-worker sole trader with $300,000 fixed costs and a $520,000 loan, that money is better spent reducing 4.6% waste and supporting the $840,000 mill than on expensive airtime.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is cheap and reaches MGK's local catchment with a short launch message. Its reach is limited relative to the 75,000-unit output and the regional retailer network, and radio cannot show the wholegrain product or fibre message as clearly as visual media, so it cannot drive the required volume alone.

Social media influencer marketing: Influencers can demonstrate fibre benefits to the 70% of 650 surveyed shoppers willing to pay $0.40 more and the 54% checking fibre content, with precise targeting, national reach and measurable engagement at modest cost. Results build slowly and rely on credibility, but the fit with survey evidence is the closest.

Recommendation: MGK should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the identified shoppers nationally, costs far less than television and supports the premium behind the $6.00 contribution per unit. Television is rejected as costly and wasteful; radio is rejected because it cannot deliver enough reach for regional retailer listings.
    Keywords: wholegrain, 70%, 54%, $0.40, 650, 75,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited MGK context. | level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in MGK's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options and recommends influencer marketing, explaining why television and radio are rejected.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: MGK's waste is 4.6% and absenteeism is 7%. Explain two benefits for MGK of using job rotation to motivate its production team.
    Answer: Point 1: Job rotation moves the 55 workers between milling and packing tasks, reducing repetition and boredom and encouraging staff to spot waste at each stage. That can lower the 4.6% waste rate and protect the $6.00 contribution on 75,000 units, making better use of the $840,000 mill without extra capital. Staff who understand several processes can cover for absent colleagues, limiting disruption from the 7% absence rate.

Point 2: Rotation develops a more versatile workforce and raises morale because employees gain new skills and variety, which supports MGK's democratic leadership. Higher motivation can reduce absence and the need to retrain the 14 of 55 staff still needing on-the-job training, where college courses cost $850 each. --- STEM ---
Kestrel Tooling Industries (KTI) is a private limited company in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2011 by Eleanor Kestrel, the firm manufactures tungsten-carbide cutting tools for aerospace and automotive clients across the region and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KTI plans to invest $820,000 in a new CNC tool-grinding cell, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $370,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: KTI plans to fund part of its $820,000 CNC grinding-cell investment with retained profit rather than the $450,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for KTI of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or capital repayments, so KTI avoids adding debt-service costs to its $264,000 a year fixed costs at a time when it already has a $450,000 ten-year bank loan commitment. Every dollar kept inside the business can instead absorb the 9.8% rise in tungsten and cobalt alloy costs, protecting the $6.00 contribution earned on each of its 80,000 cutting tools without pushing the $13.50 selling price higher for aerospace and automotive buyers.

Point 2: Using $370,000 of retained profit leaves ownership and control with Eleanor Kestrel and avoids the collateral and conditions a lender would attach to the new CNC cell. With the defect rate at 2.2% and skilled operators scarce, KTI's managers can reinvest quickly in grinding adjustments and on-the-job training without seeking lender approval. This flexibility suits its flat organisational structure and helps honour the preference of the 58% of surveyed buyers who would pay $0.50 more for precision-ground tools, supporting the launch of the new range while the automated cell beds in.

In 2025 the corresponding assets were $110,000 + $185,000 + $75,000 = $370,000; $370,000 ÷ $230,000 gives the 2025 measure. For the stock-excluding measure the 2024 numerator is $350,000 − $140,000 = $210,000 and $210,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.84; in 2025 $370,000 − $110,000 = $260,000 and $260,000 ÷ $230,000 = 1.13.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The 2024 figure of 1.40 rose to 1.61 as current assets grew while current liabilities fell from $250,000 to $230,000. More importantly the stock-excluding figure rose from 0.84 to 1.13, so KTI no longer depends on selling inventory to meet short-term debts — valuable while it funds an $820,000 cell. However, trade receivables climbed from $160,000 to $185,000, tying up cash; if aerospace buyers pay late the improvement could unravel, and inventories fell to $110,000, which may limit supply during peak orders.

Conclusion: KTI's financial position has improved. Both the 2024–2025 measures (1.40 to 1.61 and 0.84 to 1.13) show stronger short-term solvency, and the gain is not driven by stock. The residual risk is higher receivables, so KTI should tighten credit control before committing further capital.

For a 40-employee firm, the $820,000 expansion makes dependable short-term liquidity especially important, so KTI should keep monitoring its cash balance as receivables settle.
    Keywords: 1.40, 1.61, 0.84, 1.13, $350,000, $370,000, $820,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current and acid test measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether KTI's position improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KTI of introducing automated optical inspection for its cutting tools.
    Answer: Advantage: Automated optical inspection checks every tool far faster than manual viewing and can cut the current 2.2% defect rate toward the 3.6% benchmark it improved from, protecting the $6.00 contribution on each of the 80,000 units and the reputation behind the 58% of buyers willing to pay $0.50 more.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in tungsten and cobalt input costs will affect KTI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If KTI's $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, an illustrative full 0.75 percentage-point increase would add 0.0075 × $450,000 = $3,375 a year — small beside $264,000 fixed costs; the insert does not state the loan's rate type, so on a fixed rate the direct effect is zero. Higher rates may still discourage aerospace clients from expanding and raise the cost of any future borrowing.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.72 an hour): KTI employs 40 operators and the wage rise feeds into its wage bill, but the insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so no annual total can be invented honestly. The defensible test is productivity: 80,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 2,000 units per worker, so a higher wage is affordable only if productivity holds at that level or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $6.00 contribution per unit.

Input cost inflation (9.8% tungsten and cobalt): The $7.50 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is honest — if the whole variable cost rose 9.8% it would add 0.098 × $7.50 = $0.735 a unit, or about 80,000 × $0.735 = $58,800 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution and threatens the 44,000-unit break-even, though the $0.50 premium accepted by 58% of buyers offers partial recovery.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 80,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $820,000 cell, and it cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate. The interest-rate effect is a bounded $3,375 at most, and the wage effect depends on productivity, so both are smaller and more manageable than pervasive input inflation.
    Keywords: 5.0%, 5.5%, 9.8%, interest rate, $450,000, $7.50, $13.72

--- STEM ---
Rothermere Marine Instruments (RMI) is a partnership in the marine electronics sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by senior partner Innes Rothermere, the firm produces navigation displays and depth gauges for commercial fishing and leisure boats, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. RMI plans to invest $760,000 in a new display-assembly line, financed by $360,000 retained profit and $400,000 through hire purchase. It has fixed costs of $245,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. RMI faces two operational problems: a defect rate of 3.4% on assembled displays and longer delivery times, with labour turnover rising among test technicians.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: RMI plans to finance $400,000 of its $760,000 display-assembly line through hire purchase rather than retained profit. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RMI of using hire purchase.
    Answer: Advantage: Hire purchase spreads the $400,000 cost of the new display-assembly line into manageable instalments, so RMI can install the equipment now and begin producing displays rather than waiting to build up cash. This preserves the $360,000 retained profit for working capital and helps a 50-person partnership protect its $15.00 selling price and the $7.00 contribution on each of 70,000 units while it tackles the 3.4% defect rate.

Disadvantage: Hire purchase is more expensive overall than paying cash because interest is built into the instalments, raising the true cost of the $760,000 investment and adding a fixed commitment alongside $245,000 a year of fixed costs. If delivery times lengthen and cash is tied up in the 16,800 displays built last quarter, missed instalments could put the equipment at risk, reducing Innes Rothermere's control over the new line.

The partnership can therefore keep the $7.00 contribution on 70,000 displays intact while it fixes the 3.4% defect rate, rather than spending part of each sale on hire-purchase interest.
    Keywords: hire purchase, $760,000, $400,000, $360,000, retained profit, $245,000, 4.75%

It avoids print and exhibition costs and supports the launch after the 5.6-day delivery problem is fixed, though it needs digital skills and steady web traffic to deliver sales.

Recommendation: RMI should choose e-commerce through a new website. It reaches buyers cost-effectively, answers warranty questions and can be measured against the 70,000-unit target. Magazines are rejected as narrow and unmeasurable; the boat show is rejected as short-lived and expensive. RMI can add a small show presence once online demand is proven.

This top-down control suits a partnership whose senior partner must coordinate commercial and leisure customers quickly.

Point 2: Autocratic leadership enables fast decisions to clear the 5.6-day delivery backlog, for example by reallocating the 12 of 50 technicians still awaiting on-the-job training to the test rigs or authorising overtime, without lengthy consultation. Under Taylor's ideas of clear method and supervision, quicker decisions protect the $7.00 contribution on 70,000 units, though RMI should watch that rising labour turnover among technicians is not made worse by a directive style.

In a partnership the senior partner remains accountable to the other owners, so a clear chain of command also makes it easier to explain to clients why delivery times have stretched to 5.6 days and what is being done about it, supporting the 61% of surveyed owners who would pay $0.60 more for a waterproof display.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: RMI must strengthen its testing team to cut the 3.4% defect rate. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment. Which should RMI choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: Internal recruitment: Promoting an existing assembly worker into testing is cheap, quick and low-risk because RMI already knows the person's reliability and they understand the 16,800 displays built each quarter. Decision: RMI should choose external recruitment for the specialist testing roles. The technical skill gap is the direct cause of the defect problem, and internal promotion alone cannot close it; internal recruitment is rejected as too limited in skill, while short external courses at $640 can then update the whole team. RMI should still use internal promotion for supervisory positions to keep morale high.

RMI should also set a probation period with a practical test on the new rigs so the 3.4% defect rate is actually reduced, and combine it with the $640 certification courses for existing staff. Without such checks, hiring an outsider would raise costs without fixing the 5.6-day delivery problem, and the partnership would gain little from the decision.

--- STEM ---
Portview Valves & Fittings (PVF) is a public limited company in the industrial fluid-control sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 1999 by Jonas Portview, who remains chief executive, it makes brass valves and pipe fittings for water utilities and chemical plants, and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. PVF plans to invest $1,100,000 in an automated valve-testing facility, financed by a $700,000 new share issue and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: PVF plans to raise $700,000 through a new share issue to fund its $1,100,000 valve-testing facility. Explain two advantages for PVF of a share issue compared with a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue brings in $700,000 of permanent capital with no interest charges or compulsory repayments, so PVF does not add debt service to its $360,000 a year fixed costs while it equips the $1,100,000 testing facility. That protects the $8.00 contribution on each of 90,000 valves and leaves the $400,000 retained profit free for working capital as utility clients demand more reliable deliveries.

Point 2: Because PVF is a public limited company, a share issue can raise a large sum from many investors and spread the risk of the new facility beyond Jonas Portview's existing shareholders. Unlike borrowing, there is no collateral to pledge and no lender covenants, giving management freedom to set testing standards and respond to the 2.8% defect rate, while the 66% of surveyed buyers willing to pay $0.80 more for certified valves offer a return that can justify the new investment.

Shareholders also expect a return through dividends or rising value, so PVF must earn that $8.00 contribution on enough of its 90,000 units to keep the share price stable.
    Keywords: share issue, $700,000, $1,100,000, retained profit, $360,000, $400,000, public limited company

Detailed workings: In 2024 current assets were $210,000 inventories + $240,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $520,000, and $520,000 ÷ $350,000 current liabilities gives the 2024 measure. In 2025 the corresponding assets were $180,000 + $265,000 + $95,000 = $540,000, and $540,000 ÷ $330,000 gives the 2025 measure. The concern is trade receivables rising from $240,000 to $265,000; if utility clients pay slowly, the stronger position could weaken, and lower inventories of $180,000 may need watching given 6.2-day lead times.

Conclusion: PVF's financial position has improved. Both the 2024–2025 measures (1.49 to 1.64 and 0.89 to 1.09) rose and the gain does not rely on stock. The residual risk is higher receivables, so tighter credit control should accompany the new investment.

Solstice Battery Systems (SBS) is a private limited company in the rechargeable battery manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2014 by Priya Solstice, it builds lithium-ion battery packs for forklifts and grid-storage units and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. SBS plans to invest $940,000 in a battery cell assembly line with an on-site recycling unit, financed by $500,000 venture capital and $440,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. SBS faces two operational problems: a defect rate of 3.1% in cell welding and rising waste from rejected packs.

  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: SBS plans to raise $500,000 of venture capital for its $940,000 assembly line. Explain two advantages for SBS of venture capital over a bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Venture capital does not require the regular interest and capital repayments of a bank loan, so SBS can direct its $440,000 retained profit and the $500,000 raised into the $940,000 assembly line without adding debt service to $320,000 a year fixed costs. That protects the $8.00 contribution on 80,000 battery packs while the 3.1% welding defect rate is being reduced.

Point 2: A venture capital investor usually brings sector expertise and contacts as well as money, which can help Priya Solstice recruit recycling technicians and reach grid-storage clients for the 63% of 410 surveyed buyers who would pay $0.70 more for recyclable packs. The risk of the new line is shared with the investor rather than borne by SBS alone, and there is no collateral to pledge, unlike a loan secured on the company's assets.

That matters because the 3.1% welding defect rate on 18,400 packs a quarter already wastes materials, and debt service would reduce the cash available for recycling-technician courses at $860 each.

--- STEM ---
Nordic Precision Bearings (NPB) is a worker cooperative in the precision engineering sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2007 by Anders Nord, it manufactures sealed ball bearings for wind turbines and machine tools and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. NPB plans to invest $880,000 in a robotic bearing-grinding line, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $400,000 of member share capital. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and currently produces 96,000 units a year. --- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: NPB plans to raise $480,000 through a bank loan for its $880,000 grinding line. Explain two disadvantages for NPB of using a bank loan rather than member share capital.
    Answer: Point 1: A bank loan requires interest and capital repayments, so at a base rate raised to 4.9% the $480,000 borrowing adds a fixed financial burden on top of $288,000 a year operating costs. That drains cash which could otherwise cover the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 bearings and fund on-the-job training for the 11 of 48 members still learning the grinding robots.

Point 2: Lenders commonly require collateral and impose conditions, which can reduce the autonomy of a worker cooperative and put its assets at risk if the 2.6% defect rate delays returns from the $880,000 line. Member share capital of $400,000 carries no such fixed claim and keeps decision-making inside the cooperative, whereas a lender may restrict further borrowing or demand priority repayment, limiting NPB's flexibility on quality investment and the $710 robotics courses.

Interest on the $480,000 loan would also compete with the $710 robotics courses needed for the 11 of 48 members still in training, so member share capital, despite diluting ownership, better fits a cooperative's long-term aims.

    Answer: Calculations:

Current Ratio 2025 = 1.62 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.05 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.90 : 1

Detailed workings: In 2024 current assets were $130,000 inventories + $170,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $360,000, and $360,000 ÷ $220,000 current liabilities gives the 2024 measure. In 2025 the corresponding assets were $180,000 + $180,000 + $45,000 = $405,000, and $405,000 ÷ $250,000 gives the 2025 measure. For the stock-excluding measure the 2024 numerator is $360,000 − $130,000 = $230,000, and $230,000 ÷ $220,000 = 1.05; in 2025 $405,000 − $180,000 = $225,000 and $225,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.90.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. The broad coverage measure edged down from 1.64 to 1.62 as current liabilities rose from $220,000 to $250,000 and cash fell from $60,000 to $45,000. The stock-excluding measure fell more sharply, from 1.05 to 0.90, because inventories built up from $130,000 to $180,000; NPB is relying more on selling bearings from stock to meet short-term debts while servicing a $480,000 bank loan. Receivables have also risen to $180,000, so if equipment buyers pay late the position could worsen further.

Conclusion: NPB's financial position has not improved; it has deteriorated. Both the 2024–2025 measures (1.64 to 1.62 and 1.05 to 0.90) fell, with the sharpest decline in the measure that excludes stock. NPB should run down excess inventory and tighten credit control before adding to its borrowing.

With $480,000 of bank-loan commitments, NPB should prioritise rebuilding its cash balance before further borrowing, because the current position leaves little room for a delay in receiving the $180,000 owed by customers.

    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NPB of introducing computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) on its grinding line.
    Answer: Advantage: CAM can grind bearings to tighter, repeatable tolerances, cutting the 2.6% defect rate on the 23,200 bearings finished last quarter and protecting the $6.00 contribution on 96,000 units. Disadvantage: CAM adds capital cost to the $880,000 already committed and raises fixed costs above $288,000 a year, pushing the 48,000-unit break-even higher if wind-turbine orders dip.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.9%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in bearing-steel input costs will affect NPB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.1% to 4.9%): NPB has a $480,000 bank loan, but the insert does not state whether it is variable-rate, so any direct figure is only an illustrative bound: a full 0.8 percentage-point rise on $480,000 is 0.008 × $480,000 = $3,840 a year. That is modest next to $288,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the effect is zero; higher rates may still slow wind-turbine investment.

Minimum wage increase (5.2%, to $13.78 an hour): The cooperative employs 48 members and the rise lifts wage costs, but the insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual total cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 96,000 units ÷ 48 members = 2,000 units per worker. A higher wage is affordable only if productivity holds; otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $6.00 contribution.

Bearing-steel cost inflation (8.7%): The $6.00 variable cost is not decomposed, so only a bound is possible — if the whole variable cost rose 8.7% it would add 0.087 × $6.00 = $0.522 a unit, or 96,000 × $0.522 = $50,112 a year. Even a partial rise raises the 48,000-unit break-even, though the $0.45 premium accepted by 59% of buyers offers some recovery.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in bearing-steel costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 96,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution needed to service the $880,000 grinding line. The interest effect is at most a bounded $3,840 and the wage effect depends on productivity, so neither matches the reach of material inflation.

--- STEM ---
Zephyr Quay Fashion (ZQF) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2013 by Nadia Zephyr, the business sells apparel through its own e-commerce site and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ZQF plans to invest $720,000 in an automated e-commerce fulfilment and returns-processing centre, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.20 a unit and a selling price of $15.20, and produces 72,000 units a year. ZQF faces two problems: its online return rate has climbed to 18% and picking errors are rising, while late deliveries are damaging customer ratings.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: ZQF plans to fund part of its $720,000 fulfilment-centre expansion with a $420,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for ZQF of using its $300,000 retained profit instead of that loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Using the $300,000 retained profit costs ZQF no interest or capital repayments, so its cash flow is protected while it already carries $216,000 of fixed costs and an 18% return rate that ties up working capital. Every dollar not paid as loan interest stays inside the business to fund the picking-accuracy fixes needed after the 2.1% picking error rate and the rise in complaints from 46 to 71 a month. That protects the $7.00 contribution per unit earned on 72,000 units sold at $15.20 each, which is the cash the $720,000 expansion depends on.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk. If the new automated returns-processing centre fails to cut the 18% return rate, a lender could still demand repayment of the $420,000 bank loan, putting the jobs of the 40 staff and Nadia Zephyr's control at risk. Internal funding imposes no lender conditions and leaves the loan facility untouched as a reserve for a sudden spike in returns or the late-delivery problem. It also signals to staff that growth is being paid for out of trading success rather than debt, which supports morale in a flat structure where democratic leadership relies on trust.
    Keywords: retained profit, $720,000, $420,000, $300,000, 18%, $216,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to ZQF's financing, returns problem and contribution data.

    Question: ZQF is launching a faster-delivery service for its online fashion range. Consider national television advertising, paid search advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should ZQF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: National television advertising: A TV campaign would build mass awareness of the faster-delivery promise across the whole country, which could help ZQF win shoppers beyond its current customer base. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a 40-person e-commerce business already funding a $720,000 expansion with a $420,000 loan, and much of the audience does not buy online fashion. Given that market research of 500 shoppers found 68% value fast delivery, a broad TV message would waste spend on the 32% who do not, and it cannot demonstrate the 3.8-day delivery claim credibly.

Paid search advertising: Buying search terms such as 'next-day fashion delivery' reaches shoppers at the moment they are ready to buy, and spend can be capped and measured against orders. It directly targets the 68% who value fast delivery and can be switched off if the 18% return rate makes sales unprofitable. Its weakness is that it only reaches people already searching, so it does little to build the brand or explain why ZQF's delivery is better, and competition for popular terms can push the cost per click up sharply.

Social media influencer marketing: Fashion influencers can demonstrate the faster-delivery service and the new apparel range to a targeted audience, generating engagement and trust that a search advert cannot. It speaks directly to the 57% of surveyed shoppers who would pay more for better service, and it can show real parcels arriving in 3.8 days. The drawback is slower, less predictable volume and a dependence on influencer credibility, but cost per reached shopper is low and content can be reused across the site.

Recommendation: ZQF should choose paid search advertising as the primary launch channel, supported by a small influencer campaign. Search captures buyers at the point of purchase and is measurable against the 2.1% picking-error and return concerns; influencers supplement it with proof. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm with $216,000 fixed costs and a $420,000 loan, and pure influencer marketing is rejected because its results are too slow to fill the new fulfilment centre.

Because the people handling the orders know where the 2.1% picking errors occur, their suggestions can be more practical than top-down rules, and involvement raises job satisfaction and commitment under Maslow's social and esteem needs. Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 + $94,000 + $62,000 = $366,000; 2025 current assets = $186,000 + $118,000 + $48,000 = $352,000. For 2024, $366,000 ÷ $180,000 = 2.03; for 2025, $352,000 ÷ $196,000 = 1.80. Excluding stock: 2024 ($366,000 − $210,000) ÷ $180,000 = $156,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.87; 2025 ($352,000 − $186,000) ÷ $196,000 = $166,000 ÷ $196,000 = 0.85.

Evaluation: Liquidity has deteriorated on both measures. Coverage of short-term obligations fell from 2.03 to 1.80 because current assets dropped by $14,000 while liabilities rose from $180,000 to $196,000. The stock-excluding measure also slipped, from 0.87 to 0.85, showing KBO is no more able to meet debts without selling inventory, a concern while it services a $600,000 loan and commits $900,000 to a warehouse. Cash fell from $62,000 to $48,000 and inventories from $210,000 to $186,000; receivables rose to $118,000, tying up cash. The buffer at 1.80 is still adequate, so the position is not critical.

Conclusion: KBO's financial position has not improved. Both measures fell and the stock-excluding measure also weakened, so the decline is not explained by inventory alone. KBO should tighten credit control over the higher receivables and rebuild cash before drawing further on debt.
    Keywords: 2.03, 1.80, 0.87, 0.85, $366,000, $352,000, $900,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations. | level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend. | level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion that the position has not improved.

  Q4(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KBO of switching to responsibly sourced materials for its outdoor clothing.
    Answer: Advantage: Responsibly sourced materials match the 63% of 520 shoppers who would pay up to $2.00 more, protecting the $12.00 contribution per unit as textile and freight costs rise 11.2%. It supports the brand behind the $900,000 warehouse and may raise the 70,000-unit sales plan.

Disadvantage: Certified materials usually cost more than standard fabric, raising the $18 variable cost per unit unless the full $2.00 premium is accepted.   Q4(b) [12 marks]
    Question: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.8%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in textile and freight costs will affect KBO. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
    Answer: Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.8%): If KBO's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.8% of $600,000 = $4,800 a year (0.008 × $600,000). This is small relative to fixed costs of $324,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct effect is zero. Higher rates could dampen outdoor-clothing spending and raise future borrowing costs, but the risk is manageable and can be hedged by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (4.9%, to $14.48 an hour): With a workforce of 48, higher hourly pay raises KBO's wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual wages, so an annual total cannot be invented; the defensible benchmark is productivity of 70,000 ÷ 48 = 1,458.3 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it falls, the $12.00 contribution per unit is eroded.

Textile and freight inflation (11.2%): The $18 variable cost per unit is exposed, but the insert does not decompose it, so only an illustrative bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.2%, that adds 11.2% × $18 = $2.02 per unit, about $141,000 a year at 70,000 units. The $2.00 premium 63% of shoppers accept can offset part of this.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in textile and freight costs has the greatest impact. It applies to every unit sold, directly threatens the $12.00 contribution that supports the $900,000 expansion, and is only partly recovered through pricing; the interest effect is modest and the wage effect turns on unstated hours.

--- STEM ---
Quay Street Marketplace (QSM) is a private limited company in the online retail and e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 26. Founded in 2016 by Nadia Quay, the platform sells its own craft giftware range through a website and mobile app alongside independent sellers and runs a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. QSM plans to invest $520,000 in an automated stock-control and dispatch system, financed by a $320,000 five-year bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $150,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $17, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. QSM faces two problems: staff turnover is rising and dispatch errors have increased.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QSM plans to fund part of its automation with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for QSM of using retained profit to finance the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment schedule, so QSM protects the cash needed to run a marketplace with fixed costs of $150,000 a year and a $320,000 bank loan already outstanding. Cash saved can absorb the 8.7% rise in packaging and shipping costs without raising the $17 selling price for the 71% of surveyed buyers who value fast delivery.

Point 2: Using $200,000 retained profit avoids the collateral and covenants of a bank loan, so the $520,000 stock-control and dispatch system is not endangered if sales fall short. It also preserves Nadia Quay's control of the platform instead of handing influence to lenders, letting QSM respond quickly to the 46% of buyers who would pay $0.90 more for carbon-neutral shipping. Faster decisions suit a small 26-employee e-commerce firm.
    Keywords: retained profit, bank loan, $200,000, $320,000, $150,000, $520,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to QSM's costs, finance and survey evidence.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QSM is promoting its carbon-neutral shipping option. Consider a national television campaign, search-engine advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should QSM choose to promote this option? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national TV advert would give QSM's marketplace instant mass recognition and could attract new sellers and buyers. However, airtime is expensive for a 26-employee business investing $520,000 in automation, and most viewers do not shop on niche craft platforms, so the spend would be largely wasted.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search targets buyers searching for craft giftware or carbon-neutral delivery, is measurable and can be strictly budgeted, which protects cash flow alongside the $320,000 loan. Its weakness is that it only captures people already looking, so it cannot create demand for a new shipping option among the 46% of 380 buyers who would pay $0.90 more but may not yet know QSM offers it.

Social media influencer marketing: Craft and lifestyle influencers can show the carbon-neutral option to an engaged audience that already buys online, matching the 71% of buyers who value fast delivery and building trust in the platform. It is cost-effective and measurable, though results depend on the influencer's credibility and can take time to accumulate.

Recommendation: QSM should choose social media influencer marketing with a small search budget. It reaches the right online community, explains the $0.90 carbon-neutral proposition and costs far less than television, which is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted. Search alone is rejected because it cannot generate the awareness needed for a new option.
    Keywords: 71%, 380, $0.90, website, 46%, $520,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of promotional methods with minimal reference to QSM. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two methods applied to QSM's online marketplace. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three methods with a justified recommendation that rejects television and explains the limits of search advertising.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: QSM's staff turnover is rising and dispatch errors have increased. Explain two benefits for QSM of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation in its operations team.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives the 26 staff freedom to decide how they organise dispatch, which suits a flat structure and can raise job satisfaction and reduce the rising staff turnover. Skilled workers who choose their own routines are more likely to stay, cutting the cost of repeated recruitment and helping protect the 13,200 orders processed each quarter.

Point 2: Allowing staff to solve problems themselves can reduce the 1.9% dispatch error rate, because those closest to the stock-control system see faults first and can act without waiting for approval. Autonomy also makes the $680 college training more valuable, as employees apply it directly, supporting the $520,000 automation and the 2.8-day dispatch time.
    Keywords: laissez-faire leadership, staff turnover, workforce of 26, 1.9%, 13,200, $680
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of laissez-faire leadership identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to QSM's turnover, errors, structure and training.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: QSM must train 9 staff on the new stock-control system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should QSM choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Learning at the dispatch desk is tailored to QSM's own system, costs no fees, and keeps the 9 staff handling the 13,200 orders processed each quarter. It directly targets the 1.9% dispatch error rate and fits a flat structure where experienced colleagues coach others. Drawbacks are that the coach's work slows, mistakes can be copied, and no formal certificate is awarded.

Off-the-job training: College courses at $680 per employee cost $6,120 for the 9 staff, a small fraction of the $520,000 investment. They provide structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification, useful as the platform grows. However, staff are away from the dispatch desk, worsening the 2.8-day dispatch time, and generic content may not match QSM's system, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: QSM should choose on-the-job training, with short college updates later. It is cheaper, specific to the stock-control system and avoids losing output while staff turnover is a problem and dispatch errors remain. Full off-the-job training is rejected because $6,120 and the absence of 9 staff would slow the 2.8-day dispatch promise during automation, and laissez-faire leadership works best with coaching on the job.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $680, 9, $520,000, dispatch errors
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to QSM. | level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in QSM's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption, error reduction and system relevance.

The $2.50 premium 66% of shoppers accept can recover part of this.

Conclusion: The 10.4% rise in fabric and import costs has the greatest impact. It applies to every garment, directly threatens the $14.00 contribution that justifies the $760,000 hub, and is only partly offset by higher prices; the interest effect is modest and the wage effect depends on hours not given in the insert.
    Keywords: 5.25%, 5.8%, 10.4%, $460,000, $20, $14.18
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to JRC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on JRC's costs, revenue or financing in context. | level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in JRC's context with a justified greatest-impact judgement that avoids invented figures.

--- STEM ---
Xanadu Parcel Company (XPC) is a public limited company in the online gift retailing and e-commerce fulfilment sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2005 by Xanthe Xanadu, the business sells personalised gifts through its own website and packs orders for other retailers, operating a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. XPC plans to invest $810,000 in a new automated gift-wrapping and dispatch line, financed by a $510,000 ten-year bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $21, and currently produces 66,000 units a year. XPC faces two problems: absenteeism is rising and gift-wrapping quality complaints have increased.

--- QUESTIONS ---
  Q1(a) [8 marks]
    Question: XPC plans to fund part of its automation with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for XPC of using a share issue to finance the expansion instead of the bank loan.
    Answer: Point 1: A share issue raises $300,000 of equity that never needs repaying and carries no interest, unlike the $510,000 bank loan. With fixed costs of $216,000 a year and cardboard and courier costs up 9.8%, avoiding debt service protects cash flow and leaves more of the $21 selling price to absorb cost rises.

Point 2: Equity requires no collateral, so the $810,000 wrapping and dispatch line is not at risk of repossession if gift demand falls. It also strengthens the balance sheet of a public limited company answerable to shareholders before further borrowing. The 62% of 500 buyers who would pay $1.20 more for recyclable packaging give a growth chance that can be pursued without lender conditions.
    Keywords: share issue, bank loan, $300,000, $510,000, $216,000, $810,000
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to XPC's costs, finance and survey evidence.

  Q1(b) [12 marks]
    Question: XPC is promoting its recyclable packaging option for online gifts. Consider a national television campaign, search-engine advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should XPC choose to promote this option? Justify your recommendation.
    Answer: Television campaign: A national TV advert would build broad awareness of XPC's personalised gifts and could win new retail clients, but airtime is costly for a business funding an $810,000 line, and most viewers do not order gifts online, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search catches shoppers looking for personalised gifts or recyclable packaging, is measurable and can be budget-capped, protecting cash alongside the $510,000 loan. Its limitation is that it only captures existing demand and cannot create desire for the new packaging option among the 55% of 500 buyers who check delivery speed but may not know XPC's offer.

Social media influencer marketing: Gift and lifestyle influencers can demonstrate the recyclable packaging and the personalised products to a receptive audience, matching the 62% of buyers who would pay $1.20 more. It is targeted and measurable, though results depend on the influencer's credibility and may take time to build.

Recommendation: XPC should choose social media influencer marketing with a small search budget. It reaches online gift buyers, explains the $1.20 recyclable proposition and costs far less than television, which is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted. Search alone is rejected because it cannot generate the awareness needed to launch a new packaging option.
    Keywords: 62%, 500, $1.20, website, 55%, $810,000
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of promotional methods with minimal reference to XPC. | level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two methods applied to XPC's online gift business. | level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three methods with a justified recommendation that rejects television and explains the limits of search advertising.

  Q2(a) [8 marks]
    Question: XPC's absenteeism is rising and gift-wrapping quality complaints have increased. Explain two benefits for XPC of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation in its fulfilment team.
    Answer: Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets the 40 staff decide how they organise wrapping and packing, which can raise job satisfaction and reduce the absenteeism that disrupts the 16,800 gift orders packed last quarter. In a flat approach to routines, experienced packers take ownership, helping cut the 2.7% packing error rate.

Point 2: Giving staff freedom to solve problems uses their close knowledge of the wrapping line, so quality faults behind the rising complaints are corrected quickly without waiting for approval. Autonomy makes the $720 college training more useful and supports the $810,000 automation while local teams adapt the new machinery.
    Keywords: laissez-faire leadership, absenteeism, workforce of 40, 2.7%, 16,800, $720
    Mark scheme: knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of laissez-faire leadership identified (max 2). | application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to XPC's absenteeism, errors, structure and training.

  Q2(b) [12 marks]
    Question: XPC must train 13 staff on the new gift-wrapping line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should XPC choose? Justify your decision.
    Answer: On-the-job training: Coaching beside the wrapping line is specific to XPC's machinery and quality standards, costs no fees, and keeps the 13 staff packing the 16,800 orders processed each quarter. It directly targets the 2.7% packing error rate and the quality complaints. Drawbacks are that the trainer's output falls, bad habits may spread, and no certificate is awarded.

Off-the-job training: College courses at $720 per employee cost $9,360 for the 13 staff, a small part of the $810,000 investment. They give structured skills and a recognised certificate, useful for a public limited company. However, staff are away from the line, lengthening the 3.6-day dispatch time, and generic content may not match XPC's wrapping machinery, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: XPC should choose on-the-job training first, with short college updates later. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while absenteeism is rising and quality complaints remain. Full off-the-job training is rejected because $9,360 and the absence of 13 staff would slow the 3.6-day dispatch promise during automation, and laissez-faire leadership suits learning by doing on the line.
    Keywords: on-the-job training, off-the-job training, $720, 13, $810,000, absenteeism
    Mark scheme: level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to XPC. | level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in XPC's context with some judgement. | level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption, quality and machine relevance.

  Q3(a) [8 marks]
    Question: Calculate and explain how XPC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
    Answer: (i) Break-even output = 24,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 66,000-unit output; modelling the $1.20 recyclable premium; loan-service volume targets; and unit-cost benchmarking at $15.27 to monitor packing errors.
    Keywords: 24,000, $9.00, 66,000, $216,000, $12, $21, $15.27
